openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.name: OpenRouter cookbook: Jev-Verified Cascade
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.whatItDoes: A documentation recipe (not an installable package, MCP server, hook or skill). It shows TypeScript code for a RAG app: a cheap model (~openai/gpt-luna-latest) drafts an answer from retrieved excerpts, Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13) via POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions classifies the draft as supported/unsupported/declined with a confidence, and a frontier model (~openai/gpt-astra-latest) is called only if the check fails. If the verdict is supported with confidence >= 0.8, the answer is sent. If the verdict is declined, it goes to a human. Otherwise it escalates once, and a second failure goes to a human. It targets customer-support/RAG backends and has nothing to do with Claude Code, coding workflows or agent tooling.

providerSupport.evidence: Recipe page https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/jev-verified-cascade(.md): `new OpenRouter({ apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY, serverURL: 'https://openrouter.ai' })`; `decisions.alpha.decisions.create({ decisionsRequest: { model: 'typesafe/jev-1.13', state: {...}, questions: { support: { type: 'choice', instructions, criteria: {supported, unsupported, declined} } } } })`; page states the Decisions API is at https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and a client without serverURL gets a 404. Env var: OPENROUTER_API_KEY only. No TypeSafe direct endpoint or TYPESAFE_API_KEY is used (only a docs link to docs.typesafe.ai/confidence).
providerSupport.others: Uses the @openrouter/sdk (TypeScript) with an OpenRouter chat client for the draft and escalation models. Page links to the TypeSafe SDK guide (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk) for pointing the TypeSafe SDK at OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not applicable. It is OpenRouter-native already.

interface.name: draftAnswer(model, question, excerpts)
interface.purpose: openrouter.chat.send with a system prompt that says to answer only from the excerpts, plus numbered [i] excerpts and the question. Returns the text.

interface.name: verifyAnswer(question, excerpts, answer)
interface.purpose: One Jev Decisions request. State is {help_center_excerpts, customer_question, assistant_answer}. One 'choice' question with 3 labels. Returns {choice, confidence, probabilities}.

interface.name: answerWithCascade(question, excerpts)
interface.purpose: Loops [DRAFT_MODEL, ESCALATION_MODEL]. Returns {route: send|handoff, model, answer, verdicts[]}. ACCEPT_CONFIDENCE = 0.8.

interface.name: (no MCP tools, hooks, skills or CLI commands)
interface.purpose: The recipe ships no runnable artifact for Claude Code. It is meant to be pasted into an app's backend.

security: No code is installed, so there is no supply-chain, postinstall or curl|sh risk from the recipe itself.
API key is read from process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY (not argv). The recipe adds no telemetry.

Prompt-injection surface: the draft answer and the retrieved excerpts are sent to Jev as state. The recipe does not treat them as untrusted, and Jev outputs only typed labels, so injected text can at most skew the verdict.

Jev is a beta, non-reasoning classifier, and the recipe's own benchmark is small (50 questions, self-graded by an Opus judge, and the page admits 2-answer noise between runs). The 'zero wrong answers at 7% of cost' claim is vendor-authored and unverified.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.dataEgress: In the recipe as written: the retrieved excerpts, the customer question and the draft answer are sent to OpenRouter (Jev), and also to the draft/frontier models via chat completions. If it were adapted to Claude Code, whatever text is placed in `state` (code, diffs, file contents, tool output) would leave the machine to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe. The recipe itself has no Claude Code data flow.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.failureMode: No failure handling is shown. `verifyAnswer` throws on an unexpected shape, a missing confidence defaults to 0 (which fails acceptance and escalates), and there are no timeouts, retries or fail-open/closed logic. If Jev is down, answerWithCascade throws. Anyone adapting it must add their own timeout and fallback.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.latencyImpact: Not applicable to Claude Code, since nothing is wired in. In the recipe every question pays a draft call plus one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms), and an escalated question pays a frontier call plus a second Jev call. This would be serial extra latency on top of the model call, and it makes no sense when the main model is already Opus.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: 0 tools, no MCP instructions and no hook-injected text, because nothing is installed. The page itself is about 17 KB of markdown (about 4k tokens) only if the user or Claude reads it.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.autoInvocation: Not applicable: it is documentation, so it never runs unless a developer implements it in an application. It is 'only when prompted', and it cannot be triggered by Claude Code on its own.
pros: Confirms the exact OpenRouter wiring for Jev: POST /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY only, serverURL must be https://openrouter.ai (not /api/v1). This is useful as a reference when writing a custom hook or MCP wrapper.

Provides a concrete, copyable Choice request shape (state object plus criteria labels) and the response shape (answers.<name>.choice, confidence, probabilities). It also gives a threshold-tuning method (start at 0.8, adjust from logged verdicts).
Reports realistic Jev behavior: confidences are often near 0 or 1, and it discloses noise (2-answer differences) and a forced-escalation test.
Needs no install or third-party code, so there is no supply-chain risk.
cons: It is not an integration for Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, and it gives Claude Code no automatic behavior.

It targets grounded-RAG answer verification with a cheap-draft/frontier-escalate cost cut. The user's main model is Opus 5.5 on a subscription/OAuth login, where per-token cascades save nothing, and Claude Code's main loop cannot be intercepted this way without a proxy.
Verifying that an answer is 'supported by excerpts' has no clear daily-coding equivalent. It would need a source-grounded ground truth, and code tasks do not have one.
It is TypeScript-only, assumes @openrouter/sdk, and has no timeouts or fail-open handling.
The performance numbers (0 wrong at about 7% of the cost) come from a small, vendor-authored 50-question benchmark graded by another LLM.
Jev is in beta and only supports a 32k context, so large diffs or files would not fit.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-evaluate-and.verdict: Reference documentation for a support-chatbot RAG cost pattern, not a Claude Code integration. Skip it as an integration, and use it only as a wiring example for the OpenRouter Decisions endpoint. For automatic use inside Claude Code, look at the sibling OpenRouter cookbook 'Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev' (listed in llms.txt), which targets Claude Code permission prompts.

docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.name: TypeSafe agent-skill (typesafe-ai/skills, Claude Code plugin "typesafe")
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.whatItDoes: A single documentation-style SKILL.md (about 10 KB) plus plugin.json and marketplace.json. It teaches Claude how to design and write application code that calls TypeSafe System One (Jev), covering the Choice, Noul and Score primitives, composition patterns and live-doc lookup. It contains no MCP server, no hooks, no scripts and no runtime code. It never calls Jev itself, so it cannot make Claude Code use Jev for its own coding decisions.

providerSupport.evidence: grep for openrouter, base_url and api.typesafe across the clone (src/README.md, src/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md, src/.claude-plugin/*.json) found no endpoint and no OpenRouter mention. The only references are docs.typesafe.ai links (SKILL.md:32-53) and the TYPESAFE_API_KEY variable, which appears only in the docs page https://docs.typesafe.ai/agent-skill and not in the repo. The direct endpoint POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone appears only in the live docs page https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md. 'partial' means the skill only points at TypeSafe docs and its own code paths make no calls.
providerSupport.others: None. The skill has no provider code. It tells Claude to read docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and .md pages.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Nothing to patch, because the skill has no provider layer. The generated app code would target whatever endpoint the user asks for. The OpenRouter surfaces (POST /api/v1/systemone and /api/alpha/decisions) look schema-compatible with api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (state, model, questions), so it is trivial to steer Claude to write code against them. That is a prompt or CLAUDE.md instruction, not a code change.

security: No executable code: no shell, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in the repo (files: README.md, LICENSE, SKILL.md, two JSON manifests).
No API key handling in the skill. TYPESAFE_API_KEY is only mentioned in the docs page as an env var for experiments.

Prompt-injection surface: SKILL.md instructs Claude to fetch live docs from docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and *.md pages (SKILL.md:26-44). That content is remote and can change, so the vendor's docs effectively steer the agent's behavior. The risk is low, since it is a first-party domain and read-only fetching.
Plugin marketplace installs track the GitHub main branch, so a later release can change the instructions without review. Pin or read the diff on update.
The skill tells Claude to keep credentials server-side in web apps (SKILL.md:149).
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.dataEgress: The skill itself sends nothing. Claude (via WebFetch or curl) reads public docs pages from docs.typesafe.ai, so the URLs fetched leak only that a doc was requested. No code, prompts or diffs go to Jev or TypeSafe from this skill. Any Jev call happens only in application code that Claude writes and the user runs.
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.failureMode: Not applicable, because the skill has no runtime dependency on Jev. If docs.typesafe.ai is down, SKILL.md tells Claude to fall back to local docs or SDK types and state the limitation (SKILL.md:41-44). It is effectively fail-open.
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.contextCost: 0 tools and 0 MCP instructions. At startup only the frontmatter (name plus a roughly 750 char description, about 190 tokens) sits in the skills listing. The full body (about 10 KB, roughly 2.5k tokens) loads only when the skill is invoked or auto-triggered. It injects no hook text.
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.latencyImpact: None per call or turn. A one-off cost of a few WebFetch calls to docs.typesafe.ai when the skill is used to write Jev code.
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at Claude's discretion when the task is 'add AI decisions to an app'. It does not make Claude Code consult Jev during its own work. It cannot meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically.
pros: Official, MIT-licensed, tiny and safe: 12 KB of Markdown/JSON, no executables, no hooks, no MCP, no telemetry. Nothing that can break the existing Bash, Read or Grep hooks.
Near-zero context cost (about 190 tokens of description at startup, about 2.5k tokens only when loaded).

Useful for building Jev features into client apps: correct primitives (Choice, Noul, Score), the pattern of 'ask independent questions in parallel over the same state', and guidance on confidence thresholds (SKILL.md:96-148).
Points Claude at live docs (llms.txt), so guidance stays current without plugin updates.
Popular (2.4k stars in about 5 weeks), maintained by the vendor with a release bot, currently v0.5.7.
cons: It does not call Jev. It is documentation for writing Jev code, so it fails the core requirement of Claude Code invoking Jev automatically for its own decisions.

No OpenRouter awareness. Neither the repo nor the docs page mention OpenRouter, and the docs point to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Claude would default to the direct TypeSafe endpoint unless the user adds an instruction such as 'use OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone'.

The trigger is broad and semantic ('brainstorming what AI could make possible', 'LLM prompt-and-parse step'). It may load unprompted while the user works on unrelated AI features and nudge Claude toward adding Jev to client projects where it is unwanted.
Immature: 2 squashed commits, one human author, no tests or CI visible, and the version is 0.5.x. The main branch is tracked, so instructions can change on plugin update.
Depends on the live docs for the actual API contract, so behavior varies over time and needs network access during sessions.
docs-typesafe-ai-agent-skill.verdict: Safe and cheap, and worth installing only if you build Jev-powered features in your own or client apps. It is a coding-knowledge skill and not an integration, so it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically'. Pair it with a hook or MCP layer if that is the goal, and add a CLAUDE.md line to prefer the OpenRouter endpoint.

docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.name: TypeSafe cookbook: Skill suggestion (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion)
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.whatItDoes: Official TypeSafe recipe (Python, not an installable tool) that picks at most one skill per agent turn from Nous Research's Hermes 182-skill roster. Request 1 is one system_one call: a Choice over all 182 skills (option criteria = the 60-char index description) plus 3 Noul gate questions ("is an action wanted rather than explanation?"); if the mean gate is under 0.30 nothing is suggested. Request 2 re-ranks the top 3 with full descriptions plus about 700 chars of each SKILL.md and adds a per-candidate "fits" Noul; if the best fits value is under 0.30 nothing is suggested. The winner is injected as a <skill_relevance> block appended after the cached system prompt. Reported result over 488 requests against claude-haiku-4-5 (jev-1.12, run 2026-07-31): wrong-skill loads fell from 16.8% to 7.3% and needless loads from 9.8% to 4.0%. The floor with the correct answer handed over was 2.5% and 1.2%. Requests were LLM-written and self-described as easier than real user prompts. The recipe is a blueprint for a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit skill-router hook, but it ships no Claude Code hook.

providerSupport.evidence: Cookbook code (skill_suggestion.md, Setup section): `TypeSafeClient(api_key=os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_API_KEY","cache-only"), base_url=os.environ.get("TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT"), timeout=120.0)`, with `client.system_one(...)`, `pip install typesafe-sdk` and `TYPESAFE_MODEL = "jev-1.12"`. Quickstart (docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/quickstart.md:38-47) gives the direct endpoint `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with a Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The recipe never mentions OpenRouter. The base_url override (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT) is an SDK-level hook. Per the brief, OpenRouter serves a POST /api/v1/systemone System One API and typesafe/jev-1.13 model IDs. I did not verify that the SDK's request and response schema matches the OpenRouter route.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Probably trivial in the recipe, unverified end to end. Set TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT to the OpenRouter base, use OPENROUTER_API_KEY as the key, and change the model to typesafe/jev-1.13. That works only if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same shape as the SDK expects. Otherwise it is a small raw-HTTP rewrite of two functions (rank_wide, rerank), which are short.
providerSupport.others: None. Also depends on Anthropic API for the measured agent (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY), which does not apply to a Claude Code subscription login.

docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.license: Recipe code license not stated on the page. The roster data comes from NousResearch/hermes-agent (MIT). Depends on the cooksafe and typesafe-sdk packages, which I did not inspect.
security: No installable artifact. Copying the recipe adds pip deps: typesafe-sdk, cooksafe, anthropic, matplotlib, ipython. I did not vet them.
API key would be read from an env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY or an OpenRouter key). It would not appear in argv if used from a hook, as long as it is read from env.

Prompt-injection surface: the user prompt and SKILL.md excerpts are passed as state to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injected text cannot produce free-text instructions. The only text that reaches Claude is a skill name chosen from a fixed roster, so injection risk is low.
If turned into a hook, the hook itself must be written and audited by the user. Nothing here executes shell commands or telemetry.
Docs pages carry text aimed at AI agents (the 'install the TypeSafe skill' prompt in the quickstart). I treated it as data and did not act on it.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.dataEgress: In the recipe as written: the full user prompt goes to TypeSafe on every turn (and the last request only, not history). Also sent: the whole skill roster (182 names plus 60-char descriptions, about 16k chars) in request 1, and for the top 3 candidates the full descriptions plus about 700 chars of each SKILL.md in request 2. Ported to Claude Code this would send every prompt, which may contain client code or secrets, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, plus the names and descriptions of installed skills. It sends no file contents or tool outputs unless the author adds them. Pairs poorly with client projects under NDA.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.failureMode: The recipe has no failure handling. The client timeout is 120 s, there is no retry, and the code has no try/except. A port to Claude Code would need its own fail-open wrapper with a short timeout (for example 1 to 2 s) that exits 0 with no injection. Failure of the advisory hint is harmless if fail-open. Fail-closed would block prompts, which is unacceptable.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.latencyImpact: Cookbook demo timings: request 1 took 0.16 to 0.31 s and request 2 about 0.09 to 0.12 s, so roughly 0.25 to 0.45 s serial per prompt. That is a single pre-turn delay per user message, not per tool call. Numbers are from the vendor's demo and likely cached or warm. Over OpenRouter the extra hop may add more. The brief's claim is 70-500 ms.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.contextCost: If ported to a UserPromptSubmit hook: zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. It injects about 40 tokens per turn (one <skill_relevance> line, roughly 150 chars) or a short 'no skill relevant' line. Claude Code would still list its own skills, so this adds a hint and does not remove tokens. The context saving the cookbook advertises (a truncated roster) does not apply, because Claude Code already truncates skill descriptions and has no 182-skill index to trim.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.autoInvocation: Recipe only, so nothing runs automatically as shipped. A port as a UserPromptSubmit hook would be fully deterministic and automatic, needing no user prompting. The recipe's own design is a per-turn pre-processor whose output is appended to the system prompt.
pros: Official TypeSafe recipe with a fully specified, working design (thresholds 0.30/0.30, shortlist of 3, 700-char excerpts). It gives the exact confidence-gated two-stage pattern to build a real Claude Code hook.

Fits the user's requirement of automatic use: a UserPromptSubmit hook would be deterministic, so the user never says 'use jev'. Output is only a skill name from a fixed roster, so Jev cannot inject free text.
Cheap and fast per the demo: about 0.1 to 0.3 s per request, and both stages are single calls. At about $0.042/M input tokens, roughly 5k tokens per prompt costs about $0.0002 per turn.
Honest evaluation: reports a floor (2.5% and 1.2%) and admits the requests are easier than real ones. Measured error reduction was more than half (16.8% to 7.3% wrong loads).

The claimed benefits are relevant for a user with many installed skills (dougthepug-design, empat-design, gitnexus-*, caveman, anthropic-skills:* and so on), where wrong or missed skill triggers are a real annoyance.
cons: Not an integration. There is no hook, MCP server, plugin or installer, and the user would have to write, test and maintain the hook, roster extraction and thresholds themselves.

Measured on a different agent: Hermes, claude-haiku-4-5 via the Anthropic API, and a forced skill_view tool. Claude Code with Opus 5.5 already selects skills from full descriptions in its own system prompt, so the 16.8% baseline error rate likely overstates the headroom. No evidence is given for Claude Code.
Only helps skill selection, which is a small part of daily coding. It does nothing for code edits, search, planning or permission decisions, so the value per turn is small.
Sends every prompt and the skill roster off-machine on each turn. That is a concern for client projects, and the provider list is OpenRouter plus TypeSafe with a beta model.

Evaluation set is LLM-written (Sonnet 5), 'easier than real user prompts', with a Mastodon-to-X false positive showing the recipe can suggest a wrong skill for near-miss requests. Suggesting a wrong skill can mislead an agent that is told to 'ignore if it does not fit'.
Adds a 0.25 to 0.5 s serial delay before every prompt, and up to 2 s if a port uses a timeout. Needs a fail-open wrapper because the recipe has none.

Uses the TypeSafe Python SDK and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. OpenRouter support is inferred, not shown, so the recipe needs porting and testing against /api/v1/systemone. Requires Python plus pip deps, or a reimplementation as a Node or curl hook.
docs-typesafe-ai-cookbooks-skill-suggest.verdict: Useful only as a design blueprint for a custom UserPromptSubmit skill-router hook, not as something to install: there is no shipped Claude Code integration, and the measured gains come from a much weaker agent (Haiku on Hermes' 60-char index) than Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. If built, it must be fail-open, use a short timeout and go through OpenRouter, and it would send every prompt off-machine for a marginal skill-selection gain.
evidence: https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md (full recipe read; TypeSafeClient setup with TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT, rank_wide, rerank, suggest(), suggestion_block(), results table, demo timings 0.09 to 0.31 s)

docs-typesafe-ai-introduction-coding-age.whatItDoes: Official TypeSafe docs page (no code, no installable artifact). Tells coding-agent users to (a) install the TypeSafe agent skill so the agent writes correct Jev integrations into the apps they build, or (b) use Jev inside their own apps for routing, scoring, guardrails and typed extraction. The docs' skill_suggestion cookbook does show one relevant pattern: two Jev calls per agent turn pick at most one skill and inject a `<skill_relevance>` line into the system prompt. Any Jev decision layer built on the page's advice sends whatever is put in `state` plus the questions to api.typesafe.ai or to OpenRouter and its upstream provider. Text only, up to 32k tokens for state plus the longest question. In a Claude Code hook that would be the user prompt, and possibly diffs, file contents or tool outputs. The design should send a minimal state, such as the prompt plus a skill or tool index, and filter secrets first.
docs-typesafe-ai-introduction-coding-age.failureMode: Not applicable to the docs page. The Python SDK default timeout is 10 s per HTTP operation with retries and backoff, and it honors retry-after on 429. Rate limits are 100K tokens/s and 40 req/s, and the docs warn they change dynamically. Any Claude Code hook built on this must be written fail-open with a short timeout of about 1-2 s, and that has to be implemented by the user. Nothing here provides it.

The only auto element is the skill's description trigger, which makes Claude write Jev code when building an app. The docs' own advice for the agent-decision use case is that developers write their own code around Jev. That means a self-built deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse) calling OpenRouter Jev, modeled on the skill_suggestion cookbook.
docs-typesafe-ai-introduction-coding-age.latencyImpact: Nothing for the docs page. For a self-built hook, the cookbook shows about 0.31 s for a wide Choice-plus-Nouls call over 182 skills, and the brief claims 70-500 ms end to end. The cookbook's full pattern uses two sequential calls per turn, so expect roughly 0.5-1 s added per user prompt, more via OpenRouter. Running it on every tool call would add too much delay.

Points to the right architecture for the user's goal: Jev as a typed, calibrated decision layer inside hooks or apps, using confidence gating and intent routing. That is the only way to get the 'automatic' behavior without prompting.

The skill_suggestion cookbook is a working blueprint that fits Claude Code closely: inject `<skill_relevance>` via a UserPromptSubmit hook, with a 0.31 s first call. It reports wrong-skill loads dropping from 16.8% to 7.3% (Haiku 4.5, 488 requests). With the user's many plugin skills this could be useful.
Cheap: $0.042 per 1M input tokens and output is free. Hook-sized states of about 2-5k tokens cost roughly $0.0001-0.0002 per call.

cons: It is documentation, not an integration: nothing here can be installed to make Claude Code use Jev automatically, so the user's core goal is not met by this candidate.

The page and the skill cover only the TypeSafe direct API (api.typesafe.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and never mention OpenRouter. Using OpenRouter means custom code and an untested base URL and model name (typesafe/jev-1.13).

The skill activates only when Claude is building something that fits a Jev use case, so it does not touch Claude Code's own decisions such as skill selection, permission checks or routing. Nothing on it runs at runtime.

Jev 1.13 jaggedness doc: literal reading, weak on numbers and dates, weak with large irrelevant state, adversarial content, and no generation. Hooks over big diffs or repo context are the wrong shape. Good targets are short classification questions.
Beta and rate limits are unstable: the models page says limits change without notice, and the skills repo has 2 commits despite 2.4k stars.

Latency and cost accrue per prompt (about 0.3-1 s if the cookbook pattern is copied). The user already has a busy hook stack (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post, caveman), and each addition adds serial latency and a fail-open burden.
docs-typesafe-ai-introduction-coding-age.verdict: Not an integration, but the most honest guidance available. It confirms Jev cannot be plugged in as Claude Code's model, so any 'automatic' setup must be a hook-based decision layer the user builds, using the skill_suggestion cookbook as a template with OpenRouter as the endpoint. npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.name: @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai (Vercel AI SDK provider)
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.whatItDoes: A small (about 300 LOC of source) Vercel AI SDK provider that exposes TypeSafe System One (Jev) as an experimental "evaluationModel". It works with `experimental_evaluate` from the `ai` package. One POST to `<baseURL>/systemone` sends `{model, state, questions}` and maps choice, score and boolean (noul) answers to typed results with probabilities and confidence. It is a TypeScript library only. It has no MCP server, no hooks, no skill and no CLI, so it does nothing inside Claude Code unless someone writes a hook or MCP server on top of it.

providerSupport.evidence: package/src/typesafe-ai-provider.ts:26 and :36 default baseURL 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1', overridable through the baseURL setting (line 27). typesafe-ai-provider.ts:40 and typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:99 read the API key from TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY (not OPENROUTER_API_KEY) unless `apiKey` is passed. typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109 posts to `${baseURL}/systemone`. Setting baseURL to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 gives the OpenRouter System One endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone), which OpenRouter's TypeSafe SDK guide says implements TypeSafe's request and response shapes. No 'openrouter' string exists anywhere in src or dist, and the ai-sdk.dev provider page does not mention OpenRouter or AI Gateway. The candidate's 'also on Vercel AI Gateway' claim is not supported by the package. The default model id is 'jev-latest'. OpenRouter needs 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. Any string is accepted as a model id (evaluation-model.ts:26). The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported.
providerSupport.others: Any OpenAI-style gateway that exposes /systemone (for example rout.my, per search results) works through the baseURL setting. It has custom `headers` and `fetch` hooks.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no fork needed: createTypeSafeAi({baseURL:'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1', apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY}).evaluationModel('typesafe/jev-1.13'). Caveats: (1) The response schema is a zod object, which strips unknown keys by default, so OpenRouter's extra id, provider and usage.cost fields should not break parsing. This was not run. (2) The Decisions API is not covered.

interface.name: createTypeSafeAi(settings)
interface.purpose: Factory taking apiKey, baseURL, headers and fetch. Returns a ProviderV4. languageModel, embeddingModel and imageModel all throw NoSuchModelError.

interface.name: provider.evaluationModel(modelId)
interface.purpose: Returns an EvaluationModelV4 whose supportedQuestionTypes are choice, score and boolean. doEvaluate validates at most 255 choice options and at most 10 score levels, then POSTs to /systemone. Boolean is mapped to the noul type and back.

interface.name: experimental_evaluate (from 'ai', not this package)
interface.purpose: User-facing entry point. Retries 429 and 529 through the core maxRetries setting (default 2). This package has no retry loop and no timeout of its own.

security: Small surface: 2 runtime deps (@ai-sdk/provider, @ai-sdk/provider-utils), no postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json scripts are build and test only), no shell execution, no telemetry, and no process.env access other than through loadApiKey for TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY.
npm provenance is enabled (SLSA attestation, published by GitHub Actions OIDC via vercel-release-bot).
The API key travels only in an Authorization: Bearer header (no argv exposure). A key set in the environment will be visible in /proc/<pid>/environ.
A User-Agent suffix 'ai-sdk-typesafe-ai/<version>' is added, which is harmless.
Prompt-injection surface: none in the package itself, because it returns numbers and enum choices only. A future hook that feeds the result into Claude context would carry only probabilities.
Repo license is 'Other' per GitHub (Vercel AI's LICENSE), while the npm package declares Apache-2.0.
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.dataEgress: Everything the caller places in `state` and `questions` is sent to the configured baseURL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai if overridden). The package adds nothing on its own. If a Claude Code hook were built on it, whatever that hook puts in `state` would leave the machine: prompt text, file contents, diffs and tool output. That matters for client projects. The Authorization header carries the API key. No other endpoints are contacted.
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.failureMode: The library throws APICallError on failure. There is no timeout in the package, only abortSignal passthrough, and core retries 429 and 529 twice. Fail-open or fail-closed is entirely up to the consumer, for example a hook wrapper with its own AbortSignal.timeout that exits 0 on error. The library gives no default protection against a hung request.
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.contextCost: Zero on its own: no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook text. Any wrapper would add its own cost. A hook that stays silent unless it decides to intervene adds nothing. An MCP wrapper would add about 1 to 3 tools, roughly 500 to 1500 tokens of definitions.
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.autoInvocation: Not applicable: it is a library, so it only runs when other code calls it. Automatic use inside Claude Code needs a custom deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse or PostToolUse) that calls it. That is the only way to meet the 'without prompting' requirement, because an MCP tool or skill is at the model's discretion.
npmjs-com-package-ai-sdk-typesafe-ai.latencyImpact: Library overhead is negligible. One HTTP round trip to /systemone, claimed at 70 to 500 ms end to end, plus Node startup of about 100 to 200 ms if a hook spawns a fresh `node` process on every event. Pre-tool hooks run serially on every call, so this would be noticeable on Grep, Glob and Bash unless the matcher is narrow.
pros: Same Jev OpenRouter schema, trivially pointed at it: base URL override plus apiKey covers openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (evaluation-model.ts:109, provider.ts:27). No fork is needed.
Tiny, readable code (5 source files, 2 runtime deps, no install scripts, npm provenance). It is easy to audit and safe as a building block for a custom hook.
Typed handling of Choice, Score and Noul, with client-side limits (255 options, 10 score levels), rounding metadata, and confidence exposed under providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence.
Backed by Vercel and the AI SDK release process (repo has 27k stars, active pushes on 2026-09-30, unit tests for provider and model, an edge-runtime test config). 12 releases in 2 weeks.
Batches multiple questions against one state in a single request, which suits a hook that asks several gating questions at once.
cons: It is not an integration with Claude Code: it has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI. The user would have to write and maintain the hook or MCP wrapper, which is the actual hard part.

It requires the `ai` package and the `experimental_evaluate` API, which is explicitly experimental and may change. Using it in a hook script adds the ai, zod and provider-utils dependency tree to a tool that only needs one fetch call. A direct `fetch` to /systemone is about 20 lines.

Defaults are wrong for this user: the env var is TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY (the user wants OPENROUTER_API_KEY), the base URL is api.typesafe.ai, and the default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id (it needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Everything must be overridden explicitly.
Only System One /systemone is covered. There is no OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) and no Jev Router model support.
No timeout, no fail-open behavior and no caching in the package. A hung request on a PreToolUse hook could stall every tool call unless the wrapper adds AbortSignal.timeout.
The Vercel AI Gateway claim in the discovery data is not backed by the package or the ai-sdk.dev page.

pros: Official TypeSafe artifact, MIT licensed, 2.4k stars and 145 forks in 5 weeks, so it is the canonical way to teach Claude the Jev API, primitives and patterns.
Zero risk surface: no code, hooks, MCP or network calls of its own; installs via the native Claude Code plugin flow with no postinstall.
Very small resident context cost (about 230 tokens) with no tool-definition bloat, and no latency added to normal turns.

Good design guidance (SKILL.md:95-149): one narrow question per judgment, include a no-match option, treat confidence as concentration not permission to act, ask independent questions in parallel. Useful if the user ever builds Jev-backed features in an app.
Complements any transport (MCP or router): it lets Claude write correct Jev integration code in the user's own projects.
cons: Does not do what the user wants: it never makes Claude Code call Jev for its own decisions. It is documentation for building Jev apps, so 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' is not achieved.

No OpenRouter awareness at all: docs and skill only reference TYPESAFE_API_KEY and api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Nothing about openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone or typesafe/jev-1.13 model IDs, so generated code will default to the direct API and need manual steering.

The trigger description is broad ('when an LLM prompt-and-parse step could become a structured decision') and could fire in unrelated tasks, loading 2.5k tokens plus doc fetches and nudging Claude to add TypeSafe to client projects that never asked for it.
Depends on live remote docs treated as 'source of truth' (SKILL.md:28-44): mutable, an injection channel, and requires network. The skill is only a thin index and is useless offline.
Encourages giving the agent a real API key to 'run experiments' (docs), which is a cost and data-egress risk under bypass or auto permission mode on client code.

Repo has 2 commits, no tests or CI, and 5 weeks of age, and 2 open community issues report the direct API console being down (issue 10, 500s on sign-in) and a broken migration link (issue 13), which is thin signal on vendor operational maturity.

openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.name: OpenRouter cookbook: Gate Agent Tool Calls with Jev (plus sibling Claude Code permission-hook recipe)
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.whatItDoes: Documentation recipe (no installable package, no repo) showing how to gate an OpenRouter Agent SDK (@openrouter/agent, TypeScript) tool call with Jev. In onToolCalled it runs deterministic arithmetic checks, then POSTs {model, state:{policy,ticket,refund}, questions} with three Noul questions to /api/alpha/decisions, and maps probabilities to approve (all >=0.9), block (any <=0.1) or review (pause for a human). It is a customer-support refund example, NOT a Claude Code integration. The Claude-Code-relevant version is the linked sibling recipe "Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev" (cookbook/coding-agents/auto-approve-permission-prompts-with-jev), which I also read. It ships a Bun/TypeScript PermissionRequest hook for Claude Code (also Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) with a regex risk list evaluated before Jev, then two Noul questions (reversible, serves_task) with threshold 0.9. It only ever upgrades a prompt to allow. It is a copy-paste snippet, not a maintained package. Pattern is portable to a PreToolUse hook, but the port is DIY.

Sibling page, step 2 jevApproves(): same URL and env var, AbortSignal.timeout(8_000). Response schema: {model, answers:{key:{type:'noul',noul:number}}, usage:{input_tokens,output_tokens,cost}, id, provider}. No TYPESAFE_API_KEY path in the recipes. The hub page /docs/guides/community/jev.md says the TypeSafe SDK can be pointed at OpenRouter via /api/v1/systemone by changing the base URL.
providerSupport.others: Recipes mention the OpenRouter TS/Python/Go SDK Decisions clients and the TypeSafe SDK (System One path). The agent model in the example is ~openai/gpt-sol-latest via OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already OpenRouter-native, so no patch is needed. Switching to the direct TypeSafe API would be a base URL and key swap, but the recipes do not document it.

interface.name: askJev(state, questions)
interface.purpose: Fetch client for the Decisions API. Throws on non-2xx, missing answer, or probability outside [0,1], so a broken check never becomes an approval (gate-tool-calls step 1).

interface.name: gateRefund(ticket, refund)
interface.purpose: Deterministic pre-check, then Jev with 3 Noul questions (customer_asked, right_order, policy_covers). Returns approve/block/review plus reason and probabilities (step 3). APPROVE_AT=0.9, BLOCK_AT=0.1.

interface.name: tool.onToolCalled / onResponseReceived
interface.purpose: Agent SDK hooks. approve runs the side effect, block returns a refusal note to the model, review returns null and pauses with status awaiting_hitl (step 4).

interface.name: neverAutoApprove(command)
interface.purpose: Sibling recipe: regex risk list (sudo, rm -rf, git push/reset --hard, publish, deploy, .env/.ssh/.aws, sh/eval/python -c, command substitution) checked before Jev.

interface.name: jevApproves(state)
interface.purpose: Sibling recipe: two Noul questions, reversible and serves_task. Returns true only if all scores >=0.9, undefined on any error or timeout.

interface.name: Claude Code PermissionRequest hook
interface.purpose: Sibling recipe: matcher Bash, command 'bun ./path/jev-permission-hook.ts', timeout 15s. Reads stdin JSON {cwd,tool_name,tool_input.command,description} and prints hookSpecificOutput.decision.behavior=allow only when confident. Otherwise it prints nothing and the normal flow continues.

openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.install: No package. Copy the TypeScript from the docs page into your own file. Sibling Claude Code hook needs Bun, OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment Claude Code runs in, and a PermissionRequest entry in .claude/settings.json (or ~/.claude/settings.json). For this user, port to node 24 or tsx, since Bun is not in the toolchain list. Agent SDK recipe needs @openrouter/agent, zod 4 and an existing HITL agent, which is irrelevant to Claude Code.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.runtime: TypeScript on Bun or Node. The Agent SDK recipe needs @openrouter/agent and zod 4. The hook needs only fetch and node:stream/consumers.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.license: Docs page under OpenRouter's site terms. No license grant for the snippets was seen. Endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions, an alpha API, and the model is beta.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.createdAt: Recipe cites captured runs dated 2026-09-21 and 2026-09-22 (and jev-1.13 released 2026-09-18), so it is under about 2 weeks old at 2026-09-30.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.lastCommit: n/a (docs page). The sibling page was captured 2026-09-22.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.tests: None shipped. The recipe gives a "Check your work" manual checklist and captured outputs from the live endpoint. Only four gate cases and three shell commands were sampled. No CI, no benchmark, no false-negative rate for risky commands. It admits that scores drift by up to about 0.08 across identical repeats.
security: API key is read from the process env and sent as an Authorization header, so it is not in argv or the process list. Claude Code hook subprocesses inherit env, but the recipe found Codex strips *KEY* vars from hook env.

The recipe says outright that the risk list, not the threshold, is the security boundary. Jev cannot tell that `cat foo` reads a secret unless the command text shows it. Hostile repo content or a prompt-injected agent can craft benign-looking commands. The regex list is bypassable in principle (e.g. curl piped to an interpreter, python script files, `make` targets, npm scripts that do bad things).

Prompt-injection surface: the state includes the agent-written command and description (or user task), which are attacker-influenceable strings. The recipe itself warns that customer text can try to change policy, and it hardens the question wording for that. The Claude Code variant uses the agent's own description as the task, so a compromised agent can justify anything to Jev.

Fail-open risk in the recipe design: on Jev error or low confidence it prints nothing and the normal permission flow continues. Under bypassPermissions or auto mode that flow is 'run it', so the gate then adds no protection. The recipe only ever ADDS allow, and never returns deny for Claude Code. Use as a guard requires a PreToolUse rewrite that emits deny or ask.

PermissionRequest hooks run only when Claude Code is about to prompt. The user's bypass mode means they would essentially never fire, per the docs text 'runs only when it's about to ask you'. A PreToolUse hook is needed instead.
Host deny/ask rules still win over hook allow (per the recipe), which is good.
No telemetry, no shell execution beyond the hook itself, no curl|sh or postinstall, since there is no package. Every byte sent is under your control.
Jev has no explanation output, so audit is only probabilities, and reasoning cannot be inspected. Skeptic claim that it is a router around a small LLM is unverified.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.dataEgress: Per gated call, one HTTPS POST to openrouter.ai (which routes to TypeSafe as the provider) containing: model id, the full command string(s), project absolute path (cwd), and the agent description or task text (up to 2000 chars in the OpenCode variant). Extending the pattern to Write/Edit would send file paths and diffs or content. The refund example sends the whole ticket and policy. Nothing else leaves the machine. Real client project paths and command text (which may embed hostnames, table names, or inline tokens) go to two third parties, and the OpenRouter/TypeSafe data-retention policy was not confirmed in the docs I read (the hub says to check the model page).
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.failureMode: Recipe design: fail-safe toward the PROMPT, not toward a block. fetch has an 8 s AbortSignal.timeout inside a 15 s hook timeout. Any network error, non-2xx, unparsable body, or out-of-range score returns undefined, so the hook prints nothing and Claude Code's normal permission flow proceeds. In default mode this means one extra prompt. In bypass/auto mode it means the command runs ungated (fail-open). Agent SDK variant throws, and the model sees {error} and may retry, and nothing is issued (fail-closed for approvals). Cursor variant needs failClosed:true because Cursor defaults to fail-open. For a security guard the user must choose the fail policy explicitly, and the hook API supports exit code 2 or permissionDecision deny/ask in PreToolUse.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.latencyImpact: Claimed under 600 ms per Decisions request in the recipe (gate-tool-calls warning box), and the hub page claims 70-500 ms end to end. Added to every gated Bash call and serialized before the command. Static-risk-list hits skip the network. Adds Bun/Node cold start of about 50-150 ms per hook process on top. If hooks run per Bash call across a long agent session (hundreds of calls/day), that is noticeable but not blocking. Existing GitNexus and secret-guard hooks on Bash run in parallel with this one, so the worst-case hook adds its own latency. Cost is about $0.000017 per call (400-token state) or under $0.0001, roughly $0.02 per 1000 gated calls.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and zero MCP instructions, since it is a hook and not an MCP server or skill. Only hook stdout is read by the harness, and silent-exit or allow JSON adds no model-visible tokens. If ported to deny with a reason, that short string is shown to the model, which is cheap.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. Once registered in settings.json the harness runs it on every matching tool event without the model or the user having to say anything. As written in the sibling recipe it is a PermissionRequest hook (fires only when Claude Code would prompt). For the user's bypass/auto mode it must be re-registered as PreToolUse (matcher Bash, possibly Write|Edit) to fire at all.
pros: Most literally 'automatic' integration possible: a deterministic hook fires on every risky tool call with no user or model prompting, satisfying the 'never say use jev' requirement.
Zero context-window cost: no tool schemas, no MCP instructions, no injected text (unlike an MCP server).

Single OpenRouter key (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and single endpoint, https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13, confirmed in the page code. The recipe has no TypeSafe account or separate key.
Cheap: about $0.000017 per call measured and 70-600 ms, so about $0.02 per 1000 gated Bash calls.

Design is sound: static regex list first (no network), Jev only for the residue, fixed numeric thresholds, and errors handled toward 'no decision'. The gate-tool-calls recipe explicitly documents fail-closed error handling and a split of approve/block/review, which maps onto PreToolUse allow/deny/ask.
Semantic check adds something the existing regex secret-leak hook cannot: 'does this command serve the current task and is it reversible', a judgment call on the intent of the command.
Captured evidence of actual scores (bun test 0.93/0.95, bun add left-pad 0.45/0.09, wrangler deploy 0.04/0.07) shows the separation works on the samples.
Host deny rules and existing hooks stay authoritative, so this stacks on top of the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration as titled: the gate-tool-calls page targets @openrouter/agent SDK refund tools (ticket/policy/HITL). Only the sibling coding-agents page has Claude Code hook code, and nothing is packaged, versioned, or maintained. You'd be maintaining copy-pasted code.

The published Claude Code hook uses PermissionRequest, which fires only when Claude Code is about to prompt. In bypass or auto mode the user runs, it rarely or never fires, so as written it gives nothing for the daily flow. It must be rewritten as PreToolUse, and that variant has not been tested by the authors.

Its main function is to REDUCE prompts (auto-approve), not to add safety, and the user already has prompts off. For a bypass user the value is only a new deny/ask layer, which the recipe never implements, and would need new design of thresholds (asking Jev 'is this dangerous' instead of 'is this reversible').

Fail-open in bypass mode: if Jev times out or errors, the recipe's fall-through means the command just runs, so the guard silently disappears exactly when it is needed unless you add explicit deny/ask on error.

Security evidence is thin: 3 shell commands and 4 refund cases sampled, no false-negative rate on adversarial or obfuscated commands, and the authors themselves say Jev is fooled by e.g. `cat` of a secret file not on the list. Scores drift by up to 0.08 on repeated runs, and the Codex example shows a description phrased as a question dropping serves_task from >0.9 to 0.54, so it is sensitive to the wording of the state.
Data egress to OpenRouter and TypeSafe of every command line, cwd and agent description on client projects (confidentiality/contract risk). Retention policy not verified.
Bun is assumed (user has Node 24, so a port is needed), plus alpha endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) and a beta model, so the API may change. The recipe is about 2 weeks old.
Adds a serialized network round trip before each gated Bash call and one more hook process to an already busy Bash hook chain (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post, caveman).
No Read/Grep/Glob/Edit coverage in the published version, only Bash. Jev cannot judge code quality, so it does not help the actual coding work, only tool gating.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-building-age.verdict: Useful as a design reference and the only concrete route to automatic, zero-context, deterministic Jev use in Claude Code via a hook, but it is a copy-paste snippet whose stock Claude Code variant (PermissionRequest, fail-open, Bun) does not fit a bypass/auto-mode user. Worth adopting only as a self-written PreToolUse hook (node, fail-closed to ask/deny, Bash-only, after the regex guard) if the user accepts sending commands and paths to OpenRouter/TypeSafe.

openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.name: OpenRouter guide: TypeSafe SDK on OpenRouter (@typesafe-ai/sdk + typesafe-sdk)
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.whatItDoes: A documentation page (not a Claude Code integration) explaining that the official TypeSafe SDKs (@typesafe-ai/sdk on npm, typesafe-sdk on PyPI) can be pointed at OpenRouter by setting baseURL=https://openrouter.ai/api and using an OpenRouter key, so client.systemOne({model:'jev-1.13', state, questions}) POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. API key sent only as Authorization: Bearer header (js/src/client.ts:354, py transport.py:121), never in argv. Key lives in env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or constructor; a hook process inherits it from Claude Code env, so OPENROUTER_API_KEY must sit in settings.json env or shell profile (visible to every child process). Log level debug prints headers/bodies (client.ts debug logging) - keep at default warn.
SDK sends non-sensitive telemetry-like headers on every call: User-Agent, X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime (client.ts:355-358); no separate telemetry endpoint found in source.

Prompt-injection surface: any state sent to Jev is attacker-influenceable text (file contents, command strings, repo README). Jev returns only numbers, so it cannot be instructed to run tools, but a poisoned state can push probabilities (cookbook itself warns: the static RISKY list, not the threshold, is the security boundary; Jev cannot know a 'cat foo' reads a secret).

Beta model, third-party (TypeSafe) receives content via OpenRouter; OpenRouter data policy for typesafe/jev-1.13 not verified from model page (WebFetch not used); treat client code as sensitive. Existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook should also run before anything is sent.
Cookbook hook idea itself is a permission-bypass risk if misconfigured: an 'allow' from the hook grants the command; deny rules still win per doc.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.dataEgress: SDK/Decisions call sends exactly what the integrator puts in 'state' and 'questions' (JSON body, model id). In the cookbook Claude Code hook: the Bash command string, cwd (project path), and optionally tool_input.description (the agent's one-line description; not the user task on Claude Code). No file contents, diffs or transcript by default, but the state is arbitrary so a custom hook could send anything. Traffic goes to openrouter.ai then to TypeSafe as provider. Plus SDK headers (SDK version, runtime).
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.failureMode: SDK: throws on failure; defaults are 10 s timeout per attempt (retry.ts:5, py constants.py DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=10.0), maxRetries 2 with backoff 0.5-5 s on 408/429/5xx/connection/timeouts (retry.ts:10-22), so worst case roughly 30+ s before throwing; Python retry overall cap 30 s. Fail behavior is decided by the integrator's code. Cookbook hook is fail-open-to-prompt (any error/timeout 8 s returns undefined -> no decision -> normal permission flow; the hook timeout is 15 s). In headless `claude -p` / background subagents, no decision means deny. Cursor's version differs (failClosed flag).
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.contextCost: SDK itself: zero context (not an MCP server/skill). Cookbook PermissionRequest hook: zero tokens injected (prints nothing unless allowing), so no context cost. A custom MCP wrapper would cost ~1-3 small tools (~300-800 tokens).

Cookbook logged 400-token requests at ~$0.0000168 each. Only paid on permission prompts that pass the static list, so effectively zero added latency for already-allowed tools.

Via the cookbook's PermissionRequest hook: deterministic hook, fully automatic, but ONLY when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog (per the doc: hook 'never sees commands that an allow rule already covers'). In bypassPermissions mode no dialogs occur, so this hook effectively never fires; in 'auto' mode the built-in classifier handles approvals (inference; not verified for PermissionRequest firing there).
pros: Confirms the OpenRouter path is trivial and official: baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key; identical request/response schema to TypeSafe direct (doc + js/src/client.ts:321).
SDKs are clean, MIT, typed, well tested (JS ~120 test cases, dist tests, Python pytest), no install scripts, sane defaults (10 s timeout, 2 retries), Bearer key not in argv.
Gives typed Choice/Noul/Score helpers, which makes writing a robust custom hook or a tiny MCP wrapper easy (answer types inferred).

The linked cookbook provides a real, deterministic Claude Code integration pattern (PermissionRequest hook, static RISKY list first, 0.9 threshold, fail-to-prompt) that needs no model discretion and injects zero context.
Very cheap: ~$0.00002 per decision; free output tokens.
cons: Not an integration: no MCP tools, hooks, skills, or CLI in either SDK repo; the user must write and maintain everything, contradicting 'automatic integration' out of the box.
SDK reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY not OPENROUTER_API_KEY; models.list() is broken against OpenRouter; default base URL is api.typesafe.ai so a missed override sends the OpenRouter key to TypeSafe.

Repos are ~4 weeks old (created 2026-09-04), JS SDK 0.6.0 / Python 0.7.x, beta model; API is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha) and shallow public history (5-6 commits, bot-authored) offers little track record. Skeptic claim that Jev is a small flash router remains unverified.

The only automatic Claude Code use case documented (permission auto-approve) does nothing for this user: bypass mode never prompts, and 'auto' mode already uses a classifier. The hook also adds a network call per prompt and would only ever approve, not improve code quality.

Jev returns probabilities without reasoning and cannot see secrets it is not shown; the cookbook admits the static regex list is the real safety boundary. Sending client-project commands/paths to a third-party provider via OpenRouter is a data-governance issue for client work.

No obvious daily-coding value: Jev is a classifier/router, not a code model; hooks on PreToolUse would add 70-500 ms plus cold start to every Bash/Read/Grep on top of the already-loaded secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-community-type.verdict: Useful only as a low-level building block: it proves OpenRouter can host Jev with a base-URL swap, but it is a library, not a Claude Code integration, and the closest documented automatic pattern (PermissionRequest auto-approve hook) is a no-op in this user's bypass/auto workflow. Recommend using raw fetch to /api/alpha/decisions (as in the cookbook) rather than adding an SDK dependency if any custom hook is built.

security: Not on npm (package.json has private:true). Install is git clone, npm install, npm run build:web, node bin/jev.mjs install. It pulls the npm dependency tree at install time, including esbuild and @puppeteer/browsers. No curl|sh installer and no postinstall script seen in package.json.

`jev install` mutates user config: it runs `claude mcp remove/add -s user`, rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml if present, and creates symlinks in ~/.claude/skills and ~/.local/bin (install.ts:52-88). Uses execFileSync with arg arrays, not a shell.

API key handling is decent. The key is read from env or ~/.config/jev-browser/config.json (0600) and sent only as an Authorization header (client.ts:68), so it does not appear in argv. `jev settings set ... -` reads from stdin. redactConfig masks keys (store.ts:70-83). Trace store refuses to persist key-like strings (SECURITY.md). Note the resolution order: JEV_OPENROUTER_API_KEY, then config file, then OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so a shared OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var would be picked up implicitly.

Daemon listens on a 0600 unix socket and on 127.0.0.1 (port 47913 for the extension WebSocket and debug UI). The Chrome extension pairs with a one-time 6-digit code. The extension uses chrome.debugger on the user's real Chrome profile, which means full control of logged-in sessions. This is a large privilege surface, and the repo is 1 week old with 1 author.

Prompt-injection surface is real. Web page text flows into Jev prompts and into agent-visible results (jev_observe, results lists). Mitigations: hidden text and injection bait are dropped from the page model (README), secret:true params never sent to Jev, card/password values masked (src/core/safety/privacy.ts), irreversible actions require confirmation. All of this is heuristic and unaudited.

No telemetry or analytics found (grep of src). The only outbound URLs are the provider endpoints and a link builder for console.typesafe.ai playground share URLs (playground.ts:8). Those links compress the payload into the URL fragment, so the payload is not sent unless the user opens it.
Header comments say sub-decisions are labelled and stored locally in a SQLite trace, including page-derived content.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (or TypeSafe) only: POST /systemone with {model, state, questions} (client.ts:55). The state is a serialized view of the current browser page (element names and roles, region text, task goal/intent/params). Non-secret param values are included. Password, card and OTP fields are masked and secret params are excluded. Repo code, diffs and Claude Code prompts are NOT sent. Only web-page content from browsing tasks and the task text the agent writes leave the machine. Locally it stores traces, screenshots and site memory in ~/.local/share/jev-browser. Because the extension drives the user's real Chrome, any authenticated page the task visits can be sent to the provider. OpenRouter's own retention and logging apply.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.failureMode: Retry then throw, and only fail-open in the sense that Claude keeps working. client.ts:13-14 sets 20 s per-request timeout and up to 5 attempts (4 retries) with jittered exponential backoff (500 ms base, max 8 s, honoring Retry-After) on network, timeout and retryable statuses. Worst case is over 100 s for one call. A missing key gives a JevError 'config' at once. Failover to typesafe is off by default and needs a second key. It is opt-in and isolated: nothing in the coding loop depends on it, so a Jev outage only breaks browser tasks, and the MCP tool returns an error to Claude. Rate limiter defaults are 1200 requests per minute and 250k tokens per second.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.contextCost: 15 MCP tools (jev_task, status, wait, answer, control, result, trace, observe, find, ask, act, tabs, screenshot, settings, doctor). Source of the two registration files is about 34k chars, and descriptions plus zod schemas are roughly 60% of that, so about 4.5-6k tokens of tool definitions (estimate, not measured). Server instructions add about 2.5k chars, roughly 640 tokens (src/mcp/instructions.ts), and are injected every session. Total is about 5-7k tokens per session while connected (about 5% of a 200k window). Every jev tool result also gets an appended 'JEV is waiting for your answer' block when questions are pending. No hooks are shipped, so nothing is injected per prompt. The SKILL.md (119 lines, description-only in context until triggered) adds a little more. This is comparable to the existing playwright MCP, and it overlaps with it.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. No hooks and no transparent proxy. Claude will call jev_task only when a request involves operating a website, so it would never trigger during ordinary code editing, Grep, Bash or test runs. It is automatic only for browser work, and it competes with the already-installed playwright MCP for the same job.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: None on ordinary coding turns, since there are no hooks and nothing on the request path. Only tool schema tokens are added at session start. Per browser task, the README claims about 100 ms per Jev decision, 17-20 Jev calls, and 10-17 s per task. The daemon starts lazily and exits after 30 minutes idle. The 20 s timeout and retries can stall a task in a bad network.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=22.18 (TypeScript run directly), Chrome/Chromium, optional Chrome extension; ships SQLite trace store
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.tests: Substantial for a week-old repo. About 19 unit test files in test/core, 9 integration tests (Chromium, daemon, extension, MCP, runner), 2 live tests gated by JEV_LIVE=1, and a 58-case grounding eval (evals/cases/grounding.json) run against local fixture sites. No .github directory, so no CI. The commit trailers show the repo was largely written by Claude Opus 5.5 sessions. Test results were not executed by this audit (static reading only).
pros: Only candidate found that uses OpenRouter natively: default provider is 'openrouter', model typesafe/jev-1.13, base https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (schema.ts:54-56, client.ts:66). It reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it works with the user's planned key with zero patching.

Real, non-trivial Jev use. It sends typed questions with a state payload and consumes per-answer probabilities. Confidence gating (act / verify / ask), calibration reports and traces make good use of the calibrated-probability design of Jev. Also handles retry, Retry-After, rate limiting and OpenRouter usage.cost.
jev_ask exposes raw noul/choice/score primitives over page state, which is the closest thing to a generic 'ask Jev' tool among what was audited.
Clean opt-in: zero hooks, no per-prompt injection, no latency on normal coding turns, MIT license, no telemetry, key sent via header only, key input via stdin.
Good test and eval coverage for its age, with fixtures, integration tests, and a grounding eval.
Careful safety design for browsing: irreversible-action confirmation, secret params kept from the model, masking of card and password values, domain allow-lists and budgets.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It is browser automation. Jev is used to pick page elements and verify web steps, not to make coding decisions (which file, is this diff risky, which test, permission gating). It does nothing for daily coding in Claude Code and duplicates the existing playwright MCP.
Auto-invocation is only model discretion or skill trigger and only for website tasks. It cannot satisfy 'Claude Code uses Jev whenever it adds value' for code work.
Costs about 5-7k tokens of context per session for 15 tools plus instructions, for a capability that is rarely needed when coding.

Very immature: created 2026-09-23, 1 star, 0 forks, 1 author, 94 commits in 2 days, v0.1.0, mostly AI-authored, no CI, not on npm (private:true). Install is a manual clone, npm install and build. `jev install` edits Claude and Codex config and creates symlinks in the user's home.

Extension path gives chrome.debugger control over the user's real logged-in Chrome, and page content from authenticated sites goes to OpenRouter. That is risky on client projects. Prompt-injection defences are heuristic.

Uses /api/v1/systemone only and not the alpha Decisions API. Full retry cascade can block a call for over 100 s. Channels push needs --dangerously-load-development-channels, which the user's bypass workflow may accept but is a research-preview dev flag.
Claimed benchmark numbers (100% top-1, ECE 0.05, 7-step flight run) come from the author's own local fixtures, not independent validation.
gh-legostin-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-in-class for native OpenRouter Jev support and a solid code base, but it is a browser-automation server, not a coding integration. It would add about 5-7k tokens of context and overlap with playwright while never fire on ordinary code work. Only worth installing if the user wants Jev-driven web tasks. Do not use it as the primary Jev integration for coding, and if trying it, take it with a scoped, dedicated OpenRouter key and the headless Chromium driver rather than the real-Chrome extension.

openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.name: OpenRouter cookbook: Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev (reference impl: PanAchy/jevvy)
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.whatItDoes: Official OpenRouter recipe: a Bun/TS PermissionRequest hook for Claude Code (also Codex, Cursor, OpenCode plugin). A static RISKY regex list runs first. Otherwise it asks Jev two Noul questions ("reversible" and "serves_task") and auto-allows the Bash command only if both score >= 0.9. It abstains, leaving the normal prompt, on any error, timeout or low score. It only reduces permission prompts for Bash commands. It does not add reasoning, code search, routing or review. The installable reference implementation is PanAchy/jevvy (npm @jevvy/permissions v0.5.0, MIT, Claude Code plugin jevvy-permissions@jevvy). It ships its own calibrated four-question policy (harmful, sensitive, untrusted, obscured, all as max-Noul thresholds) and supports providers zen, typesafe, openrouter, vercel, laya and custom.

Note the recipe uses the /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, while jevvy uses /api/v1/systemone. Both are OpenRouter surfaces from the brief. Jevvy reads its provider from ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc and OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the environment. In the recipe, TYPESAFE_API_KEY is not used.

interface.purpose: Same review as the recipe hook. It skips visible 'ask' rules from settings, then applies a 4-question policy with a 5 s per-request timeout, a 512-entry in-memory cache and a provider cooldown after failures.

security: Recipe: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from process.env in the hook. It is not placed in argv and stays out of ps output. The hook does not run any shell command itself.

Recipe: the RISKY regex list is a heuristic denylist. Bypasses via unusual shell constructs are plausible, and the final gate is an LLM-style probabilistic score. The docs call the scores noisy (0.02-0.05 variance) and tell users to tighten RISKY themselves.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command text and description go into the Jev state. Jev returns typed probabilities only, with no free text and no tool execution, so injection can at worst bias a score. That is still a real risk when it converts a prompt into an automatic allow.

Risk to this user: an auto-allow is a security downgrade whenever a false positive gets through. The Claude Code docs page (fetched via summarizer, so unverified) says a hook 'allow' can override deny rules. The recipe claims it cannot. Check this before trusting it.

Jevvy reads a global config only (~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc). Project repos cannot override it. The key can sit in plaintext JSONC or come from env, and there is a redact helper for error text. Jevvy is a 5-week-old npm package (0.5.0). Installing it runs 3rd-party code with access to the command stream, so pin the version. The workflows pin action SHAs.
No telemetry was seen in the recipe. Jevvy telemetry was not exhaustively audited. Nothing was executed.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.dataEgress: Recipe hook sends to openrouter.ai, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe. The payload is the full Bash command string, the absolute project cwd, and (when present) the tool 'description' as the task. Only requests that would otherwise prompt are sent. It does not send file contents, diffs, the conversation or tool outputs. Command strings can still embed inline secrets or client paths. The cwd leaks client project names and paths. Jevvy sends less, only state {action:'shell', resource:<command>}. It does not send cwd or a task. Nothing leaves the machine except for prompt-eligible Bash commands.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.failureMode: Fail-open to the normal permission prompt, meaning it abstains. Recipe: network errors, non-OK responses, invalid probabilities and an 8 s timeout all return undefined, so no output and the normal prompt shows. It is never fail-closed on Claude Code. The Cursor variant has failClosed true, but the script returns 'ask' on errors. The claude hook timeout of 15 s (recipe) or 10 s (jevvy) caps the worst case. Jevvy adds a 5 s per-request timeout, an in-memory cache and a provider cooldown after auth or credit failures. Missing key gives a one-time SessionStart warning and no auto-approval.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.latencyImpact: Only on commands that would prompt: one HTTPS round trip, brief claims 70-500 ms and the worst case is 8 s (recipe). Bun or node startup adds roughly 50-150 ms. Latency does not touch the main loop, tool calls that are already allowed, or non-Bash tools. The hook never runs when no prompt would appear.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.contextCost: Zero. No MCP tools and no skill descriptions (the optional calibrate-permissions skill is separate). The hook only emits JSON or a one-time SessionStart systemMessage warning when misconfigured. The cost is about $0.0000168 per 400-token request.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest, matcher Bash). It fires automatically without any prompt, but ONLY when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog. Per the Claude Code hooks docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, fetched via summarizer, so verify locally), PermissionRequest fires in default, plan and acceptEdits modes. It does NOT fire in auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions modes.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a deterministic hook and needs no 'use jev' prompt, which matches the user's requirement in its permission mode.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected text.
Fail-open to the normal prompt. It can only remove prompts, never block work. Timeouts are bounded (8 s / 15 s).
Uses OpenRouter directly (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so nothing needs patching. Jevvy also supports openrouter natively.
Cheap: about $0.00002 per decision. Small egress compared with an MCP that sees code.

Jevvy has real engineering: 28 commits, 15+ test files, CI with pinned action SHAs, changesets releases, a calibration corpus (eval/commands.json), MIT license, and a Claude Code plugin (marketplace.json, hooks.json). It skips explicit ask rules and never overrides allow/deny.
Coexists with the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks, because it only touches the PermissionRequest event.
cons: Wrong fit for this user's mode: the user runs bypass or 'auto', and PermissionRequest does not fire in auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions, so the hook would rarely or never run. It only helps in default, plan or acceptEdits. Worse, it swaps a human prompt for a probabilistic auto-allow, which can be less safe than default mode.
It does not make Claude Code use Jev for coding decisions such as routing, review, test selection, refactor choices or model selection. It is a permission-prompt reducer only.
Only Bash is covered. There is no Edit/Write/MCP gating in the recipe or jevvy hook.
The recipe sends cwd and the description to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe). This matters on client projects. Jevvy sends the command only.
Scores are noisy (0.02-0.05 variance). The recipe's 'reversible' Noul can mis-score commands with side effects outside the repo. The user must maintain their own RISKY list.

The recipe needs Bun and a hand-wired settings.json. Jevvy needs Node >= 22.19 (the user has Node 24), but it is a 5-week-old 0.5.0 package with ~20 stars, one main author (21 of 28 commits) and no proven track record.

Docs conflict on whether a hook 'allow' overrides deny rules (recipe says no, the Claude Code hooks page says yes), and the Claude Code docs page was read through a summarizer, so it is unverified. Needs a local test in default mode.
Key handling: an API key in the hook environment or in ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc plaintext. Codex strips *KEY* env vars, though this does not apply to Claude Code.
openrouter-ai-docs-cookbook-coding-agent.verdict: This is well built, safe (fail-open, tiny egress, zero context) and OpenRouter-native, but it is a narrow permission-prompt shortcut, not a Jev integration for coding. It also does not fire in the auto or bypass modes this user normally runs. Use it only if the user moves to default or acceptEdits mode and wants fewer Bash prompts, preferably via pinned jevvy with the openrouter provider, not the raw recipe.

openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.name: OpenRouter Jev Router (typesafe/jev-router)
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.whatItDoes: A hosted OpenRouter model slug (typesafe/jev-router), not a repo or package. Jev reads the conversation, scores task type, difficulty, precision and how much a stronger model would help. OpenRouter then serves the request from the cheapest pool model that meets that bar, choosing reasoning effort too. It is described as cache-aware: it switches model only when the expected gain outweighs the lost prompt cache. It works over Chat Completions, Responses and Messages (streaming and non-streaming). Claude Code's Messages traffic can therefore hit it through OpenRouter's Anthropic-compatible endpoint with no local code. An optional `jev-router` request plugin (models / allowed_models / excluded_models, up to 1,024 wildcard patterns each) narrows the pool. The `X-OpenRouter-Metadata: enabled` header exposes the decision (resolved_models, list_fallback, list_tier_cap, max_fallback).

providerSupport.evidence: OpenRouter-native model. Docs jev-router.md: `POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions` with `"model": "typesafe/jev-router"` and `Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY`; 'works with Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages'. Public /api/v1/models lists id typesafe/jev-router (created 1790363560, about 2026-09-25, context_length 1000000, pricing prompt/completion '-1' meaning dynamic, supported_parameters [], input modalities text/image/file/audio/video, and /endpoints returns an empty array). Claude Code wiring per OpenRouter's claude-code-integration.md: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=<OPENROUTER_API_KEY>, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="", then /logout. Not offered on TypeSafe's own API, so it is only reachable through OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: Uses OpenRouter's model pool (composition not published in the docs I read). Third-party wrappers (gargpratyush/jev-router, FrancoisChastel/jev-router, Ex8-ca/jev-router) are separate candidates and not this one.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: N/A, it is already OpenRouter-native.

interface.name: plugins:[{id:'jev-router', models, allowed_models, excluded_models}]

interface.purpose: Reports which backend model actually served the request.

interface.name: OpenRouter Activity dashboard
