security: No local code is installed: no npx, hook, MCP or postinstall surface. Risk sits in the account and the network path.

The OpenRouter key goes in ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (sent as a Bearer header). It stays out of argv if set in the shell profile or the settings.json `env` block. OpenRouter's own doc warns against committing it and suggests loading it from a keychain.
Putting the key in project .claude/settings.local.json risks leaking it into a client repo. Use ~/.claude/settings.json or a shell wrapper instead.

OpenRouter docs say Claude Code + OpenRouter is only guaranteed to work with the Anthropic first-party provider. If the router picks another provider, tool-use or thinking quirks are possible. Silent switching to non-Anthropic models is a behavioural and compliance surprise.

The router decides using conversation content, including pasted logs and issues. Content in tool results could in principle steer routing (for example, low-difficulty framing pushes a cheap model). Third-party coverage says the router claims to see the conversation, so this is an untested prompt-injection surface.

Data-policy and ZDR details for the router are not stated on the doc pages I could read. The Auto Router docs mention honoring account ZDR and guardrails; whether Jev Router does the same is unverified.
No telemetry beyond OpenRouter's normal logging and Activity dashboard.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.dataEgress: Everything Claude Code sends in each Messages request leaves the machine. That is the system prompt and CLAUDE.md content, the full conversation, file contents from Read/Grep, Bash outputs, diffs and tool results, plus images if present. It goes to OpenRouter, to Jev (TypeSafe) for the routing decision (the docs say Jev 'reads the conversation'), and to whichever upstream model provider is picked. That is potentially non-Anthropic and non-US, and the pool is not enumerated in the docs I read. Versus today's Anthropic-only path, this adds OpenRouter, TypeSafe and possible extra model vendors. That is a real issue for client code. The existing PreToolUse secret guard only blocks tool input, not what tool results carry onward, and it does not reduce this exposure.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.failureMode: Fail-closed. Claude Code talks only to openrouter.ai, so an outage, 5xx or 502 upstream stops the session with no fallback to Anthropic (docs: 502 for upstream failure, 'failed generations are not billed'). Exclusion lists that empty the pool return 404, but Claude Code cannot send the plugin. OpenRouter advertises provider failover across Anthropic providers for Anthropic models. The Auto Router docs say it 'degrades gracefully' if classification is unavailable; I found no equivalent statement for Jev Router. The router's own decision latency is claimed at 70-500 ms for Jev; there is no documented timeout for it. Mitigation: keep a separate wrapper or profile so plain `claude` still uses the subscription.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.contextCost: Zero added Claude Code context: no tools, no MCP server instructions and no hook-injected text. It only changes which endpoint and model string are used. Indirect cost: Claude Code's model-specific prompt tuning, cache_control and thinking behaviour may degrade when the served model is not Opus or Sonnet. Also, supported_parameters is empty and pricing is dynamic, so tool-calling support is asserted only in third-party summaries ('streaming, tools, thinking and prompt caching pass through untouched').
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at OpenRouter and the model is typesafe/jev-router, every main-loop and subagent request is routed with no user prompting and no model discretion. It is the only candidate type that satisfies 'never say use jev' literally. The cost is that it replaces the model choice rather than adding a capability.
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.latencyImpact: Documented figures are maker-reported. Jev decision: 70-500 ms end to end (TypeSafe brief). OpenRouter claims the lowest median TTFT among the routers it tested (0.58 s on Terminal-Bench vs 2.06 s for the next fastest, per a JevMade summary). It is not independently verified. Expect a sub-second overhead on requests where a routing decision is made. Cheaper models chosen for easy turns may be faster overall than Opus 5.5.
pros: Only truly automatic option evaluated: no hook, MCP or prompt discipline. Set two env vars and the model string, and it just runs (OpenRouter claude-code-integration.md).
Zero context and zero local attack surface: no tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no installer or npm supply chain (contrast with wrapper proxies that run localhost code).

Cache-aware by design: it holds a model while the prompt cache is warm and switches only if the gain exceeds the lost cache. This addresses the biggest failure of naive per-turn routers in Claude Code's long agentic loops.
Can lower spend by sending mechanical turns to cheap models. Pricing is the underlying model's cost with no separate router fee ('costs nothing to invoke' per coverage).
OpenRouter-native, so it fits the user's OpenRouter-only constraint, with the Activity dashboard, budgets and response.model giving per-request visibility into what was chosen.
Works with the Messages API that Claude Code speaks, streaming supported, and the pool can be restricted with the jev-router plugin (for API callers).
cons: Does not work with the subscription/OAuth login. OpenRouter's guide requires blanking ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, setting ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and running /logout, so all traffic bills per token. Leaving the flat-rate Opus 5.5 subscription for a heavy all-day user could cost far more.

It replaces the user's chosen Opus 5.5 with whatever the router picks; the user would lose deterministic quality on hard tasks. Jev's role is a cheap decision model, and the benefit claimed is cost/speed, not better code.

Evidence is thin and maker-reported. The model was created about 2026-09-25, is beta, and the pool/tier composition is not documented in the pages I read. Benchmark claims conflict across sources (237 vs 130 tasks in the announcement summary; 221 vs 73 in the JevMade summary), and the skeptics' claim that it is a small-model router is unresolved.

Tool-calling support is not confirmed by structured metadata (supported_parameters is []; /endpoints returns empty). Claude Code's heavy tool-use and thinking loop on non-Anthropic models is explicitly not guaranteed by OpenRouter ('only guaranteed to work with the Anthropic first-party provider').

Cannot pass the jev-router plugin from Claude Code, so restricting the pool to Anthropic models, or excluding weak models, is not possible per-request. It would need OpenRouter account-level provider/model restrictions, and whether Jev Router honors these is unverified.

Fail-closed dependency on OpenRouter for every keystroke, and conversation content goes to OpenRouter, TypeSafe and unknown upstream vendors. That is a compliance risk for client projects, and pointing settings at a single endpoint affects all projects unless scoped.
Cache loss risk remains when a switch happens, since a switch discards the prompt cache. With Claude Code's large system prompt and tool schema, a bad switch is expensive.
Could not be tested here (no OpenRouter key; live checks limited to the public /models listing and the docs).
openrouter-ai-docs-guides-routing-router.verdict: The only genuinely zero-prompt, zero-context integration, but it swaps your model rather than adding Jev as a capability, forces API billing instead of the Opus 5.5 subscription, and sends all code to OpenRouter, TypeSafe and unknown upstream providers. Worth trying as a scoped opt-in profile (separate wrapper or settings for personal, low-stakes projects) after a small paid trial to check tool-use reliability. It is not a good global default for client work.

security: No install-time shell: package.json has only a prepare script (tsc build); CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts and npm audit; no curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry found (grep clean).

Plugin launches `npx -y github:rahulrajaram/jev-mcp#main` (.claude-plugin/plugin.json): unpinned floating branch, code fetched from a 0-star personal repo and built on first run, so any future push to main runs on the user's machine with the user's env and key. Pin a commit SHA or use a local checkout (README option 1) for client work.

API key never a tool argument and not in argv; read from env or key files (~/.config/openrouter/key, ~/.openrouter). Plugin deliberately ships no env block. Sent only as Authorization Bearer to OPENROUTER_BASE_URL (default openrouter.ai); OPENROUTER_BASE_URL is overridable so a poisoned env could redirect the key.
Sends X-Title=jev-mcp and HTTP-Referer=repo homepage to OpenRouter (app attribution, benign).

No shell execution or file reads beyond key files; MCP server only makes HTTPS calls. Prompt-injection surface: tool result is structured JSON with validated shape (answers checked against the question sent), the model cannot emit free text.

No secret scrubbing of the state: Claude decides what to put in state, so code or secrets Claude pastes go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user's existing PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tool args (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the tool's `state` and question/option text: diffs, file excerpts, claims, candidate lists, up to about 150k chars (JEV_MAX_STATE_CHARS) per call, sent via HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (which routes to TypeSafe's Jev; OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see it). Nothing is sent automatically or in the background: only on model-initiated tool calls. Also GET /api/v1/auth/key and /models/.../endpoints on jev_models. Plus API key as bearer. No telemetry. Client-project code can leave the machine, which needs a client-policy check.
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open in practice: tool errors come back as isError with classified kind/retryable/hint (authentication, rate_limit, timeout, connection, insufficient_credits, malformed_response, invalid_request), so Claude just proceeds without Jev. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), 3 attempts on 408/429/5xx/connection with 500 ms doubling backoff capped 5 s and Retry-After honoured up to 60 s, so worst case can be roughly 45+ s stall on a single call. Missing key at startup: server still starts and every call errors (does not block Claude Code). No hook involved, so nothing can block tool execution.
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Approx 16-18k chars of tool names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas, about 4-4.5k tokens loaded per session (each of 4 judgment tools carries a roughly 1.3k-char SCOPE_GUIDE plus long state/question/thresholds descriptions; jev_ask has the largest schema). Estimate from source, not measured. No MCP server `instructions` field (new McpServer({name,version}) only). Skill adds about 150 tokens of description in the listing (body loads only on trigger, about 1.9k tokens). No hooks, so nothing injected per turn. Could shrink by deferring tools via tool search.
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There is no hook, proxy or deterministic trigger. Worse, the tool descriptions and SKILL.md explicitly tell Claude NOT to use Jev for one-off judgments and to prefer its own reasoning, so for normal coding turns Claude will rarely invoke it. It only fires when Claude decides a repeated-judgment or calibrated-threshold task is at hand (e.g. triaging 40 files).
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero added latency per turn unless Claude calls a tool. Per call: claimed 70-500 ms model latency plus OpenRouter hop and Claude's tool-call round trip (one extra model turn to build the call and read the result, seconds). MCP server start via npx github: first run clones, installs and builds with tsc (tens of seconds), cached per commit thereafter; a cold start can make the server fail to connect in the first session. Timeouts up to 15 s x 3 attempts on failure.
pros: Native OpenRouter support against the exact endpoint in the brief (POST /api/alpha/decisions), default model ~typesafe/jev-latest, per-call dollar cost surfaced from OpenRouter usage: works with the user's OpenRouter-only setup with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY + JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.

Best-in-class safety design among Jev wrappers: caller owns option set, every answer validated against the question sent (malformed_response otherwise), local enforcement of real limits (10 score levels, 255 options, about 32k tokens), classified errors, retries with Retry-After, act/review/abstain gating.
Ships both the MCP server and a skill in one Claude Code plugin; skill and tool descriptions carry honest scope guidance (no computing, no dates, filter state, batch via jev_ask), reducing misuse.

Fail-open by construction (errors returned as tool results; no hook can stall a Claude Code turn); no telemetry, no postinstall, key kept out of argv and tool args, CI with ci --ignore-scripts and audit, about 1.7k lines of tests (unit + local stand-in, live e2e opt-in).
MIT, small readable code (about 1.5k lines src), easy to fork/pin/audit.
cons: Does not meet the core requirement of automatic use: it is model-discretion only, and its own SKILL.md and tool descriptions tell Claude to prefer its own answer for single judgments, so in normal edit/debug/refactor turns it will almost never fire. There is no hook or router that puts Jev in the loop.

Supply chain risk: plugin runs `npx -y github:rahulrajaram/jev-mcp#main` (unpinned branch head) from a brand-new personal fork (created 2026-09-18, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 13 commits, 2 authors in 2 days); on client projects pin a SHA or use a local build.

Repo is 12 days old, jev 'beta' upstream, and the OpenRouter Decisions endpoint is /api/alpha/: two layers of instability; the fork tracks upstream only manually and the README says npm jev-mcp is the inferior 0.4.0 without OpenRouter.
Context tax of roughly 4-4.5k tokens for 5 tools every session (long repeated SCOPE_GUIDE text) for a capability Claude is told to seldom use; jev_models is only a diagnostic.

Data egress with no guard: Claude-chosen state (diffs, code) goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; the existing secret-leak PreToolUse matcher does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and client-confidential code may not be allowed off-machine.

Tool-call overhead: each use costs an extra Claude turn to construct a large JSON call plus the state tokens re-emitted as output by Opus; worst-case failure stall about 45 s (15 s x 3 attempts). Provider auto-selection prefers TypeSafe if any TypeSafe key exists, so must pin JEV_PROVIDER.
Jev is a fixed-option chooser that cannot count/compute/compare dates; few daily coding tasks fit (triage many files, rank candidates), and Opus already handles those with an explainable answer.
gh-rahulrajaram-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-engineered and the only one found here with first-class OpenRouter support, plus a plugin and skill, but it is a passive, model-discretion tool that deliberately discourages use for one-off judgments, so it will not deliver the 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' goal alone. Reasonable as the tool layer (pinned to a commit SHA, JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter) only if paired with a hook or CLAUDE.md routing rule that deterministically triggers it for batch triage or gating tasks.

gh-jkudish-jev-browser.name: jkudish/jev-browser (@jkudish/jev-browser)
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.whatItDoes: A Jev-driven headless-browser agent (Playwright/Chromium) exposed as an MCP stdio/HTTP server with a single tool, jev_navigate, plus a CLI, a library, and an optional SKILL.md. Given a task and a start URL, code owns the loop: each step it sends page state (up to 240 clickable, typeable and selectable elements) to Jev as a typed Choice ("which action") plus goal-reached and stuck probabilities, then executes the action in the browser. Jev never writes text, so a separate small "typing model" generates any string typed into a field. It returns the final page (text, markdown, html or aria), a step trace with confidences, console errors, cost and a screenshot. It is browser automation for web tasks, not a coding-assistant helper.

providerSupport.evidence: Judgment transport lives in dependency @jkudish/jev-agent-tools@0.1.3 (same author, npm created 2026-09-24), not in this repo. dist/transports/openrouter.js:5 needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY matching /^sk-or-/; :16-17 maps jev-latest to typesafe/jev-1.13; :18 POSTs https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with body {model, state, questions}. dist/transports/typesafe.js:3-11 uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai). dist/provider.js:7 JEV_PROVIDER auto-selects in order TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Vercel. The /api/v1/systemone endpoint is not used. With only OPENROUTER_API_KEY set, judgments go via OpenRouter automatically. The typing model also uses OpenRouter (src/navigate.ts:164, default google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite per README). README 'Configuration' and 'The typing model' sections.
providerSupport.others: Cloudflare Workers AI (CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN + CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, alias typesafe/jev), Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, typesafe-ai/jev). Typing model: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (JEV_BROWSER_TYPE_BASE_URL, e.g. Ollama).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter is already supported natively. Caveat: TYPESAFE_API_KEY takes precedence, so keep it unset or set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.

interface.name: jev_navigate (MCP tool, src/index.ts:54-249)
interface.purpose: The only MCP tool. Inputs: task, start_url, max_steps (1-100, default 24), max_seconds (10-600, default 180), allow_typing, format (text|markdown|html|aria), max_chars, screenshot, password_file, password_env, cookie_file[], cookie_env[]. Returns JSON trace plus a JPEG screenshot.

interface.name: jev-browser run "<task>" <url> (CLI, src/cli.ts)
interface.purpose: Same agent from the shell. Options --format, --max-chars, --max-steps, --max-seconds, --no-typing, --screenshot, --record, --cookie-file, --password-file, --password-origin.

interface.name: jev-browser --http / JEV_BROWSER_TRANSPORT=http
interface.purpose: Stateless HTTP MCP server at /mcp with /health, bearer auth required off loopback, concurrency cap 4.

interface.name: navigate() library export (src/library.ts)
interface.purpose: Programmatic API with injectable JevTransport.

interface.name: skills/jev-browser/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Skill whose description triggers on driving a real website (forms, logins, JS flows) or choosing between jev_navigate, static fetch, and the client's own browser automation. It tells the agent to call jev_navigate for real-site interaction tasks. It is manual copy into .claude/skills and only teaches when to call the tool. It has no hook.

security: API keys are read from environment variables only and never taken from argv, but the README's `claude mcp add ... -e` and JSON config examples put TYPESAFE_API_KEY in a config file. The README notes some MCP clients filter env and drop the key.

Serious prompt-injection surface: it browses arbitrary web pages and returns their text, markdown or html into Claude's context. The SKILL.md itself says to treat the page text as untrusted. It is an active browser (click, select, submit) and can perform consequential writes on real sites.

SECURITY.md admits pages it visits can reach private endpoints, so localhost and internal services are reachable via the start URL. It says to run it in a container or restricted network. This matters for client projects.

Password and cookie handling is unusually careful: handoff files (0700 dir, 0600 files, no symlinks, one-shot delete), JEV_PASSWORD_* and JEV_COOKIE_* env allowlist, exact-origin binding, multi-encoding redaction, screenshot suppression.

Install risk: the npm package has a postinstall (scripts/ensure-chromium.mjs) that runs `npx --yes playwright install chromium`. It also has a `prepare` build script and about 13 runtime deps, including the AI SDK for four providers, @typesafe-ai/sdk and @jkudish/jev-agent-tools, a 1-week-old single-author package.
The README's recommended `npx -y @jkudish/jev-browser` runs unpinned latest code with the user's keys on every start. Pin the version if it is used at all.
No telemetry found in src (grep for telemetry/analytics only hit a code comment). OpenRouter requests send HTTP-Referer and X-Title attribution headers.
Typing-model trap: a stale OPENAI_API_KEY silently wins typing-provider detection over OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
Tests: 3 offline suites (unit 1584 lines, transports, http) plus a 1697-line live e2e suite. CI runs typecheck, build and tests on Node 22. The e2e run needs a real key.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.dataEgress: To the judgment provider (OpenRouter POST /api/alpha/decisions with this key): the task text, the current URL and page state (page excerpt text, plus descriptions of up to 240 interactive elements) and the questions, on every step (up to 24 steps by default). To the typing provider (OpenRouter google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite by default if only an OpenRouter key is set, or OpenAI/Anthropic/Google if those keys are in the env): the task and field context, once per typed field. To the visited websites: normal browser traffic from the user's IP, plus any seeded cookies or passwords for the configured origin. It does NOT read the local repo, diffs or Claude's transcript on its own. Only what Claude puts in `task` or `start_url` leaves the machine, along with what the pages contain. Local files created: ~/.jev-browser/handoff only if the password flow is used.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level, because it is an on-demand tool. If the key is missing the tool returns a config error and the server does not break Claude. If OpenRouter fails or is slow, the transport throws 'OpenRouter decisions API HTTP <status>'. The run ends with status error and the tool returns isError. Runs have a hard wall-clock deadline (max_seconds default 180, cap 600) via an AbortController (src/navigate.ts:552), a step cap, and per-action Playwright timeouts of 4-30 s. Schema-invalid Jev answers stop the run before any action executes. Nothing blocks Claude's normal work, but a hung navigation can occupy a tool call for up to 3 to 10 minutes, and the README warns that client tool-call timeouts (60 s in the TS SDK) may need raising. If the typing model fails, fields are left empty with warnings.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (jev_navigate). Its description is about 1.1k chars, and the input schema (13 params including nested cookie_file/cookie_env objects, each with long descriptions) is about 5k chars, so roughly 1.5k to 1.8k tokens of tool definition (chars/4 estimate from src/index.ts:54-154). No server `instructions` field. No hooks inject text. Each call returns a large JSON trace (page content 8k to 16k chars or up to 1MB for html, plus per-step trace) and a base64 JPEG screenshot into context, so every use costs several thousand tokens. The optional SKILL.md is 5.6k chars, and only its frontmatter description (about 350 chars) is always loaded. Playwright MCP is already installed and overlaps in role.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, plus an optional skill description trigger. No hook, no proxy. Claude Code would only call jev_navigate when Claude judges that a real-website interaction is needed, and the user already has playwright MCP, WebFetch and Chrome tools that compete for that role. The bundled SKILL.md nudges the model toward jev_navigate for forms and JS flows but only after it is manually copied into ~/.claude/skills. It does not make Jev automatically assist coding decisions such as permissions, routing, review or classification.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns, since it is on demand and there is no hook. When used, one navigation takes seconds to minutes: the README claims about 4 s for a short Wikipedia hop at $0.0016, and each step costs one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms, plus the OpenRouter alpha hop) plus a Playwright page settle of 250-400 ms or more. Default budget is 180 s. First MCP server start via npx adds a download and install of the dependencies plus a Chromium fetch of about 150MB on first run.
pros: Genuine OpenRouter support in code, not just the README: alpha decisions endpoint with typesafe/jev-1.13, and one sk-or- key also covers the typing model (openrouter.js:5-27; navigate.ts:164).

Real, well-engineered Jev use: typed Choice actions plus calibrated goal and stuck probabilities gate the loop, and the returned step trace with confidences is auditable. It is one of the few Jev integrations that uses Jev for what it is good at, structured decisions, rather than chat.
Strong credential hygiene (handoff files, env allowlists, origin binding, redaction) and a hard wall-clock and step budget; the failure mode is a clean error, not a hang of Claude Code.
Active and popular for a 2-week-old repo: 297 stars, 27 forks, 67 commits, v0.8.1 released 2026-09-29, MIT, CI, and about 3.8k lines of tests including a live e2e suite.
Cheap per run (README claims about $0.0016 for a 4 s navigation) and only a single low-cost tool definition (about 1.7k tokens).
Useful niche for a web dev: verifying a deployed page, smoke-driving a login-walled staging app or a JS-only flow with an evidence trace (screenshot, console/network errors).
cons: Not a coding-workflow integration at all: it does not touch code, diffs, tests, permissions or Claude's decisions. It fails the user's core goal of Claude Code using Jev automatically to add value in daily coding.

Duplicates tools the user already has (playwright MCP with 30+ tools, WebFetch, Chrome) and its own SKILL.md says to prefer the client's own browser automation for local dev servers and signed-in profiles, which is most of a developer's use.
Auto-invocation depends entirely on Claude's discretion and competes with playwright MCP; the SKILL.md must be manually copied. It cannot be made deterministic without a custom hook.

Heavy, brittle install: npx -y of an unpinned package with a postinstall that runs `npx playwright install chromium`, roughly 13 dependencies, and single-author deps (@jkudish/jev-agent-tools is about 6 days old). The Playwright download duplicates what playwright MCP already has.

Sends page content and element lists to OpenRouter on every step, and typing prompts to whichever provider key is in the env (a stale OPENAI_API_KEY silently wins). Client sites and staging pages would leave the machine, which is a client-confidentiality concern.

Untrusted page content is returned straight into Claude's context, which is prompt injection exposure in bypass or auto permission mode. SECURITY.md also warns pages it visits can reach private endpoints on the local network.

OpenRouter Decisions API is alpha and adds a hop (the README itself recommends direct TypeSafe). Jev 'browser use' quality is claimed on Wikipedia and DuckDuckGo tasks and the README admits rough edges and thresholds tuned on those only.
Long-running tool calls (up to 180 to 600 s) can exceed client tool-call timeouts.
gh-jkudish-jev-browser.verdict: Well built, honest and genuinely OpenRouter-capable, but it is a web-browsing agent that competes with the playwright MCP the user already runs, not a way to make Claude Code use Jev automatically for coding decisions. Skip it for the daily-coding integration. At most, install it pinned and opt-in later for occasional evidence-grade site checks, and never with client credentials.

gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.name: itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp (renamed: itsmostafa/system-one-connector), binary "evaluate"
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Single static Go binary ("evaluate") that runs as a stdio MCP server exposing ONE tool, `evaluate`. The tool POSTs {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} to Jev and returns the typed JSON (probabilities, confidence). Local extras: criteria validation, stable option ordering, client-side min_confidence abstain (`__uncertain__`), and an `items` fan-out (up to 500 records, 8 concurrent, one billed request each). Also has `setup mcp` (auto-registers with claude/codex/hermes CLIs and Claude Desktop), `setup pi`, `update` (self-update with SHA-256 check) and `version`. Routes: TYPESAFE_API_KEY -> api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (wins if both set), otherwise OPENROUTER_API_KEY -> openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest. The repo was renamed from typesafe-mcp to system-one-connector; the old URL redirects.

providerSupport.evidence: cmd/evaluate/main.go:152-158: `case os.Getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") != "": return &Client{URL: "https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions", APIKey: os.Getenv("OPENROUTER_API_KEY"), Model: "~typesafe/jev-latest", ...}`. main.go:135-151 is the TypeSafe route: TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai) joined with v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_MODEL (default jev-latest). Precedence at main.go:116-119: TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins if both are set. client.go:20-32 sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>` with the same body for both routes. docs/configuration.md notes the OpenRouter path is still /api/alpha/ and may move. It does NOT use /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL accepts any http(s) host that implements POST /v1/systemone (local CLM/Laya, Liquid AI d1 at api.liquid.ai/decisions). The OpenRouter model is hardcoded to ~typesafe/jev-latest (main.go:156); the per-call `model` argument overrides it, so typesafe/jev-1.13 can be pinned per call but not as a default. No TYPESAFE_MODEL effect on the OpenRouter route.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed: OpenRouter is already supported. Only small gaps: the default model is hardcoded, and the path is /api/alpha/decisions rather than /api/v1/systemone. Both are trivial one-line changes in route() if OpenRouter moves the endpoint.

interface.name: MCP tool `evaluate`
interface.purpose: Only tool (tools.go:104-139, annotated ReadOnlyHint: true). Inputs: state (any), questions (map id -> {type noul|choice|score, instructions, criteria?, min_confidence?}), items (map, <=500), model, include_item_usage. Returns Jev JSON, or {results, errors, meta} in items mode.

interface.name: MCP server instructions
interface.purpose: ~2.9k-char guidance block (main.go:31-47) on how to write good Jev questions: narrow judgments, evidence not verdicts, no-match option, batch questions, read confidence. Plus a tool description that lists use cases: classification, routing, scoring, extraction, branching, guardrails/judging. The `Use for...` list is what drives model-discretion invocation.

interface.name: evaluate mcp [--no-update-check]
interface.purpose: Run the stdio MCP server. Unless --no-update-check is passed, it makes a blocking GitHub releases/latest call at startup (2s budget) and appends an update notice to the instructions (update.go:146-158).

interface.name: evaluate setup mcp
interface.purpose: Registers with `claude mcp add evaluate -s user -e KEY=VAL -- <exe> mcp`, plus codex, hermes and Claude Desktop config. Bakes in all TYPESAFE_* vars and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (setup.go:36-246).

interface.name: evaluate setup pi
interface.purpose: Writes a pi extension (~/.pi/agent/extensions/evaluate.ts). Not relevant for Claude Code.

interface.name: evaluate update / version
interface.purpose: Self-update from GitHub Releases with a SHA256SUMS.txt check (checksum comes from the same release, so it protects only against corruption, not a compromised release). Prints the version.

security: API key handling: `evaluate setup mcp` runs `claude mcp add ... -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<value>` (setup.go:226-232), so the key sits in argv, visible in `ps` and /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the moment setup runs. It is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (user-scope mcpServers.evaluate.env). This is avoidable: register by hand and use `${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}` expansion in .mcp.json or an env-wrapper, so the key is never written to disk by the tool.
At runtime the key is read from the env and sent only as a Bearer header to the fixed OpenRouter URL (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). It is not logged; no `log`/print of the key is visible in the source.
No shell execution at runtime. The only exec.Command calls are in `setup` (claude/codex/hermes CLIs, with fixed args). Nothing runs during normal MCP operation.

Install: README pushes `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | sh`. The script (install.sh, 61 lines) is short and sane: it downloads the release tarball and SHA256SUMS.txt from the same GitHub release, verifies the hash, and installs to ~/.local/bin. The checksum is same-origin, so it does not defend against a compromised release. Safer path for you: `gh release download` and inspect it, or `go install` at a pinned tag and audit the source (about 1.3k lines of non-test Go). I did not run the installer.

Self-update (`evaluate update`) replaces the binary from GitHub releases with the same same-origin checksum. Releases are built by GitHub Actions with pinned action SHAs (release-please.yml), which is good hygiene. There are no signed releases and no provenance attestation.
No npm postinstall (Go binary). Dependencies are minimal: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.7.0, cobra, and their transitive deps.

No telemetry. The only third-party contact besides the Jev endpoint is the unauthenticated GET to api.github.com/repos/.../releases/latest on each server start (leaks IP and the fact you run this version; can be disabled only via the hidden --no-update-check flag, which you can put in the MCP args).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is a numeric/enum JSON (probabilities, option keys echoed from your own criteria), so there is little text for an attacker to smuggle back. Inbound risk is the reverse: whatever Claude places in `state` (file contents, issue text, tool output) leaves the machine, and the guidance itself warns that instructions embedded in state can steer Jev.

`ReadOnlyHint: true` plus `items` fan-out (500 billed requests per call) is a cost-abuse vector, and the docs admit some hosts auto-run read-only tools. `TYPESAFE_MAX_ITEMS` mitigates this per call only, so set an OpenRouter spend limit on the key.
License MIT. Author is an individual (itsmostafa/Mostafa); affiliation with TypeSafe is not verified from the repo, though the README presents the project as a connector for TypeSafe's models.
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: Everything Claude puts in the tool-call arguments (`state`, `items`, `questions.instructions`/`criteria`, optional `model`) goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your OpenRouter key, and then to TypeSafe's hosted Jev via OpenRouter (or to api.typesafe.ai on the direct route). It is only what the model chooses to send, not automatic capture: no hook reads your files, prompts or diffs. In practice that means code snippets, diffs, error logs, ticket or issue text, and anything else Claude decides to pass as `state`. There is no client-side redaction, and the secret-leak PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover MCP tool calls, so a mcp__evaluate__* call could carry a secret it has read. Provider-side data retention and logging follow OpenRouter's and TypeSafe's policies (not checked here), which matters for client projects under NDA. A second egress is the GitHub API call at every server start (IP and version only).
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open. Errors come back as an MCP tool result with IsError, and Claude just carries on without Jev. HTTP client timeout is 60 s per attempt (main.go:168); 429 and 529 are retried up to 3 times with 1s/2s/4s backoff (client.go). A hung endpoint could therefore stall a single tool call for up to about 4 minutes. A non-JSON 2xx body or a response over 16 MiB is rejected. If neither key is set, `evaluate mcp` exits at startup (route() error, main.go:164), so the MCP server shows as failed and no tool is registered, with no impact on other Claude Code functions. At server start the update check adds up to 2s, and if it fails it silently adds nothing. There is no circuit breaker, so a slow provider costs 60s per call. In items mode, one failed item does not fail the batch.
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Rough size, chars/4: server instructions about 2.9k chars (~730 tokens; Claude Code may truncate long server instructions, so the tail, including the score/confidence notes, might be cut, which I could not verify), tool description about 1.3k chars (~320 tokens), JSON schema property descriptions about 2.3k chars (~580 tokens) plus schema scaffolding (~200 tokens). Total is about 1.8-2k tokens of always-present context if the tool is loaded eagerly. With Claude Code's MCP tool-search/deferral, only the name is present until the tool is needed, but the server instructions are still injected. No hook-injected text, since there are no hooks. Small compared with gitnexus (17 tools) or playwright (~25 tools).
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The trigger is the tool description (`Use for classification, routing, scoring, extraction, branching, guardrails/judging...`) and the server instructions, which the model reads at session start. Nothing is deterministic: there are no hooks, no skill, and no proxy. Real-world firing in coding sessions is likely rare, because Opus 5.5 can classify or branch inline at no extra cost and there is no cue in normal coding work that says to call Jev. To get reliable automatic use you must add your own steering, for example a CLAUDE.md paragraph or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook that nudges use in defined situations (triaging many issues/logs/files with `items`, gating risky actions with a noul such as `does this diff touch auth/payments`). The user said they do not want to prompt it, so a CLAUDE.md rule is the practical lever.
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Per call about 70-500 ms according to the vendor (not measured here) plus MCP stdio overhead, and this is added only on turns where Claude chooses to call it. Items mode: 8 concurrent, about 20s per 500 items (from code comments). Server startup: up to +2s for the blocking GitHub update check at every Claude Code session start (skip it with the `--no-update-check` arg). No effect on turns where the tool is not called. Worst case is a stuck request, up to 60s per attempt.
pros: Is the one, Jev-specific integration that already supports OpenRouter in code: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` set and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` unset routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest (main.go:152-158). It fits your setup with no patching.
Tiny footprint: one tool, no runtime dependencies, one static Go binary with a small dependency tree, and no telemetry or hooks. Very little context cost next to gitnexus or playwright.

Well-engineered client behaviour for its size: 429/529 retry with backoff, 16 MiB response cap, rejection of non-JSON 2xx, local validation that gives clear errors, exact preservation of numbers (UseNumber), and stable option ordering.

Useful extras for agent use: `min_confidence` abstain, which turns a shaky Jev answer into `__uncertain__` so Claude escalates rather than acts; and `items` batching for cheap bulk triage (e.g. classify 200 log lines or issues in one call).

The instructions and tool description are unusually good prompt-engineering for Jev (evidence not verdicts, no-match option, do not do arithmetic). They raise the chance that Claude will use the tool correctly.

Actively maintained: 121 commits in 13 days, 8 releases (v0.4.8 on 2026-09-30), release-please with pinned action SHAs, checksummed release archives, MIT. 337 stars and 37 forks show real adoption. Tests exist: 24 Test funcs in a 940-line evaluate_test.go.
Fail-open and read-only. It cannot modify files or run commands, so a bad Jev answer costs little unless Claude acts on it blindly.
Can be installed with tighter security than the README suggests: build from a pinned tag with Go, use env expansion in .mcp.json, and pass `--no-update-check`.
cons: Only auto-invoked at the model's discretion (no hook, no skill), which is not the guaranteed 'Claude Code uses it without me asking' behaviour you want. Left alone, Opus 5.5 will probably seldom call it; you would have to add CLAUDE.md steering or a hook yourself.

Jev has no code-specific strength and no reasoning. Daily coding (edit, debug, refactor) rarely needs a calibrated classifier, and Claude can decide the same things inline. The realistic wins are narrow: bulk triage, routing, guardrail-style gates. Vendor latency and quality claims are unverified, as is the skeptics' 'DeepSeek flash router' claim.

Sends whatever Claude passes as `state` (code, diffs, logs) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. That is a compliance question for client projects. Your secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls, and there is no redaction.

`setup mcp` puts the OpenRouter key in argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. `setup` also silently re-registers with codex, hermes and Claude Desktop if they are present. Avoid `setup` and configure manually.

README's `curl | sh` installer and the self-update use a same-origin checksum only, no signatures. Sole maintainer is an individual account, so it is a supply-chain trust decision on a 13-day-old repo (contributors: itsmostafa/Mostafa are the same person under two identities, plus 2 one-off contributors and a bot).

Depends on OpenRouter's `/api/alpha/` path, which the docs say may move. The default model is hardcoded to ~typesafe/jev-latest, so pinning a version needs per-call `model` unless you patch it. The tool uses /decisions, not the /api/v1/systemone endpoint.

No CI test workflow: only release-please.yml exists, so the 940 lines of tests run only if a contributor runs them (Taskfile); a release can ship without a test gate. No timeout budget for the LLM route beyond a flat 60s, and no circuit breaker, so a slow provider can freeze a turn.

Blocking GitHub call (up to 2s) on every server start, and an 'update available' string injected into instructions for the model to relay. That is harmless, but it is unrequested outbound traffic and a prompt-adjacent channel from a third-party release feed.
`items` with ReadOnlyHint true can burn 500 billed requests per call; you need an OpenRouter spend cap. Instructions may be truncated by Claude Code's server-instructions limit (unverified).
gh-itsmostafa-typesafe-mcp.verdict: Best-fit Jev integration for you and the reference implementation to use: it already speaks OpenRouter, is tiny and fail-open, and has strong usage guidance. Two caveats: auto-invocation is model-discretion only (so pair it with a CLAUDE.md rule or a thin hook), and Jev's value for coding itself is narrow (bulk triage, gating, routing). Install it by building from a pinned tag and registering manually with env expansion and `--no-update-check`, not with `curl|sh` or `setup mcp`.

gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.name: ctmx/openrouter-jev-mcp
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Python 3.13 stdio MCP server (plus importable JevGateway client) that wraps OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint (model ~typesafe/jev-latest). It exposes Jev's Noul, Choice and Score primitives as MCP tools with input validation, bounded retries and a local diagnostic log. It is OpenRouter-only: a TYPESAFE_API_KEY is explicitly rejected. It is purely a model-discretion tool. It has no hooks, skill or plugin, and the README tells the user to prompt the agent to use it ("How to Prompt Your Agent").

It does NOT use the /api/v1/systemone endpoint. The model is overridable via the model= constructor arg, but server.py builds JevGateway() with no args, so there is no env override for the model or URL.

security: The API key is passed via env (claude mcp add -e), not argv, so it is not in the process list. However, Claude Code stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. Prefer launching through a wrapper or shell env that reads the key from a secrets file.
gateway.py:104 also reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the environment and only uses it to emit an error message. It is never sent anywhere.

The key is added to the log redaction list (gateway.py:120), and diagnostics redact keys matching authorization/api_key/token/secret/password/credential/cookie (diagnostics.py:21,248-259). This is best effort, as the README admits.

Default-on local logging of every successful call's full STATE and answers to ~/.local/state/jev-gateway (0700 dir, 0600 files, O_NOFOLLOW, 24h retention, 20 MiB cap: diagnostics.py:61,134,182-184). For client projects this puts code, diffs and log snippets on disk in plaintext for 24h. There is no env switch to disable it. Only JEV_LOG_DIR can redirect it, e.g. to /dev/null or tmpfs.

No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh in the code I read. The only network destination is openrouter.ai (hard-coded). Response size capped at 256 KiB; content-encoding forced to identity.

Install via uvx from unpinned git HEAD is a supply-chain risk: the sole maintainer can change the code, and it runs with the key in env. Pin a commit SHA or vendor a clone. Single anonymous-ish maintainer, 1 star, 1 day old at first commit.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev returns only typed values (probabilities and labels), not free text, so returned content is low-risk. But the model is invoked with attacker-influenced state (file contents, tool output), and the answers can be manipulated. The README itself says the results are advisory and give no permission to act.
Tools take state: Any and options as dicts. There is no allow-list of what goes into the payload, so the calling model decides what to send.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the Claude model puts into the `state` argument (arbitrary strings, objects or lists such as code, diffs, logs, commands, test traces) plus the question text and options is POSTed to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the model ID and Authorization: Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (gateway.py:161-163,212,221). Payload cap is 256 KiB. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool, so it is model-controlled and unfiltered. logging_exclusions does NOT strip fields from the outbound payload (README). Secret filtering exists only in the local log copy. The secret-leak PreToolUse guard the user has covers Bash/Read/Grep/NotebookEdit and will not see MCP tool arguments, so a matcher on mcp__openrouter-jev-mcp__.* would be needed. OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe (a third party), which matters for client-project NDAs. Even for client code, only a single hop to OpenRouter is added.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level. Every JevGatewayError is caught and returned as a normal result {"error":{"category","message"}} (server.py:17-21), and the README says to treat this as 'no judgement'. Claude Code is never blocked and no hook can deny anything. Timeouts: an overall asyncio.timeout of 20 s covering up to 3 attempts, with retries on 408/429/502/503/504, connect errors and timeouts, and exponential backoff from 0.25 s or Retry-After (gateway.py:213-244). At most 8 concurrent requests; excess calls error immediately. Worst case adds about 20 s to a single tool call when the API is down. A missing key returns a configuration error per call (and the MCP server still starts). The one real risk is that an error result costs a tool round-trip of context. This is the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, so contract breakage would surface as provider_response errors.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. The descriptions are short one-liners (about 100 chars each, server.py:24-47). The schemas are generated from type hints (state: Any, question: Any, options: dict[str,str|None], levels: list[str], logging_exclusions: list[str]|None), with no per-parameter descriptions. Estimate: about 5 x 130 tokens = 600-900 tokens of tool defs. The FastMCP-style server passes description=... to MCPServer, but I saw no long 'instructions' text, so there is no instruction overhead. It injects no hook text. With ToolSearch-style deferral, the cost drops to just the tool names. The cost is very low, but there are also no usage instructions to steer the model.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where the tool is unused. Per call: the provider-claimed 70-500 ms (README cites about 260 ms median), plus about 0.3-1 s of MCP round trip and Claude's own extra tool-call turn (one more sampling step, several seconds with Opus). A new httpx.AsyncClient is created per request (no connection reuse), which adds a TLS handshake. Worst case is 20 s when OpenRouter is degraded. Because it is model-discretion, the extra Opus turns are the dominant cost, not Jev.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill, plugin, CLAUDE.md snippet or transparent proxy in the repo. The README's 'How to Prompt Your Agent' section prescribes explicit prompts ('Use jev_classify to evaluate...'). With bare tool descriptions such as 'Evaluate a Noul proposition against string, object, or list state', Opus 5.5 will rarely call it unprompted, so it does NOT meet the 'never say use jev' requirement on its own. Making it automatic would need the user's own additions: a CLAUDE.md policy block, or a PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook that has Claude call the tool (hooks cannot call MCP tools directly; a hook would need to call the gateway class or the OpenRouter API itself).
pros: The only candidate I saw that targets OpenRouter natively: the hard-coded alpha Decisions URL, ~typesafe/jev-latest, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY match the user's chosen provider exactly (gateway.py:19-20,101).
Cheap in context: 5 tools, about 600-900 tokens, no server instructions, and no hook injection into every Grep/Bash call, unlike the user's existing GitNexus hooks.
Covers all three Jev primitives, plus jev_evaluate to batch several questions into one call (fewer round trips, up to 64 questions).
Fail-soft design: errors are returned as data, a 20 s hard deadline, bounded retries, an in-flight cap of 8, and 256 KiB request/response caps. A Jev outage cannot block or break Claude Code.
Sane engineering for a 1-day-old repo: ~51 offline tests including a stdio subprocess test, pinned dependencies, and owner-only 0600 log files with O_NOFOLLOW.
Small (about 1.1k lines of source), so it is easy to audit, fork and modify. MIT licensed. It supports uvx, and mcp==2.2.0 resolves on PyPI.
Egress is explicit and limited to openrouter.ai; no telemetry, no shell execution, no installers.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain MCP tool, so it needs a prompt or a CLAUDE.md rule for Claude to use it, which fails the user's core requirement. Nothing in the repo (no hooks, skill or tool-selection guidance) makes Claude call it.
Tool descriptions are generic one-liners with no guidance on WHEN to call them, and the parameters are untyped `Any`. The model has no cue for when Jev adds value in coding.
Unpinned `uvx --from git+...` recommended in the README: an unreviewed HEAD of a 1-star, single-maintainer repo would run with the OpenRouter key in its env. Vendor it or pin a SHA.
Default-on plaintext logging of full state to ~/.local/state/jev-gateway with no off switch. This is a concern for client-project data. Redirect JEV_LOG_DIR to tmpfs or /dev/null as a workaround.

Model-controlled, unfiltered egress: code and diffs can go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. logging_exclusions only affects the local log. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tools and needs a new matcher.

Hard-coded to the alpha /api/alpha/decisions (the contract may change, README admits this). There is no env var for the base URL or model (JevGateway() takes no arguments in server.py:14), and TYPESAFE_API_KEY and /api/v1/systemone are unsupported.

Python 3.13 only (<3.14 pin) and package name `src`; a git-only distribution with no PyPI release, no tags, no CI, and no verification of the request schema against the live API was possible from the source. Test claims about the live API are unverified and I did not run anything.
Each tool call costs an extra Opus turn, so it will not save time or tokens when Jev is merely 'advisory'. It is a weak fit for the coding loop unless a hook makes gating decisions deterministic.
Wide-open API key handling on the host side: `claude mcp add -e` writes the key in plaintext to ~/.claude.json.
gh-ctmx-openrouter-jev-mcp.verdict: The best OpenRouter-native Jev MCP wrapper I've audited: small, readable and fail-soft, with a cheap context footprint. But it is a passive model-discretion tool with no auto-invocation, default-on plaintext logging and an unpinned git install. Use it (vendored or pinned to a SHA, JEV_LOG_DIR pointed at tmpfs) only as the transport layer, and add your own CLAUDE.md or hook-based trigger policy on top. As shipped it does not satisfy the 'automatic without prompting' requirement.

gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.name: blakestone-x/jev-mcp
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP/mcp>=2.2) wrapping the official typesafe-sdk. Deps: mcp>=2.2,<3, typesafe-sdk>=0.6,<1 (0.7.2 current), httpx2, pydantic, msgspec. gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.install: claude mcp add --scope user jev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- uvx --from git+https://github.com/blakestone-x/jev-mcp@v0.2.1 jev-mcp  (for OpenRouter: additionally -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, untested). Better: pin a full commit SHA instead of the mutable tag and put the key in an env-wrapper rather than argv.
security: Key in argv: README states the key 'is briefly visible in the process list while claude mcp add runs' (scripts/register.sh:96 passes -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=${api_key}); the key is then stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json mcpServers env. Avoid register.sh; use an env-var-from-secret wrapper.

The server itself reads the key only from environment (client.py:41-49); it does not log it. It sets TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=warning at import (jev_mcp/__init__.py:8) so SDK request bodies are not logged, and _failure returns state-free error envelopes with truncated loc/details (server.py:140-187, SECURITY.md).

No shell execution or subprocess in the runtime package; no telemetry beyond calls to the configured base URL. Egress goes only to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL resolves to (default api.typesafe.ai). Because TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is honored by the SDK, a mis-set env would send the bearer key and state elsewhere.

Supply chain: uvx installs from a git tag (mutable, no release artifacts, single-author brand-new repo, 26 stars, 3 commits in one day) plus transitive deps mcp>=2.2, typesafe-sdk, httpx2 (unusual package name to vet). Runs unsandboxed with the user's privileges on every session start. Pin a commit SHA and review deps.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are numeric/label envelopes, but jev_ask/jev_classify echo caller-supplied labels and mapping keys back in results; jev_screen is explicitly a filter, not a security boundary (SECURITY.md, README). Output validation rejects answers outside the submitted options (server.py:374-390, 502 envelope).

Dangling risk in helper scripts: register.sh/register.ps1 write plaintext key into ~/.codex/config.toml and the Claude user config; they do validate key characters and back up configs, but apply mode modifies user config files.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the state/questions/labels/candidates/text tool arguments is serialized and sent to the Jev endpoint (up to 120,000 chars per request, JEV_MCP_MAX_REQUEST_CHARS). Nothing is collected automatically: no hooks, no file scanning. Claude Code decides what to pass, so code snippets, diffs, log text, ticket text or file contents can leave the machine if Claude includes them. With OpenRouter as the base URL that data goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe (OpenRouter's data policies apply). Also the bearer key and model name. jev_health sends only an authenticated model-list request. jev_match fans out ceil(n/window)+1 requests carrying all candidates.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open to the agent, not fail-closed to the workflow: every error is caught and returned as an {ok:false,status,error} tool result (server.py:140-187); Claude just sees a failed tool call and proceeds. Timeouts: 8 s HTTP timeout, 20 s SDK retry budget with 3 retries and 1 s to 20 s backoff honoring Retry-After (client.py:107-125), so one call can block about 30 s when degraded (README); ensemble classify about 60 s (two sequential calls); jev_match up to 45 s deadline. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY does not stop the server from starting; each call returns a 401 envelope (ConfigurationError). No circuit breaker, so a down provider makes each attempted call cost up to 30 s of wall time. It is not in the hook path, so it cannot block tool execution.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per tool call: about 130 ms claimed model latency plus SDK/HTTP and Python overhead. Server cold start via uvx (environment resolution from git on first run; cached later) adds seconds to session start, and if the server fails to start it is reported as a failed MCP connection like caveman-shrink currently is. Degraded provider: up to about 30 s per call (60 s ensemble, 45 s match). Client-side limiter caps at 8 req/s (client.py:36). Zero latency on turns where Claude does not call it. The extra LLM round trip in Claude Code (tool call plus reasoning about result) typically costs more than Jev's own latency.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.contextCost: 7 tools, all deferred-capable (Claude Code 2.1.x loads MCP tool schemas lazily via ToolSearch when many tools exist, but names appear in the deferred list). Approx tokens of names+descriptions+schemas by chars/4: docstrings about 300-500 chars each (about 100 tokens each incl. the repeated cost/confidence sentences) plus pydantic-derived input schemas (jev_ask with nested Choice/Score/Noul question unions is the biggest) for roughly 2.5k-3.5k tokens when fully loaded. No MCP server 'instructions' are set (MCPServer(name, version, description) at server.py:74-79). No hook-injected text. Small compared to playwright (26 tools) and gitnexus (17 tools) already installed.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no server instructions. The only steering is tool descriptions that say what the tools are not for ('not for text generation or numeric extraction'). Claude Code will rarely pick these on its own for coding, because there is no coding-oriented trigger; matches the user's requirement only weakly and would need extra steering (CLAUDE.md rule or a hook) that this repo does not provide.
pros: Real, readable, well-structured code: strict pyright, ruff, offline tests (about 59) and CI on two OSes; errors are state-free envelopes; out-of-set model answers are rejected (server.py:374-390).

Uses the official typesafe-sdk, whose base URL is env-configurable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and whose paths are /v1/systemone, exactly the path OpenRouter exposes at /api/v1/systemone, so pointing it at OpenRouter is plausibly config-only (unverified, needs a live test).

Sensible engineering for Jev's real quirks: token-per-minute 429 backoff with Retry-After, order-ensemble to detect position bias (README says 32 of 200 choices flipped on reversal), windowed matching with abstention, confidence bands (act at 0.90, verify at 0.50).
Key is read from env, not tool arguments; SDK logging forced to WARNING so bodies are not logged; MIT licensed; no shell exec or telemetry in runtime code.
Small footprint (about 3k tokens) and errors never crash the session; it is off the hook path so it cannot block edits.
cons: Not automatic: nothing triggers Jev unless Claude chooses to call a tool; there is no coding-specific profile (README says 'Jev intentionally does not load profiles for you'). The user's 'never prompt use jev' requirement is not met without extra CLAUDE.md steering or a custom hook.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; env override is undocumented and jev_health (GET /v1/models) likely breaks on OpenRouter's different model-list schema; model IDs differ (jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-1.13).

Very new and thin: created and last pushed 2026-09-16, 3 commits, 1 author, no release, 26 stars; 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha'. The README performance numbers come from one unnamed field-service company's ticket data, not code tasks.

Installs via uvx from a mutable git tag at every session start; unpinned transitive deps (mcp>=2.2, httpx2) widen supply-chain exposure; a different unrelated 'jev-mcp' exists on PyPI (name-confusion risk).
Plaintext key in ~/.claude.json and briefly in argv when registered via claude mcp add or scripts/register.sh (README admits it); with OpenRouter that is a general-purpose OpenRouter key.
Degraded-provider behaviour is slow: up to about 30 s per call (60 s ensemble, 45 s match) with no circuit breaker.
Any code or diff text Claude passes as state leaves the machine to a third party; the design encourages passing raw text (jev_screen, jev_classify) to be judged.

Use cases (support-ticket classify, entity match, injection screen) are generic decision primitives, not code-review, routing-of-tasks or tool-permission decisions; Opus 5.5 already answers these better in-context for small inputs.
gh-blakestone-x-jev-mcp.verdict: Clean, honest, small MCP wrapper that is probably repointable to OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus JEV_MCP_MODEL, but it is only a model-discretion toolbox with no coding triggers, so it fails the 'automatic, never prompt' requirement on its own. Useful only as a transport layer if paired with your own hook or CLAUDE.md policy (pin the commit, keep the key out of argv).

gh-davila7-claude-code-templates.whatItDoes: Marketplace/CLI repo (npm claude-code-templates v1.29.6) that vendors "Claude Mods": Anthropic function-hook plugins (register(on, options) middleware, Claude Code >=2.1.259, needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1). Five are real Jev integrations under cli-tool/components/mods/: (1) productivity/jev-model-router 0.4.2 sends each prompt to Jev (choice tier, score effort, noul risky) and rewrites subagent model at agent.spawn and main-loop effort (optionally model) at turn.step. (2) productivity/jev-skill-suggestion withholds the engine's skill listing (prompt.attachment) and at prompt.submit runs two Jev requests (rank all skills + gate nouls, then rerank top 3 with SKILL.md excerpts) and injects the winning SKILL.md as a <skill_relevance> block. (3) security/jev-auto-mode is a Jev-judged permission layer on tool.call. (4) security/jev-guardrails screens prompts/replies. (5) security/jev-vercel-sandbox. Also games/chess uses Jev. The candidate's two named items (jev-model-router, jev-skill-suggestion) both exist and are genuine. Backends are TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest) or Vercel AI Gateway (evaluation-model); OpenRouter is not coded but is a config-only change.

interface.name: jev-model-router: prompt.submit hook
interface.purpose: Classifies the prompt with Jev (tier choice fast/balanced/deep, effort score 0-3, risky noul); skips bare slash commands; result held in a single slot for the turn

interface.name: jev-model-router: turn.step hook
interface.purpose: Applies the decision to the main loop's effort (routeMainEffort, default on) and model (routeMainModel, default OFF because it invalidates prompt cache); upgrade bar 0.3 confidence, downgrade bar 0.6, risky>0.7 forces deep

interface.name: jev-model-router: agent.spawn hook
interface.purpose: Chooses the model of each subagent (haiku/sonnet/opus aliases) from the subagent prompt+description+agent type (routeSubagentModel default on)

interface.name: jev-skill-suggestion: prompt.attachment(skill_listing)
interface.purpose: Returns {text:null} so the model never sees the skill listing (saves ~5.5k tokens on a 40-skill roster per README)

interface.name: jev-skill-suggestion: prompt.submit
interface.purpose: Request 1: choice over every skill + 3 gate nouls (acts_on_user_system, would_follow_documented_procedure, prose_suffices); Request 2: rerank top 3 with 700-char SKILL.md excerpts + fits nouls; injects winner's SKILL.md as <skill_relevance> block

interface.name: jev-skill-suggestion: skill.prompt / session.end / session.compact
interface.purpose: Observation logging, injected-skill bookkeeping reset on clear/compact, and rewrites the /jev-skill-suggestion:setup command

interface.name: /jev-skill-suggestion:setup [restore]
interface.purpose: Slash command that proposes edits to ~/.claude/settings.json (skillOverrides user-invocable-only, disableBundledSkills) with backup at ~/.claude/jev-skill-suggestion.skill-overrides.backup.json

interface.name: jev-auto-mode: tool.call, tool.check, command.run, skill.prompt, turn.start, session.start
interface.purpose: JSON-policy permission layer with deny>ask>allow rules, Jev judge for unmatched actions, onError default 'ask', timeoutMs 2500

interface.name: jev-guardrails: prompt.submit, turn.step
interface.purpose: Screens prompts and replies via Jev; fail-open by default, failClosed optional, timeout 1500ms

interface.name: npx claude-code-templates@latest --mod <category/name>
interface.purpose: Installer that copies the plugin dir into .claude/skills/<name>/ (auto-loaded as <name>@skills-dir in a trusted project); alternative claude --plugin-dir

pros: Real, automatic, hook-based integration (prompt.submit/turn.step/agent.spawn) - the user never says 'use jev'; matches the stated requirement better than any MCP tool the model must choose to call.

cons: Depends on early-access function hooks: needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 and a rollout flag (tengu_plugin_hooks_modules); $ API 'may change between releases' (it already changed in 2.1.278 and 2.1.283). Silent no-op if untrusted project or flag off.

Value for this user is modest: Opus 5.5 main model on subscription, and routeMainModel is off by default, so the main saving is lowering reasoning effort and pushing subagents to haiku/sonnet. Effort/model changes are request parameters that the status line never shows (README), making behaviour hard to audit.

Sends every prompt verbatim to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe); on client projects this is a data-handling/NDA concern. Skill-suggestion also ships all skill names/descriptions and SKILL.md excerpts.

Skill-suggestion is invasive: hides the skill listing, edits ~/.claude/settings.json (skillOverrides, disableBundledSkills), injects SKILL.md out of sight of the user; a malicious client repo's .claude/skills could be injected. Open issues: second request dropped by the 800 ms default on big catalogues, HTTP 400 over 255 skills, setup wrongly blocks some skills.

Two sequential Jev calls per prompt for skill suggestion, one for router; both block prompt start, adding ~0.2-1.6 s per user message; Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' skepticism means accuracy is unproven (only vendor-cited numbers).

No OpenRouter-specific testing or env var support: key must sit in pluginConfigs under the right plugin id (@skills-dir vs @inline) or it silently falls back to the built-in classifier; OpenRouter confidence-field parity unverified.
Installer is the large npx claude-code-templates CLI with analytics/tracking code; hard rule prevented running it, so recommend copying the directory by hand.
jev-auto-mode/guardrails would send tool-call details and assistant replies to Jev and conflict with user's existing PreToolUse secret-guard/GitNexus hooks and bypass mode; not advised.
gh-davila7-claude-code-templates.verdict: Best automatic Jev integration found: jev-model-router and (optionally) jev-skill-suggestion are deterministic hooks that already speak the exact /v1/systemone wire format, so pointing typesafeBaseUrl at https://openrouter.ai/api with the OpenRouter key and model typesafe/jev-1.13 is a config-only change. Adopt model-router (subagent model + main effort, leave routeMainModel off) first, verify one live call and the log lines, then consider skill-suggestion; skip auto-mode/guardrails and be aware of the early-access flag and prompt-egress on client repos.

gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.name: darthzen/jev-mcp
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Single-file (157 LOC) Python FastMCP 3 server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards the exact body of POST /v1/systemone (state + questions + model) to TypeSafe and returns the raw JSON response. Runs only as a streamable-HTTP server (designed for a k8s deployment behind a Cloudflare tunnel with a URL path secret), not stdio.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_mcp/server.py:42 API_URL = os.environ.get('JEV_API_URL','https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'); :43 DEFAULT_MODEL = env JEV_MODEL default 'jev-latest'; :105-109 client.post(API_URL, json=body, headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {_api_key()}'}); key from JEV_API_KEY / JEV_API_KEY_FILE (:54-67). No mention of openrouter anywhere in repo. Body is {state, questions, model} (:102).
providerSupport.others: None built in; JEV_API_URL is a free-form override so any gateway with the same schema works.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change: set JEV_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_API_KEY(_FILE)=OpenRouter key (sent as Bearer, which OpenRouter accepts), JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest (the default 'jev-latest' is TypeSafe-style and likely not an OpenRouter ID). Assumes OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same body as TypeSafe's; I could not verify that from this repo. Caveat: server has only a bare `model` field, so OpenRouter-specific fields (provider routing, etc.) cannot be passed.

interface.name: evaluate (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Args: state (object|list|str), questions (map id -> {type: choice|noul|score, instructions, criteria}), optional model. Returns raw System One response (choice/noul/score + confidence + probabilities). Annotated readOnlyHint/idempotentHint/openWorldHint. Rejects empty questions.

interface.name: GET /healthz
interface.purpose: Liveness probe returning 'ok'.

interface.name: jev-mcp (CLI entrypoint)
interface.purpose: Starts the HTTP server; fails fast if no API key; binds JEV_BIND_HOST:JEV_BIND_PORT (default 0.0.0.0:8080), path /<secret>/mcp or /mcp.

interface.name: MCP server instructions
interface.purpose: ~560-char text telling the model to 'use evaluate before any decision: choosing between options, classifying, ranking, judging a condition' and to act on clear leads / gather more evidence when flat.

gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.runtime: Python >=3.12 (fastmcp==3.4.5, httpx==0.28.1 pinned); HTTP only; Dockerfile targets SUSE BCI. No PyPI package or release, so install means git clone + uv venv + uv pip install -e and running a long-lived local process.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.tests: 4 pytest tests (respx-mocked): pass-through body/auth header, upstream 401 -> ToolError, key-file handling, path-secret validation. No CI workflow (.github absent), no releases, no live test against TypeSafe/OpenRouter. I did not run them (static reading only).
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.install: Not on PyPI. Local: git clone; uv venv && uv pip install -e .; run `JEV_BIND_HOST=127.0.0.1 JEV_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 JEV_API_KEY_FILE=~/.keys/or JEV_MCP_PATH_SECRET=<24+ chars> jev-mcp` as a background service, then `claude mcp add --transport http --scope user jev http://127.0.0.1:8080/<secret>/mcp`. README's example points at the author's public URL (jev-mcp.ash4d.com), which must not be used.
security: API key read from env or *_FILE (server.py:54-67); never in argv, which is good, and never logged. The key lives in the server process, not in Claude Code config.

Server does NOT authenticate callers (README); with the default bind 0.0.0.0 (server.py:139) and allowed_hosts=['*'] (:152), anyone on the LAN can spend the key's credits unless JEV_BIND_HOST=127.0.0.1 is set and a path secret used. Without JEV_MCP_PATH_SECRET it serves unauthenticated on /mcp with only a warning (:124-126).
No shell execution, no file access beyond reading the key file, no postinstall or curl|sh. Dependencies pinned exactly.

Upstream error text (first 500 chars of response body) is returned to the model as a ToolError (:113): a small prompt-injection surface only if the upstream is compromised. Response JSON is passed through unchanged and is typed numbers/keys, so injection risk from Jev output is low.
No telemetry in code. Dockerfile runs as non-root uid 10001.

Bigger risk is the content Claude chooses to put in `state`: arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, secrets could be sent; the user's secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover this MCP tool (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in `state` and question `instructions`/`criteria` (code snippets, diffs, error logs, file contents, tool outputs, possibly client code) goes from the local server process to api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter if repointed). Also the API key (Bearer) and model name. Nothing else; no telemetry. The model decides the payload, so the volume and sensitivity are unbounded (32k ctx limit upstream). With OpenRouter, data additionally passes through OpenRouter and its provider policies, which matters for client projects under NDA.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level: on timeout (default 60 s, JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT), network error or HTTP >=400 the tool raises ToolError with a message and Claude continues on its own. But there is no retry, no circuit breaker, and 60 s is far above the claimed 70-500 ms, so a hung upstream can stall a turn for up to a minute per call. If the local server process is down, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tool is simply absent (fail-open, silent). Startup fails fast if no key (:138). Tool is stateless HTTP (stateless_http=True), so restarts are harmless.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per call: one Claude tool-call round trip (model emits tool call with a structured payload, ~1-3 s of Opus generation for the state/questions JSON) plus 70-500 ms Jev claimed plus localhost hop, so realistically 2-5 s added per use; a new httpx client and TLS handshake per call (:104) adds a few tens of ms. Zero cost on turns where Claude does not call it.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Tool description ~1,250 chars, input schema roughly 350 chars (state union, questions dict, model), plus server instructions ~560 chars: about 2,200 chars = roughly 550 tokens. Cheap. No hooks and no injected text. Deferred tool search may reduce it further.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The server `instructions` (server.py:46-51) say to use `evaluate` 'before any decision', which nudges Opus to call it, but nothing deterministic forces it, and Claude Code often truncates or deprioritises MCP instructions. No hook, no skill, no proxy. Whether Claude actually calls Jev is unreliable, and each call requires the model to compose a large typed payload, which is the opposite of the transparent System One use case. Would need a companion CLAUDE.md rule or a hook to be reliable.
pros: Very small, readable, auditable (157 LOC, pinned deps, Apache-2.0), no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry.
Exposes the full Choice/Noul/Score contract via one tool, mirroring the raw System One body, so nothing is lost.
Switching to OpenRouter needs only env vars (JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL, JEV_API_KEY_FILE) with no code patch (subject to schema parity).
Key handled via file/env, never argv; fail-fast on missing key; ToolError on failures so Claude is not blocked.
Tiny context cost (~550 tokens, one tool).
cons: Built for the author's homelab: HTTP-only, no stdio mode, must run a long-lived local process yourself (no PyPI, no npx/uvx one-liner); defaults bind 0.0.0.0 with unauthenticated MCP.
Purely model-discretion: does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' requirement; no hook or skill layer; the user would need CLAUDE.md nudges or a custom PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook on top.
Default model 'jev-latest' and default URL are TypeSafe-only; the repo has never been tested against OpenRouter and is not aware of OpenRouter model IDs (~typesafe/jev-latest) or headers.

Brand new (created and last pushed 2026-09-22, 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no CI); one commit already fixed an API-shape bug, showing the tool description is hand-maintained against a beta API.
60 s timeout with no retries; new HTTP client per call.

Claude must author the whole typed payload with state, so cost is Opus output tokens plus seconds of latency per decision, and it can leak code/secrets to a third party via `state` with no redaction and outside the existing secret-guard hook matcher.
Not really a coding accelerator: Jev returns probabilities, and in a coding agent the LLM already decides; benefit is unproven.
gh-darthzen-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, minimal, safe-to-read wrapper that would work against OpenRouter by env vars alone, but it is a homelab-shaped, HTTP-only, day-old PoC that relies entirely on Claude choosing to call it, so it does not deliver the automatic integration wanted. Useful at best as a raw building block (run locally on 127.0.0.1) beneath a hook or CLAUDE.md rule, or as a reference for a purpose-built stdio/hook integration.
