gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.name: rashedInt32/jev-mcp (npm jev-mcp)
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server (TypeScript, wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing six tools that call Jev's System One endpoint (Choice/Score/Noul). Also ships as a Claude Code plugin (plugin.json inlines mcpServers -> npx -y jev-mcp@0.5.1) plus a skills/jev/SKILL.md describing when to call the tools. Answers are validated against the question sent and gated into act/review/abstain and yes/no/uncertain. jev_triage reads files server-side (confined to roots, credential-name deny list) so file contents go to Jev but not into the agent context.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter reference anywhere in the repo. src/index.ts:226 does `new TypeSafeClient({ apiKey, timeout, logger })` and passes no baseURL. The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:58 and :513) reads env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai. It POSTs to path /v1/systemone (index.mjs:554) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (index.mjs ~ fetchWithRetries) and GETs /v1/models (index.mjs:365). Key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY, then JEV_API_KEY, then ~/.config/typesafe/key or JEV_KEY_FILE (src/index.ts:188-220). Model comes from JEV_MODEL, default "jev-latest" (src/index.ts:70).
providerSupport.others: None. No other gateways. TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL only tunes SDK logging.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and needs no code change. The SDK path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or JEV_KEY_FILE) to the OpenRouter key and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, because the default "jev-latest" is not an OpenRouter id (use ~typesafe/jev-latest for the alias). Caveats I could not verify statically: whether OpenRouter's System One request and response bodies are byte-compatible with the SDK's schema (the server's strict answer validation would turn any mismatch into malformed_response errors), and jev_models would hit OpenRouter's /v1/models, which probably returns a different shape. The plugin ships no env block, so the env has to be supplied via `claude mcp add -e ...` or the JEV_KEY_FILE route. A plain fork is also easy: add baseURL to the constructor at src/index.ts:226.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Choice: pick one of caller-supplied options; adds a 'none' option by default; returns probabilities, confidence, act/review/abstain action (src/index.ts:256)

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Score: rate on a caller-supplied ordered scale (>=2 levels); returns expected position, distribution, confidence, action (src/index.ts:322)

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Noul: yes/no question; returns P(yes) and yes/no/uncertain verdict (src/index.ts:388)

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Batch of up to 64 mixed classify/score/check questions about one state in a single request (src/index.ts:448)

interface.name: jev_triage
interface.purpose: Same question set over up to 50 items (text or server-read file path), concurrency 4, one request per item; partial failures reported in place (src/index.ts:502)

interface.name: jev_models
interface.purpose: List models available to the key and confirm the key works (src/index.ts:631)

interface.name: skills/jev/SKILL.md (skill 'jev')
interface.purpose: Description-triggered skill: use Jev tools only when the same judgment repeats across many items or a calibrated number is needed; otherwise answer yourself. Explicitly says 'Prefer an ordinary answer for a single judgment in conversation.'

gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20.12 (engines), TypeScript, ESM. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod ^3.25. Launched as `npx -y jev-mcp@0.5.1`, so the first start downloads from npm.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.install: /plugin marketplace add rashedInt32/jev-mcp ; /plugin install jev@jev-mcp (registers server plus skill). Or: claude mcp add --scope user jev -- npx -y jev-mcp. For OpenRouter you would add: -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 and supply the OpenRouter key through TYPESAFE_API_KEY or a 0600 file named by JEV_KEY_FILE (not in the README).
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.tests: About 67 node:test cases across 6 files in test/ (lib 19, tools 23, triage 12, files 9, e2e 4). The offline suite spawns the real built server over stdio against a local stand-in API and asserts on request bodies; e2e needs a live TypeSafe key. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs typecheck, build and test on Node 20/22/24, plus `npm audit --audit-level=high`, with `npm ci --ignore-scripts`. I did not run any of it, in line with the hard rules.
security: API key is never a tool argument (README design rule 3); read from env or a key file, so it does not appear in argv/ps. With `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` the key would sit in ~/.claude.json, so the 0600 key-file route (JEV_KEY_FILE) is better.

jev_triage file reads: paths must be below JEV_FILE_ROOTS (default = the cwd of the server, i.e. the project Claude Code was started in), checked lexically and after realpath. Credential-name deny list in src/files.ts:57-65 (.env*, .ssh, .aws, .npmrc, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa, credentials/secrets, ~/.config/typesafe|gh, the server's own key file). It is name-based only, so secrets in ordinary source files, config.json, or hard-coded tokens still go out. Only regular text files, no truncation, 200k chars max per item.

Prompt-injection surface: the model chooses which paths to send, and file contents go to a third-party API. The tool result never echoes file contents, only answers, so injected text cannot flow back through this tool. Result strings such as verdict and action are computed locally. The SKILL.md tells the agent to treat files as untrusted.

No shell execution, no child_process, no telemetry in the repo code. The SDK sends only User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers. No postinstall/preinstall script in package.json. `prepare` exists but does not run for registry installs.

Supply chain: plugin runs `npx -y jev-mcp@0.5.1` at every start, so it pulls an unpinned transitive tree from npm from a sole maintainer with an 8-star repo. The version is pinned but the dependency ranges (^) are not lockfile-pinned for npx users. Pin and review, or vendor it. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__ tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so jev_triage bypasses it.
Debug logging: SDK logger at TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs request bodies (state) to stderr. Headers are redacted. Default level is not debug.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state`/`question`/`options` (diffs, code snippets, file text, tool outputs) for jev_classify/score/check/ask, plus full file contents for every `path` item in jev_triage (up to 50 files x 200k chars per call, one request each), minus the credential-name deny list. Sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone by default, or to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says (OpenRouter would then receive it and route it to TypeSafe, which matters for client projects under NDA). Nothing else leaves the machine: no telemetry, no repo metadata. The API key goes in the Authorization header only.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors come back as isError results with a classified kind (no_api_key, authentication, rate_limit, server_error, timeout, connection, malformed_response, file_access) and retryable flag, so Claude just continues without Jev. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), SDK retries 2x on 408/429/5xx with 500 ms to 5 s backoff, so worst case is about 45 s+ for a single stalled call, not the claimed 70-500 ms. Nothing blocks the session and there is no hook. If the npx download fails or the key is missing the server still starts (lazy client) and each tool returns a clear error. A missing MCP connection is simply an absent tool.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call a jev_* tool (no hooks, no proxy). When called: one API round trip (claimed 70-500 ms) plus MCP stdio overhead. jev_triage runs at concurrency 4, so 50 files is about 13 sequential rounds of requests. Server cold start via npx adds a few seconds at session start (README says allow a few seconds), and much more on a first, uncached download.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Tool descriptions total about 2.4k chars, but the JSON schemas with long .describe() strings (state, question, options, levels, threshold params, the nested QuestionSpec union in jev_ask and jev_triage) push it to roughly 14-16k chars, which I estimate at about 3.5-4.5k tokens for names, descriptions and schemas. That is well below Playwright's 30+ tools. The server sets no `instructions` field (src/index.ts:252 `new McpServer({name, version})`). The skill adds a ~700-char description to the skills listing (~150-200 tokens) and the 203-line SKILL.md body (~2.5k tokens) loads only when triggered. No hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred-tool loading (ToolSearch), the schemas may only load on demand.
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There are no hooks and no proxy, so nothing is deterministic. The skill's own trigger text and body are deliberately conservative: 'Prefer an ordinary answer for a single judgment in conversation', 'Do not reach for a tool to look rigorous', and 'Do not call a tool to prototype what will become shipped code.' It steers Claude toward Jev only for repeated judgments over many items (triage of dozens of files, ranking candidates). In daily Opus coding that is rare, so expect Claude to rarely call it on its own. It will not run without the user asking, and rewriting the skill or adding a CLAUDE.md nudge is needed to make usage frequent.
pros: Best-engineered Jev MCP I inspected: answer validation against the question sent (malformed_response instead of trusting a bad label), caller-owned option sets, confidence gating, classified errors with retryable flag, stderr-only logging (src/index.ts:80-85).

Runs on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, and the base URL is read from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (SDK index.mjs:58,513) with path /v1/systemone (index.mjs:554), which lines up with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Switching to OpenRouter is env-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, key, JEV_MODEL) with no fork needed, in principle.

jev_triage keeps file contents out of Claude's context and screens up to 50 files per call for about $0.04 per 1M input tokens. This is the one workflow with a plausible coding payoff (find which files matter before opening them).

Real safety design for the file-reading tool: root confinement, symlink re-check after realpath, FIFO guard, no truncation, credential-name deny list, no file content in errors or results (src/files.ts).

Solid hygiene: MIT license, CI on Node 20/22/24 with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and npm audit, about 67 tests including an offline stdio integration suite, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec, key never in argv, and low context footprint (6 tools, no server instructions, no hooks).
Fail-open, and adds zero latency or tokens on turns that do not use it. Compatible with the user's existing hooks because it adds none.
cons: Not automatic in the deterministic sense the user wants. It is model-discretion, and its own SKILL.md and README tell Claude to answer itself for one-off judgments, so Claude will seldom call it during ordinary coding. There is no hook, transparent proxy or auto-trigger; Opus 5.5 is a better judge than a 'System One' classifier for single decisions.

No OpenRouter support in the repo: no OpenRouter env var, doc or test. The OpenRouter route depends on the OpenRouter System One schema matching the TypeSafe SDK's request and response bodies, which I could not verify statically. The wrong default model id ('jev-latest') must be overridden with JEV_MODEL, and jev_models likely misbehaves on OpenRouter's /v1/models. The plugin ships no env block, so you must hand-register the server with -e flags or a key file instead of the one-command plugin install.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-17, 10 commits, 2 contributors (9 by the author), 8 stars, 1 issue/PR, no GitHub releases, four npm versions in 9 days. Formally beta on a beta model, and the plugin runs `npx -y` at each session start, which is a live supply-chain fetch on a machine with client projects.

Data egress on client projects: jev_triage ships whole file contents to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter then TypeSafe). The deny list is name-based only, and the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not see mcp__jev__ calls. Client NDAs may forbid it; JEV_FILE_ROOTS=off or a narrow root is required.

Jev is a one-pass chooser with no reasoning and cannot compute, count or compare dates (README 'When not to reach for this'), and confidence is only distribution concentration, not correctness. This restricts it to screening and ranking, which are the least critical steps of coding work.

Failure timing is worse than the marketing: 15 s per-attempt timeout with 2 retries means a slow API can stall a tool call for tens of seconds. In the plugin, using it inside the jev-mcp checkout itself fails (README dev note).
gh-rashedint32-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-built Jev MCP and the one to use if you want Jev tools at all. It is easy to point at OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL and a key file (unverified against OpenRouter's schema, so smoke-test with jev_models and one jev_check). But it is opt-in model-discretion by design: Claude will rarely reach for it unprompted, so it does not deliver the automatic, hook-like integration the user asked for. Pin the version, restrict JEV_FILE_ROOTS, and treat it as a niche triage add-on rather than the core integration.

gh-freepik-company-jev-mcp.name: freepik-company/jev-mcp
gh-freepik-company-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Go stdio MCP server (~2.3k lines incl. tests/docs) wrapping the OpenRouter/TypeSafe System One endpoint. interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Choice question. Takes state, instructions and options (a map of key to description). Returns the winning option, per-option probabilities and a confidence.

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Score question. Takes state, instructions and 2-10 ordered levels. Returns a score and a distribution.

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Noul question. Takes state and a yes/no instruction. Returns {probability, likely}.

interface.name: jev_gate
interface.purpose: Takes action and optional context, then sends 3 questions in one call: a risk score, a touches_prod noul, and an allow/confirm/block choice. Advisory only, and it only runs if the model chooses to call it.

interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Generic multi-question call. Takes state and a free-form questions map (z.any). Returns model, answers and usage.

Any jv_live_ key auto-routes to jevtypesafeai.com, which says it is not affiliated with TypeSafe AI and whose logging and retention policy is undocumented in the pages I saw. A hosted key would send all state to that reseller.

Each call is one extra tool round trip: about 70-500 ms Jev-claimed plus a Claude turn to emit the call and read the result, realistically 2-5 s per use. Worst case is 20s on timeout. A stdio server start adds a small Node cold start, plus an npx fetch from GitHub if the cache is cold.
gh-codaaiteam-jev-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. Descriptions are about 1.3k chars and schemas (including the z.describe strings) about 2k chars, so roughly 800-1000 tokens of tool definitions per session (schemas are deferred if ToolSearch is active). The server sets no MCP `instructions` and no hook injects text.
gh-codaaiteam-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skill triggers or proxy. Claude would call the tools only if it judges them useful from their descriptions, and in practice it rarely picks a niche classifier tool unprompted. That fails the user's 'automatic' requirement unless it is paired with a hook or a CLAUDE.md instruction.
pros: Tiny, readable, dependency-light single file (src/index.js, about 250 lines) that is easy to audit and fork completely.
Covers all three Jev primitives (choice, score, noul) plus jev_decide for arbitrary multi-question calls, matching the brief's API shape.
Generic JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL overrides mean OpenRouter is reachable without code changes if the OpenRouter systemone schema matches (src/index.js:29-30).
Fail-open, 20s timeout, no telemetry, and MIT licensed. Tool outputs are small typed JSON, so little context is used.
The jev_gate concept (risk-score a shell command) is a useful pattern to lift into a PreToolUse hook.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion tools only, with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, so the user would still need to prompt or rely on Claude choosing it.

The default endpoint is api.typesafe.ai and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read. OpenRouter requires manual JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest, and the OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and schema compatibility with /api/v1/systemone is unverified.

Very immature: 3 commits over 3 days, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, not on npm, no version pinning. Installing via unpinned `npx github:` is risky for client work.
jev_gate is advisory and depends on Claude calling it, so it is no real guardrail compared with a PreToolUse hook. It would also duplicate the existing secret-leak guard hook.
No key-file support: the README's -e KEY=value approach stores the plaintext key in ~/.claude.json.
Sends whatever code, commands or diffs Claude puts in state to an external API, which is an egress concern for client projects.
gh-codaaiteam-jev-mcp.verdict: A small, readable, MIT-licensed wrapper that is useful mainly as a reference implementation. It is a manual model-discretion tool with no hooks and no OpenRouter support out of the box, so it does not give the user automatic integration. Fork or copy the ~250 lines, pin it, and point it at OpenRouter yourself rather than adopting it as-is. If used at all, pair it with a hook and avoid jv_live_ keys.

Bounded retries (408/409/429/5xx only, no retry on ambiguous network failures), 1 MB response ceiling, whole-request deadline.

Only shell-ish surface: jev_extract runs caller-supplied regexes in a node:worker_threads Worker (src/lib.ts:472) as a ReDoS sandbox with timeout; not shell execution.

No npm install scripts in the 43-package lockfile (hasInstallScript count 0); `prepare` builds only on git installs. Runtime deps: @jkudish/jev-agent-tools 0.1.3 (same author, small), @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, MCP SDK, zod. `npx -y` fetches latest of a single-maintainer package on every start unless version is pinned: supply-chain risk, pin @0.11.0.
HTTP mode is loopback by default, bearer token via timingSafeEqual, host/origin rebinding guards; irrelevant for stdio use.

Prompt-injection posture: server returns advisory numbers only; SKILL.md tells agent to treat fields as evidence; tool outputs contain caller-supplied strings (claims, ids) echoed back, low risk. jev_screen itself is a Jev model judgment, not a guarantee.

gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes as tool arguments leaves the machine, sent to openrouter.ai (POST /api/alpha/decisions) as {model, state, questions}: claims, evidence text, fetched page text for screen, candidate lists, and for jev_review/jev_gate the diff, request text, test output and completion claims. The server never reads files itself (SECURITY.md); egress is entirely model-driven, so the model can send client code or diffs to OpenRouter/TypeSafe if it decides to call review/gate. Per-tool truncation limits exist (e.g. jev_noul 150k chars, rerank 100k chars, decide evidence 12k chars). Your existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__jev__* calls unless its matcher is extended. OpenRouter also sees the key holder identity and content per its own logging policy; check OpenRouter data-policy settings for client projects.
gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level: it is an optional tool call, not a gate. If OpenRouter is down/slow, the tool call errors (fixed string like 'OpenRouter decisions API 503') after up to 3 attempts with jittered backoff within a 60 s whole-request deadline (JEV_MCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS default 60000, JEV_MCP_MAX_ATTEMPTS default 3; src/provider.ts:40-42), so a bad outage can stall one tool call up to 60 s; lower the timeout to about 10000 for interactive use. Malformed model answers fail closed per judgment (invalid_response, action review, never a clean pass). Missing/invalid key: configuration error at call time. Nothing blocks Claude Code startup except normal MCP spawn cost (npx cold start).
gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.contextCost: 12 tools. Tool descriptions plus zod schema descriptions I extracted total about 11.3k characters of literal text (about 2.8k tokens); with JSON-schema structure, property names and enums the realistic tool-definition load is about 5-7k tokens if fully loaded (jev_gate, jev_review and jev_decide are the largest, each 2.4-3.1k chars of source schema). No MCP server 'instructions' string (McpServer created with only capabilities, src/index.ts:105). No hook-injected text. The SKILL.md (7.9KB, about 2k tokens) adds only its ~70 token frontmatter description until triggered, then about 2k tokens plus reference/tools.md on demand. Claude Code deferred MCP tool loading (ToolSearch) reduces the upfront cost to names only.
gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns that do not call it. Per call: claimed 150-500 ms model time, plus OpenRouter alpha Decisions hop (README admits it adds a hop), plus one MCP round trip and the model's own tokens to build the arguments (large for review/gate since Claude must paste the diff/evidence into tool args, which costs output tokens on Opus). Realistically 1-3 s wall clock per call including argument generation; first call in a session adds npx cold start (a few seconds, and network fetch of the package unless cached).
gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. The bundled SKILL.md is aggressive ('Call the matching tool ... even when the answer looks obvious', 'Gate before done') and its description keyword-matches verify/screen/review/gate/extract/rank/classify tasks, so Claude will call jev_screen after WebFetch, jev_review/jev_gate before declaring done, etc. only if the skill is copied to ~/.claude/skills (not auto-installed by the MCP add). Even then it is probabilistic; with Opus 5.5 and 12 tool descriptions in context it will be used inconsistently. Getting real automation requires adding your own hooks (for example a Stop or PostToolUse hook that reminds the model, or a CLAUDE.md line), which the repo does not provide.
pros: OpenRouter is supported in code with the correct alpha Decisions endpoint and only OPENROUTER_API_KEY needed (src/provider.ts:293-336); no patching required.

Only candidate seen with tools aimed at coding-agent moments: jev_review/jev_gate score a diff and verify 'tests pass' claims against evidence before done, and jev_screen checks fetched pages for prompt injection, which is useful when WebFetch/Playwright ingest untrusted pages.

Ships a real agent skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) with routing policy and per-tool reference, which is the closest thing to automatic invocation in this repo; description triggers on realistic coding-agent tasks.

Careful engineering: strict zod input schemas, per-judgment fail-closed invalid_response, bounded retries/deadline/1MB body cap, redacted errors, regex worker sandbox, static tool list, sizeable mock test suite plus CI.
No install scripts, no telemetry, no shell execution, key never in argv; small dependency tree (43 lockfile packages).
Active and popular: 463 stars, 53 forks, 12 releases in 12 days, contributor PRs merged, responsive changelog; MIT licensed.
No MCP instructions string and only 12 tools, so context cost is moderate, and Claude Code's deferred tool loading lowers it further.
Cheap: about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, so tool calls cost fractions of a cent even at heavy use.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP; the user's requirement of Claude Code using Jev without prompting is only met probabilistically via the skill, and the skill must be installed separately (manual copy).

Jev cannot read code: jev_review/jev_gate require Claude to serialize the diff and evidence into tool arguments, costing Opus output tokens and 1-3 s per call, and it sends client code diffs to OpenRouter/TypeSafe (data egress on client projects, and it bypasses your Bash/Read/Grep-matcher secret guard).

Jev judgments are calibrated probabilities from a small router-like model (Theo's claim unverified); a passing jev_gate is weak evidence and could give false assurance next to real tests; the README itself says 'not infallible' and thresholds are untuned defaults.

OpenRouter path is alpha and adds a hop; on OpenRouter 'jev-latest' is hardcoded to typesafe/jev-1.13 in code (src/provider.ts:296) so it will not follow new releases without JEV_MCP_MODEL; usage tokens are not documented for the Decisions API (falls back to 0), so cost reporting is unreliable.
Silent provider precedence: if TYPESAFE_API_KEY exists in env it wins over OpenRouter; must set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter to be explicit.
OpenRouter key must be provided as sk-or- env var; `claude mcp add -e` stores it plaintext in ~/.claude.json, so use env inheritance or a wrapper instead.
Failure can stall up to 60 s with default retries/timeouts; `npx -y` unpinned means every start trusts the latest publish of a 13-day-old single-maintainer package.

Twelve tools is broad: much of it (classify, rerank, extract, compare, audit, find) is retrieval/data-pipeline oriented and duplicates what Claude, rg and gitnexus already do in daily coding; only about 4 tools (screen, verify, review, gate) matter.
Aggressive skill wording ('even when the answer looks obvious') can make Claude call Jev on every finish, adding latency and cost with low marginal value.
gh-jkudish-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-fit ready-made option so far: real, maintained, OpenRouter-native, with a skill and coding-relevant tools (screen, review, gate). It still relies on model discretion (no hooks), so treat it as the base layer: install via env-injected OPENROUTER_API_KEY with JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, pin the npm version, copy the skill globally, and add your own thin Stop or PostToolUse hook if you need deterministic triggering. Restrict or gate jev_review/jev_gate on client repos because diffs leave the machine.

Solid fail-closed design: unknown args rejected (strict schemas), malformed answers -> invalid_response + review, no retries so no double-billing, explicit timeout, key not in argv and not logged; small dependency footprint (MCP SDK + zod), no postinstall, no shell exec, no telemetry.

Ships a skill whose resident description is written to trigger automatic use ('reach for them by default', four 'not optional' moments), which is the closest thing to 'Claude uses Jev without being told' among MCP options; stdio mode available (npm run stdio) so no port/daemon needed.
MIT; 39 commits with CI (typecheck, ~1.8k lines of tests over all 12 tools, bundle + stdio smoke test), tagged releases v0.1.1-v0.1.5.
Tools return only enums/probabilities/usage JSON so results add little context and carry little injection surface; usage/cost reported per call.
cons: Extremely young and unproven: repo created 2026-09-29, 0 stars, 0 forks, single human author (34 of 39 commits by 'Alex', 5 bot), 5 releases in ~1 day; ported from jkudish/jev-mcp (463 stars) so a more-followed upstream exists. No evidence of a live end-to-end run against OpenRouter: tests use a stub endpoint and OpenRouter is only 'fixtures from docs'; OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions is itself alpha.

Automatic use is only probabilistic (model discretion via skill text); no hook-based deterministic integration (no Stop/PreToolUse hook to run jev_gate/jev_review). Author admits Claude Code drops MCP server instructions, so everything rests on a skill description that must be copied manually.

Skill mandate is aggressive and expensive for daily coding: 'even when the answer looks obvious', screen every fetched page, review/gate at the end of every non-trivial task and before pushes; Jev is a small System One model with claimed router-like quality (unverified), so it may add latency (70-500 ms claimed, but 60 s timeout) and noisy false-positive review/escalate actions that Opus 5.5 must then reason around.

Data egress risk for client projects: diffs (up to 200k chars aggregate for gate), test logs and fetched pages are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe whenever the model calls tools; the existing secret-leak guard hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* arguments, so secrets in diffs could be forwarded.

Unauthenticated localhost HTTP endpoint (no token, no Origin/Host validation) that spends the user's OpenRouter key; safer stdio config would avoid it but README steers toward the macOS tray app (Tauri, Rust 1.77+, macOS-centric docs and xattr/AppTranslocation notes), which is a poor fit for a Linux user. Must git clone + npm install (Node >=22.18) and keep a checkout path; not published to npm.

Key naming friction: uses generic JEV_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY; real env beats .env so shell exports can silently override; 12 tools cost ~4.5-5.5k tokens of definitions (mitigated by MCP tool search) and many tools (find/rerank/extract/audit/classify) are of marginal use in ordinary coding.

Skill body tells the agent to run 'npm start' in the checkout if tools are missing - an agent-initiated process start driven by third-party text; Claude Code's bypass/auto mode would follow it without asking.
gh-rtf6x-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-fitting concrete MCP candidate found so far for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (config-only endpoint, coding-relevant review/gate/screen tools, sane fail-closed code), but it is a 1-day-old single-author fork with no proven OpenRouter run, and 'automatic' is only skill-nudged, not a hook. Use stdio mode (not the HTTP tray app), pin a commit after reading it, restrict to jev_review/jev_gate/jev_screen, and pair with a Claude Code hook if deterministic invocation is required.

gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.name: ieee0824/jev-mcp
gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Rust stdio MCP server (rmcp 3.4, reqwest/rustls) that exposes TypeSafe Jev's System One API as four tools (jev.noul, jev.choice, jev.score, jev.batch). The caller (an agent) supplies `state` evidence and a closed question; the server POSTs {state, model, questions} to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, validates the response, and adds a deterministic `policy` block (accept/verify/reevaluate by confidence thresholds 0.90/0.60). Ships a Codex-oriented `jev-decisions` SKILL.md with 7 recipe references (action selection, hypothesis ranking, evidence sufficiency, trace monitoring, context selection, safety advisory, multi-axis), an offline/online JSONL eval CLI, and optional input-free JSONL telemetry to stderr. It does not read repos, collect history, or execute anything: the model must decide to call it and must hand-assemble the evidence.

The path suffix /v1/systemone and the {state, model, questions} body match the brief's OpenRouter System One API (openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone), so the schema is plausibly identical, but this is unverified against OpenRouter's response envelope. The server strictly validates the response shape (`invalid_response` error kind), so any envelope difference would fail closed.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial-to-moderate. gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into `state`, `instructions` and `criteria`, plus model id, sent by HTTPS POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (would be openrouter.ai if patched). By design that is model-selected excerpts: diffs, stack traces, test output, file snippets, work traces (the skill recipes explicitly send tool results and work history for context-selection/trace-monitoring/safety-advisory). Nothing is sent automatically; the server never reads the repo. No client-side secret redaction: the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook does NOT cover MCP tool calls (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so a secret that appears in a log the model relays into `state` would leave the machine. gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-explicit at the tool layer, fail-open at the agent layer. Missing key: tools still list, calls return isError with kind authentication. Timeouts/429/529/network/invalid response all return structured isError results with error.kind + retryable and policy `reevaluate/evaluation_failed`; never fabricates an answer. Profiles: `reliable` (default) 30s per attempt / 60s total, retries 429/529 up to 2x, no timeout retry; `interactive` 1.5s per attempt / 3s total, one retry incl. timeouts (profile.rs:59-69). Set JEV_PROFILE=interactive for a coding loop, else a hung Jev can stall a turn up to 60s. Claude must decide to continue without Jev; nothing blocks tool use or permissions (it is not a hook).
gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Only when the model chooses to call it: one extra tool-call round trip = model turn to emit the call (with its hand-written state JSON, hundreds to thousands of output tokens, i.e. seconds on Opus) + Jev 70-500 ms claimed + 3s worst case in interactive profile (60s worst in reliable). Because the calling LLM must author the evidence payload and then read the JSON, the net per-decision cost is dominated by Claude output tokens, likely making it slower than Claude just deciding itself. Zero latency on turns where it is not called. Server cold start negligible (Rust binary).
gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.contextCost: 4 tools always loaded (unless Claude Code tool search defers them). Estimated static cost: 4 descriptions ~1.1k chars + JSON schemas from schemars (Context untagged enum with Text/Object/Array, Question tagged enum with 3 variants, NoulCriteria, profile enum, repeated in $defs for batch) roughly 6-9k chars total, approx 2-2.5k tokens, plus server `instructions` ~470 chars (~120 tokens). Total about 2.2-2.7k tokens per session (estimate, I did not build the binary to dump tools/list). Optional skill: frontmatter description ~430 chars always visible (~110 tokens); full SKILL.md is 8.7 KB (~2.2k tokens) loaded on trigger, plus reference files 1-3 KB each on demand. No hook-injected text (no hooks).
gh-ieee0824-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus (optionally) skill-description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. Claude will only call jev.* if the tool descriptions/instructions/skill description persuade it in-context; the skill's own description is weakly worded ('when the user requests a Jev judgment, or when several related judgments share the same evidence') and the SKILL says 'Use Jev only when the judgment justifies an additional network call', so with Opus 5.5 it will rarely call it unprompted. To meet the user's 'never say use jev' requirement one would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule or rewrite the skill description, and even then invocation stays probabilistic.

Correct semantics for Jev: closed decision space, exposes all three primitives plus batch, preserves raw probabilities and adds a deterministic accept/verify/reevaluate policy layer (configurable thresholds) that suits Claude acting on calibrated output.

Has an `interactive` profile (1.5s/3s budget, one retry) purpose-built for coding loops, plus opt-in privacy-preserving telemetry to stderr (no state/keys) that would let you measure real latency and call rate.

Same wire path (/v1/systemone) and body ({state, model, questions}) as the OpenRouter System One endpoint in the brief, so retargeting to OpenRouter is a ~3-line const/env patch, no schema translation expected.
No shell execution, no repo reads, no install-time scripts: static analysis found nothing risky; read-only/non-destructive tool annotations.

Recipe library (action selection, hypothesis ranking, evidence sufficiency, context selection) gives concrete design ideas for where Jev could plausibly add value in agent loops, and SKILL.md is a valid Claude Code skill format after copying.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tools with no hook or proxy. Directly conflicts with the user's core requirement; Opus will seldom call a decision tool when it can answer itself, and the bundled skill explicitly discourages routine use.

Hard-coded TypeSafe endpoint (client.rs:15), no OpenRouter support: requires a local fork and Rust >=1.88 toolchain build, with no releases or prebuilt binaries. OpenRouter response envelope compatibility is unverified.
Written for Codex, not Claude Code: README documents only ~/.codex/config.toml, skill ships agents/openai.yaml, no plugin.json/.mcp.json/hooks. Claude Code setup is DIY.

Calling LLM must serialize the evidence into `state` itself: burns Claude output tokens and a full extra tool round trip per decision, so net latency/cost is likely worse than letting Opus decide; Jev's 70-500 ms advantage is swamped.
Data egress of code/diffs/logs to third parties (TypeSafe/OpenRouter) at model discretion, with no redaction and outside the existing secret-guard hook's matcher; sensitive for client projects.

Adds ~2.2-2.7k tokens of tool schema context every session for a tool that will rarely fire; README itself states real-model quality, cost and latency are unmeasured ('Evaluate ... separately') and that Jev-vs-token-savings benefit is a future question.

gh-rajasekharponakala-jev-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. The generic jev_evaluate schema is loose (state: str|dict|list, questions: dict). The estimated total is about 1.0-1.5k tokens for tool names, descriptions and the FastMCP-generated JSON schemas (about 4-5k chars). The server sets no `instructions` string (FastMCP("jev") with no instructions arg), and no hooks inject text. The cost is fixed unless the tools are deferred through ToolSearch, which is Claude Code's default for MCP tools when many are configured.
gh-rajasekharponakala-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or nudges Claude to use it: there is no hook, no server `instructions`, and no SKILL.md. The tool descriptions are terse ("Yes/no judgment...") and do not say when to use them. Without a CLAUDE.md rule or a companion hook or skill, Claude will rarely call it, which conflicts with the user's goal of use without prompting.
gh-rajasekharponakala-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero when not called. A call is a stdio MCP round trip plus one HTTPS POST: the claimed Jev latency is 70-500 ms end to end, plus the LLM turn overhead of a tool call (roughly 1-3 s of model thinking and token generation to write the arguments and read the result). A cold `uv run --with` start adds seconds only at session start.
pros: Small enough to audit completely: 193 lines, one file, no shell, no telemetry, no postinstall. It can be reviewed in five minutes.
Full coverage of the three Jev primitives, plus a batch tool with parallel questions and a models-listing tool, all in the documented request shape {state, model, questions}.
The key comes from env (with the .env fallback never overriding real env), and it goes only to hard-coded HTTPS hosts.
The design is easy to patch for OpenRouter: an existing Zen branch shows exactly where a third endpoint goes (server.py:56-66), and the /v1/systemone suffix is shared across gateways.
Also usable as a model-callable building block if you write your own hook or skill on top (the tools give the typed answers to a routing decision).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and OPENCODE_API_KEY (server.py:56-66). It requires a patch or fork, which turns you into maintainer of an AGPL fork of a 2-commit, 2-star repo.

No automatic invocation: no hook, no skill, no server instructions. It only ever runs when Claude chooses to call it, and nothing in the tool descriptions tells Claude when Jev is useful. This does not meet the requirement 'Claude must use it without me prompting'.
The 60 s no-retry timeout (server.py:75) could block a turn if Jev or the gateway is slow, and there is no circuit breaker.
Zero tests, no CI, no releases; 9 days old, one author; fastmcp>=4 is an unbounded dependency.
Nothing constrains what goes into `state`, and your secret-leak guard hook matcher does not cover MCP tools, so a secret could be exfiltrated in a Jev call.

Even when called, the value for coding is thin: Jev returns probabilities for classification or routing questions, not code, and Claude Opus's own judgment is already available for those at no extra tool round trip. Every call costs a tool turn.
AGPL-3.0 license is unusual for a tool you would use on client projects (fine to run, but avoid embedding).
The README `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` pattern stores the key in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
gh-rajasekharponakala-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, auditable but tiny and brand-new proof-of-concept wrapper. It has no OpenRouter path (needs a roughly 5-line patch whose schema compatibility I could not verify) and, more importantly, no automatic-use mechanism, so alone it does not satisfy the user's goal. It is only useful as a reference or base for a fork paired with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md routing rule.

gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.whatItDoes: Small stdio MCP server (Node, ~440 LOC) exposing two tools, jev_evaluate (mixed noul/choice/score typed questions over a supplied state) and jev_classify (batch classification of up to 100 items against predefined classes plus a mandatory none class, with review flags from probability/margin thresholds). Its server instructions tell the agent to 'use Jev proactively' for narrow semantic judgments, but it is purely model-discretion, with no hooks and no skill.

Not run by me (static audit only). Optional live smoke script. Docs claim 8 live tutorial scenarios with published evidence, including failures.
security: API key handled well: read from env, sent only as Bearer to a hardcoded HTTPS host, redirect:'error', errors never echo URL/content/key (client.mjs:73-78). Documented env-file pattern keeps the key out of argv and ps.

No shell execution, no file reads, no URL fetching, no telemetry, no logging of content (grep and SECURITY.md consistent with source). Deps are pinned; the CI and install guidance use --ignore-scripts, so no postinstall.

Prompt-injection surface is small: tool has readOnlyHint and returns only numbers and ids. The main risk is the calling agent trusting probabilities. classify wraps item text as data with 'evidence not instructions' notes (classify.mjs:60-64), which is only a soft guard.
Response body capped at 1 MiB and requests at 256 KiB; strict zod validation of response with sum-to-1 check (schema.mjs:45-64) so malformed output fails closed as a tool error.

Supply chain risk: single anonymous-ish maintainer, 4 commits, 1 star, no npm release, no signed tags. A fork should be pinned to a reviewed commit SHA. Also the README links a French article, which is untrusted data.
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.dataEgress: Only the explicit tool arguments (state, questions, item contents, class definitions and context) serialized as JSON, plus the model name and the Bearer key, go to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (would be openrouter.ai if patched, which then also sees it and its logging and retention policy applies). The server never reads project files by itself. However, because the model chooses what to put in state, Claude could send code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. Tool args and results also stay in the Claude Code transcript. Nothing is sent when Claude does not call the tool.
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, because it is an optional MCP tool: errors return isError JSON with codes (MISSING_API_KEY, TIMEOUT, NETWORK_ERROR, RATE_LIMITED, HTTP_xxx, INVALID_RESPONSE) and Claude just proceeds without a decision. There is no substitute model. The per-attempt timeout is 30 s (client.mjs:40) and there are up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx with short Retry-After honored (a delay above 5 s returns RATE_LIMITED). Network errors and timeouts are not retried. Worst case is about 90 s or more of blocking on repeated 5xx, and the README advises a 120 s MCP client timeout. If the process fails to start (bad env-file path), the MCP server shows as failed and the rest of Claude Code is unaffected (as with caveman-shrink now).
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.contextCost: 2 tools. Estimated about 6,000 chars total, roughly 1.5-2k tokens: server instructions about 1.3k chars (server.mjs:126) which are always injected into the system prompt; jev_evaluate description about 700 chars and jev_classify about 640 chars; JSON schemas from zod with nested unions and describe() strings about 3-4k chars. Under Claude Code tool search/deferred MCP tools, only the names are loaded until needed. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn.
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call it. Per call: a network round trip to Jev, claimed 70-500 ms end to end, plus the model-turn overhead of Claude building a state and rubric (extra output tokens, typically several seconds of Opus generation) and a permission prompt unless allowlisted (mcp__jev__* rule or bypass mode). Net effect is usually slower than Claude deciding itself.
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The server 'instructions' text and tool descriptions nudge 'Use Jev proactively' for classification, relevance and triage. There is no deterministic trigger: Opus 5.5 decides, and for a coding workload it will rarely see a narrow semantic-classification need, so real usage would be near zero unless CLAUDE.md rules or a hook direct it.
pros: Cleanest code of the candidate types: small (about 440 LOC), readable, pinned deps, 3 concurrent calls cap, strict input and output validation, fail-closed on malformed answers, and the tests are offline.
Good security hygiene: key via --env-file (not argv), fixed host, no redirects, no logging, no shell, no postinstall; readOnlyHint set.
jev_classify batches up to 100 items into one upstream request with a required none class and review thresholds, which is sensible design for Jev's calibrated-probability strengths.
Tool descriptions and server instructions already encode when-to-use guidance ('use proactively'), which is the only auto-invocation lever available for an MCP tool.
MIT licensed; the native /systemone shape matches what OpenRouter says it accepts, so an OpenRouter fork is a roughly 3-line patch.
Tiny context footprint (2 tools, about 2k tokens) and no per-turn hook cost.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter as shipped: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model regex rejects typesafe/ IDs, and the default jev-1.13.0 is not an OpenRouter-style ID. It needs a fork, and the OpenRouter response compatibility of the strict zod schema is unverified.

Automatic use is not guaranteed: it is model-discretion only. The instructions say 'proactively', but daily coding rarely presents narrow, pre-defined-class semantic judgments, and Claude must write a full rubric each call, which costs tokens and seconds and is often slower than deciding itself. It does not meet the goal of Claude Code using Jev automatically when needed, unless supplemented by CLAUDE.md rules or hooks.
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, v0.1.0, not on npm, so you would install from a git clone and maintain it yourself. Jev is beta and the vendor is unaffiliated.
Data egress is model-chosen: Claude may send code or client file contents to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on client projects. It needs an explicit policy for client repos.

No coding-specific features (no commit or diff triage, test-failure routing, or PR risk scoring recipes), and a generic tool needs the model to design good criteria. Interplay with existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks is neutral, but there is no hook integration.
Permission friction: without an allowlist entry or bypass mode each call prompts; timeouts up to 30 s x 3 attempts could stall a turn on bad days.
gh-mattioofr-mcp-server-jev.verdict: A well-written, safe, minimal generic MCP wrapper, and the best MCP-shaped starting point because an OpenRouter fork is nearly a 3-line patch (URL, key env, model regex). But it is TypeSafe-only as shipped, brand-new and single-maintainer, and being model-discretion it will not deliver the truly automatic, hook-like Jev use the user wants. Use it, if at all, as a forked, SHA-pinned tool paired with deterministic hooks or CLAUDE.md routing rules.

gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.runtime: Python 3.10+ with the `mcp` package (pip). It imports `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer` (mcp_server.py:27), the v2 SDK API; PyPI mcp is 2.2.0, so a v1 install would probably fail on import. No pyproject.toml, requirements.txt or lockfile, so run it by hand in a venv or uv run --with mcp. Stdlib urllib for HTTP.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.install: Clone the repo, then `pip install mcp` (INSTALL.md:46). scripts/install.sh is Hermes-specific: it runs `pip install --upgrade mcp`, registers with the `hermes` CLI, and writes /tmp/jev-install.log. For Claude Code, register manually: `claude mcp add jev -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -- python3 /path/mcp_server.py` (README shows an mcpServers JSON block). Nothing is published to PyPI or npm, so there is no uvx one-liner.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.tests: Only test_mcp_client.py, a manual e2e script that needs a live key. No unit tests, no CI (.github returns 404) and no releases. RESULTADOS_BATERIA.md is a 6-case self-benchmark: 5/6 label accuracy, tied with gpt-4o-mini, and the author says it proves nothing about calibration. The domain is customer-support ticket triage, not coding.
security: API key: read from env var, else from a plaintext file under ~/.hermes/secrets. The README's Claude Code snippet puts the key in the mcpServers env block, which lands in plaintext ~/.claude.json. Use `claude mcp add -e` or inherit from the shell environment instead. The key is never on argv in the recommended setup, and no code logs it.
No shell execution and no eval in the server. HTTP goes through urllib to hardcoded HTTPS URLs only. No telemetry. No npm postinstall.

scripts/install.sh is not curl|sh. It is local, idempotent and does `pip install --upgrade mcp` into whichever Python it finds. It writes /tmp/jev-install.log at a predictable path (minor symlink and tmp risk). It does not write the key.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever Claude passes as `state` (code, file contents, issue text) goes to Jev. Jev returns only typed numbers and enums, so the response channel is a very low injection risk. Error text `raw_error` is truncated to 500 chars and comes from the provider.

Retries: up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff, and a 120 s timeout per attempt (jev.py:77,93). A hung provider can block one tool call for a very long time (about 8 min worst case). This is a reliability risk, not a vulnerability.

Unpinned dependency (`pip install mcp`) and a brand-new single-author repo with no releases or signing. It is small enough to audit in 10 minutes, but nothing ties a future git pull to what was audited, so pin a commit.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions` and `criteria` goes to openrouter.ai over HTTPS with a Bearer key. That means arbitrary code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs if the model chooses to pass them. Nothing is sent automatically, and there is no hook that harvests content. Responses come back with model, provider, cost and request_id. jev_health sends the fixed string 'Teste de conectividade.'. OpenRouter and TypeSafe see and may log the payloads. Check OpenRouter's data-policy settings before using this on client code under NDA.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the MCP layer: config errors, HTTP errors and network errors all return a JSON {ok:false,...} tool result rather than raising, so Claude Code continues. The problem is latency. Retryable statuses (429, 500, 502, 503, 529) and URLErrors are retried 4 times with backoff of 1, 2 and 4 s, and each attempt has a 120 s timeout (jev.py:77-107). A stalled Jev can therefore hang a tool call for minutes. There is no circuit breaker and no short timeout option exposed to the tool. Non-retryable errors such as 400 or 401 return immediately. If the key is missing, the tool still registers and only fails when called.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero at session start except spawning a Python process, plus a fixed context cost. Nothing is added to Read, Edit or Bash calls because there are no hooks. Each jev_decisions call adds one Claude tool round trip (about 2-4 s of Opus time to author the question schema) plus 70-500 ms claimed network latency. Worst case with retries and timeouts is minutes. Realistically Jev's own latency is smaller than the LLM overhead of asking it.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.contextCost: 2 tools. Rough count: server instructions about 1.3k chars (about 330 tokens), jev_decisions description about 750 chars, jev_health about 300 chars, plus schemas (state: Any, questions: dict, route) and tool names, about 500 chars. Total about 2.9k chars, or about 700-800 tokens permanent. In Claude Code 2.1.x with tool search deferral, the schemas may be deferred and only the names shown, and the instructions text is always injected. Very cheap. The Portuguese description is a small quirk.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude sees the tool and the Portuguese server instructions ('use when you need semantic judgment that ordinary code cannot do'). Nothing pushes it to call jev_decisions during ordinary coding: there is no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet. Opus 5.5 already handles classification internally, so it will almost never choose to author a typed-question payload and pay a round trip, unless the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill. It does not meet the requirement of 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically without me saying so'.
pros: Correct endpoint, default route and model for the user's setup: OpenRouter POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY read from the environment (jev.py:37-39). No patching is needed.
Small and auditable: about 250 lines in mcp_server.py plus jev.py, stdlib HTTP, no shell execution, no telemetry and no postinstall. Static read shows no exfiltration beyond the declared call.

Pre-validates question contracts (choice criteria as dict, score criteria as ordered list) before spending a call, and validates response probabilities (sum to about 1, range checks), so malformed Claude-authored questions get a corrective error. This handles the trickiest part of the Decisions API.
Fail-open: all errors are returned as data, not exceptions.
Returns cost_usd, tokens and request_id per call, which is useful for auditing spend. About 700 tokens of permanent context for 2 tools.

Ships the honest guidance 'policy stays in code, low confidence is information', and a README that lists real API gotchas (no /v1, not in the models catalog, /chat/completions returns 400, noul has no confidence field).
cons: Cannot satisfy the core requirement. It is only a model-discretion tool with no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md rule, so Claude Code will not use Jev 'when needed' on its own. Opus 5.5 will normally just decide things itself.

Generic pass-through with no coding-specific value: no prebuilt questions for 'is this diff risky', 'which file matches this task', 'does this test failure look flaky', and so on. The only example is customer-ticket triage. The user or Claude must invent schemas each time, which costs more Opus tokens and time than the decision saves.

Extreme immaturity: 0 stars, 3 commits in one day, 1 contributor, no CI, no releases, no unit tests, no pyproject or lockfile. It is Hermes-first (install.sh, ~/.hermes/secrets, HERMES_HOME) with Claude Code treated as an afterthought.

TypeSafe direct route (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model 'jev-latest') is unverified in the code, and the repo has no evidence it ever worked. The /api/v1/systemone OpenRouter endpoint is not supported. Only the alpha Decisions API is used, and 'alpha' may change or break.

Retry and timeout policy is hostile to an interactive session: 4 attempts, 120 s timeout each, no way to shorten it. A Jev outage or 429 storm would stall the tool call for minutes with no circuit breaker.

README example puts the API key in the mcpServers env block, which is plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The key-file fallback lives under ~/.hermes, which is irrelevant to this user. The `mcp.server.mcpserver` import needs the v2 SDK, with no version pin, so it can break on install.

The repo's own benchmark (6 ticket cases, 5/6, tied with gpt-4o-mini) does not show Jev outperforming a plain LLM, and says nothing about code tasks. It offers no evidence for the 'router' claims, and the author admits calibration is unproven.

Client code sent as `state` leaves the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the server has no allow/deny filtering or redaction. This matters for client projects even though the existing secret-leak hook guards only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit tool inputs, not MCP calls.
gh-tmbmartell-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, honest, OpenRouter-native reference wrapper that is worth copying as a starting point. But it is a passive tool that Claude will basically never call unprompted, it has no coding-specific questions, and it is a one-day-old single-author POC with an aggressive retry and timeout policy. Use it, if at all, as the transport layer, and add your own PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hook or skill (with fixed coding questions and a short timeout) to get the automatic behaviour the user wants.

gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.name: Songokou1983/jev-mcp
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Python FastMCP server (stdio or Bearer-authed streamable HTTP) wrapping TypeSafe's direct System One API (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) as 6 MCP tools: classify (Choice), check (Noul), rate (Score), batch_judge, system_one_raw, health. Adds server-side confidence gating (act/confirm/escalate), 32k-char state cap, $0.10 per-process budget, in-memory LRU cache, tenacity retry on 429/529, and a JSONL decision log. It is a personal project whose default deployment is a home server reached over Tailscale.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.license: No LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo is null. pyproject.toml declares MIT in metadata only, so the legal position is ambiguous.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.runtime: Python >=3.10; mcp<2 (FastMCP 1.x), httpx, uvicorn, tenacity. Installed from a git clone with uv pip install -e . Not published to PyPI (README only shows clone plus editable install).
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.install: git clone, uv venv, uv pip install -e ".[dev]". Then either claude mcp add --transport http (Tailscale server plus Bearer token, README default) or a stdio registration. The README's stdio command uses odd --command/--args flags that I could not verify. Stdio mode needs no JEV_MCP_TOKEN. The key is read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY in env or ~/.jev/.env.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.tests: 142 tests claimed (120 unit with respx mocks, 6 real-API integration gated on env, 16 regression). Test files exist under tests/ (about 1500 lines). I did not run them, per the hard rules. There is no CI: .github does not exist. Latest release is v0.3.0, created the same day as the repo.

interface.name: classify(text, options[2-255], descriptions?, question?)
interface.purpose: One-of-N classification via Choice. Returns choice, confidence, probabilities, action (act/confirm/escalate), cached (server.py:119-134, :476).

interface.name: check(text, condition)
interface.purpose: Yes/no via Noul. Returns probability, verdict, action. Effective confidence is computed as |p-0.5|*2 (server.py:137-146, action_gate.py:181).

interface.name: rate(text, levels[2-10], question?)
interface.purpose: Ordered rubric scoring via Score. Returns score, score_label, probabilities, confidence, action (server.py:149-160).

interface.name: batch_judge(items[<=20], criteria[])
interface.purpose: Independent sequential API call per item, no cache, echoes each item back in the result (server.py:163-249).

interface.name: system_one_raw(state, questions)
interface.purpose: Raw passthrough to /v1/systemone with the model pinned. No cache and no gate, but budget accrual and logging still apply (server.py:252-259).

interface.name: health()
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models probe plus session stats: budget, cache, uptime, decisions_logged (server.py:262-279).

security: API key handling is sound: TYPESAFE_API_KEY comes from env or ~/.jev/.env (server.py:599-615), never argv. Under `claude mcp add`, the key would sit in ~/.claude.json env unless you use ~/.jev/.env. A hand-rolled .env parser strips quotes only.

HTTP mode enforces Bearer auth with hmac.compare_digest (bearer.py:165-174) and refuses to start without a token (server.py:579-584). But the token travels over plain http:// on Tailscale, and if you use the README's --header form the token appears in ~/.claude.json and the claude process argv.
stdio mode has no auth, which is fine because it is a local child process.
transport_security allowlist hard-codes the author's Tailscale IP 100.86.140.31 (server.py:500-505) and issuer_url 127.0.0.1:8765, so HTTP mode on another host needs code edits. stdio is unaffected.
httpx trust_env=False (jev_client.py:93,114) deliberately ignores HTTP(S)_PROXY and NO_PROXY, so it breaks in proxied or corporate networks and bypasses any egress policy.
No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, and no telemetry in the code. Its only outbound host is api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool returns only typed fields, but batch_judge echoes the submitted items back. Tool results are model-parsed dicts, so risk is low. The bigger issue is that Claude decides what state to send.

Decision log ~/.local/share/jev-mcp/decisions.jsonl holds metadata plus sha256 args_hash only by default. JEV_LOG_FULL_RESPONSE=1 stores full responses. I did not check file mode 0600 enforcement in code; the README claims it.
The cache is an in-memory LRU keyed by sha256 with no TTL, so it is lost on restart.
Budget cap of $0.10 is per process, and the budget accrue path will raise a BudgetExceeded error into the tool call once hit. Not a security issue, but an unexpected hard stop.
Unsigned commits from a single anonymous author (git identity huangqi@local). No license file, no CI, no pinned dependencies beyond lower bounds.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the tool's text/state or in system_one_raw's state and questions goes over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter). That means arbitrary code snippets, commands, diffs or file contents that Claude chooses to pass. Nothing is sent automatically from hooks, since there are none. Capped at 32000 chars per call (state_cap.py). health() sends only a GET with the key. With the HTTP deployment, the same payload first crosses Tailscale (plain http) to the home server. No third-party telemetry. Client-side text is not filtered for secrets, and the user's secret-leak guard hook covers only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* calls.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level and not fail-open at the workflow level. The client has a 30 s timeout per attempt (jev_client.py:53) with up to 3 retries on 429/529 (base 0.5 s, max 4 s), so a bad case can stall a call for about 2 minutes. Other errors (401, 422, 5xx except 529, connect errors) raise JevAPIError or httpx errors, which surface as an MCP tool error to Claude. Claude can carry on without Jev, so it is effectively soft. Nothing blocks Claude Code itself. batch_judge is sequential (about 20 x 300 ms), and a mid-batch failure loses all results. Once the $0.10 session budget is hit, tools raise BudgetExceeded. No circuit breaker. trust_env=False ignores proxies, so a network that requires one fails.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per call: the TypeSafe-claimed 70-500 ms, plus stdio process overhead (Python startup, negligible after the first call), plus the LLM turn to decide to call the tool and read the result (an extra tool round trip in Claude Code, typically 1-3 s of Opus time). Cache hits are instant. In HTTP mode it adds a Tailscale hop. batch_judge is sequential, about 0.3 s x N. Startup of the MCP server is the Python import time (mcp, httpx, uvicorn), a fraction of a second to a couple of seconds.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.contextCost: 6 tools. Descriptions total about 5,600 chars (about 1,400 tokens: classify 903, check 844, rate 736, batch_judge 1391, system_one_raw 1028, health 695), plus JSON schemas for parameters (options, descriptions, criteria, state, questions), roughly 400-700 more tokens. That is about 2,000 tokens in total, always loaded unless Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch (which the environment shows it does for MCP tools). The FastMCP instructions field is not set (no instructions kwarg at server.py:508-525). No hook-injected text. The tool descriptions are written in English as [POSITIVE]/[NEGATIVE]/[EXAMPLE]/[CONTRACT] blocks. They are wordy and tell the model when not to use the tool.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tool descriptions are the sole trigger; there are no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin manifest, and no CLAUDE.md snippet for the user's projects (the repo's own CLAUDE.md is for developing the project). The NEGATIVE text in each description actively discourages use unless the case is fuzzy, so Claude will call it rarely and unpredictably. Not deterministic and not transparent. This does not meet the user's requirement of use without prompting, other than by chance.
pros: Cleanest primitive mapping of the three Jev primitives: classify=Choice, check=Noul, rate=Score, with typed results and per-option probabilities (server.py:119-160).
Hard cost and abuse limits: 32k-char state cap, $0.10 per-process budget, LRU cache, so a runaway loop cannot burn much money (budget.py, cache.py, state_cap.py).

stdio mode works locally with no Tailscale, no bearer token and no server to run. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no shell execution, and the only egress is api.typesafe.ai. Python 3.13 and uv are already on the machine.
Sensible engineering for a PoC: retry/backoff on 429/529, health probe that costs nothing, decision log stores hashes rather than content by default, 142 tests including regression tests.
Useful pattern to steal: the action gate (act/confirm/escalate) and effective_confidence=|noul-0.5|*2 to convert Noul into a confidence. It works as a reference for writing your own thin wrapper.
Descriptions include explicit NEGATIVE guidance (do not use for regex, arithmetic, deterministic checks), which avoids paying for trivial calls.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: base URL https://api.typesafe.ai is hard-coded and never overridable (jev_client.py:51, server.py:546), key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (server.py:599-615), and the model is pinned to the TypeSafe ID jev-1.13.0. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider, so a fork is needed to switch.

Not automatic. It is a pure model-discretion MCP tool set with no hooks or skill. The NEGATIVE text deters use, and Claude Code will rarely reach for a probability tool while coding. Directly conflicts with the no-prompting requirement.

Designed for support-ticket/agent-routing use (examples: refunds, billing, customer anger) rather than coding work. Nothing in it targets code review, diff triage, test selection or command safety, so the user would have to author all the coding-specific criteria in every call, and Claude must serialise code into the text argument each time.

Every use costs a full extra Opus tool round trip (Claude decides, formats, calls, reads), which is usually slower than Jev's 70-500 ms and often slower than Claude just deciding itself. Net latency gain is negative.

Egress is uncontrolled: whatever Claude puts in text (code, diffs, secrets) goes to a third party. The existing secret-guard hook does not match mcp__jev__* tools, and there is no redaction in the server.
Sequential batch_judge, echoing items back, 30 s timeout x 4 attempts, and a per-process $0.10 cap that raises BudgetExceeded mid-session. There is no circuit breaker.

HTTP deployment code is tied to the author's home Tailscale IP (server.py:500-505) and is plain http; trust_env=False breaks proxied networks. Author's own machine paths (/home/son_goku) in the README.
Very young and single-author: 5 commits all on 2026-09-22, 2 stars, no CI, no LICENSE file, unsigned commits, docs largely in Chinese. Unverified against the current OpenRouter alpha API.
gh-songokou1983-jev-mcp.verdict: A tidy, well-tested weekend PoC that maps Jev's three primitives to MCP tools, but it is TypeSafe-direct only, takes no OpenRouter key, and relies on the model choosing to call it, so it fails both the OpenRouter and the automatic-use requirements as shipped. At best, use it as a reference or fork base (about 30 lines to retarget) and pair it with hooks or a skill, since it has neither.

License MIT. package.json marks the package private, and npm publishing is intentionally disabled.

API key is read from the process env or a plaintext ~/.jev-mcp/.env (mode 0600, dir 0700) written by the installer (installer.ts:287-301). The key is never placed in argv or in the client MCP config; the claude mcp add call has no -e flag. This is good for the process list, but the key sits in plaintext on disk, and env-file loading also reads a checkout-local .env (index.ts:44).

Recommended install is curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/.../v0.5.0/scripts/install.sh | bash. It clones the repo at a tag (a tag, not a commit SHA, so it is mutable) and runs 'npm ci' and 'npm run build'. That executes the dependency tree's install scripts on the machine. Dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0 and zod ^4.3.6, and the lockfile is committed. Do not use the curl|bash path; audit and build manually instead.

installer.ts uses spawnSync with fixed argument arrays, plus 'sh -lc command -v <fixed literal>' (installer.ts:187). I found no shell injection surface. The runtime MCP server itself does no shell execution and no file writes, only fetch. No telemetry found. Its only outbound call is fetch to the configured base URL, and there is a User-Agent jev-mcp/0.5.0.

Prompt-injection and exfiltration surface: 'state' is free-form, chosen by the host model, and forwarded to the remote API. A prompt-injected model could ship repository content out, but only to the configured endpoint. If TYPESAFE_BASE_URL were tampered with, the bearer key would go to another host, and the code accepts any http/https URL, including plain http (core.ts:75).

Tool responses include only the API JSON plus a local advisory wrapper. The model's answer is numeric or keyed, so it is a low text-injection vector. Upstream error bodies (up to 2000 chars) are echoed to the model (index.ts:160).

The host model decides the content. The server instructions say to send a minimal, redacted summary, but nothing enforces it. The server does not read files itself and does not see the transcript, diffs or tool outputs unless the model copies them into 'state'. With OpenRouter as the base URL, the data goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe/upstream, and OpenRouter's logging and privacy settings apply. That matters for client code. No telemetry.
gh-afloat16-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open. Each tool wraps callJev in try/catch and returns isError:true with the message, so the host model just proceeds without the Jev signal (index.ts:223, 173-179). The timeout is 15 s by default, configurable from 250 ms to 120 s via TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS (core.ts:81-88). There are no retries and no circuit breaker. A missing API key throws at call time, not at startup, so the server still starts and the tools appear. A bad key produces an error only when a tool is used. Nothing blocks a turn, because the call is model-initiated.

Estimated static cost is about 1.7k tokens: server instructions about 3.7k chars (roughly 930 tokens, injected every session, index.ts:56-116), tool names, descriptions and zod-to-JSON schemas about 3k chars (roughly 750 tokens). Each call returns a JSON payload of a few hundred tokens with an advisory wrapper (about 60 tokens).

The server instructions and tool descriptions deliberately ask for restraint ('only after inspecting enough context... genuine uncertainty... do not call merely because a task is complex'). It has no hooks, no skill triggers and no proxy behaviour. Claude Code will therefore call it rarely and unpredictably, and there is no deterministic trigger. It cannot be forced without editing the SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS or adding a CLAUDE.md or hook policy outside this repo. It has only the Codex-flavoured AGENTS.jev-conservative.md, which is also conservative.
gh-afloat16-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero unless the model calls a tool. When called, it adds one MCP round trip plus an HTTPS call. The claimed Jev latency is 70-500 ms; OpenRouter routing adds some overhead. The model must also spend an extra turn of output tokens to build state, options and criteria, typically a few seconds of Opus generation. There is no per-turn overhead and no hooks on the hot path. Or use a project .mcp.json with env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
pros: Small, readable, auditable code (about 500 lines of runtime logic). The request format matches OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone body and answer shapes, so OpenRouter works with three env vars and no patch.
Fail-open by design. Errors return isError text and never block the coding flow. The timeout is configurable and defaults to 15 s.

Good hygiene for secrets. The key is never in argv or in the Claude config, the .env file is 0600 with a 0700 dir, and tool annotations are readOnlyHint. It has no shell or filesystem access at runtime.
Sensible tool taxonomy. Risk score with 4 fixed levels, gate with a threshold, and choice for routing map cleanly onto Jev's Choice/Score/Noul primitives.
It has a claude-code installer target and a documented MCP-only setup, and it ships instructions that push the model toward privacy-minimal state.
cons: It does not deliver the user's core requirement. Invocation is model-discretion and deliberately conservative ('prefer zero Jev calls'), with no hook or skill to trigger it automatically. In daily coding Claude Code will almost never call it. Forcing more usage means editing the instructions or CLAUDE.md.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2 days ago, one day of history, 1 star, tests only for helpers. Pre-1.0, with tool schemas that may change in minor releases (README says so).

The default path is curl|bash, which does git clone plus npm ci plus build, and the installer targets nine clients and writes to their configs. There is no npm package, so updates are manual. Use the manual build instead.

OpenRouter is undocumented and unsupported by name. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY hold OpenRouter values, the installer writes the TypeSafe default URL into ~/.jev-mcp/.env, and JEV_MODEL must be set to an OpenRouter ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). There is no live-call verification here.

Only the /v1/systemone endpoint is used, with no Decisions API, no session_id, no trace and no provider routing. The 15 s timeout with no retry is far longer than Jev's 70-500 ms claim. Anything in 'state' goes to a third-party API, which is a client-confidentiality risk. Nothing scrubs secrets or code, and the server relies only on the model following instructions.
About 1.7k tokens of standing context per session (instructions plus tool schemas), for a tool the instructions say should rarely be used.
gh-afloat16-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, small, fail-open MCP wrapper that works with OpenRouter via env vars only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). It is an opt-in second-opinion tool that is deliberately rarely called, so it cannot give the automatic, hook-level Jev use the user wants. Build it from source after review if you want an MCP baseline, but pair it with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md policy, and treat it as young and unproven.

gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Node (ESM) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards typed Jev questions (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe's System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone) and returns the raw JSON of probabilities. Also ships `jev-eval`, an offline harness (Brier, ECE, AUC, McNemar, latency/cost) for comparing Jev vs OpenAI/Anthropic baselines on labelled noul datasets, plus `jev-mcp install` which registers the server in Claude Code/Desktop/Codex.

providerSupport.evidence: src/config.js:6-8 DEFAULT_BASE_URL="https://api.typesafe.ai", EVALUATE_PATH="/v1/systemone", DEFAULT_MODEL="jev-latest"; src/config.js:15-16,36-38 env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required) and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override (trailing slashes stripped); src/client.js:185 url = baseUrl + EVALUATE_PATH; src/client.js:220-224 sends `authorization: Bearer <key>` + JSON body {state, questions, model}. No OpenRouter string anywhere in the repo. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api yields exactly https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (the OpenRouter System One URL) with a Bearer key, so it should work unmodified by putting the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Caveats: model default "jev-latest" (tool.js:121, config.js:8) is not an OpenRouter id (typesafe/jev-1.13, ~typesafe/jev-latest), so the agent must pass `model` on every call or the default must be patched; OpenRouter's request/response schema for /v1/systemone equalling TypeSafe's is assumed, not verified in this repo.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial: config-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<openrouter key>) plus a one-line change to DEFAULT_MODEL in src/config.js:8 to typesafe/jev-1.13 (or a fork reading JEV_MODEL env). Optionally add OPENROUTER_API_KEY alias in requireApiKey (config.js:25-33). Needs the OpenRouter /v1/systemone body schema to match TypeSafe's, which is unverified.
providerSupport.others: Eval harness only: OpenAI (OPENAI_API_KEY) and Anthropic (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) baseline adapters, not used by the MCP server.
