gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20 (ESM); deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.21, commander ^14, zod ^3.25; 95 resolved packages in lockfile. Not on npm (npm view @arunav25/jev-mcp = 404); install via `npm install -g github:arunav25/jev-mcp` or git clone + npm link.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/arunav25/jev-mcp && cd jev-mcp && npm install && npm link (or npm i -g github:arunav25/jev-mcp). Then register manually with `claude mcp add jev -s user -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -- node /path/src/cli.js serve` (preferred over `jev-mcp install`, which puts the key in argv).
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.tests: 7 node:test files (client, tool, install, eval, metrics, performance, regression); GitHub Actions CI on Node 20/22/24 running npm ci + npm test (.github/workflows/ci.yml). No releases/tags. Not executed here (static audit only).
security: API key handling: `jev-mcp install` passes `-e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<value>` as argv to `claude mcp add` (install.js:130-131), so the key is visible in the process list during install and is stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (and Desktop/Codex configs, mode 0600 only for the Desktop temp file). It also copies every TYPESAFE_* var. Mitigation: register by hand or use env passthrough.

No shell execution beyond execFile (no shell) for `which`, `claude`, `codex` in install.js; no postinstall/preinstall scripts (package.json scripts only start/test/eval); no curl|sh; no telemetry found in src/ (only fetch is client.js to the configured base URL and eval/http.js for baseline LLMs).
Response cap 8 MB streamed-reject (client.js:106,268-297); timeouts via AbortSignal (90 s per attempt); 401/422 not retried.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is raw API JSON of numbers/labels (no free text from Jev), so low injection risk from output; input is whatever the agent puts in `state`, which is untrusted repo content sent off-machine.

Supply chain: single-author, 8-star repo, install from git HEAD (unpinned unless a commit is specified), 95 transitive npm packages; server name `jev` written with user scope. Baseline `bare jev-mcp` on npm is an unrelated project (README warns), a typosquat-style confusion risk.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put in `state` and `questions.instructions/criteria` (could be code, diffs, logs, ticket text, file contents) plus the model id, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default api.typesafe.ai; would be openrouter.ai with override) with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically from the machine; no telemetry, no file scanning, and it does not read hook events or transcripts. On OpenRouter, provider logging/retention settings apply; client code must be considered egressed to TypeSafe via OpenRouter.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level, never blocks Claude Code: transient errors (429/502/503/504/529/network) retried up to 4 attempts with jittered exponential backoff from 700 ms and Retry-After honoured (client.js:103,157-165,249-253); per-attempt timeout 90 s (client.js:161), so worst case a single call can stall roughly 5-6 minutes if the service hangs (4 x 90 s + backoff), which is long for a synchronous tool call, though it honours the abort signal. After exhaustion it returns an isError tool result the model can ignore. Missing key makes serve throw at startup (config.js:25-33) so the MCP server shows as failed to connect but Claude Code continues. No circuit breaker, no lower configurable timeout without editing code.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Nothing added unless the model decides to call the tool; each call = one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms) plus MCP/stdio overhead and the extra model turn to write the call and read the result (typically 1-3 s of Opus generation to write state/questions JSON). Node stdio server spawn adds ~100-300 ms at session start. Retry logic can inflate the tail badly on outages (see failureMode).
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (`mcp__jev__evaluate`). Tool description ~380 chars plus zod-derived JSON schema with long .describe() strings (~2.2k chars total, ~550 tokens) and server `instructions` ~3.6k chars (~900 tokens; config.js:53-91). Roughly 1.4-1.6k tokens permanently in context; zero hook-injected text. Small compared with the existing playwright and gitnexus servers.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no plugin, no CLAUDE.md snippet. The tool description ('Use it wherever you would otherwise ask a model for an answer and then parse the reply') and server instructions are the only nudge; Opus will rarely choose it for ordinary coding since it has no coding-shaped use case (classifying tickets/urgency is the example domain). Meets the 'no prompting jev' requirement only weakly and unreliably; would need a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook to make it deterministic.
pros: Genuinely wraps the Jev System One endpoint with all three primitives (noul/choice/score) and pre-validates criteria (tool.js:63-89), saving wasted 422 round trips.

OpenRouter is one env var away: the path /v1/systemone (config.js:7) and Bearer auth match OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api; patch is at most a one-line default-model change.

Small, readable, dependency-light code (about 900 LOC in src/), MIT, no postinstall, no telemetry, execFile not shell, response size cap, sane retry/Retry-After handling, tests plus CI on Node 20/22/24.
Single tool with ~1.5k tokens context cost; readOnly/idempotent annotations may let permission modes auto-approve it.
Server instructions contain unusually good guidance for avoiding self-confirming state (config.js:59-65), which matters for a calibrated classifier.

jev-eval offers a statistically careful way (Brier, ECE, McNemar, perf on unlabelled data) to test whether Jev beats Opus/Haiku on the user's own decisions, which is the honest way to test the 'router' skepticism.
cons: Not coding-oriented: example domain is support tickets; nothing maps to Claude Code events (edit, test failure, diff, PR risk). Automatic use is left to model whim, so the user's core requirement (automatic, no prompting) is not met.

Only OpenRouter via undocumented-in-repo override; model default jev-latest is not a valid OpenRouter id, so calls without an explicit `model` may 4xx unless patched; OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
`jev-mcp install` leaks the API key into argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and stores it plaintext in ~/.claude.json; also blanket-copies TYPESAFE_* env.
Not published to npm, unpinned git install, single author, 5 commits over 4 days, 8 stars, no releases, v0.1.0: alpha-quality supply-chain trust for client projects.
No timeout/retry configuration surface: 90 s x 4 attempts can hang a turn for minutes when Jev (beta) is down; no fail-fast for a latency-sensitive 70-500 ms model.

Every call requires the model to hand-write a typed schema and put code/context into `state`, costing Opus output tokens and time that likely exceed the value of a decision Opus could make itself; sends client code off-machine to a third party.
Eval harness scores only noul questions and needs hundreds to thousands of labelled items; large surface (about 400+ LOC of eval) unrelated to the integration goal, and pulled in by the install.
gh-arunav25-jev-mcp.verdict: The most complete existing Jev MCP wrapper and safe to read/fork, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an explicit model id, but it is only a model-discretion tool with no coding-specific triggers, so it will not give the automatic, hook-driven Jev use the user wants. Best used as a base to fork (fix default model, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY, shorter timeout/fail-fast) behind a hook or CLAUDE.md rule, or as the eval harness to test Jev; register manually rather than via `jev-mcp install` to keep the key out of argv.

gh-byk-jev-mcp.name: BYK/jev-mcp (npm: jev-eval-mcp)
gh-byk-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small stdio MCP server (Node/TS, ~48 KB source) wrapping TypeSafe's System One endpoint. Exposes 3 tools: jev_ask (prototype typed questions on one state), jev_map (run a question set over many items from a JSONL/JSON file, filter/sort, save full results to disk), jev_eval (evaluate question variants against labeled data: accuracy, Brier, ECE, AUC, threshold sweep, worst misses). It is an offline-workflow/eval tool for building and calibrating Jev classifiers and for bulk triage. It is not a runtime gate or routing layer inside Claude Code.

No OPENROUTER_* env var anywhere. Since the URL is baseUrl + /v1/systemone, setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint in the brief. I could not fetch OpenRouter docs to confirm that the request and response schema (state/model/questions -> answers/usage) is identical, and the model id would need to be typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest via JEV_MODEL or the per-call model arg.

That is likely but unverified, because the docs pages returned 404. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. The env var name is misleading but works. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported.

gh-byk-jev-mcp.lastCommit: 2026-09-18 (about 12 days before audit date; single-author project by BYK, 4 of 7 commits from devin-ai-integration[bot])
gh-byk-jev-mcp.tests: Only test/metrics.test.ts (5 test cases, unit tests of the metrics math, no network). The HTTP client, tools and schemas have no unit tests. Live scripts/smoke.ts exists but needs a real key. GitHub Actions CI runs typecheck, lint, test and build on Node 22. Release via Craft, and the publish workflow is issue-driven. One release, 0.1.0 (2026-09-17); CHANGELOG says only "No documented changes". Forks: 0.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20 (uses .ts imports at runtime for scripts, so Node 24 is fine). Install per README: `npx -y jev-eval-mcp`. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0 and zod 4.6.1, both pinned. No postinstall script.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.install: claude mcp add jev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- npx -y jev-eval-mcp   (README form). For OpenRouter, the untested variant adds -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. Better: pin the version (jev-eval-mcp@0.1.0) or clone and run dist/index.js, and put the key in an env file or wrapper rather than argv.
security: README install puts the key in argv via `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...`. That value is stored in ~/.claude.json, not in the process list. The server process reads it from its environment. Prefer the config-file env block or `${VAR}` expansion.

`npx -y` without a version pin runs whatever latest is on npm on every start, which is a supply-chain risk for a process holding an API key. The dependency set is small (MCP SDK and zod, pinned exactly) and there is no postinstall script.

Arbitrary filesystem access via tool args: dataset_path is read with readFile (src/schemas.ts:83) and save_path is written with writeFile (tools/map.ts:194, evaluate.ts:331), with no path sandboxing. A prompt-injected agent could write JSON to any path, but the content is fixed-format results. The written data is not attacker-controlled shell code, so the risk is low but real.

Read path: the dataset file's contents are sent to the remote API. A prompt-injected agent could point dataset_path at ~/.ssh or .env files that are valid JSON or JSONL and exfiltrate them to the Jev provider. This is limited to JSON-parsable files (invalid JSON throws an error that quotes only the line number). It is still a hole in the existing secret-leak guard, which only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would not see MCP calls.

No shell execution, no eval, no telemetry (grep for process.env shows only 3 vars). Calls only the configured base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is fully user-controlled, so if the env is poisoned the key goes to an arbitrary host.

Tool results contain only numeric/typed model output (no free text from the model), so the prompt-injection surface via responses is minimal. Injection inputs (state) go to Jev, whose output is typed, which is a good property. Error messages echo up to 500 chars of the API response body.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` (or in the dataset file items) plus the question instructions/criteria is POSTed as JSON to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone, for example file contents, diffs, tickets, or logs. That is entirely model-discretion, because nothing is sent automatically. With OpenRouter as the provider, the payload goes to openrouter.ai and then to TypeSafe. Nothing else leaves the machine: no telemetry, and the API key is sent as a Bearer header. Client and personal code is exposed only when Claude chooses to pass it, which is relevant for client NDAs, and that choice is not gated by the existing secret guard.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by design, because it is a tool. On error the tool returns isError text and Claude carries on. Client retries: up to 4 attempts on 408/425/429/5xx/529 and on network errors, with exponential backoff (250ms*2^n, max 8s, plus Retry-After up to 20s), and a 60s per-request timeout (typesafe.ts:88-156). Worst case a single hung call blocks that turn for about 4x60s plus backoff, which is a bad tail for interactive use. The timeout is not configurable through env. A missing key makes the server exit(1) at startup, so the MCP connection fails visibly. No hook or gate exists, so nothing can block Claude.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call a tool. When invoked, the added cost is one MCP round trip plus the Jev latency (claimed 70-500ms end to end). jev_map with concurrency 8 over N items scales with N/8 requests. The first start with `npx -y` adds a cold-start delay (registry check and download) on every Claude Code session unless pinned or globally installed.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.contextCost: 3 tools. Estimated tool defs: names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas total about 6-8k chars, so roughly 1.5-2.2k tokens. The schema is inflated by the repeated discriminated-union question schema (noul/choice/score) in each tool, plus the dataset fields. Server `instructions` is about 420 chars (about 105 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Total is about 2k tokens of standing context, which is moderate for what is a niche capability. Claude Code's MCP tool search/deferral may reduce this when many tools are configured.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tools describe prototyping, bulk triage and eval workflows, not gating routine coding actions. Claude may occasionally reach for jev_map when triaging hundreds of items, but nothing here makes Claude Code use Jev on ordinary coding turns, and the server's own instructions tell it not to use Jev for decisions it can make itself. Not a hook, skill or proxy.
pros: Only real Jev-specific MCP found here with a clean, honest design: read-only annotations, typed output, and instructions explicitly warning against oracle-style use.

OpenRouter switch is config only: baseUrl + '/v1/systemone' (typesafe.ts:130) with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and model override via JEV_MODEL, so OpenRouter can be used without patching (schema parity still to be confirmed).

jev_eval gives real calibration metrics (Brier, ECE, AUC, threshold sweep, worst misses), which is the right way to decide whether a Jev question is trustworthy and where to set a threshold before wiring any gate. That directly addresses the 'is Jev just a flash router?' skepticism with the user's own data.
jev_map keeps bulk triage (files, findings, tickets) out of Claude's context via save_path, filter and sort. It fits one-off large triage jobs.
Small, readable codebase (~48 KB), MIT, pinned exact deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec. It was easy to audit statically.
Retry and backoff logic is sane, and there is CI with lint and typecheck. Runs on Node 24 without changes.
cons: Does not deliver the user's stated goal. No hooks, skill or proxy exists, so Claude Code will not use Jev automatically on routine coding; it only appears when Claude decides an MCP tool fits, and the tool descriptions target eval and bulk triage, not everyday decisions like permission classification, commit-type choice or test triage.

OpenRouter support is undocumented and unverified. Env naming (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding an OpenRouter key) is confusing, the default model 'jev-latest' would not resolve on OpenRouter (needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and the Decisions API is not used.

Very young and thin: created 2026-09-17, 7 commits, 4 stars, one release, 12 days old, a single human author, 5 tests that cover only the metrics math and none of the HTTP client or tools. No issue history to judge responsiveness.

Unbounded file access: dataset_path reads and save_path writes any path with no sandbox. Because the MCP call bypasses the existing secret-leak hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), a JSON-parsable secret file could be sent to a third party without a guard firing.
Retry policy up to 4 x 60s can stall an interactive turn on a slow or down provider, and the timeout and attempts are not configurable via env.
Standing context tax of about 2k tokens for three tools, mostly repeated question schemas, for a niche feature; `npx -y` cold start on each session unless pinned.
Privacy: anything Claude passes in state (client code, diffs) leaves the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, at the model's discretion, which is not ideal for client projects.
gh-byk-jev-mcp.verdict: A well-built, safe-to-read eval and bulk-triage MCP for Jev, useful when building or calibrating a Jev classifier and worth keeping as an optional, pinned side tool. It cannot give the automatic, no-prompt integration the user wants, because nothing in it triggers on its own in Claude Code. Use it (via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api) to measure whether Jev is good enough on your own data, then put the measured questions into a hook or proxy.

That would go against the user's 'no prompting' requirement unless wired via hook/CLAUDE.md, which you must add yourself.

Headless `jev-mcp gate` with exit codes 0/1/2/3 can be wrapped in a Claude Code Stop hook to make the check deterministic instead of model-discretion.
Explicit security posture: no shell interpolation, key 0600, key never via MCP tool, localhost-only http, key masking.
cons: Self-attested gate: it judges what Claude WRITES about its own work (extra.summary), not the diff or test output. It does not run tests or read git (git is an empty placeholder), so it adds little independent signal for Opus 5.5; garbage-in gives 'done'.

Not automatic in Claude Code: no hook, skill or plugin manifest, Cursor-only docs; Claude will rarely call decide unprompted. Getting auto-invocation needs your own Stop hook or CLAUDE.md rule, and a Stop hook that emits fix/ask can loop Opus with extra turns.
Adds real per-task cost: Claude must generate the summary/verification JSON and take an extra tool turn; value is marginal for a senior dev on subscription Opus.
extra is sent unredacted to Jev/OpenRouter (state_builder.py:76-77), a leak risk on client projects; redaction regexes are narrow (no JWT, DB URLs, .env style unless KEY=value).

Unpublished and unlicensed in practice: PyPI name mcp-jev-mcp 404s so README install fails; no LICENSE file; 0 stars, 1 contributor, 11 commits in 9 days, v0.2.0 with policy and question set ids already churned to v3.

No OpenRouter awareness: key must be put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, `key add` and health probe use /v1/models (OpenRouter schema differs, probably breaks), default model id 'jev-latest' is wrong for OpenRouter; nothing tested against OpenRouter.
Threshold/policy values (0.6, 0.67...) are hand-picked and uncalibrated; Jev is beta and its quality is disputed.
gh-olivdx-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, small proof-of-concept for a "should I stop?" gate that can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is Cursor-oriented, self-attested (Claude grades its own summary), unpublished on PyPI and offers no automatic Claude Code invocation. Use only as a reference or wrap `jev-mcp gate` in your own Stop hook if you want that specific check; not a daily driver.

Bun is not in the user's stated toolchain (Node 24, Python, uv), so it needs to be installed. private:true, not published to npm; install is git clone plus 'bun install'.

Optionally symlink skills/ask-jev into ~/.claude/skills/. Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the MCP server env (e.g. 'claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... ' or via a wrapper reading it from a file, to avoid putting the key in ~/.claude.json/argv).

security: API key: sent as Bearer header from process.env (client.ts:140, 16), never in argv unless the user passes it via 'claude mcp add -e', which then lives in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The relay key is read from ~/.config/jev/key or JEV_OPENROUTER_KEY (jev.ts:20-28).
fetch uses redirect:'error' (client.ts:19) and a 30 s total timeout, so redirect-based key leaks are blocked.

ask_jev's `command` param executes an arbitrary shell string via child_process.exec (index.ts:64-92) with the user's env (including OPENROUTER_API_KEY and any other secrets) and a 60 s timeout. The only guard is an LLM gate: Jev classifies the command as read_only/reversible/irreversible and blocks only when irreversible confidence >= 0.6 or destructive_intent >= 0.7 (level06/bash-gate.ts:39-68). 'reversible' commands (edits, installs, curl|sh, git commit, writes, network exfiltration) pass. Yet the tool is annotated readOnlyHint:true (index.ts:116-121), so a client or the user's auto/bypass mode may auto-approve it. This effectively adds a permission-bypass side door around the user's Bash hooks (the secret-leak PreToolUse guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__*), so it would also see .env files by path.

File reading has no secret filter: readFileState accepts absolute paths and any relative path including ../ (level08/read-state.ts:29-46); SKIP_DIRS is only node_modules, .git, .sessions, dist, build, coverage, .pi (level09/prune.ts:10-18). No exclusion of .env, .npmrc, keys, or ~/.ssh. Files go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. The user's secret-leak guard would not be triggered because the read happens inside the MCP process.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents are sent to Jev as state; Jev returns only typed values (no free text), so injection can only skew probabilities (e.g., make a malicious file look 'safe' or make the gate say read_only for a destructive command in a command string that Claude itself supplies). Return values are validated strictly (client.ts:158-223), which is good.

Telemetry: none to third parties. Every call writes a JEV_EVENT JSON line to stderr including answers and the source (jev.ts:77-79), which Claude Code may capture into MCP logs; the file content is not logged.
No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh; deps are the official MCP SDK, zod and dev tooling. Not audited beyond package.json and bun.lock existence.
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.dataEgress: Whole file content (up to about (32k-4k)*4 = 112k chars per file per call, ask_jev_files up to 255 files/call, one HTTP request each), file paths, cwd, question text, command strings and captured stdout/stderr (up to 200k chars each) go to the configured endpoint: by default a localhost relay (cc-router, not publicly available), or, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and downstream TypeSafe. Egress happens on every tool call, not just once. No secret filtering. Conversation history and Claude's prompts do not leave, except whatever Claude writes into `state`/questions.
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.failureMode: Per-call fail-open for the agent: on error the tool returns isError text and Claude carries on (index.ts:58-61). Client retries 429/502/503/529 up to 3 attempts with 500 ms exponential backoff, capped 8 s delay, 30 s total deadline (client.ts:31-33, 205-241), so a hung provider can stall a tool call for up to 30 s (5 s for the command gate via withGuardTimeout, jev.ts:84-97; gate then fails CLOSED and refuses the command). Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY without a relay means ECONNREFUSED to 127.0.0.1:8792 on every call (no silent mock, by design). Because it is model-discretion, a broken server just means Claude does the work itself.
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.latencyImpact: Author claims about 300 ms per call; the code adds a local file read plus one HTTPS round trip (client claims 70-500 ms, unverified). ask_jev_files fans out one parallel request per file (up to 255), which could hit OpenRouter rate limits, so retries add seconds. Only paid when Claude chooses a Jev tool; there is no per-turn overhead beyond tool-list loading. Command gate adds one extra Jev call before every ask_jev command.
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.contextCost: 6 MCP tools, roughly 7-8k chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas in src/index.ts, so about 1.8-2.2k tokens (QUESTION_SCHEMA is repeated inside ask_jev_files' description). No MCP server 'instructions' field (McpServer constructed with name/version only, index.ts:114). No hooks, so zero injected text per turn. The optional skill adds one description line (about 150 tokens) always loaded, and the SKILL.md body (about 900 tokens) when triggered. Tool results are small structured JSON (per-file answers), which is the real context-saving point.
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a skill-description trigger. The tool descriptions actively nudge Claude ('Prefer this over reasoning out a classification, risk score, or yes/no with confidence yourself', index.ts:148-149) and the skill description lists triage/classify/score triggers, but there is no deterministic hook, so Claude will only sometimes reach for it. Nothing forces use, and grep/Read/gitnexus will usually win for daily coding tasks.
pros: Only candidate here that actually ships tools tailored to coding-agent use: judging files (bool/choice/score) and picking which file to open, with the content never entering Claude's context, i.e. genuine context savings on directory triage (index.ts:195-236).

Direct OpenRouter path is implemented in code with the alpha Decisions endpoint and ~typesafe/jev-latest alias (client.ts:19-25), so setting only OPENROUTER_API_KEY makes it work with no patching; OpenRouter is the only live provider, matching the user's requirement.

Strict response validation (envelope, usage, probabilities sum to 1, declared choice keys, score legend) fails loudly on contract drift (client.ts:158-223); redirect:'error', timeout, bounded retries.

Automatic-ish invocation: tool descriptions and the ask-jev SKILL.md description carry triggers, so Claude can use it without 'use jev' being typed; low fixed context cost (about 2k tokens, no hooks, no per-turn injection).
Clean, small, readable codebase (about 3.4k lines, mostly vendored), MIT, no install scripts; offline mock for testing with JEV_BACKEND=mock.
Reports cost (usage.cost) in every result and logs JEV_EVENT to stderr, useful for checking spend and whether Jev is actually being called.
cons: Brand new: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, created 2026-09-29 (one day old), no releases, no CI; the whole thing is a personal port of the author's demo repo ten-levels-of-jev, and src/jev/ is vendored 'do not edit'.

Defaults are wrong for this user: with no env it points to the author's private http://127.0.0.1:8792 cc-router relay (jev.ts:18, 40-44; cc-router repo does not resolve on GitHub), README install command hardcodes /Users/probello paths, and it requires Bun.
Does NOT use the /v1/systemone endpoint the README and brief mention; the direct path is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha, may change). Never verified against live OpenRouter in this audit.

Serious security gap: ask_jev `command` runs arbitrary shell via exec gated only by a probabilistic Jev classifier that lets 'reversible' commands (writes, installs, network) through, while the tool is marked readOnlyHint:true, so with the user's bypass/auto permission mode it bypasses the permission prompt and the existing Bash secret-guard hook, and the child inherits OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

No secret filtering on file reads: .env, keys and absolute/parent paths are allowed and their full contents are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every call, which is a real problem on client projects with NDA code. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools.

Not deterministic: relies on Claude's discretion, and Claude's own Grep/Read/gitnexus is usually better for coding; Jev is a probability classifier with no reasoning, so for the daily loop the value is limited to triage-style questions (which of 200 files touches billing, risk score), not edits, tests or debugging.

Unproven quality of Jev on code judgments; an LLM-router-like model (Theo's claim) may give miscalibrated probabilities, and the tools return numbers Claude may over-trust. Fan-out of up to 255 parallel calls per tool call can hit rate limits and burn credits.
Tiny test suite (about 7 cases, mock only), no live test; no automatic update path (git pull, and re-vendoring upstream by hand).
gh-paulrobello-jev-mcp-server.verdict: The most relevant Jev-for-Claude-Code MCP found: it supports OpenRouter directly (via /api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and gives model-discretion triage tools, but it is a day-old single-commit proof of concept with author-specific defaults and a serious side door (LLM-gated shell exec plus unfiltered file reads sent off-machine). Usable only after review: run it with the command param and secret-path reads restricted (or fork to drop `command`, add .env/key excludes and a deny in permissions), and treat it as an optional triage helper, not a deterministic integration.

gh-anasbekheit-typesafe-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions`/`criteria` is sent verbatim as JSON over HTTPS to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe, NOT OpenRouter) with the API key as Bearer. Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself: no file scanning, no hooks, no diffs unless Claude decides to paste code, diffs, file contents or tool output into `state`. Calls only when the model chooses, so zero overhead on turns where it is not invoked; but each invocation is an added tool-use round trip on Opus.

Estimated always-on cost (or deferred via ToolSearch if tool-search is on): tool name+description ~470 chars (~120 tok) + JSON schema for state/questions/model with enum variants and descriptions ~1.8k chars (~450 tok) = ~570 tok; MCP server `instructions` ~2.4k chars (~610 tok) injected into system prompt; skill `jev` frontmatter description ~430 chars (~110 tok) always listed, body ~1.7k chars (~430 tok) loaded only when triggered. providerSupport.evidence: src/index.ts:9-22 requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY (exits 1 if unset) and builds new TypeSafeClient({apiKey}). The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:58,513) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai), sends Bearer auth (line 581), and POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (line 554). No 'openrouter' string in the repo or the SDK. src/index.ts:21 honors TYPESAFE_MODEL for the model. list_models uses GET /v1/models (SDK line 365).
providerSupport.others: None. Only the TypeSafe direct API, plus a custom base URL through the SDK.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and untested. Put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY and set TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, because the OpenRouter model ID format is unlike TypeSafe's `jev-latest`. Returns the raw SDK response as JSON: answers keyed by id, model and usage. Choice returns choice, probabilities and confidence. Noul returns P(yes) with no confidence. Score returns a legend-index score, probabilities and confidence. Source: src/index.ts:57-98, src/schemas.ts.

gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript compiled to dist/ by tsc). Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 (pre-1.0), zod ^4. No npm package published, so you clone and run npm install and npm run build. No postinstall scripts found.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.tests: None. No npm test and no CI. Three scripts under scripts/ are manual live-API checks that spend tokens and read the author's private Obsidian vault at /mnt/d/OBS/brncx-skills. No releases or tags.

The README example puts the key in the --env argument. Passing the key on the command line is visible in argv and shell history; put it in the config env or a wrapper script instead.
security: API key comes only from the env var and is never logged. The README's `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...` puts the key in shell history and argv of the add command, but the running server gets it through env, not argv.
The server does no shell execution, no file access and no telemetry of its own. The SDK sends a User-Agent header of typesafe-sdk/VERSION and redacts authorization and x-api-key headers in its logs.
Prompt-injection surface is low. Tool output is JSON probabilities, and Jev returns no free text. The `state` and `instructions` fields are model-supplied and go straight to the API.

The MCP tool exposes no safety controls: no size cap on `state` (a large state means large token cost), no redaction, and the secret-leak guard hook cannot see MCP payloads because its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit.
Supply chain: brand-new single-author repo with 1 star, no license file, and an unpinned ^ range on a pre-1.0 SDK and the MCP SDK v2. Low bus factor.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in `state` and `instructions`/`options` of an `ask` call goes to api.typesafe.ai (or the overridden base URL, for example OpenRouter), plus the API key. Claude chooses the content, so it can include code, diffs, file contents or tool output, up to 32k context. Nothing else leaves the machine, since the server reads no files itself. For client projects this is a risk, because OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see the content, and the secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. API errors return an isError tool result (src/index.ts:45-55) that Claude can ignore. The SDK retries 408/429/5xx and connection errors twice with 0.5-5s backoff and honors Retry-After up to 60s. The per-attempt timeout is 10s with no total budget (README), so worst case is roughly 30s+ of blocking a tool call. A missing key makes the server exit at startup (shows as a failed MCP connection). Because it is model-discretion, a slow Jev only stalls turns where Claude chose to call it.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.contextCost: 2 tools. Estimated size: `ask` description (about 1.2k chars) plus a zod-derived JSON schema (state, a discriminated union of 3 question types, options and levels, all with descriptions, about 2.5k chars), `list_models` (about 0.3k chars), and server instructions (about 0.55k chars). That is roughly 4.5k chars, or about 1.1k tokens, always loaded (or deferred behind ToolSearch in recent Claude Code). No hooks and no injected text.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code invokes it when the model judges it useful, based on the tool description, which is written for classification and rating of business state (tickets, frustration, routing). Nothing pushes Claude toward coding-loop uses, and no CLAUDE.md snippet, hook or skill trigger is shipped. This is the weakest form of the user's "automatic" requirement; it would need a CLAUDE.md rule or hook added on top.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.latencyImpact: Claimed 70-500 ms per Jev call, unverified. Added only on turns where Claude calls `ask`, plus a normal MCP tool-call round trip. Startup cost is Node boot plus SDK load, and about 1.1k tokens of context per session. Worst case with retries is 30s+.
pros: Thin, readable MCP server (src/index.ts is 122 lines and schemas.ts 126), so it is easy to audit and fork. It uses the official TypeSafe SDK for retries, errors and wire format instead of a hand-rolled client.
The batched `ask` design (one state, many typed questions) matches Jev's per-input-token billing and gives choice, noul and score in one call, with rubric-style option descriptions.
The base URL is overridable through the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api probably reaches OpenRouter's /v1/systemone with no code changes, though this is unverified.
Fail-open behavior: errors come back as isError results, with sane SDK retry defaults and no shell or file access.
Small context footprint (about 1.1k tokens, 2 tools) compared with big MCP servers.
Handles both MCP protocol eras (2026-07-28 and the older initialize handshake) via serveStdio.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain tool the model may or may not call. There are no hooks, no skill and no CLAUDE.md guidance for coding use, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told.
The tool description is framed around support tickets, customer frustration and app state routing, not coding decisions, so Opus is unlikely to reach for it during normal coding.

Not OpenRouter-native. It requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY (the variable name is misleading when it holds an OpenRouter key), a manual base-URL override and TYPESAFE_MODEL. The OpenRouter schema and model ID are untested, and list_models will hit OpenRouter's whole-catalog /v1/models.

No tests, no CI, no releases, no npm package, no LICENSE file (MIT is declared only in package.json), and a single author at 1 star. The repo is 12 days old and the SDK is pre-1.0 with a ^ range, so breakage on upgrade is likely. Users must clone and build it.

Data egress is model-controlled: Claude can put code, diffs or file contents into `state`, with no redaction or size cap. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls, which matters for client projects.
The 10s per-attempt timeout with 2 retries and no total budget can stall a turn for 30s+ when Jev is degraded.
The README's install example passes the key on the command line, and the scripts are hardwired to the author's private vault paths.
gh-cbruyndoncx-askjev-mcp.verdict: A clean but tiny, unproven personal MCP wrapper for the TypeSafe direct API. It is a reasonable template to fork (rewrite it to be OpenRouter-native, add a coding-oriented description and a CLAUDE.md or hook nudge), but as shipped it is not automatic, not coding-focused and not OpenRouter-ready, so it does not satisfy the user's goal.

interface.name: jev_step
interface.purpose: Fused coding-loop router that selects among up to 32 host-prepared calls in one Jev request. Returns handoff of execute_tool, use_tools, gather_context, partner_model, ask_user, stop or review.

interface.name: jev_coding_loop
interface.purpose: Decides retry, stop or context-gathering and whether a partner model is needed (handoff and partner_model fields).

interface.name: jev_tool_route
interface.purpose: Selects among up to 32 host-prepared exact tool calls. It never generates arguments, and empty or ineligible lists return locally with no API call.

interface.name: jev_review
interface.purpose: Scores a diff on correctness, spec match, test gap and blast radius, plus a safe_to_apply noul.

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Marks each claim verified, contradicted or unsupported against supplied evidence.

interface.name: jev_gate
interface.purpose: Combines review and verify in one upstream call, giving an overall auto, review or escalate.

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Prompt-injection and relevance screening of untrusted content before the host reads it.

interface.name: jev_rank
interface.purpose: Ranks host-supplied candidates, up to 5000 in repeated rounds of 250 options.

interface.name: jev_evaluate
interface.purpose: Escape hatch for custom atomic noul, choice and score questions.

interface.name: jev://packs/{coding-loop,tool-route,step,review,verify,screen,rank,gate}
interface.purpose: MCP resources holding the exact question JSON for each recipe.

interface.name: CLI: doctor [--json], eval --stdin|--json|--state/--questions, help
interface.purpose: Diagnostics and one-off evaluation from the command line.

interface.name: skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Description-triggered guidance on when to call each tool. It is Cursor/Codex flavoured, and the user must copy it into the project or ~/.claude/skills.

The repo also contains .github/workflows/notify-jev-mcp.yml, which posts PR events to a Cursor Cloud Agent, and Windows helper scripts. The base URL is strongly hardened: HTTPS only, HTTP allowed only for loopback, custom hosts need an explicit opt-in flag, and userinfo, query strings, obfuscated IPs and private, link-local and metadata addresses are rejected (config.ts). This is unusually careful code.

Prompt-injection surface: it returns typed probabilities only, with no free text from the model. Host-supplied flags (authorized, schema_valid, preconditions_met) gate executable call dispatch, and the SKILL says never to derive them from untrusted content. jev_screen is a probabilistic injection filter, and Jev is a small classifier, so its detection quality is unmeasured.
No shell execution and no telemetry in the server. Calls go only to the configured TypeSafe or custom base URL.
gh-burnigtm-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to pass as tool arguments leaves the machine, sent to api.typesafe.ai (or to openrouter.ai if reconfigured). That means the task text, observations (command output, test results), diffs, claims and evidence, candidate tool-call descriptions and argument shapes, and candidate text (capped at 2000 characters each). State is truncated to about 32k-64k tokens. Raw host arguments stay local unless the call is selected. The server reads no files itself and has no ambient collection. Nothing is sent unless Claude invokes a tool, and no telemetry goes to any third party. Client-project code and diffs will go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter whenever jev_review or jev_gate is called. That matters for client confidentiality and OpenRouter data-policy settings.
gh-burnigtm-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft and advisory. There is no hook, so a Jev failure or timeout cannot block Claude Code. The default deadline is 30 s per tool call (JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS) and it is shared across retries. There is no fabricated verdict, and errors return isError with code CONFIG_ERROR, TIMEOUT or API_ERROR plus a retryable flag. A missing key returns CONFIG_ERROR. In the worst case Claude waits up to 30 s, so lower the timeout to about 3 s. When the SKILL guidance is not followed, nothing happens at all.
gh-burnigtm-jev-mcp.contextCost: Nine tools registered eagerly. Descriptions total about 2.8k chars (roughly 700 tokens). Input schemas are zod with nested candidate/execution objects (step.ts and tool-route.ts are about 11k chars each of source), so I estimate about 4-6k tokens of tool definitions in total. That is heavy for a marginal helper, though Claude Code's deferred tool loading (ToolSearch) reduces the standing cost. The server sets no MCP `instructions`. It has no hooks, so there is no per-turn injection. The optional SKILL.md adds only a short description (about 100 tokens) until it is triggered, and its body is about 1.4k tokens.
gh-burnigtm-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There is no deterministic hook and no proxy. Claude may call jev_review or jev_step if the SKILL/tool descriptions persuade it, but nothing forces it. The main flow (jev_step with candidates) requires Claude to prepare structured call candidates and host-fact flags first, which costs extra Claude turns and tokens and is unlikely to happen naturally in Claude Code. The user's requirement of automatic use is therefore only weakly met.
gh-burnigtm-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Each call costs one HTTPS round-trip: the claimed 70-500 ms for Jev, plus Node stdio overhead of a few ms. Claude's own extra turn to construct the arguments is the real cost, typically several seconds of generation plus the tokens for large diffs and state. jev_step and jev_gate cut two calls to one, but they still add a full extra tool round-trip to a turn. Mock-mode benchmarks exist, but no live latency or quality measurements were published (README admits live quality and cost savings are unmeasured).
pros: Most complete Jev toolkit found: 9 recipes (review, verify, gate, screen, rank, step and tool routing) with pre-built question packs and local policy thresholds (auto, review or escalate). It also refuses to auto-approve when the context is truncated.

Solid engineering for a 2-week-old repo: 19 test files (about 3.3k lines) against 3.5k lines of source, an MCP stdio transport test, an offline packed-install test, a benchmark, and CI on Node 20 and 22 across Windows and Linux. MIT licence.

Security-conscious code: env-only key handling (not in argv), a strict base-URL validator, redirect:error, logging off, and no shell execution, telemetry or postinstall. Fail-explicit errors never invent a verdict.

Config-only OpenRouter path is plausible: the SDK calls {baseURL}/v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MCP_ALLOW_CUSTOM_BASE_URL=1 and JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 would target it.
The docs name Claude Code as a supported stdio host (docs/install.md:54). jev_review and jev_gate are concrete, useful pre-completion checks that a senior dev could plausibly want.
Read-only, idempotent tools with readOnlyHint annotations, so they can be auto-allowed in the user's permission mode without prompt friction.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code. The variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the user would have to put an OpenRouter key there plus enable the custom-URL flag. Schema parity with OpenRouter is unverified, and the `doctor` models.list call may break.

Not on npm. The npm package jev-mcp is a different project (rashedInt32), so `npx jev-mcp` would run the wrong code. The user must clone, npm ci, build and pin an absolute path. There are no releases or tags and the version is 0.1.0.

Automatic invocation is weak. It is model-discretion tools only, with no hooks. jev_step needs Claude to prepare candidate calls and set host-fact flags (authorized, schema_valid, preconditions_met), which is awkward in Claude Code's native tool loop. The skill is Cursor/Codex-oriented and must be copied by hand.

Bloated for a helper: 9 tools with heavy nested schemas (about 4-6k tokens) and overlapping tools (jev_step vs jev_coding_loop vs jev_tool_route, and review vs verify vs gate). Much of its 'reduce partner-model turns' premise does not apply, because Claude Code with Opus 5.5 has no cheaper partner model to route to.

Client-project diffs and observations get sent to a beta third-party model on every review or gate. The README admits live quality and cost savings are unmeasured. Jev has no reasoning and outputs probabilities only, so its review verdict is a weak signal next to Opus's own reasoning.

gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.name: wangkuangkuang/jev-mcp-server
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.whatItDoes: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, mcp>=1.9, httpx[http2]) wrapping TypeSafe System One. Exposes 7 tools: choice, score, noul (1:1 with the official question types) plus compare (A/B choice), verify (claim vs evidence noul), classify (batch choice, sequential per item, up to 100), and setup (verify and store a key at ~/.config/jev-mcp/key). Also ships an `install <client>` subcommand for claude-code, cursor, codex, opencode and pi. It POSTs {model, state:{}, questions} to a configurable base URL with a Bearer key, validates the response (probabilities sum to about 1, choice in ids, and so on), and returns compact JSON with latency and usage. It has no hooks, skills or proxy. Claude has to decide on its own to call the tools.

security: The key is read from the env var or from ~/.config/jev-mcp/key (dir 0700, file 0600, atomic write; config.py:106-113). The installer's `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key>` puts the key in argv, so it is briefly visible in the process list (installer.py:108-121). It then persists in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, and codex and cursor configs get the same treatment.

The `setup` tool takes the API key as a tool argument. That routes the secret through the model context and the transcript, and a prompt injection could invoke it. Setting the env var means it never needs calling.

There is no shell execution at runtime. subprocess is used only in the installer, for `claude mcp add`. There is no postinstall hook and no curl|sh in the code; the README only suggests the astral.sh uv installer as an option.

There is no telemetry. The only network destination is config.base_url(), and the User-Agent header names the repo. Overriding JEVMCP_BASE_URL sends the Bearer key to whatever host is set, so it must be set correctly.

Supply chain: this is a solo-maintainer 8-day-old package, and `uvx jev-mcp-server` without a pin pulls the latest release on each run. The publish workflow uses a PYPI_API_TOKEN secret and a mutable @release/v1 action ref. Errors return only the first 200 chars of the response body, and there is no logging of the key.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Tool outputs are numeric JSON plus echoed input; classify echoes the items it was given. Jev returns no free text. The risk sits in what the model chooses to send out as context.
The cache is off by default. If JEVMCP_CACHE=1, question payloads (which can contain code) are written as sha256-named JSON files in ~/.cache/jev-mcp, unencrypted.
Version 0.2.3 fixed a real bug where the installer replaced a whole client config because of a UTF-8 BOM. The code is now safer, but the history shows immaturity.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts into tool arguments leaves the machine: question, options, levels, context, a and b, claim and evidence, or classify items. The `verify` tool is designed to carry log excerpts and diffs as `evidence`, and `context` is free text. Everything goes to the endpoint in JEVMCP_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter after an override) together with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically from the repo or from tool outputs; the model decides. Under OpenRouter, the OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies apply. That matters for client-project code, and the payload can contain snippets of it.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.failureMode: Failures are per call and non-blocking, so Claude Code keeps working. The client uses a 25 s httpx timeout, up to 3 attempts on 429, 503 and 529 with 0.5 s then 1 s backoff, and then raises RuntimeError ('TypeSafe unavailable after retries; no decision made', client.py:34-45). Connection errors raise immediately with no retry. Other HTTP errors raise with the first 200 chars of the body. FastMCP turns the exception into an isError tool result, so the model sees the failure and can proceed without Jev. There is no circuit breaker: with a dead endpoint the worst case is roughly 3 x 25 s plus backoff on each call. Malformed responses raise ValueError ('no decision returned'). classify is sequential, so one failure aborts the whole batch.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call a tool. Each call adds about 0.4-0.7 s network plus the MCP round trip, per the README's own measurements; I did not measure it. The first call also pays uvx startup and the httpx HTTP/2 client init. classify costs about 0.6 s times N items, sequentially.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.contextCost: 7 tools (mcp__jev__choice, score, noul, compare, verify, classify, setup). The docstrings from server.py come to roughly 6.5k chars, and the JSON schemas add about 1.5-2k chars, so roughly 2-2.5k tokens of tool definitions. The server sets no MCP `instructions`, and there are no hooks, so nothing else is injected. Dropping `setup` (or denying it via permissions) trims it a little. If Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch, only the tool names sit in context until they are needed.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The sole trigger is the tool descriptions, which say things like 'triage, routing, classification' and 'is this change breaking?'. There is no hook, skill, CLAUDE.md snippet or proxy, so nothing guarantees Opus will call them unprompted. Opus will mostly answer such questions itself unless CLAUDE.md, a skill, or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook nudges it. A README-style prompt ('Which of these is safest? Show me the probability split') is what triggers it in practice.
pros: Uses the official question types 1:1 (choice, score, noul). It validates responses strictly (server.py:48-97), so garbage or out-of-range output becomes an error and never silently misleads Claude.

OpenRouter is a config-only switch. JEVMCP_BASE_URL and JEVMCP_MODEL are both overridable, the auth is a plain Bearer header, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone forwards the TypeSafe body unchanged, so no fork is needed.

Small and auditable. About 17 KB of server code and no shell exec at runtime, no telemetry, and no hooks or proxy that could break the existing PreToolUse chain. It is MIT and has an offline test suite plus a cross-OS CI.

Compact JSON output and a small tool surface (7 tools, about 2k tokens). Probabilities are sorted, so near-ties are visible. compare and verify are well-shaped for code-review-style checks, such as claim vs log or A/B of two error messages.
Fails gracefully: tool errors are visible to Claude and never block the session. The cache is off by default, and the response includes latency and usage.
cons: Not automatic. It is a pure MCP toolset with no hook or skill, so it fails the user's core requirement. Claude would call it only rarely unless a CLAUDE.md rule or hook is added on top.

Has no OpenRouter support in code or docs. The key env var is hard-named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which is confusing when it holds an OpenRouter key. The default model id 'jev-latest' is wrong for OpenRouter, which needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. This is untested against OpenRouter.

A weak value proposition for a subscription-based Opus 5.5 workflow. Jev is a classifier, not a reasoner, and most coding decisions (what to edit, why a test fails) are not enumerated-option problems. In that workflow it saves few tokens and adds a network hop, an API key and a data-egress path to a third party.

Very immature: created 2026-09-22, 8 commits, 3 stars, 5 releases in 1 day. The 0.2.3 fix corrected an installer bug that crashed on every non-`--key` path, and the earlier BOM handling could wipe a user's whole client config. That does not inspire trust in the installer, so do not use it and register the MCP by hand.

The `setup` tool lets the model take an API key as an argument (a secret in the transcript, and an injection target). The installer puts the key in argv. Unpinned `uvx` means unreviewed updates run automatically on the user's client projects.

Data egress on client projects: `context`, `evidence` and `items` are free text that Claude may fill with code, diffs or logs. No redaction is applied, and the user's secret-leak guard hook covers only Bash, Read, Grep and NotebookEdit, not MCP tool args.

classify is sequential (about 1 min per 100 items) and has no concurrency. There is no circuit breaker, so a dead endpoint blocks each call for up to about 75 s. The client also cannot use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) or the Jev Router, only /systemone.
gh-wangkuangkuang-jev-mcp-server.verdict: A clean, small, well-validated Jev MCP that would work with OpenRouter by env vars alone (JEVMCP_BASE_URL, JEVMCP_MODEL, and the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY). But it is purely model-discretion, with nothing that makes Claude Code call it automatically, and it is very new. Useful only as a thin transport layer if paired with a CLAUDE.md rule or hook, and pinned by version.

Input hardening: __proto__ key stripping, 256 KiB payload cap, question-spec validation before any request (server.mjs:126-160); no shell execution, no filesystem access, no telemetry beyond SDK headers X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime

Prompt-injection surface is low: the tool only returns probabilities/option names, no free text; but the model (Claude) chooses what state to send, so injected content in state could steer questions, and answers could steer Claude's decisions

gh-clouatre-labs-decisions-judge-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the `state` and `questions` arguments of a judge call (up to 256 KiB per call) goes to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai/api if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is set), plus the bearer key and SDK User-Agent/runtime headers. The server itself reads no files, diffs or tool outputs; egress is model-chosen, so summarized repo state, file paths, diffs or code snippets could leave if Claude includes them. The flagship skill's own docs flag this as third-party transit (agentic-coder-skill SKILL.md item 9). Matters for client projects; no allow/deny filter exists and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools unless matcher is extended.
gh-clouatre-labs-decisions-judge-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every error (network, 4xx/5xx, bad key, missing key, oversize payload, malformed question) returns a normal tool result {fallback:true,error} with exit 0 (server.mjs:143-176; typesafe-api.mjs:116-143). Missing key only prints a stderr warning at startup, server still handshakes. Timeout: caller-supplied timeout_ms up to 60000, otherwise the SDK default timeout (not read from source here), SDK retries 408/5xx up to 2 times with backoff (retry list typesafe-api.mjs:45, DEFAULT maxRetries 2, backoffInitialMs 500); 429/529 rotate across configured keys with no delay. Worst case a slow Jev stalls one tool call, never the session. Because the tool is model-invoked, a fallback envelope simply makes Claude proceed without it.
gh-clouatre-labs-decisions-judge-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call it. Each call adds one MCP round trip plus Jev's claimed 70-500 ms end to end (unverified), i.e. sub-second, but also an extra model step (Claude must decide to call, compose state/questions, then read the answer), so realistically 2-5 s of model time per use. First launch via npx adds npm resolution/download time (seconds) unless installed globally or cached.

gh-pzacca-askjev.name: askjev (pZacca/askjev)
gh-pzacca-askjev.whatItDoes: Unofficial stdio (npx askjev) or hosted-HTTP (jev.zacca.dev/mcp on Cloudflare Workers) MCP server exposing one tool, `ask`. The agent passes `state` (string/object/array) plus free-text `questions` (optional `options`). The server uses @typesafe-ai/sdk to make 2 Jev systemOne calls (3 if a scale question has no options): a routing call that classifies each question as noul, score or choice, an optional call that picks one of 7 built-in rubrics, then an answer call. It returns raw probabilities, confidence and routing metadata. It has no thresholds or verdicts, and per-question errors are returned as `kind: error` entries.

providerSupport.evidence: askjev src has no hardcoded URL. src/jev.ts:16-21 wraps `new TypeSafeClient(config)` with no baseURL. src/cli.ts:124 calls createJev() with no config, so the SDK reads env vars. SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:56-62 maps apiKey to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, baseURL to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and defaultModel to TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. index.mjs:513-514 sets baseURL default `https://api.typesafe.ai` and default model `jev-latest`. index.mjs:554 POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with body {state, questions, model} and header `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (index.mjs:581). askjev README documents TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. OpenRouter's own guide (https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md) says to point the TypeSafe SDK at https://openrouter.ai/api (SDK appends /v1/systemone) with an OpenRouter key as bearer, via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The System One API doc says bare ids like jev-1.13 and jev-latest map to typesafe/. Not tested live, since running candidate code was forbidden.
providerSupport.others: Hosted mode (src/http.ts) takes the key in the x-api-key or Bearer header and forwards to options.baseURL (Worker var TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). It does not use /api/alpha/decisions (Decisions API) anywhere.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no patch is needed. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and optionally TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest (or typesafe/jev-1.13). The env var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY is misleading when it holds an OpenRouter key.

interface.name: ask (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Input {state, questions[{question, options?}]}. Output {answers[]} with kind noul|score|choice|error, answer, probabilities, confidence, legend/rubric/note, routing. Optional model/usage fields come from ASKJEV_INCLUDE. Annotated readOnlyHint and openWorldHint (src/server.ts:75-95). Input schema is in src/schema.ts.

interface.name: askjev CLI (bin dist/cli.js)
interface.purpose: Starts the stdio MCP server. Configured only by env vars TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL and ASKJEV_INCLUDE (src/cli.ts).

interface.name: POST /mcp (hosted worker)
interface.purpose: Stateless Streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint at jev.zacca.dev. Key is per request (src/http.ts, src/worker.ts).

security: No postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json). Runtime deps are only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk and zod. There is no child_process or shell use in src (grep clean).

Release workflow publishes to npm with `--provenance` (release.yml). MIT license. Single maintainer, so npx -y pulls whatever he publishes next, and the account or package is a supply-chain point. Pin the version, e.g. askjev@0.2.0.

Key handling: stdio mode reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the env, so it is not in argv. `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, but the process list only shows `npx -y askjev`. Hosted mode puts the key in a header, and the operator of jev.zacca.dev could see the key and state if malicious. Never use hosted mode with client code.
SDK debug logging redacts headers (redactHeaders, index.mjs), but debug logs print the request body (the state) to stderr. Leave TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL unset.

No telemetry in askjev source. Tool output is JSON of numbers and short strings, with label echoes only from the caller's own options. Prompt-injection surface is small, but the `state` text sent to Jev could contain injected content that skews probabilities. The `note` field is server-authored.
Not audited by a third party. The hosted worker is a personal Cloudflare deployment, and CI auto-deploys every push to main, which makes it a moving target.
gh-pzacca-askjev.dataEgress: In stdio mode, whatever `state` Claude chooses to pass (code snippets, diffs, error text, ticket text, anything) goes to OpenRouter, then to TypeSafe/Jev. Also sent are the question texts and options, and a routing call whose state is the question text. Nothing leaves automatically beyond what the model puts in `state`. There is no file scanning or hook capture. The existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it will NOT inspect mcp__askjev__ask inputs. Hosted mode would additionally send everything to jev.zacca.dev (a third party) and should be avoided for client work.
gh-pzacca-askjev.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level. The SDK default is timeout 10s and maxRetries 2, with retry on 429/5xx/connection errors and backoff (index.mjs:74, 518). Worst case is roughly 10s x 3 per Jev call, and ask() makes up to 3 sequential calls, so a hung upstream could block one turn for tens of seconds (~90s worst case). Nothing lowers the timeout except SDK config, and askjev exposes no timeout env var, so it is not tunable without patching. On failure it returns an MCP result with isError:true and a readable message (src/server.ts:100-112). Claude sees the error and continues. Auth failure gives 'Jev rejected the API key'. There is no fail-closed behaviour, and no session-blocking hook is involved.
gh-pzacca-askjev.contextCost: One MCP server with one tool (`mcp__askjev__ask`). The tool description is about 1.1k chars (server.ts:34-42 plus the describeOutput and key-hint lines), and the input and output schemas add roughly 2.5k chars of zod descriptions. Total is about 900-1,000 tokens of tool definition, or fewer when tools are deferred via ToolSearch. No MCP server-level `instructions` field is set. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. This is very light next to playwright or gitnexus.
gh-pzacca-askjev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The description says 'Use it for a quick second opinion, a classification, a rating, or a yes/no check instead of reasoning it out yourself or spawning a sub-agent', which is a soft nudge. Opus 5.5 will rarely call a probabilistic classifier for coding work unprompted. There is no hook or skill trigger, and no transparent proxy. To meet the 'never say use jev' requirement, it needs a one-paragraph rule in the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, or a separate deterministic hook or skill layered on top.
gh-pzacca-askjev.latencyImpact: Each `ask` makes 2 sequential Jev round trips (3 when a scale question has no options). At the claimed 70-500 ms per call that is about 0.15-1.5 s per ask plus MCP and npx spawn overhead, added to the normal model turn for the tool call. It adds nothing on turns where Claude does not call it.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with no code change, because it uses the official TypeSafe SDK (whose baseURL and key come from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and OpenRouter documents that exact path (/api/v1/systemone). Config is env only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest.
Tiny and auditable: 734 lines of TS across 10 src files, no shell execution, no postinstall, and only 3 runtime deps. Verified in the tree, not just the README.
Very small context footprint: one tool, about 1k tokens, no hooks and no per-turn injection.

Clean output design: raw probabilities and confidence, with no invented thresholds. Per-question errors do not fail the batch. Routing metadata makes misclassification visible. The tool description tells the agent to read the confidence and fall back to its own reasoning when it is low.

Good engineering hygiene for a young project: 35 unit tests across 5 test files, CI on lint, typecheck, tests and a 3-OS smoke run, a weekly live router eval with a human-labelled dataset (claims 42/42 routing, 16/16 rubric), npm provenance, and clear architecture and eval docs.
Fail-soft: errors surface as isError tool results and Claude continues. Batching several questions into one ask costs the same number of Jev calls.
stdio mode keeps the key in an env var, not argv, and keeps the request off any third-party host.
cons: Only model-discretion invocation: no hook, no skill, no proxy. It will not be used 'automatically when it adds value' without a CLAUDE.md rule. Even then, invocation is probabilistic and each call adds a model turn.

Wrong shape for coding. It is a generic free-text question router meant for support-ticket-style triage. It has no coding-specific rubrics, and the built-in rubrics (sentiment, frequency, agreement...) are not code-review concepts. Its own routing layer costs an extra Jev round trip on every ask, which is 2-3 sequential calls where a direct SDK call needs 1.

Ecosystem maturity is poor: 2 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor (Pedro Zaccaria), 40 commits, created 2026-09-17, only 2 npm versions (v0.1.0 and v0.2.0, the latest published 2026-09-18), and no push since. It is unofficial and not affiliated with TypeSafe. Single-maintainer supply chain, so pin the version.

Not tunable for reliability: SDK timeout 10s with 2 retries is not exposed as an env var, so a slow OpenRouter could stall a turn for up to ~90s across the 3 sequential calls. Fixing it means forking or patching.

The secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__askjev__ask (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so source or secrets Claude puts in `state` go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe unfiltered. That matters for client projects. A matcher extension would be needed.

The env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY but must hold an OpenRouter key, which is confusing. Hosted mode (jev.zacca.dev) would send code and the key to a personal third-party Worker, so it should not be used.

Uses the System One (/v1/systemone) surface, not the Decisions API. If OpenRouter's Decisions alpha is the endorsed path, that limits future alignment. Jev's quality is itself unverified, since skeptics call it a router-like model. A 5-level 'severity' score from a 32k-context model is weak evidence for code decisions.
gh-pzacca-askjev.verdict: This is the cleanest and lowest-risk way to get Jev into Claude Code as an MCP tool, and it works on OpenRouter with env vars only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest. On its own it fails the 'fully automatic' requirement, because Claude has to choose to call it. It also spends 2-3 round trips per question on generic routing that a coding-specific hook or skill could skip. Use it only as an opt-in second-opinion tool with a CLAUDE.md nudge (pin askjev@0.2.0, run stdio only), not as the core integration.
gh-pzacca-askjev.runtime: Node >=22 (TypeScript, ESM), stdio via npx -y askjev, or Cloudflare Workers for the hosted variant
gh-pzacca-askjev.install: claude mcp add askjev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest -- npx -y askjev@0.2.0

gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.name: jbt95/jev-toolkit
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.whatItDoes: Small stdio MCP server (Bun + Effect + @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing three Jev tools: typesafe_ask (raw choice/noul/score questions over arbitrary state), typesafe_rank (orders 1-20 supplied text candidates via one Noul question per candidate), typesafe_verify (labels claims supported/contradicted/unrelated/insufficient vs supplied evidence, using an evidence-matrix question pack plus a numbers-missing-from-evidence check). Writes a local JSONL event log (~/.local/share/jev/events.jsonl). Includes 'jev install claude-code|opencode|pi|omp' which registers the server (claude mcp add --scope user jev-toolkit -e JEV_HARNESS=claude-code -- bun .../jev.ts mcp). Server 'instructions' tell the model to call the matching tool before answering.

interface.name: typesafe_ask
interface.purpose: Typed judgment: args state (string/object/array), questions map of choice|noul|score, optional model, sessionID. Returns formatted per-question probabilities/confidence + usage; confidence <0.4 flagged no-signal. readOnlyHint true.

interface.name: typesafe_rank
interface.purpose: Rank 1-20 candidate texts against a query (one Noul per candidate); rejects code-like/diff/transcript text by regex, redacts credentials, 40k char cap; returns JSON ranking of relevance probabilities.

interface.name: typesafe_verify
interface.purpose: Check 1-20 claims against evidence text (40k chars, credentials redacted); returns supported/contradicted/unrelated/insufficient per claim with confidence and numbers-not-in-evidence flags.

interface.name: jev mcp (CLI)
interface.purpose: Run the stdio JSON-RPC MCP server (initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call; no resources/prompts).

interface.name: jev install claude-code|opencode|pi|omp (CLI)
interface.purpose: Register the server user-scope in the harness; for claude-code it shells out to 'claude mcp add/remove --scope user jev-toolkit'; never stores the API key.

interface.name: MCP initialize instructions
interface.purpose: ~1.4k-char routing policy: 'when a task matches a case below, call that tool before answering'; injected into Claude's context.
