security: API key read from env at call time (src/cli/jev.ts:91), never in argv; installer passes only JEV_HARNESS via -e, so key is inherited from Claude Code's environment and not written to ~/.claude.json unless the user adds it.

No postinstall scripts; no curl|sh; scripts/install.sh only mkdirs and symlinks into ~/.local/bin. Pi target runs 'pi install npm:pi-mcp-adapter' (irrelevant for Claude Code). Only child processes are 'claude mcp add/remove' and pi (install.ts:41-110).
No telemetry code; the retired Prometheus/telemetry surfaces were removed in the last commit. Only outbound calls are to the configured JEV_ENDPOINT via the SDK.

Credential redaction is a heuristic regex (src/core/text.ts:8-15) applied to rank and verify only; typesafe_ask state is sent as supplied with no redaction (docs/mcp.md: 'callers must redact'). Existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard hooks do not cover mcp__ tools (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).

Code/diff/transcript regex reject for rank (server.ts:96-106) is bypassable prose-only heuristic (README admits it); typesafe_verify has NO such reject, so Claude can pass test output, diffs or source as 'evidence' to a third party.

Prompt-injection surface: claim/evidence/candidate text is passed inside Jev questions; rank tells Jev to treat text as data. Jev outputs are only numbers/labels (no free text) so injected output risk is low; the larger risk is the server 'instructions' text pushing the model to call tools.

Tool annotations declare readOnlyHint:true (server.ts:558), so in auto/bypass mode calls are not prompted; also writes local event log (~/.local/share/jev/events.jsonl) with session id, question ids, answers, latency (no raw text for rank/verify).

Single unknown maintainer, 2 stars, unreleased; executes from a live git checkout on every Claude Code start, so a malicious or careless future commit pulled by git pull would run with the user's env (including OPENROUTER key).
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (default) or JEV_ENDPOINT: the Bearer API key; for rank: query + up to 20 candidate texts (credential-redacted, regex-filtered against code/diff/transcripts, max 40k chars); for verify: claims + evidence (credential-redacted, up to 40k chars, no code filter); for ask: arbitrary state JSON and questions exactly as Claude supplies them (no redaction). Model name and question definitions also sent. No file reads, no automatic capture of prompts, diffs or tool outputs: only what Claude explicitly puts in tool arguments. Local only: event log with metadata. With OpenRouter as endpoint, OpenRouter also sees this traffic (subject to its data policy settings).
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: every failure (missing key, API error, timeout, decode mismatch) is returned as MCP text with isError:true, logged locally, and Claude continues (server instructions say to report the limitation). SDK path timeout is 10 s per attempt with maxRetries 2 (SDK index.mjs:74,518), so a hung upstream can block a single tool call roughly 30 s+ backoff; the 120 s TIMEOUT in client.ts:21 is only for the legacy fetch transport. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY does not stop server startup; tools then error per call. Server startup failure (e.g. bun missing) only drops the MCP server. Never blocks tool execution as it is not a hook.
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.contextCost: 3 tools. Approx chars: ask schema+desc ~1.9k, rank ~2.5k, verify ~1.7k, server instructions ~1.4k, plus annotations/titles ~0.4k = ~7.9k chars = ~2.0k tokens per session (with Claude Code tool search deferral, tool schemas load lazily but the instructions text stays). No hook-injected text.
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Server instructions ('call that tool before answering') and tool descriptions ('Use whenever you need to order or prioritize...', 'especially before presenting evidence-based conclusions') nudge Claude to call it without user prompting, but there is no hook, skill trigger or proxy; behavior depends on Opus deciding a task matches. Not deterministic; not integrated into file editing, code review or routing flows.
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.latencyImpact: Zero on non-Jev turns (no hooks). Per Jev call: Bun cold start once per session (~100 ms), then one HTTPS round trip; claimed 70-500 ms plus MCP round trip and the model's own extra tool-use turn (~1-3 s wall clock of Opus overhead). Worst case ~30 s if upstream hangs (10 s x 3 attempts).
pros: Genuinely Claude Code-aware: 'jev install claude-code' registers a user-scope MCP server automatically, adding no key to argv or config.

Model-discretion auto-use is the closest available to the user's wish: server 'instructions' (directives.ts:2-9) and tool descriptions tell Claude when to call ask/rank/verify without the user saying 'use jev'.

Sensible primitive mapping: rank = per-candidate Noul, verify = 4-way claim labelling with a deterministic numbers-not-in-evidence check (server.ts:456, evidence-matrix.ts), ask = raw Choice/Noul/Score passthrough; all return numbers/labels only.

Endpoint is env-overridable (JEV_ENDPOINT, paths.ts:28) and the SDK uses Bearer auth on /v1/systemone, so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the OpenRouter key should need only env vars plus a one-line default-model patch.

Privacy-conscious design: credential redaction on rank/verify, code/diff/transcript rejection for rank, no raw claim/evidence/candidate text in the local event log, key read at call time, no telemetry, no postinstall, small auditable codebase (~2.7k src lines), MIT.
Fail-open with typed errors and bounded SDK timeout; no hook so it can never wedge Claude Code; only ~2k tokens of context; plays well with existing hooks (no hook overlap).
Good test discipline (offline fakes, e2e CLI, MCP protocol tests) and strict pinned deps.
cons: No OpenRouter support as shipped: hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY and default model 'jev-latest'; OpenRouter use is an undocumented env hack plus a source patch, and schema compatibility of OpenRouter's /v1/systemone with TypeSafe's is unverified by the repo.
Uses only System One /v1/systemone; ignores OpenRouter's Decisions API.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21, one author, 2 stars, no release, no CI, no npm publish, last commit is a large rewrite (Node to Bun, TS 7, retired most features) so churn/breakage risk is high; depends on effect 4.0.0-rc.112.
Requires Bun (not part of the user's Node/Python/uv stack) and a live git checkout executed on every session; updating means git pull + bun install with no signed releases.

Scope is narrow and not core to coding: relevance ranking of prose, claim-vs-evidence labelling, and ad hoc typed questions. It does not do code review, commit/permission gating, model routing, or edit decisions; rank explicitly rejects code-like text, which is most of a coding session.
Automatic use is only probabilistic: Opus 5.5 may rarely call it, or over-call verify on every conclusion (each an extra turn, network hop, and paid call); no hook-level determinism.

Privacy gaps for client projects: ask state is unredacted, verify has no code filter, and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools; readOnlyHint:true means in bypass/auto mode nothing prompts before data leaves the machine.
Worst-case latency 10 s x 3 attempts on a stalled endpoint; no user-configurable timeout via env.
Skeptic caveat from the brief (Jev may behave like a small router model) means verify/rank verdicts are not obviously better than Opus judging the same text itself, while adding cost and latency.
gh-jbt95-jev-toolkit.verdict: The most Claude Code-native and cleanest Jev MCP wrapper so far (auto-registers, model-discretion tool routing, small, MIT, privacy-aware), and OpenRouter is reachable via JEV_ENDPOINT plus a key alias and a default-model patch, but it is a week-old single-author Bun project whose three tools (prose rank, claim verify, ad hoc ask) add little to daily coding and whose auto-use is only best-effort. Worth forking/pinning as the MCP layer if you want Jev in Claude Code at all, but do not expect deterministic or high-value automatic behavior from it alone.

gh-simota-tenbin.name: simota/tenbin
gh-simota-tenbin.whatItDoes: A design-time toolkit for TypeSafe System One (Jev), not a runtime helper. It has three parts: a stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript, wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk) with tools to lint, evaluate, batch-evaluate, rerank and walk taxonomies; an Agent Skill (/tenbin, SKILL.md) with a procedure, templates and offline Python scripts; and docs. The intended workflow is that a human asks Claude to design a Jev integration (decompose a judgment into Choice/Score/Noul questions, lint them, measure accuracy per confidence band on labelled data, put thresholds in code), and the resulting application code calls the TypeSafe SDK directly. It does not route Claude Code's own coding decisions through Jev, and it has no hooks.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code or docs anywhere (grep -ri openrouter over the repo returns nothing). tenbin/src/config.ts:34 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. tenbin/src/client.ts:52-60 builds TypeSafeClient({apiKey, defaultModel, logger, logLevel}) with no baseURL, so the SDK default applies. In the @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 tarball (dist/index.mjs:58-59 and :514) baseURL comes from config or the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env var and defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai. The SDK then POSTs baseURL + '/v1/systemone' (index.mjs:554) and GETs '/v1/models' (index.mjs:365). skills/tenbin/scripts/evaluate.py:42,98,311 does the same with DEFAULT_BASE_URL and --base-url or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, and posts {state, model, questions} with Bearer auth. The README documents api.typesafe.ai only (README.md:106).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Probably trivial for evaluate and lint, but not verified. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would send POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is the documented OpenRouter System One path, so no code change is needed. Caveats: (1) the model id must become typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest through TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, because the default 'jev-latest' is the TypeSafe alias. (2) tenbin_list_models calls GET /v1/models, and OpenRouter's model list has a different shape, so the SDK's unwrapModels would throw. (3) The response schema on OpenRouter (usage, x-typesafe-request-id header) is unverified. (4) The hardcoded $0.042/Mtok cost math is only approximate. A cleaner patch would add an OPENROUTER_API_KEY mapping and skip list_models. I did not run anything to confirm.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct is the only documented provider.

interface.name: tenbin_lint_questions (MCP tool, offline)
interface.purpose: Static lint of a Choice/Score/Noul questions map: option and level counts, degree-only levels, compound or counting/date questions, missing state paths, unused state fields, token budget. server.ts:16-22

interface.name: tenbin_evaluate (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Lints, then POST /v1/systemone for one state and many questions. Returns answers, usage, cost_usd, request_id, latency_ms.

interface.name: tenbin_evaluate_many (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Runs evaluate over a list of states concurrently, with optional repeat for self-consistency. Returns per-question stats, for threshold calibration.

interface.name: tenbin_rank (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Reranks candidates against a query by fanning out Noul questions, or by a Choice tournament. Includes an optional existence check.

interface.name: tenbin_walk_taxonomy (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Beam-search classification down a nested taxonomy with a Choice at each level.

interface.name: tenbin_list_models (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models plus a pricing table.

interface.name: tenbin_session_stats (MCP tool, local)
interface.purpose: Calls, tokens, USD cost and remaining session budget for this MCP process.

interface.name: MCP prompts: tenbin, design_integration, design_questions, decompose_judgment (+1)
interface.purpose: User-invoked slash-style prompts. They inject guide text (suggestions, question-design, integration-design) telling the host agent to propose Jev uses or generate integration code. They work offline. prompts.ts:40-147

interface.name: MCP resources tenbin://guide/*
interface.purpose: Static markdown guides (primitives, patterns, confidence, question design and others) plus examples.

interface.name: Skill 'tenbin' (skills/tenbin/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Triggered by the description keywords (classify, route, triage, spam or injection detection, severity, rank, thresholds, guardrails, Jev, Choice/Score/Noul), or by /tenbin. It walks a 9-step design, measure and threshold procedure.

interface.name: skills/tenbin/scripts/{lint_questions.py, evaluate.py, estimate_cost.py}
interface.purpose: Offline lint, direct HTTP evaluate with stdlib urllib and a budget cap, and a cost estimator. Python only, no SDK.

interface.name: Makefile targets: install-claude, register-claude, link-claude, env-file, build-mcp
interface.purpose: Local installer: npm ci and build, claude mcp add with an env-file wrapper, and a skill symlink into ~/.claude/skills.

gh-simota-tenbin.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript 7, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod 4) for the MCP; Python 3 stdlib for the skill scripts. Not published to npm: it is installed by git clone plus make (npm ci and tsc build).
gh-simota-tenbin.install: git clone https://github.com/simota/tenbin && cd tenbin && make install-claude (env-file, build-mcp, register-claude, link-claude). I did not run it. Apart from the npm ci build and the claude mcp add wrapper, it needs no curl|sh. There is no npm package, so pin a commit SHA.
gh-simota-tenbin.tests: There are 68 test cases in tenbin/src/*.test.ts (node:test, fake fetch, no network; server.test.ts has 45) and 2 Python test files under skills/tenbin/scripts. No CI: there is no .github directory. The Makefile test target covers only the Python tests. I did not run any tests.
security: API key handling: it is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var. The Makefile registers the server as `claude mcp add tenbin -- sh -c 'set -a; . $HOME/.config/tenbin/env; set +a; exec node .../dist/index.js'`. The key stays out of ~/.claude.json and out of argv, and lives in a chmod 600 env file (Makefile:14, 66-69). This is better than most MCPs, though the wrapper sources the file as shell, so the file is executable code owned by the user.
Alternative documented registration `claude mcp add tenbin -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$TYPESAFE_API_KEY` writes the key into ~/.claude.json (README:~140).
Logging: client.ts:33-38 forces the SDK logger to warn and error only, on stderr, because debug logs would print request bodies unredacted. The README warns never to set TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug.

No shell execution in the server. grep finds no exec, spawn or child_process in tenbin/src, and there is no telemetry code and no postinstall script. The only outbound network calls go through the SDK to api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: the MCP prompts and the skill tell the agent to inspect project files and then generate code (prompts.ts, SKILL.md). Repository contents are handled as data, with an explicit note not to follow them, but the skill still steers the agent to write code with wide edit scope. Jev is also documented as weak against adversarial input.

Supply chain: a single maintainer, 7 commits, a brand-new repo with no releases, and no lockfile audit or CI. @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (created 2026-09-12, MIT) is the only third-party API dependency besides the MCP SDK and zod. A budget guard exists (default 20M tokens, about $0.84 per process, plus a per-call cap of 60k).
gh-simota-tenbin.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine unless Claude calls tenbin_evaluate, tenbin_evaluate_many, tenbin_rank, tenbin_walk_taxonomy or tenbin_list_models, or runs evaluate.py. What is sent is exactly the state and questions JSON that the agent composed for that call: it can be file contents, tickets, code snippets or candidate lists. It goes to api.typesafe.ai, or to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says, with the Bearer key. Prompts, diffs and tool outputs are not sent automatically. The lint tool, the prompts, the resources and the offline skill scripts send nothing. There are no hooks, so no passive capture of the coding session. This matters for client projects, because the agent chooses which state to send.
gh-simota-tenbin.failureMode: The server is not on any hot path and has no hooks, so the effect is per tool call. Without a key it starts in offline mode with only lint, prompts and resources (server.ts:24 returns early when the gateway is null). With a key, the SDK does automatic retries with backoff. Errors come back as an isError tool result with guidance (client.ts describeError), so it is effectively fail-open: Claude just gets a tool error and continues. Timeouts are the SDK defaults, and there is a budget, a size cap and a cancellation signal. evaluate.py uses a 60s timeout with retries. A 5xx, 429 or timeout only degrades the current design-time task.
gh-simota-tenbin.contextCost: 7 tools when a key is set (1 when there is none). Tool descriptions total about 1.7k characters, plus zod schemas for state, questions, options and so on, which I estimate at 2 to 3k tokens for the tool block. That is small compared with Playwright or GitNexus. It also registers 5 MCP prompts and about 8 resources, which are listed but not injected. The `tenbin` prompt, when invoked, injects roughly 15 to 25 KB of guides (about 5k tokens), and the skill body is 12 KB (about 3k tokens) once triggered. The skill description is a 351-char trigger string that sits in the skill listing every session. There are no hooks and no MCP server 'instructions' text.
gh-simota-tenbin.latencyImpact: None on ordinary Claude Code turns, because there are no hooks or proxying. When invoked, each tenbin_* call adds one network round trip of about 100 to 650 ms (the README sample shows 650 ms), and evaluate_many and rank fan out with up to 8 parallel requests. The MCP server process adds a small Node startup and a one-off listing cost at session start.
gh-simota-tenbin.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. Claude may load the skill on its own when the task looks like classify, route, triage, spam or injection detection, ranking or thresholds. The skill description is keyword-rich, so it will trigger on such requests without the user saying 'jev'. MCP tools are used when Claude decides to. It is never a deterministic hook, and nothing is a transparent proxy. Its trigger is 'the user is building an application feature that needs typed judgments', not 'Claude needs a decision while coding'. Most daily coding sessions will never trigger it. Its own README also says the intended entry is `/tenbin` or 'use the tenbin skill'.
pros: Real, non-trivial, well-structured code: 7 tools with lint, budget guard, per-call token caps, concurrency pool and error-to-advice mapping (client.ts, tools/*). 68 offline tests with a fake fetch.

The best key handling I have seen among these candidates. The key goes in a chmod 600 env file, the wrapper is registered so the key never lands in argv or ~/.claude.json, and SDK debug logging is forced off (Makefile:14, client.ts:33-38).
A cheap-to-run offline mode: tenbin_lint_questions, the prompts and the guides work with no key and no network, so it can be evaluated with zero spend.
Small context footprint (7 tools, about 2 to 3k tokens) compared with the user's Playwright and GitNexus MCPs.

Genuine value for one job: if the user builds apps that will call Jev, it gives measured Choice/Score/Noul design, calibration on labelled data and cost estimation, and its skill description can auto-trigger for such tasks.
Switching to OpenRouter looks nearly config-only. The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone, which maps to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (unverified against a live call).
MIT licence, a single small dependency set, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec in the server.
cons: It does not do what the user asked for. It uses Jev to help design Jev-powered application code. It does not use Jev to make Claude Code's own decisions such as which file to read, whether a command is safe, or routing, and there are no hooks. Its README states 'Everything runs at design time'.
Auto-invocation is limited to model-discretion skill or tool triggers. On most daily coding tasks it will not fire, and the workflow assumes the user asks for '/tenbin' or 'use the tenbin skill'.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs. It needs an env-var hack (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY plus an OpenRouter model id). tenbin_list_models will likely break because /v1/models has a different shape, and it is unverified. The hardcoded $0.042 price and 'jev-latest' alias assume TypeSafe direct.

Immature: created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 7 commits from 1 author, 4 stars, no releases, no CI, not on npm, so it has to be built from a git clone and pinned by SHA. The build uses TypeScript ^7.0.2.
Much of the skill and README is in Japanese in places (for example the /tenbin examples), and the skill is a heavy 12 KB SKILL.md plus about 25 KB of guides, which cost context when triggered.

Egress risk on client work: whatever state the agent packs into an evaluate or rank call is sent to a third-party service (TypeSafe or OpenRouter). The tool descriptions actively push the agent to 'put every question that uses this state here, including speculative ones', which encourages broad state.

Prompt and skill text steers the agent toward large generation tasks (design_integration writes SDK code, wiring and tests), which can conflict with the user's existing hooks and workflow if it triggers unexpectedly.
gh-simota-tenbin.verdict: The most complete Jev tooling I found, with good key hygiene and an offline mode, but it is a design-time toolkit for building Jev-powered apps. It is not an automatic Jev-in-the-loop for Claude Code, and it has no OpenRouter support out of the box (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL might make it work, untested). Keep it as an optional skill or MCP for projects that actually adopt Jev, not as the answer to 'Claude uses Jev automatically'.

gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.tests: None. There is no test dir, no test script and no .github workflows or CI. There is a CONTRIBUTING.md and a CHANGELOG. The changelog dates 1.0.0 as 2025-09-15, before Jev existed (released 2026-09-18), so it has a typo or backdating.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.install: claude mcp add jev -s user -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -- npx -y jev-flash-router. Better to pin the version and run a reviewed local copy: node /path/dist/index.js. The skill would need a manual copy to ~/.claude/skills/jev-flash-router/SKILL.md, because install-skill does not target Claude Code.
security: No third-party binary and no postinstall script (only prepublishOnly). Runtime deps are just the MCP SDK and dotenv. But the recommended `npx -y jev-flash-router` runs unpinned code from a 4-star, single-author package at every start, so pin the version or use a reviewed local clone.

The API key is read from the env var, so it is not in argv when passed via the MCP env block. The tool also accepts an apiKey argument (src/index.ts:139, 163-166), which would put the key in the model context, the transcript and tool-call logs. The README examples embed the key literally in JSON config.

dotenv.config() (:18) loads a .env from the process cwd. Claude Code launches stdio servers in the project directory, so a project .env is parsed into the server's env. It only uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY, but a client project's .env key could silently be used and billed instead of the intended one.

The prompt-injection surface is moderate. The model chooses the state, so untrusted repo, log or web content can flow into it. The output is only probabilities, which limits injection back into the agent, but the SKILL.md 'you MUST call' directive is an injected instruction and would drive frequent calls.

No shell execution and no eval. install-skill writes SKILL.md files into home directories, which is benign but writes outside the project. It calls process.exit(0) whenever the install-skill arg appears anywhere in argv.

No telemetry is sent. The 'telemetry' in responses is local. output_tokens:0 and cost:"$0.00 output" are hard-coded strings (:263-267), not read from the API, so they are marketing rather than measured.
An uncaughtException handler swallows crashes and keeps the process alive.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.dataEgress: Only what the model puts into `state`, `question` and `criteria` is sent (any code, diffs, logs or task text Claude chooses to include) to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the Bearer key and Referer/X-OpenRouter-Title headers. Nothing else leaves the machine. Nothing is sent to TypeSafe directly or to the package author. There is no redaction or size cap. The secret-leak guard hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not MCP tools, so it will not inspect what goes into state. Sending client code to OpenRouter and TypeSafe is a data-policy question for client projects.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.failureMode: Fail-open in practice but with no timeout. The fetch (:233) has no AbortSignal or timeout, so a hung OpenRouter connection would block the tool call until the client's MCP timeout. HTTP errors and network errors are caught and returned as isError text, so Claude simply continues without Jev. There is no retry and no fallback. A missing key returns an error message on every call, and the server still starts fine.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.contextCost: One tool, evaluate_decision. The description is about 250 chars and the schema (5 properties, each with a description) is about 1.2k chars, so roughly 400-450 tokens of tool definition, or even less if the tool is deferred via ToolSearch. The server sends no MCP instructions. If SKILL.md is manually installed, the frontmatter description adds about 60 tokens permanently, and the 4.2k-char body (about 1k tokens) loads whenever the skill triggers. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.latencyImpact: Nothing is added unless Claude calls the tool. Each call is one HTTPS round trip. The README claims about 150 ms, which is unverified, and it is consistent with the brief's 70-500 ms. Add MCP stdio overhead plus the model turn that emits the tool call and reads the result, so each use costs a full extra agent step (about 1-3 s wall time, plus the tokens for state, question and criteria that Opus must write out). That output-token cost is larger than the 'zero-token' claim implies. Using it saves nothing versus Opus just deciding.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, plus a skill-description trigger only if SKILL.md is copied manually into ~/.claude/skills (the bundled installer does not). There is no hook, no proxy and no deterministic path. Whether Claude calls it depends on Opus following the tool description ('Use this BEFORE generating long reasoning plans') or the skill directive. That is unreliable, and it may over-trigger and add friction.
pros: OpenRouter is the native and only provider: it hits /api/alpha/decisions with an OPENROUTER_API_KEY and ~typesafe/jev-latest, exactly the requested setup, with no patching (src/index.ts:214,233).
Tiny surface: one tool, about 317 lines, two dependencies, no postinstall or shell exec. It is easy to audit and vendor in minutes, and the ~450-token context cost is small.
Supports all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) with a correctly shaped questions.eval payload and a clean unwrap of answers.eval.
MIT license, a package that reads sensibly, and stderr redirection of console.* to protect the stdio handshake.
Ships a SKILL.md with a valid Claude Code frontmatter and examples that can be reused as the basis of a home-grown skill.
cons: Automation is weak. It is a model-discretion tool only, and the bundled install-skill writes to ~/.gemini and ~/.agents, not ~/.claude (src/index.ts:40-47), so out of the box Claude Code has no trigger. That fails the user's 'never say use jev' requirement.

Hard-coded fake telemetry (output_tokens:0, cost string) and 'zero-token' marketing are misleading. Claude must generate state, question and criteria as output tokens on Opus, so it costs more than it saves.
No timeout, no retry and no fallback on fetch. There is no model or base-URL override, and no TypeSafe direct or System One endpoint support.
The apiKey tool argument invites keys into transcripts. dotenv loads the cwd .env, which is risky across client projects.
Immature: created 2026-09-18, 4 stars, 16 commits, no tests, no CI, no releases, a backdated changelog (1.0.0 dated 2025-09-15), and it is the work of a single author.
All egress goes through model-chosen free text with no redaction, so the existing secret-guard hook does not cover MCP calls. It is a concern for client code.

The 'MUST call before reasoning' skill directive risks over-triggering, adding an agent step (1-3 s) to trivial decisions, and giving Jev's calibrated probabilities false authority over Opus's own judgement.
gh-ravinder82-jev-flash-router.verdict: A small, correct and OpenRouter-native wrapper around the Decisions API that is fine as a reference or a vendored starting point, but not something to install as-is. It cannot deliver the automatic, no-prompt integration wanted: it is only a discretionary MCP tool, its skill installer misses ~/.claude, and its claims of zero cost and telemetry are cosmetic. Prefer a self-owned copy with a timeout, a fixed key path and a hook or skill wired for Claude Code.

gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.name: King4s/Jev-AI-Skill
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.whatItDoes: Python skill plus stdio MCP server (jev-loop, 9 tools) that uses Jev via the TypeSafe direct API. It has a build/review Loop (loop_*), four stateless Gate tools (triage, verdict, decide, pick) meant to run before spending a large-model turn, and CLI helpers (route.py, git_decide.py, find_code.py, --watch). It is aimed at agent-orchestration cost saving (cron and event triage, review rounds, owner questions), not at the interactive coding decisions a Claude Code user makes all day. There are no hooks; use depends on the model following SKILL.md and the MCP server instructions.

providerSupport.evidence: jev_mcp.py:43 API = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"; key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.config/jev-loop/typesafe_api_key (jev_mcp.py:54-60); model default "jev-latest" (gate_* signatures, route.py:33 JEV_ROUTE_MODEL, git_decide.py:38 JEV_GIT_MODEL); request body {model,state,questions} with Bearer auth (jev_mcp.py:91-95). The only OpenRouter reference is legacy loop.py:28-29 (OPENROUTER_API_KEY), which uses OpenRouter for executor/reviewer chat models, not Jev; loop.py:68 still calls api.typesafe.ai for Jev. No openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone endpoint anywhere.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The API constant is duplicated in 3 files (jev_mcp.py:43, route.py:32, git_decide.py:37) and is not env-overridable. The request shape {model,state,questions} matches the TypeSafe System One schema, which is probably close to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, but that is unverified. A patch would need a configurable base URL, an OPENROUTER_API_KEY fallback, a model id mapping (jev-latest -> ~typesafe/jev-latest or typesafe/jev-1.13), and a check that the response shape (answers dict) is the same. That is about 20-40 lines across 3 files. Workaround with no code change: JEV_UPSTREAM forwards Jev calls to any HTTP endpoint that speaks POST /jev with the same body, so a small local proxy could translate to OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: Optional JEV_UPSTREAM / JEV_MCP_URL forwarding to a shared self-hosted jev_mcp.py --http server (/jev endpoint), without authentication.

interface.name: loop_start(goal_path)
interface.purpose: Start a build/review loop run from a goal JSON file. Runs the goal's shell checks once.

interface.name: loop_decide(run_id)
interface.purpose: Ask Jev for the next step: execute, review or stop.

interface.name: loop_record_turn(run_id, notes, files, executor_ok)
interface.purpose: Record an executor turn and re-run the checks.

interface.name: loop_record_review(run_id, done, missing)
interface.purpose: Record the independent reviewer's verdict.

interface.name: loop_status(run_id)
interface.purpose: Show run state.

interface.name: gate_triage(events, known, policy)
interface.purpose: For up to 40 events (cron, poll, notification), decide ignore, known, report or act, and whether an agent is needed at all.

interface.name: gate_verdict(goal, items, evidence, changes)
interface.purpose: Decide which review findings the evidence already closes, and whether the next review is none, narrow or full.

interface.name: gate_decide(question, options, context, recommended, policy)
interface.purpose: Choose among the harness's own options and say whether the owner must decide.

interface.name: gate_pick(task, candidates, context)
interface.purpose: Pick a tool, skill or file from one-line descriptions.

interface.name: route.py <request.json>
interface.purpose: CLI helper that picks a model tier (haiku/sonnet/opus/fable), a skill and whether to delegate.

interface.name: git_decide.py --repo --summary [--reviewed --checks-green]
interface.purpose: CLI helper that recommends commit, push or PR steps with hard blocks and a heuristic secret scan; it does not change git state.

interface.name: find_code.py --repo --task [--pattern]
interface.purpose: CLI helper that splits the repo into chunks of up to 2400 characters and has Jev score them all (up to 2000 chunks) for code search.

interface.name: jev_mcp.py --watch / --gate / --http / --check
interface.purpose: Agentless recurring check with Jev triage, a stdin JSON Gate CLI, a shared HTTP server, and a live self-check.

interface.name: skill 'jev' (SKILL.md, 341 lines, about 22 KB)
interface.purpose: Triggers include: Jev-AI-Skill, jev, jev-loop, jev-gate, jev-route, jev-git, plus Danish phrases (kør loopen, byg med jev, lad Jev styre, skal det pushes). The name and description are Danish/English and explicitly name-driven.

gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.tests: Yes. 8 pytest files (about 1.6k lines: test_jev_mcp, test_gate, test_decision_helpers, test_find_code, the installer tests and others). GitHub Actions runs pytest on ubuntu and windows with Python 3.12. I did not run them. Roughly 6 days of history; 62 of 73 commits are by one human, and 5 are by "Hermes Agent", so it is heavily AI-assisted and very fast-moving.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.runtime: Python 3.11+, requests, and mcp>=2.2, which it imports as mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer. That is a newer SDK layout, and an unpinned dependency may break. install.sh builds a repo-local .venv.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.install: git clone https://github.com/King4s/Jev-AI-Skill.git ~/Jev-AI-Skill && ~/Jev-AI-Skill/install.sh. It creates .venv, pip-installs requirements, and copies the skill to ~/.claude/skills/jev. It also runs `claude mcp add jev-loop --scope user` (install.sh:34). On Debian without ensurepip it downloads get-pip.py from bootstrap.pypa.io and runs it (install.sh:21-23). It does not use curl|sh for the project itself. Not executed by me.
security: API key is read from env or ~/.config/jev-loop/typesafe_api_key and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv, and the install script only passes the key as an env reference for Hermes (install.sh:64-72). No key in the process list.

Loop executes `shell=True` commands taken from the goal JSON (jev_mcp.py:109), with a 300 s default timeout. This is arbitrary code execution driven by a model-written goal file. The README admits it, and bypass mode makes it riskier.

Gate/Loop inputs are model-composed strings from Claude, so hostile repo content that reaches those strings could influence a decision. Decisions are probabilistic and low-stakes for triage, but the skill tells the agent to skip work on 'ignore' or 'known'.

The --http mode has no authentication (README and the serve_http docstring). If it is bound to 0.0.0.0, the /jev endpoint would be an open proxy that spends the key, and /mcp would let anyone start loops that run shell checks on that host. The default host is 127.0.0.1.
The MCP server is registered at user scope with an absolute path to the venv and script. Runtime pip deps (mcp>=2.2, requests) are unpinned and there is no hash pinning.
No telemetry found in the code. Run state and a decision tape are written to runs/*.jsonl next to the script, or under ~/.local/state/jev-loop/runs.
The git_decide secret scan is heuristic; the README says so.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.dataEgress: Sent to api.typesafe.ai only, over HTTPS (TypeSafe, not OpenRouter), and only when a Jev tool is called. The payload is {model, state, questions}, where state is what Claude composes. gate_* sends up to 40 events (each clipped to about 600 characters), findings, evidence tails, option labels and descriptions, and question text. loop_* sends the goal, acceptance criteria, a limited project file list, check outputs (last 2000 characters per check) and short turn notes. route.py sends the task, context and skill descriptions. git_decide.py sends repo facts (branch, commit subjects, counts). find_code.py is the biggest one: up to 2000 chunks of 2400 characters of raw source from the repo go to TypeSafe, which is unsuitable for client code. Full files and diffs are not sent by the hooks or MCP tools, because there are no hooks and nothing observes the session automatically.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.failureMode: The MCP tools return {"error": ...} through safe() when Jev fails (jev_mcp.py:~650). SKILL.md says to 'do the work the expensive way' and never treat an error as ignore, which means fail-open to normal Claude work by instruction, not by mechanism. Jev HTTP calls use a 60 s timeout with up to 4 retries and exponential sleep on 429/529 (jev_mcp.py:86-100). Worst case is several minutes blocked inside one tool call. The upstream forwarding path has a 90 s timeout and retries 4 times on connection errors. With no API key, RuntimeError is returned as an error dict. The --gate and --watch CLIs exit 2 with error JSON.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.latencyImpact: Nothing runs on turns Claude does not call it for, because there are no hooks. Each Gate call is one HTTPS round trip to Jev (claimed 70-500 ms) plus MCP stdio overhead, plus Python cold start when the server first spawns (about 0.3-1 s). On failure the retries can reach 60 s x 5 attempts. find_code.py can make hundreds of sequential or batched calls on a large repo.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.contextCost: Server: 9 tools. Tool defs (names, docstrings, schemas) come to roughly 4.6 KB of source, so about 1.2-1.8k tokens once schemas are added. The server "instructions" string is about 600 characters, or about 150 tokens. The skill adds its name and description to the listing (about 520 characters, about 130 tokens), and the 22 KB SKILL.md (about 5.5k tokens) loads whenever the skill triggers. No hooks, so nothing is injected per tool call. Total idle cost is about 1.5-2k tokens, which is moderate; 9 tools for a mostly irrelevant workflow is poor value.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger. The server "instructions" and SKILL.md tell Claude to call gate_triage, gate_verdict and gate_decide 'every time, before reasoning' in those moments. The skill description is name-driven (jev, jev-loop, kør loopen, byg med jev), so it fires mostly when the user says those words, which conflicts with the "never say use jev" requirement. There is no deterministic hook, so triggering depends on model compliance. The Gate moments (cron and poll events, review rounds, owner questions) are rare in an interactive session.
pros: Real, inspected code with 8 test files, CI on Linux and Windows, an MIT license, and releases. It is more than a README skill.

Gate design is sensible for Jev's strengths: short structured state in, calibrated probabilities out. The instructions for each question type are well framed (noul and choice primitives in jev_mcp.py:493-620).
Fail-safe wording: on an error, do the work the normal way. Errors return as dicts and do not crash the server.
Key handling is clean: env or a chmod 600 file, no argv exposure, no telemetry, and no npm postinstall. The installer never pipes to sh.
gate_decide and gate_pick could plausibly reduce 'should I ask the user?' interruptions, useful in auto mode.
JEV_UPSTREAM forwarding is a ready-made seam for a translating proxy to OpenRouter.
git_decide.py's hard blocks (no direct push to main, identity and private-pattern blocks) are a useful guard, though only if actually called.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the only endpoint is api.typesafe.ai and the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The base URL is hardcoded in 3 files, with no env override. It cannot be used with an OpenRouter key without patching.

The hooks Claude Code would need for automatic use do not exist. Triggering relies on the model reading a 22 KB SKILL.md and 9 tool descriptions. The skill description is keyword-driven ('jev', 'byg med jev', 'kør loopen'), which is the opposite of the user's wish to never say 'use jev'.

The problem it targets is agent-fleet cost (cron jobs, notifications, chat-room events, Hermes, Codex) and not interactive coding in Claude Code. In a normal Claude Code session the Gate moments barely occur. Its author's own audit says the biggest token sinks were scheduled jobs and echoed exit codes.

Loop is a whole competing orchestration protocol (start, decide, execute, record_turn, review) that overlaps with and fights Claude Code's own agent loop and plan mode. It also runs shell checks from the goal file with shell=True, which is risky under bypass permissions.
find_code.py ships raw source excerpts (up to 4.8 MB in 2000 chunks of 2400 characters) to a third party. That is unacceptable for client projects, and it is uncached and slow.

The project is 6 days old, with 30 commits on a single day. It is essentially one author with AI agents (5 commits by 'Hermes Agent'), has 3 stars and 0 forks, and is unproven. Docs and the skill are partly in Danish. mcp>=2.2 with the mcp.server.mcpserver import is a fresh, unpinned dependency.
Adds 9 tools plus a 22 KB skill to context for capabilities that are mostly irrelevant, on top of gitnexus, playwright and caveman.
--http mode has no authentication, and the shared-server setup expects a tailnet. Failure retries can stall a tool call for minutes.
gh-king4s-jev-ai-skill.verdict: Well-built for its niche, but the niche is not yours. It gates agent-fleet turns (cron, notifications, review rounds), it is TypeSafe-direct only (no OpenRouter), and its auto-trigger is a name-driven skill plus model-discretion MCP tools instead of hooks. Use it as a reference for Gate question design (noul/choice framing), not as your daily integration. If you did adopt it, install only the Gate tools behind an OpenRouter-translating JEV_UPSTREAM proxy, and skip Loop and find_code.py.

gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.name: Smith2912/jev-context-mcp
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.whatItDoes: Local Node MCP server (v0.10.0) built for OpenAI Codex CLI on Windows, not Claude Code. It calls TypeSafe's System One API (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13.0) with Score-type questions to (a) rerank redacted log/file chunks before loading them into context (triage_log, select_file_context), (b) score generated files against criteria (check_file_output), (c) recommend a model/effort/skill/execution profile for a prompt (route_task), and (d) run an optional registered-workflow and Computer Use decision mode. Everything is advisory. A deterministic local fallback works without a key. Extra machinery includes a disk cache, a 6-requests-per-minute limiter, a usage ledger and a native Codex runner.

providerSupport.evidence: Direct TypeSafe only. The URL 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone' is hardcoded at core.mjs:49 (rank), router.mjs:25 (routeTask) and decision-engine.mjs:47 (workflow). The only credential is process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.mjs:18, 29, 31; launch.mjs:10-17; workflow-cli.mjs:11). It is sent as a Bearer header. The model is the bare string 'jev-1.13.0' (core.mjs:42, decision-policy.json:3). decision-engine.mjs:25 rejects any policy whose model is not exactly 'jev-1.13.0'. The request body is {model,state,questions:{id:{type:'score',instructions,criteria}}} and the response is read as data.answers[id].{type,score,confidence} plus usage and model. No OpenRouter string appears anywhere in the source.
providerSupport.others: None. The credential can also be loaded through a Windows DPAPI file (decrypt-key.ps1 run via launch.mjs, powershell).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The request and response shape looks compatible with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (same 'systemone' path, state+questions body, answers response), so in principle it is a base-URL, key and model-ID change. But the URL is hardcoded in 3 places, the env var name is fixed, the model must be renamed to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' in payloads, decision-policy.json and the strict equality check at decision-engine.mjs:25, and the response model-equality checks (core.mjs:53, router.mjs) would report 'provider-reported-alias'. It is a fork-and-patch job, not a config switch. I did not verify that OpenRouter's response schema matches exactly.

interface.name: triage_log
interface.purpose: Deduplicate a .rpt/.log file locally and return bounded excerpts plus an omitted inventory. Optional Jev ranking of up to 24 redacted passages. The description is DayZ-specific.

interface.name: read_log_range
interface.purpose: Read original redacted lines from a triaged log by path and SHA-256. Local only.

interface.name: select_file_context
interface.purpose: Select compact evidence chunks from a large code, doc or data file for a question. Optional Jev rerank; small inputs skip Jev.

interface.name: read_file_context
interface.purpose: Retrieve redacted original lines from a selected file with a matching SHA-256. Local only.

interface.name: check_file_output
interface.purpose: Jev scores a generated file against 1-4 criteria. Typed scores only, and it needs shareWithTypeSafe=true.

interface.name: route_task
interface.purpose: Jev advisory recommendation of model tier, effort, up to 5 skills and one of 4 execution profiles for a prompt. It skips prompts under 20 characters or over 4000 characters and credential-looking prompts. It supports invocation='hook' output, but no standalone hook script is shipped for it.

interface.name: prepare_work_packet
interface.purpose: Workflow mode only (default disabled): prepare source evidence for a registered workflow.

interface.name: run_workflow_stage
interface.purpose: Workflow mode only: inspect, verify, report or finish. Runs registered tests.

interface.name: get_run_report
interface.purpose: Workflow mode only: report stage and provider receipts.

interface.name: decide_computer_step
interface.purpose: Workflow mode only: Jev picks one registered routine action ID from a text observation.

interface.name: native-global-hook.mjs (UserPromptSubmit)
interface.purpose: Codex hook. It only reacts to the literal prompt 'jev: workflow=<registered-id>' and spawns a detached native Codex runner. Everything else passes through. It is not a Claude Code hook.

security: Key handling: TYPESAFE_API_KEY comes from the MCP process env or a Windows DPAPI file. It is not passed on argv, and launch.mjs deletes it from process.env after import. Under Claude Code the key would sit in the .mcp.json env block, or be inherited from the shell.

Data leaves only if the per-call boolean shareWithTypeSafe is true. That is a tool argument the model chooses, so under bypass or auto permission mode nothing stops Claude from setting it to true. The README says redaction is best effort.
Redaction: regex cleanText/redact strips private keys and password/token/apikey/secret JSON fields. It is not a guarantee, and client code and secrets could still be sent.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted passages and prompts go into Jev's 'instructions' fields, with wording that tells the model to treat them as data. The output is typed scores only, so injection impact is limited to biasing rankings. A wrongly low score could hide relevant evidence from Claude.
File reads are confined to allowedRoots and contextRoots from a private settings.json. The shipped example grants no roots, and SHA-256 checks bind ranges to a selection.

launch.mjs can execFileSync python (refresh-catalog.py) and powershell only if configured. The native runner spawns detached Codex processes. No postinstall script, no curl|sh, no telemetry found. The only outbound URL is api.typesafe.ai.
Dependencies are pinned to exact versions (MCP SDK 1.30.0, zod 4.6.5, js-tiktoken 1.0.21). The CI actions are pinned by SHA. License is MIT.
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only, and only when shareWithTypeSafe=true and a key is present. Contents: redacted question text plus up to 24 passages of at most 900 characters each (log or file chunks), or the redacted prompt (max 4000 characters) plus skill names and descriptions for route_task, or a file's content for check_file_output. Workflow mode adds compact evidence and observations. Nothing goes to OpenRouter. Local disk holds a cache of validated typed responses only (not requests), a usage ledger and run artifacts.
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open, and timeouts are bounded. Any provider error, bad schema, oversized response (over 100 KB) or missing key falls back to local-only results, or to {continue:true} for route_task. Timeouts are 6 s for route_task, 20 s for rank and 15 s in the workflow policy. A local limiter allows 6 paid requests per minute, and 429s get 1 retry. If the MCP process fails to start (for example a missing settings.json, which launch.mjs and server.mjs read unconditionally), the tools are simply absent.
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.latencyImpact: Model-invoked only, so zero on turns where Claude doesn't call it. Each call adds one extra tool round-trip of about 70-500 ms Jev latency (per the brief) plus local file reading. route_task worst case is 6 s, and rank up to 20 s. The MCP server starts once per session, which costs Node startup plus a settings.json read. Since there is no Claude Code hook, it adds no per-prompt latency.
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.contextCost: 10 tools if the workflow mode is enabled, otherwise 6. Tool names, descriptions and schemas together are about 6 KB of source for all 10, so roughly 1.5-2k tokens. With the default 6 tools it is about 1k tokens. There is no server 'instructions' field, and no hook-injected text unless the user builds a hook themselves (route_task adds at most 800 characters of additionalContext).
gh-smith2912-jev-context-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The descriptions push Claude to call select_file_context before loading large files ('Before loading a large code, document...'), and triage_log before raw logs. Nothing deterministic ships for Claude Code. The shipped hook is a Codex hook for an explicit 'jev: workflow=' prompt prefix. The route_task hook mode has no script, so a user would have to write a wrapper that speaks MCP or reimplement the call.
pros: It uses Jev in the way the brief describes: Score questions over typed criteria, and the response validation is strict (score range, confidence 0-1, size cap). Good reference code for the request and response shape of /v1/systemone.
The select_file_context idea (rerank chunks before they enter context) is a sensible System One use, and a small file skips Jev entirely. The file tools work locally with no key.
Fail-open design with a cache, a 6 requests per minute limiter, per-run token ceilings, a usage ledger and SHA-bound retrieval. Little risk of runaway spend or of blocking the session.
Pinned dependencies, SHA-pinned CI actions, MIT license, an extensive test suite (14 test files), and no postinstall or telemetry. The sharing opt-in is per call.
It has a tiny context footprint in the default mode (6 tools, roughly 1k tokens).
cons: Built for Codex CLI on Windows. The install docs are `codex mcp add` and PowerShell, the DPAPI credential path is Windows-only, and the hook and its output projection target Codex's parser. The native runner is Codex-only. Roughly 10-15 of about 50 files are Codex or Windows specific, so it needs a rework for Claude Code on Linux.

No OpenRouter support. The TypeSafe URL is hardcoded in 3 places, the env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the model 'jev-1.13.0' is checked by strict equality in decision-engine.mjs:25. Switching to OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-1.13, /api/v1/systemone) needs a fork patch, and the schema match is unverified.

The auto-invocation the user wants doesn't exist for Claude Code. It relies on the model deciding to call tools and setting shareWithTypeSafe=true. The route_task hook mode has no script, and the native-global-hook only fires on the explicit prefix 'jev: workflow='.

It leans on a narrow pipeline: rerank files or logs, route models. route_task recommends models that Claude Code cannot switch mid-task, and its tier table and skills come from a local catalog that is empty in the tracked template. The docs are DayZ-flavored (triage_log is for .rpt logs). The value for general daily coding is small.

gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.name: pedroknigge/mcp_jev
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) wrapping the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. Exposes 5 tools: a catalog of 13 hand-written "packs" (review_diff, code_audit, command_risk, verify_gap, boundary_check, model_router, skill_router, i18n_copy, etc.) plus a generic run_questions tool for custom Choice/Noul/Score calls. It also ships a CLI (doctor, dogfood, smoke, scan, urlcheck, hosts write, config set-key) and a very large SKILL.md (about 51 KB) meant to teach agents when to call it. There are no hooks, so it never intercepts tool calls. Everything is model-discretion or skill-triggered.

So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the documented OpenRouter System One endpoint.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, no code change: set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and set JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), because the default 'jev-latest' is TypeSafe's own model ID rather than an OpenRouter slug. Remaining gaps: (1) the OpenRouter request/response schema for /v1/systemone must match TypeSafe's, which I did not test; (2) OpenRouter attribution headers cannot be set from env (SDK defaultHeaders is not wired); (3) a key stored in ~/.mcp_jev/.env takes precedence over the process env (user-config.ts:118-125), which is a footgun; (4) install.sh/doctor and the docs assume a TypeSafe key from console.typesafe.ai.

security: MIT license. Not published to npm (README says so; npm view mcp_jev returns 404), so the install path is git clone + scripts/install.sh, which runs npm install && npm run build. That pulls transitive deps and the package.json 'prepare' script (tsc) at install time. Nothing is pinned by a signed release.

API key handling is mostly decent: stored in ~/.mcp_jev/.env at chmod 600 with the dir at 700 (user-config.ts:72-97), host mcp.json stays keyless, and ping and errors never echo the key. Weaknesses: install.sh passes $TYPESAFE_API_KEY on argv to 'config set-key' (visible in ps briefly), the 'config set-key <key>' argv form is supported (cli.ts:305), and the generated wrapper does `source ~/.mcp_jev/.env` (executes it as shell), so anything written there runs.

hosts write modifies ~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/settings.json by read-modify-write with a non-atomic writeFileSync (hosts.ts:255-278). This is risky on a live ~/.claude.json that holds OAuth and project state. Do the registration manually or with `claude mcp add` instead.
Key precedence quirk: the stored ~/.mcp_jev/.env key overrides the process env key (user-config.ts:118-125), so an OPENROUTER key exported in the environment can be silently ignored.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool outputs are typed JSON (probabilities), which is small. But run_questions/run_pack take free-form 'instructions' and state built by the model, so untrusted repo content flowing into state can steer Jev's answers. No shell execution in the server tools. urlcheck makes HTTP requests to user-supplied bases only when invoked from the CLI.
No telemetry found in src. Outbound calls go only to the configured TypeSafe base URL. There is no fetch( in src; the network client is the SDK.
Single-maintainer, agent-authored code (Cursor Agent co-authored 8 of 34 commits); the repo is 11 days old with 1 star.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden): exactly the `state` JSON plus the typed questions that the model builds for each run_pack/run_questions call. The model chooses what goes into state. The pack schemas ask for diff summaries, file lists, commands, claims and evidence names, and code_audit accepts an `excerpt` of file text (src/scan.ts:522-533 slices raw file content to MAX_EXCERPT_CHARS). The CLI 'scan' command reads files up to 1 MB, skips .env files and applies .gitignore (scan.ts:238,414), and sends path, signals and optional excerpts to code_audit. Nothing is sent automatically: no hook or proxy reads prompts, tool outputs or files. On client projects, egress happens only when the model decides to call the tools. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard will not see the MCP call's payload (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so state could carry secrets that pass unchecked.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.failureMode: Fail-open relative to Claude Code: a slow or down Jev only makes that MCP tool call return isError JSON (server.ts:21-27), and the model carries on. Timeout is a hard-coded 20 s (config.ts:9, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS, no env override). The SDK also has retry maxRetries: 2 by default (sdk dist/index.mjs:74). A dead endpoint can therefore stall a turn for roughly 20-60 s per call before the error comes back. A missing key returns a friendly error, not a crash. If the MCP server fails to start, Claude Code just shows it as failed and nothing else breaks.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.contextCost: 5 MCP tools: list_packs, describe_pack, run_pack, run_questions, ping. Tool names+descriptions+schemas are about 3,000 chars (server.ts:36-129), roughly 750 tokens. The server sets no `instructions` field. The skill adds its frontmatter description (about 1,300 chars, roughly 330 tokens) to every session's skill list. When triggered, the SKILL.md body is about 51 KB (roughly 13k tokens), and it points to a 54 KB pack-catalog.md (roughly 13k more tokens) if read. Every use starts with list_packs (a catalog of 13 packs) and, when unfamiliar, describe_pack (full JSON schema): a further 2-5k tokens per use. No hook-injected text. Baseline about 1k tokens; a real use costs 5-30k tokens, which is heavy.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. Two mechanisms: (a) the MCP tool descriptions, which are generic and steer the model to use them only for typed judgments; (b) the skill description trigger, which fires on keywords like 'Jev', 'PR audit', 'review diff', 'code audit', 'model router'. Since the user does not want to type "jev", and ordinary coding prompts rarely contain those words, this will fire rarely and unpredictably. There is no deterministic hook, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse integration and no transparent proxy. Making it automatic would need a CLAUDE.md rule or hooks written by the user.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.latencyImpact: Nothing added to turns where the model does not call it. Each call is stdio to Node, then a request to Jev (claimed 70-500 ms, which I did not measure), plus about 1-2 model round-trips of overhead for list_packs, describe_pack, run_pack and the state-building tokens the main model must emit (a few hundred to 2k output tokens). Realistically 3-15 s of added wall time per Jev use, dominated by Opus, not Jev. Worst case with a dead endpoint is 20-60 s.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript compiled by tsc, ESM), deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod. Runs via ~/.mcp_jev/bin/mcp_jev wrapper (bash) or node dist/index.js from a git checkout.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.install: git clone + scripts/install.sh (npm install && npm run build, writes ~/.mcp_jev/bin/mcp_jev and ~/.mcp_jev/.env). It is not on npm. `npx -y github:pedroknigge/mcp_jev` is also documented. Manual Claude Code registration: `claude mcp add mcp_jev -- node /path/to/dist/index.js` with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL in env (or the ~/.mcp_jev/.env store). I did not run any of this.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.tests: 26 test files under test/, about 154 it()/test() cases (tsx --test). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) on Node 20 runs npm ci, npm test, typecheck, a stdio MCP smoke and a mocked all-packs smoke. All tests mock TypeSafe, so no live-API coverage. There is a release workflow. Latest release v0.0.9 while package.json is 0.0.11.
pros: Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so the wire format is TypeSafe's own. The SDK POSTs /v1/systemone with a Bearer token, which lines up with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone once TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api is set. OpenRouter therefore works via env vars only, with no fork.
The tool surface is small: 5 tools, about 750 tokens of definitions, no server instructions, no hook text. That is cheap to keep loaded.
Typed run_questions is a general Choice/Noul/Score escape hatch, so it does not lock the user into the 13 packs.

Reasonable engineering hygiene for its age: MIT, 26 test files, CI, typed inputs validated with zod, strict validation of Choice/Noul/Score shapes (custom-questions.ts), key stored chmod 600 and never echoed.

Packs that map to coding decisions (review_diff, command_risk, verify_gap, boundary_check, code_audit, skill_router, model_router) could serve as building blocks for a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy later, and the pack question definitions are a useful reference for writing your own.
Nothing runs unless invoked; there is no telemetry and no background process.
cons: No automatic integration. It ships no hooks, no PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit wiring and no proxy. It only fires when the model reads the tool descriptions or the skill triggers, and the skill's triggers are keywords like 'Jev', 'TypeSafe' and 'PR audit'. That directly fails the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told.

Explicit OpenRouter support is absent: 'openrouter' appears nowhere in the source, docs or scripts. It relies on the undocumented-here TYPESAFE_BASE_URL trick plus a manual JEV_MODEL slug (the default 'jev-latest' is a TypeSafe ID, not an OpenRouter one). The OpenRouter payload compatibility is unverified. The installer and doctor also insist on a TypeSafe console key.

The workflow is token-heavy for a 'fast decision' tool: list_packs, then describe_pack, then run_pack, with a 51 KB SKILL.md and a 54 KB pack catalog to load. The main model (Opus) must hand-build state JSON, so a call adds seconds of Opus latency and thousands of tokens, which cancels Jev's 70-500 ms advantage.

The 13 packs are speculative, agent-authored guesses at judgment tasks (the repo's own docs say 'invent questions' and 'dogfood'), with no evidence that Jev outperforms a plain Opus judgment on review or command risk. The `command_risk` pack states it is not an allowlist, so it cannot replace a real guard.
Sends model-chosen code/diff/command summaries to a third party on client projects, and the user's secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool payloads.

Very new and immature: 11 days old, 1 star, single maintainer with Cursor-agent commits, releases v0.0.x, and an install path (clone, npm install, build, wrapper that sources .env) with no signed artefacts. `hosts write` rewrites ~/.claude.json non-atomically, so registering by hand is safer.
Hard-coded 20 s timeout with SDK retries (2), and no env override, so a slow endpoint can block a turn for up to about a minute.
Stored-key-over-env precedence (user-config.ts:118) makes swapping providers error-prone.
gh-pedroknigge-mcp-jev.verdict: Cleanly written, small MCP wrapper around the official SDK, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with env vars alone (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). But it is a passive toolbox with no hooks, and its skill triggers on keywords, so it will not deliver the "Claude uses Jev automatically" goal. It also carries heavy skill and catalog token costs for every real use. Treat it as a reference or a fallback tool, not the primary integration. Automatic behaviour would need a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy built on top.
