interface.name: jev_verify (MCP)
interface.purpose: Claims vs evidence: verified / contradicted / unsupported. No length bound on input.

interface.name: jev_gate (MCP)
interface.purpose: Ship check: patch, completion claims and test log checked in one call -> auto / review / escalate. At most 16 claims and 16 evidence items.

interface.name: jev_review (MCP)
interface.purpose: Score a diff against the request: correctness, spec match, test gap, blast radius, safe_to_apply.

interface.name: jev_screen (MCP)
interface.purpose: Prompt-injection and relevance screen of fetched or pasted text: pass / review / block / skip.

interface.name: jev_compare (MCP)
interface.purpose: Two passages: same_fact / contradicts / different_facts, with optional per-aspect checks.

interface.name: jev_find (MCP)
interface.purpose: Pick the best of at most 250 candidates and report whether any matches.

interface.name: jev_rerank (MCP)
interface.purpose: Relevance score for every candidate (up to 250), fully ordered.

interface.name: jev_classify (MCP)
interface.purpose: Bucket up to 64 items into a class catalog.

interface.name: jev_decide (MCP)
interface.purpose: One choice among 2-6 options, with ask_user / investigate / none escape hatches.

interface.name: jev_extract (MCP)
interface.purpose: Regex proposes candidates, Jev picks one, value returned verbatim (local regex worker pool).

interface.name: jev_score (MCP)
interface.purpose: Grade on a 2-10 level ordered rubric.

interface.name: jev-skill://jev-mcp/SKILL.md and jev-skill://jev/SKILL.md (MCP resources and prompts)
interface.purpose: Routing skill for the tools, and a cookbook for building apps on the Jev API. They are served over MCP, not installed as Claude Code SKILL.md files.

interface.name: jev-judge-mcp hook gate (opt-in PreToolUse command hook)
interface.purpose: Judges each proposed Bash/Write/Edit action with a Choice allow/deny. Emits only deny or ask, never allow. Sample matcher Bash|Write|Edit, timeout 30 s (docs/harness/gate.hooks.json).

interface.name: jev-judge-mcp completion-hook (opt-in PreToolUse hook)
interface.purpose: On Bash commands matching git push / gh pr create / gh pr merge, runs jev_gate in process using JEV_COMPLETION_DIFF, JEV_COMPLETION_CLAIMS and JEV_COMPLETION_TESTS files. Asks unless the result is auto (cli.py:570-617).

interface.name: jev-judge-mcp setup | install | doctor | judge <tool> | gate | calibrate
interface.purpose: Store the key, write MCP entries into agent configs, offline config check, CLI access for non-MCP clients, and threshold calibration.

gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.install: No package install is needed for the OpenRouter path. Register by hand in ~/.claude.json or via claude mcp add: command uvx, args [\"--python\",\">=3.12\",\"--from\",\"jev-judge-mcp==0.7.0\",\"jev-judge-mcp\"], env {\"OPENROUTER_API_KEY\":\"${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}\",\"JEV_PROVIDER\":\"openrouter\",\"JEV_MCP_MODEL\":\"typesafe/jev-1.13\"}. The [typesafe] extra is only needed for the TypeSafe direct path. The documented flow is `uvx --from 'jev-judge-mcp[typesafe]' jev-judge-mcp setup`, then `install`, then `doctor`. Setup and install are TypeSafe-key oriented. PyPI has versions 0.1.0 to 0.7.0, and 0.7.0 was published 2026-09-29.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.runtime: Python >=3.12 (mcp>=2.2,<2.3, httpx, pydantic, pydantic-settings, tomlkit), launched via uvx; POSIX only; stdio transport (streamable-http is experimental).
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.tests: Large suite of about 80 unit files plus contract, parity (frozen recorded fixtures against the TS reference), property (hypothesis), security, load and integration tests, with pyright, ruff, actionlint and a parallel CI matrix (.github/workflows/ci.yml). Release-please releases 0.1.0 to 0.7.0 in 7 days. I did not run any of it (static read only).
security: API key handling is careful. Keys come from env only, plus an optional 0600 key file in a 0700 dir (keyfile.py, fsutil). Every SecretStr setting is redacted from logs and error text (ADR-0008/0017, settings.py:250-276). Provider URL, model and key can never be set by tool arguments (ADR-0008), which closes an SSRF and key-exfiltration route.

Key is passed via env reference (${VAR}), never argv. setup refuses a key on the command line (setup.py). The one exception is the Claude Desktop --desktop-key flag, which writes the key in plaintext to that app's config, but that is not relevant to Claude Code.

No curl|sh, no postinstall (PyPI wheel via uvx). subprocess use is limited to: a fixed-argv git diff for the gate CLI (cli.py:150,207), a sandboxed regex worker for jev_extract (extract/worker.py:229), and the installer's verify/launch --version checks. Regexes run in a worker pool with stdlib re (ADR-0004/0018), so ReDoS is contained.

No telemetry phone-home. Telemetry is local spans/metrics. Prompt payload capture is off unless JEV_MCP_TELEMETRY_PAYLOADS is set (SECURITY.md). The response cache is off by default. If enabled it writes judged state to ~/.cache/jev-mcp at mode 0600.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool arguments are model-authored and can contain attacker text from fetched pages. The repo itself admits that jev-1.13 does not treat state as hostile and that injected instructions can move an answer (skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md, verify anti-injection ADR-0068). The jev_screen tool is itself a Jev judgment, so it is not a hard security boundary.

Supply chain: a single maintainer (elkaix, 203 of 210 commits, remainder bot) and an account about a week old. Hard version caps on mcp and typesafe-sdk because it uses their private internals (pyproject.toml comments). Pin ==0.7.0 and review before bumping.
hook gate treats a provider failure as ask (not allow), and never emits allow. In the required mode this can interrupt work, and in bypass mode it may prompt you unexpectedly.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.dataEgress: MCP tools: only the arguments the model puts into a tool call go to the provider (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions). That is evidence text, diffs, test logs, candidate lists and fetched pages, plus the question and options. Jev never sees the wider conversation. Nothing is sent automatically for a turn you did not trigger. OpenRouter therefore receives whatever the agent chooses to pass, which can be client code, since jev_gate, jev_review and jev_verify take raw diffs and logs. The verify and screen tools have no size cap. Headers sent: Bearer key, HTTP-Referer = the GitHub repo URL, X-Title jev-mcp. Optional hook gate: sends cwd, permission mode, tool name, and the full Bash command or Write/Edit input (through redact_action pattern redaction, hook.py:170-192) to the provider on EVERY watched tool call, so Write/Edit file contents leave the machine per edit. No other network destinations found in the code (grep of URLs).
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.failureMode: MCP tools fail closed and visibly. A missing key returns an error in the tool result, an invalid provider answer becomes invalid_response, and an unknown confidence never reaches auto (policy). Claude then falls back to normal checks, as the agent rules tell it to. Timeouts: each attempt has a 30 s timeout, up to 3 attempts with backoff, inside a 90 s budget (retry.py, README operator notes). Over stdio there is no whole-call deadline (ADR-0021 stdio-attempt-deadline), so a call can stall Claude for up to about 90 s in the worst case; cancellation is propagated. hook gate: missing credentials or bad stdin are fail-open (silent), but a provider error or timeout gives ask with a 30 s hook timeout, and JEV_HOOK_REQUIRED=1 makes missing credentials ask too. completion-hook: fail-open on provider errors, silent on non-push commands.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.latencyImpact: Jev itself: median 464.6 ms, p90 1245 ms, p95 1469 ms over 157 calls (repo's bench150). Each MCP call is also an extra Claude tool turn. The repo's own agent studies measured +4.6 s median wall time per task for Claude Code and +10.4 s for forced calls on Pi. First launch through uvx has a cold build and download cost (their smoke test needs a 'cold-build budget'), and the server pre-warms a regex pool at startup (ADR-0058). The opt-in hook gate adds about 0.5 to 1.5 s (plus a Python process spawn) to EVERY Bash/Write/Edit, which on an all-day session is significant. completion-hook only costs time on git push and PR commands.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.contextCost: 11 tools. The repo's frozen snapshot of the 10 original tool definitions is 18,353 JSON chars (about 4.6k tokens); jev_score adds roughly 0.6-0.8k, so about 5.2-5.5k tokens if tool schemas are loaded eagerly. Claude Code's tool search defers MCP schemas, so the steady-state cost is 11 tool names plus the server 'instructions' string. That string is about 1.5k chars (about 375 tokens), built in instructions.py, and includes the on-demand policy text. The optional hooks inject no text into context (they emit only a permission JSON). The jev-mcp skill is an MCP resource/prompt, so it costs nothing unless read. The recommended CLAUDE.md rule block adds about 700 tokens if the user pastes it in.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools. Guidance arrives through the server instructions (instructions.py: 'jev_gate is the recommended final judgment before claiming done... unless tests... already settle completion'; jev_screen before reading external text; jev_verify for other agents' reports), an optional CLAUDE.md rule block (docs/agent-rules.md) and MCP-served skills. There is no deterministic trigger by default, and install does not enable hooks. Deterministic triggering exists only via two opt-in PreToolUse hooks: hook gate (Bash|Write|Edit, all actions) and completion-hook (git push / gh pr create / gh pr merge, but it needs pre-made claims and tests files from env vars, so it is awkward to run automatically). The repo's own bench shows that when the agent is left to choose, it called Jev on 0 of 150 tasks (Pi/DeepSeek), and one Pi pair never called it at all. Claude Code's selection behavior with these instructions is only measured on a tiny study.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (providers/openrouter.py:18, resolver.py:138), using the alpha Decisions API with slug typesafe/jev-1.13. Only OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... plus JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is needed, and no TypeSafe account is required.

The most complete and best-documented Jev integration found. It covers 11 tools that map onto real coding steps (done-claim gate, patch review, injection screen, docs-vs-code drift, candidate rerank), plus a policy layer that fails closed (unknown confidence never returns auto).

Strong secret hygiene for a week-old project: env-only credentials, redaction derived from the settings schema, no per-call provider override (SSRF closed), key file 0600, no telemetry phone-home, no curl|sh or postinstall.

Unusually honest evidence: the README itself reports the agent was slower with Jev (Claude Code +4.6 s, 6/9 solved both ways) and that automatic use left Jev uncalled on 150/150. It says to skip Jev when tests, types or lint already settle the answer. This matches a senior dev's 'add value or stay out of the way' need.

Provides real deterministic hook hooks (hook gate, completion-hook) that can only deny or ask (never allow), so they can add a safety net on top of the user's existing hooks. The hooks live in separate opt-in JSON fragments (docs/harness/*.hooks.json) that can be merged by hand, and they do not break the existing secret-guard or GitNexus hooks since PreToolUse hooks compose.
Large test suite and CI (unit, property, parity against a frozen TS reference, security, load), pinned dependency bounds, and a version-pinnable uvx launch (==0.7.0).
cons: Automatic use is not really delivered by the MCP alone. The model decides whether to call the tools, and the server's own studies show it often does not (0/150 on Pi). To make Claude Code use it reliably the user must add CLAUDE.md rules and/or hooks, and the repo has no plugin manifest or Claude Code SKILL.md, so it is not a one-step 'automatic' integration.

Its own numbers argue against heavy use in daily coding: slower with Jev on every solved pair, no accuracy gain measured, 140k vs 36k tokens per solved task in the 2026-09-27 study, and no certified operating points (docs/EVIDENCE.md). The policy thresholds are inherited parity defaults, not calibrated on Jev.

The opt-in hook gate would send every Bash command and every Write/Edit body (after pattern redaction) to OpenRouter and add roughly 0.5-1.5 s per call, all day, on client projects. It turns provider errors into 'ask', which in an unattended bypass/auto session may block or interrupt.

Client-code egress: jev_gate/review/verify take raw diffs and logs, and jev_verify/jev_screen have no size cap. On client projects, model-chosen tool calls can ship proprietary code to a third party (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe). The user needs a per-project disable or a permissions deny rule.
completion-hook is hard to use automatically: it needs JEV_COMPLETION_CLAIMS and JEV_COMPLETION_TESTS files that something must produce before every push.

Setup tooling assumes a TypeSafe key: setup verifies against TypeSafe, and install writes ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} references (install/launch.py:25,186). The OpenRouter route needs a hand-written MCP entry, and an unset ${VAR} reference can break server start.

Young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-23, 29 stars, 3 forks, 7 releases in 7 days, 203 of 210 commits from one author), with private-API dependence on the mcp SDK (bounded to >=2.2,<2.3). It uses only the alpha Decisions endpoint, pins 'jev-latest' to jev-1.13 in code, and POSIX only.

Injection weakness is acknowledged: jev-1.13 does not treat state as hostile, so jev_screen is a soft filter. The Jev model may also be a cheap router (unverified skeptic claim), and this repo's quality numbers (89/92 on the JevBench subset) are self-run and small-n.
gh-pymodel-jev-judge-mcp.verdict: The best-engineered and only OpenRouter-native Jev MCP found, and the most sensible base for a Claude Code integration: register it by hand with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, and pin the version. It only gives model-discretion, not guaranteed, automatic use. Its own benchmarks show Jev makes the agent slower with no measured accuracy gain, so limit the automatic part to the tools plus a short CLAUDE.md rule (jev_gate before done/PR when tests do not settle it, jev_screen for fetched web text), and skip the per-action hook gate on client work.

gh-abhishekashokvkumar-jev-mcp-dispatche.whatItDoes: Despite the candidate label "mcp-server", this is NOT an MCP server. It is a standalone Python CLI/REPL (jev_mcp_dispatcher.py, 751 lines) that acts as an MCP CLIENT: it spawns a stdio MCP server (default: a bundled song-player demo, overridable via MCP_SERVER_COMMAND), lists its tools, then routes a typed-in natural-language command to a tool using Jev Choice/Noul primitives (tool pick, per-word yes/no highlighting for argument extraction, enum Choice, compound-command splitting) and calls the tool. It is a proof of concept demonstrating Jev-only tool dispatch, and has no Claude Code integration (no hooks, no skill, no plugin, no .mcp.json).

The README is honest about its limits, including a clear caveats list, with pinned dependencies and .env gitignored.

Cannot fulfil the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told). It has no integration surface and does not sit in Claude Code's loop.

Solves a problem Claude Code does not have: Opus already does tool selection and argument extraction natively, with far better accuracy than per-word yes/no highlighting. Its own README admits the design cannot handle pronouns, computed values, optional parameters, nested types, or paraphrase.

OpenRouter is not supported in code. Only the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override might make it work, and model naming and auth were not verified.

gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.name: chy4pro/jev-in-mcp
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP relay/gateway (TypeScript, 858 LOC). Sits between Claude Code and your real MCP servers: it connects to them as a client (config in ~/.config/jev-in-mcp/config.json), re-exports every downstream tool as <server>__<tool>, adds <server>__use_jev(goal) per server plus one global use_jev(goal) and jev_status. use_jev runs a loop (via jev-dev-kit runLoop): each step POSTs a Choice decision to Jev (candidates = that server's tools, plus enum/boolean params as extra choices), executes the chosen tool on the downstream server, and repeats up to max_steps (default 20). String/number params that Jev cannot choose are written by the calling Claude model via MCP sampling or a needs_input/session round trip. It is NOT a hook or a code-aware tool: it only routes tool calls among MCP servers.

Key is sent only as Bearer header (jev.ts:11), never argv. Setup page is plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 random port with no CSRF/Origin check (a malicious local web page could POST and switch provider/model, but cannot read the key); form values are reflected unescaped (setup.ts model value attribute) minor self-XSS.

'import' copies every server's env and headers (GITHUB_TOKEN etc.) from ~/.claude.json, including all per-project sections, into a second plaintext file config.json (mode 0600) - secrets duplicated at rest; the importer reads ~/.claude.json wholesale.

Bypass surface: replacing your MCP servers with the relay moves them behind a gateway. Downstream tools run with the relay's process env (downstream.ts:20 merges process.env). use_jev lets a 300 ms classifier auto-execute tool calls; the only guard is per-tool deny lists (delete_repository etc. must be listed by hand); Claude Code permission prompts see only 'use_jev', not the underlying tool, so hooks/permissions keyed to mcp__gitnexus__* or mcp__playwright__* would not apply to calls made inside use_jev.

Prompt-injection: downstream tool results (first 800 chars) are fed back into Jev state and drive next tool choices, and result text is returned to Claude; Jev can only pick among listed tools, but a poisoned web page/file could steer which tools run in the loop.

Dependency jev-dev-kit pulled from a GitHub tag (github:chy4pro/jev-dev-kit#v0.4.0), 'prepare' script builds on install (arbitrary build-time code from a 1-star repo). Not on npm (404), so 'npx -y jev-in-mcp' in README does not work today; install requires npm install -g github:... . No telemetry found.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (or the endpoint override) on every use_jev step: the goal text, the server/tool names and descriptions (candidate sentences), plus the last calls with arguments and results truncated to result_chars=800 each (relay.ts:210, 238; encode() actually sends all recorded calls of the run, results 800 chars each). Tool results can contain file contents, page snapshots, code, and secrets that pass through the downstream servers. Nothing is sent when Claude calls the passed-through <server>__<tool> tools directly. With sampling, values are written by the Claude model (already Anthropic). HTTP-Referer/X-Title identify the app to OpenRouter.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude level in the sense that Claude can still call the pass-through tools directly, but weak handling inside: jev.ts:17-30 retries 429/503/529 up to 3 times with 0.8/1.6/3.2 s backoff, other errors throw; there is NO fetch timeout or AbortSignal anywhere (grep found none), so a hung connection would hang the use_jev call until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout. If no key is set, use_jev returns an explanatory error (relay.ts:165) and pass-through still works. A downstream server that fails to connect is recorded and skipped (downstream.ts:30-32), but the relay is now a single point of failure for ALL migrated MCP servers: if it crashes at startup (e.g. missing dist/jev-dev-kit build), gitnexus, playwright, etc. all disappear.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.contextCost: Tool count = N downstream tools (all re-exposed under longer names, so no savings and they add a 'mcp__jev__server__' prefix) + one <server>__use_jev per server + global use_jev + jev_status. For gitnexus (~17) + playwright (~26) + caveman-shrink: about 45 passthrough tools (roughly equal to today's token cost, plus a few tokens each for longer names and '[server]' prefixes) plus about 5 new tools. Each use_jev description is ~330 chars plus a list of all usable tool names (playwright's would be ~500+ chars) and a ~700 char JSON schema, so roughly 200-300 tokens each: about 1.0-1.5k extra tokens total. No server 'instructions' field, no hook-injected text. Claude Code tool-search deferral would hide them anyway, but the value is negative: it also prevents the built-in per-server deferral grouping.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.latencyImpact: Per use_jev step: about 270-730 ms Jev latency observed by author (median ~300-485 ms) plus tool execution plus, for text params, an extra Claude sampling/needs_input round trip; author's live runs took 4.5-10 s per simple filesystem task (mostly the writer model). Pass-through calls add one extra stdio hop (small). Nothing runs automatically per turn, so no added latency on turns that do not call use_jev. For a single-step task Claude calling the tool directly is faster than use_jev.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill, or proxy. Claude decides whether to call use_jev based solely on the tool description ('Use it for multi-step tasks whose every value is in the goal'). Since Claude has direct access to the same tools (pass-through) and is a stronger planner, it will rarely prefer use_jev; this does not meet the 'used automatically when useful, without asking' requirement and gives no deterministic trigger. It also would not intercept built-in tools (Read/Edit/Bash/Grep), only MCP tools.
pros: Genuine OpenRouter support in code: default endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, accepts OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/jev.ts:10, config.ts:44,80); endpoint is overridable so it can follow /api/v1/systemone if needed.
Small, readable codebase (858 LOC), MIT, key stored 0600 and not in argv; setup page keeps key out of chat.

Sensible design for a niche: Jev only chooses among enumerated tools/enums, the calling model writes free-text values, deny/allow lists and per-tool description overrides exist, max_steps cap, stuck/repeat detection via the kit.
Handles sampling and a needs_input/session fallback; skips servers that fail to connect.
Author documents a live 6/6 run on OpenRouter (and Vercel gateway) with Jev per-step latency ~300 ms.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for daily coding: it automates chains of MCP tool calls (filesystem, github, browser) that Claude already does better; Claude Code's core work uses built-in Read/Edit/Bash/Grep which the relay cannot see. Only evidence is a 6-task filesystem demo; 'Other servers have not been tried yet' (README).
Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with no hook; Claude has the raw tools too and will rarely pick use_jev. Fails the user's key requirement.

Invasive install: you must replace gitnexus/playwright/caveman-shrink entries with a single 'jev' server, changing every tool name to mcp__jev__<server>__<tool>. This breaks existing hooks/matchers, skills (gitnexus-* skills reference mcp__gitnexus__*), permission allowlists, and makes the relay a single point of failure for all MCP servers.

Security regression: use_jev executes downstream tools autonomously inside one opaque call; permission prompts and PreToolUse hooks (secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit; GitNexus hooks) never see the inner calls (e.g. playwright browser_run_code_unsafe is a candidate unless denied). Tool results (page/file contents) are sent to OpenRouter.

Immature: created 2026-09-20, 9 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 0 forks, no CI (.github absent), 3 test files, v0.1.1, not on npm (npm view 404, so README's 'npx -y jev-in-mcp' fails), depends on a 1-star github-only package jev-dev-kit#v0.4.0 built at install ('prepare').

No fetch timeout/AbortSignal; retries only on 429/503/529; worst case hangs until Claude Code's MCP timeout. Setup page has no CSRF protection; import duplicates all secrets into a second plaintext file.

Jev's Choice primitive over dozens of Playwright/GitNexus tools degrades with candidate-set size (DESIGN.md admits this), yielding a global two-stage workaround; browser and graph tools require object/array params that Jev cannot express and are excluded from use_jev (candidates.ts unsupportedReason).
Context: +5 tools with long descriptions and full duplicate re-export of ~45 existing tools, with no saving.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.verdict: A well-scoped proof of concept that really does talk to OpenRouter Jev, but it is an MCP-to-MCP tool-routing gateway, not a coding assistant: it is model-discretion only, requires replacing your existing MCP servers with a single relay (breaking hooks, skills and tool names, and hiding inner calls from your permission/secret-guard hooks), and is one-star, one-week-old, unpublished on npm. Do not adopt it for daily Claude Code use; at most study it as a reference for how to format Choice requests against /api/alpha/decisions.
gh-chy4pro-jev-in-mcp.install: Not on npm (npm view jev-in-mcp: 404). gh-ndolinschi-mcpmatch.name: ndolinschi/mcpmatch
gh-ndolinschi-mcpmatch.whatItDoes: Not an MCP server, hook or skill. It is a private Next.js 15 demo web app (UI in src/app/page.tsx plus one POST route, /api/decide) that takes a typed user goal and picks from a hard-coded catalog of about 40 fake MCP tools. It uses a two-stage Jev Choice: first a category, then a tool within that category. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY it silently falls back to local softmax heuristics and reports mode "demo". It has no Claude Code integration and does not read the user's real installed MCP servers. The README is 6 lines.

gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.name: agent-fastpath (abhishekswe/agent-fastpath, npm: agent-fastpath)
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server that wraps TypeSafe Jev (System One) behind opinionated presets (ship_gate, risk, severity, ambiguity, relevance, verify_claim, classify, intent, rank, compare, extract_fields). Deterministic regex rules run first (failing test logs, git push --force, rm -rf, DROP TABLE); otherwise one Jev call, then a local confidence gate maps the answer to accept/review/escalate. It also offers server-side file triage (reads up to 500 files locally, sends 4,000-char redacted excerpts to Jev, returns top-N snippets) and a Playwright headless browser with SSRF proxy and an irreversible-action gate. It is a caller-driven decision tool, not a router or a transparent proxy.

providerSupport.evidence: packages/provider-typesafe/src/client.ts:30-32: apiKey = options.apiKey || process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY; endpoint = options.endpoint || 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'; model = 'jev-latest'. packages/mcp-server/src/server.ts:41-45 createJudgmentProvider reads only env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY and never passes an endpoint, so no env var can override the URL. grep for openrouter, api/alpha and OPENROUTER finds nothing in packages/ or docs/. Only TypeSafe direct plus a keyword mock (FASTPATH_JUDGMENT=mock). Payload is {state, model, questions:{k:{type,instructions,criteria}}} with Authorization: Bearer (client.ts:52-75). Answers are parsed from data.answers (client.ts:91), normalized in questions.ts:42-76.
providerSupport.others: None. docs/providers.md documents a JudgmentProvider interface for swapping implementations, but only TypeSafe and mock ship.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, roughly a 10-20 line fork. Add OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_ENDPOINT/JEV_MODEL env handling in server.ts:41-45 and client.ts:30-33. Change the endpoint to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and the model to typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. This assumes OpenRouter's System One API uses the same {state, model, questions} in and {answers} out schema as the TypeSafe direct API. I could not verify that: the OpenRouter docs URL I tried returned 404. The Decisions API at /api/alpha/decisions is a different surface and would need a real adapter. Because the endpoint is hardcoded, using it as-is means a TypeSafe key and console.typesafe.ai, not OpenRouter.

interface.name: fastpath_evaluate
interface.purpose: Typed choice/score/noul questions over text. Takes a preset or custom questions plus a confidence policy. Returns status accept/review/escalate, answers, reasonCode, recommendedAction and a traceId. Deterministic rules run before any Jev call (server.ts:93-101, tools/evaluate.ts).

interface.name: fastpath_triage
interface.purpose: Ranks up to 500 files or inline items against a query. The server reads files inside FASTPATH_ROOTS (default cwd), 64KB each, sends 4,000-char redacted excerpts to Jev with 8-way concurrency, and returns the top-N snippets (tools/triage.ts:16-24).

interface.name: fastpath_browser
interface.purpose: Headless Playwright, one step at a time (modes open/observe/act/choose/check/run_bounded/close). Returns a compact element table with obs_id:n refs. SSRF-checked egress proxy; irreversible actions need allowIrreversible. Needs `npx playwright install chromium`.

interface.name: fastpath_evidence
interface.purpose: Looks up a previous result by traceId (last 500 traces held in memory).

interface.name: fastpath_capabilities
interface.purpose: Reports the active provider, presets, limits and security config, without secrets.

interface.name: CLI: start | doctor | install-config <client>
interface.purpose: start runs the stdio MCP server. doctor checks Node, the key and the browser. install-config prints client configs for 12 clients. No hooks, no skills, no plugin.json, no .mcp.json.

gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.runtime: Node >=20.12 (TypeScript, esbuild bundle), deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, commander, playwright, zod. Runs via `npx -y agent-fastpath start`; Playwright Chromium is downloaded separately for the browser tool.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.install: claude mcp add agent-fastpath -s user -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key> -- npx -y agent-fastpath start   (README:27). The key lands in ~/.claude.json env, not in the npx argv. It needs a TypeSafe key, not OpenRouter, unless forked.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.tests: About 52 test cases: unit tests for deterministic rules, gate, network policy and normalization; integration tests for evaluate and triage; e2e browser tests; a CLI smoke test. A live-scenario suite and a benchmark need a real key. CI runs Node 20/22/24 with Playwright, plus CodeQL and dependency-review workflows. Only 3 tags and 2 npm versions (0.1.1, 0.2.0). No GitHub release object.
security: The API key is passed by env (`-e TYPESAFE_API_KEY`), stored in ~/.claude.json, and sent as a Bearer header. It does not appear in the npx argv. It is redacted from state by the TypeSafe key pattern in deterministic_engine.ts:210.

Redaction is regex-based (deterministic_engine.ts:169-247): private keys, ts_/apikey_ keys, sk-ant, sk-, ghp_, AKIA, xox, Bearer, *_API_KEY= assignments and JSON password fields. It does not cover an OPENROUTER key format (sk-or-v1-... matches the generic sk- rule only if 32 or more chars, which is likely) or arbitrary proprietary secrets. The docs admit it is not DLP.

No postinstall or preinstall scripts and no telemetry found by grep. `npx -y` runs the latest published version unpinned, so a compromised release would auto-execute. Pin agent-fastpath@0.2.0 to mitigate.

cli/src/index.ts:13-22 calls process.loadEnvFile on ./.env in the cwd, so a project's .env is loaded into the server process env. It is not sent anywhere, but it can pull in a client project's TYPESAFE_API_KEY or FASTPATH_* overrides. This is odd behaviour for client work.

Prompt-injection surface: the browser tool feeds page text to the judge (acknowledged in SECURITY.md) and triage feeds file content. Impact is limited to skewing a decision, and the confidence gate escalates on low confidence. Filesystem access is confined to FASTPATH_ROOTS with symlink resolution. Browser SSRF is enforced by a per-session egress proxy. Chromium runs with its sandbox on, unless FASTPATH_BROWSER_NO_SANDBOX=1.
Single maintainer, 3 stars, project 9 days old. The supply-chain trust level is low for use on client code.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone only (hardcoded, client.ts:31): the redacted `state` string the calling agent passes to fastpath_evaluate (logs, diffs, requirements, up to 262,144 bytes by default) plus the question definitions. fastpath_triage sends the first 4,000 redacted chars of each ranked file, up to 500 files per call, read from disk by the server. That is source code excerpts leaving the machine, though they stay out of Claude's context. Browser page text may go to Jev for choose/check. Deterministic verdicts stay local. No prompt/conversation data is sent unless Claude puts it in `state`. Playwright itself does normal web browsing. There is no other telemetry. For client projects, note that source excerpts go to a third-party (TypeSafe today, OpenRouter after a patch).
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.failureMode: Fail-open, advisory. Retries: 2 with 100/200ms backoff on timeout, 429 and 5xx. A 4xx fails immediately (client.ts:62-110). Default timeout is 5000ms per attempt, so worst case is about 15s plus backoff unless the caller sets deadlineMs. On failure or a missing key, the tool returns status 'error' (PROVIDER_ERROR) or 'escalate' (JUDGMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE) with recommendedAction 'fallback_large_model' (capability_router.ts:103-129). Claude just proceeds on its own. Nothing blocks the session and there are no hooks to hang. Deterministic rules keep working offline. A dead Jev costs Claude a wasted tool call and up to about 15s.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.latencyImpact: Deterministic path is under 1 ms plus MCP stdio overhead. A Jev call is one HTTP request (claimed 70-500 ms; README says "milliseconds to a couple of seconds"). Triage runs at most 8 concurrent calls, one per file, so 500 files is about 63 sequential batches. Cold start via `npx -y` adds a registry check and maybe 1-3 s at session start. The browser tool adds Chromium startup. It adds no latency to normal turns because nothing is on the hot path, since there are no hooks.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.contextCost: 5 tools, all always loaded (no MCP server instructions, no hooks, no skill). Estimated 2,000-2,800 tokens for names, descriptions and zod schemas. fastpath_evaluate has a large schema (discriminated union of questions, policy object, presets) at about 900 tokens, fastpath_browser about 600, triage about 400, evidence and capabilities about 100 each. Each call's result is compact JSON, but the evaluate result carries full answers and traces. Claude Code may defer these via ToolSearch, lowering the idle cost. Compared with the existing gitnexus (17 tools) and playwright (26 tools), this is small, but fastpath_browser duplicates the playwright MCP already installed.
gh-abhishekswe-agent-fastpath.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions ("Answer typed questions about a piece of text...", "Rank files... without reading them into your context") are the only trigger. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no proxy. Opus will call them only when it judges them useful, and in practice it is unlikely to volunteer a ship-gate/risk call on its own, especially when it can read a log directly. Reliable automation would need a user-written PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook or CLAUDE.md rules, which this project does not provide.
pros: It is the only candidate here that is a real Jev consumer with a working, tested wrapper: presets, normalization of choice/score/noul into one confidence scale (questions.ts:42-76) and a margin/confidence gate (escalation_gate.ts). This is a sensible pattern for using System One.
Deterministic rules run before any API call (deterministic_engine.ts). `git push --force`, rm -rf, DROP TABLE and failing test logs cost nothing and never leave the machine.
Fail-open, honest degradation: missing key or outage yields escalate/error with 'fallback_large_model' and never a fabricated answer (capability_router.ts:103-129). No hook can hang the session.
Small tool surface (5 tools, about 2-3k tokens), no postinstall and no telemetry found. Secret redaction runs before egress. Triage roots are confined by symlink-resolving checks.
MIT licensed, small readable codebase (about 4.4k lines TS) with CI on Node 20/22/24, CodeQL and dependency-review. Easy to fork and patch for OpenRouter.
The JudgmentProvider interface (docs/providers.md) is a clean seam for adding an OpenRouter provider.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and there is no env override (client.ts:31, server.ts:43). It needs a TypeSafe key, or a fork to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. The wire-schema equivalence is unverified.
Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool, with no hook or skill. Claude must decide to call it, which the user explicitly does not want to depend on.

Value proposition is thin for a senior dev on Opus. The typical Claude Code workflow already reads test output directly and has permission and secret-guard hooks. Ship-gate and risk regexes duplicate what Claude sees, and a Jev call adds a network hop and trust in a beta model (Theo's 'flash router' claim is unverified).

fastpath_triage sends 4,000-char source excerpts per file, up to 500 files per call, to a third party. That is a real code-egress path that is a problem for client projects (redaction is regex-only), and it contradicts the 'keeps files out of context' framing (README acknowledges this).
fastpath_browser duplicates the already-installed playwright MCP and adds a second Chromium.
Immature and single-maintainer: 9 days old, 3 stars, 24 commits, 2 npm versions, no releases. `npx -y` is unpinned, and cli/index.ts:15-21 loads the cwd .env into the server process.

Worst-case failure latency is about 15s (5s timeout x 3 attempts) unless deadlineMs is passed, wasted whenever Jev is down. Score dimension is 0-based and preset outputs are opinionated, so custom needs mean writing question schemas anyway.

It is a reasonable code reference or fork base for an OpenRouter-backed hook or MCP, but I would not install it as-is for daily client work because of triage code egress, unpinned npx and overlap with existing tools.

gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.name: VishiATChoudhary/toolJev
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.whatItDoes: Python MCP gateway (FastMCP) that sits in front of your other MCP servers and replaces their tool lists with just two tools: search(query) and execute(code, session). search does BM25 + bge-base embedding recall, then one Jev call to rerank and score fit. execute runs agent-written Python in a Pydantic Monty sandbox where upstream tools are mcp.<server>.<tool>() and jev.choice/noul/score/ask/map do bulk typed decisions. Aimed at 100s of tools and bulk per-item triage, not at general coding assistance.

providerSupport.evidence: tooljev/decider.py:37-68 HostedJev wraps typesafe_sdk.AsyncTypeSafeClient(api_key=None, model='jev-latest', ...) and calls client.system_one(state, questions); no openrouter string anywhere in repo (grep). Key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (README:86,106; decider.py:38). SDK typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 sdist: constants.py:15 DEFAULT_BASE_URL='https://api.typesafe.ai', constants.py:6 BASE_URL_ENV='TYPESAFE_BASE_URL'; _core/constants.py:5 SYSTEM_ONE_PATH='/v1/systemone'; transport.py:121 header 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'; transport.py:134 URL=base_url+path. So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with a Bearer key. Model passes through config: make_decider(**cfg.decider) (server.py:29) so [decider] model='typesafe/jev-1.13' is forwarded to HostedJev(model=...). Response-schema parity with OpenRouter's /systemone is unverified.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: trivial in theory, zero code change: env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, and [decider] model='typesafe/jev-1.13' (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Risks: OpenRouter's /systemone request/response shape must match TypeSafe's (unverified, not tested by me), and SDK strict pydantic parsing could reject extra/missing OpenRouter fields (e.g. usage/provider metadata). If it breaks, a ~30-line httpx subclass of HostedJev.decide is a moderate fix. Not running code, so untested.
providerSupport.others: Local 'nanojev' backend (separate repo VishiATChoudhary/nanojev, git dependency, torch/transformers, NLI encoder or small LM) needs no key but was measured much less accurate (README:53, config.py comments).

interface.name: MCP tool search(query: str)
interface.purpose: Finds up to 5 upstream tools for a plain-language request; returns Python signatures plus per-tool fit probability and an in_catalog warning when nothing fits. Uses BM25+dense recall then Jev rerank (server.py:48-58, search.py).

interface.name: MCP tool execute(code: str, session: str|None)
interface.purpose: Runs agent-written Python in a Monty sandbox with mcp.<server>.<tool>(**kw), jev.choice/noul/score/ask/map, FINAL(), print(); limits 120s wall, 20s CPU, 256MB, 2000 calls, 16 concurrent, stdout 4000 chars; optional named REPL sessions (max 8) (server.py:60-66, sandbox.py:36-66).

interface.name: CLI tooljev --config FILE [--transport stdio|http] [--host] [--port 8765]
interface.purpose: Starts the gateway; needs a TOML listing upstream servers (server.py:71-82).

interface.name: Config [decider]/[servers.*]/[search]/[sandbox]
interface.purpose: Upstream servers as command/args/env or url/headers with optional allow-list; decider backend hosted or nanojev (config.py).

gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.runtime: Python >=3.11 (uv), deps fastmcp>=4.0, pydantic-monty>=1.0, typesafe-sdk>=0.7; optional sentence-transformers (torch) for dense recall, nanojev via git. Install from git clone + uv pip install -e; not on PyPI.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.install: git clone https://github.com/VishiATChoudhary/toolJev && cd toolJev && uv venv && uv pip install -e ".[retrieval]"; write tooljev.toml listing upstreams; claude mcp add tooljev -- uv --directory /path/to/toolJev run tooljev --config /path/to/tooljev.toml
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.tests: 4 test files, about 44 test functions (sandbox 20, search 15, decider 6, server 3), fake decider and in-process servers; CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs pytest -m 'not slow and not hosted' on py3.11/3.12. Hosted tests skipped without TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Large bench/ directory with results; benchmark upstreams are mocks; agent runs 36 tasks per setup, 1-2 reps (own caveat in README).
security: No API key in argv: key read from env by the SDK; SDK logging redacts Authorization headers (logging.py:45).

Upstream server secrets (e.g. GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN) live in plaintext in tooljev.toml env/headers tables; you would have to duplicate every upstream (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) into this file and they would be spawned as children of tooljev.

README states 'The sandbox is not authorization': agent-written Python can call any allowed upstream tool, including destructive ones (playwright run_code_unsafe, gh tokens), with no per-call approval prompt per tool; Claude Code's normal per-tool permission/hook gates (secret-leak guard PreToolUse on Bash|Read|Grep, GitNexus hooks) would not see the inner mcp.* calls, only the single execute call. In bypass/auto mode this is a large hole.
Monty sandbox has no filesystem/network/env access per README/sandbox.py:9; bounded by CPU/mem/call caps. Sandbox escape risk is that of a young third-party interpreter (pydantic-monty).

Persistent unredacted JSONL trace of every search query, every executed code string and every host-call args/results at ~/.tooljev/traces/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (trace.py:11-18, server.py:57,64), on by default with no rotation; would accumulate client code/secrets returned by tools.
Prompt-injection surface: upstream tool results flow into sandbox variables and Jev state; Jev returns only typed probabilities so it cannot inject text, but agent-written code acts on them.

No postinstall/curl|sh; install is git clone + uv. Unpinned dependency on git repo nanojev (pyproject tool.uv.sources) only for the local extra. Single-author 2-day-old repo, no releases, no security policy.
No telemetry in tooljev itself; TypeSafe SDK sends User-Agent/SDK/runtime headers.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint only: search query text plus the top-15 candidate tool names/descriptions (search.py) and, in execute, whatever state you pass to jev.* (tool results such as ticket bodies, file/issue text, arbitrary JSON) along with question instructions. Not sent automatically: Claude Code prompts, repo files, diffs, unless the agent's code passes them to jev. Local disk: full traces of queries, code and tool call args/results to ~/.tooljev/traces. Embeddings (bge-base) run locally. Upstream servers see calls as normal.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.failureMode: Fail-closed per call: HostedJev.decide retries 429/529 via SDK (max_retries=3) plus 4 attempts with 1s/2s/4s backoff on 5xx/timeout, client timeout 30s (decider.py:43-68), then raises DecisionError. In search this makes the search tool error (no visible fallback to retrieval-only found in decider.py; search.py not exhaustively audited for try/except); in execute it surfaces as an exception in agent code. Worst case a single call can block roughly 30s x 4 plus 7s backoff. Because all upstream tools are hidden behind tooljev, if the gateway process or an upstream fails to start, the tools vanish from Claude Code entirely.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.latencyImpact: Per search: local BM25/embedding few ms + one hosted Jev round trip, README measured about 285 ms p50 (74 ms local). Extra turn cost: Code Mode needs search then execute, so 2 model turns before any real tool call; README's own agent bench shows 34 s vs 18 s for Claude Code's native tool search. First start loads bge-base embeddings (torch, seconds) and spawns all upstream servers.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.contextCost: Tiny: 2 tools (search, execute). execute description is PRELUDE_DOC about 2.3k chars (~600 tokens) plus schema; search doc ~350 chars; server INSTRUCTIONS ~500 chars (~125 tokens). Total roughly 800-1000 tokens. No hooks inject text. But adopting it would mean hiding the existing gitnexus, playwright and caveman-shrink servers behind the gateway, changing their tool naming (mcp__gitnexus__* no longer native) and breaking skills/hooks that reference them.
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. Claude Code decides whether to call search/execute; it only replaces upstream tools if you route them through it. Does not make Claude Code call Jev on its own for coding decisions.
pros: Genuine, working Jev integration with real benchmarks (MCPToolBench++, LiveMCPBench, When2Call, 400-ticket triage): 98.8% accuracy for $0.063 vs $0.332 with Haiku (README:20-30, bench/RESULTS.md).
Very small context footprint (2 tools, ~1k tokens) and pays off at scale: with 612 tools it cut input tokens 77% and cost 28% vs Claude Code's native tool search.
Clean decider abstraction (decider.py) so backend swap is a small change; SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and model config, so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is plausibly env-only.
Honest README: states when not to use it (<100 tools, latency-sensitive), documents negative results and that sandbox is not authorization.
MIT, CI on 3.11/3.12, ~44 offline tests with fake decider, sandbox resource limits, per-server allow-lists, confidence-gated hand-back to the LLM.
cons: Wrong problem for this user: solves large-tool-catalog overload and bulk triage; user has only 3 MCP servers (~50 tools) where README says direct calling is more accurate and cheaper (87 tools: 0.94 vs 0.89).

Not automatic Jev usage in Claude Code: model-discretion tool, and to benefit you must proxy gitnexus/playwright/caveman-shrink through it, breaking native mcp__gitnexus__* names, GitNexus PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks and gitnexus-* skills that match those tools.

Bypasses existing safety: inner mcp.* calls run inside one execute call, so the secret-leak guard hook and Claude Code per-tool permissions do not see them; risky in bypass/auto mode with playwright browser_run_code_unsafe.
Adds latency and turns: search then execute (2 extra turns), README's agent bench 34 s vs 18 s.
Plaintext unredacted local traces of all code and tool results in ~/.tooljev/traces by default; upstream secrets copied into a TOML.

Very immature: created 2026-09-28 (2 days old), 8 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, no release, not on PyPI, alpha classifier; benchmarks use mock upstreams and 1-2 reps of 36 tasks (89% vs 81% is 3 tasks, author's own caveat).

Heavy optional deps (torch, sentence-transformers) for dense recall; OpenRouter response-schema compatibility with typesafe-sdk untested; if Jev fails, search errors with no clear fallback and tools disappear.
Does nothing for the user's actual daily coding decisions (which file to edit, whether to run tests, permission classification).
gh-vishiatchoudhary-tooljev.verdict: A well-built but narrowly scoped Code Mode gateway for hundreds of MCP tools or bulk triage; not a coding-workflow Jev integration and not automatic. For a 3-server setup with permission hooks it adds latency and bypasses guards, so skip it, though its decider.py plus the SDK base_url/env pattern is a useful reference for pointing typesafe-sdk at OpenRouter.

gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.name: Dharundp6/jev-carryforward (npm: carryforward)
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.whatItDoes: Cross-session memory ledger for Claude Code, shipped as a plugin (MCP server + skill + SessionStart hook). Two MCP tools: record appends facts (constraint, correction, decision, measurement, thread) to ~/.carryforward/<project>.jsonl; recall(task) returns pinned rules (constraint/correction) in full and asks Jev one boolean question per remaining entry ("is this still live for the task starting now?"), bucketing by probability (>=0.60 full, 0.30-0.60 one line, else omitted). Jev is only a relevance ranker over the user's own notes. It does not review code and does not route decisions for Claude Code.

providerSupport.evidence: src/gateway.ts:13 MODEL = "typesafe-ai/jev"; gateway.ts:20 requires env.AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; gateway.ts:23,37 calls experimental_evaluate from the Vercel `ai` npm package (^7.0.107), so the repo contains no URL or fetch. grep for openrouter/OPENROUTER/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/fetch( over src/ returns nothing. recall.ts:298 note says AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY not set -> unscored. SECURITY.md confirms Vercel AI Gateway is the only route. server.ts:149 hardwires gatewayAsker().
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway only (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY). Library users can pass a custom Asker(ask(state, questions)) to recall(), but the CLI/MCP server do not expose it.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. Change is confined to src/gateway.ts (46 lines) behind a clean Asker interface, and the question shape (boolean + instructions + criteria) maps well onto OpenRouter Noul/System One. But it is not a base-URL swap: you would replace the `ai` SDK experimental_evaluate call with a hand-written fetch to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or /api/alpha/decisions) using OpenRouter's request/response schema, plus fork and maintain it (or use the library Asker in a wrapper). Roughly 30-60 lines of code.

interface.name: MCP tool record
interface.purpose: Append one fact to the project ledger (kind, obtained, text, ref?, refresh?, supersedes?). Local file write only, no network. Description instructs the model to call it after user rules, corrections, decisions, measurements, parked work.

interface.name: MCP tool recall
interface.purpose: recall(task?) returns pinned constraints/corrections in full plus Jev-scored other entries; falls open to everything if no key, no task or scorer error. Only network call in the package.

interface.name: Skill carryforward (skills/carryforward/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Description-triggered: instructs model to call recall before any non-trivial task and record on rules/corrections/decisions. Model-discretion.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart (startup|clear|compact)
interface.purpose: Runs `npx -y carryforward recall` (25s timeout) to inject pinned rules; the only deterministic path. Note the plugin's hooks.json omits --quiet (README settings snippet uses it).

interface.name: CLI carryforward serve|recall [--quiet] [task]|path
interface.purpose: Run MCP server over stdio; print brief; print ledger path.

security: No shell execution, no postinstall script (package.json scripts are build/typecheck/test/prepublishOnly only); reads/writes only ~/.carryforward/*.jsonl (plain text, unencrypted, ledger.ts:117-118).

Key handling: AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY via env; README install command `claude mcp add carryforward -e AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=$AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY -- npx -y carryforward` expands the secret into argv/shell history and into ~/.claude.json.

Runs via `npx -y carryforward` on every session start (hook) and MCP spawn: unpinned npm fetch of a 2-star, single-maintainer package (dharun7). Supply-chain exposure on every startup; pin a version or vendor if used.
Repo/registry inconsistencies: latest release URL points at github.com/dharun-cohere/jev-carryforward (org rename/transfer), and npm latest is 0.1.0 while repo/plugin manifests say 0.1.1.

Prompt-injection surface: ledger contents are model-authored and are re-injected into context as trusted-looking text, and SKILL says treat 'Always' as binding. A poisoned record (e.g. from a fetched web page or untrusted repo content the model summarised) persists across sessions and is re-injected by a SessionStart hook. Ledger is per-project but global home dir, no integrity or provenance beyond obtained field.
No telemetry in code. SECURITY.md is honest and accurate about egress.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.dataEgress: Only recall(task) with AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY set: the one-sentence task string plus all non-pinned ledger entries (id, kind, obtained, date, text, ref, refresh), batched 25 per request, to Vercel AI Gateway model typesafe-ai/jev (recall.ts:263-272). Constraints and corrections are never sent. No source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent unless the model wrote them into an entry text or ref. record never touches the network. Note: the SessionStart hook runs recall with no task, so no network call there.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.failureMode: Fail-open. No key, no task, or any scorer exception returns the whole ledger unscored with a note (recall.ts:286-320). No explicit timeout on the Jev call; the SDK default applies (the hook has a 25s cap, but the MCP recall tool has none besides the client's). If npx cannot fetch the package (offline/npm down), the hook simply fails non-blocking and the MCP server would fail to start.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.contextCost: 2 tools. Approx 650-800 tokens of tool defs (record description ~1.0k chars, recall ~0.7k chars, schemas ~0.8k chars), plus the skill description (~60 tokens, ~2k chars body loaded when triggered), no MCP server instructions field. SessionStart hook injects the pinned rules (size grows with user's ledger; plugin hooks.json without --quiet also prints the 'ledger is empty' message at every start/clear/compact). Each recall result is a markdown brief of variable size.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.autoInvocation: Mixed. Deterministic only for SessionStart hook (pinned rules injection, no Jev call, no task known). recall/record are model-discretion MCP tools nudged by tool descriptions and a skill description. The project's own eval (README 'What the eval suite found') reports the agent called recall 0 out of 4 runs even with skill installed, so the author himself concedes automatic invocation is unreliable.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.latencyImpact: Per recall with a task: one Jev round trip per 25 non-pinned entries (README claims about 1.4 s for 9 entries; 'about a second' per 100 entries, unverified). Zero latency on record, on ordinary tool calls and on turns. Hook adds npx startup time (node cold start plus possible npm resolution) to every session start/clear/compact.
pros: Genuine, well-scoped Jev use: boolean relevance scoring per entry is the type of typed-decision task Jev is designed for (no free text needed), and it fails open cleanly.
Small, readable codebase (~600 LOC src, 3 test files, CI on Linux+Windows, Node 22/24, MIT). Constraints/corrections never sent to any network.
Clean Asker abstraction (types.ts / recall.ts) makes swapping the scorer to OpenRouter a localized rewrite of src/gateway.ts.
Ships as a proper Claude Code plugin (plugin.json with mcpServers, skills, hooks) and a SessionStart hook that re-injects rules after compaction, which is actually useful for a long-running user.
Honest README: admits 9-entry sample is not proof and that the agent skipped recall 0/4 times.
cons: Not OpenRouter-compatible: hardwired to the Vercel AI Gateway via the `ai` SDK experimental_evaluate; needs a second key and account, or a code fork.

Does not meet the goal of automatic Jev use: Jev is invoked only inside recall, which the model must choose to call; the author's own eval shows 0/4 calls. The one deterministic hook does no Jev scoring (no task at session start).

Solves a memory problem, not a coding-decision problem: Claude Code already has CLAUDE.md, auto-memory and compaction; the user already has GitNexus for graph context. Adds a second, parallel memory store that the model must manually curate via record.
Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 6 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, 0 forks, v0.1.x; npm latest (0.1.0) lags repo (0.1.1); no accuracy evidence, only a 9-entry, 3-task anecdote.

Persistent-injection risk: model-written ledger entries are re-injected as binding 'Always' rules across sessions and hooks; risky on client projects with untrusted content. Ledger also lives in the home dir, unencrypted, shared across all client work unless CARRYFORWARD_PROJECT is managed.
Runtime `npx -y carryforward` unpinned on every session start adds startup latency and supply-chain risk; plugin hooks.json lacks --quiet so empty ledger prints noise.
Adds about 700 tokens of tool defs to every session for a tool that the model tends not to call.
gh-dharundp6-jev-carryforward.verdict: A tidy but early-alpha memory ledger where Jev is a niche relevance ranker, wired only to the Vercel AI Gateway and reachable only if the model chooses to call recall (author's eval: 0/4). It does not deliver automatic OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code; skip it, or at most borrow the Asker pattern.

gh-kierandotai-jev-scout.name: kierandotai/jev-scout
gh-kierandotai-jev-scout.whatItDoes: Node MCP stdio server that replaces Claude Code's WebSearch/WebFetch with guarded_search, guarded_fetch and research_report. interface.name: guarded_search
interface.purpose: Input: query, goal, max_results. Searches through SearXNG, Brave or DDG. Judges the top-k results (default 8) with Jev and returns them with relevance (0-2), credibility (0-2) and worth_fetching. In gate mode it drops results below the thresholds and lists them in `dropped`.

interface.name: guarded_fetch
interface.purpose: Input: url, goal. Runs an SSRF-guarded fetch and text extraction, then one Jev call returning answered, content_class and steering_risk (advisory prompt-injection flag). Judgment fields are emitted before the text.

interface.name: research_report
interface.purpose: Session aggregates by goal: domains with mean credibility, flagged domains, spend, budget, thresholds, dashboard URL.

interface.name: npm run drift

gh-kierandotai-jev-scout.failureMode: Fail-open. A Jev error or timeout delivers the result unscored (`scored:false`), and the budget reservation is refunded (pipeline.ts ~230, catch block). An exhausted budget passes results through with budget_exhausted:true. The per-call timeout is 30 s (DEFAULT_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS at pipeline.ts:147). jev-client retries on RETRY_STATUSES with backoff, MAX_ATTEMPTS attempts. Judging is sequential (`for` loop with await, pipeline.ts ~253), so with 8 results and a slow Jev a single search could take up to 8 x 30 s. Session caps are 300 calls and $0.05. If the search backend chain fails, guarded_search returns a backend_chain_failed error. The DDG fallback is often blocked.

gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.name: TheBous/jev-flash-review (mirror of lucvalse/jev-flash-review)
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also Codex/Cursor/OpenCode manifests) shipping one local stdio MCP tool, review_diff, plus 3 skills (review-pr, review-free, review-loop). The agent supplies a unified diff plus title/description/taskContext. The engine chunks the diff and asks the TypeSafe System One API about about 447 built-in rules across 19 JSON files. Each rule is a Choice question (YES/NO/N/A) sent in batches of 80 rules per call, per diff chunk, in parallel. Then a second Choice picks the evidence hunk, a third confirms it, and a fourth rates impact. Output is JSON with the full rule matrix, confirmed violations and a summary with a blockers count. It is a rule-based code-review gate, not a general decision helper. A Cloudflare Worker remote variant and a CLI (npm run review -- PR) also exist.

The SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 (dist/index.mjs:56-61) reads env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai) and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL (default 'jev-latest'). systemOne() POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (index.mjs:554, 581). providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no code change is needed for the local stdio server if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same request/response schema as TypeSafe's /v1/systemone. That is unverified here. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (the SDK appends /v1/systemone), TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, because the SDK default 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter model ID. Nothing is hardcoded. The env has to reach the MCP process, e.g. via ~/.claude/settings.json env or the plugin .mcp.json, which currently has no env block. security: API key is read from env by the SDK and sent only as a Bearer header over TLS. It is never placed in argv, and the stdio server takes no key arguments, so it is not visible in the process list. The SDK redacts the authorization header in debug logs (index.mjs:285-287).

No shell execution inside the engine (it never reads the repo or runs git). The skills do instruct the agent to run gh/git commands. `gh pr diff` for client PRs pulls the diff into the agent's context and out to the API.

Supply chain: private package with no published npm release. Building needs npm install of a large dev tree (wrangler, release-it, commitlint, husky with a `prepare` script, esbuild allowScripts). No curl|sh installer.

Prompt-injection surface: diff text and taskContext go into the typed-question state. Jev outputs only typed probabilities, so it cannot emit instructions. The tool result contains the rule question text and locations, all from static rules, so the injection risk to Claude is low. The bigger risk is a review-loop skill that pressures the agent to obey the engine's verdicts, including the 'rationalizations' table.
Remote Worker: a single static bearer token; POST-only; the Worker holds TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Not needed for local use.

Provenance oddity: the repo owner is TheBous, but all 37 commits are by lucvalse, and the README, manifests and CHANGELOG point to lucvalse/jev-flash-review and TheBous/review-blaster. The install command targets the lucvalse repo, not this one, so this is likely a mirror or transfer. Verify which repo you actually trust.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.dataEgress: On every review_diff call, the full diff (all added and removed lines, chunked), title, description and taskContext are sent to the configured Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden). The same content is re-sent in each of the parallel calls: roughly 6 rule batches per chunk (447 rules / 80 per call), then the evidence, confirm and impact calls. Rule text is sent every time. Nothing is read from disk by the engine. The agent decides what goes in the diff, and the README asks the user to never send secrets, .env files or lockfiles. For client projects, this means client source diffs go to TypeSafe and, via OpenRouter, to OpenRouter as well. This is a privacy and contract risk. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it does not inspect this MCP call.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.failureMode: There is no hook, so nothing blocks the session. Per-attempt timeout is 60 s (judge.ts:13) with the SDK default of 2 retries, so a hung API can stall one tool call for about 3 minutes plus backoff. Failures are all-or-nothing: engine.ts uses Promise.all and throws on any judge error or missing answer (engine.ts:38-43, 119), which the MCP SDK returns as an isError result. Effectively fail-open for Claude Code, since the session continues. The skills, however, say STOP and never do a manual review when the tool is missing, so Claude will halt the review workflow rather than degrade. The fan-out of parallel calls (chunks x 6 batches, plus evidence, confirm and impact) risks 429s or rate limits on OpenRouter. There is no client-side concurrency cap.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.contextCost: Low static cost, high per-call cost. Static: 1 MCP tool. The description is about 540 chars and the schema has 4 fields with descriptions (about 900 chars), so roughly 350-400 tokens. No server-level 'instructions'. The 3 skills add about 3 short descriptions (about 60 tokens each) to the skill list. Loading a skill body costs about 400-800 tokens. No hooks and no injected text. Dynamic: the tool returns JSON.stringify of the entire matrix, `results` for all 447 rules plus `violations`. Each entry carries rule_id, the question text, severity, answer, probability, confidence, evidence and impact, roughly 60-100 tokens each. That is an estimated 25-45k tokens returned into the main context per call (my estimate from the code; not run). review-loop repeats this every iteration, so it can burn 100k+ tokens quickly. A subagent would be needed to contain it.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.latencyImpact: Each review is a multi-stage pipeline: Promise.all over chunks x 6 batches, then evidence, then confirm and impact, so at least 3 sequential API round trips of 70-500 ms claimed each, with larger payloads (8k+ tokens of rules per call). Realistically several seconds to tens of seconds per review for a modest diff, and more for large diffs (many chunks). Nothing is added to ordinary tool calls or turns, because there is no hook. The latency hits only when the skill fires, and review-loop multiplies it per iteration.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.autoInvocation: Model-discretion via skill description triggers only. There are no hooks, no proxy and no server instructions. review-loop's description ('Use when implementing a nontrivial change and the project's rule engine should gate it') is the only broad trigger. review-pr and review-free fire when the user asks for reviews. Whether Claude picks review-loop unprompted in daily work is not deterministic and cannot be relied on. Getting deterministic behavior would need a user-written Stop or PreToolUse hook or a CLAUDE.md rule, which the plugin does not provide.
pros: Genuinely integrates Jev's Choice primitive through the SDK: ('select instead of generate' evidence location, confidence gating at 0.55, confirm pass). This is the closest real example of Jev as a typed decision engine rather than a chat model.

Provider is configurable with zero code changes via the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL / TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL env vars (index.mjs:56-61), so OpenRouter routing is plausible: base https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model ID like typesafe/jev-1.13.
Only one MCP tool, so the always-on context cost is small (about 400 tokens) and there are no hooks to slow down your existing Grep|Glob|Bash hooks.
Engine never reads the repo, key never goes through argv, and the SDK redacts auth headers; the architecture is clean (Judge port, tests for engine and diff, CI running tsc and npm test).
Includes a Claude Code marketplace plus plugin manifest, skills and slash commands, so nothing needs writing to try it. Also has a Worker option if you want the key kept off the laptop.
cons: Wrong shape for the goal: it is an explicit code-review gate, not a background helper. Claude only calls it if the skill description matches or you ask; there is no hook, so 'automatic whenever useful' is not met.

Likely broken on a plain /plugin install: .mcp.json runs dist/server.js, but dist/ is gitignored and not in the repo. You must npm install and npm run bundle in the plugin cache (executes third-party build scripts, incl. husky prepare), and re-run after every update.

Heavy result payload: the tool returns the full 447-rule matrix as JSON, an estimated 25-45k tokens per call into Opus's context, and review-loop re-runs it each iteration. This is a big cost for daily use.

Sends whole diffs plus taskContext to TypeSafe/OpenRouter several times over per review. For client projects this is a data-handling and NDA problem, and your secret-guard hook does not cover MCP tool calls.

Very immature and low-trust: 1 star, 1 author (lucvalse), 37 commits over 2 days, last push 2026-09-19, no release, no LICENSE file (plugin.json claims MIT). The repo is owned by TheBous while the docs point to lucvalse, so the provenance is confusing.

Rule set is opinionated and huge (447 rules over 19 files, a mix of security, ai-generated-code and others). Expect noise for personal projects and a rule-tuning burden. The confidence thresholds (0.55, 0.1 margin) are admitted guesses ('tune from field data, not theory').

Failure handling is all-or-nothing (Promise.all), with 60 s x 3 attempts and no concurrency cap, so a Jev hiccup or OpenRouter 429 can hang or fail a whole review. The skills forbid falling back to manual review, so Claude stalls instead of degrading.
The Worker variant hardcodes the TypeSafe key path and has no base URL passthrough, so OpenRouter would need a patch there.
gh-thebous-jev-flash-review.verdict: A real, sensibly built Jev integration, but a niche rule-based review gate rather than an always-on assistant. It is opt-in by skill description, ships unbuilt, dumps a huge JSON into context, and sends full diffs out. Worth trying only as an optional pre-merge review on personal repos (with OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). Do not treat it as the main automatic Jev integration, and keep client code out of it.

Best-effort secret redaction only (scan.py:40-140); README/SKILL.md admit it does not anonymize proprietary source
Prompt-injection surface: it deliberately ingests untrusted third-party skill text; mitigated with a BOUNDARY prompt and SKILL.md 'treat as data', but the results feed Claude's report
No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry other than the TypeSafe calls; single 1-commit repo, no release, no signed tags, so supply-chain trust is only 'read it yourself' (small, 1200 lines)
Author is an individual (win4r), 11 stars, unaudited
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.dataEgress: Only in jev mode: redacted source snippets (12k-char chunks, up to 400 files/8MB, up to 80 HTTP attempts) of the scanned Skill/MCP target plus relative filenames, to api.typesafe.ai. Not the user's own project, prompts, diffs or tool outputs unless the user points it at their own code. Local mode makes zero network calls. Normal OS proxy settings still apply.
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.failureMode: Fail-open/soft at the tool level: it is a manual CLI, not in any request path, so Jev downtime cannot block Claude Code. Inside the scan: 45s timeout, one retry on 429/5xx after 2s, 401/403/redirect disables client; failures recorded as errors and reported as coverage gaps (exit 3), falling back to static findings; unverified triage hits become 'verification_unavailable' review findings.
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.contextCost: Very low: no MCP tools, no hooks. One skill whose frontmatter description (~200 chars, in Chinese) sits in the skill listing (~60 tokens); the 4.5KB SKILL.md body (~1.1k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. Nothing injected per turn.
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion): Claude may load it when the user asks to review/vet a skill or MCP for malicious behavior or before installing one. The Chinese description and narrow scope mean it will rarely trigger, and SKILL.md wants an explicit user request to authorize sending source to TypeSafe. Not a hook, not proactive.
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.latencyImpact: None on normal Claude Code turns. When invoked, a jev scan is many sequential HTTP calls (2 per flagged chunk, up to 80 attempts, 45s timeout each); wall time is seconds to minutes depending on target size (validation: about 8 calls and 20k input tokens per small specimen round).
pros: Genuine, well-engineered Jev use of both Noul and Choice primitives with a two-pass triage/verify design and strict schema validation (jev_client.py:22-52), a good reference implementation of the System One request shape {model,state,questions}
Very safe to install: stdlib-only, ~1200 lines, no hooks, no MCP server, no context bloat, key never in argv, redirects blocked, 29 offline tests + pinned CI

Real value for this user specifically: he installs third-party MCP servers/skills/plugins (gitnexus, caveman, playwright) and works on client projects, so vetting them is a legitimate security task; local mode is fully offline and free
Honest calibration language and coverage reporting (skipped files, failures, exit 3), no overclaiming
MIT, easy to fork; OpenRouter port is a few lines if the OpenRouter /v1/systemone envelope matches
cons: Not an MCP server and not for coding: it audits other people's skills/MCPs, so it adds no Jev value to daily edit/debug/refactor work
Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai with TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter support at all, contradicting the user's requirement, and needs a local fork with unverified response-schema compatibility

Cannot be automatic: it is an occasional, explicit-consent, manual scan; SKILL.md tells Claude to explain the source transfer and the Chinese description makes auto-triggering unlikely; no PreToolUse/install hook to vet MCPs on add

Immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 11 stars, no releases, 11 days old; only 4 self-authored synthetic specimens as validation, no accuracy data; author's own docs say two Jev passes are not independent verification
Sends source to a third party (redaction best-effort), a concern for client-owned code; Jev-specific gain over the static regex checks is unproven (Jev sometimes only downranks or reconfirms)
Fixed 45s timeout with sequential calls; large targets can consume up to 80 calls and unknown billing
gh-win4r-jev-security-scan.verdict: A tidy, safe, single-purpose Jev skill for vetting third-party Skills/MCPs, not a coding integration and not an MCP server; it is TypeSafe-only (hardcoded endpoint) and manual, so it fails the automatic and OpenRouter requirements. Worth a look only as a reference client or an optional forked pre-install audit tool, not as the core Jev integration.
