gh-bartlomein-oko.name: bartlomein/oko
gh-bartlomein-oko.whatItDoes: Local Rust binary (oko) that runs an MCP stdio server exposing a single code-search tool (mcp__oko__search). It does local ripgrep/BM25/tree-sitter retrieval to build up to 60 candidate snippets (max 32,000 bytes per request), then asks Jev via the System One API (/v1/systemone) one Noul yes/no relevance question per candidate and returns the top ~3 excerpts with line numbers. `oko setup --client claude` also writes a managed section into CLAUDE.md, adds SessionStart/SubagentStart/PreToolUse hooks to .claude/settings.local.json, and allow-lists mcp__oko__search. Also has CLI (oko ask/rank/auth) and a --deep multi-step mode.

providerSupport.evidence: src/ranking.rs:432 `env_value("TYPESAFE_BASE_URL").unwrap_or_else(|| "https://api.typesafe.ai")`; ranking.rs:438 model from TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL default "jev-latest"; ranking.rs ~468 `.post(format!("{}/v1/systemone", base.trim_end_matches('/'))).bearer_auth(api_key)`; key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/auth.rs:58; env > cwd .env > OS keyring). Request is {model,state,questions{candidate_N:{type:noul,instructions}}}, response read as answers.candidate_N.{type:noul,noul:float} (ranking.rs:261-330). No OpenRouter string anywhere in src/. docs/configuration.md: 'TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL may be set in the process environment ... not read from .env'.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change, if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same answers/noul shape (unverified by me, plausible since the path and primitive names match). Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (Bearer auth). BASE_URL and MODEL must be in the process env, so put them in the env block of the MCP server config (claude mcp add-json ... "env":{...}), not in .env. Risks: OpenRouter model-id format, extra field `model` handling, and different rate limits (oko throttles at 200k tokens/s assuming TypeSafe's limit).
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai) by default; any base URL via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.

interface.name: MCP tool `search` (mcp__oko__search)
interface.purpose: Only tool. Params: question, symbols (exact names), mode (usages/enumerate/unused), questions[] (up to 8 parallel), directory, intent (implementation/explanation/general/callers), deep, max_steps. Marked read-only, alwaysLoad via _meta anthropic/alwaysLoad (src/mcp.rs:~1817-1830).

interface.name: Hook SessionStart / SubagentStart (`oko hook session-start|subagent-start`)
interface.purpose: Injects additionalContext (~600 chars) stating that mcp__oko__search is loaded. Timeout 10s, never blocks (src/hook.rs, setup.rs:~430).

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse matcher ^(Bash|Grep|Glob|Agent|mcp__oko__.*)$
interface.purpose: On grep-like Bash/Grep/Glob, injects a reminder every 4th non-Oko code search; on Agent calls to Explore/Plan/general-purpose subagents it rewrites tool_input.prompt via updatedInput to append a line telling the subagent to use mcp__oko__search. Keeps per-session counters in ~/.cache/oko/hooks. Timeout 5s.

interface.name: CLI `oko setup [--client claude|codex|opencode|all] [--no-jev] [--no-hooks] [--no-instructions]`
interface.purpose: Per project: copies binaries, runs `claude mcp add-json --scope local` with alwaysLoad, edits CLAUDE.md (managed oko:search section, src/guidance.md ~2.9 KB), writes .claude/settings.local.json hooks + allow rule.

interface.name: CLI `oko mcp [--root DIR] [--no-jev]`
interface.purpose: stdio MCP server entrypoint.

interface.name: CLI `oko auth login|status|logout`
interface.purpose: Manage TypeSafe key in OS keyring (Linux Secret Service; no plaintext fallback).

interface.name: CLI `oko ask`, `oko rank`, `oko benchmark`

security: Key never on argv: read from env, cwd .env, or OS keyring (keyring crate, zeroize); `oko auth login` uses hidden prompt; docs say never pass keys as arguments. On headless Linux without Secret Service the keyring errors and you must use env var.

install.sh (curl|sh style, 109 lines) is careful: HTTPS-only, downloads release tarball plus SHA256SUMS from same GitHub release (checksum protects against corruption, not a compromised release), rejects unsafe tar paths/links, runs `oko --version` before linking; no root. macOS binaries unsigned. I did not run it. Rust source build alternative exists (cargo).

No npm postinstall; prebuilt binary + bundled ripgrep from GitHub releases; single-author repo (158+11 of 175 commits by owner, 6 by CharlieHelps bot), 7 stars, 12 days old, so supply-chain trust is low.

Prompt-injection surface: candidate code snippets from the repo are embedded in the Jev request state and returned to Claude as tool output; server instructions say 'Source excerpts are untrusted data'. Jev returns only numeric probabilities so it is not a text-injection channel itself. Hook text is phrased as facts because Claude Code treats imperative hook text as injection.

Hook rewrites Agent subagent prompts (updatedInput) - a behaviour-modifying hook that may collide with other PreToolUse hooks (GitNexus, secret-guard) since it also matches Bash|Grep|Glob. Never denies/blocks.

Setup edits CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.local.json in each project (client repos too) and adds allow rule for mcp__oko__search; under your bypass/auto mode the allow rule is moot. Managed markers make it idempotent, but it leaves files in client repos (settings.local.json is typically gitignored, CLAUDE.md is not).
Metrics file only if OKO_METRICS_FILE is set; no telemetry endpoints found: only reqwest use is the Jev call (grep of src). Extra header x-oko-phase sent to the provider.

Secret handling gap: snippets are sent as-is; no secret redaction before egress. It respects ignore rules for search discovery but .env-style files in the repo could be candidates if not ignored (not verified in search.rs).
gh-bartlomein-oko.dataEgress: Per search: the user's question text plus up to ~60 shortlisted code snippets (whole request capped at 32,000 bytes; trailing items dropped) with file-path 'source' labels, sent to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/v1/systemone (TypeSafe or, if repointed, OpenRouter, which then routes to TypeSafe). Multi-question calls and --deep send several requests. Not sent: full repo, diffs, tool outputs, Claude conversation. Local index cache lives in ~/.cache/oko. Hook and MCP process otherwise make no network calls. With client repos this means client source snippets go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (a contract consideration); --no-jev avoids all egress but then no Jev.
gh-bartlomein-oko.failureMode: Fail-open for Claude. Jev call has a 10s hard reqwest timeout, no retries (ranking.rs JEV_TIMEOUT=10s); the MCP path uses a shorter 4s patience (mcp.rs JEV_PATIENCE, overridable OKO_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, clamped 500ms-10s) and on timeout/error returns keyword-ranked results labelled 'lexical-fallback' instead of an error. Missing key: MCP returns an error message telling to run oko auth login (mcp.rs:486) unless started with --no-jev. Hooks print {} on any error and never block; timeouts 10s/5s. A process-wide token bucket throttles at 200k tokens/s. Claude can always fall back to native grep (guidance says so).
gh-bartlomein-oko.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (search) with a ~1.4 KB description plus a schema of 8 params (~700 chars incl. doc comments) => roughly 500-600 tokens always loaded (alwaysLoad meta forces it out of deferred ToolSearch). MCP server instructions ~500 chars (~125 tokens). Per project CLAUDE.md managed section ~2.9 KB (~750 tokens) added every session. SessionStart hook ~600 chars (~150 tokens) once; subagent-start hook ~500 chars per subagent; PreToolUse reminder ~250 chars every 4th grep/Glob; ~200 chars appended to each exploring subagent prompt. Total baseline about 1.5k tokens per session per project, plus tool results up to 16,000 bytes (~4k tokens) per search (MAX_MCP_RESULT_BYTES).
gh-bartlomein-oko.latencyImpact: Claimed Jev ~0.5s typical (mcp.rs comment); worst case capped at 4s then lexical fallback. Local retrieval on big repos: first request reads/hashes all files (docs say cache helps later); hook process spawn adds a few ms per Bash/Grep/Glob/Agent call (compiled Rust, trivial). Up to 8 questions ranked in parallel. Net latency per search likely 0.6-2s, but it replaces multiple grep/read turns.
gh-bartlomein-oko.autoInvocation: Hybrid, mostly model-discretion. The MCP tool is alwaysLoad'ed (visible to main agent and subagents) and steered by CLAUDE.md guidance + SessionStart/SubagentStart context + PreToolUse reminder every 4th grep + deterministic rewrite of Explore/Plan/general-purpose subagent prompts. Nothing forces or intercepts Grep/Glob; Claude may still grep. No user prompting needed after `oko setup`, but setup is per-project (CLAUDE.md + settings.local.json in each repo).
pros: Only Jev integration found whose whole purpose is automatic use inside a coding agent: Jev is on the hot path of every search and the user never has to say 'use jev'.

Correct use of Jev's strengths: independent Noul yes/no relevance per candidate, numeric output only (ranking.rs:261-330), no free text from Jev, cheap at ~$0.042/1M input tokens with 32KB caps per request.

Provider layer is one function: base URL, model and bearer key are all env-configurable, path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so OpenRouter is likely a pure config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY).
Fail-open design: 4s patience then labelled lexical fallback, hooks never block, native grep remains available; no dependence on Jev availability.
Key handling is good: OS keyring/env/.env, hidden prompt, zeroize, nothing in argv; no telemetry endpoints; only one outbound call site.

Sophisticated auto-adoption: alwaysLoad meta, subagent prompt rewriting, grep reminders, guidance in CLAUDE.md; tool results returned as exact current file text with line numbers so Claude can edit directly; result stub dedup and 16KB result cap.

Substantial test suite (~330 #[test], big tests/mcp.rs 2.7k lines) and CI with build workflow; published benchmarks with raw results (author claims 17-27% fewer tokens, 32-53% fewer tool calls); MIT license; MCP works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode; single static binary, no Node/Python runtime.
Supports TS/JS/Python/Go/Rust/Ruby/Java/Kotlin via tree-sitter for caller/usage queries.
cons: Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-18, 175 commits in 12 days, 7 stars, 0 forks, 6 releases; v0.6.0 'prerelease' per README. Expect breaking changes and bus-factor 1.

Not natively OpenRouter: only TYPESAFE_* env vars; OpenRouter compatibility is my inference from matching path/schema, not tested (I did not run it). BASE_URL/MODEL are not read from .env so must go in the MCP env block; the key variable name is misleading (OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY).

Sends user questions and up to 32KB of code snippets per search to OpenRouter and TypeSafe: a real client-confidentiality issue for the user's client projects, with no redaction and no per-project allowlist besides --no-jev.

Overlaps with existing GitNexus (graph query/context/impact) and Claude Code's own Grep/Glob; the user now has two code-navigation MCPs competing for the agent's attention, and oko's PreToolUse matcher (Bash|Grep|Glob|Agent) stacks on GitNexus and the secret-guard hooks on the same events. Its Agent-prompt rewrite may fight GitNexus guidance.

Setup is per project and mutates repos: CLAUDE.md managed section (committed file), .claude/settings.local.json hooks, `claude mcp add-json --scope local`; must be repeated for every repo and can leave diffs in client repos. --no-hooks/--no-instructions reduce this but also reduce auto-invocation.
Auto-invocation is still model-discretion: nothing intercepts Grep; adoption depends on guidance text. Under Opus 5.5 it may or may not prefer it; the author's benchmarks are self-run.

Jev only reranks a lexical shortlist, so recall is bounded by BM25/ripgrep retrieval; skeptics' claim that Jev is a router-ish model is irrelevant here but quality of Noul vs a local reranker is unproven independent of author benchmarks.
install.sh is curl|sh style with checksum from same release origin; unsigned macOS binaries; needs glibc>=2.35 (fine on Debian 13). Linux keyring needs Secret Service/D-Bus, else must use env var.
Context tax of about 1.5k tokens per session per project plus up to ~4k tokens per search result.
gh-bartlomein-oko.verdict: Best candidate found for genuinely automatic, everyday Jev use in Claude Code: a real, well-tested, fail-open MCP server with hooks and guidance whose provider layer looks repointable to OpenRouter with three env vars. Adopt it cautiously (try with --no-hooks first, verify the OpenRouter /v1/systemone response shape on a scratch repo, and keep it off client repos unless snippet egress to OpenRouter/TypeSafe is acceptable), given its age, single maintainer and overlap with GitNexus.

gh-greenyamao-antigravity-mcp-semantic-s.name: greenyamao/Antigravity-mcp-semantic-search-with-TypeSafeAi (TypeSafe Code Guard)
gh-greenyamao-antigravity-mcp-semantic-s.whatItDoes: Single-file Python MCP server (stdio, mcp_server.py, ~670 lines) with two tools. typesafe_find_code: walks the project tree, builds up to 25 candidate files (path plus ~160 chars of first lines), asks Jev (Choice plus Noul) which file matches a natural-language query, then splits that file into blocks (label = path/signature only), asks Jev for the best block, and returns a ~15-line snippet. typesafe_audit_diff: runs git diff HEAD (or takes a diff), truncates it to 12k chars, and asks Jev one Score and four Noul questions (scope_alignment, touches_state, breaks_contracts, removes_defenses, leftover_debug). It returns a markdown report with the probabilities and threshold-based advice. Ships an Antigravity-style AGENTS.md rule and a SKILL.md that tell the agent to call the tools "before grepping" and "before finishing edits".

providerSupport.evidence: mcp_server.py:20 uses typesafe_sdk.TypeSafeClient(api_key=os.environ['TYPESAFE_API_KEY']) (mcp_server.py:118-127). No base_url or model is passed in the repo, so the SDK env fallbacks apply. typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 (sdist inspected): constants.py:6 TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, constants.py:9 TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, constants.py:15 DEFAULT_BASE_URL='https://api.typesafe.ai', constants.py:18 DEFAULT_MODEL='jev-latest', _core/constants.py:5 SYSTEM_ONE_PATH='/v1/systemone', transport.py:121 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'. The SDK therefore POSTs {base}/v1/systemone. With TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api it hits https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is OpenRouter's System One endpoint. Error text hard-codes api.typesafe.ai (mcp_server.py:190,194) but is cosmetic. Whether OpenRouter's response JSON matches the SDK's pydantic parsing is not verified.
providerSupport.others: None. The repo has no gateway abstraction.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change: set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (the server only reads this name at mcp_server.py:118), and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) in the MCP 'env' block. The only risk is schema or response drift between OpenRouter and the direct API, and that would need a live test. The SDK also lacks OpenRouter-specific headers, which are optional.

interface.name: typesafe_find_code(query, directory='.', file_extensions=None)
interface.purpose: Two-stage Jev semantic locator. Stage 1 picks a file from up to 25 candidates, stage 2 picks a block, and the tool returns file, line and a ~16-line snippet with confidence (mcp_server.py:200-455).

interface.name: typesafe_audit_diff(task_description, git_diff='', directory='.')
interface.purpose: Runs git diff HEAD (subprocess, list argv, no shell) or takes a supplied diff and asks Jev 5 typed questions. Returns metrics and advice (mcp_server.py:490-665).

interface.name: AGENTS.md rule (Antigravity)
interface.purpose: Says 'Always call typesafe_find_code before grepping' and 'call typesafe_audit_diff before finishing edits'. Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md natively, so it must be copied into CLAUDE.md.

interface.name: Skill typesafe-code-guard (.agents/skills/.../SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Query-writing guidance and metric thresholds. It has a frontmatter description trigger and is Antigravity-oriented, so it would need copying to ~/.claude/skills.

security: TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read from env or a repo-local .env (load_dotenv, mcp_server.py:22-25). It is never put in argv, and .env is gitignored. Any OpenRouter key would sit in the MCP env block or .env in plaintext.

directory is an arbitrary model-controlled path (mcp_server.py:225). The tool scans any directory the model names, so first lines of many files leave the machine. Hidden dirs and node_modules etc. are excluded, but .json/.yaml/.yml/.sh/.md files are included. Their first 30 lines (8 non-comment lines, 160 chars) are sent to Jev, which could include config values or secrets.
git diff is sent verbatim (12k chars, mcp_server.py:571). Any secret in a diff goes to the provider. There is no redaction, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this MCP call path.

subprocess.run(['git','diff','HEAD'], cwd=repo_dir) uses list argv with no shell, so no injection. git diff runs in a model-chosen directory, so repo-local git config or hooks could be involved (low risk).

Prompt-injection surface: file paths, first lines and the diff are interpolated into Jev state and instructions (mcp_server.py:283,287). Jev only returns typed probabilities, so the output surface is small. The snippet returned to Claude is raw file content, as with any read.

No curl|sh installer, no postinstall, no telemetry in the repo. Dependencies: typesafe-sdk>=0.6.0, mcp>=2.2.0, python-dotenv>=1.2.0, all unpinned and with no lockfile. No license file, so legal reuse in client work is undefined. Single anonymous-ish author, 2 stars.
gh-greenyamao-antigravity-mcp-semantic-s.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is repointed). find_code sends the query, up to 25 relative file paths plus ~160 chars of each file's first non-comment lines, then the chosen file path plus one line label (path/signature, max 80 chars) per block. It does not send code bodies; the local snippet is read locally and returned only to Claude. audit_diff sends the task description, changed file names and up to 12,000 chars of raw diff (code contents; lockfiles, minified files and images are stubbed out by _clean_diff). Nothing else, and no telemetry. The SDK logs only if TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL is set.
gh-greenyamao-antigravity-mcp-semantic-s.failureMode: Fail-open: every SDK exception is caught and returned as a plain-text error string to the model (mcp_server.py:295-296,402-403,605-606), so the tool never crashes the session and Claude just proceeds. There is no explicit timeout or retry setting in the repo. SDK defaults are 10 s per HTTP operation and max_retries=2 with 0.5-5 s backoff (constants.py:21, retry.py:52), so a hung provider can block a call for roughly 30 s. The server is synchronous, and os.walk over a large monorepo blocks the stdio loop. A missing key returns an error string instead of a hard failure. A 'no relevant file' result silently steers the agent to grep. Malformed Jev output would raise KeyError or ValueError outside the try (mcp_server.py:298,306), so some paths can raise after the API call.
gh-greenyamao-antigravity-mcp-semantic-s.contextCost: 2 MCP tools. Tool defs (name, docstring, schema) are about 2.4k chars, roughly 600-700 tokens per session. No server-level 'instructions' field. No hooks inject text. Each find_code result adds about 200-400 tokens (snippet plus header), and each audit report about 250 tokens. gh-123wwwa-jevtrace.name: JevTrace (123wwwa/JevTrace)
gh-123wwwa-jevtrace.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) that, given a plain-language JS/TS coding task, uses the TypeScript compiler (call hierarchy, references, types, tests) plus Jev Noul/Choice judgments to select the relevant functions and their callers/callees/types/tests within a token budget, returning source text to the agent instead of grep/read loops. Multi-stage pipeline: scope check (is the task specific?), directory/file/symbol discovery via Jev, compiler expansion, Jev context ranking. Falls back to lexical/structural ranking if Jev stages fail. JS/TS/Vue only.

Local: usage log with task+project path.
gh-123wwwa-jevtrace.failureMode: Mostly fail-open with degradation. postJson uses 30 s default timeout (15 s for scope and choice calls), one retry on 408/425/429/5xx/network error (decision-backends.ts:87-121). Discovery stage failure -> falls back to lexical top-k leads with a warning (discovery.ts:540-544); scope-check failure -> treated as specific (task-pipeline.ts:136-140); Stage 4 ranking failure -> structural order (task-pipeline.ts:409-411). Missing API key or no provider configured -> tool returns isError with 'run jevtrace setup' (judges.ts:334-336), not a crash; there is no automatic offline fallback (--offline is CLI flag only). Worst case a single tool call can block for tens of seconds (up to 30 s x2 attempts per batch stage) before degrading; the agent can still fall back to Grep.

Each call returns up to maxChars=30000 (~7.5k tokens, default tokenBudget 8000) as BOTH content text and structuredContent.context (server.ts:139-149) - Claude Code passes one of them to the model, but the duplicate payload may inflate transcript size. First call also builds a file index (about 5.5 s for 5,400 files cold, 0.6 s after per docs/usage.md). gh-bentlybro-siftr.name: Bentlybro/siftr
gh-bentlybro-siftr.whatItDoes: Stdlib-only Python CLI plus stdio MCP server exposing four read-only tools (semantic_search, focused_read, pick_relevant, filter_output). Each tool packs code outlines or chunks into batches, asks Jev a `noul` question ("is this relevant to the query?") per item through hundreds of parallel requests, and ranks or filters the returned P(yes). It is a real, purpose-built Jev integration: Jev is used as a cheap relevance judge, not as a chat model. `siftr agents install` also rewrites the MCP config files of many coding agents.

providerSupport.evidence: siftr/jev.py:26-29 OPENROUTER_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, TYPESAFE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_MODEL=jev-latest. jev.py:50-53 uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY if set (preferred), else jev.py:54-57 TYPESAFE_API_KEY. SIFTR_MODEL env overrides the model id. Request body {model,state,questions} with questions of type noul (engine.py:155-158); the response is read from payload['answers'][id]['noul'] (engine.py:165). jev.py:9-10 comment states OpenRouter chat-completions returns HTTP 500 for this model, so the Decisions API is required. The code never uses /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe native only as fallback when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is absent.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already supported natively; no patching needed.

(Not executed during this audit.)
gh-bentlybro-siftr.tests: 4 offline unittest files, about 526 lines (test_agents, test_hedging, test_search, test_tools). CI (.github/workflows/test.yml) runs a matrix of ubuntu, macos and windows on Python 3.10-3.13 plus an install smoke test. Benchmarks are in bench/ with a frozen dev/test split on SWE-bench Lite (README: search hit@5 82% vs BM25 52% and grep 22%; read 92% kept at 59% cut; pick 81% vs BM25 38%). These are the author's own numbers on Python-only repos and are not independently verified. Nothing was run here.
security: API key handling is good. The key is read from env or from a 0600 file (config.py:64), sent only as a Bearer header (jev.py:71) and never put in argv. `siftr agents install` writes only command=siftr and args=[mcp], with no key in the MCP config, so nothing shows in ps or ~/.claude.json.

config.load_env (config.py:40-48) runs at CLI start and loads the first `.env` found in the CWD or any parent directory into os.environ via setdefault. Under Claude Code the CWD is the project, so a client project's .env containing OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY would be picked up, and the key used would depend on the project. Real env vars win over it. Setting the real env or the user config avoids the surprise.

No secret redaction before upload. scan.py TEXT_EXT includes .json/.yaml/.toml/.ini/.cfg/.conf/.sh/.tf. .env itself is skipped (no extension match) and dot-directories are skipped, but config files with embedded credentials can be sent as chunks (up to 1600 chars each). The existing PreToolUse secret guard does NOT cover this, because the MCP server reads files itself and does not go through the Read tool.

The MCP tools are read-only and accept arbitrary absolute paths (semantic_search path, focused_read path, filter_output path) with no root confinement (mcp.py:131, 150-155). A prompt-injected agent could point them at ~/.ssh or ~/.aws text files, which would upload contents to OpenRouter. Extensions like .json/.conf/.txt are only filtered in the directory scan, not in focused_read/filter_output, which read any file.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Jev returns only probabilities, so tool output is scores and file:line ranges plus the first line of chunk text as a preview (search.py:110-111), which is repo-controlled text echoed to the agent (minor).

Installer risks: curl|sh for siftr and, transitively, for uv. The default source is the unpinned main.zip, so a compromised repo or account gives code execution at install time. No npm-style postinstall. Runtime shell use is limited to `git ls-files` (scan.py:104).

No telemetry. The only network destination is openrouter.ai, or api.typesafe.ai in fallback. X-Title: siftr and User-Agent are sent. `siftr agents install` edits many configs (with backups), a large blast radius for a 5-star project, though the by-hand `claude mcp add` path avoids it.
Single maintainer, 8 commits on one day, no releases, and a 'jgrep' to 'siftr' rename in progress. Supply-chain trust is low.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.dataEgress: Yes, code content leaves the machine. Per semantic_search: (1) every file's relative path plus its symbol-name outline, in batches of up to 150 files or 24k chars, for the whole tree minus gitignored and skipped dirs; (2) the top 30 files' chunks, up to 1600 chars of raw source each, sent verbatim, plus the query text. focused_read sends chunks of the target file. pick_relevant sends the item strings. filter_output sends log chunks. Everything goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, which forwards it to TypeSafe (README 'Privacy and cost' warns not to use it on code you can't send to a third party). Nothing goes out for diffs, prompts or tool outputs unless the agent passes them as query/items. Outlines are cached locally in ~/.config/siftr/cache/. This conflicts with client-project confidentiality unless the client permits OpenRouter and TypeSafe processing; OpenRouter data policy and ZDR settings should be checked.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.failureMode: Fail-open and bounded. Per-request timeout is 6s (engine.py:24), with 2 retries (RETRIES=2, so up to 3 attempts) and a hedged duplicate after 2s (engine.py:63-91). A request that still fails becomes {} and its items get None scores, which are dropped from results (search.py:78). In the worst case a search can take about 18s or more before returning 'No confident matches', which is misleading because it does not say Jev was down. A missing key raises JevError, surfaced as an isError tool result (mcp.py:223-224). An HTTP 401/403 gives 'API key rejected'. The server itself never crashes, since exceptions are caught in the serve loop. Claude falls back to Grep/Read because each tool description says to. There is no stalling or blocking of the main flow because these are opt-in tool calls, not hooks. The 64-thread fan-out can hit OpenRouter rate limits on large repos, and that would appear as silent partial results.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. Tool definitions total about 4,000 chars (about 1,000 tokens), and the server `instructions` string adds about 430 chars (about 110 tokens), for about 1.1k tokens always resident, or less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Tool results are compact: 10 hits at about 100 chars each.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill or proxy. Claude will call semantic_search only if its description, plus the optional CLAUDE.md snippet from docs/agents.md, convinces the model to prefer it. Its descriptions do say 'Use it FIRST when you don't know the exact identifiers', which nudges usage. The project itself recommends adding a CLAUDE.md block to make agents use it, so unprompted usage is probabilistic and not guaranteed. With existing GitNexus and Grep/Glob tools, Opus 5.5 may often pick those instead.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.latencyImpact: Only when the tool is called. Author-reported: search about 2s (p90 2.9s) on a 4,000-file repo; read and pick under 0.5s. Local scan is cached by mtime, and the first run on a big tree is slower. The tool blocks the agent turn for that time, with worst-case about 18s+ during OpenRouter problems. There is nothing on non-calling turns.
pros: Only candidate found so far that ships a working, benchmarked Jev to OpenRouter path: correct OPENROUTER_URL and typesafe/jev-1.13 model, OPENROUTER_API_KEY preferred (jev.py:26-53). It needs no patching to match the user's provider choice.

Uses Jev for what it is actually good at, cheap parallel calibrated yes/no relevance judgments, rather than as a chat replacement. The batching design (150 items per request, 64 threads, hedged duplicates) fits Jev's 70-500ms latency.
Directly addresses a real daily-coding token sink: semantic 'where is X' search and partial reads of large files, at about 1-2 cents per big-repo search and under a cent for read/pick.

Zero dependencies, stdlib-only, about 2.8k lines of readable Python. The auditing burden is small and the runtime footprint is tiny (no npm, no build). Only ~1.1k tokens of always-resident tool definitions and no hook overhead.

Well-documented fail-open behaviour and honest limits: docs say to use grep when exact strings are known, and filter_output is labelled experimental. Results are suggestions with a map of omitted sections, so a wrong answer costs one extra read.
API key is never in argv or MCP config. It sits in a 0600 file or the env. The MCP server does not execute shell commands (deliberate design noted in mcp.py:7-10).
Frozen dev/test benchmark methodology on SWE-bench Lite, with raw result JSONs in bench/results, is more rigorous than typical for a repo this small. It is still Python-only and self-reported.
MIT license. Manual install is easy and reversible with `claude mcp add -s user siftr -- siftr mcp` and `claude mcp remove`.
cons: Not automatic. It is model-discretion only. The author's own docs say to paste a CLAUDE.md block to get agents to use it, and there are no hooks. It cannot satisfy 'Claude must use it without my prompting' deterministically, and it competes with the built-in Grep/Glob and the user's GitNexus graph tools.

Sends raw source (up to 1600-char chunks) plus all file paths and symbols to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every search. There is no redaction, no path allowlist and no project opt-out. This is a real problem for client projects under NDA, and the existing secret-leak hook never sees these reads because the MCP server reads files itself.

MCP tools take arbitrary absolute paths with no project-root confinement (mcp.py:131, 150-155), so a prompt-injected agent could exfiltrate any text file to a third party via focused_read/filter_output.
Project `.env` in cwd or parents is auto-loaded into the environment (config.py:40-48), so a client repo's own OPENROUTER_API_KEY could silently override the intended key or billing account.

Very immature: 11 days old, 8 commits all on 2026-09-19, 1 contributor, 5 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, and mid-rename (jgrep to siftr, legacy cleanup code). Expect API churn. Depends on the OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, which is alpha and could change.
Install path is curl|sh (twice: siftr, then uv) against an unpinned main.zip. `siftr agents install` edits many agent configs. Use a pinned git commit and add the MCP by hand instead.

Search cost and latency scale with repo size: about 2s and 1-2 cents per search on 4k files, and every call re-sends the full outline of all files (cached only locally). A heavy day of searches costs cents but not zero. Silent partial results under rate limiting look like 'No confident matches'.

Benchmarks are self-reported, Python-only (SWE-bench) and unverified by third parties, so quality on the user's TS/JS/other stacks is unproven. Redundant with GitNexus (which already gives graph and semantic query context) for indexed repos.

Skeptic caveat about Jev itself (possible 'flash router' behaviour, unverified) applies because the whole tool's quality depends on Jev's relevance probabilities. The benchmark was run on jev-1.13, which is the model the code pins.
gh-bentlybro-siftr.verdict: Best-fit Jev-on-OpenRouter integration found so far: a small, readable stdlib-only MCP server that already targets /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and it uses Jev sensibly for relevance ranking. It is still model-discretion (needs a CLAUDE.md nudge, not truly automatic) and uploads raw code chunks to a third party without redaction or path confinement, so adopt only on personal or approved repos, pinned to a reviewed commit and installed by hand rather than via curl|sh.

gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.name: kinde-starter-kits/jev-agent-authorization (Jev Gatehouse)
gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.whatItDoes: Not an MCP server and not a Claude Code plugin. It is a Next.js + Convex + Kinde reference web app ("Jev Gatehouse") that puts a server-side guard in front of a demo SaaS workspace API. Agent tool calls reach the guard through Kinde's hosted Secure MCP connection. The guard verifies the Kinde JWT and permissions, then sends non-read calls to Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via the OpenRouter System One endpoint) with 4 Noul questions (matches_intent, destructive, injected, exfiltration), 1 Score (risk) and 1 Choice (verdict_hint: allow/step_up/deny). Policy code turns the signals into allow, step_up or deny. Low-confidence calls go to an LLM judge. Every decision is written to a ledger before the call runs. Held calls need a fresh-sign-in approval page. It includes a 300-case benchmark and an attack playground. It is the best public worked example of Jev typed signals for tool-call authorization on OpenRouter, but it is a design pattern to copy, not something to install into Claude Code.

security: Not installable into Claude Code, so no direct attack surface on the user's machine. Repo has husky 'prepare' script (dev-only, standard) and no postinstall or curl|sh installer.
MIT license. Single author (sholajegede, 120 of 121 commits), Kinde starter-kit org, CODEOWNERS present.
OPENROUTER_API_KEY is held server-side in Convex env (never in argv), sent as a Bearer header. This is a good pattern.

Prompt-injection design is the main strength. The Jev state marks the user request as verified by the server, marks the agent's stated reason as unverified, and includes recent content the agent read. There is a specific 'injected' Noul question and a fail-closed design (ledger write must succeed before the call runs).
Any local reuse must not send whole files or secrets to OpenRouter. Redaction exists in convex/lib/redact.ts, which I did not review in depth.
Repo benchmark is self-authored (their own 300 cases and labels), so the 0.0% false-allow and 83.7% accuracy figures are unverified vendor-style claims.
gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.dataEgress: In the app: to OpenRouter (then TypeSafe) it sends a JSON 'state' with the tool call (operation, method, arguments), the verified user request text, the agent's stated reason, excerpts of content the agent recently read, and the user's recent call history. To Kinde it sends token verification and permission lookups. To Convex it sends everything, including the ledger. If the pattern were ported locally to Claude Code, the egress would be the tool-call arguments (Bash commands, file paths, edit diffs) plus the user's prompt, unless the user filters it.
gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.failureMode: Fail-closed by design. A Jev error or 3 s timeout gives step_up with reason jev_unavailable (convex/guard/judgment.ts:28). Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives step_up (jev_not_configured). An unset judge model holds low-confidence calls (judge_not_configured). Any guard exception gives a 503 and the call does not run (handler.ts handleApiRequest catch). That is right for a production API gate, but a fail-closed local hook would stall the user's Claude Code whenever OpenRouter is down, unless changed to fail-open.
gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.contextCost: None for Claude Code, since nothing is installed. Kinde's MCP would add one tool per OpenAPI operation of the demo workspace API, which is irrelevant to the user's own repos. Zero hook-injected text.
gh-kinde-starter-kits-jev-agent-authoriz.autoInvocation: Not applicable to Claude Code. Inside its own architecture the guard is a transparent server-side proxy that runs deterministically on every non-read tool call, with no model discretion. That is the property the user wants, but it works at the API layer, not as a Claude Code hook.
pros: Uses Jev via OpenRouter System One (POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13) with a complete request and response contract in ~100 lines (convex/jev/client.ts), including the questions schema for Noul, Score and Choice, the answers shape, and usage.cost.

Shows the strongest idea for this user: a deterministic gate that treats Jev's calibrated probabilities as inputs to policy code (convex/guard/policy.ts) rather than trusting a single verdict. Their own benchmark reports that the multi-signal approach has less false-allow than a single Jev verdict (0.0% vs 12.4%). The numbers are self-authored, not independent.
Concrete latency and cost data: p50 205 ms and about $0.029 per 1,000 calls for Jev signals, against about 2 s and $0.93 for a Sonnet judge. This is useful for sizing a PreToolUse hook.
Ready-made question set (matches_intent, destructive, injected, exfiltration, risk, verdict_hint) that could be ported almost verbatim into a Claude Code PreToolUse hook.
Sound failure handling patterns: 3 s timeout, explicit reason codes, cascade to a stronger judge only on low confidence.
Decent hygiene for a starter kit: MIT, CI (format, lint, typecheck, test, build), 140 test cases across 20+ test files, CHANGELOG, CODEOWNERS.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook or skill for Claude Code. There is no install path into Claude Code, and it cannot be made automatic without a rewrite.

Requires Kinde (a business account), Convex, and Next.js. It guards a demo SaaS API reached through Kinde's hosted MCP, not the user's local Bash/Edit/Write tools, so it does not protect Claude Code sessions.

The authorization flow depends on server-verified user intent from the in-app console (KINDE_WEB_CLIENT_ID azp check, convex/guard/handler.ts:200-212). An external MCP client such as Claude Code gets intent source 'none', where the client.ts question text says to answer no for matches_intent, so most non-read calls would be held.
Fail-closed step_up on any Jev problem would stall an interactive coding session if ported unchanged.

gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.name: seb4ez/jevguard-mcp
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Python stdio MCP server (PyPI jevguard-mcp) that wraps TypeSafe's System One endpoint. It exposes 7 tools: 3 atomic ones for command safety, patch verification and option choice, plus 4 low-level ones for generic evaluate, calibrate, prune_state and cache_fingerprint. It prunes state, injects an UNRESOLVED_OR_OTHER escape option, caches results in local SQLite, and applies its own calibration thresholds. The repo also ships an Antigravity-style SKILL.md that tells the agent to call the tools before risky shell commands and large diffs. It is not a hook. The tools are only called if the model decides to call them, or if the skill is copied in and triggers.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jevguard_mcp/tools.py:1772 and :1866: endpoint = TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT or JEVGUARD_ENDPOINT or 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'; api_key = TYPESAFE_API_KEY (:1773, :1865). tools.py:76-105 is_authorized_endpoint: https-only, host allowlist {api.typesafe.ai, typesafe.ai} plus hostnames from JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS (no wildcards). _dispatch_upstream (tools.py:2543-2639) sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' and POSTs JSON {model, questions, state}, then reads data['answers']. The model defaults to the hard-coded 'jev-latest' (tools.py:1758, :1859, :1296), and there is no env override. It is only a per-call tool argument, so a model or a patch must supply 'typesafe/jev-latest' or 'typesafe/jev-1.13'. No 'openrouter' string appears anywhere in the source.
providerSupport.others: Smithery config (smithery.yaml) passes only TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No other gateways.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate to trivial for the endpoint and key, but not verified end to end. Setting TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS=openrouter.ai, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> passes the allowlist and sends the same Bearer header. Two things remain. First, the hard-coded model 'jev-latest' would need to become 'typesafe/jev-latest'; that is a 1-2 line patch, or a wrapper that fixes the model. Second, the OpenRouter System One request and response schema (questions/state/answers) is unverified against this wire format. It must be checked against the OpenRouter docs before relying on it. The cache fingerprint includes the endpoint, so switching endpoints does not collide.

interface.name: jevguard_evaluate_command_safety
interface.purpose: Sends a shell command string (plus working_dir and elevated flag) to Jev as 3 questions: Noul is_destructive, Score risk_score, Choice execution_policy. Returns ALLOW_AUTONOMOUS, REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL or DENY_DESTRUCTIVE. Alias evaluate_command_safety.

interface.name: jevguard_verify_code_patch
interface.purpose: Sends a unified diff and target_file to Jev with a risk_tolerance of strict, balanced or permissive. Returns approved, recommendation (APPROVE, REQUEST_CHANGES, REJECT) and risk_level. Alias verify_code_patch.

interface.name: jevguard_evaluate_decision
interface.purpose: Sends context, a decision_question and a flat options list to a Jev Choice question, with an injected UNRESOLVED_OR_OTHER escape. Returns selected_option, confidence, is_escape_selected and status (CONFIDENT or AMBIGUOUS_STATE). Alias evaluate_decision.

interface.name: jevguard_evaluate
interface.purpose: Generic pipeline: state plus a dict of noul/score/choice questions. It prunes, fingerprints, checks the cache, dispatches upstream, then calibrates.

interface.name: jevguard_calibrate
interface.purpose: Local only. Applies thresholds to supplied answers: top_prob under 0.40, gap under 0.15, or noul within 0.12 of 0.5.

interface.name: jevguard_prune_state
interface.purpose: Local only. Strips nulls and empties, collapses whitespace, breaks cycles, and estimates tokens.

interface.name: jevguard_cache_fingerprint
interface.purpose: Local only. Returns a SHA-256 over the state with volatile keys such as timestamp and trace_id masked.

interface.name: skills/jevguard/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Description-triggered skill: call evaluate_command_safety before rm, dd, mkfs, systemctl, kill, pip install and git reset; call verify_code_patch before big diffs to auth, DB or concurrency files; call evaluate_decision when choosing between technical options. Only usable if the user copies it into ~/.claude/skills. There is no plugin.json, hooks.json or .mcp.json, and no CLI beyond the jevguard-mcp entrypoint.

gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.runtime: Python >=3.10, stdlib only (no dependencies). Started with `python -m jevguard_mcp.server` or the `jevguard-mcp` script. PyPI has 1.0.2 (2026-09-23), while the repo is at 1.1.0 and the latest GitHub release tag is v1.0.1, so PyPI lags the audited source.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.install: pip install jevguard-mcp (or uvx jevguard-mcp). Then register with `claude mcp add jevguard -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- python -m jevguard_mcp.server`. Optionally copy skills/jevguard/SKILL.md into ~/.claude/skills/jevguard/. No installer script or postinstall.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.tests: 134 unittest cases in test_mcp_server.py (2907 lines, stdlib unittest, mock-based, no network). There is no CI (no .github directory), so the claim 'all pass in 0.6s' is not verified here. I did not run them, per the hard rules.
security: The API key is read only from the env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv, but it sits in the MCP env config in ~/.claude.json.

Good hygiene in the code: NoRedirectHandler blocks redirects to prevent Authorization leakage (tools.py:64-70), https only, no userinfo in the URL, and a host allowlist with wildcards rejected. The response is capped at 10MB. Unknown tool arguments are rejected.

The endpoint can be changed through env (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT or JEVGUARD_ENDPOINT), but only to allowlisted hosts. Adding hosts requires JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS, which is env-controlled, not model-controlled.

No subprocess or os.system, and no shell execution. It never executes the commands it evaluates; it only classifies them. No telemetry beyond the upstream call. The 'telemetry' field in results is local latency data.

The local SQLite cache at ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db (TTL 3600s default, JEVGUARD_CACHE_PATH and JEVGUARD_CACHE_TTL) stores the full wire_payload in plaintext. That includes evaluated shell commands, diffs and states, so pasted secrets in commands or diffs would persist on disk for an hour. The cache also keys on the tenant (a SHA-256 prefix of the API key).
A mock_answers argument is refused unless JEVGUARD_TEST_MODE=1. This is fine in production but is a test-only bypass toggle.

Prompt-injection surface: the diff or command being judged is untrusted content placed into the Jev state. Jev has no free-text output, so injection can only skew the probabilities. Because verdicts are advisory and Claude decides what to do with them, a poisoned diff could push toward APPROVE or ALLOW_AUTONOMOUS.

Provenance concerns: the README and GitHub description say 'Official MCP server for JevGuard and TypeSafe AI', yet the README also calls itself 'an independent open-source runtime'. It was written by an anonymous individual (seb4ez), 0 stars, 1 contributor, and created 10 days before the audit date. The upstream 'jevguard' repo is the same author's. There is no evidence of TypeSafe affiliation. The 'Official' claim should be treated as unverified marketing. The README benchmark uses a hard-coded endpoint, https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, not the OpenRouter one.
The PyPI 1.0.2 artifact was not diffed against the repo, so supply-chain equivalence is unverified.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.dataEgress: On a cache miss, the full JSON {model, questions, state} is POSTed over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (or the configured endpoint). For command_safety, state is the command, working_dir and elevated flag. For verify_code_patch, it is the complete patch content and the target file path. For evaluate_decision, it is the context text, the question and the options. For jevguard_evaluate, it is whatever the model puts in state. Only what Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine; the server does not read files. Cache hits send nothing. Anything in a command or diff is sent to a third party, including secrets and client code, which is a real issue for client projects, and the existing secret-leak guard would not see this MCP traffic unless its matcher covers mcp__jevguard__ tools.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open for the workflow but fail-closed in the advisory verdict. On timeout, HTTP error, missing key or network error, a tool returns isError JSON with verdict/fallback_action MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED, and the stdio connection stays up. The default per-call timeout is 10s (parameter up to 300s). _dispatch_upstream retries up to 3 times on 429/5xx/timeouts with exponential backoff inside that total deadline. Client-side rate limit is 120 requests/min. Because nothing is enforced at the harness level, a failure can only make Claude ask you for confirmation (per SKILL.md) or ignore the result. In bypass mode there is no hard block. In the worst case a slow or down upstream stalls a turn for up to about 10s per checked command.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.contextCost: 7 tools. The tool definitions (names, descriptions, JSON schemas, lines 1268-1560 of tools.py) come to about 15.8k characters, or roughly 3.9k tokens, and that is loaded into every session unless tool search defers it. Tool descriptions are long, disambiguation-style ('Use ONLY for... Do NOT use for...'). The server sends no MCP 'instructions' field (server.py:270-310 has only the tools capability). No hooks and no injected text. If SKILL.md is installed, add about 100 tokens for the description at discovery, and about 1.2k tokens when loaded. Each actual call costs a model turn for the tool call plus a JSON result with echoed wire_payload, calibration and telemetry, so it is verbose.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.latencyImpact: Cache miss: about 700-750 ms upstream per the README's own benchmark against api.typesafe.ai (not the claimed 70-500 ms), plus the Python startup and the Claude tool-call round trip (a full extra model turn, likely 2-5 s). Cache hit: about 0.1 ms locally. Because it is model-invoked, the extra cost lands on every risky command or patch that Claude chooses to check.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The tool descriptions tell the model when to use them, and the optional SKILL.md description triggers on 'evaluating terminal command safety, verifying code diffs, making architectural decisions'. There is no deterministic hook and no PreToolUse integration, so it is not guaranteed and not automatic. The user would have to write their own PreToolUse hook to force it.
pros: Only candidate here whose code and SKILL.md are aimed at coding-agent use: command safety, diff verification, and decision choice map directly onto Jev's Noul, Score and Choice primitives.
Zero dependencies, pure stdlib Python 3.10+, and no postinstall or shell execution; the source is small enough to read and even pin (one 2.6k-line tools.py).
Endpoint hardening is better than typical MCP servers: https only, host allowlist, redirects blocked, response size cap, key only in env and never in argv.

Endpoint and key are env-overridable, and a JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS=openrouter.ai plus TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone gets past the allowlist with the same Bearer scheme. So a patch to reach OpenRouter is small.

Local SQLite cache with 1h TTL and volatile-key masking avoids repeat spend for identical commands. It also has a 134-test suite, and failures come back as structured errors and never crash the stdio session.
Escape-option injection (UNRESOLVED_OR_OTHER) and dispersion checks are a reasonable defence against a forced-choice classifier.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code: model is hard-coded 'jev-latest' with no env override, no openrouter references, and TypeSafe direct is the only documented path. The OpenRouter wire format is unverified for this payload.

Not automatic. Pure model-discretion tools plus an optional skill; nothing runs unless Claude decides to. No hooks.json, no plugin.json, no PreToolUse integration, which is exactly what the user asked for (automatic use without prompting).

Duplicates what Claude Code already does. Claude Code has its own permission system, and the user runs bypass or auto mode with an existing secret-leak hook. A probabilistic classifier's advisory verdict cannot block anything in bypass mode, and judging 'is this command destructive' with a 32k-context router model is weaker than the main model's own judgment.

Sends every checked command and full diff to a third-party endpoint on cache miss, which conflicts with client-project confidentiality. The cache also keeps the payloads in plaintext on disk for 1 hour.
Costs about 3.9k tokens of tool definitions per session, plus a whole extra model turn per check, and the verbose output echoes wire_payload.

Provenance and maturity risk: brand-new (created 2026-09-20), one anonymous author, 0 stars, no CI, no issues, and versions inconsistent (PyPI 1.0.2, repo 1.1.0, latest release tag v1.0.1). It claims to be 'Official' while calling itself independent. The author churned about 4 'hardening' commits in one day (2026-09-25), so the code is still changing.

Custom calibration thresholds (0.40, 0.15, 0.12) are admitted heuristics rather than fitted, and the README benchmark measured only 5 hand-picked cases against TypeSafe direct, with a 730-750 ms latency far from the claimed 70-500 ms. The safety claims are unproven.
Prompt-injection risk: the untrusted diff or command is what gets judged, so an adversarial patch can bias the verdict, and the harness does not enforce the outcome.
gh-seb4ez-jevguard-mcp.verdict: A small, reasonably hardened but very young and unaffiliated MCP wrapper that only supports TypeSafe direct. Reaching OpenRouter would need env tweaks plus a model-name patch, and it is model-discretion only, so it does not deliver the automatic, no-prompt integration the user asked for. It is worth using only as a reference for wire format and calibration ideas, or as a base for a custom PreToolUse hook. It is not worth installing as-is.

gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.name: jimmyhealer/jevex
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.whatItDoes: Python stdio MCP server exposing one tool, codebase_investigate. It indexes the repo into heuristic chunks (at most 48 lines each, BM25 seeds, import/call/test/doc edges). It then walks a graph frontier and sends each candidate chunk (question, excerpt, signature, neighbors) to Jev through typesafe-sdk system_one. Jev answers with Choice (role), Score (relevance), Noul (is_source_of_truth) and Choice (next_edge). The server returns an evidence packet of ranked file and line regions for the agent to Read. It is read-only and does not edit files. A --no-jev lexical mode exists.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_explorer/jev_client.py:7 imports AsyncTypeSafeClient from typesafe_sdk. jev_client.py:178 builds AsyncTypeSafeClient(api_key=self._key, timeout=60.0) with no base_url or model argument. config.py:147 reads JEV_API_KEY, falling back to TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The string openrouter appears nowhere in the repo. In the typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 sdist (from PyPI): constants.py:6 defines TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and :15 DEFAULT_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai. constants.py:9 defines TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and :18 DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest. _core/constants.py:5 sets SYSTEM_ONE_PATH=/v1/systemone. _core/config.py:61 resolves base_url from the env var. _core/transport.py sends an Authorization Bearer header.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and probably needs no code change. The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and posts to {base}/v1/systemone with a Bearer key, which matches OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone. In principle: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and the OpenRouter key passed as JEV_API_KEY. This is unverified. The OpenRouter response schema may differ from the SDK's SystemOneResponse pydantic models, and the SDK's models.list() may not exist on OpenRouter. It was not run, per the static-only rule. security: Not a curl|sh installer and has no postinstall hook. Nothing runs shell commands (no subprocess use seen in mcp_server, investigate, jev_client or index). Read-only tool.

The API key lives in the MCP env (claude mcp add -e), stored in ~/.claude.json and not in argv. load_dotenv also reads .env from the cwd and the package root, which could pick up a project's .env with unrelated vars. That is override=False, so it is low risk.

redaction.py gives partial secret protection: skips .env*, credentials.json, secrets.json, id_rsa and .pem/.key/.p12/.pfx files, and applies 4 regexes (key/secret/token assignments with quoted values of 8+ chars, sk-..., apikey_..., PEM headers) before sending. The regexes miss unquoted values, YAML and env style KEY=value, AWS AKIA keys, ghp_ tokens and JWTs, so real secrets can still leak in code excerpts. That matters for client projects.

looks_like_injection() is defined in redaction.py:68, but the two-second check found it used only as a helper. Repo text is fed to Jev, whose typed output cannot carry instructions. The returned packet includes raw excerpts that the agent reads, so a malicious repo file could still inject text into Claude's context (normal Read risk).
Writes .jev-index.json into the repo root only if the user runs the dump command. It is not auto-written by the MCP. The in-process _INDEX_CACHE (index.py:271) never invalidates.
No telemetry found in jevex. The typesafe-sdk sends SDK and runtime headers only. Single-maintainer, 4-commit, 11-day-old repo with no security review or CI. SECURITY.md is only a stub.
PyPI typesafe-sdk is the official SDK (github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python), a reasonable dependency.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.dataEgress: On each codebase_investigate call, for every evaluated chunk (up to max_nodes=18 chunks per call, plus 1-3 gap evaluations) it sends to Jev: the user's question, the chunk excerpt (up to about 40 lines), the signature and path, neighbor names, and already_collected summaries (up to 12). Gap calls send all collected evidence. Everything passes through the regex redact() first. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (and then the Jev provider behind it) if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden. Whole-repo contents are not sent, only shortlisted chunks, but that is client source code leaving the machine. Conversation history, diffs and tool outputs are not sent.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.failureMode: Fail-closed per call. There is no try/except around the Jev calls (investigate.py:222-300 has no except). A Jev outage, 4xx or timeout makes asyncio.run raise, so the MCP tool returns an error to Claude, which then falls back to Grep/Read. The SDK has a retry policy (transport.py send with Retrying). Client timeout is 60s per request, with concurrency 6 and up to about 18-24 sequential-ish requests, so a slow Jev could take tens of seconds. A missing API key raises RuntimeError at JevJudge() construction, so use_jev=True fails even for lexical use unless the model passes use_jev=false. The MCP server itself starts fine without a key. The index cache is per process, so edits made during a session are not re-indexed, and a stale packet can point at wrong line ranges.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.latencyImpact: Model-invoked, not per turn. The first call builds the index (regex scan of files up to 1 MB each, seconds on a large repo). Each investigation runs about 2-6 batches of parallel Jev calls, at 70-500 ms claimed each plus network, so roughly 1-5 s typical, maybe 10 s+ on a big repo or a slow Jev. The README claims a 160s to 69s agent-time gain on SWE-bench with a cheap Gemini Flash agent, which is not measured with Opus. No latency is added to turns where Claude does not call the tool.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__jevex__codebase_investigate). Estimated about 550-700 tokens for the tool description, the 13-parameter schema and the server instructions (about 330 chars). Nothing injected by hooks. Each call returns an evidence packet with excerpts, which can be a few thousand tokens. That is likely not smaller than a targeted GitNexus query result.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. There are no hooks, skills or plugin manifests. The server instructions and tool docstring say to call it before grepping, so Claude Opus will use it for "where is X enforced" questions, but nothing is deterministic. It competes with the already-installed gitnexus MCP (query, context, explain) and the GitNexus Grep|Glob hook for the same job, and Claude may prefer those. README mentions a skills/jev-explorer/SKILL.md (config.py:127), but that file does not exist in the repo.
pros: Genuinely Jev-shaped use case: it uses all three primitives (Choice for role, Score for relevance, Noul for source-of-truth) with a fixed-schema, low-cost typed judgment, which is what Jev is good at, instead of a wrapper around free text (jev_client.py:75-109).
Cheap: about $0.0015 per question claimed. At OpenRouter's $0.042 per 1M input tokens, the 80k token cap per call is at most about $0.003.

Very likely OpenRouter-compatible by environment only. The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, and the path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so the user needs no fork (needs a live test).
Single tool, small context footprint (about 600 tokens), read-only, with no shell execution, no postinstall and no curl|sh.

Server instructions explicitly tell the agent to call the tool before grepping, so there is a reasonable chance Claude Code uses it automatically without being told to use Jev. Tool-level fallback to grep is natural.
MIT, small codebase (about 3.7k lines), easy to read and fork. Redaction and skip lists for .env, key and pem files exist.
cons: Very immature: 1 star, 1 contributor, 4 commits all on one day (2026-09-19), no release, no tests directory despite pytest config, no CI. The benchmark numbers (n=16, n=5) are self-reported and unreproducible, and used a cheap Gemini Flash agent rather than Opus.
Not installable from PyPI (name jevex is taken by an unrelated package). Must git clone plus pip install -e and keep it updated by hand.

Overlaps with the existing gitnexus MCP and the GitNexus graph-context hook, which already give graph-aware code search. Jevex's index is a regex heuristic (no AST) and is weaker than GitNexus. It adds a second source of code-location truth that Claude has to choose between.

Fail-closed with no error handling: no try/except around Jev calls, up to 60 s timeout per request, so a Jev outage or slowness yields a slow tool error and a wasted turn. It only falls back if Claude itself decides to grep.

Stale index: the per-process _INDEX_CACHE is never invalidated, so after Claude edits files the packet points at outdated line ranges during a long session. A .jev-index.json on disk is never auto-refreshed. This is bad for an edit-heavy daily workflow.

Sends source excerpts to a third party (OpenRouter and the Jev provider) with only regex redaction (quoted assignments, sk-, PEM). It misses many secret formats and, more importantly, it is client code leaving the machine, which needs client sign-off. There is no allowlist or per-repo opt-out.
JEV_EXPLORER_REPO is a single fixed path, so a global install needs cwd fallback to work across many repos, and the MCP process cwd is not guaranteed to be the project root.

Skill reference (skills/jev-explorer/SKILL.md) is dangling. Only the server instructions steer the model, and Opus 5.5 tends to prefer native Grep and the GitNexus tools, so 'automatic' use is not guaranteed. The README notes its own 160s to 69s gain is for a weak agent and the value for a strong agent with GitNexus is unproven.
The key has to be passed as JEV_API_KEY, and the code has no OpenRouter key name, base URL or model docs. The user must set three env vars by hand, and the OpenRouter response shape is unverified.
gh-jimmyhealer-jevex.verdict: A real, on-topic and thoughtfully designed Jev MCP tool (Choice/Score/Noul reranking of code chunks) that would probably work against OpenRouter through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL alone. It is a 4-commit, untested, 11-day-old single-maintainer PoC that duplicates GitNexus, goes stale in long sessions and fails closed. Worth a sandbox trial or as a design reference, not for client projects or as the primary integration.

gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.name: caiovicentino/jev-shield
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.whatItDoes: Semantic security layer built on Jev (model 'typesafe-ai/jev' via Vercel AI Gateway, using the Vercel `ai` SDK's experimental_evaluate). Ships four pieces in one repo. (1) A stdio MCP firewall proxy (`jev-shield wrap -- <cmd>`) that screens tools/list descriptions for poisoning, tool calls for exfiltration/destructive/injection/credential hazards, and tool results for injection/secrets, with taint tracking and JSONL audit. (2) A CLI `jev-shield verify` (JSON on stdin, typed verdict on stdout). (3) A Claude Code skill (SKILL.md) that tells the model to call the CLI before risky actions. (4) An opt-in Claude Code PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook, plus an opencode plugin. It is a security guardrail, not a coding-assist integration. It uses Jev Choice/Noul/Score-style questions (boolean and score) over tool-call and tool-output state.

providerSupport.evidence: Only the Vercel AI Gateway is supported. src/verify.mjs:1 `import { experimental_evaluate as evaluate } from 'ai'`; verify.mjs:141-148 runEval calls evaluate({model,state,questions}) with model string from config/policies.json:2 "typesafe-ai/jev", which resolves through the `ai` package's default gateway (package-lock.json:22 pulls @ai-sdk/gateway 4.0.85). The only credential named anywhere is AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (.env.example:2, hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs:4, install-hooks.mjs:81). No fetch() calls, no openrouter.ai URLs, no OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY anywhere (grep over all .mjs/.js found none). README:125 says 'the model layer is abstracted so providers can be swapped', but the code has a single runEval seam, not a provider abstraction.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway only (repo topic vercel-ai-gateway; README links vercel.com/ai-gateway/models/jev).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. runEval (verify.mjs:141-148) is one seam, so a patch is a rewrite of about 10 lines: POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with an OPENROUTER_API_KEY bearer header and map the answers back to {answers[id].probability/score}. However, the code depends on the Vercel `experimental_evaluate` request and response shape (questions map with type boolean/score, criteria, state object, answers[id].probability/.noul/.score, usage.inputTokens). That must be re-mapped to OpenRouter's Decisions API schema (Choice/Noul/Score), and the shape mapping has to be verified against the OpenRouter docs. The `ai` and MCP SDK dependencies would then only be needed for the proxy. You would be maintaining a fork of a 4-star, 8-commit repo.
