interface.purpose: stdio MCP firewall proxy (src/firewall.mjs). Handles tools/list (poison scan, annotate/hide) and tools/call (structural rules, Jev call battery, forward, Jev result battery, redact or annotate, 5-minute taint escalation). It exposes no tools of its own; it re-exports the wrapped server's tools.

interface.name: jev-shield verify
interface.purpose: CLI (src/verify-cli.mjs). Reads {kind:call|result,...} JSON on stdin and prints {decision:block|annotate|pass, triggered, hazards, severity, ms, usd}.

interface.name: jev-shield install-skill / install.sh
interface.purpose: Writes SKILL.md into ~/.claude/skills and ~/.config/opencode/skills, with the repo path injected via sed.

interface.name: install-hooks (node install-hooks.mjs)
interface.purpose: Copies hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs to ~/.claude/hooks/, merges PreToolUse (Bash|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit|MultiEdit|WebFetch|WebSearch|mcp__.*) and PostToolUse (Bash|WebFetch|WebSearch|Grep|mcp__.*) into ~/.claude/settings.json, and installs the opencode plugin. Not exposed in bin/jev-shield.mjs; must be run via `npx github:...` or `node`.

interface.name: uninstall-hooks
interface.purpose: Removes the hook and plugin and strips jev-shield entries from settings.json.

interface.name: Skill 'jev-shield' (SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Model-triggered by description: use BEFORE destructive commands, external sends, credentials/PII, and untrusted content. The model runs `echo JSON | npx -y jev-shield verify` via Bash.

interface.name: Claude Code hook: PreToolUse
interface.purpose: Deterministic. Maps Bash/Write/Edit/WebFetch/mcp__* to a call payload, runs verify, and emits permissionDecision deny (block), ask (annotate, or verifier unavailable), or nothing (pass).

interface.name: Claude Code hook: PostToolUse
interface.purpose: Screens tool output. If contains_injection or contains_secrets >= 0.7 it returns decision:block with a reason telling the model to treat the content as untrusted.

interface.name: Env switches
interface.purpose: JEV_HOOK_OFF=1 (kill switch), JEV_FAIL_MODE=open|closed, JEV_SHIELD_CONFIG, JEV_AUDIT_VERBOSE=1, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.

security: MIT licensed, no telemetry code of its own. All screened data goes to Vercel AI Gateway and then to TypeSafe/Jev.
No curl|sh and no npm postinstall script (package.json has only demo/eval/install-* scripts). install.sh is local-only and uses sed with the repo path.

The hook has a fallback to `npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield verify` when LOCAL_SRC is empty (hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs:23). That would be an unpinned run of GitHub HEAD code on every tool call. With install-hooks the path is rewritten to the local checkout, so it is only a risk if the hook is copied by hand.

The SKILL.md tells the model to run `npx -y jev-shield verify` and falls back to `npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield`. That is an unpinned, mutable dependency executed by the agent. The unscoped npm name `jev-shield` is not shown to be owned by the author, so it is a typosquat or dependency-confusion risk.

install-hooks.mjs rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json wholesale (JSON.parse then JSON.stringify). This would silently drop comments or unusual formatting, and it edits user config without a backup. It also stacks with existing hooks: PreToolUse Bash and mcp__.* would run alongside the user's secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.

verify-cli.mjs:198-202 loads a .env file from the repo root into process.env. That is benign, but it is a secrets file read outside the user's control. The API key is in the environment, not in argv, so it is not visible in `ps`.

audit.jsonl is written inside the repo dir (verify.mjs:240) with args_preview (300 chars of tool args) and output_preview (300 chars of tool output). That can persist commands, secrets, and PII in plaintext. It is gitignored, but it is unmanaged and never rotated.

Prompt-injection surface: the attacker-controlled text (commands, file writes, tool outputs) is fed as `state` to Jev and can try to steer the probabilities. The README itself says 'This is not a security boundary'. The eval reports 94% block recall, but it is self-reported on a curated set of about 60 cases (eval/report.md), with no independent validation.

Known evasion: in eval/report.md, injection at the end of a ~36k-character output passes because text is cut to 12k for screening (verify.mjs:190). The hook keeps the first 8000 and last 4000 characters.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.dataEgress: Everything screened goes to Vercel AI Gateway and then to the Jev provider. PreToolUse sends the full tool_input JSON (ev.tool_input) with no truncation for calls: entire Bash commands (which can contain inline secrets), full Write/Edit/MultiEdit content and diffs (i.e. source code, including client code), WebFetch/WebSearch URLs and queries, and all mcp__* arguments. PostToolUse sends the first 8000 and last 4000 characters of every Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, Grep and mcp__* result (file contents, command output, search hits). The MCP proxy mode sends the full tools/list schemas plus up to 12k characters of each result. The prompts and chat are not sent. On the user's setup this covers personal and client code, and Vercel becomes an additional data processor, a contractual issue for client work. Vercel's data retention is not documented in this repo.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.failureMode: The hook and CLI fail open by default, but the user experience of that is poor. If verification errors (no key, network down, Vercel outage, or a 30 s timeout on execFileSync), then in PreToolUse the hook does not silently pass. It emits permissionDecision 'ask' with 'verification unavailable' (hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs:84-90). In a session without AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, every Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call would therefore raise a confirmation prompt, which also undermines the user's bypass mode. In PostToolUse, failure means exit 0 (pass). JEV_FAIL_MODE=closed makes it exit 2, which blocks. The timeout is 30 s per call with the local checkout, or 60 s via the npx fallback, and it is synchronous, so an outage or hang stalls the agent for up to 30 s per tool call. The MCP proxy's verifyCall catch block fails open as 'annotate' (verify.mjs:180); with fail_mode closed it blocks.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.contextCost: Near zero context by default. The hooks add no tool definitions, and the MCP proxy adds no tools of its own, only wraps the ones you give it. The only context cost is the skill description, roughly 100 tokens (SKILL.md:3, about 430 chars). If the skill body is invoked, it adds about 1.1k tokens (4.4 KB). Hook text is injected only on a flag: a deny/ask reason (short) or a PostToolUse block reason (about 60 tokens). Flagged MCP tool descriptions get an appended warning line.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.autoInvocation: Mixed. (a) The opt-in PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks are deterministic and fully automatic: no user prompting, and they cover all Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch and mcp__* calls. (b) The skill is a description-triggered skill for risky actions only, and it is cooperative and unreliable. (c) The MCP proxy is transparent per wrapped server, but Claude Code's .mcp.json must be edited to wrap each server. Only (a) satisfies the requirement 'Claude Code must use it when needed' with no prompting, and only for security screening, not general decision-making.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.latencyImpact: Documented at about 0.5 to 1.3 s per screened tool call (README:99), p50 437 ms and p95 1042 ms for the model call only (eval/report.md). The hook also spawns a fresh `node` process for the hook and a second `node verify-cli.mjs` via execFileSync on every event, importing the `ai` SDK each time. That likely adds several hundred more ms of cold start. Pre plus Post on the same Bash call means roughly 2 x (0.5 to 1.3 s) plus process overhead, serialized with the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Estimated 1 to 3 s added to every Bash, Edit, Write or MCP call in a day of heavy agentic coding, which is significant. Read, Grep and Glob are exempt in PreToolUse, but Grep is still screened in PostToolUse.
pros: The only candidate found so far with a fully deterministic, no-prompt Claude Code integration of Jev: the PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks in hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs need no 'use jev' from the user, which matches the automatic-integration requirement.

Makes real use of Jev's calibrated probabilities as a typed decision engine (boolean and score questions batched in one call, policy thresholds review 0.35 / action 0.7 / severity_block 2.0 in config/policies.json). This is a legitimate System One use case rather than a chat replacement.
Has a working opt-out (uninstall-hooks.mjs, JEV_HOOK_OFF=1) and a documented kill switch. Cost is tiny (about $0.00002 to $0.00003 per check, 4.2e-8 USD per input token in verify.mjs:7).

Ships an eval harness (eval/run.mjs, about 23 KB) and a candid report with documented limitations (truncation bypass, over-blocking of .env to internal recipients, PII in support tickets) instead of only marketing numbers.

The prompt-injection screen of PostToolUse results (WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP output) is genuinely useful for a client-work setup that runs in bypass or auto permission mode, where nothing else checks fetched content.

MIT license, no telemetry code, no install-time code execution beyond the explicit install scripts. The code is small (about 135 KB total, of which 46 KB is the lockfile) and quick to audit in full; I read all of the runtime code.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the only provider is the Vercel AI Gateway (verify.mjs:1, policies.json:2, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY everywhere). The user must create a Vercel account and key, or fork and rewrite runEval against openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, which contradicts the OpenRouter-hosted Jev requirement.

Wrong job for daily coding: it is a security gate that adds a verdict only on risk, not a decision helper that improves coding (no routing, triage, or 'does this test need to run' style use). It helps with injection defense but does not make Claude Code faster or better at coding.

Heavy per-call overhead: two hook events, each spawning node plus the `ai` SDK and a network round trip, adding about 1 to 3 s to every Bash/Edit/Write/MCP call, on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. That is a large cumulative cost for all-day agentic sessions.

Broad data egress to a third party: every Bash command, full file write/edit content and 12k characters of every tool result go to Vercel and TypeSafe. Unacceptable by default for client projects under NDA, and it works against the user's own secret-leak guard hook, which exists to keep secrets off the network.

Fail-open is actually fail-to-prompt: when the key is missing or the gateway is down, the PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision 'ask' for every call (jev-shield.mjs:86-89). In the user's bypass or auto mode this creates constant prompts, or is ignored, so the result is either friction or silent no-op. There is no local timeout shorter than 30 s.

False-positive risk in normal dev work: its own report shows `.env` or customer exports to internal recipients, and PII, scored payload_sensitivity 0.92-0.93 and blocked. A coding agent routinely touches .env, migrations, curl calls and git push --force, so 'annotate' becomes 'ask' and 'block' becomes deny, which would collide with the user's workflow.

Immature: 8 commits over one day (2026-09-16 to 2026-09-17), single contributor, 4 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, no unit tests (only a self-run eval against the live API), and nothing since 2026-09-17. README explicitly says it is not a security boundary.

Installer hazards: install-hooks.mjs rewrites the user's ~/.claude/settings.json without backup, the hook has an unpinned `npx github:` fallback, and the skill recommends `npx -y jev-shield` (unverified unscoped npm name). audit.jsonl in the repo dir logs command and output previews in plaintext.

Its own truncation is a known bypass (injection past 12k or after the 8000+4000 hook window is missed), so the security value is partial. Also, the hook classifies Bash as a generic 'shell_exec' with the description 'Execute a shell command on the host', with no repo context, which limits precision.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.verdict: The only concrete, automatic (hook-based) Jev integration for Claude Code found in this audit, but it is a security-screening gate and not a coding aid, and it is hard-wired to the Vercel AI Gateway, not OpenRouter. Its latency cost of roughly 1 to 3 s per tool call and its broad data egress make it a poor fit for this user's all-day client work. It is worth reading as a reference hook design, or forking to OpenRouter's Decisions API for a narrow use such as PostToolUse injection screening of WebFetch/WebSearch only, but not worth installing as-is.
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.install: npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield install-hooks (opt-in hooks; needs AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY); npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield install-skill (skill); or `jev-shield wrap -- <upstream-cmd>` as an MCP server command
gh-caiovicentino-jev-shield.tests: None besides eval/run.mjs, a live-API eval harness with about 60 curated cases and a self-reported result (94% block recall, 0 false positives on benign, 15/15 consistency across 3 runs). There is no unit-test suite and no CI (.github absent).

gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.name: agent-chaperone
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.whatItDoes: A "calibrated firewall" for agent tool calls. It is both an MCP stdio/HTTP proxy that wraps other MCP servers and a Claude Code plugin whose PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure hooks screen Claude Code's own built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch, Read, Grep, NotebookEdit). Each screen combines deterministic rules (allow/deny lists, secret regexes, shell rules) with a small battery of typed Jev questions: destructive, exfiltration, severity, instructs_reader (prompt injection), secret_in_args, plus optional off_task and policy_violation. Thresholds live in a YAML policy. Modes are shadow (default, blocks nothing, logs only), enforce and strict. Held calls return permissionDecision "ask" and can be released with `agent-chaperone approve <id>`. Withheld results are replaced through updatedToolOutput. It also keeps a local digest of MCP tool lists to detect rug-pulls.

providerSupport.evidence: Jev path: src/backends/typesafe.ts:222-262 builds TypeSafeClient from @typesafe-ai/sdk and calls client.systemOne(). The SDK (sdk/package/dist/index.mjs:56-62,513,554,581) reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai) and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL (default jev-latest), POSTs {state, questions, model} to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. chooseBackend (src/cli/main.ts:496-509) picks TypeSafe first and calls createTypeSafeBackend() with NO options, so no baseUrl is passed from code, but the SDK still honors the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env var. OpenRouter path in the tool itself: src/backends/openai.ts:27,285-291 uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY against https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with default model openai/gpt-4o-mini (AGENT_CHAPERONE_MODEL overrides). That is an ordinary chat-completions call to a general model, NOT Jev and NOT /api/v1/systemone or /api/alpha/decisions. src/cli/main.ts:501-508 marks it `uncalibrated: true` and prints a warning on every start. README states those probabilities are not calibrated and no thresholds were measured for them.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Probably trivial with no code change: set TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. The SDK would then POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with a Bearer token, which matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint in the brief. UNVERIFIED: I could not fetch OpenRouter's schema (docs URL 404), so request and response body parity with api.typesafe.ai and the model-id handling are assumptions. The fetch would need a live test with a real key, which I did not run. An alternative is a 5-line patch passing baseUrl to createTypeSafeBackend. Any setting of TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes chooseBackend prefer this Jev path over the uncalibrated OpenRouter chat path.
providerSupport.others: Also supports Vercel AI Gateway through AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (uncalibrated chat completions, src/backends/openai.ts:28,296).

interface.name: Claude Code plugin hooks (hooks/hooks.json)
interface.purpose: PreToolUse matcher Bash|PowerShell|Monitor|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit|WebFetch runs `node scripts/plugin-hook.mjs pre`. PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure matcher Bash|PowerShell|Read|Grep|WebFetch runs `... post`. It launches a global `agent-chaperone` if one is on PATH, otherwise it does an npm install of the matching version into the plugin data dir on first use (~13s, README) and then runs that copy (~0.15s per call, README).

interface.name: agent-chaperone hook pre|post
interface.purpose: Reads the Claude Code hook JSON on stdin and writes a decision on stdout: permissionDecision deny/ask, updatedToolOutput, or additionalContext. It always exits 0 (src/cli/main.ts:648).

interface.name: agent-chaperone [opts] -- <cmd>
interface.purpose: stdio/HTTP MCP proxy that screens tools/call arguments, results and tool-list changes for the wrapped server. No MCP tools of its own are exposed to the model.

interface.name: agent-chaperone wrap <config> [--write|--unwrap|--header-env]
interface.purpose: Edits an MCP config to put the proxy in front of each server, keeps a .before-agent-chaperone backup.

interface.name: agent-chaperone log [--follow] | show <id> | approve <id> | trust <server> | report | replay [--policy] | task "..."
interface.purpose: Audit log viewing, one-shot approval of a held call, accepting a changed tool list, summary of what enforcing would stop, re-deciding under another policy, and recording the current task for the off_task question.

interface.name: skills/agent-chaperone/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Tells the agent what held or withheld notices mean and not to route around them. Installable via `npx skills add`. It ships with the plugin.

interface.name: Jev question battery (src/screens/questions.ts)
interface.purpose: destructive (noul), exfiltration (noul), call_severity (score), instructs_reader (noul), result_severity (score), secret_in_args (noul), policy_violation and off_task (optional, unmeasured), description_steers (off by default).

gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript, ESM). Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (MIT, published 2026-09-15 by TypeSafe maintainers), yaml, zod. A Python bench harness exists but is not used at runtime.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.install: /plugin marketplace add agent-chaperone/agent-chaperone; /plugin install agent-chaperone@agent-chaperone (or `npm install -g agent-chaperone` plus hand-written hooks in ~/.claude/settings.json). Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY (and, for OpenRouter, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL) in the environment Claude Code launches hooks from.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.tests: 42 vitest files under src/ (about one per module, including hooks, proxy framing, redaction, plugin matcher parity). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs lint, format check, typecheck, build and tests on Node 24, plus a release workflow with changesets. The bench/ folder holds recorded Jev responses (1,947 requests) and methodology in ADR-0004. I did not run any of it.
security: Key handling: src/backends/typesafe.ts:6-8 says the package never reads the key. The SDK takes it from TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so there is nothing in argv or the process list. SDK logLevel is pinned to 'off' (typesafe.ts:224) because debug logging would print request bodies. src/proxy/upstream.ts:27 strips TYPESAFE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY and AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY from the environment of wrapped MCP servers.

Response bodies from the backend are never copied into failure messages or the audit log (typesafe.ts:8-14, 118-160), which limits injection back through the log. Zod validation and size guards at entry points; SECURITY.md says no eval or shell interpolation of content.

Supply chain: the plugin's first hook call runs `npm install agent-chaperone@<version>` at runtime (scripts/plugin-hook-lib.mjs:111-140, plugin-hook.mjs) with its own npm cache. There is no curl|sh and no postinstall script. It is still a runtime fetch from npm of a 3-week-old, 2-maintainer package, and its transitive deps run on every tool call.
No telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics returned nothing). The only network calls are to the configured model backend and npm on first install.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is sent to Jev as data. README admits adaptive attacks will get through, the model does not treat input as hostile by default, it is not a sandbox, and 8-13 of 68 benign 'discusses injection' items are false positives. A fail-open screen is a second opinion, not a control.
Audit log stores arguments and results locally unless AGENT_CHAPERONE_STORE_CONTENT=0 is set. Secret patterns are redacted before send and before write, which is regex-based and best-effort.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.dataEgress: Every screened Claude Code tool call leaves the machine to the configured backend (api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai if repointed): for pre hooks the Bash command, Edit/Write file paths and content, WebFetch URL and prompt; for post hooks the full Bash stdout/stderr, Read file contents, Grep matches and WebFetch results (long results are screened by first and last chunks). This is source code and command output from personal AND client projects. Secret-shaped strings are regex-redacted first. Results the allow/deny lists settle never reach the model. Per-server `screen_calls/screen_results: false` opt-outs exist in the policy file. With `agent-chaperone task` or the suggested UserPromptSubmit hook, the user's prompt is also sent with every call. With the OpenRouter chat path, content goes to openrouter.ai and then to openai/gpt-4o-mini. Nothing else is sent, and there is no telemetry.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.failureMode: Fail-open in shadow and enforce, and fail-closed only in strict mode (SECURITY.md, src/screening/gate.ts and src/hooks/run.ts failure handling). SDK per-attempt timeout is 10s and 2 retries with a 30s total budget (typesafe.ts:36-40). The OpenAI-compatible path has a 20s timeout (openai.ts:32). A dead or slow Jev therefore stalls each Bash/Read/Grep call for up to 30s before failing open. A missing key means rules-only and every judgment records that no model was asked. An unreadable policy file makes the pre hook return 'ask' (main.ts:660-678), which prompts on every screened call, so a broken policy is loud. An npm install failure lets calls through and is not retried for 10 minutes. Session-scoped caching avoids repeat asks for identical state.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.latencyImpact: Hooks are synchronous and block the tool. Per screened call: Node process start plus the plugin launcher, roughly 0.15s (README's own measurement), plus one Jev request (claimed 70-500ms, avg 754 input tokens per README). Expect about 0.3-0.7s added to every Bash/Edit/Write/WebFetch call (pre) and every Bash/Read/Grep/WebFetch call (post), so Bash, Read and Grep pay twice. It runs beside the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks, and hooks for the same event run concurrently, so wall-clock stacking is partial. The first call after install waits about 13s for npm. Latency on a long agent session is significant: hundreds of extra round trips. Deterministic allow-lists skip the model.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.contextCost: Very low. It exposes no MCP tools, so tool-definition cost is 0 in plugin mode (the proxy adds none of its own either). The plugin adds one skill; the description is short, about 100-150 tokens (SKILL.md not sized precisely). Hooks inject nothing when a call passes. Injected text appears only for held/withheld/annotated calls (a notice of about 50-100 tokens) or a policy-load failure. Setting a task via UserPromptSubmit adds nothing to context. It does add an audit log on disk.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure matchers fire on every matching built-in tool call with no model discretion and no user prompting. For MCP tools, the proxy is transparent only after the MCP config is rewritten with `wrap`. The screens are automatic, but they are a security gate. They do not give Claude decision-making help, and Claude never calls Jev itself.
pros: Only candidate here that is truly automatic: plugin hooks fire on every Bash/Edit/Write/WebFetch/Read/Grep call with zero prompting, which is exactly the 'Claude Code uses it without me asking' requirement.

Uses Jev for what its typed, calibrated probabilities suit: yes/no and ordinal judgments (destructive? exfiltration? does this tool output instruct the AI?). Published benchmark on jev-1.13: AUC 0.976 on InjecAgent, 0.993 on hand-labeled tool calls, 1,947 requests for $0.062 total, so per-call cost is negligible.

Direct Jev code path: uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk /v1/systemone. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL are read by the SDK, so repointing to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is likely env-only (needs a live test).
Safe rollout: default 'shadow' mode blocks nothing and logs what it would have done; `report` and `replay` let the user tune thresholds from their own traffic before enforcing.
Context-cheap: no MCP tool defs; nothing injected on pass. Coexists with existing hooks (matchers overlap on Bash but it never auto-approves, and the README/ADR describe coexistence with ECC).

Fixes a real gap for a bypass/auto-permission user: content-aware second opinion on rm -rf, force-push, curl-with-secrets and prompt-injected WebFetch/Read/Grep results, which permission prompts cannot see.

Careful engineering: fail-open launcher that never crashes a call, response-body text never copied into the log, redaction before send, SDK debug logging pinned off, the plugin's matchers tested against docs, 42 test files, CI, and an honest 'what it is not' section and known false positives.
cons: Sends the full stdout of Bash, Read file contents and Grep matches, plus Write/Edit content, to a third-party API on every screened call. That is client source code on client projects, and regex redaction is the only protection. This is a real confidentiality and NDA problem unless the client work is excluded through policy.

OpenRouter is not a first-class provider. The tool's own OPENROUTER_API_KEY path calls chat completions on openai/gpt-4o-mini with uncalibrated probabilities, not Jev, and the README says so. Getting Jev via OpenRouter depends on the untested TYPESAFE_BASE_URL trick, and the model-ID mapping (typesafe/jev-1.13 vs SDK 'jev-latest') is unconfirmed. If you set OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone you silently get GPT-4o-mini.

Per-call latency of roughly 0.3-0.7s on every Bash/Read/Grep (twice, pre and post), with a worst case of 30s per call if Jev is slow. Over a full day of agent work this is noticeable, and it stacks with the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.

It is a guardrail, not a coding accelerator. It does not use Jev to route, pick files, decide next steps or review diffs, so it does not deliver the 'Jev adds value to coding' idea beyond safety. Because the user runs bypass/auto mode, enforce-mode 'ask' prompts would reintroduce interruptions.

Immature and low-adoption: created 2026-09-18, 21 stars, 2 real contributors, v0.3.3, API churn likely. The plugin does a runtime `npm install` on first use. Unmeasured questions (off_task, policy_violation, description_steers) are not benchmarked. Author-run benchmark only: 8-13 false positives out of 68 benign security-doc samples, and recall of 0.805 for InjecAgent at threshold 0.5. It is not a sandbox and adaptive attacks pass through.
Duplicates part of the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and adds a second 'ask' source on overlapping matchers. The plugin hook wrapper spawns Node per call.
Shadow mode's default value is only diagnostic: until the user reads the logs and switches to enforce, it protects nothing. Enforce needs tuning.
gh-agent-chaperone-agent-chaperone.verdict: The strongest genuine, automatic, Jev-based Claude Code integration found so far: a deterministic hook plugin with an honest shadow-first design that uses Jev for calibrated safety judgments. It is not an OpenRouter-native tool, though: the OpenRouter route in code is an uncalibrated GPT-4o-mini fallback, and using real Jev via OpenRouter means an untested TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override. Its egress of all Bash output and file contents is a real cost on client projects, and it adds safety rather than coding help. Try it in shadow mode on personal projects first, and exclude client repos via policy.

gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.name: NiazMorshed2007/jev-review
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (Node, TS bundled to dist/server.js) exposing one tool, jev_review. The coding agent sends task, diff, files and repositoryContext. The server builds 57 typed questions (19 quality metrics x [Noul applicable, Score 1-10, Choice weakness]) and POSTs them with the state to TypeSafe's /v1/systemone using model jev-latest. It maps the Score/Noul/Choice answers to per-metric 1-10 scores, confidence, up to 5 rubric-derived priorities, and deltas versus previousEvaluation. A bundled SKILL.md plus MCP server instructions tell the agent to run an iterative implement, score, improve, rescore loop on every nontrivial task. It is a quality-score feedback loop and does not provide Jev as a general decision router.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev/client.ts:13 `JEV_API_ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"` (hardcoded, no base-URL env override; same in dist/server.js:37030). client.ts:14 `JEV_MODEL = "jev-latest"` hardcoded. src/config/environment.ts:4 reads only `JEV_API_KEY` (not TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY). client.ts:61-67 sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and body `{state, model, questions}`. README 'Security and privacy' confirms only api.typesafe.ai is contacted.
providerSupport.others: None. Only the TypeSafe direct endpoint; no gateway abstraction.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in wire terms but requires a fork and rebuild. OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone takes the same {model, state, questions} body with a Bearer OpenRouter key (per OpenRouter TypeSafe SDK docs). The patch is 3 constants: endpoint to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model to typesafe/jev-latest or ~typesafe/jev-latest, and env var to OPENROUTER_API_KEY. dist/server.js is a committed 1.39 MB esbuild bundle, so either hand-edit lines ~37030-37031 and the env lookup there, or run npm install and npm run build (that means running third-party build tooling). Any upstream update would overwrite the patch. Whether OpenRouter's response shape is exactly what jevResponseSchema (src/jev/schema.ts) expects is not verified; the schema is passthrough and only requires model, answers and usage.input_tokens/output_tokens.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_review (src/mcp/server.ts:29-58)
interface.purpose: Only tool. Input {task?, diff?, files?[{path,content}], repositoryContext?, previousEvaluation?}; at least one context field is required. Output is a structured Evaluation with 19 metrics (applicable, score 1-10, confidence, summary, issues), priorities (max 5, score<8), and comparison/improvements/regressions if previousEvaluation is given. Annotations: readOnlyHint true, openWorldHint true. Errors come back as isError text.

interface.name: MCP server instructions (src/mcp/server.ts:9-19)
interface.purpose: About 1.1k chars injected into Claude Code's system context. Says 'For every nontrivial coding task, call jev_review after the first coherent implementation... then call it again after each meaningful improvement' and 'A single baseline call is not completion: continue while important weak metrics remain'.

interface.name: Skill jev-review (skills/jev-review/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Description-triggered skill (not a slash command by default in Claude Code auto mode). Defines the loop implement, validate, score, inspect, improve, rescore, and stopping conditions. Tells the agent 'Never send secrets'.

interface.name: Hooks
interface.purpose: None. No hooks.json, no settings snippets. Automation relies only on model compliance with instructions and the skill.

interface.name: Install: npx plugins add NiazMorshed2007/jev-review --target claude-code
interface.purpose: Uses the third-party 'plugins' CLI (Agent Plugins 1.0). Manual alternatives: claude --plugin-dir <clone>, or claude mcp add --scope user jev-review -- node /abs/dist/server.js. The .mcp.json runs `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/server.js` with no env block, so JEV_API_KEY is inherited from Claude Code's process environment.

gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.install: Recommended for this user if used at all: git clone, read the diff, then `claude mcp add --scope user jev-review -- node /abs/path/dist/server.js`, with the key exported in the shell environment. security: API key is read from env JEV_API_KEY and used only in the Authorization header (client.ts:62-65). It is not in argv unless the user puts it there. Manual `claude mcp add` without --env keeps it out of the process list.
No shell execution, no postinstall (package is private, no scripts run at install), no telemetry, no other network endpoints found in src or by grepping dist (only api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone).
Error handling does not echo response bodies (client.ts:105-128), only mapped messages, so the key does not leak in errors.

Supply-chain: the committed dist/server.js is 1.39 MB, bundled with the MCP SDK and zod. It cannot be fully audited by reading and is not built by CI. Only the JEV constants were confirmed to match src. Running it means running an unaudited bundle.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool takes agent-chosen diff and files, and Jev returns only typed numbers, so response injection is minimal (fixed rubric strings from metrics.ts). The main risk is the reverse, an injected agent exfiltrating file contents via the files[] argument to a third party. Only the model decides what to send.

The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it does NOT cover mcp__jev-review__jev_review inputs. Secrets already in context (from Read) could be forwarded without a check. Only SKILL.md's advice 'Never send secrets' applies.
The install path `npx plugins add` runs an extra unaudited third-party CLI.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in task, diff, files[].content and repositoryContext leaves the machine as JSON to api.typesafe.ai in the unmodified version (or to OpenRouter, then TypeSafe, if patched). That is source code, diffs and requirement text, and the SKILL loop calls it repeatedly (baseline, then after each improvement), so the same code is sent many times per task. Also sent: 57 static question definitions (about 20 KB, roughly 5k tokens) per call. previousEvaluation is compared locally and not sent. No automatic repo reads, telemetry or other endpoints. Client-project code goes to TypeSafe/OpenRouter under their retention terms, which conflicts with typical client NDAs unless approved.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.failureMode: Fail-open. Errors are caught in the tool handler and returned as isError text (mcp/server.ts:50-56), so Claude continues without a score. Client timeout is 30 s per attempt (client.ts:51), with 2 retries on 429/529/5xx and backoff up to 5 s (client.ts:52,80-83,144-153). A worst-case hang can therefore be about 90 s+ of blocked agent turn. A missing JEV_API_KEY gives an error only at first call (the server still starts and lists the tool). There is no circuit breaker, so the agent may retry the tool on later turns.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.latencyImpact: Only when the model decides to call. Each call is one Jev request with 57 questions plus the diff, and the claimed 70-500 ms is likely stretched by the large question set and network. Realistic 1-3 s per call (unmeasured). The bigger cost is the loop design: the instructions push 2+ calls per nontrivial task plus extra Opus turns to inspect and rework code, which adds minutes of agent time and Opus tokens per task. There is no per-tool-call overhead for Read/Edit/Bash since there are no hooks.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.contextCost: 1 tool, jev_review. Tool description is about 900 chars (about 225 tokens). Input schema includes the nested previousEvaluation with 19 metric objects (the schema may be $ref'd or inlined; inlined would be much larger), estimated 1.5-3k tokens. Server instructions are about 1.1k chars (about 280 tokens), always injected. The skill description is about 450 chars (about 110 tokens) in the skill list. Total estimated roughly 2-3.5k tokens of standing context, moderate for a single tool. Hooks add no text. Every tool call adds the returned Evaluation JSON, which is large (19 metrics with fields, about 1-2k tokens), plus the diff/files the model must write into the call as output tokens on Opus, which is the real recurring cost.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus skill-description trigger, reinforced by strongly worded server instructions ('For every nontrivial coding task, call jev_review...'). It is not deterministic. There is no hook, so Claude Code will not always call it, and in a session with many other instructions and tools it may be skipped or over-used. It does not require the user to say 'use jev', but nothing guarantees it will fire.
pros: Truly automatic in the sense the user wants: server instructions and the skill description tell Claude to call it on nontrivial tasks without being asked (src/mcp/server.ts:9-19, SKILL.md). No hooks needed, so it does not collide with the existing GitNexus/secret-guard hooks.

Uses Jev in the way it is designed: only typed Score/Noul/Choice primitives, no free text, and it says explicitly that Jev cannot explain root causes (README 'How it works'). Honest about limitations.

Small, readable codebase (about 1.3k lines of TS excluding tests). client.ts is easy to audit and shows a single outbound endpoint, no telemetry, and key only in the Authorization header. Fail-open with mapped errors.
OpenRouter port is small: endpoint, model and env constants (client.ts:13-14, environment.ts:4) since OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone uses the same {model,state,questions} body.
MIT, 231 stars and 20 forks in 13 days suggest community interest and some eyeballs on it. Cost per call is negligible ($0.042/1M input, output free).
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint, model and key var are hardcoded to TypeSafe direct, so the user's stated goal needs a fork/patch plus editing or rebuilding a 1.39 MB committed bundle, and the patch has to be maintained.

Very young and single-author: 4 commits all on 2026-09-17, 1 contributor, no releases, no CI, about 13 unit tests with fakes only, and no evidence the live OpenRouter or TypeSafe schema was tested beyond the author's own runs.

Value is doubtful for daily coding: it returns 1-10 scalars on 19 dimensions from a model with no reasoning, and priorities/reasons are canned rubric text (transform.ts:39-43, metrics.ts), so the agent must still diagnose everything itself. The score is unvalidated as a predictor of code quality, and the skeptic 'cheap router model' claim is unaddressed.

Token and time burn: the SKILL demands a loop of score, inspect, improve, rescore ('A single baseline call is not completion'), which on Opus 5.5 means the model re-emitting diffs/files as tool arguments several times per task, plus about 1-2k tokens of JSON per result. This is likely to exceed the savings from a $0.042/M scoring model many times over.

Code egress with no guard: diffs and full file contents go to a third party under the model's own choice. The user's secret-leak hook does not match MCP tool names, and client-project code would be sent to TypeSafe/OpenRouter. There is no allowlist, redaction or size limit (README: 'does not impose an additional character... limit').

Auto-invocation is only advisory prose; behavior will be inconsistent, and a bypass/auto-permission session would let it fire on every task without a check. There are 57 questions per call that add payload and latency for every review.
Recommended install path (`npx plugins add`) adds another unaudited third-party installer; the bundle is not reproducibly built.
gh-niazmorshed2007-jev-review.verdict: A tidy, auditable single-tool MCP that auto-nudges Claude toward a Jev score loop, but it is TypeSafe-only (needs a fork to use OpenRouter), 13 days old with one author, and its output is canned scores rather than actionable review. It burns Opus tokens and ships client code out with no guard, so use it only as a patched, optional experiment and not as the core Jev integration.

gh-brainwires-jevwire.name: Brainwires/jevwire (npm jevwire, Claude Code plugin "jev")
gh-brainwires-jevwire.whatItDoes: Third-party (Brainwires, single author Josh Guyette) Claude Code plugin plus MCP server plus library built on TypeSafe's System One /v1/systemone endpoint. It has 7 MCP tools (jev_rank, jev_pick, jev_verify, jev_evaluate, jev_gate_action, jev_next_step, jev_list_models), and a large hook suite that runs without the user or model asking. The hooks: a PreToolUse gate on Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit/Agent/Task/mcp__*; a semantic lint of edits; a git-commit diff scope and staged-secret check; a PostToolUse prompt-injection screen on WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__*; a Stop-hook check that the final message is not unfinished and that its claims match git diff HEAD; and UserPromptSubmit bookkeeping. Hot-path hooks are type:"http" posts to a loopback daemon on 127.0.0.1:10522. It is a guardrail and verifier, not a coding accelerator.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.install: /plugin marketplace add Brainwires/jevwire ; /plugin install jev@brainwires-jevwire ; then export TYPESAFE_API_KEY or set the plugin api_key option, then /reload-plugins. Bare MCP: claude mcp add jev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- npx -y jevwire. Not executed in this audit.

GitHub Actions CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs type-check, tests and build on Node 20 and 22. It also checks that the committed bundle is fresh and runs the daemon e2e twice concurrently. I did not run any of it. The project is 9 days old with no GitHub releases (latestRelease null) and 0.x churn: six releases in about four days, and its own changelog notes it blocked its author falsely twice.

providerSupport.evidence: The base URL is configurable but the wire path and key are TypeSafe-shaped. src/config.ts:33 sets DEFAULTS.baseUrl to https://api.typesafe.ai, and config.ts:109 reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. src/hooks/config.ts:99 and :252 do the same for the hooks, via the plugin option base_url or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. src/jev/client.ts:DEFAULT_BASE_URL is https://api.typesafe.ai, and evaluate() posts to the hard-coded path "/v1/systemone" (`${baseUrl}${path}`) with Authorization: Bearer <key>. listModels does GET /v1/models. The key is read from JEV_PLUGIN_API_KEY, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY (config.ts firstKey). The model default is the pinned "jev-1.13.0" (config.ts:33-40) and is overridable via the plugin option model or JEV_MODEL. A grep for openrouter across the repo has zero hits. OpenRouter's documented surface is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api would produce exactly that URL. The request body is {state, model, questions}, and the client validates answers[id].type against each question. I could not confirm that OpenRouter's body and response schema is identical: the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404. plugin/hooks/hooks.json also hard-codes the header X-Jev-Env-Key: $TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key would have to be exported under that name.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only, and no gateway abstraction.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Probably trivial config-only, unverified. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, then TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (or the plugin api_key option), and JEV_MODEL/plugin model=typesafe/jev-1.13. The model id must change because jev-1.13.0 is TypeSafe's id and OpenRouter uses typesafe/jev-1.13. Two risks remain. First, if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone envelope differs from TypeSafe's (answers/usage field names, Noul/Score answer shapes), client.parseEvaluateResponse throws JevProtocolError, and every hook then fails open, so the plugin would look installed but do nothing. Second, GET /v1/models (used by jev_list_models and the smoke script) probably does not exist at that path on OpenRouter. If the schemas differ, patching src/jev/client.ts is a small change (one file, about 100 lines) but means forking and rebuilding the committed plugin/dist bundles.

interface.name: MCP jev_rank
interface.purpose: Rank candidates, or files given as paths/glob that the server reads itself, against a query. Returns path:start_line-end_line plus a relevance score, without echoing file text. Needs a fairly specific, model-discretion trigger.

interface.name: MCP jev_pick
interface.purpose: Choose 1 of 2-240 candidates (grep hits, symbols, test names) with a 'none' escape hatch. Returns per-candidate fits.

interface.name: MCP jev_verify
interface.purpose: Check claims against evidence text or an evidence_path file. Returns supported / contradicted / not_addressed / conflicting per claim.

interface.name: MCP jev_evaluate
interface.purpose: Raw batched Choice/Noul/Score questions over a state.

interface.name: MCP jev_gate_action
interface.purpose: Second opinion on an irreversible action, returning allow / confirm / block.

interface.name: MCP jev_next_step
interface.purpose: Choose a next step after a confusing tool failure.

interface.name: MCP jev_list_models
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models, listing the models the account may send.

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse (Bash|Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|Agent|Task|mcp__.*)
interface.purpose: Deterministic prefilter, then optional Jev judgment of destructive/outward/credential/scope risk. It can add a post-hoc note or a one-time deny 'tripwire' that Claude can answer with a '# jev:intended <reason>' marker. It never emits allow. Hard-coded regex tripwires cover rm -rf ~, force-push to main, DROP TABLE and similar. Also runs semantic lint on edits (regex gate, then Noul: swallowed error, hardcoded secret/URL, removed test, CLAUDE.md convention breaks), and on git commit judges pr_scope, message_describes_diff and a staged secret.

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse (WebFetch|WebSearch|mcp__.*)
interface.purpose: Injection screen: chunks the whole tool result (up to about 128k chars) to Jev, and adds a context line if it reads as instructions to an AI or contradicts the request.

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure (Approval / async ledger)
interface.purpose: Bookkeeping: records whether the last test/build/lint passed.

interface.name: Hook Stop
interface.purpose: Blocks the stop, at most once per prompt, if the final message admits unfinished work or claims checks pass while the ledger says they failed. Also checks file/identifier claims against git diff HEAD.

interface.name: Hook UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Records the last 3 prompts (2,000 chars each). Optional route_prompts classifier (off by default).

interface.name: Hook SessionStart / SessionEnd
interface.purpose: Starts and registers the loopback daemon on 127.0.0.1:10522 and reports missing-key config. A watchdog in the MCP server re-checks it every 10s.

interface.name: Skill jev-decisions
interface.purpose: Description-triggered guidance on when to call the MCP tools and how to read the [jev] lines.

interface.name: Slash commands /jev:on, off, status, why, calibrate, daemon
interface.purpose: Control and audit (why shows the '# jev:intended' audit trail; calibrate replays the local decision log).

security: No curl|sh installer, no postinstall script, and no telemetry found. The only child_process use is src/hooks/daemon/control.ts spawning its own daemon, and the Stop claim check runs git via execFile with an argv array and GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF/GIT_PAGER stripped (SECURITY.md). The committed bundles (hook.mjs, mcp.mjs at 40k lines) are not auditable line by line, but CI checks they match the source.

The API key is sent to a local HTTP daemon on a fixed port. Every http hook sends Authorization: Bearer $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY and X-Jev-Env-Key: $TYPESAFE_API_KEY to http://127.0.0.1:10522 (hooks.json). SECURITY.md itself lists the residual risk that another local user who binds 10522 first receives the key and the hook payloads, and says multi-user hosts are unsupported. That is fine on a single-user box.

The daemon authenticates with a sha256 timingSafeEqual key comparison. But a hook post with no matching key is still served if its body names a known session id (SECURITY.md), and a keyless daemon runs unauthenticated. /v1/health is unauthenticated and leaks no secret. The key is never logged, and redact() in server.ts masks it in errors.

The key does not appear in argv. The MCP server receives it via env (JEV_PLUGIN_API_KEY), which is visible to the same UID via /proc/<pid>/environ. The bare-MCP install form `claude mcp add ... -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...` stores the key in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

Jev is explicitly not injection-hardened (SECURITY.md). Text in a fetched page or file that argues for its own approval can shift the probabilities, and the plugin is advisory only. It can never emit permissionDecision allow, and Claude itself can bypass a tripwire by re-issuing the call with '# jev:intended <reason>'. It does not deliver security enforcement. Under bypassPermissions, ask_on_trip does nothing, so the only effect is that Claude sees a deny or note.

Its notes and tripwires inject text into Claude's context that is shaped by untrusted content (tool inputs and results). The README says the wording is deliberately declarative to avoid tripping Claude's injection defenses. That adds noise and gives the user's existing GitNexus, caveman and secret-guard hooks a new interaction surface.

Redaction of secrets before sending or logging is regex-based (sk-, ghp_, AKIA, Bearer, PEM, password=...). SECURITY.md calls it 'a net, not a guarantee'. A sensitive-path predicate (src/util/sensitive-path.ts) refuses .env*, ssh keys and .claude/settings*.json for the file-reading tools and hooks.
A local plaintext decision log (decisions.jsonl, session files) is kept under ~/.claude/plugins/data/... and holds redacted excerpts of prompts, actions and emitted notes.

Small single-author project, 9 days old. The user works on client projects, so a new third-party plugin that sees all Bash commands, edits and MCP results carries supply-chain risk. Updates come via the plugin marketplace from a repo branch with no signed releases.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.dataEgress: Sent to the configured Jev endpoint (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if repointed), per SECURITY.md and the source. (1) PreToolUse: the tool name plus a redacted excerpt of the arguments, capped at 4,000 chars (Bash commands, file paths, Write/Edit content excerpts, and MCP tool inputs), together with the last 3 user prompts (2,000 chars each) and the captured Agent/Task subagent prompt. The gate is skipped for read-only and allowlisted calls (prefilter). (2) Edit lint: the edit content, the current file for a Write, and up to 12 rule lines extracted from CLAUDE.md. (3) git commit: the staged diff (git diff --cached). (4) PostToolUse screen: the whole WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__* result in 16,000-char chunks, up to about 128k chars, which covers all GitNexus, Playwright and other MCP outputs. (5) Stop: the final message (tail 6,000 chars) plus the git diff HEAD and the extracted claim sentences. (6) Explicit MCP calls: file contents when jev_rank paths/glob or jev_verify evidence_path are used (up to 512 KB per file). Redaction is regex-based. Nothing is sent to any third party other than the Jev endpoint, and no telemetry was found. Through OpenRouter, that traffic also goes to OpenRouter and its upstream provider under OpenRouter's data policy. For client projects this is a real confidentiality concern: diffs, code excerpts and MCP outputs leave the machine on every judged call.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every hook exits 0 with empty output on any error, and the http hooks are ignored if the daemon is down or the connection is refused. The hook Jev timeout is 1,500 ms with 0 retries (src/hooks/config.ts:99-104), under a 5 s Claude Code hook timeout. The MCP server uses a 30 s deadline with up to 3 retries and jittered backoff (429/5xx/network only), so an explicit tool call can stall up to 30 s. A missing key means the judgment hooks are inactive; only the deterministic regex checks (rm -rf ~, force-push main and similar) still run. A retired or wrong model id (for example jev-1.13.0 on OpenRouter) or a schema mismatch fails silently as error records in the log, so there is no visible breakage, and no protection either. The one fail-closed-like behavior is the Stop block, at most once per prompt; false positives have happened (0.6.3 fixed a case where the check blocked its own author). Port 10522 in use means the hooks are inactive for the session, with a warning.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.latencyImpact: Per the README and docs/BENCHMARKS.md, measured by the author against TypeSafe direct (not OpenRouter). Prefiltered calls (ls, git status, reads, tests, in-project edits) cost about 3 ms p50 through the daemon (8 ms p95). Judged calls take p50 about 210 ms warm and 536 ms overall (p95 1,168 ms) over 740 real calls, blocking the tool call because these are synchronous PreToolUse hooks. The Stop check adds a call at the end of a turn. The screen adds one or more sequential-or-parallel calls per WebFetch/MCP result. Memo hits within 5 minutes cost about 5 ms. The author's live log shows 689 gate records for 1,017 total, of which roughly 500 were allow. Expect about 0.2-1.2 s added on only a fraction of tool calls. OpenRouter adds a routing hop, so its latency is unknown. The daemon start costs about 0.4-0.6 s on the first SessionStart. If the daemon is down, the command-hook fallback pays a 0.16-2 s node cold start per hook. The cost is about $0.064 for a heavy dev day at $0.042/Mtok, which is negligible.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.contextCost: MCP: 7 tools. By source, description plus zod schemas total roughly 25-35k chars, so about 6-9k tokens of tool definitions loaded every session. The rank tool's description and schema are the biggest, and the whole rank.ts file is 26 KB. This is an estimate: I did not run the server, and 2.3-26 KB per tool file includes code. The plugin manifest passes 13 env vars. No MCP server 'instructions' text was found. The skill jev-decisions adds one description line (about 100 tokens), with the body loaded only on trigger. Hook-injected text: notes are capped at 5 per prompt, deduped for 30 min, and described as rare in advisory mode, with the sample messages 40-80 tokens each. Tripwires and stop blocks are a few lines plus an extra Claude turn to re-issue the call. Six slash commands are also registered. Each judged hook also registers a statusMessage that flashes in the UI.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks, which is what the user asked for. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop/UserPromptSubmit fire automatically with no prompting and are gated by a deterministic prefilter (no model call on read-only or in-project ordinary calls). The 7 MCP tools plus the jev-decisions skill are model-discretion (description trigger) and Opus may rarely choose them. So the automatic part is guardrail work (risk notes, injection screen, stop check, lint, commit scope), not acceleration of coding tasks such as ranking files. Hook types are 'http' and 'command', and both run for all of the user's Bash/Edit/MCP calls in addition to the existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks.
pros: It is the only candidate found that delivers what the user literally asked for: automatic use via hooks, with no 'use jev' prompt. The PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop and SessionStart hooks in plugin/hooks/hooks.json fire on their own, and a deterministic prefilter keeps most calls at about 3 ms and $0.

The base URL is an env var (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, config.ts:109 and hooks/config.ts:252). OpenRouter's documented path /api/v1/systemone matches the client's hard-coded /v1/systemone when the base is https://openrouter.ai/api, so the switch is likely config-only. The body {state, model, questions} is plain.
Careful engineering against Jev's limits: it never asks Jev to count or reason, uses regex gates plus Noul questions, and pins the model version to avoid probability drift (config.ts:33-40).
Fail-open everywhere, with a 1.5 s hook timeout, 0 retries, a memo and a loopback daemon that keeps the TLS connection warm. Cost is negligible: about $0.064 for a heavy day.

The Stop verify catches a real class of Claude errors: claiming tests pass when the ledger says they failed, and claiming files that do not exist (git diff HEAD check). Commit checks (staged-secret tripwire, pr_scope, message vs diff) fit daily work.

Never prompts the user and is compatible with bypass mode: notes go to Claude and denies are answerable by Claude, and it never returns allow, so it cannot override the user's permission rules. Kill switches are simple: JEV_HOOKS_DISABLE=1, gate=off, /jev:off.
MIT license, dependency-free hook bundle, no postinstall, no telemetry found, extensive tests and CI, transparent SECURITY.md, and it honestly admits it is advisory.
cons: The default target is TypeSafe direct. Nothing in the code knows OpenRouter, and I could not verify that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone envelope matches; the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404. A mismatch means parseEvaluateResponse throws and every hook silently fail-opens. The model id also has to be changed to typesafe/jev-1.13, and the hooks.json header X-Jev-Env-Key is hard-wired to $TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key must be exported under that name.

Data egress is large and broad for client work: Bash commands, edit contents, staged diffs, git diff HEAD, the final message, prompts, and the whole output of WebFetch and every MCP tool (GitNexus, Playwright) go to a third party (and via OpenRouter, to a further one). Redaction is a regex 'net, not a guarantee'. This may conflict with client NDAs.

The value is guardrails, not coding acceleration. Under bypass/auto permission mode the user has chosen no gating, and this adds a classifier whose output goes only to Claude, which can override with '# jev:intended'. It is not a security boundary, and Jev is not injection-hardened (SECURITY.md). It overlaps the user's existing secret-leak guard and adds another PreToolUse layer on the same Bash calls as GitNexus and the secret guard.

Synchronous PreToolUse hooks add about 0.2-1.2 s to judged calls (p95 1.17 s), plus a Jev call on Stop, on top of the 3 ms prefilter cost. OpenRouter's extra hop is unmeasured. False positives and extra Claude turns are possible (0.6.3 fixed a Stop check that falsely blocked its own author twice; SECURITY.md notes trips add turns).

Context and complexity cost: 7 MCP tools (about 6-9k tokens estimated) that Opus will rarely call, 6 slash commands, 13 plugin env vars, and a resident daemon on a fixed port 10522 with the API key sent in headers. The port-squat risk is documented, and a port conflict silently disables the hooks.

Immature: created 2026-09-17, 32 commits, one contributor, 22 stars, no GitHub release, six 0.x releases in four days. It comes from a third party that could ship breaking changes or malicious code via the marketplace, and Jev itself is a beta model that Theo-style critics call a flash-router. Bundles are 40k-line minified-style artifacts that are hard to audit.

Some hooks are noisy by design (routing, lint, commit note) and the user cannot easily tell whether fail-open silence means 'fine' or 'broken'. /jev:status is the only visibility, with no OpenRouter smoke check.
gh-brainwires-jevwire.verdict: This is the best fit found for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement, because it does everything through deterministic hooks with prefilters, fail-open behavior and negligible cost, and OpenRouter is probably reachable with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model id change. But it is a young single-author guardrail plugin (not a productivity booster) that sends diffs, commands and all MCP output to a third party. Pilot it on personal projects only, after verifying the OpenRouter schema with one manual call, and consider disabling screen_results and lint for client repos.

gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.whatItDoes: Unofficial community Claude Code / Codex plugin: a zero-dependency Node stdio MCP server plus 3 skills wrapping the TypeSafe System One endpoint. Exposes 8 MCP tools (route, rank, extract, verify, judge, usage_summary, session_mode, escalation_gate) that turn a bounded decision into Choice/Score/Noul questions and return probabilities, confidence and a proceed/review recommendation. Claude itself decides when to call them, guided by skill descriptions. Tools are read-only; no hooks.

security: Key handling: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.config/typesafe-as-a-judge/token (chmod 600, setup.sh uses hidden prompt). The key is never in argv; .mcp.json passes it via env_vars.
Setup token validation makes a live call (validate-token.mjs).
No child_process, exec or shell use in server or scripts (only tests/mcp.test.mjs spawns node). Zero runtime dependencies. package.json has no install or postinstall scripts, and no curl|sh.
No telemetry to third parties. Usage stats are in-memory only. The only network destination is api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool arguments are composed by Claude, so any injected repo content can flow into the request. The output is typed probabilities and a recommendation only, so there is little to inject on return. There is no redaction, only a 256KB payload cap (judge.mjs:3) and a 'don't send secrets' instruction in the skill. That instruction is not enforced in code, and the user's secret-leak hook would not cover MCP tool args.
Apache-2.0. Sole maintainer, unofficial, no security audit. The SECURITY.md is only a policy.
Supply-chain: it is a plugin that runs local unreviewed code, so pin the commit if forked.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the tool args goes to api.typesafe.ai (or openrouter.ai after a patch): 'state', 'source', 'evidence', 'claim', candidate lists and criteria. Sizes are capped at 256KB. In practice this means code excerpts, file paths, test output and diffs that Claude chooses to include. Nothing is sent automatically, since there are no hooks, and there is no redaction. The model name and a Bearer key go with each call. Client work sent to a third-party beta model may breach client NDAs, so decide this per project.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. On network error the code retries up to 3 attempts total with 250/500 ms exponential backoff, and only on network errors, HTTP 429 and 529 (judge.mjs:4, 101-118). Each attempt has a 30 s AbortSignal timeout (judge.mjs:111), so the worst case is roughly 90 s of stall on a hang. A final failure returns an isError text result to Claude, which just carries on without Jev. A missing key returns an error immediately. Nothing blocks the session. There is no circuit breaker, so a slow API can stall turns. The 30 s timeout is too generous for a 70-500 ms service.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.contextCost: 8 tools. The tool definitions are about 8.3k chars in server/index.mjs (lines 1-98), so roughly 2.1k tokens of names, descriptions and schemas, some of it repeated per tool (comparison_model appears 5 times). Server instructions are one short sentence (about 30 tokens). The 3 skills add about 150-250 tokens of descriptions. Total is about 2.3-2.5k tokens of always-on context, which is moderate. Claude Code may defer MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch, lowering the constant cost. No hook-injected text.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.latencyImpact: None on turns where the tools are unused. Each call is claimed at 70-500 ms for the API. The README's own measurement is 0.861 s for one rank call (README 'Measured development-planning comparison'). Also add one extra model turn (tool_use plus result) in Claude Code, typically 2-5 s with Opus. So the net effect is usually slower, not faster, versus Opus deciding inline. Worst case with retries is about 90 s.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus skill description triggers. There are no hooks and no proxy. The tools are read-only and Claude Code will call them when the skill description (or tool descriptions) match. The 'auto' policy in the session-control skill encourages Jev for bounded semantic decisions. Nothing is deterministic, so invocation reliability depends on Opus choosing to call it. With Opus 5.5, expect it to mostly do these micro-decisions itself (file ranking, claim checks) and rarely call Jev. The skills also explicitly steer away from open-ended coding work, which is most of a daily session.
pros: Purpose-built for the exact use case (Claude Code decides when to call Jev). It is the only candidate found that ships both MCP tools and a skill trigger, with no need for the user to say 'use jev'.
Typed, calibrated outputs with a proceed/review recommendation and a deterministic escalation gate. Sensible guardrails: refuses to be an authority for security, permissions, or destructive actions.

Clean, small codebase: zero dependencies, no shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry, and all network I/O funnels through one function (judge.mjs:83), so it is easy to audit and patch for OpenRouter (about 5 lines).
Sound token handling: setup.sh uses a hidden prompt and a 0600 token file, and the key is not in argv. Retries with backoff on 429/529. Input validation and a 256KB payload cap.
Session-mode tool gives an in-session kill switch (disabled), and the local usage summary is honest about 'theoretical' savings.
Apache-2.0 license, with tests (9 test cases across 4 files), a CHANGELOG and a v0.1.0 release.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and no env override. The user must fork or edit locally (about 5 lines), and the OpenRouter response shape is unverified.

Very immature: repo created 2026-09-21 (9 days old), 11 commits all on one day by one author, 2 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues, no CI workflows (no .github/workflows), and only about 9 tests. The unofficial status is stated in the README.

Value for daily coding is doubtful. The README's own benchmark is a single hand-picked case (which file to inspect first) that Opus would answer inline for free. Extra tool-call round trip plus 0.86 s API call, so it is likely slower and costs money (a separate Jev API bill) while the main model is on a subscription. The savings claims are self-declared 'theoretical'.

Invocation is at the model's discretion, so it is not deterministic. Opus is unlikely to route trivial choices through an external tool, so the 'automatic' integration would be weak and hard to observe.
Costs about 2.3-2.5k tokens of constant context for 8 tools, 3 of which (usage_summary, session_mode, escalation_gate) are meta or local-only and add no Jev value in daily coding.

Data egress risk on client projects: no redaction (only a prompt-level 'do not send secrets'); the existing secret-leak guard hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would not see MCP tool arguments. Code, diffs and test output would go to a third-party beta model.
30 s per-attempt timeout with 3 attempts (up to ~90 s stall) is badly tuned for a sub-second service, and there is no circuit breaker.
The declared 'comparison_model' savings narrative is Codex/GPT-centric (gpt-5.6-luna) and irrelevant to Claude Opus.
gh-e-fl-typesafe-as-a-judge.verdict: The closest thing to an agent-facing Jev integration, and clean, dependency-free code that could be patched for OpenRouter in about 5 lines. It is a 9-day-old, single-author PoC whose model-discretion tools add context and latency for micro-decisions Opus already handles well. Worth forking as a low-risk experiment, but not a solid basis for automatic daily use.

gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.name: Project1Dev/Jev-MCP (jev-control-plane)
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Python stdlib-only MCP server (17 tools) plus a 7-event Claude Code hook suite (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd) and status line. The hooks send small bounded decisions to typesafe/jev-1.13 on the OpenRouter Decisions API: task class, worker model, subagent tier and count, verification level, whether Bash output should be trimmed, which file or function a task will touch, whether to /clear or /compact, and progress checkpoints. It then enforces some of the results through hook outputs. It can deny or rewrite Agent calls, replace large Bash output with a trimmed version, block Stop once when tests are missing, and (in tmux only) paste /model and /clear into the pane. It is a router and gate for the agent, not a code-quality helper.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.runtime: Python 3.9+ (stdlib only, no pip). Node is not needed. Hooks run as `python3 ~/.claude/jev/scripts/jev-cc-hook`.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/Project1Dev/Jev-MCP && ./install.sh --hooks. This copies code to ~/.claude/jev, writes ~/.claude/jev/.env (mode 600) and prompts for the key, runs `claude mcp add --scope user jev-control-plane -- python3 ~/.claude/jev/run_server.py`, and merges 7 hooks plus a statusLine into ~/.claude/settings.json (timestamped backup first). No curl|sh, no npm or pip step. `./install.sh --uninstall` reverses it.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.tests: 322 test functions across 32 test files, all mocked (no network). Run with `python3 run_tests.py`. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs Python 3.9/3.11/3.12/3.13 plus a secret scan with gitleaks. I did not run the tests (static review only).

providerSupport.others: No other gateway. DeepSeek direct and an OpenRouter model-escalation pool exist as optional worker-routing pools, not as Jev providers.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart
interface.purpose: Initialise session state and sweep old state and spill files; recheck the autopilot default.

interface.name: Hook UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Classify intent locally. Start a background Jev route call and a location chain (which file or function). May ask Jev whether to continue, /compact or /clear (only when context is over 100k tokens). May BLOCK the prompt when autopilot wants /clear or /model (tmux only, up to a 4 s wait). Injects a one-line [jev] hint into context. #nojev bypasses.

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse (Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|Bash|Agent|Task)
interface.purpose: Apply the pending route at the first substantive action. For Agent or Task calls, enforce the subagent cap (permissionDecision deny) and rewrite the subagent model via updatedInput. Runs progress checkpoints every 12 actions.

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure
interface.purpose: Record tests and edits. Ask Jev whether large Bash output (12k chars or more) should be trimmed, then replace it with updatedToolOutput. Detect repeated failures (loop guard) and inject checkpoint advice.

interface.name: Hook Stop
interface.purpose: Block the stop once per task ({decision:block}) if code changed without a passing test after the last edit, a test failure is outstanding, or the route demanded an Opus review subagent.

interface.name: Hook SessionEnd
interface.purpose: Finalise the outcome and audit records.
