interface.name: MCP jev-completion-check / jev-guard / jev-review / jev-context / jev-context-budget / jev-loop-guard / jev-select-environment / jev-models / jev-bypass / jev-audit
interface.purpose: Bounded decisions: test depth, risky-action policy, diff verdict, context assembly under a budget, retry loops, tool selection, model registry, bypass and audit.

interface.name: CLI jev-claude and jev-dashboard
interface.purpose: Launcher that starts Claude Code on the model Jev routes to; a TUI showing calls, cost and savings.

security: Key handling is decent. The key is read from env or ~/.claude/jev/.env (mode 600) and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv (jev/client.py, jev/config.py). Errors are redacted (client._redact), and policy.redact_text scrubs prompt text and secret-shaped strings before egress.
No curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found. The only outbound hosts are openrouter.ai (Decisions API and the /api/v1/models feed).

HIGH RISK: the hooks can alter agent behaviour. They deny Agent calls (scripts/setup_claude_code.py registers PreToolUse for Agent|Task; claude_code.py:1908), rewrite the subagent model via updatedInput, and replace Bash tool output via updatedToolOutput (claude_code.py:1261). They also block Stop once (claude_code.py:2275-2300). The tests are mocked only, and the code base is 2 days old.

HIGH RISK: jev/autoclear.py spawns a detached process that runs `tmux paste-buffer` and `send-keys` into $TMUX_PANE to type /model and /clear plus the user's held-back prompt. It also edits ~/.claude/settings.json to restore the default model (autoclear.py:242-250). This is on by default inside tmux and is disabled with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0 or JEV_AUTOMODEL=0. A wrong or manipulated Jev answer could clear the conversation or switch the model. /clear needs at least 0.8 confidence.

The prompt-injection surface is moderate. The Jev response is a constrained choice validated against a shortlist and confidence floors, so injected text cannot produce free text. Tool output content is not sent to Jev, but the command string and the size and shape of the output are. Prompts, subagent briefs and repo text can still bias the classification.

scripts/setup_claude_code.py rewrites the user's global ~/.claude/settings.json (backup written). It adds 7 hook groups and a statusLine. It uses `python3 <path>` and a fixed timeout of 10-30 s per hook.
Writes state under ~/.claude/jev/state (audit.jsonl, spill files holding full Bash output, per-session state); the docs say they are redacted, but the spill files hold raw output.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai only. (1) Task text: the user prompt, secret-redacted and capped at 2000 chars (claude_code.py:274-279, TASK_TEXT_CAP), plus prompt size, intent and risk tags. Also up to 700 chars of Claude's last reply for follow-up prompts (_last_reply). (2) Subagent briefs: description plus prompt, capped at 1500 chars, plus 400 chars of parent task (agent_tier). (3) Bash trim: the command (redacted, 400 chars), the output size, line count and error-like line count, plus 600 chars of task. Output content is NOT sent (claude_code.py:1213-1220). (4) Location chain (locate.py): file paths and one-line summaries (docstring, first comment, top-level names) for up to 400 files, plus 12-line code snippets (160 chars per line) of candidate functions or files for the beam step (EVIDENCE_LINES = 12). So client repo structure and small code fragments leave the machine. (5) Checkpoint evidence counters (files changed, tests run and failed, repeats). Whole files, diffs and tool outputs are not sent in the hook path. The MCP tools jev-review and jev-context can send model-supplied diffs or text if Claude calls them. Retention is per OpenRouter and TypeSafe policy, which I did not check. Client work in the 12-line snippets and file-path lists is a real exposure to consider.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.failureMode: Mostly fail-open. jev-cc-hook always exits 0 and catches BaseException (scripts/jev-cc-hook). Handlers record an error and let the tool call proceed (claude_code.py docstring). HOOK_JEV_TIMEOUT defaults to 20 s (JEV_HOOK_TIMEOUT), and the hooks have 10-30 s timeouts in settings. The route call runs in a background process. The prompt waits at most 4 s (autoclear.WAIT, locate.MAX_WAIT = 4.0). apply_pending_route waits for the job at the first Agent/Task call or Stop, up to about JOB_TIMEOUT*2+5 s, then falls back to a default route (job_timeout). A missing key marks the task bypassed with a warning. JEV_OFFLINE=1 or JEV_HOOKS=0 disables it. Two things are not fail-open: the Stop hook blocks once by deterministic rule (not a Jev outage), and the subagent cap denies only on a real Jev 'no'. The default retries count is 0, so one transient error simply skips that decision.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per hook event this adds a Python process start of about 20-50 ms with lazy imports. Background Jev calls take roughly 0.1-4 s (a TLS handshake of 0.6-4 s is noted in client.py). Steady-state prompt overhead is up to 4 s only when the autopilot or location step waits; otherwise the route lands on a later hook. Bash PostToolUse adds one synchronous Jev call for outputs over 12k chars, and subagent launches add one Jev call each, plus up to 12 calls per normal task (CALL_LIMIT_NORMAL). Expect roughly 50-100 ms of local overhead on ordinary tool calls and 0.5-4 s on trim, Agent and prompt-submit paths. This is estimated from the code, not measured.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.contextCost: The MCP server exposes 17 tools. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 20.4k chars in jev/server.py lines 44-515, roughly 5.1k tokens. It sets no server-level `instructions` field. Hooks inject at most one short `[jev] ...` line per task (route_context, for example "run the tests for changed code after your last edit"), plus occasional checkpoint, location ("likely file X") and context-advice lines. Notes shown to the user use systemMessage and cost nothing. The design deliberately keeps injected text small, so I estimate less than 300 tokens per task. Trimming Bash output can reduce context. With hooks alone (no MCP registration), the token cost is near zero. The MCP server is optional and could be skipped.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for 7 events, so Claude Code runs Jev without the user or the model asking. This is the only candidate style that satisfies 'no prompting'. The MCP tools are model-discretion and are not needed. Hooks activate automatically after `./install.sh --hooks`.
pros: Only candidate seen that is truly automatic: 7 command hooks fire without any 'use jev' prompt (scripts/setup_claude_code.py EVENTS).

Native OpenRouter: defaults to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (jev/config.py:13-17). JEV_ENDPOINT and JEV_MODEL are overridable, so ~typesafe/jev-latest works.
Uses Jev the way it is designed: typed Choice questions with probabilities, validated against shortlists and confidence floors, with deterministic fallbacks (decide_route, _pick, confident()).
Fail-open hooks with bounded timeouts, a 4 s max prompt wait, background route jobs, and kill switches: JEV_OFFLINE=1, JEV_HOOKS=0, #nojev in a prompt, JEV_TRIM=0, JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0.

Egress is designed to be small and redacted: capped prompt text, and Bash output content not sent for trimming. Zero-dependency Python with no install-time code fetch. Uninstall is supported (`install.sh --uninstall`).
Cheap: about $0.00005 per route call per the code comments. Useful for subagent-tier downgrades, Bash trimming of 12k+ char logs, and stop-gate tests on code changes.
Has an audit log and TUI dashboard to measure whether Jev actually saves anything.
cons: Very young and unproven. Created 2026-09-29, 4 commits, 2 authors, 0 stars, no releases, and the last commit dropped OpenCode support and reworked the install layout. Expect breakage.

Optimised for saving subscription tokens by routing to cheaper models, which conflicts with a user running Opus 5.5 as the main model. It routes workers and subagents to Sonnet/Haiku tiers and can paste /model and /clear into tmux. That trades output quality for cost and changes behaviour silently.

Invasive hooks. It denies or rewrites Agent/Task calls, replaces Bash output with a trimmed version, blocks Stop once, and edits ~/.claude/settings.json. These stack with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman) which also touch the same tool matchers, so conflicting updatedInput or updatedToolOutput results are possible.

Autopilot (autoclear.py) drives tmux with paste-buffer and send-keys and rewrites the default model in settings.json. It is on by default inside tmux and is risky in bypass or auto permission modes. It must be disabled with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0.

Sends prompt text (2000 chars), the last reply (700 chars), subagent briefs, and a file-path and summary index plus 12-line code snippets to a third party (OpenRouter, TypeSafe). That may be a problem for client projects.

Assumes the user has a Claude Code subscription pool and a `claude` CLI (Sonnet worker, Opus reviewer defaults). It does not use the TypeSafe direct API or the /api/v1/systemone endpoint, only the alpha Decisions API, which may change.

Benefit for an Opus-main, senior-dev workflow is modest: the routing, trimming and location hints save tokens, not correctness. Jev's ability to classify tasks better than a heuristic is unproven (skeptics' router claim). The repo is 19k lines for a job that mostly could be done by 2 or 3 hooks.
The MCP server adds about 5k tokens of tool schemas if registered and not deferred, and the tools are redundant when hooks are installed. Install it with hooks only.
Tests are mocked only; no measured latency or quality data was verified.
gh-project1dev-jev-mcp.verdict: The only reviewed candidate that is truly automatic and OpenRouter-native, but it is a brand-new cost-router that rewrites subagents, trims Bash output, blocks Stop and can drive tmux, so it fits an Opus-first, hook-heavy setup poorly. If trying it, install hooks only with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0, JEV_AUTOMODEL=0 and a low-spend key, and skip the MCP server, or cherry-pick its ideas (Bash trim, subagent tier, stop gate).

gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.name: brunopivetta88/jev-claude (plugin "jev-guard")
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also Codex hook pack) that installs hooks on SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop. Before Bash/Write/Edit/NotebookEdit/WebFetch/Task/mcp__* calls it runs ~35 regex rules ("deterministic floor") and asks Jev 6 Noul questions plus 1 Score question (destructive, secret_exposure, exfiltration, prompt_injection, scope_creep, prod_impact, severity). It merges them with max() and maps the result through thresholds to allow/warn/ask/block. It ships in shadow (log-only) mode. PostToolUse asks 3 questions only on failure or when an action repeats 3 or more times. Stop asks 2 questions (goal_incomplete, unverified_claim) and can force the turn to continue. It is a safety guardrail, not a coding-assist feature. It is not an MCP server and has no skills that call Jev.

providerSupport.evidence: Default Jev target is TypeSafe direct: src/config.mjs:11 apiBase 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone', model 'jev-latest'. src/providers/index.mjs:31-36 preset 'jev' with keyEnv TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The 'openrouter' preset (index.mjs:88-93) is kind 'openai', pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model null. That preset sends a chat-completions JSON-schema prompt to a general LLM, NOT the Jev System One endpoint, so it would not use typesafe/jev. The jev adapter (index.mjs:160-165) POSTs {model,state,questions} with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' to apiBase and parses json.answers[key].type 'noul'|'score' (src/jev-client.mjs:60-72). Nothing in the code references openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone or /api/alpha/decisions. jev-client.mjs:88-96 lets an explicit JEV_GUARD_API_BASE or JEV_GUARD_MODEL override the preset. jev-client.mjs:90-97 and config.mjs:141-145 read the jev key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or JEV_GUARD_API_KEY, and there is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY fallback for kind 'jev'. Tests only hit a local mock (test/core.test.mjs:37). The training/ dir has a local 'jevlab' server that mimics the Jev wire format.
providerSupport.others: Openai-compatible presets (openai, deepseek, kimi, grok, mistral, groq, together, openrouter), Anthropic Messages, Gemini, and local ollama/lmstudio/vllm/jevlab. A second 'compare' provider can run in parallel (JEV_GUARD_COMPARE_*).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate and unverified. On the code side it is probably 3 env vars: JEV_GUARD_PROVIDER=jev, JEV_GUARD_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_GUARD_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and JEV_GUARD_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>. That works only if OpenRouter's System One request body and response match TypeSafe's {model,state,questions} -> {answers} shape. I could not verify this: the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404, and the repo has no OpenRouter test. If the schemas differ, a small new adapter is needed in ADAPTERS (about 10 lines). One risk: putting an OpenRouter key in JEV_GUARD_API_KEY mixes credential names, and the plugin's own userConfig field is named typesafe_api_key.

interface.name: hook SessionStart
interface.purpose: bin/claude-hook.mjs records a session line in the state JSONL. No network.

interface.name: hook UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Stores the user's prompt (redacted, first 1500 chars) as the session 'goal' (src/run.mjs:80-85). No network, but the prompt is later sent to Jev as user_goal.

interface.name: hook PreToolUse (matcher Bash|Write|Edit|NotebookEdit|WebFetch|Task|mcp__.*)
interface.purpose: Runs rules plus a Jev call with 7 questions. Emits permissionDecision 'deny' (block) or 'ask', or additionalContext (warn or shadow note). Never emits 'allow'. hooks/hooks.json timeout 15s, statusMessage 'jev-guard: checking action'.

interface.name: hook PostToolUse (same matcher)
interface.purpose: Jev call only when the tool failed (looksFailed regex on output) or the same summary appeared 3 or more times. Emits additionalContext or decision:'block'.

interface.name: hook Stop
interface.purpose: Jev call with goal_incomplete and unverified_claim. On ask/block it exits 2 with the reason on stderr, which forces Claude to keep going (adapters/claude-code.mjs:54-57). No stop_hook_active guard was found in the code (grep returned nothing).

security: API key is sent as an Authorization: Bearer header from env vars (jev-client.mjs:135, index.mjs:161). It is not put in argv. The hook command line is only node bin/claude-hook.mjs, so no key appears in the process list.

Redaction of outbound payloads (src/redact.mjs:5-13) is regex-based: private keys, AKIA/ASIA, gh*_ tokens, sk-*, xox*, JWTs, KEY=value. It misses arbitrary secrets, DB URLs with passwords and proprietary source code. Each string field is truncated to 4000 chars and objects to 50 keys.

Egress is limited to the configured apiBase, with no telemetry beyond that. But the state dir defaults to '.jev-guard' resolved against the CWD (config.mjs:60, entry.mjs:37) unless CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA is set. In a client repo that could drop .jev-guard/ (session logs, decisions.jsonl, response cache) into the working tree, and it is only gitignored inside this repo.
JEV_GUARD_COLLECT=1 (off by default) writes full redacted tool inputs to disk for training.

A per-project jev-guard.config.json in cwd can override apiBase and provider (config.mjs:106-113). A malicious repo could point the hook's traffic, including your key and code snippets, at an attacker URL. The key is only sent when the URL is chosen via config, since it is attached in the adapter headers.

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs, and on failures tool outputs, are embedded in the Jev state JSON. Jev has no free text output, so the injection risk is mostly bypass of the classifier, and the deterministic floor still stands. With provider openai/anthropic the prompt-injection risk is higher.
The skill and the /jev-mode command ask Claude to write jev-guard.config.json. That is low risk but it modifies project files.
No shell execution beyond the hook itself. The status command runs a local node script. No curl|sh, no postinstall.

One-person project, 0 stars, 3 commits, and the maintainer identity is inconsistent (brunopivetta88 on GitHub vs bruno-ship-it in the README, package.json and marketplace). That is a supply-chain trust issue: install from a pinned commit after reading it.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.dataEgress: To the configured Jev endpoint, per evaluated call: the session goal (your prompt, redacted, max 1500 chars), the proposed tool name and its full tool_input (redacted, max 4000 chars per string field, so Bash commands, Write file content, Edit old/new strings and MCP arguments), the last 8 action summaries (200 chars each), and the cwd path. PostToolUse on failure or repeat also sends the tool result (last_result, sanitised) and the Stop hook sends the goal plus the action summaries. Read, Grep and Glob are never sent. Note the matcher mcp__.* also covers gitnexus and playwright calls (URLs, page content arguments). Whole file contents from Write/Edit leave the machine, so this is a real concern for client code under NDA. The local-only route is provider ollama or jevlab.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.failureMode: Fail-open by default (JEV_GUARD_FAIL_OPEN=1). Jev calls time out at 1500 ms (JEV_GUARD_TIMEOUT_MS), with an abort controller and a HARD_DEADLINE 8 s watchdog that exits 0 (entry.mjs:6-25). Internal exceptions become allow (run.mjs:63-72). A 200 with no parseable answers counts as a failure, not an all-clear. The deterministic floor still applies when Jev is down, and with failOpen=0 the outcome becomes 'ask'. Unparseable input exits 0. It is a well-designed failure path. Caveat: the Stop hook can exit 2 repeatedly to force continuation and I found no stop_hook_active loop guard.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool definitions and no server instructions. Two slash commands and one skill (descriptions about 300 chars, roughly 100 tokens) are added to the listing. The real cost is hook-injected text: in shadow mode, every action that would have warned or blocked injects an additionalContext line of the form 'jev-guard [shadow: would ask]: secret_exposure=0.62 (jev) -> ask...'. That is about 30-60 tokens, and only on non-allow outcomes. Enforce mode adds deny/ask reasons. The status message 'jev-guard: checking action' appears on each hooked call. Small overall.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.latencyImpact: Each Bash/Write/Edit/Task/mcp__ call pays node cold start (~40-80 ms) plus one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms, capped at 1.5 s, cached 60 s on disk for identical bodies). That is roughly 150-600 ms typical per hooked call, and it is serial with your other PreToolUse hooks only if Claude Code runs them sequentially. It adds nothing on Read/Grep/Glob, and the PostToolUse call is only made on failures. The Stop hook adds one call at the end of each turn. Across a session of hundreds of tool calls that is tens of seconds of added waiting.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. Claude Code runs it on every matching event without any prompting, which is exactly the "automatic" behaviour you asked for. However, it is purely a passive guardrail; Claude never consults Jev for coding decisions.
pros: Fully automatic: five hook events wired through hooks/hooks.json. No prompt like 'use jev' is ever needed.
Well-engineered failure semantics (fail-open, 1.5 s per-request timeout, 8 s watchdog, cache, deterministic floor with Jev only able to raise signals), so a slow Jev cannot wedge Claude Code.

Never emits permissionDecision 'allow', so it cannot widen your permissions or interfere with your existing hooks. It only adds deny/ask/context. It uses Jev's real strengths: typed Noul/Score primitives, calibrated probabilities, no free text.
Shadow mode by default plus a decisions.jsonl audit trail and /jev-status help you tune thresholds. Only the risky tool set is evaluated, so read-only tools cost nothing.
Zero dependencies, Node >=20 only (you have Node 24), and no argv key leak or postinstall. It is fully readable in about 1750 lines.
Multi-provider abstraction lets you run the same hook against a local model (ollama/jevlab) for the sensitive client repos.
cons: OpenRouter is not first-class. The 'openrouter' preset talks to a chat-completions LLM rather than to Jev, and you would need to override JEV_GUARD_API_BASE and JEV_GUARD_MODEL and reuse JEV_GUARD_API_KEY for the OpenRouter key, all on the assumption that OpenRouter's System One schema equals TypeSafe's. That is unverified, and the repo has no test for it.

It only gives you a security guard, not Jev-assisted coding (no routing of tasks, no test-failure triage, no code-review scoring, no next-step decisions). Value beyond safety is low. In your bypass/auto permission mode that safety layer is arguably the most valuable piece, but only in enforce mode. In bypass mode I have not verified that a hook 'ask' still prompts.
Sends Write/Edit file content, Bash commands and MCP args to a third party on every evaluated call. That is a real NDA/client-code concern, and its regex redaction is incomplete.

Overlaps your existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) and the GitNexus hooks. The matcher mcp__.* adds a network call on every gitnexus and playwright MCP call, which are frequent.

Extremely immature: 3 commits over 3 days, one author, 0 stars, no releases, and an unclear maintainer identity (README/marketplace slug bruno-ship-it 404s vs brunopivetta88). The thresholds are guesses, never calibrated on real traffic. Jev is itself beta and Theo's claim that it is a 'flash router' is unverified.
Stop hook exit-2 can trap Claude in a continuation loop (no stop_hook_active guard), and can be a noisy and costly false-positive source ('goal_incomplete' judged from 8 action summaries only).
Default state dir '.jev-guard' resolves against cwd if CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA is missing, which may pollute client repos.
Repo-level jev-guard.config.json can redirect the endpoint, a supply-chain risk when opening untrusted repos.
License is a modified MIT with an attribution request and is not clean for client work.
gh-brunopivetta88-jev-claude.verdict: The only candidate here that gives truly automatic, hook-driven Jev use in Claude Code, with sound fail-open engineering, but it is a 3-day-old solo guardrail with no OpenRouter-native path and heavy code egress. If you try it, install it pinned and read, run it in shadow mode, route through OpenRouter via env overrides only after you verify the System One schema, and keep it off client repos (or point it at ollama/jevlab) until it has matured.

Gateway binds 127.0.0.1 by default; non-loopback HOST refused without ROUTER_API_KEY+UPSTREAM_API_KEY; Host and Origin header checks (app.ts:265-275) mitigate DNS-rebinding/browser CSRF against localhost.
systemd unit is sandboxed: NoNewPrivileges, PrivateTmp, ProtectSystem=strict, ReadWritePaths only the state dir, RestrictAddressFamilies.

No postinstall hooks (installs with --ignore-scripts; runtime deps only hono + @hono/node-server; SDK is a types-only devDependency). No curl|sh installer. No telemetry found besides Jev calls; OpenRouter receives http-referer/x-title attribution headers.

install.py edits user config: rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json hooks, ~/.claude.json, adds rules/skill files; backs up first, validates plan before writing, supports --dry-run, removes only its own managed hooks/blocks. It is a real global-config mutation the user must review.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev outputs typed decisions only (no free text), and gateway prepends 'treat state as untrusted data'; but the hook injects mandatory-instruction text into every prompt and the Bash gate lets a Jev classification influence permissionDecision ('ask'), and can DENY commands touching the gateway. Jev verdicts are not authoritative and no allow decision is ever emitted.

Secret redaction is best-effort regex (README admits 'pattern matching, not a guarantee'); user prompts/commands/last assistant message can carry secrets or client code snippets to OpenRouter/TypeSafe.
Hook writes per-session state JSON under ~/.local/share/master-jev-hook/state (0700, 7-day cleanup); JEV_LOG_FILE keeps dashboard history of queries on disk.
Single anonymous-ish author, 4 days old, 0 stars, no CI/signing: supply-chain trust is entirely on reading this code yourself; the hook and MCP script run with your user privileges on every session.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (or TypeSafe/Vercel) only, over HTTPS from the local gateway. Per path: (1) MCP tools - exactly what Claude puts in the args (objective, candidate texts, evidence, items up to 8000 chars each, 64KB cap; Claude is told to send ids/short snippets). (2) Bash gate - only for regex-risky commands: command (<=4000 chars), cwd, Claude's description, and the last 3 user prompts (<=700 chars each), redacted. (3) Stop check - user's last request (<=2000), edited file paths, commands run after last edit, Claude's final message (<=3000). (4) PreCompact - up to 32 of the user's own messages (<=1500 chars each) sent as separate Noul questions. (5) Drift detector every 30 tool calls - last request + 4 earlier requests, last 1000 chars of prior assistant reply, and tool names + file paths/commands (<=200 chars) with error flags; no file contents or tool output. (6) SessionStart self-test - a fixed 'water boils at 100C' probe. No whole files or diffs by design, but user prompts on personal AND client projects, client file paths and commands do leave the machine. Redaction is best-effort regex. Local copies only if JEV_INSPECT_INPUTS/JEV_DEBUG_DUMP_DIR set (off by default); dashboard log on disk if JEV_LOG_FILE set.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. claude_jev.py catches all exceptions and exits 0; gateway() returns None on any error or >64KB body; per-hook Jev timeouts 3-8s (self-test 3s, Bash gate 5s inside an 8s hook, Stop 6s/10s, PreCompact 8s/12s, drift 5s/8s); gateway->Jev timeout default 8s (max 15s), retries only on 429/503/529/connection-refused (x2, honoring retry-after up to 5s); low confidence -> abstain -> continue locally. MCP adapter returns 'Gateway unavailable. No decision was applied.' isError with a 17s fetch timeout. Only fail-closed behavior: a Bash command that does systemctl stop/disable/mask/kill master-jev-hook is denied unless Jev says the user requested it (abstention also denies). If gateway is down, SessionStart still adds a status line and instructs Claude to print an error block, and each hook silently degrades.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.contextCost: 5 MCP tools, all marked alwaysLoad (per-tool _meta plus server-level alwaysLoad:true written to ~/.claude.json): tool names+descriptions+schemas approx 3.7k chars = ~920 tokens; MCP server instructions 783 chars = ~200 tokens; rule file ~/.claude/rules/master-jev-hook.md 2.4k chars = ~590 tokens always loaded; skill SKILL.md description ~100 tokens (body 7.7k chars ~1.9k tokens when triggered); UserPromptSubmit reminder ~900 chars = ~230 tokens injected on EVERY prompt (duplicates the rule); SessionStart adds ~1.5k chars (~400 tokens) for tool-load request + print-status instruction + status block, and asks Claude to run a ToolSearch turn and print a verbatim status block at the top of the first reply. Roughly 1.7k tokens standing overhead plus ~230 tokens per prompt (cached mostly), plus 'announce with 🔷 lines' text before and after each Jev call. Author measured ~2.8k extra cached tokens per turn.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.latencyImpact: Model-invoked Jev call: author reports 0.7-1.7 s per query plus MCP/gateway hop, plus Claude must author the structured query (output tokens) and wait; deferral ToolSearch turn at session start. Hooks: a Python process spawns on EVERY tool call (PostToolUse drift, no matcher; also scans/writes the state dir each call, ~30-60 ms each), on every prompt (UserPromptSubmit), and on every Bash call (regex only, no network unless risky). Network waits: SessionStart self-test up to 3 s blocking (~300 ms typical per README); drift Jev call every 30 tool calls up to 5 s; Bash gate up to 5 s on risky commands; Stop check up to 6 s after edit turns without tests; PreCompact up to 8 s. Cold gateway start after systemd restart adds nothing else. Existing global PreToolUse Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus) will run alongside the new Bash gate; hooks in the same event run in parallel.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.autoInvocation: Mixed but strongest of the candidates: (a) deterministic hooks that fire without any user prompt (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit reminder, Bash gate, Stop, PreCompact, drift) - these call Jev themselves; (b) model-discretion MCP tools driven by a mandatory-rule text injected in three places (rules file, skill, per-prompt reminder) - adherence is model-dependent, and the author's own experiments.md admits 0 model-side calls in 10 real sessions after a rule wording change, restored by making the trigger mandatory again, with no post-fix measurement published; (c) skill description trigger. Optional proxy launchers (not needed, and not usable with OAuth login) are not part of the Claude Code path.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code (providers.json:11-17, jev.ts) with unit tests; switching from TypeSafe is two env vars in the gateway.env, no code patch. Model typesafe/jev-1.13 and endpoint /api/alpha/decisions match the brief.

Only candidate here that delivers true 'no prompting needed' automation: hooks fire deterministically and the rule is injected on every prompt, so Claude is pushed to call Jev without the user saying so.

Sensible Jev use-cases mapped to real Claude Code events: triage of 3+ grep hits/files (jev_rank), risky-Bash second opinion tuned to bypass/auto workflows (asks only at >=0.80 confidence that a command is severe, irreversible and beyond the request), completion-without-verification check, compaction 'what to keep' scoring.
Fail-open design with bounded timeouts and a hook that swallows all exceptions; never emits an 'allow' decision so it cannot widen permissions.

Good local engineering: typed input validation, 64KB caps, Host/Origin checks, loopback default, hardened systemd unit, keys not in argv, --ignore-scripts install, no runtime deps beyond hono, idempotent installer with backup and --dry-run.
Substantial tests (~190 vitest cases, 51 Python) and a candid experiments.md documenting failures and cost-weighted measurement; local dashboard gives visibility into every Jev call and cost.
Jev cost is negligible (~$0.042/M input, small queries ~600-950 tokens) so paid hook calls are not a budget concern.
cons: Heavy, invasive footprint for a 4-day-old, 0-star, single-author, no-CI, alpha project: requires building a Node service, running a systemd daemon, and rewriting global ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude.json, rules and skills. Must be reviewed line by line.

Spawns a Python process on every tool call (PostToolUse with no matcher) and every prompt just to count to 30, on top of the user's existing GitNexus/caveman/secret-guard hooks; small but constant latency tax on a heavy all-day workflow.

Sends user prompts (last 3-32 messages), commands, file paths and Claude's final message to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on hooks the user never triggers manually; regex redaction is best-effort. Client projects with confidentiality obligations need explicit sign-off; the guide even states 'by installing, you authorize paid queries'.

Permission-mode interplay uncertain: the Bash gate can return permissionDecision 'ask' (and 'deny' for gateway-off commands), which may interrupt bypass/auto sessions; whether 'ask' overrides bypass mode in Claude Code 2.1.285 was not verified. The Jev's 'routine vs confirm' verdict comes from a probabilistic model (Theo's 'flash router' skepticism applies) and gates only regex-flagged commands, overlapping the user's existing secret-leak guard.

The model-side tool value is questionable for Opus 5.5: Claude must spend output tokens writing structured candidates/evidence, wait 0.7-1.7 s per call, and then only gets a probability; author's own log shows Claude ignored the tools entirely (0 calls in 10 sessions) when the wording allowed opt-out, and the mandatory wording can force calls where Claude's own judgment would be cheaper and better.

Standing context overhead ~1.7k tokens plus a ~230-token reminder on every prompt (duplicating the rule), a forced ToolSearch turn plus a verbatim '🔷 status block' printed in the first reply of every session, and 🔷 announcement lines around each call: noisy and counter to the user's own strict CLAUDE.md efficiency rules.
SessionStart makes a blocking live paid self-test (up to 3 s) every startup/resume/clear/compact/fork.

Drift/stop/compact hooks' benefit is speculative: Jev is a typed-decision model with a 32k window judging transcript summaries; no published evidence they improve outcomes. Stop check is limited to 3 nudges and skipped if any test/lint command ran.

Not packaged as a Claude Code plugin/marketplace or npm package: no update path, manual clone/build/systemd setup, Claude Desktop-oriented workarounds (deferral bugs) add complexity; the OpenRouter alpha endpoint schema was not verified live by me, only via mocked tests.
gh-sophia-phillipa-master-jev-hook.verdict: The only reviewed candidate that natively supports OpenRouter (JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter + OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and truly auto-invokes Jev via hooks, with solid fail-open engineering and tests, but it is a 4-day-old single-author alpha that installs a daemon, rewrites global Claude Code config, adds a Python spawn on every tool call, and ships transcript snippets to a third party. Worth a sandboxed trial (install with --dry-run, disable the drift/UserPromptSubmit/SessionStart hooks, keep the MCP tools plus Bash-gate/Stop only), not a drop-in all-day default, especially for client projects.

gh-compozy-yoshi.name: compozy/yoshi
gh-compozy-yoshi.whatItDoes: Local Bun HTTP proxy on 127.0.0.1:8790. You point Claude Code at it with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. It intercepts POST /v1/messages and, above a ~50k-token size gate, splits old completed Bash/Write/Edit inputs, tool results and teammate reports into ~1,200-char spans. It asks Jev (as a typed evaluator) whether each span is still needed, and replaces spans judged unneeded with omission markers. Verdicts are frozen in .yoshi/decisions.json. It then forwards the rewritten request to api.anthropic.com and streams the response back. It also proxies the OpenAI Responses API for Codex. The README labels it an experimental POC that is moving into CompozyOS.

providerSupport.evidence: The only Jev path is Vercel AI Gateway. src/judge.ts:1 imports createGateway from @ai-sdk/gateway. src/judge.ts:37-50 builds createGateway({apiKey}).evaluationModel("typesafe-ai/jev"). Calls go through the Vercel AI SDK experimental_evaluate (src/judge.ts:3-5, 96, 205). The key comes from AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (src/server.ts:96). No openrouter.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY or console.typesafe.ai reference exists anywhere in src/ (grep). YOSHI_UPSTREAM (server.ts:97) and YOSHI_CODEX_UPSTREAM (server.ts:138) only redirect the Anthropic and OpenAI upstreams, not the judge. Cost is read from providerMetadata.gateway.cost (judge.ts:274). package.json pins @ai-sdk/gateway 4.0.85 and ai 7.0.105.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway only, model id typesafe-ai/jev. Upstream LLM targets are Anthropic (api.anthropic.com) and the Codex backend (chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, not trivial. It is not a base-URL and key swap. The code depends on the Vercel-specific evaluationModel and experimental_evaluate protocol, and on the Gateway cost metadata. You would replace src/judge.ts with a custom client for POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That means translating semantic.ts's boolean and choice question schema (semanticQuestions, semanticDecision) into Noul and Choice primitives, and re-mapping the answer and usage shapes. The rest of the proxy is provider-agnostic, so it is a bounded change of about 100-200 lines. Model IDs, thresholds and the 0.2/0.7/0.95 calibration were tuned on typesafe-ai/jev via Vercel and would need re-validating on typesafe/jev-1.13.

interface.name: HTTP POST /v1/messages (Anthropic Messages)
interface.purpose: Intercepts the request, judges and prunes old spans, then forwards to YOSHI_UPSTREAM (default api.anthropic.com). Other paths and unparseable bodies are passed through unchanged (server.ts:196-230).

interface.name: HTTP /responses and /v1/responses (OpenAI Responses)
interface.purpose: Same pruning for Codex, forwarded to chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex.

interface.name: CLI: bun start / bun run dev
interface.purpose: Starts the proxy. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill.

interface.name: CLI: bun run summary
interface.purpose: Reads the runtime log to account for savings.

interface.name: Env knobs (YOSHI_*)
interface.purpose: YOSHI_DRY_RUN=1 evaluates and logs without applying omissions. YOSHI_JUDGE=0 disables Jev. Others: YOSHI_MIN_CONTEXT_TOKENS (default 50000), YOSHI_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS (default 45000), YOSHI_JEV_MODE (atomic|choice|legacy), YOSHI_PORT, YOSHI_DECISIONS, YOSHI_LOG.

security: README labels it an experimental proof of concept. It is package.json private:true with no npm release.

Judge key handling: AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY comes from env or .env (server.ts:96), not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The Anthropic auth header (authorization or x-api-key) passes through the proxy. It is included in a sticky-cache key in lifecycle.optimize (server.ts, roughly line 250), so check whether it is hashed. The README says credentials are never logged.
Listens on 127.0.0.1 only (Bun.serve hostname, server.ts:~191), which is good. But any local process can use it as an authenticated Anthropic relay, because the client's auth header is forwarded.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output, which may be untrusted, is fed to the judge as state. The judge prompt does say the candidates are untrusted data. Jev returns typed probabilities only, so the injection impact is limited to wrongly keeping or dropping a span. A wrong drop silently removes context from the main model, which is a correctness risk rather than code execution.

No shell execution, curl|sh installer or postinstall found in the src/ files I read (grep for env and http only). Runtime is Bun, and the project needs bun install with two deps, ai and @ai-sdk/gateway.
Telemetry: no phone-home in src. Local logs .yoshi/requests.jsonl and .yoshi/decisions.json hold metadata and hashes only. Benchmark runs save raw traces locally.
Repo is 12 days old with 5 commits, 1 contributor and no CI, so supply-chain and audit confidence is low.
gh-compozy-yoshi.dataEgress: Above the size gate, each Jev call sends the current task and earlier user constraints, the action chronology, and the candidate spans (source code from Write/Edit/Bash arguments, tool results, teammate reports). Spans are up to ~24KB per request. It also sends a byte-bounded set of retained evidence. All of this goes to Vercel AI Gateway and then TypeSafe (README Privacy: no zero-data-retention option requested). The full Anthropic request itself goes to api.anthropic.com as normal via the proxy. On OpenRouter this would go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe instead. That is a real concern for client projects.
gh-compozy-yoshi.failureMode: Fail-open for correctness: failed, invalid or timed-out judgments keep the span (README; judge.ts catch blocks at ~lines 120-137 and 232-243). With no key, requests pass through unchanged. It is NOT fail-fast for latency: an outage can hold a request up to the 45s judge deadline (YOSHI_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS default 45000 in conversation scope, server.ts:115). Judging runs on the request path, which blocks the request. The proxy itself is a single point of failure: if bun start is not running, claude fails with a connection error because ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at a dead port.
gh-compozy-yoshi.latencyImpact: Large and measured by the authors. Fable diagnostic: baseline 39.77s vs Yoshi 210.54s (about 5x slower), with 301 Jev calls and 3 failures. Sonnet mixed session: 35.14s vs 171.99s (about 5x slower), with 142 calls and 3 failures. The README itself warns both trials were slower than baseline. The cost is per-turn while a large history is being judged, so it will not show on short sessions below the 50k gate.
gh-compozy-yoshi.contextCost: Adds no MCP tools, hooks or injected text, so it costs zero tokens of tool definitions. It works in the opposite direction: it rewrites the request history sent to Anthropic, and the goal is to reduce input. Real results: Fable diagnostic showed 34% accumulated-input reduction with the gate disabled, while the Sonnet mixed session showed -0.03%, meaning no savings. Rewriting old history can also invalidate Anthropic prompt-cache prefixes, and cache-write behavior differs between arms in the README table. The authors say there is no single validated savings percentage.
gh-compozy-yoshi.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set and the proxy is running, it applies to every request with no user prompting and no model discretion. That is the closest fit to the user's automatic-integration requirement. However it is context pruning, not a general Jev decision tool.
pros: It is the only candidate here that is truly automatic and invisible to Claude Code: a transparent proxy, with no prompt or model discretion needed.
Cheap failure semantics for correctness: failed or timed-out judgments retain the span, and an omitted span is replaced with an explicit marker. Tool IDs and paths are kept byte-identical.
Passes auth headers through, so it should work with OAuth or subscription auth (I have not verified this with a real login; the transport is plain passthrough in server.ts).
Benchmarks are unusually honest (two studies, hashes, and explicit statements that no single savings number is validated). MIT license.
The semantic.ts question design (boolean Noul-style plus choice) maps conceptually onto Jev's Noul and Choice primitives, so a port to OpenRouter is plausible.
Includes a YOSHI_DRY_RUN mode to evaluate decisions without applying them.
cons: No OpenRouter support: Jev is reached only via Vercel AI Gateway (typesafe-ai/jev) through @ai-sdk/gateway evaluationModel. Using it needs a Vercel key, or a custom judge.ts rewrite against openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions.
Measured to be about 5x slower than baseline in both trials (39.8s vs 210.5s and 35.1s vs 172.0s), with judge failures in each. A judge outage can stall a request up to 45s.

Savings are unproven. One study showed 34% input reduction with the gate disabled, while the other showed zero. Single trial per arm. Rewriting history may break Anthropic prompt caching, and the Yoshi cost totals are unknown.
Sends source code and tool output from your project to Vercel Gateway and TypeSafe with no ZDR option. That is a poor fit for client projects.
Silently deletes context from Opus's view, so a wrong verdict causes hard-to-diagnose task errors. That is a correctness risk for daily coding.
Solves a narrow problem, context pruning, not the broader uses Jev could serve in Claude Code (permission and risk decisions, routing, and so on). Only relevant in long sessions above 50k tokens.

Requires running a separate Bun daemon and launching claude with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. If the daemon dies, Claude Code breaks. A Claude Code session started normally will bypass it, and the Bun runtime and a second process need managing.

Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 5 commits, 1 contributor, no CI, no releases, and the README says the real version is moving into the CompozyOS repo. The maintainer intends to move away from this standalone form. Already 27 stars and 2 forks, so early interest.
gh-compozy-yoshi.verdict: Automatic and transparent, but it targets context pruning only and does not support OpenRouter. It needs a custom Decisions-API port, and it measured about 5x slower with unproven savings. Treat it as an interesting reference for a Jev judge design, not a daily driver. Do not point client code at it.

gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.name: tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.whatItDoes: Claude Code function-hook plugin (early-access, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, types generated from CC 2.1.274) plus an npm-style library. It hooks session.compact: pairs tool_use/tool_result, sends Jev the whole conversation as state (tool results replaced by "ok, N chars (omitted)"), asks two noul questions per non-pinned call (keep call? keep result verbatim?), and drops/truncates tool calls/results below keepThreshold 0.5. It replaces the built-in LLM summary with the original messages minus stale tool calls. A second hook, turn.complete, auto-triggers $.session.compact() when context reaches 60%. It falls back to the built-in summary on any error or if reduction is under 25%.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The library already has a baseUrl option (src/request.ts:60,67); the hook only needs about 3 edits: pass baseUrl in jevAsker/buildJevRequest calls (hooks/fast-jev.ts:94, 171), read OPENROUTER_API_KEY in getApiKey (:235), and use model typesafe/jev-latest (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) instead of 'jev-latest'. If OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same {model,state,questions} noul schema, that is all it takes. That is plausible given the shared endpoint name, but I could not verify it. interface.name: hook session.compact
interface.purpose: Replaces the built-in compaction. Sends state plus noul questions to Jev, prunes tool calls/results, and returns {messages}. Falls back with next(event) on error or if reduction is under minReductionRatio. Shows a toast and logs a decisions line (hooks/fast-jev.ts:263-290).

interface.name: hook turn.complete
interface.purpose: After each turn it reads $.session.usage(). If context.percent >= compactAtPercent (60), it calls $.session.compact(), with an in-flight guard. Errors are logged and ignored (hooks/fast-jev.ts:292-307).

interface.name: library compactMessages / compact / JevClient
interface.purpose: npm API for other agents: compactMessages(transcript, opts), reductionRatio, buildJevRequest, parseJevResponse, fitState, batchCalls, decideCall, applyDecisions. It is not published as a release, and package.json 'files' points to dist/.

interface.name: plugin userConfig
interface.purpose: apiKey (sensitive), keepThreshold, preserveRecentMessages, compactAtPercent, minReductionRatio, maxStateTokens, maxRequestTokens, truncateHeadChars, model (.claude-plugin/plugin.json). No baseUrl option.

interface.name: npm scripts
interface.purpose: build, typecheck, test (vitest), demo (live API), validate:plugin. There is no MCP server, no skill and no slash command.

The library needs Node >=18. Dev deps: tsx, typescript, vitest, @types/node. Zero runtime dependencies.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.install: export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 and TYPESAFE_API_KEY in ~/.claude/settings.json env; claude plugin marketplace add tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction; claude plugin install fast-jev-compaction@fast-jev-compaction; /reload-plugins. Or claude --plugin-dir <checkout> from the repo root.
security: No shell execution, no child_process, no postinstall, no telemetry, no curl|sh installer (grep finds none in src/ and hooks/). Only network egress is via host $.http.fetch to the configured URL.

Plugin sandbox per types/claude-code.d.ts:21: no fs, network or exec of its own, and everything goes through the host. This limits blast radius, but the function-hooks API is early access and can change.

API key is sent as an Authorization Bearer header inside the host fetch, so it is not in argv or the process list. The apiKey plugin option is marked sensitive: true. But the hook also reads $.settings.read() env (hooks/fast-jev.ts:236-243) to fetch the key. The key would live in ~/.claude/settings.json env, and that env is also exported to every Bash tool call, so the existing secret-leak hook should watch for it.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns only numeric noul probabilities and the parser rejects anything else (request.ts:96-122). But adversarial text in the transcript could steer the score, so an injected page could cause a tool result about a constraint or instruction to be dropped. Dropped results are irreversible within that session context (the original messages are replaced).

Integrity risk: it deletes tool calls and results with only a probabilistic 0.5 threshold. There is no user confirmation. Truncated results keep 300 chars plus a note. Context loss can cause silent regressions such as forgotten error details or file contents, though the assistant can re-read files.

Repo is 13 days old with 17 AI-authored commits and 7.2k stars in a day; a supply-chain risk for a plugin that runs in-process on every compaction. Pin a commit and audit before install (and re-audit any update: marketplace add tracks the default branch).
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.dataEgress: On each compaction, one or more requests (the full state is resent per request) go to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. The state contains: all user and assistant text (long ones abridged to 400 head + 150 tail chars, pinned messages likely full), the goal (last 3 user prompts), and each tool call's name and input (Bash commands, file paths, Edit/Write inputs and grep patterns, truncated to 1000, then 200, then 60 chars). Tool RESULT contents are NOT sent (only 'ok, N chars (omitted)', src/state.ts header + README step 2). So file contents read via Read/Bash output are not sent, but Bash commands (may contain inline secrets or tokens), paths, client project names, and pasted prompts are. That matters for client projects: the data goes to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if patched), with no redaction. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover this channel.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.failureMode: Fail-open for correctness: any Jev error, HTTP failure, malformed JSON, missing key or non-fitting state throws, and the hook catches it and calls next(event) to use Claude Code's built-in summary (hooks/fast-jev.ts:283-289). There is no explicit timeout or AbortSignal anywhere in the repo (grep for timeout/AbortSignal finds only the toast timeout), so a hung request depends on the host $.http.fetch default and could stall the compaction. turn.complete errors are swallowed. The hook is not on the per-tool path, so a Jev outage does not block coding.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.contextCost: None added: no MCP tools, no skills and no hook-injected text into the model context (it is a function hook, not a prompt injection). A toast and a ui.log decisions line appear only in the UI. The plugin actually reduces context: compaction keeps the original messages minus stale tool calls/results instead of an LLM summary, and it triggers at 60% context (versus the default of about 90% or so). Side effect: the pruned history is likely larger than a summary, so it may compact more often. Its hidden cost is cache invalidation on rebuilt messages.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.latencyImpact: Per-tool-call: zero. Per compaction: N concurrent HTTP requests (one per batch of questions, each carrying up to 25k tokens of state), claimed 70-500 ms each, so about 0.5-2 s total when everything fits in one or two requests. Cost per compaction is roughly 25-30k input tokens times the number of requests at $0.042/1M, about $0.001-0.005. Compaction cost is negligible either way. It also replaces the built-in summarization call (which takes many seconds on Opus), so compaction could be faster.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: session.compact (manual /compact and auto-compaction) and turn.complete (proactive compaction at 60% context). No prompting is needed, and it is fully automatic once installed. It needs the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS flag.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks session.compact and turn.complete, so the user never prompts for Jev (hooks/fast-jev.ts:263, 292).
Uses Jev for what it is designed for: typed noul yes/no probabilities with no free text (src/request.ts noulAnswer), and it maps well onto Jev's calibrated decisions.
Fail-open design: any error, missing key or low reduction falls back to Claude Code's built-in summary (fast-jev.ts:283-289), so it cannot block work.
Zero context-token overhead, no MCP tool definitions, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry; runs in the CC function-hook sandbox with network only via the host fetch.
Tool RESULT contents are never sent to Jev (only length notes), which limits egress of source code and file contents.
Compaction is verbatim: user and assistant text is kept unmodified, so there is no lossy summary, and it compacts at 60% instead of near the limit.
Has a library baseUrl option (request.ts:60,67), so retargeting to OpenRouter is a small patch; MIT license; the tests mock Jev so the logic is covered.
cons: No OpenRouter support: hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; the hook does not even pass baseUrl (fast-jev.ts:94,171), so OpenRouter use requires a fork or local patch, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema compatibility is unverified (docs pages 404, not in llms.txt).

Depends on the early-access, unstable CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS feature; types were generated from CC 2.1.274 and the user runs 2.1.285, so behavior on the current version is untested and may break on any release.
Only helps at compaction time (rare in a day of coding, and the user runs Opus 5.5 with a large window). It does not give Jev a role in routing, permission decisions, or code review.

Irreversible probabilistic deletion at 0.5 threshold with no confirmation; context loss can silently drop constraints or error detail, and prompt-injected tool text can bias which calls get dropped. Jev claims (per Theo) may just be a fast flash router, and no benchmark of compaction quality is in the repo.

Sends prompts, assistant text and Bash commands and file paths (inputs up to 1000 chars) of client projects to a third party with no redaction, every compaction, up to N times per compaction (state is resent for each request).

Immature and hype-driven: 13 days old, 30 commits (17 by Devin AI), no CI, no release, version mismatch (0.2.0 vs 0.3.0), an unrelated macOS SwiftUI demo bundled, no timeout on the fetch, and a 7.2k-star/463-fork count reached in one day.

May conflict with the user's existing setup: replaces built-in compaction wholesale, does not interact with the GitNexus and secret-guard hooks, and the sensitive key would need to sit in settings.json env, which is exposed to Bash subprocesses.
gh-tamaratran-fast-jev-compaction.verdict: The only candidate that is fully automatic (deterministic session.compact and turn.complete hooks, zero context cost, fail-open), but it is narrow, not OpenRouter-ready without a patch, and built on an early-access feature and an untested 13-day-old repo. Worth a pinned, audited fork (baseUrl plus OPENROUTER_API_KEY plus typesafe/jev-latest) as an optional experiment for compaction only, not as the main Jev integration.

gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.name: tamaratran/jev-pruner (plugin id: fast-jev-output)
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin built on Claude Code's early-access "function hooks" (a TypeScript module registering on('tool.call', {tool:'Bash'}) that wraps next()). After a Bash command runs and before the result reaches the main model, if stdout exceeds 10,000 estimated tokens it splits the output into 20-line chunks (max 200) and sends conversation history plus chunks to Jev. It asks one noul question per chunk: does any line here need to remain available. Chunks with a low keep probability become "[N lines omitted]" markers. The full output is archived under .claude/fast-jev-output/ with a recovery footer. Errors, diagnostics, JSON/XML/diffs, source, docs, and cat/jq/git diff output are protected. On any failure the original output is returned. It also ships an opt-in Codex wrapper and an eval/training harness (a Kev-0.8B fine-tune pipeline, marked superseded).
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.runtime: TypeScript module run inside Claude Code's function-hook runtime (Node >=18 declared). hooks/hooks.json is {"modules":["./fast-jev-output.ts"]}. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. The installed claude 2.1.285 binary contains that flag string (grep count 10), so the mechanism exists there, but it is early access and the README says the API may change between releases (types generated from 2.1.274).
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.install: Add CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 and TYPESAFE_API_KEY to the settings env. Then run: claude plugin marketplace add tamaratran/jev-pruner; claude plugin install fast-jev-output@fast-jev-output. There is no build step on the Claude path. Local alternative: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 claude --plugin-dir . (not executed in this audit).

security: Plugin code runs with hook privileges (fs read/write, http.fetch, session.messages, settings.read) inside Claude Code. It is TypeScript from a 12-day-old, largely AI-authored repo, so review before enabling. I did not audit the whole of src/output.ts (26 KB).
API key: read from plugin option, env, or settings.env, and sent only as a Bearer header via $.http.fetch. The key is never in argv or a process list. The apiKey option is marked sensitive.
The hook reads the entire settings via $.settings.read() but takes only env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

Prompt-injection surface: Bash output and history are sent to Jev, which returns only numeric probabilities, so injection can at most bias which lines are dropped. A crafted output could hide lines from the main model (integrity risk), mitigated by the archive footer and protection of error and result lines.

Secret handling is weak. looksSecret (src/secrets.ts) is a regex that only suppresses local archiving. The README says it does not redact or prevent sending content to Jev. Output from cat .env or printenv still goes to the remote API, and the pruned result then states 're-run the command'.
Writes .claude/fast-jev-output/bash-*.txt (full stdout+stderr) in every project, with a self-gitignore. Client-project output persists on disk unencrypted.

No curl|sh, no postinstall (package.json has no install scripts), no telemetry in the hook. The dev dependencies are tsx, vitest and typescript. The demo/ folder holds a macOS Swift app plus .agents skills for Claude subscription login and Modal login (login.py) that are dev tooling, not part of the plugin runtime. Not audited further.
Early-access function hooks: the plugin trust and permission model for them is not documented in the repo. The `claude plugin eval --trust-plugin` flag suggests trust prompts exist.
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.dataEgress: Per pruned Bash call, Jev receives {context, task, history, command, chunks, category}. That is the command string, the full stdout or stderr split into chunks (up to about 25k state tokens per request, several parallel requests), the last three user prompts (500 chars each), and the session history from $.session.messages() (up to the newest 4096 messages): user and assistant text, complete tool inputs, and tool-result text and structured data. That includes file contents Claude has read and earlier command output. Requests go to api.typesafe.ai, or to OpenRouter if baseUrl is set, and OpenRouter forwards them to TypeSafe. Requests are not sent for output at or below 10,000 tokens. Most Bash calls are small, so egress happens only for large outputs (builds, test logs, large greps). When it does trigger, it can send a large slice of the whole conversation, code and client data included, to a third party. That is a significant concern for client projects. History is re-sent per request and per history segment.
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.failureMode: Fail-open, by design. Any exception, missing key, HTTP error, archive-write failure, or unfittable budget returns the original result (catch at hooks/fast-jev-output.ts:283 returns answer). Jev is called only after Bash has finished. However, I found no explicit timeout or AbortSignal in the plugin code (grep for timeout, AbortSignal and Promise.race hits only the toast timeout). It relies on the host's $.http.fetch timeout, so a hung Jev could stall the tool result for the host timeout. The retry policy is a max_tokens_exceeded retry twice with a halved budget, and request count is capped at min(12, ceil(visibleChars/192)). With the key unset, pruning is silently skipped ("missing_key"). Whether the host's function-hook API changes and breaks the plugin is untested, but the try/catch means it degrades to passthrough.
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.latencyImpact: Zero for the 95%+ of Bash calls with output at or below 10k tokens (a pure JS estimate, no network). For large outputs it adds one or more Jev round trips: author-reported mean 240 ms per decision on synthetic tests, but there are up to 12 requests, run partly in parallel, plus a local archive write and history read. Real-world cost is probably 0.3 to several seconds on rare huge outputs, and could be longer with a long history (many partitions x output batches). The pruned result cannot be shown to the model until scoring finishes.
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.contextCost: Zero added tool definitions: it is not an MCP server, has no skill, and injects no system prompt or instructions. It only shrinks tool results, adding a short footer ("[fast-jev-output full output: <path> ...]") and "[N lines omitted]" markers to pruned results. Net effect on context is negative. The author reports about 83% reduction on synthetic tests and 54% on real captures, but only when a single Bash output exceeds 10,000 tokens (about 40k chars). Claude Code already truncates or persists such outputs to a file with a head preview, so the real saving is mostly about surfacing the relevant part instead of the head, which is the plugin's stated use case (76k-char log example).
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. It triggers on every Bash tool call with no user or model action, gated internally by output size. This is exactly the "automatic, user never asks" behavior, and Jev is used as a real classifier in the hot path.
pros: It is truly automatic: a tool.call hook wrapping Bash, with no prompting or model discretion, which matches the user's requirement. Jev's noul primitive is an apt fit for a per-chunk 'keep or drop' decision (hooks/fast-jev-output.ts:162; src/output.ts).
Fail-open everywhere: try/catch returns the original result, and a missing key means silent passthrough. It adds no context tokens, since there is no MCP or skill (contextCost zero).

Conservative retention design: errors, diagnostics, test totals, artifact paths, source, docs, JSON/XML/diffs and cat/git diff output are never pruned, dropping requires keep-probability <=0.1, and the full output is archived so the model can Read it (README 'Information retention rules').
OpenRouter-compatible via configuration: baseUrl plus apiKey are already plugin options, and OpenRouter's System One endpoint claims TypeSafe-SDK compatibility with jev-latest mapped to typesafe/.

Already tuned for Claude Code: it handles Claude's persisted-output files (fixing the 'head preview hides the error' problem), uses a native-preview budget cap, and includes a recursion guard for reading archives.
Active development (164 commits, MIT), with extensive tests and evals including paired native-vs-pruner arms.
Cost is small: about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, and it fires only on rare huge outputs.
cons: Depends on the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS API, which the README says may change between releases. The flag string exists in the installed 2.1.285 binary, but the plugin's types were generated from 2.1.274, and behavior on 2.1.285 is unverified. It could break silently, and fail-open would then hide that.

Data egress is broad. When it fires, it sends the command, the full output and much of the session history (file contents Claude read, tool results) to a third party. Its own README says the secret check does not stop content being sent to Jev. This is risky for client projects, and there is no per-project disable other than not setting the key.

There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support. The key must be given as the apiKey option or by putting the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Live OpenRouter compatibility is untested by the author, whose tests target api.typesafe.ai only.

Narrow value: it only helps on the rare single Bash output above 10k tokens (about 40k chars). Claude Code already persists and previews such output, and cat/git diff/JSON/source are excluded. Most daily coding therefore sees zero effect. Real captures showed only 54% reduction, and the savings are a small share of tokens in an Opus session.

Lossy pruning risk: chunks that look like progress noise but hold the needed fact are dropped (the 0.1 threshold is 'a retention policy, not a measured error guarantee'). The model may not know to look at the archive.
History partitioning can generate up to 12 Jev requests with re-sent history, so latency and cost on big logs are unbounded by any explicit timeout. There is no explicit timeout in the plugin code.

Immature and largely AI-written: 12 days old, 3 contributors (98 of 164 commits are Devin AI), 0 releases, no CI, and a 2,000+ line eval scaffold. The repo mixes in unrelated material (Codex, training, macOS demo, login skills). The plugin name (fast-jev-output) does not match the repo name.

Writes full command output, including possible secrets, to .claude/fast-jev-output/ in each project, which is a client-data hygiene concern. It also overlaps with existing hooks: the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard and GitNexus post-Bash hook also touch Bash results, and ordering or interaction with them is undefined.
Requires modifying settings env (a flag plus the key). Being a TS module loaded by the CLI, it is not sandboxed.
gh-tamaratran-jev-pruner.verdict: The only candidate that genuinely uses Jev automatically inside Claude Code, as a deterministic fail-open hook with zero context cost, and it can point at OpenRouter through the baseUrl and apiKey options. The value is narrow (rare >10k-token Bash outputs), it depends on an early-access hook API, and it ships large slices of session history to a third party. It is worth a trial on personal projects only, not client projects; verify the OpenRouter baseUrl and response shape before relying on it.

gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.name: GhalebDweikat/winnow
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (v0.5.1) that acts as a context sieve. A function-hook TypeScript module (hooks/winnow.ts) wraps every Read/Bash/Grep tool result over 1500 chars. It posts the result plus the current task (last user request, last assistant sentence) to a resident local Python sidecar on 127.0.0.1:47311. The sidecar splits the text into ~25-line blocks and asks Jev one Noul yes/no question per block ("is this block needed for the current task?"). Blocks with P(needed) < 0.1 are replaced by a 3-line stub (summary by Claude Haiku plus a recall key). Full text is cached in ~/.winnow/cache. Nothing is hidden if the output looks like an error. A second hook (prompt.submit) ranks the project memory files and WINNOW_CONTEXT_DIRS against the prompt with Jev and injects up to 3 files (8000 chars max). It also ships an MCP server with winnow_recall and winnow_stats, a SKILL.md explaining stubs, and offline replay/benchmark/labeling CLIs.

providerSupport.evidence: winnow has no OpenRouter code. sidecar/src/winnow/judge.py:67-83 builds typesafe_sdk.TypeSafeClient(model=..., retry=RetryPolicy(max_retries=1,timeout)) and calls client.system_one(state, questions) with no base_url argument. Keys are read via config.py:119 (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) and the ~/.winnow/env loader (config.py:82-111) copies any KEY=VALUE into os.environ. The PyPI sdk typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 (which I statically read) resolves base_url from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (constants.py:6, default https://api.typesafe.ai) and POSTs to base_url + '/v1/systemone' (_core/constants.py:5, endpoints.py:31) with Authorization: Bearer <key> and body {state, model, questions}. OpenRouter's System One API is POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and WINNOW_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 should route it there. This is unverified: I did not run it, and OpenRouter's request/response schema, model-id format and error codes may differ from TypeSafe's. Summaries and the 'adapter' judge need ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (judge.py:86-99, summarize.py) and are separate from OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: Adapter judge: system-one-adapter emulates System One via Claude Haiku 4.5 or OpenAI (WINNOW_ADAPTER_PROVIDER). Summaries use the Anthropic API (WINNOW_SUMMARY_MODEL).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, with no code change. Put TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and WINNOW_MODEL in ~/.winnow/env, and set WINNOW_SUMMARY=0 because the user has no Anthropic API key. It only works if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same {state, model, questions} body and returns answers[].noul plus usage; the response parser at judge.py:39-64 depends on that. Needs a one-call smoke test (winnow demo without --fake) before relying on it. If the schemas differ, the fix is a small subclass of TypeSafeJudge that posts with httpx.

interface.name: function hook tool.call (Read, Bash, Grep)

interface.name: function hook prompt.submit
interface.purpose: hooks/winnow.ts:147-160. Posts the prompt (12+ chars) to /hook/user-prompt-submit. Appends Jev-selected memory/context files to the prompt context.

interface.purpose: mcp_server.py:40. Tokens saved, outputs rewritten, regret rate.
