interface.name: CLI winnow doctor/demo/stats/recall/serve/bench/clean/mcp/hook/replay/review
interface.purpose: sidecar/src/winnow/cli.py. Diagnostics, offline benchmark against the user's own transcripts, hand-labeling, and regret review.

security: API keys live in plaintext in ~/.winnow/env (home dir chmod 0o700 at config.py:72) or in settings.json env; no keys in argv. The sidecar reads the file and injects it into os.environ.

Sidecar HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:47311 (serve.py:236) has no auth token. It rejects requests carrying an Origin header or a non-JSON Content-Type (serve.py:160-182) to block browser CSRF. Any local process or user can still POST to it and spend the judge key. SECURITY.md lists this as in scope.

The SessionStart hook runs 'uv run' on the plugin's pyproject, so each new plugin version resolves and installs dependencies from PyPI (typesafe-sdk, system-one-adapter[anthropic], anthropic, mcp>=2.0) at session start with a 600s timeout. That is a supply-chain surface, and dependencies are unpinned except by uv.lock.

Prompt-injection surface: it rewrites what Claude sees. A crafted tool output, or the judge being wrong, can hide a block the model needed. Recovery is by winnow_recall. The prompt.submit hook injects file contents into the prompt context from memory files, so a poisoned memory file becomes a context-injection vector.

Uses Claude Code early-access function hooks (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1), an in-process TypeScript module with access to session messages, cwd and http.fetch. It is not sandboxed from the session.

No telemetry found in the source. Only the judge and summarizer endpoints are contacted (grep shows no other outbound URLs). No postinstall, no curl|sh installer. The sidecar is spawned detached (serve.py:302-311).
MIT, single maintainer, 2 contributors. SECURITY.md documents the threat model and a private disclosure channel.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.dataEgress: The README table says winnow sends the following to the judge (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed). (1) Every Read/Bash/Grep tool output over 1500 chars, chunked into blocks and capped by WINNOW_MAX_STATE_CHARS=120000 chars per call. In practice that is source code, command output, grep hits and possibly secrets in files, plus the tool arguments (paths and commands). (2) A task description: the last user request (up to 1500 chars) and the last assistant sentence. (3) On every prompt of 12+ chars, the prompt text plus the first 600 chars of each candidate memory or context file (up to 60 files). Hidden blocks (up to 20000 chars per group, up to 4 groups) also go to Anthropic for summaries when WINNOW_SUMMARY=1 and an Anthropic key exists. The full text of hidden outputs is stored locally in ~/.winnow/cache with no eviction. For client projects this means routing a large share of client code through a third-party judge. The existing secret-leak guard is a PreToolUse hook, so it does not filter what winnow sends after a tool has run.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.failureMode: Fail-open by design. hooks.py docstring: every failure degrades to pass-through. The TS module returns the original result if the sidecar is unreachable, non-2xx or returns non-JSON (winnow.ts:74-110). A missing key posts one 'judge can't start' notice per session. Judge timeout is WINNOW_JUDGE_TIMEOUT=15s with max_retries=1 (judge.py:74-78), so a hung Jev call could stall a tool result for roughly 15-30s before passing through, with no circuit breaker on the tool.call path (serve.py has next_build_attempt backoff only for judge construction). If Jev is slow but not down, every large Read or Bash pays the wait. The function-hook path also depends on an early-access flag: without CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 the module silently never loads.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.contextCost: Small static cost. 2 MCP tools (winnow_recall, winnow_stats), about 250-350 tokens for names, descriptions and schemas, plus a server instructions string of about 40 tokens. The skill description is about 90 tokens, with the full SKILL.md (about 500 tokens) loaded only on trigger. Per-turn injection: on prompt.submit up to 8000 chars (about 2k tokens) of memory files when P(relevant) >= 0.5 (top 3), and this hook can conflict with or duplicate the user's existing memory. Stubs replace hidden blocks (about 100 tokens each), so the net effect is fewer tokens only when a rewrite happens. The DESIGN measurements show only about 2% (default question set) to 4.6% (structured set) of text is hidden at the only clean threshold (0.1), so real savings are small, and most results are skipped by the 0.2 minimum prune ratio.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.autoInvocation: Deterministic and fully automatic. tool.call function hooks wrap every Read/Bash/Grep call and prompt.submit runs on every prompt, with no model discretion or user prompting. The SessionStart hook starts the sidecar. Only the winnow_recall MCP tool and the skill are model-discretion, and those are used only when a stub appears.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.latencyImpact: Measured by the author: sidecar overhead about 16 ms per judged call versus 381 ms for per-call Python startup (README/bench). Jev median 86 ms per case in the author's 300-case run (docs/DESIGN.md:75-86), plus a network hop. Through OpenRouter, add its routing overhead (unmeasured). Results under 1500 chars skip the round trip. Prompt-time selector adds one Jev call per prompt when candidate files exist. Summaries call Haiku serially or in parallel only when something was hidden (hundreds of ms to seconds). Worst case is the 15s-plus-retry timeout.
pros: It is the only candidate here that does what the user asked: it is a deterministic, hook-based integration that fires on every Read/Bash/Grep without any 'use jev' prompt (hooks/winnow.ts:120-160).

It fails open. Sidecar down, judge error, missing key or odd tool shape all return the original result, and there is a shadow mode (WINNOW_MODE=shadow) to observe decisions for a week before changing anything.

It uses Jev in the way the model is designed for: batched calibrated Noul yes/no probabilities with thresholds decided in code. Published numbers in the repo: Jev ECE 0.14 versus 0.31 for a lexical baseline, median 86 ms, $0.036 for 300 cases; the most confident bin (p<0.1) had 0% needed on 97 hand labels.

The Jev call goes through the official typesafe-sdk, which honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. The /v1/systemone path matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so OpenRouter routing is likely a config-only change (unverified).

It has real tests, and CI covers Ubuntu and Windows on Python 3.10 and 3.13, plus 'claude plugin test' for the function hooks. It ships a replay tool to score the judge on the user's own transcripts, and a recall cache so hidden text is recoverable (nothing deleted).
No obvious telemetry, no curl|sh installer, no postinstall, and MIT licensed. SECURITY.md is unusually explicit about the threat model.
Judge cost is tiny (about $0.0004 per 10k-token result).
cons: Little benefit at the safe operating point. At WINNOW_DROP=0.1 the author's own data show only about 2-5% of text is hidden, and results below the 20% minimum prune ratio are not rewritten at all. At 0.3, regret is about 21% of needed blocks (upper bound). Above 0.1, Jev is described as under-confident. For a user on a subscription with Opus, tokens saved translate into little.

Depends on Claude Code's early-access function hooks (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, 2.1.260+). The README says the surface may change between releases, and without the flag it silently does nothing. It has not been tested against this user's other hooks (GitNexus post hook on Grep|Glob|Bash, the secret guard, caveman) and may interact with them, since both rewrite or annotate the same tool results.

High data-egress risk for client work. Nearly all large code and command output plus every prompt (when memory files exist) is sent to Jev/OpenRouter, and the secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover post-tool output sent by winnow. Stubs also alter Read results: line numbers are renumbered from 1 (SKILL.md), which can confuse edit and navigation workflows.

Requires an Anthropic API key for summaries. The user's OAuth subscription does not provide one, so summaries must be turned off (WINNOW_SUMMARY=0), which degrades stubs to a deterministic digest. The 'adapter' fallback also needs an Anthropic key.

Alpha and young: created 2026-09-16, 29 commits over 2 weeks, effectively 1 maintainer (28 of 29 commits), version 0.5.1, and it has been rewritten once already (PostToolUse to function hooks). Hand labels were made by Claude, not a human, and are self-reported.

Extra moving parts: a resident local server without auth on port 47311, an unpinned dependency resolve via uv at every plugin update, a plaintext ~/.winnow/env, an unbounded ~/.winnow/cache (no eviction), and a worst-case 15-30 s stall per tool call when Jev is slow.
Official OpenRouter path is not tested by the project; the README only documents TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so OpenRouter use is on the user to verify.
gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.verdict: The only fully automatic, deterministic Jev integration among the candidates, and technically sound and fail-open. Its practical payoff is small: about 2-5% of text hidden at the safe threshold, an early-access hook dependency, and a lot of code egress. Worth running in shadow mode against OpenRouter (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, WINNOW_SUMMARY=0) on personal projects to measure it, but not enabling active mode on client code.

gh-ghalebdweikat-winnow.tests: 16 pytest files in sidecar/tests plus tests/winnow.test.ts (claude plugin test). GitHub Actions CI on ubuntu and windows, Python 3.10 and 3.13. I did not run them, per the static-reading rule.

gh-bytebell-jev-filter.name: ByteBell/jev-filter
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace "bytebell", plugin jev-filter 0.1.0) bundling a single-file, stdlib-only Python MCP server (also usable as a CLI), a skill, and a /jev-find slash command. After the agent chooses a grep regex, the server runs git grep / rg / a Python walk (or takes paths the agent already has) and sends EACH candidate file's full text (up to 24k tokens) as a separate call to OpenRouter's Decisions API with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and one Choice question with yes/no criteria ("is this file part of this feature / would a dev edit it"). It keeps files with p(yes) >= 0.7, lists borderline ones (0.5-0.7), caches decisions on disk, and reports Jev's billed cost versus an estimated Claude cost. It replaces only the "which grep hits matter" step; the LLM still picks the pattern and reads the kept files.

Also fetches https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models (:35,:149) for price comparison. No TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no /api/v1/systemone, no other gateway anywhere in source.
providerSupport.others: None. Only the OpenRouter alpha Decisions endpoint; DECISIONS_URL is hard-coded (not env-overridable), JEV_MODEL is overridable.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: N/A (already OpenRouter-native). Pointing it at TypeSafe direct would be a small edit of the hard-coded URL and key env var, if TypeSafe's schema matches, which is unverified.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_grep_filter
interface.purpose: Args question, pattern (required); root, threshold, include_tests, glob, compare_models. Runs git grep -l -I -i -E (else rg -l -i, else Python os.walk regex) with the agent's exact pattern, skips test files by default, sends each hit to Jev, returns kept files with p_yes, borderline, Jev cost/latency, and Claude cost estimates (server :68-90, :123-125).

interface.name: MCP tool jev_filter
interface.purpose: Args question, paths (required); root, threshold, compare_models. Classifies an explicit list of files the agent already found (:92-108, :126-127). Accepts arbitrary absolute paths.

interface.name: Skill jev-filter (skills/jev-filter/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Description-triggered: 'Use when you need to find which files implement or belong to a feature (how does X work, where is Y handled, which files would I change for Z) and grep would return many candidates.' Body says: use when grep returns >10 files, threshold 0.5 for impact analysis/refactor, read only kept files, and tell the user the cost in one line.

interface.name: Slash command /jev-find <question>
interface.purpose: Explicit trigger: pick grep regex, call jev_grep_filter, read kept files, answer, end with cost comparison line.

interface.name: CLI python3 jev_filter.py grep|files
interface.purpose: Terminal use without an agent (--root, --glob, --include-tests, --threshold, --compare, --no-cache, --json).

interface.name: Hooks
interface.purpose: None. No hooks.json, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse, no proxy.

gh-bytebell-jev-filter.tests: One offline unittest file (tests/test_jev_filter.py, ~11 tests with a faked Jev API: truncation, cache, cost math, missing key, MCP handshake). No CI (.github absent), no releases, no tags. Not executed by me (static review only).
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.runtime: Python 3.9+ stdlib only (python3 invoked from plugin/.mcp.json). No pip/npm deps, no postinstall, no build step. User has Python 3.13 so compatible.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.install: export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... (in the shell that launches Claude Code); claude plugin marketplace add ByteBell/jev-filter; claude plugin install jev-filter@bytebell
security: API key is passed via MCP env (${OPENROUTER_API_KEY} expansion in .mcp.json) and used in an Authorization header only; never in argv, so not visible in the process list. It must exist in the environment that launches Claude Code (not in a settings env file by default).

No shell=True; subprocess is called with an argument list (git -C root grep -l -I -i -E <pattern>, rg ...). The agent-supplied pattern is passed as a positional arg after -E without a '--' separator before it, so a pattern beginning with '-' could be parsed as an option by git/rg (minor argument-injection surface, low impact). Glob is appended after '--' for git but as '-g <glob>' for rg.

jev_filter accepts arbitrary absolute paths and reads them server-side with open(); root is arbitrary. This bypasses the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), which does not match mcp__ tools. A prompt-injected or careless agent could ship ~/.ssh keys, .env, credentials files (any UTF-8 text) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. No path allow-list, no secret filter.

Even jev_grep_filter can hit secrets: git grep only covers tracked files, but the rg fallback (no --no-ignore, so honors .gitignore) and the pure-Python _walk_grep fallback (skips only .git/node_modules/vendor/... dirs) read untracked files such as .env in non-git dirs. Pattern such as 'key|token|secret' would select exactly secret-bearing files.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output returned to Claude contains only file paths, probabilities and cost numbers (no file content), so injection via returned text is small; but file contents go to a third-party model whose only output is a number. A hostile file could try to game its own p(yes) but that only affects ranking.
Disk cache at ~/.cache/jev-filter (decisions and prices) keyed by sha256 of model, question, path and content; stores only p_yes/cost/latency, not file text. Default perms, minor.
No telemetry beyond sending HTTP-Referer/X-Title headers to OpenRouter. Also unauthenticated GET to openrouter.ai/api/v1/models for prices. No curl|sh, no postinstall.
Tool description/README contain marketing claims ('better and 1% of cost') that steer the model to call it; that is a persuasion-in-description surface but benign here.

1 star, 1 author (deusmachinea/ByteBell), created the day before audit; supply-chain trust is low. Since it executes as a local process with your OpenRouter key and reads your source, pin a commit after reading it (this audit read the whole 25 KB file).
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.dataEgress: Full text of every candidate file (up to 24,000 estimated tokens = 84k chars each, truncated beyond that; 70% shrink retry on 400 context errors), its relative path, and the natural-language question the agent wrote, sent file-by-file to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (then routed by OpenRouter to TypeSafe). Up to 400 files per call (JEV_MAX_FILES). Personal and CLIENT code both leave the machine; README itself warns 'Your code leaves your machine... sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe.' Client NDA/data-processing concerns apply; OpenRouter data-policy/ZDR settings and TypeSafe retention unverified. Not sent: prompts, diffs, tool outputs, conversation. Also OPENROUTER_API_KEY to openrouter.ai and a GET of the public model list.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.failureMode: Fail-open at the agent level, fail-soft per file. No hooks, so nothing blocks Claude's normal tools. Missing key: tool returns isError 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set' and Claude can fall back to plain grep/Read. Per-file errors are collected in result.errors, other files still judged; 401/402/403 return clear messages without retry. Timeouts: 120s per HTTP request (:222); 429/5xx/network errors retried up to 5 times with exponential backoff capped at 30s plus jitter (:263-266), so a single failing file can stall ~2-3 min; a full 400-file call with 8 workers has no overall deadline, and the MCP server handles tools/call synchronously in its main loop (serve() is single-threaded), so one long call blocks all other requests to this server (and may exceed Claude Code's MCP tool timeout). Failed files are silently absent from 'kept', so a partial outage yields a thin result that looks like a real answer (only a trailing 'N files failed' line). Cost cap: none other than the 400-file limit; no per-call budget guard.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.latencyImpact: Per Jev call the README claims sub-second; server does 8 parallel requests. 231 files was reported (README) with 726k input tokens; wall time not stated in README (summary prints it). Estimate: 50 files about 5-15 s, 200-400 files about 30-90 s, plus retries on 429. Cached repeats near-instant. Only paid on turns where Claude chooses to invoke it; no cost on other turns. Beats a serial Opus read of hundreds of files but is slower than a single grep and adds to turn time where grep returns 10-30 files.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.contextCost: 2 tools. Tool defs: jev_grep_filter about 1.4k chars (description ~520 + schema ~880) and jev_filter about 0.9k chars, roughly 600-700 tokens total (deferred via ToolSearch in recent Claude Code so often only names are in context). No MCP server 'instructions' field returned (initialize returns only name/version/tools capability). Skill adds name+description frontmatter (~470 chars, ~120 tokens) always in the skill listing; SKILL.md body (~1.8k chars, ~450 tokens) loads only when triggered. /jev-find command listing ~60 tokens. Hooks inject nothing. Each tool call returns TWO text blocks (summary plus the full indented JSON) plus structuredContent, so a 43-kept/231-candidate result can be several thousand tokens of duplicated output (kept + borderline + errors + cost tables), which partly cancels the token-saving pitch.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only, steered by the skill description ('how does X work / where is Y handled / which files would I change') and the MCP tool descriptions. Not deterministic: there is no hook, so Claude Code decides. The skill's own guidance (>10 grep hits) and Claude's strong preference for built-in Grep, Glob, Explore subagents and the user's existing GitNexus graph hooks means invocation will be inconsistent, and subagents (Explore) may not use it. Satisfies 'user never says use jev' partially; cannot guarantee it fires. Each invocation also makes Claude add a cost-comparison line to its answer (SKILL.md step 5), which is noise for daily work.
pros: Only candidate here that is actually wired to OpenRouter's Decisions API with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, in ~250 lines of readable stdlib Python; entirely auditable (I read all of it), no deps, no install scripts, no hooks.

Uses Jev for what it is designed for: a typed Choice with per-option probabilities for a yes/no relevance decision, not free-text generation. Request schema (state + questions.choice + criteria) matches the brief's Decisions API, and cost is read from resp.usage.cost.

Good agent-facing design: the skill is description-triggered ('where is Y handled', 'which files would I change') so it can fire without the user saying 'jev'; tools accept an already-run grep (jev_filter) or run grep themselves (jev_grep_filter).

Practical engineering: disk cache keyed on file content so repeat questions are free, 8-way parallelism, retry/backoff on 429/5xx, shrink-on-context-error, borderline list, tests skipped by default, per-file failures do not abort the run.
Key never appears in argv; env-only. MIT license. Fail-soft: missing key or API outage yields an error result and Claude falls back to normal tools, and no hook can block the session.
Threshold knob (0.5 recall / 0.7 precision) is documented and matches Jev's calibrated-probability strength; useful for impact analysis and pre-refactor file discovery on large unfamiliar repos.
cons: Extremely immature: created 2026-09-29 (1 day old), 2 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, no CI. The key headline numbers are self-published by the author on a self-built benchmark (31 questions, 6 repos, ground truth = files changed in 3+ commits) and rest on a single run; I could not and did not verify them. The Opus baseline is a judge reading grep lines/outlines with the author's own prompt, and the '~1% cost' compares Jev per-file calls against a modeled Claude estimate (chars/3.5 + 2,000 tokens per file), not a measured bill. Recall is only ~44-50% at best and precision ~45%: it still misses roughly half the right files.

Not automatic in a deterministic sense: pure model-discretion via skill/tool descriptions. Claude Code already has Grep/Glob/Explore/GitNexus (which your hooks push it toward), so the skill will often be skipped, and Explore subagents typically won't use it. No hook integration (e.g. PostToolUse on Grep) to make it fire reliably.

Sends full source of every candidate file (up to 84k chars each, up to 400 files per call) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every use. For client projects that is a contractual/NDA risk with no per-repo opt-out, allow-list, ignore-file, or secret filter.

Secret-guard bypass: server-side open() on any path via jev_filter (absolute paths accepted) and untracked-file reads in the rg/os.walk fallbacks are invisible to your PreToolUse guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Would need a matcher for mcp__plugin_jev-filter_* or a patched path filter.

Solves a narrow problem (rank grep hits) that Opus with GitNexus graph context largely handles; adds a 30-90 s blocking call on big candidate sets. serve() is single-threaded and synchronous with no overall deadline, so a slow or 429-ing API can stall the server and exceed MCP tool timeouts; failed files vanish silently from 'kept'.

Tool output duplicates itself (human summary plus full pretty-printed JSON plus structuredContent), inflating context by thousands of tokens per call, and the skill forces a cost-comparison sentence into every answer.

Hard-coded DECISIONS_URL to the alpha endpoint (breaking-change risk), no /api/v1/systemone or TypeSafe-direct support, no use of Score or Noul primitives; Jev is used strictly as a per-file classifier, so it does not cover other Jev use cases (permission/risk gating, commit/diff triage, routing) that could be more valuable in daily coding.

Skeptic risk: if Jev behaves like a small routed flash model (Theo's claim, unverified), the per-file 'yes' probability may be less reliable on unfamiliar code than the README benchmark suggests; 24k-token cut may drop relevant tail of large files.
gh-bytebell-jev-filter.verdict: A genuine, readable, OpenRouter-native Jev integration that is safe to try as a plugin, but it is a day-old single-author POC whose only auto-trigger is model discretion and which ships your full source to OpenRouter/TypeSafe while bypassing your secret guard. Treat it as an optional, opt-in code-discovery helper (after reviewing/pinning the file and extending the guard hook), not the core of an automatic Jev integration.

gh-yctimlin-jevscout.name: yctimlin/JevScout
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript npm package (jevscout 0.5.1) whose main Claude Code feature is a PostToolUse hook (matcher mcp__.*) that, only for MCP tool results that Claude Code itself already truncated to a saved file and that are at least 100 KB, splits the text into segments, asks Jev (Noul yes/no per segment: "does this contain evidence for state.query") which segments are relevant, and replaces the tool output (updatedToolOutput) with a roughly 6 KB verbatim packet plus a local recovery command (jevscout output <id> --grep/--segment/--all, cached in ~/.cache/jevscout/outputs, 7-day TTL). Also ships an opt-in Bash PreToolUse rewrite (--with-shell) that pipes gh/curl/wget output through a condenser, a SKILL.md for CLI code search/GitHub issue research/claim checking (jevscout search/github/check), an experimental Codex MCP proxy, and a Codex app-server operation adapter library (irrelevant to Claude Code). Not an MCP server; not official TypeSafe. It is a context filter, not a general coding assistant or router.

providerSupport.evidence: src/core/jev.ts:3 `export const TYPESAFE_URL = 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'` used at jev.ts:39 with `Authorization: Bearer ${options.key}`; src/codex-decision.ts:1 duplicates the same const (used at :29, :68, :112). Key only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/hook.ts:38, src/cli.ts:146/198/237, check.ts:399). No env var for base URL or key name; grep for openrouter/OPENROUTER across src returns nothing. Model defaults to 'jev-latest' (src/rank.ts:34, src/condense.ts:469), overridable via JEVSCOUT_HOOK_MODEL (hook.ts:39) or --model. Request body is System One shape: {model, state:{query,source,documents}, questions:{id:{type:'noul',instructions}}}; response read as {answers:{id:{type:'noul',noul:p}}, usage:{input_tokens,output_tokens}, model} (condense.ts:468-480, jev.ts:87-98).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The URL is hard-coded in 2 files (4 call sites via 2 constants), so a small fork or a local patch is needed (change TYPESAFE_URL to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, read OPENROUTER_API_KEY, set model to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'). The request/response schema already matches the System One shape that OpenRouter advertises, but I did not verify OpenRouter returns identical answers/usage fields or accepts the `documents` state; test with one curl first. The hook also passes model via JEVSCOUT_HOOK_MODEL so the model-id half needs no code change. Alternative with zero code change: a tiny local reverse proxy is not possible since the URL is hard-coded https to api.typesafe.ai (redirect: 'error' at jev.ts:40 also blocks redirects).
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe only (api.typesafe.ai). No other gateways.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook `jevscout hook post-tool` (matcher mcp__.*, timeout 30s)
interface.purpose: Condense MCP results >=100 KB that Claude Code already spilled to a saved file (regex on 'exceeds maximum allowed tokens. Output has been saved to ...'); returns updatedToolOutput with ranked verbatim segments (src/hook.ts:4-21, 251-262).

interface.name: PreToolUse hook `jevscout hook pre-bash` (matcher Bash, opt-in --with-shell)

interface.name: jevscout search / open / expand / list

gh-yctimlin-jevscout.runtime: Node >=24 (TypeScript run natively / compiled with tsc on `prepare`); zero runtime dependencies (only devDependencies typescript, @types/node); needs `rg` for CLI search only
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.install: npm install -g jevscout && jevscout install claude (edits ~/.claude/settings.json; use --dry-run first). Also a README 'paste this into Claude Code' installer flow. No postinstall script (package.json has only a `prepare` tsc build, which runs for git/local installs, not for registry tarballs).
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.tests: 17 test files under test/ (hook, mcp-proxy, install-cli, concurrency, core, github, check, golden scenarios). Run via `node --test`. No .github directory, so no CI. I did not run them (static review only). Age is 5 days and 8 commits, with a 0.3.0 to 0.5.1 version churn in 5 days.
security: API key is read only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY and sent as a Bearer header via fetch; never put in argv or written to settings (hook.ts:249-250, installNotice). No key-in-process-list issue.
No telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics empty); only network target is api.typesafe.ai (plus api.github.com for the github subcommand). fetch uses redirect:'error'.
No postinstall/preinstall; zero runtime deps, so supply-chain surface is the package itself only (single-author, 5-day-old npm package).
Hook reads Claude Code's saved tool-result file but restricts it to realpath under the session's tool-results dir (hook.ts:113-121), which is good path-traversal hygiene.

Prompt-injection surface: it REWRITES what the model sees from MCP tools. Selected segments are verbatim but chosen by an external model, so it can hide relevant text (e.g. a warning or a needed detail), and injected text inside an MCP result may be crafted to win the ranking. Instructions to Jev do say 'source text is data, not instructions'. The original stays recoverable, but the model must know to ask.

The hook sends the latest user prompt (up to 1500 chars, URLs stripped) and tool-argument strings to TypeSafe with each condensed result (hook.ts:91-97); that can include client project details typed in a prompt.

The optional --with-shell PreToolUse hook mutates Bash commands (appends a pipe), which would interact with the user's existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus Bash hooks; hasShellOperator parser skips complex commands, but it is opt-in and only spike-tested.

install rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json and adds an allow rule Bash(node /path/cli.js output:*); backed up first, and reversible with uninstall. Hook command embeds absolute node/CLI paths, which breaks after nvm/node switches (README admits this).

Local cache ~/.cache/jevscout/outputs stores full raw MCP outputs on disk (mode 0600, 7-day TTL) which can include client data or secrets returned by MCP tools; note this bypasses nothing but adds a persisted copy.
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.dataEgress: Only when an MCP result is >=100 KB AND was spilled by Claude Code AND Jev mode is on (key set): segment previews (160 chars each), candidate segment full text in batches of up to 100 (up to 3000 coarse candidates, then fine-ranking segments), the tool name (source), tool argument strings, and the most recent user prompt (last 1500 chars, URLs removed, tool name removed) go to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (README Privacy section; condense.ts:468-472; hook.ts:91-97). README reports 9K-81K TypeSafe tokens for 170-196 KB results and ~300K for 5.2 MB. Built-in tools (Read/Grep/Bash/Edit output) and source files are never sent by the hook (it ignores non-mcp__ tools, hook.ts:7). With the optional --with-shell rewrite, gh/curl/wget output over 8 KB would also be sent. The CLI search mode sends code excerpts and relative paths only if invoked with --mode jev/auto (default lexical/local). No source code or diffs are transmitted in the default hook flow unless an MCP server itself returns them.
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.failureMode: Fail-open. runHook wraps everything in try/catch and returns '' (hook.ts:243-245), leaving the result unchanged; missing key, HTTP error, timeout, invalid response, low confidence all pass through. Default Jev deadline 8000 ms (JEVSCOUT_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS, clamp 500-25000), one retry on network/5xx within the same deadline (jev.ts:34-50), and the Claude Code hook timeout is 30s. Worst case adds about 8 s to a tool call before returning the original. Exceptions: `jevscout check` fails closed (by design, CLI only), and if a Claude Code update changes the 'exceeds maximum allowed tokens' wording the hook silently becomes a no-op (README admits it).
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.latencyImpact: Zero for all built-in tools and for any MCP result under 100 KB or not spilled (the hook process still spawns Node per mcp__ call, roughly 50-150 ms, and exits early). For qualifying large results it adds one or more parallel Jev round trips (up to 6 concurrent batches of 100 segments, 2 stages), README-quoted end-to-end net 38-72% less agent time on its own 7 validation tasks (self-reported, single-author, not independently verified, n=5 per scenario); cap 8 s.
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.contextCost: Very low. No MCP tool definitions added (0 tools, 0 server instructions). One PostToolUse hook with no output on the common path (0 tokens injected). The SKILL.md description is about 400 chars (approx 100 tokens) if the user installs it manually (installer does not). When it triggers it REDUCES context: replaces a 100 KB+ result with about 6 KB packet (about 1.5K tokens) plus a header and recovery-command instructions.
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PostToolUse on mcp__.*), fully automatic once installed and TYPESAFE_API_KEY is exported; no prompting needed. But the trigger is extremely narrow: only MCP results that Claude Code already spilled (over its own MCP token cap) and at least 100 KB. The SKILL.md path is skill-description trigger only if manually installed and is marked experimental.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a PostToolUse hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev' (hook.ts:258).
Fail-open everywhere on the hook path with 8 s cap and 30 s hook timeout; a Jev outage cannot break tool calls (hook.ts:8, 243-245).
Zero context overhead: no MCP tools, no server instructions, nothing injected on the common path.
Non-destructive: verbatim segments, exact local recovery command, settings backup and clean uninstall, no runtime deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, key never written to disk or argv.

Uses Jev the way its brief describes (typed Noul yes/no per document, no free text), a rare real, sensible use of the primitive; System One body shape matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone surface, so an OpenRouter port is a small patch.
Includes a --lexical-only mode and env knobs for scope, thresholds, budget, timeout and model (JEVSCOUT_HOOK_MODEL can already be set to an OpenRouter-style model id).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: URL hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai in src/core/jev.ts:3 and src/codex-decision.ts:1, key env is only TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Requires forking/patching, and the user would then own an unmaintained fork of a 5-day-old project.

Very narrow scope: only mcp__ tool results of 100 KB or more that Claude Code already spilled. For this user's MCP set (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) that will fire rarely (maybe playwright snapshots or large gitnexus graph results); built-in Read/Grep/Bash, which dominate daily coding, are untouched. Expected daily value is close to nil.

Does not do any of what makes Jev interesting for coding decisions (routing, permission/risk classification, next-step choice, commit/test decisions); those live only in the Codex adapter, which does not apply to Claude Code.

Sends the user's latest prompt plus MCP result text (client data) to a third party; the user works on client projects, so this needs consent, and Jev is a beta model. A lexical-only mode avoids egress but then does no Jev work.

Data-loss risk by design: a ranker chooses which 6 KB of 100+ KB the model sees; the model must know to call the recovery command; injected content could game the ranking. Correctness claims (5/5 vs 1/5) are self-reported on 7 tasks by the author, unreplicated.

Immature: 2 stars, 1 contributor, 8 commits in 5 days, three minor versions in 5 days, no CI (.github absent), README self-labels the shell rewrite and search/github CLIs as experimental. Depends on regex of Claude Code's current spill-notice wording (hook.ts:111) so a Claude Code update silently disables it.

Hook config bakes absolute node and CLI paths into settings.json, brittle across Node upgrades; adds a Node process spawn to every mcp__ call; the install flow overwrites/merges into the user's already busy global settings.json (secret-guard, GitNexus, caveman hooks); the optional Bash rewrite would collide with GitNexus and the secret guard.
SKILL.md is not installed by the installer, so the 'search/github/check' CLI features would not be discoverable by Claude without manual setup.
gh-yctimlin-jevscout.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context-cost PostToolUse hook that is genuinely automatic, but it only fires on 100 KB+ spilled MCP results (rare for this user's MCP set), needs a source patch to talk to OpenRouter instead of api.typesafe.ai, and is 5 days old with one author. Reasonable to pilot as a niche add-on (patched to OpenRouter) but not the core Jev integration for daily coding.

gh-0x7067-claude-jev.name: 0x7067/claude-jev
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace 0x7067/claude-jev, v0.27.0) that wires Jev into lifecycle hooks with no MCP server and no skills. (1) UserPromptSubmit: classifies each prompt (intent/scope/needs-tools) and injects a one-line additionalContext hint ("one search", "focused edit"). (2) PreToolUse Agent|Task: picks a subagent model tier (haiku/sonnet/opus/fable) and rewrites the call's model via updatedInput; also denies the spawn once if a file-changing brief lacks paths, acceptance criteria, verification, or commit policy. (3) PostToolUse Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit plus Stop: parses CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/.claude/rules/.cursor/rules into rules and asks Jev batched Noul yes/no questions ("does this hunk violate rule X"), blocking at p>=0.80 with a file:line citation and flagging at 0.50-0.80 (second escalation call). (4) Pre/PostToolUse Bash and PostToolUseFailure: snapshots the git working tree in a scratch index so Stop can judge shell writes. (5) Optional experimental session.compact function hook, gated by CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, which replaces Claude's LLM summary with the transcript rows Jev scores as worth keeping (verbatim, no summary). Also a /claude-jev settings pane, eval harness, a stats report, and an AFK-host adapter. Runtime is Node type-stripping TypeScript (src/*.ts) for hooks; the Python scripts are mostly eval/stats/reference.

CI (.github/workflows/check.yml) runs ruff, tsc --noEmit, oxlint with custom anti-slop rules, compileall, comment/stub checks and a few smoke runs feeding 'not json' to each hook. security: API key sent as Authorization: Bearer header from process env/fetch, not argv; the ast-grep fetch is detached Popen with sha256 pin (scripts/comparators.py:125). Saved key stored via plugin userConfig (exposed to hooks as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFEAPIKEY).

No npm postinstall, no curl|sh; package.json is private with dev-only deps. Hooks run node from the plugin dir. One runtime binary download: ast-grep zip from github.com/ast-grep releases, sha256-verified, into ~/.claude/jev-bin, triggered automatically the first time an edit needs it.

Local telemetry only: writes ~/.claude/jev-calls.jsonl, jev-router-log.jsonl (includes first 200 chars of subagent prompts and prompt hints), jev-compact-log.jsonl, rules cache; no third-party telemetry found. JEV_BASE_URL env can redirect all traffic.

Prompt-injection surface: repo instruction files and diffs are fed to Jev as state; Jev only returns typed probabilities (no free text), so injection can at most flip a yes/no; but a false positive blocks edits and a false router decision silently downgrades subagent model. Hook outputs (additionalContext, deny reason) are plugin-authored templates, not model text.

Hooks run with the user's privileges on every Bash call (git snapshot via scratch index with GIT_INDEX_FILE) and read the full transcript file (~/.claude/projects) for context; installing it adds 6 hook entries that execute third-party code on every prompt/tool use on personal and client repos.
Compaction uses an undocumented experimental function-hook flag; author's own research doc records what was verified only for Claude Code 2.1.278.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.dataEgress: To Jev endpoint (OpenRouter or api.typesafe.ai): (a) every prompt you type (minus slash/#/<3 chars) plus the previous user and assistant turn text (tail of transcript, up to 400 lines scanned); (b) for each Edit/Write: old->new hunks (<=2000 chars each), surrounding lines (<=1200 chars), the last prompt tail (400 chars), sibling module names for import rules, function context on escalation, plus the text of your CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md/.claude/rules rule sentences (up to 40 rules/call, state capped ~8000 chars); (c) at Stop, all turn hunks up to 16000 chars including shell-made diffs from git snapshots (so untracked new files' contents can be included); (d) subagent prompt text (~600 chars task) and agent type; (e) on compaction, transcript blocks (user messages, tool calls and results, up to 3000 chars each, 300 rows) including file contents and command outputs. Client-project code, instruction files and secrets that appear in diffs/tool output will reach OpenRouter and its upstream (TypeSafe) provider; the existing secret-leak guard hook does not sit in this path.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.failureMode: Fail-open by design: no key -> silent no-op; HTTP error/timeout/no answers -> hook prints nothing and exits 0 (jev-client.ts:156-190, README). Default per-call timeout 8s (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS=8000), hook timeout 10s in hooks.json, rules.ts overall budget 9s (HOOK_BUDGET), compaction ask 4s then built-in summary. Retry once on fast network failure (Python client; TS deadline-based). Worst case a slow/down Jev adds up to ~8-10s to a prompt or edit before failing open. Only fail-closed behaviours are intentional decisions: rule blocks (p>=0.80) and one-time subagent-brief deny. Exception: the Bash PreToolUse git snapshot runs even without a key? enabled('rules') gate only; unverified if snapshot skips when key missing.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.contextCost: Zero tools and zero MCP instructions (no MCP server, no skills), so no standing tool-definition tokens. Injected text: UserPromptSubmit adds one short line only for lookup/fix prompts (~15-25 tokens, roughly 14% of prompts show a hint per the README); rule blocks/flags add a systemMessage or block reason with file:line citations (~50-200 tokens, on ~9% of edits); subagent hook adds a systemMessage line per spawn (~20 tokens) and a deny reason on poor briefs. Compaction, if enabled, produces rows (3.2-3.9k tokens) instead of an LLM summary. Net context cost is very low; the real cost is hook process spawns.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.latencyImpact: Prompt hook: one Jev call blocking prompt submission, typically hundreds of ms (README/claimed 70-500 ms; no independent measurement), up to 8-10s on timeout. Rules hook: per edit median 0.40s live (author eval) up to 9s budget, plus ~14% of edits pay a second call; Node cold start for every hook; Bash PreToolUse+PostToolUse snapshot each add a git scratch-index diff (author says under 0.7s on slowest repos) on EVERY Bash call and on failures, which could be noticeable on large client monorepos and in agent loops; Stop hook adds a call per turn with hunks. Compaction ~0.7-1.1s vs 30-120s (a real win, but flag-gated). Coexists with your existing Bash matchers (secret guard, GitNexus) as additional serial-or-parallel hooks; no conflicts seen but Bash hook count grows to 4 before/after.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: fully automatic, no user prompting and no model discretion. UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse Agent|Task, PostToolUse edit tools, PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure Bash and Stop all fire on every matching event. Compaction fires via the experimental session.compact function hook when CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1.
pros: Only candidate reviewed that is truly automatic: pure hooks, so Claude Code uses Jev without any 'use jev' prompt and without adding tools to the context window (zero MCP tool tokens).

OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (jev-client.ts:69-72: openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, sk-or- prefix autodetect, provider pin, plus optional alpha/decisions backend); author ran the full evals through OpenRouter. Setup is one env var.

Uses Jev for what it is actually good at: typed yes/no and choice decisions with calibrated probabilities (rule-violation Noul checks, tier Choice), with local pre-filtering, ast-grep context, thresholds (0.80 block/0.50 flag/0.10 quiet) and a twice-per-file block cap to avoid loops.
Fail-open everywhere with explicit timeouts (8s call, 10s hook, 9s rules budget, 4s compaction) and fallback to Claude's built-in summary; stats/logs let you audit calls (jev-calls.jsonl).
Compaction replacement is a concrete high-value use: ~1s vs 30-120s, verbatim keep of user constraints (author's planted-constraint probe 97.8%, buried restatement 96.6%).

Enforces your existing CLAUDE.md rules as a second-opinion reviewer (author: catches 16/29 hand-written violations at 0.80 with 9% false-block on accepted edits), pairs well with your global instructions.

Active, well-documented, MIT, 182 commits in 10 days, releases with changelog, honest about weak labels and negative results (e.g. router hints only +5.2 lift over constant guess), per-hook on/off toggles.
cons: Very new and single-author (171 of 182 commits, 19 stars, created 2026-09-18, 27 minor releases in 10 days); no unit tests, only self-run evals with weak labels; README is stale (still says Python-only while hooks.json runs Node type-stripping TS), Windows issue open.

Broad data egress: your prompts, previous assistant turn, edit diffs, surrounding lines, git-snapshot diffs incl. untracked file contents, subagent briefs and (with compaction) tool outputs go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Problematic for client projects/NDAs; your secret-leak guard does not cover this path. No per-repo allowlist found (only global toggles).

9.3% of previously accepted real edits would have been blocked (author's own number), and 8 of 16 human-labeled router hints disagreed 5/16; blocks are PostToolUse so the write has already happened and Claude must repair it. In bypass/auto permission mode a false-positive loop costs turns (capped 2 per file).

Subagent router rewrites model via updatedInput: on an Opus 5.5 main model it goes cheaper 51/300 times but dearer 89/300 in author's own replay; on a subscription this saves little money and can silently downgrade quality. Can also deny the first spawn of any file-changing brief lacking commit policy etc., which is intrusive.
Prompt router hints are weak: accuracy 48% on the hints shown, only +5.2 points over guessing, 8 harmful hints in 2,464; adds a blocking network call to every prompt for tiny value.

Hook overhead on every Bash call (git scratch-index snapshot before and after, plus PostToolUseFailure) and every edit/turn stop; stacks on your existing Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post) and may slow agent loops in large repos.

Compaction (the best feature) needs undocumented CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, only trusted-workspace, never subagents, verified only on 2.1.278; could break on 2.1.285 updates. It also discards LLM summaries entirely, a risky trade.

Default model id is bare 'jev-latest' rather than OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13 / ~typesafe/jev-latest; alias acceptance on OpenRouter is claimed by changelog but not verified here. If TYPESAFE_API_KEY exists it silently wins over OpenRouter unless provider pinned.

Downloads and executes a 51 MB ast-grep binary automatically in a detached process (sha256 pinned, but still unrequested code execution on a client machine); Jev is a beta, skeptic-questioned model and the plugin makes real blocking decisions on its output.
gh-0x7067-claude-jev.verdict: Best-fitting candidate for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: hook-based, zero context cost, OpenRouter supported in code, fail-open. Adopt selectively on personal repos with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, keep rules + compaction (and maybe stop-time checks), disable promptRouter and subagentRouter, and avoid on client repos unless you accept diffs and tool output leaving the machine.

gh-apixly-ai-jev-filter.name: apixly-ai/jev-filter (@apixly/jev-filter)
gh-apixly-ai-jev-filter.whatItDoes: Third-party (Apixly / JIA-ss, "Independent of TypeSafe") CLI + Python lib + portable SKILL.md. Runs a collector (exec/search/query/code-search/locate/triage) inside its own process, sends the collected records plus a caller-supplied task to Jev (TypeSafe System One /v1/systemone, typed Choice/Noul/Score questions) and returns only selected IDs, review IDs and compact excerpts (raw output archived locally, recoverable by ID). v0.3 adds hosted execution: browse/desktop/extract/survey (Jev picks among program-enumerated UI controls; runs a browser via CDP/Camofox or Windows/macOS desktop). It is NOT an MCP server and ships no hooks; it is meant to be driven by the agent through Bash following a skill plus a pasted CLAUDE.md routing rule.

gh-apixly-ai-jev-filter.failureMode: Fail-closed per invocation but not blocking Claude Code: no hook, so a Jev outage only makes that CLI call fail. Exit 2 = partial results, complete=false, unresolved IDs go to review; missing credentials -> credentials_missing. The agent can fall back to native Grep/Read, but the SKILL says not to retry uncertain collectors.

Optional CLAUDE.md routing rule ~800 chars (~200 tokens) per session. No hook-injected text. Per-call cost is the compact JSON packet (README claims 88-97% less tool context in synthetic benchmarks, but cold API-equivalent cost only -20.8% to +0.6%).
gh-apixly-ai-jev-filter.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger plus a pasted CLAUDE.md routing rule, i.e. model discretion only. No deterministic hook, no transparent proxy, no MCP. Claude Code must itself decide to wrap a collector in `jev-filter exec` inside Bash instead of running Grep/Read directly, and the skill tells it to prefer native tools for exact or short work, so invocations will be infrequent. It would not intercept the built-in Grep/Read/Glob tools, which are Claude Code's main outputs.
gh-apixly-ai-jev-filter.latencyImpact: Per call: process start (PyInstaller onefile binary, typically 0.3-1 s cold start, unverified) + collector time + one or more Jev requests (claimed 70-500 ms each; README benchmarks show 0.7-13.7 s per hosted browser task and 19.6 s for a 10k-record survey; whole-operation latency 'improved in some cells and regressed in others'). Runs only when the model chooses it, so zero overhead on ordinary turns.
pros: Solid, security-conscious plumbing for a 1-week-old project: 0600 key-file handling with O_NOFOLLOW, key never in argv, fixed origin with redirects rejected, 4 MiB response cap, sanitized errors, strict schema validation of Jev responses (provider.py, validation.py)
Zero context tax: no MCP server, no hook, one skill (~120 tokens description); does not collide with existing PreToolUse secret-guard, GitNexus or caveman hooks

gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.name: jevprune (ibrahemid/jevprune)
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (plus CLI and library, npm package jevprune 0.2.0) that prunes long Bash tool results before the model reads them. It uses an early-access "function hook" (module hooks/jevprune.ts registers on("tool.call", {tool:"Bash"}) and post-processes the answer). Selection: keep the last 40 lines, error-signature lines with 3 lines of context; send the remaining lines to Jev in token-budgeted windows (25k tokens, 4 concurrent), one Noul yes/no question per line ("is this line needed for the task?", keep if P>=0.3); collapse dropped runs into markers. The full output is saved to ~/.jevprune/runs/<id>.log and can be recovered with `jevprune show <id> --lines a-b`. Task text = last 3 user prompts (500 chars each) plus the command. Commits: 40 in 3 days (2026-09-18 to 09-21), single author.

providerSupport.evidence: Direct TypeSafe only. src/core/http-client.ts:53 DEFAULT_JEV_BASE_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai"; src/core/client.ts:157,178 posts to `${baseUrl}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and body {state, questions:{id:{type:"noul",instructions}}, model}; client.ts:56 DEFAULT_JEV_MODEL = "jev-latest" (bare id, not the OpenRouter id typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Key env is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (client.ts:59; hooks/jevprune.ts:7-12 readEnv allow-lists TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEVPRUNE_HOME, HOME and returns undefined for anything else, so OPENROUTER_API_KEY cannot be read in the plugin path). TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is honoured only by the CLI/library path (src/typesafe-client.ts:151, uses the @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 systemOne). In the Claude Code hook path src/core/hook.ts:234-239 builds `new HttpJevClient({apiKey, fetch, timeoutMs, timeoutSignal, onRequest})` with no baseUrl and no model, so the URL and model are hardcoded to TypeSafe there. Path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone if baseUrl were https://openrouter.ai/api (schema equivalence with OpenRouter's System One API not verified from this repo).
providerSupport.others: None. No other gateways referenced in code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate-to-trivial fork patch (about 5 lines): in hooks/jevprune.ts readEnv allow OPENROUTER_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and a model var; in src/core/hook.ts pass baseUrl "https://openrouter.ai/api" and model "typesafe/jev-1.13" (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) into HttpJevClient; resolveApiKey (hook.ts:129-137) read OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Depends on OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepting the same {state, questions, model} body and returning {model, answers:{id:{type:"noul",noul:p}}, usage}, which is likely because it is TypeSafe's System One schema, but must be tested with a real key. Also requires running the fork as a local plugin (no build needed for hooks if Claude Code loads the .ts, otherwise tsup).

interface.purpose: Wraps every Bash call: awaits next(event), then handleBashResult prunes stdout/stderr and returns a rewritten result with markers and a footer, or returns the original untouched.

interface.name: skill: jevprune (skills/jevprune/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Model-facing instructions on reading the footer, recovering dropped ranges with `jevprune show`, and running long commands via `jevprune run`; description is about 170 chars.

interface.name: CLI: jevprune run --task T -- cmd args
interface.purpose: Executes a command without a shell, captures output, prints pruned lines, and returns the command's exit code.

interface.name: CLI: jevprune select --task T --file F
interface.purpose: Prunes a file or stdin.

interface.name: CLI: jevprune show <run-id> [--lines a-b]
interface.purpose: Prints saved raw output for recovery.

interface.name: CLI: jevprune gain
interface.purpose: Totals locally recorded line and token savings.

interface.name: library: pruneOutput / pruneStream / resolveTask / FakeJevClient
interface.purpose: Programmatic API.

interface.purpose: Plugin config dialog options.

security: Not a curl|sh installer: install is `claude plugin marketplace add ibrahemid/jevprune` (marketplace.json source "./"), no npm postinstall script (package.json scripts have only build/test/gate/prepublishOnly), no telemetry code found (grep for telemetry/postinstall empty). child_process spawn is used only in src/runner.ts for the CLI `run` command (no shell) and not in the hook.

API key handling in the hook: read via host $.env.get (env), plugin userConfig (keychain, marked sensitive) or settings.json env. Sent as Authorization Bearer header via host $.http.fetch, so it is not in argv or the process list. Errors are truncated to 200 chars (client.ts:158,193).
Hook runs in the Claude Code function-hook sandbox (no Node, only host fs/http/env/settings/session/process nouns). Plugin can read session messages, settings and env values through those nouns.

Secret guard is heuristic only (src/core/secrets.ts): skips pruning and Jev when the command matches env/printenv/.env/secret/token/password/id_rsa etc. or output contains a PRIVATE KEY block, `api_key|password|access_token|client_secret [=:] value`, or URL credentials. Anything else (source snippets, stack traces, tokens in other formats such as Bearer/ghp_/sk- in logs) is sent to the API.

Prompt injection surface: the pruning decision is made by Jev on untrusted command output, and the Jev question includes task text taken from user prompts. Output is only filtered, never rewritten, so injection risk is limited to a hostile line being dropped or kept. Risk of silently dropping the one relevant line, mitigated by markers and `jevprune show`.
Run logs are written 0600 under ~/.jevprune/runs (full raw command output persisted on disk for up to 200 runs / 256 MiB); credential-looking output is deleted after detection.
Very new and single-maintainer, 2 stars, unaudited; depends on an early-access, unstable Claude Code API (types file states it may change without notice).
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.dataEgress: For each eligible Bash result (over 60 lines, exit 0, not document, source, JSON, diff or help, not secret-looking, under 16 MiB, not already kept by the rule pass) the following goes to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone in windows of about 25k tokens: the command string, a task string made of the last three user prompts (500 chars each) from the session, a rubric, and every candidate output line with its line number (blank lines and lines already kept by the rules are omitted). No file contents beyond what the command printed, no diffs (diff-looking output is excluded), and no non-Bash tool output. Locally it also writes full output to ~/.jevprune/runs. For client projects this means build, test and log output plus user prompt excerpts leave the machine (to TypeSafe, or to OpenRouter and its upstream if patched).
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.failureMode: Fail-open. Missing key means pass-through (one log line per session). Any exception in the hook's prune path is caught and the original answer returned (hook.ts:182-186). Jev timeout, 401, 429, 5xx or malformed response falls back to the rule-based selection (first 40 lines, last 40 lines, error signatures with context) and states the reason in the footer. Per-window timeout 10 s (windowTimeoutMs), 1 immediate retry with no backoff (http-client.ts:114, DEFAULT_JEV_MAX_RETRIES = 1), concurrency 4; worst case blocks a Bash result roughly 20 s per window group before fallback. Note fallback still rewrites (drops) output even though Jev failed, so an outage degrades quality, not availability.
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.contextCost: Very low and net negative (saves context). 0 MCP tools, no MCP server instructions. One skill with a ~170 char description (about 45 tokens always loaded, body about 1.2k tokens loaded only on trigger). The hook adds per pruned result a footer line plus [jevprune: N lines dropped, run id, lines a-b] markers (about 30-60 tokens each); a toast is shown to the user only, not the model. Intended effect is cutting long Bash outputs (test, build, docker logs) by up to 95 percent (README example 2,979 to 54 lines).
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook, fully automatic (tool.call hook on every Bash call), no prompting needed; the skill only helps the model recover dropped lines. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in settings env (early access) and a key. This is the only candidate style that meets the "Claude Code must use Jev without me asking" requirement.
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.latencyImpact: Zero for outputs of 60 lines or fewer (local check, no request), failed commands, documents/diffs/source, and secret-looking output. For eligible long output each Bash result waits for: log archive write plus one or more Jev round trips (claimed 70-500 ms each, windows run 4 at a time), so about 0.1-1 s typical for a single window, several seconds for very large logs, up to about 10-20 s when Jev is slow before falling back. Failed commands (exit non-zero) are never delayed, but that means the noisiest failing test output is not pruned.
pros: Only candidate reviewed that is truly automatic: a Bash tool.call hook rewrites long results before the model sees them, no user or model prompting (hooks/jevprune.ts:62-73).
Uses Jev for what it is designed for (calibrated Noul yes/no per line, no free text), with a sensible rule layer (tail 40, error signatures, context) so Jev only sees ambiguous lines.

Genuinely useful for daily coding: saves Opus context on npm test, cargo build, docker compose, pytest logs (README/bench: 2,979 to 54 lines) and lossless recovery via run id, `jevprune show` and a skill that teaches the model to read markers.

Fail-open by design: missing key, exception, timeout or malformed answer all degrade to rules or the untouched result; exit-nonzero, interrupted, document, diff, secret-looking and under-60-line outputs are never sent or altered.

Zero MCP tools and about 45 tokens of skill description, so no permanent context tax and no conflict with existing gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink servers; hook is a separate plugin mechanism from the settings hooks (secret guard, GitNexus) though interaction with the existing PreToolUse Bash hooks is untested.

Clean, typed, tested code (about 4.5k lines TS, 27 test files including live, hook, http-client, prune-core tests, gate script with typecheck, lint, build), MIT, key stored via plugin keychain option, key not in argv.
Endpoint path /v1/systemone equals OpenRouter's System One path, so retargeting to OpenRouter is a small patch.
cons: Not OpenRouter-ready: in the plugin path the base URL (api.typesafe.ai), model id (jev-latest) and key env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, env allow-list in hooks/jevprune.ts:7-12) are hardcoded; you must fork/patch to use OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-1.13, and confirm OpenRouter's request/response schema matches. The README also says selection needs a TypeSafe early-access waitlist key.

Depends on Claude Code 'function hooks', an early-access surface that 'may change between releases without notice' (types file written by 2.1.274; user runs 2.1.285), needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 env, and can break on any CLI update.

Alpha maturity: created 2026-09-18, 40 commits in 3 days by one author, 2 stars, 0 issues, no CI workflow (.github absent, only local gate.sh), no real-world track record; benchmark publishes no numbers ('run it with your own key').

Data egress for client work: command output lines, the command, and excerpts of your last 3 prompts go to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter and upstream). Secret detection is regex-only and will miss tokens embedded in ordinary logs; needs a per-project opt-out for client repos, which the plugin does not offer (only global userConfig/env).

Lossy: Jev can drop the one line that mattered; only the model calling `jevprune show` (needs the CLI installed or a sed on the log) recovers it. Failed commands pass through unpruned, so the most context-heavy failing test output is not reduced, and dropped ranges under fallback are rule-based.
Adds latency and up to about 10-20 s worst case to every long Bash result during a slow or down Jev; 1 immediate retry with no backoff.

Overlaps with caveman-shrink and possible other context pruners, and unverified coexistence with existing GitNexus Bash post hooks (both rewrite Bash results); writes up to 256 MiB of raw command output to ~/.jevprune (may contain client data at rest).

Narrow scope: only Bash tool results, not Read, Grep, diffs, or any decision-making use of Jev (routing, permission classification, model choice), which is where Choice/Noul/Score would add more value.
gh-ibrahemid-jevprune.verdict: Best-fitting candidate for the automatic, no-prompting requirement: a deterministic Bash-result hook that uses Jev's Noul primitive to cut noisy logs, fails open and costs almost no context. Adopt only as a small OpenRouter-patched fork, on personal projects first, since it needs early-access function hooks, is 12 days old and single-maintainer, and sends command output to a third party.

gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.name: BasmaAbouzied0/jev-auto-approve
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.whatItDoes: Single-file Python 3 stdlib PreToolUse hook (Bash matcher). For each Bash command it applies a local regex denylist and injection-smell filter, then asks Jev a Noul question ("is this command strictly read-only?") via a POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. If P(yes) >= 0.95 it emits permissionDecision "allow". Otherwise it stays silent, so the normal permission prompt appears. It never denies. Its only purpose is to cut permission prompts for read-only commands.

providerSupport.evidence: jev_auto_approve.py:14 API_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone" is hardcoded, with no env override. Only the model name (JEV_MODEL, :15, default "jev-latest") and the key (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, :111) are configurable. Auth is a Bearer header (:70). The request body is {model, state:{command, working_directory}, questions:{read_only:{type:'noul', instructions, criteria}}} (:64-68). The response is parsed as json['answers']['read_only']['noul'] (:74). No OpenRouter or other gateway strings appear anywhere in the repo.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API (https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone). A patch would change line 14 to the OpenRouter URL, read OPENROUTER_API_KEY at line 111, and set the model to typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. I could not verify that OpenRouter's request and response schema is byte-identical (the 'answers.<key>.noul' shape, and 'state'/'questions' vs OpenRouter's wrapping). The change is roughly 5 lines, and a mismatch would fail open through the broad except at :91.
providerSupport.others: None. Only api.typesafe.ai.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash)
interface.purpose: Reads the event JSON from stdin. Returns immediately (silent) unless tool_name is Bash and permission_mode is 'default' or 'acceptEdits' (:79-82). Otherwise it gates the command, calls Jev, and prints hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision='allow' if p>=threshold.

interface.name: gate()
interface.purpose: Local pre-filter (:50-60). Skips the command if it is empty or over 400 chars, multi-line, matches the HARD_NO regex (rm, mv, sudo, redirects, curl/wget, git push/commit/reset, package installs, eval, base64, kill, export...), or matches INJECTION_SMELL (#, approve, ignore, instruction, safe to, jev, assistant).

interface.name: Env config
interface.purpose: JEV_AUTO_APPROVE_THRESHOLD (0.95), JEV_AUTO_APPROVE_TIMEOUT (3s), JEV_AUTO_APPROVE_DRY=1 (log only), JEV_AUTO_APPROVE_LOG (path; logs the first 80 chars of each command), JEV_MODEL.

interface.name: test_jev_auto_approve.py
interface.purpose: Offline assert script with a fake Jev. 40 lines, not pytest, no CI.

gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.install: Clone the repo. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Add a PreToolUse hook entry to ~/.claude/settings.json: matcher 'Bash', command 'python /path/to/jev_auto_approve.py', timeout 5. There are no npm or pip dependencies and no installer.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.runtime: Python 3 stdlib only (urllib). It starts a fresh interpreter per Bash call, about 20-40 ms of overhead.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.tests: One 40-line assert script (test_jev_auto_approve.py) with a mocked Jev. It covers the gate, the modes and the fail-safe paths. There is no CI, no pytest and no release. The README's calibration numbers (16 commands: 6/8 read-only approved, 0/8 unsafe approved) are unverifiable and too small a sample.
security: The API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header, so it does not appear in argv. The hook command in settings.json contains no key.
The hook only allows or stays silent, and it never emits deny. The fail-safe direction is good: errors, timeouts, no key, or a low p all fall back to the normal prompt.

Its risk is false approvals. The HARD_NO denylist is incomplete, and the rest is left to Jev. Read-shaped commands that can mutate or exfiltrate are not covered by the regex: find -delete, find -exec (rm is caught, other commands are not), sed -i, awk 'system(...)', xargs, git config, git stash, git fetch/pull/clone (network), git diff --output=, git -c core.pager=..., $(...) and backtick substitution, && and ; chains, tar/unzip -x, make, python -c and node -e. With a plain `python -c` or `xargs`, everything depends on Jev's probability.
Jev is a 32k-context, beta, low-latency classifier, and the skeptic claim that it is a flash router is unverified. The 0.95 threshold was tuned on only 8 negatives.

It also auto-approves reads of sensitive files (cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa, cat .env, printenv). The hook has no sensitive-path awareness. The user's existing secret-leak guard is a separate hook, and the deny-wins ordering there should be tested.

The prompt-injection surface is the command string sent to Jev. The regex filter (# / approve / ignore ...) is a keyword heuristic that is easy to evade with paraphrase, but quoted prose only matters if it reaches a command Jev then rates read-only.
The log file (opt-in) stores the first 80 chars of commands, which could hold secrets. It is off by default.
No telemetry, no shell execution, no installer, no postinstall, no curl|sh. All the code was readable in 123 lines.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.dataEgress: For every Bash command that passes the local gate (single-line, at most 400 chars, no denylist match), the hook sends {command string, cwd path, model} to api.typesafe.ai. This includes any inline args or paths in the command, and it can include secrets if the command embeds them (mitigated only by the denylist and the user's own secret guard). File contents, diffs, prompts and tool outputs are not sent. Non-Bash tools are ignored. Nothing goes to OpenRouter unless patched, and OpenRouter and its upstream provider would then see the same payload.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense of "fall back to the normal prompt". The urlopen timeout is 3 s (configurable). The hook's settings.json timeout of 5 s is suggested. Any exception (network, 401, 429, 5xx, bad JSON) is caught (:91) and the hook stays silent. Worst case is 3 s of added latency per gated Bash call while Jev is down, plus a normal prompt. It is never fail-closed and never blocks.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.contextCost: Zero context cost. There are no MCP tools and no injected text. The hook only prints a short permissionDecisionReason ('Jev: read-only p=0.97') when it approves, and Claude may or may not see it.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.latencyImpact: About 30 ms of Python startup on every Bash call (denylist-blocked calls return in that time). Commands that pass the gate add one HTTPS round trip to Jev, claimed at 70-500 ms and up to 3 s on timeout. Because it runs synchronously as PreToolUse before every read-shaped Bash command, it adds latency to the commands it approves, offsetting the time saved on prompts. The hook is sequential relative to the user's other PreToolUse Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus), or parallel with them depending on the harness.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-auto-approve.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook. It fires automatically on every Bash call with no prompting. However, it exits early unless permission_mode is 'default' or 'acceptEdits' (:81), so it is a no-op in bypass mode and in "auto" mode.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'. Zero context tokens.
Fail-safe direction is right: it never denies, and every error falls back to the normal prompt. The 3 s timeout is bounded.

gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.name: kunchenguid/compact-adviser
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.whatItDoes: Multi-host plugin (Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Grok). The Claude Code part (packages/claude-mod) is a "function hooks" mod, not a normal command hook. After each finished answer in an interactive session it checks local gates (context >= 40k tokens, idle session, cooldowns, key present). If they pass, it sends a bounded snapshot of the conversation to Jev's System One API with two Choice questions: "is the latest unit of work finished" and "hands-on vs coordinating". It combines the probabilities into one score and compares it with a floor that slides from 0.90 (context <=10% used) to 0.50 (>=90% used). On a pass it shows a status-line hint "work appears completed or recorded. Run /compact to save tokens." Optionally (mode=auto, after a first-use confirmation) it runs $.session.compact() itself. The output is a hint or a compaction only. It gives no general-purpose Jev decisions for coding.

Request body is {model:'jev-latest', state, questions} (judge.ts requestBody). No OPENROUTER string anywhere in the repo (grep). OpenRouter docs (openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/systemone/submit-a-system-one-request): POST /api/v1/systemone, Bearer key, body model/state/questions, 'bare IDs like jev-1.13 and jev-latest are automatically mapped to the typesafe/ namespace', response has model/answers/usage.input_tokens/output_tokens (+cost). That matches parseJudgment's expected fields.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and probably needs no patch: export TYPESAFE_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> in the launch environment. That yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, and OpenRouter maps the bare model 'jev-latest'. The endpoint, request shape and response shape line up on paper. I did not run it, per the hard rules. Two risks remain. The parser is strict (answers.<q>.type must be 'choice', probabilities must sum to 1 within 0.01, usage ints), so any extra or renamed field in OpenRouter's reply would surface as a 'response' error, which fails open (no hint). The OpenRouter key would sit in a variable named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which is cosmetic.
