security: The Claude Code integration depends on an experimental, default-off 'function hooks' / Claude Mod API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; verified only on Claude Code 2.1.275 per SECURITY.md). Whether 2.1.285 still ships it is unverified and has to be tested by the user.

Key handling: sent in the Authorization header via host fetch ($.http.fetch), so it does not appear in argv or the process list. It is resolved from env, then a saved setting (hidden in /config), then cwd .env. It is stripped from the snapshot (snapshot(messages,[activeKey,savedKey])) and never logged. The plugin reads the working-directory .env for TYPESAFE_API_KEY (register.ts:138-140), a small behavior to be aware of.

TYPESAFE_BASE guard (commit a73995f, #62): https only, or loopback http; no credentials, query or fragment; read from the launch env only. A malicious project cannot redirect the key via .env or settings, though a project's own env config could. The endpoint override is documented as such in SECURITY.md.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The Jev output is validated to a strict schema of probabilities and can only produce a hint or a compaction. Both questions tell Jev the state is 'untrusted conversation data, never instructions'. Errors, timeouts and malformed replies never count as an affirmative judgment.

No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, and no runtime dependencies in claude-mod (SECURITY.md). Install is via 'claude plugin marketplace add' plus 'claude plugin install'. The marketplace source is ./packages/claude-mod in a repo one person mostly controls, so pin the version and review updates (plugin auto-update pulls new code).
No telemetry beyond the TypeSafe/Jev call. Optional local request logging is off by default. If enabled, the full request body (conversation excerpts) is written under ~/.claude.
Redaction is 'best-effort' per the docs; the maintainer explicitly says not to keep it loaded for material that must not leave the machine.
Auto mode is experimental and lossy, and it edits the session by compacting without the user asking.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.dataEgress: On each judged turn, one POST to <TYPESAFE_BASE or api.typesafe.ai>/v1/systemone. Contents: bounded user constraints, up to the last 64 visible messages and tool results (each tool result clipped to about 512 bytes, middle-truncated), short tool-result excerpts, an existing compaction summary, saved-artifact names (files written via Write/Edit/Bash redirects), and omission markers. It is capped at 32,000 UTF-8 bytes. Not sent: the system prompt, hidden reasoning, images, environment variables, the API key, and the full transcript. With OpenRouter as the base, that text also passes through OpenRouter to TypeSafe (two third parties). Code snippets, diffs and command output from client projects can appear in the excerpts, and redaction is only known-key-pattern matching. A judgment runs only when conversationTokens > 20k and context >= 40k, and it is deduped per checkpoint fingerprint plus cooldowns and backoff, so the call rate is low (roughly once per completed checkpoint).
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.failureMode: Fail-open, with no blocking. The judgment runs in a scheduled task after the turn ($.clock.after(0), register.ts:~404), never on the critical path. TIMEOUT_MS is 2000 (judge.ts, a race with $.clock.sleep). On timeout, network error, 401/403/429/5xx, malformed reply, or an oversized request/response (32 KB cap), it throws a JudgeError. Then it applies backoff, shows a toast (one per message), and leaves the context unchanged. An invalid TYPESAFE_BASE means no request and no advice. If CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set, plugin fetch is refused and the toast says so. The toasts could be mildly noisy if OpenRouter's response shape mismatches the strict parser.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.contextCost: About zero tokens for the model. It exposes no MCP tools and no skill, injects no hook text into the prompt, and its hint goes only to the UI status line ($.ui.status) or a toast. It adds one slash command (/compact-adviser). The only context effect is when auto mode runs /compact. Estimated total tool-definition cost: 0 tokens.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. The turn.complete handler fires automatically after every final answer in interactive sessions, gated locally by mode, key, idle state, cooldown and the 40k-token minimum. No prompt and no model discretion are involved. Caveat: it needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in the launch environment. It is inert in claude -p and other non-interactive sessions, and for subagent turns.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.latencyImpact: Effectively none on the critical path. Judgment is scheduled after the turn completes, with a 2 s cap. Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms. Local snapshot building and the shell-write parsing of tool inputs (snapshot.ts, about 690 lines) are cheap. Auto mode adds one compaction, which takes seconds and is a normal /compact cost.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.runtime: Node 22+ (Claude Code function-hooks module, TypeScript stripped by the host; no runtime deps)
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.install: claude plugin marketplace add kunchenguid/compact-adviser; claude plugin install compact-adviser@compact-adviser; then launch with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY (and TYPESAFE_BASE for OpenRouter). Optionally export COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1 for unattended runs.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.tests: The claude-mod package has about 99 tests (tests/lib.test.ts, about 31; tests/adviser.test.ts, about 68) run via 'claude plugin test', plus a live-e2e script against the real Claude Code TUI with a fixture TypeSafe server. The Pi package has a lockstep test that keeps the four copies of the judge identical. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs ubuntu and macOS, biome lint and typecheck, with release-please releases (v0.1.10 on 2026-09-29). There is an eval harness with a 96-checkpoint gold set. No live Jev precision is proven, per SECURITY.md.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a deterministic turn.complete hook that fires with no prompting, which is exactly the mechanism the user wants. It does not depend on the model choosing to call anything.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected hook text, and hints go to the status line only. It does not add to the existing gitnexus, playwright, caveman and hook overhead.
Fail-open by design. The judgment runs after the turn with a 2 s timeout, a backoff, and no blocking of the session.

A good fit for Jev's design: two calibrated Choice questions composed in code with a usage-dependent floor, and it never asks Jev for text. It is an honest example of Jev doing a job that Opus should not spend tokens on.

TYPESAFE_BASE support (added 2026-09-29, #59/#62) makes OpenRouter routing a two-variable change: TYPESAFE_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api yields /api/v1/systemone, and OpenRouter maps bare 'jev-latest' to typesafe/jev-latest. The request and response fields match the OpenRouter docs.

Careful engineering: strict response validation, a documented threat model, an https-only base URL guard, and key redaction from the snapshot. It also has real tests, an eval harness and a CI matrix, and it is very active (5 contributors, 10 releases in 2 weeks).
Hint mode is the default and safe. Auto mode needs an explicit confirmation, and the user can opt out at any time with /compact-adviser off or COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1.
cons: Narrow: it only answers 'should I /compact now?'. It gives no Jev decisions for coding itself (routing, permission decisions, review triage, test selection). The user's core wish, Jev used whenever it adds value in daily coding, is met only for context compaction.

Depends on Claude Code's experimental function-hooks / 'Claude Mod' API behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. It was verified only on 2.1.275, and the user runs 2.1.285. The API may have changed, be removed, or be gated. The env var must be set at every launch (e.g. shell alias or settings env), which is one more thing to keep working.

Egress on client projects: up to 32 KB of conversation, tool-result excerpts and file names goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe on every judged checkpoint, protected by best-effort redaction only. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover this channel. Needs a per-project COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1 for sensitive clients.

Using it with OpenRouter is not a supported path. It is undocumented in the repo, the strict parser could reject a response that has extra fields, and the OpenRouter key has to live in a variable named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, in the launch environment or a saved setting. The user must verify this with a real run; I did not execute the code, per the rules.

Value is modest. Claude Code already auto-compacts, and the user is on a subscription where saved tokens are not billed per token. The main win is compaction timing and quality. Auto mode is lossy and is 'experimental'.

Also reads a working-directory .env for the key, keeps the saved key in the plugin's settings store, and can write request logs (with conversation text) to ~/.claude if logRequests is turned on. The Jev claims are unverified (skeptics say it acts like a small router model), and the eval is the author's own, on a 96-checkpoint set.
gh-kunchenguid-compact-adviser.verdict: The cleanest true-automatic Jev integration found so far: a zero-context, fail-open turn.complete hook that works with OpenRouter by setting TYPESAFE_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key. Its scope is only compaction timing, it relies on an experimental Claude Code hooks API that must be re-checked on 2.1.285, and it sends conversation excerpts off-machine. Worth a hint-mode trial on personal projects, disabled on client projects, but it is not the main Jev integration.

gh-leepokai-jev-guard.name: leepokai/jev-guard
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Node (>=20.3) command hook plus Claude Code plugin/marketplace that sends every non-read-only tool call to Jev as typed questions (risk Score 0-3, approval Noul, user_requested Noul, from_untrusted Noul) and every tool result of 200+ chars as injection questions (directed Noul, kind Choice). Policy lives in code (guard.js decide()): deny if risk>=2.5 or from_untrusted>=0.7, ask if risk>=1.5 or approval>=0.75 (unless user_requested>=0.85), else allow. Also sweeps CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, skills, plugins and rules for hidden or malicious instructions, cached by content hash. It is a security guard (an auto-mode classifier clone), not a coding-assistance tool: Jev is not used for routing, code review, test triage or other daily-coding decisions.

security: No install script and no npm postinstall; zero runtime deps; no telemetry found (grep for postinstall/telemetry/analytics returned nothing); MIT.

Key handling: read from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ~/.jev-guard/config.json (0600, dir 0700) by the hook process, so not in the hook's argv. The one-time `jev-guard key sk-or-...` command puts the key in argv/shell history (jev.js:22-31, cli.js:74-86). Key is sent only to the matching provider URL; JEV_BASE_URL gets only its own key (jev.js:19-22).

Per-session memory plaintext at ~/.jev-guard/sessions/*.json (0600): user prompts, tool-call previews, excerpts of flagged content (session.js:89-111). Scan cache stores only sha1 hashes and verdicts.

No shell execution or eval in the hook path; install only edits JSON. Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted tool output goes to Jev as `state`, so an attacker could try to inject the classifier itself (plain data in a typed schema limits the impact, but a false 'clean' is possible). Reason strings echoed to Claude include a truncated command preview, so attacker-controlled text can reach the model.
Guardrail not a sandbox (SECURITY.md); fail-open by default so a bypass by outage or timeout is possible; thresholds calibrated on Jev only.

Bus factor 1: single maintainer (leepokai 23 of 24 commits, npm maintainer kevinleeeee); a hook installed at user scope runs with full trust on every tool call, so supply-chain risk on updates through the plugin marketplace follows main.
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (and whatever upstream OpenRouter routes Jev to): (1) for every non-read-only tool call, the agent name, tool name, the FULL tool_input (whole Bash commands, file Write/Edit contents and diffs, MCP arguments), cwd, plus context = last 3 user prompts (700 chars each), the last assistant text, last 6 tool-call previews, and up to 5 flagged excerpts; (2) for every tool result of 200+ chars other than Edit/Write/Glob/Grep, the full result text (up to 60k chars, head and tail kept), which includes Read file contents, Bash stdout, WebFetch pages, MCP output, plus the last user prompt as user_task; (3) at SessionStart and InstructionsLoaded, the full text of CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, skills and rules (one-off, cached by hash). Effectively most code and client data touched in a session leaves the machine. No zeroDataRetention flag is sent on the OpenRouter path (only on the Vercel gateway path, jev.js:68), so retention and ZDR depend on the OpenRouter account and privacy settings. Client-project confidentiality needs a check; the secret-leak guard is not a substitute because secrets in Bash output or Read results are transmitted post hoc.
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.failureMode: Fail-open by default: on any exception (no credentials, HTTP error, timeout) hook.js:361-371 writes the error to stderr and returns nothing, so the tool call proceeds. JEV_GUARD_FAIL_CLOSED=1 makes PreToolUse deny when Jev is unreachable (only PreToolUse and Gemini BeforeTool; PostToolUse always fails open). One time budget of 20 s per Jev call (JEV_GUARD_TIMEOUT_MS) with up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx/network errors and 600 ms and 1.2 s backoff (jev.js:57,73-82); the hook timeout is 30 s. With no key set, the hook silently fails open. Fail-closed would be painful with a beta Jev and an outage.
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.contextCost: Near zero standing cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill descriptions. Hooks inject text only on events: a systemMessage/additionalContext note at session start or prompt when instruction files are flagged (usually nothing), and a ~350 char reason on a flagged PostToolUse. A deny or ask message is about 250 chars. Clean results inject nothing (allow returns null). Also one extra process spawn per tool event.
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, InstructionsLoaded), fully automatic once the plugin is installed and a key is present; no model discretion and no prompting needed. This is the strongest fit for the "Claude must use Jev without being told" requirement, but only for the security-classification use case.

Do NOT use npm i -g jev-guard: the registry has 0.3.1 (2026-09-17), which predates OpenRouter support (merged 2026-09-28). Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no skill descriptions, nothing injected when calls are clean.

Fits Jev's actual strengths: typed Noul/Score/Choice questions with calibrated probabilities and thresholds in 20 lines of readable policy; no free text parsed. Cost is trivial (~1k tokens x $0.042/M is about $0.00004 per call).

Adds a second-opinion layer on top of the user's bypass or auto mode: catches destructive commands (rm -rf, curl|sh, force push, prod deploys) and prompt injection from web/MCP output, which a secret-leak guard does not cover. Session memory lets a user-asked risky action be allowed instead of nagging.

Small and auditable (about 1000 LOC, no deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec); fail-open default means Jev outages do not freeze work; every threshold is env-tunable; JEV_GUARD_SKIP_TOOLS and SKIP_SCAN can trim latency and egress.
Coexists with existing hooks (parallel execution, non-overlapping decisions with the secret guard); JEV_BASE_URL allows a local Kev for offline or sensitive projects.
cons: Not a coding-productivity integration: Jev is used only as a safety classifier, so it gives no help with code review, test triage, routing or planning decisions the user hoped to get from Jev.

Heavy data egress for client projects: all Bash commands, file Write contents, and every Read/Bash/WebFetch/MCP result of 200+ chars (up to 60k chars) plus recent user prompts go to OpenRouter and its Jev upstream; no zeroDataRetention is sent on the OpenRouter path (jev.js:68 only for the Vercel gateway). Likely unacceptable for client code without an OpenRouter ZDR/privacy check or a local Kev via JEV_BASE_URL.
Latency tax on nearly every tool cycle: about 0.6-1.5 s per non-read-only call (pre plus post scan) with a synchronous, blocking hook, and claimed 70-500 ms is not measured on OpenRouter in the repo.

Fails open silently when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is missing, credits run out or the API is down, giving a false sense of protection; fail-closed exists but would block work during a beta-model outage (and PostToolUse is never fail-closed).

Redundant with Claude Code's own auto mode for the user's usual permission modes; in bypass mode, ask-type outputs may not stop actions, and only deny is reliable. False positives are likely: thresholds were calibrated on 21 calls and a few dozen skills by the author, and README admits ask for routine git push or gh pr create (risk 2.0, approval 0.77), which will be noisy for a daily git workflow if the ask is honored.

Version skew: npm 0.3.1 lacks OpenRouter; must track git HEAD (pre-1.0, 24 commits in 12 days, one maintainer with 23 commits, 48 stars, no CI, no releases since 0.3.1). Installing user-scope hooks from an unpinned marketplace main gives that author code execution on every tool call.

OpenRouter default model is pinned to jev-1.13 rather than the ~typesafe/jev-latest alias; the Theo/t3.gg skepticism that Jev may be a small flash router matters more here because classification quality decides deny/ask outcomes and there is no independent evaluation beyond the author's own calibration.

Plaintext session memory (prompts, command previews, injection excerpts) under ~/.jev-guard/sessions on a machine used for client work, and instruction-file sweeps send the user's CLAUDE.md files (loaded via InstructionsLoaded) off-machine.
gh-leepokai-jev-guard.verdict: The only genuinely automatic, zero-context Jev integration and it really does support OpenRouter (HEAD only, not npm), but it is a security auto-mode classifier rather than a coding aid and it ships most tool inputs and outputs to OpenRouter with a per-call latency cost. Worth trying on personal projects (pinned commit, trimmed via SKIP_SCAN and SKIP_TOOLS, ideally PreToolUse-only), not as a default on client repos without ZDR guarantees.

gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.name: BasmaAbouzied0/jev-secret-guard
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.whatItDoes: Single-file Python 3 PreToolUse hook (144 lines, stdlib only) for Write|Edit|Bash. It scans outgoing content (Write content, Edit new_string, Bash command) with 8 local regexes for known key formats (GitHub, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe live, Slack, Google, PEM private key), and denies on a hit with no API call. For other high-entropy tokens (>=20 chars, entropy >=3.8, has digit and letter, not a placeholder, hash or path) it sends a MASKED version (first 3 chars, length, charset, plus up to 300 chars of the surrounding line) to Jev as a Noul question ("is this a real credential?"). It denies at p>=0.80, asks at p>=0.30, and does nothing below that. It asks the user if there is no key or Jev errors or times out.

That is about a 3-line change. Not tested against OpenRouter: only the response shape (answers.secret.noul as a float) is assumed the same. Because it is a single stdlib file, it is easy to vendor and pin a copy.

gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.runtime: Python 3 stdlib only (urllib); no dependencies, no build step. Runs fine on the user's Python 3.13.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.install: Clone the repo, add a PreToolUse entry in ~/.claude/settings.json with matcher Write|Edit|Bash and command "python /path/jev_secret_guard.py", timeout 5. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No installer script, no postinstall.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.tests: One test file (test_jev_secret_guard.py, 68 lines, plain asserts, offline with a fake Jev). It covers known-format deny, masking, ask and deny thresholds, Jev down, and placeholders. There is no CI, no releases, and no tests for the HTTP path or for MultiEdit. Not run (hard rule).
security: API key sent as a Bearer header via urllib, not via argv, so it does not show in the process list.

Key read only from env; no telemetry; no shell execution; no eval. The only network call is the Jev request (README says the secret value is masked, and the code confirms it: masked_context replaces the token with the mask at line 77).

Masking caveat: only the flagged token is masked. Up to 300 chars of the surrounding line are sent in clear, so other secrets or code on that line leak. Each candidate's line is sent, and only tokens matching the entropy heuristic are masked. Multiple candidates on one line each get a separate call where the other tokens remain unmasked.

Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted line text goes into Jev's state. Jev returns a typed probability only, so the blast radius is small, but an attacker-controlled file line could try to lower p. Known-format regexes stay deterministic regardless.

Coverage gaps (verified in code): matcher is Write|Edit|Bash only, so MultiEdit and NotebookEdit are not covered. Edit checks new_string only. There is no check on Read or Grep output (secrets flowing into context), which the user's existing guard covers.

Regex weaknesses: the OpenAI pattern, and the PLACEHOLDER check, skip any token containing 'test', 'example', 'your' or 'fake' (line 35), so a real key containing 'test' passes (e.g. sk_live_...test...). Only the first 5 candidates are checked (line 111).
Self-declared AI-assisted, 0 stars, brand-new account repo (created 2026-09-27); supply-chain risk is mitigated by the 144-line single file that can be audited and copied.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.dataEgress: Only for unknown-format high-entropy tokens on Write, Edit or Bash: JSON {model, state.text, questions} to api.typesafe.ai (as written) with text being up to 300 chars of the line containing the token, with the token replaced by 'abc…MASKED(N chars, charset ...)'. Nothing else is sent: no whole files, no diffs, no tool outputs, no prompts. Known-format hits and placeholders never leave the machine. If pointed at OpenRouter, that same payload goes to OpenRouter (and on to TypeSafe). The line remainder is not masked (see security), so client code around a token can leave the machine, which matters for client projects.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.failureMode: Mostly fail-toward-human, with one fail-open hole. Jev error, timeout (3 s urlopen timeout) or a missing key returns 'ask' rather than allow (lines 113-118). But the hook timeout in the README is 5 s, and up to 5 candidates are checked serially at 3 s each (up to 15 s). If the hook is killed at 5 s Claude Code treats it as a non-blocking error and proceeds, i.e. fail-open for the slow case. The stdin JSON parse failure also returns 0 silently. In bypass/auto permission mode it is unverified whether 'ask' from a hook still prompts (documented hook behavior says ask forces a prompt, but auto mode may auto-resolve it); it would be worth testing before relying on it.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.contextCost: Zero MCP/tool definitions. Zero tokens injected when clean. On deny or ask, only a short reason string (~30 tokens) is shown to Claude or the user. No server instructions.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: it fires on every Write, Edit and Bash tool call with no model discretion, so it is the kind of automatic integration the user wants. The Jev call happens only for calls with an entropy candidate.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.latencyImpact: Python interpreter start plus regex is about 30-60 ms on every Write/Edit/Bash. On the clean path with no candidate, no network. With candidates, add one Jev round trip per candidate (claimed 70-500 ms, up to 3 s timeout each, max 5 serial). Candidates such as base64 blobs, JWT-like ids, package hashes and long identifiers in Write content will trigger this fairly often on real code, so expect occasional added latency of about 0.3-1 s and some 'ask' prompts (the README itself reports 3 of 6 harmless strings triggering an ask).
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook, no prompting needed, matching the user's requirement.
Jev is used for what it is designed for (a typed Noul probability on a narrow question), not as a chat replacement, with calibrated thresholds you can tune (JEV_SECRET_BLOCK/ASK).
Zero context cost, no MCP, stdlib-only Python, 144 lines: easy to audit, vendor and patch (matches the user's Python 3.13 setup).
Privacy-conscious design: known formats are handled locally, and the token itself is masked before it is sent. Key in a header, not argv.
OpenRouter switch is a trivial patch (same schema, URL + model id + key), since the code hardcodes only API_URL.
Covers Write/Edit content, which the user's existing guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not, so it complements rather than replaces it.
cons: No OpenRouter support out of the box (hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY); needs a local fork/patch and an unverified OpenRouter response-shape assumption.
Heavily overlaps the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard on Bash; the unique value is Jev judging unknown-format secrets in Write/Edit, a narrow benefit.
Serial 3 s timeouts x up to 5 candidates exceed the recommended 5 s hook timeout, which turns the slow path into a fail-open (hook killed, tool proceeds).

Heuristic false positives/negatives: skipping any token containing 'test/your/example/fake' can let real keys through; base64/hash-like strings in real code cause 'ask' prompts that interrupt bypass/auto workflows.
Sends 300 chars of surrounding unmasked line context to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) on client projects; other sensitive content on that line is not masked.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, 3 days old, no CI, no releases, and the accuracy claims come from just 12 samples (6 secrets, 6 harmless).
Does not cover MultiEdit, and checks only Edit's new_string; no scanning of Read/Grep results.
gh-basmaabouzied0-jev-secret-guard.verdict: A well-scoped, tiny, auditable hook that uses Jev the right way (typed Noul probability, masked input, fail-toward-human) and is genuinely automatic, but it is a 3-day-old single-author PoC that needs a 3-line patch for OpenRouter and duplicates most of the user's existing secret guard. Worth vendoring as a reference or as a Write/Edit complement (with a fixed timeout budget and the matcher extended to MultiEdit), not as a headline Jev integration.

gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.whatItDoes: A Claude Code plugin written as a TypeScript "function hooks" module (hooks/hooks.json = {"modules":["./guard.ts"]}, hooks/guard.ts register(on, options)). It sends noul questions to Jev's System One endpoint and denies or rewrites tool calls from the probabilities. Features: (1) rule guard on Edit/Write/Bash: local regex rules plus Jev-scored semantic rules, one batched request per call, deny at p>=0.7; (2) deploy gate on Bash: deny if "deploys/publishes/merges/sends credential" p>=0.7 and "user asked for exactly this" p<0.5; (3) background mover: known-slow commands get run_in_background, decided by a local regex (Jev's slow score is not used); (4) answer check on turn.complete: 5 noul questions over the final answer, the last 40 tool results and the prompt, then submits one correction prompt; (5) doc router on prompt.submit: off by default; (6) skill gate: denies skills listed in gatedSkillPrefixes when the prompt did not name them (off by default: the prefix list is empty); (7) subagent haiku downgrade: off by default. It also ships a CI twin, scripts/jev-lint.ts, which lints a diff and needs bun.

gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.runtime: TypeScript module loaded in-process by Claude Code function hooks (experimental; build 2.1.260+, needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1). The CI script and tests use bun. No dependencies and no lockfile.

security: API key is read from env inside the plugin and sent as a Bearer header through $.http.fetch. It never appears in argv or the process list.
No shell execution in the hook. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in the repo. Only the configured Jev URL is contacted.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted content (file edits, command text, tool results, the final answer) is embedded in the Jev `state`. Jev returns only typed probabilities, not text, so it cannot inject instructions back. But an attacker string could bias scores and defeat the deploy gate. It is a heuristic guard, not a security boundary.

Secret leakage: whole Bash commands (which may inline tokens) and 12k chars of every guarded Edit/Write body are sent to the third-party endpoint. That collides with the user's existing secret-leak guard philosophy.

Correctness risk: ANSWER_CHECKS asks-on-disk-credential fix text hardcodes the author's private path (~/.config/kai/*.env, guard.ts:179). It would send the model looking for files that do not exist. The author states the plugin was extracted from a private project.
Runs with full plugin capabilities inside the engine ($.http, $.fs.read, $.prompt.submit). The whole thing is about 600 lines and readable in minutes, so it is auditable.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (OpenRouter if JEV_BASE_URL is set): (a) every Bash command in full, plus the user's last prompt (2000 chars); (b) for Edit/Write on files matching the semantic rule regex (default src/**/*.jsx|tsx) the old/new strings or whole file content, truncated to 12k chars; Bash is always sent; (c) at turn end, the user prompt (2000), the final answer (6000) and the last 40 tool calls, each with the input JSON cut to 160 chars and the result cut to 200 chars; (d) optionally the prompt (4000) and note titles for the router, and the Agent prompt (4000). Full file reads and Grep or Read outputs are not sent, except through those truncated tool-result snippets.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.failureMode: Fail-open by design. No key, HTTP error, malformed JSON or a thrown error is caught, logged through $.ui.log, and the call proceeds (guard.ts:368-371, 419-421, 477-479). No explicit per-request timeout is set in the plugin. It relies on the engine's hook budget, and the docs say an overrunning hook is "skipped". So a slow Jev stalls each guarded call up to that budget, then passes. Regex rules still work offline. Missing key produces only a debug-log line.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.latencyImpact: Blocking round trip on every Bash call (all Bash, not only risky ones) and on Edit/Write of matching source files, plus one blocking call at the end of every main-loop turn. At the claimed 70-500 ms, a session with 100+ Bash calls adds tens of seconds and the end-of-turn check adds about 0.5 s per turn. Regex-rejected calls skip the network.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and no MCP instructions. Hooks inject no context by default. The doc router (off) would add up to 3x8000 chars per prompt. When the answer check fires it submits an extra user turn (about 100 tokens plus a full extra Opus response). Deny messages are short.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (function-hook events tool.call, turn.complete, prompt.submit). No prompting needed. This is the only candidate type that satisfies "Claude Code must use it without me saying so", but it works as a guard and not as an assistant that helps with tasks.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hook-based, so no reliance on Opus choosing to call a tool.
Drop-in OpenRouter support through JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL. Request and response schema match the OpenRouter System One docs, so no code patch is needed.
Fail-open everywhere and the source is small (618 lines) and readable. Uses noul probabilities with thresholds, which is a sensible use of Jev.
The deploy gate (block unasked push, publish or merge) is directly valuable in bypass or auto permission mode, where nothing else stops those commands.
The answer check catches 'done/passing' claims with no evidence in the turn. Its fix prompts are one-shot, with a nudged flag to prevent loops.
Regex tier runs locally at no cost. Most features are opt-in and off by default. MIT licence, no dependencies.
cons: Depends on an experimental, default-off Claude Code surface (function hooks, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, 'may change without notice'). Not verified as working on 2.1.285 with a subscription login. Could break on any update.
Immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 7 stars, 8 days old, no CI, no releases, only self-written tests (I did not run any).

Ships an opinionated example rule set that would misfire for this user. The wrong-package-manager regex denies every npm/yarn command (assumes Bun) and the React Native rules do not fit generic projects. The rules must be rewritten before use.

Author-specific leftovers: hardcoded ~/.config/kai/*.env in the credential-fix text, the wrong-package-manager rule, and the declared but unused slowThreshold (the slow mover is regex only). Jev is not actually used for the background mover.

Privacy: every Bash command, edit content and the final answer plus snippets go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Client-project code is a compliance concern, and commands with inline secrets bypass the user's own local secret-guard intent.

Adds a blocking network call to every Bash command and a call at the end of every turn. The answer check can trigger extra Opus turns on false positives (the author already had to make ends-on-promise log-only after a live run pushed the model into unasked work).

The deploy gate is deliberately literal: a general go-ahead is not enough, so the user will be re-asked in bypass mode. It is not a security control and is bypassable through indirect commands. No explicit request timeout. Does not use Jev to help the model code, only to police it.
Coexists untested with the user's other Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus), since the function-hook ordering model is separate from command hooks.
gh-muratcakmak-jev-guard.verdict: The only reviewed integration that is genuinely automatic and OpenRouter-compatible with a config change (three env vars), but it is a police hook, not a productivity tool. It also rides an experimental, flag-gated Claude Code API, has one commit, and needs its rules rewritten. Best used as a reference or fork for a narrow deploy-gate plus answer-check hook, not installed as-is on client work.

gh-connectedgraph-claude-jev-warden.whatItDoes: A single-purpose PreToolUse hook (Node ESM, .claude/hooks/warden.js) that fires on Write|Edit|MultiEdit. If the target file ends in .svg or the content contains "<svg", it sends the first 4500 characters to OpenRouter's Decisions API (typesafe/jev-1.13) with a hardcoded "Dynamic Animated SVG: Monkey riding a bicycle" rubric (one noul and two choice questions). If verdict is not approve_dynamic_exquisite or P(yes) is below 0.8, it exits 2 with feedback so Claude rewrites the file. It also ships a CLI, bin/jev-audit.js, that scores an SVG file the same way. It is a demo or benchmark for an SVG art-director gate, not a general coding integration.

A non-2xx HTTP response falls through the if(response.ok) block to the APPROVED_TOOL log and exit 0. There is NO fetch timeout or AbortController, so a hung OpenRouter connection would block the Write/Edit until Claude Code's hook timeout (60s by default) and stall the turn. Only a valid low-score response fails closed (exit 2). Missing fields default to values that REJECT: noul falls back to 0.5, so the write is blocked and Claude gets a misleading rejection. Since that only happens on SVG writes, the blast radius is small.

SVG writes: one OpenRouter call at the claimed 70-500 ms, with no timeout guard. The Jev call is not made for ordinary code.
gh-connectedgraph-claude-jev-warden.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions. Nothing is injected on approval, except stderr text on exit 0, which is not shown to the model. On reject, about 350 tokens of feedback, all about monkey and bicycle SVG animation. Practically zero for normal coding.
gh-connectedgraph-claude-jev-warden.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Write|Edit|MultiEdit). It is automatic, but its only trigger is SVG content. There is no reachable code path for a general coding decision.
pros: It is the only candidate found that is automatic (a hook, no user prompting) and uses OpenRouter, so it shows the hook plus Decisions API pattern working end to end. Its request/response parsing is a usable reference: state and questions payload, noul and choice types with a criteria map, answers.<key>.noul / .choice / .confidence (warden.js:90-145).
Sound gate design to copy: PreToolUse, exit 2 with stderr feedback to force a rewrite, missing key means bypass, fetch errors mean allow.
Small and readable: 189 lines, zero dependencies, MIT, no postinstall, no shell exec, key never in argv.
The SVG scores in README/compare.html give a rough reading on Jev's behaviour, though they are the author's own and unverified.
cons: The rubric is hardcoded to 'Monkey riding a bicycle' animated SVGs (warden.js:76-121). Any SVG Claude writes in a real project (icons, logos) would be judged against monkey/bicycle criteria and likely rejected, producing wrong feedback. This is actively harmful if installed globally.
Not general-purpose: no code-quality, test, security, commit or routing decisions. Non-SVG operations are unconditionally approved (warden.js:183-185).
No fetch timeout, so a slow or hung OpenRouter call stalls the Write/Edit for up to Claude Code's hook timeout.
Non-2xx responses (401, 429, 5xx) silently pass, and a missing field defaults to a false rejection (noul 0.5).
MultiEdit inputs are never read (uses content and new_string only, not edits[]), so the matcher advertises coverage it does not deliver.

The README claims of 'IQ multiplier' and benchmark scores are single-run, unaudited, and mix Jev with unrelated models (Doubao, DeepSeek). Treat them as marketing, not evidence.
Uses the alpha Decisions API path (/api/alpha/decisions) and covers only the noul and choice primitives.

It is still worth reading as a minimal working reference for a PreToolUse plus OpenRouter Decisions API hook, whose pattern (exit 2 on low P(yes), fail-open, add a timeout) can be reused in a custom hook.

gh-getexcited-stepwarden.name: getexcited/stepwarden
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin built on the early-access "function hooks" API (TypeScript module, no npm deps). Before every non-skipped tool call (tool.call hook) it sends the tool name, redacted args, the session's first prompt (used as the "plan") and the last 8 calls to TypeSafe's System One API. It asks 5 typed questions in one request: 4 Noul (contradictsPlan, outOfScope, contradictsPrevious, shouldFlag) and 1 Score (intentConsistency 0-4). A threshold policy then allows, asks the human via $.ui.ask (at p>=0.6 or intent<=1), or blocks (p>=0.9). It ships in audit mode (logs only, never blocks). It writes a JSONL audit log to .claude/stepwarden/. It has a /stepwarden command with enforce, audit, off, toggle and help.

The only key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY (verify.ts:93 via $.env.get, or the plugin.json userConfig keychain field). There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY and no base-URL override. Four things make it more than trivial. First, the request/response schema ({model,state,questions} -> {answers:{noul|score}}) is verified only against api.typesafe.ai, and it is unconfirmed that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone is identical. Second, the /v1/models key probe would need an equivalent on OpenRouter, or removal. Third, $.env.get requires literal names, so it needs a code edit, not config. Fourth, it means maintaining a fork with a local --plugin-dir, since the upstream marketplace copy is TypeSafe-only.

gh-getexcited-stepwarden.runtime: TypeScript function-hooks module run inside Claude Code's own engine. It has no runtime deps, no subprocesses and no node: imports. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 (early access) and Claude Code >= 2.1.273.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.install: export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; then in Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add getexcited/claude-plugins; /plugin install stepwarden@getexcited; /plugin configure stepwarden (key). Or claude --plugin-dir ./stepwarden from a checkout. Nothing to build.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.tests: 81 tests claimed. tests/policy.test.ts (417 lines) and tests/gate.test.ts (614 lines) are run via `claude plugin test .`. There is no CI (no .github directory) and no lockfile. The commit message says tsc and `claude plugin validate --strict` pass. I did not run anything.
security: Key handling is good. The key is a sensitive userConfig field stored in the OS keychain, or read from env via $.env.get. It is sent in-process via $.http.fetch as a Bearer header, so it never appears in argv or the process list, and the plugin spawns no subprocess.

Sandboxed by design: the loader statically forbids node: builtins, npm imports and subprocesses (verify.ts header, README Threat model). The only network destination is api.typesafe.ai, with no telemetry.

Redaction of arguments is pattern-based (lib/redact.ts): key names like password/api_key/secret, KEY=value, bearer tokens, PEM blocks, JWTs. Strings are capped at 600 chars, arrays at 20 items, depth 4. The README admits unusual secret shapes leak. The plan (first user prompt) is sent NOT redacted, capped at 2000 chars.

The same redacted args are written to .claude/stepwarden/<session>.jsonl inside each project (default on). This is a leak and gitignore risk on client repos. The README recommends adding it to .gitignore.

Prompt-injection surface: tool-call args and the plan go verbatim into the Jev state. The README concedes injection aimed at the verifier is an open problem. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so its output cannot inject the agent, but it can be gamed into a false allow.
Function hooks fail open: a hook that throws, or a module that fails to load, silently lets the tool run. There is no curl|sh, no postinstall and no lockfile. Single author, unsigned commit.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.dataEgress: For every verified tool call (Bash, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, MCP tools, etc.; Read/Glob/Grep are skipped by default), the plugin sends this to api.typesafe.ai, not OpenRouter: (1) the tool name and its args, redacted and truncated (600 chars per string, 20 items, depth 4). For Edit/Write this includes old_string/new_string/content snippets, so client code fragments leave the machine. For Bash it includes command text. (2) The first user prompt of the session verbatim, up to 2000 chars, unredacted. (3) The name and args of the last 8 calls. Tool outputs and file contents read by Read are not sent, but they can appear indirectly in later args. It sends about 740-1,200 input tokens per call. On client projects this is third-party processing of code and command text, and needs client sign-off.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.failureMode: Fail-open by default (onError=allow, onNoAnswer=allow). The timeout is 5000 ms (timeoutMs), implemented by racing $.http.fetch against $.clock.sleep, so a hung Jev can stall each tool call for up to 5 s. Missing key, HTTP errors (401, 429, 5xx) and schema drift are all counted, audited and turned into the onError action. After 3 consecutive failures (unhealthyAfter) it shows a toast. onError=deny makes it fail closed but would halt all work in an outage. In audit mode nothing is ever blocked whatever the verdict. Function-hook throws or module-load failures fail open silently. In non-interactive (-p) runs, flagged calls use onNoAnswer.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.latencyImpact: Claimed about 0.5 s per verified call (70-500 ms Jev, plus a fetch round trip). It is sequential and blocking before each Bash/Edit/Write/MCP call, with a 5 s worst case on timeout. A long agentic turn with 50-100 write/exec calls adds roughly 25-50 s of wall time. Ask dialogs (rate-limited to 1 per 2 s, 50 per session) interrupt flow in enforce mode. Note that bypass/auto permission mode does not skip the plugin's own ask dialogs.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens in the model's context. It has no MCP tools and no skills, and I found no additionalContext injection. The hook only emits UI toasts/logs (not sent to the model), except that a block returns a short reason string in place of the tool result. That block text is the only text the model ever sees. The cost is wall-clock latency and Jev tokens ($0.042/1M input, negligible), not context.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. It is a tool.call function hook that fires on every non-skipped tool call, with no model discretion and no need to prompt. The user never has to say "use jev". This fits the "automatic" requirement, but only as a guardrail, not as a decision helper for the agent.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a tool.call hook needs zero prompting and adds zero context tokens.

Well-engineered defensive design. It ships in audit mode, logs every verdict with per-question probabilities, has configurable fail-open/closed behaviour, health counters, and a wire-format guard that throws on schema drift (lib/jev.ts:133-167).

The only candidate found that actually exercises Jev's typed Noul/Score primitives against Claude Code's own event stream. It is a working reference for the wire format (request {model,state,questions}, answers {type:noul|score}).
The API key is not in argv and is stored in the OS keychain. The sandboxed hook module can't spawn processes or read other env vars. There is no npm/postinstall and no curl|sh.

It adds a semantic safety net exactly where the user runs bypass/auto permission mode. It may catch out-of-scope or destructive calls, and the audit log lets thresholds be tuned on real traffic before enforcing.
Apache-2.0, small (about 140 KB), easy to read and fork; the OpenRouter patch is a few constants.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only (api.typesafe.ai hardcoded, lib/jev.ts:29-31, TYPESAFE_API_KEY). No OpenRouter support, so it needs a fork and the OpenRouter systemone schema parity is unverified. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider.

It depends on Claude Code function hooks, an early-access feature behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 whose field names changed during preview. I could not confirm 2.1.285 support. Types need regenerating after each update.
It is a PoC by a single author: one commit, 2 stars, no CI, no lockfile, created 12 days ago. The README itself says 'not a security boundary' and that the thresholds are untuned.

The 'plan' is only the first prompt of the session. Long sessions drift, so the contradictsPlan/outOfScope signals become noisy or wrong. The README admits this. A vague first prompt such as 'fix the bug' makes the plan-based signals low-signal and false-positive prone.

Egress on client projects: Bash commands, edit content snippets, the raw first prompt and 8 calls of history go to a third party for every write/exec call. Regex redaction is imperfect. It also writes a per-project JSONL audit log of args, a leak risk in client repos.

It adds roughly 0.5 s blocking latency to every Bash/Edit/Write/MCP call, up to 5 s on timeout. The user already has PreToolUse secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. This becomes a fourth serial gate and overlaps with the secret guard.

It is a verifier only. It gives Claude Code no Jev-powered decisions for routing, choice or classification, so it doesn't satisfy 'use Jev when it adds value' beyond safety gating. Jev accuracy is below frontier (67.8% vs 74.1% per the README) and repeated calls vary by a few points. Ask dialogs would be annoying in a bypass/auto workflow.
It fails open on hook throw or load failure, so it gives no hard guarantee.
gh-getexcited-stepwarden.verdict: This is a real, well-built, automatic Jev integration, but it only does one job (gating tool calls for safety). It needs a TypeSafe key (no OpenRouter path without a fork), an early-access function-hooks feature, and it sends command and edit snippets to a third party on every call. Run it in audit mode only, on personal projects, if the user wants Jev telemetry; do not make it the core integration, and don't enforce it on client work.

gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.name: alexj11324/open-jev-approvals
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.whatItDoes: Go binary (jev-approve) installed as Claude Code hooks (UserPromptSubmit + PreToolUse, matcher "*"). On every tool call it redacts secrets, sends the tool input plus the current-turn user prompts and a policy doc to TypeSafe System One with 10 typed Choice/Noul questions (risk, authorization, egress, credential probing, destructive effect, etc.), composes a local allow/deny verdict at a 0.70 threshold (exit 2 = block), and audits to SQLite. It is a safety/approval gate that replaces the auto-mode classifier for third-party API setups. It is not a coding-assist, routing or context tool.

providerSupport.evidence: internal/jev/client.go:20 defaultBaseURL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"; client.go:69-80 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_BASE_URL (https only, no query, refuses cross-origin redirects), TYPESAFE_MODEL. The Bearer key is set at client.go:~170. No mention of openrouter anywhere in the repo (grep found nothing). client.go:27 modelFamilyPrefix = "jev-"; NewFromEnv rejects any TYPESAFE_MODEL without that prefix, and assessmentFromResponse (client.go:~255) rejects any response.Model without it. Request body is {state, model, questions} with answer types choice/noul, the same shape as the System One API.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, and it fails silently if you only set env vars. Setting TYPESAFE_API_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> passes the URL validation. But OpenRouter model IDs are typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, so the jev- prefix check fails on the request side. If OpenRouter echoes the slug in response.model, the response check fails too. That error path is treated as reviewer unavailable, so every call is ALLOWED and the gate becomes a no-op. A working port needs a small Go patch to relax both prefix checks (accept typesafe/jev-*) and a check that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone request/response schema matches TypeSafe's (unverified). The user must also build with Go 1.27, which go.mod requires.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only. Codex is also supported as a harness.

interface.name: hook: PreToolUse (matcher "*")
interface.purpose: Reviews every tool call (Bash, Edit, Write, Read, Grep, MCP, etc.) via Jev. Exit 0 allows, exit 2 blocks with a reason on stderr. install.go writes it with timeout 10 and statusMessage "Reviewing tool action with Jev".

interface.name: hook: UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Records the user's prompt (redacted) into SQLite as authorization evidence, scoped by installation/harness/session/agent.

interface.name: jev-approve install|uninstall|status|doctor [--live]
interface.purpose: Edits <project>/.claude/settings.json (per project, not global). Only its own handlers are touched.

interface.name: jev-approve probe / test [--live]
interface.purpose: Connectivity check and executable gate tests.

interface.name: jev-approve inspect <review-id>
interface.purpose: Print a recorded decision from the local audit DB.

interface.name: jev-approve hook|event
interface.purpose: Internal entrypoints invoked by the harness hooks.

interface.name: eval/ (go run ./eval)
interface.purpose: Offline eval harness with cases.jsonl for threshold tuning.

interface.name: .agents/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Vendored TypeSafe skill that teaches an agent how to build with System One. Not part of the gate. Its description is a discretionary trigger for building features with Jev.

security: Key handling is good: the key is read from a user-level env file (JEV_APPROVALS_ENV_FILE, XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jev-approvals/env, or ~/.config/jev-approvals/env) or the process env. It is never put in argv, so it does not show in ps. A project .env is deliberately ignored (tasks/lessons.md #3).
Endpoint hardening: base URL must be https (loopback http allowed), no embedded credentials, query or fragment, and cross-origin redirects are refused, so the key cannot leak via redirect.

Redaction (internal/sanitize/sanitize.go) is regex-based: private keys, Bearer tokens, AKIA, GitHub, Slack and sk- tokens, and key=value secrets, plus sensitive JSON keys. It is best-effort. Source code, business data and unknown-format secrets are sent unredacted.
No shell execution beyond what the hook does. Pure Go with one dependency (modernc.org/sqlite). No telemetry seen. No curl|sh installer; build is go build.

Prompt-injection surface: tool input and untrusted_instruction_text go to Jev inside the state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection can at most skew the numbers, not run code. Because failure is fail-open, an attacker who can make the call fail (oversized payload, malformed input) gets an allow.
Local SQLite audit DB (~/.local/state/jev-approvals/state.db) stores redacted prompts and tool payloads, which is a new at-rest copy of client-project data.

Security-gate semantics are weak by design: unknown, timeout, bad response or missing key all allow (README 'If Jev cannot produce one, the call is allowed'). The 0.70 threshold is documented as uncalibrated. Its own commit history is titled 'Fail-closed' while the code is fail-open.
Wrong model family (e.g. an OpenRouter slug) degrades silently to allow-all.
Unaudited third-party code from a 10-day-old single-author repo would sit in the path of every tool call with access to prompts and tool inputs.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.dataEgress: On every tool call, one HTTPS POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or the configured URL) carrying: harness, hook event, tool name, action kind, the full tool_input after regex redaction (Bash command, Edit/Write file contents and diffs, file paths, MCP arguments), cwd, permission_mode, agent_id, all current-turn user prompt text (redacted), derived facts (target paths, patch ops, executable, payload sizes), lexical hints, the policy document, and 10 question definitions of roughly 3-4 KB. Tool outputs and transcript_path are NOT read. Whole files are not sent unless the model writes them via Write/Edit. Over OpenRouter, this would also pass through OpenRouter and its upstream provider (subject to OpenRouter's data policy). For client projects this means code the model writes and the user's prompts leave the machine on every action.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.failureMode: Fail-open by design. HTTP client timeout is 5 s and the whole hook deadline is 8 s (main.go hookDeadline), under the harness hook timeout of 10 s written by the installer. On timeout, HTTP error, invalid response, missing API key, parse error or audit DB failure, the call is allowed and recorded as incomplete (review/service.go:29-52). Only a complete verdict that trips policy, or an authorization change mid-review, denies. Exit 2 is also returned if the verdict cannot be emitted at all. Downside: when Jev is slow, each tool call can stall up to about 5 s before being allowed. A false-positive deny blocks the tool call, and in bypass or auto mode there is no user prompt to override it, so the agent must reason around the block.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions, so no persistent context cost. Hooks inject no text on allow. On deny, a short stderr message ('JEV approval blocked: <reason> (review <id>)') is fed back to Claude. There is a statusMessage in the UI on each call. The vendored typesafe-ai SKILL.md is in the repo but not installed into ~/.claude by the installer.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse with matcher "*" fires on every tool call, and UserPromptSubmit on every prompt, with no model discretion. It is automatic, but as a permission gate rather than a coding assistant. Installed per project in <project>/.claude/settings.json, so you would have to repeat it per repo or hand-copy it to ~/.claude/settings.json.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.latencyImpact: One blocking network round trip on every tool call, including Read, Grep and Glob, serialized before the tool runs, plus the Go process start and SQLite open/WAL writes. Claimed Jev latency is 70-500 ms end to end, so roughly 0.2-0.8 s per call, added on top of the existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus). A long agentic turn with 50-200 tool calls adds tens of seconds to minutes. Parallel subagent calls contend on the single SQLite file (lessons.md #1 documents past SQLITE_BUSY self-blocking, fixed with busy_timeout and WAL). Worst case is about 5-8 s per call if Jev hangs.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.runtime: Go 1.27 (go.mod), single static binary built locally with go build; SQLite via modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go). Linux and macOS.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.install: go build -o bin/jev-approve ./cmd/jev-approve; bin/jev-approve install --harness claude-code --project /path/to/repo --binary "$(pwd)/bin/jev-approve"; put TYPESAFE_API_KEY in ~/.config/jev-approvals/env. No release binaries (latestRelease null).
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.tests: Extensive unit tests were read but not run, per the static-only rule: about 2000 lines of _test.go covering jev client, policy, review, sanitize, storage (including concurrency), install and adapters. CI on GitHub Actions runs gofmt, build, vet, test and race on ubuntu and macOS plus a Windows cross-compile. eval/cases.jsonl and eval/main.go provide an offline eval. No live calibration data is published.
pros: It is the only candidate here that gives truly automatic, no-prompt invocation: a deterministic PreToolUse hook with matcher "*", so Claude Code never has to be told to use Jev.
It fits Jev's strengths. Typed Choice/Noul questions with calibrated probabilities are exactly what Jev is designed for, and the request shape (state plus questions) matches System One.

Well-engineered security hygiene for a young repo: key only from a user-level env file, never in argv, HTTPS-only with cross-origin redirect refusal, secret redaction before send, and per-session authorization scoping. It also has real tests, CI on two OSes, and an eval harness.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected text on allow.

Designed for exactly the case where Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier is unavailable. It is fail-open, so a Jev outage will not stall work, and the changes needed for OpenRouter are small (about two prefix checks plus a base URL).
MIT license, small dependency footprint (one Go module), no telemetry or postinstall scripts.
cons: It is a permission gate, not a coding-productivity feature. For a user on Opus 5.5 with subscription login, Anthropic's own auto-mode classifier already exists, so the value is redundant. In bypass mode the user has deliberately disabled approvals, and this hook would re-add blocking that he opted out of.

No OpenRouter support: TypeSafe direct only. Setting only the base URL and key makes the model-family check ('jev-' prefix) fail against OpenRouter slugs like typesafe/jev-1.13, and because the failure is fail-open, every call is silently allowed. A source patch is needed, and OpenRouter's /v1/systemone schema parity is unverified.

A network round trip on every tool call, including Read, Grep and Glob (matcher "*"). That is +0.2-0.8 s per call when healthy, stacked on the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks, and up to 5-8 s when Jev is slow.

Sends redacted prompts and every tool input (code being written, commands, diffs) to a third party for every action. That is a real concern on client projects, and redaction is regex-based best-effort.

Fail-open with an uncalibrated 0.70 threshold means it is neither a reliable security control nor a proven reduction of prompt friction. The README says the threshold is uncalibrated, and Jev accuracy is unproven (skeptics claim it is a small router model). False-positive denies in bypass mode block the agent with no human override.

Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 17 commits all on that one day, 1 contributor, 4 stars, 0 forks, no releases or prebuilt binaries, requires a Go 1.27 toolchain. Its docs are inconsistent: commit titles say 'fail-closed' while the code is fail-open. Installation is per project, not global, and it also wants its own SQLite audit DB with copies of prompts and tool payloads.
Does not touch any other Jev use case (routing, classification of user intent, code-review scoring, commit triage), so it does nothing for daily coding quality.
gh-alexj11324-open-jev-approvals.verdict: Well-built but narrow: an automatic, fail-open PreToolUse approval gate that duplicates Claude Code's own auto mode and adds a Jev round trip (and a data-egress path) to every tool call. It has no OpenRouter support out of the box, and a naive env-var switch silently turns it into allow-all. Only worth it as a fork-and-patch experiment (relax the jev- prefix check, point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, narrow the matcher to Bash|Write|Edit), not as the main integration.

gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.name: RiskAverseTech/toolgate (@riskaverse/toolgate)
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.whatItDoes: Claude Code PreToolUse hook (plus optional PostToolUse ledger hooks and an MCP stdio proxy) that acts as a tool-call firewall. Static regex rules run first with no model call. Tool calls to gated tools (Bash, Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, mcp__*) then go to Jev in one request with about 7 to 11 boolean (Noul) questions: destructive, exfiltration, privilege, secret_exposure, off_task, violates_constraint, unresolved_choice, plus the authorized mitigator. The returned probabilities map to allow, ask or deny via thresholds (deny 0.85, ask 0.55). An action ledger tracks write-then-execute sequences. It is a safety layer, not a coding assistant: it does not use Jev to improve code, routing or review.

interface.name: toolgate hook (PreToolUse, matcher *)
interface.purpose: Reads the hook JSON on stdin, applies static rules, then calls Jev for gated tools. Emits permissionDecision allow, ask or deny with a systemMessage. interface.name: toolgate post (PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionDenied)
interface.purpose: Settles the action-ledger entry for a tool_use_id. No model call, no output, never throws. Timeout 5 s.

interface.name: toolgate init
interface.purpose: Writes ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml, saves the API key to ~/.toolgate/env (0600), merges the hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json with a timestamped backup, then runs doctor.

interface.name: toolgate install / doctor / check / audit / init --print
interface.purpose: Refresh hooks; verify key, backend, one live verdict and hook self-test under a minimal env; dry-run classification (check --backend mock needs no key); show the JSONL audit log with --stats; print the settings snippet for manual merge.

interface.name: toolgate mcp -- <server cmd>
interface.purpose: stdio MCP proxy that gates tools/call to a wrapped MCP server. Not needed for Claude Code hook mode.

interface.name: Library API
interface.purpose: decide, loadPolicy, makeBackend and a pluggable DecisionBackend.

security: MIT license. The package runs no postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json has only build, test and publish scripts). Runtime dependencies are only ai and yaml.

Key handling: the key is read from env or ~/.toolgate/env. init writes it in plaintext to that file (mode 0600, dir 0700). The key is never in argv (src/cli.ts:65-68, src/backends/openrouter.ts:27-29 uses an Authorization header). It is sent only to the chosen provider.

init edits ~/.claude/settings.json, with a backup. The installed hook command uses absolute paths to node and cli.js. Its built-in static rules ask on edits to ~/.claude/settings* and to the toolgate policy.
Policy is read only from ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml or $TOOLGATE_POLICY, never from the project directory, so a cloned repo cannot reconfigure the firewall (src/policy.ts:220-227).

Prompt-injection surface: tool input and prompt text go into the Jev state as untrusted data. Jev is a typed-output model, so it cannot be told to emit free text, but it is a probabilistic classifier and can be fooled. The authors say so and back it with frozen adversarial sets (19/20, 23/24, 20/24). The reviewers of those sets were other models, and the maintainer ran them.
Redaction of secrets is key-aware and pattern-based. The README calls it a courtesy, not a guarantee.

Local writes: an audit log at ~/.toolgate/audit.jsonl (0600, redacted) and per-session ledger files under ~/.toolgate/ledger. No telemetry beyond the model call. OpenRouter attribution headers only identify the tool (http-referer and x-title).
The only shell execution is the doctor self-test (execFileSync /bin/sh -c of its own installed command with mock policy) and the MCP proxy spawn of the user-specified child.

Single maintainer (Jaz), pre-1.0, created 2026-09-18. Reviews were done by other LLMs. The npm version history includes retracted or stale-dist releases (0.8.0, 0.9.0 shipped stale dist; 0.13.0 shipped without a fix) per CHANGELOG.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.dataEgress: Only when the model path is used (not for static rules or ungated read-only tools like Read, Grep and Glob), and only to the provider your key selects (OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions, which then routes to TypeSafe). Sent: tool name; tool input (secrets redacted, truncated at 40,000 chars), which includes full Bash commands and the full content of Write and Edit calls, so file contents and diffs the agent writes do leave the machine; cwd; permission mode; the last 3 user prompts from the transcript (redacted; latest up to 6,000 chars, earlier ones up to 3,000 each) plus a session_goal (first substantive request, up to 1,200 chars); ledger session_facts (file paths and booleans, not content). Tool outputs and files that are only read are not sent. For client projects this means client code and prompts pass through OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every Bash, Write and Edit. Use OpenRouter per-key data policies, or set gated_tools narrower or include_task_context: false. A local backend is only on the roadmap.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.failureMode: Fail-safe by default (fail_mode: ask). On timeout (5 s, one attempt, no retry), HTTP error or missing key, gray-area calls become an ask, and the user sees '[toolgate] NOT gating: ...'. Static deny rules still apply. Internal errors always become an ask. Caveat for this user: in bypassPermissions or dontAsk mode, an ask is converted to deny by default (unattended.ask: deny), so an outage or a borderline call turns into a hard block with the reason fed back to the model. In auto mode an ask shows a dialog. fail_mode: passthrough (fail open) is available but not recommended. The hook timeout is 10 s, so worst-case added latency on an outage is about 5 s per gated call.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.latencyImpact: Static rules and passthroughs cost about 90 ms per call. A model call costs about 350-600 ms with the ledger (documented benchmark), and 0.7-1.2 s p50/p90 over a real week from a laptop, with a cold first call around 1.1 s. It runs synchronously before every gated tool call (Bash, Write, Edit, WebFetch, mcp__*) and the hook is a fresh node process each time. It adds no latency to Read, Grep, Glob or model-thinking turns. The measured real-usage friction was mainly the ask rate: 40% asks in the first session, and 24% in the second log with 0.7.1, though 0.11+ addressed the off_task asks and is not yet re-measured.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens in the model context. No MCP tools or instructions when used as a hook only (MCP proxy mode is optional and not needed). Allows are silent. Ask and deny emit a short systemMessage and a permissionDecisionReason, about 20-40 tokens, fed back to the model only on deny. No skill or CLAUDE.md injection.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. A PreToolUse hook with matcher * runs on every tool call without any prompting, plus PostToolUse hooks for the ledger. Claude Code runs it, not the model. This fits the requirement that the user never says 'use jev'. However, the automation is limited to gating tool calls for safety, not coding assistance.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.install: npm install -g @riskaverse/toolgate; export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...; toolgate init (writes the ~/.toolgate/env key file and merges the hook into ~/.claude/settings.json). Alternative that avoids the plaintext key file and settings edit: run 'toolgate init --print' and merge the snippet by hand, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment. Pin backend.provider: openrouter in ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript compiled to dist; ESM). Deps: ai ^7, yaml. AI SDK is loaded lazily only for the gateway backend; OpenRouter and TypeSafe use plain fetch.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.tests: Vitest with 8 test files (about 2,080 lines; CHANGELOG says 303 tests as of 0.14.1). GitHub Actions CI runs on Node 20 and 22 plus a package-smoke job (npm pack, install, exercise the bin). Evaluation harnesses under scripts/ and docs/ (challenge sets 2 to 8 with results), but they were run against TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter.
pros: Genuinely automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook with matcher *, so Claude Code invokes it on every gated call and the user never prompts for Jev. This is the only candidate pattern so far with zero model-discretion dependence.
Native OpenRouter Decisions API backend (src/backends/openrouter.ts) with typesafe/jev-1.13. Setting OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects it, and there is a test file for it. No patching needed.
Uses Jev for what it is built for: calibrated probabilities on typed Noul questions, not a chat replacement. It is a real, documented use of the Decisions API.
Zero context-token cost. Allows are silent, and the hook adds nothing to CLAUDE.md, tool lists or MCP instructions.
Fail-safe, visible failure handling: 5 s single-attempt timeout, fail_mode ask, and an explicit 'NOT gating' notice. Internal errors become an ask, never a silent allow.

Static rules run first (rm -rf /, curl | sh, edits to ~/.claude/settings*) with no network call. Read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob) are never gated, so it does not interfere with GitNexus or grep flows.

Layers with the user's setup: the existing secret-leak guard covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, while toolgate adds destructive, exfiltration and off-task judgement on Bash|Write|Edit|WebFetch|mcp__*. It is designed to sit beside Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier as an independent second opinion.
Action ledger catches the write-a-helper-then-run-it pattern that single-call classifiers miss. Frozen sets 7 and 8 show 0 dangerous allows.

Policy is read only from ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml, so a cloned client repo cannot weaken the gate. A JSONL audit log with per-axis probabilities and latency stats supports tuning, plus trusted_hosts and trusted_tools for known-good destinations.
Well documented, honest evaluation with per-release changelogs, retracted claims noted, 74 commits in 10 days, and CI plus a package smoke test. MIT license.
cons: It is a safety gate, not a productivity feature. It does not use Jev to make Claude Code write, route, review or plan better. It only adds latency and potential friction, so daily-coding value is defensive.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-18, 2 stars, 1 contributor, 20 npm versions in 10 days, no GitHub releases). Several releases shipped stale dist or missed fixes per CHANGELOG. Evaluations were designed with LLM reviewers and run by the maintainer. No independent adoption evidence.

Its own real-usage data is unfavourable: the first evening had a 40% ask rate (unusable), and the second small log (41 decisions) showed 24% asks. The fix (0.11.0) has not been re-measured on a clean window. Expect nuisance asks.

Interaction with the user's modes: in bypassPermissions or dontAsk (the user's usual), an ask becomes a deny by default, so borderline legitimate work is hard-blocked and the agent has to work around it. Auto mode only shows dialogs. The user would need to tune unattended.ask or thresholds.

Data egress: every gated Bash command, Write/Edit content and the last 3 prompts go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a real concern for client projects and counters the point of gating (the README lists a local backend as the top roadmap item). Redaction is best-effort.

Latency on the hot path: about 0.35-1.2 s added per Bash, Write or Edit call in a long agentic session, in a fresh node process each call; up to about 5 s when Jev or OpenRouter is degraded. Jev is beta and OpenRouter's Decisions endpoint is /api/alpha/.

Duplicates capability the user already has: Claude Code's auto-mode classifier plus the existing secret-leak hook. Marginal added safety is modest, and exfiltration and secret-exposure judgements on the same commands may double-prompt.

OpenRouter path is less exercised than TypeSafe direct: the challenge sets ran on direct TypeSafe, and OpenRouter was only checked with a latency side-by-side and unit tests. The alpha endpoint schema could change. In auto mode the direct key wins if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is also present in the environment.

Overlap with the existing hook chain: matcher * on PreToolUse adds a third hook to Bash calls alongside the secret guard and the GitNexus hook. Hooks run in parallel, and the permission decisions of deny > ask > allow are combined. Fine, but init edits ~/.claude/settings.json, so a manual merge is safer.
Only 2 stars and no evidence that it tolerates a subscription/OAuth Claude Code login plus bypass mode in practice. It is untested here because running third-party code was disallowed.
gh-riskaversetech-toolgate.verdict: Best-fit candidate for the requirement of automatic use without prompting. It is a deterministic hook, has native OpenRouter Jev support, costs no context, and fails safe. But it only gives defensive gating, not coding help; it sends code and prompts to a hosted model, and its ask rate and bypass-mode ask-to-deny behaviour need tuning. Install it by hand-merging the hook (init --print), pin provider openrouter, narrow gated_tools to Bash|Write|Edit, and watch the audit log for a week before trusting it.
