gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.name: muse0509/jev-preflight
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (Go binary, invoked via bash wrapper) with two hooks. UserPromptSubmit takes a private git snapshot of the working tree. At Stop it diffs against that baseline, filters and best-effort redacts the diff, then makes one POST to TypeSafe's System One API with 8 fixed Noul questions (behavior regression, auth boundary, input validation, data integrity, error handling, compatibility, lifecycle, regression tests). If any P(yes) is at or above 0.85 (uncalibrated), it returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext asking Claude to investigate once more, at most once per prompt. Modes are assist, report and off. It is fully deterministic and needs no prompting.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.runtime: Go (static binaries darwin/linux/windows x amd64/arm64 shipped in a release zip). Bash wrapper scripts/run. Marketplace source is an archive with a pinned SHA-256. No runtime install is needed beyond git and bash.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.install: claude plugin marketplace add muse0509/jev-preflight; claude plugin install jev-preflight@jev-preflight; claude plugin enable jev-preflight@jev-preflight (defaultEnabled false). The key comes from the sensitive plugin option typesafe_api_key or the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.tests: About 108 Go test functions, including fake-server client tests and hook protocol/failure tests. A live_test exists but is disabled by default. CI covers ubuntu/macos/windows, go test -race and a cross-build matrix (11 jobs, reported passing in docs/verification.md). Verification was done with synthetic code only, against Claude Code 2.1.267.

providerSupport.evidence: internal/jev/client.go:18 `const Endpoint = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"` is hardcoded. docs/security.md:57 says repository settings cannot override it. internal/config/config.go:110-115 reads only CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFE_API_KEY, then TYPESAFE_API_KEY. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY and no base-URL env var. client.go:77 sends model "jev-latest", a bare TypeSafe ID, not typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. jev.New(endpoint, client) accepts an endpoint, but hook/runner.go:139 calls it with jev.Endpoint, so it is test-only injection.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The path is /v1/systemone, the same as OpenRouter's System One API, and the request is {state, model, questions} with a Bearer header. The body is probably close to compatible, but I could not verify OpenRouter's schema because the docs URL I tried returned 404. A patch means a fork and Go rebuild: change the Endpoint constant to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, add an OPENROUTER_API_KEY lookup in config.APIKey, and change the model string to typesafe/jev-latest. You would also need to confirm that the answers.{id}.{type:noul, noul:float} response shape matches OpenRouter's. The plugin ships as a pinned-hash zip, so you would have to self-build and self-host it as a local plugin (scripts/package exists). The patch is small, roughly 10 lines, but it is not zero-config, and every upstream update needs a re-merge.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only.

interface.name: Hook UserPromptSubmit (hooks/hooks.json)
interface.purpose: Runs `bash scripts/run hook user-prompt-submit`, timeout 90 s. Creates the private git baseline snapshot. Makes no network call. Duplicate submissions do not move the baseline.

interface.name: Hook Stop (hooks/hooks.json)
interface.purpose: Runs `bash scripts/run hook stop`, timeout 90 s. Diffs against the baseline, redacts, and does one POST to TypeSafe. At risk >= threshold it emits hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, at most 3 axes plus the file list, once per prompt. In report mode it emits a systemMessage.

interface.name: Config .jev-preflight.json (repo root)
interface.purpose: mode (assist|report|off), riskThreshold (0.85), timeoutMs (2000), maxDiffBytes (65536), exclude[] path globs. Strict parsing; invalid config fails open.

interface.name: policies/default.json
interface.purpose: Eight embedded Noul questions with instructions plus true/false criteria: behavior_regression, auth_boundary, input_validation, data_integrity, error_handling, compatibility, lifecycle, regression_tests.

interface.name: CLI jev-preflight hook <event>
interface.purpose: Internal entrypoint used by the hooks. No MCP tools and no skills are exposed.

security: API key goes only in the Authorization: Bearer header. It is read from the env or a sensitive plugin option, never from argv, and diagnostics use fixed error classes only (client.go:43-48).
The endpoint is fixed and the client refuses redirects (client.go:65). There are no retries. Responses are capped at 64 KiB and strictly validated.

Best-effort regex redaction (internal/redact/redact.go, 8 rules for PEM keys, auth/cookie headers, *password/secret/token/api_key assignments, AWS keys, Bearer, sk-/ghp_/xox tokens, JWT). It is explicitly not DLP. Business logic, file names and unknown secrets go out. Snapshots of the working tree, including untracked files, are held unredacted in a private git object store on disk until cleanup, with a 24 h fallback TTL after crashes.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Only the diff is sent and only fixed-format numbers come back. The injected additionalContext is templated from the axis IDs, probabilities and quoted file paths, with no model free text. A malicious file name is strconv.Quote'd.

The wrapper is a small bash script that execs a prebuilt binary. There is no curl|sh, no postinstall and no telemetry. The marketplace pins the release-zip SHA-256, but the binaries are opaque unless you build them yourself. Single unknown maintainer, no signed release, 1 star.
Repo config cannot change the endpoint, which avoids a malicious repo redirecting the diff. It can set mode off or add excludes only.

Uses Git plumbing on your repo (temp index and object store). Client work on the personal AND client repos means client source would be sent to a third-party US-hosted service; ZDR is enterprise only.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.dataEgress: The redacted unified diff of the turn's changes, plus the changed-file list, sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (US-hosted) at every Stop that has a non-empty diff. Diff context lines and removed lines carry surrounding old code. Eight fixed question texts and model=jev-latest go with it. The user prompt, transcript and tool outputs are not sent. Git-classified binary files send path and status only. Tracked files matching .gitignore are still eligible. Default excludes cover lockfiles, build/vendor dirs, minified files and docs/media. The cap is 64 KiB of state, and an oversized diff skips evaluation entirely. The key leaves only in the auth header. Client repos would send code to TypeSafe unless excluded via .jev-preflight.json or mode off.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. A missing key, network error, timeout, non-200, invalid response, oversized diff, bad config, missing binary or unsupported platform all exit 0 and let Claude finish. The API call has a 2000 ms default timeout (configurable to 60 s) inside an 80 s runner deadline and a 90 s hook timeout. It makes at most one request per Stop, with no retry. A non-blocking systemMessage notice is shown once per session and error class. One risk: the persist-before-call design means an interrupted evaluation is not retried, so that turn is simply unchecked.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.contextCost: Zero tool definitions (no MCP, no skill), so idle context cost is 0 tokens. Hooks inject text only when triggered. That is roughly 150-250 tokens of additionalContext (up to 3 axis lines plus the file list plus a fixed paragraph) on the minority of turns at or above the 0.85 threshold, and one extra Claude investigation round on those turns (real token cost, not Jev cost). A report-mode systemMessage is about 40 tokens. Otherwise nothing is injected.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.latencyImpact: UserPromptSubmit: local git snapshot of the working tree, typically tens to hundreds of ms and more on large repos with many untracked files. It is synchronous before the prompt is processed. Stop: git snapshot and diff, plus one HTTPS call (claimed 70-500 ms for Jev, 2 s cap), so about 0.3-2.5 s per turn end when a diff exists, and zero API calls for read-only turns. At threshold, one extra investigation turn, which is more latency and Opus tokens. Not measured by the author (the docs say the timeouts are limits, not performance claims). It will also run alongside your existing hooks, without a conflict on the same events.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. UserPromptSubmit and Stop fire on every turn with no user prompting and no model discretion. Once enabled it is fully automatic. It ships defaultEnabled false and needs an explicit `claude plugin enable`.
pros: It is the only candidate here that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement by design: deterministic Stop hook, turn-scoped diff, at most one continuation per prompt (runner.go, protocol.go).

It matches Jev's actual design of typed Noul probabilities. It sends 8 calibrated yes/no questions and gets back numbers, with no free text to hallucinate or inject, and this is a natural cheap pre-merge risk screen for Opus.
Fail-open with tight bounds: 2 s timeout, single request, no retry, no redirect, 64 KiB response cap, and empty or read-only turns make zero calls.
Zero idle context cost (no MCP tools, no skill descriptions), and the additionalContext is templated and short.

Careful engineering: strict config parsing, a repo config that cannot redirect the endpoint, key never in argv, path/lock/TTL cleanup, a real Go test suite (about 108 tests) and cross-OS CI, a pinned-SHA archive marketplace, and honest docs (threshold 'uncalibrated', redaction 'not DLP').
The endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so an OpenRouter port is a small patch.
MIT, and small enough (about 2.3k non-test Go lines) to audit fully and fork.
Per-repo .jev-preflight.json lets you set mode off or exclude paths on client projects.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and it needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY. That contradicts the user's stated goal of an OpenRouter-hosted Jev, and it needs a fork plus Go build plus local plugin hosting to fix.

Model is the bare `jev-latest`, not OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-latest or ~typesafe/jev-latest, so the model string must change too. I could not verify that OpenRouter's request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's (the docs URL returned 404).

Sends source diffs (with surrounding context and removed lines) of personal and client repos to a third-party US service on every code-changing turn, with only regex redaction. Client work needs per-repo mode off or exclusions, or explicit consent.

Very immature: 3 commits over 2 days (2026-09-18 to 2026-09-20), 1 contributor, 1 star, prerelease v0.1.0, 'independent, not affiliated', the README says CI was pending when it was finalized, verified on synthetic code only, and no real-world signal quality.

The 0.85 threshold is explicitly uncalibrated. The 8 fixed generic questions on a diff-only view, with no repo context, may produce false-positive or always-low scores, and each positive triggers an extra Opus investigation round (cost and time). The skeptic claim that Jev is a small router model is relevant to how well it judges code risk.

UserPromptSubmit does a synchronous git snapshot of the whole working tree, including untracked files, on every prompt. Unredacted copies sit in a private git object store, which is heavy on big repos or repos with large untracked assets.
Binary releases are prebuilt and opaque, from a single unknown maintainer with no signing. Safe use means building from source yourself.
In bypass/auto permission mode the Stop feedback only nudges. It is not a gate, and there is no MCP tool for on-demand or in-loop use of Jev (for example for planning or routing).
It covers only one Jev use case (turn-end diff risk). Other Jev-fitting uses (task routing, confirmation classification) are not addressed.
gh-muse0509-jev-preflight.verdict: The best-engineered and only truly automatic Jev-in-Claude-Code integration so far: a deterministic Stop-hook risk gate, fail-open, with zero idle context cost. But it is TypeSafe-direct only, so it needs a small fork (endpoint, key env var, model ID) to use OpenRouter, and it is a 3-commit, 2-day-old one-maintainer beta that ships client source diffs off-machine. Use it as a template or fork rather than installing it as-is, and enable it only on personal repos.

gh-dr-dimitru-claude-jev-plugin.name: claude-jev (dr-dimitru/claude-jev-plugin)
gh-dr-dimitru-claude-jev-plugin.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (no MCP server) that wires TypeSafe System One (Jev by default) into hooks. PreToolUse on Bash|Write|Edit asks 4 typed questions in one request (destructive? exfiltration? beyond requested scope? impact score) and warns (shadow mode, default) or returns permissionDecision "ask" (enforce mode). PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure on Bash checks output for leaked secrets (replaces output via updatedToolOutput on success) and classifies failures into fixed local advice. UserPromptSubmit stores a bounded copy of the user prompt as context for the gate. Also ships a `claude-jev` CLI (check/ask/status/...) and two skills (jev, and user-only decide).

security: Sound internal design: grants are HMAC-signed, single-use, bound to canonical action fingerprint; unhandled MCP methods fail closed rather than pass through; _meta stripped before forwarding upstream; prompt-injection instruction in every Jev question says state is data, not instructions.

Explicit self-admission (README): early release, no external security review, dataset labels self-authored; mcp-guard mode is not a boundary against the local machine (policy lives in the same process).

API key passed via env in the MCP config (not argv), good; but Claude Code project cwd .env gets auto-loaded by 'import dotenv/config' in scripts/mcp-guard.ts:1, and the child upstream gets a full copy of process.env (stdio.ts spawn env: {...process.env}).
Spawns an arbitrary upstream command from UPSTREAM_COMMAND with args split on spaces (no quoting), so paths with spaces or quoted args break.
Adopted upstream tools default to REVERSIBLE_WRITE with a generic semantic policy; risk classes are guesses (docs say so).

No telemetry in the guard path (OTLP/webhooks exist only in the API server); no postinstall found in the guard path but a full pnpm workspace install (Next.js, Fastify, drizzle, etc.) pulls a large dependency tree.

Intent comes from _meta 'actiongate/intent' (packages/proxy-core/src/enforce.ts:91-96); Claude Code never sets it, so text becomes 'No user intent was relayed with this MCP tool call.' with source workflow, which defeats the alignment/target-match questions that are the whole point.
gh-omkarghugarkar007-actiongate-jev.dataEgress: To OpenRouter per guarded tools/call: model id plus a minimal state (buildMinimalState in packages/core/src/state-builder.ts) containing the proposed tool name, whitelisted argument fields (target, transaction, order, recipient, record, semanticLabel), the tool's semantic policy statements, and user_intent text (in Claude Code just the placeholder string, since no intent is relayed). Six question definitions. Not the full prompt, repo, diffs, or tool outputs in normal operation, but argument values of the guarded MCP tool leave the machine. Nothing is sent for non-guarded (built-in) tools. Fake provider makes no network calls.
gh-omkarghugarkar007-actiongate-jev.failureMode: Fail-closed. If Jev errors, times out, or returns invalid output, decision-engine.ts:53-58 applies failureDecisionForRisk(riskClass, failOpenReadOnly default false), so the call is REVIEW/BLOCK and the tool is not forwarded. Embedded timeout 10 s (sdk-js/src/embedded.ts:99), API server 2 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS). OpenRouter adapter has no retries; TypeSafe adapter retries 429/529 up to 2. A Jev outage therefore breaks every guarded MCP tool, including read-only ones adopted at REVERSIBLE_WRITE. Also each spawn of mcp-guard runs upstream.listTools at startup, so a slow/failed upstream delays MCP connect.
gh-omkarghugarkar007-actiongate-jev.contextCost: Adds no tools of its own; it re-exposes the wrapped server's tools under a new server name. However tools/list emits inputSchema as {type:'object'} only (proxy.ts:100, since PolicyRegistry and StdioMcpUpstream drop upstream inputSchema, stdio.ts:89-92 and 122-131), so Claude sees no parameter schema for the wrapped tools, cutting context but making tools hard or impossible to call correctly. No server instructions. No hook-injected text. Roughly 0 extra tokens beyond the wrapped server's (degraded) tool list.
gh-omkarghugarkar007-actiongate-jev.latencyImpact: Per guarded tools/call: one OpenRouter Decisions call with 6 questions, documented sample 733 ms (docs/a-real-refusal.md), claimed 70-500 ms upstream; plus MCP startup listTools of upstream on every session. Zero latency for built-in tools (Bash/Edit/Read) since they are not intercepted.
gh-omkarghugarkar007-actiongate-jev.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy for MCP tools only: once mcp-guard replaces a server entry in .mcp.json/settings, every tools/call to that server is intercepted deterministically with no prompting. It does not cover Claude Code built-in tools and requires editing/replacing each existing MCP server config (gitnexus, playwright).
pros: Real, working OpenRouter Jev integration using the alpha Decisions API with typesafe/jev-1.13, with a live test fixture and a recorded live decision (733 ms, $0.000049); useful as a reference implementation of Choice/Noul/Score request shapes and toWireQuestion translation (openrouter-jev.ts:52-62).
Deterministic + Jev design where the model only supplies evidence and code holds authority; fail-closed on provider errors; single-use grants; honest docs about limits.
Fully config-only stdio integration path with no code (mcp-guard.ts), Apache-2.0, sizeable test suite (~45 test files across TS and Python, CI with Postgres/Redis, CodeQL, e2e).

Useful pattern if the user later wants a policy gate around a risky MCP server (e.g. playwright browser_run_code_unsafe), and the code could be mined for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls the Decisions API.

Cannot gate built-in Claude Code tools (Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch), which are where the risk is in daily coding; only MCP tools of a single wrapped server, and one guard process per wrapped server.

Claude Code does not relay the actiongate/intent _meta, so every call is judged against the placeholder 'No user intent was relayed', making the semantic alignment questions meaningless (enforce.ts:91-96); with default REVIEW/BLOCK thresholds this likely blocks or reviews many legitimate calls, and REVIEW has no human-review UI in stdio mode.

Wrapped tools lose their input schemas (inputSchema forced to {type:'object'}, proxy.ts:100), so Claude cannot see parameters for gitnexus/playwright tools; also a Jev call per MCP tool call adds ~0.5-1 s and cost, and Jev outage fail-closes all wrapped MCP tools.

Not installable via npx/uvx: must clone the repo and pnpm install a whole monorepo (Next.js, Fastify, Postgres drivers); README says not on npm/PyPI. Pins node>=22, fine with Node 24, but heavy for a hook.

security: MIT license. Repo created 2026-09-17, so it is 13 days old. Latest commit 2026-09-28. 153 commits from 2 authors (Basit Mustafa 124, 'Cursor Agent' 29). 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases. package.json is private:true, so it is not published to npm.

Installing it means git clone + npm install of a Next 16 / React 19 / shadcn app (about 390 KB package-lock). That is a large dependency surface for a hook, and npm install can run dependency postinstall scripts. package.json itself has no postinstall.
API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, .env.local) in the sidecar process and sent as a Bearer header via fetch. It is not put in argv. The hook script itself carries no secret.

The sidecar listens on an unauthenticated localhost HTTP port (43147). It is bound to 127.0.0.1 in the npm scripts. Any local process can POST to it and spend the Jev key, and can read scoring responses.
claude-hook.sh runs curl --data-binary @- with input from stdin, so payloads stay out of argv. No shell execution of untrusted input was found in hooks/*.sh. hooks/run.ts uses JSON.parse only.

The tool_input and prompt sent to Jev are untrusted data placed in Jev's 'state'. The answers are typed probabilities and cannot inject free text. Deny and steer messages to Claude are fixed constants (AGENT_DENY / AGENT_STEER), so there is no free-text injection path back into Claude.
No telemetry was found in the code. Outbound calls are only to TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT.

The README (1 MB) and SKILL.md (1.2 MB) are auto-generated by hourly commits titled 'fold(hourly-...)'. They contain thousands of lines of third-party repo summaries. The docs are untrusted and huge, so treat the skill body as a prompt-injection and context-bloat surface if it is ever loaded.
Its detectors are regex heuristics (protected paths such as eval/hidden, grader, answer_key, .claude/hooks). They are easy to evade and are unrelated to normal-development risk.
gh-24601-rh-guard.dataEgress: To the local sidecar, on every matched event: the entire raw Claude hook JSON (prompt text, Bash commands, Edit/Write tool input including file contents and patches). To api.typesafe.ai (or the overridden OpenRouter endpoint) on each non-structural-deny event: a packed 'state' JSON with tool_name, the parsed command, target paths, a diff summary (patch clipped), the user prompt (clipped to 4000 chars, 800 if the state is over 12000 chars), the artifact role, and about 16 question definitions. That is code and command content from personal and client projects leaving the machine via UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse (src/lib/risk/jev.ts:97-147, 316-338). Structural denies skip the Jev call. The secret-leak guard is not integrated: secrets pasted in prompts or in Bash commands are sent as-is.
gh-24601-rh-guard.failureMode: Mixed, and worse than the docs suggest. Jev call: 1200 ms AbortController timeout (jev.ts:77). On timeout, HTTP error or missing key, collectNeural falls back to lexical scoring, so Jev failure is fail-open to regex only. Sidecar: the UserPromptSubmit and Stop HTTP hooks are fail-open (Claude Code ignores non-2xx and timeouts). The PreToolUse command hook claude-hook.sh is deliberately FAIL-CLOSED. If the sidecar is not running or is slow (curl --max-time 8), it prints a deny and exits 2, which blocks every Bash/Edit/Write/StrReplace call. The plugin does not start the sidecar, so a fresh session, a reboot or a crashed 'next dev' would stop all editing and shell work until the user runs 'npm run dev' by hand. Any handler exception in the route also returns a fail-closed deny (route.ts:29-41). Default mode is enforce, so false positives on words like 'grader' or 'hidden test' could block real work.

The skill's frontmatter description is about 400 chars (roughly 100 tokens) and lists eval-design topics only, so it rarely triggers in daily coding. If the skill did trigger it would load a 1.2 MB SKILL.md (roughly 300k tokens), which does not fit in the context window. That is a real risk if the description matches.
gh-24601-rh-guard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse on Bash|Edit|Write|StrReplace, Stop). It fires automatically with no user prompting, but it is a gate/scorer only and adds no capability. The skill is description-triggered and rarely relevant.

The repo's README cites 230-460 ms Jev latency for OpenRouter (from a different project). The Jev calls run sequentially before the tool executes. Cold 'next dev' route compilation on the first hit can be several seconds. Expect 0.3-1.5 s added per tool call, which is heavy for a session with hundreds of Bash/Edit calls. claude-hook.sh also forks mktemp and curl each time.

gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.name: choiyounggi/jev-gate
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (v0.3.1, installed via marketplace choiyounggi/groundwork) that uses a Jev-compatible System One endpoint (default: LOCAL ollaya server at http://localhost:11435/v1/systemone serving Gemma-4-based winnow:e4b) for three things: (1) PreToolUse Bash gate: hard regex denylist (exit 2 in strict mode), read-only fast path (allow, no model call), then a model layer asking a Choice (risk clear/caution) plus a Noul (destructive) on the command, mapping to allow/ask/exit-2; (2) Stop/SubagentStop gate that blocks a turn once if the last message claims done (p>=0.8) with no verification evidence (p<=0.2); (3) `decide` MCP tool (from the ollaya binary) plus a jev-decide skill telling the agent when to hand classification/ranking/yes-no to the model. It is a safety/guardrail layer, not a productivity assistant. Written for a Korean-speaking macOS user (Korean stop-gate message, Korean docs).

providerSupport.evidence: Default and only tested target is local ollaya (not hosted). hooks/jev-bash-gate.sh:29 URL="${JEV_GATE_URL:-http://localhost:11435/v1/systemone}"; hooks/jev-stop-gate.sh:17 same. README.md:80 says JEV_GATE_URL can point to hosted Jev. Request body is {model,state,questions:{id:{type:choice|noul,instructions,criteria}}} POSTed via `curl -sS --max-time $TIMEOUT -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$BODY" "$URL"` (jev-bash-gate.sh:220, jev-stop-gate.sh:55) with NO Authorization header anywhere (grep for authorization/bearer/api_key/openrouter across repo returns nothing; only TYPESAFE_API_KEY=local appears in eval/eval.py:4 and skills/setup/SKILL.md:52 for the SDK harness). Response parsing expects .answers.<q>.choice / .confidence / .probabilities and .answers.<q>.noul (jev-bash-gate.sh:224-226). eval/eval.py:8 mentions TYPESAFE_API_KEY=ts_... with model jev-latest against hosted TypeSafe via typesafe-sdk, but that is the eval harness only, and no hosted run is recorded in eval/results.
providerSupport.others: Local ollaya (Ollama-like server from ollaya.dev) is the only wired backend; models winnow:e4b, decider, decider:0.8b, laya.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial-to-moderate. Set JEV_GATE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and JEV_GATE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (env-only, works today for URL and model), but auth is missing: need to add `-H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"` to the two curl calls (2 one-line edits, or fork). Caveat: putting the key in curl -H puts it in argv/process list (use `-H @file` or `--config -` instead). Unverified whether OpenRouter's /systemone body/response shape is identical to TypeSafe's (state/questions/answers) that this code assumes; the README's 'TypeSafe-compatible' claim is based on the local server passing typesafe-sdk, not on OpenRouter. Also the prompts, thresholds (0.8) and Korean-tuned eval were calibrated only for winnow:e4b, not for typesafe/jev-1.13, so thresholds would need re-measuring with eval/eval.py.

interface.name: SessionStart hook: hooks/preflight.sh
interface.purpose: Silent if local server + model healthy; otherwise prints an onboarding block (missing ollaya / server / model, recommended model for the machine via scripts/recommend-model.sh) into session context. With OpenRouter and no local ollaya this would print every session (noise) unless ollaya is installed or the hook is removed.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash): hooks/jev-bash-gate.sh
interface.purpose: Deny regexes -> exit 2 (strict default JEV_GATE_STRICT=1); read-only fast path -> allow with no model call; else one model call (risk choice + destructive noul) -> allow / ask / exit 2 / no decision. Timeout 10s in hooks.json, curl --max-time 6. Override marker '# jev-gate: override' only honored by model layer for user-allowlisted one-line commands.

interface.name: Stop + SubagentStop hooks: hooks/jev-stop-gate.sh
interface.purpose: Sends last assistant message (last 4000 chars) to model; blocks the stop once (JSON decision:block, Korean reason) if status=done_claimed p>=0.8 and has_evidence<=0.2; skips when stop_hook_active. Timeout 15s.

interface.name: MCP server 'ollaya' (.mcp.json -> scripts/ollaya-mcp-launch.sh -> `ollaya mcp`)
interface.purpose: Tools decide(state, questions|preset, model), list_models, show_model, pull_model. Requires the third-party ollaya binary; talks to the local ollaya server, NOT to OpenRouter, so it would need separate re-pointing.

interface.name: Skill jev-decide
interface.purpose: Description-triggered instructions telling the agent to call decide for 3+ same-criteria classification/ranking/yes-no judgments; falls back to curl to 127.0.0.1:11435. Hard-coded to local ollaya.

interface.name: Skill setup (/jev-gate:setup)
interface.purpose: Onboarding: recommend model, AskUserQuestion, run scripts/setup-ollaya.sh (downloads ollaya via curl https://ollaya.dev/install.sh then sh, pulls up to ~8 GB model, writes LaunchAgent on macOS or nohup server on Linux).

interface.name: scripts/setup-ollaya.sh, recommend-model.sh, eval/eval.py
interface.purpose: Installer (curl|sh with sha256 claim), hardware-based model recommender, 50-item Korean eval harness using official typesafe-sdk.

security: MIT license; no npm postinstall or package manifest. README.md declares no telemetry; none found in hooks. Logs every decision (full Bash command text, cwd) to ~/.local/state/jev-gate/decisions.jsonl and last-message head to stop-decisions.jsonl, unbounded and world-default perms; could persist secrets typed inline in commands.

scripts/setup-ollaya.sh downloads https://ollaya.dev/install.sh and runs it with sh (curl|sh pattern, script says 'sha256-verified' but that verification is inside the third-party installer); pulls a multi-GB model; starts a background server. Only runs if the user invokes /jev-gate:setup, but the SessionStart hook and setup skill description actively steer the agent toward it. Not executed by me.
Third-party binary 'ollaya' is launched as MCP server by .mcp.json with plugin-provided launcher; unaudited.

Prompt-injection surface: command text and the agent's own last message are fed to the model, mitigated by 'treat as data' instructions and by design where the model can only return allow/ask/block, never widen permissions beyond fast-path/allow; but model 'allow' (clear p>=0.8 and destructive<=0.2) does emit permissionDecision allow, which in normal (non-bypass) mode can auto-approve commands, though README reports the model produced 0 allow in field data because clear confidence maxed at 0.77.

Regex denylist is bypassable by design (README/NOTES admit 18 bypasses found in review, e.g. node -e rmSync); author is candid about this. Fast-path allowlist includes grep/rg/find/sed -n etc. with a global escape-token screen.
Auth: hooks send no credentials at all today; a patch for OpenRouter would put the bearer token on curl's argv (visible in /proc) unless done via -H @file or --config.

Hard-deny list includes sudo, curl POST/-d to non-localhost, gh release create, etc. with exit 2 in strict mode, which will block legitimate work for this user (client projects); override needs a user-maintained allowlist file, so the agent cannot self-override at the model layer.
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.dataEgress: With default config nothing leaves the machine (local ollaya on localhost:11435). If pointed to OpenRouter/TypeSafe: every non-fast-path Bash command (up to 3000 chars: first 2000 + last 800), its description field and cwd are sent per call, plus the last 4000 chars of every assistant final message at each Stop/SubagentStop (this can include code, diffs, file paths, client names and any secrets echoed in commands or output summaries). Read-only fast-path commands are not sent. The existing secret-leak guard hook would need to run before this one to be useful; hook ordering is not controlled. Bash commands inline-containing tokens (e.g. curl -H 'Authorization: ...') would be sent to a third party for client projects. Local logs keep the full command text.
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere for the model layer: missing jq, curl error or timeout (default 6s Bash, 6s Stop), unparseable JSON, empty fields all exit 0 with a log line and no decision; the model never auto-allows on error. Deterministic denylist stays fail-closed (exit 2) independent of the model and will block matching commands even if Jev is down. Hook timeouts in hooks.json are 10s (Bash) and 15s (Stop), so worst case adds 6s to a non-fast-path Bash call and 6s to every turn end when the endpoint hangs; with an unreachable localhost it fails instantly.
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.latencyImpact: Per source: read-only fast path about 50 ms (many bash/jq/grep forks), model path about 250-760 ms per Bash call with local winnow:e4b (README: p50 763 ms; 0.9-2.4 s longest of the day; 3.5-4.3 s under 4 concurrent requests); hosted Jev claimed 70-500 ms plus network but not measured by this repo. Additionally one model call at EVERY Stop and SubagentStop (turn end), so each turn/subagent completion gains roughly 0.3-0.8 s. Blocked stop forces an extra agent turn (3/344 in field data).
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.contextCost: Low. One MCP server 'ollaya' with 4 tools (decide, list_models, show_model, pull_model): roughly 600-1000 tokens of definitions (estimate, tool schemas live in the ollaya binary, not readable statically); no server-level instructions in repo. Two skills add descriptions to the skill list: jev-decide (~450 chars) and setup (~400 chars), about 200-250 tokens in total, in Korean. Hooks inject text only on SessionStart when unhealthy (~600-900 chars, about 200 tokens per session) and on block/ask messages. Note the MCP server starts a third-party binary each session and fails with stderr if ollaya is not installed, showing a failed-MCP entry.
gh-choiyounggi-jev-gate.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks (PreToolUse Bash, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart): these fire automatically with no prompting, which matches the user's goal of not saying 'use jev'. The decide MCP tool is model-discretion, reinforced by the jev-decide skill description trigger (Korean trigger phrases plus 'three or more items with same criteria'); the author also had to add a line to global CLAUDE.md to make it reliable (hooks/NOTES.md:16), so unprompted use of decide is weak.
pros: Genuinely automatic: hooks fire on every Bash call and every turn end with no user prompting, and the code is fail-open on Jev errors (jev-bash-gate.sh:220-223, 252-253; jev-stop-gate.sh:55-56).

Well-designed pattern for using Jev typed decisions: Choice+Noul question schema, thresholds, deterministic layer first, model can only escalate, full JSONL decision log for tuning (jev-bash-gate.sh:45-51, 206-219). Good reference code for a custom hook against OpenRouter.

Unusually honest engineering: README documents field data from 1,023 Bash decisions and 344 stop decisions, admits model produced 0 useful allows (clear p max 0.77), discloses 18 regex bypasses found in review, and keeps regression tests for them.

Most tests of any candidate here: about 73 pytest cases (test_gate.py 45, test_stop_gate.py 11, test_recommend 7, test_eval 7, test_preflight 3) with a fake TypeSafe-compatible server (tests/conftest.py), so the hooks can be tested without a model.
Env-configurable URL/model/thresholds/timeouts (README table) so pointing at hosted Jev needs little more than an auth header.
Stop-gate 'done claimed without evidence' check is a plausible daily-coding quality feature: 3 blocks in 344 turns, 2 made the agent quote real output.
cons: Does not work with OpenRouter as shipped: no Authorization header is ever sent (curl at jev-bash-gate.sh:220 and jev-stop-gate.sh:55) and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY handling; the whole design is built around a local ollaya server and an ~8 GB Gemma-4 model download, not around hosted Jev. Unverified that OpenRouter's /systemone request/response shape matches.

Thresholds and prompts calibrated only for local winnow:e4b on a 50-item Korean, single-labeler dataset (README limits section); no measurement of typesafe/jev-1.13. Even for winnow the model never produced a confident allow, so the model layer adds only 'ask' friction.

Wrong problem for the user's goal: it is a safety gate, not something that makes Claude Code use Jev where Jev adds value. In bypass/auto mode, model 'ask' just runs the command interactively (README: 41/41) and is denied headless, so the useful path is exit 2 hard blocks, which the user did not ask for and will cause friction on legitimate client work (sudo, curl POST, git push -f, gh release create, crontab, git restore, checkout --).

Overlaps with and adds a second PreToolUse Bash hook next to the user's existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks; with hosted Jev it would send every non-trivial Bash command and every final assistant message to OpenRouter, including possibly client code and inline secrets.
Latency tax: a model call on every Stop/SubagentStop and on non-read-only Bash calls; heredoc denylist false positives (3 of 1,023) and known regex bypasses.

Do not install as-is; at most borrow the hook structure and the Stop-gate idea into a custom OpenRouter hook.

gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.name: rashedInt32/jev-gates
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (pure Node ESM, zero deps) with nine Jev-judged "gates" implemented as hooks. As of v0.9.0 only the claims gate is on and only the Stop hook is wired. After each turn it sends the last prompt, final reply and this turn's tool calls and outputs to Jev. Jev says whether each reply sentence claims an action or result, and whether the turn's tool output supports it. Unsupported claims block the stop (exit 2, reason on stderr) once, so Claude corrects itself or actually runs the check. Opt-in gates (done, proof, rules, scope, intent, prompt check, bash guard, commit guard) need env flags and, for most, hand-wired hooks.

providerSupport.evidence: lib/jev.mjs:22-23: model = env.JEV_GATES_MODEL || "jev-latest"; baseUrl = env.JEV_GATES_BASE_URL || "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone". lib/jev.mjs:83: key = env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY || env.JEV_API_KEY, else file ~/.config/typesafe/key (JEV_KEY_FILE). lib/jev.mjs:153,187-190: POST {model,state,questions} with Authorization: Bearer <key>. Body is validated as answers[id].noul / choice+probabilities (lib/jev.mjs:129-145). The word openrouter appears nowhere in the repo (grep). The broker only forwards to config.baseUrl (lib/broker.mjs:121,178), so an override is honoured. OpenRouter's docs (guides/community/typesafe-sdk) say the System One API at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone is wire-compatible with the TypeSafe SDK: change base URL and key only, and bare IDs like jev-latest are mapped to typesafe/. Not run, so the OpenRouter path is untested by the author.
providerSupport.others: Any URL via JEV_GATES_BASE_URL. Non-https is allowed (http.request used in the broker for tests).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only, no code change. Set JEV_GATES_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (the full path, since the code does not append /v1/systemone). Put the OpenRouter key in JEV_API_KEY (env block of ~/.claude/settings.json, since hooks do not inherit the shell) or in ~/.config/typesafe/key. Optionally set JEV_GATES_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 to pin the version. Caveat: the OpenRouter response must match TypeSafe's shape (answers.<id>.noul); OpenRouter's docs claim it does, but that is unverified here.

interface.name: Stop hook: hooks/stop-gate.mjs (wired in hooks/hooks.json, timeout 20s, status message "Jev: checking the reply")
interface.purpose: Claims gate (on by default): splits the reply into sentences, asks two Noul questions per sentence (is it a claim, is there evidence), blocks once via exit 2. Also done gate (JEV_GATES_DONE=on) and proof gate (JEV_GATES_PROOF=on), which share the same request.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook: hooks/intent-guard.mjs (NOT wired; manual settings.json entry)
interface.purpose: Intent guard (question vs change request) and prompt check (missing outcome, location, or finish line), opt-in via JEV_GATES_INTENT/CHECK=on.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook: hooks/rule-guard.mjs (NOT wired)
interface.purpose: Rule guard and scope guard on Edit|Write|MultiEdit and file-writing Bash; checks the change against CLAUDE.md rules and the user's ask. Asks or denies.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook: hooks/bash-guard.mjs (NOT wired)
interface.purpose: Noul risk check on non-read-only shell commands; asks above threshold 0.7.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook: hooks/commit-guard.mjs (NOT wired)
interface.purpose: On git commit, checks that message claims match the staged diff.

interface.name: lib/broker.mjs (detached local process)
interface.purpose: Keep-alive connection proxy over a 0600 Unix socket at ~/.claude/jev-gates/broker.sock. Saves about 650 ms of TLS per hook call. Exits after 1h idle.

interface.name: Env config JEV_GATES=active|shadow|off, JEV_GATES_CLAIMS=off, JEV_GATES_TIMEOUT_MS, thresholds
interface.purpose: shadow mode logs would-block decisions to ~/.claude/jev-gates/decisions.log without intervening.

security: Key is read from env or a 0600 file, never argv (lib/jev.mjs:81-91), so it does not appear in the process list. It is sent per request over a private Unix socket to the broker, which holds no key (lib/broker.mjs:76-79) and refuses a different baseUrl (line 178).

Regex secret redaction (lib/redact.mjs) is applied to everything sent and logged: PEM keys, URL passwords, Bearer/Basic, key=value pairs for api key/token/password names, and sk-, ghp_, AKIA, AIza, glpat, npm_ and JWT shapes. Best effort only. Source code, business data and unlabeled secrets pass through.

Data dir ~/.claude/jev-gates is chmod 0700 and files 0600. It keeps decisions.log, cache, last-*.json and proof/*.json, which hold redacted excerpts of prompts, replies, tool outputs and diffs persistently on disk. The broker socket and process are user-scoped.

No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev API. Zero npm dependencies. package.json is private with only a test script. Install is via the /plugin marketplace, which runs plugin files as the user.
Shell execution: only execFileSync("git", args) in lib/git.mjs, and spawn(process.execPath, [broker]) detached. The rest is static parsing of commands.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompt, reply and tool outputs are labelled as untrusted data in the questions. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection can at worst flip a gate decision. Every gate only escalates and never approves.
Single unaudited maintainer, 12 days old, no releases, no CI, no signed tags. The plugin cache path changes per version. It runs with the user's full privileges on every turn.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.dataEgress: With the default claims gate, each Stop sends to the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter then TypeSafe): the last user prompt (up to 8k chars), the final assistant reply (up to 12k chars), this turn's tool calls and their outputs (Bash commands and output, file reads and edits, subagent reports), and the last three earlier assistant replies. The total cap is 48k chars (JEV_GATES_MAX_CHARS). Redaction removes the recognizable secret shapes. With JEV_GATES_PROOF=on it also sends git diff excerpts against HEAD. Client source code, file contents and command output leave the machine on every turn that used tools. Only the first 100 chars of decisions are logged locally. With OpenRouter, the request goes through OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, so check OpenRouter's data policy and the per-provider ZDR settings. Client NDAs may forbid this.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. Missing key, HTTP error, malformed answer, timeout (8 s default, JEV_GATES_TIMEOUT_MS), oversized state (>48k chars), no tool activity recorded, or any thrown error all mean exit 0 with no output, so Claude stops normally (stop-gate.mjs:52-55, 92-95, 244-246; lib/jev.mjs header). Hook timeout is 20 s in hooks.json. Worst case is about 8 s of added wait per turn when Jev hangs. A block is issued once only, because stop_hook_active short-circuits the second stop (stop-gate.mjs:34-37). A false positive costs one extra Opus turn of tokens. Broker failure falls back to a direct call.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.latencyImpact: Stop hook runs synchronously at the end of every turn. Per the README, about 0.45 s per hook with the warm broker, about 1.1 s cold. The first call in a session starts the broker and is cold, and the broker has a 1 h idle exit. The author measured calls at about 0.9-1.3 s in the calibration table, above the 70-500 ms claimed for Jev. Zero added latency on prompts and tool calls in the default config, since no other hooks are wired. Node startup (about 50-100 ms) is added per Stop. If the user enables the PreToolUse gates, that adds one round trip per edit or Bash, and the author says they were not worth it.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no MCP instructions, no tool defs. Nothing is injected on normal turns. Only when a claim is blocked does a short stderr message (about 100-300 tokens) get fed back to Claude. Opt-in UserPromptSubmit gates would inject a one-line note per flagged prompt. Effectively free for context.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: a Stop event fires on every turn with no model discretion, so it is fully automatic and needs no prompting. Only the Stop hook is wired by the plugin. Other gates need hand-edited settings.json hooks.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a plugin-shipped Stop hook (hooks/hooks.json), so the user never says "use jev".
Makes sound use of Jev's strength (calibrated Noul probabilities, no prose). Fail-open, escalation-only design with thresholds, shadow mode and a decision log.
Works with OpenRouter by config alone: JEV_GATES_BASE_URL plus JEV_API_KEY, because OpenRouter's System One endpoint mirrors TypeSafe's wire format. No fork needed.
Zero context cost, zero dependencies, no argv key exposure, 0600 files, secret redaction. Small, readable code (about 3k lines).
Reasonable test suite (about 120 test cases across 13 files against a local stand-in API). The author already cut noisy gates after a week of real use (v0.9.0), which shows honest calibration.
Complements the user's existing setup: the secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks are PreToolUse/other events, so the Stop hook does not overlap with them.
Addresses a real pain point: Opus claiming "tests pass" without running anything.
cons: Sends prompts, replies and full tool outputs (code, command output) to a third party on every turn. On client projects this is a real confidentiality and NDA issue. Regex redaction is best-effort, and it adds a hop through OpenRouter.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18, 24 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, and it has already changed defaults once (0.9.0 breaking). Expect churn.
Not tested against OpenRouter by the author, and the docs mention only api.typesafe.ai. The full base-URL path must be set by hand, and a shape mismatch would just silently fail open.
Stop-hook latency of about 0.5-1.3 s per turn (measured by the author, slower than Jev's claimed 70-500 ms). The first call in a session pays for a cold connection and broker spawn.

The claims gate judges sentence by sentence and has documented false positives and blind spots (long outputs truncated, restated results, lagging transcript). It can trigger an extra Opus turn. The 'wrong' costs are small but nonzero.
Narrow value: it catches unsupported 'I ran X' claims only. The other eight gates are opt-in, need manual hook wiring, and by the author's own account mostly interrupted without catching anything.
It runs a persistent detached background Node process (broker) plus a growing decisions log and last-*.json files holding redacted excerpts on disk.
Bypass/auto permission mode: a Stop-hook block still works, but PreToolUse 'ask' gates lose their force in bypass mode. Only the Stop gate is relevant, which is the one with value.
gh-rashedint32-jev-gates.verdict: The best automatic, zero-prompt Jev integration found so far: a deterministic Stop hook that uses Jev the way it is meant to be used, fails open, costs no context, and can be pointed at OpenRouter with two env vars. It is too young to trust blindly, and it ships full tool outputs to a third party each turn. Run it in JEV_GATES=shadow on personal projects first, and keep it off on NDA client repos.

gh-noplan-inc-limpet.name: noplan-inc/limpet
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.whatItDoes: Claude Code (and Codex) plugin that installs a Stop hook (single stdlib-only Python file, limpet.py, ~600 lines). When the agent is about to stop, it sends the last 3 messages, this turn's tool-call one-liners and the final message to Jev, asking one yes/no (Noul) question per plain-language rule in ~/.limpet/rules.md ("Is the agent violating this rule? Rule: ..."). If a rule's P(violation) exceeds a per-rule threshold (LIMPET_BLOCK), the hook exits 2 with a stderr line and the agent is sent back to work once. Default is shadow mode (log only, never block). Also ships `suggest` and `calibrate` CLI commands that mine your past transcripts to propose rules and thresholds.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.runtime: Python 3.9+ stdlib only (python3 on PATH); no npm/pip deps; no postinstall
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.install: In Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add noplan-inc/limpet ; /plugin install limpet@limpet (prompts for typesafe_api_key / ai_gateway_api_key / block; keys marked sensitive, stored in secure storage). CLI: claude plugin install limpet@limpet --config typesafe_api_key=... (key then visible in argv at install time only). Manual alternative: clone and add a Stop hook running python3 ~/limpet/limpet.py (timeout 30).

interface.name: Config env vars
interface.purpose: TYPESAFE_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, LIMPET_KEY_CMD, LIMPET_PROVIDER, LIMPET_BLOCK, LIMPET_RULES, LIMPET_LOG, LIMPET_JEV_MODEL, LIMPET_DEBUG; plugin options exposed as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_*.

security: Key handling is good: plugin userConfig marks keys sensitive (secure storage), `key set` uses getpass/keychain so the key never appears in argv; the hook reads the key from env/keychain and sends it in an Authorization header via urllib (no key in process list at runtime). Only `claude plugin install --config typesafe_api_key=...` puts it in argv once.

LIMPET_KEY_CMD is executed with shell=True (limpet.py ~139) with an 8 s timeout; only sourced from env/plugin config/~/.limpet/env, so not remotely injectable, but ~/.limpet/env is plain text and any writer to it can set it.
Keychain lookup spawns `secret-tool lookup` on every stop (2 s timeout); on headless Linux without a Secret Service this is a no-op after timeout.

Prompt-injection surface: assistant/user text and tool-call strings (up to 200 chars each) are interpolated into the Jev state as data, and Jev only returns probabilities (no free text), so injected text can at worst flip a probability and cause a false block/pass. The stderr block message is limpet-authored plus rule text and percentages, not model output.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no telemetry other than the Jev call; stdlib only so no supply-chain deps. But the plugin is fetched live from a 1-contributor, 2-week-old GitHub repo and runs on every stop, so pin a commit or vendor the file. CI workflow pullfrog.yml references many provider secrets but is workflow_dispatch only (repo-side, does not affect users).

Local log ~/.limpet/log.jsonl stores session_id, cwd, transcript_path and first 500 chars of every final assistant message in plain text (retained indefinitely, not rotated). For client projects this leaves client-derived text on disk outside the project.

`suggest` and `calibrate` read transcripts of every Claude Code project and Codex session on the machine and ship excerpts (including your own replies) to the provider; running them would send client-project conversation content to a third party.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.dataEgress: Per stop, to the chosen provider only (api.typesafe.ai or Vercel gateway; OpenRouter after patching): up to 3 previous messages (each truncated to 2000 chars, newest first, user and assistant text), the final assistant message (2000 chars), and up to 40 one-line tool-call summaries from the current turn ("Bash: <command up to 200 chars> -> ok/error", or file_path/pattern/url first string arg), plus the rule texts. File contents, diffs and tool outputs are not sent, but Bash commands and prompts/assistant prose can contain client names, paths, hostnames and inline secrets in command strings. The user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover this channel. suggest/calibrate additionally send stop/reply pairs from all projects over the last N days.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.failureMode: Fail-open. main() returns 0 on missing key, API error, timeout, malformed answers (probabilities None are ignored) and any top-level exception (limpet.py 331-360, 600-605); urllib timeout is 20 s, hook timeout 30 s, keychain 2 s and key cmd 8 s inside that budget. Worst case Jev hangs: the agent stop is delayed up to ~20 s, then proceeds. Default with no LIMPET_BLOCK is shadow mode (never blocks). Push-back is capped at once per stop chain via stop_hook_active. Errors are only recorded to the log unless LIMPET_DEBUG=1.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.contextCost: Zero tools, zero MCP instructions, zero tokens on normal turns. Only when it blocks does it inject one stderr line (~40-80 tokens: 'limpet: this response may violate: "<rule>" (91%). If it does, follow the rule and keep working. If it does not, say why in one line, then stop.') which forces at least one extra assistant turn (real cost is the follow-up turn's tokens, and a possible spurious 'no, this is fine' reply on false positives, which the README says are ~5% by design).
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook: fires on every agent stop with no prompting and no model discretion. This is exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' shape, but it only covers the single decision point 'is the agent stopping too early'.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.latencyImpact: Added only at end of turn, not per tool call: Python startup + transcript tail read (last 512 KB) + one HTTPS call with N parallel yes/no questions; author claims ~0.7 s per stop. Through OpenRouter's claimed 70-500 ms Jev latency expect ~0.3-1 s per stop. Up to 20 s if the provider stalls. No effect on PreToolUse/PostToolUse or existing GitNexus/secret-guard hooks (different event).
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a Stop hook with no prompt changes, matching the user's 'never say use jev' requirement; verified in hooks/hooks.json and limpet.py main().
Uses Jev for what it is actually good at (typed probability judgments, no free text) with cost ~ $0.0001 per stop, i.e. a few cents per heavy day; one call carries all rules in parallel.
Fail-open on every error path and shadow mode by default, so it cannot wedge a client-project session; push-back capped once per stop via stop_hook_active.
Zero context cost on normal turns (no MCP tools, no injected text) and no conflict with the user's existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
Small, auditable single stdlib Python file (~600 lines, MIT), no deps, no postinstall; keychain-based key storage via secret-tool works on Linux.
Existing 'typesafe' provider already speaks the System One request shape, so retargeting to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a ~10-line patch.
calibrate gives honest, data-driven thresholds and reports AUROC per rule, which is a rare, credible way to evaluate whether Jev helps at all.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only api.typesafe.ai and Vercel AI Gateway (limpet.py:35-38); user would need a TypeSafe key or a fork/patch, and I could not verify OpenRouter's exact response field for Noul.

Modest measured effectiveness by the author's own numbers: AUROC 0.50-0.64, catches only 5-12% of bad stops at 5% false positives ('a cheap nudge, not a wall'), and labels are noisy. Opus 5.5 with a strong system prompt may stop early less often than the author's mixed agents, so benefit for this user is unproven.

Solves only one problem (early stopping / handoff); it does not give Claude Code Jev-based routing, permission decisions, tool selection or code-review scoring, which is what the user's broader integration goal implies.

Sends conversation excerpts and Bash command lines (including possible client names/paths/inline secrets) to a third party on every stop; the user's secret guard does not cover this and it is a compliance question for client projects. Local log also stores 500 chars of each final message plus cwd/transcript path in plaintext.

Very immature: 1 contributor, 13 commits all on one day (2026-09-17), 5 stars, no releases/tags, 13 days old, only ~5 test functions (no API-call tests). Plugin installs float on the default branch of a personal repo, so supply-chain pin is manual.

Exit-2 Stop blocking forces an extra full Opus turn on each hit (and false positives force a pointless 'it's fine' reply), which costs subscription usage and can annoy in bypass/auto mode where the user already wants uninterrupted runs.

Default rules are tuned to the author's habits (e.g. 'Don't hand work to human', 'give time estimate') and some rules like 'Don't say done without running tests' show AUROC 0.50 (no signal); requires the calibrate step before it is worth turning blocking on.
suggest/calibrate read every project's transcripts on the machine (including client projects) and send them to the provider, an unsafe default for a mixed personal/client workstation.
gh-noplan-inc-limpet.verdict: The only real, deterministic auto-invoked Jev integration in Claude Code I found here: a safe, fail-open Stop hook that costs nothing in context. But its value is a narrow anti-early-stop nudge with weak measured lift, it lacks OpenRouter support (needs a ~10-line fork), and it ships conversation and Bash-command excerpts off-machine, so run it in shadow mode from a pinned, patched local copy rather than installing the marketplace plugin as-is.

security: Age: repo created 2026-09-24, npm first published 2026-09-25, 6 days old on 2026-09-30. 302 commits by ONE author (Ciprian Ursu), no other contributors, 3 stars, 0 forks. The GitHub release is titled v0.16.0 but tagged v0.15.0 (npm is at 0.16.0). Very high churn: 85 commits on 2026-09-29 alone, and 'fix(gate): tamper check ...' bypass fixes on the day of audit.
MIT license. No npm postinstall/preinstall script (package.json scripts are test/eval only). package.json declares no runtime dependencies, and I saw none in the manifest.

Key handling is careful: the key travels in the Authorization header, never in argv (install.mjs and hook commands take only flags like --mode). keyRouteError pins the OpenRouter key to https://openrouter.ai. fetch uses redirect:'error'. Errors log the HTTP status only, and the key is scrubbed from error text (providers.mjs:166-190). The plugin key is a sensitive userConfig option kept in system secure storage.

Fail-closed design: hook.mjs and failsafe.mjs exit 2 or answer ask if the script fails to load. In enforce mode, Jev errors, timeouts or malformed answers give the policy fallback (ask), never a pass. The default never emits allow, so a wrong Jev answer can only add a prompt.

Installers: README offers `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash` and `npx @ursuciprian/reflex setup`. Neither is needed for the plugin route (/plugin marketplace add ursuciprian/reflex). install.sh runs `npm install --global` into ~/.local/share/reflex. `reflex setup` edits ~/.claude/settings.json (hooks plus permissions.ask rules) and writes ~/.config/reflex/config.json. The plugin route changes no settings.

Prompt-injection surface: the guard ingests web pages and MCP results and sends them to a hosted model (Jev), which adds an attacker-influenced-input path into the judge. The 'injection' question exists for this. Mitigations: typed outputs only, and the model cannot emit shell. The README admits the guard is a heuristic filter and the rules are pattern matching, not a shell parser ('treat as a strong filter'). The SECURITY policy lists the known bypasses (scripts changed between check and run, nesting deeper than 2 levels, >256KB).
Reflex is not a sandbox. Scripts are read at hook time, not at run time (a TOCTOU that the GUIDE admits).

Shell execution: gate.mjs shells out for context (git, and optionally `terraform show -json`, off by default), and spawns a detached copy of itself for shadow-mode Jev. Telemetry: none found. The only outbound calls are to the chosen Jev provider, the optional System 2 judge, the optional Slack/json webhook (notify.mjs:71), and npm at install time.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.dataEgress: With engine=jev, ONLY for commands the rules, read-only list and fast lane do not settle: the redacted command; the cwd path; environment names (AWS profile, region, kube context, terraform workspace, git branch); the agent's last message and last 5 commands (redacted and truncated); and the first 16 KB of a local script the command runs (make recipe, npm script), never .env or credentials files. The injection guard additionally sends, per inspected result of WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP tools, network-command Bash output, or a Read of a file outside the project, up to 8 chunks x 3000 chars redacted, the tool name, a redacted origin and the last 1000 chars of the user's prompt (docs/GUIDE.md:1493-1497). Conditional instructions send the first 4000 chars of the prompt only when a fragment is undecided. Redaction is a regex list (AWS/GitHub/Slack/OpenAI tokens, bearer headers, *SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD=, JWTs, private keys), which the GUIDE itself calls 'not DLP'. Via OpenRouter, the data goes to OpenRouter AND is passed on to TypeSafe, so two processors' terms apply; the GUIDE tells users to check both before rollout. That matters for client projects. With engine=local (the default) nothing leaves the machine. Logs stay local in ~/.local/state/reflex/.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.failureMode: Fail-closed in enforce mode. One deadline (REFLEX_TIMEOUT_MS, default 3000 ms) covers all retry attempts of a Jev call. 408, 409, 429 and 5xx are retried, at most 3 attempts with jittered backoff, only if the wait still ends before the deadline. Network errors are not retried. A timeout, an HTTP error or a malformed reply gives the policy fallback `ask`, so a human is prompted, never a silent pass. Rules, the read-only list and the fast lane keep working locally. An internal error gives ask in enforce mode and pass in shadow mode. The Claude Code hook timeouts are 10s (PreToolUse) and 15s (guard PostToolUse), and Claude Code's own handling then applies. Consequence for this user: an OpenRouter outage in enforce mode turns into more permission prompts on uncertain commands, which is annoying in bypass mode. A missing key in the plugin does not error; the engine silently degrades to local (plugin.mjs default).
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.contextCost: MCP server: 5 tools. Names, descriptions and schemas total about 4.8 KB in the source lines 28-70, so roughly 1.2-1.5k tokens, plus the server instructions (about 100 tokens) telling the model to call reflex_check before shell commands. That instruction is redundant with the enforcing hook, and it makes the model spend extra turns calling reflex_check (each call runs the gate again, so possibly a second Jev call). The skill description adds about 60 tokens. Hooks inject text ONLY on findings: PostToolUse additionalContext on an injection warn/block, and UserPromptSubmit additionalContext when a conditional instruction fragment matches. Otherwise pass is silent. About 4 hook entries fire on Bash calls (PreToolUse, PostToolUse gate, PostToolUse guard, PermissionRequest), each a fresh `node` process. The plugin is a large code bundle (gate.mjs is ~228 KB) but it costs no context.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks, with no user prompting. PreToolUse fires on Bash, Task, Agent, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and every mcp__ tool. PostToolUse guard fires on WebFetch, WebSearch, Read, Bash and mcp__ tools. UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt. The MCP tools and the skill are additionally model-discretion. This is the only fully automatic Claude Code path among the candidates I would expect for OpenRouter-Jev, but what it automates is risk-gating of shell commands, not general coding decisions.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.latencyImpact: Local-only decisions (read-only, rule and fast-lane, about half of commands per the author's replay) cost one `node` process start, roughly tens of ms (my estimate, not measured). A Jev-classified command adds one HTTP round trip: the README reports 0.35-0.42 s in scenarios, the GUIDE about 0.7 s in enforce mode, and a 3 s ceiling before falling back to ask. In shadow mode Jev runs in a detached background process, so the agent does not wait. Identical commands are cached for 24h. OpenRouter adds a proxy hop over direct TypeSafe (the GUIDE says so). The injection guard runs after every WebFetch/WebSearch/Read/Bash/MCP result. With jev it can add a Jev call per network result (up to 15s hook timeout). With the local engine it is local regex only. The extra PreToolUse hooks for Edit/Write/MCP calls add node-start overhead to nearly every tool call.
pros: Truly automatic: the plugin registers PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest and UserPromptSubmit hooks (hooks/hooks.json), so Claude Code invokes it with no 'use jev' prompt. That is exactly the auto-invocation requirement.

OpenRouter is first-class in code, not just docs: providers.mjs:26-29 targets openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, a host-pinned key, and attribution headers. It also has mock tests for the request shape and the retry/timeout paths.
Well-built failure semantics: a single 3 s deadline across retries, ask on any Jev error in enforce mode, malformed answers treated as unavailable, and hook.mjs/failsafe.mjs exit 2 on load failure.

Uses Jev for what its typed Choice/Noul/Score outputs suit (calibrated probabilities from a policy.json, not free text), so it is a genuine System One use case. Default never emits allow, so Jev can only add prompts.

Cheap: about 1k input tokens per uncovered command, roughly $0.04/M, and the author's replay estimates about $0.47 per week of 13,743 commands. The rules layer cuts about half of calls before they reach the API.

Safe rollout path: the plugin starts keyless in shadow mode, and `reflex replay claude --since 7d` reads your existing transcripts with nothing executed, so you can see what it would have flagged before sending anything to OpenRouter.
Stands down if the same hooks are also in settings.json, so no double-judging. It coexists with your other hooks: Claude Code runs hooks in parallel, and Reflex only tightens (ask/deny).
Key hygiene: sensitive plugin option, never in argv, and no telemetry found.
cons: Its value is command-risk gating, not 'Jev makes coding better'. For a senior dev on personal + client repos with no prod/terraform/kubectl focus, most commands are read-only or ordinary build/test, so Jev calls will be rare and the benefit modest. The project is aimed at infra teams (terraform, kubectl, freezes, SOC2 audit).

Duplicates existing safeguards: overlaps with your PreToolUse secret-leak guard (both see Bash|Mcp), and with Claude Code's own auto mode and permission classifier. In bypass mode, whether a hook 'ask' still prompts is not verified by me. If it does, an uncertain command in bypass mode now produces prompts you deliberately turned off; if it does not, the gate is moot.

In plugin mode the key MUST be entered through the /plugin Configure dialog. An exported OPENROUTER_API_KEY is deliberately ignored and scrubbed (plugin.mjs). Without the key the plugin silently runs local-only, so it is easy to think Jev is active when it is not; `reflex doctor`/status is needed to confirm.

Client-code exposure: with jev, command text, cwd paths, the agent's last message and 5 previous commands, 16 KB of script bodies, and up to 24 KB (8 x 3000 chars) of every web/MCP/out-of-project-Read result go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. Redaction is regex-only ('not DLP'). That may breach client confidentiality terms, so the guard would need to stay local-engine for client repos.

6 days old, single author, 3 stars, 302 commits (85 in one day), a live bypass-fix stream, and a release tag that does not match the version. Docs and code disagree on scope: README says only shell tools are gated while the hook matcher includes Edit/Write/MCP. Expect breaking changes.

Per-call overhead: about 4 hook processes per Bash call plus PreToolUse on Edit/Write and every mcp__ call. The MCP server adds about 1.3-1.5k tokens per session, and its instruction ('call reflex_check before running a shell command') is redundant with the hook and can add extra model turns and duplicate Jev calls.

Not verified against OpenRouter live: all published accuracy numbers (171/171 tool gate, 97%/100% injection) are for TypeSafe-direct jev-1.13.0. The OpenRouter route is tested only against a mock. Jev on OpenRouter is beta on the /alpha/ endpoint, so a path change would break it (OpenRouter returns HTTP errors, which mean ask). Pinned to minor jev-1.13 (no 'latest' alias).
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.verdict: The only real candidate that fully automatically wires OpenRouter-hosted Jev into Claude Code (deterministic hooks, first-class openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions support, fail-closed, cheap). But it is a week-old, single-author, infra-safety gate rather than a general coding aid, it duplicates your secret-guard and permission modes, and it ships up to ~24 KB of tool results and command context per event to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Try it in plugin shadow mode plus `reflex replay` on personal projects first, with the local engine for client repos.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.install: Claude Code plugin route (no settings edits, no curl|sh): `/plugin marketplace add ursuciprian/reflex` then `/plugin install reflex@reflex`, then /plugin -> reflex -> Configure: set Jev provider=openrouter, paste the sk-or- key into 'Jev API key', engine=jev, mode=shadow. Alternative (edits ~/.claude/settings.json): `npx @ursuciprian/reflex setup --provider openrouter` with JEV_OPENROUTER_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY exported. I did not run any of these.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.runtime: Node.js >=18 (hooks and MCP server run with plain `node`, zero runtime deps). Optional Python 3.9+ for LiteLLM routing and 3.10+ for Laya.
gh-ursuciprian-reflex.tests: Offline self-checks in test.mjs (1935 lines) plus embedded selfchecks in gate.mjs, providers.mjs, mcp.mjs and install.mjs. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs `npm test` on Ubuntu with Node 18/22 and Python 3.9/3.12, and on macOS with Node 22; it has a plugin job, plus publish.yml and pages.yml. Live evals against Jev are not run in CI. I did not run any tests.

gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.name: jonathanavis96/jev-kit
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.whatItDoes: A monorepo "kit" for TypeSafe Jev + Claude Code. Core is "Airlock": a stdlib-only Python PreToolUse hook registered for every tool (matcher "*"). A local rules table (airlock/rules.py) pre-filters each call in microseconds. Only ambiguous cases (R2 Skill load, R4 long bare shell, R8 sub-agent tier guard, R8 tool-choice/disk-crawl guard, R10 catch-all general-risk) send a redacted typed question to Jev (POST /v1/systemone, model jev-latest, 1.5 s budget) and then allow, warn, deny or rewrite. Pure-code rules cover secret exposure, sudo, destructive commands, commit-secret and Playwright-MCP calls. Also ships: SessionStart health check, warm unix-socket daemon (systemd --user), a Stop-hook wrapper (belay, pinned third-party jev-belay), a 1-tool stdio MCP "browse" (vendored browser-use/jev-ultrafast), and opt-in compaction, review, tuning loop and other extras. Install is a bash script that only prints the settings.json block unless --wire is passed. Not an OpenRouter integration.

providerSupport.evidence: airlock/client.py:17 API_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"; client.py:18 MODEL = "jev-latest"; client.py:39-48 body {state, model, questions} with Authorization: Bearer <key>; airlock/daemon.py:52-54 imports API_URL and splits it for the pooled HTTPS connection; vendor/jev-ultrafast/jev_ultrafast/model.py:283 hardcodes https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with os.environ["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"]. Key is read only as TYPESAFE_API_KEY (env or ~/.config/jev-kit/env, airlock/keyfile.py). No OPENROUTER_API_KEY or openrouter.ai reference for Jev anywhere; the only openrouter.ai hit is TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 for the browse agent's text-writer LLM (tests/test_browse.py:687), unrelated to Jev.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate but mostly mechanical for the guard: change API_URL in airlock/client.py:17 (daemon.py inherits it) to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, set MODEL to typesafe/jev-latest (client.py:18), and put the OpenRouter key in a TYPESAFE_API_KEY= line (the name is only a label). It only works if OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same {state, model, questions} body and returns the same response shape as api.typesafe.ai, which I could not verify from this repo. A second hardcoded URL in vendor/jev-ultrafast (model.py:283) and the belay third-party clone would need separate patches. It is a fork to maintain, not a config switch.
