security: API key never placed on argv: urllib Authorization header built in-process (airlock/client.py:39-48), key read from env or a mode-600 file by plain file I/O (airlock/keyfile.py); browse passes it via the subprocess env (browse/server.py:751), not argv.

Redaction (airlock/redact.py) of token-shaped strings before egress, truncation after redaction; a 13-rule redactor in belay. Regex redaction is best-effort, so client code or secrets in unusual formats could still leak in the ambiguous slice.

Everything fails open on error, timeout, budget or missing key, so a guard/deny is advisory rather than a hard security boundary. R11 deliberately ignores the airlock-ok stamp and loop allowance (strict).

install.sh: no sudo, writes only under $HOME per README/header, prints the settings.json block unless --wire; but it git-clones pinned third-party repos (jev-belay, and compaction plugin if enabled), enables systemd --user units (daemon, monitoring, filesearch, claude-update) and the claude-update component runs npm install -g when idle; no curl|sh seen in install.sh grep.

Prompt-injection surface: verdicts come from a model reading tool-call text, and a user_requested question reads recent user prompts (softening only, guarded by a code belt in context.py). Tool results are not sent (except the opt-in compaction plugin, which sends up to about 25k tokens of raw UNREDACTED tool inputs and results per request, per docs/components.md).
No telemetry to a third party by default; optional Uptime-Kuma push (opt-in, status word only). Third-party code pulled in: vendor/jev-ultrafast (browser-use, MIT), valentynkit/jev-belay.
Hook is registered for every tool: every Bash/Read/Edit/MCP call spawns a Python process running the rules prefilter, and its deny output can block calls.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter): for the ambiguous minority of tool calls, a redacted, truncated summary of the call (Bash command text + description + cwd/scope, Skill name/purpose, Agent dispatch description and prompt) plus, for the user_requested softening check, recent user prompts (redacted, truncated). Belay (Stop hook, opt-in) sends task text, final assistant message and check command lines (1,500 + 2,000 char caps, redacted). Tool results, diffs and file contents are not sent by the default guard. Opt-in extras send more: compaction up to about 25k tokens of raw unredacted tool inputs/results per request; browse sends page state and goals to TypeSafe and, with plan=true, to Claude; review sends diffs. No egress for pure-code rules, session check, file search, monitoring. A local log of verdicts is written under ~/.config/airlock.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.failureMode: Fail-open by design. client.py DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5 s, but enforce.py budget AIRLOCK_BUDGET_MS defaults to 1500 ms (2000 ms on Windows); any exception, malformed answer, budget overrun, missing key or daemon down means ALLOW, logged with error set. Deny/rewrite additionally require confidence >= 0.8 and margin >= 0.4 (0.9/0.5 for rewrite). Default mode is shadow (log only, nothing blocked) until you write "enforce" to ~/.config/airlock/mode. Daemon connect timeout 0.2 s with fallback to a direct HTTPS call. SessionStart check warns once per 6 h when the guard is not judging. Worst case with Jev down is a session with no guard beyond code-only rules, not a stall.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.contextCost: Very low for the default hooks: no MCP server, no tool definitions, no skill descriptions. Hooks inject text only when a rule warns or denies (a few lines, e.g. the 2-line tier advice note) and SessionStart is silent when healthy. Optional browse MCP adds 1 tool (description about 1,000 chars plus schema, roughly 400-500 tokens) and the R11 suggestion text when triggered. The repo's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md only matter inside the repo checkout.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PreToolUse with matcher "*" fires on every tool call without any prompting; SessionStart, PostToolUse/Failure and (opt-in) Stop hooks likewise. No model discretion needed. This is the closest match found to the user's requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically, but Jev acts as a guard/judge on tool calls rather than a general coding helper.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.latencyImpact: Code-only path: Python interpreter startup per tool call (est. tens of ms; the prefilter itself is microseconds) on EVERY tool call because the matcher is "*". For the ambiguous slice (README claims about 7 percent of calls, 93 percent pass straight through) add about 0.3 s warm via daemon or about 0.9 s cold, hard-capped at 1.5 s then fail-open. Numbers are the repo's own measurements (docs/measurements.md), not independently verified. Belay adds a Jev call at Stop time only when a change lacks a passing check.
pros: Only candidate seen that satisfies the hard requirement literally: a PreToolUse matcher-* hook plus SessionStart/Stop hooks run automatically with no 'use jev' prompt.

Respects Jev's actual nature (typed decisions with probabilities, no free text): it asks typed Choice/Noul/Score questions and applies confidence and margin thresholds (>=0.8 / >=0.4) before acting, instead of treating Jev as a chat model.

Safe rollout: default shadow mode logs what enforce would do, python3 -m airlock.report reviews it, kill switch AIRLOCK_DISABLE=1, per-rule rules.json overrides, install.sh --check-only and wire only with --wire, rollback.sh.
Fails open everywhere with a hard 1.5 s budget and a 5 s ceiling; a Jev outage cannot stall the session, and SessionStart warns when the guard silently stopped judging.
Cheap by design: rules table pre-filters most calls locally, only the ambiguous slice reaches Jev, Jev call skipped when a deny is unreachable, 5 percent sampling for tuning.
stdlib-only Python hook, key never on argv, redaction before egress, egress documented per component in docs/components.md (unusually candid, flags compaction as 25k-token unredacted exposure).
Large test suite claimed and present (about 50 test files in tests/, README says 1310 passing) and labelled eval cases for each rule; 64 commits in 11 days, active.
Tier guard (R8) could reduce Opus 5.5 sub-agent spend if the ladder is configured in tiers.json for the user's agent names; belay Stop hook catches overclaimed 'done' messages.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL and model are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and jev-latest (airlock/client.py:17-18, vendor model.py:283); key only read as TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Using OpenRouter needs a local fork/patch and depends on OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepting the identical request/response schema (unverified); the user's stated provider requirement is not met out of the box.

Mostly a guard, not a coding accelerator: its value is blocking/warning on risky tool calls and steering cost, not writing or reviewing code better in daily work. Much overlaps with things the user already has: R1 secret guard duplicates the existing PreToolUse secret-leak hook, R9 commit-secret overlaps too.

Direct conflict with existing setup: R11 (strict, no override stamp) denies every Playwright MCP browsing call and points to its own 'browse' tool, which the user's installed playwright MCP would hit unless R11 is turned off via rules.json; R8 grep/disk-crawl steering may interact with the GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks (a raw-grep steer toward graphify only when graphify-out exists, so likely inert).

Hook on matcher '*' adds a Python process spawn to every single tool call, stacked on the user's two existing hook chains (secret guard, GitNexus pre+post, caveman); mostly milliseconds but cumulative.

Tier guard is built around a custom ladder (scout/workerS/worker/director/fable) and Agent subagent_type names; low value unless the user's agents are configured into it. Rewrite mode silently downgrades sub-agents and is a real risk on client work.

Heavy footprint for a hook: systemd --user daemon, monitoring and filesearch timers, an idle auto-updater that runs npm install -g claude, cloned third-party repos (jev-belay, vendored jev-ultrafast), Windows/WSL/tuning extras. Large surface to audit for client machines; a personal project (about 50 stars, 3 contributor identities, mainly one author, no releases, no CI config in the repo).

Data leaves the machine to a beta third-party API: redacted bash commands, cwd, Agent prompts and recent user prompts. Regex redaction is not a guarantee; on client projects this is a confidentiality question. Fail-open means the guard is not a real security control, and README claims (93 percent pass-through, 0.3 s) are self-reported.

Depends on an unverified vendor product (Jev beta, skeptics say it is a router-like model); calibration thresholds in the kit were tuned against the author's own eval data and workflow, and its installer defaults (belay, auto-updater on, daemon) suit the author's machine.
gh-jonathanavis96-jev-kit.verdict: The best structural fit for "automatic, no prompting" because it is a deterministic PreToolUse/SessionStart/Stop hook set with shadow mode and fail-open. But it is TypeSafe-direct only (hardcoded URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY), so OpenRouter needs a small unverified fork. It is a guard, not a coding helper, and it clashes with the user's Playwright MCP (R11) and secret hook. I would cherry-pick the pattern (a minimal shadow-mode hook on selected matchers), not install the whole kit on client projects.

gh-nanako0129-stingray.whatItDoes: Claude Code (and Codex) Stop hook, one bash script (hooks/stingray.sh, 646 lines) using jq, curl and perl. When a turn ends, it redacts the last assistant message and POSTs it to TypeSafe System One (model jev-1.13.0) with Noul questions from questions.json. Questions: no_action, broken_promise, watch_claim, watch_mismatch and wrong_language. If a score is at least tau (0.5), it exits 2 with a fixed nudge on stderr, so Claude keeps working. The nudge covers a turn that did nothing, an announced action never carried out, a promise to watch CI with nothing running, or a reply in the wrong language. The hook is off by default and needs env switches (STINGRAY, STINGRAY_SHADOW, STINGRAY_SHAPE3, STINGRAY_LANG). It is a follow-through guardrail, not a general Jev integration.

The response is read as .answers.<question>.noul (:611, :628). There is no mention of openrouter anywhere in the repo.
providerSupport.others: None. The Codex hook (hooks/stingray-codex.sh) uses the same TypeSafe endpoint.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial on paper, unverified in practice. STINGRAY_ENDPOINT and STINGRAY_JEV_MODEL are already env overrides. Set STINGRAY_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and STINGRAY_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, and put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (the only variable read besides ~/.config/typesafe/api_key). Whether the OpenRouter System One API accepts the same request shape ({model,state,questions{...instructions,criteria}}) and returns the same .answers.X.noul shape is not confirmed. If it wraps the response, jq paths at lines 611, 628 and 664 need editing. This is a small edit to one file. No code change is needed for the key or URL.

interface.name: Stop hook (hooks/hooks.json)
interface.purpose: Runs /bin/bash ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/stingray.sh at every turn end, with timeout 10. Exit 2 plus stderr text sends Claude back to work. Every failure path exits 0 (fail-open).

interface.name: shape 1 no_action (STINGRAY=1 or SHADOW)
interface.purpose: Noul question: the turn stopped without doing anything it could have done.

interface.name: shape 2 broken_promise (STINGRAY=1 or SHADOW)
interface.purpose: Noul question: the final message declared an action that the turn's tool names do not account for.

interface.name: shape 3 watch_claim / watch_mismatch (STINGRAY_SHAPE3=1, STINGRAY_SHAPE3_JUDGE=1)
interface.purpose: Promised to watch CI, a build or a PR with nothing in background_tasks, session_crons or pending SendMessage handoffs. Judge mode also checks whether the running work is the thing promised.

interface.name: shape 4 wrong_language (STINGRAY_LANG=1)
interface.purpose: Final message not in the language from settings.json. Irrelevant for an English user.

interface.name: Tuning env vars
interface.purpose: STINGRAY_TAU=0.5, STINGRAY_TIMEOUT=6, STINGRAY_MAX_BLOCKS=3 per session, STINGRAY_STATE_DIR, STINGRAY_REDACT_WORDS, STINGRAY_ENDPOINT, STINGRAY_JEV_MODEL.

interface.name: decisions.jsonl
interface.purpose: Local log at ~/.local/state/stingray/decisions.jsonl with shape, score, would_block, model, qset_hash and secs.

interface.name: Plugin install

gh-nanako0129-stingray.runtime: bash + jq + curl + perl + shasum; no Node or Python needed at runtime (python3 is used only by the tests)
gh-nanako0129-stingray.install: claude plugin marketplace add Nanako0129/stingray && claude plugin install stingray@stingray --scope user. Then set STINGRAY_SHADOW=1 (and the key) in the settings.json env block. Also needs jq, and a key file ~/.config/typesafe/api_key or TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.tests: Large for its size. tests/acceptance.sh (339 lines, stubs, no network), network.sh (fail-open paths and a --live mode), mutants.sh (mutation checks of the guards), and hook-shell, codex-hook, version-bump and show-payload scripts. Live calibration fixtures: 50 labelled watch lines and 22 labelled promise turns. CI (.github/workflows/tests.yml) runs on ubuntu and macOS with SHA-pinned actions. I did not run any of it. The README's own numbers on 124 turns are precision 81.8%, recall 14.1%, FPR 3.3% (jev-1.13.0, 2026-09-21). The author admits the labels undercount, the test script and turns were not kept, and the wording changed after the measurement.
security: API key appears in curl argv: hooks/stingray.sh:562 uses -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY", so the key is visible in ps and /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the duration of each call (up to 6s). The README says nothing about this. It matters on a shared machine.

Key is read from ~/.config/typesafe/api_key or TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The README prefers the file because env vars leak to child processes. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the settings.json env block, as the README suggests for the switches, exposes it to every tool subprocess.

Outbound guard: STINGRAY_ENDPOINT must be https or loopback (:552-557). The request body is scanned for sk-, gh*_, github_pat_, AKIA and PEM patterns before sending (:~529), and a match cancels the request. It is a good defensive design, but a regex denylist.

Redaction (perl, hooks/stingray.sh:~395-450) strips fenced code, inline code, URLs, block quotes and any line containing a path or filename. It masks SHAs, issue numbers and project names derived from cwd and the git remote. The README states plainly that redaction does not achieve zero private content and that the substance of the work survives.

Prompt-injection surface: Claude's own final message goes to Jev, and the nudge sent back is a fixed paragraph, not model or Jev generated. The Jev result is only a numeric score, so injection can at worst cause a spurious block (limited to 3 per session) or suppress one. Cron prompts and background task descriptions are also sent.
Shell execution: none beyond the script itself. No eval, no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry other than the call to api.typesafe.ai. The state dir holds decisions.jsonl and counters.

The README says TypeSafe processes requests in the US and publishes no retention limit, and that its MCA caps liability low. Third-party processing of the last ~2400 bytes of every turn is a real concern for client projects.

Supply chain: a 5-star, 8-day-old repo with 2 real contributors (70 + 17 commits under two names of the same person, plus 1 other). Plugin install runs the script from a mutable branch or tag with no lockfile. It is a single readable file, so review is easy.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.dataEgress: Only when a key is set and a switch is on: one POST per turn (that has a non-empty last message) to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or STINGRAY_ENDPOINT). Payload: the last assistant message after redaction (code, paths, URLs, quotes and SHAs removed), truncated to the last 2400 bytes; the tool NAMES used this turn (no arguments); for each background task its status and description; for each cron its prompt; the name of a pending handoff session; and the language name for shape 4. User prompts, tool arguments, file contents, diffs and command lines are not sent. Redaction leaves the substance of the work readable, which the README admits. Nothing goes to OpenRouter today.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.failureMode: Fail-open on every path (README section "Friction only ever goes up"): no key, no jq, no questions.json, secret pattern in payload, network error, non-200, malformed JSON, score outside [0,1], loop guards (stop_hook_active plus MAX_BLOCKS=3 per session). curl --max-time defaults to 6s (:561). The author measured 6.15s for a hung endpoint against a 10s hook timeout, so at worst the turn end is delayed about 6s and never blocked. It cannot make Claude do less, but the check silently does not run when Jev is down, and there is only a stderr note.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.contextCost: Zero MCP or tool definitions and no server instructions. The hook injects no text on a normal turn. On a block it injects a fixed stderr nudge of about 100-150 tokens, and the model is then forced through one extra turn (extra Opus cost). If the OpenRouter response does not match the parser, the hook fails open and prints a short "(stingray: unavailable ...)" line to stderr.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.latencyImpact: Adds one blocking round trip at every turn end (Stop) when a switch is on and the message has prose: the README measures p50 0.74-0.76s and p95 0.82-0.89s from Taiwan, 0.68-1.03s for a single question. Roughly 1s per turn, not per tool call. Add up to 6s if the endpoint hangs. A block causes one more full model turn. Nothing runs when the switches are unset.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: registered on the Stop event, so it fires automatically at the end of every turn with no prompting, once installed and a switch is set. It does not use Jev to help with coding decisions, only to police Claude's own turn endings.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a Stop hook, so Jev runs without any prompt from the user. It also adds no tool definitions and no context cost at all.

Real, sensible Jev use of the Noul primitive (P(yes) with a threshold), with an offline mutation suite and a fixture-based calibration harness. Unusually honest README, with precision/recall/FPR published and limits listed.

Fail-open everywhere, with a per-session cap of 3 blocks and a double loop guard, so it cannot trap a session. It is off by default, and STINGRAY_SHADOW=1 gives log-only records in decisions.jsonl for a safe trial.
Single readable bash file (646 lines), MIT, no npm or pip install, no telemetry. A SHA-pinned CI on Linux and macOS. The dependencies (bash, jq, curl, perl) are already present on this Linux machine.

STINGRAY_ENDPOINT and STINGRAY_JEV_MODEL overrides make an OpenRouter switch a config change if the request and response shapes match. It targets a real annoyance: Opus stopping with 'I'll now do X' or 'I'll watch CI' and nothing done.
cons: Wrong provider out of the box: only api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. OpenRouter needs the untested override (endpoint, model ID typesafe/jev-1.13, OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and possible jq path edits. The 8-day-old repo has never been tested with OpenRouter.

Narrow scope: it only judges Claude's own turn endings. It gives no Jev help for routing, choosing between options, or coding decisions, so it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev whenever it adds value'. It covers one use case.

Prompts are calibrated on Traditional Chinese: questions.json criteria are in Traditional Chinese, and the README says English criteria have zero live measurements. The 81.8% precision comes from the maintainer's own Chinese transcripts. For an English-speaking user, accuracy is unknown, and recall was only 14.1% in the maintainer's own data.

Sends every turn's redacted final message (last 2400 bytes) to a third party that publishes no retention limit. Redaction leaves the substance of the work readable by the author's own admission. This is a compliance risk on client projects, and it happens on every turn even in shadow mode.

API key passed on the curl command line (visible in ps). Adds about 0.7-1s at each turn end, and a false positive costs a whole extra Opus turn. There is a 'watch' shape that assumes the background_tasks payload and SendMessage transcript formats of a specific Claude Code version (2.1.278 measured, transcript format 2026-09-26). It may break on 2.1.285.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 5 stars, 1 fork, 88 commits by essentially one person. Mutable install from GitHub, and the model is pinned to jev-1.13.0, while OpenRouter naming and behavior differ.
gh-nanako0129-stingray.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context Stop hook that really does run Jev automatically, but it only polices half-finished turns, is tuned on Traditional Chinese, targets TypeSafe direct (OpenRouter needs an untested env override), and ships every turn's redacted message to a third party. Worth a shadow-mode trial on personal projects only, not a core Jev integration.

gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.name: VladyslavHontar/clear-head
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.whatItDoes: Claude Code Stop hook (single Python stdlib script, 484 lines). At the end of each substantial turn that used tools, it reads the session transcript, splits the final answer into sentences, uses Jev Choice/Noul primitives to classify which are factual claims about the codebase, retrieves keyword-matched tool-output lines as evidence, then asks Jev if each claim is supported/contradicted/not addressed. It blocks the turn (decision:block) with a list of [CONTRADICTED]/[UNSUPPORTED]/[STALE]/[RELAYED]/[UNVERIFIED] claims so Claude must verify or downgrade them. It is a hallucination/claim-verification guard, not a general decision router.

Optional local backend kev() at :95-108 (127.0.0.1:8009/v1/systemone, model kev-latest). No OPENROUTER reference anywhere (grep empty).

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. The wire contract is the System One shape ({model,state,questions} -> answers[q].probabilities / .noul), which is the same schema OpenRouter exposes at POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. Change API (line 36), key() to read OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model to typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest (line 74), and add an HTTP-Referer/X-Title header if wanted. Caveat: the OpenRouter response envelope is not verified here (assumed identical to TypeSafe's answers key); also the Cloudflare UA/WAF workarounds may differ, though the explicit User-Agent stays harmless. About a 5-line patch, or a 15-line new 'openrouter' backend entry.

gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.dataEgress: Per turn, to api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter if patched): (1) up to 60 sentences of the assistant's final answer plus the first 12,000 chars of the full answer (pass 1, stop_verify.py ~L330); (2) per factual claim, up to 12 keyword-matched tool-output lines / 1,200 chars (LINES_PER_CLAIM, CHARS_PER_CLAIM at :37), i.e. excerpts of file contents, grep results, command output; (3) up to 120 commands/paths used (READS_CAP) unless the WAF rejects, then omitted; (4) up to 3,000 chars of doc comments from files read (DOC_CHARS). Not sent: user prompt in general (only user-message numbers are used locally), whole files. Everything sent is mirrored to sent.jsonl (L373). For client projects this is code leaving the machine to a third party; the README itself warns about this. Zero Data Retention terms on OpenRouter/TypeSafe are unverified.
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: any exception is logged and swallowed (stop_verify.py:477-482) unless JEV_FAIL_CLOSED is set; per-request timeout 30s (jev) / 50s (kev), hook-level timeout 60s (180s for kev) so the harness kills it and proceeds. Exception: local Kev backend down blocks once (BackendDown). Observed real-world failure: Cloudflare WAF 403s silently disabled checks until a User-Agent fix and a retry-without-commands fallback were added, i.e. silent degradation is a known risk. False positives can block the turn and force Claude to do an extra round (one extra turn maximum thanks to stop_hook_active guard).
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.contextCost: Zero tool/MCP definitions and no server instructions. A Stop hook adds no per-turn prompt tokens except when it blocks: the reason text (~100-400 tokens plus the listed claims) is injected and triggers an additional Claude turn (extra Opus tokens for verification reads and rewrite). Silent when passing.
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: registered as a Stop hook in settings.json, runs automatically at the end of every turn (that produced an answer and used tools). No prompting needed. Fully matches the user's 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement, but it fires at end-of-turn, not for choosing options mid-work.
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.latencyImpact: Jev path: README reports about 1 s for an 18-sentence answer (two to three batched calls: sentence classification, mutable-state noul, claim verification in chunks of 25), within the 30s per-call timeout. Adds roughly 1-3 s at end of qualifying turns via OpenRouter (claimed 70-500 ms per call, several sequential calls). Retry after 403 adds one more call. Local Kev path is 44 s per long answer (not relevant here).
pros: Only candidate found so far that is a real deterministic Stop hook: fires automatically on every turn, satisfying 'Claude Code must use it without me asking'.

Good fit for the Jev use case: uses Choice and Noul primitives with calibrated probabilities and thresholds (JEV_CONTRA, JEV_FIRM, JEV_FACT) instead of free text, playing to Jev's strengths as a cheap judge (about $0.042/M input tokens).
Zero context cost in the normal path, no MCP tool definitions; pure Python stdlib, no dependencies, no postinstall; easy to audit (484 lines).
Provider swap to OpenRouter is a few lines because the code already targets the System One /v1/systemone wire contract with a pluggable BACKENDS dict.

Thoughtful engineering born from real dogfooding: STALE rule for outside-world status, RELAYED for subagent claims, numeric claims not found in output, evidence floor to avoid blocking derivations, loop guard via stop_hook_active, per-tool-call-id evidence tagging, and it logs every payload to sent.jsonl for auditing.
Fail-open by default with 30s timeout and 60s hook timeout, so a slow or down Jev/OpenRouter will not wedge the session; JEV_HOOK=off per-shell kill switch (useful for client work).
Has offline unit tests (test_stop_verify.py) and a replay harness with measured agreement numbers, unusual for a 12-day-old repo; MIT license.
cons: Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; needs a small patch (base URL, key var, model id typesafe/jev-1.13) to use OpenRouter, and the OpenRouter response envelope compatibility is unverified.

Sends excerpts of code, tool outputs, doc comments and the assistant's answer to a third party on every qualifying turn; problematic for client projects and it bypasses the user's PreToolUse secret guard since secrets already in tool output would be shipped and stored in sent.jsonl.

Purpose is narrow: catches unsupported claims in final answers; it does not help with routing, permission decisions, tool selection or code choices. Value depends on how often Opus 5.5 makes false codebase claims.

Keyword-based retriever (not semantic), so false positives/negatives; the README admits that true claims not read this session are flagged, and blocks force extra Claude turns that cost Opus tokens and interrupt flow, especially annoying in auto/bypass mode.

Immature: 2 stars, 1 fork, single author (two git identities), 23 commits in 6 days (2026-09-18 to 09-24), no CI, no releases; hand-tuned thresholds that need per-project tuning; the WAF/User-Agent breakage shows brittleness of the direct API and it silently stopped checking before being noticed.

Relies on Jev being good at entailment judgments, an unproven use of a beta model; skeptics claim Jev is just a small router; the author's own Kev comparison shows judges disagree heavily (Kev agrees with Jev only 12% on contradicted).
Stop hook does not check claims made in the turn that answers a block (stop_hook_active exemption), nor Claude's mid-turn decisions; log.jsonl/sent.jsonl grow unbounded with code excerpts.
Would co-exist with the user's existing Stop/PreToolUse hooks but adds another Python process per turn; no OpenRouter attribution headers.
gh-vladyslavhontar-clear-head.verdict: The best fit found for 'automatic, no prompting': a small, auditable, deterministic Stop hook that uses Jev's Noul/Choice properly and fails open. With a ~5-line patch to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and OPENROUTER_API_KEY it is viable, but treat it as an opt-in claim-checker (disable with JEV_HOOK=off for client repos) because it ships code excerpts off-machine and its value is narrow.

gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.name: vinilana/jev-gateway (jev-claude launcher)
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.whatItDoes: Local Hono/Node HTTP proxy (127.0.0.1:8789 for Claude) that sits between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. On each POST /v1/messages carrying tools it flattens system prompt plus conversation into a Jev "state" and asks Jev one Choice question (which tool, including no_tool_needed) plus a Noul (needs tool?). It also asks speculative arg questions for closed-set params. If Jev is confident (default >= 0.7) it either forces tool_choice, answers directly with a synthesized tool_use, or (for Claude Code, since thinking is on and prompts are cached) appends a hint as a text block styled as a system-reminder to the last user message. Otherwise the request is forwarded unchanged. It is not a hook or MCP server. It does not cover subagent or plan-time reasoning, only the next-tool pick. Bench results are mixed (see verdict).

interface.purpose: Routed endpoint. Adapter src/adapters/messages.ts. Modes: passthrough, none, forced, hint, direct. Response headers x-jev-gateway-mode/reason/tool/confidence/latency-ms.

interface.purpose: Dry-run: returns the Jev decision for a request body without calling upstream.

security: API key: entered via hidden prompt, stored in ~/.jev-gateway/.env with mode 0600 and dir 0700 (bin/setup.mjs:38-40). Sent only as a Bearer header to the provider URL, not in argv. The daemon inherits the env from launcher (process.env), so OPENROUTER_API_KEY is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, not in argv.

Your Anthropic OAuth bearer token from Claude Code transits the local proxy on every request (forwarded untouched, src/upstream.ts:311-316). It is bound to 127.0.0.1 by default (config.ts:69), with no auth on the local port unless ROUTER_API_KEY is set; any local process/user can hit it, and the daemon persists after sessions close.

Prompt-injection surface: hint mode injects a <\system-reminder> block into the last user message that Claude treats as harness text (messages.ts:490-502; open issue #40). Tool names are sanitised to /^[\p{L}\p{N}_.:/-]{1,128}$/ (decide.ts:55) so an MCP tool name cannot break out. Jev picks only a tool name from the client's own roster, so it is a steering nudge, not arbitrary text. In forced/direct mode the gateway can synthesise tool_use calls with Jev-chosen enum/boolean args, bypassing model reasoning. Direct is disabled when thinking is on (decide.ts:197), so with Opus 5.5 it stays hint mode.

No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no telemetry found (grep). Only runtime deps hono and @hono/node-server. Published to npm via trusted publishing (no token), GitHub Actions pinned by SHA in ci.yml. Single maintainer (Vinicius Lana, 54 of 74 commits), brand-new 12-day-old package and a 265-star, 36-fork repo. No curl|sh installer. Opt-in JEV_DEBUG_DUMP_DIR writes full conversations to disk (headers redacted).
Detached daemon spawn and xdg-open of the dashboard are the only process execution. No shell strings.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.dataEgress: To the Jev provider (OpenRouter if configured) on every request that has tools, which is nearly every Claude Code turn: system prompt truncated to 4000 chars, the newest conversation turns up to 60k chars total and each message/tool_call args/tool_result clipped to 4k chars (state.ts, messages.ts:429-465), i.e. user prompts, assistant text, Bash commands and tool outputs including file contents read, plus every tool name and description (up to 1024 chars each, 48k budget) and questions (questions.ts). A second shortlist call is made when tools > 120. Issue #24 measured a median of ~34.5k input tokens per call (max 49k). Images and thinking blocks are stripped and become a placeholder. The full unmodified request also flows to api.anthropic.com as before. OpenRouter sees code and secrets that show up in tool results. The existing PreToolUse secret guard does not protect this path, since it runs before tool output enters the conversation but not on the proxy. The response contains only probabilities. Local logs at ~/.jev-gateway/claude.log store metadata, not prompts. Cost is roughly $0.042 per 1M input tokens, so ~34k tokens per turn is about $0.0015 per turn (my estimate from the brief pricing).
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.failureMode: Fail-open by design and tested (test/failopen.test.ts). Jev timeout is 4000 ms (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS) with one 100 ms retry on 408/429/5xx/network error (jev.ts:200-257), so the worst case before falling back is about 8.1 s of added delay per request (a slow but not dead Jev is the risk). Any Jev error, unexpected answer, low confidence, unparseable body, adapter exception or 400/422 from the upstream on a rewritten request leads to the original bytes being forwarded (app.ts:214-234). Missing key stops the launcher and exits 1 when non-TTY. If the daemon is not running, plain claude with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set in settings.json would get ECONNREFUSED with no fallback, so it is fail-closed at the transport level unless the launcher or a hook keeps it alive. A daemon started with a different upstream refuses to start.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-definition tokens, no MCP instructions, no hooks. Only added tokens are the hint block on hint turns (about 50 tokens, roughly 200 chars, appended after the cache breakpoint at messages.ts:497, so the prompt cache prefix stays intact). Because it changes the last user message, the hint is replayed as part of history on later turns. Issue #37 reports Claude Code showing "Compacting conversation..." immediately when routed through the gateway on a 250-tool profile. The reporter found the same with routing off, and later evidence points to a 429 rate-limit from upstream rather than a gateway bug, so it is unresolved and worth testing.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.latencyImpact: Synchronous and on the critical path: the Jev call completes before the request is forwarded to Anthropic. The README claims 70-500 ms, but issue #24 live-measured a median 1,329 ms and max 3,938 ms per turn with OpenRouter and a 127-tool roster, and 88% of those calls were discarded for low confidence (median confidence 0.48). With ~250-tool Claude Code profiles a second shortlist Jev call is added first (tools > 120, decide.ts:136), possibly doubling this. Bench (README): Opus 5 in Claude Code on the feature task was +22% output, +61% input tokens, +83% time with routing on. On bugfix it was -7% / -22% / +2%. Sonnet 5 feature was +9/+16/+37%. Only Fable 5.1 improved on both. Benchmark sample is 5 runs per cell.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at the local gateway (via jev-claude wrapper, shell alias, or env in ~/.claude/settings.json) every /v1/messages call is routed automatically with no user prompting. However the daemon is not auto-started by Claude Code: it is started only by the jev-claude launcher (or `jev-claude --start`). Truly automatic use needs a wrapper alias for claude or a SessionStart hook plus systemd user unit, otherwise ECONNREFUSED. It steers next-tool choice only. It does not give Claude Code any new capability, and Claude may ignore the hint.
pros: Only candidate that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: transparent proxy, zero context cost, no MCP tools or hooks, so it does not clash with the existing gitnexus/playwright/caveman/secret-guard setup.

OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (providers.json:105-111, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, typesafe/jev-1.13) and issue #24 shows it live with Claude Code; setting JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is all that is needed.

Designed around Claude Code constraints: hint mode when thinking or cache_control is present, never direct-answers when thinking is on (decide.ts:197), hint is appended after the cached prefix, and it keeps the OAuth login (only ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set, ~/.claude untouched).

Robust fail-open engineering with tests: 20 test files covering failopen, router, messages, and CI on Node 22.15 and 24 with SHA-pinned actions, plus a dry-run /router/decide, routing on/off toggle and a dashboard for A/B token comparison.

Small, readable codebase (about 3.2k lines TS, 2 runtime deps), MIT, no postinstall/telemetry, npm trusted publishing, key stored 0600. Easy to audit and to fork/patch (e.g. add a confidence-based or timeout tweak).
cons: Value for Opus 5.5 is unproven and possibly negative: the project's own benchmark shows Opus 5 in Claude Code +22% output tokens and +83% time on the feature task and only marginal gains on bugfix. Only Fable 5.1 clearly improved, and the README itself says expect better tool picks, not lower cost or latency.

Adds real latency on the critical path on every tool-bearing turn: issue #24 measured 1.3 s median (up to 3.9 s) with ~34k input tokens per Jev call, 88% of results thrown away as low confidence. Worst-case fail-open delay is about 8 s (4 s timeout x2 attempts).

Data egress is broad: conversation text, bash commands, file contents from tool results and full tool descriptions go to OpenRouter on nearly every turn, which matters for client projects and bypasses the local secret-leak guard's intent. Would need a per-project opt-out (x-jev-gateway: off header or a scoped env) for client repos.

Not integrated as a Claude Code plugin/hook: requires a background daemon that only the jev-claude wrapper starts, and a settings.json ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with no daemon means every request fails (ECONNREFUSED). Needs your own systemd user service or launcher alias, and the OAuth bearer transits an unauthenticated localhost port.

Immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 74 commits, 54 by one author, 0.5.0, open issues include #37 (Claude Code compacts/disconnects on large tool roster, unresolved), #40 (hint disguised as a harness <\system-reminder>, a prompt-injection-style trust channel), and #24 (cost of roster re-send). OpenRouter endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha) and the README admits OpenRouter path was tested only with mocks in the README. The advertised 250-tool MCP roster triggers a two-stage (shortlist then decide) call.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.verdict: Technically the best fit for 'automatic, never say use jev' since it is a transparent local proxy with OpenRouter support, fail-open behaviour and zero context cost, but its own benchmarks and issue #24 show it is slower and no cheaper for Opus 5 in Claude Code (hint-only, 1.3 s per turn, 88% discarded), so treat it as an opt-in experiment behind a wrapper with routing off for client repos, not a default. Measure with `jev-claude --routing off/on` and the dashboard before adopting.
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.install: npm install -g jev-gateway (npm 0.5.0, Node >=22.15), then run `jev-claude`; the first run asks for provider (choose OpenRouter) and key, saved to ~/.jev-gateway/.env. To make plain `claude` use it, `jev-claude --start` plus env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8789 in settings.json (`--print-config`).
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.runtime: Node.js >=22.15 (TypeScript compiled to dist/, Hono + @hono/node-server), background daemon
gh-vinilana-jev-gateway.tests: 20 vitest files (about 3.4k lines: failopen, router, messages, responses, opencode, gemini, kilo, launcher, setup, usage, dashboard, exa fuzz, wire) using fake Jev and provider transports; CI runs typecheck, test, build and npm pack --dry-run on Node 22.15 and 24; I did not execute any of them. Real-API verification is partial per README (TypeSafe and OpenCode verified, OpenRouter path only mocked per README although issue #24 shows live use); Gemini path is unit-tested only.

gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.name: valentynkit/jev-belay
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin with one Stop hook (node belay.mjs, zero dependencies). At the end of each turn it reads the local transcript slice since the last user prompt and uses regex belts to detect (a) file edits and (b) a passing test/build/lint runner. Only if files changed and no check passed afterwards does it make one Jev System One call (4 questions: claims_done, claims_verified, verification_applies, outcome). If Jev says the closing message is an unverified "done", it exits 2 with a reason on stderr, so Claude keeps working and runs the tests. It fails open on every error. Also ships shadow mode, a decision log, a TUI (watch/stats/last/doctor) and two skills (why, doctor).

providerSupport.evidence: belay.mjs:500 `const base = env.JEV_BASE_URL || "https://api.typesafe.ai"`; belay.mjs:501 key = option(env,"TYPESAFE_API_KEY","TYPESAFE_API_KEY","JEV_API_KEY"); belay.mjs:503 `Authorization: Bearer ${key}`; belay.mjs:504 body {model: env.JEV_MODEL || MODEL, state, questions}; belay.mjs:510 POST `${base}/v1/systemone`; belay.mjs:18 MODEL default "jev-1.13.0" (TypeSafe-native ID). No OpenRouter string anywhere in code or README. Test test/client.test.mjs:29 asserts url = base + /v1/systemone. OpenRouter docs (via web search: openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk) say the SDK appends /v1/systemone to base https://openrouter.ai/api, same body (model, state, questions), Bearer OpenRouter key, model typesafe/jev-1.13.
providerSupport.others: JEV_BASE_URL can point at any shim (tools/fake-jev.mjs for tests).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only, no code change: set JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or JEV_API_KEY), set JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Path /v1/systemone and Bearer auth already match OpenRouter's System One API. Caveats: the response shape parsed is answers.<q>.noul / answers.<q>.choice+confidence/probabilities (belay.mjs decide()); OpenRouter is documented as near-identical but I could not verify byte-level response parity from OpenRouter docs. The README's calibration numbers were measured on jev-1.13.0 direct, not the OpenRouter route. With the plugin userConfig, the field is named typesafe_api_key, so env-block setup is simpler for an OpenRouter key. Note runHook lets the hook run with JEV_BASE_URL set even without a key (belay.mjs:693), harmless.

security: API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header via fetch (belay.mjs:503); not in argv or process list. Plugin userConfig marks it sensitive (Keychain). Manual setup puts it plaintext in settings.json env block.
Zero npm dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh installer, no child_process/exec/spawn in belay.mjs (grep found none); static-only audit, I did not run anything.

Outbound payload is redacted before sending (belay.mjs:52-76 SECRET_RULES: private keys, Authorization/bearer, api_key/password/token=..., URL creds, sk-, ghp_, npm_, AKIA, xox, AIza, JWT), home dir rewritten to ~. Regex redaction is best-effort, so secrets pasted in prose prompts could still slip through.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompt and final assistant message go into Jev state; Jev returns only typed probabilities (no free text), so output cannot inject instructions. The nudge text is fixed template plus the failed check command string from the transcript.
Writes only under ~/.claude/belay (sessions/*.json always; decisions.jsonl only if log=on, 5 MB rotate). Decision log stores task and final_message text locally.
No telemetry beyond the Jev call. Endpoint overridable via JEV_BASE_URL (whoever controls that env controls where prompts go).
Single author, no independent review; 20 stars. Plugin install requires trusting the marketplace repo (hook runs arbitrary node code with user privileges on every Stop).
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.dataEgress: Per gated stop only: user task text (first 1500 chars of the last prompt, redacted), the assistant's closing message (last 2000 chars, redacted), file_changes count, and a list of check commands with passed/failed (e.g. "npm test -> passed"). No diffs, file contents, tool outputs or paths beyond ~ (belay.mjs buildState 465-478; README 'What leaves your machine'). Model and question definitions are also sent. Stops with no edits or with a passing check make no network call. Client-work risk: the user's prompts and Claude's summaries can contain client names, code identifiers, and business detail, and they would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe on ~18% of turns (author's corpus). Redaction is regex only.
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. No key, unparseable payload, no readable transcript, gate says nothing to check, network error, HTTP error, garbage answer, or any uncaught exception all lead to exit 0 (belay.mjs main() catch, runHook returns). Retries up to 3 attempts with 600ms*2^n backoff on 429/5xx inside one shared budget, default 20000 ms (JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS), under the hook timeout of 25 s. So a hung Jev/OpenRouter can stall the end of a turn for up to about 20 s before failing open. stdin read timeout 10 s. Loop protection: stop_hook_active, one block per prompt, 60 s cooldown, max 3 blocks per session, host cap of 8. Recommend lowering JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS to about 5000 for OpenRouter.
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no MCP server instructions, no tool-definition tokens. Two skills (why, doctor) add only two short description lines to the skill listing (about 30 tokens). The hook injects text into context only on a block: about 90 tokens (the nudge, roughly 350 chars) at most 3 times per session. Silent otherwise (exit 0 with no output unless shadow mode or DEBUG).
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook, fired by the harness on every turn end with no model discretion and no need for the user to say anything. Jev is consulted automatically, but only on turns where files changed and no passing check followed (author measured 17.7% of stops).
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.latencyImpact: Zero on ~82% of stops (local transcript read only, plus a 300 ms flush wait on older hosts that lack last_assistant_message; Claude Code 2.1.285 sends it). On the gated ~18%: about 350 ms median, 433 ms p90 (author-measured direct to TypeSafe; via OpenRouter expect a bit more), worst case about 20 s if the endpoint hangs. When it blocks, Claude does an extra test-run round trip, which is the intended cost.
pros: Truly automatic: a Stop hook, so the user never prompts for Jev; matches the requirement exactly.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to (typed noul/choice decisions with calibrated probabilities, no free text), with code owning thresholds and evidence, so Jev is not asked to reason.
Same wire format as OpenRouter's System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone, Bearer, {model,state,questions}), so OpenRouter works by three env vars, no fork needed.
Very cheap and low overhead: about $0.00005 per gated stop, no network on ~82% of stops, zero context tokens from tool definitions.
Fail-open by design with loop caps (1 per prompt, 60 s cooldown, 3 per session); a wrong call costs one extra test run.
Zero dependencies, no exec/spawn, no postinstall, readable 800-line single file; 13 test files run offline against a fake Jev, CI matrix Node 20/22.

Shadow mode plus decision log and stats let the user trial it for a week with no behavioral change; complements rather than collides with the existing PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus hooks (different event).
Egress is narrow and documented (prompt, closing message, counts), with redaction before send, better than any tool that ships diffs or file contents.
Useful for the user's Opus 5.5 in bypass/auto mode, where nobody watches each turn and false 'tests pass' claims are the main risk.
cons: Very new (created 2026-09-18, 12 days old, 37 commits in 3 days, single author, 20 stars, 2 forks, 0.2.0), so it is likely to churn.
Only ONE use case (unverified-done gating); it does not give Claude general access to Jev for routing, classification or other decisions. It is a narrow win, not 'Jev integrated in Claude Code'.

OpenRouter path is not implemented or tested by the author: default is api.typesafe.ai, model pin jev-1.13.0 must be overridden to typesafe/jev-1.13, and the key env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY (an OpenRouter key goes in a misnamed variable). The README AUROC 0.976 was measured on a TypeSafe direct call on n=100 with 12 positives and proxy labels from Sonnet (wide CI 0.915-1.0).

Sends the user's prompt and Claude's closing message off machine on ~18% of turns; for client projects this is a confidentiality issue and redaction is regex-only. Could be mitigated by a per-project disable, but the hook has no per-repo allowlist (only the global key/plugin toggle).
Misses read-only turns (no edits, so no check) and custom test scripts unless the check regex is set; only one of four thresholds is empirically swept.
Hung endpoint can hold the end of a turn up to ~20 s (default budget) before failing open; needs JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS tuning.

The plugin's install instructions use the plugin marketplace, which pulls third-party code executed on every Stop; with bypass permissions on, pin a commit SHA or vendor and read it. I did not run it.

Redundant with the user's own habit or a plain command hook running tests; the value depends on whether Opus 5.5 actually falsely claims done (unknown), and only about 8% of turns get blocked in the author's corpus.
Beta model with skeptic claims that Jev is a router in disguise; the hook's value rests on Jev calibration being real, which only the author's small corpus supports.
gh-valentynkit-jev-belay.verdict: Best-fit auto-invoked Jev integration seen so far for daily coding: a deterministic, fail-open, dependency-free Stop hook that already speaks the OpenRouter System One wire format, so it works with OPENROUTER_API_KEY through JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 and a lowered timeout. It is a narrow single-purpose guard from a 12-day-old solo repo, so run it in shadow mode first, pin a commit, and disable it on confidential client repos.

gh-kevnk-jev-claude-statusline.name: kevnk/jev-claude-statusline
gh-kevnk-jev-claude-statusline.whatItDoes: Claude Code status-line add-on. A Node hook (hooks/jev-progress.mjs, 328 lines) runs on UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse and Stop. It builds a small state object (task text, last 15 tool summaries, latest assistant message, turn status) and POSTs it to Jev System One with three questions: phase (Score 0-5), done (Noul) and waiting_on_user (Noul). Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command, edit content and the last assistant message are sent as 'state' to Jev. Injected text can try to sway the verdict, but Jev returns only typed values, which limits the impact. Rules are checked by a model whose fail-open behaviour means an attacker who crashes or slows the verifier removes enforcement.

Unpinned trust: plugin auto-loads from GitHub main. A 1-star, 1-commit, 1-author repo could push a malicious hook update that runs with hook privileges. The hook runs arbitrary node code on every tool call.
/jevguard:rule is model-invocable and can edit rules.json, so the agent could weaken its own rules. Only pause/resume/init are blocked from model invocation.
Without a configured key it sends no Authorization header, gets a 401 and fails open silently, so it can look like it is protecting when it is not.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.dataEgress: To the configured base URL (OpenRouter after switching): rule text (instructions and criteria) plus the full state of each matching event. For scope bash that is the entire Bash command string, including any inline secrets or tokens. For scope edit it is the full tool_input, meaning entire Write file contents, Edit old_string and new_string, and file paths. For scope response it is the entire last assistant message. Scope 'other' tools (Read, Grep, MCP calls) send their tool_input only when a rule has scope 'all'. File contents returned by Read are not sent (PreToolUse only). Nothing is redacted or truncated (verify.ts and hook.ts), and this includes client project code, so it needs client consent. It also bypasses nothing in the existing secret-leak guard, but that guard only protects reads, not what this hook forwards. Requests to OpenRouter are also seen by OpenRouter and TypeSafe, per their retention policies.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.failureMode: Fail-open on errors: main().catch writes {} to stdout and the reason to stderr, and the exit code is 0 (bin/jevguard-hook.ts:37-40). HTTP errors, 401s, parse errors and answer-type mismatches all allow the call (verify.ts:63). BUT there is no fetch timeout or AbortSignal (grep found none). A hung or slow connection stalls every tool call until Claude Code's own hook timeout kills the process, which is long by default. A killed hook is treated as a non-blocking error, so the call proceeds, but only after that delay. No retry. If the rules file is invalid, the parse error is thrown inside main and swallowed, also fail-open. Pause is done by the flag file .jevguard/paused.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Skills add four descriptions, about 150-250 tokens in total, and init/pause/resume are excluded from model invocation. The hook injects text only when a rule warns (additionalContext) or denies (reason string), which is a few lines. No server 'instructions'. Rule-block reasons and warnings are the only in-context cost, but repeated denial-retry loops can waste turns.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.latencyImpact: Cold node start (about 50-100 ms, estimated) on every tool call, since the hook has no matcher. If no rule applies to the scope, it returns without any network call (verify.ts:70). For Bash/Edit/Write with rules, one blocking round trip to OpenRouter on each call (claimed 70-500 ms plus network). Over a day of hundreds of tool calls that adds up to minutes. Stop adds one more call per turn. There is no local cache, no async mode, and no timeout cap.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse and Stop are registered by hooks/hooks.json and fire without any prompting. The user never has to mention Jev. Only setup (key/URL, /jevguard:init per project) is manual.
pros: Only candidate here that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: a real PreToolUse/Stop hook backed by Jev, not a tool the model must choose to call.
Uses the exact OpenRouter System One contract; OpenRouter works by changing two env vars plus the model string, with no fork required (client.ts:42, config.ts:23-27).
Batches all rules into a single Jev request and skips the network call entirely when no rule matches the scope (verify.ts:70).
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions.
Fail-open on every error path, so an OpenRouter outage will not brick the session (bin/jevguard-hook.ts:37-40, verify.ts:63).
Key handling is sound: sensitive userConfig in the keychain, never in project files, and the design explicitly keeps it out of argv.
Per-project pause, and per-rule action of block, warn or off; rules are human-readable and diffable in .jevguard/rules.json.
MIT licence, small (about 400 LOC of source), easy to audit and to fork with a timeout added.
cons: Very immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 2 stars, created 2026-09-21, no releases, no CI. Auto-updating a hook from an unpinned GitHub source that runs on every tool call is a supply-chain risk for client work; fork and pin a commit instead.

Exfiltrates full Bash commands, entire Write/Edit contents and the last assistant message to a third party, unredacted. That is a problem for client projects with NDA or code-confidentiality terms. The secret-leak guard does not cover it.
No fetch timeout (no AbortSignal in source). An OpenRouter stall delays every Bash/Edit/Write call until Claude Code's hook timeout, so 'fail-open' is only eventual.
PreToolUse has no matcher, so a node process starts on every tool call including Read/Grep/MCP, even though it exits early when no rule applies.
Adds a network round trip to every Bash/Edit/Write call under bypass or auto mode. The value is a guardrail (rule adherence), not an improvement to coding quality or speed.

Judgment quality is unproven. Rules are passed as prose instructions, Jev has no reasoning, and the thresholds are crude (noul >= 0.5). Expect false-positive denies that make the agent retry, burning tokens. Skeptics call Jev a small-model router.
Stop hook does not check stop_hook_active, so a block on Stop can loop; the default is warn but that warn output shape (hookSpecificOutput additionalContext on Stop) is likely ignored by Claude Code.
README references build-docs/ and a ~/.claude/plans path that are not in the repo, and it says PostToolUse is handled, but the hook is not registered. Small signs of an early draft.
Overlaps with, and adds another blocking hook next to, the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Ordering and combined latency are unknown.
Needs per-project /jevguard:init and rule curation, and /jevguard:rule is model-invocable so the agent can edit its own rules. Silent no-op without a key.
gh-jhonnyr97-jevguard.verdict: The only reviewed integration that is actually automatic, and it works with OpenRouter by setting two env vars and jev.model=typesafe/jev-latest, but it is a 1-commit proof of concept that streams your commands and edited code to a third party with no timeout or redaction. Worth using only from a fork pinned to a commit, with a fetch timeout and rules narrowed to bash/edit, and probably only on personal projects.

gh-qkal-canny.name: qkal/Canny (canny-warden)
gh-qkal-canny.whatItDoes: Supervision layer for Claude Code and Codex CLI built purely from hooks (zero runtime deps, plain Node ESM, compiled dist committed). Keeps an append-only ledger of edits and commands under ~/.canny/sessions. A deterministic Stop hook blocks the agent from finishing when code files changed but no test/build/lint check has passed since the last edit. Pattern checks deny secret-shaped strings on write, ask on test removal or skips, and rewrite `npm test | tail` to run with pipefail. Jev is used only as an optional advisor through the Noul (yes/no) primitive. (1) After each edit, one Noul per project rule (bullets extracted from CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, up to 24) asks whether the diff breaks it; a p>=0.9 yes becomes an additionalContext note. (2) At Stop, when unverified edits exist, one Noul asks whether the final message claims the work is done; p<=0.1 can only relax the block. Jev never blocks anything itself. Answers are cached by content hash on disk and logged so `canny replay` is offline and deterministic.

interface.purpose: Uninstall, hash-trust .canny.json (the verify, ignore, rules and allow fields are inert until trusted), inspect the ledger, offline re-derivation of Stop verdicts, and the hook entrypoint that reads one event on stdin.

gh-qkal-canny.install: No npm package. Clone https://github.com/qkal/canny to ~/.canny/src (the compiled dist/ is committed), then run `node ~/.canny/src/dist/cli.js init --global`, which writes to ~/.claude/settings.json (or run `init` in a single project). The README's default path is a 'paste this prompt to your agent' install. Requires Node >= 22, and the user has Node 24. Then set CANNY_JEV_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, CANNY_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> in the Claude Code environment. Pin a reviewed commit rather than tracking `git pull --ff-only` on main.
gh-qkal-canny.runtime: Node >= 22 (TypeScript compiled to committed dist/*.js, ESM, zero runtime dependencies, devDependencies only). One short-lived `node dist/cli.js hook --agent claude` process per hook event.
gh-qkal-canny.tests: Vitest with 12 test files (hook, checks, events, ledger, jev with mocked fetch, install, cli e2e via the real child process, robustness sweep over malformed payloads, ReDoS guard, and real Claude Code and Codex fixture payloads with snapshots). Coverage thresholds are enforced in CI (lines 97, branches 90). CI runs static gates, a Node 22/24/26 matrix, a smoke test, weekly cron, a `git diff --exit-code dist` check so the committed dist matches the source, and CodeQL. There is also a bench harness (5 tasks). The README's own A/B result shows no measurable outcome improvement (25 of 25 passes in both arms) and admits benefit is unmeasured. The Jev path has no test against the live endpoint.
security: API key handling: read from an env var and sent in the Authorization header only (src/jev.ts:88-96). It is never in argv or the process list, and the hook command line holds only the node path plus `hook --agent claude`.

No telemetry and no other network calls. fetch appears only in src/jev.ts. The only child process is `git check-ignore` with a 2s timeout (src/checks.ts:178). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no npm dependency chain. The install is a git clone that runs the committed compiled dist/, so the supply-chain risk is trusting the author's repo and pulling main.

The README install is 'paste a prompt into your agent', which is a prompt-injection-shaped habit. Clone and init manually, and review dist/ at a pinned commit. dist is committed and CI verifies it matches src, but that is only as strong as the repo owner.

Local plaintext storage. ~/.canny/sessions ledgers hold full command lines, and the README admits a secret on a command line lands in the ledger. ~/.canny/jev/<hash>.json caches the full request body, meaning clipped diffs up to 4000 chars per side plus the agent's final message, in plaintext at mode 0600 (dir 0700). Client code therefore persists on disk.

The hook rewrites Bash commands (updatedInput) and can deny or ask. This is a large behavioural surface layered on the user's existing PreToolUse hooks, with unknown ordering and merge semantics when multiple hooks return updatedInput or decisions.
The .canny.json trust model is a speed bump. The loosening fields are inert until `canny trust`, keyed by content hash, but the README concedes that an agent with shell access can run trust itself.

Jev output is treated as untrusted advisory, and only p>=0.9 or p<=0.1 is acted on. Notes are a fixed template that includes the rule text from CLAUDE.md, so the prompt-injection surface is small. The rule text and diff are user or repo content sent to the model as `state`, not executed.
The repo is 19 days old, has effectively a single author, and is not on npm. Bus-factor and stability risk.
gh-qkal-canny.dataEgress: With a key set: (a) after every Edit, Write, or shell-written file, for each changed file not matching config ignore, the state {rules[] (up to 24 bullets extracted from CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md), change:{file relative path, added text clipped to 4000 chars, removed text clipped to 4000 chars}} plus one question per rule goes to the endpoint, which would be OpenRouter, which forwards to TypeSafe. (b) At Stop, only when code was edited and no check has passed, the agent's final assistant message goes as {message}. Not sent: prompts, whole files, Read or Grep outputs, or tool results (src/hook.ts:194-232). Without a key, nothing leaves the machine. Requests are skipped when no rules are found (`if (!rules) return allow`), when the file matches ignore, or when allow:['rules'] is set, but those fields need `canny trust`. This is real client code egress to a third party for the rule check. It can be constrained by allow:['rules'], which leaves only the Stop message, or by adding `ignore` regexes for client repos.
gh-qkal-canny.failureMode: Fail-open on all Jev failures. There is no key, or an HTTP non-2xx, a timeout (AbortSignal.timeout of 3000ms by default, configurable via CANNY_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), or a network error. Each returns null (src/jev.ts:89,102,112-122), the error is logged to the ledger, and the deterministic rules stand alone. A crash anywhere in the hook is caught, logged to ~/.canny/errors.log, and answers `{}`, so Canny cannot block the user (src/cli.ts:86-98). The hook timeouts are 10s for PreToolUse and 15s for PostToolUse and Stop. The deterministic Stop block is by design fail-closed when there are unverified code edits, and it is capped by Claude Code at 8 consecutive blocks and relaxes on a repeated Stop unless strict is set. That block does not depend on Jev.
gh-qkal-canny.contextCost: No MCP tools, so no tool-definition or server-instruction tokens. Five hook events are registered. Always injected: the SessionStart note, about 60-80 words or ~100 tokens per session. Conditional injections: a rule-violation note per broken rule (~50-150 tokens, only when Jev p>=0.9), a repeat-failure note, a pipefail-rewrite additionalContext line (~30 tokens each time the agent pipes a check into tail), and the Stop block reason (~80 tokens, plus one extra turn when the agent has not run checks). Overall it is very low context cost and never bloats the tool list.
gh-qkal-canny.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop) run on every relevant event with no model discretion and no need for the user to say 'use jev'. This is the strongest fit for the 'automatic, never prompted' requirement. However, Jev's role inside the hooks is narrow: two fixed Noul questions, and the Jev call only happens when rules exist or the Stop is unverified.
gh-qkal-canny.latencyImpact: Node cold start plus ledger I/O is about 40ms per hook call (README claim, plausible for zero-dep Node). Every edit, write, and shell call triggers PreToolUse plus PostToolUse processes, so roughly 80ms of overhead per tool call even without Jev. The Jev rule check awaits inside PostToolUse, in parallel across changed files: about 70-500ms claimed per call on a miss, hard capped at 3s (the default timeout), and 0ms on a cache hit. The tool result is delayed by that wait on every edit and shell-written file when CLAUDE.md has rules. If OpenRouter is slow, each edit can stall 3s, and the timeout is per request rather than per turn. The Stop-time call happens only on an unverified stop. Expect ~0.3-0.6s added per edit when the API is healthy.
pros: It is the only candidate here that gives truly automatic Jev use with zero prompting: registered hooks fire on every edit and Stop, and Jev is called without model discretion (src/install.ts:58-62, src/hook.ts:185-233).

Jev is used in the 'right' System One way: narrow atomic Noul questions, thresholds at 0.9 and 0.1 that are wider than the ~0.05 drift, and a content-hash cache so identical inputs give identical answers (src/jev.ts:11-13,39-41,77-87). It can never block on Jev alone.

OpenRouter switch is config-only: request and response shape match OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone OpenAPI example (state, model, questions with type noul, and answers[id].noul). Only the key variable name is hard-coded to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which can be set in the Claude env block.

Fail-open everywhere on the Jev path (3s timeout, errors logged, null answers), and a hook crash returns {} so it cannot brick the session (src/cli.ts:86-98). Jev-down means the deterministic guard still works.

Actually useful for daily coding regardless of Jev: a done-gate that catches 'Done' with no test run, test-skip and removal guard, and a pipefail rewrite for `| tail`. Fits Opus in auto or bypass mode, where nobody watches every step.
Zero runtime dependencies, no telemetry, no postinstall, one fetch call site, and a small readable codebase (about 2,000 lines of TS) that is easy to audit and fork.

Testing above its age: 12 test files, coverage gates, CodeQL, dist-drift check in CI, real Claude Code and Codex payload fixtures. It also honestly reports that its own bench showed no outcome change and only avoided overhead.

Per-project .canny.json (verify, ignore, rules, allow:['rules']) lets you turn off code egress for client repos while keeping the deterministic gates. It also has an SessionStart hook that tells the agent the rule up front, which avoids wasted blocked turns.
cons: Jev is a minor, optional part. All blocking is deterministic and works without any key, so Canny does not deliver 'Jev deeply integrated into Claude Code'. It adds a rule-violation note and one relax-only claims_done check.

It sends real code diffs (up to 4000 chars per side per file per edit) and the final message to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every edit, and caches them in plaintext under ~/.canny/jev. That is a serious concern for client projects, so you would need allow:['rules'] or ignore lists, which themselves need `canny trust` per repo.

The rule check fires up to 24 Noul questions per edited file, derived from heuristically extracted bullets in CLAUDE.md. Your global CLAUDE.md has many instruction-like bullets, so quality and hit rate are uncertain and there is no evidence of value. The README says the effect on agent quality is unmeasured, and Jev is unverified in this role.

Stacks a lot of hooks on top of yours. It registers PreToolUse and PostToolUse on the edit and shell tools, which overlaps with the existing secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) and GitNexus (Grep|Glob|Bash pre and post), and it rewrites Bash commands through updatedInput. Interaction and ordering with other updatedInput or additionalContext hooks is untested, so there is a real chance of conflict.

The Stop-block can add extra turns and tokens on Opus 5.5 subscription usage, and its ledger heuristics (regex-based shell parsing) can misjudge. The README itself lists commands it does not see (xargs rm, python -c writes) and its 'ask' decisions may behave differently in bypass or auto permission mode (not verified).

The OpenRouter key must be stuffed into TYPESAFE_API_KEY because the variable name is hard-coded. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support, no live-endpoint test, and the README explicitly notes the Jev half is built against docs and mocks.

Young and single-author: 23 commits over 19 days, 106 stars, not on npm, and installed by a 'paste this prompt to your agent' flow with `git pull --ff-only` updates from main. That is a supply-chain and stability risk unless pinned to a commit.
Latency is added on every edit and shell tool call: two Node process spawns (~80ms) plus up to a 3s Jev wait per edit when OpenRouter is slow, and the wait is not bounded per turn.
Claude Code 2.1.285 was not verified against it. Fixtures come from an unspecified older Claude Code version and the bench used 2.1.278.
gh-qkal-canny.verdict: Canny is the only audited option that uses Jev truly automatically, through deterministic hooks with fail-open behaviour, and it is config-only to point at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (URL, model and the key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY). But Jev only adds a small advisory layer to a mostly non-Jev done-gate, and every edit's diff leaves the machine and is cached in plaintext, which is risky for client repos. Adopt it as a pinned, per-project or personal-project guard with allow:['rules'] for client work, and watch for hook conflicts with your existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
