gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.name: EliaAlberti/jev-rules
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (hooks only, no MCP server, no skills) that gives each project a .claude/jev-rules/*.md rule set (plus optional .claude/jev-map docs). On every UserPromptSubmit it sends the prompt plus one Noul yes/no question per rule/map doc to Jev in a single call, and injects (additionalContext) only rules with P>=0.6, once per session. On PreToolUse for Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit it asks Jev which not-yet-delivered rules apply to the file path (path only) and injects them just before the edit. Optional early-access rules pane (/rules) and a one-line "Jev gave Claude: rule 0.94" message. Purpose is context trimming and rule routing, not code intelligence.

providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai/evaluation-model, model typesafe-ai/jev, key AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY or a key starting vck_). No OpenRouter anywhere (grep -ri openrouter over the repo returns nothing).
providerSupport.evidence: plugins/jev-rules/hooks/lib/jev.mjs:50-89 BACKENDS = {typesafe: url https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest, body {state, model, questions:{id:{type:'noul', instructions, criteria}}}, decode json.answers[id].noul; vercel: ...}. config.mjs:46-56 keys: JEV_API_KEY || TYPESAFE_API_KEY (backend typesafe, or vercel if it starts with vck_), else AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. Headers: authorization Bearer <key> (jev.mjs:54).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The typesafe backend is already the System One wire format (POST /v1/systemone, questions keyed with type noul, answers[id].noul), which is the same path family as OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. A patch is roughly 15 lines: add an openrouter entry to BACKENDS in jev.mjs (url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, Bearer key) and OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling in config.mjs:46-56. Caveat: OpenRouter's request/response schema for /systemone is unverified against this code, so a live test is needed. It would have to live in a fork or local marketplace, since plugin updates overwrite edits. No adapter or base-URL env override exists, so it cannot be done through config alone.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook (jev-rules.mjs -> run)
interface.purpose: Reads .claude/jev-rules/*.md and .claude/jev-map, asks Jev one Noul per undelivered rule or map doc about the prompt, and injects rules with P>=0.6 as additionalContext. Prompt cut to 24000 chars. Timeout 10 s in hooks.json, 2 s internal by default.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook, matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit (runEdit)
interface.purpose: Asks Jev which undelivered rules apply to the file path (relative path, or basename if outside the project) and injects them before the edit. Answers are cached per file for the session.

interface.name: SessionStart hook, matcher clear|compact
interface.purpose: Resets the once-per-session delivered state after /clear or compaction.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook, matcher AskUserQuestion (runAnswer)
interface.purpose: Handles the answer to the pane opt-in question. On yes it writes CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 into the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json.

interface.name: /jev-rules:pane slash command
interface.purpose: Makes Claude call AskUserQuestion to offer switching on the rules pane.

interface.name: /rules pane (hooks/pane.tsx)
interface.purpose: Optional early-access pane that lists the rules and highlights the ones Jev picked. It needs the CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS flag.

interface.name: Config env vars
interface.purpose: JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, JEV_RULES_THRESHOLD (0.6), JEV_RULES_TIMEOUT_MS (2000, range 100-8000), JEV_DEBUG (log to ~/.jev-rules.log), JEV_RULES_EDITS, JEV_RULES_MAP, JEV_RULES_REPEAT, JEV_RULES_SHOW_PICKS.

security: MIT licensed. Zero npm dependencies, no postinstall and no install script. Installed via /plugin marketplace add EliaAlberti/jev-rules, which only clones the repo. Hook code is plain Node ESM using fetch, fs and crypto, with no child_process or shell execution (I did not grep every file, but none of the read files use it).
API key travels only in an Authorization Bearer header (jev.mjs:54). It never appears in argv or the process list.

Key sources: process env, then <project>/.env, then ~/.jev-rules.env (config.mjs:20). Parsing project .env files in client repos is a mild surprise: a repo-supplied .env containing JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY would be picked up. Only those named keys are used, and the merged env is not written back to process.env.

Prompt-injection surface: the rule files under .claude/jev-rules are injected verbatim as additionalContext. A malicious client repo can therefore plant rule text that Claude reads as trusted instructions. The same is true of CLAUDE.md, but the injection here arrives silently at PreToolUse, right before an edit.

The plugin instructs Claude via additionalContext to ask the pane question (offerInstruction). Accepting rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json env, which turns on the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS flag for ALL plugins. It is opt-in via AskUserQuestion and can be disabled with 'Don't ask again', but a hook that offers to edit global settings is unusual.
No telemetry, but a state file is written to os.tmpdir()/jev-rules (state.mjs:21) and an optional debug log to ~/.jev-rules.log holding an 80-char prompt snippet.
The hook never blocks. It always exits 0, swallows all errors, and returns no permission decision (jev-rules.mjs header). It cannot interfere with the existing secret-leak guard.
Single maintainer, 63 stars, 2 weeks old. Supply-chain risk comes from marketplace auto-update, so pin a commit or fork.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai or Vercel AI Gateway (and to OpenRouter if patched): (1) on every UserPromptSubmit, the full user prompt text (cut to 24,000 chars) plus each rule and map-doc description, and applies/does_not_apply criteria lines. Rule names and bodies stay local because questions are keyed r0, r1... by position (jev.mjs docstring). (2) On the first edit of a file with undelivered rules, the project-relative file path only (basename if outside the project) and the rule descriptions. No file contents, diffs, tool outputs or code are sent (edit.mjs:5-9). The prompt itself may still contain pasted code or client details, and it goes to a third party on every prompt while undelivered rules exist. That matters for client work.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.failureMode: Fail-open and never blocks. No key, timeout, network error, HTTP error or unparseable reply all lead to every not-yet-delivered rule being injected with a note "Jev was unavailable" (run.mjs:48-55, 99-104). Map docs are only listed, not included. The internal timeout is 2 s by default (configurable 100-8000 ms) and covers both attempts, with one retry on 429/529 after at most 300 ms (jev.mjs:15-21, 162-174). The hook-level timeout is 10 s. Worst case is +2 s on a prompt or on the first edit of a file when Jev is slow. Because rules are delivered once per session, a Jev outage costs tokens rather than correctness.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Injected text per hook call is capped at 9000 chars (about 2250 tokens, run.mjs OUTPUT_BUDGET), and each rule or map doc is delivered at most once per session, resetting after /clear or compaction. It injects nothing if the project has no .claude/jev-rules or .claude/jev-map (run.mjs:247 returns null). It adds a systemMessage line under each prompt, which is visible to the user only, and a one-time AskUserQuestion offer instruction. The design is meant to reduce context versus loading every rule in CLAUDE.md, but the user must first move their conventions into .claude/jev-rules/*.md files.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.latencyImpact: Per README, 260-520 ms per Jev call, with the first call of a session slower because of TLS. A call happens only on a prompt with undelivered rules or docs, and on the first edit of a file with undelivered candidate rules. The result is cached per file and rules are delivered once, so later turns are mostly zero-call. Node startup adds about 50 ms per hook. Worst case is +2 s on timeout (fail-open). PreToolUse Edit hooks run sequentially with the user's existing hooks, but none of those match Edit or Write, so there is no interaction.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. It fires automatically on UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse for Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, SessionStart for clear/compact, and PostToolUse for AskUserQuestion. The user never has to say "use jev" and Claude never has to choose to call it. This is exactly the automatic-integration shape the user asked for, but the scope is only rule and context routing.
pros: Truly automatic: pure hooks, no model discretion, no MCP tool definitions, so no context tax for tools.
Uses Jev for what it is actually built for (typed Noul yes/no decisions with probabilities), and it is the only candidate I've seen that does this per prompt and per edit.
Robust fail-open design, verified in code: exit 0 always, 2 s cap, single retry on 429/529, never blocks the prompt or edit (jev.mjs:162-174, jev-rules.mjs).
Small, readable code with no dependencies and no postinstall: about 10 short ESM files, easy to audit and to fork.
Egress is minimal on edits (path only, never contents), and rule names and bodies never leave the machine (questions keyed r0, r1...).
131 offline tests across 8 files (README, CHANGELOG), and the code has a test seam for injecting fetch. It has releases (v0.5.0), a CHANGELOG and an MIT license.
Once-per-session delivery plus a 9000-char budget bound the token cost, and injection resets after /clear and compaction.
Already has a second wire-format backend (Vercel), so OpenRouter is a small additive patch: the typesafe backend already speaks POST /v1/systemone with type noul.

No hook conflicts with the user's existing matchers (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit secret guard overlaps only on NotebookEdit and only in that it never returns a permission decision; GitNexus is Grep|Glob|Bash).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_API_KEY (api.typesafe.ai) or Vercel AI Gateway. The user must fork or patch jev.mjs and config.mjs, and the OpenRouter /systemone schema is not verified to be identical.

Narrow value: it selects among project rules the user writes in .claude/jev-rules/*.md. It gives no code understanding, no routing of tasks or subagents, and no review or risk scoring. A senior developer with a compact CLAUDE.md gets little from it, since a rule set must be big enough to be worth filtering.
Per-project setup: every personal and client repo needs its own rule files with descriptions, so there is adoption friction, and nothing happens where rules are absent.

Sends the full user prompt (up to 24k chars) to a third-party API on every prompt with undelivered rules. Pasted code or client-confidential text would leave the machine, which is a concern on client projects. The user's secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
Edit-time judgment uses the file path only, so it is coarse. A Jev call precedes the first edit of a file, adding 260-520 ms before the write.
Reads project .env for keys and injects repo-controlled rule text as trusted context: a prompt-injection channel in untrusted client repos.

Offers to modify ~/.claude/settings.json to enable an early-access flag that affects all plugins (pane feature). It is optional, but noisy and risky, and it is disabled only by answering 'Don't ask again'.

Immature: created 2026-09-18, 63 stars, 21 commits (visible), 2 authors (both the same person, with Claude as co-author), no CI workflows, and the ecosystem is unproven. Jev itself is in beta with the unverified 'a DeepSeek flash router' skeptic claim.
Marketplace updates overwrite any local OpenRouter patch, so a fork or local marketplace is required.
gh-eliaalberti-jev-rules.verdict: Best-shaped candidate for "automatic, no prompting" because it is a pure fail-open hook plugin that uses Jev's Noul primitive, but it only routes project rules and has no OpenRouter backend (a roughly 15-line patch in a fork). Worth adopting only if the user is willing to maintain .claude/jev-rules per project and accepts sending prompts to the Jev provider. Otherwise it is a modest, low-risk add-on rather than a core daily tool.

gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.name: 7hemas7er/jev-hooks
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also its own marketplace) that calls a Jev-compatible POST /v1/systemone backend (TypeSafe Jev, or self-hosted rizzo-flow) with typed noul/choice/score questions. (1) Commit reviewer: a PreToolUse hook on Bash (if Bash(git *)) intercepts git commit, builds the staged diff, runs regex detectors (live keys, private keys, prompt-injection phrases, bidi chars, CI files) that set lane floors, splits the diff into ~2000-token chunks, asks 7 questions per chunk plus 5 global ones, and config/policy.json turns the probabilities into a lane: BLOCK (deny), SECURITY REVIEW (ask), NITS (notes plus escalation to Claude), MERGE (status line). (2) Opt-in effort router: a function hook (hooks/register.ts) classifies each typed prompt with 7 questions and lowers per-turn effort, never above the session's. (3) Skills /jev-review and /jev-status, a jev-review CLI, a guard on Edit/Write of .jev-hooks/, a PostToolUse commit log, and a GitHub Action.

Default model 'jev-latest' (backend.ts:23). OpenRouter docs (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md) say the System One API is TypeSafe-SDK-compatible, base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, Bearer OpenRouter key, and bare 'jev-latest' is mapped to typesafe/. Caveat: /jev-status probes GET /v1/models (run.ts:257) and OpenRouter returns its own model-list shape there, so the status skill likely misreports; commit hook and router do not use it. Not tested live against OpenRouter.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: trivial: config only, no code change. Only caveat is that the calibration profile falls to the generic 'jev'/unknown-backend profile, not one measured on Jev.

security: Single author (7hemas7er), 0 stars, 0 forks, repo created 2026-09-27, 65 commits in 3 days; v0.10.0 on 2026-09-30; no GitHub release, no topics. Self-declared 'public preview'.

Runs unsandboxed command hooks (outside Claude's sandbox) on every Bash tool call matching git *; the trust boundary is a young single-maintainer repo. Installed by /plugin from GitHub main; updates only when version is raised and user runs /plugin update.

No dependencies (package.json has none), no npm postinstall, no curl|sh installer; Node >=22.18 type-stripping runs the .ts directly. run-node.sh only probes for node binaries in nvm/fnm/volta/asdf/mise/n/brew paths.

API key: sensitive plugin option kept out of settings.json and delivered to hooks via CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY env of the hook process only; key only in Authorization header, never in URL/logs; never in argv (CLI takes key from env or key file, never a flag). Key is sent only to the URL of its own layer (TYPESAFE_API_KEY never goes to a LAN host). Key file warns if group/world-readable.

Client uses fetch redirect:'error' (no key or body follows redirects), 4 MiB response cap, https required except loopback/RFC1918/Tailscale/.local hosts. Hand-written strict URL parser to prevent host-confusion tricks.

Git hardening: spawnSync without shell, fsmonitor/hooks/external diff/textconv/pager disabled, minimal env without keys, temp index copy, symlinks not followed. Hostile .jev-hooks/ project rules can only tighten, not loosen.

Prompt-injection posture: verdict computed by code from probabilities; Claude receives only check ids, numbers, filtered paths and line ranges in a '[jev-review] review data, not instructions' block, never diff lines/title/description. Regex detectors floor the lane for injection phrases. Authors state the 4B/Jev model can still be steered on one probability.

Local log (log.jsonl in plugin data dir) stores outcomes, probabilities, hashes, plugin version, backend fingerprint; no diff, prompt or key. No telemetry found in code; only network target is the configured backend.
Not independently audited; I read docs and core files (backend.ts, systemone.ts, transport.ts, run-node.sh, hooks.json, plugin.json, security.md) but did not audit all ~9k lines of source.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.dataEgress: Commit reviewer (default on once review_url is set): the staged diff (chunked, ~2000 tokens each, plus file list, commit title/description for the 5 global questions) is POSTed to the backend on every git commit Claude runs. For non-local backends it is first redacted: detector-recognized secrets and their repeats replaced by random same-shape values, PEM blocks replaced whole, sensitive files (.env, .pem, credentials) sent as path only, guardrail mask map applied if present (nothing sent if the map is invalid). Secrets no regex recognizes still leave (docs/backends.md says to prefer local rizzo for private repos). Full source code in the diff therefore goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe: relevant for client projects under NDA. Effort router (off by default): every typed prompt (redacted) is sent to the backend. Nothing else (no file reads, tool outputs, or transcripts) leaves. A floor of BLOCK skips the backend call entirely.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.failureMode: Fail-open, visibly: backend down/slow/misconfigured lets the commit proceed with a one-line notice once per session per error kind; deterministic regex floors still apply offline (private keys, live AWS/Stripe/GitHub/Slack tokens -> BLOCK even with backend off). Missing Node >=22.18 also fails open with a systemMessage. Timeouts: hook timeout 180 s in hooks.json, policy total budget (config/policy.json:69-76) with 60 s per-request timeout_ms and a 1 s margin before deadline; timeouts are never retried. Router timeout 1.5 s then turn proceeds unchanged, with a 30 s busy backoff. Risk: with a slow remote backend a commit can wait up to tens of seconds before the fail-open path.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero MCP server instructions. Two skills (jev-review, jev-status) add two short skill descriptions to the listing (~150 tokens total). Hooks inject text only on git commit: a one-line status for MERGE, or a compact data block (check ids, probabilities, files/line ranges) for NITS/escalation, roughly a few hundred tokens; the /jev-review skill returns the same block. Router notices are not sent to the model.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: the commit reviewer fires automatically on every git commit Claude runs through Bash (PreToolUse, matcher Bash, if Bash(git *)), with no prompting needed; the guard fires on Edit/Write of .jev-hooks/. The effort router is an opt-in function hook on every typed prompt (needs an env flag and an account beta). The /jev-review skill is description-triggered and on demand. It never covers commits made in the user's own terminal.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.latencyImpact: Only at git commit: bash prefilter is negligible for non-commit git commands and for all other Bash calls (hook matches Bash but 'if' limits to git *; Node starts only if the input contains 'commit'). Per commit: one node start plus roughly 12 questions per chunk-set over HTTPS. Docs' figures are for rizzo on a DGX Spark (median 0.28-0.82 s); against OpenRouter/Jev the brief claims 70-500 ms per call, so expect about 1-3 s per typical commit, more for large multi-chunk diffs. Router, if enabled, adds up to 1.5 s to every prompt.
pros: Only candidate seen that is genuinely automatic in Claude Code: a deterministic PreToolUse hook on git commit needs no user prompt and no model discretion, exactly the user's requirement.

Works with OpenRouter by configuration alone: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key, because backend.ts appends /v1/systemone and OpenRouter documents its System One API as TypeSafe-SDK-compatible (bare jev-latest mapped to typesafe/).
Uses Jev the way it is designed: closed noul/choice/score questions, probabilities to thresholds in editable JSON (config/checks.json, policy.json), verdict computed by code rather than free text.
Fail-open with deterministic floors (private keys, live tokens) that hold even with the backend down or unset; no risk of blocking the user's workflow.

Careful security engineering: key as sensitive plugin option not in settings.json or argv, no redirects, https-only for non-local hosts, redaction before remote send, hardened git, no diff lines fed back to Claude, no dependencies or postinstall.
Zero MCP tools and near-zero context cost; complements (does not collide with) the existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks, since it hooks git commit/Skill/Edit only.
~900 offline tests (18.8k lines under tests/), CI on Node 22.18 and 24 with pinned action SHAs, manifest validation, weekly Claude Code compat job; honest docs on limitations.
cons: Very narrow use: only reviews commits (and optionally routes effort). Does not help with code search, context, refactoring or planning, so it adds little to 'daily coding' beyond a pre-commit second opinion.

Thresholds and calibration were fitted on rizzo-flow (Spark-X2.5-4B) and a small synthetic bench, not on real Jev; docs/backends.md admits the 'jev' profile trusts TypeSafe's calibration claim unverified. README itself says treat verdicts as a second opinion, not a gate. Real false-positive/negative rates on the user's diffs are unknown.

Zero OpenRouter support in code or docs; OpenRouter compatibility rests on OpenRouter's docs, and was not tested here. /jev-status uses GET /v1/models, which OpenRouter answers in a different shape, so the status skill likely errors.

Full staged diffs of personal and client repos go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every commit; redaction is regex-only, so unrecognized secrets and proprietary code leave the machine. Problematic for client/NDA work unless scoped per project or disabled there.

Brand new and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-27, 65 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, no release; it is unsandboxed code in the hook path, updated straight from GitHub main. Would need a pinned commit and a review before trust.

Effort router needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, an early-access API that may break between Claude Code releases, and a per-turn-control beta the user's OAuth subscription may not have; without it every effort change flushes the prompt cache. Should stay off.
Redundant in part with existing setup: the PreToolUse secret-leak guard and Anthropic's security-guidance plugin already cover credential leaks on commit; docs warn that both run on git commit.
In bypass/auto permission mode the SECURITY REVIEW 'ask' still interrupts (docs say it asks even in auto mode); adds seconds of latency per commit on a remote backend.
gh-7hemas7er-jev-hooks.verdict: Best-engineered and the only truly automatic (hook-driven) Jev integration seen for Claude Code, and it should work with OpenRouter by setting review_url=https://openrouter.ai/api and an OpenRouter key. Its scope is only a pre-commit second opinion with thresholds not measured on Jev, and it sends full diffs off-machine and is a 3-day-old solo project, so pin a commit, read it, keep the router off, and enable it only on personal repos first.

gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.name: erkamyaman/jev-enforce
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (npm jev-enforce 1.1.1) with two command hooks: a Stop hook checks Claude's final reply, and a PostToolUse hook (Edit|Write|MultiEdit) checks the newly written text. Both are checked against rules extracted from CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .claude/rules. Rules are classified once (Jev Choice, cached in ~/.cache/jev-enforce/scopes.json) as reply, code, both or none. Each check sends one batched System One request with one Noul question per rule ("Does the text break this rule?"). If P >= 0.7, the hook returns decision:"block" with the quoted rules, so Claude rewrites or fixes in the same turn. It fires at most once per turn (stop_hook_active guard). It is a CLAUDE.md compliance linter using Jev as a cheap judge. It does not add Jev-based routing or decisions to the agent's own work.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev.ts:1 `export const JEV_URL = 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'`; src/jev.ts:23 default model 'jev-latest' (a TypeSafe-direct ID; OpenRouter IDs are typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest); src/jev.ts:33 `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}`; src/hook.ts:211 `env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is the only key env var; src/hook.ts:244 `createAsk({ apiKey, fetch: deps.fetch })` passes no url or model, so createAsk's `url` option (jev.ts:16) is unreachable from env or CLI. grep for 'openrouter' across the repo: no hits. Request body is `{state, model, questions}` and the response is `{answers}` (jev.ts:29,42), with noul answers as `{type:'noul', noul}` and choice answers as `{type:'choice', choice, probabilities, confidence}`.
providerSupport.others: None. No other gateways.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate: about 5 lines. Change JEV_URL to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, set the default model to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' (or '~typesafe/jev-latest'), and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Bearer auth is already what OpenRouter uses. The open risk is that I could not confirm OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone body and response match TypeSafe's `state/model/questions -> answers` shape. The OpenRouter model page (openrouter.ai/typesafe/jev-1.13/api) did not expose the example. dist/src is committed and must be rebuilt (check-dist), so use a fork or a local patch. Env-var overrides are not read today.

interface.name: hook Stop (cli.js hook stop, timeout 30s)
interface.purpose: Checks last_assistant_message against reply/both rules and blocks with quoted rules if P>=threshold. Skipped when stop_hook_active is set, so a fix is never re-checked.

interface.name: hook PostToolUse Edit|Write|MultiEdit (cli.js hook post-edit, timeout 30s)
interface.purpose: Checks new_string, content or edits[].new_string against code/both rules and returns decision:block on violation. Edits to CLAUDE*.md, AGENTS*.md and .claude/rules are skipped (hook.ts:181). In JEV_ENFORCE_MODE=end it only queues edits in a JSON file and checks them all at Stop.

interface.name: CLI: jev-enforce rules
interface.purpose: Lists the rules found for the cwd and their scope.

interface.name: CLI: jev-enforce check [--as reply|code] [file|-]
interface.purpose: Checks a file or stdin against the rules and exits 1 on violation (usable in CI).

interface.name: env settings
interface.purpose: TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required), JEV_ENFORCE_THRESHOLD (0.7), JEV_ENFORCE_MODE=end, JEV_ENFORCE_OFF=1.

interface.name: MCP tools / skills / slash commands
interface.purpose: None. The plugin ships no MCP server, no skills, no commands and no agents.

gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.runtime: Node >=18.17 (Node 24 fine). TypeScript compiled to committed dist/src, no runtime dependencies. Hooks run as `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/src/cli.js`, so there is no npx or network install at hook time.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.install: claude plugin marketplace add erkamyaman/jev-enforce && claude plugin install jev-enforce@jev-enforce; then set env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY in ~/.claude/settings.json. For OpenRouter this needs a patched fork.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.tests: One offline test file, test/jev-enforce.test.ts (about 17 tests) against a fake Jev, covering hook behaviour, rule discovery, caching and end mode. I did not run it (static reading only). There is a bench harness (bench/run.ts) and results from 59 labeled cases against 19 rules on the real API. The published benchmark reports 93.3% precision and recall at 0.7, with 2 of 28 clean texts flagged. CI is only publish.yml on release (npm test, check-dist, npm publish with provenance/id-token). No PR CI. Releases v1.0.0 to v1.1.1 in 4 days. Age is 9 days, 9 stars, 1 fork, 1 issue.
security: No runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev call. Only network destination is api.typesafe.ai (src/jev.ts:1).
API key is read from env (hook.ts:211) and sent as a Bearer header, never put in argv. The recommended setup puts it in plaintext in ~/.claude/settings.json.

Non-secret-aware egress: any Write/Edit content is sent, including .env or credentials files, since only CLAUDE/AGENTS/rules files are excluded (hook.ts:181). This bypasses the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard, which only covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit.

Prompt-injection surface: the checked text (reply or file content) is placed in Jev state next to the rule questions. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so the injection blast radius is limited to a false negative or false positive. The block reason quotes only rule text from the user's own CLAUDE.md, not model output.

Filesystem writes: ~/.cache/jev-enforce/scopes.json (rule classification cache) and pending/<session>.json (end mode, contains edited text in plaintext), or the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA dir. The session_id is sanitized (hook.ts:188).

Plugin executes committed dist/src/*.js, which is only verified in CI by check-dist. Anyone installing trusts the repo owner; a single-maintainer, 9-day-old repo with auto-updating plugin marketplace is a supply-chain risk for client work.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on every Stop and every Edit/Write/MultiEdit: the full last assistant message (up to 60k chars, head+tail truncated, check.ts:65-78), and the newly written text of each edit, meaning the code content Claude just wrote (new_string or content) plus the file path. Rule text extracted from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, project CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .claude/rules, once for classification and then again in every question. It does not send the user prompt, tool outputs, or the existing file contents around an edit. For client projects this means client code and the user's global CLAUDE.md go to a third party (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter plus its upstream provider if patched). README states this too ("Your reply text, edits and rules go to TypeSafe's API").
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.failureMode: Fail-open. With no key or JEV_ENFORCE_OFF=1 the hook returns null. Any thrown error is caught in cli.js:40-45, written to stderr and exits 0 with no output, so Claude proceeds unblocked. Timeout is 15s per fetch (jev.ts:26) with up to 2 retries on 429/529 (400ms then 800ms backoff), while the hook is hard-killed at 30s by hooks.json; a killed hook is a non-blocking error. Worst case a slow Jev stalls each edit or turn end for up to 15-30s. There is no circuit breaker: if Jev is down, every edit pays the timeout. The first call in a new project also does a classification pass. The one-block-per-turn guard and stop_hook_active mean it cannot loop.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.latencyImpact: Claimed and benchmarked p50 348ms and p95 464ms per check (bench/results.md), added synchronously after every Edit/Write in default `turn` mode. That is roughly 0.35s per edit, plus 0.35s at every turn end. A 20-edit turn costs about 7s. JEV_ENFORCE_MODE=end cuts this to one check per file at Stop, run in parallel. Local rule-file scanning is negligible. When a violation is found, Claude gets an extra fix turn (Opus tokens and seconds). About 1 in 15 flags is a false positive, and it forces a needless rewrite.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.contextCost: Zero tool or MCP definitions, no server instructions, no skills, so a baseline cost of 0 tokens. Hook text is injected only on a violation: a reason of about 100-300 chars (about 25-75 tokens) quoting the broken rules, plus a systemMessage to the UI. The Stop block forces an additional assistant turn.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (Stop and PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit). Fully automatic with no prompting, which matches the user's requirement in form. But the only Jev use is a CLAUDE.md compliance judge, not a general decision aid for Claude Code.
pros: Truly automatic: two deterministic hooks, no prompting, zero context-token overhead (no tools, no skills), with the block message shown only on a violation.
Small, readable, dependency-free code (about 450 lines of src). Static audit is easy, and there is no postinstall or shell exec.
Fail-open by design (cli.js:40-45): missing key, network error or bad JSON never breaks a session.

Well-chosen Jev use: one batched Noul request per check with one question per rule matches Jev's typed-decision strength. Cost is about $0.0027 per 59-case benchmark run, and the input is cheap at $0.042/M tokens.
Honest, reproducible benchmark (93% precision and recall at 0.7) and a README section on limits. Rule scope classification is cached, and it respects CLAUDE.md precedence, including AGENTS.md.
Fits the user, who already keeps a long ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md of rules. It adds enforcement that a plain CLAUDE.md lacks, and the CLI `check` can run in CI. MIT licensed.
The endpoint is one hardcoded URL and one body shape, so a fork that points at OpenRouter is a small diff.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter: TYPESAFE_API_KEY and api.typesafe.ai only, model 'jev-latest'. The url option exists in createAsk but is never wired to env, so OpenRouter needs a forked and rebuilt committed dist. OpenRouter's request and response schema equivalence is unverified.

Sends every edit's new code and every assistant reply to a third party, including for client projects and including .env or secret writes (not excluded). It sidesteps the existing PreToolUse secret guard, which does not cover Write/Edit content.
Synchronous latency on every edit (about 0.35s p50, more if degraded) with no circuit breaker. Worst case 15-30s stalls when Jev is slow or down. Retries are only on 429/529.

Only judges style and rules that fit in one snippet. It cannot see the surrounding file or repo state (README: 'never add a dependency' scored 0.56, editing an old migration scored 0.06). About 7% false positives, so needless Opus rewrite loops. The fix is not re-checked.

Narrow value for a senior dev who already has caveman/GitNexus/secret hooks: it enforces prose and style bullets, and most of this user's CLAUDE.md is workflow rules (classified 'none'). Linters and tests already cover code rules better. It does nothing for routing, planning, permission or tool-choice decisions, which is where Jev would add real value.

Very immature: 9 days old, 9 stars, 1 open issue, 2 contributors, 25 commits, release tags v1.0.0 to v1.1.1 in 4 days, no PR CI, sole maintainer. Supply-chain trust risk for client work. Committed dist/ must be trusted.
Plaintext API key in settings.json, and pending edits stored in plaintext in ~/.cache in end mode.
gh-erkamyaman-jev-enforce.verdict: Clean, small, fail-open hook plugin that is genuinely automatic, but it is a CLAUDE.md compliance checker rather than a general Jev integration, and it is hardwired to TypeSafe's direct API. Using OpenRouter needs a fork (about 5 lines plus rebuild, schema parity unconfirmed), and it ships all written code and replies to a third party. That last point is a real problem for client work. It is optional and low priority, best run in `end` mode after a patch, and only on personal projects.

security: No MCP server, no hooks, and no postinstall or curl|sh installers. package.json has only build, typecheck, test and prepack scripts.
API key comes from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and goes only in the Authorization: Bearer header (src/jev.ts:382). Not in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
Third-party code is spawned only through execFile/spawn with argv arrays (git, cargo, go, and the user's --exec command). No shell is involved, so there is little command-injection surface.

The full unified git diff is sent to a third party, including any secrets or client code in the changed lines. The runtime code has no redaction. secretlint appears only as a devDependency and pre-push hook for the repo itself, and test code has an onRequest leak assertion (src/jev.ts:105). This matters for client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: diff text is sent to Jev, but Jev returns only typed scores, so injected text in a diff cannot drive tool calls. It could at worst sway the scores and deselect a test. Test names and files are also embedded in questions.
Writes .jev-test-filter/*.json into the repo (untracked noise unless gitignored). Records contain test names and answers, not the diff.
No telemetry found in the source. Only outbound calls are to the Jev base URL.
Deps: @ast-grep/napi and lang packages (native binaries). Lockfile present.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.dataEgress: The whole `git diff` (working tree vs HEAD, or vs --base), capped at 96k chars (src/state.ts), plus `git diff --stat` and the changed file list. Each test's file path, title path and line range go into the questions (src/questions.ts). Test bodies and unchanged files are not sent, but any file whose lines are in the diff is sent with context. The destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says (OpenRouter if you set it, so OpenRouter also sees it). Nothing leaves the machine unless the tool is invoked. Chat prompts and other tool outputs never leave.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.failureMode: Fail-open by design: no API key, a Jev error, a missing answer, no tests found, or a diff too large all fall back to "run everything", with the reason on stderr and in the result (src/run.ts:186-232, 257-266). Request timeout is 60 s (src/jev.ts:286), with 4 retries for network/5xx using exponential backoff up to 20 s, and up to 8 retries on 429. A worst-case outage could therefore stall for minutes before falling back, but the fallback is safe. The one fail-closed case is exit 1 on a repo with more than one framework and no --format. Selection is nondeterministic near the cutoff. The truncated-diff guard forces a full run when less than 50% is selected.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.latencyImpact: Only when invoked, never per tool call. The author claims about 1.3 s and $0.00098 for a 110-test suite, and the code comments say 260 ms plus 5.7 ms per 1k tokens per request. A large suite plus a big diff can send 2M+ tokens (about 4 s at 32-way concurrency, measured by the author on typesafe direct). Cost is about $0.04 per 1M input tokens. This is negligible per run, but it only pays off when the test suite takes longer than a few seconds.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.contextCost: Tiny: no MCP tools and no hook-injected text. The plugin adds one skill whose frontmatter description is about 1,000 chars (about 250 tokens), plus /filter-tests (about 60 tokens of description). The SKILL.md body (about 6 KB, about 1.5k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger only: Claude loads SKILL.md when the description matches ('only run affected tests', 'which tests does this PR need') or the user runs /filter-tests. There are no hooks and no proxy, so nothing runs deterministically. Without a wrapper (e.g. a PreToolUse hook rewriting `vitest run`, which the repo does not provide), Claude will not use it on its own for every test run. The skill also does not install the CLI. Claude would call `npx jev-test-filter`, which downloads and runs npm code at runtime.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.runtime: Node >=24 (TypeScript run via node --test/tsc build). Dependencies: @ast-grep/napi, lang-go, lang-rust.

pros: Genuinely uses Jev's real strength: a typed Score primitive, one state plus N questions in one round trip, with per-test calibrated confidence. It is the most idiomatic Jev use case found (src/questions.ts).
Endpoint and key are env-configurable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_TEST_FILTER_MODEL), so pointing at OpenRouter needs no code change, if OpenRouter's System One schema matches.

Robust fail-open: every error runs the full suite. A wrong selection is the only real risk, and the tool guards against it (touched tests always chosen, unsure band, dynamic titles always chosen, truncated-diff guard).
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, one skill description of about 250 tokens. No hook overhead on the existing Bash/Grep hooks.
Does not use a shell (spawn/execFile with argv) and passes the key in a header, not argv. No postinstall scripts and no telemetry.
Broad runner support (vitest, jest, node, bun, Playwright, cargo, go) and offline --replay for tuning without paying again.
MIT license, readable code, a substantial test suite.
cons: Not automatic. Autonomy is only through a skill description, at the model's discretion. Claude will normally just run `npm test`. There is no hook that rewrites test commands, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic use without prompting.

Narrow use case: test selection only. It does not help with general coding, review, routing or planning. Its value depends on slow suites (Playwright, integration tests); for fast unit suites the author himself says the overhead can exceed the saving.

Sends the full working-tree diff to Jev or OpenRouter with no redaction. That conflicts with client-project confidentiality and the user's secret-leak-guard posture. The user's PreToolUse guard would not see this network egress, since it happens inside the CLI.

TypeSafe-only in code and docs. The SKILL.md and /filter-tests command insist on TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the command stops if it is unset. OpenRouter use would be a hack (a TYPESAFE_* var holding an OpenRouter key), and the schema match with /api/v1/systemone was not confirmed.
Very young and single-author (58 of 59 commits by mizchi, created 2026-09-21, v0.1.3). It has no CI, no releases and 31 stars. It is alpha quality and the behaviour will churn with Jev's beta API.
Selection is nondeterministic near the cutoff, and a wrong deselection can hide a regression. The skill itself says never to use it as a merge gate.

Requires Node >=24, npx downloads at runtime, and it writes .jev-test-filter/ record files into each repo. The CLI needs installing separately from the plugin, which creates an unpinned supply-chain hop.
Retry and timeout budget (60 s timeout, 4 retries, 8 rate-limit retries) means a Jev outage can delay the fallback by minutes.
gh-mizchi-jev-test-filter.verdict: A well-built, honest Jev consumer that is fail-open and cheap in context. But it is a narrow, manually-triggered test-selection tool, not an automatic Claude Code integration. It is TypeSafe-direct, so OpenRouter would work only via a base-URL/key env override that I could not verify against OpenRouter's schema. It is worth an optional per-project install for repos with slow Playwright or integration suites, not as the primary Jev integration.

gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.name: kyu1204/oh-my-harness
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.whatItDoes: npm CLI (omh / oh-my-harness) that generates a per-project Claude Code guardrail harness (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json hooks, bash hook scripts) from harness.yaml/presets. Jev is an optional layer. (1) `omh init "description"` and `omh modify "request"` call Jev once to choose or edit catalog blocks (Noul per block, Choice for strictness). (2) Rules marked `enforce: true` produce a `semantic-rule-guard` PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Edit|Write|MultiEdit). On every such call it POSTs the tool input to the System One endpoint with one Noul question per rule, and blocks at p>=0.9, asks at 0.6-0.9, and allows below that. (3) An optional `semantic-diff-gate` shells out to the separate `jgrep` tool.

The key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or a project .env (lines 35-39), and the model is hardcoded as `model: "jev-latest"` (line 62). src/nl/typesafe-chooser.ts:17-18 hardcodes `TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"` and `TYPESAFE_MODEL = "jev-latest"`, with no env override for the TS chooser (fetch at ~line 56, Bearer header, 15s timeout). The only env override is OMH_TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT, in the bash hook only. OpenRouter appears in the code only as an LLM provider for NL intent parsing (src/nl/provider-registry.ts:110-120, openrouter-oauth.ts:3), not for Jev.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate but small. The hook is nearly there: set OMH_TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, since the Bearer header is identical. Two things remain unverified or blocking. First, the model is hardcoded as "jev-latest", whereas OpenRouter needs "typesafe/jev-latest" or "~typesafe/jev-latest", so line 62 of the template needs a one-line edit or an env var. Second, the request body `{model,state,questions}` and the response `answers.{key}.noul` are assumed to match OpenRouter's System One API, which I did not verify. The TS chooser (init/modify) needs a source patch because it has no endpoint override. Fork/patch effort is roughly 5-10 lines. Alternatively, run a tiny local proxy that rewrites the model id.

interface.name: omh init [description...] [--preset]
interface.purpose: Detects the project, then generates harness.yaml plus .claude/settings.json hooks, scripts and CLAUDE.md. With TYPESAFE_API_KEY, Jev picks the blocks.

interface.name: omh modify [request...]
interface.purpose: Edits harness.yaml from a sentence, using Jev to choose enable/disable/ask/keep per block. Needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

interface.name: omh sync / diff / doctor / explain / test / uninstall / config / stats / update / catalog list|info / hook add|remove / loop start|run|stop|status|clean
interface.purpose: Harness lifecycle, drift checks and stats. The loop subcommands are an autonomous agent loop engine.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook semantic-rule-guard (Bash|Edit|Write|MultiEdit)
interface.purpose: Sends each tool call to Jev with one Noul per enforced rule; blocks at p>=0.9, asks at 0.6-0.9, and otherwise allows. Fails open.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook semantic-diff-gate
interface.purpose: Runs `jgrep --diff --staged` before git commit and blocks on a hit. Needs the jevgrep npm package.

interface.name: Deterministic hooks (branch-guard, command-guard, path-guard, secret-file-guard, tdd-guard, sql-guard, lint/format/test-on-save, commit gates, stop gates, no-verify/force-push guards)
interface.purpose: Non-Jev guardrails from the catalog. The 17 selectable blocks are listed in src/nl/typesafe-chooser.ts.

security: Key visibility: the hook passes the key to curl as `-H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"` (semantic-rule-guard.ts:69), so the OpenRouter/TypeSafe key is visible in the process list (ps/proc cmdline) for the length of each call.

Key sourcing: the hook falls back to grepping TYPESAFE_API_KEY out of the project's .env via sed (lines 36-38). This is a read of a secrets file, and it will collide with a secret-leak guard that watches .env reads only if that guard matches the hook's own shell, which it should not.

The prompt-injection surface is narrow. Jev returns only probabilities, and rule text comes from harness.yaml. However, attacker-controlled content in the tool call (new_string, content, command) goes into the Jev `state`, and a Noul on it can be gamed, so this is a soft guard. The README states it never relaxes deterministic guards.

Shell execution: the hooks are generated bash scripts, and the rule text is embedded via a quoted heredoc so it is safely quoted. jq is required. The TS `omh` CLI does not exec third-party code besides optional `jgrep`.

No npm postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json scripts are only build, test and prepublishOnly). It is installed with `npm install -g oh-my-harness`, not via curl|sh. Only the file list dist/, presets/ and README is published.

Telemetry: none found (grep for telemetry/analytics only hit an unrelated stats TUI label). The TUI init has a one-time prompt that offers to star the repo via gh (src/cli/github-star.ts), which is opt-in.
License: MIT. Single maintainer (483 of 485 commits are from one author), 17 stars, 2 forks, repo created 2026-03-16.
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.dataEgress: For semantic-rule-guard, on every Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit call the hook sends to api.typesafe.ai, or to OpenRouter if repointed: tool name, the full Bash command, the Bash description, the file_path, old_string truncated to 2000 characters, and new_string and content each truncated to 4000 characters, plus the enforced rule texts (semantic-rule-guard.ts:52-66). No prompts, no conversation history, no file reads and no tool outputs are sent. Edited code fragments and shell commands, which may contain inline secrets or client code, DO leave the machine on every write. For init/modify, the project description plus the detector facts (languages, package managers, etc.) go to TypeSafe. The request is not sent to Anthropic. There is no telemetry.
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.failureMode: Fail-open by design. There is no key, no curl, a non-200 response, curl failure, or no answers, and in each case the hook logs `skipped` and exits 0 (semantic-rule-guard.ts:39-40,71,74). curl has a hard `-m 10` cap, so the worst case adds 10 s to a single tool call when Jev hangs. The hook script has no set timeout in settings.json, so Claude Code's default hook timeout applies as an outer bound. The TS paths (init/modify) use a 15 s AbortSignal and print a fallback message. A slow or down Jev never blocks the user, but the guard silently disappears in that case.
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.contextCost: There are no MCP tools or server instructions, so tool-definition cost is 0. The hooks inject text only on block/ask, as a short reason string of roughly 30-60 tokens. The generated CLAUDE.md section from harness rules adds a small managed block per project, roughly a few hundred tokens depending on the rules. The hooks are per-project (.claude/settings.json), not global.
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook. The harness fires semantic-rule-guard automatically on every Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit call in a project where `omh init` has been run and a rule has `enforce: true`. No model discretion and no prompting is needed. The hook only asks Jev a rule-compliance question; it does not provide general decision-making help to Claude. Setup is per project, and it writes .claude/settings.json, harness.yaml and CLAUDE.md into each repo, which is intrusive for client repos.
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.latencyImpact: One synchronous curl per Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit call plus bash+jq startup. The vendor claim is 70-500 ms and the README says about 500 ms per init call. Expect roughly 0.3-0.8 s added to every write or shell tool call, up to 10 s on a timeout, and zero on reads or greps. Over a day of 500-1000 mutating tool calls this adds up to several minutes of wall time. Cost is about 1-2k input tokens per call at $0.042 per 1M tokens, which is negligible.
pros: It is the only candidate here that actually wires Jev into Claude Code with a deterministic PreToolUse hook. No 'use jev' prompting is needed, which matches the user's automatic-integration requirement (semantic-rule-guard.ts:11-17).

A sensible use of Jev's strengths: a Noul with calibrated p, block at >=0.9, ask at 0.6-0.9. It emits a real permissionDecision:"ask" for the middle band (lines 88-91). It uses Jev the way the model was designed, with typed questions and no free text.
Robust fail-open: no key, curl failure, non-200 or timeout all allow with a log, and the hard 10 s curl cap. It is additive to the deterministic guards.

It sends only the tool input, truncated (2-4k characters per field), rather than transcripts or file reads. The hook also has a test with a fake local endpoint (OMH_TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT), and an endpoint override already exists in the bash hook.

The repo is active (v0.25.0 released today, 485 commits since March 2026, CI on Node 20/22, 100+ unit test files with recorded Jev fixtures) and MIT licensed, with no postinstall scripts and no telemetry.
The OpenRouter path is nearly free: it needs a base-URL env var plus a one-line model-id patch, since the Bearer auth scheme is the same.
cons: No native OpenRouter support: the model is hardcoded to `jev-latest` (semantic-rule-guard.ts:62; typesafe-chooser.ts:18), and the TS init/modify endpoint is hardcoded with no env override. OpenRouter needs a model id such as `typesafe/jev-latest`, and the OpenRouter System One request and response shape parity is unverified. The key must be supplied under the name TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

The scope is a rule-compliance gate, not a general Claude Code decision helper. It only adds value if the user writes natural-language `enforce: true` rules. It does not route models or pick tools, or triage anything else.

Per-project install: `omh init` writes harness.yaml, .claude/settings.json hooks, scripts and CLAUDE.md into each repo. This is intrusive and may need committing on client projects, and it does not give a global user-level integration. It also merges with existing settings and may interact with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus).

Latency and egress on every mutating call: roughly 0.3-0.8 s per Bash/Edit/Write, and client code fragments (up to 4000 characters per field) and shell commands go to a third-party model on each write. That is a compliance concern for client projects, and the guard can be gamed by adversarial content in the call.
Key handling: the Bearer key is in curl's argv, so it is visible in ps, and it is read from a project .env by sed.

Single-maintainer project (483 of 485 commits) with 17 stars, at v0.25.0 and 6 months old. It bundles a lot of scope (loop engine, TUI, Codex/Pi generators) unrelated to Jev, and it is coupled to the beta Jev API (Jev is early access, so the guard is only as good as p-calibration, since the skeptics' 'flash router' claim is unverified).
gh-kyu1204-oh-my-harness.verdict: The strongest concrete example of automatic, hook-based Jev use in Claude Code, and it is worth stealing the semantic-rule-guard pattern. It is not a drop-in for OpenRouter (hardcoded model and endpoint) and is too intrusive and latency-heavy to adopt wholesale across client repos. The better plan is a small custom global PreToolUse hook that reuses this Noul design and a hardened curl, pointed at OpenRouter.

It always exits 0. Suppress it with --no-triage or JEV_TRIAGE_SKIP in the command.

security: API key is read only from the environment and sent in an Authorization: Bearer header via http.client, so it does not appear in argv or the process list.

Hard-coded host allowlist (api.typesafe.ai) with a DNS check that rejects private, loopback and link-local addresses. It does not follow redirects and refuses non-https. This is a reasonable SSRF defense but blocks OpenRouter until patched.

Secret redaction before egress: 9 regexes cover GitHub tokens, sk- keys, api_key/password/token=, bearer tokens, DB URLs, JWTs and AKIA keys. It is best-effort and pattern-based, so client-specific secrets can leak. The test-output text can also contain PII or proprietary code snippets from assertions.

The prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns typed probabilities, not free text. The hook prints only fixed advice strings plus a root-cause reason from local rules, so injected text in logs cannot easily steer Claude. The 'likely root cause' line is rule-derived, not model text.

No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh. The only file writes are ~/.jev-triage/ledger.jsonl (no raw log text) and ~/.claude/settings.json on --install. --install modifies the user's global settings, which is acceptable but should be done by hand here.
Single anonymous author with an unknown identity. The account and repo are 9 days old and have 1 star. Supply-chain trust is low, but the code is about 2.2k lines of readable stdlib Python.
The hook regex list has known false-positive paths (for example a test that asserts on the string ModuleNotFoundError), which the README itself admits.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.dataEgress: The only external call is the Jev request, and only for failures the local rules cannot resolve. It sends the parsed failure fields (test name, error type, location, message, stage, summary line) and a compacted log excerpt of up to 9000 characters, with the first and last parts of the log and every failure block, after regex secret redaction. The API key goes in the Authorization header. Nothing else leaves the machine: no repo files, diffs or non-test command output. It is limited to test commands that fail.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.failureMode: Fail-open by design. run_hook() catches BaseException and always returns 0. Jev call timeout is 8 s (hook timeout 15 s in settings), with a single retry after 0.35 s on 429, 5xx and TLS errors, so the worst case is roughly 16 s or more. A timeout, a bad key, a missing key or a network error yields a degraded verdict and prints nothing. There is a design flaw: the retry can add to blocking time on the hook's synchronous path, and Claude waits for the hook to finish.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions, so no per-session token cost. It is a hook only, and text is injected only when a test command fails: about 3-4 lines (about 60-100 tokens). Caveat: see autoInvocation. If Claude Code does not feed PostToolUse plain stdout to the model, the injected cost is 0 and so is the benefit.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.latencyImpact: Nothing on passing runs or non-test commands (a Python process start of about 30-80 ms). On a failing test run: rule-resolved cases (44% of the author's corpus) add about 0 ms. Jev-resolved cases add a measured median of about 1.1 s, a typical 0.8-2.5 s, and a worst case of about 6.5 s, plus up to 8 s on timeout. The author measured this and says it does not match the advertised 70-500 ms. The ledger write and Python startup add small overhead.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PostToolUse on the Bash tool), so it needs no prompting. However, there is a likely integration bug that I did not verify by running it (third-party code is not to be run). Per my knowledge of Claude Code hook semantics: (1) plain stdout from a PostToolUse hook on exit 0 is shown in the transcript/verbose view and is not added to the model's context; only JSON with hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (or UserPromptSubmit/SessionStart stdout) reaches the model. hooks.py:_emit() writes plain text at lines 89-93 and 168-170, and a grep for additionalContext or hookSpecificOutput finds no match anywhere in the repo. (2) A failing Bash command (non-zero exit) is generally reported as a tool error, which fires PostToolUseFailure rather than PostToolUse. The installed matcher is registered only under PostToolUse, and extract_output() reads tool_response/tool_result keys that the failure payload may not contain. Both points need a live check in Claude Code 2.1.285 before relying on it. Treat 'the model sees the verdict automatically' as unproven.
pros: Truly automatic trigger model: a deterministic PostToolUse hook restricted to failing test commands (12 runner regexes), so the user never has to prompt 'use jev'. Zero MCP tools means zero standing context cost.

Sensible, cheap architecture: local parser and rule layer resolve 7 of 16 real logs (44%) with no network call, and Jev is only called for ambiguous failures, so cost and latency stay low ($0.000334 for 16 logs per the ledger).
Fail-open discipline is real: BaseException is caught, the exit code is always 0, and tests cover the hook and security paths (111 offline tests; 7 test files, about 1.5k lines).

Honest README: it discloses measured Jev latency of 0.8-2.5 s against the advertised 70-500 ms, admits the 16-log eval was written by the prompt author, and records the earlier 76.9% score. This is useful independent evidence for the latency and calibration skepticism.
Good egress hygiene: secret redaction before sending, SSRF and redirect protection, a 9000-character cap, no raw logs in the ledger, and no key in argv.
It matches a legitimate System One use case (a typed 3-way Choice plus a Noul), so it doubles as a working reference for building a request payload.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the host allowlist is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai (triage.py:36, 109-120), the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and the model is jev-latest. It must be forked and patched, and the OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified. This conflicts with the user's stated requirement to use OpenRouter.

The value proposition is narrow: it only helps after a test failure. The rules already do the obvious cases, and Claude Opus 5.5 reading the same traceback usually classifies it correctly without a second-hand hint. Jev adds 1-6 s of hook wait on a failing run in exchange for a hint the main model rarely needs.

Probable delivery bug: plain stdout from a PostToolUse hook is likely not injected into the model's context, and a non-zero Bash exit likely triggers PostToolUseFailure instead. Nothing in the repo uses additionalContext or PostToolUseFailure, so the advertised 'agent sees it as context' behaviour is unverified and may be a silent no-op on Claude Code 2.1.x.

Quality signal: 2 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no CI, no release, no PyPI package, 9 days old, described as Alpha. Only a self-reported 16-log evaluation, which the author admits is not field accuracy. Jest is not covered by a real fixture.

Risk of wrong-direction advice: the hook says 'do not re-run the suite unchanged' on FIX_CODE and FIX_ENV. Rule false positives (for example 'timed out' or 'permission denied' matching assertion text) could mislead a model into skipping a valid retry.

--install edits ~/.claude/settings.json, which the user manages with existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman). It is safer to add the entry manually. It also requires a global pip install that puts a jev-triage binary on PATH.

Leaks part of client test output (assertion text, stack traces, paths) to a third party, only partly mitigated by regex redaction. This matters for the client projects; on the OpenRouter route, prompt logging and retention policy would need checking.
gh-ccai40359-wq-jev-triage.verdict: A small, carefully written and honestly documented test-failure triage hook, and it is the only candidate here that gets automatic invocation from a deterministic hook rather than model discretion. But it is TypeSafe-only (needs a fork for OpenRouter), the payoff is marginal for an Opus-class main model, and the hook likely fails to inject its output into Claude's context on current Claude Code. It is worth borrowing as a design pattern (rules first, Jev for the ambiguous remainder, fail-open) rather than installing as-is.

gh-ckorhonen-jev-lint.name: ckorhonen/jev-lint
gh-ckorhonen-jev-lint.whatItDoes: Fuzzy linter for coding agents. A Claude Code/Codex PostToolUse (or PreToolUse with --pre) hook takes the code each Write/Edit/MultiEdit adds, gates ~170 built-in rules (TS/React, Swift, Kotlin, Rust, Python, Ruby, Bazel; security, tests, performance packs) plus repo rules in .jev-lint/ by regex, and sends the remaining rules as Jev "noul" (yes/no) questions in ONE POST /v1/systemone call. Risk: src/cli/loadEnv.ts:59-77 auto-loads the nearest `.env` between cwd and repo root into process.env for any variable not already set. A cloned client/untrusted repo could ship a .env setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (jevClient.ts:120) to redirect the user's globally-set API key plus hunk text to an attacker host. Prompt-injection surface: hunk text (untrusted code/comments) goes into the Jev question, but Jev returns only a typed choice validated against a fixed label set (validateChoiceAnswer), so injection can at worst flip include/exclude for a hunk; low-confidence falls back to 'mixed' and unstaged. Plan is verifiable via `git diff --cached` before commit.
Atomic staging with stale-snapshot check protects the index; the tool never writes working-tree files and never commits.
Skill's allowed-tools pre-approves `git commit *` and `git add *`, which widens auto-allowed permissions for the skill (moot in bypass mode).
Single maintainer, 2 stars, 12 days old, package published 2026-09-18; supply-chain trust is low. Pin a version and read the diff before installing.
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.dataEgress: Per README 'What leaves the machine' and code: the staging sentence, optional exclusion sentence, changed file paths, hunk headers and full hunk text (added/removed lines with 6 lines of context, plus neighboring same-file hunks as context) for all unstaged tracked changes are POSTed to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). No tool outputs, no whole files, no conversation. Untracked files excluded. With OpenRouter, the same payload would go to openrouter.ai and be subject to its provider/logging policy. For client projects this means proprietary diff content leaves the machine on every invocation.
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.failureMode: Fail-open at the classification level but not silent: a missing key with --yes/--json exits 1 (MissingApiKeyError); interactive without key asks per hunk; missing/invalid/low-confidence/too-large answers become 'mixed' and are left unstaged (policy.ts). Request errors throw ProviderError. SDK timeout is 60 s with 2 retries (jevClient.ts:23-24), so worst case is minutes of blocking on a slow endpoint (Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms). Requests are windowed and run 4 concurrently (windowing.ts DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY=4). Nothing is staged if the snapshot goes stale (exit 3). Never blocks other Claude Code tools since it only runs when the skill invokes it.
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.latencyImpact: Only when a staging request occurs: one or a few concurrent HTTP calls (one question per hunk, batched into windows), so roughly 0.1-1 s of Jev time plus git snapshot/apply and Node startup; larger diffs add windows. Zero overhead on normal turns (no hook, no MCP, no proxy).
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.contextCost: Near zero. No MCP server (0 tools, no server instructions) and no hooks. Only the skill listing entry: name + description (~290 chars, roughly 70 tokens) is always in context; the SKILL.md body (~3.3k chars, roughly 800 tokens) loads only when the skill triggers.
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model-discretion): Claude loads the skill when the user asks to commit/stage part of the working tree. It is not a deterministic hook, and it does not fire during ordinary coding, only on partial-staging requests; with a broad 'commit everything' request Claude will just use git add/commit.
pros: Genuine, well-fitted use of Jev's Choice primitive: per-hunk include/exclude/mixed with calibrated probabilities and a confidence threshold, so uncertain hunks are left unstaged rather than guessed.
Ships as a real Claude Code plugin+skill with a description trigger, so Claude can pick it up automatically when the user says 'commit just the auth fix' without naming Jev.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no hooks, no proxy; ~70 tokens of always-on listing.

Uses the System One endpoint, and the SDK path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key is a plausible zero-code switch apart from the model id.
Provider abstraction (JevProvider interface, baseURL/model constructor options) makes an OpenRouter wrapper via the library trivial.
Safe engineering: atomic index update with lock and stale-snapshot check, never commits, never touches working files, --dry-run and --json modes, fail-soft to 'mixed'.
Unusually thorough tests and fixtures and a CI matrix for a 12-day-old repo; MIT license; tiny dependency footprint (one first-party SDK).
No prompt-injection amplification: Jev output is a validated enum plus probabilities.
cons: Narrow scope: it only helps with selective hunk staging, an occasional task, not daily coding flow; Claude already stages via git add -p or explicit file lists.

Model id blocker for OpenRouter: hard-coded 'jev-latest' is always sent (jevClient.ts:22,84) and overrides TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL; the CLI has no model flag/env, so OpenRouter's 'typesafe/jev-latest' needs a patch or the library API.
README and SKILL.md only document TYPESAFE_API_KEY from a waitlist key; no OpenRouter support or docs, and OpenRouter response compatibility is untested.
Sends full diff hunks (proprietary client code) to a third party on every call; problematic for client projects without approval.
`.env` auto-loading from the repo tree (loadEnv.ts) lets an untrusted repo redirect key and diff via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.
Skill only triggers on explicit partial-commit phrasing; it is not a deterministic hook, so 'automatic' integration is limited to that niche and Claude may not choose it over plain git.
Immature: 1 contributor, 2 stars, 22 commits, v0.1.1 from 2026-09-18, and no history of external use; Jev itself is beta and skeptics doubt it is more than a small router model.
Skill pre-allows `git commit *`/`git add *`, and --yes stages without review, so a wrong include silently lands in the index (mitigated by the confidence threshold and Claude's diff --cached check).
Requires global npm install of a 12-day-old package on PATH (plus Node 22+), extra supply-chain surface.
gh-ibrahemid-git-jev-stage.verdict: A well-built, legitimately Jev-based skill for one niche job (stage only the hunks matching a sentence), auto-triggered by the skill description with negligible context cost, but it is a narrow, alpha, single-author tool that only speaks TYPESAFE_* today. OpenRouter works only with a small patch or library wrapper (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus model typesafe/jev-latest); use it as an optional add-on for personal repos, not as the core Jev integration, and avoid it on client code without approval to send diffs out.

security: MIT license. The repo was created 2026-08-23, so it is about 5 weeks old. It has 141 stars, 5 forks, 604 commits (603 by one author, Domas Bitvinskas, 1 by a contributor), and latest release v2.0.1 published 2026-09-25. Last push was 2026-09-27.

API key is read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header via ureq (quality.rs:1332). I found no --api-key CLI flag, so the key does not appear in argv or the process list. The endpoint check rejects plain http except for localhost (quality.rs:148-158), and redirects are disabled (max_redirects(0), :1315), so the key cannot be redirected elsewhere. Response size is capped at 1 MiB and the schema is validated against the request (:1186+).

The plugin is only markdown (skills and commands). There are no hooks, no MCP server, and no shell execution beyond the commands the agent runs. The commands use allowed-tools Bash(npx supercov quality:*) and Bash(npx supercov docs:*). The skill text tells the agent to run scans without asking again when the key is set, which is a consent shortcut. It is not an injection vector, but it does mean code egress happens without a prompt.

npx pulls the supercov package, whose bin/native.js resolves a prebuilt native binary from optionalDependencies (@supercov/cli-linux-x64-gnu etc.). There is no postinstall script, as package.json only has build/test/prepack scripts. Still, `npx supercov` downloads and runs an opaque native Rust binary from npm at 2.0.1, so it is unaudited supply-chain surface. The Homebrew, cargo and go run install paths also exist. Version pinning would be prudent.

The coverage mode executes the user's own test command in an isolated workspace and instruments code. That is a large attack surface (lots of instrumenters and runtimes) if run on untrusted repos, but it is unrelated to the Jev path.
Telemetry: none found. A grep for telemetry/analytics/posthog/sentry found no hits in the source, and SECURITY.md says coverage sends nothing.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents go to Jev, which returns only typed probabilities (no free text), so Jev output cannot inject into the agent. The one exception is that `security` output includes the line and code where a finding is confirmed, taken from the local file rather than from Jev.
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.dataEgress: Only `supercov quality` and `supercov security` (and `review`, which uses them) send data, and only when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set. Per SECURITY.md:15 and quality.rs, the request body is the full source file content (or a split slice of it when a request would exceed the 30k token budget, MAX_REQUEST_TOKENS = 30_000, with files over 4 MiB skipped) plus the question set, and the model name (quality.rs:186-201). For `patch` mode it sends the before/after versions of the changed files. It sends no test outputs, prompts or conversation. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the env override. This means whole-repo source, including client code, goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user should check OpenRouter's ZDR and data-retention policy and the client contracts. `--dry-run` prints the exact requests. A local response cache (`.supercov/`, self-gitignored) makes repeat runs on unchanged files send nothing. Coverage runs send nothing. Cost is about $0.01 per MB of source, so a normal repo costs a few cents per full scan.
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.failureMode: Fail-open in practice, because it is invoked on demand as a CLI and not in a hook path. On transport failure or timeout it returns an error ("transport failed... retry the command"). The per-request global timeout is 45s (quality.rs:1314), with up to 4 attempts on 429/5xx, backoff capped at 30s and honoring Retry-After. If Retry-After is longer than 30s it errors out immediately. A missing key gives an error message, and the skill tells the agent to fall back to reading the code by hand and say that Supercov did not check it. A failed scan never blocks a tool call. However, a full-repo scan with retries could hang a turn for minutes.
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.contextCost: Very low at rest. There are no MCP tools and no server instructions. Two skills (about 1.7 KB and 0.9 KB of SKILL.md, of which only name+description sit in the always-loaded listing, about 150-200 tokens total) and 4 slash commands with disable-model-invocation (about 3 KB, loaded only when typed). No hook-injected text. Cost per use is the CLI output the agent reads, which is designed to be short and paginated (`gaps --limit 5`, `--json`).
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). It fires when the user asks for tests, coverage, refactoring or a security scan, and the skill then tells the agent to run the Jev-backed scan without asking again. It does not fire on ordinary edits, commits or reviews unless the user says so. The slash commands are user-typed only. There is no deterministic hook, so it is not the always-on "Claude Code uses Jev whenever useful" behaviour the user asked for. It could be made deterministic only by adding your own PostToolUse or Stop hook that calls `supercov quality patch`, which you would write and own.
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.latencyImpact: None on ordinary turns; per scan, roughly one to a few System One calls of 70-500 ms each for patch scope, minutes for a cold full-repo scan, 45s cap per request.
pros: It is the only candidate I saw with a real, tested OpenRouter path in code: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 hits /api/v1/systemone with a Bearer sk-or- key (quality.rs:136-158, tests/typesafe_base_url.rs, docs/quality.md:41-47). A mock server checks the exact path, header and model, and ~typesafe/jev-latest is tested.

It uses Jev for what it is designed for. Jev returns typed Noul probabilities and the CLI does the arithmetic, so no free text comes back and the results are checkable. The design fits the System One model, and the cost is tiny at about a cent per MB.

Skills auto-trigger from the description, and the skill says to run without re-asking once the key is set. That is close to the "no prompting" wish for the specific case of security-scan, refactor and add-test requests.

Very low context footprint, with no MCP tool schemas and no hook-injected text. There is no telemetry, no postinstall, and no key on argv. Redirects are disabled and https is enforced. The --dry-run flag shows the exact payload before egress.

Content-hash cache, per-model cache keys, and `quality patch` scoped to uncommitted work or branch diff make repeated use cheap. It also gives real local coverage/MC-DC tooling, which is useful independently of Jev and aligns with daily test-writing work.
Actively maintained, with 604 commits in 5 weeks, a large CI workflow set, and 1002 `#[test]` functions counted in the crates.
cons: Not automatic in the sense the user wants. It is a skill triggered only by explicit test, coverage, refactor or security requests, not a hook that runs Jev on every edit, commit or plan. Jev never helps with general routing or decisions in Claude Code, only with this tool's own file scoring.

It ships whole source files, including client code, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every uncached scan, and the skill instructs the agent to do so without asking again once the key is set. With bypass permissions on, this happens silently on client repos. Per-project gating of the env var (direnv) would be needed. The user must check OpenRouter data policy and client contracts.

The user must export a key named TYPESAFE_API_KEY containing an sk-or- OpenRouter key, plus 2 more env vars, before Claude Code starts, and it is set globally unless scoped. The system One path only. A live end-to-end run against OpenRouter was not shown (only a mock).

Young, single-maintainer project (603 of 604 commits by one person, first commit 2026-09-01, 141 stars) with a huge codebase (789 files, 8 languages of instrumenters). The npx binary is an opaque native download. Jev's quality and security judgments are weakly validated: the CHANGELOG itself reports security F1 0.47 (precision 54%, recall 41%), and its own docs say no score threshold has survived calibration.

Answers are only as good as Jev, which the brief says may behave like a routed cheap model. The calibrated catalog targets model jev-1.13.0, and when the model is overridden to typesafe/jev-1.13 the scores may drift, with the cache and diff keyed per model.

The main CLI value (coverage and MC/DC) has nothing to do with Jev. Full-repo scans are slow on a cold cache and cost real minutes and retries on 429, so they are unsuitable for a per-turn hook without wrapping.
gh-supercorp-ai-supercov.verdict: Best-evidenced OpenRouter-compatible Jev consumer found so far. It is a real, tested integration with a tiny context footprint and useful quality, security and coverage output. But it is skill-triggered (only on test, refactor or security requests) rather than an always-on hook, and it exports full source files to OpenRouter without further prompting, so use it as an opt-in per-project add-on (pin the version, scope the env vars with direnv) and not as the main way to get automatic Jev use.

gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json + .mcp.json + skill + subagent) for Rust-only code review.
