Also the response parser accepts a `usage` object with input_tokens/output_tokens; OpenRouter may differ but usage is #[serde(default)] so it tolerates that. No OpenRouter integration test exists (tests/jev_http.rs mocks only local wiremock).

interface.name: MCP tool cargo_diagnostics(repo_path?, scope?)
interface.purpose: Runs cargo clippy --all-targets --message-format=json (plus ~10 off-by-default lints) or cargo check; returns errors anywhere and warnings on changed lines, semver-checks verdict, Miri suggestion. Executes project build scripts/proc macros.

interface.name: MCP tool evaluate_rust_changes(repo_path?, scope?, dry_run?, profiles?, max_units?)
interface.purpose: Collects diff, splits into units, sends typed questions to Jev per unit, returns flagged (unit, dimension) pairs, tool_covered, project facts, cargo facts, redaction counts, token usage and cost. dry_run returns exact request bodies.

interface.name: MCP tool verify_rust_findings(findings[1..20], repo_path?, scope?, dry_run?)
interface.purpose: Re-reads claimed code (plus definitions of named items) and asks Jev support/severity/category; returns verdict report|insufficient_context|uncertain|dismiss|not_material|tool_reported.

interface.name: Skill /jev-rust-review:rust-review [scope] [--no-cargo] [--dry-run] [--json]
interface.purpose: Orchestrates the 7-step review: cargo facts, Jev triage, tests, inspection, verification, report. Description: 'Use when asked to review Rust code or Rust changes.' allowed-tools pre-approves the 3 MCP tools, Read/Grep/Glob, cargo test/nextest, git diff/show/log.

interface.name: Subagent rust-reviewer (tools: Read, Grep, Glob)
interface.purpose: Dispatched by the skill to inspect flagged units and return candidate findings; 'not for general use'.

interface.name: scripts/launch.sh
interface.purpose: MCP launcher: cached binary, PATH binary, checksum-verified prebuilt download from GitHub releases, else background cargo build --release --locked. Flags --install.

gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.runtime: Rust (edition 2024, MSRV 1.88, rmcp 3.4 stdio MCP server, reqwest rustls, tokio); POSIX sh launcher; requires cargo/clippy on the host, and there are no prebuilt binaries yet (first run compiles from source, 65-75 s)
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.install: export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... ; claude plugin marketplace add kindintelligence/jev-rust-review ; claude plugin install jev-rust-review@jev-rust-review  (first start fails the 30 s MCP timeout while cargo builds from source; then /mcp reconnect)
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.tests: Substantial for a 1-week-old repo: ~9.3k lines Rust; tests/ has e2e, eval, jev_http (wiremock), pipeline, plugin_files, stdout_guard, tool_diagnostics; 33 fixtures with before/after crates and recorded Jev answers; CI on ubuntu+macos (fmt, clippy -D warnings, test, smoke.sh, fresh-install test incl. tampered checksum), MSRV job, plugin manifest job; release workflow. Author-run eval (eval/2026-09-21-three-mode.md, claude-sonnet-5): Claude-only 45/48 vs Claude+Jev 47/48 seeded bugs found, 0 false positives on clean fixtures in either, Claude cost $7.08 vs $8.08 (Jev itself $0.013). The eval shows Jev adds a marginal recall gain on an author-built benchmark, not a large one. Self-authored, not independent.
security: API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY / JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_KEY), never argv; .mcp.json passes it via env from plugin userConfig (sensitive:true, keychain). Client uses bearer_auth; no key in process list. Config test asserts the secret is not Debug-printed (config.rs ~196).
Redirects disabled (jev.rs redirect Policy::none) so a 307/308 cannot re-post key and code elsewhere; endpoint must be https unless loopback (endpoint_error).

src/redact.rs skips secret-named files (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, .npmrc, *credential*, *secret*) and regex-redacts token shapes (AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Google, sk-, JWT, private keys) before sending; heuristic, not a guarantee, and does not match OpenRouter sk-or-v1 explicitly except via generic sk- rule (sk_token needs 20+ chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-], which sk-or-v1-... satisfies).

Shell execution: server spawns git and cargo via tokio Command with argument vectors, no shell, no stdin (cargo_tools.rs ~372-410, clippy.toml disallows other spawns). BUT cargo clippy/check executes the repository's build.rs and proc macros: running on an untrusted/client repo is arbitrary code execution by design; the skill tells Claude to ask first in untrusted repos and offers --no-cargo, and JEV_RUST_REVIEW_CARGO=0 disables. With bypass/auto permission mode, that asking is weak.

launch.sh: curl/wget only from https GitHub releases (--proto =https, tlsv1.2), verified against SHA256SUMS from the same release (same trust origin as the binary, so protects against corruption/tamper of the asset, not a compromised repo owner); falls back to cargo build --release --locked of the plugin's own source. No curl|sh, no npm postinstall. Dependency surface is a normal Rust crate tree (Cargo.lock committed, #![forbid(unsafe_code)]).

Prompt-injection surface: diff text goes into Jev state and Claude's context; DESIGN.md/eval include a prompt_injection fixture (3/3 found). Jev outputs are typed numbers, so Jev cannot inject text back; Claude reads only structured fields plus the diff.
No telemetry claimed and none found in the source (only one outbound host: the configured Jev URL; plus GitHub release download in launcher).

Third-party plugin from a 2-star, 1-week-old single-author repo: installing it means running its compiled binary with your API key and your source code on every review. Pin the tag/commit and read/build yourself.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.dataEgress: On evaluate_rust_changes and verify_rust_findings: JSON {model, state, questions} with changed Rust code hunks plus enclosing items (units up to 6000 tokens, up to 400k tokens and 60 units per evaluation), file paths/line ranges, project facts (edition, MSRV, runtime), and for verification the claimed lines plus definitions of items named in the claim from elsewhere in the repo, after secret-file skipping and regex token redaction. Sent directly (no proxy, no telemetry) to {JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_URL}/v1/systemone (TypeSafe by default; would be OpenRouter, an additional third party that sees code, if repointed). Not sent: whole repo, non-Rust files, Claude's conversation, tool outputs from other tools. cargo_diagnostics sends nothing off-machine. GitHub releases download only at first launch. Dry-run mode returns request bodies without sending. Client-project code leaving to Jev/OpenRouter is a contractual concern for client repos.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.failureMode: Fail-open by design. No key or unauthorized/insecure endpoint: status jev_unavailable, skill falls back to a Claude-only review with a banner (verify tool still does tool_reported dedup without a key). Per-request timeout 30 s (JEV_RUST_REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECS), connect timeout 10 s, up to 3 retries (max 10) with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After capped at 30 s, on 408/429/529/5xx/network; other 4xx are non-retried errors; per-unit failures give status partial. So a dead Jev can stall a review for minutes worst-case (30 s x 4 attempts + backoff per request, concurrency 4) but never blocks Claude Code itself. cargo runs are bounded by a 600 s timeout, which can be long. First-run: MCP server fails the 30 s startup window while building (documented) and needs a manual /mcp reconnect.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns (the tools are only called inside the rust-review skill). A full review adds cargo clippy time (up to 600 s cap, project dependent, an extra full build if using a separate target dir), plus per-unit Jev fan-out (claimed 70-500 ms per call, concurrency 4, so seconds for a modest diff), then a second Jev round for verification. The author's eval measured ~29-30 min wall for 60 runs = roughly 30 s per full agentic review in the J mode, dominated by Claude, not Jev. First launch: 65-75 s source build.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.contextCost: 3 MCP tools; tool descriptions total roughly 3.8k chars (grep of description strings = 3,780 chars) plus JSON schemas for scope/findings inputs, so approx 1.3-1.8k tokens always resident (if MCP tool search/deferred loading is active it drops to names only). Server instructions string about 600 chars (~150 tokens). Skill: name+description in the always-loaded listing (~450 chars, ~110 tokens); SKILL.md body is 16 KB (~4k tokens) loaded only when invoked, plus per-dimension reference files (16 dimensions + 3 frameworks) loaded only when flagged; agent rust-reviewer.md 5 KB. No hooks, so nothing injected on ordinary tool calls. A review's tool results (flagged lists, facts) add more per invocation. Total resident cost is about 2k tokens, all for a Rust-only feature.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.autoInvocation: Model-discretion, two paths: (1) skill description trigger 'Use when asked to review Rust code or Rust changes' so it fires only if the user asks for a Rust review, not on every edit or commit; (2) the three MCP tools with server instructions, which Claude could call unprompted but nothing forces it. No hooks (no PostToolUse on Edit, no pre-commit/Stop hook), no proxy. So it does not meet 'Claude uses Jev automatically when it adds value' beyond Rust review requests; it is Rust-specific and review-triggered.
pros: Best-engineered Jev integration of its kind: uses Jev exactly as its brief says (typed Noul/Choice/Score questions in bulk, no prose), with two concrete uses (cheap triage, verification gate) and Claude keeping the reasoning; DESIGN.md documents Jev's weak spots and works around them.
Jev cost is negligible ($0.013 for 60 eval runs, jev.rs ~$0.042/M tokens) and calls are fast, so the Jev part is not the bottleneck.

Endpoint path is /v1/systemone and URL/model/key are env-configurable (config.rs:112-117), so pointing at OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone is a 3-env-var change, no fork needed, provided OpenRouter's schema matches.

Safety hygiene above typical: no shell, argv vectors, redirects disabled, https enforced, secret-file skipping and token redaction, dry-run mode that shows exact outgoing payloads, checksum-verified downloads, forbid(unsafe_code).
Fail-open with a clear banner, and tool_reported dedup works without any key, so it degrades gracefully to a Claude-only review.
Real test suite and CI (wiremock HTTP tests, 33 recorded fixtures, install/tamper tests, macOS+Linux, MSRV), MIT license, no telemetry, no hooks that could slow or break every tool call.
Low always-on context cost (~2k tokens) and it does not interfere with the existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
cons: Rust-only: every question, lint, and reference is Rust (clippy, cargo-semver-checks, syn). Useless for non-Rust personal/client work; no evidence the user's daily stack is Rust.

Not automatic: triggers only when the user asks for a Rust review (skill description) or when Claude elects to call the MCP tools. No hook fires on edits, commits or Stop, which fails the user's core requirement of Claude using Jev by itself when needed.

Marginal value on its own benchmark: author's eval shows Claude alone 45/48 vs Claude+Jev 47/48, and the one hard fixture (symlink_check_then_delete) went 0/3 to 2/3, at +$1 Claude cost per 60 runs. Self-run and self-built fixtures; no independent validation.
Alpha and tiny: 33 commits over 3 days by one author, 2 stars, v0.1.0, explicitly 'in active development' with interfaces/thresholds that may change; not affiliated with TypeSafe or Anthropic.

No OpenRouter support tested or documented; whether OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the identical body, model id typesafe/jev-1.13, and returns the same answer shape is unverified. Key env naming is confusing (OpenRouter key goes in the 'typesafe_api_key' userConfig or JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_KEY; TYPESAFE_API_KEY overrides).

Source-build friction: no prebuilt binaries yet, needs Rust toolchain, first launch takes 65-75 s and exceeds the 30 s MCP startup timeout, so the server shows failed until manual /mcp reconnect. Ships and runs an unaudited compiled binary with your key.

cargo clippy runs the target repo's build.rs and proc macros; on client repos with bypass/auto permission mode the 'ask first if untrusted' guidance is effectively unenforced, so it is arbitrary code execution from the reviewed repo. Must use --no-cargo or JEV_RUST_REVIEW_CARGO=0.
Sends client source code (hunks plus related item definitions) to a third-party model API (TypeSafe or OpenRouter); redaction is regex-based best effort. Relevant for client NDAs.
Review latency and clippy build cost can be significant (up to 600 s cargo cap), and it competes with the user's own cargo build lock unless an extra target dir (an extra full build) is configured.
gh-kindintelligence-jev-rust-review.verdict: High-quality but narrow reference implementation of Jev for Rust PR/diff review only; patchable to OpenRouter via env vars, but it is a review-on-request skill, not an automatic, language-agnostic Jev integration, and it is v0.1 from a one-person repo. Worth borrowing as a design pattern (triage plus verify gate, dry-run, redaction) or installing only if the user does substantial Rust work and pins the tag.

gh-doeixd-jev-pref.name: doeixd/jev-pref
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.whatItDoes: Node CLI (npx jev-pref, MIT) that acts as a semantic "AI linter" over git diffs. The user defines checks in jev-pref.json (Noul conditions and Choice classifications, e.g. "does this change introduce shared mutable state?"). `review` collects the working, staged, PR or arbitrary diff, splits it per hunk or per file, sends state and questions to Jev via the `advocaat` SDK in one batched call, then maps P and confidence to approve/advisory/fix_now with exit codes 0/1/2. Also has `setup` and `sync` (agent-facing protocol text), `tune` (calibrates thresholds on labeled evals), `doctor`, `examples`, plus a GitHub Action for PR review. It is not an MCP server and not a hook. It ships one thin skill (skills/jev-pref/SKILL.md) that only says to run `npx jev-pref setup`. The integration intended for Claude Code is a paragraph the agent writes into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md telling itself to run `npx jev-pref review --hunks` after substantial implementation work.

providerSupport.evidence: Default is TypeSafe direct. advocaat dist/index.mjs:33 baseURL = options.baseURL ?? env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL ?? 'https://api.typesafe.ai'; :60 POST baseURL + '/v1/systemone' with Bearer key; :34 default model 'jev-latest'. There is also a Vercel AI Gateway path (:29-31, 65-73, ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai/evaluation-model). jev-pref exposes JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL, JEV_PROVIDER (typesafe|vercel, validated in config.js:385) and JEV_API_KEY (packages/jev-pref/src/config.js:86-88, 308; jev.js:49-50 forwards baseURL/model to advocaat). No mention of 'openrouter' anywhere in the repo (grep over js/md/json/yml returned nothing). Because the OpenRouter route /api/v1/systemone is the same path and Bearer scheme the SDK appends, `JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 JEV_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY` should work with no code change (a web search result claims OpenRouter has parity with the TypeSafe System One schema). I did NOT test this live, and I did not confirm OpenRouter's response shape or its use of the /api prefix from OpenRouter's own docs (the docs URL I tried returned 404).

gh-doeixd-jev-pref.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and probably config-only. Set JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) and JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>. Passing an explicit apiKey forces advocaat's non-gateway branch (advocaat :29), so the request goes to POST {base}/v1/systemone with a Bearer token. Caveats: (1) the repo pins advocaat 0.0.2, whose relevant code matches 0.0.6; (2) the JEV_PROVIDER=vercel path is irrelevant; (3) OpenRouter's response must match the shape advocaat parses (answers[name].type noul/choice/score), which is unverified; (4) OpenRouter may add headers or rate limits that the retry logic only partly covers (it retries only 429 and 529).
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.others: Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY / VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN, zeroDataRetention flag) as an alternative gateway.

interface.name: jev-pref review [--staged|--pr|--diff REF|--diff -] [--hunks|--files] [--json|--raw|--dry-run] [--fail-on] [--include/--exclude] [--model/--base-url/--provider/--timeout-ms]
interface.purpose: Core linter. Sends the diff plus configured questions to Jev and returns a verdict. Exit 0 accepted, 1 failOn policy triggered, 2 config/infra/usage failure.

interface.name: jev-pref setup
interface.purpose: Prints a long agent-facing onboarding protocol (setup.js is 517 lines). It inspects the repo and env var presence, and tells the agent to write jev-pref.json and CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md instructions.

interface.name: jev-pref sync
interface.purpose: Read-only printout of a protocol for reconciling AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md guidance with the Jev checks.

interface.name: jev-pref tune [--sweep] [--check=N] [--dry-run]
interface.purpose: Scores checks against labeled evals/*.json (one Jev call per case) and proposes a gateThreshold.

interface.name: jev-pref doctor / examples
interface.purpose: Environment and config diagnostics, and copyable recipes (agent-loop, pre-commit, github-action, review-script).

interface.name: skills/jev-pref/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: A discovery-only skill (about 20 lines). Its description triggers on setting up jev-pref or reviewing changes in an already configured repo.

interface.name: actions/review (GitHub Action)
interface.purpose: Bounded per-file PR review with a sticky comment and annotations. Needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

interface.name: agent handoff config (jev-pref.json agent.command)
interface.purpose: Optional argv array executed after a verdict, with stdin JSON that includes the full diff. Uses execFile, no shell.

gh-doeixd-jev-pref.lastCommit: 2026-09-18 (docs: center explainer above README title). Latest release v0.4.1 on 2026-09-18. No pushes for 12 days as of 2026-09-30.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.runtime: Node >=20, ESM, one runtime dependency (advocaat 0.0.2, MIT, by pi0/pithings, first published 2026-09-16). Invoked via npx.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.install: No install needed for basic use: `npx jev-pref setup`. Optional `npx skills add doeixd/jev-pref --skill jev-pref`. Per the README, the agent then writes jev-pref.json and a "Semantic review" section into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md. `npx` fetches and runs the latest published npm package unless the version is pinned, so there is a supply-chain surface. I did not verify whether the npm package exists at a matching version (static review only).
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.tests: 10 test files, about 1,100 lines, using node --test. They cover args, config, hunks, render, scope/budget, setup, suites, the CLI and the action. jev.test.js is 11 lines, so the live client, retry and timeout paths are thin. CI (.github/workflows/validate.yml) runs skill validation, npm ci, tests, doctor, and `tune --dry-run`. The last 5 runs succeeded. There are no live Jev calls in CI. The repo also has a self-review workflow (jev-review.yml). 1 open issue.
security: API key is env-only by design (config.js:6-8, 308). It is never accepted via flags or files, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. That is good.

Data is sent to whatever JEV_BASE_URL points at (config.js:87). The config layers also accept baseUrl from jev-pref.json and jev-pref.local.json, and from a fenced ```jev-prefs block inside CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (config.js:3, 116-140). A malicious or untrusted repo could therefore redirect diffs to another host. It could not steal the key from a file, but the Bearer key from the env would be sent to that host. This matters on client projects.

Repo-controlled command execution: `agent.command` in jev-pref.json (or the fenced block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) is run with execFile whenever the outcome matches agent.on (agent.js:55, config.js:389-403). No shell is used, but any cloned repo's config can run an arbitrary binary with the full diff on stdin. Never run this in untrusted repos.

Prompt-injection surface: diff and file contents go to Jev, which has no free text output and returns only probabilities, so injection can bias verdicts but cannot cause text-based hijack. However the `setup` and `sync` output is instruction text the agent obeys, and it is generated from repo content (AGENTS.md etc.). That is a mild surface.
No postinstall scripts. Runtime dependency is a single 260-line SDK (advocaat), which I read in full. It only does fetch to baseURL, with no telemetry and no filesystem or exec use.
No telemetry found in jev-pref src (no calls other than the Jev request, plus local git and `gh pr view`).

npx usage means the latest published package runs unpinned unless the user pins the version (the pre-commit example itself says to pin). The package is brand new, from a single author, 12 days old. I did not verify the npm tarball matches the GitHub source.
The 'secrets' suite is itself a Jev question (a diff sent to a remote model to look for secrets). It is not a local scanner and offers no protection against sending secrets.
No timeout or sandbox concerns beyond a 60s per-call timeout and 5 overload retries.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.dataEgress: Per Jev call the payload (review.js:395-430, git.js:133-204) contains: the config prefs (ids, questions, labels, guidance), git status, diff --stat, the branch name and scope, and the diff text. That text is the full tracked diff, split per hunk or file and capped at 20,000 chars per request (30k-token Jev input limit). Untracked files that are not gitignored (git ls-files --others --exclude-standard) are also read and sent in full, up to 100 files and 20k chars each. A `.env` that is not ignored, or scratch files, would be sent. Binary files are skipped. `--staged`, `--pr` and `--diff` scopes send the corresponding diffs. Nothing is sent from Claude Code conversation, prompts or tool outputs, only git state. Destination: api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if JEV_BASE_URL is set, in which case OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see client code. Supports a zeroDataRetention flag for the Vercel gateway only. Pricing is about $0.042/M input tokens, so a review costs fractions of a cent, but per-hunk mode can make up to 10 calls (maxHunks) per review.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.failureMode: Fail-closed by contract for the CLI: exit code 2 on config, infra or timeout failure, and the docs state that 'exit 2 is never approval'. Timeouts are 60 s per call (AbortSignal.timeout, jev.js:52), and 429/529 are retried up to 5 times with backoff 500ms doubling, capped at 30s (jev.js:26-28, 62-66). Worst-case stall is therefore roughly minutes per call. Other HTTP errors fail immediately. Because it is not a hook, nothing blocks Claude Code on its own: the agent just sees a failed command and, per the recommended CLAUDE.md snippet, treats it as 'not approval', and there is a 3-loop limit. If wired as a hook, fail-open versus fail-closed depends on the user's wrapper script, and the default `jev-pref review` exit codes would block in a Stop hook if used naively.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.latencyImpact: Zero per-turn latency unless invoked. Each `review` costs one Jev call per scope (Jev claims 70-500 ms end to end), plus npx startup (about 0.5-3 s cold, if it is fetched from the registry) and git collection. With --hunks and maxHunks=10 there can be up to 10 sequential or batched calls. Since the model is only invoked on demand, the practical cost is a few seconds per invocation, but the calls are not run in parallel as far as I could tell from the review.js structure (I did not confirm). If a Stop or PostToolUse hook were added, latency would land on every turn or edit.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.contextCost: Near zero tools: 0 MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. Skill description is about 35 tokens, always listed. The CLAUDE.md snippet the agent writes is about 150-250 tokens permanently in context for that repo. `npx jev-pref setup` prints a very large protocol once during setup (setup.js is 517 lines, so roughly 5-8k tokens, one-time). Each `review` prints a short verdict, about 100-800 tokens depending on findings. No hook-injected text.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only, via instructions in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (the "After a substantial bout of implementation work, run npx jev-pref review --hunks" snippet) plus a discovery-only skill trigger. There is no shipped Claude Code hook, MCP server or proxy. Automatic in the sense the user wants (never say "use jev") only works if the snippet exists in each project's CLAUDE.md (or the user's global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) and the model follows it, which is probabilistic. Deterministic automation would require the user to add a Claude Code Stop or PostToolUse hook that runs `jev-pref review --json` themselves, which the repo does not provide (it offers a git pre-commit example only).
pros: Actually uses Jev's real primitives (Noul, Choice, and batched questions) for a well-scoped, well-fitting job: classifying diffs against project-defined semantic rules. This is what a System One model is good at, unlike chat-style uses.

Provider indirection is nearly complete in code: JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL, JEV_API_KEY are all honored (config.js:86-88; jev.js:49-50), and the SDK posts to {base}/v1/systemone, the exact OpenRouter route, so pointing it at OpenRouter is likely env-only.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, tiny skill, one CLAUDE.md paragraph. Works with the user's existing hooks and MCP without conflict.
Sane security defaults for keys: env-only, never in argv; execFile without shell; no telemetry; one small dependency I read in full.

Machine-readable interface: --json output plus stable 0/1/2 exit codes, --dry-run to preview what would be sent, --raw for numbers, and `tune` to calibrate thresholds on labeled diffs. This is easy to wrap in a hook.
Cheap: about $0.042/M input tokens on OpenRouter, so a review of a 20k-char diff is a fraction of a cent.
Bounded input handling: 20k-char per-request budget, hunk/file splitting, and a pre-flight check against the 30k token limit, so calls do not fail on big diffs.
MIT licensed, has tests and passing CI, and a clearly documented boundary of what Jev should and should not judge (docs/principles.md).
cons: Not automatic. There is no hook, MCP server or proxy. Invocation relies on Claude following a CLAUDE.md sentence, so it is model-discretion and can be skipped, which conflicts with the user's stated 'Claude Code must use it when needed' goal unless the user writes their own Stop/PostToolUse hook wrapper.

OpenRouter support is undocumented and unverified: the string 'openrouter' appears nowhere in the repo, the README/`doctor`/`setup` all steer to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and `doctor` only recognizes JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN (doctor.js:34-39). It is a diff linter, not general assistance: value only appears where the user has authored good semantic rules (jev-pref.json) per project. On client projects that means writing and maintaining checks and modifying their repo or CLAUDE.md, which some clients will not want.

Data egress: full diffs plus non-ignored untracked files (up to 100 files, 20k chars each) leave the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. That is a compliance question for client code, and there is no local secret redaction; even the secrets suite works by sending the diff to the model.

Repo-controlled behavior: baseUrl and agent.command can be set by files inside the reviewed repo (jev-pref.json, jev-pref.local.json, or a fenced block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), giving a repo the ability to redirect the diff and the Bearer key or execute a binary. Unsafe to run automatically in untrusted client repos.

Very young and single-author: 12 days old, 46 commits in 2 days, 1 contributor, 11 stars, no pushes since 2026-09-18, tests mostly don't exercise the live client, and the tool is pinned to the 0.0.x SDK. High breaking-change risk in a beta-model ecosystem.
`npx` unpinned means running whatever is newest on npm each time (supply-chain exposure, plus multi-second cold-start latency). Pin the version or vendor it if used.

Calibration is unproven: the Jev model is beta and skeptics claim it resembles a small router model. Semantic-lint verdicts (P>=0.7 gating) may be noisy, and the tool's own docs admit thresholds need calibration on labeled diffs.
gh-doeixd-jev-pref.verdict: The only candidate here that puts Jev to a job it suits (typed Noul/Choice judgments about code changes), and it is probably switchable to OpenRouter via JEV_BASE_URL plus JEV_MODEL plus JEV_API_KEY, though I did not test that live. It is not automatic on its own: the intended integration is a CLAUDE.md instruction, so the user would need to add a Stop/PostToolUse hook wrapper for deterministic use, and should pin the version and avoid running it in untrusted client repos because repo config can set the endpoint and execute a command.

security: API key is read only from env (src/jev.ts:36) and sent in an Authorization header (src/jev.ts:361-366), so it is never in argv. A literal apiKey in the config file is a hard error (config.ts:160).

Runs `npx -y jev-lint` (unpinned fetch of the latest npm version) in the slash commands and in the git hooks docs. That is a supply-chain surface on every hook run. The author's own hook uses the checked-out CLI instead.
No postinstall or preinstall scripts in package.json. No telemetry found in src/ (grep). Shell execution is limited to execFile of git and ast-grep with argument arrays, with no shell string.
The verdict cache .jev-lint/baseline.json is trusted input, and the docs say so: anything that can edit it can silence a rule.

Prompt-injection surface: the code, comments and commit messages being judged are sent to the model, and it returns only numbers. So a comment cannot inject text into Claude from Jev. The slash commands do make Claude read the findings and open code, which is normal.

The `baseUrl` config key can redirect all source to another host. A malicious repo .jev-lint.yaml could set baseUrl to exfiltrate code to an attacker host whenever the user's key env var is present; the key is sent as a Bearer token to that host. This matters for client repos (check with --base-url and the config before running).
Author reports about one finding in five is wrong; the cache and --retry mitigate but do not remove this.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.dataEgress: Full source text of each judged file (state.source, enclosing_code, symbols, imports, module identity), related test excerpts, the git diff and stat plus commit message for commits mode, the full AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md text, and rule-declared context documents. Each request goes to the configured base URL (default api.typesafe.ai) as {model,state,questions}. Nothing is sent from Claude's own prompts, tool outputs or conversation, because it is not a proxy. It sends whole files, so `check src` on a client repo ships the entire codebase to a third party. Suppression comments (jev-lint-ignore-file) skip sending. There is no built-in secret redaction, and .env files could be sent if included in files:.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.failureMode: The CLI is fail-open for hooks. It retries 5xx or network errors 4 times with backoff, uses a 60 s per-request timeout (src/jev.ts timeoutMs=60_000) and retries 429 separately. On failure it exits 3 (requests failed), and the shipped git hooks deliberately let exit 3 through, and also exit 0 when no key is set. In the slash commands, Claude just reports the failure. The whole-run wall time can be long: about 5 s for 2,300 subjects with 32 in flight, per docs/cost.md. Because it is not in Claude's tool loop, a Jev outage never blocks Claude.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.latencyImpact: None on normal Claude turns, because nothing runs automatically inside Claude Code. When run, review on a small diff takes about seconds (docs/cost.md: 3 commits reviewed in 8 s; full-repo self-lint 5 s over 32 concurrent requests). Startup includes npx -y resolution and Node 24, roughly a second or more per invocation. The git pre-commit hook would add several seconds to each commit.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.contextCost: Very low. There is no MCP server, so 0 tool definitions. The skill adds about 700 chars of description (roughly 175 tokens) to the always-on skill list. The body is about 10.5 KB, roughly 2.6k tokens, and loads only when triggered. The plugin also registers 4 slash commands with a short description each (about 100 tokens in total). No hook-injected text.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.autoInvocation: Skill-description trigger only. It fires when the user or code mentions jev-lint or .jev-lint.yaml, and, per the description, on 'any request to check code for something a conventional linter cannot decide'. It is NOT triggered by Claude editing code. The slash commands are manual. The only deterministic automatic path is the git pre-commit or pre-push hook, which fires when any tool (including Claude's Bash git commit) commits. That is a git hook, not a Claude Code hook, and it would cover Claude-made commits.
pros: Uses Jev exactly as designed: typed score/noul questions with calibrated cutoffs, so it exercises the primitive well and Jev's cheap latency ($0.042/M input; a full 2.3k-subject self-lint cost $0.09).

Base URL and model are already overridable via env or config (src/jev.ts:269-270, config.ts:236-246), so pointing at OpenRouter's /v1/systemone should need only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_LINT_MODEL and apiKeyEnv, with no fork.
Ships a real Claude Code plugin (plugin.json and marketplace.json valid) with a skill and slash commands, so install is two /plugin commands.

The git pre-commit hook is the one truly automatic path: it triggers on Claude's own `git commit` without any prompt to Claude, reviews staged lines only (a fraction of a cent) and judges the staged diff against the repo's AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md.

Careful failure design: hooks fail open (skip on no key, tolerate exit 3), never block by default (no shipped rule has severity error), verdict cache and --retry to tame noise, and --dry-run prices a run without any request.
Key never in argv or config file; no postinstall or telemetry; CI uses SHA-pinned actions and a keyless replay test; 36 test files; MIT.
Catches real AI-coding failure modes that tsc/eslint miss: stale comments, names that overclaim, tests that do not test what they claim, and a diff violating CLAUDE.md.
cons: Not an automatic in-session integration. No MCP tool and no Claude Code hooks (PostToolUse/Stop) ship, so Claude will not call Jev while coding. The skill only triggers when jev-lint is mentioned or the user asks to 'check code for something a linter cannot decide', which contradicts the requirement to never prompt.

It is a batch reviewer of whole files and diffs, not a decision-helper Claude can consult mid-task (routing, classification, yes/no gates). Only a fraction of Jev's Choice/Noul/Score value is exposed, and only through fixed rules.
Author-measured precision is about 80% (one finding in five wrong) and scores near cutoffs move by hundredths between runs. A noisy reviewer in an all-day bypass-mode workflow adds triage work.

Sends whole source files and diffs (and CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) to a third party; on client projects this is a real confidentiality question, and no redaction exists. A hostile repo .jev-lint.yaml can set baseUrl to redirect code and the Bearer key.
Slash commands and docs use `npx -y jev-lint` (unpinned latest) and Node 24 with an ast-grep binary; every run resolves a fresh package, a supply-chain and startup-latency cost.
OpenRouter path is undocumented and untested by the author (no 'openrouter' in src). Model id 'jev-latest' must be overridden. The response schema match is unverified from code.
Very new (11 days old, 209/237 commits by one author, releases page stale at v0.2.1 vs 0.7.0). API and rules are churning (threshold migration, rules by language in a week).
Rules are code-quality oriented (naming, comments, tests, prose, shell), useful in review but only a small slice of daily coding.
gh-mizchi-jev-lint.verdict: A well-built, low-context Jev linter that could be pointed at OpenRouter with three env settings. But it is not an automatic Claude Code integration: it is a skill plus manual slash commands, and only a git pre-commit hook fires on its own. Use it at most as an optional commit-time reviewer on personal repos, and weigh the code-egress risk before enabling it on client projects. It does not meet the goal of Claude using Jev by itself when useful.

gh-buchmark-claude-jev.name: buchmark/claude-jev
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json) that bundles a stdio MCP server (committed, esbuild-bundled dist/server.js, TypeScript source, uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk) exposing 5 Jev tools, a "jev" SKILL.md with a description-based trigger, and 4 slash commands. Four tools are presets (review findings, hypothesis ranking, option picking, file-relevance filtering) with question texts and verdict thresholds hardcoded in code; jev_ask is a generic escape hatch. The server reads source snippets from disk itself (line ranges), so code does not pass through Claude's context, and sends them plus typed questions to Jev.

providerSupport.evidence: src/infrastructure/typesafe-jev.ts:134-138 builds TypeSafeClient with only apiKey/defaultModel(/fetch); no baseURL passed and no OpenRouter string anywhere in src/ or README. The bundled SDK (dist/server.js:37584-37590, 37950) reads env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai) and POSTs {baseURL}/v1/systemone (dist/server.js:37991) with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (38018) and body {state, questions, model}. Key env: src/infrastructure/config.ts:190 JEV_API_KEY ?? TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Model: config.ts:191 JEV_MODEL default 'jev-latest'; plugin.json passes JEV_MODEL from a userConfig enum [jev-latest, jev-preview, jev-1.13.0]. So OpenRouter would be reachable by TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, matching the brief's System One endpoint), TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. Not verified: OpenRouter's request/response schema equality with TypeSafe direct, and whether the env var reaches the MCP child (plugin.json env block only sets JEV_*; inherited env is expected but untested).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate, config-only (no code fork): set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or the plugin apiKey option), and override the model to an OpenRouter ID. Catches: (1) plugin.json always injects JEV_MODEL (default 'jev-latest', enum-restricted UI options) which takes precedence over nothing else, so the OpenRouter model ID 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest' must be entered via plugin config/settings and may be rejected by the enum options; (2) if OpenRouter's System One schema differs even slightly, toDomainAnswer() throws MalformedAnswerError; (3) --check calls GET /v1/models, which OpenRouter may serve differently (only affects the manual check). A 3-line source patch (pass baseURL from env in typesafe-jev.ts) plus rebuild would be needed only if env inheritance does not work, but rebuilding means a local fork.
providerSupport.others: None. Only api.typesafe.ai (default) is supported natively.

gh-buchmark-claude-jev.runtime: Node >=20 (bundled ESM single file dist/server.js, ~1.4 MB, no runtime deps; user has Node 24). Requires Claude Code >=2.1.269 (user has 2.1.285).
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.install: claude plugin marketplace add buchmark/claude-jev && claude plugin install claude-jev@claude-jev  (then /reload-plugins). dist/server.js is committed; no postinstall or build needed. NOTE: not run by this audit.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.tests: 72 vitest tests in tests/ (budget, catalog, config, format, fs-source-reader, typesafe-jev, use-cases) using a fake Jev and fake reader, no network; no .github directory so no CI; no releases/tags; package.json private:true v0.1.0. README shows real output from live runs but the one showed a planted false positive being kept (0.57), i.e. filter quality is modest.
security: No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh; install is a committed prebuilt bundle. Downside: dist/server.js (1.4 MB, bundled MCP SDK + TypeSafe SDK + zod) is an unreviewable blob that must match src; README itself warns it must be rebuilt and committed manually, so it can drift from source.

API key handling: plugin option marked sensitive (README says macOS Keychain; on Linux this likely falls back to plaintext credentials storage - unverified). Key is passed via env (JEV_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY), not argv, so not visible in the process list arguments. SDK logger at debug level logs headers/bodies (dist/server.js ~38000) but default log level is not debug.

Filesystem guard in src/infrastructure/fs-source-reader.ts:14-32: hard denylist for .env*, .git, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .gcloud, .npmrc, .netrc, credentials*, secrets.*, *.pem/*.key/etc; realpath + containment check against client MCP roots; 4 MB ceiling; binary refusal. It is filename-based only: secrets hardcoded inside ordinary source files (config.ts, settings.py, terraform.tfvars, docker-compose.yml with passwords) are still sent. Complements but does not replace the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, which will NOT fire on MCP tool calls (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so files read by the MCP server bypass that hook.

Prompt-injection surface: source content is sent to Jev as data and Jev returns only numbers, so injection can at worst skew a probability (README admits this). Jev's numbers then feed Claude, but output is compact text of numbers/labels, not free text. Verdict labels come from fixed code thresholds. Low risk of instruction injection into Claude; moderate risk of manipulated verdicts (a malicious comment could make a real finding get dropped).

Model-supplied `path` arguments: Claude (or injected content) can request any in-root file, so untrusted repo content that steers Claude could cause exfiltration of any non-denylisted in-root file to the Jev provider. Bounded to session roots.

No telemetry in plugin code; SDK sends User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers. Single author, 7 stars, brand-new: supply-chain trust rests on one unknown GitHub account (owner name 'oxdev' in manifests vs GitHub user buchmark).
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.dataEgress: With source reading on (default true): file contents of the line ranges / files named in each tool call (up to 64 KB per source, 20 sources per call, default; up to 1 MB / 200 via options), plus the task text, finding claims/failure descriptions, hypothesis text, option summaries, and question text, go to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default; would be openrouter.ai and then OpenRouter's upstream if patched via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). The full state is re-sent with every request of a fan-out (up to 8 requests per call). Only what Claude explicitly puts in a tool call leaves the machine; nothing is sent automatically on prompts, diffs or tool outputs unless Claude calls a tool. Set JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false to send only text passed in the call. Relevant for client projects: client code goes to a third party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter), and OpenRouter data-retention/logging policy applies.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: errors are caught in src/adapters/respond.ts:15-21 and returned as isError text (missing key, budget, forbidden path, HTTP error, MalformedAnswerError), so Claude just sees an error and proceeds. Missing key does not crash the server; it errors on first call with an explanatory message (typesafe-jev.ts:6-13, 133). SDK defaults (dist/server.js 37955, 37599): 10 s request timeout, maxRetries 2 with 0.5-5 s backoff and Retry-After up to 60 s on 408/429/5xx, so a worst case for a slow/down endpoint is roughly 30+ s blocking per tool call (requests in a fan-out run in parallel). Being an MCP tool, not a hook, it never blocks tool execution or prompts; Claude can ignore failure. If server process fails to start, only the tools disappear.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Estimated tool defs: 5 descriptions of roughly 500-700 chars each (about 3k chars) plus zod-derived JSON schemas with .describe() text for sources, questions (nested discriminated union), findings, hypotheses, options, candidates (about 6-8k chars) - approx 2.5k-3.5k tokens total in the tool list (deferred/ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.x may reduce this to names only until needed). Skill: description frontmatter ~800 chars (~200 tokens) always listed; the full SKILL.md (~4.5 KB, ~1.1k tokens) loads only when triggered. 4 slash commands add ~4 short one-line descriptions. No MCP server 'instructions' field is set (server.ts:14 constructs McpServer with only name/version). No hook-injected text. Per-call output is a compact block of numbers.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.latencyImpact: No hooks, so zero latency on ordinary tool calls or prompts. Each Jev tool call adds one MCP round trip: claimed 70-500 ms (README says ~150 ms) network plus local file reads; fan-out requests run in parallel via Promise.all (src/application/fan-out.ts:23). Worst case with retries about 30 s. Also adds Claude-side turns: Claude must first assemble structured findings/hypotheses/options (extra output tokens, one extra tool-call turn) before Jev is consulted, which is the larger cost than the Jev call itself.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.autoInvocation: Model discretion only, via two soft channels: (1) MCP tool descriptions that say 'Run it on your own candidate findings before presenting a review', 'Use it right after a broad grep, glob...' etc. (src/adapters/tools/*.ts); (2) the jev skill whose description triggers on code review, false positives, why is this failing, which approach is safer, is this reachable, which files matter. There are NO hooks, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no deterministic trigger. The four slash commands are manual. With Opus 5.5 in bypass/auto mode it will sometimes call them during reviews/debugging/planning, but nothing guarantees it, and the skill itself says 'not for every step'. To make it more automatic the user would need to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a small hook/SessionStart reminder.
pros: Purpose-built for Claude Code and Jev: presets for the exact moments Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives fit (review finding triage, hypothesis ranking, option choice, grep-hit filtering), with prompt text and thresholds kept in reviewable code (src/domain/catalog/*).
Best auto-invocation story among plugin-style options: both skill description triggers AND tool descriptions steer Claude to call it during review/debug/plan without the user saying 'use jev'.
Server reads files itself from line ranges, so source never enters Claude's context, and the filter tool triages grep hits cheaply.
Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so wire format tracks TypeSafe's real API; SDK already honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, making OpenRouter (/api + /v1/systemone) a config-level switch rather than a fork.

Decent engineering hygiene for a week-old repo: hexagonal layout, strict TS, 72 offline tests, budget planner that refuses instead of truncating (src/domain/budget.ts), explicit fail-safe error responses, MIT, single-file committed bundle with no postinstall.

Sensible egress controls: hard secret-file denylist, realpath containment against client roots, size caps, JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING kill-switch for client repos, per-call request cap (JEV_MAX_REQUESTS).
Non-blocking design: no hooks means no interference with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks, and no added latency when Jev is unused.
Honest README about limits (kept a planted false positive at 0.57; Jev weaknesses), and skill rule that Jev output is never authorization for destructive actions.
cons: Not OpenRouter-native: hardcoded to TypeSafe direct by default; OpenRouter requires undocumented env override TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model ID (typesafe/jev-1.13) that plugin.json's enum-restricted JEV_MODEL option does not list, and schema parity with OpenRouter's System One API is unverified.

Auto-invocation is only model-discretion: no hook, so use will be inconsistent; it depends on Claude choosing to assemble structured findings first. The added workflow (Claude writes candidates, Jev filters) costs extra Claude tokens/turns on top of Jev's cost.

Value is unproven and skeptical: Jev is a beta model, filter quality is modest (the README's own demo kept a planted false positive), and the calibration claim is a property of aggregates. Gating review findings on it can drop real bugs (an injected comment or a bad prior can lower `real`).

Bypasses the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit does not cover MCP tools); only a filename denylist protects hardcoded secrets in source files. Client code leaves the machine to TypeSafe/OpenRouter and upstream, a compliance question for client projects (mitigable with JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false, which weakens the main benefit).

Brand-new, single-author (8 commits all on 2026-09-18, 7 stars, no releases, no CI); committed 1.4 MB dist bundle must be manually rebuilt so it can drift from src; plugin is 'private: true' with mismatched owner name (oxdev vs buchmark).
Context tax of about 3k tokens for 5 tools plus skill description on every session, for capabilities that only cover four narrow scenarios.
Retry/timeout defaults (10 s x up to 3 attempts) mean a degraded endpoint can stall a tool call for tens of seconds; not configurable through plugin options.

README says the sensitive API key goes to the macOS Keychain; on this Linux machine the storage behavior is unclear, so the safer path is an env var, which leaves the key in plaintext shell profile/settings.
gh-buchmark-claude-jev.verdict: The most complete and best-designed Jev integration for Claude Code found so far (skill plus tools plus presets, sane guards, offline tests), and the closest to 'Claude uses it on its own'. But it is TypeSafe-direct with an untested OpenRouter path via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and the model enum, auto-use is only soft (no hook), and it is a week-old single-author project, so pilot it on personal repos with source reading toggled per client project.

gh-kyu1204-jgrep.name: kyu1204/jgrep (npm: jevgrep)
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.whatItDoes: A zero-dependency Node CLI (`jgrep`, npm package `jevgrep`) that does semantic grep. It splits files (git ls-files) or git diff hunks into 5-60 line chunks and packs 16 chunks plus 16 Noul yes/no questions into one System One request ("does this code match: <description>"). It prints file:line hits above a probability threshold. It also has --diff (lint a diff with English rules), --tests (predictive test selection, name + import graph in code, rest via Jev) and --rows (score CSV/JSONL). A bundled SKILL.md (also a Claude Code plugin via .claude-plugin/) teaches the agent when to call the CLI through Bash. There is no MCP server and no hook.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jgrep.ts:13-19: ENDPOINT=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (MODEL jev-latest); OPENROUTER_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, OPENROUTER_MODEL=~typesafe/jev-latest. resolveProvider() at src/jgrep.ts:339-349 reads env / ./.env / ~/.config/jgrep/env. TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins over OPENROUTER_API_KEY when both are set, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects the OpenRouter endpoint and model id. JGREP_ENDPOINT and JGREP_MODEL override both, and http:// is only allowed on loopback (checkEndpoint, :328). src/providers.ts:149-159 adds OpenRouter attribution headers (HTTP-Referer, X-OpenRouter-Title, X-Title, X-OpenRouter-Categories: cli-agent) only for openrouter.ai hosts. The key is sent as a Bearer header. Only /api/v1/systemone is used, not /api/alpha/decisions; the only primitive used is Noul.
providerSupport.others: JGREP_ENDPOINT/JGREP_MODEL work with any server speaking System One, including local Ollama on loopback with no key (README 'Other endpoints').
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed: OpenRouter is already first-class. Setting OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and not TYPESAFE_API_KEY) is enough.

interface.name: jgrep "<desc>" [paths]
interface.purpose: Semantic grep over a tree. Prints file:start-end p=.. lines above -t (default 0.7); flags -C, -a, --json, -b, -c, --timeout, --retries, --rate, --estimate, --no-cache.

interface.name: jgrep --diff [ref] [--staged] "<rule>"
interface.purpose: Lint a git diff (working tree, staged, or vs a ref) with an English rule. Exit 0 means the rule matched.

interface.name: jgrep --tests [ref] [--staged]
interface.purpose: Predictive test selection (name, import graph and package-root in code, the rest via Jev). Default threshold 0.5.

interface.name: jgrep --rows file.csv|.jsonl [--questions q.json --out f]
interface.purpose: Score table rows with Noul/Choice/Score questions.

interface.name: jgrep init
interface.purpose: Interactive setup: verifies the key against the API, writes ~/.config/jgrep/env (chmod 600) or ./.env, installs SKILL.md into ~/.claude/skills/jgrep and/or ~/.codex/skills/jgrep, and opens the GitHub star page (xdg-open, opt-in prompt).

interface.name: skills/jgrep/SKILL.md (skill 'jgrep')
interface.purpose: Skill description tells Claude to use jgrep when locating code by behavior, before opening 5+ files, and to self-lint the staged diff before committing. It first runs `command -v jgrep`, never installs anything itself, and tells the user if there is no key.

interface.name: .claude-plugin/plugin.json + marketplace.json
interface.purpose: Plugin manifest so `/plugin marketplace add kyu1204/jgrep` and `/plugin install jgrep@jgrep` install the skill (no hooks, no MCP).

gh-kyu1204-jgrep.lastCommit: 2026-09-30 (v0.6.0 release, same day as the audit)
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.tests: Bun test suite with about 120 tests in 8 files (http, isolation, pool, cli, tests, jgrep, errors, provider), all offline with a fetch stub. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs the tests, builds, and does a Node-runtime smoke test with a bad key. npm publish uses OIDC trusted publishing on release-PR merge. The bench/tests directory has a retrospective benchmark of --tests on five OSS repos. It has 0 open issues and 5 npm versions in 11 days. I did not run any of it.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.runtime: Node >=18 (bundled with bun build, zero runtime deps; @clack/prompts is a dev-dep bundled for init). The build/test toolchain is bun.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.install: npm i -g jevgrep && jgrep init, or export OPENROUTER_API_KEY, then /plugin marketplace add kyu1204/jgrep and /plugin install jgrep@jgrep. The skill can also be installed by `jgrep init`. Both need the global npm binary.
security: No shell string execution: git is called via execFileSync with array args (src/jgrep.ts:91,103) and xdg-open via execFile. No postinstall script in package.json. The npm tarball ships dist/skills/README/LICENSE, published via OIDC trusted publishing.

The API key is sent only in the Authorization header and never in argv, so it is not visible in the process list. It comes from the env var, ./.env, or ~/.config/jgrep/env (written 0600, dir 0700). readVar also reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the cwd's ./.env, so a client repo's .env could inject a key or JGREP_ENDPOINT (mitigated: non-loopback http:// is rejected; an https endpoint attacker-controlled by a malicious repo's .env would still receive the key, and this is a real but narrow risk).
jgrep init can append the key to ./.env in a project (only if the user picks it) and warns if .env is not gitignored.
No telemetry beyond the API call. OpenRouter attribution headers (Referer/Title jgrep) are sent, which identifies the app, not the user. init asks to open the GitHub star page (opt-in).

Prompt-injection surface is small: the model returns only probabilities, never text, so injected text in scanned code can bias a score but cannot make the tool run commands. The bigger risk is the SKILL.md instructing the agent to trust or ignore hits. The SKILL.md itself is benign and says not to install anything.

No secret filtering. The file walker uses `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` (tracked plus untracked-not-ignored) and skips only binaries and files over 1 MB. An unignored .env, key file or credentials JSON inside the scanned path is chunked and uploaded. The user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard only sees the Bash command line and will not stop jgrep from reading files itself.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.dataEgress: Raw source text leaves the machine: every 5-60 line chunk of every scanned file (or every diff hunk with +/- lines and 3 context lines), plus file path, line range and the English query. It goes to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai, or JGREP_ENDPOINT) in request bodies of about 16 chunks (src/jgrep.ts buildRequest, :131-141). For --tests it also sends the compacted source diff and each test file's imports and test names. --rows sends full CSV/JSONL rows. Nothing is sent for cache hits. The local cache is ~/.cache/jgrep/cache.json, a plain JSON of sha1(query+chunk text) mapped to probability, with no code stored. Scanning a whole client repo means the whole repo goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. This matters for client NDA projects and for anything with unignored secrets.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense that nothing is in Claude's critical path: it is a CLI the model chooses to call. The CLI is resilient: 5 attempts, full-jitter backoff (500 ms base, 30 s cap), a per-batch deadline of 15 s including retries, a per-attempt timeout of 30 s, and a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive fatal errors. On failure it exits 2 (distinct from 1 for no match), keeps partial hits, and prints a typed error summary on stderr. The SKILL.md says never to treat exit 2 as clean. If jgrep is missing, the skill tells Claude to ask the user to install it. A missing key gives a 'No API key' message and Claude is told not to work around it. Worst case is a wasted Bash call of up to about 15 s, and there is no hang.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens and no server instructions. No hook-injected text. The skill frontmatter (name plus description, about 509 chars) adds roughly 130 tokens to every session. The SKILL.md body (4.1 KB, about 1.1k tokens) loads only when Claude invokes the skill. Results are compact file:line lines, and the skill tells Claude to Read only the listed ranges. Output tokens are small compared with a multi-file grep/read exploration.
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.latencyImpact: Claimed and self-benchmarked at about 1.6-2 s for 500-900 chunks (README timing table, unverified by me), with 0 s on a cache hit. Batches are 16 chunks with 16 in parallel by default, so a large repo of 10k+ chunks needs 600+ requests and could hit the 15 s batch deadline or rate limits; --rate exists. The cost is about $0.01 per 900 chunks at $0.042/M input tokens. There are no hooks, so zero latency on non-jgrep turns. Each invocation adds one Bash tool call and roughly 2 s only when Claude chooses it. Chunks are judged in isolation, so cross-file questions do not work (README Tips).
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, i.e. model discretion. The description (skills/jgrep/SKILL.md frontmatter) says to use jgrep when locating code by behavior, before opening many files, and as a self-check of the diff before committing. Claude Code would load the skill and then run the CLI through Bash. There is no hook, no MCP tool and no proxy, so there is no deterministic trigger. With Opus 5.5 and built-in Grep/Glob/Explore plus the user's GitNexus MCP and hooks, the model may often prefer those, and the reliability of the skill trigger is unproven. To make it deterministic, the user would need to add their own PreToolUse/Stop hook or a CLAUDE.md rule, which is not shipped. The skill depends on a globally installed npm binary and a key in ~/.config/jgrep/env or the env.
pros: It is the only candidate here with real OpenRouter support in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with model ~typesafe/jev-latest (src/jgrep.ts:18-19,345-346). The user needs no patching or proxy.
Zero context overhead: no MCP tools and no hook text. It costs about 130 tokens of skill description per session, unlike MCP servers that add tens of tool schemas.

Uses the 'System One' strength directly: batched Noul yes/no questions (16 chunks in one request) at $0.042/M input, about $0.01 per 900 chunks, with output free. This is a sensible use of Jev, whose decision output is cheap and typed.

The self-lint idea (`jgrep --diff --staged "<rule>"` before commit) gives a second-model check on Opus's diffs, and `--tests <ref>` narrows test runs. Both are workflows that built-in grep and GitNexus do not cover.

Robust engineering for a 11-day-old tool: typed errors, retries with jitter, per-batch deadline, circuit breaker, exit 2 distinct from 1, and a cache. About 120 offline tests plus CI that smoke-tests under Node. The key is never in argv, the config file is chmod 600, there is no postinstall, execFile is used with arrays, and non-loopback http endpoints are refused.

Non-invasive integration: a plain skill copied to ~/.claude/skills or installed as a plugin, with no settings.json edits. It does not interfere with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks, and it is trivially removable.
Has a `--estimate` dry-run that shows requests, tokens and cost without a key or a call. The SKILL.md tells Claude to stop and tell the user rather than install software or work around a missing key.
cons: Not deterministic. It is a skill-description trigger via Bash, so it does not meet 'Claude Code must use it when needed'. With GitNexus (graph/semantic query), the built-in Grep/Glob and Explore agents already available, Opus will often pick those. Nothing forces Jev use, and there is no hook to make it automatic.

Sends raw source to a third party (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe): every scanned chunk, file path and diff hunk (src/jgrep.ts buildRequest). There is no .env or secret filtering; `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` includes untracked non-ignored files, so an unignored .env or key file is uploaded. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover file reads made by the CLI itself. This is a real problem for client projects.

Chunks are judged in isolation by a heuristic column-0 splitter (a 'ponytail' comment in the code admits tree-sitter is not used), so cross-file or flow questions do not work (README Tips). The probability quality (p>=0.9 reliable) is self-reported, and the bench covers only --tests, with no precision/recall for grep. The Theo 'flash router' skepticism is untested here.

Very young: created 2026-09-19, 23 commits, 2 committers (effectively one author, 22 commits), 57 stars, v0.6.0 and 5 versions in 11 days. Expect churn. The System One endpoint is beta. The README says it 'appears in OpenRouter's app rankings' (attribution headers are sent by default), and init nags for a GitHub star.

Requires a global `npm i -g jevgrep` binary and a separate key file (~/.config/jgrep/env or ./.env), so there is a second place for the OpenRouter key to live. The cache key uses the constant MODEL 'jev-latest' (src/jgrep.ts key()) rather than the resolved model id, so the README claim 'cached per model id' looks inconsistent for JGREP_MODEL or OpenRouter runs. A project ./.env can also supply the key or JGREP_ENDPOINT (a supply-chain risk on untrusted repos).

Scope mismatch with 'Jev decides things in the workflow': this is a grep replacement and a diff linter, not a general router or decision layer for Claude Code (permission decisions, task routing, and so on). It also scans whole directories, so cost and time grow with repo size (600+ requests on a 10k-chunk monorepo; a 15 s batch deadline).
gh-kyu1204-jgrep.verdict: A well-built, low-footprint skill and CLI with genuine OpenRouter support, and the best 'drop-in' Jev candidate for optional semantic search, diff self-lint and test selection. But it is model-discretion only (not automatic), it uploads raw code with no secret filtering, and it competes with GitNexus and built-in Grep. Use it as a complement (skill plus a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge you add yourself, restricted to non-client repos), not as the core Jev integration.

It prints lines whose P(yes) >= threshold, with grep-style flags (-v, -n, --score, --json, --threshold) and grep-style exit codes. Shows a useful System One pattern with evidence: naming lines (lines.line_01) instead of list indices raised mean F1 from 0.75 to 0.90 by removing answer bleed between batched items. This applies to any custom Jev wrapper.

Honest documentation of Jev's weaknesses: literal reading, fuzzy 'real error' F1 0.80 versus Haiku 0.92, numbers and dates, and susceptibility to text that describes itself (0.97 score on an injected line).
Low-risk footprint: key from env, no shell exec, no telemetry, no hooks, no context cost, MIT.

Cheap (about $0.004 per 1,000 lines) and fast (about 0.4 s per request), and it is a useful manual tool for triaging long logs, CI output, or journalctl/kubectl streams that Claude Code would otherwise read fully.
Sound streaming and retry design: micro-batches, order preserved, LRU cache, 4 retries, and clean exit codes that let Claude tell 'no match' from 'error'.
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so nothing triggers it automatically. The user's requirement of 'Claude uses Jev when needed without prompting' is not met without hand-written CLAUDE.md or skill glue.

Narrow scope: one job, per-line yes/no filtering of text streams. Claude Code's daily work (Grep/Glob/Read on source code) is already served by rg, which is free and instant, and by GitNexus. The README itself says to use grep if a regex works.
Only Noul, and only for lines. It does not expose Choice or Score, so it cannot be used for routing, gating or triage decisions.

Data egress: any piped content (logs with secrets, client code) goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That clashes with client-project confidentiality and with the user's existing secret-leak guard hook. --explain also sends data to Anthropic via OpenRouter.
Immature: 1 star, 1 author, 8 commits, created 9 days before the audit date (2026-09-21), version 0.1.0, alpha. The benchmark is one small synthetic log labelled by the author.

Reported accuracy limits: it loses to Haiku/Sonnet on fuzzy questions, and it is vulnerable to self-describing injected text (0.97 false positive), so its verdicts are not safe as a security or filtering gate.
Depends on typesafe-sdk (httpx2, pydantic), which adds a new Python tool install. A duplicate-idea competitor exists (keltokhy/jgrep, jev-grep), and jev-cli offers a general MCP server.
gh-allebee-jevgrep.verdict: A clean, honest, well-tested small CLI that shows how to call Jev via OpenRouter and how to batch Noul questions, but it is a manual pipe tool, not a Claude Code integration, so it gives no automatic invocation. Worth reading for its request-shape lessons (keyed line names, cost from usage.cost) or installing as an optional log-triage helper that Claude calls only if the user writes a rule for it; it should not be the primary Jev integration.

Ships a Claude Code plugin/marketplace with one skill (using-jevr) whose description tells Claude to use jevr instead of grep/glob for conceptual code search. Not an MCP server and no hooks.

Uses Noul and Choice primitives correctly, with pinned model, 3x retry, sha256 response cache (content-keyed so never stale), gitignore-aware walking, stateless (no index dir).
Apache-2.0, small readable Rust codebase (~30 files), 30ish unit/integration tests including captured wire-format replay (tests/wire.rs), cargo-installable binary, no shell exec or telemetry.
Fail-safe for Claude Code: if it errors, Claude simply uses grep; no hooks that could block tool calls.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read; user wants OpenRouter as provider, so needs a fork/patch (likely small but schema equivalence unverified).
Uploads raw source windows of many files to a third party on each cold query, with no secret redaction; risky for client projects and only partially aligned with the user's secret-guard hooks.

Solves search, not the broader 'decision' use cases (e.g., routing, permission triage, commit/PR classification) where Jev's typed decisions could add value in Claude Code.
