gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.name: onesie (frodi-karlsson/onesie)
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.whatItDoes: Go CLI (single static binary) that is a Unix filter over the System One API (Jev). You pipe text in, ask a yes/no, --pick or --rate question, and get a probability/option/level with scriptable exit codes; it also has a batch/stream mode, calibrate, caching, and built-in gates (shell-safety, prompt-injection, personal-data, moderation). It ships a Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json) made of 6 skills (onesie, onesie-gate, onesie-calibrate, onesie-patterns, onesie-setup, onesie-stream) and one SessionStart hook. It has deliberately NO MCP server (README "Why no MCP server"). The plugin teaches Claude how to write correct onesie invocations; it does not by itself route Claude Code's own decisions through Jev.

providerSupport.evidence: HTTP layer is in the sibling SDK github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie-go v0.1.0 (go.mod:6), which I cloned and read. onesie-go/provider.go:42-52 OpenRouter(): BaseURL "https://openrouter.ai/api", EnvAPIKey "OPENROUTER_API_KEY", requestIDHeader X-Generation-Id, modelsPath "/v1/models?output_modalities=decisions". client.go:22 systemOnePath = "/v1/systemone", so the call is POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (the System One API, not the alpha Decisions API). Default TypeSafe: option.go:13 DefaultBaseURL "https://api.typesafe.ai", env TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Also Berget (provider.go:55-66, BERGET_API_KEY). Selection: --provider openrouter or ONESIE_PROVIDER=openrouter (internal/cli/root.go:236, cli/auth.go:24). Key resolution internal/cli/auth.go:498-540: provider env var first, then OS keychain or credential file via onesie auth set. Default model = DefaultModel (jev-latest alias per README; calibrate example uses -m jev-1.13.0).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: n/a, already native: set ONESIE_PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
providerSupport.others: Berget (api.berget.ai, own System One models, no jev-latest).

interface.name: onesie QUESTION [--pick a,b,c | --rate low,mid,high] (stdin or --state/--state-file)
interface.purpose: Core ask: yes/no probability, one-of-N choice, or rubric level. -r prints raw answer, -o json/values/csv/markdown, --assert EXPR, --threshold, --min-confidence, --fallback, --abstain-if.

interface.name: onesie -f shell-safety -q --state CMD
interface.purpose: Built-in gate: exit 0 = run, 1 = block, 7 = abstain/ask a person, other = no answer. Thresholds: destroys<0.25, secrets<0.3, network<0.5; abstain if destroys<0.5 and secrets<0.67 (examples/questions/shell-safety.yaml).

interface.name: onesie --ask NAME=Q ... / -f NAME
interface.purpose: Several named questions in one request; question files in .onesie/questions/*.yaml; --print-questions to save.

interface.name: onesie calibrate
interface.purpose: Run questions over labelled JSONL, report catch/false-alarm rates per cut, --offline + --require for CI.

interface.name: onesie questions / auth set|status / cache / --print-request / --mock FILE (ONESIE_MOCK)
interface.purpose: List question sets, store key in keychain, disk cache (ONESIE_CACHE, 24h TTL), free dry-run of the exact request, mock answers.

interface.name: -i jsonl|lines|csv|tsv|request, -j N, --out, --resume
interface.purpose: Streaming/batch mode with concurrency and resume.

interface.name: Skill onesie
interface.purpose: Trigger: script needs a onesie judgment on one text (probability/option/rubric), before prompting a general model and parsing its reply. allowed-tools Bash(onesie:*).

interface.name: Skill onesie-gate
interface.purpose: Trigger: a onesie answer decides whether a command runs / step continues / build fails; warns about a common wrong gate recipe.

interface.name: Skill onesie-calibrate
interface.purpose: Trigger: choosing a --threshold/--assert cut, labelled records, CI guard.

interface.name: Skill onesie-patterns
interface.purpose: Trigger: >255 options, shortlist, low-confidence to human, several questions on same text.

interface.name: Skill onesie-setup
interface.purpose: Trigger: onesie not on PATH / no key / hook reports either. Walks install and auth without key entering the conversation.

interface.name: Skill onesie-stream
interface.purpose: Trigger: more than one record, JSONL, tail -f, jq over output, exit 6/3.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart hooks/preflight.sh (timeout 10s)
interface.purpose: Injects one line: onesie on PATH?, does a key resolve (provider+source), binary vs plugin version mismatch, list of saved question files (max 20). Always exits 0. NOT a PreToolUse hook.

security: MIT license (LICENSE, GitHub licenseInfo mit).

API key never in argv: read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY env, or from OS keychain (zalando/go-keyring) or credential file via onesie auth set (internal/cli/auth.go:498-540, internal/creds). No --key flag found. onesie-go redacts headers in debug logs (client.go:388 redactedHeader) and copies http client so Authorization is not leaked on redirect (client.go:77).
However the question text and the state (e.g. the shell command in `onesie -f shell-safety --state 'cmd'`) DO appear in argv/process list and shell history when passed via --state; stdin avoids that.

install.sh (curl|sh from main): well written, set -eu, everything in main(), verifies sha256 vs checksums.txt and, if gh is logged in, `gh attestation verify` build provenance; installs to ~/.local/bin. Still a curl|sh path; alternatives are brew tap or go install (go.mod says go 1.27.1, needs a very new toolchain). I did not run it.
No npm postinstall, no telemetry/analytics code found in Go sources (grep). Only network egress is to the chosen provider plus optional schema URL references.

Prompt-injection surface: text handed to Jev is data classified into typed output (no free text), so the model cannot emit instructions back; risk is limited to a attacker steering the probability (e.g. crafted command hiding intent). The shell-safety gate is a probabilistic classifier, not a sandbox: the README's own worst miss is `echo hello > notes.txt` answered destroys=0.37 (abstain band).
Hook preflight.sh only runs `onesie auth status`, `onesie --version`, `onesie questions` and sed/awk on local files; sanitises control chars in output injected into context.
Plugin marketplace entry pins ref v0.4.3 (tag), good supply-chain hygiene. Dependabot configured, releases have build provenance attestation (release.yml).
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.dataEgress: Only what you pass to onesie: stdin / --state / --state-file text plus the question wording and option lists, sent over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai). Nothing is sent automatically by the plugin; the SessionStart hook is fully local (no network, per its own comment). With --cache, responses are stored on local disk (XDG cache, 24h TTL for aliases). If wired into a PreToolUse gate, every Bash command string (which can contain inline secrets, tokens, client hostnames) would go to OpenRouter unless pre-filtered; file contents/diffs only leave if a script pipes them.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.failureMode: CLI is fail-closed by exit code contract: any exit other than 0/1/7 means 'no answer' and README's recipe blocks on it (`*) echo 'no answer, blocked'`). Per-attempt HTTP timeout 10s (onesie-go option.go:20), 2 retries (option.go:25), Retry-After honoured up to a cap (--max-retry-after), all overridable via --timeout/--retries. Worst case for a hook using defaults is about 30s+ before failure, so a custom hook should pass --timeout 2 --retries 0 and map non-{0,1,7} to allow. The plugin SessionStart hook is fail-open (always exit 0, 10s timeout) and does no network calls. Because the plugin has no PreToolUse hook, a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code by itself.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 tool definitions. 6 skills: description lines are 251, 330, 402, 295, 328, 298 chars (about 1.9k chars, roughly 500 tokens always in the skill listing); SKILL.md bodies load only on trigger (onesie 13.3k chars, onesie-gate 14k, onesie-stream 15.8k, onesie-calibrate 8.4k, onesie-setup 6.5k, onesie-patterns 5.4k, i.e. roughly 3-4k tokens each when loaded). SessionStart hook injects one line of about 100-300 chars (key status, plus up to 20 saved question names). Very cheap versus an MCP server.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.autoInvocation: Skill description triggers (model discretion) plus one SessionStart hook that only reports status. The descriptions trigger when Claude is WRITING a script/pipeline that needs a judgment ("when a script needs a onesie judgment", "before writing `if onesie`", "before prompting a general model and parsing its reply"); they do not make Claude route its own coding decisions or tool-call approvals through Jev. Nothing is deterministic: there is no PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. To get truly automatic behaviour the user must add their own hook, e.g. a PreToolUse Bash hook calling `onesie -f shell-safety -q --timeout 2 --retries 0 --state "$cmd"` and mapping exit 1 to deny, 7 to ask/permission prompt, others to allow.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.latencyImpact: SessionStart: a few local process spawns (onesie auth status/--version/questions), tens of ms, no network. Skills: no per-turn latency beyond loading SKILL.md when triggered. Any Jev call adds a network round trip to OpenRouter (claimed 70-500 ms end to end for Jev) plus Go binary start (~ms); with default 10s timeout and 2 retries a degraded provider could stall a hook for 30s+ unless flags are tightened.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.runtime: Go single static binary (go.mod go 1.27.1); releases via goreleaser for linux/darwin amd64/arm64 with checksums and build provenance attestation; brew tap, install.sh, go install. Plugin is skills + shell hook (POSIX sh).
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.install: Binary: `brew install frodi-karlsson/tap/onesie`, or `go install github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/cmd/onesie@latest` (needs Go 1.27.1), or release tarball verified by sha256 (prefer manual download over curl|sh). Key: `export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...` and `export ONESIE_PROVIDER=openrouter` (or `onesie auth set` after `--provider openrouter`). Plugin: `/plugin marketplace add frodi-karlsson/onesie` then `/plugin install onesie@onesie`. Not executed by me.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.tests: Extensive: 121 *_test.go files across internal/, cmd/, examples/; onesie-go SDK also has unit + integration tests; CI workflows ci.yml, integration.yml, release.yml, history-lessons.yml; skillcheck/skilleval tooling verifies skill examples against the binary; golangci config. Committed calibration data (examples/data) backs the shell-safety thresholds (40 labelled commands, AUC 1.00 for destroys). I did not run any of it.
pros: Native, code-verified OpenRouter support: same System One wire protocol at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY (onesie-go provider.go:42-52); one env var switches the provider, no patching needed.
Zero MCP tool-definition cost: 6 skill descriptions (about 500 tokens) and a one-line SessionStart hook; bodies load only when triggered. Explicit design decision against an MCP server.

Ships a ready-made, calibrated gate: `onesie -f shell-safety -q` returns exit 0/1/7 (run / block / ask a human), which maps 1:1 onto a Claude Code PreToolUse hook decision (allow / deny / ask). Also prompt-injection and personal-data gates that could screen tool outputs or fetched web content.
Good security hygiene: key from env/keychain, not argv; redacted debug logs; install.sh verifies sha256 and build provenance; plugin pinned to tag v0.4.3; no telemetry found.
Timeout/retries/cache/mock knobs (--timeout, --retries, ONESIE_CACHE, ONESIE_MOCK, --print-request free dry-run) make it easy to build a fail-open hook and to test it without spending tokens.
Only Jev-specific tool found with a calibration workflow (`onesie calibrate` with --offline --require for CI) which is valuable given skeptic claims that Jev may just be a small-model router.
Well tested for a 9-day-old project (121 test files, CI, releases with attestation, 200 commits).
cons: Not automatic as shipped: the plugin has only skills and a status-only SessionStart hook. Skills trigger only when Claude is writing scripts that need a judgment, not on Claude's own edit/run/review decisions. The user's goal of 'Claude Code uses Jev without being told' needs a custom PreToolUse hook the project does not provide.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 2 stars, 0 forks, 1 human contributor (plus dependabot), v0.4.3, still churning (7 tags in 9 days); pre-1.0 flag/API breakage likely. Repo is a Show HN project.

Requires building/installing a Go binary; go.mod requires Go 1.27.1 for go install, and the README's main path is curl|sh (mitigated by checksum and attestation). User has Node/Python/uv, not necessarily Go.

Shell-safety gate is probabilistic: README's own worst miss is `echo hello > notes.txt` at 0.37; calibrated on only 40 labelled commands, mostly synthetic; would also produce many exit-7 prompts in bypass/auto mode where user wants fewer interruptions. Adds 70-500 ms+ network latency to every Bash call if used as a PreToolUse gate, and sends every command string to OpenRouter.

Commands passed via --state appear in argv/process list; hook must use stdin. Default timeout is 10s with 2 retries so an unconfigured hook can stall ~30s; must set --timeout/--retries itself and map errors to allow.
Overlaps with the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard and permission mode: a Jev gate would be an additional, non-deterministic layer, not a replacement.
Depends on the separate onesie-go SDK (v0.1.0, created 2026-09-29, 0 stars) for all HTTP behaviour, so audit surface is two young repos.
gh-frodi-karlsson-onesie.verdict: Best building block found for a DIY deterministic Jev integration (OpenRouter-native, shell-safety gate with exit 0/1/7, near-zero context cost, no telemetry), but the plugin itself is only skills and does not make Claude Code use Jev automatically. Use the binary plus your own PreToolUse hook (tight timeout, fail-open, stdin only) rather than relying on the skills, and treat the project as an early-stage, single-maintainer dependency.

gh-tumf-jev-cli.name: tumf/jev-cli
gh-tumf-jev-cli.whatItDoes: Unofficial community Python package (PyPI jev-cli 0.6.3) that installs two commands: `jev` (CLI for noul/choice/score/run) and `jev-mcp` (stdio MCP server exposing the same four operations as tools). Also bundles an Agent Skill (`jev install-skills --claude [-g]`). Thin urllib client over the System One request schema (state + questions map) with selectable providers: official TypeSafe, Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter, custom. No hooks, no auto-invocation logic. The README calls it 'dependency-free' but that only holds for the CLI; the MCP server depends on `mcp>=2.2.0,<3` (pyproject.toml).

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_cli/__init__.py:18-39 PROVIDERS table: openrouter -> endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, key_env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13; official -> https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, jev-latest; vercel -> ai-gateway.vercel.sh with a request/response translation (lines 221-250); custom -> JEV_ENDPOINT/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL (lines 253-271). Provider selected by JEV_PROVIDER env or per-call `provider` arg (mcp_server.py:146-151). Bearer auth header at __init__.py:280. Tests cover openrouter default model and endpoint (tests/test_jev.py:185,219; tests/test_mcp_server.py:337,374). README documents an MCP config with env JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter + OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The /api/v1/systemone OpenRouter endpoint is not used; only alpha/decisions. Request body is the native System One shape, sent unchanged to OpenRouter; I could not confirm the OpenRouter schema line-for-line (docs page only lists model/state/questions/noul-choice-score), and there is no live test in the repo.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (typesafe-ai/jev), custom Jev-compatible proxy
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already supported; nothing to patch. Minor: default model is pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13, not ~typesafe/jev-latest (overridable via `model` arg or JEV_MODEL only for the custom provider).

interface.name: MCP tool noul(state, question, [provider, model, endpoint])
interface.purpose: One yes/no judgment returning P(yes)

interface.name: MCP tool choice(state, question, options{key:desc}, ...)
interface.purpose: Pick one option; requires >=2 options; returns per-option probabilities and confidence

interface.name: MCP tool score(state, question, levels[], ...)
interface.purpose: Score against >=2 ordered levels; zero-based, possibly fractional

interface.name: MCP tool run(request{state, questions, model?}, ...)
interface.purpose: Send a complete multi-question System One request; unknown fields are forwarded

interface.name: CLI jev noul|choice|score|run
interface.purpose: Same judgments from the shell; --value, --pretty, --json-state, --provider, --model; state via arg, @file or stdin; exit codes 0/1/2/3 (auth)/4 (retryable)

interface.name: CLI jev auth set|status|test
interface.purpose: Store the key at ~/.config/jev-cli/credentials.json (0600, dir 0700) via hidden prompt or stdin; check or verify it

interface.name: CLI jev install-skills [-g] [--claude]
interface.purpose: Copy the bundled jev-cli SKILL.md into .claude/skills or .agents/skills; refuses to overwrite unmanaged dirs

interface.name: Skill jev-cli (SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Description 'Use when classifying or scoring state with the jev CLI or the jev-mcp stdio MCP server'; tells the model to prefer MCP tools, send only necessary state, never send secrets

gh-tumf-jev-cli.runtime: Python >=3.13, uv (uv tool install jev-cli or uvx --from jev-cli jev-mcp); depends on mcp>=2.2.0,<3; the CLI part is stdlib only (urllib)
gh-tumf-jev-cli.install: uv tool install jev-cli  (then: claude mcp add jev -e JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -- jev-mcp; optionally jev install-skills --global --claude). Never run by me; static review only.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.tests: 3 unittest files (about 920 lines: test_jev.py, test_mcp_server.py, test_skill.py), covering providers, credential store, MCP framing and cardinality. CI on GitHub Actions matrix ubuntu/macos/windows with Python 3.13 (`make check`), release workflow builds a wheel and smoke-tests it. Not executed by me. No live API integration test.
security: API key never in argv: `auth set` reads from a hidden prompt or stdin, and MCP takes the key from env. Credential file is written atomically with 0600 in a 0700 dir (__init__.py:117-138). It is plaintext JSON.
Only if you put OPENROUTER_API_KEY in `claude mcp add -e` or in .mcp.json, it sits in ~/.claude.json or the project file; use env expansion or export it in the shell instead.
Env var wins over the credential file. The key is sent only as a Bearer header to the selected endpoint.

Per-call `endpoint` and `provider` tool arguments exist. A prompt-injected model could point the `custom` provider at an attacker URL, but it would send JEV_API_KEY (not the OpenRouter key) and the state. With `endpoint` overridden while provider=openrouter, the OpenRouter key would go to the arbitrary endpoint (call() uses api_key(provider) with whatever endpoint is passed, __init__.py:280). This is a real key-exfiltration vector via injected tool args, and is not mitigated by the code.

No shell execution, no subprocess, no eval; the MCP server calls the library directly. No telemetry. No postinstall. Pure Python wheel from PyPI, published from a single maintainer account; release workflow uses no trusted-publishing step that I could see (upload done outside the visible workflow).
install-skills copies files into ~/.claude/skills with a managed marker and rmtree only on directories it marked. Low risk.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is numeric probabilities plus error strings that echo the API error body (could carry text), otherwise low. Bigger risk is the SKILL.md steering the model.
Single maintainer, 1 week old, unofficial and not affiliated with TypeSafe; supply-chain trust is low but the code is about 740 lines and easy to audit.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.dataEgress: Exactly what Claude puts in the `state` and `question`/`criteria` arguments is POSTed as JSON to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or the chosen endpoint), verbatim. Nothing is read from disk by the MCP server (no @file or stdin expansion in MCP mode). Nothing leaves automatically beyond what the model chooses to pass, so code, diffs, or file contents are sent only if Claude puts them in `state`. The CLI does read @file/stdin. OpenRouter also sees the model ID, key and usage.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level: any HTTP error, timeout or bad JSON raises a ToolError returned to Claude, which can continue without it. Fixed 60 s urllib timeout (__init__.py:288), no retry and no circuit breaker. No hook is involved, so a Jev outage never blocks a tool call or the session. A hung call can stall a turn for up to 60 s, and there is no tunable timeout. If the MCP process fails to start (uv/python/mcp version) the server just shows as disconnected, as caveman-shrink does now.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (noul, choice, score, run). Estimated about 6,500-7,000 chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas, roughly 1.6-1.8k tokens if loaded eagerly. Server instructions add about 330 chars (about 80 tokens). Smaller if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch (only names loaded). The `run` schema is the heaviest (nested QuestionSpec with extra=allow). Bundled SKILL.md: the description is about 1 line always in context, and the body loads on trigger. No hook-injected text.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus an optional skill description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. The tool descriptions are generic ('answer one yes/no question about the state'), with no guidance on when a coding agent should use them, so Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for them unprompted. Achieving the user's 'automatic' goal requires adding your own steering (a CLAUDE.md rule, a custom skill, or a hook) on top.
gh-tumf-jev-cli.latencyImpact: Per call: process is long-lived stdio, so no spawn cost after startup (first start is a uv/python import of mcp, maybe 0.5-1.5 s). Each tool call is one HTTPS request via urllib with no connection reuse: about 70-500 ms Jev-claimed plus TLS setup and the OpenRouter hop, and plus model round trip for Claude to decide and read the result. Zero latency on turns where it is not called.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code, with the correct endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions), OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and model typesafe/jev-1.13 (__init__.py:29-33). Works with the JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter env only, no patching.
Exposes all three primitives plus batched `run`, with sensible validation (>=2 options/levels), giving Claude a ready MCP surface for Jev in an hour.
Small and auditable: about 740 lines of source, only stdlib plus the official `mcp` SDK. No shell exec, no telemetry, no postinstall.
Key handling is careful: no key in argv (env or hidden prompt), 0600 credential file, MCP stdout kept for protocol only.
Tools return errors as ToolError instead of crashing, and never block the session (no hooks). Fail-soft.

Ships a Claude-targeted SKILL.md (`install-skills --claude`) that tells the model to send minimal state and not to send secrets, which is a useful base to extend into a proper 'when to consult Jev' skill.
Has tests and cross-OS CI, and the openspec change history shows deliberate design, which is unusual for a 1-week-old repo.
Vercel and custom providers give a fallback if OpenRouter's alpha endpoint changes.
cons: Does not solve 'automatic': no hook, no routing, no trigger guidance. The user must add their own steering, so as-is Claude will use it only rarely.

Tool descriptions are generic ('the text or JSON value to judge') and say nothing about coding scenarios such as commit risk, test-need classification, or PR triage. There are no ready-made decision templates or presets.

Per-call `endpoint` and `provider` arguments let a prompt-injected model redirect the request, and call() attaches the selected provider's key to whatever endpoint is given (__init__.py:274-284), so the OpenRouter key could be sent to an attacker URL. Under bypass or 'auto' permissions this matters. Mitigate by denying/removing those args, which needs a fork or a wrapper, or by a scoped low-limit OpenRouter key.
Key must be provided through MCP `env` or the shell. `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plain text in ~/.claude.json unless you use ${VAR} expansion.

Requires Python >=3.13 and the `mcp>=2.2.0,<3` package; 'dependency-free' in the tagline is false for the MCP path. Fine for this user (Python 3.13 and uv installed), but cold start pulls a dependency tree.
Single maintainer, 14 stars, created 2026-09-17, unofficial, version 0.x alpha; the OpenRouter alpha API and the beta model may change. Default model is pinned to jev-1.13, not ~typesafe/jev-latest.
Fixed 60 s timeout, no retries, no per-call timeout config; a hung call can stall a turn far beyond the claimed 70-500 ms.
No urllib connection reuse, no usage/cost reporting except through the raw response, and only /alpha/decisions (not /v1/systemone).

Sends `state` verbatim, so the only guard against leaking client code or secrets is the model's judgment (SKILL.md text), and the user's existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* by its matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
gh-tumf-jev-cli.verdict: Best-in-class as a plain MCP transport for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (native OpenRouter provider, small auditable code, fail-soft), so it is a reasonable building block, but it gives no automatic invocation on its own. To meet the goal you would pair it with your own CLAUDE.md rule, a custom skill or a hook, and ideally fork or wrap it to drop the `endpoint`/`provider` overrides before running it in bypass mode with a real OpenRouter key.

gh-omni-ask-jev.name: omni-/ask-jev
gh-omni-ask-jev.whatItDoes: Windows-only PowerShell UserPromptSubmit hook for OpenAI Codex (not Claude Code). When the user types ':jev' or ':jev ask <question?>', it reads the local Codex rollout JSONL transcript, redacts and truncates it (48 KiB evidence, 64 KiB request), and sends it to TypeSafe /v1/systemone with 13 Noul checks plus one Choice outcome. It shows a probability report through the hook's blocking reason without starting a model turn. It is an explicit, user-typed audit of whether the agent verified its work, at most once per turn. It is not automatic.

providerSupport.evidence: lib/Jev.psm1:130 hardcodes PostAsync('https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone') with Bearer auth. The key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY (ask-jev.ps1:34, lib/Jev.psm1:112). The model is TYPESAFE_MODEL, default 'jev-latest' (lib/Jev.psm1:43-44). The model regex allows '/' (lib/Jev.psm1:45), but the base URL and env var names are not configurable. grep -ri openrouter over the repo returns nothing. Request body is {model, state, questions{id:{type,instructions,criteria}}}. Response is validated as {model, answers{id:{type,noul|choice,probabilities,confidence}}, usage{input_tokens,output_tokens}} (Assert-JevResponse, lib/Jev.psm1:56-88).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: The endpoint swap alone is trivial. The URL is one literal at lib/Jev.psm1:130. OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-1.13 is probably close to the same schema, but that is unverified. The strict validator would fail closed on any envelope difference. Overall it is hard, because the tool is Codex-specific. It depends on the Codex rollout path (~/.codex/sessions/rollout-*.jsonl), the Codex hook payload, Windows PowerShell 5.1 paths and a Windows registry-style env lookup. Running it under Claude Code would need a new transcript parser and hook adapter. That is the repo's own unchecked TODO.md item.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only.

security: API key is read from the process env or the Windows user env, and sent only as a Bearer header via HttpClient. It is not in argv, and the code redacts configured-key matches from output (lib/Jev.psm1:100, 141).
HTTP redirects are disabled (AllowAutoRedirect=false, lib/Jev.psm1:122). Errors are bounded and sanitized. The response is strictly validated.

Transcript content is treated as untrusted in the policy prompt (lib/Jev.psm1:4). It has no shell execution beyond the PowerShell hook launcher, and no telemetry or curl|sh installer. The worker is killed after 28 s.
Redaction is heuristic. The README says it is not comprehensive secret removal, so code, tool output and secrets in the transcript can reach TypeSafe.
The installer edits hooks.json with a custom JSON text patcher. Codex hook trust is required, and a changed hook needs a new review.
Marker files in the OS temp directory are empty and hashed. Real rollouts and reports are gitignored.
gh-omni-ask-jev.dataEgress: On explicit ':jev' or ':jev ask' only, selected conversation text, user instructions, assistant messages and tool calls/results from the Codex rollout are sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Evidence is capped at 48 KiB and the full request at 64 KiB, after credential redaction (lib/Jev.psm1:42-49, README). Binary/base64 payloads and encrypted reasoning are omitted. Nothing is sent for ordinary prompts or help. Adapted to Claude Code, this would include file contents and diffs seen in tool outputs.
gh-omni-ask-jev.failureMode: Fail-closed for its own command only. On any handled failure (missing key, HTTP error, timeout, malformed response) it blocks the ':jev' command and shows an error, with no retries. It uses a 15 s HTTP timeout and an 8 s internal deadline for transcript work. The supervisor kills the worker at 28 s, and the hook timeout is 40 s. Ordinary prompts are never affected, since they pass through with no network call. If the hook is untrusted or fails to launch, the command simply falls through to the model.
gh-omni-ask-jev.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped, because it does not run there. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions and no injected text. In the original Codex design, the blocking report never enters model context, since it costs zero host tokens and is not sent to the model.
gh-omni-ask-jev.latencyImpact: None on ordinary prompts. A ':jev' command adds about 0.4 s of Jev request time plus transcript parsing (README and docs/verification.md say 0.4 s on Windows/Codex, with a 15 s cap and 28 s supervisor kill). It is not measured under Claude Code.
gh-omni-ask-jev.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. The user must type ':jev'. It is a UserPromptSubmit hook keyed on an exact typed token and does no automatic per-turn or per-tool triggering. The README explicitly says 'no per-turn audits'. This directly contradicts the user's requirement of automatic use.
pros: Concrete, working design of a Jev use case: an independent typed judge of whether an agent's work was actually verified, using Noul and Choice with strict response validation. The question set in lib/Jev.psm1:11-38 is reusable prompt material.
Sound engineering: redirects disabled, bounded errors, 64 KiB request cap, a policy prompt that treats transcript text as untrusted, no telemetry, and a per-turn atomic once-marker.

Real request/response contract against api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (model jev-1.13.0, usage tokens) is documented in code and verification.md, and is useful as a reference for building a Claude Code hook.
MIT license. It is small (about 1,100 lines of PowerShell) and readable, so porting the question set and validator is feasible.
The hook shows results without a host model turn, so it costs no Claude tokens.
cons: Does not support Claude Code at all. TODO.md lists Claude Code as an unsupported, unverified port, and the README says 'Claude Code and OpenCode are not implemented'.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 only. The installer hardcodes System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe (install.ps1:8), and the env lookup reads the Windows user environment. Linux is unverified and the paths and launcher would not work as-is.
Explicit and manual only (typed ':jev'). Not automatic, which fails the user's core requirement.
TypeSafe direct only. The endpoint is a hardcoded literal at lib/Jev.psm1:130, and it uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The OpenRouter route is not implemented.
Depends on the Codex rollout JSONL format, which the README itself calls 'not a stable Codex API'. Claude Code transcripts have a different format and location.
Immature: a single commit on 2026-09-16, 1 author, 2 stars, no releases and no CI. Tests are Windows-only, and there is no accuracy calibration ('smoke tests, not calibration').
Sends the full conversation, including tool outputs and code, to a beta third-party model. Redaction is explicitly not comprehensive, which matters for client projects.
Audits after the fact, so it does not steer coding decisions during a session. It also adds no value for routing or choosing actions.
gh-omni-ask-jev.verdict: Not usable for this user. It is a Windows-only, manual ':jev' audit hook for Codex with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint. It has no Claude Code support, and no automatic invocation. Only the question set, response validator and request shape are worth borrowing as reference material for a custom Claude Code hook.

gh-eugeniughelbur-jev-engineering.name: eugeniughelbur/jev-engineering (jev-gate plugin + layer + MCP server)
gh-eugeniughelbur-jev-engineering.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin whose core is jev-gate: a deterministic PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit, 8s timeout) that runs hard-deny regexes, then a read-only fast-path allowlist, then ONE POST to OpenRouter System One asking two typed questions (Noul 'destructive' and Choice allow/ask/deny), and maps the probabilities to allow/ask/deny by thresholds. Modes: observe (default, log only), auto, guard, enforce. Also ships an optional 5-tool MCP server (check_action, route_turn, keep_context, rank_options, gate_stats), a layer.py CLI (route/rank/keep), slash commands, a local HTTP service, a GitHub Action (review-router) and use-case scripts (inbox triage, etc.). It is a permission/safety gate, not a coding-productivity tool.

Honest, reproducible public benchmarks including one where Claude Code's auto mode wins on smoothness (12/12 safe vs 9/12) and its own misses, plus tests in CI
Zero context cost (no MCP server needed); observe-by-default lets user measure decisions in ~/.jev-gate/decisions.jsonl before enabling; cost ~$0.00002/check
Quick to trial: two plugin commands, and can be disabled with /jev-off or removing the plugin
cons: It is a safety/permission gate, not a Jev value-add for coding quality: with the user in bypass/auto permission mode its 'allow' output is largely moot and only its 'deny' has any effect, so benefit reduces to a second, weaker secret-leak/destructive-command guard that overlaps the existing PreToolUse secret guard
Extra 280-500 ms (p95 ~530 ms, timeouts to 5 s) on every non-allowlisted Bash, and on every Edit/Write/NotebookEdit since fast-path is Bash-only; noticeable in long agentic loops

Sends every ambiguous Bash command string and the last user prompt (2000 chars) from personal AND client repos to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; commands with inline secrets are exposed, and the same commands are written unredacted to ~/.jev-gate/decisions.jsonl

Model step is manipulable and noisy: authors' own test shows 1-3/30 dangerous commands allowed under polite authority injections, blunt injection flips safe commands to deny, and a real miss (cat ~/.aws/credentials) was patched only after a benchmark; scores drift between model versions (force push returned deny 0.94 then ask 0.78)

Hook runs arbitrary code from a week-old repo on every tool call; must pin a commit and audit updates

route_turn and keep_context are irrelevant/impossible inside Claude Code (a tool cannot switch the main model or prune the harness context); rank_options/check_action rely on model discretion and the README concedes MCP tools are not enforceable

Much of the value (review-router GitHub Action, inbox triage, Slack follow-ups) is outside Claude Code daily coding; nothing here uses Jev for code intelligence, test selection or edit decisions inside a session (ci-test-selection is a CI script)

Worth a pinned, observe-only trial (or cherry-picking its hard-deny rules and the Noul/Choice question pattern into the user's own hook), not an install-and-enable for daily use.

gh-pkcoulon-jev-for-flutter.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse Read rewrite, UserPromptSubmit prefetch, PostToolUse edit guard) for the narrowing and guard features; find_code MCP is model-discretion but off by default. Other hooks add Python startup (~30-60 ms each) on every Read/Grep/Glob/Bash/Agent/Task PostToolUse and prompt submit (code_context.py, 3s timeout) even in non-Dart projects (they exit early on policy/config). pros: Genuinely automatic: PreToolUse Read hook rewrites the tool input (updatedInput offset/limit) with no user prompting, exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' behavior requested.
Good use of the right Jev primitives: choice over 200 chunks for locality, noul for 'is this a focused question', with thresholds (0.6/0.85) so uncertain cases leave the Read unchanged.
Fail-open design with breaker, short hook timeouts, and per-session request caps (hookio.py, jev.py, config.py:27); will not hang Claude.
Strong privacy tooling for client work: deny_paths / deny_remotes policy, secret-file globs, regex redaction, per-project opt-in default off (policy.py, USAGE.md Privacy).
Endpoint and model overridable via JEV_FLUTTER_JEV_URL / JEV_FLUTTER_JEV_MODEL, so OpenRouter is plausibly a config-only switch; small readable stdlib Python, easy to audit and fork.
Ships a reusable pattern (typed Jev client, breaker, redaction, Read-narrowing hook) that could be copied into a language-agnostic hook.
Honest docs: benchmarks labeled exploratory, n=3, unblinded, +7% runtime; context prep disabled by default after unfavorable results.
cons: Dart/Flutter only: every feature checks .dart suffix or Dart outline (narrow.py:read, lens_nudge.py:99). Useless for a general multi-language workflow unless forked.
Native to TypeSafe API only; zero OpenRouter references. Key env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY; OpenRouter parity with the /v1/systemone body is unverified and would need a live test.
Repo is 2 days old, 0 stars, 1 author, 21 commits, no tests directory, no CI (.github absent), no releases beyond own tags; v0.3.6 rebrand from 'dartlens' with legacy shims - churn risk.

Measured benefit is weak: 3 questions, one run each, unblinded; 23% fewer tokens but 7% longer runtime; author's own context-prep feature was turned off after unfavorable results. Opus-class Claude reading 400+ line files rarely needs Jev.
Read narrowing can silently omit relevant code (a 'selected region'), risking wrong answers; also affects Claude Code semantics via updatedInput on a client codebase.
Sends client source (redacted chunks, edit diffs) to a third-party gateway; project-committed config can flip jev.enabled, and redaction is regex-only.

Installing adds ~10 hook registrations (PostToolUse on Read|Grep|Glob|Bash|Agent|Task, Stop, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, 3x UserPromptSubmit) that spawn python3 on nearly every tool call, alongside user's existing GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks and secret guard; potential interaction/ordering with the secret-leak guard (both on Read) and GitNexus.
Messages injected into Claude are in French; user-facing errors mixed French/English.
Does not use Jev's strengths for general coding decisions (permission gating, model routing, commit/PR triage); it only ranks code chunks.

gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.name: adarshmishra07/jcm-router
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.whatItDoes: Bun/TypeScript local HTTP proxy on localhost:8787. Claude Code is pointed at it via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. For each new user turn on /v1/messages (requests with tools), it sends Jev the user message (max 6000 chars) and the previous assistant reply (max 2000 chars). Three questions: model (choice: fable/opus/sonnet/haiku), effort (choice: low..max) and is_followup (noul). It then rewrites the model and output_config.effort in the request and forwards it to api.anthropic.com with the original OAuth headers. A cost guard always routes subagents, but only switches the main chat when the prompt-cache re-write is cheap (under 100K context and under $0.25 extra). The default ROUTER_UPGRADES=off means it can only downgrade. It includes a supervisor with passthrough fallback, a dashboard, a statusline script, an eval harness and a tuner.

security: No third-party runtime dependencies, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry. The only network calls are to Anthropic and TypeSafe.

Jev API key is read from env and sent as a Bearer header in fetch (not in argv). The key is never logged, and /healthz exposes only a jev_key boolean (src/env.ts:96-97). If it is placed in .env, it is stored on disk in plaintext.

The proxy forwards Claude Code's Authorization / OAuth headers to ANTHROPIC_UPSTREAM (src/proxy.ts:92-100). The upstream is env-configurable, so a poisoned env would exfiltrate the subscription token. It listens on localhost:8787 with no auth, so any local process or browser page that can reach it can use it as an authenticated Anthropic relay (but cannot read the token).

Bun.serve({port}) without an explicit hostname binds all interfaces by default, so the unauthenticated relay may be reachable from the LAN (src/server.ts:150-152). This is not verified at runtime, but it is a real concern on a shared network.
scripts/env-on.sh edits ~/.claude/settings.json with jq (backup made first, atomic mv). It is a global change that affects every Claude Code session, including client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev sees the user message and the previous assistant reply, which can contain tool-derived text. Jev only returns typed choices and probabilities, gated by confidence thresholds, and the model alias must be in the allowlist, so the damage is limited to a wrong model or effort pick. The default upgrade-off means it cannot escalate spend.

Local logs at ~/.claude-router/decisions.jsonl contain the first 300 chars of every prompt (ROUTER_LOG_PROMPTS=1 default), which is a client-confidentiality leak into the home directory. Set ROUTER_LOG_PROMPTS=0 to turn it off.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.dataEgress: To TypeSafe (or OpenRouter after a patch), once per new user turn: latest_user_message (first 6000 chars of the prompt) and previous_assistant_reply (first 2000 chars), plus the previous routing, alongside the policy questions (src/routing-policy.ts:166-186, src/server.ts:63-71). This does not include diffs, file contents or tool outputs, unless the user pastes them into the prompt or the assistant's previous reply quotes them. To Anthropic: the full original request, unchanged except for model/effort. Locally: 300-char prompt previews in ~/.claude-router. Not sent for continuations (tool loops), for turns skipped by the context gate, or when both model and effort are overridden with !flags. Client code snippets in prompts would go to a third party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter), which matters for client work.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.failureMode: Jev side is fail-open: askJev never throws, has a 2.5 s timeout (src/jev.ts:4,57), and any HTTP error, bad shape or timeout forwards the request unchanged. Rewrites rejected by Anthropic with a 4xx (except 401/403/429) are retried once with the original request. Proxy side is fail-closed by design: with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at localhost and nothing listening (supervisor killed, reboot, sleep, port conflict), Claude Code cannot reach the API at all. A supervisor respawns the router and after 3 crashes in 60 s degrades to plain passthrough. Recovery from a hard kill is manual (env-off.sh plus restart). The proxy is a new single point of failure for the entire Claude Code session. It streams the response body, so streaming works.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.latencyImpact: One synchronous Jev call before each new user turn is forwarded, up to a 2.5 s timeout. The README estimates 0.3 to 1 s per turn (against Jev's claimed 70-500 ms). Continuations and tool-loop steps add only a localhost hop, and skipped and cached decisions add no Jev call. For the main chat with a large context (over 100K), Jev is not called at all. A subagent spawn adds a Jev call each time.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.contextCost: Zero tokens in Claude Code's context: it is a transparent proxy with no MCP tools, no skill and no hooks. The optional statusline command adds no model context. Cost side effects: changing the model or effort mid-conversation invalidates the prompt cache (documented $19.53 loss on 309 requests), which the guard mitigates by mostly refusing main-chat switches.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (fully automatic, no prompting needed). It sits in the request path once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set, and every new turn and every subagent is classified automatically. Overrides via !opus etc. are optional.
pros: Truly automatic and zero-prompt: a transparent proxy needs no CLAUDE.md, skill or tool-call cooperation from the model, which is exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' requirement (src/server.ts:79-148).
Works with the subscription OAuth login: it forwards Claude Code's own headers, and the README explicitly says ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not needed (README Install/Environment).
Zero context tokens: no MCP tool defs, no hook-injected text. It does not interact with the existing PreToolUse secret-guard, GitNexus or caveman hooks.

Honest, evidence-driven design: it documents a measured $19.53 loss from routing the main chat, then adds a cache-aware cost guard (src/cost.ts, routing-policy.ts:150), subagents-only scope (ROUTER_SCOPE=subagents), upgrades off by default, and confidence gates (0.7). It is the only candidate that uses Jev's calibrated probabilities as designed (Choice/Noul with confidence thresholds).

Robust operational design: Jev calls are fail-open with a 2.5 s timeout, 4xx rewrite rejections retry with the original request, and the supervisor falls back to passthrough. Plus /healthz, ROUTER_DRY_RUN for observing without acting, a dashboard and a tuner.
Small, readable codebase (~1.5k lines of src), MIT, no runtime dependencies, no postinstall or telemetry; a decent test suite with a fake-upstream integration test and CI.
Configurable endpoint (TYPESAFE_API_URL) with the same /v1/systemone path as OpenRouter's System One API, so the OpenRouter patch is about 3 lines.
cons: No OpenRouter support today: it hard-requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY with an 'apikey_' prefix (src/env.ts:57-59) and sends model 'jev-latest' (src/jev.ts:56). It needs a local patch or fork (prefix check, model id 'typesafe/jev-latest'), and the OpenRouter response schema is unverified.

Its value proposition (saving cost by downgrading to Haiku/Sonnet) is weak for this user: a single long Opus session in the main chat, where its own README says 'Probably not' and the guard refuses most switches, so it adds Jev latency to every turn for mostly no-ops. It only pays for subagent-heavy fan-out.

Routes between Claude models, which is a different problem from making Claude Code decisions better. Downgrading the main model away from Opus 5.5 risks quality on client work, and the hardcoded model IDs (claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-fable-5-1, src/routing-policy.ts:9-33) may not match the user's Opus 5.5 setup, causing 4xx rewrite rejections and fallbacks.

Single point of failure for the whole Claude Code session: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to localhost fails closed on reboot, sleep or supervisor kill. It requires Bun (not in the user's stack) and a process kept alive (no systemd unit; only a macOS launchd plist is documented, and the README targets macOS: brew, launchd). On Linux you write the systemd unit yourself.

Global change affecting every session, including client projects: scripts/env-on.sh mutates ~/.claude/settings.json, and the proxy sees all Anthropic traffic and OAuth headers. The unauthenticated relay on localhost:8787 may bind to all interfaces (Bun.serve default). Client prompt text goes to a third party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter), and 300-char prompt previews are written to ~/.claude-router by default.

Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 32 commits all on one day by a single author, 9 stars, no releases, and not battle-tested. The README claims (savings, 41-case eval) are self-reported. New-turn detection is tied to Claude Code 2.1.x request shapes and may break on 2.1.285.
Adds 0.3-1 s of blocking Jev latency to every new turn and every subagent, which is directly felt in daily interactive use.
gh-adarshmishra07-jcm-router.verdict: Well-engineered but narrow: a transparent auto-invoking Jev proxy that routes Claude model and effort. It only really helps subagent-heavy cost saving, which fits poorly with a subscription plus Opus 5.5 main-chat workflow, and it needs a small patch for OpenRouter (prefix check and model id). Worth considering only as an opt-in, subagents-scope, dry-run experiment, and not as the primary Jev integration, because of the fail-closed proxy risk and the client-prompt egress.

gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.dataEgress: Safety hook: for non-routine Bash/Write/Edit calls only, the redacted command string, contents of any local script it runs, and a redacted content excerpt for out-of-project edits go to the Jev endpoint. Supervise hooks: every turn end with repo changes sends first/latest prompt from transcript, up to 20k chars of git diff and 12k chars of recent tool output; every 10 tool calls sends the last 30 tool-call summaries. Manual commands send whatever files/logs/diffs you pipe. Routine read-only commands, project tests/builds and in-project edits stay local. With the OpenRouter base-URL trick the traffic goes to OpenRouter (and its upstream), not api.typesafe.ai; the only other outbound call is the npm version check.
gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.failureMode: Mostly fail-open with one fail-closed default. Hook API timeout 6s (HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS, hook.ts:45), stop 10s, maxRetries 0; settings hook timeouts 15s/20s. Missing key, timeouts, network errors: fall through to normal permission flow (source=error, decision allow). HTTP 403 (API firewall rejection) is denied by default (--on-error auto, hook.ts:86,128), which could block legitimate calls, especially if OpenRouter returns 403 for a key/credit/region/moderation problem; set --on-error allow to avoid. Supervise hooks stay silent on any error. Git hooks skip quietly if unreachable. Manual CLI uses a 60s client timeout (client.ts) and a 24h response cache.
gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.latencyImpact: Node process start (roughly 100-300ms, not measured) on every Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit call and on every tool call for the PostToolUse hook (no matcher; it only calls the API every 10th call but still spawns Node each time). Local fast-path decisions add no network. Non-routine Bash calls add about 0.4-0.5s (README: roughly half a second). Stop hook adds up to 10s worst case at turn end when the repo has changes. Git hooks add about 1s per commit/push. Compounded on top of existing GitNexus and secret-guard hooks that already fire on Bash.
gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.contextCost: Hooks: zero tokens when silent; PostToolUse injects a short additionalContext note only when concern is flagged; SessionStart hooks (jev-axi setup hooks, optional) inject a jev-axi status/command summary each session. No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. Two skills add only their name+description to the listing (roughly 100-150 tokens each, descriptions are about 500 chars); full SKILL.md bodies (~7.3KB, ~1.8k tokens, and ~7.6KB) load only if invoked. Deny/ask reasons are short strings.
gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse safety, PostToolUse and Stop supervision, git hooks) fire automatically with no prompting; the skills and the CLI commands (triage/diff/files/guard) are model-discretion only. The author's own benchmark (docs/skills-do-not-get-used.md) found 0 of 22 free-choice runs loaded the skill, even with a SessionStart hook or custom subagent, so only the hook layer is truly automatic.
pros: Only candidate reviewed so far that is genuinely automatic: real PreToolUse/Stop/PostToolUse hooks, so Claude Code never has to be told to use Jev (hook.ts:16-30, 210-264).
Fast local pre-filter means routine calls (read-only, project tests/builds, in-project edits) never touch the network, cutting cost, latency and egress; only risky-looking calls reach Jev.

Never auto-approves and only returns deny/ask or silence, so it composes with the bypass/auto permission mode as an extra brake without weakening existing guards; redacts secrets before sending and skips .env/*.pem/.npmrc.
OpenRouter reuse is plausible with zero code change: the SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's System One path.
Honest author: benchmark shows Jev did not lower agent cost and the skill goes unused; ships warn-only defaults and advises running supervise warn-only before --block.
MIT, idempotent installer with --remove, no postinstall, no telemetry beyond an opt-out npm version check, sensible tests and cross-OS CI, local audit logs of every decision.
Extra useful commands for manual use: triage of failing logs, diff review before commit, guard for fetched web content (relevant to playwright use).
cons: Not OpenRouter-native: TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming, default model jev-latest vs OpenRouter typesafe/jev-1.13, error hints point to api.typesafe.ai; OpenRouter compatibility is inferred from source and untested.
Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-16, 26 stars, 68 commits, one main author; fast-moving API (0.7.x) and pinned to a beta model.

Jev is a classifier, not a reasoner; the author's own benchmark found no reliable cost or file-read savings and that the skill was never used, so for daily coding the value is mostly the safety net, not productivity.

Safety hook is redundant or overlapping for this user: already has a secret-leak PreToolUse guard and runs in bypass/auto mode where the author's ask/deny semantics would interrupt flow; adds another Node spawn on Bash alongside GitNexus hooks.
Default 403-means-deny policy fails closed and could block legitimate calls if OpenRouter returns 403 for credits/key/region issues, and the reason text tells the agent to hand it to the user.

Data egress on client projects: supervise sends prompts, up to 20k chars of diff and 12k chars of tool output per turn to a third-party (OpenRouter and upstream); redaction is pattern-based only, a compliance concern for client code.
PostToolUse hook has no matcher, so a Node process spawns on every tool call of every session even when it does nothing; Stop hook can add up to 10s at turn end.
Supervise verdicts are admittedly uncalibrated (README) and reading the job from the transcript relies on an unguaranteed format; --block can send the agent back to finished work.
Skeptic caveat on Jev quality (router-like behavior) applies to every judgment it makes; no independent validation beyond the author's 44-case safety set.
gh-shiftynick-jev-axi.verdict: Best automatic-integration candidate found so far because it ships real PreToolUse/Stop/PostToolUse hooks with local fast-path, redaction and fail-open behavior, and it can plausibly be pointed at OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (untested). Its value is a cheap safety/supervision layer rather than coding productivity, so install it only user-level PreToolUse with --on-error allow (skip supervise on client repos) after a manual curl test against OpenRouter.

gh-francoischastel-jev-router.name: FrancoisChastel/jev-router
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.whatItDoes: A local Node HTTP relay (127.0.0.1:4141) that sits between Claude Code (also Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Pi, Cursor) and the model provider. On each request it picks a model tier (fast/mid/frontier) and reasoning effort and rewrites ONLY the model field. It uses tool-outcome heuristics (NVIDIA Switchyard style) and, when the situation is ambiguous or a new user turn arrives, one Jev call. Jev answers 5 task questions or 3 execution questions about a bounded summary. Claude Code is pointed at it via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-code/auto written into ~/.claude/settings.json. It is a cost-saving downgrade router, not a way to give Claude Code Jev-as-a-tool. Jev only judges which model to use.

Request body {model, state, questions, session_id}, Bearer auth, response {answers, usage}. Generated policy also uses OpenRouter for inference (openai/gpt-6-luna, anthropic/claude-sonnet-5, anthropic/claude-opus-5.5). README states mechanics verified live against OpenRouter, but not live against Vercel or TypeSafe.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: n/a, OpenRouter Decisions is already the default/primary transport

security: Not an MCP server and no Jev tool for the model. It is a transparent proxy in the path of EVERY Claude Code inference request (all prompts, code, file contents, tool results pass through a local Node process). This is high blast radius for a 3-star, 3-day-old, single-author project.

OAuth handling: with a claude.ai login it forwards Claude Code's own bearer token unchanged to api.anthropic.com (docs/harnesses.md, SECURITY.md). It does not store the token, but a third-party process now handles the subscription OAuth bearer in memory. Routing subscription traffic through a non-official base URL may also conflict with Anthropic terms/behavior; unverified.

Judge key stored in plaintext in ~/.jev-router/env (mode 600). The key is not in argv unless the user passes --judge-key (setup flag, visible in ps/shell history). The systemd unit and hooks run node with a script path only.

Writes ~/.claude/settings.json (env block ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/ANTHROPIC_MODEL, modelPicker, statusLine, hooks) with .bak backup. It would collide with the user's existing hooks and env configuration, and changes the global model to claude-code/auto for ALL projects including client work.

Claimed redaction hook is a no-op: src/core/dossier.ts:38 defaults redact to identity, and the daemon/relay never passes dossier.redact (decide.ts:364 uses input.dossier ?? {}; grep finds no other caller). SECURITY.md line says 'A redaction hook runs before anything leaves the process', which is misleading. Secrets in the last user message or tool-output excerpts would be sent to OpenRouter/Jev unredacted. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this path.

Hardening present: loopback bind by default, --token required for non-loopback, content-type application/json required on POST (CSRF defense in 0.3.0). Publishing via `jev-router expose` creates a public cloudflared/ngrok tunnel (Cursor only, opt-in).

No telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics returned nothing). No npm postinstall script. The repo also commits a stray francoischastel-jev-router-0.1.0.tgz binary. Install is npm install -g of a brand-new npm package (published 2026-09-30) from an unknown author, so supply-chain risk is high; not executed by this audit.
Tunnel dependency and a background service that runs continuously and keeps a session store and decision log at ~/.jev-router/decisions.jsonl (digests, not prompt text).
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.dataEgress: Judge (OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions): a bounded dossier of at most 12,000 chars: the harness name, the last user message (first 2000 chars), the tail of the assistant's intent (400 chars), up to 40 tool names, up to 8 recent tool outcomes with 200-char excerpts, and an images flag. It never sends the full conversation, file contents or system prompt, but the excerpts of tool output and the user's task text can contain secrets or client code, unredacted (redaction is not wired). Plus session_id. Inference: the relay forwards the ENTIRE request (full conversation, files, tool results) to whichever upstream the policy selects. With the OAuth egress it goes to api.anthropic.com, so nothing new leaves; with a gateway key it goes to OpenRouter (and to non-Anthropic models such as openai/gpt-6-luna on the fast tier). Local disk: ~/.jev-router/decisions.jsonl with digests and token counts.
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.failureMode: Documented and coded as fail-open for the judge: 1500 ms per-attempt timeout, 1 retry (250 ms x 2^n jittered backoff) for 429/5xx/timeout/network, then falls back to tool-signal-only routing or the default model (src/judge/http.ts, policy timeout_ms 1500). Missing key means deterministic routing only. Hooks have a 2 s timeout and never block tools. BUT the relay itself is a single point of failure: if the local daemon or systemd service is down, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=127.0.0.1:4141 gets connection refused on every request (fail-closed for Claude Code), and there is no bypass. Recovery means removing env keys from settings.json. Cascade retry is off by default.
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.latencyImpact: Steady state: one extra loopback proxy hop, a few ms, plus streaming pass-through. Judge call only on new user turns or ambiguous signals (not per tool call; holds and leases reuse the last decision): about 70-500 ms typical, worst case about 1.5 s x 2 attempts plus backoff (about 3.3 s) on a bad turn, blocking the first token of that request. Hooks: up to 2 s per event only if the relay is stalled; otherwise about ms per tool call. Model switches invalidate the prompt cache; the design partly mitigates this with a cache_penalty guard.
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero server instructions. Hooks are HTTP hooks with no injected additionalContext text, so no context tokens. Only 1 slash command (/jev-router:status, about 100 tokens in the command list). The real cost is not context but quality and cost of the MODEL: the default claude-code/auto policy starts on Sonnet 5 and routes routine turns to the fast tier (Haiku on a subscription; openai/gpt-6-luna on a gateway), escalating to Opus only when it deems it necessary. That silently DOWNGRADES the user's chosen Opus 5.5 main model.
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy plus HTTP hooks (sensors). Fully automatic once setup runs, with no prompting needed. Every Claude Code request passes through it. Jev is called by the relay deterministically on new user turns or ambiguous signals, not at Claude's discretion. It is the only candidate type that fits "automatic without prompting", but what it automates is model selection, not giving Claude Jev decisions for code tasks.
pros: Genuinely automatic and Jev-native: Jev is the judge for model routing via OpenRouter Decisions (src/judge/http.ts openrouter transport, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), one key for judge and inference, and the user's no-prompting requirement is met.

Careful engineering for a young repo: 46 test files, CI (typecheck, biome, bun test, build, cancel smoke, npm pack install test), 19k LOC, MIT, detailed DESIGN.md/SECURITY.md/CHANGELOG, and honest 'unproven savings' disclaimers.

Judge fail-open with 1.5 s timeout and retries; the judge is called sparingly (holds/leases, tool-signal shortcut, judge only on new user turns or ambiguity). Cost of Jev is negligible (about $0.00003 per decision).

Subscription-aware: reads Anthropic 5h/7d rate-limit headers and caps tier at 80%/95% of window. Also adds statusline, stats/replay/why for cost auditing, and --shadow mode that serves one model while logging what the router WOULD have done. That last is a safe way to evaluate without changing behavior.
No context-window cost (no MCP tools, no injected hook text), local-only, no telemetry, .bak backups on settings edits, an uninstall path documented.
cons: It solves a different problem than the user's goal: it routes to cheaper models (Haiku/Sonnet/gpt-6-luna) to save money. The user runs Opus 5.5 as the main model on a subscription, so the default policy will silently downgrade quality on personal and client work. Savings are also weak on a flat-rate subscription.

Sits in the critical path of every Claude Code request as a localhost proxy and rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json globally (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-code/auto). If the daemon dies, Claude Code is dead (fail-closed at the transport level), and it competes with the user's existing settings and hooks.

Handles the claude.ai OAuth bearer for the subscription and forwards it to api.anthropic.com from a 3-day-old, 3-star, single-author project. Client code and prompts transit the relay, and for client projects this needs explicit consent. The router might also send inference to non-Anthropic models via OpenRouter, changing the data-processing chain on client code.

SECURITY.md claims a redaction hook, but redact is identity by default and never wired (src/core/dossier.ts:38; no caller sets dossier.redact). The Jev dossier can carry the last user message and 200-char tool-output excerpts, potentially secrets, to OpenRouter unredacted; the user's PreToolUse guard does not cover it.

Very young and alpha: repo created 2026-09-27, v0.3.0 on 2026-09-30, 46 commits by one author, 3 stars. Benchmarks have not been run (README: 'treat any savings figure as unproven'), and live runs against TypeSafe direct and Vercel have not been done. The OAuth-relay approach depends on Claude Code internals (modelPicker/behavesAs, gateway hint headers) that may break across Claude Code releases.

Does not give Claude Code Jev's typed decisions for coding tasks (e.g., 'is this change risky', 'which file to edit'); Jev is used only internally as a router judge, so it does not deliver the broader 'use Jev whenever it adds value' goal. Model switching also risks losing prompt cache and mid-session behavior consistency; cascade/retry semantic side effects.
Adds up to ~3.3 s worst-case latency on turns where the judge times out twice; it can also conflict with the user's Opus-first workflow through effort/model changes mid-task.
gh-francoischastel-jev-router.verdict: Technically the most complete and automatic Jev integration (OpenRouter Decisions as judge, transparent proxy, fail-open judge, tests and CI), but it is a cost-saving downgrade router that would swap the user's Opus 5.5 for cheaper models and puts a 3-day-old third-party proxy in front of every request and the OAuth token. Do not install it as-is; at most try it in --shadow mode or borrow its judge client and question design.

gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.name: shaharia-lab/jev-cli
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.whatItDoes: Unofficial, Rust (2 crates: jev-client, jev-cli) command-line tool for TypeSafe Jev. It does three things. (1) CLI: `jev noul|choice|score|eval|validate|batch run` sends state plus typed questions to POST {base}/v1/systemone with Bearer auth and returns probabilities. Exit codes make it usable as a semantic `if` (0 = ok, 10 = gate false, 11 = abstain band). (2) `jev mcp serve`: a hand-written stdio JSON-RPC MCP server with 6 tools (7 with --allow-dir). (3) A Claude Code plugin and skill (skills/jev-cli/SKILL.md, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json) that teaches the agent the workflow. It ships no hooks and no proxy. It is not affiliated with TypeSafe.

providerSupport.evidence: Code only knows the TypeSafe contract: DEFAULT_BASE_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai" (crates/jev-client/src/base_url.rs:9). The endpoint path is fixed at "v1/systemone" (crates/jev-client/src/http.rs:298) and is joined onto the base URL. The key is read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (crates/jev-cli/src/credentials.rs:24) or the `jev auth login` credentials file. The base URL is overridable with --base-url, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (crates/jev-cli/src/config/settings.rs:106) or a profile. Auth is `Authorization: Bearer` (http.rs:389). The Response struct has no deny_unknown_fields (response.rs:19-31), so OpenRouter's extra fields (id, provider, usage.cost) should be tolerated. OpenRouter's doc page https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk says: set the base URL to https://openrouter.ai/api, the SDK appends /v1/systemone, use the OpenRouter key as Bearer, and the model names `jev-latest` -> ~typesafe/jev-latest and `jev-1.13` -> typesafe/jev-1.13 are mapped server-side. That is exactly the jev-cli contract, so `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api` plus `TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<openrouter key>` should work with zero code changes. I could not run it (static audit only), so this is unverified live. The repo has no OpenRouter mention (issue #105 is about Cloudflare hosting, and the maintainer bot said any non-TypeSafe contract is out of scope). Known breakages on OpenRouter: (a) `list_models` and `jev models list` GET /v1/models, and OpenRouter's shape differs, so they will fail; (b) the price table only knows the id `jev-1.13.0` (pricing.rs:29), and OpenRouter's id is `jev-1.13`, so --max-cost-usd-per-call and cost_usd are unavailable for OpenRouter ids unless you set the pricing_usd_per_mtok override in config.toml.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial for the evaluation path, because it is config only: a profile or env with base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, the OpenRouter key and model jev-latest. No patch is needed for evaluation. The models listing and the spend cap need a tiny patch or config: use the pricing override, or fork the price table to add jev-1.13.
providerSupport.others: Cloudflare-hosted Jev is a different contract (issue #105). Any --base-url that speaks TypeSafe's /v1/systemone shape and Bearer auth works.

interface.name: Skill: jev-cli (plugin jev@jev-cli)
