It teaches the discover, author, validate, run and branch loop. It tells the agent to ask the person before installing jev and never to handle the key.

gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (dual; GitHub reports apache-2.0; LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE both present)
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.runtime: Prebuilt Rust binary (cargo, brew, or the install.sh curl|sh from GitHub Releases). Single static binary, no Node or Python runtime. MCP over stdio.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.install: Options: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shaharia-lab/jev-cli/main/install.sh | sh` (SHA-256 check always, minisign check if minisign is installed, no sudo, installs to ~/.local/bin and edits the shell profile PATH unless --no-modify-path); `brew install shaharia-lab/tap/jev`; `cargo binstall jev-cli`; `cargo install jev-cli --locked`. Then `claude mcp add jev -- jev mcp serve` (scope user), optionally `claude plugin marketplace add shaharia-lab/jev-cli && claude plugin install jev@jev-cli`. For OpenRouter: `jev profile create openrouter --base-url https://openrouter.ai/api --model jev-latest`, run `jev auth login` with the OpenRouter key (or export TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the shell that starts claude), then register `jev mcp serve --profile openrouter`. Do not put the key in `claude mcp add -e`, because that writes it into ~/.claude.json.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.tests: About 493 #[test] functions across 24 integration test files plus unit tests, snapshot tests for help and the spec, secret-leak tests, MCP protocol tests (tests/mcp.rs), and cargo-fuzz targets including an MCP fuzz target. CI runs fmt, clippy -D warnings and tests on Linux, macOS and Windows. It also runs a nightly live-smoke test against the real API, cargo-deny and audit, and pins actions to commit SHAs. Releases use release-please and minisign signing. The CI and tests are unusually thorough for an 11-day-old repo.
security: API key handling is good: it comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or a 0600 credentials file in a 0700 dir (credentials.rs). It is never accepted as an argv value, so it does not appear in `ps` or shell history. It is held in a zeroize-on-drop type with a redacting Debug, and response bodies are scrubbed of the key. Redirects are never followed, so the Authorization header cannot be replayed to another host. HTTPS is enforced except for loopback, and TLS uses rustls with the platform verifier. There is no project-local config, so a repo cannot redirect the key.

MCP file access is deny-by-default. batch_run exists only with --allow-dir, paths are canonicalized (symlinks and .. resolved), and the output file must not already exist. Without --allow-dir the server touches no files.
No telemetry. The two hosts contacted are the API base URL and GitHub Releases for self-update (docs/development/threat-model.md, README).

Self-update: a detached background `jev update --background` runs at most once every 24h. It downloads a release from GitHub, verifies it against minisign keys compiled into the binary (crates/jev-cli/keys/*.pub) and swaps the binary in on the next run with a rollback self-test. This is a supply-chain surface (a compromised release key or repo would give code execution on a dev machine). It can be turned off with `jev config set update.auto false` or update.pin_version. On a client-work machine, turn it off and pin the version.

The installer is curl|sh, but the script is verified: SHA-256 always and minisign only when minisign is installed (--require-signature enforces it). Prefer cargo install --locked, or a manual download of the release plus checksum, over piping to sh.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are numeric JSON (probabilities), not free text, so a Jev response cannot carry injected instructions. The inbound direction is the risk: the agent chooses what to send as `state`, so injected content in a file could steer what gets sent. The blast radius is small, because it is read-only, has no shell execution and no file writes unless --allow-dir is set.
Terminal-escape neutralisation is implemented for human output, and error text from the server is never echoed verbatim.

Governance risk: the project is unofficial, has one main human maintainer (55 of 67 commits) plus bots, and is 11 days old. The AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files in the repo are contributor instructions for that repo, not for us.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.dataEgress: On every noul, choice, score or evaluate call: the `state` text or JSON, plus the question instructions and criteria, plus the model name. All of it is chosen by Claude as tool arguments, so it can be code snippets, diffs, logs, file contents or a tool output. It goes over HTTPS to {base_url}/v1/systemone, which is OpenRouter and then TypeSafe as the inference provider, so it crosses two third parties. The Authorization header carries the API key. `validate` sends nothing. `list_models` sends only the GET with the key. The auto-updater makes a request to GitHub Releases at most once a day and sends no code. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry. Bodies are logged only with --debug-bodies. For client projects this is a real consideration, because the model decides what to send and no hook or allowlist restricts it. OpenRouter's data-policy setting for the account should be checked.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.failureMode: Fail-open in practice. The MCP server starts even without a usable key, and each evaluating call then returns a tool error (JSON error object with code and hint, e.g. no_api_key, exit class 3). Claude sees the error and carries on. Nothing blocks the session and there are no hooks to hang. Per attempt the HTTP timeout is 30 s with a 10 s connect timeout (retry.rs:65, http.rs:32), and there are 2 retries with 0.5 to 5 s backoff. Timeouts are retried and Retry-After is honoured up to 60 s. So a hung or slow Jev could stall a single tool call for about 90 s plus backoff before erroring. This can be tightened with --timeout and --max-retries or a profile. A 429 or 5xx becomes a tool error. Validation errors are caught offline before any request is spent.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.latencyImpact: Nothing is added to calls that do not use Jev, because there are no hooks or proxying. Each Jev call is one HTTPS round trip. The claimed 70 to 500 ms end to end holds for the model, but through the OpenRouter routing layer it is likely to be a few hundred ms, plus MCP stdio overhead (negligible) and a Rust process start once per session. The README demo shows 1 ms for a mocked call. Batching is encouraged: `evaluate` answers many questions in one call.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.contextCost: There are 6 tools by default (evaluate, noul, choice, score, validate, list_models) and 7 with --allow-dir. A static estimate from the source is about 5 to 7k tokens (about 22 to 28k chars) if the tool definitions are loaded in full. The evaluate, validate and batch_run descriptions are 0.9 to 1.6k chars each and embed the full request JSON schema (schemas/request.schema.json is 6.5k chars). The noul, choice and score tools carry smaller per-question schemas plus a shared ~600-char JEV_LIMITS/RESULT boilerplate in each description. The server sends an `instructions` string of about 800 chars (mod.rs INSTRUCTIONS). Claude Code here defers MCP tool schemas behind ToolSearch, since deferred tools appear by name only, so the resident cost drops to a few hundred tokens of names plus the ~800-char server instructions. The plugin skill adds only its description line (~800 chars) to the skill listing, and its ~16.5 KB body loads only when triggered. No hook-injected text.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.autoInvocation: The MCP tools are model-discretion: Claude calls noul, choice, score or evaluate only if it judges they fit. The descriptions are well written for this ('Choose noul for an absolute judgment', 'ask one snap judgment per question'), and the server-level `instructions` explains when to use it. The optional plugin skill is a description-triggered skill, so it fires on 'semantic judgment about content (classify, route, detect, rate, verify)' tasks. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no CLAUDE.md wiring. Real auto-use will be sparse and unpredictable, because Opus 5.5 can classify text itself for free with the reasoning it already has, and nothing in a coding session specifically calls for a calibrated probability. The most reliable way to make it fire more is to add a short CLAUDE.md rule, or to put the calls in a PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook that runs `jev noul ... --fail-under` (a CLI call, deterministic, but you must build the hook yourself).
pros: Best-engineered Jev integration found so far. It is the only candidate here that combines an MCP server, a CLI (usable from hooks and CI), a skill/plugin, offline validation and batch mode, all Jev-native. It has a real test suite (~493 tests, fuzzing, 3-OS CI, nightly live smoke test).

OpenRouter works with config only. The client builds `{base}/v1/systemone` with Bearer auth, and OpenRouter documents `https://openrouter.ai/api` plus `/v1/systemone` as TypeSafe-compatible with the same body (state, model, questions -> answers, usage). So: `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api` with the OpenRouter key. `jev-latest` maps server-side to ~typesafe/jev-latest.
A profile (`jev profile create openrouter --base-url ...`) plus `jev mcp serve --profile openrouter` keeps the OpenRouter settings and key out of ~/.claude.json.

Safe by default: read-only tools, no shell execution, file access only via --allow-dir, key never in argv, no telemetry, results are numbers (no injection channel), and failure never blocks Claude (tool error only).

Tool descriptions and server instructions are written so that a model knows when to pick a tool (prefer evaluate for several questions, always include an escape option, Jev cannot count). Because MCP schemas are deferred in this Claude Code setup, the resident context cost is small.

Offline `validate` catches the API's silent failure modes (unknown fields inside questions are silently accepted and bill you) before spending money. The CLI is scriptable: `jev noul ... --fail-under 0.8` gives a hook-friendly exit code, so a deterministic PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook (e.g. 'does this diff touch auth/secret handling?') is possible.
Apache-2.0/MIT license, signed releases, cargo-deny and audit in CI.
cons: Automatic use is the weak point. It is pure model-discretion. Nothing makes Claude reach for Jev during coding, and a frontier model can usually answer 'is this a bug fix?' at zero marginal cost. Expect it to be called rarely unless you add CLAUDE.md rules or build your own hooks.

The OpenRouter path is untested by the project. The repo never mentions OpenRouter. It depends on OpenRouter's compat shim, which is beta. `list_models` and `models list` will break because the OpenRouter models shape differs, and cost estimates come back null. `--max-cost-usd-per-call` only knows the id `jev-1.13.0`, while OpenRouter expects `jev-1.13`, so the spend cap needs the pricing override in config.toml or a small patch. The response-parsing assumption (extra OpenRouter fields tolerated) comes from a lack of deny_unknown_fields, not from a test.

It is a new (11 days), 33-star, community, single-maintainer project (55 of 67 commits from one person, the rest bots) that is explicitly unofficial. If TypeSafe changes the API the tool may lag, though the nightly live smoke test helps. The API itself is beta.

The background self-updater (daily GitHub check, staged binary swap) is a supply-chain and surprise-behavior risk for a machine that holds client work. It must be disabled with `update.auto false`. The recommended installer is curl|sh, and its signature check is skipped when minisign is not installed.

Data egress goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the agent picks the payload. On client projects, code, diffs and logs could be sent to third parties with no hook to filter them. It bypasses your secret-leak guard, because the guard matches Bash, Read, Grep and NotebookEdit, not `mcp__jev__*`. You would need to add an MCP matcher.
Worst-case stall is about 90 s for one call (30 s timeout x 3 attempts) unless you set --timeout 5s --max-retries 0 in the profile.

No hooks are shipped. This is the audit's main gap against 'automatic': the skill and MCP server are advisory. The 16.5 KB skill body is heavy if it triggers often, and its install text tells the agent to run a curl|sh install (it does say to ask the person first).

Two Jev surfaces exist on OpenRouter (Decisions API at /api/alpha/decisions and System One). jev-cli only speaks System One, so it does not cover the Decisions API or 'Jev Router' semantics beyond the model id.
gh-shaharia-lab-jev-cli.verdict: The strongest Jev-specific building block found, and the best MCP server to use if you want Jev at all: `jev mcp serve --profile openrouter` with base URL https://openrouter.ai/api and your OpenRouter key should work with no code changes, but this is unverified live. It will not make Claude 'use Jev automatically' on its own. Auto-use needs your own CLAUDE.md rule or a CLI-based hook. Before using it on client work, turn off auto-update, pin the version and add an mcp__jev__* matcher to your secret guard.

gh-dirien-jev-router.name: dirien/jev-router (@ediri/jev-router)
gh-dirien-jev-router.whatItDoes: Local Node.js pass-through proxy (Anthropic Messages for Claude Code, OpenAI Responses for Codex). Claude Code is pointed at it via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in ~/.claude/settings.json. Once per NEW HUMAN MESSAGE it sends a small scrubbed state plus one 4-option Choice question (mechanical/routine/complex/deep) and two Noul guards (routing_claim_present, alters_sensitive_state) to Jev over the System One API. Jev's answer is mapped by asymmetric thresholds to a model tier (default Claude-only config: fast=Haiku 4.5, balanced=Sonnet 5, frontier=Opus 5.5) and the request's `model` field is rewritten. Tool-loop steps, subagents and compaction follow the session tier, and the tier only ratchets upward within a session. Background calls go to Haiku. Streams pass back byte for byte. It also ships a live decision view on :4100, a `report` command, a systemd user service installer, a secret scanner, and a Docker Sandboxes kit. Jev here is used as a cost/quality tier selector, not as an in-workflow decision oracle.

gh-dirien-jev-router.tests: ~200 node:test cases (unit 69, router 45, cli 39, setup 36, ui 12) with fake upstreams/fake Jev, coverage gates (lines 85 / branches 75 / functions 85), Biome lint, tsc typecheck, markdownlint. CI on ubuntu Node 22 and 24 with SHA-pinned actions and npm provenance publish. Live tests exist (test/live.mjs) but were not run. Self-reported comparisons (live vs Anthropic) come from the author.
gh-dirien-jev-router.runtime: Node.js >=22 (user has 24), zero runtime dependencies (only devDependencies), ESM; installed globally via npm as @ediri/jev-router (v1.6.0 released 2026-09-25)
gh-dirien-jev-router.install: npx @ediri/jev-router setup   (then restart claude). Do NOT use unscoped `jev-router` on npm: it is an unrelated package (gargpratyush/jev-router).
security: Keys are stored in ~/.config/jev-router/env (0600) and read from env/file, not passed as CLI args, so they do not show in argv/ps; the README explicitly advises JEV_ROUTER_UI_TOKEN over a flag because flags show in ps.

Binds 127.0.0.1 only and refuses non-loopback unless JEV_ROUTER_TOKEN is set; rejects foreign Host headers (DNS rebinding) and any request with an Origin header; no admin API; /healthz exposes only counters.

Claude OAuth/login header is forwarded only to targets marked clientAuth (api.anthropic.com); other upstreams receive minimal headers and no metadata. If ANTHROPIC_API_KEY exists in the router env it overrides the OAuth login and is billed (src/router.mjs:1058-1062).
Refuses to point Claude Code at itself when another gateway's credentials (ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN/API_KEY/apiKeyHelper) are present, so foreign creds are not leaked to Anthropic.

Deterministic secret scanner (src/secrets.mjs, includes sk-or-v1 pattern) on human messages; a hit pins the session to the 'trusted' target and redacts bodies for untrusted upstreams (Ollama). Regex list is admitted to be 'a floor, not a guarantee'.

Prompt-injection surface: the routed text steers Jev; the author cites an independent eval where one sentence moved Jev's answer 73.5%. Mitigated by 'text is data' framing, routing_claim guard and sensitive-state override, and impact is bounded to picking among Anthropic tiers (cost/quality), not tool execution.

Setup modifies ~/.claude/settings.json (with backup and a setup.json manifest for clean uninstall), writes a systemd user unit, and runs `npm install -g` when launched via npx. It uses spawnSync/spawn with argument arrays, not shell strings. No curl|sh, no postinstall script, no telemetry found in src.

Single maintainer, repo 6 days old, 118 commits in 2 days: a supply-chain risk because it sits on the path of ALL Claude traffic including the OAuth bearer token. Package is npm-provenance-published and has no runtime deps, which limits transitive risk. I did not run any code.
gh-dirien-jev-router.dataEgress: To Jev (TypeSafe/OpenRouter), once per human message: a scrubbed state with the latest human message (harness text removed, secrets scrubbed, code blocks replaced by one-line summaries like '[code block (python), 40 lines]', cut to 4,000 chars), up to two earlier human messages (600 chars each), the last assistant message only when the new message is under 30 words, and session metadata (harness name, depth bucket, recent tool-call counts). Never tool output, file contents, diffs, or the system prompt. Claude traffic itself (full prompts, code, tool results) flows through the local proxy to api.anthropic.com only, same data as today; there is no other third-party egress unless the Ollama option is chosen (then fast-tier prompts go to Ollama Cloud with redaction). Local logs hold routing metadata, hashes and costs, not prompts.
gh-dirien-jev-router.failureMode: Jev failure is fail-open with soft fallback: 1.2 s timeout per attempt, 2.5 s deadline per decision, one retry, TypeSafe then OpenRouter, timeout channel skipped 30 s, 401/402/403 skipped 5 min. A new session falls back to the default tier 'balanced' (Sonnet 5, NOT Opus) and stays provisional (retries Jev up to 3 times); an ongoing session keeps its tier. policy.failClosed=false by default. BUT the router itself is a hard single point of failure: setup points ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at 127.0.0.1:4000 for every session, and when nothing listens Claude Code fails with connection errors (docs/activation.md:235). Mitigated by systemd user service with Restart, but it gives up after 5 failed starts in a minute; and the service only runs while logged in unless linger is enabled. Per-session `launch claude` avoids the global dependency.
gh-dirien-jev-router.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no hooks, no skills, no server instructions: nothing is injected into Claude's context by the router. It only changes settings env vars. Side effect: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true is forced (to keep MCP tool search on behind a gateway) and CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=160000 which makes auto-compaction occur earlier than with Opus 5.5's native window. Claude sees no text about Jev at all.
gh-dirien-jev-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: fully automatic on every human message once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points to it. No user prompting, no model discretion, no hook. Deterministic, code-driven.
gh-dirien-jev-router.latencyImpact: Local proxy overhead is negligible; streaming is byte-for-byte. One Jev call per human message adds roughly 0.2 to 0.65 s (docs cite median 0.23 s on OpenRouter, 0.44-0.65 s from Europe), bounded by a 2.5 s deadline, and the call is awaited before the request is forwarded. Tool-loop steps, subagents, compaction and count_tokens add no Jev latency. Switching model tier cold-starts the prompt cache for that model, which can cost latency and tokens on the first request after a tier change (ratchet limits this to upward moves).
pros: Only candidate that meets the 'fully automatic, never say use jev' requirement with zero prompting and zero context cost: it is a transparent proxy, not an MCP tool or skill Claude must choose to call.

Real OpenRouter support in code (channel 'openrouter', https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), usable as the sole Jev provider; TypeSafe direct optional as failover.

Works with subscription/OAuth login: the client's own credential is passed through to api.anthropic.com only, no Anthropic API key needed (README + src/router.mjs:1058-1062). Claude Code 2.1.285 exceeds the required 2.1.273.

Careful design: decides only at human turns, ratchets upward only, keeps prompt cache, routes background calls to Haiku, adapts 5 request shapes that break on Haiku 4.5 (thinking, effort, max_tokens, system-message folding, 1M beta), which is the hard part of Claude Code model routing.

Sends Jev only a small scrubbed state (never tool output/file contents/system prompt) and has a deterministic secret scanner pinning secret-bearing sessions to a trusted target: reasonable for client projects.

Good hygiene: zero runtime deps, Apache-2.0, ~200 tests with coverage gates, SHA-pinned CI, npm provenance, loopback-only with DNS-rebind/Origin protections, keys not in argv, clean `uninstall` that restores settings.json, `launch claude` for per-session opt-in, and a live decision view plus `report` for auditing.

Composes cleanly with the user's existing hooks and MCP servers: it touches none of them (no PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman interaction), and it forces ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH which helps the user's several MCP servers.
Explicit manual overrides (#frontier, /model opus, x-jev-tier) let the user pin Opus when they want it.
cons: Its value is cost/quota saving via downgrading, not extra intelligence: with Opus 5.5 as the user's main model, easy turns get silently rerouted to Sonnet 5 or Haiku 4.5. A senior dev prioritising quality on client work may not want that; a mis-route to a cheap tier hurts the whole session (author's own data: all 12 observed Jev misses were too cheap).

Very young and single-maintainer: repo created 2026-09-24, v1.6.0 on 2026-09-25, 118 commits in 2 days, 6 stars, 1 contributor, SECURITY.md still lists 1.5.x as latest supported. It sits on the path of every Claude request and the OAuth bearer token, so any bug or compromise is high impact; no third-party audit.

Global router is a hard single point of failure: if the service is down or crash-loops (systemd gives up after 5 starts/min) every claude session fails to connect, and the user must undo ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Mitigation is `launch claude` per session, but then it is not automatic for plain `claude`.

Changing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL alters Claude Code behaviour: forces CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=160000 (earlier compaction than Opus 5.5's native window), ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, and uses undocumented gateway hint headers. Anthropic states model routing through gateways is unsupported for non-Claude models; behaviour with subscription OAuth may change with Claude Code updates.

Unverified quality claims: the routing accuracy figures come from the author/LiteLLM benchmark on author-written prompts, and the Jev prompt-injection sensitivity (73.5% flip in an independent eval) plus Theo's skepticism mean thresholds need tuning on the user's own prompts (docs/evaluation.md).

Sends the user's (scrubbed, truncated) prompts to a beta third-party model on each human turn; for client projects with confidentiality terms this is extra egress beyond Anthropic, though limited to text of the messages, not code or tool output. Regex secret scanning is admitted incomplete.
Tier switch invalidates prompt cache for that model (first request after an upward move is cold), and the ratchet means long sessions drift to Opus anyway, reducing savings.

Setup mutates ~/.claude/settings.json, installs a global npm package and a systemd user unit (bypass-permission users get no prompt on these). Codex and Ollama parts add unused surface; Jev is not exposed to Claude for in-task decisions (no Choice/Score/Noul tools for e.g. permission gating).
gh-dirien-jev-router.verdict: The only reviewed option that is truly automatic with zero context cost and first-class OpenRouter support, but it is a cost-downgrade router on the critical path of all Claude traffic, from a 6-day-old single-maintainer project. Worth trying via per-session `jev-router launch claude` (or with the Fable/Opus-biased config and #frontier override) rather than a global settings.json install, and it does not give Claude access to Jev decisions for hooks or permission gating.

gh-xafold-jev-router.name: xafold/jev-router
gh-xafold-jev-router.whatItDoes: Rust binary (jev-router 0.5.8) that wraps `claude`. `jev-router claude` starts a loopback HTTP proxy (127.0.0.1:random) and launches Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointed at it and a sentinel model "jev-router". On the first request of each user turn the proxy calls TypeSafe Jev (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13.0) with about 40 Noul/Choice/Score questions. It maps the answers through rule trees to a model and effort (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5/5.5, Opus 5.5), rewrites the /v1/messages body, and forwards it to api.anthropic.com. It reuses Claude Code's own auth headers (API key or OAuth). It also has cache-aware switching, safety floors (security, concurrency and irreversible work get at least Opus), per-message effort system messages, a local dashboard, a status line wrapper, and feedback-based auto-tuning. It uses Jev only for model and effort routing. It gives Claude Code no Jev tool for decisions.

gh-xafold-jev-router.license: None. GitHub reports licenseInfo null and there is no LICENSE file in the tree, so it is all rights reserved by default. Do not fork or redistribute without asking the author. Personal patching is a grey area.
gh-xafold-jev-router.tests: 25 unit tests in src/*.rs plus tests/golden.rs and tests/parity.rs. Golden fixtures are 110 labelled prompts; the README claims v2 rules put 96% in the acceptable range against 67% for v1. There is no CI (no .github directory). Tests were not run, per the static-only rule. The repo is 5 days old with 8 tags (v0.5.0 to v0.5.7; the latest release is 0.5.7 while Cargo.toml is at 0.5.8). It has 5 stars and 0 forks, and it is a Rust port of a Python reference by gargpratyush.
security: The proxy sees every Claude Code request in full: prompts, file contents, tool results, and the Authorization or x-api-key header (the OAuth token for a subscription login). It forwards them unchanged to the upstream, api.anthropic.com or the user's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (src/main.rs:111-112, src/proxy.rs:826+). Risk is contained by binding only to 127.0.0.1 with a random port (src/proxy.rs:714). Any local process can still reach that port and use the proxy as an authenticated relay.

The TypeSafe key is read from env or ~/.config/jev-router/.env and sent as a Bearer header via ureq. It is never put in argv, so it does not show in the process list. It is in the environment of the jev-router process only. Claude Code is spawned with the parent env, so it inherits TYPESAFE_API_KEY from `jev-router claude` if it was exported.

Prompt egress is partly redacted by regex only, which the source calls a 'ponytail' shortcut (src/jev.rs:35-46). It catches key=value pairs, common token prefixes and 40+ character tokens. It will miss many secrets, so it is not a substitute for the user's existing secret-leak guard hook.

It writes full Jev state and answers (prompts, up to 7 turns) to ~/.local/share/claude-router/decisions.jsonl at mode 0600, plus proxy.log and usage.jsonl. That is a persistent local plaintext prompt log, including for client projects.

It modifies ~/.claude/settings.json on exit: restore_saved_model rewrites the 'model' key if it equals 'jev-router' (src/main.rs:27-46). A crash could leave 'jev-router' as the saved default model. It also injects a statusLine via --settings and runs the user's own statusLine command through `sh -c` (src/main.rs:167). That command comes from the user's own settings, so it is not third-party code execution.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no telemetry other than Jev and Anthropic calls, and no build.rs. The dashboard is loopback-only with Host and Origin checks. The only shell execution is the user's statusline command. The Anthropic /v1/models lookup reuses the user's auth headers against the same upstream. It has no license, and the release tarball was not inspected or verified.

It rewrites request bodies (model, effort, system messages, cache breakpoint move, MCP tool-schema sanitization) and forces a beta header. That is a fragile, version-coupled integration with Claude Code 2.1.x and the Anthropic API. A body-rewrite bug is guarded by catch_unwind, which forwards the request unmodified.
gh-xafold-jev-router.dataEgress: To Jev (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if patched) on each user turn: the new user message (clipped to 2000 chars, regex-redacted), up to 7 earlier user and assistant text turns (2000 chars each, no tool output), the repo folder name, and the first up to 800 chars of CLAUDE.md or README.md (redacted). The last is off with JEV_ROUTER_REPO_SUMMARY=off (src/jev.rs:73-125, README 'What goes to api.typesafe.ai'). Internal side requests and 'continue'-style replies skip Jev. No code, diffs or tool output are sent to Jev unless the user pastes them into the prompt. Everything else, including the OAuth or API credentials and the full conversation, flows unchanged through the local proxy to Anthropic as usual. With OpenRouter as the provider, the same prompt text would also pass through OpenRouter and is subject to its logging policy. That matters for client projects.
gh-xafold-jev-router.failureMode: Fail-open. Jev has an 8 s timeout per attempt with 1 retry after 500 ms (408, 429, 5xx and transport errors), so a hung Jev costs up to about 16.5 s on that turn (src/jev.rs:25-26, 155-176). On error, the failure is logged to proxy.log. The turn uses the previous rung if one exists, else Sonnet medium for agent turns (AGENT_FALLBACK = S_MED) or Haiku for tool-less auxiliary calls (src/proxy.rs:28-31, 641-657). Nothing is retried per turn, so each new turn pays the timeout again while Jev stays down. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes `jev-router claude` start plain claude with no proxy. If the local proxy process dies mid-session, Claude Code gets connection errors because its base URL is dead, so this part fails closed. Upstream transport errors return 502.
gh-xafold-jev-router.latencyImpact: About 0.4 s per user turn (the README's figure; the brief says 70-500 ms), plus a proxy hop. Only the first request of a turn is routed; the tool loop reuses the rung. Continuations, retries and Claude Code's internal calls skip Jev. The worst case is about 16.5 s when Jev is down. Model switches can also force a prompt-cache rewrite, which the cache guard partly mitigates. The extra latency is small relative to Opus turn times.
gh-xafold-jev-router.contextCost: Zero MCP or skill context: no tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text. It does inject effort-only role:system messages mid-conversation and moves the cache breakpoint on Opus 5.5. It sets CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=200000, which caps the context window (a shrink if the user runs a larger-window Opus). It also replaces the status line, wrapped around the user's own.
gh-xafold-jev-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Once Claude Code is started via `jev-router claude` (the user would alias claude to it), every turn is routed with no prompting and no model discretion. It is not a hook, MCP tool or skill. Plain `claude` is not covered, and there is no installer that wires it into settings.json. It only chooses which Anthropic model and effort serves the turn. It does not give Claude Code access to Jev decisions for other purposes, such as tool-use gating, commit or test triage, or risk scoring.
pros: The only candidate seen that is truly automatic and prompt-free: it sits at the API layer, so no 'use jev' phrasing is ever needed.

Uses Jev's strengths correctly: about 40 typed Choice, Noul and Score questions per turn (request type, depth, breadth, security, failed-fix) turned into a deterministic rule ladder, with logged probabilities and a dashboard for auditing each decision.
Fail-open on Jev errors (8 s timeout, 1 retry, fallback rung), loopback-only bind, log files 0600, and catch_unwind around the rewrite so a bug forwards the request unmodified.

Cache-aware switching, safety floors (security, concurrency and irreversible work get at least Opus) and a manual /model override that passes through. This is careful engineering for the prompt-cache cost problem.
Zero context tokens: no MCP tools, no schemas, no hook text.
Small, readable single-purpose Rust codebase (about 4.6k lines with tests) that is easy to audit. One file, src/jev.rs, holds all Jev I/O, so an OpenRouter patch is a few lines if the schema matches.
Works with a subscription/OAuth login: auth headers are passed through unchanged, and the /v1/models lookup uses the same OAuth beta header.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter. The URL, model id (jev-1.13.0, not typesafe/jev-1.13) and key (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) are hardcoded, and the TypeSafe key is waitlisted. Using OpenRouter means a local fork built with cargo, and OpenRouter's System One schema match is unverified.

No license (licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file), so forking or patching it is legally unclear. It is also 5 days old, with 5 stars, 0 forks, no CI, and no independent review. It shipped 8 releases in 5 days and depends on undocumented Anthropic betas and Claude Code behavior, so it is likely to break on Claude Code updates.

Not really 'inside' Claude Code: the user must always start Claude Code with `jev-router claude` (or an alias), and there is no hook, settings or plugin install. Any plain `claude`, IDE or Desktop launch bypasses it. It also runs as an extra wrapper process for every session.

It downgrades the user's chosen Opus 5.5 to Haiku 4.5 or Sonnet for 'simple' turns, and it overrides the user's model choice, effort setting and /model default. That changes quality and behavior on client work. The 200k CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS cap can also shrink the window. The value is mostly cost saving, which matters little on a flat subscription, so the payoff is uncertain for this user.

Sends recent conversation text and the repo folder name plus CLAUDE.md/README.md intro to a third party on every turn. The only redaction is regex ('ponytail') redaction. That is a real concern for client projects, and it comes on top of the existing secret-guard hook. The prompts are also logged in plaintext to decisions.jsonl.

Sits in the path of the OAuth credentials and all traffic, so a bug or supply-chain compromise of the binary would expose the Anthropic credentials. The prebuilt release binary would need trust, or a source build.

Modifies ~/.claude/settings.json on exit (model key restore) and replaces the status line; it may interact badly with any existing statusLine or with the hooks the user already has. Interaction with the GitNexus and caveman hooks is untested. Sub-agent turns may share one status file.
It exposes no Jev decision to the agent (no tools or hooks), so it cannot serve other uses such as risk scoring or gating tool calls. It is model-routing only.
gh-xafold-jev-router.verdict: The closest thing to hands-free Jev in Claude Code, and the only router found that does model and effort switching silently. It is TypeSafe-only, unlicensed, days old, and does not support OpenRouter without a Rust fork. For a Opus 5.5 subscription user its payoff is mostly cost routing with some quality risk, and it sends prompts to a third party on client work. Treat it as a reference design to patch or reimplement (hooks or a minimal proxy) rather than something to install as-is.

gh-drewpayment-jev-route.name: drewpayment/jev-route
gh-drewpayment-jev-route.whatItDoes: Claude Code "hooks module" plugin (TypeScript, early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1). On every eligible prompt it sends the redacted prompt (<=20k chars) plus previous tier to Jev's /v1/systemone with a Choice question (tier fast/balanced/powerful) and a Noul question (risky). It then rewrites model (and optionally effort) of every API request of that turn via turn.step (fast->haiku, balanced->sonnet, powerful->opus), with hysteresis, prompt-cache-aware switch lock (downgrades blocked above 50k context) and risky>=0.7 forcing powerful. It is a cost/capability router, not decision support for coding actions. Fails open to the session model.

gh-drewpayment-jev-route.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: every hook is wrapped in try/catch; any error, non-2xx, unparseable response, or timeout means no decision and the session model runs (register.ts:236-253, prompt.submit catch). Hard deadline timeout_ms default 800 ms (clamped 50-5000) covering fetch+body+parse with AbortController. Status line shows 'route: on' and /route status shows last error. If Jev is slow every prompt is delayed by up to 800 ms before failing open.
gh-drewpayment-jev-route.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens; no server instructions; no text injected into the model context (prompt passed through untouched, only status line/toasts in the UI). Registers one slash command (/route) only. Effectively 0 context tokens. Side effect: switching model per turn can invalidate prompt cache (mitigated by switch lock and hysteresis).
gh-drewpayment-jev-route.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (engine-level prompt.submit/turn.step hooks module): runs automatically on every prompt with no model discretion and no user prompting. This is the only candidate style that fully matches 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so', but it uses Jev only as a model-tier router.
gh-drewpayment-jev-route.latencyImpact: Adds one Jev round trip before the first request of each eligible prompt: README says typically 0.4-0.6 s via gateway, capped at 800 ms default (max 5 s). Nothing added to subsequent steps of the turn. Not per tool call.
pros: Only candidate that is fully automatic and deterministic: prompt.submit/turn.step hooks fire every turn with no user 'use jev' prompting and no MCP tool-choice by the model.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected text.
Fail-open with hard timeout (default 800 ms), so Jev/OpenRouter outage never blocks coding.

Clean, small, readable code (1448 lines, no deps, no shell exec); wire format uses Choice+Noul primitives exactly as Jev is designed (typed tier + risky probability), a genuinely good use of Jev's strengths.
OpenRouter reachable via provider=custom with base https://openrouter.ai/api (yields /v1/systemone) and typesafe/jev-1.13 model id; parser lenient about response keys.

Sensible engineering: secret redaction, cache-aware hysteresis and switch lock, subagent turns untouched, /route kill switch, decision toasts, per-tier model mapping configurable, defaults already use claude-sonnet-5-5 / claude-opus-5-5.
Can save quota/cost by sending trivial prompts to Haiku while keeping Opus for risky work; MIT license.

Does not use Jev for anything besides picking Haiku/Sonnet/Opus. For a user whose main model is Opus 5.5 on subscription, downgrading turns to Haiku/Sonnet may lower quality and, on OAuth subscription, saves little money (only rate-limit quota); Jev latency +0.4-0.8 s per prompt with a benefit only if routing helps.

Routing model classifier judges only the prompt text ('yes', 'continue' rely on previous_tier), with no repo/context awareness; skeptics say Jev behaves like a small router, so tier quality is unproven.
Switching models per turn breaks prompt cache in the first turn of a switch (mitigated but not eliminated) and downgrades stop after 50k context, so it is most useful in short sessions.
Client-project prompt text goes to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe); redaction is regex best-effort only.

gh-gargpratyush-jev-router.whatItDoes: Node CLI wrapper (jev-claude, jev-codex) that starts a loopback HTTP proxy on 127.0.0.1:<random port>, launches the real `claude` with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointed at it, and registers a "Jev Router" sentinel model (jev-router) in /model. For each fresh user turn the proxy makes one Jev System One call (choice over the account's exact Claude model ids plus 3 score questions: task complexity, reasoning, tool complexity), applies a policy (explicit "use opus" override, low-confidence no-downgrade, no downgrade if context >20k tokens, tier clamping) and rewrites body.model to Haiku/Sonnet/Opus (Fable opt-in) before forwarding to api.anthropic.com with the CLI's own auth headers. It routes the main model per turn (cost saving), it does not give Claude a Jev tool. It injects a status line showing the chosen model, and bundles a user-only /jev-explain skill.

Genuinely uses Jev for what it is good at (typed choice + score primitives, calibrated confidence) with a well-designed policy: low confidence never downgrades, downgrade refused when context >20k tokens to avoid cache rebuild (config.mjs THRESHOLDS), explicit overrides win, tool-loop turns keep the tier, sub-agents pinned separately.
Fail-open with tight timeouts (1.5 s/3 s deadline, 1 retry) rather than the SDK default 10 s x2 retries (router.mjs comments).
Near-zero context cost: no tools, no hook injection; all changes are outside the context window.

OpenRouter works with env-only config: SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and bare 'jev-latest' id, so no fork needed (SDK dist/index.mjs:513,554; OpenRouter docs).

MIT, small readable codebase (~1.4k lines src), no postinstall, no telemetry, decent unit tests (65+), clean revert (just run plain claude).
Handles real compatibility problems (MCP schema exclusiveMinimum, stripping thinking/effort for Haiku), and provides /jev-explain and a status line so routing is auditable.
cons: Its value is cost/speed saving by downgrading models, not better decisions inside a coding session. For a user who chose Opus 5.5 as main model on client work, silent per-turn downgrades to Sonnet/Haiku are a quality risk; benefit on a flat-rate subscription is mostly usage-limit headroom.

Routing is only first-turn-of-prompt and cache-sensitive; downgrades refused once context >20k tokens (config.mjs:downgradeMaxContextTokens), so in long daily sessions it will mostly stay on Opus anyway - small realised savings.

Likely silently broken for this setup: issue #48 (open) - Claude Code >=2.1.283 appends hook output as trailing system messages so newTurnPrompt returns null and Jev is never called; user runs GitNexus/caveman/secret-guard hooks on 2.1.285. Loads cwd .env into environment inherited by Claude Code (jev-claude.mjs:75-85,113) - leaks client project env vars and lets a repo's .env redirect Jev traffic; bad for client projects.
Bypass/auto permission mode is unaffected but the proxy sees all Anthropic traffic in cleartext and writes prompts to /tmp/jev-claude/*.json and optionally ~/.jev-claude.log.

gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.name: satviksinha/jev-model-router (jev-router)
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.whatItDoes: Claude Code "hooks module" plugin (TypeScript, early-access function hooks). On every user turn (turn.start) it POSTs the raw prompt text to Jev /v1/systemone with two typed questions: a Choice "tier" (haiku, sonnet, opus, fable, each with a criteria string) and a Score "effort" (5 levels). In turn.step it rewrites the model request to the chosen model id and effort level (MODEL_OF: claude-haiku-4-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5, claude-fable-5-1) for all steps of that turn. It also prefixes the reply with a route line, appends a footer with usage and cache ratio, adds a SessionMode footer label, and registers a /jev command (status, on/off, quiet/loud, sticky). This is a model router, not a decision-support tool for code tasks. It fits the "automatic, no prompting" requirement well, but it changes which Claude model answers, which is a big behavioural side effect.

gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.dataEgress: Only the text of each human-typed user turn (e.text, plus <\task-notification> XML text for background-agent wake-ups) plus static tier and effort criteria strings and the API key. No code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs, or transcript history are sent (register.ts:197 state: e.text). Subagent loops are not sent. But whatever the user pastes into a prompt (code, secrets, client data) leaves for Jev via the provider. With OpenRouter this means OpenRouter plus TypeSafe see it; check OpenRouter data-policy settings for client projects.
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.failureMode: Fail-open. Missing key: no request is made. Timeout default 1500ms (JEV_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_MS), implemented as a Promise.race against $.clock.sleep (jev.ts:251-261; note the fetch is not aborted). HTTP error, non-JSON, no answers, or a tier not offered means the turn runs on the session model unchanged, with an '⚠️ unrouted · reason' line in the reply. Worst case adds 1.5s to the turn. Blocking: turn.start awaits Jev before the turn proceeds.
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool definitions, no server instructions, no skill descriptions. The only cost is text it writes into the conversation: one route line per reply (~20-30 tokens) plus a fenced footer (~40 tokens) per finished reply, both persisted in the transcript and seen by the model; /jev quiet removes them. Also registers one slash command. Much larger indirect cost: switching model per turn invalidates the per-model prompt cache (README documents 4% cache hit after a switch on 128k context), so mixed routing on big contexts can cost more tokens/quota than staying on Opus.
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.latencyImpact: Blocking Jev call once per user turn (not per tool step): README measured 402-839ms on 10 live calls via the TypeSafe/Vercel gateway on 2026-09-20; cap 1500ms. Expect similar (claimed 70-500ms) via OpenRouter, unmeasured. Additional cold-cache latency on turns that switch model. Not applied to subagents.
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.autoInvocation: Deterministic engine hook (turn.start/turn.step modules) that fires on every user turn with no model discretion and no user prompting. Requires only the plugin installed plus CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in env.
pros: Truly automatic: turn.start/turn.step hooks fire on every prompt, zero prompting, zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition context cost.
Uses Jev exactly as designed: typed Choice plus Score with calibrated probabilities, no free text, tiny payload (prompt text only).
Fail-open with named reasons, 1500ms cap, one call per turn (not per step), tests for policy/provider/jev/register/status (5 test files, ~60KB) using injected fetch and fake engine.
OpenRouter reachable with config only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api yields openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (provider.ts:55); at worst a one-line model id patch.
Policy is a plain editable table (TIER_CRITERIA, policy.ts:384) and JEV_ROUTER_EXCLUDE can drop tiers, so it can be tuned to only route between opus and lower tiers or only adjust effort.

Sticky mode (/jev sticky) holds shaky switches to protect prompt cache; /jev shows history, actual answering model and cache ratio, so effect is measurable. Key never in argv; no shell exec; no postinstall.
Secondary value for a subscription user: routing trivial prompts to haiku/sonnet can save quota.
cons: Not a decision-support integration for coding tasks (no branching, gating or review decisions); it only picks a Claude model, and could downgrade the user's Opus 5.5 main model: MODEL_OF maps opus to claude-opus-5 (policy.ts:373-378), and haiku/sonnet tiers will answer real work at lower quality. Model ids are hardcoded and must be edited to match the user's models.
Model switching per turn busts the prompt cache (per README, cache 4% after switch), which can cost more than it saves in long client sessions; requires sticky tuning.
Writes a route line and footer into the assistant's reply text, which is recorded and re-read by the model; noisy for a daily driver (mitigated by /jev quiet).

Depends on an early-access engine API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, hooks modules, 'claude-code' types) that can break across releases; README targets 2.1.275, installed is 2.1.285, so compatibility is unverified.

Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 7 commits, 1 contributor, 4 stars, no releases, no CI, tests not run by me. Heuristic tier criteria were tuned on 10 prompts; Jev quality is unverified (Theo's 'flash-router' claim is unverified) and the sample shows odd combos such as haiku·xhigh.
Adds 0.4-0.85s blocking latency to every human turn (up to 1.5s); the fetch is not aborted on timeout.
Ships the whole prompt to a third party with no redaction; for client projects this needs OpenRouter/TypeSafe data-policy consideration.
No native OpenRouter support: the env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY and errors say 'gateway'; the model id 'jev-latest' is untested on OpenRouter. Subagents are never routed.
gh-satviksinha-jev-model-router.verdict: The only candidate here that meets the "fully automatic, never say use jev" requirement, via a deterministic turn hook with no context cost and a fail-open design, and it can reach OpenRouter by setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. But it is a model router that swaps the Claude model per turn, so it needs its model table and sticky settings tuned to avoid downgrading Opus 5.5 or breaking cache, and it sits on an early-access API and week-old code. Try it only as an opt-in experiment (fork it, fix the model ids and the OpenRouter model name, use sticky mode).

First-class OpenRouter support: config.ts:170-179 hits openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest using OPENROUTER_API_KEY - matches the user's intended provider with no patching; TypeSafe direct also works.
Safe design: read-only tools, no shell execution, no hooks that can block your session, fail-open to offline heuristic, key passed by env not argv, keychain-stored userConfig, MIT license.
Reasonably tested for a new project: ~135 test cases across 9 test files (node --test), CI on ubuntu/windows/macos x Node 22/24 plus Node 20 bundle job, dist-must-match-source check, secrets scan.
Low cost: about $0.08 per 1,000 decisions per the author; negligible standing context (~2k tokens) and zero per-turn overhead.
Delegation path exists (/jev-model-router:delegate sets Agent tool model alias) - the only way this can act on a recommendation inside a subscription session.
cons: Solves a different problem than 'use Jev automatically when it adds value': it routes tasks to an LLM (haiku/sonnet/opus/fable) rather than giving Claude Code calibrated yes/no or choice decisions (e.g. is this diff risky, which file to open) during coding.

With a Claude subscription/OAuth login and Opus 5.5 as the fixed main model, there is nothing to route per turn: Claude Code cannot switch main model mid-turn from a tool, so the output is advice the user must apply manually via /model and /effort, or via subagent alias.

Not automatic: no hook, no proxy. Firing depends on Opus choosing to call the tool when the user asks 'which model'; the user explicitly does not want to prompt for it, so it will mostly sit idle while costing ~2k standing context tokens.

Extra hop is often net-negative: an extra Opus tool round-trip to choose a cheaper model for a task Opus is already executing; its own cost-saving claims (-4% vs Opus 5 high, -49% vs Fable) are modelled by the author on 42 tasks and are irrelevant on flat-rate subscription.
Data egress through the LLM-authored task string (6k chars) to OpenRouter is not covered by the user's secret-leak hook (matcher excludes MCP tools) - risky for client projects.

Immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 2 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, version 1.0.0, Jev/OpenRouter Decisions API itself is alpha/beta; committed 1.7 MB bundle and daily remote intel JSON from the author's main branch are unreviewed supply-chain trust.
Config gotcha: a TYPESAFE_API_KEY in env silently takes priority over OpenRouter unless JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter; worst-case fallback latency ~36s on outage.

Model catalog/score data contains fictional-looking or fast-moving entries (e.g. 'Claude Fable 5.1'); recommendations depend on the author's curated scores that may drift from what the user has access to.

Worth at most a manual /delegate experiment for cost-tiering subagents; not the core integration.

gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin built on the early-access "function hooks"/mods API (TypeScript module hooks/register.ts, needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1). On every user prompt (turn.start) it POSTs the prompt to Jev's System One endpoint with a Choice question (tier haiku/sonnet/opus/fable) plus a Score question (effort), then rewrites the model and effort of every request in the turn (turn.step), also routing subagents (agent.spawn). Policy layers: confidence bar 75% (90% for upgrades past 100k ctx), prompt-cache price checks, $1 upgrade cap, context-window guard, effort ceiling xhigh, named-tier override ("use opus"), go-ahead shortcut. Optionally replaces Claude's summary compaction by asking Jev (noul questions) whether each tool call and output still matters. Prints a route line plus cost summary in each reply. Fork of satviksinha/jev-model-router; compaction vendored from tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction.

gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.dataEgress: To the configured provider only (TypeSafe direct, Vercel gateway, or OpenRouter if overridden): (1) each user prompt, first 12,000 chars (hooks/jev.ts:37); (2) each subagent task text as the model wrote it; (3) one-line finished-task summaries only if JEV_ROUTER_NOTIFY_CONTINUE=0; (4) at compaction (on by default with a TypeSafe/OpenRouter key): conversation text messages plus each tool call's input truncated to 1,000 chars, which includes Write/Edit content, i.e. code; tool result contents are not sent, only size and error flag. gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.failureMode: Fail-open. Default 1500 ms timeout (JEV_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_MS, clamp 100-8000). On timeout, HTTP error, bad JSON or missing key the turn stays on the tier already running (or session model if none) and the route line states the reason (jev.ts:257-372). Caveat: engine $.http.fetch takes no abort signal so a timed-out request still completes and is billed (~$0.00003). Hook budget is 10 s. Compaction falls back to engine summary on >8 s, error or <25% reduction. Silent total no-op if function hooks flag is missing or the module fails to load.
gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.latencyImpact: One blocking Jev round trip at the start of each typed prompt (README/jev.ts comment measured 402-839 ms on 10 prompts, capped at 1.5 s by default). No call for go-aheads, named tiers, wake-ups from background tasks, or turn.step iterations after the first (decision cached per turn). Extra Jev call per subagent spawn. Compaction adds up to 8 s but replaces the engine's own summary LLM call. Model switches can also add cost: a tier change invalidates the prompt cache (mitigated by its price checks).
gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.contextCost: Effectively zero tool-definition cost: no MCP server, no tools, no server instructions, no skill descriptions loaded into context. Cost is output-side: a route line (~20 tokens) at the start of each reply and a summary line (~30 tokens, more with agents) at the end are written into the reply text and so remain in conversation history; /jev quiet hides them. No text injected into the system prompt found.
gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.autoInvocation: Deterministic engine-level hooks (turn.start, turn.step, agent.spawn, session.compact) that fire on every turn without any prompting or model discretion. This is the only fully automatic, zero-prompt integration style, but requires function hooks enabled.
pros: Truly automatic: fires on every prompt via engine hooks, the user never says 'use jev', which matches the stated requirement exactly
Uses Jev for what a System One classifier is good at (Choice tier + Score effort in one request, typed probabilities, ~0.4-0.8 s, ~$0.00003 per call) rather than as a chat model
Economically aware routing: price checks against prompt-cache warmth, $1 upgrade cap, window guard, sticky 75% bar; avoids the classic router failure of cache-thrashing model switches
Fail-open with named reasons and 1.5 s cap; nothing blocks Claude if Jev/OpenRouter is down
Zero MCP context cost, no tools registered, does not collide with gitnexus/playwright/caveman MCPs or the existing classic PreToolUse/GitNexus hooks (function hooks are a separate mechanism)
Provider is code-level compatible with OpenRouter via env-only override (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + ALLOW_CUSTOM_BASE + pinned model), with compaction following the same endpoint
Strict env-based key handling (not argv), key scrubbing in errors, base-URL allowlist
Broad test suite (~695 cases, register.test.ts drives real hooks), detailed README, per-session /jev controls, tiers can be excluded (e.g. JEV_ROUTER_EXCLUDE=fable,haiku) and ceiling capped
Optional Jev-based compaction keeps conversation verbatim and prunes only tool calls, potentially better than lossy summaries
cons: Depends on Claude Code's early-access function-hooks API ('may change between releases without notice'); unverified that 2.1.285 with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 loads it, and an update can silently turn it into a no-op

It overrides the model for every request: the user's chosen Opus 5.5 gets downgraded to haiku/sonnet or bumped to fable per Jev's opinion, which changes quality/behaviour and, on a subscription login, whether fable/haiku are even allowed on the plan is unverified; it hardcodes model IDs claude-haiku-4-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-opus-5-5, claude-fable-5-1
Value is mainly cost/usage savings; benefit is unproven and Jev's quality is contested (Theo claims it behaves like a small flash router); tier/effort calibration is only tuned on ~6 sample prompts

OpenRouter is not a first-class provider: needs 4 to 5 env vars incl. a misleadingly named TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding an OpenRouter key and the ALLOW_CUSTOM_BASE flag that widens key exfiltration risk; OpenRouter response compatibility and model-id spelling (jev-1.13 vs typesafe/jev-1.13) untested by me

Sends every prompt (12k chars) and, at compaction, Write/Edit tool inputs (1k chars each) to a third party on client projects; also stores 400 chars of every prompt on disk; needs client-confidentiality sign-off
Very young and low-trust: created 2026-09-22, 2 stars, single main author, mostly AI-written commits, no CI, no marketplace packaging; unusual install path (~/.claude/skills/) from README
Adds 0.4-1.5 s blocking latency to every typed prompt, plus visible route line and cost summary noise in every reply (hideable with /jev quiet)
Bug class where a module load error silently disables everything; ~8k lines of TS in a hot path is a large surface for a tool that just picks a model
Free-form Jev limits: it only sees the first 12k chars of the prompt, not repo state, so routing is on prompt wording alone (a short prompt about hard code can be routed cheap; README admits this)
gh-flam1ngfir3ball-jev-claude-router.verdict: The only candidate that is genuinely automatic and uses Jev as a typed classifier at the right moment (per-turn model/effort routing, zero context cost, fail-open), and it should work with OpenRouter by env vars alone. But it needs an experimental engine API, overrides the user's main-model choice, sends prompts and some code to a third party, and is an 8-day-old AI-heavy project, so pilot it read-only first (e.g. JEV_ROUTER_EXCLUDE to limit tiers, /jev compact off, personal projects only) before trusting it on client work.

gh-wxk-ai-jev-opus.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI (npm jev-opus, v0.4.8) that wraps Claude Code. `jev-opus claude` starts a local 127.0.0.1 gateway, sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to it (plus a token header), adds a "Opus 5.5 · Jev" entry to /model and launches the normal interactive claude with --model jev/claude-opus-5-5. Fail-CLOSED for the gateway itself: if the local gateway crashes, Claude Code loses its ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL target and all requests fail; if journal write or journal recovery fails, the request is NOT forwarded and an error is returned (README lines on prepared-decision flush and corrupt-journal replay). gh-wxk-ai-jev-opus.verdict: The only candidate here that is truly automatic and OpenRouter-ready, but it does one narrow thing (Jev picks Opus effort) by inserting a fail-closed local proxy in front of all Claude traffic from a week-old single-author package. Worth trying on personal projects via `jev-opus claude`, not something to make the default for client work, and it does not replace a broader Jev decision-hook integration.

gh-chrishan17-claude-jev-mod.whatItDoes: A Claude Code "mod" plugin (function-hooks module, not an MCP server or proxy) that registers a single engine.create hook adding a `$.jev.ask({state, questions})` noun to the plugin engine interface. Other plugins' hooks can then call Jev (Choice/Score/Noul) via six providers and read back typed probabilities. By itself it decides nothing and calls nothing: it is a client library with no consumer hooks, no MCP tools, no skills. The candidate summary "router-proxy" is a mislabel; it is a plugin-host SDK.

Whether a failure blocks or passes the tool call is decided by the consuming hook (README: 'failing open is usually right for a guard'). gh-chrishan17-claude-jev-mod.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill descriptions, and the mod injects no text into the model context. Only adds the engine.create hook at startup.

README's examples (risk score of Bash commands, destructive-command noul) are illustrative, not shipped. So it is a building block toward the user's goal of hook-driven, no-prompt invocation, not the integration itself.

gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.whatItDoes: Local FastAPI proxy (127.0.0.1:9099) meant to sit at ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. For each /v1/messages request it sends the last user message as plain text to a Jev /chat/completions endpoint, then prepends a "SYSTEM EXECUTION CONTEXT" system message containing the raw Jev reply and forwards a rebuilt, stripped-down payload to Anthropic using a stored API key. It does not use the Jev Decisions/System One primitives (Choice/Noul/Score). The "needs_generation" bypass is a substring check for "needs_generation=false" in Jev text, and even then the proxy returns a stub reply rather than skipping generation properly. The 3x faster / 80% cheaper claims are unsubstantiated.

gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.dataEgress: The last user message text goes to the Jev endpoint (default api.typesafe.ai/v1, user-configurable) on every turn: the whole message, not only a snippet. Then a rebuilt request goes to api.anthropic.com. Because the payload is rebuilt from Message(role, content: str), other parts are dropped: system prompt, tools, tool_use/tool_result blocks. In practice tool results are not sent to Jev, only the last user-role message text. Claude Code turns with tool_result arrive as user messages with list content, which would fail pydantic validation.
gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.failureMode: Intended fail-open: Jev timeout (0.8s default) or exception yields needs_generation=True and the request passes through (jev_client.py:64-77, proxy.py:87-89). The proxy itself is a single point of failure: if it is not running, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set gets connection refused, so the whole session is fail-closed. Malformed bodies (content as a list of blocks, which Claude Code always sends) raise a 422/500. Non-streaming requests (Claude Code's small-model background calls, title generation, token counting) return an error object. Anthropic upstream errors are streamed through without status handling.
gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks, no skills, so 0 tool-definition tokens. But the proxy prepends a system message with the raw Jev reply on every request (variable, maybe 50-300 tokens per turn), and it invalidates prompt-cache prefix stability, since a new system message is inserted at position 0 that varies per turn. This wrecks Anthropic prompt caching, which is costly for long Claude Code sessions. The proxy also drops the Claude Code system prompt and tools when rebuilding the payload (proxy.py:142-149), which effectively breaks Claude Code.
gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9099). Automatic in principle, no model discretion, but Jev is called on every user message whether or not it adds value, and it must be started manually in a separate terminal.
gh-j1s4nn-jevxagent.latencyImpact: Adds one blocking Jev round trip (up to 0.8s timeout) before every /v1/messages request, serialised before the Anthropic call, with no caching or skipping of tool-loop turns. Net effect is added latency, not the claimed speedup: Jev does not shorten Opus's output, and the proxy cannot skip generation (bypass returns a stub string).

gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.name: MongLong0214/jev-gate
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.whatItDoes: Single Claude Code plugin (also native Codex) that uses Jev (System One, Choice/Score questions) for cost-oriented task routing rather than code intelligence. Five parts: Gate (Jev admits a request as direct/single/orchestrated, then dispatches to subagent workers and denies the root session's own tools while a job is admitted), Router (changes root-turn effort and subagent model/effort per decision), Compact (local extractive compaction, no Jev), Output (folds passing vitest logs, no Jev), Evidence (MCP tool jev_evidence: semantic source-window search, Jev-ranked). The aim is to save tokens by delegating to cheaper models.

No endpoint override env var exists.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The request body ({model,state,questions}) and the response shape ({model,usage,answers}) look like the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone schema, so the wire format probably matches. But the endpoint is hardcoded in at least 3 files (src/jev.ts, mods/router/hooks/client.ts, src/evidence). The model ID 'jev-1.13.0' would have to become 'typesafe/jev-1.13'. The plugin also ships as a pinned, sha256-checked release archive (.claude-plugin/marketplace.json), so you would need a fork and a rebuild, and would give up the marketplace install and its updates. Feasible with about 5 edits, but you would carry a fork of a fast-moving codebase with no license file.

security: No LICENSE file and GitHub licenseInfo is null. That means all rights are reserved, which is a problem for client projects.

Gate 'auto' sends the user request and the composed task contract, which can include source excerpts, file names and constraints, to TypeSafe. docs/advanced-usage.md states: 'There is no secret scrubber and no zero-retention promise.'
Router does screen outbound strings with looksSecret (mods/router/hooks/client.ts:~148) and sends nothing if a match is found. It is a pattern filter, not a DLP.

The API key goes in the Authorization header only (src/jev.ts). It is not in argv. It comes from the env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or the sensitive plugin option (kept in secure storage). Traces are documented as not receiving the key.

A project-level .claude/settings.json can set TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_EVIDENCE_CONFIG, so a hostile repo could redirect the key or the Evidence config (README). pluginConfigs in project settings are ignored.

fetch uses redirect:'error', a 128 KB request cap, a 1 MB response cap, and strict validation of the response (probabilities sum, argmax). Jev output is typed, so the injection surface is small. However, Evidence returns raw source text into the model context, and the skill tells the model to treat it as source, not instructions.
Local dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1:4731 and reads only metadata. Job state files hold the plan AND the user request verbatim under ~/.local/state/jev-gate/jobs/ (7-day cleanup).

Plugin installs as a release zip with a pinned sha256 (marketplace.json). No npm postinstall. package.json is private with only devDependencies. Runtime child_process is limited to spawnSync of `claude auth status` (shell:false) in the CLI doctor. No telemetry found beyond calls to TypeSafe.
Root guard is an execution boundary that denies the main session's Edit/Write/Bash while a job is admitted. It is not a sandbox, but it can block the user's normal flow.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only (no OpenRouter path). Gate auto: the user's prompt verbatim at admission, and the task contract plus predecessor summaries at each planner/worker dispatch (can include source excerpts and file names). Router: the text of the decision being asked (a root-turn prompt or a subagent prompt), after the looksSecret check. Evidence semantic: goal, constraints, and a page of source windows (only when remote is true, which is the default when a key is present; exact-symbol and read-back are not sent). Compact and Output send nothing. Whole repos and transcripts are not uploaded. In lean mode, prior conversation-history groups are sent.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.failureMode: Fail-open by design. callJev is one POST, one deadline, zero retries. Router preparation budget is 800 ms by default (routerTimeoutMs); past it the request runs natively. No key, timeout, 4xx/5xx, malformed answer, low confidence or a tie all mean the call stays native. After a 401 or 402 the Router stops asking for the rest of the activation. Hook timeout is 5 s. The exception is that a Gate job that is already admitted keeps the root guard on. If the host cannot run a foreground worker, the doctor warns, and 'auto' skips the request instead of failing.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.contextCost: One MCP tool (jev_evidence) with a large schema (goal, constraints, roots, queryTerms, exactSymbols, mode, limit, offset, expectedSnapshot, sources), plus a dynamic description listing the allowed roots. Estimate is about 800-1,200 tokens (src/evidence/server.ts is 11.6 KB, with most of the schema and description being tool text). The skill is disable-model-invocation, so it costs 0 in the listing. The MCP server sets no 'instructions' field (capabilities: {tools:{}}). Hooks add additionalContext only when Gate admits a job (a coordinate directive, size not measured). Plugin agents (planner, workers) add a few agent descriptions to the Agent tool listing. Each admitted job also spends worker-subagent context and cost. Real cost driver: it changes how the session runs (root guard, delegation), not just tokens.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks, which suits the goal of no prompting. UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse hooks run on every prompt and every tool call. Router and Compact are transparent function hooks that patch requests and compaction. Evidence is a model-discretion MCP tool: the model may call it, and nothing forces it. The skill is manual-only.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.latencyImpact: A `node dist/entry.js` process is spawned on every UserPromptSubmit AND every PreToolUse (unmatched), and on Stop and SessionStart. Roughly 40-100 ms per tool call (estimate, not measured). Gate A adds a Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms, batched) on eligible prompts. Router preparation is bounded to 800 ms per decision, and this happens in the request path of a turn. Admitted jobs add subagent latency (bench: a delegated run was sometimes slower, sometimes faster).

pros: It is the only candidate that fits the wanted model (automatic, with no prompt to Claude): deterministic UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hooks and transparent Router/Compact function hooks. It is also the most thought-out design for using Jev as a typed decider (Choice/Score with calibrated-probability thresholds, uncertainty means native).

Strict fail-open client: one POST, deadline, zero retries, 128 KB request cap, 1 MB response cap, strict validation of the answer schema (src/jev.ts). Every uncertain, timeout or key-less path keeps the native behavior, and 401/402 trips a circuit breaker.

Explicitly supports the subscription OAuth login (src/auth.ts isSubscriptionOAuth) and warns on ANTHROPIC_* conflicts, which matches the user's setup. Each of Gate, Compact, Output and Router has its own off switch, and the Router never changes the root model unless routeMainModel is true.

Unusually honest documentation: it publishes unfavorable results (V4 forced delegation cost more, the depth ladder was withdrawn, no saving guaranteed), with a local dashboard, doctor and trace explain. Router does a local looksSecret check before sending anything.
Native Codex support also ships, and 58 test files plus CI show engineering discipline.
cons: Wrong problem for this user: it optimizes token cost by downgrading effort/model and delegating. The user runs Opus 5.5 on a subscription and wants Jev value in daily coding, not cheaper models. Open issue #132 records that the Router cut effort xhigh to medium/low and 'savings come from doing less work' (55 s/$1.02 vs 462 s/$5.60 for a review with a shorter output), and #135 records that Gate A predicts tool calls at about 1/10 of the measured value and never delegated in the bench.

OpenRouter is not supported. The endpoint api.typesafe.ai and the model 'jev-1.13.0' are hardcoded, and a strict model-equality check would discard OpenRouter's 'typesafe/jev-1.13' answers. Using OpenRouter needs a fork and a rebuild of at least 3 files, and loses marketplace updates. The user would need a separate TypeSafe key and billing.

Invasive to a bypass/auto-permission workflow: while Gate admits a job, the root session's tools are denied by PreToolUse (only read/task/Agent/MCP tools pass), the work goes to subagents, and Gate requires foreground workers (CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1), which changes how all subagents run. Each of those can conflict with the existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks.

Depends on CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, an experimental host feature verified only against Claude Code 2.1.282-2.1.284 types. It may break on 2.1.285 or later, and the README says the mode resolver was checked on 2.1.284 only.

Data egress on client projects: the user prompt, task contracts and source excerpts are sent to TypeSafe with no scrubber in Gate and no retention promise (the docs say so). Evidence semantic search is on by default when a key exists. The repo has no license, which is unsuitable for client work.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-17, 61 commits in 13 days, 1 contributor, 4 stars, v0.7.0 released hours ago; it changes fast (6 policy fixes on the last day). A node process is spawned on every tool call (unmatched PreToolUse), and the marketplace release is a pinned zip you cannot inspect from the marketplace entry alone.
The Evidence tool duplicates Grep, the existing GitNexus graph and local search. Its value is low next to GitNexus, and being a model-discretion tool it is not guaranteed to be used.
gh-monglong0214-jev-gate.verdict: The most complete automatic (hook-based) Jev integration for Claude Code, but it is a cost-routing and delegation harness pointed at TypeSafe's own API. It does not fit an Opus-on-subscription user who wants Jev as a decision oracle, it has no OpenRouter path (a fork is needed), and its root guard and effort downgrades conflict with a bypass-permission daily flow. Mine it for design ideas (the strict fail-open client, and thresholding of Choice/Score probabilities) rather than installing it.

Default mode is hybrid with an on-device classifier and Claude advise/clear-gate off, so with defaults and no key almost nothing is sent to Jev; with a key and the Claude clear gate or advise enabled, code snippets and tool outputs from client projects go to Jev/OpenRouter.
