gh-nekowasabi-jev-routing.failureMode: Jev side: 20s HTTP timeout (jev.go:56), errors returned to caller, and README states a fail-safe design (uncertain -> do not narrow tools, unsupported history shapes pass through unrewritten, compaction reply falls back to upstream when reduction under 25%). Mostly fail-open for Jev slowness. But the local proxy itself is a hard single point of failure: if it is not running or crashes, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to it gets connection errors (fail-closed for all model traffic). A 20s Jev timeout on the request path can stall a turn.
gh-nekowasabi-jev-routing.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no MCP instructions, no hooks, no skills. It does not add tokens to the tool catalog (for Claude it deliberately does not narrow tools because that breaks the prompt cache). When advise is enabled it appends a short next-tool reminder to the last tool_result (opt-in, off by default). Net context cost about 0; the proxy's stated effect is to reduce context, but with the author's own data: Claude Code native clear edit gives only about 6.3% real-session ceiling, and advise gives about +1.67% (noise) on opus-5-5.
gh-nekowasabi-jev-routing.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Fully automatic once claude is started through jev-routing run claude (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL exported globally in settings.json env / shell alias plus a daemon); no prompt changes needed. But it must sit in front of every request, and Jev is called only when the proxy decides (hybrid/local classifier default).
gh-nekowasabi-jev-routing.latencyImpact: Local proxy hop on every model request (sub-ms to few ms, streaming reverse proxy). When Jev is consulted (clear gate: once per conversation; advise: per tool result when enabled; selection paths) adds one blocking Jev round trip, claimed 70-500 ms, worst case 20s timeout. Author notes that rewriting history/tools can disrupt the Anthropic prompt cache (raising cost/latency), which is a risk for Opus 5.5 sessions with an ~80k-token fixed prefix.
pros: Truly automatic and prompt-free: transparent ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy, no MCP tools, no context tokens added, no skills to trigger, matches the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' requirement mechanically.

Jev endpoint and model are env-configurable (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL, key sent as plain Bearer), so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with an OpenRouter key is plausibly a zero-code change (schema equality unverified).

Sane defaults for Claude Code: tool catalog not narrowed (protects prompt cache), advise and clear-tool-uses default OFF, on-device classifier in hybrid mode so nothing goes to Jev without a key, compaction replacement falls back to Claude's own when savings under 25%.
Well-tested Go (about 464 Test funcs), single static binary, MIT, tiny dependency set, no npm/postinstall/curl|sh; loopback dashboard shows exactly what was rewritten.

The archived RESEARCH.md is unusually honest, paired/pre-registered data on Jev in Claude Code: a valuable negative result and a design reference (native context editing + one Jev gate call is the only approach that held up, about 8-11% on same-path, about 6% real ceiling).
cons: ARCHIVED 2026-09-26 (8 days after creation, 1 star, no releases, no CI): author explicitly concluded Jev tool selection/steering does not reduce tokens; no maintenance or bug fixes will come.

Its own Claude Code data: Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool_choice under any thinking mode, advise gave +1.67% (3 better/3 worse, noise) and Sonnet 5 advise was an increase up to -27% (99% of it Jev cost). The one working feature (clear_tool_uses gate) is default-off with a ~6% real-session ceiling. Little coding benefit to gain.

Puts a custom rewriting proxy in the path of ALL Anthropic traffic including the subscription OAuth token and client-project code; single point of failure (proxy down = Claude Code down), plaintext loopback with no local auth, and it drops ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/AUTH_TOKEN from the child env. Unsuitable for client work without an audit.

Requires launching via 'jev-routing run claude' or a global ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL plus a supervised daemon; Claude Code 2.1.285 compatibility is unverified (benchmarks used claude-opus-5-5 and sonnet-5 on an older CLI); it also rewrites history/compaction, which risks prompt-cache misses and quality loss on an 80k-token-prefix Opus session.

Not a coding-quality tool: Jev only guides tool choice/erasure for cost; it does not add review, routing-to-cheaper-model, or code intelligence. Env var naming (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and default model 'jev-latest' need remapping for OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-latest) and OpenRouter schema parity is unconfirmed.

Coexistence unknowns with existing setup: caveman-shrink MCP, GitNexus/secret-guard hooks operate on tool calls and are unaffected, but the wrapper approach conflicts with subscription features if the proxy mishandles streaming/headers.
gh-nekowasabi-jev-routing.verdict: Technically the only candidate that is truly automatic (transparent proxy, zero context cost) and it can likely be pointed at OpenRouter via JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_MODEL, but the author archived it after measuring that Jev steering does not help Claude Code (advise about 0%, context-clear about 6% real ceiling). Do not adopt for daily or client work; treat RESEARCH.md as a reference and, at most, borrow the 'native clear_tool_uses + one Jev gate call' idea.

interface.name: Skill: jev-decide

interface.name: Skill: claude-subagent-model
interface.purpose: Policy text (10 KB) routing subagents to haiku/sonnet/opus/fable; opinionated, tied to the author's setup.

interface.name: Agents: mech/bulk/deep/oracle

gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.runtime: Node >= 20 (plain ESM .mjs, zero npm dependencies, global fetch); bash install.sh; pi extensions in TypeScript
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.install: git clone to ~/workspace/jev-agent-hooks; ./install.sh (symlinks hooks to ~/.claude/hooks, skills to ~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills, agents to ~/.claude/agents, jev CLI to ~/.local/bin/jev; does NOT edit settings.json); then manually merge config/claude-settings.snippet.json into ~/.claude/settings.json and export TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.tests: None. No test files, no CI workflows, no releases, no issues. Quality evidence is only an offline replay in the README (34 turns, 20 dispatches, n=1 user).
security: API key is read from env only and sent as an Authorization header via fetch; never appears in argv/process list. Good.

No telemetry to third parties; only api.typesafe.ai is contacted. Local JSONL logs in ~/.claude/logs include the first 200 chars of every prompt (jev-skill-suggest.jsonl) and the subagent task description; jev-cli log omits state.

install.sh is local-only (no curl|sh, no postinstall). BUT link() does `rm -rf` on any real directory at the destination (e.g. an existing ~/.claude/skills/jev-decide or ~/.claude/agents/<name>, and ~/.agents/skills/<name>) and it links every skills/* dir and agents/*.md into your dirs; the README instructs cloning and running it. Review before running; destinations are fixed from $HOME.

Injected additionalContext is a fixed template with only the skill name interpolated from the local roster; low prompt-injection surface. Roster contents (third-party plugin SKILL.md text) are sent to Jev as criteria, so a malicious skill could bias the pick but only to another local skill.
alreadyDenied() writes a JSON state file at os.tmpdir()/jev-agent-gate-denied.json (predictable shared path in /tmp, read-modify-write without locking; low-risk on a single-user box).
Hooks run with bypass-mode user privileges; code is small and readable (read all of jev-lib, jev-skill-suggest, jev-agent-gate in full).
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe direct; would be openrouter.ai if patched, adding OpenRouter as a second processor): (a) every user prompt, truncated to 6000 chars; (b) the last assistant text message from the transcript, last 1500 chars; (c) descriptions (250 chars each) of ALL installed skills/plugin skills on the first call, and 700-char SKILL.md body excerpts of the top 3 on the second; (d) for each Agent dispatch: the subagent prompt (up to 8000 chars), description, agent name/description, which routinely contains code snippets, file paths and task details. README itself warns not to put secrets in agent prompts. No file contents or diffs are sent directly, but prompts and subagent prompts on client projects can contain client code/IP. There is no secret redaction, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this path because it runs inside the hook process, not via a Bash/Read tool call.
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.failureMode: Jev-dependent hooks fail open: skill-suggest wraps main in .catch(() => {}) and returns silently without key/CLAUDECODE (jev-skill-suggest.mjs:165-183); agent-gate catches Jev errors and allows (jev-agent-gate.mjs ~line 124-128). Per-request timeout 4 s (jev-lib.mjs:11), two sequential requests for skill suggest, hook timeout 10 s in settings snippet, so worst case a prompt is delayed ~8 s before proceeding without suggestion. Agent-gate is fail-open but can deny (once per session/agent/tier; identical resubmission passes). NOT fail-open: subagent-model-gate.mjs is a pure rule gate that denies any Agent call lacking an explicit haiku|sonnet|opus|fable alias and preset mismatches, with Chinese denial text; independent of Jev availability, it changes Claude Code behavior for every subagent spawn. Can be disabled with CLAUDE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_GATE=off.
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.latencyImpact: Skill suggest is synchronous on UserPromptSubmit (prompt does not reach the model until it finishes): README states 2-3 s per turn live (two round trips), offline p50 ~1 s; gate short-circuits after call 1 if gate score < 0.3 (rare per its own data). Agent-gate adds ~400 ms per Agent dispatch. Rule gates negligible. Plus Node startup ~50 ms and roster scan of all plugin skill dirs each prompt (sync fs reads).
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server: 0 tools, 0 server instructions. Always-loaded skill listings: jev-decide description ~430 chars (~110 tokens), claude-subagent-model description ~120 chars (~30 tokens) plus 4 agent descriptions (~470-1230 bytes each incl. Chinese, ~250 tokens total in Agent tool listing). Per-turn hook injection: one ~45-token line only when best fit >= 0.7 (README: ~3 of 34 turns, so rare). Full jev-decide body (~1k tokens) loads only when invoked; claude-subagent-model body is 10 KB (~2.5k tokens) if the model loads it.
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse Agent, SubagentStop): run without user prompting on every event, but their effect is advisory (one-line ignorable suggestion) or a one-time deny. Plus jev-decide skill: skill-description trigger, Claude's discretion to shell out to `jev` CLI via Bash. So it satisfies 'automatic' in a limited way, but the automatic Jev uses are skill routing and subagent model routing, not code decisions.
pros: Genuinely automatic: UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse hooks fire with no user phrasing, matching the 'never say use jev' requirement; hooks return additionalContext / permission decisions per the real hook protocol.
Fail-open on every Jev path (try/catch, AbortSignal 4 s, missing key => no-op), so a Jev/OpenRouter outage will not block Claude Code.
Tiny, readable, dependency-free code; all Jev traffic funnels through one function (hooks/jev-lib.mjs:6), so retargeting to OpenRouter is a ~4-line edit.

Uses Jev for what a calibrated classifier suits (pick a skill from a roster, tier fit), following TypeSafe's own skill-suggestion cookbook; has shadow mode (JEV_SKILL_SUGGEST=shadow, JEV_AGENT_GATE=shadow) to log without acting, which is the safe way to trial it.
Honest README: reports its own weak results (gate barely separates, near-duplicate skills split probability, misfires on short phrasing) and raised threshold to 0.7 from real data.
Low context cost (no MCP tools, ~100-400 tokens of always-on listings, injection only on ~10% of turns); API key not in argv; MIT license.
jev-decide skill gives a model-discretion path for act-or-ask and verify-before-done checks, closest thing in this repo to Jev helping actual coding decisions.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only (https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model 'jev-latest' at jev-lib.mjs:6-10); zero OpenRouter support, so it needs a fork/patch, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified from source.

Value is narrow for this user: skill-suggest only helps when you have a large skill roster, and the author's own data show it is marginal (3 suggestions in 34 turns, near-duplicate skills confuse it, 'correct' labels are just what the agent loaded). Claude Code already auto-selects skills from descriptions; the hook adds 1-3 s blocking latency to EVERY prompt for a rarely-shown hint.

Sends every prompt (6000 chars), last assistant reply (1500 chars), and full subagent prompts (8000 chars, often containing client code) to a third party; no redaction; risky on client projects and duplicates exposure if routed via OpenRouter.

Bundled subagent policy is the author's personal workflow and is intrusive: rule gate hard-denies any Agent/Workflow call without an explicit haiku|sonnet|opus|fable alias, references a 'fable' tier and Chinese-language deny messages/agent prompts, and would fight the user's Opus 5.5 setup and existing workflow scripts; the Jev tier-gate can also veto subagent dispatches (a wrong answer costs a retry turn).
Overlaps/conflicts with existing hooks: adds a second UserPromptSubmit hook and Agent PreToolUse hooks next to the caveman and gitnexus hooks; roster scan reads all enabled-plugin skills each prompt.
install.sh does `rm -rf` on real directories at link destinations and symlinks skills/agents into ~/.claude and ~/.agents; must be reviewed/adapted rather than run blindly.
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 10 commits over 4 days, 2 stars, 1 fork, no tests, no CI, no releases, single-user evaluation; latency and accuracy claims are not reproducible.
Does not use Jev where it would help daily coding most (commit/PR classification, risk gating of destructive Bash, test triage, retrieval reranking); those would need to be built on top.
gh-onlyjq04-jev-agent-hooks.verdict: Useful as a reference implementation of the correct hook shape (UserPromptSubmit additionalContext plus PreToolUse gate, fail-open, shadow mode) and a one-function patch point for OpenRouter, but not worth installing as-is: TypeSafe-only, marginal skill-suggest value at 1-3 s per prompt, unredacted prompt egress, and an opinionated Chinese-language subagent-model policy that would fight this setup. Cherry-pick jev-lib.mjs plus jev-skill-suggest.mjs in shadow mode (or the jev-decide skill) with the URL/key patched to OpenRouter, and skip the model gate, agents and install.sh.

gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.name: BeLazy167/typesafe-mod
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin using the early-access "function hooks" feature (TypeScript module running inside the agent loop, not a shell hook). Two routers calling Jev via POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. (1) Decision router on tool.call for AskUserQuestion (on by default): sends the agent's this-or-that question and its options to Jev, then shows per-option probabilities as a transcript line and a panel over the dialog, and can auto-answer via deny when TYPESAFE_AUTO_ANSWER=1 and confidence >= 0.75. (2) Skill router on prompt.submit (opt-in, TYPESAFE_SKILL_ROUTER=1): ranks all installed SKILL.md descriptions against the user prompt (Choice plus a Noul "needs a procedure") and injects one advisory context line naming the winning skill if confidence >= 0.6. Fails open everywhere.

providerSupport.evidence: hooks/suggest.ts:27 endpoint: 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'; hooks/suggest.ts:28 model: 'jev-latest'; hooks/register.ts:81 and :140 read env TYPESAFE_API_KEY; register.ts:95 and :148 send Authorization: Bearer ${key}. No mention of openrouter anywhere in the repo (grep clean). Body shape is {model, state, questions:{id:{type:'choice'|'noul', instructions, criteria}}} and response is read from root.answers (suggest.ts:507-509) which is the TypeSafe v1 schema.
providerSupport.others: None. Hardcoded single endpoint.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial if OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone accepts the same request/response schema (very likely, since it is named System One): change endpoint (suggest.ts:27) to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model (suggest.ts:28) to typesafe/jev-latest (or typesafe/jev-1.13), and the env var name at register.ts:81/:140 to OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Response envelope on OpenRouter is unverified and could differ (e.g. answers nesting), which would need small parser edits in readDecisions/pickWinner. Requires maintaining a fork or a local --plugin-dir copy, since it is not configurable by env.

interface.name: session.start (function hook)
interface.purpose: If TYPESAFE_SKILL_ROUTER set, runs sh -c 'find -L ~/.claude/skills ~/.claude/plugins -name SKILL.md | head -2000 | sed -n 1,60p each' via $.process.run (8s timeout), parses name+description, caches roster in $.store (register.ts:45-66)

interface.name: prompt.submit (function hook, opt-in)
interface.purpose: Sends the user prompt plus ~all skill names/80-char descriptions to Jev (~6.8k input tokens on 194 skills), and appends one advisory context line for the winning skill (register.ts:68-118). Skips prompts <12 chars or starting with /.

interface.name: tool.call {tool:AskUserQuestion} (default on)
interface.purpose: Batches all questions in the dialog into one Jev request with cwd; logs probabilities; stores DecisionViews; with TYPESAFE_AUTO_ANSWER=1 and a single question returns {deny: note} to answer for the agent (register.ts:122-200). Multi-select steps are skipped.

interface.name: ui.render {component:AskUserQuestion}
interface.purpose: Wraps core dialog with a TUI panel of probability bars (max 4 rows) (register.ts:205-290)

interface.name: env switches
interface.purpose: TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required), TYPESAFE_SKILL_ROUTER, TYPESAFE_DECIDE_OFF, TYPESAFE_AUTO_ANSWER, plus required CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1

security: API key read via $.env.get from Claude Code's env and sent as a Bearer header via $.http.fetch inside the engine; never placed in argv or a subprocess command line (the only subprocess is the fixed find/sed scan, register.ts:50, suggest.ts:51-58)
Only shell execution is a static hard-coded sh -c find/sed command; no user or model input interpolated into it
No install scripts, no npm deps, no postinstall, no curl|sh; plugin is pure TS loaded by Claude Code (hooks.json -> ./register.ts). No telemetry beyond calls to TypeSafe

Prompt-injection surface: skill router injects only a skill name chosen from the local roster (advisory line); the decision router only accepts an answer that is one of the offered options (README 'checks that the answer is one of the options'). SKILL.md descriptions are sent to Jev as criteria, so a malicious skill description could skew ranking but not inject free text back
Auto-answer mode uses deny so the agent sees an error string; that text is built locally by decisionNote, not from Jev free text (Jev returns none)

Author is one small maintainer (BeLazy167) with a collaborator merging PRs; unaudited third-party code that runs in-process with hook privileges inside Claude Code and can run processes ($.process.run) and read env; pin a commit and review before enabling
Function hooks are an early-access, env-gated Claude Code feature; the plugin's own tests only run in the engine's offline harness
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.dataEgress: Decision router (default): question text, option labels/descriptions for every AskUserQuestion dialog, and the working directory path, sent to api.typesafe.ai (README/register.ts:150-155). Roughly 374 input tokens. Skill router (opt-in): the full raw user prompt text on every submit (register.ts:96, buildRequest state.user_request) plus the names and first 80 chars of description of every locally installed skill/plugin SKILL.md. No code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs leave. For a client-project user, prompts and cwd paths (client names in paths) go to a third party, TypeSafe (or OpenRouter after patching), when the skill router is on.
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.failureMode: Fail-open on every path: missing key, HTTP error, JSON parse failure, throw, or timeout all fall through to next(e) (register.ts:82, :141, :101-114, :194-199). Each call races $.clock.sleep(4000) (budgetMs 4000 in suggest.ts:43) because the engine has an uncatchable 10 s dispatch budget. So worst case per affected event is a 4 s stall, then continue. Below-threshold confidence also falls through to asking the user. Auto-answer edge: only a lone confident question is answered.
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no tool definitions. No server instructions. Default mode injects nothing into model context (advisory output goes to the transcript UI/log only). With skill router on, one short advisory line is appended per confident prompt (a few dozen tokens); the skill list itself is unchanged so prefix caching is preserved (README). Auto-answer adds a short deny note as a tool error. Negligible context footprint overall.
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.latencyImpact: Decision router: runs only when the agent calls AskUserQuestion (rare, and blocked on a human anyway); one round trip, up to 4 s cap. Skill router (opt-in): README measures +166-420 ms on every prompt, with a one-time ~1.1 s scan per session; 6.8k input tokens per prompt on a 194-skill install. Cost negligible ($0.00028 per prompt at $0.042/M).
gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks, no model discretion and no user prompting needed: the Claude Code harness fires prompt.submit and tool.call(AskUserQuestion) function hooks automatically once the plugin is installed, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 is set and a key is present. The skill router still needs TYPESAFE_SKILL_ROUTER=1 to be on. Jev's output is advisory only by default.
pros: Genuinely automatic: registered as in-process function hooks, so Jev is invoked with no 'use jev' prompt, which matches the user's core requirement

Correct conceptual use of Jev's typed decisions (Choice + Noul with calibrated probabilities) rather than free-text; sensible confidence floors (0.6 skill, 0.75 auto-answer) and a check that the answer is one of the offered options
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no schema tokens, no server instructions; advisory output goes to the UI, prefix cache preserved
Fail-open everywhere with a self-imposed 4 s race under the engine's 10 s budget; cannot wedge a turn

No dependencies, no install scripts, no argv secrets; static ~590-line pure-function core with about 7 test files (batch, edge, render, scan, suggest, switches) and CI running 'claude plugin validate' and 'claude plugin test'

MIT license, tiny surface (3 source files) so a fork pointed at OpenRouter is a few-line patch; installed Claude Code 2.1.285 binary contains the CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS gate, so the mechanism exists on the user's version (string found in the binary)
Complements, rather than conflicts with, existing Bash/Grep PreToolUse hooks: different events (prompt.submit, AskUserQuestion), so no interaction with the secret guard or GitNexus hooks
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint, model id and key env var are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (suggest.ts:27-28, register.ts:81,140); needs a fork or local patch, and OpenRouter's response envelope is unverified

Relies on early-access function hooks (env flag CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1), an unstable API that can change or break with any Claude Code update; the README itself notes loader restrictions on '$'

Low value for this user's daily flow: the default-on decision router only fires on AskUserQuestion, which is rare, and in bypass/auto permission mode is often not asked at all; the skill router (the only frequent path) is off by default and adds 166-420 ms to every prompt for a one-line hint the model mostly gets from skill descriptions already
Does not touch the high-value decisions in coding (permission/safety classification of Bash commands, plan-vs-act, which file to edit, commit-worthy?), so Jev is used only for weak advisory signals
Auto-answer is awkward: it must use deny, so a successful decision renders as a red error and the agent may argue with it (author admits this); and it only handles a single non-multiselect question

Skill router sends every raw user prompt plus the whole installed-skill list to a third party on every turn; on client projects this is a data-handling concern, and it is ~6.8k input tokens per prompt

Very young, effectively a proof of concept: created 2026-09-17, last push the same day, 25 commits by 2 people (18/7, the second mostly merging PRs), 4 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no tagged versions (plugin.json 0.5.1), no issues history; cookbook-derived design with no evidence of use at scale
Runs arbitrary in-process code with $.process.run and $.env access in the user's session; needs a personal review and pinned commit before trusting on client machines

gh-belazy167-typesafe-mod.verdict: The only candidate here that hooks Jev into Claude Code with no prompting, and with zero context cost and fail-open behavior. But it is a day-old POC on an early-access hook API, hardcoded to TypeSafe direct (not OpenRouter), and its default path (AskUserQuestion) rarely fires. Best treated as a reference implementation to fork for OpenRouter, not something to install as-is.

gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.name: JevRouter (BillionsBobby/JevRouter)
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI + SDK + stdio MCP server ("jevrouter" npm-style package, installed via npx github:) that asks Jev one typed Choice question ("which tool/model/subagent should handle this?") over a caller-supplied candidate list, then applies local policy (permissions, risk, confirmation, confidence gate) and writes a JSON receipt to .jevrouter/decisions. It is decision-only: it never executes the selected capability. For Claude Code it installs, per project, a /jevrouter Skill, a CLAUDE.md rule block telling the agent to route "meaningful capability choices", a route.mjs helper, and optionally a .mcp.json entry exposing jev_route and jev_capabilities. Also has plan (multi-step), discover, evaluate (Choice/Score/Noul), a local dashboard, and an HTTP serve mode.

Does NOT use /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter, only the alpha Decisions route. functions/api/jev.js:1-2 (their website playground) also uses the alpha decisions endpoint.

interface.name: Skill /jevrouter (skills/jevrouter/SKILL.md, description: "Use Jev to choose the next tool, model, or subagent when a task has competing capability choices, the user asks for routing, or the next step is uncertain")
interface.purpose: Instructs Claude to announce 'JevRouter: routing the next step', hand-assemble the real tool/model/subagent candidates as JSON and pipe them into a Bash CLI call (route --stdin), then report decision_id/status and follow the result. Model-discretion via skill description.

interface.purpose: Project-level rule appended to CLAUDE.md: before the first meaningful choice between tools/models/subagents read the skill and run the CLI route; re-route when observations change. This is the only 'automatic' trigger and it is prompt-based, not a hook.

interface.purpose: Lists locally registered capability manifests.

interface.name: CLI route / plan
interface.purpose: One Choice decision or multi-step plan (serial, batch, decompose, beam); exit 0 selected, 2 review/no-decision, 1 error; stdout JSON.

interface.purpose: Builds manifests from skills dirs, MCP config (spawns each server for initialize + tools/list), CLI --help output, DSH manifests (src/discovery.ts).

interface.purpose: Writes skill, helper, CLAUDE.md block, .jevrouter/integration-v2.json, .gitignore entry into the current project; start also spawns the host (claude) with inherited env, shell:false (cli.ts:231-232).

interface.purpose: Programmatic use; evaluate() batches Choice+Score+Noul questions on one structured state.

gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript, single dep: yaml). Installed via npx --yes github:BillionsBobby/JevRouter (runs prepare -> tsc build on install, needs devDependencies). No npm registry release.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.tests: About 89 node:test cases in 10 files (router, plan, planning, primitives, agent-flow, mcp-discovery, endpoint-security, inline-candidates, dashboard, cache-model); GitHub Actions CI runs typecheck, test, build on Node 22 for every push/PR. All tests use stubs/mock MCP fixtures, no live Jev calls. Not executed by me (static audit only).
security: API key handling is good: read from env only, never written to files or argv (credentials.ts:6-20, secret entered via raw-mode TTY prompt; agent-setup.ts:88 writes "${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}" placeholder into .mcp.json). Caveat: docs/cookbook/05-mcp-adapter.md shows a literal key in .mcp.json env, which would land in a client repo if copied.
HTTPS enforced for custom endpoints, cleartext only on loopback (provider.ts:77-94, tested in endpoint-security.test.ts).

No postinstall script, but package.json has a prepare script (tsc build) that runs on git install; quickstart is npx --yes github:... straight from the default branch of a 1-week-old, unpinned repo (supply-chain risk; pin a commit SHA if used). No curl|sh installer found.
No telemetry in src; the only extra outbound call is the Cloudflare playground function for their website. Dashboard binds 127.0.0.1 and is read-only.
discover --mcp spawns every configured MCP server (executes commands from the config) and discover --cli runs `<cmd> --help`; not part of the default agent setup path but a shell-exec surface.

Setup writes into the project tree (CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills, .mcp.json, .gitignore, .jevrouter/) with backup-and-append and refusal to follow symlinks (agent-setup.ts:187-206). Safe for the user's files but pollutes client repos with files that embed an absolute path to the installed dist/cli.js (agent-setup.ts:109), which points into the ephemeral npx cache and goes stale.

Prompt-injection surface is low: Jev returns only a constrained choice among caller-supplied IDs, and the router hard-filters on permissions/risk. Candidate descriptions from third-party MCP servers or skills do flow into Jev, but cannot make it execute anything; nothing is auto-executed.
Decision receipts store the full request/state and raw Jev response under .jevrouter/decisions in each project (gitignored by setup, but plaintext on disk).
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai): whatever Claude puts into the route call, i.e. a task summary/request string, optional context object, and the candidate list (tool names, descriptions, input schemas) as JSON state plus the choice criteria. Content is authored by the model at call time (via the Bash heredoc or MCP arguments), so it can include file paths, snippets or client details if the model decides to include them; the tool does not itself read source files, diffs or tool outputs. Sent with Authorization: Bearer key and referrer headers identifying 'JevRouter'. Local: full request and raw response persisted to .jevrouter/decisions/*.json per project. No other network destinations found in src.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.failureMode: Fail-open by construction (advisory). Provider timeout (20s OpenRouter / 15s direct), HTTP or auth error is caught and returned as status no_decision with fallback.type provider_error (router.ts:328-330, 430-436); CLI exit code 1 or 2; Claude simply carries on per SKILL.md ('explain the fallback and gather better inputs'). Nothing blocks tool use because nothing is a hook. Worst case is a 20 s wait plus a wasted turn. Missing key throws 'Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY' (runtime.ts:26). CLI runs with the cache disabled, so no offline fallback unless the SDK cache flag is set.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.contextCost: Skill mode (default): skill listing entry about 230 chars description (~60 tokens) always loaded; CLAUDE.md block about 690 chars (~170 tokens) always loaded per project; SKILL.md body ~3.2k chars (~800 tokens) when invoked, plus each route call costs output tokens for the model to hand-write candidate JSON (100-500+ tokens) and a JSON result echoed back (decision includes raw_jev, candidate list, probabilities; often 1-3k tokens). MCP mode (--with-mcp): 2 tools, ~1.5k chars of names+descriptions+schemas (~400 tokens) plus server instructions ~470 chars (~120 tokens); jev_route result is pretty-printed JSON both as text and structuredContent (duplicate payload). No hooks, so nothing injected per tool call.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.latencyImpact: Per route call: Jev itself claimed 70-500 ms, their own benchmark shows 1.58 s per serial task and 10.6 s for decompose+thread (README Benchmark table); plus node cold start, plus a full extra model turn for Opus to author the Bash/MCP call and read the result (several seconds and tokens). Applies every time the model chooses to route; not on every tool call. Net effect for a subscription Opus session is added latency with no cheaper alternative displaced, since the routing target (Claude Code's own tool choice) is already made by Opus in the same turn.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: CLAUDE.md rule plus skill-description trigger (and optional MCP tool with server instructions). No hook, no transparent proxy. Whether Claude routes at all depends on Opus following the prompt text; the README concedes explicit /jevrouter invocation for the first task. Decision is never enforced or used to change the main model, spawn agents or gate tools ('does not switch the host underlying model', SKILL.md).
pros: Native OpenRouter support against the correct endpoint (POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, ~typesafe/jev-latest) with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the user's chosen provider works without patching (provider.ts:156, runtime.ts:28).
Only real Claude Code integration of the three routing ideas found here that ships an end-to-end Skill + CLAUDE.md + optional MCP installer, with doctor --live connectivity check.

Careful engineering: keys never in argv/disk, HTTPS-only endpoints, symlink refusal, backup-then-append of CLAUDE.md, decision-only with policy gates, append-only receipts, ~89 tests and CI, MIT, single small dependency, ~3k lines readable in an hour.
Fail-open advisory design: provider error just yields no_decision, cannot break a coding session.

Exposes all three primitives via evaluate()/questions (Choice, Score, Noul) and a reusable SDK, so pieces (provider.ts, buildQuestions) are a good reference for a custom hook that asks Jev Noul/Score questions.
Own benchmark is honest that it measures next-tool prediction, not task completion (README), with Jev beating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on cost and first-5 hits.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: it routes among tools/models/subagents, but in Claude Code Opus already picks tools in the same forward pass; a Jev call to pick a tool costs an extra turn and tokens for a benchmark accuracy of 38-44% position-wise hits versus an unbenchmarked Opus baseline. Nothing enforces or consumes the result; Opus can ignore it.

Not truly automatic: relies on the model reading a CLAUDE.md sentence and a skill description and deciding to route. No PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook, so the 'never prompt use jev' requirement is only probabilistically met, and the README recommends invoking /jevrouter explicitly first.

Model must hand-author the candidate JSON each call (no automatic enumeration of Claude Code's real tool list), burning output tokens and risking wrong or invented candidates; the skill itself warns against reusing example catalogs.

Per-project install writes CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills/jevrouter, .mcp.json (with --with-mcp), .jevrouter/ and a .gitignore edit into every repo, including client repos, and helper scripts embed an absolute path to an ephemeral npx-cache dist/cli.js that goes stale (agent-setup.ts:109). There is no user-global (~/.claude) install path.
Data egress of task text and tool descriptions to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on client work, chosen by the model at runtime, plus plaintext receipts per project.

One-week-old, alpha (v0.1.0, no releases, no npm publish), installed with npx from the default branch of GitHub with a build step on install; 301 stars mostly hype-driven; author-run benchmark on 10 tasks only; alpha Decisions endpoint may change.
Extra Bash/MCP round trip on every routing decision adds seconds plus 1-3k tokens of pretty-printed JSON result (with raw_jev) to context; MCP result duplicates payload in text and structuredContent.

Interacts awkwardly with existing hooks: its Bash-invoked CLI call would pass through the user's PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus Bash hooks each time, adding further latency, and in bypass/auto mode nothing distinguishes it from any other command.
gh-billionsbobby-jevrouter.verdict: Well-built, OpenRouter-native and safe (fail-open, decision-only), but it is a prompt-driven advisory router for a decision Opus already makes, so it adds latency, tokens and per-project repo clutter for little proven gain and does not deliver deterministic automatic use. Worth reading as a reference for provider.ts and the primitives, not worth installing as the daily Jev integration; a small custom global hook calling Noul/Score/Choice on specific gates is the better route.

gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.name: lomeshdutta/skill-router
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.whatItDoes: Python CLI (skill-router 0.2.0) plus a Claude Code SessionStart hook. The hook injects an instruction telling Claude to establish a one-sentence session goal and run `skill-router intent set "<goal>"`. That command lists all installed skills (project, user, plugins, built-ins) and calls Jev's System One endpoint once, with 3-4 questions in parallel: needs_skill (Noul), task_kind (Choice), installed_skill (Choice over every skill, plus a "none" option) and skills_sh_topic (Choice). It prints one of three outcomes: load skill X, search skills.sh via find-skills, or no skill needed. It only does skill routing. It is not a general coding-decision layer. An opt-in per-prompt UserPromptSubmit hook exists but is off by default. A mock keyword mode runs when no key is set.

providerSupport.evidence: No URL or endpoint is hardcoded in skill-router itself. src/skill_router/router.py:28 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and router.py:134-146 calls typesafe_sdk.TypeSafeClient(...).system_one(state=..., questions=...). The pinned SDK typesafe-sdk 0.6.0 (uv.lock:243, sdist inspected) defines DEFAULT_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai (constants.py:15), reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (constants.py:6, _core/config.py:51), reads TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL (default 'jev-latest', constants.py:12/18), uses path /v1/systemone (_core/constants.py:5) and sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (_core/transport.py:114). OpenRouter is never mentioned in the repo. scripts/check_invariant:19 allowlists only api.typesafe.ai, skills.sh, github.com and similar, but it only scans src/, so an env override is not blocked. The SDK path matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone.
providerSupport.others: skills.sh via `npx -y skills find <query>` (skills_sh.py:299), used only for discovery of uninstalled skills.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, with no code change: set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Set them via the `env` block in ~/.claude/settings.json so the hook inherits them. Caveats: not tested here. It assumes OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's. Also, router.py:37-51 load_dotenv only fills unset vars, so the env wins over .env. Risk: Bearer key and payload go to OpenRouter, so any OpenRouter key rules apply.

interface.purpose: List discovered skills, search skills.sh, show ~/.cache/skill-router/decisions.jsonl, and print or write the hook config (--event SessionStart|UserPromptSubmit, --settings, --write).

gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.runtime: Python >=3.12 (uv project; the user has 3.13 and uv). Single dependency: typesafe-sdk>=0.6.0 (httpx2, msgspec). Runs from a local git clone and .venv. It is not published on PyPI or npm. The optional skills.sh step needs npx.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.tests: 24 test functions (tests/test_router.py 16, tests/test_invariant.py 8). GitHub Actions CI runs ruff, pytest, scripts/check_invariant and a mock-mode eval. Eval harness evals/run_eval.py with 19 cases. Reported live results on the author's machine (~130 skills): 9/10 goal to installed skill, 4/5 search, 3/4 none, 10/10 single-prompt. An independent run found two bugs (fixed) and a median latency of ~5 s vs the author's ~0.36 s. No releases, no tags.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or a .env in the project root or ~/.config/skill-router/.env (router.py:34-51). It is sent as an HTTPS Bearer header by the SDK and is not put in argv. A test asserts the key never reaches the decision log.

Prompt-injection surface: hook output is instruction text injected into Claude's context. Installed skill names and descriptions from third-party plugins are sent to Jev as data. Claude is told to relay the output and to 'load skill X' from Jev's choice, and the SKILL.md forbids installing anything without a yes. The outcome-B text lists skills.sh search results (package names) as optional installs.

Shell execution: subprocess `git rev-parse` (context.py, 1.5 s timeout) and `npx -y skills find <query>` (skills_sh.py:299). The `npx -y` runs a remote, unpinned npm package (skills) at hook time, only in outcome B. It uses a scrubbed env {DISABLE_TELEMETRY, PATH}. The query is built from the user prompt or goal and passed as an argv element, with no shell.
No curl|sh and no npm postinstall. Install is git clone + uv sync + writing the hook into settings (`install-hook --write` edits ~/.claude/settings.json).
No telemetry of its own. Local writes go to ~/.cache/skill-router/ (decisions.jsonl stores the first 160 chars of prompts in per-prompt mode, plus cwd and goal).
Single maintainer, 12 days old, 3 stars, and depends on an early typesafe-sdk 0.6.0. The invariant script checks hosts in src/ only, not payloads.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points at, e.g. OpenRouter). Per SECURITY.md and context.py:160-184, the payload is: the session goal (or, in per-prompt mode, the prompt plus up to 3 earlier user messages at 400 chars each), the project directory name (not the full path), file counts by extension (top 8, depth <=2), which marker files exist, the git branch name, the first 500 characters of the project's CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md), and the name and description of EVERY installed skill (about 9,100 input tokens per call at ~130 skills). It does not send source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. It does send the CLAUDE.md head and the goal text, which for client projects may include confidential project descriptions. To skills.sh via npx, only a search query built from the goal. There is no per-project opt-out except the SKILL_ROUTER_DISABLE=1 env var.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.failureMode: Fail-open. Hooks are wrapped in catch-alls and return 0 (hook.py:388, cli.py session-start). `intent set` catches all exceptions and prints 'Could not get a routing decision... proceeding without a suggestion' (cli.py:~120). SDK timeout is 8 s with max_retries=1 (router.py:29,145), so the worst case is about 16-17 s of blocked Claude tool execution inside the `intent set` Bash call. The SessionStart hook itself never calls Jev, so session start is not delayed. Without a key it silently falls back to a keyword mock, labelled 'mock', which gives low-quality picks. A misconfigured OpenRouter base URL, model or schema mismatch would surface as an error string and no suggestion.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.latencyImpact: Session start: about 0 ms (the hook only prints text). Once per session (or on /intent): one Bash tool call, adding about 0.4-5 s of Jev latency plus Python startup, git and skill-catalog scan, plus one extra model turn. The author measured a median of ~0.36 s from US West Coast; an independent reviewer measured a median of 4.96 s and max 8.4 s. No per-turn cost by default. Per-prompt mode would add the Jev round trip to every prompt.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.contextCost: No MCP tools, so no tool-definition tokens. The SessionStart hook injects about 720 characters (~180 tokens) of instruction each session. Each `intent set` result adds ~100-200 tokens. Reading the injected instruction and running the extra Bash call costs one turn. The optional /intent skill adds a ~60-token description to the skill list. In per-prompt mode, ~100-250 tokens per prompt.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.autoInvocation: Hybrid. The SessionStart hook is a deterministic hook, but it only injects text. The actual Jev call happens only if Claude obeys the instruction and runs `skill-router intent set` via Bash, so it is model-discretion. In a session where the first message already states a goal, Claude infers one; otherwise Claude asks the user 'What are you trying to get done this session?', which is a user prompt the user wanted to avoid. Later task pivots need the user to type /intent, so nothing is automatic after the first call. The opt-in UserPromptSubmit hook is fully deterministic but noisy.
pros: Real, working Jev integration in code. It uses System One with Noul plus Choice over up to 255 options, which is exactly the primitive Jev is designed for (router.py:133-167, questions.py). It is a real example of the kind of decision Jev is good at.

OpenRouter switch needs no code change. The SDK it depends on reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, and uses path /v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone surface (verified in the SDK source, not yet tested end to end).

Fail-open everywhere, with an 8 s SDK timeout, catch-alls on hooks and a SKILL_ROUTER_DISABLE kill switch. The failures found by independent reviewers were fixed with regression tests. It has CI, an invariant script and an eval harness with reported accuracy.
Cheap: about $0.0004 per call (~9k input tokens at $0.042/1M). A once-per-session call means negligible spend and context (~180 tokens).
Small codebase (about 1.5k lines of Python), MIT, no install script, no postinstall, no telemetry, and the code is easy to audit and fork.
Useful for a user with many skills and plugins (caveman, gitnexus-* and others), where a semantic pick can surface a relevant skill Opus would otherwise not load.
cons: Narrow scope: it routes skills only and does not touch daily coding decisions (which file, which tool, whether to run tests, risk gating). Opus 5.5 already sees the skill list and descriptions in-context and can pick skills itself. The marginal value is small.

Not truly automatic for this user. The Jev call happens only if Claude follows an injected instruction to run a Bash command. If the first message has no clear goal, Claude asks the user a question first, and later pivots need a manual /intent. This contradicts the 'never prompt' requirement.

Once per session, based on a one-sentence goal, so it cannot react to what happens mid-session. The per-prompt mode that would is opt-in and was judged noisy by the author (repeated skill-creator suggestions).

Privacy risk on client projects: it sends the first 500 chars of CLAUDE.md, directory name, git branch, extension counts and all installed skill names and descriptions (~9k tokens) to the Jev provider on every call. There is no per-project allowlist, only a global env kill switch.

Immature: 12 days old, 19 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, alpha classifier. It depends on typesafe-sdk 0.6.0 (Sept 2026). The eval set is small (19 cases) and was tuned on the author's machine, and the independent reviewer saw ~5 s latency.

Installation is clumsy. It needs a git clone with a local venv and writes an absolute path to a .venv/bin into ~/.claude/settings.json. The bundled /intent skill runs `uv run skill-router` from the repo root, so it breaks in other project directories. `npx -y skills find` pulls unpinned remote code in outcome B.

OpenRouter path is untested. If the OpenRouter response schema differs from TypeSafe's (e.g. the model name prefix, wrapper fields), typesafe_sdk parsing would fail and the tool would silently degrade to 'no suggestion'. Also, with the key missing, it silently falls back to a keyword mock.
gh-lomeshdutta-skill-router.verdict: A tidy, honest, well-tested proof of concept for Jev-based skill routing that could be pointed at OpenRouter by setting three env vars, but it is narrow, alpha, and not truly automatic: it relies on Claude choosing to run a Bash command once per session and may ask the user a question. It also leaks CLAUDE.md excerpts and the full skill catalogue to the provider. Treat it as a reference implementation of the Jev System One call pattern, not as the main integration.

gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.runtime: Python >=3.10, stdlib only (urllib). Not on PyPI; install via pip install -e from a clone, and the hook script is referenced by path in the clone.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.install: git clone, then python -m pip install -e /path/to/jev-skill-selection. Merge adapters/claude_code/settings.example.json into settings.json (UserPromptSubmit, command 'python3', args [hook.py], timeout 30). Set JEV_MODE=jev and TYPESAFE_API_KEY to use Jev. The example uses ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/adapters/... so the path must be edited to an absolute one for global use.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.tests: About 49 test functions (unit tests plus a harness with a mock LLM server). Live host e2e is gated behind JEV_HARNESS_LIVE=1. No CI workflow (.github absent). Not executed per hard rules.
security: API key is read from env and sent as a Bearer header, never in argv, so there is no process-list leak (jev_client.py:90,128).

Hard mode mutates files on every prompt: it rewrites <cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json in client and personal projects, and merges 'on' for kept skills, so it can clobber the user's own skillOverrides. Writes are non-atomic-safe only via tmp+replace, and unparseable JSON is silently replaced with {} (common.py:257-285), which can wipe a user's settings.local.json (permissions, env).

Prompt-injection surface is low: Jev returns numeric probabilities and there is no free text back into context in hard mode. SKILL.md bodies (400-char excerpts) are sent to Jev, but the output is only used for thresholding.
No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall. Uses stdlib urllib only.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is env-overridable, so a poisoned env could redirect the prompts.
JEV_E2E_LOG, if set, appends the first 500 chars of every prompt to a file.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.dataEgress: In jev mode only, per user prompt, to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter after patching): the full user prompt text (state={'message': prompt}), plus for each candidate skill (up to 32 after local prefilter) its name, description and a 400-char body excerpt. It sends no code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs, since it only fires on UserPromptSubmit. In the default local mode nothing leaves the machine.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but slow. hook.py:25-29 catches any exception, logs to stderr and exits 0, so the prompt proceeds. There is no local fallback when the Jev call fails, so no filtering happens that turn. The HTTP timeout is 30 s (models.py:52), matching the 30 s hook timeout in the example settings, so a hung API can block every prompt for up to 30 s. There is no retry or circuit breaker.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Hard mode injects no text (empty hookSpecificOutput). Soft/both modes inject up to ~9000 chars (~2.2k tokens) per prompt. Net effect is a potential reduction, since dropped skills are hidden. The skill listing is only ~100 tokens per skill, so savings are modest unless the user has hundreds of skills.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.latencyImpact: Local mode: python startup of about 50-100 ms per prompt. Jev mode: adds one HTTPS round trip per user prompt (claimed 70-500 ms, up to 30 s on failure), blocking prompt submission. It does not fire per tool call.
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), fully automatic with no prompting. It only gates the skill list, though. It does not give Claude a general Jev decision capability for coding.
pros: It is a real, automatic, deterministic hook that needs no 'use jev' prompt, and it uses Jev's Noul primitive as intended (one yes/no per skill).
Stdlib-only Python with no dependencies, MIT licensed, and no telemetry or installers. The code is small (about 60 KB of source) and easy to audit or fork.

Endpoint, key and base URL are env-driven, so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13) provided the schema matches.
The default local mode works offline with no key. Jev mode has a local prefilter (top 32) to bound the payload.
Fail-open exception handling at hook.py:25-29 means a broken hook will not block the user.
cons: It solves a narrow problem (trimming the skill list) that Claude Code already handles with progressive disclosure (about 100 tokens per skill), so the gain is small. Its own README demo saves about 1 KB of characters.
It never asks Jev to make coding decisions (model routing, risk gating, permission decisions, test selection), so it does not deliver the user's goal of Jev being used when it adds value.

It mutates <cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json on every prompt in client projects, and overwrites unparseable files with {} (common.py:257-285). This can wipe permissions or env and creates config churn. It also forces 'on' for kept skills, overriding user preferences.

The hard filter takes effect after prompt submit, so a settings reload may lag by one turn. It only sees ~/.claude/skills and ./.claude/skills, so plugin and marketplace skills (caveman, gitnexus) are not covered.
Jev mode sends every user prompt to a third party, which is a concern for client projects. It has a 30 s timeout with no local fallback and adds a blocking round trip per prompt.
It has no OpenRouter support in code (only the TypeSafe env names), and the OpenRouter schema is unverified. Model-id mapping (jev-1.13.0 vs typesafe/jev-1.13) is not handled.

It is very immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 2 stars, created 2026-09-21, no CI, no releases, and not on PyPI. The example settings use a non-portable ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} path. The author is inconsistent (the repo owner is redreamality; pyproject URLs point to i3u8).
gh-redreamality-jev-skill-selection.verdict: Skip it as the main integration. It is a genuine but tiny hook that only prunes the skill list, it mutates project settings files on every prompt, and Jev mode ships every prompt off-box for negligible savings. It is worth borrowing only as a reference for the UserPromptSubmit-to-System One call pattern (Noul per option over env-configurable base URL) when building a custom OpenRouter hook.

gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.name: ShivamPansuriya/jev-skill-gate
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.whatItDoes: Node CLI (zero deps) that registers a Claude Code SessionStart hook (optionally UserPromptSubmit). At session start it discovers all installed skills, builds a project-signal state (stack, top-level dirs, branch, last 12 commit subjects, deps, 1200-char README excerpt), sends one Jev request with one noul question per skill ("is this skill relevant"), then writes skillOverrides (name-only / user-invocable-only) into .claude/settings.local.json to shrink the skill manifest. Falls back to a local TF-IDF scorer with no key. It is a context-trimming tool, not a general Jev decision integration: Jev is not used to gate tool calls, route models or make coding decisions.

Base URL and model are user-overridable (README 'config --provider typesafe --base-url ...', config.mjs:23-27, README stuntd section used exactly this trick).
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (gateway provider), Open-Jev self-hosted HTTP, laya (python subprocess), laya-mlx, stuntd via typesafe provider, local TF-IDF fallback, user plugin providers in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate/providers/*.mjs (arbitrary code loaded via dynamic import, providers/index.mjs:53).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, unverified in practice: set provider=typesafe, providers.typesafe.baseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (path becomes /api/v1/systemone, matching the OpenRouter System One endpoint), model=typesafe/jev-1.13, and supply the OpenRouter key via TYPESAFE_API_KEY (envKeys lacks OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so you would alias the env var or write apiKey into the 0600 config file). Works only if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone has the identical request/response schema as TypeSafe's (state/questions/noul -> answers.noul); this was not confirmed from source here. A proper fix is a ~30-line openrouter.mjs provider file dropped in the plugin dir or PR'd.

gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.runtime: Node >=18 (user has Node 24), zero npm dependencies; not published to npm, installed via git clone or curl|bash install.sh
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.tests: test/run.mjs (886 lines, node built-in, commit msg says 69 pass; README badge stale at 43). No CI workflow (no .github dir). Eval harness in eval/ but only 4 of 20 cases ran against live Jev (free-tier 429s); rest uses local scorer. Not executed by me.
security: API key: env var wins; config --api-key stores in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate.json mode 0600, but passing it as a CLI arg exposes it in argv/ps and shell history during that one command (bin/jev-skill-gate.mjs:299). Hook itself reads key from env/file, not argv.
Sends Authorization: Bearer key over HTTPS via node:https (http.mjs) to the configured baseUrl; a repointed baseUrl (or plain http) would leak the key, but that is user-controlled.

User provider plugins in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate/providers/*.mjs are dynamically import()ed and executed on every hook run (providers/index.mjs:53): arbitrary code by design, only from user's own dir.

Self-update (update.mjs) downloads main-branch tarball from codeload.github.com and then executes the fetched code with --check/--help: unpinned auto-updating of code that runs in a SessionStart hook on every session = supply-chain risk if author account is compromised. install.sh is a documented curl|bash of raw.githubusercontent main.
No npm postinstall, no telemetry beyond the scoring call; stats ledger local in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate/stats.json.

Prompt-injection surface: skill descriptions (from third-party plugins) go into Jev as claim parameters, but Jev returns only probabilities, so injection can only bias which skills show, not execute anything. UserPromptSubmit mode injects skill name+description text into the model context (additionalContext) from local skill files only.

Writes .claude/settings.local.json inside every project (including client repos) at session start; normally gitignored by Claude Code but it is a write into client working trees. Reads only the first 8000 chars of SKILL.md files, README 1200 chars.
Positive: never writes 'off', snapshots original skillOverrides, atomic writes, tracks managed keys, preserves user-set overrides.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.dataEgress: SessionStart mode (once per session, or when cache misses): to the Jev endpoint, the full name+description of every discoverable skill (user, project and plugin skills, including any private/client-specific ones) plus project state: project directory basename, detected stack labels, top-level directory names (max 25), git branch, last 12 commit subjects, up to 40 dependency names from package.json, and first 1200 chars of README (signals.mjs:52-106). No source code, diffs or tool outputs. Client repo names, commit subjects and README text do leave the machine, which matters for client projects under NDA. UserPromptSubmit mode additionally sends the user's prompt (first 4000 chars) on every prompt with no cache (signals.mjs:113, gate.mjs useCache:false). Cache key includes state JSON (branch and recent commit subjects), so each new commit changes the key and forces a fresh paid call (cache.mjs:24-26), despite the 7-day TTL.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Provider error/timeout falls back to local TF-IDF (gate.mjs:221-228); scores that don't separate or thin state leave every skill visible (gate.mjs:49-69); unscored skills stay visible; hook errors are caught and session continues ungated (bin ~L251). Caveat: per-request timeoutMs 20000 with maxRetries 4 and exponential backoff (config.mjs:81-82, runner.mjs:44-69) can exceed the hook's 30s timeout when Jev is slow or 429ing, in which case Claude Code kills the hook and session start is delayed up to 30s before proceeding ungated. Free-tier 429s were documented by the author.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.latencyImpact: SessionStart blocks on the hook (one Jev call over ~217 questions, ~17.7k input tokens; author reports cost ~$0.0007-0.0009 but gives no latency figure). Cache hit is near-instant, but cache key includes recent commit subjects/branch so active repos miss often. Worst case about 30s stall at session start. Zero per-turn latency in SessionStart mode; the opt-in UserPromptSubmit mode adds a full Jev round trip (no cache) to every prompt.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.contextCost: Adds nothing: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no always-on text. Net negative context: claims 12,750 -> ~3,185 tokens on a 217-skill install (author's own estimate, /context showed 9.9k baseline, so real saving ~7k). User's real saving depends on skill count; with the user's skills (gitnexus x9, design skills, caveman etc., roughly 50-60 listed) saving is likely 1-3k tokens, small versus Opus context. UserPromptSubmit mode injects up to 5 skill descriptions per prompt (about 300 tokens) when triggered.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (SessionStart, optional UserPromptSubmit). Fully automatic after one-time install, no prompting needed. But Jev is used only for skill-manifest relevance, not for any general coding decision.
pros: Genuinely automatic (SessionStart hook, no 'use jev' prompt) and the only candidate seen so far that has a real measured Jev use case with cost figures (~$0.0007/session at $0.042/M).
Very well-engineered safety: fail-open at every level, never writes 'off', atomic writes, exact restore, preserves user-set overrides, unscored skills stay visible.

Zero dependencies, readable ~4.5k lines of Node, MIT, provider abstraction with base URL + model override so OpenRouter can be added with one small provider file or config (typesafe provider + baseUrl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, model typesafe/jev-1.13).

Uses Jev exactly as designed (typed noul questions, calibrated probabilities, single parallel pass over 200+ options) and honestly reports a committed eval, a local no-key fallback and its own limits (README 'Known limits of this evidence').
Composes with the user's existing hooks: only adds a SessionStart entry, merges into settings.json, does not touch PreToolUse (secret guard, GitNexus) matchers.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code (zero 'openrouter' matches); env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY/AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY only, so it needs aliasing or a custom provider, and OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified.

Solves a narrow, small problem: trims skill descriptions (~10k tokens on a 217-skill library; the user has far fewer, and Opus context and prompt caching already absorb the cost). Does nothing for code decisions, routing, permission approval, or task classification, which is what the user meant by integrating Jev.

Sends skill catalogue plus repo name, branch, last 12 commit subjects, dependency names and README excerpt of every project (including client repos) to a third party on each cache miss; UserPromptSubmit mode sends the user's prompt every turn. Poor fit for client/NDA work without care.
Cache key includes recent commit subjects and branch, so in an actively committed repo the 7-day cache misses often, adding a blocking network call to session start.
Retry budget (20s x 5 attempts with backoff) exceeds the 30s hook timeout: a slow or rate-limited Jev can stall session start ~30s before failing open.

Evidence is thin: 4 of 20 eval cases ran against real Jev (429 free-tier), 1 contributor, 12 commits, 8 stars, 13 days old, no CI, stale test badge; verified only against Claude Code 2.1.274 and relies on skillOverrides/reloadSkills semantics that may change.

Self-update pulls and executes unpinned main-branch code inside a hook that runs every session; writes .claude/settings.local.json into every project including client repos; hiding skills is silent so a miss costs quality unnoticed.

Hidden skills reduce auto-discovery of the user's own skills (gitnexus-*, design systems) in projects where the state signal is weak or the vocabulary doesn't match; the 0.15 nameOnly threshold survives one labeled skill by 'exactly zero' margin per README.
gh-shivampansuriya-jev-skill-gate.verdict: Well-built, safe, genuinely automatic hook, but it only uses Jev to trim skill descriptions, which yields a small saving for a user with a modest skill set while shipping repo metadata (commit subjects, README, branch) off-machine, and it has no native OpenRouter support. Treat as an optional, low-priority experiment (with provider=fallback or a patched OpenRouter provider), not the core Jev integration.

gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.name: eran-broder/jev-skills
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.whatItDoes: Claude Code (and Codex) plugin that moves skills out of the model's always-on skill listing into ~/.jev-skills/library. On UserPromptSubmit and after Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/WebFetch/WebSearch tool results, a Node hook sends the prompt, the last 3 assistant turns and the tool output to Jev as one "noul" (yes/no) question per skill. Skills with P>=0.6 (max 3, once per session) have their SKILL.md body injected as additionalContext. It is a skill router only: it does not help with code review, model routing or other coding decisions.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev/client.ts:3 const ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone" (hardcoded, no env or config override; same string at dist/hook.js:19890). Auth is `authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}` (client.ts:51). Key sources are CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY or config.json apiKey (src/config.ts:97-107). Default model "jev-latest" (config.ts:78). grep for openrouter in src/ and README returns nothing.
providerSupport.others: None. Codex is supported via ~/.codex/hooks.json (src/codexInstall.ts).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, close to trivial. The path suffix /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, and the request body is {state, model, questions:{id:{type:'noul',instructions,criteria}}}. To switch, change ENDPOINT, set model to typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, and read the OpenRouter key from an env var. Two open risks: (1) I could not verify that OpenRouter's response schema matches the strict zod schema (answers.{id}.noul plus usage.input_tokens/output_tokens), and a mismatch would make every call fail silently; (2) dist/hook.js is committed as a 20k-line esbuild bundle, so you would have to rebuild it (npm ci; npm run build) or hand-edit line 19890. It needs a fork or local patch, and upstream has no provider switch.

gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.tests: 5 unit test files (transcript, select, prefilter, frontmatter, fanout) run with node:test through tsx. Only pure functions are covered, and there are no HTTP client tests and no hook-level tests. scripts/e2e.ts spawns headless claude and codex against canary skills and is manual, not in CI. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs typecheck, tests and build on ubuntu and windows with Node 20 and 22, and fails if committed dist/ is stale. I did not run any of it.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.runtime: Node >=20 (you have 24). Plugin hooks run `node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/hook.js`. The bundle is committed, so no npm install is needed at runtime. Only dependency is zod, which is bundled.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.install: claude plugin marketplace add eran-broder/jev-skills; claude plugin install jev-skills@jev-skills --config typesafe_api_key=<key>. Optionally `node dist/cli.js migrate --apply` to move skills into the library. I did not run these.
security: plugin.json declares typesafe_api_key as sensitive userConfig, which Claude Code stores in its credential store and passes to the hook as an env var. This is the better path. Inside the hook the key is only in the environment, not in argv.
`jev-skills setup <key>` puts the key in argv, visible in the process list and shell history, and writes it in plaintext to ~/.jev-skills/config.json with no chmod (cli.ts:29, config.ts:114-118).
Each request carries the Authorization Bearer header to the hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint. There is no TLS pinning or host override. Retries go up to 3 attempts on 429/502/503/529.
No shell execution in the hook path, no eval, no postinstall script and no curl|sh installer. package.json has only dev scripts. The only child_process use is scripts/test.ts (dev).
No telemetry beyond Jev calls. The local log ~/.jev-skills/log.jsonl records event names, skill names and probabilities, not prompt text.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output (web pages, files) is sent to Jev as state. Adversarial content can raise a skill's probability, but the injected text only comes from your own local SKILL.md files, so the impact is low. The injected header says 'Follow their instructions', so a malicious skill dropped into the library gets full trust.
dist/hook.js is a 20k-line committed bundle. It matches the source on the endpoint string, but reviewing it fully is impractical. CI enforces freshness, not provenance.
The user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard does not cover this path. It runs before tools, while this hook sends PostToolUse output outward.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on every non-empty prompt, and on every PostToolUse of Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/WebFetch/WebSearch with output of 200 chars or more (observeToolResults defaults to true). Payload (state.ts): the user prompt clipped to 6000 chars, the last 3 assistant text blocks plus tool names, the basename of the project directory, and for tool results the tool name, the full tool_input (Bash commands, file paths, grep patterns, URLs) and the tool_response clipped to about 3000 chars. That is file contents, command output and possibly secrets or client code. It also sends every skill's name and description, once per question. Diffs are not sent as a separate item, but they appear whenever a Bash git diff or Read result goes through. In practice this is a near-continuous stream of client-project content to a third party. If pointed at OpenRouter, it would go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe under their data policies. Injected skill bodies stay local.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.failureMode: Fail-open. main().catch logs the error to log.jsonl and exits with no output (hook.ts:206), so the prompt is never blocked. A missing key throws MissingApiKeyError and is also swallowed. The per-request timeout is 6000 ms (configurable), with up to 3 attempts on 429/502/503/529 and backoff of 300 ms x 2^n or Retry-After. A network error or timeout is not retried and throws, which fails open. The worst case is a slow hook: the hook timeout is 15 s, and a degraded Jev could add several seconds to each prompt and each Read/Bash/Grep call, because the hook is synchronous. There is no circuit breaker or negative cache. Errors are silent (logged only), so a wrong OpenRouter response schema would leave the plugin quietly doing nothing.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.contextCost: 0 MCP tools, no MCP server and no server instructions. Always-on cost is 0 tokens from the plugin, and it also removes skill listings once skills are migrated (README claims about 1,350 tokens per 13 skills). Hook-injected text: a one-line header plus up to 3 full SKILL.md bodies, capped at 24,000 chars (about 6k tokens) per call and once per skill per session, plus a one-line systemMessage 'jev-skills loaded: ...'. Nothing is injected when no skill scores at or above 0.6. Gain for you is modest: your listed skills (about 30 descriptions, roughly 3-4k tokens) are already a small share of the context. Plugin-provided skills (caveman, gitnexus) are not moved by migrate, which only handles ~/.claude/skills.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.latencyImpact: Synchronous hook on every user prompt and on every qualifying tool result. Costs: Node cold start (~50-100 ms), library scan (cached), then one Jev request. The README measures 250-450 ms for 23 skills, 700-830 ms for 624 and 2.2-2.7 s for 3,024. Through OpenRouter, add its proxy hop (unmeasured). In a tool-heavy agentic turn with many Read/Bash/Grep calls this adds roughly 0.3-0.5 s per call, and it can stack to tens of seconds per turn. It is worse on failure: 6 s timeout, retries and a 15 s ceiling. The README's own figures are self-reported, and I did not verify them.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, SessionStart, PostCompact) with no model discretion. The user never has to say 'use jev'. This is the automatic pattern the user wants, but the only thing it decides is which skill to inject.
pros: Truly automatic: hook-based (hooks/hooks.json), no prompting, and it fails open (hook.ts:206) so it cannot block work.
Zero MCP tools and zero always-on tokens, unlike an MCP server.
Correct use of Jev's strength: many parallel yes/no questions that come back as calibrated probabilities. The threshold, cap and once-per-session dedup are sensible (select.ts, session.ts).
Small, readable TypeScript (about 1,000 lines), MIT license, no postinstall, no shell exec, no runtime dependencies. The key is a sensitive plugin option that is not written to settings.
Exact-form hooks (command + args) and CI on ubuntu and windows with a stale-dist check. Useful reference implementation for a custom Jev hook.
Endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so a fork is a small change.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai (client.ts:3) with no override, and the key is TypeSafe-only. You would need a fork and a dist rebuild, and the response-schema match with OpenRouter is unverified. This contradicts the requirement that OpenRouter be the provider.

Data egress is large: prompts, assistant text and the full tool_input plus about 3k chars of every Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/Web tool output are sent to a third party on nearly every step. That is a serious concern for client projects and bypasses your secret-leak guard's intent. You would have to set observeToolResults=false to reduce it, which removes the mid-task value.

Narrow value: it only routes skills. It does nothing for permission decisions, model routing, review triage or other coding decisions. Your skills are few and mostly small, so the token saving is a few thousand tokens per session at best. Plugin skills are not covered by migrate.

Latency tax: a synchronous network call on every prompt and on every Read/Bash/Grep result (about 0.3-0.5 s each, up to 15 s if Jev is degraded), on top of your existing GitNexus and secret-guard hooks that fire on the same tools.

Requires moving skills out of ~/.claude/skills into ~/.jev-skills/library. This breaks the /skill and Skill tool discovery you use today and makes skill invocation depend on a beta model's probabilities (a miss means the skill silently never appears).

Very immature: 7 days old, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 6 stars, no releases. Tests cover only pure helpers, with no client or hook tests. Committed 20k-line bundle. The Theo/t3.gg skepticism about Jev's quality is unverified, but false negatives here would be invisible.
Fail-open errors are silent (log only), so a misconfiguration or API schema drift looks like 'works, injects nothing'. `setup <key>` leaves the key in argv and in a plaintext config.json.
gh-eran-broder-jev-skills.verdict: Best-in-class example of an automatic, deterministic Jev hook for Claude Code, but it solves a small problem (skill-listing tokens) at the price of continuously sending client code and tool output to a third party, with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint. Not recommended for daily use. Worth reading as a template if you build your own hook, and only if you fork it to OpenRouter and turn off tool-result observation.

gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.name: Akramovic1/jev-pilot (jev-pilot Claude Code plugin)
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin built on Claude Code's early-access "function hooks" (TypeScript hook module, no MCP server). Before every user prompt it POSTs the prompt, the last 4 messages (max 2000 chars, text plus tool names only), and some counters to Jev at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. It then uses the typed answers to (a) set the main conversation's reasoning effort per turn (low..xhigh, raised to max after 2 failed tool calls), (b) pick the model (haiku/sonnet/opus) and effort of each spawned subagent, (c) pick one skill and attach its SKILL.md to the prompt while hiding Claude Code's own skill listing, (d) attach advice blocks (strategy direct/delegate/parallel/graph, ask-first for vague requests, failing-test-first for bugs, design pack). It also has an optional "crew" layer: a local 127.0.0.1 proxy (jev-router) that sends jev-<slot> model requests to OpenRouter and Codex/OpenCode CLI reviewers, an animated terminal pet, and a decision ledger/report. Jev is used only as a routing classifier; it never writes code or text.
