security: API key: declared sensitive:true userConfig in plugin.json; install.sh passes it as 'claude plugin install ... --config openrouterApiKey=<key>' (install.sh ~line 260-262), so the key is briefly visible in argv/ps during install; a safer path is to install by hand or set it via Claude Code's own prompt. In clone mode the key is written in plaintext to ~/.claude/settings.json pluginConfigs (with backup). The key is sent only as Authorization Bearer to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai / ai-gateway.vercel.sh if those keys are chosen); it is never put on argv by the plugin at runtime.

Advertised install is curl|bash of a 13 KB install.sh from a 1-week-old single-author repo; it runs claude CLI, python3/node JSON edits, creates a symlink in ~/.local/bin. Read it before running; no sudo, no postinstall scripts, no npm deps.

Function hooks run arbitrary TS inside Claude Code with the plugin's $ API (http, fs, process.run, env, store, session.messages, agent.register). Observed uses are benign: process.run only for 'codex login status', 'opencode --version/auth list/models', 'codex debug models'; fs writes under ~/.claude/jev-pilot/ and skill-override files; fetches only to openrouter.ai, api.typesafe.ai, ai-gateway.vercel.sh, and raw.githubusercontent.com/VoltAgent/awesome-design-md (the design pack tells Claude to fetch DESIGN.md files from there, a small prompt-injection surface). No telemetry endpoints found (grep of all URLs in hooks/, router/, bin/, install.sh).

jev-router (only when started by claude-jev): listens on 127.0.0.1:8799, requests must carry a 32-hex secret path from ~/.claude/jev-pilot/router-secret (chmod 600), browser requests with Origin are refused; nohup+setsid supervisor loop keeps it alive after the terminal closes; it sits in the path of ALL Anthropic traffic including the user's OAuth bearer token (streams unchanged, key never crosses over per code comments). Adds a persistent local daemon and a single point of failure; can be disabled with JEV_ROUTER=off.

Prompt-injection surface: injects extra context blocks into user prompts (strategy/quality/design advice, full SKILL.md of the Jev-picked skill, a session note telling Claude not to pin subagent models). A skill wrongly picked because of a manipulated prompt could load the wrong SKILL.md, but Jev output is a constrained typed choice, so it cannot inject free text itself.

/jev-pilot:setup (opt-in, asks first) rewrites skill overrides to hide every skill from the model, with a backup and a restore command; if a user runs it and later uninstalls without restore, skills stay hidden (README warns).
Supply chain: MIT, 1 contributor, no signed releases, marketplace installs track main; claude-jev self-update fetches from GitHub. Pin a reviewed commit.
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (and then TypeSafe/Jev host) on every prompt: the full user prompt text (any pasted code, stack traces, client names or secrets in it), up to 4 prior messages / 2000 chars including assistant prose and tool NAMES (never tool inputs or outputs, per hooks/context.ts header), counters (prompt length, files mentioned, has_code_or_error, tool-kind counts), the name plus description of EVERY skill and command available (about 300 chars of each SKILL.md opening; excerptChars default 300), custom-agent info, and file-name-derived platform hints (cdk.json, vercel.json, Dockerfile). Per subagent spawn: the entire subagent prompt/brief, description and agentType (briefs can contain code and file contents). Not sent: file contents read by tools, diffs, tool outputs, the OAuth token. Optional and off by default: Codex/OpenCode reviewers (own CLIs, own accounts) and custom OpenRouter model slots, which would send whole task context to those models. OpenRouter logs/prompt-retention settings and provider routing for Jev apply; client-project prompts leave the machine on every turn, so check client contracts and the OpenRouter data policy.
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.failureMode: Fail-open. askJev (jev-model-router.ts:127-165) races the fetch against io.sleep(timeoutMs) (default 1500 ms, installer sets 1500); on timeout, non-2xx, network error or unparsable answer the decision is null and the turn/subagent proceeds unchanged (effort and model left as Claude Code chose), with a routine note in the pet/log. Missing key falls back to Claude Code's built-in $.model.classify classifier. The router proxy also falls back to Sonnet on Anthropic if a custom slot fails. Weak spot: prompt.submit is awaited, so a slow Jev costs up to 1.5 s before every prompt and up to 1.5 s per subagent spawn; there is no circuit breaker seen, so an outage repeats the wait each time. Also fail-open in the negative sense if the hooks module is not enabled: silently does nothing until CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1.
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.latencyImpact: README claims about 0.5 s per prompt (single merged request; earlier versions were 1.5 s with three calls); worst case adds the 1500 ms timeout per prompt and per non-fork subagent spawn (awaited, blocking). Pure prompt/effort decisions happen before the main-model turn, so this is perceived as time-to-first-token added on every prompt. 'continue/keep going' prompts skip the call. Extra proxy hop only if claude-jev router is used (local, negligible).
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. Per-prompt injected text: a session note on the first prompt and after compaction listing what jev-pilot controls, plus conditional blocks (strategy advice, quality advice, design pack, step-back notes, full SKILL.md of the picked skill, which can be thousands of tokens). With hideListing=true (default) it REMOVES Claude Code's skill listing from context, which can save tokens for a user with many skills, but takes skill discovery away from the model and depends on Jev's pick. Under claude-jev, sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (deferred tool schemas) because a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL otherwise inlines every tool schema. Transcript lines only if display is transcript/both (default is the pet UI, which only draws in the interactive terminal).
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: fully automatic without any prompt mention. Runs on prompt.submit, turn.step and agent.spawn events, so it fires on every prompt and every subagent spawn regardless of what the user or model says. This is the only integration style in this audit that meets the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' requirement, but it applies Jev only to routing decisions (effort/model/skill/strategy), not as a tool Claude can consult about the code.
pros: Only candidate that is truly automatic: deterministic hooks on prompt.submit/turn.step/agent.spawn, no need to ever say 'use jev' (hooks/jev-pilot.ts registers all modules).

OpenRouter is first-class: hooks/model-router.policy.ts:209-253 posts TypeSafe-shaped {model,state,questions} to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with ~typesafe/jev-latest by default and pinnable typesafe/jev-1.13; it exactly matches the brief's System One surface, and per-answer confidence is used for thresholds (raise at 0.3, lower at 0.6).

Uses Jev for what it is built for (typed choices with calibrated probabilities), not as a chat model: Choice for effort/tier/strategy/skill, Noul for risky/underspecified/bugfix/design, so the design fits the primitives.
Fail-open with a 1500 ms hard timeout and built-in classifier fallback; a Jev or OpenRouter outage degrades to stock Claude Code behavior (jev-model-router.ts:127-165).

Data minimisation is considered: tool inputs/outputs are never sent (hooks/context.ts), subagent briefs are sent without conversation, context capped at 4 messages / 2000 chars, all configurable via contextMessages/contextChars.

Every part has a live kill switch (/jev effort|subagents|skills|strategy|quality|design|pet off, /jev all off) and plugin.json exposes ~50 options, so the risky parts can be disabled while keeping effort and subagent-model routing.

Hooks are separate function-hook modules, not settings.json hooks, so they should not collide with the existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus pre/post hooks or caveman hooks; installed 2.1.285 binary does contain the CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS gate the plugin needs.

Reasonable engineering hygiene for a 1-week-old repo: about 320 test cases in 15 files, CI, CHANGELOG with measured numbers, a decision ledger and /jev-pilot:report to check whether it pays off, MIT license, no telemetry endpoints found.
Sensible defaults for Opus 5.5: starts at xhigh at most, needs 0.6 confidence to downgrade, raises effort on repeated failures, and keeps an explicitly named subagent model.
Works with a subscription/OAuth login per README (effort changes keep the cache), and does not need ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
cons: Depends on Claude Code 'function hooks', which the installed 2.1.285 binary itself labels early access ('hooks modules are not turned on for installed plugins ... set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1'); API can change any release and it would silently stop working; needs the env var in settings.json (plain claude) or the claude-jev wrapper.

Very immature: created 2026-09-23, 36 commits in 7 days by a single author, 6 stars, 1 fork, plugin.json 0.12.0 ahead of latest release tag 0.11.0, about 12 releases in a week. Benchmarks (76 labelled prompts, 40 briefs, jev-bench 8/8) are self-run and unverified.

Every prompt and every subagent brief goes to OpenRouter/Jev, including client-project text; skill names and descriptions plus 300-char SKILL.md excerpts of all your skills (dougthepug, empat, gitnexus etc.) also leave the machine. There is no per-project exclusion switch, so client work needs a contract/policy check or a per-project disable.
Blocking latency: awaited request before every prompt (claimed 0.5 s, up to 1.5 s timeout) and again per subagent spawn; no circuit breaker, so an OpenRouter incident costs 1.5 s repeatedly.

The value is mostly cost/effort routing; on a subscription (Opus 5.5, OAuth) the savings show as quota rather than money, and jev-pilot's own changelog concedes Opus 5.5 did the right thing with or without its advice on the quality tasks (9-vague, 10-transfer), with only 11% cheaper. Jev never sees the repo, so it cannot improve code quality directly.

Invasive by default: hideListing=true removes Claude Code's skill listing and replaces it with a Jev-picked SKILL.md injected into the prompt; wrong or missed picks mean the model cannot discover skills itself, and it interacts with the existing skill-heavy setup (gitnexus-*, caveman, design skills). Also injects advice blocks into prompts that change Claude's behavior (ask-first, failing-test-first, subagent strategies) without an explicit user choice.

Adds a session note telling Claude not to set subagent models or create agent types to pin them, which conflicts with custom workflows the user or CLAUDE.md may define, and overrides subagent model choices except explicitly named ones.

claude-jev launcher starts a persistent detached local proxy on 127.0.0.1:8799 and repoints ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL through it, putting the OAuth traffic through third-party code and a daemon (secret-path protected, but a new failure/attack surface); needs JEV_ROUTER=off, or use plain claude with the env var instead. Also sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true globally for the session.

Install path is curl|bash and puts the key on argv (claude plugin install --config openrouterApiKey=...), visible to other local users in ps for the duration; clone mode stores the key plaintext in ~/.claude/settings.json.

Scope creep: pet UI, Codex/OpenCode reviewers, custom OpenRouter model slots, design pack, tuning ledger. Large surface (8.4k lines of hooks) to audit for a router that only needs ~3 hooks; the user can disable most, but must review them.

Only uses /api/v1/systemone, not the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions); it cannot be extended to arbitrary decisions in the user's own workflow without editing the plugin. It also cannot provide a 'consult Jev on X' tool, so it is not a general Jev integration.

Unverified claim that Jev behaves like a DeepSeek-flash router (per skeptics) means the routing quality rests entirely on the author's threshold tuning; user-side ledger review is required to trust it.
gh-akramovic1-jev-pilot.verdict: The only real candidate that gives automatic, no-prompting Jev use in Claude Code (deterministic function hooks) and it supports OpenRouter's /v1/systemone natively with a fail-open 1.5 s timeout. It is a one-week-old, single-author, early-access-API plugin that sends every prompt and subagent brief to OpenRouter and hides your skill listing by default, so if you try it, pin a reviewed commit, install by hand with the env var in settings.json (skip the curl|bash and claude-jev proxy), and disable skill-hiding, design pack and crew features, keeping only effort and subagent-model routing.

gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.name: abgregs/jev-skill-router
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (and own marketplace) with two hooks. UserPromptSubmit reads ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md (name+description only), sends the prompt + last ~2000 chars of transcript + every skill as one Jev Noul each (sharded 250/request, parallel) to TypeSafe systemOne, thresholds probabilities (invoke >=0.85, suggest 0.80-0.85, cap 6), and injects 'Skill routing verdict ... do not select skills yourself: Invoke: ...' as additionalContext. A PreToolUse matcher=Skill gate denies Skill calls not on the approved list (fail-open on missing/stale state). Defaults to a keyword mock judge with no network; real Jev only if .skillrouter.json has {"judge":"jev"} plus a key. Skill routing only, not general coding decisions. Also ships CLI (route, doctor, install claude) and a static demo site.

Prompt-injection surface: additionalContext is generated from skill ids only (no user text echoed), but skill names/descriptions from ~/.claude/skills are sent to Jev and used verbatim in Noul instructions; low risk. The gate is a policy layer and can deny legitimate Skill calls when the judge returns an empty verdict (README admits this regime).

gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.dataEgress: With judge=jev (opt-in; default is mock with zero network): on every user prompt, sent to the Jev endpoint: full prompt text, last ~2000 chars of recent user+assistant text turns from the transcript, and name+description of every skill in ~/.claude/skills (repeated per shard; one Noul per skill). openFiles/projectRules fields exist but the Claude Code hook does not populate them. No file contents, diffs, or tool outputs are sent. Prompts on client projects therefore leave the machine on every turn (to TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed).
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.failureMode: Fail-open by design: any exception in the UserPromptSubmit hook -> exit 0 silently (hooks/user-prompt-submit.ts:132-135); gate allows on missing/stale state or error (pre-tool-use-gate.ts:84). But the hook has no internal timeout ("Claude Code's own hook timeout is the bound", :11-12) and hooks.json sets no timeout; the SDK default is 10s per attempt with 2 retries (408/429/5xx) and backoff, so a slow/down Jev can stall each prompt for roughly 30s+ before failing open. Missing key with judge=jev throws -> silent no-op. Real gap: a fully empty verdict makes the gate deny agent-chosen skills not named in the prompt (README documents this), which is fail-closed for skills.
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no server instructions, no tool schemas. Hook injects only when verdict non-empty: ~300-500 chars (~75-125 tokens) per turn plus a short user-visible systemMessage; silent on conversational turns. Side effect: instructs model 'do not select skills yourself', and obedient models load every invoked skill (~2k tokens each, up to 6 = ~12k tokens/turn by README's own estimate).
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit + PreToolUse on Skill) once plugin is installed; fully automatic, no prompting. Real Jev is off by default and needs a per-project .skillrouter.json {"judge":"jev"} (or ~/.skillrouter.json for global) plus key in env.
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.latencyImpact: Added on every prompt submit, blocking before the model sees the turn. Author's measurements: Jev call 132-306 ms for 51 skills, 479-545 ms for 1,064 skills in 5 shards; whole hook wall ~0.5 s, paired spawn-to-init overhead 0.5-0.7 s (bench/results/README.md); later live topic-switch session reported 2.4-3.1 s to first skill. Node cold start adds ~100 ms. No per-tool-call latency except negligible gate on Skill calls. Worst case ~30 s if Jev hangs (see failureMode).
pros: The only candidate seen here that is a truly automatic, hook-based Jev integration: user never types 'use jev'; runs on every prompt (hooks/hooks.json) with fail-open behavior.

Uses Jev for what it is designed for: many independent Noul yes/no judgments sharded across parallel requests; measured 132-306 ms for 51 skills; good reference implementation of toState()/noul() usage and the currentRequest vs earlierConversationBackground framing lesson.
No MCP tools and near-zero context cost when no skill matches (~100 tokens injected); no argv key exposure; no telemetry or postinstall; MIT.
Safe trial path: defaults to free mock judge (no network), config-gated real Jev, clean uninstall, per-project exclude/alwaysAllow/threshold knobs.
SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and Bearer auth, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api with an OpenRouter key is plausible with zero code changes (needs a live test).
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: only skill selection. Opus 5.5 already picks skills reasonably; benchmark evidence is Sonnet on bare Claude Code, n=3 per cell, 61% vs 33% hit rate, and author admits cost/turn deltas unsupported and junk counts confounded.

Only routes ~/.claude/skills (user-prompt-submit.ts:71); skills delivered by plugins (caveman, gitnexus-*, etc.) are never on verdicts, so the gate can deny them unless named or in alwaysAllow; with an empty verdict the gate blocks the agent's own correct skill choices (README documents this failure).

Sends every prompt plus recent transcript and the whole skill catalog to a third party on every turn, including client-project prompts; plaintext prompt also cached in /tmp/jev-skill-router/turn-*.json for 24h.
No internal timeout: SDK 10 s x 3 attempts can stall each prompt ~30 s when Jev/OpenRouter is degraded (jev is beta); adds 0.5-3 s to every prompt when healthy.

Recall-biased default (0.85) makes obedient frontier models load up to 6 skills (~12k tokens) per turn; injected text tells the model not to choose skills itself, conflicting with user's existing hook/plugin stack behavior.

Immature: created 2026-09-21, 16 commits in 9 days, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests or releases; runs unaudited committed dist bundles (supply-chain risk if repo updates); OpenRouter path untested by the author; response-shape compatibility unverified.
Does not use Choice/Score or general code decisions (e.g. should-I-run-tests, is-this-secret, risk gating) that would benefit daily coding.
gh-abgregs-jev-skill-router.verdict: A well-engineered but narrow proof-of-concept: automatic, fail-open hooks that use Jev Noul fan-out for skill routing, and the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL should let it run against OpenRouter. It adds latency, sends every prompt off-machine, misses plugin-provided skills, and can block skills via its gate, so for Opus 5.5 daily coding it is at most a pattern to copy, or a ungated (UserPromptSubmit-only) experiment from a pinned fork.

gh-kitze-skillbox.name: kitze/skillbox
gh-kitze-skillbox.whatItDoes: Self-hosted (Docker + Bun + Hono + PostgreSQL + React UI) versioned skills library exposed to agents over HTTP MCP and a Node stdio bridge (cli/skillbox.mjs). Jev is used in exactly one place: the recommend_skills MCP tool, which sends the task text plus all authorized skill descriptions to Jev as Score questions (one per skill, 0-4 scale) and returns skills scoring >=3. It is a skill-picker, not a general code-decision layer. It is not a plain "skill"; it is a server app whose bootstrap SKILL.md tells agents to call search_skills at the start of each task. The Jev key is entered in the Skillbox web UI and stored server-side, not read from the environment.

gh-kitze-skillbox.dataEgress: Claude Code -> your Skillbox server: task strings passed to recommend_skills/search_skills (<=2000 chars), model/harness identity headers (X-Skillbox-Model), and skill-use reports. No code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent to Jev by design, though the task text is whatever the model writes as the task, which could contain client project detail. Results cached 5 minutes in server memory.
gh-kitze-skillbox.failureMode: Fail-open. recommend_skills falls back to deterministic lexical search with an explicit fallbackReason (timeout, rate_limited, unavailable, authentication_failed, invalid_response, catalog_limit, busy) and noMatch=null. Deadline 8000 ms (DEADLINE_MS), rate cooldown from Retry-After, max 10 model calls/min per scope, max 2 concurrent, one failed OpenRouter batch fails the whole request to fallback (recommendations.ts:10-14, :335-398). If the Skillbox server itself is down, the MCP tools error and the bootstrap skill says to report it.
gh-kitze-skillbox.latencyImpact: Only when the model calls recommend_skills: one cold OpenRouter batch (Jev claimed 70-500 ms per call, plus 1-3 sequential rounds for catalogs over 32 skills at 2 concurrent) up to an 8 s cap, then cached 5 min. Plus one search_skills call at each task start as mandated by bootstrap SKILL.md. Nothing is added to Bash/Edit/Read calls; no hooks.
gh-kitze-skillbox.contextCost: 5 base MCP tools (search_skills, recommend_skills, load_skill, read_skill_file, report_skill_use) plus up to 4 write tools (upsert_skill, propose_skill_update, list_skill_proposals, archive_skill) depending on permissions; est. roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens of tool definitions (recommend_skills description alone is about 620 chars). The bootstrap skill adds a short description (about 60 tokens) always and about 700 tokens when triggered. search_skills at every task start injects the full skill index (up to 220 chars per skill, so 200 skills is about 11k tokens), which grows with library size. No hook-injected text.
gh-kitze-skillbox.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger plus model-discretion MCP tool. The bootstrap SKILL.md description says 'ALWAYS browse the Skills Library at the start of a task', which prompts Claude to call search_skills; recommend_skills is explicitly additive and optional ('still call unqueried search_skills once'). Jev is not invoked by any deterministic hook and is never used for coding decisions.

It is a working, tested reference for the Decisions API Score request/response shape.
Careful failure handling: 8 s deadline, fail-open to lexical search, rate limit cooldown, batch limits, cache, no partial ranking, redirect:'error', bounded response size.
Key is encrypted server-side and never enters Claude Code's env, argv or context.
Uses Jev for what a calibrated scorer suits (rank N candidates against a task) with an injection-resistant rubric.
MIT, clear SECURITY.md, ~74 tests, mocked-provider tests for OpenRouter batching.
Bootstrap skill gives genuinely automatic behavior for the skill-discovery step without the user prompting.
cons: Jev only ranks skills in a library the user would have to build and host; it adds no Jev value for code edits, tool routing, permission decisions, or commit/PR choices, which is what the user wants.
Heavy infrastructure for a personal setup: Docker Compose + PostgreSQL + Bun server + admin UI, versus the user's existing Node/uvx-only tooling.
Jev call is behind an optional recommend_skills tool the model must choose to call; the mandated flow is search_skills, which does not use Jev, so Jev is often skipped. Not deterministic.

Key entered through the web UI and no env var support (no OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so it cannot be wired into Claude Code settings or hooks; the candidate's TYPESAFE_API_KEY evidence is wrong for the code.
Sends task text and all skill descriptions to OpenRouter on each cache miss; client-project task text leaves the machine (via your server).
Every task start pays for search_skills output in context that grows with library size, and installs a ALWAYS-trigger skill that will fire on all tasks including trivial ones.
Skill bodies are remote instructions followed by the agent, a prompt-injection channel that conflicts with the user's secret-guard hooks and client-work confidentiality.
Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-17, 11 commits, 1 contributor (3 identities), no releases, no CI, version 0.1.0; stars are likely hype-driven.
Adds nothing to existing setup that Claude Code's built-in Skills and skill descriptions do not already do locally at zero latency.
gh-kitze-skillbox.verdict: Real and Jev-integrated (OpenRouter Decisions API supported natively, fail-open), but Jev is confined to ranking skills in a self-hosted library, which is a poor match for automatic Jev use inside daily Claude Code coding. Worth reading as a reference for the Score request shape; do not install it as the integration.

gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.whatItDoes: Local Python (stdlib+httpx+PyYAML) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, skill_router, plus an optional Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook. gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.install: Download source ZIP, run python Install.py (venv in ~/.jev-skill-router/runtime), or uv tool install '.[secure]'; then jev-skills setup --root <skills> --client claude [--hook]; jev-skills auth or set TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No PyPI package.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.tests: About 2,570 lines across 12 test files (API mock transport, cancellation, catalog, MCP client, protocol/setup, retrieval, upgrade, release). GitHub Actions test matrix on ubuntu 3.11/3.13, windows 3.12, macos 3.12, with SHA-pinned actions and read-only permissions. I did not run them. VALIDATION.md:60 admits live Jev auth, selection quality, latency and cost were never measured (no key available), and the 96-case comparison was local only ('Live Jev was not run').
security: API key sent only as Bearer header to a fixed HTTPS host, redirects not followed (jev.py:160). Key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or a supported OS keychain; no plaintext file fallback (config.py:91-111). Key never appears in argv.

No shell execution in the server; MCP is stdio only, read-only tool. Only subprocess use is setup calling 'claude mcp add' with a fixed argument list (integrations.py:136). Install.py runs pip in a venv (network installs from PyPI), no curl|sh, no npm postinstall.

Setup mutates user state: writes ~/.claude.json via claude CLI, writes a skill into ~/.claude/skills, and with --hook merges a UserPromptSubmit entry into ~/.claude/settings.json (with backup). park --apply moves your skill folders to a vault (interferes with existing skills and plugins).

Prompt-injection surface: skill text is sent to Jev as evidence and then returned verbatim to the main model as instructions; SECURITY.md concedes this is not a sandbox and that injection defense is incomplete. Only trusted skill roots are safe. Path reads block traversal and symlinks.

Hook path is worse for secrets: every raw user prompt (up to 64KB read) goes off-machine to the provider, and there is no redaction (SECURITY.md admits it cannot reliably detect secrets). This bypasses the intent of the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, which does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
No telemetry uploader; in-memory cache only. Single-author repo, 9 days old, no independent audit.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter as shipped): the focused task text (with the hook, the entire raw user prompt on every turn; with the MCP tool, whatever task/context the model chooses to pass), all skill names and descriptions in the catalog (batched, up to 24KB per request), and up to 900-char excerpts of shortlisted skill bodies (SECURITY.md: excerpts may include interior and final portions). Does not send code files, diffs, tool outputs or the full conversation unless Claude places them in the task/context fields. Local skill files are read but only descriptions and excerpts leave the machine.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking. The hook catches RouterError and prints an additionalContext line saying routing is unavailable and to continue under ordinary rules (cli.py:138-146), exit 0. MCP returns isError text. Bounds: 15 s per HTTP request, 45 s per route deadline, 32-request cap, 2 retries on 429/5xx with capped backoff (max 8 s, honors Retry-After), no retries on network errors (jev.py:246-250). The hook is registered with timeout 120 s (integrations.py:152), so a slow or down Jev can stall each prompt for up to 45 s before the turn proceeds. No fallback to another model or keyword routing in live mode (by design).
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.contextCost: 1 MCP tool. Tool name+description (~300 chars) + inputSchema (7 properties, ~1,100 chars) + annotations, about 1,500 chars, roughly 400 tokens. Server 'instructions' BOOTSTRAP ~480 chars (~120 tokens). Bridge SKILL.md adds a ~80-token description to the skill list. Total about 600 tokens fixed. The project's own benchmark (README) says this is a net loss for small catalogs (-27% at 5 skills) and only pays off at 50+ skills. With the hook, each prompt gets an injected additionalContext of either the selected skill JSON (up to 12,000 chars = about 3k tokens, max_output_chars) or a ~150-char status line every turn.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.autoInvocation: Two modes. (a) Default: model-discretion MCP tool, nudged by the server instructions and a bridge skill; not deterministic, and Claude Code lazily lists MCP tools so it can be skipped. (b) Optional --hook: deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook that routes on every submitted prompt, but only ever selects SKILL.md files, so it automatically 'uses Jev' for skill selection only, not for any coding decision.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.latencyImpact: Hook mode adds 2+ sequential logical Jev calls (rank, then verify; more for large catalogs, up to 3 concurrent) to EVERY prompt before Claude starts, plus Python interpreter startup (~100-300 ms) and file scan; separate hook processes share no cache. Even at the claimed 70-500 ms per call that is roughly 0.3-1.5 s per prompt best case, up to 45 s worst case. MCP mode adds the same only when Claude chooses to call it. Real latency is unmeasured by the author (VALIDATION.md:60).
pros: Genuinely uses the System One primitives the way Jev is meant to be used (Choice for ranking at router.py:42, Noul plus Score for verification at router.py:51-52) and enforces confidence and fit gates (min_fit 0.65, min_confidence 0.5), so it is a real, non-toy Jev integration with typed decisions and strict response validation (jev.py:29-55).
Ships an actual deterministic auto-invoke path for Claude Code (UserPromptSubmit hook), so no 'use jev' prompting is needed; fails open with clear status text.
Careful engineering: request/time budgets, cancellation, byte caps, no redirects, keychain-only key storage, SHA-pinned CI on 4 OS targets, 2.5k lines of tests, backups before editing client configs.
MIT licensed, small readable code (about 1.5k lines), no telemetry, no shell tool exposed.
The endpoint, key var and model are three isolated constants, so an OpenRouter fork is a small diff (jev.py:15, config.py:34, config.py:92).
cons: Wrong problem for this user: it only decides which SKILL.md to load, so it adds nothing for daily coding decisions (test triage, permission or risk gating, routing, code review verdicts). Value exists only if the user has 50+ skills; at small catalogs it costs more context than native progressive disclosure (README's own table, -27% at 5 skills).

No OpenRouter support as shipped: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, contradicting the user's requirement for an OpenRouter-hosted Jev. Needs a fork, and the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone schema equivalence is unverified.

Hook mode sends every raw prompt (possibly containing client code, paths or secrets) to a third party with no redaction, on personal AND client projects, and runs before the user's PreToolUse secret guard could act; plus 2+ Jev calls and a Python process launch on every single turn.

Never validated live: author states Jev accuracy, latency, cost and real model task success are unmeasured; the 3-star, 9-day-old, single-author project has no field use. Jev's claimed accuracy here rests on a possibly-router-like model (Theo's claim) and is untested.

Invasive setup: park moves existing skill folders out of discovery paths, writes ~/.claude.json, ~/.claude/settings.json and a bridge skill, and pip-installs a private venv; conflicts with the user's plugin-managed skills (caveman, gitnexus), which park does not manage. Native skills stay visible unless removed, negating the context savings.
Injects selected skill text (which may carry prompt injection) as additionalContext each turn; 45 s route deadline with 120 s hook timeout can noticeably stall interactive typing when Jev is slow.
gh-himomohi-jev-skill-router.verdict: A well-built but narrow tool: it uses Jev solely to pick SKILL.md files, needs an OpenRouter fork (hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint and key), and its hook ships every prompt to a third party and adds Jev latency each turn. Only worth considering as a reference implementation of Choice/Noul/Score usage, or if the user later accumulates a very large skill library; not recommended for this user's daily coding.

gh-govindup63-skillpick.name: govindup63/skillpick
gh-govindup63-skillpick.whatItDoes: Bun/TypeScript CLI that installs a UserPromptSubmit command hook into ~/.claude/settings.json (also Codex, Gemini, Droid, OpenCode, Amp). On every submitted prompt it scans SKILL.md files (project and home dirs), sends the prompt plus skill descriptions to Jev via @typesafe-ai/sdk in two /v1/systemone calls (call 1: Choice over all skills plus 3 Noul gate questions; call 2: Choice plus a Noul per shortlisted skill), and injects a one-line <skill_relevance> block via hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext naming the suggested skill, or saying none is relevant. It only nudges skill selection. It does no code analysis, routing, review or decision work.

providerSupport.evidence: src/config.ts:47 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or file apiKey); src/pick.ts:124-128 builds new TypeSafeClient({apiKey, defaultModel: config.model, timeout: 15_000}) with no baseURL passed; src/config.ts:48 model defaults to 'jev-latest' (override via SKILLPICK_MODEL). README and code never mention openrouter (grep for openrouter across src/adapters/bench returned nothing). The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:56-58) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai (line 513), and posts to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (line 554) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (line 581). So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> plus SKILLPICK_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 should hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with no code change.
providerSupport.others: None. Only TypeSafe direct, or anything that speaks the /v1/systemone shape.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, in theory, and it needs no code change: set env vars only. The body is {state, questions, model}, which matches the System One API surface described in the brief. Unverified: whether OpenRouter's /systemone accepts the SDK's exact request and response schema (choice/noul answer types, usage.input_tokens), and whether it wants the model id 'typesafe/jev-1.13' rather than 'jev-latest'. Env vars must be visible to the hook process. They can go in settings.json 'env' or the shell profile, and the ~/.config/skillpick/config.json 'apiKey' has no baseURL field. Because the key env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, there is a risk of mixing it up with a real TypeSafe key. I did not test it, per the no-execution rule.

gh-govindup63-skillpick.tests: Two small bun test files (test/roster.test.ts 53 lines, test/hook-format.test.ts 33 lines), covering roster parsing and hook output formatting. Nothing tests Picker or the API path. No CI (no .github, 0 workflows), no releases, no tags, 1 contributor, 5 commits, 11 days old (v0.1.0). It ships a self-run benchmark (bench/RESULTS.md) on 140 skills and 85 labeled requests, done by the author on one machine: 93.3% correct on covered requests, 24% needless suggestions on uncovered ones, p50/p95 latency 805/1812 ms, $0.00076 per prompt.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.runtime: Bun 1.x (the package is executed as TypeScript source via `bun run src/cli.ts`; the hook command is `"<bun path>" run "<cli.ts>" hook --agent claude`). Dependency: @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 (MIT, TypeSafe's official SDK). The user has Node 24, not Bun, so Bun would have to be added.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.install: git clone https://github.com/govindup63/skillpick && cd skillpick && bun install && bun link && skillpick set-key <key> && skillpick install --claude. This is a manual clone plus bun install, with no curl|sh and no postinstall script. It needs Bun, and it edits ~/.claude/settings.json, so back that file up first. For OpenRouter, export TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<openrouter key> and SKILLPICK_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 through settings.json env.
security: API key: TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env, or plaintext in ~/.config/skillpick/config.json (mode 600, chmod set in cli.ts). `skillpick set-key <key>` puts the key in argv and shell history. The hook itself passes no secrets in argv.
No shell execution of prompt content: the hook only reads stdin JSON and the skill files, and calls fetch through the SDK.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the output is only a skill name that must be one of the roster keys (Jev returns a choice from the supplied options), inside a fixed template. But SKILL.md files in cloned client repos (project .claude/skills, .agents/skills) are read and their descriptions and 700-char body excerpts are sent to the API, so an untrusted repo can shape ranking or exfiltrate its own text only to Jev.
install rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json (idempotent, leaves other hooks alone per README). Hooks run in parallel with the user's existing UserPromptSubmit hooks, if any.

No telemetry in skillpick code. TypeSafe states it does not train on requests, per the README. With OpenRouter as gateway, OpenRouter and TypeSafe's provider policies would both apply and are unverified here.

Supply chain: one dependency (the official SDK), a bun.lock, no postinstall, a 1-person 11-day-old repo. Read-only audit of the source found nothing malicious. The install-for-me agent prompt in the README makes an agent clone and run third-party code, so do it by hand.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.dataEgress: Per submitted prompt (unless it starts with '/' or is under 12 chars): the full user prompt text, plus the name and description of every SKILL.md found in the cwd and in the home skill dirs (call 1). Call 2 adds the full description and the first 700 chars of the body of the top 3 skills. It runs about 18k input tokens per prompt on a 140-skill roster. No code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs or assistant messages are sent, only the current prompt with no conversation history, so follow-ups like 'yes do it' under 12 chars are skipped. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (and its upstream provider) if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is set. Client-project prompts can contain confidential specifics, so this needs a per-project SKILLPICK_DISABLED=1.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.failureMode: Fail-open, but it blocks first. Any thrown error is caught and only written to stderr, exit 0 (src/cli.ts:106-110), and no key or empty roster returns silently. The SDK timeout is 15 s per request with 2 retries and backoff (SDK maxRetries: 2), against a 15 s hook timeout. A hung Jev can therefore stall every prompt for up to about 15 s until Claude Code kills the hook, and the hook then adds nothing. There is no circuit breaker and no cache. Bun stdin read has no guard. Gating decisions are also silent, since a failed call injects nothing rather than 'none relevant'.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.latencyImpact: The hook is synchronous, before the model sees the prompt. Author benchmark: p50 805 ms, p95 1812 ms for both calls on 140 skills (roster scan plus Bun startup extra, probably about 100-200 ms). Claimed cost is $0.00076 per prompt, so about $0.08 per 100 prompts. It is paid on every prompt, not every tool call. It adds no per-tool-call latency, but it stacks with the user's other UserPromptSubmit hooks and with OpenRouter overhead, which is unmeasured.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.contextCost: 0 MCP tools and no server instructions. The hook injects a fixed block per prompt (about 40-55 tokens when a skill is picked, about 20 for 'No installed skill appears relevant'). That accumulates across a long session, roughly 5k tokens per 100 prompts, and it defeats no prompt caching because it sits at the end. The roster in the system prompt is untouched. Nothing else is added.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: a UserPromptSubmit command hook fires on every prompt with no user or model action. This is the auto-integration the user asked for, but it only affects skill selection, not coding decisions.
pros: It is truly automatic: a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never says 'use jev', and it writes to settings.json idempotently with uninstall and a SKILLPICK_DISABLED=1 kill switch.

It is the only candidate here that is a real, working Jev application with a documented measurement: 93.3% correct on covered requests, and the same pick on 3 repeat runs (24/24). Its design follows TypeSafe's official skill-suggestion cookbook.
OpenRouter looks trivial to swap in: the official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to {base}/v1/systemone, so base=https://openrouter.ai/api needs zero code changes.
Fail-open by design: it never blocks a prompt on an error, and it uses stdin rather than argv for prompt data.
Small footprint: no MCP tools, no server instructions, about 20-55 tokens injected per prompt, one official dependency, no postinstall, MIT.
Useful for this user only if their roster is big: they have gitnexus-* (about 9), caveman (about 8), design and other skills, so it may reduce wrong skill loads.
cons: It solves a narrow problem: picking which skill to load. Claude Code already lists skill descriptions natively and Opus 5.5 loads them well, so the marginal gain is unproven for this user, and the author's own benchmark shows 24% needless suggestions and confident wrong picks that can mislead (cookbook: 37 fixed, 7 broken).
Blocking latency on every prompt: p50 0.8 s, p95 1.8 s. A slow OpenRouter call can stall up to 15 s with 2 retries, and there is no caching or circuit breaker.

Data egress on client projects: every prompt plus skill descriptions and body excerpts go to a third party (and through OpenRouter). Client confidentiality needs a per-project disable, and nothing automates that.
Requires Bun, which the user does not list (Node 24 only), and depends on an absolute bun path baked into settings.json, which breaks if the clone moves ('STALE').

OpenRouter is unsupported in the documented config: the key variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model default is 'jev-latest' (the OpenRouter id is typesafe/jev-1.13), the schema equivalence with OpenRouter's /systemone is unverified, and the config-file key has no baseURL. The author has never tested OpenRouter.
Immature: 1 author, 5 commits, 11 days old, 2 stars, no CI, no releases, tests cover only roster parsing and hook formatting, and the benchmark was self-run on one machine (skills the author owns).
Adds a plaintext key file, and set-key puts the key in argv/shell history. Small rosters (<8 skills) make the nearest skill win even when nothing fits.
It does not touch the higher-value Jev uses (permission decisions, risk gating, routing subagents, review triage) that this user wants.
gh-govindup63-skillpick.verdict: A working, honest, low-context and fail-open Jev hook, and the only one of its kind found here, but it only nudges skill selection, which Claude Code already does well natively. Its cost is 1-2 s of blocking per prompt plus egress of every prompt, and the project is 11 days old with no OpenRouter test. Worth trying with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api on personal projects, not as a core piece of the daily setup or on client repos.

gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.name: Dicklesworthstone/skillranker (sr)
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.whatItDoes: Standalone Rust CLI (binary `sr`, ~150k LOC) that, on each Claude Code UserPromptSubmit, reads the session transcript plus the visible skill roster, asks Jev two typed questions (a wide Choice over up to 254 skills plus "none", then a rerank with Choice/Noul fit checks on a shortlist), and injects at most one "Suggested skill for the next step: X" line as additionalContext. Advisory only; abstains silently. Also ships eval/replay/ledger/feedback tooling.

providerSupport.others: Cloudflare Workers AI hosted Jev (SR_PROVIDER=cloudflare, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN). No OpenRouter string anywhere in the repo (grep -ri openrouter is empty).
providerSupport.evidence: src/jev/endpoint.rs:26 DEFAULT_TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://api.typesafe.ai; :32 SYSTEMONE_PATH=/v1/systemone; :143-150 any non-root path in TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT is rejected (NonRootPathForbidden); :329-347 Cloudflare endpoint is special-cased as https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{id}/ai/run; src/config.rs:304-309 env vars TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT, SR_PROVIDER, SR_MODEL; src/jev/wide.rs:25 and src/config.rs:25 DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest; src/jev/client.rs:381-392 sends Authorization: Bearer <key>, origin-scoped.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, not a config change. OpenRouter's surface is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, but sr accepts only a root origin and appends /v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api is rejected by design. Loopback-proxy tricks fail too, because credentials are refused over plain HTTP. A patch needs a new Provider variant and EndpointConfig (like the Cloudflare one) with target https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, an OPENROUTER_API_KEY env mapping, and SR_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (slash is allowed by valid_id). The wire codec (model/state/questions, Bearer auth) is likely reusable if OpenRouter's System One schema matches TypeSafe's, but I could not verify that: the OpenRouter docs URL I tried returned 404. Requires building a Rust 1.95 / edition 2024 fork and maintaining it, on a repo with fast-moving history.

Then `sr ledger init`, set network.enabled=true in ~/.config/sr/config.toml, export TYPESAFE_API_KEY into the environment Claude Code launches with, and run `sr install-hook claude --apply`.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.tests: 152 files under tests/, several of them 1-3k lines, plus in-source unit tests and Python contract validators in scripts/ with a prepush_gates.sh. There is no .github directory, so no CI is visible. I did not run anything.
security: API key is read from the environment only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), so it does not appear in argv. The key is origin-scoped: it refuses to emit the Authorization header to any other origin (src/jev/endpoint.rs:13, :413-426).
Redirects are hard failures, ambient HTTP(S)_PROXY variables are not trusted, and HTTP is allowed only for loopback and never with a credential. unsafe_code is forbidden (Cargo.toml).
Networking needs explicit opt-in (network.enabled in trusted user config), and a project-level file cannot enable it. Credential presence alone does not enable it.
Outgoing context is redacted, but the README admits it cannot catch all confidential prose. Dry-run and disclosure receipts let you inspect the payload.

Hook installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json (preview first, backup, lock, digest check). It also drops a usage skill and shell completions via install.sh, which is a curl|bash installer with SHA256 verification. The fallback source build pulls git-pinned dependencies.

Prompt-injection surface: skill bodies and descriptions from the roster, and transcript and tool output, go into the Jev request. Jev returns typed decisions, not free text. The injected output is a locally validated skill ID within a 1,024-character cap, so the injection risk is low.
No telemetry or remote feedback sink is claimed (README Privacy section). The ledger is local SQLite, owner-only permissions, 30-day default retention.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.dataEgress: On each user prompt, and only if network is enabled, the standard profile sends the newest prompt, recent conversation history, recent tool calls and results, project signals such as dirty paths, plus every candidate skill's description and body excerpts (up to 254 candidates and a 96 KiB request) to the provider. Everything is redacted first. Minimal profile and --no-tools reduce this. Without a code diff step, file contents appear only where tool results are in the recent transcript. Because the destination would be a patched OpenRouter endpoint, this content of client-project sessions would transit OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Local state: SQLite ledger and response cache (at most 10 minutes) under ~/.local/share/sr.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.failureMode: Fail-open. The hook never blocks: errors give empty stdout, a sanitized stderr line, and exit 0. Internal deadline is 3000 ms from process entry with 200 ms reserved for cleanup; the installed harness timeout is 4 s. Per-invocation budget is 2 logical requests and 4 HTTP attempts, with retry and Retry-After honored inside the deadline. Stale or late responses are not published. A circuit breaker and shared attempt allowance are optional. The worst case is a UserPromptSubmit that takes up to about 3-4 s before Claude starts.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. The hook injects at most one short line per prompt (typically 20-40 tokens, 1,024-character cap), and injects nothing on abstention or failure. The installed usage skill adds one skill description to the skill list. That is the lowest context cost of any Jev integration, but it also gives the smallest benefit.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.latencyImpact: Added to every user prompt, synchronously, before Claude sees it. README targets (unmeasured, self-declared): exact cache hit p95 at most 100 ms; warm network p50 at most 600 ms, p95 at most 1,500 ms; hard cap 3 s. Two sequential Jev calls are made unless the need is low. Local roster discovery, transcript parsing, and Quill indexing add to this. Under bypass or auto mode with many short prompts, the cost is felt on every turn.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: UserPromptSubmit with an empty matcher, so it fires on every user prompt with no user or model action. It is advisory: Claude may ignore the suggested skill. It fires only on user prompts, not on mid-turn tool calls or subagent steps.
pros: The only candidate seen so far that is truly automatic and deterministic: a UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to (typed Choice and Noul with calibrated probabilities and a 'none' abstention), following TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook.
Very small context cost: no MCP tools, at most one injected line, silent on abstain.
Strongly fail-open with a 3 s deadline, a 4 s harness timeout, bounded retries and a circuit breaker, so it cannot wedge Claude Code.
Careful key handling: env-only key, origin-scoped bearer, no redirects, no proxy trust, network opt-in, redaction and dry-run disclosure receipts.
Hook installer is safe: previews, backs up, and merges without touching the existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. It is also cleanly uninstallable.
Substantial engineering: 731 commits in 13 days, 152 test files, replay and eval tooling, and a written design plan.
Already handles Claude Code specifics: transcript parsing, skill roster with override and shadow resolution, and explicit 'don't use skill X' handling.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the code accepts only a root origin plus /v1/systemone, or Cloudflare. Using OpenRouter needs a source patch and a fork to maintain (moderate effort).

It only picks skills. The user's stated goal was to use Jev where it adds value in daily coding. It provides no code-level decisions such as risk of an edit, whether a command is safe, or which file to read. Value depends on having a large skill library; with a handful of skills it gains little.
Adds a synchronous network round trip (two sequential Jev calls, unmeasured p50 about 0.6 s, up to 3 s) before every prompt.
Sends conversation history, tool results and skill bodies from all projects, including client work, to a third party. Redaction is best-effort, and the flow would add OpenRouter to the data path.

Very new and alpha: created 2026-09-17, no release, no visible CI, one dominant author, main is moving daily, and CHANGELOG Unreleased lists many correctness fixes (for example large-roster live ranking was failing). The dependency stack (asupersync, frankensearch, git-pinned) is niche.
Non-standard license with an Anthropic/OpenAI rider whose terms (execute, benchmark, 'on behalf of') are ambiguous for a Claude Code user on client work.
Installer is curl|bash (with checksum), and there is no prebuilt release, so a source build needs Rust 1.95 and Git and pulls git dependencies.

Requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or a patched equivalent) to be exported into the environment Claude Code is launched from, which is awkward for a GUI or launcher and for subscription/OAuth users who have no such key setup.
The hook fires only on UserPromptSubmit, so it never helps during long autonomous runs in bypass or auto mode, where most of the tool calls happen.
gh-dicklesworthstone-skillranker.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context UserPromptSubmit hook that is genuinely automatic, but it only recommends skills, is TypeSafe-direct or Cloudflare only (an OpenRouter patch is needed), is very young, and adds a network round trip to every prompt. Treat it as a reference design for a hook-based Jev integration, not something to install as is.

gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.name: weiping/jev-claude-code
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace jev-engineering, plugin jev v0.2.1) that wires TypeSafe Jev into deterministic hooks. Python hooks call Jev via typesafe-sdk with typed Choice/Noul/Score questions and keep all thresholds in code/config: (1) PreToolUse(Bash) permission gate: hard deny regexes, readonly allowlist, else Jev decides allow/ask/deny plus egress and network-requested checks; (2) PostToolUse(Bash) output ladder: chunks output of 80+ lines and shows each chunk in full, excerpt or hidden, saving the original for recall; (3) UserPromptSubmit: conditionally loads project guidance files and suggests project tools per rules.json/tools.json; (4) PreToolUse(Agent) router: downgrades mechanical subagent work to haiku, blocks sensitive work on cheap models, denies duplicate subgoals; (5) skills /jev:init, /jev:stats, /jev:snapshot, /jev:recall plus cheap-worker and readonly-reviewer agents. Defaults to shadow mode (calls Jev and logs, changes nothing) until mode=enforce.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code. plugins/jev/scripts/jevlib.py:313-324 builds TypeSafeClient(model=cfg['model'], timeout, retry) with no base_url and calls client.system_one(state=, questions=). requirements.txt pins typesafe-sdk==0.7.1. The SDK (inspected wheel typesafe_sdk/constants.py:3-15, _core/constants.py:5, _core/transport.py:121,134) reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai), posts to base_url + '/v1/systemone' with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'. config/default.json:2 sets model 'jev-1.13.0'.
providerSupport.others: None. Mock transport via JEV_MOCK for tests only (jevlib.py:280-321).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, no code edit needed: export TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (SDK path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, Bearer auth), and set model to typesafe/jev-1.13 in .claude/jev/config.json (config is deep-merged). Unverified: whether OpenRouter's System One request/response schema is byte-identical to the SDK's (questions/criteria/answers/usage) and whether SDK validates model names against /v1/models. Needs one live smoke test; the env var leaks the OpenRouter key under a TypeSafe name, harmless but confusing.

security: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY by SDK and sent as Bearer header; never in argv. Repo's own .claude/jev/config.json adds a deny rule for echoing the key.

Fixed pip install of pinned typesafe-sdk==0.7.1 at first SessionStart via setup.sh (runs pip install in a venv; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall); transitive deps are unpinned (httpx2>=2, pydantic, tenacity) - supply-chain surface.

Hook input passes untrusted text (commands, script contents, command output, subagent prompts) into a model only for typed classification; no free text returned, so prompt injection can only flip a probability, but a crafted command/output could bias allow/hide decisions. Deny regexes run before Jev.

Permission gate returns permissionDecision 'allow' in enforce mode when Jev confidence >= 0.85: this can auto-approve commands and bypass the user's normal prompt; an attacker-influenced command could be judged benign. Deny-regex list is weak (bypassable by obfuscation, e.g. variable indirection).

Output ladder can hide up to all chunks of long Bash output from the model (only if no error detected at 0.5), a correctness risk not a security one; original saved unencrypted under .claude/jev/state/outputs (gitignored via auto .gitignore) and may contain secrets.
Local logs .claude/jev/logs/decisions.jsonl record full commands and answers, incl. anything secret in commands.

Executes only its own scripts; reads script files named as argv[1] of python/bash/node/sh/ruby (up to 4000 chars) and sends them out. No telemetry beyond Jev calls seen in plugin code; SDK sets a User-Agent header only.
Single anonymous maintainer, 0 stars, 3 days old, no releases beyond v0.1.0 tag (plugin now 0.2.1): high unreviewed-update risk since plugins auto-execute on every Bash call.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.dataEgress: Sent to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if repointed) on every non-trivial event: (a) each Bash command not matching the readonly allowlist or a deny regex: command string, cwd, repo_root, the latest user prompt (last_prompt.txt) and the first 4000 chars of any script file it runs (python/bash/node/sh/ruby X); (b) every Bash output of 80+ lines: up to 3000 chars per 25-line chunk (up to 60 chunks, so up to ~180 KB of tool output) plus the command and user prompt; (c) every user prompt in projects with rules/tools.json: full prompt text and list of up to 200 changed file names (git diff --name-only, untracked); (d) every Agent dispatch: up to 6000 chars of subagent description+prompt, and up to 50 prior subgoal texts (300 chars each). Not sent: full file contents via Read/Edit, diffs, and the main model context. Note the secret-leak deny patterns only cover .ssh and .env in the command string; secrets echoed in command output (env dumps, logs) would go to the provider.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.failureMode: Fail-open (no decision, exit 0). guard() in jevlib.py:332-342 swallows all exceptions; permission_gate/output_ladder/agent_router catch Jev exceptions, log, and emit nothing, falling back to Claude Code's normal permission flow / unmodified output. Client timeout is 4s per attempt with 1 retry and 8s total budget (jevlib.py:316-319, default.json timeout_s 8), hook timeouts 15-20s. So a slow/down Jev costs up to ~8s per Bash call before falling back; no circuit breaker, so every Bash call pays this while Jev is down. Also silent until venv install finishes (run-hook.sh) and if TYPESAFE_API_KEY missing, SDK raises and hook fails open. Caveat: fail-open on the gate means outage = default permissions, which is safe.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.latencyImpact: Claimed Jev 70-500 ms per call. Adds one blocking Jev round trip (plus python venv interpreter startup + SDK/pydantic import, roughly 150-400 ms estimated, not measured) before every non-allowlisted Bash command, one after every Bash output of 80+ lines, one per user prompt (only if project has rules/tools), one per Agent dispatch. In a bypass/auto-permission session this is pure added latency on every Bash call (~0.3-1 s), with worst case 8s during outage. Approve-latency is not saved because the user is already in bypass/auto mode.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no MCP server instructions. Skills: 4 skill descriptions (init, stats, snapshot, recall; recall description ~250 chars) plus 2 agent descriptions, roughly 300-500 tokens total in the system prompt. Hooks inject no text in shadow mode; in enforce mode UserPromptSubmit injects up to 9000 chars (~2.2k tokens) of guidance per prompt only where rules.json matches, and the output ladder shrinks Bash output (net negative context, plus a footer of ~200 chars per trimmed output). Denial/reason messages add small text.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse on Bash and Agent, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart); the user never has to say 'use jev'. Skills /jev:recall is also description-triggered. Ships in shadow mode: nothing changes behavior until mode=enforce.
pros: Truly automatic: all behavior is hook-driven (hooks.json:1-28), matching the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being asked, with zero MCP tools and near-zero standing context cost.

Right primitive-to-task fit: uses Choice/Noul/Score for classification decisions (permission risk, output relevance, model tier, sensitivity, dedupe) with thresholds in config, which is exactly what a probability-only model is suited for.
Fail-open everywhere: guard() and per-hook try/except emit nothing on Jev failure (jevlib.py:332-342; permission_gate.py:76-80), so an outage or beta breakage cannot brick Claude Code.
Shadow mode by default plus /jev:stats lets the user log Jev decisions for a week against real work before enabling enforce, a sane rollout for a beta model.

Only reads the SDK-level knobs: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and configurable model make OpenRouter repointing a config-only change (SDK constants.py:6, transport.py:134) - no source edits or fork needed if OpenRouter's schema matches.
Subagent router (haiku downgrade, sensitivity gating, duplicate-subgoal denial) and output ladder target real cost/context savings for a heavy Opus 5.5 subagent user.
Reasonable engineering hygiene for a 3-day-old repo: ruff + shellcheck + unit + e2e CI, MIT license, no postinstall/curl|sh, output originals recoverable via recall.py.
cons: Project is 3 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 8 commits, single-author unreviewed hooks running on every Bash call; plugin update pulls new executable code automatically.

Hardcoded to the TypeSafe SDK (typesafe-sdk==0.7.1); no OpenRouter code or docs. Works with OpenRouter only if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + model name override behave identically; untested by the author and unverified by me. Model default 'jev-1.13.0' is a TypeSafe name, OpenRouter uses 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Weak value for this user: the permission gate is redundant in bypass/auto permission mode (user is not prompted anyway), and its 'allow' output can only bypass prompts, while its 'deny/ask' would newly interrupt bypass-mode sessions and break unattended agent runs.

Adds a blocking network call plus Python venv startup on every non-allowlisted Bash command; overlaps and stacks with existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard and GitNexus Bash hooks (ordering/updatedInput/permissionDecision conflicts possible).

Large data egress for a client-work user: commands, script contents, up to ~180 KB of raw command output, subagent prompts and every user prompt go to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe). Client code/secrets in output would be transmitted; only .ssh/.env command-string regexes protect it. Needs NDA/client-policy review.

Output ladder is risky: can hide relevant lines from Opus based on a beta model judgment (no-error case only); a 'router-like' model (Theo claim) deciding what the coding agent sees could silently degrade quality.

Operational sharp edges documented in GOTCHAS.md: silent no-op until venv installs (first session does nothing), stale .installing lock blocks forever, no circuit breaker so outage costs up to 8s per Bash call, Python 3.10+ checked silently.

Python subagent-router downgrade assumes the user uses cheap haiku subagents; with Opus main and OAuth subscription the cost saving is not billed per token, so the 'cheaper' benefit mostly doesn't apply; prompt_context needs per-project /jev:init and rules.json curation to do anything.
gh-weiping-jev-claude-code.verdict: Best-in-class example of how to integrate Jev automatically (hooks, typed questions, fail-open, shadow mode), and it is repointable to OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model override, but it is a 3-day-old single-author alpha whose main features (permission gate, model downgrade) add little in bypass mode on a subscription, with heavy data egress. Worth installing only in shadow mode as a measurement tool, or forking/borrowing its hook patterns rather than enforcing it on client projects.

security: License MIT. 426 stars, 48 forks, no GitHub releases (latestRelease null), created 2026-03-18, last push 2026-09-30 (very active). Effectively a single-maintainer project: git shortlog of the 200-commit shallow clone shows 197 commits by notque; 3 other contributors with 2-3 commits each.

Key handling is careful: API key sent only as an Authorization header via stdlib urllib, never in argv; the Vercel bridge gets a minimal env allowlist (jev_vercel.py:33-49, NODE_OPTIONS deliberately excluded); error receipts never include request bodies (jev_vercel_gateway.mjs safeErrorReceipt).

scripts/jev_redact.py and plugins/jev-auto-compact/hooks/redact.mjs strip secrets before anything goes to Jev (states 'nothing goes to api.typesafe.ai with a secret in it'). Tested (redact.test.mjs). This is a redaction layer, not a guarantee against leaking client code or names.
Reads the key from ~/.env via python-dotenv (jev_transport.py:22-23), from the process env, or from Claude settings env (jev-auto-compact.mjs:732-733).

install.sh is not curl|sh (run locally after clone) and uses npm ci --ignore-scripts, but it is invasive: it takes over ~/.claude by default (TAKEOVER=true: 'trash and replace' unowned entries at desired paths), symlinks about 86 agents / 62 skills / ~100 hooks, merges 70+ hook registrations across 10 events into settings.json, and runs chmod 600 on history.jsonl. Conflicts with the user's existing PreToolUse guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks are likely; --no-takeover and --dry-run exist.

Prompt-injection surface: hooks inject the JEV_RESULT JSON and many other advisory strings into model context; the pretool-prompt-injection-scanner.py and posttool-bash-injection-scan.py hooks exist. Also runs Python subprocess with list-argv (no shell) for the route script.
Vercel path adds a Node dependency tree (ai, @ai-sdk/gateway) run by the bridge; lockfile present, install scripts disabled.
Local telemetry only: SQLite learning.db and Jev call-log/cache with sha256 payload hashes and answers, 'without raw request text'. No third-party analytics found by grep.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.dataEgress: For /d: the user's request text (after redaction) plus a 'project' field (detected languages/frameworks/datastores from marker files in cwd) plus the routing questions with the agent/skill manifest descriptions (jev-route.py:614-643). The intent-alignment call also sends the model's proposed-intent restatement. Not file contents or diffs in the /d path. For the optional auto-compact plugin: message text and tool inputs and tool results (truncated to head/tail snippets, redacted) from the live transcript, i.e. real code and command output, are sent to api.typesafe.ai every time it compacts. Browser/design/compact scripts send page text or evidence packs. Everything goes to TypeSafe direct or Vercel AI Gateway, never OpenRouter, in the shipped code. Nothing else leaves the machine except the toolkit's unrelated integrations (Reddit, WordPress, GitHub) which are opt-in.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. The UserPromptSubmit hook returns nothing on any error, timeout or non-zero exit and falls back to SKILL.md Phase 1 running the script itself; 4s per attempt, up to 3 retries on 429/529 with jittered exponential backoff capped at 5s, 24s hook budget inside a 26s host timeout. jev_router_common has a circuit breaker on 401/402 (persisted across processes for JEV_BREAKER_TTL_S) and a SQLite response cache (JEV_CACHE_TTL_S default 120s). README says 'if npm unavailable, /d falls back to /do'. Auto-compact falls back to the built-in summarizer on missing key or low reduction, and returns skip for self-triggered compactions. Worst case is added latency of up to about 24s on a /d turn when Jev is down.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.contextCost: Very high if installed as designed. Installer registers 86 agents and 62 skills (each with a name and description in the system prompt, roughly 20-40k characters of listings, i.e. an estimated 6-12k tokens; skills/meta/d/SKILL.md alone is 15 KB, about 3.8k tokens, when loaded), plus about 70 hooks across SessionStart (16), UserPromptSubmit (7), PreToolUse (18), PostToolUse (16), Stop, SubagentStart/Stop etc. Several hooks inject text on every session or prompt (session-context, afk-mode, retro-knowledge-injector, rules-distill-injector, pending-advisory-injector) and /d additionally injects the JEV_RESULT JSON and mandates further scripted steps. No MCP server, so zero tool-schema cost. Cherry-picking only the /d skill plus the one hook would cost about 1-4k tokens.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.autoInvocation: Mostly only when prompted. The only Jev entry point on the prompt path is the explicit '/d' command (regex ^\s*/d\b in jev-route-injector-userprompt.py); a normal prompt never touches Jev. The skill description ('Jev request router...') does not make Claude choose it on its own. The one genuinely automatic Jev use is the jev-auto-compact function-hook plugin (turn.complete at >=60% context), which is a deterministic hook but needs the experimental function-hooks runtime, TypeSafe key, and only affects compaction, not coding decisions.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary prompts. On a /d turn: one or two Jev round trips for routing (claimed 70-500 ms each, timeout 4s per attempt) plus a second intent-alignment call, plus Python startup for pre-route.py (30s subprocess timeout) and jev-route.py; typically low single-digit seconds, worst case about 24s if Jev is down. Vercel path adds Node startup and the SDK on every call. Auto-compact adds sequential batched Jev calls (up to 4 requests per compaction) at each compaction.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.tests: Extensive: about 265 test files under scripts/tests, hooks/tests and plugins/jev-auto-compact/tests (node tests for redact and call-log); GitHub Actions test.yml, pr-ai-review.yml and claude.yml; routing benchmark and eval fixtures. Not executed by me (static audit only).
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.install: Not recommended wholesale. Wholesale: git clone https://github.com/notque/vexjoy-agent && ./install.sh --dry-run (then --no-takeover); this rewrites ~/.claude. Cherry-pick alternative: copy only skills/meta/d, hooks/jev-route-injector-userprompt.py, the jev_* scripts and agent manifests, then point TYPESAFE_URL at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (patch required).
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.runtime: Python 3 (stdlib urllib for direct Jev calls; python-dotenv, requirements.txt), Node (Vercel gateway bridge with npm ai + @ai-sdk/gateway; jev-auto-compact .mjs function hooks), bash installer
pros: Real, working Jev integration with production hardening: retry/backoff on 429/529, circuit breaker on 401/402, SQLite response cache, request-size splitting against Jev's documented limits (jev_limits.py), secret redaction before egress (jev_redact.py, redact.mjs), cost/latency stats scripts.

Direct-path wire format ({state, model, questions} with Bearer auth to /v1/systemone) is the same as OpenRouter's documented System One API, so an OpenRouter switch is a small patch of about 3 constants, not a rewrite.
Fail-open design: hook never blocks a prompt, so a Jev outage costs latency, not correctness.
Good reference material: skills/meta/building-with-jev and jev-production-lessons.md document Choice/Noul/Score usage, calibration and decision cards, useful for writing our own hooks.

jev-auto-compact is the one piece that fires automatically and deterministically (function hooks at 60% context) and applies Jev to a real Claude Code problem, pruning tool calls verbatim instead of LLM-summarizing.
MIT, very active, decent tests and CI; keys kept out of argv and the Vercel bridge gets a minimal env.
cons: Not automatic for the user's goal: Jev is only invoked when the user types /d (jev-route-injector-userprompt.py DETECT_PATTERN = ^\s*/d\b). Ordinary prompts, edits and Bash calls never call Jev, which is exactly what the user said they do not want.
No OpenRouter support at all (grep finds zero 'openrouter'); only api.typesafe.ai direct or Vercel AI Gateway. URL is a hardcoded constant; key env var checked in about 10 scripts.

Jev is used as a router over this toolkit's own 86 agents/62 skills. Without that agent ecosystem, /d has nothing to route to, and Opus 5.5 with plain Claude Code already delegates fine, so the value for a senior dev is low and unmeasured (repo's own what-didnt-work.md records routing reversals).

Installer takes over ~/.claude (trashes unowned entries by default) and registers about 70 hooks across 10 events; high collision risk with the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks, and heavy per-session context injection.
Bus factor of one (197 of 204 commits by a single author), no tagged releases, fast churn (204 commits in 3 months), opinionated persona/voice/Reddit/WordPress content unrelated to daily coding.

Auto-compact plugin sends redacted transcript content (tool inputs and results, including client code fragments) to TypeSafe on every compaction, and depends on the experimental function-hooks runtime and a hardcoded TypeSafe URL; concern for client projects.
The intent-alignment step relies on the model obediently running another script after /d, so it is only partly deterministic; adds up to two Jev calls plus Python and Node startup per /d turn.
Subscription/OAuth main model is unaffected, but /d dispatch relies on the Task/Agent flow of the toolkit's own agent files, so it does not integrate with plain Claude Code sessions.
gh-notque-vexjoy-agent.verdict: A serious, well-engineered Jev consumer, but Jev is wired to an explicit /d command inside a huge opinionated toolkit and only to TypeSafe or Vercel, so it fails the user's core requirement (automatic use, OpenRouter). Do not install it; mine it for patterns (redaction, breaker/cache, size splitting, the auto-compact function-hook idea) and consider the jev-auto-compact idea only after re-pointing its URL to OpenRouter.

gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.name: yusupsupriyadi/jev-skill (jev plugin for Claude Code)
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also cross-agent skills) with 3 hooks and 5 skills. A UserPromptSubmit hook sends the prompt plus names and descriptions (truncated to 200 chars) of every installed skill, command and subagent to Jev as a 'choice' tournament (chunks of 200 options, then a run-off, plus a triage noul/score call). It injects a "[jev] Suggested skill / close second / suggested subagent / workflow size" block into Claude's context. A Stop hook judges each turn that changed files or ran commands. It sends the final message, changed paths, shell commands run and by default a git diff (12k char cap, untracked files included). Findings (unverified claim, needs tests, secret, risk, reviewer) are parked on disk and replayed at the top of the NEXT prompt. Everything is advisory and fail-open.
