security: API key handling is good: config store written with mode 0o600 plus chmod (lib/setup.mjs:50-53); setup skill pipes the key via stdin (--key -) so it is not in argv; env var wins over store; a key is only sent to its own provider; key is verified before it is saved.

But /jev:setup asks the user to PASTE the key into the chat, so it enters the Anthropic conversation context and transcript; env var OPENROUTER_API_KEY avoids this and is the better path for this user.
Plugin option mirroring copies /plugin-entered keys into the plaintext config.json (0600) on every session start.

No curl|sh, no postinstall, zero runtime dependencies for the plugin. The installer (cli/) has 2 npm deps and runs spawnSync('claude ...', {shell:true}) with fixed args; the plugin route needs none of it.
Hooks only shell out to git (spawnSync with arg array, 5s timeout, path filtered to inside cwd). No eval, no user-controlled shell strings.

Prompt-injection surface: output is templated from numeric answers and skill ids/descriptions taken from local skill files (200-char cap) and injected into context as additionalContext. Model output is typed so Jev cannot inject prose, but a malicious third-party skill description is echoed into context (low risk). Injected text says 'not an instruction'.
No telemetry beyond calls to the chosen provider; sends HTTP-Referer/X-Title headers to OpenRouter (attribution).
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.dataEgress: Per prompt (routing): full user prompt text, project hint (cwd basename, git_repo flag, detected languages), and id + first 200 chars of description of EVERY installed skill/command/agent (about 27k tokens for 537 entries per the README; 3 to N parallel calls). Per turn (judge, Stop hook): Claude's final message (up to 4000 chars), list of changed file paths (max 40), every Bash command the turn ran (with failed flag; commands can embed secrets or client paths), and by default the git diff of changed files (12k chars) including untracked files up to 64KB each (new .env-like files are not excluded by name, only by .gitignore). All of it goes to openrouter.ai (and OpenRouter's upstream provider TypeSafe). For client projects this is source-code egress to two third parties unless send_diff=false / judge_enabled=false. There is no per-repo allowlist or secret redaction; the plugin's own secret-check runs in the model, not before sending.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: runHook swallows all errors and exits 0 (hook-io.mjs:84-94); no blocking decision is ever emitted. No key means completely idle. Per-call timeout defaults 2500 ms (judge min 4000 ms) via AbortController; failed chunks are dropped via Promise.allSettled; failed triage defaults to 'is task'. Hook timeouts (8s route, 15s Stop) are in hooks.json. Worst case the user waits about 2.5 s (parallel calls) + 2.5 s (sequential run-off) ~5 s before the prompt goes through with no suggestion. Stop hook is synchronous at end of turn (up to 4+ s). Bad keys or no credit (402) just silently yield no suggestion, so it can rot unnoticed unless /jev:doctor is run.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.contextCost: Static: 5 skill entries (name + description each ~250-400 chars, ~400-500 tokens total in the skills listing), zero MCP tools, zero MCP server instructions. Dynamic: UserPromptSubmit injects ~120-200 tokens ([jev] pick + description + close second + subagent + size + disclaimer) only when a suggestion clears the threshold (relevance>=0.5), plus 50-100 tokens of judgment recall at the next prompt when findings exist. Negligible compared with other MCPs. Note the important side effect: suggestions on every task prompt add a small nudge that may conflict with the user's existing hooks (GitNexus) or skills. The 27k-token figure is what is sent to Jev, not to Claude.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit + Stop + SessionStart) via plugin hooks.json, with no user prompting needed. Only after a key is present; skills (/jev:*) are extra and manual. This directly meets the 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so' requirement, although the value is limited to advisory hints (skill suggestion, post-turn nag), not delegating actual work.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.latencyImpact: Adds synchronous latency to EVERY qualifying prompt: README measures 1.5-4 s routing against 537 skills (2.1 s in the example, 758 ms probe); code path is parallel chunk calls then a sequential run-off, each capped 2.5 s, hook timeout 8 s. Stop hook adds up to ~4 s (min 4000 ms timeout, 15 s cap) at end of every turn that touched files, before control returns. With a smaller catalog (~50-100 skills, single chunk) expect roughly 0.5-1.5 s. The Stop-hook cost is felt every turn in bypass/auto mode. No caching (deliberately), so cost scales with catalog size ($0.0004 per route per README).
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.runtime: Node >=20, zero npm dependencies for the plugin (Node 24 fine); installer in cli/ has 2 deps
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.install: claude plugin marketplace add yusupsupriyadi/jev-skill ; claude plugin install jev@jev-skill ; export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... (preferred over pasting via /jev:setup). Set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter to be explicit. npx jev-ai is NOT yet published to npm.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.tests: 12 node:test files in tests/ (jev-client, providers, route, judge, hook-integration against a mock Decisions server, installer, catalog, transcript, questions, format, frontmatter, platforms); no network needed. No CI workflow (.github absent). Tests not run (hard rule). README says verified live only on Claude Code on Windows.
pros: Only candidate found that gives truly automatic, deterministic Jev use in Claude Code via hooks (UserPromptSubmit + Stop), with no 'use jev' prompting, matching the user's core requirement.

Native OpenRouter support with correct alpha endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions) and ~typesafe/jev-latest slug, auto-selected when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set; also TypeSafe direct as fallback; JEV_API_URL/JEV_MODEL overrides in case the alpha path moves (providers.mjs, config.mjs:80-130).
Strictly fail-open and advisory: every hook error is swallowed, exit 0, never blocks a tool call (hook-io.mjs:84-94), so it cannot break the bypass/auto workflow; idle with no key.
Zero MCP tools and near-zero static context cost (5 short skill descriptions); dynamic injection ~150 tokens and only when confident.

Sensible design for Jev's strengths: typed choice/noul/score questions, tournament for >255 options, gate on 1-P(none), judge compares claim vs commands actually run (the 'claimed done, ran nothing' check) - a genuine use of a calibrated classifier.
Key hygiene: 0600 store, stdin-based key entry, key verified before save, env var precedence; granular kill switches (JEV_ROUTE, JEV_JUDGE, JEV_SEND_DIFF, JEV_ROUTE_EXCLUDE, JEV_TIMEOUT_MS).
Clean small codebase (~2.3k lines incl. skills), readable, no dependencies, MIT, good test coverage of hook path with mock server.
cons: Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-22, 18 commits in 2 days, 1 star, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, version 0.4.0 labelled by author's README as only verified on Windows; expect breakage.

Value is modest: with this user's small catalog (a few dozen skills: gitnexus-*, caveman, dougthepug, etc.) skill routing adds little; the README itself says it is not worth it for a handful of skills. Claude already sees skill descriptions.

Data egress is heavy for client work: whole prompts, all skill descriptions, Claude's final messages, every shell command run and a git diff (incl. untracked new files) go to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every turn by default (send_diff=true). Needs send_diff=false or per-project disabling for client repos; no secret redaction, no repo allowlist.
Latency tax: 1.5-4 s (README) synchronous on every task prompt plus up to ~4 s on the Stop hook each file-touching turn; run-off call is sequential. Noticeable in a daily workflow.

Judgment verdict only surfaces on the NEXT prompt (Stop hook cannot inject), so 'unverified claim' warnings arrive late and may be stale; threshold heuristics (0.7/0.4/score>=2) are untested against real-world false-positive rates; Jev has no reasoning trace so findings are just labels.

Silent failure mode: expired credit (402), rate-limit or alpha API path changes result in no output at all, so the integration can die unnoticed; /jev:setup asks user to paste key into chat (enters transcript) unless env var is used.

Overlap and interaction risk with existing hooks (GitNexus graph-context pre/post hooks, caveman hooks): another UserPromptSubmit additionalContext injector and a Stop hook adding latency; the suggested-skill hint may fight with the user's own skill conventions.

Depends on the alpha OpenRouter Decisions API and on Jev quality (skeptic claim it is a flash router unverified); uses 3-N parallel requests per prompt which multiplies rate-limit exposure. Tests were not run and live behaviour not verified here.
gh-yusupsupriyadi-jev-skill.verdict: Best-fit integration found for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: hook-based, native OpenRouter, fail-open, negligible context cost. But it is a 2-day-old single-author alpha whose benefit is small with a small skill catalog, adds seconds of latency per turn and ships prompts/diffs to third parties by default. Install with OPENROUTER_API_KEY in env, set JEV_SEND_DIFF=false (or judge_enabled=false) and consider judge-only, and verify with /jev:doctor before relying on it for client projects.

gh-arnab621-typesafe-jev-plugin.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (2 skills, 2 agents, 1 PostToolUse hook, 2 Python scripts) for batch analytics: the user builds a reusable .sig.json 'solution signature' (state schema plus Choice/Score/Noul questions plus Excel output template), then runs a CSV/Excel/txt dataset row by row through TypeSafe's System One API and exports results to Excel. It is a data-labelling pipeline tool, not a coding-assistant integration. The only hook validates .sig.json files after Write and never calls Jev.

gh-panachy-jevvy.name: PanAchy/jevvy (@jevvy/permissions)
gh-panachy-jevvy.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also OpenCode) with one function: a PermissionRequest hook (matcher Bash) that asks Jev four Noul questions (harmful <=0.35, sensitive/untrusted/obscured <=0.50) about the complete shell command and emits an allow-only decision when all pass. Otherwise it stays silent and Claude Code's normal permission flow proceeds. A SessionStart hook only prints setup warnings. It is a permission auto-approver, not a general Jev assistant for coding decisions.

Also zen, vercel, laya, custom endpoint. It uses the System One API (/api/v1/systemone), not the alpha Decisions API. Request body is {model, state:{action:'shell',resource:<command>}, questions:{...noul}} (system-one.ts:164-171). Provider is selected explicitly with no fallback.
providerSupport.others: OpenCode Zen, Vercel AI Gateway, Laya (local), custom System One-compatible endpoint
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already supported, so no patch needed. The only requirement is provider=openrouter in ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc plus OPENROUTER_API_KEY, which must be visible to the hook process (Claude Code's env or the config file).

interface.name: Hook PermissionRequest (matcher Bash), timeout 10s
interface.purpose: Reads the hook JSON, skips if the command matches a visible permissions.ask rule (ask-rules.ts), otherwise queries Jev and emits {hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName:'PermissionRequest',decision:{behavior:'allow'}}} or nothing. It never emits deny, ask or updatedInput (claude/AGENTS.md).

interface.name: Hook SessionStart (startup|resume|clear|fork), timeout 10s
interface.purpose: Emits a systemMessage warning if no config or credential exists or the config is invalid. Makes no network call.

interface.name: CLI npx @jevvy/permissions init (bin jevvy / permissions)
interface.purpose: Interactive setup that writes ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc with mode 0600 and runs 'claude plugin marketplace add' / 'claude plugin install'.

interface.name: CLI jevvy-calibrate
interface.purpose: Runs the eval/commands.json corpus against the provider to validate thresholds.

interface.name: Skill calibrate-permissions (optional, installed via npx skills add)
interface.purpose: Guides an agent through designing and validating custom approval questions. Triggered by description, only for policy calibration.

interface.name: MCP tools
interface.purpose: None. There is no MCP server.

security: MIT licence; TypeScript with the Effect library; no MCP server, no daemon, and no telemetry found (grep of src for network calls: only system-one.ts fetch to the selected provider URL).

API key is read from env (Config.redacted) or ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc, which init writes 0600 and config.ts:115 re-chmods to 0600 if it is looser. The key is sent as an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. The hook command is plain 'node dist/claude-hook.js'.

Only one global config file is read; project repositories cannot override it, which blocks a malicious-repo config attack. It does read project .claude/settings*.json ask rules and shells out to 'git rev-parse' with cwd.

Fail-closed on approval: every error, timeout, malformed output or provider failure gives silent abstention, and it can only ever emit allow. The risk is the opposite, a wrong allow. The decision comes from a probabilistic model with calibrated thresholds on a small eval set (eval/commands.json), and Theo's skepticism about Jev's quality is unverified. Command text is attacker-influenced input to the judge (prompt-injection-like surface, though the judge outputs only probabilities).

Existing allow, deny and configured ask rules stay authoritative. Managed, CLI and session-only ask rules are invisible to the hook (README), so Jev could approve something the user meant to be an ask.

Install path: marketplace source is npm @jevvy/permissions, so it pulls a third-party npm package into Claude Code. The published package has no postinstall or preinstall scripts (npm view scripts: build/prepack/postpack/prebuild only). The 'init' CLI spawns 'claude'/'opencode' installer commands. Single maintainer (Youssef Achy, 21 of 28 commits) plus release bot; CI actions are SHA-pinned; Dependabot is on. Uses release-candidate Effect 4.0.0-rc.112.
gh-panachy-jevvy.dataEgress: On each Bash PermissionRequest that reaches the hook, the full command string (action='shell', resource=<command>) plus the four fixed question texts go to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. This is not conversation text, file contents, diffs, tool outputs, or cwd. Commands can still embed inline secrets, tokens, hostnames or client paths, and no redaction is applied to outbound commands (the redact function only scrubs the API key from output). OpenRouter can log request bodies depending on the account's privacy settings. Verdicts are cached in memory per process, and each hook call is its own process, so there is effectively no cross-call cache.
gh-panachy-jevvy.failureMode: Fail-open to Claude Code's normal flow: any error, HTTP failure, malformed body, missing key or bad config gives exit 0 with empty stdout and stderr, and the permission flow is unchanged. There is a 5 s internal timeout (engine.ts:135) inside a 10 s hook timeout. On 429 or credit exhaustion it sets a cooldown, but that lives only in the process memory of a short-lived hook, so it does not persist. When Jev is slow, each prompt is delayed up to about 5 s and then falls back to a normal prompt. Under bypassPermissions the hook is not expected to fire at all.
gh-panachy-jevvy.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens. There are no MCP tools, no server instructions and no skill in the default install. The hooks inject no model-visible text except a SessionStart systemMessage warning shown only when setup is broken. The optional calibrate-permissions skill adds one skill description line.
gh-panachy-jevvy.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest matcher Bash). Fully automatic with no prompting, but it triggers only when Claude Code was about to show a Bash permission dialog. It never fires for allowed or denied commands, non-Bash tools, or (expected, from the PermissionRequest semantics) bypassPermissions mode where nothing is prompted.
gh-panachy-jevvy.latencyImpact: Per Bash permission prompt only: Node cold start plus a bundled Effect runtime (roughly 100-300 ms, an estimate not measured), plus one HTTPS round trip to OpenRouter (claimed 70-500 ms), for about 0.3-1 s typical and a 5 s worst case before falling back to the prompt. Zero added latency for non-prompted tool calls.
gh-panachy-jevvy.runtime: Node >=22.19 (TypeScript compiled and bundled with esbuild; npm package @jevvy/permissions 0.5.0). Compatible with the user's Node 24.
gh-panachy-jevvy.install: /plugin marketplace add PanAchy/jevvy ; /plugin install jevvy-permissions@jevvy (marketplace source is the npm package). Alternative: npx @jevvy/permissions init. Then set provider=openrouter in ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc and export OPENROUTER_API_KEY where Claude Code can see it.
gh-panachy-jevvy.tests: About 2,350 lines of vitest tests in packages/permissions/test plus core tests, including claude-hook, engine, providers and openrouter tests. CI (ci.yml) runs 'npm run check' on PRs, with package-smoke matrix jobs across Linux and Windows for release PRs and a Claude Code smoke script pinned to CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION 2.1.278. Changesets-based release workflow. Supply-chain hardening: pinned action SHAs. I did not run any tests.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code (openrouter.ts:5-17, System One endpoint /api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13), using OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it needs no patching for the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev.
Truly automatic: a deterministic PermissionRequest hook, with no model discretion and no 'use jev' prompting.
Very small footprint for Claude Code: zero context tokens, no MCP server, and the key is not in argv (Authorization header; config file 0600).

Conservative design: allow-only output, never denies, honours existing allow/deny/ask rules, single global config that repos cannot override, and every failure abstains silently. This is the only candidate found that uses Jev for a task matching its strengths (a typed probabilistic yes/no over app state).

Well engineered for a 12-day-old project: typed errors, 5 s timeout, rate-limit cooldown, calibration tooling and an eval corpus with a rule that any must-ask auto-approval disqualifies a run, and SHA-pinned CI.
Provider-agnostic, so it can be switched between OpenRouter and TypeSafe direct without code changes.
cons: Narrow scope: it only reduces Bash permission prompts. It does not give Claude Code Jev for routing, code review, test selection, or any coding decision.

Little to no value in the user's modes: in bypassPermissions nothing prompts, so the hook has nothing to review (the schema accepts the bypassPermissions mode literal, but the hook is a PermissionRequest event). In 'auto' mode Claude Code's own classifier already handles most approvals. The value is mainly in default or acceptEdits mode.

Sends full shell commands to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe) with no redaction. On client projects, commands can carry inline tokens, internal hostnames and paths, which conflicts with the user's existing secret-leak guard philosophy.

Security-decision correctness rests on a beta probabilistic model that skeptics compare to a small router. A false allow on a destructive or exfiltrating command is possible, and calibration covers only the shipped eval set. Managed, CLI and session ask rules are invisible to it.
Immature and a single maintainer: 20 stars, 28 commits (21 by one author), 12 days old, on release-candidate Effect 4.0.0-rc.112, with breaking policy changes already in the changelog (0.4 to 0.5).

Each hook call is a fresh Node process, so there is no cache or persistent cooldown and it adds a cold start plus a network round trip (up to 5 s) to each prompt. It could also interplay with the existing PreToolUse secret-guard and GitNexus hooks (ordering, not conflict). Unverified: I could not check actual Claude Code semantics for PermissionRequest under auto mode.
gh-panachy-jevvy.verdict: Best-executed and the only truly automatic, OpenRouter-ready Jev integration for Claude Code, but it is a narrow permission auto-approver that mostly does nothing in bypass/auto mode and sends every reviewed command to OpenRouter. Install it only if the user runs default or acceptEdits mode and accepts the command egress. Otherwise treat it as a reference recipe for building a custom Jev hook.

gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.name: skylence-org/claudecode-jev-marketplace
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.whatItDoes: Claude Code marketplace with two plugins. "core" is an opinionated Claude Code baseline (fork of core-claude 0.9.8). It bundles a regex judge-hook rules engine, writing-guard, statusline and CLAUDE.md guidelines, plus a POSIX-sh `jev` helper (curl + jq) that calls TypeSafe's System One API. Two hooks use Jev. jev-intent-gate (PreToolUse) asks two Nouls, "was this pinned dependency version backed by a registry or lockfile lookup" and "does this edit raise a version", and blocks with exit 2 if the version looks recalled from memory. jev-research-nudge (Stop) asks one Noul, "did the last assistant turn hedge a checkable fact", and blocks the first stop once to ask for verification. "herdr-agent-org" is a multi-agent org for the Herdr multiplexer. It uses Jev for a tier gauge on dispatch and a review-gate check at accept, and needs herdr >= 0.7 plus HERDR_ENV=1. The repo also carries herdr-plugins (a Rust relay daemon, waker, aw-context). The Jev surface is narrow: two rare-event gates, not a general coding assistant.

No OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only, through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate, and UNVERIFIED end to end. The base URL is env-overridable and the path is hardcoded to /v1/systemone. So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's System One endpoint. The key is a generic Bearer, so an OpenRouter key can go in TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.config/typesafe/api_key. JEV_MODEL would need to become typesafe/jev-1.13, because OpenRouter model IDs are namespaced. It works with no code change only if OpenRouter's System One request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's ({state, model, questions} in, .answers out). That is not confirmed from this repo. `jev doctor` would fail because it calls /v1/models and expects a .models[] shape. If the schema differs, the patch is a small edit to one file, scripts/jev lines 183-225. The twin copy at plugins/herdr-agent-org/scripts/jev must be changed too, because tools/check-parity.sh enforces byte-identical twins.

interface.name: hook PreToolUse: judge-hook.sh (all tools)
interface.purpose: Regex rules engine with deny/allow/gated/escalate classes over tool inputs (rm -rf, sudo, curl|sh, git-destructive and so on). Inherited from core-claude. Not Jev. Runs on every tool call.

interface.name: hook PreToolUse: jev-intent-gate.sh (Bash|Edit|Write|skyline_*)
interface.purpose: A regex pre-match on npm/pnpm/yarn/composer pinned installs or package.json/composer.json edits. Then a lookup-regex short-circuit over the last 12 commands. Only if both pass does it make one Jev call (set deps-pin: lookup_seen, raises_version). It blocks with exit 2 if the pin looks recalled from memory.

interface.name: hook PostToolUse: writing-guard.sh (Write|Edit)
interface.purpose: Flags AI writing tells in newly written content. Regex only.

interface.name: hook Stop: jev-research-nudge.sh
interface.purpose: A hedge-word grep on the last assistant text. Only if it matches does it make one Jev Noul call (hedged_fact >= 0.7). It then blocks the first stop once with a templated reason telling Claude to verify via WebSearch/WebFetch.

interface.name: skill /core:setup
interface.purpose: One-shot no-prompt installer. Rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json (statusLine, permissions.defaultMode=bypassPermissions, disableWorkflows, awaySummaryEnabled=false, promptSuggestionEnabled=false, env CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADAPTIVE_THINKING=1, DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1, DISABLE_ORG_MEMORY=1). Edits ~/.bashrc and appends a guidelines block to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Strips legacy hook entries that match judge-hook.sh, writing-guard.sh and research-nudge.sh.

interface.purpose: Read-only audit of the whole core install, including a live Jev probe.

interface.name: skills /core:session-handoff, /core:uninstall-claude, /core:purge-claude-user-scope
interface.purpose: Unrelated utilities inherited from core-claude. The uninstall and purge skills are destructive.

interface.name: CLI scripts/jev (ask|threshold|sets|doctor|cache-clear)
interface.purpose: The Jev client. `ask <set>` takes JSON state on stdin and prints typed answers. It is fail-open, has a sha256 request cache in /tmp/jev-cache-UID, appends an audit line to ~/.claude/jev-audit.jsonl, and has a JEV_STUB_ANSWERS test mode. Question sets and thresholds live in scripts/jev-questions.json, with an overlay at ~/.claude/jev-questions.json.

interface.name: plugin herdr-agent-org: tier-gauge, review-gate-check, dispatch-worker, 7 role skills, 4 session hooks, .mcp.json relay
interface.purpose: Herdr-specific agent org. Its .mcp.json points at a local HTTP MCP at http://127.0.0.1:7431/mcp (the org-relay daemon). Irrelevant unless the user runs Herdr.

security: API key handling is good. The key goes only in an Authorization header via curl; no key appears in argv. It is read from env, a chmod-600 file (with a perms warning) or the macOS Keychain (scripts/jev:71-92, :218).

The cache dir is mkdir -m 700 and only trusted if it is owned by the user and is not a symlink (scripts/jev:206-215). The audit log stores answers plus a checksum of the state, not the state itself (:22-24).
There is no curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall and no telemetry. It is pure sh + jq + curl. Install is via /plugin marketplace, ref main (a moving target, not pinned to a SHA).

The /core:setup skill is invasive. It sets bypassPermissions, disables adaptive thinking, auto-memory and org-memory, sets disableWorkflows, edits ~/.bashrc, appends to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and deletes other hook entries by regex (judge-hook.sh, writing-guard.sh, research-nudge.sh). It also installs its own judge-hook that fires on every tool call. This would collide with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks and conflicts with their CLAUDE.md conventions. It is avoidable by installing only the two Jev hooks by hand.

Prompt-injection surface: transcript content (user messages, commands, assistant text) is sent to Jev as DATA in a typed-answer model, so injection can at most flip a probability. It fails open, so injection cannot cause a lockout. It could steer a block/no-block decision. No shell execution of untrusted data was seen in the Jev hooks; the tool input is passed through jq --argjson.
The regexes are a safety net, not a security boundary. The repo says so in judge-rules.json `_caveats`.
Single maintainer, no license file at repo level (GitHub reports licenseInfo null), though plugins/core/.claude-plugin/plugin.json declares MIT. There is no LICENSE file to rely on for client work.
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.dataEgress: Per README "What leaves the box" and the code. jev-intent-gate sends the tool_input (the full Bash command or the Edit/Write content and path, which can include file contents being written to package.json/composer.json), the last 3 user messages (each truncated to 1500 chars) and the last 12 shell commands (400 chars each). It sends these only after a regex pre-match on a pinned dependency install or a package.json/composer.json edit. jev-research-nudge sends the last assistant turn (up to 12000 chars). It sends it only when that turn contains a hedge word (might, may, probably, likely and so on), which is common in prose. The herdr tier gauge sends the lane brief. The review gate sends file paths, commit subjects and the --stat summary; the diff is sent only if JEV_SEND_DIFF=1. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai today (or the OpenRouter host after patching). This is client-project data leaving the machine. JEV_DISABLE=1 per repo turns it off. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover these hooks; user messages or commands containing secrets would be sent.
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. With no key, JEV_DISABLE=1, a timeout, a non-2xx status, an unparseable reply or missing jq/curl, `jev` prints nothing and exits 0, and the hooks allow (scripts/jev header :15-19, :186-189, :203-204, :228-238). Timeout is JEV_TIMEOUT, default 5 s (curl -m), applied to the whole request. A worst case of 5 s is added only on a slow or down Jev at a matching event. Caller bugs (unknown set or invalid state) exit 2, which for a hook means block, but the bundled hooks pass fixed sets. The hooks themselves fail open on missing jq or transcript. The only new blocking behavior is exit 2 when Jev answers below its thresholds.
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.contextCost: Very low. There are no MCP tools in the core plugin. The Herdr plugin adds a relay MCP (http://127.0.0.1:7431/mcp) that will not connect unless the Herdr daemon runs. core adds 5 skill descriptions (setup, doctor, session-handoff, uninstall-claude, purge-claude-user-scope). gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.latencyImpact: The regex pre-match costs a few ms and exits before any network. That covers the intent gate on all non-dependency tool calls and the nudge on stops with no hedge word. On a match the cost is one HTTPS round trip. The README measures 1.1-1.5 s from Western Europe, and TypeSafe claims 70-500 ms. This is synchronous inside the hook, with a cap of JEV_TIMEOUT=5 s. The judge-hook is the only thing that runs on every tool call (bash plus jq, about tens of ms, no network). The Stop hook can force one extra model turn whenever the nudge fires (hedge word plus P >= 0.7), which is a real latency and token cost.
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. Once the plugin is enabled, the PreToolUse jev-intent-gate and the Stop jev-research-nudge fire automatically, with no user prompt and no model discretion, and hooks.json registers them from the plugin. Both are gated by a regex before Jev is called, so Jev is actually invoked only on dependency pins or manifest edits, and on stops with hedged prose. This is the closest of any candidate to the user's "Claude Code must use it when needed" requirement. The use cases are narrow, however.
pros: The only candidate seen that is truly automatic, through deterministic hooks (plugins/core/hooks/hooks.json), with no user prompting and no reliance on model discretion.

Reusable pattern. scripts/jev is a small POSIX sh + curl + jq client. Base URL and model are env-overridable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL), and questions and thresholds are externalized in jev-questions.json with a per-box overlay. It is easy to retarget to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.
The key is never in argv and can live in a chmod-600 file, which fits the user's security posture. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry.

Version pins recalled from memory are caught before they land, and the intent gate is deterministic-first (a lookup-regex short-circuit skips Jev when `npm view` was run). Its comments note that judge-hook's `claude -p` escalate path is inert on OAuth logins, which matches the user's login type.

cons: No OpenRouter support at all. The repo has zero mentions of openrouter, and it uses TypeSafe direct with a TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The OpenRouter patch needs TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, an OpenRouter key in place of the TypeSafe key, and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. It relies on OpenRouter's System One schema matching TypeSafe's ({state, model, questions} in, .answers out), which is unverified. `jev doctor` would break (it calls /v1/models).

The Jev use cases are tiny and niche. Two Nouls decide a dependency-pin check that a plain regex plus the lookup short-circuit mostly handles. One Noul decides a hedged-fact nudge. Neither adds much to a senior dev's daily flow, and the hedge Stop hook can be false-positive noise, forcing an extra Opus turn (hedge grep matches 'may', 'likely' and 'might' constantly, which triggers Jev on many turns).

/core:setup is heavy-handed and conflicts with this user's environment. It forces bypassPermissions, disables adaptive thinking and both memory systems, disables workflows, writes ~/.bashrc, appends a large block to the global CLAUDE.md and strips hook entries by regex. It also adds a second judge-hook PreToolUse rules engine on every tool call beside the user's existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks. To use it safely the user would have to cherry-pick the two Jev hooks and skip the setup skill. The plugin also asserts it 'replaces core-claude' (a plugin the user may not have), and the hooks.json ships judge-hook unconditionally, so installing the plugin alone gives the extra hook.

Immature and single-author. It was created 2026-09-19 (11 days old), has 14 commits, 1 contributor (Jonas Vanderhaegen), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no license file (GitHub licenseInfo null; only plugin.json says MIT) and the plugin version is 0.2.4. Data egress of client code and conversation. The last 3 user messages, the last 12 shell commands, manifest edit contents and the last assistant turn (up to 12 KB) are sent to a beta third-party endpoint. This is unsuitable for confidential client projects without a per-repo JEV_DISABLE=1, and it is outside the existing secret-leak guard's coverage.

Half of the marketplace (herdr-agent-org, org-relay, org-waker, aw-context) is irrelevant unless the user runs the Herdr multiplexer. It adds 7 skills and a local MCP entry that will just fail to connect.

Thresholds (0.6, 0.7) are uncalibrated 'starting points' from vendor cookbooks, not measured. A false-positive block at PreToolUse under bypass mode interrupts flow. The model is pinned to jev-1.13.0 with a 5 s timeout, and the README measured 1.1-1.5 s, well above the claimed 70-500 ms.
gh-skylence-org-claudecode-jev-marketpla.verdict: It is the best reference for automatic, deterministic Jev use inside Claude Code: fail-open hooks behind regex gates, and a clean env-configurable `jev` shell client. Do not install the plugin as shipped. /core:setup would override the user's permission mode, memory and thinking settings and add a competing judge-hook, and there is no OpenRouter code. Instead lift scripts/jev and the two hooks (jev-intent-gate, jev-research-nudge) into a personal plugin, point them at OpenRouter's System One endpoint with typesafe/jev-1.13 after a real schema check, and accept that the payoff is narrow.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook permission_gate.py (matcher Bash|Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit, timeout 10)
interface.purpose: Layer 1 regex hard deny (secret read plus network send, curl|sh, rm top-level, mkfs, fork bomb, ...) or ask (force push, reset --hard, sudo, terraform/kubectl apply, rm -r outside cwd, editing secret files); layer 2 silent fast-allow for known read-only/routine commands; layer 3 Jev (4s timeout, 1 try) for unclear commands, reading up to 8000 chars of a referenced script. Emits only deny/ask, never allow. JEV_GATE=off keeps hard denies only.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook prompt_router.py (timeout 15, internal 8s deadline)
interface.purpose: Skips prompts <15 chars, filler words, harness tags, and slash commands except /goal; otherwise asks Jev (5s timeout) a Choice over the skill roster plus needs_skill noul plus one noul per user-defined condition; optional second call re-ranks top 3 skills; injects <skill_relevance> hint and/or condition text/file contents as additionalContext. JEV_ROUTER=off disables.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook dispatch_router.py (matcher Agent|Task)
interface.purpose: For jev-* subagent dispatches only, Jev re-picks tier (4s timeout); applies via updatedInput with permissionDecision allow only on same read/write side, depth confidence >= 0.6, never to debugger, honours [jev:keep]. JEV_DISPATCH=apply|shadow|off.

Key name is hard-coded: hooks/runner.ts:147 reads env['TYPESAFE_API_KEY'] and client.ts:168 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (the same header OpenRouter uses). No 'openrouter' string exists anywhere in the source. The README documents only TypeSafe. OpenRouter docs (openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/systemone/submit-a-system-one-request) show the same body {model, state, questions}, and answers {type:'choice',choice,confidence,probabilities} / {type:'noul',noul}, plus usage.input_tokens/output_tokens. So the wire schema matches.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and it needs no code change. Set SKILLFUL_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, SKILLFUL_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<the OpenRouter key>. The variable name is misleading but the key is only sent as a Bearer header. Two risks to verify with one live call: (a) skillful omits 'criteria' on noul questions (types.ts:15 optional, questions.ts:119-122) and OpenRouter's docs describe noul criteria {true,false}, so a 422 is possible. A 422 would fail open into a degraded reminder. It is a one-line fix to add criteria. (b) the response 'model' string differs, which is harmless. Env vars must reach the hook process: put them in the ~/.claude/settings.json 'env' block, or wrap the hook command in a small shell script that exports them from a 0600 file.
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct is implemented. Pi, OMP and Codex are other host runtimes, not other providers.

interface.name: skillful hook (UserPromptSubmit, matcher '*')

interface.name: skillful install / uninstall [--runtime --dry-run --json]
interface.purpose: Merges or removes its hook in the settings files for Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OMP. It makes a timestamped backup and an atomic write, and removes only its own entries (json-hook.ts). It writes a ~40-line TS extension for Pi and OMP.

interface.name: skillful doctor [--offline]
interface.purpose: Checks that the hook works, including a live trial route.

interface.name: skillful route --prompt --explain [--model --no-prompt-upload]
interface.purpose: Routes one prompt manually and shows the shortlist, BM25 scores and noul ranking.

interface.name: skillful catalog [--summary --kind --runtime]
interface.purpose: Lists the capabilities found on the machine.

interface.name: skillful eval [--recall-only --replay --record --sweep]
interface.purpose: Scores the router against fixtures.

interface.name: skillful bench
interface.purpose: Runs the SWE-bench A/B outcome benchmark in Docker. It has never been run.

interface.name: skillful report / dashboard / telemetry
interface.purpose: Writes a self-contained HTML report from the local events.jsonl.

interface.name: skillful export-case
interface.purpose: Exports a redacted routing case for a bug report.

interface.name: No MCP tools, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json

gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.lastCommit: 2026-09-17 (bcea00b, CI release via npm trusted publishing)
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.runtime: Node >=20, TypeScript compiled with tsc, ESM, pnpm workspace. No runtime dependencies (only devDependency @types/node). Version 0.2.0.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.install: The README says `npx @mrgoonie/skillful install`. The package is NOT on npm: `npm view @mrgoonie/skillful` returns E404 on 2026-09-30, and GitHub has no releases or tags. The release workflow exists but appears never to have published. The only route today is clone, `pnpm install && pnpm build`, then `node packages/cli/dist/bin.js install`. The hook command is hard-wired to absolute node and dist paths (installers/types.ts:56), so the built checkout has to be kept in place.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.tests: 15 vitest test files (route, retrieval, bm25, hooks, redact, telemetry, config, catalog, eval metrics, bench analysis). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs typecheck, test, build and a CLI smoke test with least-privilege permissions. There is also an eval-gate workflow. I did not run anything. The 'live Codex session receiving an injection' is admitted as unverified in the README.
security: No runtime dependencies and no postinstall/preinstall scripts, so the npm supply-chain surface is small. The release workflow uses npm trusted publishing (OIDC) with provenance.

API key is read only from the environment: never a CLI flag (so it is not in argv or `ps`), never a config file (config/resolve.ts:39 rejects key fields), and client.ts:4-8 states it is never put in an error message. Sent only as an Authorization Bearer header.

Install modifies the shared ~/.claude/settings.json (timestamped backup, atomic write, idempotent, remove-only-own-entries). If the JSON is unparseable it writes nothing. It also silently installs into Codex, Pi and OMP configs if those are present, unless --runtime claude-code is passed.

Prompt-injection surface: the injected text contains the skill or MCP name and a 140-180 char description taken from SKILL.md frontmatter (render.ts:73), i.e. attacker-influenced content from any installed plugin or project-local .claude/skills or .mcp.json flows into model context. It is capped at 480 chars and prefixed '[skillful]', so the risk is low but not zero.

The live request has NO secret redaction. redact.ts is only used for `export-case`. MCP entries are described as 'MCP server (transport): <url or command>' (collect.ts:107-112). A URL containing a token or query key, or a project .mcp.json in a client repo, would be sent to the provider if that server makes the shortlist. The prompt is truncated to 1000 chars (thresholds.ts:51) but is otherwise sent raw, so a pasted secret would leak. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover UserPromptSubmit.

Local files: ~/.cache/skillful/routes.json (stores a prompt hash, not the prompt) and ~/.local/state/skillful/events.jsonl (0600, hash and char count only). No telemetry leaves the machine and there is no update check (docs/telemetry.md).
Child-process use is limited to the Pi/OMP extension source, the bench Docker runner and `dashboard` opening a file. None of it is on the Claude Code hook path.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.dataEgress: Per prompt, on a cache miss, to the configured base URL (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter with SKILLFUL_BASE_URL): (1) the user's prompt text, truncated to 1000 chars (route.ts:194-197), unless SKILLFUL_UPLOAD_PROMPT=false, which sends '(prompt withheld...)' and lets Jev choose only from the locally chosen shortlist; (2) about 15 candidate capabilities from the local catalog: id, kind, name and a description of up to 200 chars. The id embeds runtime and scope; MCP descriptions carry the server URL or command string. Never sent: file contents, diffs, tool outputs, the conversation transcript, sourcePath, MCP args or env. With OpenRouter the same payload also transits OpenRouter, and OpenRouter's docs list optional session_id, user and trace fields that skillful does not set. Because the prompt goes to a third party on client projects, that is a confidentiality decision.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.failureMode: Fail-open by design, and this is the strongest part of the code. The hook has a 2000 ms total budget (SKILLFUL_BUDGET_MS, thresholds.ts:50), a 1800 ms per-attempt HTTP timeout, and up to 2 retries with backoff only on 429 and 529, all bounded by an AbortSignal (client.ts, route.ts:206-221). A top-level catch in runner.ts:227 guarantees a return, exit 0 and nothing on stderr. Caveat: on every degraded path (timeout, 401, 5xx, network, malformed, missing key) it injects one line into context: '[skillful] Could not resolve a capability suggestion... run: npx @mrgoonie/skillful' (degrade.ts:131). With no key configured, or with the key or endpoint wrong, every single prompt gets that noise line and a wasted scan. The prompt is never blocked. A skipped or none decision injects nothing.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens and no server instructions. Hook-injected text is at most 480 chars, about 120 tokens, only when a capability is chosen with sufficient probability (noneThreshold 0.4, minWinnerProbability 0.25). Most trivial or local-edit prompts inject nothing by design. On any degraded path it injects a 150-char (about 40 token) reminder every prompt. Net context cost is very low, but the user's CLAUDE.md-style skill list is already in Claude Code's context, so the benefit is also low.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: a UserPromptSubmit command hook that runs on every user prompt with no model discretion and no need to say 'use jev'. That matches the user's automatic-integration requirement. Scope limit: it only fires on user prompts. It does not see tool calls, plans, diffs or subagent decisions.
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, with no prompting needed and no MCP tools to bloat context.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, code is small and readable, and the fail-open design is genuinely careful (top-level catch, exit 0, budget-bounded aborts, retries only on 429/529).

Key handling is disciplined: env-only, never argv, never logged. Install is idempotent with backups and only removes its own hook entries, so it is safe next to the existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
Provider switch to OpenRouter is a pure config change (SKILLFUL_BASE_URL + SKILLFUL_MODEL + key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), because the wire schema matches OpenRouter's System One API.

Honest about its limits: README publishes recall 0.60 holdout / 0.82 dev, says the outcome benchmark was never run, and makes no unproven claims. Good use of Choice with a 'none' option and per-candidate Noul, which is a proper fit for Jev's primitives.
Has privacy knobs (SKILLFUL_UPLOAD_PROMPT=false, SKILLFUL_DISABLE=1) and local-only telemetry.
cons: Solves a marginal problem for this user: Claude Code already lists installed skills and agents with descriptions in context. There is no evidence that a hint improves task outcomes (benchmark never run), and holdout recall is only 0.60 against its own 0.90 target, so it will often miss or suggest the wrong capability.

Not published on npm (E404) and has no releases, so the advertised `npx @mrgoonie/skillful install` fails today. It needs a clone and build, with the hook pinned to an absolute checkout path. Very young (13 days), 15 commits, one author, 5 stars, and its own docs admit Claude Code's OAuth session was untested for the bench.

Adds synchronous latency to EVERY prompt, up to a 2 s budget (README cold route 1446 ms), on top of Node startup and a catalog scan across a large plugin tree. That is a poor trade for a daily-driver workflow.

Sends the raw prompt (up to 1000 chars) plus catalog names and MCP URL/command strings to a third party with no secret redaction on the live path (redact.ts is export-case only). That is risky for client projects, and the existing secret guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit. The upload can be disabled but then the model sees no task text.

Key variable is hard-coded as TYPESAFE_API_KEY (runner.ts:147), so OpenRouter use needs an alias, and there is no first-class OpenRouter support or test. noul criteria omitted might 422 on OpenRouter (unverified). Env must reach the hook via settings.json env (plaintext key) or a wrapper.

Degraded/no-key state injects a nag line into context on every prompt, which is the opposite of unobtrusive. Only routes to skills, MCP servers, agents and commands. It does not use Jev for other coding decisions (permission risk, commit/PR gating, test selection, code-review triage), which is where a fast typed-decision model would add real value.
gh-bestagentkits-jev-skillful.verdict: Well-engineered, safe-to-fail hook that gives the automatic no-prompting integration the user wants and can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars. But it is unpublished, unproven on outcomes (recall 0.60 holdout), adds up to about 1.5 s to every prompt, sends prompts to a third party unredacted, and only routes skills and MCPs, which Claude Code already lists. Treat it as an optional experiment or as a reference implementation of Jev-in-a-hook (Choice plus Noul with a 'none' option), not as the daily driver.

gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.name: darwintechlab/claude-jev
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace "openjev", plugin "claude-jev" v0.1.1) bundling a local stdio Node MCP server "jev" with 5 tools (jev_choice, jev_noul, jev_score, jev_ask, jev_doctor) that POST {model,state,questions} to the TypeSafe System One endpoint, plus a skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) that tells Claude to prefer Jev for bounded decisions. Adds client-side validation, retries, confidence gating (auto/escalate), criteria linting, head+tail truncation at 60k chars and a stderr audit log (state hash only). It is a mirror of the author's opencode-openjev; no hooks, no proxy. Built plugin/runtime/*.mjs is a committed esbuild bundle (about 950 KB total, dominated by the MCP SDK and zod/ajv chunks).

providerSupport.evidence: mcp-server/src/client.ts:51 default baseURL `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`; client.ts:117-118 body `{model,state,questions}` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; mcp-server/src/index.ts:17-19 reads only CLAUDE_JEV_API_KEY / CLAUDE_JEV_MODEL / CLAUDE_JEV_BASE_URL, injected by plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json userConfig (api_key, model default `jev-latest`, base_url) -> env mapping. index.ts:32 hardcodes backend label "typesafe" (audit cosmetic only). No occurrence of openrouter anywhere in the repo (grep). Explicit no-fallback: README says shell TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_API_KEY are NOT read by the installed plugin.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same {model,state,questions} body and returns {model,answers,usage} (the URL suffix /v1/systemone matches TypeSafe's, which suggests it does, but I could not verify OpenRouter's schema from this repo). No code change needed: in the plugin config set base_url=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, api_key=OpenRouter key, model=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Caveats: the key is entered via an interactive userConfig prompt (not an env var), so OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the shell is ignored; tool descriptions mention model 'jev-latest'; the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported.

interface.name: skill jev (/jev)

gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.runtime: Node >=20 (stdio MCP server, TypeScript bundled with esbuild into committed plugin/runtime/*.mjs; deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, zod, ajv bundled)

Or `claude --plugin-dir ./plugin` from a clone of claude-jev. Then enter the API key in the userConfig dialog and run jev_doctor.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.tests: 5 offline node --test suites (plugin, metrics, gate, client, baseline; about 22 KB) that spin a local test endpoint; no CI workflow (.github absent); no releases or tags. Not run by me (static reading only).
security: API key handled well: marked sensitive userConfig, passed to the MCP process via env CLAUDE_JEV_API_KEY (plugin.json mcpServers.jev.env), never in argv; no .env auto-load or fallback to shell keys in the shipped runtime; errors do not print the key (client.ts:129 prints only status and up to 800 chars of the response body).

No child_process/spawn/exec in the shipped runtime (grep of index.mjs and chunk-A3CL7OOL/LX7VSNGJ/QTEOOZ7M found none; the only fetch is client.mjs chunk line 125 to baseURL). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the configured endpoint. Bundled node_modules code is minified-free but large (about 750 KB of vendored MCP SDK/zod/ajv), hard to audit; THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES included.
base_url is user-configurable and receives both the Bearer key and all decision text; a wrong/malicious base_url exfiltrates key + state. Default is the legit typesafe host.

Prompt-injection surface: tool result is model-authored-free JSON (choice/probabilities) so low; but `state` is attacker-influenceable content (repo text, tool output) and Jev has no reasoning trace, so a gate decision on injected text is manipulable. SKILL.md encourages Claude to auto-act on 'auto' results; the README itself says keep irreversible actions behind human approval.
Audit log goes to MCP stderr (Claude Code debug log) and uses a 32-bit FNV hash of state: not a security hash, weak for low-entropy text but no raw state is logged.
Release files are committed generated bundles (no reproducible-build CI), so the runtime cannot be trusted to match TS source without rebuilding; spot-check of endpoint/env/tool text matched source.

Single anonymous author group ('OpenJev Contributors', darwintechlab), 4 days old; supply-chain trust is low. Marketplace install instructions point at a different repo (claude-openjev) than the one audited.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.dataEgress: On every jev_* call the full `state` string (up to 60k chars; whatever Claude puts in it: code, diffs, commands, file contents, ticket text) plus the question schema (instructions, criteria) and the API key are sent over HTTPS to base_url (default api.typesafe.ai, or openrouter.ai if reconfigured). Nothing is sent automatically by the plugin itself; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool. No telemetry elsewhere. README warns not to send secrets, but nothing in the code scrubs secrets; the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tool inputs unless its matcher is extended.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: on error/timeout the tool returns isError JSON {ok:false,error} (index.ts:168-170) and Claude just continues with its own judgment; no hook is in the path so nothing blocks. Client timeout 15 s per attempt, 2 retries with exponential backoff on 429/529/5xx/timeouts/network errors (client.ts:39-41,121-163), so the worst case for a hung endpoint is about 45 s plus backoff of one stalled tool call. Missing key throws immediately 'API key is required'. Invalid JSON in criteria/questions strings throws (caught).
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.latencyImpact: Per tool call: one extra model turn for Claude to emit the call plus the network round trip. Author's claim p50 about 300 ms API latency (README 307 ms, bench says 223 ms in another spot); the total added to a turn is dominated by Claude's own tool-call generation (1-3 s of Opus output) and result read, so Jev is net slower than Claude deciding inline unless the decision would otherwise need a separate LLM call. Zero cost on turns where Jev is not called; no hooks, so no per-tool-call overhead. Node MCP server startup about 100-300 ms once per session.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Tool names+descriptions+schemas total about 2.9k chars, roughly 700-800 tokens permanently in the tool list (unless Claude Code tool-search defers them). No server-level 'instructions' field. Skill adds only its frontmatter description (about 400 chars, about 100 tokens) always; the SKILL.md body (about 3.3k chars, about 850 tokens) loads when triggered. Zero hook-injected text. Each result is pretty-printed JSON (JSON.stringify(...,null,2)), typically 150-600 tokens; jev_ask echoes the full answers map.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: an MCP tool set plus a description-triggered skill. There is no hook, proxy or router, so nothing is deterministic. Whether Opus 5.5 calls jev_* for a given decision depends on it judging the skill description/tool descriptions relevant; for a general coding agent, bounded classification decisions rarely arise as explicit steps, so calls will be sporadic. Could be made deterministic only by adding your own PreToolUse hook that calls Jev (not provided; gateGuardrail is exported but unused).
pros: Cleanest integration mechanism of the kind: proper Claude Code plugin with userConfig, sensitive key storage, and a stdio MCP server; base_url and model are user-configurable (plugin.json userConfig), so pointing at OpenRouter needs no code change if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body.

Reasonable engineering: input validation before network, retry/backoff, 15 s timeout, head+tail truncation, confidence gating with asymmetric fail-closed guardrail helper, key never on argv, no shell execution, no postinstall, MIT license.
jev_ask batches up to 32 typed questions in a single call, which suits a future hook that asks several safety/routing questions at once.
Small footprint: 5 tools (about 750 tokens) and a short skill; no per-call hook overhead so it cannot slow normal coding.
Ships a skill description that explicitly nudges Claude to reach for Jev on bounded decisions without the user saying 'use jev'.
cons: Only model-discretion invocation: no hook, so it does not satisfy 'Claude Code must use it when needed' deterministically; in practice Opus will mostly decide inline and rarely call jev_* for routine editing/search tasks.

No OpenRouter support in code (zero references); works only via manual base_url override to an endpoint whose schema I could not verify; key must be typed into a plugin config dialog, OPENROUTER_API_KEY env is ignored, which is awkward for headless/scripted setups. Does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) or model ids beyond a free-text model field.

Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-24, 7 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, no CI; README and marketplace instructions reference a different repo (claude-openjev), and the description calls itself a 'mirror of opencode-openjev', so upstream provenance is confusing.

Benchmarks are self-authored (115 cases, vendor-adjacent), README claims of 90% accuracy, 'calibrated' probabilities and 1/128 cost vs Opus are unverified; author's own severity scoring accuracy is 67%. Latency claims are inconsistent (307 ms vs 223 ms).
Unused value: guardrail gate (gate.ts:200-218) that would be the most useful piece for a PreToolUse safety check is not wired to anything; user would have to build the hook himself.

Sends full state (code, diffs, command text) to a third party with a beta model; no secret scrubbing; on client projects this is a data-handling/NDA concern and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* inputs.
Each Jev call costs an extra Opus turn to write the call and read JSON, so net latency and tokens are usually worse than letting Opus decide inline; up to about 45 s stall if the endpoint hangs.
Committed 950 KB bundled runtime is hard to audit and not reproducibly built in CI; 32-bit FNV 'hash' in audit log.
gh-darwintechlab-claude-jev.verdict: A tidy, safe-looking but very new and self-benchmarked MCP plugin that gives Claude typed Jev tools; it is only model-discretion (no hook), has no native OpenRouter support (needs a base_url override that is unverified against OpenRouter's schema), so it does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' requirement on its own. Useful as a transport/reference for a custom PreToolUse hook or as an optional MCP tool, not as the primary integration.

gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.name: DarioFontanel/jev-claude-code
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.whatItDoes: Not a plugin or package: a repo of three Italian-language copy-paste prompts (prompts/01-model-router.md, 02-context-compaction.md, 03-code-review.md) that make Claude Code generate the integration inside the user's project. 01 builds a Claude Code "function hook" TypeScript module (.claude/skills/jev-router/) that calls Jev once at the first prompt of a session (plus once per subagent spawn) to pick the model tier (Sonnet/Opus/Fable) and effort, then overrides them on turn.step. 02 builds a function hook on session.compact that replaces native compaction: it sends tool-call contents to Jev in batches with a noul "still needed?" question and drops or truncates the rest. 03 builds a Python jev-review/review.py that sends a diff plus 14 typed questions to Jev in one call, computes a verdict (BLOCK, SECURITY REVIEW, NITS, MERGE) from JSON thresholds, plus a /jev-review skill. No source code exists in the repo; only README, LICENSE and 3 prompt files (56 KB total).

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, and the work is done by prompt edit rather than code patch. The request body (model, state, questions with type/instructions/criteria; response answers.<id>.noul/choice/score/confidence) is the System One schema, so it should be the same shape at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. Changes needed: replace the URL, use OPENROUTER_API_KEY as the Bearer key, and use model id 'typesafe/jev-latest' or 'typesafe/jev-1.13' instead of 'jev-latest'. Caveat: OpenRouter's request/response wrapper is unverified here, so the prompts' 'follow the live docs' clause would need to point at OpenRouter docs. The bigger blockers are not the provider, see cons.

interface.name: function hook prompt.submit (generated by prompt 01)
interface.purpose: On first prompt of a session, POST the prompt text to Jev with choice(tier fast/balanced/deep), score(effort 0-3) and noul(risky) questions; timeout 1500 ms; decision cached for the whole session

interface.name: function hook turn.step (main loop only)
interface.purpose: Apply the cached model and effort decision to every step via next({...e, model, effort}); thresholds: raise needs confidence >= 0.3, lower needs >= 0.6, risky > 0.7 forces deep tier and effort >= high

interface.name: function hook agent.spawn / session.start (prompt 01)
interface.purpose: Classify each subagent's {prompt, description, agentType} with its own Jev call and set its model alias; session.start resets the decision

interface.name: function hook session.compact (generated by prompt 02)
interface.purpose: Replace native /compact and auto-compact: batches of tool calls (state capped 25k tokens, request 30k) sent to Jev with a noul keep question (KEEP_THRESHOLD 0.5); the last 6 messages are preserved; discarded results are truncated to 300 chars; falls back to native compaction on any failure; timeout 8 s; CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE sets the trigger threshold

interface.name: /jev-review skill + jev-review/review.py --diff|--git|--working|--json|--escalate (prompt 03)
interface.purpose: Send a diff with 14 typed checks in one call; code computes the verdict from a JSON policy; the skill description triggers on phrases like 'review these changes with Jev', 'can I merge?', 'check the diff before commit'

interface.name: CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 (project .claude/settings.json env)
interface.purpose: Enables the early-access function-hook engine that 01 and 02 depend on; the prompt also asks to blank CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC if the user has it set

gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.runtime: No runtime shipped. Generated code: TypeScript function-hook modules run in-process by Claude Code (01, 02); Python 3.10+ stdlib-only script (03).
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.install: No install. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY, open claude in the project, paste the prompt block, and Claude generates .claude/skills/jev-router (or jev-compact, jev-review) plus a project .claude/settings.json env entry CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. Per-project by default; the prompt says the folder can be moved to ~/.claude/skills for global use.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.tests: None in the repo (no code). The prompts instruct Claude to write tests (hooks/*.test.ts with the claude-code/testing kit, plus 'claude plugin validate/test') in the generated output, but those are not reviewed or shipped artifacts. No CI, no releases.
security: No shipped executable code, so no postinstall, curl|sh or telemetry in the repo itself. All risk lives in the code Claude generates from the prompts at paste time, which is non-deterministic per run and must be reviewed by the user.

API key read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or settings env; README says never paste it in chat. Bearer token goes in an HTTP header via $.http.fetch, not in argv. In 03 the Python script reads os.environ, so no argv exposure.

Hook 02 exfiltrates tool-call content (file reads, Bash output, possibly secrets or .env contents that the user's existing secret-guard would otherwise block) to a third party; nothing in the prompt redacts secrets before sending.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs and the user prompt are placed in Jev's 'state'. Jev returns only numbers, so injection can at worst skew keep/drop decisions or tier choices, not run commands. However, a poisoned prompt or tool result could trick the router into a low tier or the compaction into dropping safety-relevant results.
Router hook silently downgrades the model to a smaller tier on Jev's decision; policy thresholds are hardcoded in the generated code.

Relies on an early-access, undocumented function-hook API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS) that the README itself says changes between releases; the prompts tell Claude to regenerate types from the local build and trust those over the prompt.
Requires disabling CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC if the user has set it, a broadening of network egress.
Author's own Italian marketing footer and social links; low trust signal (1 author, 7 stars, 1 week old). Referenced upstream: an X post by Paolo Rosson for the review schema.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.dataEgress: 01 router: the full text of the first user prompt of each session, plus each subagent's prompt, description and agentType, sent to api.typesafe.ai (would be openrouter.ai after patching). 02 compaction: the contents of tool calls and results from the conversation (file contents, command output, search results; up to 25k tokens of state per request, 30k per request, several batches) at every /compact or auto-compact. 03 review: the entire git diff plus title and description, on each /jev-review. Nothing is sent when the key is missing. On OpenRouter this data would also transit OpenRouter, so it is subject to that gateway's logging and provider policies. This matters for client projects.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.failureMode: Fail-open by design for 01 and 02. Router: 1500 ms Promise.race timeout, any error means no decision, the session keeps its native model, and it retries at the next prompt. Compaction: 8 s timeout (under the hook's 10 s budget), any error, missing key or a reduction under 15% delegates to native compaction (next(e)). Review (03) is on demand; a missing key exits with code 4 and Claude stops and says where to set it. A failed Jev call in the review does not block a commit because it is not gated by a hook. The hook engine can also skip a hook if it exceeds its budget; the prompt notes 'delegates to native without saying so'.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.contextCost: Near zero permanent context: no MCP server, no tools. Hooks inject no text into the model context; only a single transcript UI line ('[jev-router] sessione: sonnet · effort low') appears, plus a status bar and toast during compaction that are UI-only. The /jev-review skill adds one skill description (~50 tokens) to the skills list. The one-time generation cost is high: pasting a 12-20 KB prompt (about 3-5k tokens each) plus Claude building files with tests is a long agentic turn. Compaction can even reduce context, replacing the summary with verbatim pruning.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.latencyImpact: Router: one call per session at the first prompt (claimed 300-800 ms, 1.5 s hard cap) plus one call per subagent spawn; nothing on later turns. Compaction: adds about 1 s per Jev batch (several sequential batches, 8 s cap per request) at compaction time only, replacing the native LLM summary call (which is itself slow), so it may be net faster. Review: one call per /jev-review, roughly 1 s plus git diff time.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for 01 and 02: prompt.submit, turn.step, agent.spawn and session.compact fire without user prompting once the project has the folder and the env flag. 03 is a skill triggered by its description ('can I merge?', 'check the diff before commit') or /jev-review, so it is model-discretion, not deterministic. All of it is per-project unless the user moves it to ~/.claude/skills, and a project's .claude/skills is only loaded after the trust prompt is accepted.
pros: Only candidate here that actually hooks Jev into Claude Code deterministically (prompt.submit, turn.step, agent.spawn, session.compact), which matches the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement better than an MCP tool the model must choose to call.

Correct System One request/response contract with concrete typed questions (choice/score/noul), thresholds kept in code rather than in the model, and a documented 1500 ms/8 s timeout with fail-open fallback to native behaviour.
Design is sound for cache: decides the model once per session because switching invalidates the prompt cache; subagents get their own classification. Zero tool-definition context cost.
Prompt-form means auditable: the user reads the full spec before pasting, and generated code lives in the user's own repo with no third-party runtime, no npm/pip dependency and no postinstall.
Provider swap to OpenRouter is a URL, key and model-id edit (openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, typesafe/jev-latest), as the schema is the System One shape.
MIT license; prompt 03's policy-in-JSON review design (14 checks, BLOCK/SECURITY REVIEW/NITS/MERGE) is a reusable pattern.
cons: It is not an installable integration: 2 commits, 1 author, 7 stars, created 7 days before the audit date, no code, tests or CI in the repo. Output varies per Claude run and needs review each time.

Depends on the early-access, unstable function-hook engine (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1) that could break on any Claude Code update; I could not verify that it exists in Claude Code 2.1.285. It must be enabled through the settings env.

Router value is doubtful for this user: on a subscription/OAuth login with Opus 5.5 as the main model, auto-downgrading to Sonnet or overriding effort can reduce quality on client work, and the hardcoded model IDs (claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5-5, claude-fable-5-1) may not match the account. The saving of tokens is small on a flat-rate plan.

Compaction hook sends raw tool outputs (files, command output, possibly secrets) to a third party at every compact; there is no redaction, which is a bad fit for client projects, and it would bypass the intent of the user's PreToolUse secret guard.

Compaction replacing native summaries is a risky semantic change: dropping tool results by a noul probability can remove context the model needs, and the 'still needed?' judgement is by a small non-reasoning model.
Hardwired to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (which requires early-access approval); the prompts do not mention OpenRouter, so the user must edit each of the three prompts.
Prompts are in Italian only, and everything is per-project by default (must be moved to ~/.claude/skills for global use), with a project trust prompt gating .claude/skills.
Review skill (03) is model-triggered and needs a manual key; the diff (full client code) leaves the machine.
gh-dariofontanel-jev-claude-code.verdict: A well-designed but immature set of copy-paste prompts, not a maintained integration; its hook-based, fail-open architecture is the right shape for automatic use, but it depends on an unstable early-access hook engine and has no OpenRouter support out of the box. Use it as a reference design (especially the session-start tier router and the policy-in-code review), not as a drop-in; skip the compaction hook for client repos because of data egress.

interface.name: mcp__jev__jev_rank
