security: No postinstall/preinstall/prepare scripts in package.json; only prepublishOnly. Runtime deps are just @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod (small surface).
Runtime server makes exactly one outbound HTTPS POST per tool call to the host the key belongs to; never reads files, git state or session on its own (SECURITY.md, client.ts). No telemetry found.

Key routing guard: key sent only to the host matching its prefix; a mismatched TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is refused; custom proxy needs JEV_CODE_PROVIDER for non-TypeSafe keys (config.ts:292-303). Good design.

Key exposure: `setup` copies the key into `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...` (src/setup/index.ts:329,296) so the key appears in argv (visible in ps for the moment the child runs) and is stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. Redaction is applied to printed output only (index.ts:311-318). Avoid by using the plugin route + shell-exported env, or --no-env.

Tool results are JSON of numbers/labels computed locally from the model's typed answer; no free text from Jev returns, so Jev itself is a weak prompt-injection channel. Class labels/ids echoed back come from the agent's own input. Injection-into-Jev risk (untrusted text making it label wrongly) exists but consequences are limited to bad decisions; skill says keep destructive actions behind confirmation.

Tools annotated readOnlyHint/idempotentHint but openWorldHint true (server.ts:46); with bypass permissions they run without prompts, so any content the agent chooses to classify (code, diffs, logs, possibly secrets) is sent to OpenRouter -> TypeSafe with no gating.

Supply chain: launched via `npx -y` at pinned 0.3.0 (good vs floating), but the package is a 3-day-old npm publish (created 2026-09-27, 2 versions) from a single individual maintainer, not affiliated with TypeSafe (README says so). Pin and review before trusting with an OpenRouter key that also funds other models.
Setup writes config with timestamped backups and leaves malformed JSON untouched; runs harness CLIs via spawn without shell (setup/exec.ts). No curl|sh installer.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.dataEgress: Only what the model puts in tool arguments (items[].text up to 4000 chars each, state/diff/log excerpts, class/question text, candidate excerpts; up to ~120k chars per request, src/core/limits.ts) is POSTed to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with Bearer key plus HTTP-Referer/X-Title attribution headers (identifies the app as jev-code to OpenRouter). Passes through OpenRouter to TypeSafe. Nothing is read from the repo, session or files automatically; no telemetry. Note the skill actively encourages sending raw diffs, logs and file excerpts, which for client projects means client code leaves the machine via two third parties (OpenRouter, TypeSafe); check client NDAs and OpenRouter data policy settings.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: client errors are caught and returned as an MCP isError text result "jev_x failed: ..." (server.ts:52-57), so the agent just continues and falls back to its own reasoning; no hook blocks anything. Client is lazy: a missing key surfaces as a tool error, not a server crash (server.ts:32-37), but an MCP server that fails to start (e.g. npx offline on first run) just leaves the tools absent. Default per-attempt timeout 30 s with 2 retries on 408/425/429/5xx/timeouts and exponential backoff (500 ms to 8 s, honours Retry-After capped at 30 s) (client.ts:30-33,99-103), so worst case a single tool call can stall ~90+ s before failing (tune JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES=0/1 for interactive use). Local input validation rejects oversized requests before spending a call.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.contextCost: 5 MCP tools always present in the tool list (deferred loading via ToolSearch may reduce this in Claude Code 2.1.x). Estimate from source: tool descriptions ~550-800 chars each (~3.3k chars) plus zod-derived JSON schemas for 5 tools (src/tools/schemas.ts 6.8k chars plus per-tool schema code; generated JSON schema with descriptions likely 8-12k chars) -> roughly 3,000-4,500 tokens for tool defs. MCP server 'instructions' = USAGE_GUIDANCE, 6 sentences ~1.2k chars (~300 tokens), injected into system prompt every session (server.ts:30). Skill: name + ~1,000-char description always in the skill listing (~250-300 tokens); full SKILL.md (~7.5k chars, ~1.9k tokens) loads only when triggered, references on demand. No hook-injected text (no hooks). Total steady-state overhead about 3.5-5k tokens/session.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.latencyImpact: Zero on turns that don't use it (no hooks, nothing on the critical path). Per call: npx cold start once per session for the stdio server (fast when cached, slow/needs network on first run), then one HTTPS round trip to OpenRouter: claimed 70-500 ms model latency plus OpenRouter hop, so roughly 0.3-1 s typical; unbounded by the 30 s timeout x3 attempts in worst case. Batching means one call regardless of item count.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.autoInvocation: Model-discretion. The MCP tools sit in the tool list and the /jev skill has a long description with explicit triggers ('labelling or routing many items', 'yes/no checks', 'ranking candidates', 'prefer over eyeballing, regex, one frontier-model call per item') plus MCP server instructions and per-tool descriptions written as 'use instead of X' nudges. There is no deterministic hook, so Opus 5.5 decides; it will fire on batch-triage-shaped tasks (CI failures, many files, issue labelling) but never automatically on ordinary edits, and Opus may often judge it can do the classification itself. README's own example still prompts explicitly ('Triage the failing tests...'). For a stronger guarantee the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or their own hooks.
pros: Native OpenRouter support verified in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY / sk-or- prefix auto-routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (providers.ts:42-55, client.ts:27,93), no patching needed, and the correct System One surface is used.

Best-fit packaging for the 'automatic, no prompting' goal among file-based options: MCP tools plus a skill whose description is written as concrete triggers, plus server-level instructions and 'use X instead of Y' tool guidelines; installs as a Claude Code plugin marketplace (single command, auto-updatable) or `claude mcp add`.
Zero hook overhead: no latency on normal turns, and no interference with existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, GitNexus graph hooks or caveman hooks (none installed).
Thoughtful key safety: key never sent to a host that didn't issue it, proxy override rules, masked logging, backups of edited configs, no shell in setup, no postinstall script.

Well-designed local policy layer: batching (64 items/250 candidates per request), local input validation and size budget before spending a call, thresholded auto/review decisions, any_relevant on rank so a top hit isn't mistaken for an answer; fail-open errors returned as tool results.
Tools annotated readOnlyHint/idempotentHint, sensible for permission modes; retries with Retry-After honoured; version-pinned npx launch.
Large test suite with CI across Node 20/22/24, npm provenance, active same-day releases, responsive single maintainer; MIT license; Node 24 on user's machine is supported.
Jev's use cases (CI failure triage, rank candidate files, verify PR claims, injection screening of fetched pages) map to real coding-agent chores; cost ~$0.04/M input tokens is negligible.
cons: Not truly automatic: purely model-discretion (skill/tool description). No hook, so Opus 5.5 will frequently just do the triage/ranking itself; auto-invocation will be inconsistent and only for batch-shaped tasks. True guarantee needs extra CLAUDE.md rules or custom hooks.

Very young and single-maintainer: repo created 2026-09-19, npm package created 2026-09-27 with only 2 versions, 23 commits, 1 human contributor, 32 stars, unofficial and unaffiliated with TypeSafe. API/tool shapes may churn (0.x).

Key handling in setup: passes key via `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` (argv briefly visible; stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json). Plugin route avoids this but then the key must be in the environment Claude Code inherits; whether Claude Code forwards that env var to the plugin MCP process was not verified (README itself warns some harnesses filter env).
Sends raw code/diffs/logs to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no confirmation under bypass permission mode; relevant for client projects under NDA. Skill actively encourages passing raw evidence.

Sends bare model alias 'jev-latest' to OpenRouter rather than documented IDs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest; unverified live here. Easy override via TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL but a possible first-run 400.
Default failure timing is generous (30 s x 3 attempts) so a degraded Jev could stall a turn ~90 s; should set JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES.

Context tax of ~3.5-5k tokens/session (5 tool schemas + server instructions + long skill description) for tools that may fire rarely; jev_rank/jev_ask overlap with GitNexus/grep for code search, and skeptic claim that Jev is 'a flash router' means classification quality is unproven on code.
Jev is classification only (no free text), so value in daily coding is narrow (triage, gating, ranking); it does not replace any editing/reasoning workflow.
Uses npx at each MCP start: needs network/cache; cold start latency and supply-chain exposure to npm for a young package.
gh-francoischastel-jev-code.verdict: Best-packaged and most complete option for using OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code: native OpenRouter routing, MCP tools plus a trigger-rich skill, no hooks, fail-open behavior, good tests. Its limits are that invocation is model-discretion only (not deterministic), it is a 3-day-old single-maintainer package, and the value is limited to batch-classification chores. Install via the plugin route with OPENROUTER_API_KEY exported in the shell and short timeouts, and add a CLAUDE.md nudge or a small custom hook if you want stricter automatic use.

gh-shitianfang-jev-use.dataEgress: To the configured provider (OpenRouter https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, or TypeSafe/Vercel if their keys are set and take priority): for jev_judge, whatever `state` string the model chooses to paste (tool output, file excerpts, diffs, logs, up to 30k tokens) plus the questions. For the optional gate hook, on EVERY Bash/Write/Edit call: cwd, permission mode, optional JEV_GATE_STATE, tool name and the full tool_input JSON (entire shell command, and for Write/Edit the full file content / old_string / new_string) after regex secret redaction (hook gate, src/cli.ts:170-176; judge.ts:198-201). No truncation of tool_input found before send except the 30k-token oversized check. Client source code from personal and client projects therefore flows to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on each write when the gate is on; retention/training policy is the provider's.
gh-shitianfang-jev-use.failureMode: Timeout per attempt 10s, 2 retries with 0.5-5s jittered backoff, honors Retry-After up to 60s (src/backends/http.ts:11-16,34-83). Worst case ~31s+ can exceed the hook's 30s timeout, in which case Claude Code treats the hook as a non-blocking error (effectively fail-open). MCP tools: provider failure becomes escalate:true reason 'unreachable' ('proceed as if Jev didn't exist'), so the model continues. Gate hook: fail-open (exit 0, no output) if stdin invalid or credentials missing/backend construction throws; but if the provider is unreachable at call time the engine returns an escalate verdict, which the hook maps to permissionDecision 'ask' (cli.ts:158,182-186), meaning a Jev outage/429 would prompt the user on every Bash/Write/Edit call (issue #1 raises the doc/behaviour mismatch). Not fail-closed, but not silently open either.
gh-shitianfang-jev-use.contextCost: Two MCP tools (jev_judge, jev_gate). Description+schema text in src/server.ts is ~7.4 KB source, roughly 4.5-5 KB of model-visible text, approx 1.2-1.6k tokens always loaded (if MCP tool search/deferred loading is on, only names until needed). Plugin form also adds the skill: front-matter description ~1 KB (~250 tokens) always in the skill list, body ~3.4 KB (~900 tokens) loaded only when triggered. No MCP server-level 'instructions'. The gate hook injects no text into context (silent on allow; short reason on deny/ask). Total steady-state overhead roughly 1.5-2k tokens. Also every jev_judge call pays context tokens for state pasted as tool input plus verdict JSON back (SKILL.md admits it is a rate win, not a token win).
gh-shitianfang-jev-use.latencyImpact: MCP jev_judge: author-measured p50 ~223-274 ms, p95 ~364 ms per batched call (bench/RESULTS.md), but measured via Vercel AI Gateway from a dev container, not OpenRouter, plus the LLM turn to emit the tool call and read the result. Gate hook: each Bash/Write/Edit call adds an `npx -y jev-use@0.8.0` Node process spawn (npx resolution/cold start, typically several hundred ms to seconds, uncached case much worse) plus a network round trip (~200-300 ms author-measured; 17.1 s for 24 gated commands = ~0.7 s each) sequentially before each tool call, stacked on user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Tail case on outage: up to ~30 s per call.
gh-shitianfang-jev-use.autoInvocation: Mixed. (1) Model-discretion: jev_judge/jev_gate MCP tools, nudged by the description and by the jev-use skill (skill-description trigger) when installed as a plugin; Claude Code may or may not choose to call them, and no permission mode auto-allows MCP tools so the user must add `mcp__jev` to permissions.allow (in bypass mode this is not needed). (2) Deterministic: the optional PreToolUse `hook gate` runs automatically on every Bash|Write|Edit call, but is not enabled by install and the user must merge gate.hooks.json into settings.json.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class backend in code: /api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY and default model typesafe/jev-latest (src/backends/openrouter.ts:16-50); user only needs to export OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and not have TYPESAFE_API_KEY set, since auto-detect prefers it) or set JEV_BACKEND=openrouter.
Only project found offering a truly automatic path: skill description trigger plus a real deterministic PreToolUse hook, matching the user's 'Claude must use it without being told' requirement.

Gate is designed to only tighten (deny/ask, silent on allow), never bypasses the existing permission flow, and costs zero LLM tokens; useful safety net in the user's bypass/auto permission modes where nothing else asks.

Careful engineering of failure semantics: typed escalate reasons (unsure/oversized/unreachable/writing), separate confidence thresholds for reported vs estimated confidence, retry/backoff, 30k-token state cap, server starts without credentials and reports a named error.

Credential redaction for gated actions (src/redact.ts) with its own test file; SECURITY.md is explicit about what leaves the machine; no telemetry; version pinned in .mcp.json/hook (jev-use@0.8.0); mock backend for keyless dry runs; MIT; small readable codebase (~2.6k lines TS).
Ships a bulk path (`jev-use judge` CLI) so large lists of items can be classified without passing through the conversation.
cons: Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-19, 18 commits, 1 contributor, 31 stars, last push 2026-09-22; README admits it is substantially AI-written; performance numbers are self-reported and measured through Vercel AI Gateway, never through OpenRouter, and uses the alpha endpoint that may move.

Gate hook sends the full tool_input of every Bash/Write/Edit call (entire file contents being written, commands) to a third party; redaction is regex best-effort and applies only to the action, not the state. Risky for client projects under NDA.

Gate hook launches `npx -y jev-use@0.8.0 hook gate` for every Bash/Write/Edit call: added latency (npx startup plus ~0.25-0.7 s network) per tool call on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks; provider outage/429 turns into an 'ask' prompt on each such call rather than fail-open.

Its safety judgment is generic (state given to Jev is just cwd + permission mode + the action) so it duplicates and is weaker than the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard; 'allow' falls through to bypass mode, so the gate mainly adds a probabilistic deny on destructive commands, with unknown false-positive rate on real dev work (author tested only 12 commands for accuracy).

The MCP tool path is model-discretion, not deterministic: Jev is a rate win, not a token win (SKILL.md), pasting state into jev_judge costs Opus context both ways, and for a coding session most steps (edit, refactor, debug) are generation which the tool explicitly excludes; realistic value is limited to occasional triage/classification/verification steps.

Adds ~1.5-2k tokens of tool/skill definitions to every session; CI shows action_required (not really run), open unmerged external fix PRs (#2, #3), and `prepare` build script issue on production installs; supply-chain exposure via npx on every hook invocation.
Dependence on Jev quality itself is unverified (Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim), and beta Decisions API on OpenRouter.
gh-shitianfang-jev-use.verdict: The most complete and OpenRouter-ready Jev integration for Claude Code, and the only one with both a skill trigger and a deterministic hook, but it is a 10-day-old single-author project whose real daily benefit is narrow (optional gate plus occasional batched triage) and whose gate sends every Bash/Write/Edit payload to a third party. Reasonable to try MCP + skill with OPENROUTER_API_KEY; enable the gate hook only after reviewing data-egress, per-call npx latency and outage-becomes-ask behaviour, ideally pinned and scoped to personal projects.

gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (v0.3.5) that grades the developer's own prompts against seven "good prompt" habits (named target, success condition, bounded scope, constraints, repro, plan-first, verification) using Jev Noul questions via the TypeSafe SDK POST /v1/systemone. Bundled SDK (dist/dist-MER3SDQ4.js:53,438) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, default https://api.typesafe.ai; path POST ${baseURL}/v1/systemone (line 479, 504); auth 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (line 506). gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.dataEgress: On-demand default: nothing leaves the machine per prompt; the hook only writes a redacted prompt line to ~/.claude/jevpromptcoach/prompts.jsonl (0600). Sent to api.typesafe.ai (or the base URL you set) only when you run score/report/backfill: redacted prompt text. In always mode, sent on every prompt: the redacted prompt plus up to the last two exchanges of context, meaning the user's earlier prompts and Claude's closing reply text, also redacted (replies can be disabled with JEVPROMPTCOACH_SESSION_REPLIES=0). Never sent: file contents, diffs, tool calls or tool outputs, or project code apart from what the user pasted into prompts or Claude quoted in its closing text. Client-project names and code snippets in prompts and replies could leak under redact mode; metadata_only sends nothing.
gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. hook.ts:96-99 always exits 0; a missing key, network failure or bad response yields no output. In always mode a hard timer (default 4000 ms, config.alwaysTimeoutMs) resolves null via Promise.race (inline.ts:127-133), so the prompt proceeds with no notice. The SDK is configured with retry maxRetries=2 and 30 s default timeout for commands, but the inline race abandons after 4 s. The hook is also capped at 10 s in hooks.json.
gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.contextCost: Zero tokens of tool definitions (no MCP server, no skills the model can call; 3 slash commands are disable-model-invocation, so their descriptions are not loaded into context). The hook injects no additionalContext. In always mode it emits only a systemMessage, which is shown to the user and is not fed to the model. Effectively 0 context tokens.
gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.autoInvocation: Deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook that fires automatically on every prompt. But its output is a coaching notice for the human and a local log; Claude's behavior never depends on Jev. Slash commands are user-only.
gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.latencyImpact: On-demand: about 27-31 ms of Node startup per prompt (README-measured, not independently run). Always mode: blocks up to 4 s (default) per prompt while awaiting Jev; the claimed 70-500 ms Jev latency would give roughly 0.1-0.5 s added, and 4 s on a timeout. The README claim of "zero added latency" applies only to on-demand mode.
pros: It is the only candidate here with a working, automatic Jev hook (UserPromptSubmit) that costs nothing in Claude's context: 0 tool-definition tokens and no additionalContext.
Fail-open by design: it never exits 2, has a hard 4 s inline budget, and a test asserts the wire payload is redacted (test/hook-privacy.test.mjs).

Uses the same POST /v1/systemone Bearer-auth surface as OpenRouter, and the bundled SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so an OpenRouter switch is a small change (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model-id patch).

A good reference implementation of Jev Noul usage: batching seven questions in one call, calibrated thresholds and a labelled eval, all under a bundled, no-install, MIT-licensed dist with no postinstall.
On-demand default keeps data local and is cheap (about $0.06 for 1,000 prompts).
cons: It scores the user's prompt quality, not code, plans or tool calls. Jev never influences what Claude Code does, so it does not meet the goal of Claude Code using Jev when it adds value. It is a personal analytics tool for a senior developer, not a coding aid.
Not OpenRouter-native: the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY, the model id 'jev-latest' is hardcoded (jev.ts:13), and OpenRouter's response schema is unverified. It needs a fork or patch plus a live test.
Always mode adds a blocking network call of up to 4 s to every prompt for a notice that a senior dev will mostly ignore. On-demand mode gets no scores until a command is run.

Always mode sends the redacted prompt plus the last two exchanges of Claude's replies to a third party. On client projects this could leak code snippets or names despite shape-based redaction, which the README concedes.

Very immature: 3 stars, 1 author, 24 commits in 12 days, no releases, no lockfile, and a committed dist/ that has to be trusted. Slash-command surface and behavior are documented against Claude Code 2.1.277 and were not verified on 2.1.285.
The author's own outcome-signal study found the checks do not predict fewer corrections (docs/OUTCOME-SIGNAL.md), so the score's value is unproven.
Adds another UserPromptSubmit hook next to the existing secret guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. That is low risk, but it still spawns Node on every prompt.
gh-crowdlinker-jevpromptcoach.verdict: Well-built and safe (fail-open, redacted, no context cost), but it is a prompt-coaching plugin, not a Jev integration that helps Claude Code decide anything, so it does not fit the goal of automatic Jev use inside Claude Code. It is optional and only worth installing on-demand as a curiosity or as a code reference for a hook-plus-/v1/systemone pattern against OpenRouter.

gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.name: claude-jev-funnel (jev-funnel plugin)
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin with one skill (jev) plus a zero-dependency Python 3.9+ CLI (skills/jev/scripts/jev.py, about 2500 lines). It sends batches of items with typed noul/choice/score questions to Jev and bands the answers into confident and uncertain groups (the "funnel"). Confident answers are handled in code; only the uncertain band goes to Claude or a human. The skill has two modes: A) judge many items during a session, B) help write Jev integrations in apps (Kotlin, Swift, Python references). It is NOT an MCP server and ships no hooks.

gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.runtime: Python 3.9+ stdlib only (urllib, sqlite3); no npm or pip dependencies
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.install: /plugin marketplace add Shakibuzzaman3104/claude-jev-funnel ; /plugin install jev-funnel@claude-jev-funnel ; export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-v1-...

CI on Python 3.9, 3.11 and 3.13 runs compile, unit tests and mock/dry-run examples; release.yml tags releases. v1.0.0, 1.1.0 and 1.2.0 were all published within about 2 days, and the live benchmark has one dated result file.
security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from the environment only and sent in the Authorization header, so it is not in argv or the process list (jev.py build_headers).
Redirects are refused (NoRedirect handler) so the bearer token is never resent elsewhere; response size is capped at 8 MB.

Outgoing state, questions and criteria are scanned for secret patterns (OpenRouter, Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Google and Slack tokens, private-key blocks) and refused on a match. --lenient does not relax this. This is a partial substitute for the user's own secret-guard hook.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no os.system in jev.py (grep found none). No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry code found.

Local artifacts: usage ledger at ~/.config/jev/usage.jsonl and sqlite answer cache at ~/.cache/jev/cache.sqlite. The cache stores item payloads, so client code may persist on disk. Ledger can be disabled with JEV_NO_LEDGER=1 and the cache dir is set with JEV_CACHE_DIR.

Prompt-injection surface: none in the plugin itself (no hooks and no MCP). Jev returns numbers only, so returned data cannot inject text. The skill runs jev.py via Bash, which is trivial to do in bypass mode.

The plugin is single-author, brand new and 2-star. The whole plugin (SKILL.md and jev.py) is executed as user-level code, so pin a commit SHA and read jev.py before installing. The README recommends a credit limit on the OpenRouter key because a leaked key can call all models.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.dataEgress: Only when the skill runs: the state (item text such as log lines, diffs, file contents or review text) and the typed questions are POSTed to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (default), plus the API key in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent on session start or on ordinary prompts, and nothing is sent automatically for arbitrary tool output. OpenRouter's data policy applies. Client code could be sent if Claude chooses to triage client files or diffs, so the user has to steer that. Local ledger and sqlite cache keep copies of the payloads on disk.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.failureMode: Fail-open by nature. It is a skill run on demand, not a gate, so Claude Code is never blocked when Jev is down. jev.py has a 30 s per-attempt timeout and up to 5 attempts with backoff on 408/429/5xx/529 (worst case several minutes for one call). It honors Retry-After up to 60 s and gives typed errors for 402 (no credit), 403 and 404 (the alpha endpoint may change). When it fails, Claude can fall back to judging the items itself.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tool definitions). Passive cost is one skill entry: name plus a description of about 1000 characters, roughly 250 tokens in the skill listing every turn. When triggered, SKILL.md (about 23 KB, roughly 5.8k tokens) loads, and Claude may also read references/*.md (question-design.md is about 32 KB, api.md about 20 KB, roughly 5-8k tokens each). No hook-injected text and no server instructions.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, at model discretion. It fires on bulk classify/score/rank/triage tasks, or on mentions of Jev, TypeSafe or noul. It is not deterministic. The README suggests adding a CLAUDE.md rule (Closed-set bulk judgments over ~20+ items go to the jev skill before any cheap LLM subagent) to make the routing explicit.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns (no hooks). When invoked: skill load plus a Bash call, then a Jev round trip. The repo's own benchmark measured about 2.3 s p50 for a packed 40-item request, 3.92 s for 500 items in 13 requests, and $0.006 total. The vendor claims 0.27 s for 13 questions in one request. The skill's own text says single judgments should be made by Claude itself.
pros: Uses OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY by default (jev.py:65-70), so it works with the user's chosen provider with zero patching; TypeSafe direct is a flag away.

Truly automatic invocation with no user prompt: the skill description triggers on bulk classify/triage tasks, and the README offers a CLAUDE.md snippet to make routing explicit. This is the only kind of automatic integration the candidate offers, and it adds no hook latency to ordinary turns.
Very low always-on context cost: no MCP tool schemas, only about 250 tokens for the skill description, versus thousands for an MCP server.

Codes real Jev pitfalls: keyed rather than positional item references (the docs quote 29/320 wrong positionally, 0/320 keyed), a required no-match option on every choice, per-type calibration bands (noul ECE 0.012, choice 0.086, score 0.254), 32k context enforcement, and a dry-run cost estimate.

Sound engineering hygiene: stdlib only, no subprocess or shell, no redirects, 8 MB response cap, an outgoing secret scanner, a resumable batch with sqlite cache, a usage ledger showing real usage.cost, about 205 tests, CI on 3 Python versions, and Apache-2.0.

Honest 'When not to use it' section: it says a Jev skill router inside Claude Code adds little, and that file-relevance screening on a manageable codebase showed no effect in a 390k-line benchmark. It also says single judgments should be left to Claude.
cons: Its use case is bulk (about 20+ items) closed-set judgments such as triaging logs, lint warnings, review comments or PR diffs. Typical daily coding (edit, debug, refactor, run tests) rarely triggers it, so it will mostly sit idle. This is not a general Jev integration for coding decisions.
Model-discretion skill trigger, not deterministic. Opus may skip it or judge items itself; there is no hook that forces routing, and the bypass/auto permission mode does not change that.
Not an MCP server and no hooks, so it cannot intercept tool calls or gate actions with Jev (for example a risk score on a Bash command). Only a separate hook or MCP tool could do that.

Data egress risk on client projects: when triggered it POSTs file, diff or log content to OpenRouter and keeps the payloads in ~/.cache/jev/cache.sqlite and a usage ledger on disk. The regex secret scan is not a substitute for the user's own PreToolUse secret guard, which does not cover this Bash-invoked script's payloads.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-24, 10 commits, 2 stars, 1 contributor, three releases in two days, no external adoption or issue history. Its code is executed by Claude via Bash, so it needs a read-through or SHA pin. The upstream /alpha/ endpoint may change.

Retry policy of 5 attempts with a 30 s timeout could stall a turn for minutes when OpenRouter is degraded; there is no fail-fast option seen in the code. Skepticism about Jev's real quality (Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim) is unaddressed here, and the vendor-favouring benchmark citations (Greenberg A/B) are not independently verified.

Loading the full SKILL.md (about 5.8k tokens) plus references when triggered is heavy for a single small classification, and the skill mixes in app-building content (Kotlin/Swift) that this user will not need.
gh-shakibuzzaman3104-claude-jev-funnel.verdict: The best-built and lowest-overhead option for an OpenRouter-hosted Jev with automatic skill triggering, but it only fires on bulk closed-set triage, so it barely touches everyday coding. Treat it as a cheap, optional add-on (pin the commit SHA, read jev.py first, set JEV_NO_LEDGER and JEV_CACHE_DIR, and put the CLAUDE.md routing rule in place) rather than the core of the Jev integration.

On every Stop it runs the checks, sends a curated state to Jev (System One choice/noul/score questions: which phase, phase done, stuck, off-goal, claims-done, progress) and a pure-code policy decides allow-stop / block-with-next-step / advance phase. security: API key: read only from plugin userConfig (sensitive, stored in credential store, passed as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_JEV_API_KEY to hooks) or JEV_API_KEY env; sent only in the Authorization header, not argv (jev_client.py:70,173); redacted from error bodies and repr (:80,:133). gh-parth1811-jevflow.dataEgress: Only to the configured Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai today) on Stop and optional gates: goal (verbatim user prompt in auto mode), phase names + done_when, check exit codes and output tails (can contain code, test output, secrets printed by tests), last 4k chars of Claude's last message, changed file names with line counts from git (no contents unless privacy.send_diff=true), last 5 decisions. Optional gates additionally send Bash command lines (best-effort regex redaction) and WebFetch results. Nothing is sent when no key is set or in a project without .jevflow (except no-op hooks). Client-side, per-session budget max_jev_calls default 200.
gh-parth1811-jevflow.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Launcher hooks/jevflow prints {} and exits 0 on any crash and maps only the deliberate code 42 to exit 2; handle() catches all exceptions and returns {}. Jev errors, missing key or malformed answers give a degraded 'checks only' path that never blocks without evidence (docs/REFERENCE.md conditions degraded_*). Client timeout 15s, up to 3 retries with backoff (max 8s) => worst case roughly 1 minute per Jev call inside the Stop hook (hook timeout 600s); gate calls use shorter timeout/retries. Hard caps: max 6 blocks per session, 7 consecutive-block cap below Claude Code's 8, draft plan blocks at most 3 times, then archived as abandoned. Exception: a Stop with a failing user check does block (intended behaviour) and a corrupt flow.json yields a systemMessage disabling it for that stop.
gh-parth1811-jevflow.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tool defs). One skill: description ~330 chars (~80 tokens) always listed, body ~1.1k tokens loaded on trigger. Five slash commands add small listing entries. Hook-injected text: no-flow projects get a ~600 char SessionStart hint (~150 tokens) per session; every task-like prompt (>=8 words) gets a ~600 char nudge (~150 tokens) in projects with .jevflow but no active flow; active flows inject goal + phase table at SessionStart and a one-line [jevflow] message per phase change, plus block-reason text on each blocked Stop. Claude must also author flow.json phases, which costs output tokens per task.
gh-parth1811-jevflow.latencyImpact: Hooks are spawned as a Python process on every SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop and every PostToolUse (matcher '*') and every Bash PreToolUse: roughly 30-80 ms interpreter startup each even when the plugin is inactive (returns {} when no .jevflow). Jev call only on judged Stops: README claims 0.3-0.6 s, more when checks (test suites) run first; stops decidable by checks alone skip Jev. Optional pre_tool gate adds a Jev round trip to non-read-only Bash commands. A worst-case Jev outage adds ~1 min per judged Stop.
gh-parth1811-jevflow.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for the enforcement side (Stop/PostToolUse/SessionStart run with no user prompt), but the entry point is model-discretion plus heuristic nudges: without `jevflow auto on` Claude is merely told (SessionStart hint / UserPromptSubmit additionalContext) that it may run `jevflow start`; with auto on, task-like prompts create a draft flow deterministically and Stop blocks until Claude writes a valid plan. The Jev call itself is fully automatic once a flow is active; it is a Stop-time judge, not a general-purpose decision helper for coding steps.
pros: Genuinely automatic: no 'use jev' prompt needed; hooks fire on their own, and `jevflow auto on --project .` makes every task-like prompt start a tracked flow (README 'Many flows'; auto.py:1-20).

One of the few Jev integrations that actually exploits Choice/Noul/Score primitives with calibrated probabilities as a typed decision (judge.py:227-256: current_phase choice, stuck/off_goal/claims_done nouls, progress score) instead of using it as a chat model.

Sound safety design: 'Jev informs, code decides', checks always outrank Jev, fail-open launcher (hooks/jevflow), degraded checks-only mode, block budgets under Claude Code's 8-block cap, per-flow max_jev_calls=200, key redaction.

Zero dependencies (stdlib Python; user has 3.13), no MCP server so zero tool-schema context cost, no postinstall or curl|sh; small readable code (~5.8k lines) with 356 claimed tests incl. hook fixtures.
Directly addresses a real daily pain (Opus declaring 'done' with red tests, drift after compaction), and re-injects goal after compaction.
Small OpenRouter patch: only jev_client.py:24-25 (plus key) needs to change since the key is a generic Bearer token.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL and model are hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai and jev-latest (jev_client.py:24-25), no env override. User must fork/patch, and plugin updates would overwrite a patch; OpenRouter request schema equivalence is unverified.
Very immature: created 2026-09-24, 45 commits in 4 days by one author, 7 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, README says 'Status: MVP'; 356-test badge is self-reported and I did not run them.

Heavyweight workflow imposition: makes Claude write phased plans with shell checks for every 'real task', blocking Stop up to 6 times per session; for a senior dev on Opus 5.5 this can be friction, extra tokens and false-positive blocks, especially in bypass/auto mode where unattended loops may burn turns.

Only judges at Stop time; it does not help with mid-task decisions (which file, risk of an edit, when to run tests). Jev's value here is largely a verifier over Claude's last message tail, and the checks (deterministic shell commands) do most of the work; Jev is only used to confirm.

Spawns a Python process on every PostToolUse '*' and Bash PreToolUse for every tool call, stacking on top of the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks (added latency, hook-ordering interactions). Stop hook may also conflict with caveman/other Stop hooks.

Security tradeoffs for client work: flow.json checks and notify commands run via shell=True inside hooks, outside Claude's permission layer; data egress includes test output tails and Claude message tails to an external API (not okay for confidential client code without consent); SessionStart writes a symlink into ~/.local/bin; the SessionStart hint and per-prompt nudge inject text into context in every project.
Auto-planning uses a crude word-count/question heuristic (auto.py looks_like_task), so behaviour is unpredictable; .jevflow/ directories dirty client repos unless gitignored.
gh-parth1811-jevflow.verdict: The only candidate here that fires automatically (Stop/SessionStart hooks) and really uses Jev's typed probabilities, with a careful fail-open design, but it targets a task-completion-verifier workflow rather than general coding help and has no OpenRouter support (hard-coded api.typesafe.ai), so it needs a small fork. Treat as an opt-in per-project experiment (auto mode on, pre_tool gate off) rather than a global default, given its youth, hook stacking and the data it sends externally.

Returned steer text is injected into worker context.
Plugin hooks are global-scope once installed but self-filter on agent_type; parses transcript file (first 20 lines) for JEV-SLICE marker.

gh-damian87x-jev-claude-orchestrator.dataEgress: Only in slice-worker flows: acceptance criteria, gate stdout/stderr tails (~1.5 KB+), the full git diff of the slice (up to 60k chars, untracked files included via git diff --no-index), and every 8th tool call a summary of last 12 worker actions (tool name, target command/path up to 160 chars, first 200 chars of result) go to BASE/v1/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if switched, which then also passes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe). gh-damian87x-jev-claude-orchestrator.failureMode: Fail-closed by design for approval: any Jev error, timeout (30s default), malformed answer, HTTP error => escalate (mark slice for conductor), never approve; up to 3 retries on 429 honoring Retry-After (bounded by timeout). Health check and PostToolUse hook are fail-open no-ops (never block a tool, exit 0 on any exception). Fallback servers opt-in and cannot approve. SubagentStop hook timeout is 900s, so a bad network could stall worker stops for a long time (30s timeout x calls plus 600s gate). Outside slice-worker flows nothing can block.

Hooks inject nothing except the occasional steer inside slice workers (a short string every 8 calls when Jev flags stuck/off-track).
gh-damian87x-jev-claude-orchestrator.autoInvocation: Mixed. Hooks (SubagentStop, PostToolUse) are deterministic once installed but self-filter to slice-worker subagents, so they never fire in the user's normal coding. The skill is model-discretion by description ('large goal that decomposes into many small independently testable changes'), and the whole flow only engages when the main model chooses to run /conductor-max and dispatch workers with the JEV-SLICE marker. It is not an automatic Jev integration for daily coding.
gh-damian87x-jev-claude-orchestrator.latencyImpact: Normal sessions: one python3 process start (~20-50 ms, est.) on every tool call because PostToolUse has no matcher, then immediate exit for non-workers (it still reads stdin and parses agent_type). Slice workers: health check every 8 calls (~0.7 s claimed) and at each stop: gate runtime + QA call + 2 review calls (a few seconds plus gate time). Unbounded worst case on Jev outage: 30s per call with retries.
pros: Real, working use of Jev decisions inside Claude Code hooks: SubagentStop can block a worker from stopping (exit 2) based on gate + Jev QA + staged review, and PostToolUse injects steering via additionalContext (hooks/subagent_stop.py, post_tool_use.py).
Uses exactly the /v1/systemone endpoint and Bearer auth that OpenRouter exposes; only base URL + key + model id need changing (env vars TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL), no code edits.

Careful engineering: fail-closed policy in stages.py, vetoes before Jev, strict response validation (jevlib.malformed), redirect refusal, 429 handling, key not logged, stdlib-only, no installer scripts.

Has ~1050 lines of unit tests (6 test files) including regression tests from live runs; README includes measured Jev accuracy per stage (QA 96.3%, health 95.3%, triage 46.3%, review 9.5%), which is honest and useful evidence about where Jev is and isn't reliable.
Concrete, reusable ideas: typed triage/QA/health question sets in skills/conductor-max/references/jev-questions.json that can be lifted into a custom lightweight hook.
MIT license, tiny footprint (no MCP tool token tax, ~400 tokens always-on).
cons: Wrong shape for the user's goal: it is a parallel-subagent orchestrator that only engages inside /conductor-max slice workflows; no Jev help during ordinary daily coding, which the user explicitly wants automatic.

Author's own measurement shows Jev triage 46.3% and review 9.5% agreement with frontier majority (README table), so two of the four judgment stages are weak; system is 'starting guesses, not calibrated', v0.2 label vs 0.4.1 manifest (npm shows 0.4.0, manifest 0.4.1).

PostToolUse hook has no matcher, so a python3 process spawns on every tool call in every session even though it is a no-op outside slice workers; user already has several hooks (secret guard, GitNexus) adding latency.
Sends full diffs and gate output to a third party (TypeSafe, plus OpenRouter if routed there): risky for client projects (README says so itself).

OpenRouter compatibility is untested by author (no OPENROUTER references; env var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY would carry an OpenRouter key; model id must be changed to typesafe/jev-1.13); a schema mismatch would silently degrade to escalate on every call.

Costs and complexity of madmax orchestration (up to 50 subagent slices, worktrees, opus/sonnet/haiku workers) are heavy for a subscription user and overlap with Claude Code's native subagents; requires disciplined slice packets (JEV-SLICE marker) that the main model must be told to produce.
gh-damian87x-jev-claude-orchestrator.verdict: Well-built but narrow: a slice-conductor for large parallel refactors, not an always-on Jev layer for daily coding, and its hooks are inert outside /conductor-max slice workers. Worth mining for its typed question sets, hook exit-2 gate pattern and OpenRouter-compatible /v1/systemone call (config-only switch), but not worth installing as the main integration.

gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.name: jsk4581/jev-blindspot
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.whatItDoes: A UserPromptSubmit hook plus a local daemon (127.0.0.1:7461) and browser side panel. For every prompt you type, it sends the prompt, the last 2 exchanges and repo metadata to Jev as one System One call with 6 typed questions: worth_checking (Noul), risk (Score, 5 levels) and 4 knowledge-gap Nouls. If worth_checking is at least 0.65, it spawns a headless `claude -p --model sonnet --effort low` with Read/Grep/Glob in the project directory. That run returns up to 5 "blind spots" for the prompt, shown as cards in the panel. Nothing is injected into Claude's context and the prompt is not modified. It is a human-facing prompt-quality aid, not a way for Claude to consume Jev decisions.

Default model is `jev-1.13.0` (config.ts:170). OpenRouter would need `typesafe/jev-1.13`, set via JEV_MODEL in the env file. gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript compiled to dist/), npm package jev-blindspot 0.1.1, single dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. Linux and macOS only.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.install: npm install -g jev-blindspot; write TYPESAFE_API_KEY to ~/.config/jev-blindspot/env; jev-blindspot install-hook (edits ~/.claude/settings.json). It also needs a `dist/` build when installed from git.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.tests: 6 test files in test/ (transcript, thresholds, state, runner, parse, codex-trust) using node --test, plus gate fixtures that need a real key. There is no CI directory (no .github), no GitHub release, and 6 commits from a single author within 2 days (created 2026-09-22, last push 2026-09-24).
security: No curl|sh installer and no postinstall script in package.json. There is a single dependency, the official SDK, and no telemetry was seen in the source.
The daemon binds 127.0.0.1 only unless JEV_BIND_EXTRA is set. The panel exposes every prompt, so a LAN bind without JEV_TOKEN leaks all of them. The settings route accepts any allowed host.
Prompt text is put in argv of `claude -p` (brainArgs, src/brain/runner.ts:36), so it is visible in `ps`/procfs to other local users. The API key stays in a 0600 env file and is not in argv.

The Claude brain runs with the user's own settings, hooks and CLAUDE.md. Only the jev-blindspot hook is suppressed (JEV_BLINDSPOT_CHILD=1). The GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks would fire inside every brain run and add side effects and cost. Read/Grep/Glob are allowed and Bash/Edit/Write/WebFetch are disallowed, but the secret-leak guard hook is the only barrier against the brain reading .env or credentials, whose content would go to Anthropic.

The prompt-injection surface is the gate `state` (prompt and history are treated as data, per the comment in state.ts) and repo files read by the brain. The brain output is only rendered in the panel, not fed back to Claude, so the blast radius is small.
The hook edits ~/.claude/settings.json (with a backup) and spawns a detached daemon that persists for up to 30 idle minutes.
The .jev-blindspot-off marker file and JEV_BLINDSPOT_DISABLE=1 provide per-repo and per-shell opt-out. It is opt-out per repo rather than opt-in, so client repos would need the marker created first.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.dataEgress: To Jev (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter if repointed), per prompt: the prompt (cut at 6000 characters), the last 2 exchanges (user text cut at 500 characters, assistant reply text last 1500 characters), and project metadata (dir name, languages, frameworks, has_tests, has_ci, git branch, is_git_repo). No file contents or diffs are sent unless a reply quoted them. When the gate passes, `claude -p` sends the prompt, the history, the gate flags, the project directory contents it chooses to read, and CLAUDE.md to Anthropic under the user's subscription. Locally, prompts and results are stored in ~/.local/share/jev-blindspot/sessions/*.jsonl for 30 days. Client-project prompts would be sent to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every prompt.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.failureMode: Fail-open. Hook stdin is read for at most 800ms, the POST to the daemon has a 400ms timeout and the hook always exits 0 with no stdout. Gate timeout defaults to 2000ms with retry disabled (JEV_GATE_TIMEOUT_MS). On failure the card shows "gate unavailable" and no analysis runs, unless JEV_GATE_FALLBACK=brain. The brain has a 90s limit. Nothing blocks the prompt, apart from `/blindspot`, which is intentionally blocked.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.latencyImpact: See above: about 100ms in the hook on the prompt path. Gate 70-500ms plus brain tens of seconds, all off the critical path.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.contextCost: Zero for Claude's context. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions, and the hook prints nothing to stdout. The only exception is /blindspot, which is blocked and shown to the user. It adds one command file, ~/.claude/commands/blindspot.md, which adds a slash command entry to the list. Extra cost is the separate `claude -p` brain runs, which spend subscription usage on every analyzed prompt and load the user's CLAUDE.md and hooks each time.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit on every human-typed prompt). It is fully automatic, but the consumer is the human via a browser panel, not Claude. Claude never sees or uses Jev's output.
pros: Truly automatic: a UserPromptSubmit hook with no 'use jev' prompting, and it fails open (hook exits 0 with a 400ms cap).

It uses Jev's intended primitives well: Noul and Score in a single System One call with 6 typed questions (src/gate/questions.ts), returning probabilities with no free text. The design is a reasonable reference for a Jev gate, with a threshold (JEV_WORTH_MIN) that can be tuned by running `jev-blindspot gate`.
Nothing is injected into Claude's context and the token cost to the main session is zero. The hook is async in effect and never edits or blocks the prompt.

The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and uses the same /v1/systemone path as OpenRouter's System One API, so repointing to OpenRouter needs only env vars and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, not a code patch.

Clean, small codebase (about 3.1k lines of TypeScript), MIT, one official dependency, no postinstall or curl|sh, per-repo opt-out via .jev-blindspot-off, and Jev model pinned by default rather than jev-latest.
Its architecture (small typed gate first, expensive model only when the gate says so) is a pattern worth copying for a custom hook.
cons: It does not make Claude Code use Jev. The output is a browser side panel for the human, which conflicts with the user's goal of Claude using Jev when it adds value. It only reviews prompt quality and makes no coding decision for Claude.
It sends every prompt, recent assistant replies and the git branch/dir name to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every prompt, including client projects. It is opt-out per repo, not opt-in.

When the gate passes, it spawns a separate `claude -p` Sonnet run that reads the project. That costs subscription usage and load, and loads the user's CLAUDE.md. It also fires the user's GitNexus, caveman and secret-guard hooks inside each brain run (only its own hook is skipped), risking interaction with existing hooks.
Prompt text sits in the argv of the `claude -p` child, visible in the process list.
It needs a person to watch a browser tab. Blindspot cards are easy to ignore, and the value for a senior developer who already knows the work is questionable.

The OpenRouter path is untested and unverified: response schema parity, model ID and the misleading env var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The panel's model validator also rejects the slash in 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Very immature: 6 commits, a single author, 20 stars, 8 days old, no CI, no releases, version 0.1.1. It edits ~/.claude/settings.json and also targets Codex, which adds code and surface the user does not need.
Linux and macOS only, and it requires Claude Code 2.1.278 or newer. It relies on flags such as --permission-prompts and --json-schema that could break on updates.
gh-jsk4581-jev-blindspot.verdict: Not a fit as the integration. It is an automatic UserPromptSubmit hook, but it feeds a human-only side panel, sends every prompt to a third party, and spawns extra Sonnet runs on the subscription, so Claude never uses Jev's decisions. Its only value to this user is as a code reference for building a Jev gate: the six-question Noul/Score set and the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL repoint to OpenRouter.

gh-47vigen-catherd.name: 47vigen/catherd
gh-47vigen-catherd.whatItDoes: A Bun/TypeScript Claude Code plugin (skill + slash commands + 26-tool stdio MCP server) that orchestrates multi-agent autopilot builds: Claude plans/verifies, Codex/opencode/Cursor/Grok/Antigravity/headless-Claude workers write code. Jev is used only internally as a small classifier: 3 typed question sets (route-v2: work kind + difficulty for a lane; finding: design vs code defect; same-defect: yes/no) posted to TypeSafe's /systemone to choose which worker model/effort rung to use. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration for Claude Code sessions.

So planning prose and finding text leave the machine, not raw code or diffs by design. Also unauthenticated GETs of public model catalogs. Worker CLIs separately send whatever they see to their own vendors (Codex/OpenAI, etc.). Local jev.jsonl stores only a state hash, not the state.
gh-47vigen-catherd.failureMode: Fail-open. jev-client.ts retryingFetch: 10 s per attempt, 2 retries with 500 ms doubling backoff and Retry-After (capped 10 s), 25 s total deadline. No key, HTTP error, timeout or unparsable reply returns answers=null and routing falls back to the lane file's Kind/Difficulty, else the profile default rung (routing-service.ts route()); jev.use='off' skips the call. Worst-case added stall on a Jev outage is about 25 s per route call, plus route waits up to 5 s on model-discovery refresh. Answers are cached per run by request key (same model/state/questions).

gh-borislemeec-jev.name: BorisLeMeec/jev (Claude Code plugin + Go CLI "jev")
gh-borislemeec-jev.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (skill + one PreToolUse hook) around a Go CLI that calls the TypeSafe System One API with Noul/Choice primitives. `jev find` ranks files/lines by natural-language description, `jev ask` sweeps yes/no questions across files, and the hook rewrites Read calls on files of 400 lines to 80 KB into a window of about 1/5 of the file centred on the line Jev picks for the user's last message. It also has an opt-in lint (not wired into hooks.json), plus scan/probe/gain helpers.

providerSupport.evidence: internal/typesafe/client.go:23 hardcodes `endpoint = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"` (const, no base-URL env override). Key: client.go:31 reads TYPE_SAFE_AI_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY. Model: client.go:24 DefaultModel "jev-latest", override via JEV_MODEL (client.go:63). Bearer auth at client.go:247. No 'openrouter' string anywhere in the repo (grep -i over *.go and *.md returned nothing).
providerSupport.others: None. Only api.typesafe.ai.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. OpenRouter's docs (guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md) say the System One API at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone is TypeSafe-SDK compatible: 'change the base URL and the API key, everything else stays the same', and bare ids like jev-latest map to typesafe/. The client uses the same path shape and request/response schema ({model,state,questions} -> {answers,usage}), so it is a one-line change to the endpoint const plus an OPENROUTER_API_KEY lookup. Caution: do NOT put an OpenRouter key into TYPESAFE_API_KEY unpatched, because the client would send it to api.typesafe.ai. Response decoding was written from docs, not live output (probe.go:18), so run `jev probe` against OpenRouter after patching. You would need to fork or vendor the plugin, since the marketplace install pulls upstream.

interface.name: hook: PreToolUse matcher=Read (hooks/hooks.json), command `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/jev hook read`, timeout 20
interface.purpose: Deterministic. For a Read with no offset/limit on a file of 400 lines to 80 KB, calls Jev (Choice over ~200 chunks, plus Noul) using the last user message from transcript_path as the goal. If chunk confidence is 0.60 or higher, it returns updatedInput {offset,limit} (window is max(150, lines/5)) and an additionalContext note. Every other case passes through.

interface.name: skill: jev (skills/jev/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Model-discretion trigger through its description: locating a feature whose name is unknown, grep returned nothing, or checking a property across many files. Tells Claude to run the Bash CLI. The skill body also says to report a missing key to the user rather than fall back silently.

interface.name: CLI: jev find "<desc>" [path...]
interface.purpose: Screen every file (one Noul request per file over a code skeleton), re-score the leaders on full contents, then chunk the winner and pick the line with a Choice. Prints score and file:line. About 13 s per call in the author's timing.

interface.name: CLI: jev ask "<yes/no q>" <file|dir...> [-q]
interface.purpose: Per-file probability plus line for a yes/no question. About 2 s and $0.0016 per question.

interface.name: CLI: jev scan
interface.purpose: Dry run showing bytes, tokens and cost with no API call.

interface.name: CLI: jev probe
interface.purpose: Sends one request with all three primitives and prints the raw response, to verify the API contract.

interface.name: CLI: jev gain [--history]
interface.purpose: Report from ~/.jev/usage.jsonl on tokens examined out of context versus returned.

interface.name: CLI: jev lint (internal/run/lint.go)
interface.purpose: Checks an edit's diff against rules in .jev-rules.json. Off unless JEV_LINT_ENABLE is set, and not registered in hooks.json, so it is inactive by default.

interface.name: env knobs
interface.purpose: JEV_HOOK_DISABLE, JEV_HOOK_DEBUG, JEV_HOOK_MIN_LINES (400), JEV_HOOK_MIN_CONF (0.60), JEV_MODEL, JEV_DATA, JEV_NO_STATS, JEV_LINT_ENABLE/DISABLE.

Concern: hooks.json and the skill both need bin/jev, but .gitignore excludes `bin/`, and the repo has no SessionStart build hook, no release binary and no install script. The Makefile `sync` target comments only a local build. A plain marketplace install therefore very likely has no binary, so the hook errors (non-blocking) and `jev` is not on PATH. gh-borislemeec-jev.tests: 3 Go test files (10 Test funcs: scan_test 6, hook_test 2, permute_test 2). No .github directory, so no CI. Extensive benchmark harnesses and result markdown in bench/. The benchmarks are self-run on a few repos (mostly Go plus Flutter/React, plus Hugo and Prometheus). The find/ask query sets come from private repos and are unpublished, and samples are tens of queries.
security: Key handling is good: read from env, sent only in an Authorization Bearer header (client.go:247), never in argv. The `Debug` writer prints raw response bodies, not the key. Request bodies are not logged.

No shell execution in the Go code (no os/exec). No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry. The only network call is the hardcoded POST to api.typesafe.ai. Local writes: ~/.jev/usage.jsonl (command, token counts, bytes; disable with JEV_NO_STATS).

Data egress bypasses your secret-leak guard: the Read hook itself reads the file (os.ReadFile) and sends its contents to a third party. Claude Code runs matching PreToolUse hooks in parallel, so the secret guard's deny does not stop jev from having already uploaded a 400+ line file. Sensitive large files (dumps, key bundles, client code under NDA) are exposed on every Read.
The hook also reads transcript_path (the full session JSONL, up to 8 MB per line) and takes the last user message (first 600 chars) as the 'goal' sent to the API.

Prompt-injection surface: file content is sent as model state, but Jev returns numbers only, so injection cannot produce instructions. The worst case is a manipulated ranking or window, which could hide the relevant part of a file from Claude. additionalContext is generated locally from numbers and the file basename.

Integrity risk: the Read hook silently rewrites tool input, so Claude sees only about 1/5 of a large file. It can miss code (author measured 50/50 targets kept, but on small samples and Go repos only), and Claude may edit with incomplete context. Only partially mitigated by the note and the ability to re-read with offset.
Sending your OpenRouter key via TYPESAFE_API_KEY unpatched would leak it to api.typesafe.ai (client.go:31 vs :23).
Supply chain: single-day, single-author repo, no releases, no signed binaries. You would have to build it yourself, so read the source and pin a commit.
gh-borislemeec-jev.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter once patched): for the hook, the full contents of every file the agent Reads that is 400 lines to 80 KB with no explicit offset/limit, cut into chunks with the file's basename and the user's last message (600 chars max, from the transcript). For `find`, code skeletons of every file in scope, then full contents of the top candidates. For `ask`, whole files in scope. Not sent: Bash output, diffs (unless lint is enabled), other tool outputs, or the whole transcript. Local: ~/.jev/usage.jsonl.
gh-borislemeec-jev.failureMode: Hook fails open. Any error, missing key, unreadable payload, low confidence, or a Jev failure returns an empty decision, so the Read proceeds unmodified (hook.go:53-58, 125-130). If the binary is missing, the hook command errors non-blockingly. The client retries 429 and 5xx up to 5 times with exponential backoff and jitter (client.go:190-213), with a 120 s HTTP timeout (client.go:69) but a 20 s hook timeout in hooks.json, so a slow or down Jev can stall a Read for up to 20 s before Claude Code kills the hook and continues. Normal cost is +1.25 s per qualifying Read (the author's number). `find` and `ask` are CLI calls where errors are surfaced to Claude as text and it can fall back to grep.
gh-borislemeec-jev.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens. The skill description costs roughly 170-200 tokens in the always-on skills list (about 700 chars). The full SKILL.md body is about 6.5k chars, roughly 1.7k tokens, loaded only when the skill is invoked. The hook adds about 60 tokens of additionalContext only on a narrowed Read (and top-level additionalContext may not even be honored by Claude Code, since it sits outside hookSpecificOutput, hook.go:40-43). `find` and `ask` output is a few lines, and the README claims about 40 tokens per search. The net effect on context is negative, by design: it shrinks large reads.
gh-borislemeec-jev.latencyImpact: Read hook: +about 1.25 s (author-measured) on every synchronous Read of a 400-line to 80 KB file with no offset, and a few hundred ms extra on the hook's local file and transcript parsing. It never gives back a turn, because the agent was going to read the file anyway (bench/TIMING.md). `jev find` about 13 s repo-wide, about 2.5 s when scoped to a directory, because it sends one request per file. `jev ask` about 2 s per question. Author's paired runs show median wall-clock ratio 1.03 (a wash); the token savings come from fewer later turns re-sending context.
gh-borislemeec-jev.autoInvocation: Hybrid. (1) Deterministic PreToolUse hook on Read, which runs with no prompting and transparently rewrites offset/limit. (2) A skill whose description triggers at Claude's discretion to run `jev find` or `jev ask` through Bash; there is no MCP tool and no CLAUDE.md nudge, so the trigger rate is uncertain. Opus 5.5 tends to prefer Grep, and you have the GitNexus graph hook already steering search.
pros: The only Jev candidate with a genuinely automatic mechanism: a PreToolUse hook that fires on every Read without any prompt. That matches your 'never say use jev' requirement more literally than skills or MCP tools.
Hooks fail open by design (every gate returns the read untouched on error, timeout or doubt), and JEV_HOOK_DISABLE=1 is a clean kill switch. Explicit offset/limit reads are never altered.
No MCP servers, so no schema-token tax and no extra process. Small footprint of a skill description plus one hook.
Clean, readable Go with no shell exec, no telemetry and no curl|sh. Bearer auth via env only. Easy to audit in an hour (about 1.5k lines).

Real, honest benchmarks with harnesses in-repo, including a candid TIMING.md that admits the median wall-clock effect is a wash. `find` P@1 0.96 vs grep 0.08 on vocabulary-gap queries and `ask` precision 1.00 are useful specifically when names are unknown, such as unfamiliar client codebases.

Uses the same System One endpoint shape that OpenRouter exposes, so porting to OpenRouter is a one-line endpoint change plus a key env, and the client already handles 429/5xx backoff and the 32k-token limit (80 KB cap).
Cost is negligible ($0.042/M input, roughly $0.0016 per ask).
cons: No OpenRouter support today (endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, no base-URL override). You would have to fork and maintain a patched copy, and the marketplace install would pull upstream.

Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 6 commits in a single day, one author, no releases, no CI, about 10 tests, no issues or activity since 2026-09-18. Benchmarks are self-reported, small (tens of queries) and on Go/Flutter/React repos only.

Install looks broken for a plain marketplace install: bin/ is gitignored and nothing builds the binary, so hook and skill probably have no `jev` to run until you build it yourself. go.mod requires Go 1.26.1 while the README says 1.22+.

The Read hook is the dangerous part: it hides about 80% of a large file from Claude, and Claude edits code that way. The author admits recall was measured only on 50 targets, and in your bypass/auto mode nobody reviews those reads. On client work a silently missed guard clause is costly.

Sends full contents of every large file Claude reads, plus your last prompt, to a third party. It runs in parallel with your secret-leak guard, so the guard cannot prevent the upload. This matters for client NDA code.

The hook pays about 1.25 s on every big-file Read and returns no turns, so on the Read hook alone it is pure latency; the token saving mostly matters for API-billed users, and you are on a subscription where the win is only context and rate-limit headroom.

`find` and `ask` depend on the model choosing to invoke the skill, with no MCP tool or hook to force it. `find` takes about 13 s repo-wide and makes one request per file, which is heavy for big monorepos. This overlaps with the GitNexus graph search you already use and with Grep.

The hook's `additionalContext` is emitted at the top level, not inside hookSpecificOutput, and it uses updatedInput without a permissionDecision. I could not verify how Claude Code 2.1.285 treats either; the narrowing note may be dropped, so Claude may not know its Read was cut short.

Goal quality: the hook uses the last typed user message as the search goal. In long agentic runs with subagents or 'continue' style messages, that goal is stale or vague, so the window can point at the wrong region (it then passes through only if confidence is under 0.60).
gh-borislemeec-jev.verdict: The most 'automatic' Jev integration found (a real PreToolUse hook plus a skill), and it is easy to patch to OpenRouter with a one-line endpoint change. But it is a 1-day-old single-author POC whose install does not obviously ship the binary. Its headline hook silently truncates Reads and uploads file contents past your secret guard, so use it only as a forked, audited, pinned build, ideally with the Read hook disabled or limited and the skill/`ask` used for repo-wide audits.

gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.name: yonatangross/orchestkit
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.whatItDoes: OrchestKit is a very large Claude Code plugin (107 skills, 36 agents, about 170 hook entries across ~30 hook events) that has two opt-in, env-flagged Jev seams inside its hooks. (1) Session-category classifier: on the first prompt of a session it asks Jev for one typed Choice over 8 work categories (branch name plus first 600 chars of the prompt), used to color/label the session. (2) Route judgment (ORK_ROUTE_JEV=shadow|steer): every build-shaped UserPromptSubmit prompt is sent to Jev as a Choice over 19 route classes plus 4 side judgments (worktree, browser, mutation risk, operator); in steer mode a one-line reminder such as "route: dev_fix -> /ork:fix-issue (conf 0.83)" is injected as prompt context. A third Python lane (skills/expect/scripts/jev_shadow.py) is a shadow classifier for the /ork:expect browser-testing skill. Jev is used purely as a hidden, deterministic-hook classifier; it is not a general coding tool and the value only exists if you adopt the entire OrchestKit skill catalog (route classes map to /ork:* skills).

Python lane: jev_shadow.py:39-40 ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY and ORK_EXPECT_JEV_ENDPOINT (endpoint from env or expect config). Zero mentions of openrouter anywhere in the repo (grep).

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The route seam can be pointed at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with ORK_ROUTE_JEV_ENDPOINT and an OpenRouter key placed in ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY (Bearer auth and the /v1/systemone path look identical), but the request body carries model 'jev-1.13.0' from route-judgment.defaults.json, whereas OpenRouter expects 'typesafe/jev-1.13'; that needs a JSON edit plus a rebuild of the bundled plugins/ork/hooks/dist/*.mjs (or editing the installed dist copy). The session-category seam needs a source edit for both endpoint and model. So a fork or local patch is required; there is no config-only route. Request/response schema (state, model, questions{type:choice,...}; answers.<id>.choice/probabilities/confidence) matches the System One shape, but whether OpenRouter's API is byte-compatible is not verified from this repo.
