security: MIT license (LICENSE, GitHub licenseInfo).

Key handling: read from env ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY only; never logged (comments 'Error text only, never the request'). Sync steer path spawns `node -e <script>` and passes key and endpoint via the child's env and body via stdin, explicitly not on argv (route-judgment.ts:~515-570); child env is scrubbed to PATH plus these vars. Good practice; no key in the process list.

Egress guard on route seam: redacts secrets, emails, phone numbers, 9-digit ids, op:// refs and clients/<dir> names, rescans the serialized request in raw and JSON-decoded form, and refuses the call if anything survives (fail closed on egress). The session-category seam is weaker: raw git branch plus first 600 chars of the first prompt with only whitespace normalisation, no redaction (README itself says its egress posture differs from the expect/route lane).

Prompt-injection surface: Jev output is a closed enum/probabilities parsed against a fixed set (parseWorkCategory / parseRouteIntent), so a malicious reply cannot inject free text into Claude's context; the injected nudge is built from a static class-to-executor table.

The plugin as a whole is a huge attack/behavior surface: ~170 hook entries incl. PreToolUse x20, PostToolUse x28, PermissionRequest x4, Stop x12, SessionStart x21, plus a bundled minified dist (plugins/ork/hooks/dist/*.mjs) that a reviewer must trust; it would be stacked on the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks with unknown ordering/interaction. It also has PermissionRequest and PermissionDenied hooks that could interfere with the user's bypass/auto permission mode.

Telemetry: README states no analytics ping, no crash reporter; optional telemetry sinks only fire if user sets ORCHESTKIT_HOOK_URL / ORK_HQ_TELEMETRY_URL. Dockerfile and postinstall not observed as required for plugin install (no postinstall in package.json grep).
Per-session Jev answers and hashes (not prompt text) are written to the session data dir; route log stores sha256 of redacted text only.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.dataEgress: Default: nothing (both Jev lanes are off unless ORK_SESSION_CATEGORY_PROVIDER=jev|shadow or ORK_ROUTE_JEV=shadow|steer AND ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY are set). When on: (a) category lane sends git branch name plus the first 600 chars of the session's first prompt, un-redacted, to api.typesafe.ai; (b) route lane sends, for every build-shaped prompt, the first 1,500 chars of the prompt after redaction (secrets, emails, phones, ids, op://, clients/ dir names replaced by tokens) plus the repository basename (max 40 chars) and an opening_turn flag. No code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent. (c) expect lane sends goal, last verify result, page elements and candidates. Everything goes to api.typesafe.ai by default (a third-party processor); it would go to openrouter.ai only if the endpoint is patched. Client-project caveat: the category lane's lack of redaction and the redactor's Israeli-phone-specific and clients/-directory-specific patterns mean prompts on client projects can still contain client identifiers.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.failureMode: Fail-open on routing: no key, timeout (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS / ORK_ROUTE_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS default 3000 ms), non-2xx, malformed body, confidence below floor (0.5 route, 0.8 category), or daily token budget (2M) exhausted -> existing path runs untouched (decided_by=table/haiku); 402/429 trips the seam off for 24 h. Fail-closed only on egress-scan hits (call refused, nothing sent). Costs when slow: category lane makes the first prompt of a session wait 1.1-1.7 s cold, up to 3 s; steer mode blocks the synchronous UserPromptSubmit handler on a spawned node child for up to 3 s (+1 s child timeout margin) per build-shaped prompt. Shadow-route mode keeps the hook process alive until the call settles.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 MCP tools and no server 'instructions'. The cost is the plugin itself: 107 skills whose frontmatter descriptions total about 34.7k chars (~8.7k tokens) always loaded in the skill list, plus 36 agent descriptions (extra, not measured), plus plugin CLAUDE.md. Hooks inject context: the route steer adds one short line (~20-30 tokens) per build-shaped prompt; the once-per-session executor reminder is a one-liner; many other OrchestKit hooks inject additional prompt context (not audited in full). Net: roughly 10k+ tokens of standing context for the catalog, alongside the user's existing skills, for a Jev feature that contributes a ~25-token nudge.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit and session-identity hooks fire automatically, no model discretion), but the Jev part is dormant until env vars are set, and its only effect is a routing hint (steer) or session color/log (shadow/jev category). It never decides tool use or code changes on its own.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.latencyImpact: Category lane: +1.1-1.7 s (max 3 s) once at first prompt of a session when enabled (self-measured in the README, cold Node fetch to api.typesafe.ai). Route lane: shadow is fire-and-forget within the hook process (hook stays alive until it settles); steer is synchronous, adding roughly 0.3 s warm to 1.7 s cold, 3 s worst case, per build-shaped prompt because it spawns a fresh `node -e` child. Baseline OrchestKit dispatcher overhead from ~170 other hooks is unmeasured here.
pros: Genuinely wires Jev into Claude Code via deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, so no 'use jev' prompt is ever needed; a real, working reference for the classify-the-prompt use case.

Well-engineered failure semantics: everything fails open with 3 s timeout, daily token budget, 24 h circuit-breaker on 402/429, and egress fail-closed with a two-pass redaction scan (route-judgment.ts:235-300).
Key never hits argv: sync path passes key via child env and body via stdin (route-judgment.ts ~515-570). Jev replies are parsed against closed enums, so no prompt-injection channel from the model.
Route seam endpoint is env-overridable (ORK_ROUTE_JEV_ENDPOINT), so OpenRouter is a small patch away; request format is standard System One (state/model/questions).

Active project: 286 stars, MIT, commits daily through 2026-09-29, releases (v9.8.1 on 2026-09-29), CI workflows, dedicated Jev tests (tests/unit/test-jev-*.mjs, executor-route-nudge-jev.test.ts, mock_jev.py fixtures) and held-out eval numbers documented (93.5% at >=0.8 confidence).
Pins model jev-1.13.0 for reproducibility and logs one auditable line per prompt plus jsonl records (labels and sha256 only).
cons: Does not support OpenRouter as shipped: zero 'openrouter' in the repo; category seam has hardcoded endpoint and model (session-category-provider.ts:53,56); route model 'jev-1.13.0' is not env-overridable and OpenRouter wants 'typesafe/jev-1.13'; requires forking/patching source and the bundled dist, and the patch must be redone on each of the near-daily releases.

Not a general Jev integration: the only Jev use is classifying prompts into OrchestKit's own /ork:* route classes and session colors. Without adopting the whole toolkit (107 skills, 36 agents) it is useless; it offers no decision primitives (Noul/Score) for coding tasks like risk-gating edits, test selection, or commit/PR triage.

Enormous blast radius for a small benefit: ~170 hook entries incl. PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PreToolUse x20 and Stop x12 would be layered on the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus hooks and caveman plugin, with likely conflicts, overlapping context injection and a bypass/auto permission-mode interaction; ~8.7k tokens of skill descriptions added to every session.

Jev's value here is tiny: a 20-token routing hint that the main model (Opus) can already derive; the README's own comment says steer mode 'the model still reads the /ork:auto table and says whether it agrees'.

Latency: category lane blocks first prompt 1.1-1.7 s cold; steer blocks each build-shaped prompt by up to 3 s via a new node process, contradicting the 70-500 ms claim (they measured cold-start and TLS overhead of a fresh process).

Privacy on client work: category lane sends un-redacted first prompt and branch to a third party; route redactor patterns are tailored to the author (Israeli phone numbers, clients/ directory names), not the user's environment.

Route classes and the 'executor reminder' logic are specific to author's telemetry ('think skills 141x vs executor skills 6x'), i.e. an opinionated workflow; the Jev features are marked opt-in/shadow/experimental with issue references (#4233), so they can change or vanish.
Single dominant author (125 of 200 sampled commits, remainder bots); large surface (299 MB clone) and rapid churn make auditing the bundled dist impractical.
gh-yonatangross-orchestkit.verdict: A well-engineered but narrow, TypeSafe-direct-only Jev classifier embedded in a huge opinionated plugin; it proves the hook pattern (UserPromptSubmit + fail-open + redaction) is viable but is not worth installing for this user, and OpenRouter needs a source patch. Best used as a design reference for a small custom hook rather than as a dependency.

gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.runtime: Python 3 stdlib only (urllib); no MCP server, no hooks, no dependencies. Installed via 'npx skills add' or git clone into a skills directory.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.install: npx skills add poiuyjie/jev_project_context --agent claude-code -y, or git clone into ~/.claude/skills/project-context-v2. Then set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment or in .env. (Not executed.)
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.tests: None: no test files and no CI (.github absent). No releases. All 13 commits are from a single author on a single day, 2026-09-22, eight days before the audit date, and several are README diagram tweaks and promotion housekeeping.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or a .env file, which is searched in cwd, the scripts dir and the skill root (jev_client.py:25-49). It is sent in an Authorization header, not in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
The cwd .env search means any project .env containing TYPESAFE_* is loaded. It uses os.environ.setdefault, so real env vars win. It parses only KEY=VALUE lines and does not read other variables.
No shell execution: no subprocess or os.system (grep). HTTP only via urllib to a single configurable URL. No telemetry.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is honored without validation, so anything that can set the env or .env can redirect state payloads (including CURRENT.md content) and the bearer key to an arbitrary host.

Prompt-injection surface is moderate: memory-file content (experiment headings, CURRENT.md) is sent as Jev state and returned only as numeric scores. The manifest is printed as file names and numbers, so Jev cannot inject free text. SKILL.md instructs the agent to relay SURFACE lines, which come from local regex matches.
Install is the third-party 'npx skills add', a curl-free flow. There are no postinstall or curl|sh scripts in the repo.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.dataEgress: Only when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set and one of the Jev scripts is run. jev_context.py sends the task string (the user's request), up to 6k chars of CURRENT.md, and one-line 'cards' (file name, heading up to 110 chars, status/validity/protocol) for up to 60 memory items, capped at 24k chars total. jev_doctor.py sends record text and claims rows, capped at 24k chars per call (STATE_CAP, plus CLAIMS_CAP). It does not send source code, diffs or tool outputs. It only sends the research-memory markdown of the project. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or wherever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.failureMode: Fail-open by design. With no key, or on any JevError (HTTP error, URLError, timeout, OSError), the scripts print a [FALLBACK] line and exit 0, and the agent uses the fixed reading order. A malformed or unexpected-shape response is not wrapped in a try: json.loads errors outside the caught types are not handled, but answer_value tolerates missing keys. Timeout is 60 s (jev_client.py system_one timeout=60), which is long; a hung API could stall the agent's Bash call for up to a minute, with no retry.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. The skill's frontmatter description costs about 130 tokens (about 520 chars) in the Claude Code skills listing. When SKILL.md is triggered it loads about 222 lines (roughly 3.5-4k tokens), plus references/schemas.md (319 lines) and lifecycle.md on demand. No hook-injected text.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only. Claude decides to load the skill when the conversation is about long-term research experiments (initialize research memory, record experiment results, resume work, handoffs). The Jev scripts run only if the model follows SKILL.md instructions in start/doctor/claim-audit/synthesize AND the env key is set. There is no deterministic hook, and the skill never triggers for ordinary coding tasks such as editing, debugging or reviewing.
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.latencyImpact: Zero on normal coding turns, since it is not triggered. In research sessions: one script call at 'start' of about 70-500 ms claimed API latency plus Python start, and 60 s worst-case timeout. The script call is an extra model tool step, which adds one Claude turn of overhead, so the saving is dubious.
pros: Concrete, readable, working example of using Jev's Score primitive for a real triage task (relevance scoring of memory items with confidence, using a 3-level ordered scale). It is a useful reference for the request shape: {state, model, questions:{id:{type:score,instructions,criteria}}}.
Zero dependencies (stdlib urllib), no shell execution, no telemetry, small enough to audit in about 15 minutes; key goes in a header, not argv.
Cleanly fail-open (FALLBACK, exit 0) with a --dry-run preview mode; SKILL.md explicitly says Jev is 'never a capability gate'.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override makes retargeting at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone a one-line env change if the schemas match.
MIT license.
cons: Domain mismatch: it targets scientific experiment logging (EXPERIMENTS.md, hypotheses, claims, provenance). It gives no value to everyday coding in client and personal projects, and would impose a research-memory file layout if it triggered.

Jev is not an automatic layer: only a skill description trigger plus SKILL.md prose telling the model to run a script. Claude Code will not call Jev for ordinary coding, which is the user's requirement.

Direct TypeSafe only. No OPENROUTER_API_KEY support, no 'openrouter' string in the code; requires a hack of putting the OpenRouter key into TYPESAFE_API_KEY and overriding the model name via --model. The OpenRouter response shape is unverified against the parser.

The Jev output is used for a task Claude can do by reading a few files, and it adds a model step (Bash call) to save a few file reads. Value is low; the maintainers themselves call it a 'fallback, not degradation'.
Very immature: 13 commits by one author in one day, created 2026-09-22, no tests, no CI, no releases, 9 stars; half the commits are README diagram polishing/promotion.
60 s timeout with no retry, and the .env loader picks up a .env from the cwd, which in client projects may contain unrelated secrets (only TYPESAFE_* are consumed, but the file is read).
gh-poiuyjie-jev-project-context.verdict: Not an integration for daily coding: it is a niche research-experiment-memory skill that uses Jev only as an optional relevance and audit triage scorer, is direct-TypeSafe-only, and is triggered only by the model matching its description. Skip it for the OpenRouter/Claude Code goal; at most, treat jev_client.py as a small reference for the System One request/response shape.

gh-nidhi-singh02-agent-router.name: nidhi-singh02/agent-router
gh-nidhi-singh02-agent-router.whatItDoes: A Node/TypeScript CLI (`router run "<task>"`) that picks which coding agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode), model and reasoning effort to use for a task. It filters subscriptions by quota and policy, then asks Jev through the TypeSafe SDK (`systemOne`) to classify the task and rank the remaining candidates. It then launches the chosen agent in a Herdr terminal-multiplexer pane. It is not an MCP server or a hook, and it does not proxy Claude Code's own traffic. It is an external orchestrator that starts agents, and a Claude Code skill (`skills/model-router`) tells an agent to call the CLI.

providerSupport.evidence: packages/router/src/semantic/typesafe-client.ts:1-27 imports `TypeSafeClient` from `@typesafe-ai/sdk` and builds it with `new TypeSafeClient({ apiKey })`. No `openrouter` string appears anywhere in packages/router/src. The key is read in packages/router/src/commands/runtime.ts:190-200 from `keychain:model-router-typesafe` (macOS `security`) or the env var `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:56-58, 513) defaults to `https://api.typesafe.ai` and reads `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`. The calls use the SDK's `systemOne` wire format, which is TypeSafe's own API.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The SDK honours `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and an `apiKey` config, so pointing it at `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` with an OpenRouter key might work with no code change, if OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same request and response schema as the SDK. That was not verified. The SDK's request path was not confirmed, and OpenRouter may need a `typesafe/jev-1.13` model ID, because the SDK defaults to model `jev-latest` (dist/index.mjs:59). The key lookup is also macOS Keychain-first, though the env var fallback works on Linux. Worth a small experiment, not guaranteed.
providerSupport.others: None. The SDK is TypeSafe-only. The agent CLIs it launches use their own subscription logins.

security: The README says pre-release. It is 13 days old, 128 commits by 1 person (two git identities), 99 stars, one v0.1.0 release. There is no .github directory, so no CI.

API key handling is good. It supports a macOS Keychain reference (`keychain:NAME`) or an `env:NAME` reference. Config forbids secret values, and launched Herdr commands get an allowlisted environment (docs/privacy.md). The Keychain path is macOS-only.

Client-side guard `assertSafeState` (typesafe-client.ts:29-45) regex-rejects sk-, Bearer, GitHub, Slack, AWS, Google, private-key and URL-with-password strings before any Jev call. It is best-effort and does not catch arbitrary secrets in free text.

It shells out. It runs the `herdr` CLI, git worktree commands, the agent CLIs, and Keychain/official usage CLIs (collectors/verified-command.ts, launch/herdr-client.ts). The pane-text reading and keystroke injection for `/effort` (live-effort) is fragile and UI-coupled.
The build runs `npm ci` and compiles better-sqlite3 natively. Dependencies are few (commander, zod, better-sqlite3, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0).
Optional Cloudflare coordinator and Hermes heartbeat packages are off by default. The README says not to deploy them without approval.
Browser dashboard collectors scrape usage pages. The docs say they never copy cookie databases.

Prompt-injection surface is the SKILL.md instruction telling agents to run `router run` and `router effort` with no user confirmation for effort switches. The task text goes to Jev, but Jev returns typed output only, so injection through Jev output is limited.

Enrichment is bucketed and sends no paths or repo names.","`router effort --session` sends a one-line sub-step (at most 500 characters), the phase, the current effort, and bucketed signals.","No file contents, diffs, tool outputs or conversation are sent.","It does not send Claude Code's own traffic. gh-nidhi-singh02-agent-router.failureMode: Fail-closed for routing. The README says "Routing always calls TypeSafe; there is no fallback". If the call errors, decision-engine.ts returns `typesafe-unavailable`, and only two task families (routine-transformation and metadata) get a deterministic fallback (semantic/fallback.ts:5-24). The router never sits in Claude Code's own request path, so a slow or failed Jev call does not break Claude Code itself. It only blocks a `router run` launch. No custom Jev timeout was found. The SDK has its own timeout and retry policy, and the router uses its defaults.
gh-nidhi-singh02-agent-router.contextCost: No MCP tools and no hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. The only cost is the skill: a SKILL.md of 59 lines (about 1,000 tokens once triggered), with a short description always in the skill list (about 100 tokens). Skill loading is on demand.
gh-nidhi-singh02-agent-router.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger and only when prompted. The skill fires when the user asks to pick a model, subscription or effort, or when an agent launched by `router` reaches the end of a phase. The launching side requires a Herdr pane (HERDR_ENV=1). It never triggers on ordinary coding, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
pros: The Jev questions are well designed for a real use case. It uses several Jev primitives (Choice for ranking, Score for complexity and consequence, and a confidence policy that asks the user when confidence is below 0.75 on high-consequence tasks). This is useful as a reference for how to call Jev.
Privacy design is thoughtful. Bucketed signals, a local secret-pattern guard, a Keychain reference for keys, and a 0700/0600 state directory.
Large test suite (about 25k lines of TS and tests, vitest, a routing evals JSON) and detailed design docs and specs.
MIT license. The TypeSafe SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so OpenRouter may be reachable with little change.
Includes real Claude Code specifics, such as the CLAUDE_EFFORT variable and Opus 5.5 effort levels.
cons: It does not integrate into Claude Code. It launches Claude Code as one target among four agents inside Herdr. It is not a hook, MCP server or proxy, and it cannot make the user's existing Claude Code session use Jev.
It requires Herdr (HERDR_ENV=1) to launch anything. The user's workflow shows no Herdr.

The only automatic behavior comes from a skill that needs the user to run the router flow first. It is also written around routing between paid subscriptions (Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Claude), which this single-subscription user does not need.
TypeSafe-direct only, with no OpenRouter code. Switching to OpenRouter is unverified and depends on SDK path and model-ID compatibility. The key resolution is Keychain-first (macOS).
Every run sends the task text to a third party, and routing is fail-closed with no general fallback.

gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.name: Larkspur-Wang/Jev_steer_or_queue
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (plus a Codex variant) with five hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, StopFailure) that all run one stdlib-only Python script. When you type a message while Claude is mid-turn, the script calls Jev (Choice timing: steer/queue/interrupt/unclear, plus a Noul explicit_stop) and either lets it through (steer), blocks it and replays it from the Stop hook after the turn (queue), or blocks it and returns continue:false at the next tool boundary (interrupt). Messages sent while idle never reach Jev. It defaults to shadow mode, which only logs. It does not help with code, review or model routing. It only decides how to handle the user's own interjections.

providerSupport.evidence: claude-code/scripts/jev_router.py:28 DEFAULT_URL = https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Line 168 reads the URL from option('TYPESAFE_API_URL'), so JEV_ROUTER_TYPESAFE_API_URL overrides it (README env table). Line 67 api_key() reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Line 138 model default is 'jev-latest' via JEV_ROUTER_JEV_MODEL. Line 170 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'. The request body is {model, state, questions{type: choice|noul, instructions, criteria}} and the response is parsed as answers.timing.{choice,probabilities} and answers.explicit_stop.noul (lines 137-187). There are no OpenRouter strings anywhere in the repo.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in config, unverified in wire format. The client already uses a System One style body, and the URL, key and model are all overridable through env vars with no code change. Set JEV_ROUTER_TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and JEV_ROUTER_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). The risks are (1) that OpenRouter's /systemone request/response schema (state/questions/answers, noul key) matches TypeSafe's direct one exactly, which I could not confirm from this repo, and (2) that the model id needs the typesafe/ prefix. Reusing TYPESAFE_API_KEY to hold an OpenRouter key works but is confusing. Because the script fails open on HTTP 4xx, a wrong schema would silently degrade to native steering, so check log.jsonl for jev errors.
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe direct only by default. No other gateways.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook
interface.purpose: Detects mid-turn messages by comparing prompt_id with the stored active turn. It calls Jev only for mid-turn messages, and in active mode blocks queue/interrupt ones. On a new turn it drains leftover queue items and shows a systemMessage listing dropped ones.

interface.name: PreToolUse hook (matcher *)
interface.purpose: If an interrupt is pending, returns continue:false with stopReason and drains the queue. Otherwise it only reads and saves session state.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook (matcher *)
interface.purpose: Same as PreToolUse: performs the hard stop at the tool boundary.

interface.name: Stop hook
interface.purpose: In active mode, pops one queued message and returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext so Claude handles it as a continuation. Otherwise it marks the session inactive.

interface.name: StopFailure hook
interface.purpose: Resets the session's active/stop flags.

interface.name: plugin userConfig
interface.purpose: typesafe_api_key (sensitive, keychain) and mode (shadow|active, default shadow).

interface.name: env options
interface.purpose: JEV_ROUTER_MODE, _QUEUE_THRESHOLD (0.9), _INTERRUPT_THRESHOLD (0.9), _TIMEOUT_S (2.0), _JEV_MODEL, _TYPESAFE_API_URL, _LOG_PROMPTS. Optional ~/.jev-steer-or-queue/config.json is also read.

gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.runtime: Python 3.8+ stdlib only (python3 on PATH); uses fcntl, so POSIX only. Distributed as a Claude Code plugin marketplace.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.install: /plugin marketplace add Larkspur-Wang/Jev_steer_or_queue ; /plugin install jev-steer-or-queue@jev-steer-or-queue (needs Claude Code >=2.1.196 for the prompt_id hook field)
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.tests: None. The repo has no test files and no CI. docs/test-results.md holds manual tmux e2e notes on Claude Code 2.1.280 and Codex 0.156.1 (in Chinese), covering about 25 Jev calls at 438-660 ms, with occasional 1.5 s calls and one timeout at a 3 s limit.
security: API key is sent in the Authorization header via urllib, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. Plugin userConfig marks it sensitive (keychain). Alternatively it can sit in plaintext in ~/.jev-steer-or-queue/config.json or in env.
No shell execution, no eval, no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry beyond the Jev call. The script is about 300 lines and easy to audit.
Hook command is python3 on PATH, run for every tool call and prompt. A rogue update to the plugin would be arbitrary code in your hooks, so pin a commit.
Prompt-injection surface: queued user text is re-injected as Stop additionalContext, but it is only the user's own text. Jev output is numeric probabilities, so it cannot inject text.

log.jsonl under ~/.claude/plugins/data/... stores the first 300 chars of every prompt by default (LOG_PROMPTS=true), including client-project text. Session state files store the first 500 chars of the task and the full queued messages, unencrypted.
Blocking on UserPromptSubmit erases the message from the transcript. A misclassified 'queue' or 'interrupt' can silently lose or delay user input, and dropped items are only shown on the next prompt.
Hard-coded Chinese-language classification criteria and user notices. English behavior is unvalidated.
Single author, 3 commits, unaffiliated with TypeSafe, and the repo is 7 days old.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.dataEgress: Only for mid-turn user messages (not idle ones): new_message (up to 2000 chars) and active_task (first 500 chars of the turn's initial prompt), sent to the TypeSafe endpoint (or OpenRouter if repointed). Nothing else is sent: no transcript, files, diffs or tool output (jev_router.py:137-143). Note the first 500 chars of your prompt can contain client details, and OpenRouter would see them and may log them depending on your data policy settings.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.failureMode: Fail-open. A missing key, HTTP error, timeout or exception returns an error and the action becomes steer, which is native Claude Code behavior (lines 134-136, 177-180, 230). The default timeout is 2.0 s (JEV_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_S). The hook's own timeout is 10 s for UserPromptSubmit and 5 s for the others. main() wraps everything in try/except and exits 0 (lines 305-308). One caveat is that a silent failure looks like success, since the test notes say only 'jev: null' in the log reveals it. Another is that queued items are lost if the turn ends abnormally.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.latencyImpact: Mid-turn messages only: about 0.45-0.65 s per message, up to 2 s on timeout, and the user waits on it before the message is injected. Every other hook event (each PreToolUse and PostToolUse with matcher *, plus Stop) spawns a python3 process that takes an flock and reads and writes the session JSON. That is roughly 20-60 ms per tool call by estimate (I did not measure it), and it stacks with your existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. There is no network call on those events.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.contextCost: Zero tools, no MCP instructions, so 0 tokens of tool definitions. Hook-injected text appears only when a queued message is replayed from Stop (one short Chinese preamble plus the message, about 50 tokens), or a Chinese systemMessage when dropped items are reported. In shadow mode nothing is injected at all.
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. It runs on every UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop with no user prompting. It only calls Jev when you type while a turn is running.
pros: Genuinely automatic: hook-based with no model discretion, and zero context or tool-definition cost.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to, a cheap typed classification (Choice plus Noul with calibrated probabilities) with no free text, at 0.4-0.7 s latency.
Safe defaults: shadow mode out of the box, 0.9 confidence thresholds, and fail-open on every error path. Shadow mode lets you audit decisions in log.jsonl for days before enabling it.
Small, dependency-free, readable code (about 300 lines) with no installers or postinstall steps. The API key is in a header, not argv.
OpenRouter repointing is almost config-only: URL, key and model are all env-overridable (jev_router.py:168, :67, :138).
Payload is minimal: only the mid-turn message and a 500-char task snippet, with no code or tool output. Cost is negligible, at about $0.04 per 1M input tokens.
cons: Solves a narrow UX problem (mid-turn interjection timing), not daily coding help. It does not route models, review diffs, or gate tool calls, so its value is small for a senior dev who mostly waits for turns.
The user runs bypass/auto mode and long Opus turns, so mid-turn typing may be occasional. Claude Code's native steering already handles most of these cases.

Active mode can lose or delay input: blocked messages are erased from the transcript, only one queued item replays per Stop, there is an 8-continuation cap, Esc fires no hook so queued items are dropped, and a wrong interrupt call stops work at the next tool boundary. Jev is admitted to be weak on negation and multi-intent messages.
Prompts and criteria are in Chinese and only tested by the author on Chinese and simple English sleep-loop scenarios. English classification quality on real coding messages is unverified.

Registers PreToolUse/PostToolUse with matcher * and spawns python3 on every tool call, adding a small per-call cost next to your secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Ordering relative to the existing PreToolUse hooks is untested.
Immature: 2 stars, 3 commits, 1 contributor, no tests, no CI, no releases, created a week ago. The repo describes only a manual macOS test on Claude Code 2.1.280, not your 2.1.285 on Linux.
Native TypeSafe API only, and OpenRouter /systemone schema compatibility is unverified. Under a wrong schema it fails open silently, so the plugin would appear installed while doing nothing.
Logs the first 300 chars of every prompt to disk by default, which is a concern on client projects (set LOG_PROMPTS=false).
gh-larkspur-wang-jev-steer-or-queue.verdict: A clean, safe-by-default hook that is genuinely automatic, but it only manages mid-turn message timing and is a 1-week-old single-author PoC that talks to TypeSafe direct. Try it in shadow mode via the URL/key/model env overrides if you like, but do not count it as a core Jev integration for daily coding, and do not enable active mode without validating English classification in the logs.

Eval suite: 6 tasks x 10 runs x 3 arms, self-reported 0.96 vs 0.65 no-skill vs 0.77 official skill; graders are partly LLM judges, and this measures code the agent writes, not runtime behaviour.
security: No executable code in the Claude Code install path: plugin has no hooks, no MCP servers, no commands; skill is inert markdown (.claude-plugin/plugin.json and marketplace.json contain only metadata).

Only curl|bash is scripts/install_muse.sh (README for Muse): curl -fsSL codeload.github.com ... | tar -xz, rewrites frontmatter, rm -rf/mv into ~/workspace/skills. Muse-only, not needed for Claude Code, but it is a pipe-to-bash install path advertised in the README.

Key handling guidance is good: SKILL.md:20-24 says never print/echo/log/commit the key, never hardcode api_key=, do not search .env/profiles for it, warns TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs bodies unredacted. It does have the agent run live probes (up to ~10 calls per task) when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is in the shell, so state sent to Jev in probes is whatever the agent chooses.

Prompt-injection surface: skill instructs the agent to fetch https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and .md pages and treat live docs as winning on conflict (SKILL.md line 10), so third-party doc content becomes trusted instructions; minor but real. Prior-art files are 73 KB of links to unvetted community repos.

Supply chain: single maintainer, 4 days old, 1 open issue; marketplace may be set to auto-sync, so a later malicious commit would flow into a global skill. Plugin skill can be pinned by commit SHA to mitigate.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no network calls from the plugin itself.
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from the plugin itself. The agent may fetch docs.typesafe.ai pages (outbound GET, no user data). If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set, the agent may issue small live probe calls to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone containing whatever state/questions it designs for the code being built (potentially snippets of the user's project data); it will not do so with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY set. In no case are Claude Code prompts, diffs or tool outputs forwarded to Jev automatically.
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.failureMode: Not applicable at runtime: no Jev call path exists. If docs.typesafe.ai is unreachable the skill says to read installed SDK types and tell the user. If no key is set it designs from api-reference.md and says so (fail-open, no blocking). No timeouts to configure.
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.contextCost: 0 tools, 0 MCP instructions, 0 hook-injected text. Always-resident cost is only the skill name+description (~600 chars, about 150 tokens). On trigger, SKILL.md loads ~11.9 KB (about 3k tokens); api-reference.md (11.6 KB, ~2.9k tokens), patterns.md (9.2 KB, ~2.3k) and a prior-art shape file (~6 KB each, ~1.5k) load on demand. Typical triggered turn: 3-8k tokens. Description is broad ('classify, route, triage, filter, extract, score, rank') so it may load on unrelated NL-classification coding tasks and add noise.
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion) only, and only when the user's task is BUILDING an app/feature that uses Jev or NL judgments. It does not make Claude Code call Jev for its own decisions (permission gating, commit classification, context routing); SKILL.md itself states Jev 'is not a chat or coding LLM and cannot power a coding agent'.
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.latencyImpact: Zero added latency to normal Claude Code turns (no hook, proxy, or tool). Only skill file load on trigger; live probes, if any, are single Jev calls (claimed 70-500 ms).
pros: Zero risk and zero runtime footprint: no hooks, MCP server, postinstall or network from the plugin, so it cannot conflict with the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus hooks, or caveman plugins.

Genuinely useful when the user (senior dev, client projects) writes code that calls Jev: encodes rules like one snap judgment per question, batch all questions in one call, Score levels as situations, deterministic denylist before Jev, never let a Jev answer alone authorize a side effect. Rules cited in SKILL.md:26-60 are specific and consistent with the Jev brief.

Includes a gates.md shape with a concrete Bash-command gate (DENY regex first, then Noul flags + severity Score, block/review/allow bands) plus a 'Stop hook completion gate' variant: a ready design sketch for the user's own DIY Jev-in-Claude-Code hook. Also references OpenRouter cookbooks 'Gate Agent Tool Calls' and 'Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts' (gates.md:83) as prior art to mine.
Documents OpenRouter usage (base_url https://openrouter.ai/api, model ~typesafe/jev-latest) and Vercel gateway, and pins-to-model-version advice (jev-1.13.0), so generated code can target OpenRouter.

Good hygiene and CI: MIT, plugin validated with claude plugin validate --strict on pinned Claude Code, leaked-key scan, eval harness with isolated containers and a public ledger; code samples were validated against the live API per commit #3.
Cheap idle cost (~150 tokens of description) and installs with two claude plugin commands.
cons: It is not an integration. It never makes Claude Code invoke Jev; it does not meet the core requirement (automatic Jev use inside Claude Code without prompting). It only changes how Claude writes code when the task is already about Jev/NL classification.

API-reference is TypeSafe-direct-centric: default base URL api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, key env TYPESAFE_API_KEY; the live-probe behavior is gated on TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it won't probe using OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and it does not document OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone paths, or OpenRouter key/header conventions beyond one line (api-reference.md:130).

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-26, 8 commits, 1 contributor (aaddrick), no releases, 1 open issue; stars (125) driven by Jev hype. Content may drift from the beta API; it defers to live docs, which are fetched at runtime (untrusted-text-as-authority risk).

Broad trigger description (classify/route/triage/filter/extract/score/rank) can fire on ordinary app work, spending 3-8k tokens on a skill irrelevant to the task; non-Jev tasks may get nudged toward Jev.
Eval claims (0.96 vs 0.65) are self-measured, judged partly by LLMs, on agent-written code without an API key; says nothing about real Jev accuracy or the Theo 'flash router' skepticism.
README advertises curl|bash install (Muse only) and auto-sync marketplace option; single-maintainer auto-updating global skill is a supply-chain consideration for client work (pin a commit if used).
gh-aaddrick-building-with-typesafe-jev.verdict: A well-made, safe, inert knowledge skill for writing code that uses Jev, not a way to have Claude Code use Jev automatically. Worth installing as a cheap companion only if the user builds Jev-backed apps; otherwise it does nothing for the stated goal, which needs a hook or proxy that calls OpenRouter's Jev directly (its gates.md pattern is a good blueprint for that).

gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.tests: None in repo: no tests directory, no CI (.github absent), no releases. 'Tested' claims refer to the author's own lab logs (not included).
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.runtime: Python 3 stdlib only (urllib, concurrent.futures); no dependencies, no package manifest, no MCP server, no hooks
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.install: git clone https://github.com/marcodicesare-dev/jev-skill.git ~/.claude/skills/jev ; export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... (and call with --via openrouter)
security: API key read from env var only (jev.py:28) and sent as Bearer header; never placed in argv or process list. Good.

No shell execution, no eval, no subprocess, no telemetry; CLI only contacts the chosen endpoint (plus api.llmapi.ai/v1/credits for 'credits'). Comment at jev.py:49-51 says exp/tag are not sent or logged.
No curl|sh, no postinstall, install is plain git clone.
State (potentially code/text) is passed on the command line via --state '<json>' (visible in argv/process list to local users) unless a file path is given; load_json accepts a file.
Default route is llmapi.ai, a third-party gateway not otherwise vetted; an agent following SKILL.md example might send data to the typesafe or llmapi routes rather than OpenRouter.
Retries up to 8x on 429/5xx/timeouts with backoff up to 20 s and 30 s timeout per attempt: worst case minutes of blocking.
Skill text itself is benign (no instructions to exfiltrate); SKILL.md rule 5 says apply data-sharing rules and never send secrets, but nothing enforces it.
Author is single individual, 3 days old repo; supply-chain risk if you clone and later git pull (skill content can change under you).
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.dataEgress: Only what the agent chooses to put in --state/--questions is POSTed to the selected endpoint (OpenRouter with --via openrouter): arbitrary text/JSON, up to ~32k tokens. Nothing automatic; no hook or proxy captures prompts, diffs or tool output. Author notes Jev is on OpenRouter ZDR list (reference/api.md:82, unverified by me).
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.failureMode: Not applicable as a hook (none exists). CLI fails open in the sense that a failed call just returns non-zero exit and error JSON to the agent; but retry loop (jev.py:30-42, up to 8 attempts, 30 s timeout each, exponential backoff capped at 20 s) can block a Bash call for several minutes when Jev/OpenRouter is down. Missing key -> sys.exit with message.
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.contextCost: Very low. One skill: frontmatter description ~700 chars (~180 tokens) always listed in the skills roster. Full SKILL.md body ~7.2k chars (~1.8k tokens) only when the skill is loaded; reference/*.md loaded on demand (api.md ~10k chars, capabilities ~6k). No MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text.
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.latencyImpact: Zero unless the skill is invoked. When invoked: skill load (+~2k tokens) plus a Bash call to python3 with Jev latency (author reports 0.3-1.6 s for multi-question calls; brief claims 70-500 ms). Each use is an extra model turn to write state/questions JSON.
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). The description says 'Load when the user asks to use or test Jev, or when a workflow needs semantic classification, routing, scoring, rule checks...' so Claude may load it on such tasks, but it then only gets documentation and a CLI; nothing makes Claude call Jev during ordinary coding. No deterministic hook, no proxy.
pros: Only candidate here with an explicit, code-level OpenRouter route matching the brief: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY (tools/jev.py:20).
Near-zero context cost (~180 tokens roster entry) and zero latency when unused; no MCP server to run or fail.
Stdlib-only, ~110-line CLI, easy to audit fully; no shell exec, no telemetry, key via env not argv.

Valuable practical knowledge: question shapes, pitfalls (option names reach the model, Noul vs negation not summing to 1, overconfidence by 3-20 points, 1 text per call) and calibration data that would help Claude write correct Jev calls in application code.
Honest about limits (says not to use Jev for writing/explaining; injection flag is not a security boundary), MIT license.
cons: Not an automatic integration: it is documentation plus a manual CLI. Nothing makes Claude Code consult Jev during normal coding; at best the model may load the skill on classification/routing tasks. Fails the user's core requirement.
Aimed at building Jev-powered pipelines (hotel marketing, ad scoring, ticket routing), not at improving an AI coding assistant; none of the 5 recipes address code tasks (recipes/*.json).

Default route is llmapi.ai (third-party gateway, LLMAPI_API_KEY) and the SKILL.md/README quickstart uses --via typesafe; OpenRouter needs explicit --via openrouter, and 'credits' only works for llmapi. An agent following the docs literally will not use OpenRouter.
Does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) that the brief lists, only /api/v1/systemone.
Very young and thin: 1 star, 1 contributor, 11 commits over 2 days, no tests, no CI, no releases; performance claims come from the author's private lab logs not in the repo.
Retry loop (8 attempts, up to 20 s backoff, 30 s timeout) can stall an agent's Bash call for minutes on outage.
--state passed inline in argv would expose content to the local process list; cloned skill directory can change on git pull (unpinned supply chain).
Vendors ~18 MB of PNG/JPG marketing assets and blog-style guides with author promotion (Lumina) into a skills directory, which is noise for a dev tool.
gh-marcodicesare-dev-jev-skill.verdict: Useful as a reference and as a tiny OpenRouter-capable CLI, but it is a manually-triggered skill, not an automatic integration, and it addresses app pipelines rather than coding. Reasonable optional companion for writing Jev calls; not the answer to 'Claude Code must use Jev on its own'.

gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.whatItDoes: A Claude Code / ZCode skill (SKILL.md plus a 108-line stdlib-only jev.py) that calls Jev's System One endpoint through OpenCode Zen, using the free model jev-1.13-free. The SKILL.md description tells the model to use it automatically for classify/route, batch screen, score/rank and verify tasks. The author adapted it from the official typesafe-ai/skills SKILL.md. Its examples and showcase are about triaging e-commerce comments for the author's Taobao shop, and the README links that shop.

providerSupport.evidence: jev.py:27 ENDPOINT = os.environ.get('JEV_ENDPOINT', 'https://opencode.ai/zen/v1/systemone'); jev.py:28 MODEL = os.environ.get('JEV_MODEL','jev-1.13-free'). Key lookup at jev.py:32-43 reads only ZEN_API_KEY, ~/.jev/zen.key, a zen.key next to the script, or ~/.zcode/skills/typesafe-ai/zen.key. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY handling. jev.py:59 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>'. references/api-notes.md:15 says JEV_ENDPOINT/JEV_MODEL can be overridden for paid models.
providerSupport.others: OpenCode Zen only, which is the free gateway. Nothing else is supported in code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and it needs no code edit. Export JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 and ZEN_API_KEY=<the OpenRouter key>. Bearer auth and the request body ({state, questions, model}) are the same. I could not confirm that OpenRouter's response envelope (answers, usage, cost) matches Zen's, but the Jev brief says it is the same System One API. Cleaner is a 5-line patch that adds an OPENROUTER_API_KEY lookup and changes the defaults. The 'curl/8.9.1' User-Agent (jev.py:63) is a Zen WAF workaround and is unneeded, arguably undesirable, for OpenRouter.

interface.name: SKILL.md (skill name 'jev')
interface.purpose: The description frontmatter acts as the auto-trigger. It says 'Use AUTOMATICALLY, without the user asking' for classify/route, batch-screen, score/rank and verify tasks. The body documents the request schema for noul, choice and score, plus pitfalls.

interface.name: python jev.py [--raw] [request.json]
interface.purpose: Reads a request JSON from stdin or a file, adds the model field, POSTs it to the endpoint, and prints compact per-question lines plus a usage/cost line. Exit codes are 0 ok, 1 API error, 2 no key. It retries 3 times with backoff on 429/500/502/503/529 or network errors and uses a 60 s timeout.

interface.name: jev.call(req, retries=3)
interface.purpose: Importable Python function (jev.py:46), used by examples/comment_triage.py.

interface.name: examples/comment_triage.py
interface.purpose: Batch triage example for Chinese shop comments. It asks is_question, category, priority and compliance_risk. It is not useful for coding.

security: API key is sent in the Authorization header from a file or env var. It never appears in argv, so there is no process-list leak. There is no file permission check on ~/.jev/zen.key.
jev.py:63 deliberately spoofs the User-Agent 'curl/8.9.1' to get past the gateway WAF. That is a smell, and it only matters for the Zen route.
There is no telemetry, postinstall, curl|sh installer or shell execution in jev.py. It is stdlib only with a single HTTPS endpoint, and the ENDPOINT is env-overridable.

The prompt-injection surface comes from the skill's design. It tells the agent to feed raw untrusted content (comments, logs, messages) to Jev and consume the probabilities, which are typed and cannot carry free text. That is lower risk than a free-text model, but the agent decides what goes into 'state'.
The SKILL.md and README promote the author's Taobao shop (self-promotion). It is not malicious, but it is the marketing of an unrelated business.
The free tier depends on a claimed loophole: the /v1/systemone endpoint bypasses the free-tier client fence that applies to chat endpoints (api-notes.md:70-74). It could be closed at any time.
gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in the 'state' and 'questions' JSON goes to opencode.ai/zen, or to openrouter.ai if you override the endpoint. That could be code snippets, logs, diffs, commit messages or file contents if the model chooses to send them. There is no built-in redaction, size cap or allowlist. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background. Data leaves only when the agent decides to run jev.py. With the free Zen route, data goes to a third-party gateway on a free tier, which is a client-confidentiality concern.
gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.failureMode: Fail-open at the process level. jev.py returns {'error': ...} after 3 attempts (backoff 1s, 2s, 3s, 60 s timeout each, so worst case is about 3 minutes plus sleeps). It exits 1 on API error or 2 if there is no key, and Claude just sees the error text. Nothing blocks the session because there is no hook. A stalled call can hold a Bash tool call for up to 3 minutes, though. There is no circuit breaker.
gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.contextCost: There are 0 MCP tools and 0 hook-injected text. gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.autoInvocation: Skill-description trigger only. It is model-discretion, and Claude decides from the description whether a task matches. There is no deterministic hook and no transparent proxy. The triggers (tickets, comments, batch screening, scoring, verifying claims) are generic and business-flavored, so Claude will seldom hit them during normal coding work.
gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.latencyImpact: Only when Claude invokes it. The README claims about 2 s end to end for the Zen free route (README.en.md:20), which is slower than Jev's claimed 70-500 ms. Each call spawns a Python process plus a Bash tool round trip. gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.tests: None. There is no test suite and no CI. The claims are backed only by the author's benchmark write-up, which covers about 18 calls, and by that report's own numbers.
pros: Zero-dependency 108-line jev.py that is easy to audit. I read the whole thing: no shell execution, no telemetry, and the key stays out of argv.

The endpoint, model and key can be pointed at OpenRouter with no code change: JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, ZEN_API_KEY=<openrouter key>. A hard-coded key lookup is the only oddity.
Context cost is tiny, about 225 tokens for the listing, and there are no MCP tools. It also does not touch the existing PreToolUse, GitNexus or caveman hooks.
It uses Claude Code's native skill mechanism, so the trigger is truly automatic and needs no user prompting. That is the user's stated wish, and it is done in the least invasive way.
It has practical retry and backoff logic, and it merges several questions into one request for parallel execution.
The batch pattern (raw items stay in the script, only conclusions return to context) is a sensible use of the skill if a bulk task ever arises.
cons: Wrong domain for coding. Triggers are ticket/comment/log triage, candidate screening and claim verification. Examples and showcase are Chinese Taobao shop comments, so Claude will rarely or never match it during real coding tasks, or will match it on the wrong things.

Provider is hard-wired to OpenCode Zen. Nothing in the code mentions OpenRouter, so the user must know about the env overrides. The default model jev-1.13-free is a Zen-specific name that does not exist on OpenRouter.
The free tier relies on an unofficial loophole (api-notes.md:70-74). Sending client code and logs to a free third-party gateway is a confidentiality risk if it is left on the default endpoint.

It never says what to give Jev in a coding session (for example diff classification or test-failure triage). It offers no coding-specific question templates, and the model would have to hand-build the JSON each time.
Single author, 4 commits in a single day, 0 stars, no tests or CI, no releases. It is a personal utility that advertises the author's shop.
No timeout budget or fail-fast: 3 retries with a 60 s timeout each can block a Bash call for up to about 3 minutes if the gateway hangs.
Spoofing the curl User-Agent to get past the WAF is fragile and ethically dubious.
Adds nothing beyond the official typesafe-ai/skills SKILL.md apart from the Zen workaround, since the author adapted that skill.
gh-yuyang2230-jev-agent-skill.verdict: This is a thin, safe-to-read wrapper adapted from the official skill, and it is tuned to shop-comment triage on OpenCode Zen. It works on OpenRouter with three env vars, but the triggers rarely match coding work, so it is marginal for this user. If the user wants a Jev skill, fork it and rewrite the description around coding judgments, or use the official typesafe-ai/skills version, rather than adopting this one as is.

gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.whatItDoes: Automatic per-project memory for Claude Code (also Cursor/Codex). Claude Code plugin + CLI (jevmem) with 3 hooks and a 4-tool stdio MCP server. Stop hook (async) queues each finished turn and asks Jev typed questions (choice/noul/score via POST /v1/systemone) to decide whether it holds a decision/constraint/bug/todo, then appends one line (max 200 chars, extracted by code, not LLM) to JEVMEM.md in the repo and marks contradicted lines [superseded]. UserPromptSubmit hook makes one Jev call to pick the ~5 most relevant memory lines and injects them as additionalContext. Lines not written on this machine (e.g. from git pull) are checked by Jev noul for prompt-injection before being injected. Unreleased main (0.6) adds a PreToolUse guard (Bash|Edit|Write vs saved constraint rules) and dead-end lines. Jev is used as a fast classifier/ranker, which is exactly the System One use case.

Deps minimal: zod, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (MIT), @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No curl|sh installer; install is `npm install -g jevmem` (user runs the global CLI, so hooks execute code from npm on every prompt: supply-chain trust in a 1-week-old, 1-author package).

Key handling: read from env / ~/.jevmem/env (0600, dir 0700 via `jevmem key`, hidden prompt) / plugin sensitive userConfig; key not in argv. The plugin MCP entry passes it via env (CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFE_API_KEY), not argv. JEVMEM_DEBUG=1 logs only 'set'/'missing'.

Real past vuln: GHSA-2r3p-5hmg-46p5, fixed 0.5.8 (2026-09-28): PGPASSWORD=/"password": values were NOT scrubbed before being sent to TypeSafe in <=0.5.7. Scrubbing is regex-based; names, phones, addresses, unknown secret shapes not caught.

Prompt-injection surface: JEVMEM.md is git-committed, so PR/teammate lines are injected into context. Mitigated by Jev noul gate (author's own eval: blocks 20/22 planted lines, 2 missed) and a data-not-instructions frame; still a filter not a guarantee. JEVMEM.md header tells AIs not to edit it.

Shell execution: launcher hooks/jevmem-hook.sh (POSIX sh) locates node and runs dist/cli.js; always exits 0. Spawns a detached daemon process. Opt-in per project (does nothing without jevmem.config.json). Hook stores scrubbed turn text in .jevmem/ (gitignored) and stop-hook input in system temp.
No telemetry (PRIVACY.md; source checked by a test). Only network calls: TypeSafe (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), optionally OpenAI/Anthropic if writer configured.

Existing hooks compatibility: it does not touch Bash|Read|Grep guard matchers in released 0.5.10; the 0.6 PreToolUse Bash|Edit|Write guard would run alongside the user's secret-leak guard (both allowed to deny).
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.dataEgress: Only from projects containing jevmem.config.json (opt-in via `jevmem enable`). Sent to TypeSafe (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so to OpenRouter and onward to TypeSafe if rerouted), after regex scrubbing of secrets/emails/16-digit numbers: (Stop) the user's message for each turn, previous 2 turns (shortened), up to 200 memory lines, and the assistant reply only when the message looks like a question/bug report; (UserPromptSubmit) the full user prompt plus up to 60 memory lines (250 on main); (MCP/CLI) memory lines, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md statements on import, and for audit file names to depth 3, package.json fields, first 3000 chars of README. Guard (0.6): bash command or file path + <=600 chars new/300 chars old text of edits, only when overlapping a constraint rule. Not sent: whole files, diffs beyond guard snippets, tool outputs. Client-project prompts (which may contain proprietary detail) would leave the machine to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, and JEVMEM.md gets committed into repos.
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.failureMode: Fail-open. Hook launcher always exits 0; missing node/CLI/key just prints a notice and no-ops. Stop hook is async (process exits ~12-14 ms per author's measurements) and turns are queued to .jevmem/queue.jsonl; on Jev timeout/408/429/5xx retried with backoff 15s..10min for 24h/200 turns; other errors (400, 401 bad key) drop the turn silently to log (a wrong key drops every turn). Prompt hook: Jev budget 2 s (jev.timeoutMs) in 0.5.10, 1 s recallTimeoutMs on unreleased main; on timeout/error falls back to word-match recall from lines the poisoning gate serves; unverified lines are withheld (fail-closed for those) when Jev cannot check them. SDK maxRetries 1, hook hard deadline 12 s for queue drain, hook timeout 5 s. The 0.6 guard PreToolUse has timeout 3 s.
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (search_memory, add_memory, list_memory, audit_memory): descriptions+schemas ~3.5k chars, roughly 900 tokens always loaded (add_memory description alone ~1.1k chars); no server-level 'instructions'. Hook-injected text: per prompt a <jevmem-memory> block = ~55-token frame + up to 5 lines (~30-60 tokens each) + hands-off line, about 150-350 tokens when relevant lines exist, nothing when none. Additionally a one-time 'CLI not found / no key' notice. With OpenRouter-only MCP use, add_memory/list/search are largely redundant with the hooks, so the MCP server could be omitted (hooks are what matter).
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit + Stop, plus PreToolUse guard in unreleased 0.6). No model discretion or user prompt needed after `jevmem enable` in each project. MCP tools are model-discretion extras; the add_memory description tells the model not to call it when hooks are active.
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.latencyImpact: UserPromptSubmit is synchronous: typically ~0.3 s Jev p50 per author's benchmark (direct TypeSafe; via OpenRouter add its hop, plausibly 0.1-0.3 s more), worst case capped at 2 s (0.5.10) then word-match fallback, plus node start / warm daemon (auto-started, exits idle). Cache of identical answers under .jevmem/cache. Stop hook adds ~0 to the turn (async, detached). PreToolUse guard (0.6, unreleased) adds up to 3 s only for calls overlapping a saved constraint rule; otherwise no network.
pros: Only candidate found so far that really delivers 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically': deterministic UserPromptSubmit/Stop hooks, no 'use jev' prompting, opt-in per repo, and it uses Jev exactly as intended (typed choice/noul questions -> thresholds in code, no free text).

Trivial-looking OpenRouter path from code: SDK posts baseURL+'/v1/systemone' with Bearer key and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is officially read from ~/.jevmem/env (src/env.ts:12), matching OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone; just add jev.model typesafe/jev-latest.

Sensible engineering for hooks: async Stop with detach launcher, disk queue with backoff, warm daemon, answer cache, word-match fallback, 2 s timeout, always exit 0; fail-open so it cannot break a coding session.

Solid test culture for a 9-day-old repo: ~75 test files (vitest), CI on ubuntu+macOS x Node 20/22, a check-claims script tying README numbers to result files, npm provenance, published SECURITY.md/PRIVACY.md, self-disclosed vuln advisory and honest 'limits' section (benchmarks are author-written).

Real, useful value for a long-running senior workflow: cross-session decisions/constraints recall and [superseded] handling, plus a memory-poisoning gate for a git-committed memory file; also in Anthropic's Claude plugin directory (marketplace listing) with per-project opt-in.
Cheap: ~$0.000127/decision at Jev pricing, hook overhead negligible in tokens (~150-350 tokens/prompt).
cons: Not OpenRouter-native: no mention of OpenRouter for Jev in code or docs; README only names TypeSafe direct and Vercel AI Gateway. The reroute via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is my inference and needs a live smoke test (response shape, 'jev-latest' vs '~typesafe/jev-latest' model id, OpenRouter beta alpha status); OpenRouter routing is also 'Jev Router'/DeepSeek-flash-skeptic uncertainty.

Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-22, 207 commits in 8 days (up to 46/day), 1 contributor, 99 stars, 16 npm versions in a week, 0.5.x with author-only evals. Expect churn; user-facing docs even describe unreleased 0.6 features mixed with 0.5.10, and the checked-out main manifests (0.5.7 strings) lag npm 0.5.10.

Narrow scope: it is a memory layer, not general coding-time decision support. It does not use Jev for routing, permission decisions, test selection, code-review triage etc. (except the unreleased guard). Adds JEVMEM.md and jevmem.config.json into every enabled repo, which is intrusive in client repos unless git-ignored.

Privacy for client work: every enabled-project prompt (regex-scrubbed only, names/addresses/unknown secret forms pass through) goes to TypeSafe/OpenRouter every turn; a real scrub bug leaked PGPASSWORD/password JSON values until 0.5.8. Rerouting through OpenRouter adds another third party.

Installs a global npm CLI that runs on every prompt (supply chain trust) and a background daemon; needs Claude Code >= 2.1.273 for directory install (user is on 2.1.285, fine). UserPromptSubmit is synchronous, so slow Jev/OpenRouter delays every prompt up to 2 s.

Key handling nuance: a 401 or 400 from the endpoint drops turns silently (only logged), so a mistaken OpenRouter key/model id produces a plausible-looking but dead integration until `jevmem doctor`/stats is checked. MCP server (4 tools, ~900 tokens) is mostly redundant with hooks and add_memory/audit are marked destructive/open-world, which can trigger permission prompts outside bypass mode.

Possible overlap/interference with user's existing hooks and memory tooling (caveman, GitNexus, Claude's auto memory): another additionalContext injection every prompt and (0.6) another PreToolUse guard on Bash|Edit|Write.
gh-avinash-jetwani-jevmem.verdict: Best-fit automatic Jev hook integration seen so far: deterministic hooks, opt-in, fail-open, and using Jev for what it is good at (typed classification), with a likely 2-env-var path to OpenRouter (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + jev.model). But it is a week-old single-author memory tool, not a general Jev coding integration, and OpenRouter compatibility must be smoke-tested and client-project data egress accepted before use.

pros: Small footprint: about 250 tokens of always-on context, no MCP tools, and no hooks, so it cannot slow or break the existing gitnexus/secret-guard setup.
Fail-open: the only live Jev call is optional and skips cleanly (exit 3) without a key.

Useful reference if the user later builds their own Jev integration. jev-lens/jev-rules.md and jevaluate/rubric.md distil TypeSafe's guidance (atomic questions, Choice order rotation, confidence thresholds, treating untrusted text as data). The Choice-rotation averaging in jev_check.py is a sound pattern to copy.

No OpenRouter support anywhere. jev_check.py is hardwired to typesafe-sdk and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the model ID is jev-1.13.0, not typesafe/jev-1.13.

Skill scope is niche (image decoding and rating other people's repos). Jevaluate would fetch untrusted repos and READMEs, which is an injection surface, and it writes a private library to ~/.claude.
Its heavy workflows are expensive (about 55k tokens of overhead per subagent) and irrelevant to day-to-day edit/debug/test loops.

gh-thehan-co-jevriel.name: thehan-co/jevriel
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + skill + zero-dependency stdio MCP server, node ESM) bundling a "jevriel" skill and 9 MCP tools that call TypeSafe Jev through a selectable provider (OpenRouter Decisions API, TypeSafe direct, Cloudflare, custom HTTPS endpoint, local adapter). Tools wrap Jev's primitives as route/rank/extract/verify/judge helpers and write a local usage ledger. Its "Deep" adoption mode appends a pointer block to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md telling the agent to assess each task for Jev-suited decisions. It also ships a Python benchmark ("Flight Test") comparing Jev vs LLMs. It is designed mainly to help you build Jev into apps and agent workflows, not to accelerate Claude Code's own coding loop.

gh-thehan-co-jevriel.tests: 8 offline node:test files (~38 test cases: providers, runtime, installer, adoption, mcp, policy, costs, critic) + Python benchmark tests; CI .github/workflows/tests.yml runs npm test, python unittest and npm pack --dry-run on push/PR (offline, mocked fetch). Only 2 days of history apart from the initial week; no real-world usage evidence beyond the author's own morning agent.
security: API key never in argv: setup rejects keys as arguments (bin/jevriel.mjs:42), hidden TTY prompt; env OPENROUTER_API_KEY takes precedence. Positive.
Saved key is plaintext JSON at ~/.config/jevriel/provider.json (0600, dir 0700); SECURITY.md admits plaintext. --key-command (argv, no shell) supports secret managers.
fetch uses redirect:'error' (providers.mjs/runtime.mjs:153) so the bearer token cannot be redirected; compatible endpoint must be credential-free HTTPS (providers.mjs:32).
Error handling deliberately hides provider response text and input content (runtime.mjs:174-176). Ledger stores metadata only (no prompts/answers), 0600.
Adapter/key-command run local executables from config with your env (spawnSync shell:false, timeouts 30s/15s); trusted config, low risk unless provider.json is tampered with.

Deep mode edits ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (writes .jevriel-backup, 0600 mode on writeFileSync) and points the model at a policy file under ~/.agents/skills; this is a persistent prompt-injection/instruction surface owned by the plugin and would load in every session including client projects. Note writeFileSync mode 0600 only applies on creation.

Install is `npx --yes github:...` (unpinned HEAD of a 6-star single-author repo; runs arbitrary code on install/setup) and marketplace add from the same git URL; no npm postinstall script, no curl|sh, no telemetry (SECURITY.md, package.json scripts only test/start). Recommend pinning to a commit/tag and reading before install.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are advisory JSON; skill text says to treat documents as untrusted. Jev outputs are typed so return channel is low-risk. Main risk is the agent sending sensitive file content to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe) because the policy encourages it.
Bulk of code is dense minified-style JS (long one-liners), harder to audit; I read all ~250 lines of server/ and installer.
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put into tool arguments: state / candidates / evidence / source / claim / route rubrics (any code, diffs, file text, notes the agent decides is relevant) go via HTTPS POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your OpenRouter key, and OpenRouter forwards to TypeSafe. Payload capped by assertPayloadSize (judge.mjs). Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself; there is no telemetry and no hook that captures tool traffic. Setup sends one 'green/red' connection-check request. Local ledger records metadata only. With Deep mode, the agent is encouraged to send excerpts autonomously, so a secret-leak guard hook would not see these MCP calls (your guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jevriel__*), meaning client code could reach OpenRouter/TypeSafe unreviewed.
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, by design: one attempt (maxAttempts:1, no retries), 30 s AbortSignal.timeout in judge.mjs:111, HTTP errors mapped to short messages returned as MCP isError text (runtime.mjs:154-176); skill policy says report once and fall back to code/LLM/manual. Nothing blocks Claude Code because it is not on the critical path (no hook, no proxy). Downside: a hung Jev can stall a single tool call for up to 30 s, and the ledger must be writable or the call is refused before sending (runtime.mjs:137-138). Missing config yields 'Provider setup required' error. Invalid/unnormalised responses are rejected by validateAnswers (server/validation.mjs).
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call it (no hooks, no proxy). When called: one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms; the project's own 1,708-chunk run reports median 0.422 s) plus an extra model turn to build the tool call and read the result, so realistically 1-3 s per use. Server start adds a Node cold start (~50-100 ms, no deps). Deep mode adds a small per-task cost: model must read adoption.json + policy file at start of each task (extra Read calls and ~700 tokens of policy).
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.contextCost: 9 MCP tools; tool defs measured at 7,455 chars (about 1,860 tokens) via JSON size of definitions, plus namespace overhead, so about 2k tokens if not deferred; Claude Code 2.1.x tool search defers MCP tool schemas so real baseline is less. Server 'instructions' string about 60 tokens (tells model to run jevriel_status first, which itself is an extra call per session). Skill: frontmatter description about 60 tokens always loaded; SKILL.md body ~1.3k tokens plus references when triggered. Deep mode adds a CLAUDE.md block (~100 tokens) and forces reading adoption.md (~700 tokens) each task. No hook-injected text.
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. Light (default): the skill triggers via description only when the user talks about Jev/integration/benchmarks, and MCP tools are called only if the model decides. Deep (opt-in): a CLAUDE.md pointer instructs the model to read the policy and 'assess every workflow' and use Jev when useful; docs/adoption.md states plainly this is prompt-guided, 'not interception of every tool call, a daemon, or a scheduler'. No deterministic hook, no proxy, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse. So it cannot guarantee automatic use and will often not fire in pure coding turns.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class, code-verified provider: hits /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (providers.mjs:12,16,30); no TypeSafe account needed.
Safe secret handling for a hobby-grade project: no key in argv, hidden prompt, redirect:'error', errors scrubbed of content, key-command support for secret managers.
No hooks, no proxy, no telemetry, no postinstall: it cannot break or slow existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.

Response validation is rigorous (validateAnswers checks answer IDs, normalised distributions, choice/argmax consistency, score vs expectation) so malformed Jev/OpenRouter output is rejected rather than trusted.

Only real attempt at the 'automatic' requirement in Claude Code so far: Deep mode gives persistent CLAUDE.md-level policy with an explicit skip-trivial rule and code/LLM/human/Jev triage, plus local metadata ledger for auditing what fired and what it cost.
Useful as a design/evaluation aid when you want to add Jev decision points to an app you build (opportunity map, shadow test, Flight Card); benchmark scaffolding is reusable.
Zero-dependency Node server is easy to read and vendor; Apache-2.0.
cons: Does not deliver truly automatic invocation: Deep is a prompt pointer in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, explicitly not enforcement (docs/adoption.md, SECURITY.md); Opus 5.5 will decide case by case and mostly skip Jev on ordinary coding.

Its job is 'help you build Jev into apps', not 'make Claude Code faster'. Tool set (route/rank/extract/verify) is generic; there is no coding-specific decision (e.g. which files matter, whether a command is safe, commit-message routing) shipped.

Deep mode writes to your global CLAUDE.md, so the behaviour applies to client projects too, and it will encourage sending excerpts of client code to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; your secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jevriel__* tools.

Each use costs an extra model turn (tool call + result) that likely exceeds the latency and cost of Opus deciding directly; Jev is only worth it for bulk/batched semantic classification, not per-step agent decisions.

Immature: 12 commits over ~9 days, one author, 6 stars, v0.2.0, alpha OpenRouter endpoint, tests are all mocked/offline; README's own 429-document benchmark shows Jev had 12 invalid batches of 489 vs 2 for GPT, and no accuracy result yet (human scoring pending, frontier eval 'pending').
Install path is unpinned `npx github:` HEAD plus setup that stores the API key plaintext on disk; the setup verification call is billed.
Default model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13 (no jev-latest); .mcp.claude.json passes no env, so env must be exported in the shell that launches Claude Code or a plaintext file used.
~1.9k tokens of tool definitions plus skill and policy reads for something that will fire rarely; server instructions demand a jevriel_status call each session.
Dense one-line JS style and vendored code from a community connector make audits/upgrades harder.
gh-thehan-co-jevriel.verdict: Best-documented OpenRouter-capable Jev package and safe enough to read and try, but it is a builder/evaluation kit with prompt-based 'Deep' adoption, not a deterministic Claude Code integration, so it will not reliably give you Jev without prompting. Use it at most as a pinned, Light-mode skill+MCP for experiments; do not enable Deep globally and do not rely on it as the daily integration.
