gh-lazniak-jevskill.name: lazniak/jevskill
gh-lazniak-jevskill.whatItDoes: Agent Skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md, Claude Code plugin marketplace "jevskill" plus npx skills) that teaches the model when and how to call Jev for bounded decisions (route, triage, classify, gate, rank, and a reversible REDUCE that shortlists large logs/data before they reach the main model). It bundles a stdlib-only Python caller (scripts/jev_query.py), a bigger optional pip package/CLI (jevskill: ask/batch/plan/doctor/stats, ledger, disk cache, localhost web console, hot-loop client, Windows-only computer-use module), and a lot of reference docs. Jev is called via OpenRouter (default) or TypeSafe vendor API. It is NOT an MCP server and installs no hooks.

providerSupport.evidence: skills/jev/scripts/jev_query.py:47-48,60-75 and jevskill/config.py:36-60: PROVIDERS['openrouter'] = base https://openrouter.ai, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, key_env OPENROUTER_API_KEY/OPEN_ROUTER_API_KEY/JEVUSE_API_KEY; DEFAULT_PROVIDER = 'openrouter' (jev_query.py:76-77, config.py). PROVIDERS['typesafe'] = https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest, keys JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY. jev_query.py:395-412 POSTs with Authorization: Bearer plus OpenRouter attribution headers (HTTP-Referer, X-Title). Base URL overridable via --base-url / JEVSKILL_BASE_URL; provider via --provider / JEVSKILL_PROVIDER / ~/.jevskill/config.json. Does not use /api/v1/systemone or the ~typesafe/jev-latest or Jev Router IDs (model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13). Caveat (README, SKILL.md s5): with no provider stated, the first key found BY NAME wins, vendor names first, so an added JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently moves traffic off OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: Only the two endpoints; JEVSKILL_BASE_URL allows any custom base.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: n/a - OpenRouter is already the default and first-class; just set OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and JEVSKILL_PROVIDER=openrouter to pin it).

interface.name: skill jev (SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Model-discretion skill; description-triggered on classify/categorize/which of these/route/triage/gate/should we/rank/prioritize/grade/too many logs/reduce the data/save tokens/batch decisions/is it safe to. allowed-tools: Bash(python:*) Bash(python3:*) Bash(jevskill:*)

interface.name: scripts/jev_query.py
interface.purpose: Zero-install stdlib caller: single noul/choice/score question or --questions JSON bundle; --state-file; --reduce --keep N (gate each line/block, keep hits, stash rejects); --blocks; redaction flags (--no-redact, --redact-emails, --redact-extra); --provider, --base-url, --retries 2, --timeout 60; --json. Exit 0 decided, 2 needs review, 3 over token budget, 1 error

interface.name: scripts/jev_recovery.py
interface.purpose: Read back items REDUCE cut (--grep) from <cwd>/.jevskill/recovery/<handle>.json

interface.name: scripts/jev.py
interface.purpose: Small entry shim (doctor etc.)

interface.name: jevskill CLI (optional pip install)
interface.purpose: ask, batch, plan (free offline advice), doctor (key/endpoint check), stats/outcome/advice (ledger), web (127.0.0.1 console), patterns, cu (Windows UIA computer-use)

interface.name: MCP tools
interface.purpose: none

interface.name: Hooks
interface.purpose: none (no hooks.json, no settings snippets)

security: API key: read from env only (no --api-key CLI flag found in jev_query.py or cli.py grep), sent as Authorization Bearer over HTTPS via urllib; not visible in argv/process list. Skill instructs the agent to check key presence only via `jevskill doctor` (8-hex fingerprint), never print it.

Redaction by default: regex scrub of private keys, sk-/sk-or- keys, AKIA, gh*_ tokens, slack, JWT, bearer, password=/token= params before state leaves the machine (jev_query.py:88-100, jevskill/redact.py). Credential-shaped only; no PII/source-code protection; emails opt-in. Regex coverage is limited (e.g. no generic high-entropy secrets, .env style values under other names).

Prompt-injection surface: log/diff/ticket text goes into the state sent to Jev; SKILL.md itself warns Jev is advisory and manipulable by state content and must not authorize irreversible actions. Since Jev only returns typed decisions, injection can bias REDUCE (hide the relevant line) but cannot produce text/commands. Risk is silent omission of important lines.

Shell exec: skill declares allowed-tools Bash(python:*) Bash(python3:*) Bash(jevskill:*) which pre-approves arbitrary python execution when the skill is loaded (broad); in bypass/auto mode moot. No subprocess/os.system in package (grep clean).

Writes to disk in the CURRENT PROJECT: REDUCE stores rejected items under <cwd>/.jevskill/recovery/*.json; ledger and optional cache also at <cwd>/.jevskill/ (jev_query.py:626-631, stats.py:58-83, cache.py:57-64). On client repos this leaves log/state copies in the working tree unless gitignored; ~/.jevskill/config.json and global ledger also used.

No telemetry found; only network destinations are openrouter.ai / api.typesafe.ai (plus HEAD warm-up). OpenRouter requests send HTTP-Referer/X-Title attribution headers naming the project. Web console binds 127.0.0.1 only with Host/Origin checks.

Install: `npx skills add lazniak/jevskill -g` (third-party registry CLI) or /plugin marketplace add; install.ps1 is Windows/PowerShell only. No curl|sh, no postinstall; pyproject has zero required dependencies. Anyone can push to main of a 10-day-old, 2-star, single-author repo (supply-chain risk for a skill with broad Bash allowance): pin a commit.
docs/install.md tells an agent to fetch and follow raw GitHub instructions - instruction-following of remote content; do not use that route.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in --state / --state-file: log lines, diffs, ticket text, file contents, tool output, plus the question text and option criteria, after regex credential redaction (on by default). Sent to openrouter.ai (default) or api.typesafe.ai; OpenRouter routes to TypeSafe. Also a client-identifying Referer/X-Title header. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when the model chooses to run the script. For client projects, code/diffs/logs leave the machine to two third parties (OpenRouter + TypeSafe); check client NDAs. No local file is uploaded outside what the agent selects.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.failureMode: Fail-open in effect but soft: nothing blocks Claude Code because there is no hook. Script: default 60 s read timeout, 2 retries with 0.25-2 s backoff on 429/5xx/transport (jev_query.py:671-672, 395-430), so a hung/slow Jev can stall a Bash tool call up to roughly 3 minutes worst case; errors raise SystemExit exit 1 with a message. Package hot path uses 1.5 s read timeout, 0 retries, hedged request (config.py:123-135) but that is only for the optional Python API, not the skill default. Exit 3 means nothing sent because state exceeds token budget (default 8k). SKILL.md says API errors must be reported, not simulated. Missing key: skill tells the agent to STOP and ask the user (A get a key / B judge yourself), which is an interactive interruption, not silent.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. Always-on: skill frontmatter name + description = about 660 chars description (~165 tokens) plus name/listing, roughly 200 tokens per session. On load: SKILL.md is 11,595 chars (~2.9k tokens) each time the skill triggers, plus optional reference files (api.md 26 KB, act.md 47 KB, patterns.md 30 KB etc.) if the model opens them. No hook-injected text. The skill's trigger words are very generic ('should we', 'is it safe to', 'rank', 'route') and may cause frequent loads of the 3k-token body.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.latencyImpact: Per Jev call about 300-370 ms via OpenRouter (README-measured, vendor-claimed 70-500 ms) plus Python process startup and tool-call round trip of an extra model turn (LLM must write the Bash command, then read the result: seconds, not ms). Only incurred when the model decides to use the skill. No per-tool or per-turn latency added otherwise. Worst case 60 s x 3 attempts on a hung endpoint.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger: Claude Code loads the skill when its description matches the task (keywords like classify, triage, gate, rank, too many logs, is it safe to), then the model decides to run python scripts/jev_query.py. Not deterministic: no hook, no MCP tool, no proxy. Reliability of firing without the user saying 'use jev' is uncertain and unmeasured; the model must also judge Jev worthwhile vs. just grepping, and the skill itself says to prefer regex/grep when possible.
pros: Only candidate in this class that is genuinely OpenRouter-first: default provider openrouter, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, key OPENROUTER_API_KEY (config.py:36-45; jev_query.py:60-66). Drop-in for the user's setup.
Zero-install path: the bundled jev_query.py is stdlib-only Python, no npm/pip needed; Python 3.13 present. No required dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh (Linux path).
Skill approach costs almost no context when idle (~200 tokens) and adds no MCP tool schema tax; no hooks so it cannot interfere with the existing secret-guard / GitNexus / caveman hooks.

Sound Jev usage guidance codified in SKILL.md: decision-not-text, fan out many questions in one call, name the target value (avoids flat ~0.74 output), budget state to 8k tokens, escape-hatch options, thresholds as policy, never authorize irreversible actions from Jev output. Encodes Jev pitfalls accurately relative to the brief.

Default-on credential redaction of state before egress (private keys, sk-*, AKIA, gh tokens, JWT, bearer, password=) - meaningful for client projects, and a reason it complements the user's secret-leak guard.
REDUCE for big logs/test output is a plausible real use for daily coding: shortlist 900 log lines to ~8 before the Opus context sees them; reversible via jev_recovery.py.

Honest docs: README publishes a YAML failure, says grep/regex ties Jev on its own benchmark (18/18 both), labels savings modelled vs measured, and says use a regex if one suffices. Large offline test suite (1533 test functions counted; CI on py3.9/3.11/3.13; suite fully offline).
MIT license, key handled via env with fingerprint-only doctor; no telemetry; no key in argv.
Unpinned upgrade path is mitigated by Claude Code plugin marketplace/skill install being git-based, so a commit can be pinned.
cons: Not automatic in the deterministic sense the user asked for: it is a description-triggered skill, so Claude may or may not load it, and even then must choose to shell out. No hook or MCP tool means no guaranteed use; e.g. it will not intercept a big Bash/Read output before it enters context (REDUCE only helps if the model already decided to run it, after the tokens were often already read or must be piped through the script).

Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 26 commits in 10 days, 2 stars, 1 fork, effectively single author (24 commits lazniak + 2 Paul Lazniak), 4 issues total, latest release v0.10.2 while pyproject/marketplace say 0.15.1. Rapid churn; pin a commit before trusting it with client repos.

Sprawl: much of the 3.3 MB tree is off-topic for a Linux coding user (Windows-only UIA computer-use `cu/` module ~300 KB Python, web console, install.ps1, 47 KB act.md, benchmark fixtures). Marketing-heavy README (YouTube live banner, modelled $ savings per year, '99.3% fewer tokens' from n=3 per cell, one cheap answering model).

Broad tool permission: frontmatter allow-list Bash(python:*) Bash(python3:*) Bash(jevskill:*) pre-approves arbitrary Python when loaded; combined with bypass/auto mode it widens blast radius if the repo is ever compromised.

Data egress on client projects: logs/diffs/file text go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe; redaction is regex credential-only, no PII/source protection. Also writes .jevskill/recovery, ledger, cache into the current project working tree (not the home dir), which can leave copies of client log data and dirty git status.

Default provider selection is name-based and can silently flip to the vendor if a JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY exists; must set JEVSKILL_PROVIDER=openrouter to pin. Model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13, not ~typesafe/jev-latest or Jev Router.

Failure/latency: default 60 s timeout x 2 retries can stall a Bash call for minutes on a hung endpoint; no circuit breaker across calls. Each use costs an extra LLM turn (write command, read output), so for Opus 5.5 the seconds cost far exceeds Jev's 300 ms; benefit is only for large-data cases.

SKILL.md body is ~2.9k tokens on every load and trigger words are generic ('should we', 'rank', 'is it safe to'), risking frequent irrelevant loads; 'no key' path makes the agent stop and ask the user, an interruption.

Value is unproven for this user: the primary benefit (context reduction) matters less if grep/head/GitNexus already narrow the data; author's own benchmark shows a structural filter equals Jev. Jev cannot help with code, summaries, or reasoning, which is most of daily coding.
Jev is beta, and Theo's skeptic claim (cheap router in disguise) is unaddressed; the repo's accuracy evidence is self-reported.
gh-lazniak-jevskill.verdict: Best-in-class as a low-friction, OpenRouter-native starting point (skill only, no hooks/MCP, near-zero idle context, default redaction), but it is not the deterministic automatic integration requested: firing depends on model discretion and the payoff is limited to large-log reduction and gating. Try it pinned to a commit with JEVSKILL_PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and expect to pair it with a hook (e.g. PostToolUse on big Bash output) if real automation is needed.

gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.name: UditAkhourii/quicksilver
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.whatItDoes: Claude Code skill (SKILL.md plus one zero-dependency Node script, qs.mjs) that lets Claude offload bulk judgment work to Jev. Claude runs `node qs.mjs filter|classify|rank|find|ask ...` through Bash. The script reads files, dirs, logs or JSONL, sends each item (or packed batches with --fast) to POST {API}/v1/systemone using noul, choice and score questions, and prints a compact shortlist. The output marks borderline items with `?` and ends with a token-savings footer. The idea is that Jev rules out items so Claude never reads them.

providerSupport.evidence: skills/quicksilver/scripts/qs.mjs:10 `const API = (process.env.QUICKSILVER_API_BASE || 'https://api.typesafe.ai').replace(/\/$/, '')`. Routes are hard-coded as `/v1/systemone` (qs.mjs:241, 443, 504) and `/v1/models` (qs.mjs:542, 556). Auth is `Authorization: Bearer ${key}` (qs.mjs:91). Key sources are JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, then ~/.quicksilver/config.json (qs.mjs:61). Model is --model, QUICKSILVER_MODEL, config, or default 'jev-latest' (qs.mjs:65). OpenRouter is not mentioned anywhere in the repo (grep -rli openrouter returned nothing). OpenRouter's model page (openrouter.ai/typesafe/jev-1.13/api) documents POST /api/v1/systemone with model, state and questions (type/instructions/criteria) and a response with answers and usage. That is the same schema qs.mjs uses.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no source patch is needed, only env vars. Set QUICKSILVER_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api, so that API+'/v1/systemone' becomes https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. Set JEV_API_KEY to the OpenRouter key, since it is only sent as a Bearer token. Set QUICKSILVER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, because the default 'jev-latest' is a TypeSafe-direct ID and probably not valid on OpenRouter. All three can go in the `env` block of ~/.claude/settings.json so the Bash tool inherits them. Two caveats: `setup` and `status` call GET /v1/models, which OpenRouter also serves at /api/v1/models but with different content (only an HTTP 200 is checked), and I did not test that OpenRouter's response fields (usage.input_tokens, answers.qN.noul/choice/probabilities/score/legend) match byte for byte. I could not run anything, and the OpenRouter docs pages returned 404 or partial content.
providerSupport.others: QUICKSILVER_API_BASE accepts any base URL, so any gateway that exposes /v1/systemone works.

interface.name: skill: quicksilver (SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Model-invoked skill. The frontmatter description tells Claude to use it BEFORE reading many files, long logs or big lists just to decide what matters. It also fires on the words 'quicksilver', 'jev', 'save tokens' and 'delegate'. It excludes generation, editing, math, counting, dates and small inputs.

interface.name: qs filter "<yes/no>" <inputs> [--lines --threshold --fast]
interface.purpose: One noul question per file or line. Prints P(yes) per item, borderline band (threshold +/-0.15) flagged with `?`, and repeated log lines collapsed.

interface.name: qs classify --labels a,b,c <inputs>
interface.purpose: Choice question per item. Prints ids per label and lists low-confidence items (<0.6) with the runner-up label.

interface.name: qs rank "<query>" <inputs> --top N
interface.purpose: Score question on a 5-level relevance rubric. Prints the top N.

interface.name: qs find "<what>" <files>
interface.purpose: Chunks large files (150 lines per chunk) and asks a choice question for the best line number plus a noul question for existence. Prints the top hits with file:line.

interface.name: qs ask "<q>" --state @file | ask spec.json
interface.purpose: One-off raw System One request with noul, choice or score.

interface.name: qs setup [KEY] / setup --remove / status
interface.purpose: Verifies the key via GET /v1/models and saves it to ~/.quicksilver/config.json with mode 0600. `status` prints local lifetime stats.

interface.name: bin/quicksilver.mjs (npx github:UditAkhourii/quicksilver)
interface.purpose: Installer. Copies skills/quicksilver to ~/.claude/skills/quicksilver and prompts for the key. Also has `uninstall` and a passthrough to qs commands.

interface.name: .claude-plugin/plugin.json + marketplace.json
interface.purpose: Plugin install path: /plugin marketplace add UditAkhourii/quicksilver. There are no hooks, no MCP server, and no agents.

security: Key handling: read from the JEV_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var, or ~/.quicksilver/config.json written with 0600 plus chmod (qs.mjs:36-40, 548). It is sent only as an HTTPS Bearer header via fetch, so it never appears in the process list during normal use. Exception: `qs setup <KEY>` and `install --key KEY` put the key in argv and shell history. The SKILL.md even tells Claude to run `qs setup <KEY>` if the user pastes the key in chat, which puts it in the transcript and argv. With env vars from settings.json this path is avoided.
No telemetry. The only network calls go to API (default api.typesafe.ai) and GET /v1/models. Local stats are written to ~/.quicksilver/stats.json (counts only).

No curl|sh, no postinstall script, and no npm dependencies. `npx github:UditAkhourii/quicksilver` runs unpinned code from a 2-commit, 5-day-old repo on main, and the recommended install fetches whatever is on main. Safer: clone, read, then copy the skill dir by hand, or pin a commit SHA.
Only child process is `git ls-files` via execFileSync with an argument array, so no shell injection. Writes are limited to config, stats and the optional --save FILE.

Secret guard: SECRET_RE (qs.mjs:19) skips .env*, *.pem/.key/.p12/.crt, id_rsa*, .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, credentials.json and secrets.*, and .gitignore is respected inside git repos. Hardcoded secrets inside ordinary source files, config.yaml, docker-compose, CI files and logs are still uploaded. The --no-secrets-guard flag exists. The directory walk fallback ignores dot-dirs, but files given explicitly, stdin and --items bypass path checks (paths still go through the regex, stdin does not).

Prompt-injection surface: file and log text is sent to Jev, which only returns typed probabilities, so the injection blast radius is limited to skewed verdicts (a file can trick a filter into hiding or surfacing itself). Output printed back to Claude is only ids, numbers and clipped line text (the log/line text is attacker-controlled and is read by Claude). The skill itself instructs Claude to treat results as a shortlist.
MIT license. Author is a single individual and the repo says it is not affiliated with TypeSafe or Anthropic.
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.dataEgress: The content of every file, line or item you point it at leaves the machine. This is full file text up to 60k chars per item (--max-chars), with files up to 2 MB read, sent as `state.content` plus the file's relative path as `state.source`, together with the question text. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai/api if QUICKSILVER_API_BASE is set. This covers source code, logs, tickets and contracts. Excluded: .env, keys, certs, credential-like filenames, .gitignored files, lockfiles, minified files, binaries. Not excluded: hardcoded secrets inside normal source or log files. Nothing is sent unless Claude runs qs. Claude's own prompts and transcript are not sent. For client projects there is a real NDA and data-processing question, and with OpenRouter the content also passes through OpenRouter's provider routing.
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, because qs is just a Bash command. Nothing blocks Claude if Jev is slow or down, and Claude reads the files itself. The exit codes are: 3 for a missing or rejected key (401 or 403), 4 for a bad request (400 or 422), and 5 for exhausted retries. Each request has a 60 s AbortSignal timeout (qs.mjs:93). It retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff (500 ms x 2^n, honoring Retry-After) on network errors and 408, 409, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 and 529. A dead endpoint therefore costs around 5 minutes wall clock per request, with 16 concurrent requests, before qs dies. One failed request aborts the whole run (die exits the process), so there is no partial result. If Claude hits an error it can just fall back, but nothing enforces that. The skill does say to rephrase or lower the threshold when nothing matches.
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks and no injected hook text, so zero tool-definition tokens. Always-on cost is the skill name plus description in the skill listing, about 1,050 chars, or roughly 260 tokens. When Claude triggers it, the full SKILL.md body loads: about 163 lines and roughly 6.5k chars, or about 1.7k tokens. Each run adds a short output of about 1 to 4k tokens (id lists, footer). qs.mjs itself is not read into context (it is only executed). Per-turn cost with the skill idle is negligible.
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger via the SKILL.md description. It is not deterministic, because there is no hook or proxy. The README claims 'Claude uses the skill on its own', but with Opus 5.5 and existing habits (Grep/Glob, GitNexus graph hooks, subagents) it may frequently not fire, or may pick grep or GitNexus instead. The description is well written, with explicit 'use BEFORE reading many files/logs' triggers and clear skip conditions. Reliability could be raised by a one-line reminder in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, or by a UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook nudge, but that is extra work the repo does not provide.
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.latencyImpact: Jev latency is 70-500 ms per request, and the README reports 3-8 s for 40-3000 items at 16 parallel requests. By default it is one item per request, and concurrency is 16 (pool). Whole-repo filter on 187 files took about 6 s in their benchmark, 3k-line log about 64 s, and lodash find about 39 s. Benchmarks show no wall-clock gain on huge scans, and --fast packs 40 items per request for about 10x speed at lower accuracy. Nothing is added on turns where the skill is not invoked, because there are no hooks.
pros: Only candidate here that is a working, end-to-end Jev integration built around Claude Code, and it works purely from source-verified schema: the noul/choice/score request bodies in qs.mjs:327, 367, 414 and 443 match the System One shape (state + questions -> answers/usage) that OpenRouter's Jev page documents.

OpenRouter switch is config-only, with no patching: QUICKSILVER_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and QUICKSILVER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 in the settings.json env block. The code appends /v1/systemone, giving exactly the documented /api/v1/systemone.
Zero deps, about 590 lines of readable Node, and no postinstall, no curl|sh and no telemetry. It was easy to audit end to end, and needs Node >= 18 (user has 24, so globs work).

Skill design is right for this user: no MCP server and no hooks, so it adds about 260 tokens of always-on context, no per-turn latency, and cannot break or slow normal tool calls. It does not collide with the existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks.

Good ergonomics for an LLM caller: compact output, repeated log lines collapsed into ranges, a `?` borderline band that tells Claude to double-check, per-item requests by default (they measured packing hurting accuracy 100% -> 76%), and honest guidance on when not to use it (grep for exact matches, tiny inputs, generation).
Sensible safety defaults: secret-file name regex, .gitignore respect, 2 MB cap, and the 60k-char truncation marker `~`.

Useful jobs for daily coding: repo-wide 'which files handle X' funnels, log triage, bulk ticket/test-failure labelling, and needle-in-large-file search. The benchmark reports 100% F1/hit@k on several of these with 77-96% fewer Claude tokens, at a median Jev cost of about $0.004 per task.
MIT licensed; the skill can be copied and pinned locally so it can be maintained by the user.
cons: The benchmark is self-reported by the author on 12 tasks with a Claude subagent as baseline, and the repo has 2 commits, 1 contributor, no tests, no CI and no releases (created 2026-09-25, 5 days before the audit). It also shows failures: BGL log triage F1 23% vs 54%, commit classification 76% vs 83%, and security shortlist 89% vs 100%.

Automatic invocation is only a skill-description trigger. It is model-discretion, and with the user's Grep/Glob/GitNexus habits it may often not fire. There is no hook or enforcement, so the 'never prompt Claude to use Jev' goal is met only probabilistically.

Data egress is the whole content of files, up to 60k chars each, to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter plus its provider). The guard is filename-regex only, so hardcoded secrets in ordinary source, YAML or logs still go out. This is a real problem on client projects under NDA, and the user's secret-leak hook does not inspect what qs uploads.

Not natively OpenRouter: the default model 'jev-latest' and the default base URL are TypeSafe-direct. Config-only fix, but I could not test that OpenRouter's response envelope matches exactly, and `status` only tests reachability via /v1/models.

The scope of value is narrow. It saves Claude tokens on bulk reading, but the user is on a subscription (OAuth) where the savings are usage-limit headroom rather than dollars. Opus with Grep/GitNexus is already strong at file discovery, and the results are only a shortlist, so Claude still has to read survivors and check the `?` items.

Failure handling is blunt: up to 5 retries with 60 s timeouts (about 5 minutes worst case), and any single failed request kills the whole run with no partial output. Jev is beta, so 429 and 529 are likely on large scans at 16 concurrency.

Install path risk: `npx github:UditAkhourii/quicksilver` executes unpinned main from a brand-new single-author repo. The `setup <KEY>` path puts the key in argv and Claude's transcript if used as the skill suggests.
Wall-clock is no better than Claude on huge scans (their own benchmark: 56 s vs 64 s, 39 s vs 39 s), and cost scales with content size (lodash find $0.21, log scan $0.04).
gh-uditakhourii-quicksilver.verdict: Best-fit, lowest-overhead Jev integration found so far for Claude Code. It is a lean skill with no hooks and no MCP tool-schema cost, and OpenRouter works through three env vars. The catch is that auto-triggering is probabilistic, it uploads full file contents to a third party with only a filename-based secret guard, and the project is 5 days old with self-reported benchmarks. Use it on personal projects after auditing/pinning a local copy, and treat it as opt-in per repo for client work.

gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.name: reiswaffel78/jev-agent-toolkit (skill + npm MCP bridge jev-agent-toolkit-mcp)
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.whatItDoes: Two independent parts. (1) A portable Agent Skill (skills/jev-agent-toolkit/SKILL.md, ~9.3 KB plus 11 reference files) that teaches an agent when and how to use Jev as a bounded judgment layer (decision gate, Choice/Score/Noul, batching, confidence thresholds, limitations) and adds generic guidance on browser research, tool orchestration, Blender, Unreal and multi-agent work. (2) An optional stdio MCP server (npm jev-agent-toolkit-mcp 0.1.0, TypeScript, ~340 lines) exposing exactly one tool, jev_evaluate, which forwards {state, questions, model?} to POST /v1/systemone through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. It is not a hook or router: nothing intercepts Claude Code traffic. Automatic use depends entirely on the model deciding to call the tool.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.runtime: Node >=22 (engines). MCP server run via npx -y jev-agent-toolkit-mcp (Node 24 on user's box is fine). Skill is plain Markdown. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod ^4.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.install: Skill: `npx skills add reiswaffel78/jev-agent-toolkit` or copy skills/jev-agent-toolkit/ to ~/.claude/skills/. MCP: `claude mcp add --transport stdio --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$TYPESAFE_API_KEY jev -- npx -y jev-agent-toolkit-mcp` (note: expanding the key on the command line puts it in Claude's own argv; prefer the .mcp.json form with "${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}" env interpolation shown in examples/mcp-configs/claude-code.npm.mcp.json). No release tags on GitHub; npm has a single 0.1.0 publish (2026-09-20) by maintainer bastidd84, a different handle than the GitHub owner reiswaffel78.

gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.tests: 35 node:test tests (errors 97 lines, schemas 106, protocol round-trip 278 against a local mock upstream) plus GitHub Actions CI (skill validation, tsc typecheck, build, npm test, npm audit --audit-level=high, SHA-pinned actions, contents:read). No automated live TypeSafe test. Manual one-off live checks on 2026-09-19/20 are self-reported in docs/compatibility.md, including Claude Code 2.1.275 with 810 ms tool latency and jev-1.13.0. I did not run any of it (static review only).
security: API key read only from env (index.ts:48), never a tool arg; no shell/child_process code; tool schema has no url/endpoint field so the destination is fixed at startup by TYPESAFE_BASE_URL; single POST /v1/systemone only.

No postinstall/preinstall scripts in mcp/jev/package.json or in @typesafe-ai/sdk package.json; no telemetry found in SDK dist grep. Runtime dependency surface is small (3 deps) but @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0 is a very new major.

npx -y fetches latest matching version at each launch (supply-chain exposure); single-maintainer, 1 contributor, npm publisher handle (bastidd84) differs from GitHub owner (reiswaffel78); package 10 days old; version not pinned in shipped configs. Pin exact version or vendor a clone if adopted.

Key visible in argv only if the documented `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$TYPESAFE_API_KEY` form is used; the .mcp.json ${VAR} interpolation form avoids it. Key does appear in the child process environment (normal for MCP).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is bounded numeric/enum-like JSON (choice key is echoed from caller-supplied criteria), so return channel is low risk. The skill text instructs 'never install anything silently' and treats state as untrusted data, which is benign. Skill contains generic behavioural instructions (e.g. 'batch speculative questions', 'confirm before destructive') that would sit in Claude's context whenever loaded.

User's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would NOT cover mcp__jev__jev_evaluate calls, so any secret Claude puts in `state` would leave the machine unchecked unless the matcher is extended.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put in the jev_evaluate `state` and question instructions/criteria goes to the configured base URL (TypeSafe direct by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden), plus the API key as a Bearer header. Nothing is sent automatically: no prompts, diffs or tool outputs are forwarded unless Claude copies them into `state`. The skill's own guidance says to keep state minimal. Local logs on stderr contain metadata only (duration, model, token counts, question ids). Through OpenRouter, the request would additionally be subject to OpenRouter and upstream provider data-retention policies, which matters for client projects.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: SDK default timeout 10 s (index.mjs:518, overridable by JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS) with maxRetries 2 (index.mjs:74), so worst case could stall a single tool call for tens of seconds before returning an isError result with a retryable hint; Claude then just continues without Jev. If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset the server process exits at startup (index.ts:49-52) and appears as a failed MCP connection, again non-blocking. Nothing in the flow can block or deny Claude Code actions since it is not a hook.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.contextCost: MCP: 1 tool. Description ~1.5 KB plus zod-generated JSON schema (nested union of 3 question types, descriptions on state/questions/model) roughly 2.5-3 KB total, so about 700-900 tokens; no MCP server `instructions` field is set (server.ts constructs McpServer with only capabilities.tools). In Claude Code 2.1.x MCP tools are typically deferred and loaded via ToolSearch, so the eager cost is closer to a tool-name line. Skill: frontmatter description ~0.7 KB (~180 tokens) always listed; full SKILL.md body ~9.3 KB (~2.3k tokens) loaded only when the skill triggers, with 11 reference files (~1,900 lines total) loaded on demand. No hook-injected text.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns (no hooks, no proxy). When Claude decides to call the tool: the repo's own manual measurements are 713-1130 ms per call across hosts (810 ms in Claude Code, self-reported), plus one extra model round-trip for Claude to decide, format the call and read the result, so realistically 2-5 s per use. Cold start of npx -y adds several seconds at MCP server launch (npm resolve/fetch) unless installed locally.
gh-reiswaffel78-jev-agent-toolkit.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. The MCP tool is just available, and the skill description triggers when the task looks like building a classifier/router or mentions Jev/TypeSafe. Neither contains a mechanism that makes Claude Code call Jev during ordinary coding. The bundled coding.md only suggests ideas (triage, change risk, review property checks, test-failure classification) and itself says most work should stay deterministic. Expect rare organic invocation; getting consistent use would require adding your own CLAUDE.md rules or hooks.
pros: Cleanest and most auditable Jev MCP bridge found here: one tool, ~340 lines of TS, no shell, no arbitrary URL, key from env only, metadata-only logging, 401 bodies suppressed, SHA-pinned CI with npm audit.

Works with OpenRouter with zero code changes in principle: it delegates to @typesafe-ai/sdk which honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and hits /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, matching OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone (config: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key=OpenRouter key, model typesafe/jev-1.13).
Fail-open, non-blocking design: errors come back as isError tool results, so a slow or down Jev never blocks Claude Code; timeout tunable via JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS.
Small context footprint (1 tool, no server instructions, skill body loads on demand) and honest documentation of limitations (literal reading, counting, dates, adversarial state).
Ships a Claude Code .mcp.json using ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} interpolation so the key stays out of files; 35 offline tests including an MCP protocol round-trip.
The batching advice (many questions per call, questions are parallel) and the decision-gate guidance are practical and match Jev's primitives.
cons: Not automatic: no hook, no proxy, no CLAUDE.md snippet; Claude only calls jev_evaluate if it chooses to. This fails the user's core requirement ('Claude Code must use it when needed, without prompting') unless supplemented with custom CLAUDE.md rules or a hook.

Documented coding use cases (triage, diff risk score, review Noul questions, test-failure classification) are illustrative only; Claude Opus can answer these itself at similar cost in a single turn, and Jev adds a 1-5 s round trip and a second failure point. No evidence anywhere of accuracy gains.

Zero OpenRouter awareness: no string 'openrouter' in repo, no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) support, default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID, and the OpenRouter path was never tested by the author. Schema/response compatibility with the SDK's parser is assumed, not proven.

Very immature and single-author: 10 commits over 2 days, 2 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub release, one npm version published by a maintainer handle different from the repo owner, dependent on a brand-new @modelcontextprotocol/server v2 and an SDK at 0.6.0. npx -y at each launch means unpinned supply-chain exposure.

Bridge-level retries (SDK maxRetries 2 with 10 s timeout) can stall one call for ~30 s in the worst case, and the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not match mcp__ tools, so state contents are unguarded and would go to a third party (OpenRouter plus provider) on client projects.

Much of the repo is generic non-Jev agent boilerplate (Blender, Unreal, browser research, multi-agent) that would bloat context if the skill triggers and duplicates behaviour Claude Code already has; README itself defers to TypeSafe's official skill (typesafe-ai/skills) as canonical.

gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.name: chayan-bit/jev-harness
gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.whatItDoes: Independent (non-official) Python library plus a small CLI that wraps Jev-Frame (chayan-bit's own framework over the typesafe_sdk). It builds four Jev Choice questions (task difficulty, reasoning effort, skill, compaction) from a bounded HostSnapshot that the host must fill in, and returns an advisory-only AdviceReport. It also has a Decisions engine with 7 shadow-judgment families, offline threshold calibration, and a hook renderer that speaks the OpenAI Codex command-hook protocol (PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PreCompact, PostCompact). It is not an MCP server, a Claude Code plugin or a skill. It does not gather host state itself, so something else must write the snapshot and the report file.

security: Key is read from an environment variable, never from argv (cli.py:236, providers.py:94), so it does not appear in the process list.
The library has no shell execution: grep of src/ found no subprocess or os.system. Reports are written atomically with mode 0600 (cli.py:50-63).
No MCP server and no prompt-injection surface toward the model, except the additionalContext text the hook emits. The text is built from validated enum options and digests, not free text.

Installs via pip from a git tag, and its dependency jev-frame is also a git URL pin (pyproject.toml). This means no PyPI provenance and a supply-chain trust in one individual's two repos. The transitive typesafe_sdk comes from the Jev-Frame lock.
The hook itself never allows anything and can only deny through a user-supplied exact deny list. This is a good authority design.
SECURITY.md exists with a private vulnerability reporting channel. Actions are SHA-pinned in CI. No telemetry found.
gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine in hook mode, because the hook is offline. Live 'analyze' sends only the minimized HostSnapshot (at most 16 KiB): task_summary, phase, counts, token usage and the option ids and descriptions the host supplies. This goes to TypeSafe's endpoint through typesafe_sdk, not OpenRouter. The docs explicitly say not to include code, prompts, file contents or commands. The shadow-judgment path sends at most 16 KiB of digest-bound evidence per question, and refuses evidence that matches private-key or API-token patterns. The design is privacy-conservative, but someone must build the snapshot.
gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.failureMode: Fail-open for advice. Any provider error, a low confidence below 0.55, or a stale snapshot gives an 'unresolved' report, and the hook then emits {}. The analyze timeout defaults to 8 s and max_attempts is 1, with no retries. Hooks have a 2 s timeout in the generated config. Fail-closed applies only to the user's own deny policy: a malformed policy file or input makes the hook exit 2, which blocks. That is intended, but a corrupt file would block every tool call if matcher '*' is used.
gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero server instructions. The hook adds a short additionalContext line to PreToolUse only when a fresh report matches the session, and it is empty otherwise. In Claude Code the payload mismatch below would break this in practice.
gh-chayan-bit-jev-harness.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook in principle. The hook is a PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/PreCompact/PostCompact command hook. However, it only reads a pre-written report file. Nothing in the repo refreshes that report automatically. The 'analyze' call is a separate manual or cron step, and the report expires after 5 minutes. It is also targeted at the Codex hook schema. Claude Code has similar PreToolUse JSON, but the code validates Codex-specific fields (turn_id, model, permission_mode, and so on at hooks.py:59-83), and PermissionRequest and PreCompact/PostCompact are not equivalent in Claude Code. So it is not usable as-is.
pros: Well-designed safety model: advice-only, no allow decisions, expiring reports, digest-bound context, and secret-pattern refusal before dispatch.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, and the hook is offline with no network calls.
Real tests (about 1,270 lines of tests across 5 files, run in CI), README snippets executed in CI, lint plus mypy, SHA-pinned actions, release-please and MIT license.
Choice questions like 'which reasoning effort or skill' are a good conceptual fit for Jev's System One.
The API-key handling is clean: env var only, never argv, and reports are written 0600.
Library-level base_url support in Jev-Frame's TypeSafeProvider makes an OpenRouter experiment possible.
cons: Targets Codex, not Claude Code. The hook code validates Codex payload fields and events, and README FAQ and features say Codex. Nothing in the repo mentions Claude Code.
No OpenRouter support: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and the bare 'jev-1.13.0' model, hard-coded in two places, with no base URL option in the CLI.
Not a turnkey integration. There is no snapshot producer and no refresher, so the hook only relays a report file that you must generate. The 5-minute TTL makes this a cron or wrapper build.
Advisory outputs (reasoning effort, difficulty, skill, compaction) cannot be applied by Claude Code hooks. The hook cannot change the model, effort or skill, only add a context line.

Installs from git URLs (Jev-Frame is also a 5-day-old personal repo), not PyPI. Two layers of unaudited wrapper sit between the user and Jev.
Would add nothing over a simple custom PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.

gh-barakchamo-jev-kit.name: BarakChamo/jev-kit
gh-barakchamo-jev-kit.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (marketplace "jev", plugin "jev" v0.3.0) that ships three skills (jev-fit, jev-questions, jev-eval) teaching an agent how to WRITE well-formed Jev question maps (state + noul/choice/score questions) for application code, plus two dependency-free Node scripts: jev-run (sends labelled test cases to a Jev endpoint) and jev-audit (offline analysis of results, confidence-threshold fitting). pros: Well-researched, evidence-backed guidance for Jev question design (16 rules from 57 labelled suites); README claims wrong decisions dropping from 15.6% to 1.1% on a held-out SLA task when agents use the skill. Genuinely useful IF the user builds Jev-backed features in their own projects.

Scripts are single-file, dependency-free and readable; API key comes from the environment and is not put on argv; retry/timeout handling is sane; MIT licensed.

gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.name: nanoDBA/jev-agent-kit
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.whatItDoes: Independent Python 3.11+ package (zero runtime deps, ~7.6k LOC in src/jev_kit) that wraps TypeSafe's Jev (System One API) as a cautious "typed judgment" layer for coding agents. Ships a PreToolUse hook for Claude Code (python -m jev_kit.hooks.claude) that asks Jev tool-call-gate Noul questions (destructive? exfiltrates? widens permission?) about each Bash/PowerShell command after heavy egress minimization (command cut to basename, path hashed with HMAC, cmd_* boolean facts computed locally, secret-pattern scan). Also a jev-runtime SKILL.md (prompt guidance, no auto-trigger logic), a CLI (jev-kit), question sets (preflight-route, postflight-verify, stop-or-continue, tool-call-gate), receipts (JSONL), calibration tooling, and a `jev-kit audit` static scanner for skills. By design, hooks start in shadow mode (record only, never change behavior), Jev can never grant/approve, and only tool-call-gate is wired to a host event. The other question sets (routing, verify claims, stop/continue) are NOT wired automatically ("Nothing calls them automatically"). Added value for this user is therefore essentially a second, model-based safety gate on shell commands, and only after per-question calibration with labeled data.

Transport hardened: fixed HTTPS destination, redirects refused (Authorization not forwarded), env proxies ignored, 1 MiB response cap, TLS default context (transport.py). Note ProxyHandler({}) means corporate proxies unsupported.

Egress minimisation is strong: command reduced to basename, path -> HMAC keyed hash, cmd_* booleans, secret-pattern scan on exact outgoing bytes (egress.py, 790 lines), refuses request on match; source-code fields refused. But the free-text `context` (tool name + Claude's Bash `description`) is plain text and can contain project/client names; live gate requires JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST=agent_context and a JEV_KIT_ATTESTATION JSON file (inventory/DPA attestation) - i.e. heavy compliance ceremony, no telemetry.
Hook runs engine via subprocess `python -m jev_kit.cli` (watchdog.py), no shell; child gets key via inherited env.

Prompt-injection surface small: Jev output is only probabilities validated against a schema; hook can only add friction (ask), never allow. Untrusted description text goes to Jev but cannot cause execution.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found; pure stdlib. CI pins actions by SHA, permissions: contents read. Receipts written to disk (per-user data dir) contain digests/distributions, not raw state.
Repo contains .beads/ git hooks (dev tooling for the author's issue tracker), irrelevant at runtime but note they exist if cloned.
Author states test data/labels were written by Claude and the project is agent-developed (CLAUDE.md, docs/handoffs Codex reviews); no independent human audit.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.dataEgress: Per gated Bash/PowerShell tool call, to api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter): JSON with `command` = executable basename only (e.g. "rm"), ~11 cmd_* boolean/null facts, `target` = keyed hash of file path/URL, `context` = "tool=Bash; description=<Claude's description string>" with emails/IPs/phones masked. Never full command line, args, file contents, diffs, tool outputs, transcript, or cwd. Requests matching credential patterns are refused, not sent. Nothing is sent unless JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST includes agent_context and an attestation file exists; otherwise live gate calls are refused before sending (so, out of the box, the hook collects no evidence). ~300-390 input tokens per call.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.failureMode: Fail-safe by design. Shadow (default): any error/timeout/unparsable event returns {} so Claude proceeds untouched. Enforce: any failure, timeout, uncalibrated question, or non-cleared gate returns permissionDecision "ask" (prompts user), and with the shipped uncalibrated thresholds EVERY checked call including `ls` asks, so enforce is unusable until you calibrate on labeled data. Timeouts: hook self-deadline 8 s (hooks/core.py:34) with a watchdog killing the child process; engine per-call deadline ~10 s with retries/rate budget; recommended Claude hook timeout 30 s. Hook always exits 0. In bypass/auto permission mode, an "ask" decision from a PreToolUse hook still prompts the user, which would break the unattended flow in enforce mode.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.latencyImpact: Measured by the author: ~2.3 s per tool call end-to-end in each host (Python process start + spawning child engine + key fetched via TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND), Jev call itself typically 0.17-0.31 s, with occasional 4-7 s outliers and 3/60 over 10 s deadline in the first run. Hook is synchronous PreToolUse on every Bash call, so a 100-command session adds ~4 min of wall clock, on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks (hooks run in parallel per event but the slowest gates the call). Author itself notes it 'saves nothing unless it replaces work you would otherwise do'.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.contextCost: Near zero tokens injected into the Claude context in hook-only setup: no MCP server (0 tools, no server instructions), hook emits {} or an ask reason string only. If the optional skill is installed, only its name+description enters the listing (~60 tokens); loading it pulls the ~90-line SKILL.md plus references/evidence-contracts.md on demand.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Bash|PowerShell) - fully automatic once registered, no prompting needed. But automatic only for tool-call gating; routing, claim-verification and stop/continue question sets are not wired to any hook (no Stop / UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse adapter), and the skill has no concrete trigger.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.runtime: Python >=3.11, stdlib only, hatchling build; run as python -m jev_kit.hooks.claude (needs pip install -e from a git clone; a plain wheel does not ship the skill/question-set folder)
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.install: git clone https://github.com/nanoDBA/jev-agent-kit && python -m pip install -e . ; export TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND, JEV_KIT_HMAC_KEY, JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST=agent_context, JEV_KIT_ATTESTATION=path); add PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|PowerShell) to ~/.claude/settings.json with absolute --question-set-path. Not on PyPI, no releases.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.tests: 34 test files under tests/ (tests never call live API; mock transport), CI matrix ubuntu/macos/windows x py3.11-3.13 with pytest, ruff, mypy --strict, packaging smoke. Not executed by me. Author's own live eval: ~300 calls synthetic, labels written by Claude, not human-verified.
pros: Only candidate here that is a genuinely deterministic, automatic Claude Code integration (PreToolUse hook): no 'use jev' prompting needed, zero context-token cost, no MCP tool bloat.

Very careful security engineering: fixed HTTPS destination, no redirects, key never in argv/body, secret-pattern scanner blocks send, command reduced to basename + local cmd_* facts, path HMAC-hashed, stdlib-only (no supply-chain deps), no telemetry/installer scripts.
Fail-safe semantics: shadow default, hook can never emit allow (only ask), always exit 0, 8 s self-deadline with child kill; cannot break or silently widen permissions.
Honest documentation with measured numbers (latency, cost ~$0.000015/call, variance) and explicit caveats; receipts JSONL give an audit trail for evaluating whether Jev adds value.
Solid test/CI discipline for a young repo (34 test files, mypy strict, SHA-pinned actions, cross-OS matrix); MIT license.
Reusable design ideas (egress allowlist, command_properties parser, question-set + calibration workflow) even if not adopted wholesale.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai (transport.py:86), key env is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, model pinned by regex jev-X.Y.Z that rejects typesafe/jev-1.13 and jev-latest aliases (engine.py:884-890). User wants OpenRouter as provider, so needs a fork of transport + model-pin logic.

Value proposition is narrow for this user: only a Bash tool-call safety gate is wired. The user already has a PreToolUse secret-leak guard and runs in bypass/auto mode; the gate can only ADD friction ('ask'), which is the opposite of what bypass/auto users want, and in enforce mode with shipped uncalibrated thresholds even `ls` prompts. In shadow mode it is pure logging with no user-visible benefit.

No calibrated thresholds ship; calibration requires labeled data from your own commands and per-question/model-version registration - a substantial ongoing workflow before any answer can be acted on. Routing/verify/stop-continue question sets are not auto-invoked at all, so the broader 'Jev when it adds value' goal is not delivered.

Compliance ceremony before any live call: JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST=agent_context plus an attestation JSON (inventory/DPA) are required, otherwise the live gate is refused and no data is collected. Whether this fits client projects is the user's problem to attest; free-text `description` can still leak client/folder names to a third party.

Latency: author measured ~2.3 s overhead per tool call (Python cold start + child process + key command), with 4-7 s Jev outliers, on every Bash call, stacked on existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post).

Very immature: created 2026-09-27, 173 commits in ~2 days by one author (largely AI-generated per CLAUDE.md/handoffs), 1 star, no releases, not on PyPI, version 0.1.0; 'wheel install does not ship skill folder' so requires editable install from a clone. Eval labels written by Claude, not independent.
Uses Python subprocess per hook call and ignores env proxies (ProxyHandler({})), which may break behind corporate proxies.
Skill description is generic (no concrete trigger phrases), so model-discretion invocation of Jev would be unreliable; skill is guidance text only.
gh-nanodba-jev-agent-kit.verdict: Well-engineered, safety-first but pre-alpha hook that only gates Bash commands via TypeSafe's direct API; it lacks OpenRouter support and, for a bypass/auto-mode user, adds ~2 s per call and only friction. Worth mining for ideas (egress minimization, shadow-mode receipts), not worth installing as the Jev integration.

gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.name: AntonioCoppe/jev-harness
gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.whatItDoes: Unofficial TypeScript library (v0.1.0, not published to npm as far as inspected; clone or install from git) wrapping @typesafe-ai/sdk. DecisionHarness.run() sends state plus choice/score/noul questions to /v1/systemone, aggregates a mean confidence, applies a user-written policy (default minConfidence 0.55, low-confidence result becomes review/escalate/suppress), and supports a shadow mode (returns shadow_noop) and JSONL/OTEL/PostHog decision loggers. It also ships about 40 copy-paste TS recipes (shell-command-gate, pr-risk-gate, done-claim-check, tool-exec-gate and others) and an offline/live eval CLI (jev-eval). It has no MCP server, no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json and no Claude Code integration. The README states it is not a Claude Code /compact replacement. It is a building block for writing your own gate, not a ready-made integration.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter reference anywhere in the repo (grep for openrouter over src/eval/examples found nothing). src/harness.ts:53-58 builds new TypeSafeClient({apiKey: options.apiKey ?? process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY, defaultModel: options.defaultModel ?? 'jev-latest'}). The dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 (dist/index.mjs:56-62) reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL. Default base URL is https://api.typesafe.ai (index.mjs:513). It POSTs to baseURL + '/v1/systemone' (index.mjs:554) with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (index.mjs:581), timeout 10 s per attempt (index.mjs:518), maxRetries 2 (index.mjs:74). README 'Other backends' documents TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Also supports a custom DecisionBackend via options.client (harness.ts:27-30, 44).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial by config, unverified live. OpenRouter's System One endpoint is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and the SDK appends /v1/systemone to baseURL. So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> plus TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) should work with no code change, assuming OpenRouter's request/response schema is identical to TypeSafe's (unverified). The model id must be overridden because the default 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id. Alternatively write a ~30-line DecisionBackend with fetch to OpenRouter. The SDK sends only Bearer auth, so OpenRouter's optional HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers would need defaultHeaders.
providerSupport.others: Self-hosted or local /v1/systemone server via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL; custom in-process DecisionBackend (rules or local SLM). PostHog and OTEL are log sinks only.

gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in `state` and `questions` is sent to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter, which then forwards to TypeSafe). For a Claude Code hook built on the recipes, that would be the full Bash command string, cwd and user goal (shell-command-gate), or diffs and PR text (pr-risk-gate), or the assistant's done-claim and evidence (done-claim-check). Nothing leaves automatically, because the library has no Claude Code wiring. Decision logs, if enabled, contain only ids, action, confidence and usage. The client is a plain fetch and adds no telemetry of its own.
gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.failureMode: Library-level: the SDK uses a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries on connection errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx (index.mjs:74, 518). run() has no try/catch, so it throws on failure. Fail-open or fail-closed is therefore left entirely to the caller's wrapper. Worst case is about 30 s or more of stall if used naively in a hook, so a tight timeout (about 1-2 s) and retry 0 would have to be set. The recipes default to fail-closed-ish low-confidence handling (shell-command-gate: suppress), which in a PreToolUse hook would block commands, so a fail-open wrapper would be needed. Logger errors are swallowed.
gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.contextCost: Zero as shipped: no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text. A custom hook built on it would inject only what the developer chooses (for example a one-line permissionDecisionReason).
gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.autoInvocation: None as shipped. It is a library only ("only when prompted" / code you write). It could power a deterministic hook (PreToolUse, Stop) if the user writes a small Node wrapper around it, so it is a possible engine for a hook, not the integration.
gh-antoniocoppe-jev-harness.latencyImpact: None as shipped. If wrapped in a hook, each gated call would add one network round trip. The README's own claim is 1.3 s for 24 rows at concurrency 8, and the brief says 70-500 ms end to end. Node cold start (about 100 ms) plus TLS setup per hook invocation would add to that, since each hook is a new process with no connection reuse.

run() throws on network errors and the SDK retries twice with a 10 s timeout. There is no built-in fail-open behaviour, which is dangerous for a blocking PreToolUse hook unless wrapped.
Default logger writes JSON to stdout, which can pollute hook output
Aggregate confidence is a naive mean, and noul confidence is a stand-in (|p-0.5|*2). Gate quality depends on Jev's calibration, which is beta and disputed (Theo's 'flash router' claim).

It has no MCP, hook, skill or plugin, and it supports only TypeSafe directly, though OpenRouter is likely reachable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. It is useful mainly as reference code (shell-command-gate, done-claim-check, shadow mode) if you write your own small fail-open hook, but it is too young and unproven to depend on.

security: API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), sent as Bearer header; never placed in argv, so not visible in the process list.

No shell execution, subprocess or os.system anywhere; pure urllib + stdlib; no npm postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev call itself. Whole codebase is about 1,000 lines of Python and easy to audit (jev.py, shortlist.py, triage.py, hooks/rerank_search.py read fully; logscan.py partly).

Hook output is constrained: it only permutes an existing string array in filenames, so a hostile payload cannot inject text into Claude context through the hook. Jev returns numbers, no free text, so prompt-injection surface via the model response is minimal.
Prompt injection into Jev itself is possible (file names or log lines placed in state could bias ranking), but the worst effect is a mis-ordering; nothing is dropped.
Egress of possibly sensitive data (see dataEgress); logscan and triage do no secret redaction.

No LICENSE file in repo (GitHub licenseInfo null) although README and plugin.json say MIT; legal ambiguity for client work. Single author, 1 star, no releases: supply-chain trust is low, though pinning a commit SHA and reading the 1k lines mitigates it.
Documentation mismatch: SKILL.md says low-scoring files are moved 'under a heading' but hook code only reorders; minor accuracy concern.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.dataEgress: Hook (automatic path): on every Grep/Glob with >=12 results, sends to Jev the last user prompt text (first 600 chars, from transcript) plus the full list of matched file paths (indexed). No file contents, no match lines. Manual scripts: shortlist sends the task sentence plus paths (grep match lines only with --context); triage sends up to 1500 chars of each item plus optional context (may include code or diffs); logscan sends one raw representative log line per template (up to 300 chars, unredacted, may contain tokens, hostnames, emails). All goes to the configured BASE (if patched, OpenRouter and its upstream TypeSafe see it). File paths and user prompts from client projects leave the machine, which may matter for client NDAs.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.failureMode: Hook fails open: no key, unparseable payload, non-dict response, <12 files, no user message, any exception -> exit 0 with no stdout so the original output is kept (hooks/rerank_search.py:33-36, 66-102, 116-121). Harness timeout is 15 s, but jev.py uses urlopen timeout=120 with 3 attempts and 2s/4s sleeps and calls die() (sys.exit(1)) on 401/403/other 4xx/unreachable; the 15 s hook timeout caps worst-case added latency at about 15 s per Grep/Glob during an outage (not 0). Manual scripts fail closed with an error message and non-zero exit (no fallback ranking except logscan --no-jev). A bad OpenRouter key means every big search pays a wasted round trip, then exits.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.latencyImpact: Claimed 0.38 s for small batches and 0.72 s for 256 questions on TypeSafe direct (author-measured, not independently verified; OpenRouter adds a hop). Hook is synchronous PostToolUse, so each Grep/Glob returning >=12 files adds roughly 0.4 to 1 s plus Python startup (~50 ms). Manual skill runs add a Bash call and a model turn.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.contextCost: No MCP tools, no server instructions. Three skill entries (name plus multi-line description, about 700 to 900 chars each, roughly 2.3k chars total, approx 550 to 650 tokens) in the skill listing permanently. Invoking a skill loads its SKILL.md body (about 3 to 4k chars each, roughly 800 to 1000 tokens). The hook injects no text; it only permutes filenames. Script output adds a small block per use.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.autoInvocation: Mixed and weaker than advertised. (1) Skill description triggers: model-discretion; Claude may invoke jev-shortlist/triage/logscan when descriptions match, but the skills run through Bash scripts and Opus will often just read results itself. (2) The PostToolUse Grep|Glob hook is defined in skill frontmatter, so it registers only after jev-shortlist has been invoked in that session (SKILL.md: 'for the rest of the session'); it is not installed by plugin.json and there is no hooks/hooks.json. For a truly automatic hook the user must copy it into ~/.claude/settings.json (or a fork's hooks/hooks.json) as a global PostToolUse matcher Grep|Glob. The user's existing GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks fire on the same tools; two PostToolUse hooks both emitting updatedToolOutput may conflict (ordering unspecified, unverified).
pros: Only candidate so far that actually turns Jev into an automatic, deterministic-capable hook in Claude Code (PostToolUse on Grep|Glob with updatedToolOutput), matching the 'no prompting' requirement once installed globally.

Same wire schema as OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone: pure env-var switch (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), no code patch needed.
Small (~1k LOC), stdlib-only Python, no shell exec, no installers, key via env not argv: easy to audit and safe to run.
Hook is conservative: reorder only, never drops or rewrites content, preserves schema, fails open on all errors, MIN_RESULTS=12 avoids wasteful calls.
Uses Jev where it fits (Noul relevance, batched shared state at ~$0.042/M input, output free): cost is negligible.

Unusually honest evidence: ships eval harness and a measured calibration curve (Noul ECE 0.169, Choice ECE 0.226, recall@10 0.69 vs 0.53 search order), reports negative results and corrected its own default from 0.7 to 0.9.
Zero context bloat compared with an MCP server: no tool schemas, roughly 600 tokens of skill descriptions.
cons: Measured benefit is modest: reordering Grep/Glob file lists improves recall@10 from 0.53 to 0.69 on the author's own 102 cases; Opus 5.5 with ripgrep and GitNexus graph context rarely reads whole file lists blindly, so real gain for this user is doubtful.
The 'automatic' hook only activates after the jev-shortlist skill is invoked (skill-scoped frontmatter hook); out of the box it is not automatic. Needs manual copy into settings.json to be always-on.

Likely overlap or conflict with the user's GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash pre/post hooks and secret-leak guard: another PostToolUse rewriting Grep output may clash, and GitNexus already enriches search context.

Sends the user's last prompt (600 chars) and all matched file paths to a third party on every big search; client-project paths and prompts leave the machine; no redaction, allowlist or per-project opt-out. logscan sends raw log lines.
Task relevance signal is only the last string user message from the transcript; in long agentic turns or slash-command flows it may be stale or empty, degrading ranking.
Outage behaviour is not zero-cost: up to the 15 s hook timeout per Grep/Glob during slow or failed API; a wrong key wastes an HTTP call every time; no circuit breaker.
Jev is unreliable mid-range (author's own numbers: says 0.45 when reality is 11%); Choice confidence separates only above 0.9, so jev-triage has limited use for code-review-type judgments.

Weak maturity: created 2026-09-21, 5 commits, 1 author, 1 star, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file despite claiming MIT, unaffiliated with TypeSafe; '360x cheaper' marketing compares against a use Opus would not need for such tasks.
OpenRouter path untested by the author; TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming is confusing when holding an OpenRouter key.
gh-wanlanglin-jev-skills.verdict: The most concrete Jev integration for Claude Code so far (real PostToolUse hook, stdlib-only, repointed to OpenRouter by three env vars), but it is a small single-author POC whose gain (reordering Grep/Glob results) is marginal for an Opus + GitNexus workflow, and its hook is only auto-registered after the skill is invoked. Worth cherry-picking the hook and jev.py into a self-owned global hook (with an allowlist/redaction and a circuit breaker) rather than installing the plugin as is.

security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts and no runtime dependencies (package.json), so npm supply-chain surface is small; no curl|sh installer.

API key is read from environment only (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and sent in an Authorization header, so it never appears in argv; the generated MCP snippets carry only JEV_LAYER_PROVIDER. Caveat: with Claude Code the key must be exported in the shell or in the .mcp.json env, and the second option would put it in a plain file.
No shell execution in the core. child_process is used only in the OMP adapter (integrations/omp/extension.js) to spawn node. No telemetry found by grep.
Egress goes only to the configured endpoint. The endpoint is overridable via OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_ENDPOINT, so a poisoned env could redirect the key and payload.

Prompt-injection surface: the request intent, context and capability descriptions go to the model. The model output is an ID chosen from the closed set, and the host validates it against eligible[] (route.mjs:81-97). Data flowing back is bounded, but a wrong pick is possible. SECURITY.md itself says it is not a security boundary and that it does not detect injection.

Writes plaintext JSONL receipts at ./.jev/replay/cases.jsonl in the cwd. They can contain intent, context and host results (result is bounded to 8000 bytes, receipts.mjs:5). In client repos this means sensitive data on disk and a risk of committing it, so it needs .gitignore. src/context-filter.mjs has a sanitizeContext redactor, but I did not audit its coverage.
Single maintainer (typakon4, npm email [email removed]), 1 other commit author, and 4 stars. Hobby-scale provenance, so pin the version and review the tarball before use.
The npm tarball metadata is odd: the description is HTML from the zh-CN README. This is cosmetic.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, per call: model id, and state = {intent string, context object projected/capped to about 6,000 bytes by projectState (route.mjs:16, maxContextBytes 6_000), actor/permissions}, plus questions.tool.criteria = {id: {name, kind, description, risk}} for each eligible candidate. Nothing is sent unless the calling agent (Claude) chooses to call jev_route and passes intent/context, so what is sent depends entirely on what Claude puts in the arguments. There is no automatic capture of files, diffs or tool outputs; the tool takes only what the model supplies. The Codex SKILL says "never send secrets or full transcripts", which is prompt guidance only. If supervision, shadow_compaction or browser_step are used, host-supplied observations and context (which can include page text and file content) are sent too. The demo provider sends nothing. Locally it appends to .jev/replay/cases.jsonl.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Any provider error, timeout, HTTP non-2xx or malformed answer returns a status 'fallback' envelope with fallback.type (route.mjs:70-79), and confidence below policy.min_confidence also gives fallback. No retries. Timeouts: 5s OpenRouter, 2s TypeSafe via AbortSignal.timeout. A missing key returns fallback without an HTTP call. JEV_LAYER_ENABLED=0 disables it. Caveat: the fail-open only means the MCP tool returns a fallback JSON; whether Claude then proceeds normally depends on Claude reading it. MCP-level failures (server crash) surface as a failed tool call. The server has no per-tool-call timeout beyond the fetch timeout. Note that a server startup failure only produces an MCP connection warning, not a blocked session.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Tool definitions are about 4.1k chars, roughly 1,000 tokens of names, descriptions and schemas (src/mcp-server.mjs lines 15-123). The server declares no 'instructions' field. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. The schemas are loose (capabilities: array of object), so Claude gets little guidance on how to build valid inputs. If you rely on CLAUDE.md or a skill to trigger it, add a few hundred more tokens.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.latencyImpact: One HTTPS round trip per jev_route call. The brief claims 70-500 ms end to end for Jev, plus the MCP tool-call overhead and the Node process. Worst case is a 5 s timeout, then fallback. The important cost is on top of that: Claude has to spend a whole extra LLM turn to compose the capabilities[] list and to read the result, which adds seconds and thousands of tokens per invocation on Opus. That is far more than the Jev call itself. It is only paid when Claude decides to call it.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no Claude Code hook, no skill, no plugin and no transparent proxy. The only trigger prose is the tool description plus a Codex-specific SKILL.md and AGENTS.md, which cannot be used as-is in Claude Code. The user's goal of never having to prompt 'use jev' is NOT met. You would have to add a Claude Code skill or CLAUDE.md rule, and even then the invocation depends on Claude's judgment. A UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook could be added by the user, but the hook would need its own code to build the candidate list, since the tool cannot discover Claude Code's capabilities by itself. There is a src/discovery.mjs that has explicit capability discovery for skills, MCP, CLI and so on, which I did not verify against Claude Code's layout.
pros: Native OpenRouter support that matches the Decisions API contract: endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and optional HTTP-Referer / X-Title headers (typesafe.mjs:59-125). No patching needed for the user's chosen provider.
Fail-open by design with tests: every error path returns a fallback envelope, there are no retries, and the timeout is 5s. A dedicated fail-open-smoke script runs in CI.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry and no shell exec in the core. The key comes from env, not argv. MIT license.

Host-side policy is deterministic (risk levels, permissions, min_confidence, and the selected ID must be in the eligible set), so a Jev answer cannot escalate privileges; it can only pick among options the host offered.
Standard stdio MCP with JSON-RPC 2024-11-05, so it loads in Claude Code via a plain .mcp.json entry. The context cost is small at 6 tools (about 1k tokens).
Receipts and replay (.jev/replay/cases.jsonl) allow offline evaluation of whether Jev's routing choices were any good, which is useful for testing the Theo 'flash router' skepticism.
cons: No Claude Code integration at all. Adapters exist for Hermes, OMP and Codex only, and 'claude' appears nowhere in the repo. There is no hook, skill or plugin.json for Claude Code (the only plugin.json is for Codex).

Invocation depends on Claude's discretion, so it cannot satisfy 'use Jev automatically without me prompting'. The Codex SKILL.md even restricts it to closed-set capability routing and forbids open-ended planning, coding, research or recovery.

The use case is routing among capabilities the host already knows. Claude Code already picks tools and skills natively with a strong model, so routing through a second model adds a hop and two extra model turns to build and read the candidate list, with no gain in coding quality. The sweet spot (Noul/Score/Choice calibrated probabilities on daily-coding decisions such as 'should I run tests now', 'is this a risky edit') is not addressed.

Only the Choice primitive is used by the router. The Decisions API's Noul and Score primitives, which are Jev's more interesting outputs, are not exposed as a generic tool. The tools are opinionated wrappers, not raw Jev access.

Very immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-19, 15 commits, 2 authors, 4 stars, 1 fork, 2 releases, and the MCP serverInfo still says version 0.1.0 while the package is 0.2.0. Several features are marked experimental or shadow-only (browser step, model route, shadow compaction). The tests are offline-only, with no live OpenRouter validation.

Plaintext receipts with intent/context are written to the cwd (.jev/replay/cases.jsonl). On client projects this creates sensitive artifacts inside repos, and the user's global secret-leak guard does not cover this file.
Unused surface: the model-routing, compaction, browser and supervision tools duplicate things Claude Code already does, and add attack/confusion surface and tool-name noise for little value here.
Uses the alpha OpenRouter endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) which may change, and the 5s default timeout can stall a tool call in the worst case.
gh-typakon4-jev-layer.verdict: A clean, safe, fail-open Node MCP wrapper that already speaks OpenRouter's Jev Decisions API, but it is a router for Codex, Hermes and OMP and has no Claude Code hook or skill, so it only fires when Claude chooses to call it. It fails the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement and adds little for daily coding. At best it is a reference for the request/response shape (a provider class you could crib) or an opt-in experiment behind a custom hook, not something to install as the main Jev integration.
