gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.name: RevocGG/typesafe-jev-bridge
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Node (>=18) localhost bridge (127.0.0.1:8399) that translates OpenAI POST /v1/chat/completions and /v1/responses into TypeSafe's native POST {TYPESAFE_API_BASE}/v1/systemone with body {state, model, questions}, and renders the typed answers back as text. Also ships CLIs: ask-jev.cjs (typed question about file/dir/stdin), audit.cjs (Jev judges every file), autofix.cjs (judge, fix via a separate chat model on a 9Router endpoint, re-judge). It is NOT an MCP server, hook or skill; the only Claude Code integration is pasting a text block into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md telling the model to shell out to ask-jev.cjs. Claude Code cannot use it as a model backend anyway (it speaks Anthropic Messages API, the bridge speaks OpenAI format), and README itself says never route coding to Jev.

providerSupport.evidence: Only TypeSafe is coded. bridge.js:84 `new URL(process.env.TYPESAFE_API_BASE || "https://api.typesafe.ai")`; bridge.js:443 path `${UPSTREAM.basePath}/v1/systemone`; bridge.js:446 `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}`; key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (bridge.js:203). No 'openrouter' string anywhere in the repo (grep). Upstream payload bridge.js:751 `{ state, model, questions }` (TypeSafe native schema). Model is forced to bare `jev-latest` unless the client id starts with 'jev' (bridge.js:556-561), so 'typesafe/jev-latest' passes through as-is and 'typesafe/jev-1.13' would be sent verbatim.
providerSupport.others: 9Router (OpenAI-compatible router) documented as the main consumer; autofix uses ROUTER_9_BASE_URL for the fixer chat model. Official typesafe-sdk used only by demo.py.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Probably trivial-to-moderate, unverified. Base URL is env-configurable and path is /v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, exactly the OpenRouter System One endpoint from the brief. Unknowns: (1) whether OpenRouter's request/response schema equals TypeSafe's native {state,model,questions}; (2) model id must be typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, but the bridge may send 'jev-latest' or the mapped alias (small patch to resolveUpstreamModel); (3) setup/doctor key-shape checks are informational only but the live-check may misbehave with sk-or- keys; (4) the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported at all. No code change needed for the env path, but nothing in the repo tests or documents it.

security: Binds 127.0.0.1 only, rejects non-loopback Host (DNS-rebinding guard), rejects any browser Origin unless allow-listed (bridge.js:226, README security model)
No auth by default: any local process of the user can call the bridge and spend the API key unless BRIDGE_TOKEN is set (SECURITY.md admits this)

API key is read from env or typesafe-bridge/.env, sent only as upstream Bearer header, not in argv; setup takes the key via hidden prompt or --key-stdin, so no key in process list. Client tokens are not relayed by default (BRIDGE_ALLOW_KEY_PASSTHROUGH=0)
Regex redaction (lib/redact.cjs) is applied by the CLI by default but bridge-level redaction is OPT-IN (BRIDGE_REDACT=1) so router/agent traffic goes out unredacted by default
Sensitive path denylist (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, .npmrc, .git, *.log) enforced in ask-jev/audit/autofix (lib/sensitive.cjs) but not for content that arrives via HTTP
setup.cjs uses child_process.execSync/spawn (git ls-files, ps, python -m venv, pip install -r requirements.txt) on user machine; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found by grep
autofix.cjs rewrites source files using LLM output (dry-run default, backups) - a prompt-injection to file-write surface if enabled
Very new single-author project (3 stars, 1 fork), unofficial and self-declared unaffiliated with TypeSafe; supply-chain trust rests on one anonymous GitHub account. Not executed by me.
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.dataEgress: Upstream (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_API_BASE points to) receives: the API key as Bearer, the full `state` (flattened chat messages, or file contents with line numbers for --file/audit/autofix; directory listing names for --dir), the question map, and model id. Nothing else; no telemetry. With the CLI, secret-like values are masked first; via the HTTP bridge masking is off unless BRIDGE_REDACT=1. autofix additionally sends flagged files to the 9Router fix model. Truncation limit 200k chars per request (BRIDGE_MAX_STATE_CHARS). Sending client source to a third party (and via OpenRouter, a second party) is a real concern for the user's client projects.
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but not blocking: the bridge/CLI is invoked only when the model runs it, so nothing is blocked if it is down. bridgeFetch retries 429/529/network errors 2x with backoff (max 4s waits, Retry-After capped 10s); upstream timeout 60s default (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS) times up to 3 attempts = worst case ~3 minutes per call; CLI exits 1 with 'cannot reach the bridge' if the bridge process is not running. The bridge must be started manually or via setup --background; no autostart/systemd unit, so after reboot it is silently down and the CLAUDE.md block would make the model hit connection errors.
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.latencyImpact: Only when the model shells out: one Bash call per ask (node startup ~50ms + bridge hop on localhost + Jev 70-500 ms claimed; README sample shows ~412 ms). Per-turn cost is the extra model tool-call round trip (seconds), not Jev. No cost on turns where Jev is not invoked.
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.contextCost: 0 tools and 0 MCP server instructions. The cost is the pasted CLAUDE.md block (~2,000 chars, ~500 tokens) loaded every session, plus the tool-call/result tokens of each ask (small, a few lines). Cheapest of any integration style but only as reliable as the model's willingness to follow the prose.
gh-revocgg-typesafe-jev-bridge.autoInvocation: Model-discretion via CLAUDE.md prose only: Claude Code has to decide by itself to run `node .../ask-jev.cjs ...` through Bash. No hook, no MCP tool, no skill, no transparent proxy. Nondeterministic and, since Opus rarely needs a probability oracle for typical coding, it will seldom fire. Also the block hardcodes repo-relative paths (`node typesafe-bridge/ask-jev.cjs` 'from the repo root'), which do not resolve inside the user's other projects; it would need rewriting to absolute paths.
pros: Genuinely reads/implements the real System One request path: minimal, auditable ~1000-line bridge.js plus small libs, zero dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, no curl|sh (grep of repo)

Decent local security hygiene for a v0.2: loopback-only bind, Host + Origin checks, constant-time BRIDGE_TOKEN, key not relayed from clients, sensitive-path denylist, regex secret redaction in the CLI, offline test suite and CI on Node 18/20/22 x Linux/Windows

TYPESAFE_API_BASE is env-configurable with path /v1/systemone, so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api (-> /api/v1/systemone) is a plausible env-only switch to OpenRouter using OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY

Useful reference for how to phrase typed questions and read probabilities (0.35-0.65 uncertain band, exit code 3 on low confidence, choice/score handling), which can be lifted into a custom hook/skill
Honest about limits: README says Jev is not a chat model, warns against routing code generation to it, labels itself unofficial
cons: Wrong shape for Claude Code: it exposes OpenAI chat/responses, but Claude Code speaks Anthropic Messages to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and the user is on OAuth subscription; the 'Claude Code' topic is marketing, the real integration is a CLAUDE.md text block
No automatic invocation: no hook, no MCP, no skill. Relies on Opus choosing to call a CLI, which contradicts the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told)

No OpenRouter support in code (zero 'openrouter' matches); env-only switch is unverified and the model id mapping (bare jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest) and the OpenRouter response schema are unconfirmed; the Decisions API is unsupported

Chat-to-typed-question translation is heuristic (regex to guess yes/no vs choice, pickQuestionText scraping JSON spec fields, IS_IT_RE) - the bridge infers a question when none is supplied and README admits a coding prompt gets a meaningless 'yes'
Must be started manually (no service/systemd), no autostart; bridge down means silent failures; unauthenticated by default so any local process can burn the key
Bridge-level redaction is off by default, so agent/router traffic sends raw state (code, diffs) to a third party; highly relevant for client projects under NDA

security: API key is read from env only (kit/src/config.ts) and never put in argv. The README's 'Bearer' header goes over HTTPS to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is, so a wrong base URL sends the key elsewhere. The plugin.json userConfig.apiKey (sensitive) is declared but the hook code never reads it (grep of hooks/*.ts finds only process.env), so the userConfig key is dead config and only the env var works.

Hook redaction is on by default (core/src/redact.ts: AWS keys, JWTs, private keys, GitHub/Slack tokens, sk- keys, auth headers, env assignments, URL creds, connection strings, emails). It is regex-based, fail-open (if redaction throws, the original state is sent, client.ts), and the MCP path deliberately disables redaction.

Hard rule for gate: hook DENIES (not asks) on p>=0.5, so any false positive blocks Claude with no escape path other than editing env. core/src/patterns.ts:279-286 itself documents that a plain 'python3 script.py' was blocked at 0.84 by the single-noul gate. The repo has a judgeDestructiveDual (block/confirm/allow) but the CC hook uses the single-noul judgeDestructive.
Fail-open by construction means an attacker or outage bypasses the gate; it is advisory, not a security control. It also does not replace your secret-leak guard.

Prompt-injection surface: the model output is only numeric probabilities used against a threshold. The hook and MCP never feed free text from Jev back except a fixed template, which is a small surface. The tool_input being judged is attacker-controllable text that could argue for its own classification; the repo has a 'steering' slice in its holdout set, self-reported.
No telemetry, postinstall scripts or curl|sh found (grep). Only child_process is execSync git diff in the CLI jev-gate, not in the CC plugin or MCP server.

gh-talya1412-jev-harness.failureMode: Fail-open on all errors: every path exits 0 with no output. But there is no fast-fail. Default timeout is 15 s per attempt (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), maxAttempts 3 with 250*n^2 ms backoff on 429, 5xx, and network/timeouts (client.ts), so an outage or stall can block each Bash/Write/Edit call for about 46 s (worst case) before it proceeds. No circuit breaker in the CC hook (each hook call is a fresh process, so the in-memory cache, coalescer and budget guard from core are not in use and there is no persistent cache in the hook). No hooks.json timeout is set, so Claude Code's default applies. Mitigation: set JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=1500 or so. A missing key makes the hooks silent no-ops with no network call.
gh-talya1412-jev-harness.latencyImpact: One synchronous HTTPS round trip per Bash/Write/Edit/NotebookEdit call (claimed 70-500 ms for Jev, plus Node process start of about 40-80 ms and OpenRouter hop), i.e. an estimated 0.2-0.8 s added to every mutating call, and hooks in the same matcher run in parallel with your secret guard and GitNexus hook, but Jev's latency can dominate. There is no prefilter: harmless calls such as 'ls' or 'npm test' are still sent. UserPromptSubmit adds nothing while no roster is configured. MCP adds no latency unless the model calls a tool.
gh-talya1412-jev-harness.contextCost: Hook path: zero tool definitions and zero context text on allow; a deny adds one short reason line; skill advisor adds one line per prompt only if a roster is set. MCP path: 12 tools, about 16.9k characters in the TOOLS array (server.ts:296-664), roughly 4.2k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas on every session (less with deferred tool search); no MCP server 'instructions' string (Server created with capabilities.tools only). Most of the 12 tools (browse_action, classify, escalate, prune, finding_realness, refute) are irrelevant to daily coding, so the MCP server is poor value per token unless trimmed.
gh-talya1412-jev-harness.autoInvocation: Hook: deterministic PreToolUse on every Bash|Write|Edit|NotebookEdit call, which is the only truly automatic path and the closest thing to 'Claude Code uses Jev without being asked'. Skill advisor: deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, but useless until you hand it a roster. MCP: model-discretion only; nothing tells Claude when to call jev_* tools (no server instructions, generic descriptions), so it would rarely be used without a prompt or a CLAUDE.md rule.
pros: Only candidate so far with a real Claude Code plugin using command hooks (PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit) that runs automatically with no 'use jev' prompt, using the documented hooks.json/permissionDecision contract (hooks/hooks.json, jev-hook.ts).

Config-only OpenRouter route: baseUrl is overridable and the path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + model typesafe/jev-1.13 should work with no code change (unverified against the live API).
Bundled hook (esbuild, core inlined, dist/hooks/jev-hook.js committed) has no runtime dependencies, and fail-open on every error path, missing key = silent no-op.
Redaction on by default in the hook, and input capped at 4000 chars, reducing what leaves the machine; stdin-only key handling, no telemetry or postinstall.

Most complete Jev toolkit around: 23 patterns, eval and threshold tuning tools, decision log, benchmark with a separate holdout split, and a claimed holdout AUC 0.998 for the destructive gate; the docs candidly note calibration is not correctness.
Apache-2.0, active (79 commits, releases, CI on 3 Node versions, dependabot).
cons: Value is narrow for this user: the destructive gate duplicates protection that permission mode and your secret-leak guard already partly give, and under bypass/auto mode a Jev deny is one of the few things that would stop a bad command, but a single-noul hard deny with no 'ask' path will produce false-positive blocks (repo admits 'python3 script.py' scored 0.84 in core/src/patterns.ts:279-286) that interrupt agent loops.

Hook has no prefilter, cache or budget: every Bash/Write/Edit call, including 'ls' and 'git status', pays a network hop; each invocation is a fresh process so core's cache and budget guard never apply; worst-case stall about 46 s during an outage unless JEV_TIMEOUT_MS is lowered.

Sends Bash commands and full Write/Edit content (to 4000 chars) of client projects to OpenRouter and upstream, with regex-only redaction that fails open; for client code that is a real data-handling issue.

Documented install is likely broken: no root .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, only under packages/claude-code, so 'marketplace add Talya1412/jev-harness' probably fails; plugin userConfig.apiKey is never read by the hook code so only the env var works, and a subscription/OAuth user must export the key in the shell that starts Claude Code.
Skill router is inert by default (needs a hand-maintained JEV_SKILLS_JSON roster) and Claude Code already routes skills via descriptions, so it adds little.

MCP server: 12 tools and about 4k tokens of definitions with generic descriptions and no server instructions, so Claude will not call them on its own; most tools target OMP/browser/review-pipeline workflows.

Immature and single-author: created 2026-09-19, 0 stars, 0 forks, README table says 7 MCP tools but ships 12, SECURITY.md supported-versions table stale, hook test covers only pure helpers, and the benchmark numbers are self-reported on ~170 hand-written cases; no OpenRouter mention anywhere, so OpenRouter compatibility rests on my inference from the endpoint path.
Overlaps and can interleave with your existing PreToolUse hooks on Bash (secret guard, GitNexus), adding a third network-bound hook on the same matcher.
gh-talya1412-jev-harness.verdict: The only candidate here that gives truly automatic (hook-based) Jev use in Claude Code and it can likely be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars. But it is a narrow destructive-command gate that sends Bash and file-write content to a third party on every call, has no prefilter, a slow worst-case timeout, and a hard-deny false-positive risk. Treat it as a reference implementation to copy or fork (add a cheap local prefilter, short timeout, ask instead of deny), not something to install as-is on client projects.

The bearer key is sent as 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (src/client.mjs:180) from SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY or SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY_FILE (src/config.mjs:58, 70); TYPESAFE_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_API_KEY are NOT read implicitly (README says so), so it needs SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Non-loopback needs SYSTEM_ONE_ALLOW_REMOTE=1 (endpoints.mjs:12). The only documented hosted target is TypeSafe: examples/jev.config.json:2 url https://api.typesafe.ai, README 'Jev - hosted TypeSafe API' section, model jev-latest, provider jev. Caveats: (1) the request body is {state,questions,model} (client.mjs:144) and the response must contain answers{} and a model string (client.mjs:157). Whether OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone uses that same envelope was not verified. (2) GET /v1/models is expected to return a 'models' array (providers.mjs:275); OpenRouter's model list uses 'data', so system_one_status and the 'doctor' command would fail, but ask() never calls models(), so real judgments are unaffected. (3) The jev profile validates Score<=10 levels and demands confidence with 2-decimal rounding (providers.mjs:240-243, 260-268); use provider generic if OpenRouter's rounding differs.
providerSupport.others: Local: Kev (:8009 default), Laya, Decider, Shisa (vLLM or llama.cpp), OpenJev GGUF through llama.cpp. Generic: any System One compatible service.

gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.openrouterPatchability: Trivial for the transport: it is configuration only, with no code change (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, model typesafe/jev-1.13, key mapped via SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY). The residual risk is unverified wire compatibility with OpenRouter's response envelope and the failing /v1/models probe (doctor/status only). If the envelope differs, a small edit to src/client.mjs would be needed, since the code is compact and readable.

interface.purpose: Compare two passages overall and by aspect

interface.purpose: Regex candidates in a worker, then choose a verbatim substring per field

interface.name: MCP system_one_review
interface.purpose: Score a diff for correctness, spec match, test gap, blast radius and safety

interface.name: MCP system_one_gate
interface.purpose: Combined diff review plus completion-claim verification in one request

interface.name: MCP system_one_query
interface.purpose: Raw System One request with arbitrary state and questions

interface.purpose: Verbatim tool-pair compaction of supplied messages (returns a new transcript only)

interface.name: MCP system_one_status
interface.purpose: Check /v1/models and report capabilities

interface.name: Hook Stop
interface.purpose: Belay completion check, then Jev gate review after fresh passing checks; can return decision:block with a follow-up request (capped at 3 blocks per session)

interface.name: Hook SubagentStop / TaskCompleted
interface.purpose: Same check for child agents; TaskCompleted blocks via exit 2

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse / PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure

interface.name: Skills system-one-judgments, system-one-compaction, system-one-belay

gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.license: MIT (retains Apache-2.0 OpenJev notices under licenses/)
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.runtime: Node >=22.16, zero npm dependencies; optional Python sidecars (not needed here). Not on npm ("private": true); it runs from a git checkout or as a local plugin.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.install: git clone, then export the SYSTEM_ONE_* variables and run 'node bin/open-jev-bridge.mjs install --host claude --url https://openrouter.ai/api --model typesafe/jev-1.13 --provider generic --allow-remote'. This runs 'claude mcp add --scope user', appends 10 hook entries to ~/.claude/settings.json, and copies 3 skills to ~/.claude/skills. Alternative: 'native-claude' installs it as a local plugin via 'claude plugin marketplace add'. The user must review and trust the hooks. It has to be run from a cloned checkout, and it cannot be uninstalled cleanly if the checkout is moved.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.tests: 26 test files (about 348 test() calls), an offline CI matrix (ubuntu and macOS, Node 22 and 24) via .github/workflows/ci.yml, and Python adapter tests. docs/CI.md admits a CI failure on the same day (stale duplicate suite) that was fixed on 2026-09-30. All tests are offline fixtures. Nothing was ever tested live against OpenRouter, and I found no test of the real Claude Code hook runtime. Not run by me (static reading only).
security: API key is read from env (SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY) or from a 0600 regular non-symlink key file (config.mjs readSecret, lines 98-109), so it is never in argv. install.mjs:79 deliberately never persists an env key to config.json. Key is sent only as a Bearer header. redirect:'manual' is set, so redirects are refused (client.mjs:181).

Upstream error bodies are never echoed back (client.mjs:186). Request and response byte caps, concurrency and queue limits and a circuit breaker exist. The circuit breaker is per process, so it does not persist across hook invocations, which are each a fresh node process.

No telemetry, and no curl|sh or postinstall (no npm dependencies, package private). Shell execution is limited to execFile of 'claude'/'codex' CLIs during install (install.mjs:15-16). MCP tools are readOnlyHint and never execute commands.

Writes to ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.claude/skills (install.mjs:24). It merges rather than replaces and has rollback, but it is still a global settings edit with a hard-coded absolute path to the checkout.

Prompt-injection surface: the PostToolUse hook injects 'additionalContext' built from Jev's action label (a fixed template, not model free text), so the risk is low. The policy strings injected at SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/SubagentStart are static. Screening is documented as advisory only (SECURITY.md).

Local state: ledgers and checkpoints under ~/.local/state/open-jev-bridge (0700/0600). They hold verbatim tool inputs and results and user prompts (prompts are passed through redact(); tool inputs in ledger are stored raw), so they may contain secrets or client code at rest. redact() is a best-effort regex (pure.mjs:34-41).
The SECURITY.md itself states there has been no external security audit and no contact address. The hooks read transcript files (bounded regular reads, no symlink following).

The repo's doc set is very large relative to 2.2k dense lines of code (heavily minified single-line style), which makes review harder. The code was probably AI-generated ('ZIP', 'release overlay' language in docs).
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.dataEgress: With hosted Jev via OpenRouter and defaults (autoVerify/autoReview/autoScreen/autoCompaction all true), the following is sent to OpenRouter and on to TypeSafe: (1) Stop gate after passing checks: the redacted original user task, the edit tool inputs (diffs, i.e. Write/Edit contents), check commands and their output, and the final assistant message (hooks.mjs:110, automation.mjs:295-299, up to 50k chars per field). (2) Belay on Stop when verification is missing or stale: the message ledger with tool uses and results. (3) PostToolUse screen: WebFetch and MCP fetch|search|read_resource results up to 3000 chars. (4) PreCompact: historical tool calls and results of the whole session in batches of up to about 7.6k tokens, which is the largest leak of file contents and command output. (5) Any explicit system_one_* tool call, which carries whatever the model supplies. Redaction is regex-only, and the docs admit it. Nothing is sent to anyone other than the configured URL. For client projects with confidentiality obligations this is a real problem, because OpenRouter's own routing and logging policies then also apply. Everything can be turned off with SYSTEM_ONE_AUTO_*=false but that removes the point of the plugin.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.failureMode: Fail-open for hooks. Every hook error, timeout, invalid response or lock conflict is caught and returns {} with a stderr note, and main() also prints '{}' on any config error (hooks.mjs:130-136, bin:63). Unavailable review returns only a systemMessage saying that no verification was certified. Default request timeout is 20 s (config timeoutMs, must be <=20000 for install) inside a 25 s host hook timeout, retries 0, so if OpenRouter or Jev hangs, each Stop, SubagentStop or PreCompact can stall the session by up to 20 s; connection refusals or HTTP errors fail fast. There is no persistent circuit breaker across processes. MCP tool calls fail closed with an explicit isError result and action 'review'. The Stop hook can also fail 'closed' in a productive sense: it returns decision:block up to 3 times per session when Jev's probabilities cross belayThreshold 0.7, which could cause spurious continuation requests, especially in bypass mode where the user is not watching.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.latencyImpact: Per matched tool call (Bash, Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, WebFetch and every mcp__* tool, before and after): one node process spawn plus a file-locked read and rewrite of a JSON ledger of up to 1 MB. My estimate is 50-150 ms per event, so 100-300 ms per tool call, and no Jev call is made for these except the WebFetch/MCP fetch screen (about 100-500 ms plus network). Read/Grep/Glob are not matched. On Stop: one Jev request after passing checks (claimed 70-500 ms, but a gate request with diffs is larger, plus OpenRouter hop) or up to 20 s if the endpoint stalls. UserPromptSubmit adds a node spawn (~50-100 ms) each prompt. PreCompact adds one or more Jev batches. These hooks run alongside the user's existing Bash/Grep hooks, so hook cost stacks on Bash/mcp calls (the GitNexus and secret guard also match Bash). Not measured; inferred from the code.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.contextCost: 14 MCP tools (about 4.4k chars of schema source, expanding to roughly 8-12k chars of JSON schema and descriptions, so about 2-3k tokens if loaded, less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind tool search) plus a one-line server instruction (~150 chars). 3 skill descriptions (~150 tokens total). Hook-injected text: about 480 tokens at SessionStart, again after each compaction, and at each SubagentStart; about 85 tokens on every user prompt; occasional one-line notes after fetch results. Overall about 3k tokens up front and about 100 tokens per turn, which is moderate. It also adds pressure toward proactive tool calls ("use system_one_* proactively") that can waste turns and tokens.
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks, which matches the user's requirement, plus model-discretion MCP tools nudged by injected policy and skill descriptions. Deterministic without model choice: Stop, SubagentStop, TaskCompleted completion check and gate review, PostToolUse external-content screen, PreCompact checkpoint, evidence recording. Model-discretion: the other tools (find, rerank, classify, decide, compare, extract, verify, review). The authors say explicitly that there is no deterministic event for semantic tool selection. It is the only candidate I have seen that installs real automatic hooks, but its uses are review and safety nets, not "make Claude's decisions with Jev".
pros: Genuinely automatic: 10 lifecycle hooks fire without the user ever saying 'use jev' (Stop/SubagentStop completion gate, WebFetch and MCP fetch/search injection screen, PreCompact checkpoint). This is the exact integration style requested (hooks.mjs:11-13, hooks/claude.json).

OpenRouter works with configuration only: SYSTEM_ONE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api resolves to /api/v1/systemone (endpoints.mjs:15-19), and any bearer key works, so a separate TypeSafe account is unnecessary (wire envelope compatibility still unverified).

Robust fail-open design: every hook error, timeout, bad JSON or lock conflict returns {} and never blocks the host (hooks.mjs:130-136); the evidence ledger refuses to certify a pass when events are missing or oversized; it never auto-approves or rewrites tool calls, so it does not conflict with the user's existing secret-guard or GitNexus hooks.

Good hygiene for a young project: zero dependencies, key never in argv and never persisted by the installer, no redirects followed, error bodies not echoed, byte limits, owner-only state files, clean uninstall that preserves other hooks, MIT license, offline CI on 2 OS and 2 Node versions.

Uses Jev for what it is actually designed for: typed Noul/Choice/Score decisions (is the completion claim supported, should this tool output be kept, is this text an injection), with no free-text generation.
Can be trimmed: SYSTEM_ONE_AUTO_VERIFY/REVIEW/SCREEN/COMPACTION each toggle a hook family, and SYSTEM_ONE_BELAY_SHADOW=1 gives a shadow mode that logs would-be blocks without enforcing.
cons: 8 days old, single author, 0 stars, 0 forks, 10 commits, no releases, apparently AI-generated dense one-line code; the docs record a red CI run on the day of the latest release. No evidence anyone has run it on a real Claude Code session with hosted Jev.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs: the only tested hosted target is api.typesafe.ai /v1/systemone. Response envelope on OpenRouter is unverified, and the GET /v1/models expectation (a 'models' array, providers.mjs:275) does not match OpenRouter's 'data' list, so 'doctor' and system_one_status will fail even if judgments work.

Data egress is heavy and on by default: edit diffs, test output, fetched web content and whole-session tool results at each compaction go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a problem for client projects, and redaction is regex-only. Ledgers on disk also store raw tool inputs and results.

The value is narrow: Stop-time gating of 'is this done' with a probabilistic model can produce false blocks (up to 3 forced continuations per session, at belayThreshold 0.7) that burn Opus tokens, especially in bypass or auto mode where the user is not watching. Screening only covers WebFetch and MCP fetch/search, not Read, Bash curl, or Grep.

Hook overhead on the hot path: PreToolUse and PostToolUse spawn node for every Bash, Write, Edit and every mcp__* call, on top of the user's existing Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus). Stop or PreCompact can stall up to 20 s if the provider hangs, because the circuit breaker is per process and retries are 0.

Broad global footprint for a 0-star project: edits ~/.claude/settings.json, installs 3 skills, and injects a 'use system_one_* proactively' policy on every session, prompt and subagent, which pushes Opus into extra tool calls that add context and cost; 14 tools add about 2-3k tokens of definitions.

Most of the repo (Kev, Laya, Decider, Shisa, OpenJev GGUF adapters, Python sidecars, Codex support, function-hook plugin) is irrelevant to an OpenRouter-hosted Jev user, increasing the audit surface. The install is tied to a git checkout path (not on npm).
gh-louis-szeto-open-jev-bridge.verdict: The closest fit so far to "Claude Code uses Jev by itself", because it works through real lifecycle hooks, and pointing it at OpenRouter is only a config change. But it is an 8-day-old, unproven, single-author project with no OpenRouter testing, default-on egress of diffs and tool output, and a narrow use (completion gating, injection screening, compaction), so I would treat it as something to trial with only AUTO_SCREEN and shadow-mode AUTO_VERIFY on personal projects, not as a default for client work.

Grade counts are 18 official, 206 observed, 542 inferred and 57 unverified. There is no runtime component, no MCP server, no hook and no skill, so nothing can be installed into Claude Code. Its value is as a discovery index. The "Agent tooling: MCP, hooks, gates and coding agents" category has 251 entries. Claude-Code-relevant leads from data/entries.json: typesafe-ai/skills (official), TypeSafeAI/jev-harness (official), GhalebDweikat/winnow (Claude Code context sieve), tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction (Claude Code compaction plugin), gargpratyush/jev-router (model routing in Claude Code), xafold/jev-router (automatic model and effort switching for Claude Code), Dicklesworthstone/skillranker, jkudish/jev-mcp, burnigtm/jev-mcp, freepik-company/jev-mcp (OpenRouter or TypeSafe), BYK/jev-mcp (eval-first), clouatre-labs/decisions-judge-mcp, King4s/Jev-AI-Skill and tiffygk/jev-mode (Claude Code skills). gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.name: NicolasRisso/JevMCP
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.whatItDoes: Python (mcp>=2.2, httpx) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, jev_ask. The agent passes typed questions (noul/choice/score) plus file paths, globs, dirs or inline texts. The server reads the files locally, chunks them (60k chars), POSTs one request per file with all questions to Jev (OpenRouter Decisions endpoint or TypeSafe direct), and returns compact confidence-scored answers plus an unsure list. Goal: fan-out classification of many files without loading them into Claude's context. Note the candidate summary says "has hooks": that is wrong. The only hook is a git pre-push test runner; there are no Claude Code hooks.

security: API key is read from the process environment and sent as a Bearer header (client.py:160). The installer explicitly never puts keys in argv or on the command line (cli.py:169-177), so keys are not in the process list. The key must be exported in the shell profile (README suggests ~/.bashrc), which leaks it to every child process.

Server reads ARBITRARY local paths/globs/dirs the agent supplies, with no root confinement, allowlist or secret-file denylist (sources.py:34-49 uses glob/open directly). It can read .env, ~/.ssh, credentials, and uploads the contents to OpenRouter. Your existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would NOT cover mcp__jev__jev_ask, so this bypasses that protection. Mitigate with a matcher on mcp__jev__.*.
Only guard is JEV_MAX_ITEMS=500 (server.py:142). Binary files are skipped by a NUL-byte sniff.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents go to Jev and Jev's answers come back to Claude. docs/limitations.md admits Jev trusts instructions hidden in text. Answers are typed numbers or enum values (no free text), so injection can flip an answer but cannot inject instructions into Claude's context. Choice values echo criteria keys that Claude itself supplied.

No shell execution besides subprocess.call of the `claude` CLI in install/uninstall, with a fixed argv (cli.py:36). No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh. README's install is git clone plus pip install -e into a venv, i.e. running unaudited code from an editable checkout; a later `git pull` changes the code with no review. Zero stars, single author, 8 days old.

No telemetry found (grep for telemetry and other network calls; only the configured Jev endpoints are used). httpx INFO logging is suppressed (server.py:25). Error strings include the first 300 chars of a response body (client.py:174), which is low risk.
Dependency mcp>=2.2,<3 and httpx>=0.27 are unpinned by lockfile (no lockfile in repo). Supply-chain risk is modest but real. MIT license.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (and via it TypeSafe): the full text of every file/chunk the agent points at (up to 60k chars per request, up to 500 items per call), plus the question instructions and criteria, plus the model name. The API key goes in an Authorization header. Nothing else: no prompts, conversation, diffs or tool outputs unless Claude passes them via `texts`. Files are sent in whole, including secrets if Claude names them. OpenRouter data policies apply to client code, so check for client contract restrictions. Response usage reports input_tokens only.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level, not a hook, so Claude is never blocked. httpx timeout is 30s per request (client.py:127). Retries on network errors and on 429/502/503/529 with 1s, 2s, 4s backoff, up to 4 attempts (about 7s of waiting, worst case about 2 minutes total per item with timeouts). 401/402/403 mark the provider dead and 400/413/422 fail immediately. Per-item failures come back as {"error":...}; if all items fail with the same error the call raises one ToolError (server.py:65-68). Missing key gives ConfigError only at call time, not at server startup, so a misconfigured server still loads its tool definition and wastes context every turn. With JEV_FALLBACK plus both keys it switches providers after 2 attempts. No circuit breaker across calls.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.latencyImpact: Only when Claude chooses to call it. Roughly 70-500 ms per file request per Jev's claims, concurrent up to 16 requests (JEV_CONCURRENCY). Plus one MCP round-trip and local file read. A 300-file batch is about 19 waves, so several seconds. Nothing is added to turns where the tool is not called; startup of a Python MCP server adds a small cold start.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.contextCost: 1 tool. Description is 503 chars and the hand-written schema is 425 chars in compact JSON, so about 930 chars, or roughly 250-300 tokens per session including the tool name (the README says about 1 KB). It is a deferred tool in Claude Code, so it may only cost the name until loaded via ToolSearch. No MCP server "instructions" field found. No hook-injected text. Results are a few chars per answer.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no Claude Code hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no plugin manifest (repo ships CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md for its own development only). Claude calls jev_ask only if the tool description convinces it, so it will be used rarely and unpredictably. Getting reliable automatic use requires you to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill, or a UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook nudging use on bulk file scans. Note that Claude's own Grep already covers most "which files mention X" cases cheaply.
pros: Native OpenRouter support: with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY set it uses https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.py:15-19), matching your provider choice with no patching.

Tiny footprint: one tool, about 930 chars (roughly 250-300 tokens) of definition, hand-trimmed schema, structured_output=False to avoid duplicate results (server.py:119,149). This is the leanest possible way to expose Jev.

Well matched to Jev's real strengths: batches all questions per file into one request, fans out concurrently, and passes on uncertainty via [value, conf, top2] and an unsure list so Claude re-checks only doubtful items (compact.py, server.py:60-61).
Sensible resilience: retries with backoff, per-item errors, dead-key detection, optional cross-provider fallback (client.py); the tool never blocks a Claude turn beyond its own call.
Key never in argv: installer omits keys and the server reads env (cli.py:169-177); `jev-mcp check` gives a cheap connectivity test.
Honest docs on limits (counting, dates, injection) in docs/limitations.md; MIT license; small readable codebase (about 600 lines) that is easy to audit or fork.
cons: It is NOT automatic. Pure model-discretion MCP tool with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, which fails your core requirement of Claude using Jev without being told. The 'has hooks' claim in discovery is false (only a git pre-push test hook).

Reads arbitrary paths with no confinement or secret denylist and uploads whole files to a third party. Your secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover mcp__jev__jev_ask, so it creates a hole for client projects; you would need to extend the hook matcher.

Use case is narrow: bulk classification of many files. Typical Claude Code work (edit, debug, refactor) rarely needs 'which of these 300 files...' and Grep/GitNexus already handle it locally, free and exact. Jev cannot count, do arithmetic or reason, and is easily fooled by injected text.

Very immature: 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor, 16 commits all on 2026-09-22 (8 days old), version 0.1.0, no releases, no CI (no .github), no lockfile, README says API may change. Tests exist (6 files, 40 test functions) but were not run per the rules.
Depends on the OpenRouter alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), which may change or break without notice; does not use the more stable /api/v1/systemone.

Install path is git clone plus pip install -e (editable, unpinned mcp>=2.2), not a published PyPI/uvx package; needs the key exported in shell profile, and misconfiguration only surfaces at call time.
Chunk results are not aggregated (docs/limitations.md open items), so large files return path#N entries that Claude must merge by hand; character-based chunking rather than token-based.
Added latency and cost are small but every call moves client code to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, a compliance question for client projects.
gh-nicolasrisso-jevmcp.verdict: The cleanest and cheapest Jev MCP wrapper, with genuine OpenRouter support and a very small context cost, but it is an opt-in model-discretion tool: nothing makes Claude Code use it automatically, and it has an unrestricted file-upload path that bypasses your secret guard. Treat it as a reference implementation to fork or wrap behind hooks and a path denylist, not something to install as is for daily work.

It ships a discovery-only Agent Skill ("awesome-jev", SKILL.md, also at skills/awesome-jev/SKILL.md) that tells an agent to fetch the public JSON catalog, llms.txt and llms-full.txt and rank projects by fit. The repo runs 6-hourly GitHub Actions radar jobs plus Issue-based submissions, and takes no PRs. It never calls Jev, OpenRouter or TypeSafe. Its main value for this task is as a curated index of Claude Code x Jev integrations. Many pinned entries are not itself usable as an integration.

Near-zero risk: MIT, a Markdown-only skill, no keys, no shell, tiny context cost. Actively maintained (214 commits in 12 days, updated 6-hourly by bot) and has a security policy.
The AGENTS.md and SKILL.md untrusted-data stance matches how this audit should treat the entries.
cons: It is not an integration. Installing it gives Claude Code no Jev capability, no OpenRouter path and no automatic behavior. It cannot satisfy the no-manual-prompt requirement.
Its skill fires only on 'find Jev projects' style requests, which this user will rarely make once the integration is chosen. Permanent value after selection is roughly zero.

Quality signal is weak. 739 of 799 repos were created in 2026-09, 529 have 10 or fewer stars, and 479 summaries are auto-extracted from READMEs. Only 232 of 799 are source-verified, none is runtime-verified, and 503 have no confirmed license. The 7131 stars on fast-jev-compaction after about 2 weeks looks like inflated or anomalous attention.

Marketing claims in the README ('Sub-100ms', 'Zero Vaporware', 50-100ms) conflict with the brief's 70-500 ms end-to-end and are not measured here. The 1.5-5 s vs 50-100 ms comparison table is unsourced. Do not rely on them.
The catalog is huge (README.md 522 KB, four 470-550 KB READMEs) and full-text projects.json is 799 entries. Reading it naively would burn context, so it needs jq or subagent filtering.
Small maintainer group (2 humans plus a bot). It has a strict no-PR policy, sponsorship slots and analytics, so it is a curated but commercially-flavored directory.
The 'npx skills add' install path adds a third-party CLI dependency for zero benefit here. The skill file can simply be ignored.
gh-logicrw-awesome-jev-projects.verdict: Do not install it as the integration. It is a Jev ecosystem index with a discovery-only skill, no Jev calls and no automatic invocation. gh-miaopj0325-collab-jev-mcp.name: miaopj0325-collab/jev_mcp (jev-mcp)
gh-miaopj0325-collab-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Minimal single-file (307 lines) Node CommonJS stdio MCP server exposing 4 tools (jev_noul, jev_choice, jev_score, jev_batch_decisions). Each tool wraps caller-supplied context plus an instruction into a POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and returns the JSON result. It is a passive tool that Claude must decide to call; it has no hooks, no skill and no proxy.

package.json has no postinstall or install scripts and there is no shell execution. The only network call is the one fetch (src/index.js:33). There is no telemetry beyond the HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers, which OpenRouter uses for attribution and which advertise this repo.

Prompt-injection surface is low: responses are numeric or typed JSON from Jev (probabilities plus echoed option keys). But the option keys are chosen by Claude, and the verdict is only as trustworthy as the caller's framing.

Gotcha: if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is also set in the environment it wins over OPENROUTER_API_KEY; the key-file route is the recommended dependable one because MCP servers do not reliably inherit shell env.
providerSupport.others: None; Codex and pi supported as clients, not other gateways. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL allows any compatible gateway.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed: OpenRouter is natively supported by key prefix.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Choice primitive: pick one caller-supplied option (adds 'none'), returns probabilities, confidence, act/review/abstain gate

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Score primitive: rate on an ordered scale, expected position and distribution

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Noul primitive: yes/no with P(yes) and verdict yes/no/uncertain

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Several questions of all three primitives about one state, or about files via `paths` read server-side

interface.name: jev_triage
interface.purpose: One question set over up to 50 items (text or server-read file paths), one result per item; file contents never enter Claude's context

interface.name: jev_locate
interface.purpose: Windowed pass over one big file: returns line numbers answering up to 16 questions

interface.name: jev_search
interface.purpose: Runs ripgrep server-side over a dir, Jev ranks candidate lines with neighbours; returns path:line hits (grep replacement)

interface.name: jev_extract
interface.purpose: Picks a value (port, version, URL, date, setting) among regex-found candidates in a file; cannot invent values

interface.name: jev_rank_pages
interface.purpose: Fetches up to 20 https URLs server-side (SSRF-guarded; trafilatura/markitdown converters), ranks pages per question, returns best-page sentences plus per-page injection signal

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Four Noul injection signals plus invisible-Unicode count on untrusted text before reading it

interface.name: jev_models
interface.purpose: Verify key/model (one minimal request on OpenRouter)

interface.name: hook UserPromptSubmit (cli.js prompt-hook)
interface.purpose: When on: injects ~1 KB additionalContext each prompt telling Claude which jev tool replaces which read; sets per-session turn marker

interface.name: hook PreToolUse matcher Grep|Read|Bash|WebSearch|WebFetch|mcp__plugin_jev_jev__.* (cli.js tool-hook)
interface.purpose: When on: DENIES the first Grep or Bash rg/grep/ag/ack per prompt (redirect to jev_search; the retry is allowed); denies first WebFetch after a WebSearch; adds a hint for whole-file Reads over 16 KB; any jev tool call clears the markers

interface.name: command /jev:jev on|off|status
interface.purpose: Global switch file ~/.claude/jev-think/state.json and ledger.jsonl (calls, tokens, cost, latency by tool); disable-model-invocation so only the user toggles it

interface.name: skill jev-tools
interface.purpose: Description-triggered guidance: which jev tool replaces which read, batching, confidence handling, do-not-send-secrets

security: No API key in argv: key from env or ~/.config/jev/api_key, file must be 0600 and owned by user or server refuses it; key never a tool argument; key file itself is on the tool file-read deny list. Plugin.json env block deliberately omits the key.

Server-side file reads are confined to allowed roots (default = server cwd, plus ~/.config/jev/roots), containment checked before and after symlink resolution, credential files refused by name (.env*, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa, credentials.json). Name-based only: secrets hardcoded inside ordinary source files are still sent.

Prompt-injection surface: file paths and questions come from the model; fetched pages and grep windows are wrapped with 'treat as data' guards; jev_screen and per-page injection signal withhold sentences from suspicious pages. Jev is a probabilistic classifier, not a guarantee.

jev_rank_pages SSRF protections: https only, refuses private/loopback/link-local hosts on connection and each redirect, JEV_ALLOW_HOSTS opt-out; converters (trafilatura, markitdown) get bytes on stdin only. Shell execution limited to execFile of rg/trafilatura/markitdown (no shell string).

install.sh is a curl|sh installer that also does 'curl astral.sh/install.sh | sh' for uv and 'uv tool install' of ripgrep, trafilatura, markitdown; it is optional (plugin can be added via 'claude plugin marketplace add'). No npm postinstall; CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts and npm audit.

Committed 1.8 MB esbuild bundle (bundle/index.js, cli.js, pi.js) is what actually runs, including the vendored @typesafe-ai/sdk and MCP SDK; CI checks git diff --exit-code bundle/ against a rebuild, but a reviewer cannot practically audit it. Single maintainer, 5-day-old repo, so supply-chain trust is entirely in one GitHub account (marketplace add pulls main).
No telemetry found; only outbound hosts in code are api.typesafe.ai/openrouter.ai and user-supplied URLs for jev_rank_pages. Local ledger records tool, tokens, cost, ms, never content.

Hooks run with the user's full privileges on every Grep|Read|Bash|WebSearch|WebFetch call (node process spawn), and can deny tool calls; interaction with existing GitNexus and secret-guard PreToolUse hooks is unverified. cli.js reads only session_id, tool name and command.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.dataEgress: While switched on: (1) jev_search sends ripgrep candidate lines with neighbouring lines, in windows, from the searched directory (credential file names filtered) plus questions; (2) jev_locate/jev_extract/jev_ask paths/jev_triage send the entire text of the named files in windows (up to 200k chars per state), never truncated; (3) jev_rank_pages sends fetched page text; (4) jev_classify/score/check/ask send whatever `state` Claude passes. Destination is OpenRouter then TypeSafe (with an OpenRouter key) or TypeSafe directly. Not sent: the user's prompts or conversation as such (unless Claude puts them in state), diffs, or the API key. Source code of client projects is sent as file content, filtered only by file name. README/CLI warn 'Keep it off for private work'. The on/off switch is a single global file, not per project, so client-project safety depends on the user toggling it.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open for hooks: cli.js hook path wraps everything in try/catch and outputs nothing on error; hooks stay silent when switch is off or absent (src/cli.ts:140-151); hook timeout 3 s. The MCP tools fail as classified isError results (authentication, rate_limit, connection, malformed_response, file_access, disabled) and the skill tells Claude to carry on without Jev; defaults are JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 and JEV_MAX_RETRIES=0 (src/lib.ts:46-47), so a slow Jev costs at most ~5 s per request then an error. The search hook is designed so a failed jev_search still lets the retried Grep run (only the first search per prompt is denied), i.e. at most one wasted turn. Missing key means every call errors, hooks would still deny the first grep and redirect to a broken tool if the switch is on.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.contextCost: 11 MCP tools; tool defs (title+description+inputSchema+outputSchema strings in src/index.ts registerTool blocks) about 19.7k chars, roughly 4.9k tokens, plus JSON-schema overhead so likely 5-7k tokens if not deferred (Claude Code tool search may defer them). No MCP server `instructions`. Skill: description ~700 chars always loaded, body ~4.5k chars (~1.1k tokens) when triggered. UserPromptSubmit hook injects about 1.0 KB (~250 tokens) as additionalContext on EVERY prompt while on. Deny messages ~500 chars each, and each tool result returns full probability distributions (extra tokens per call). Nothing injected while off except the tool defs and skill description.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Mixed but strongest of the candidates: deterministic hooks (PreToolUse deny of first Grep/rg/grep per prompt and of WebFetch after WebSearch; UserPromptSubmit reminder) plus skill description trigger and model-discretion MCP tools. Requires a one-time manual '/jev:jev on' (off by default by design); after that no user prompting. Read hints are advisory only.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Claimed API 70-500 ms per window; tools add one MCP round trip (jev_search: rg + one or more Jev requests, jev_rank_pages: parallel fetch of up to 20 pages plus 10 s per-page cap and 5 s Jev timeout). Every Grep/Read/Bash/WebSearch/WebFetch call spawns a node hook process (roughly 40-80 ms each, my estimate, even when the switch is off since the switch is checked inside the process) with 3 s timeout. Each prompt's first grep is denied and re-issued, costing one extra model turn (seconds) when Claude does not use jev_search. Net effect on turn time is likely neutral to slightly negative for small repos.
pros: Only candidate seen that is genuinely automatic: PreToolUse hook (src/cli.ts:90-93) deterministically steers the first grep of each prompt to jev_search, plus a UserPromptSubmit reminder and skill trigger, so the user never has to say 'use jev' after one /jev:jev on.
OpenRouter supported natively and verified in code: sk-or- key -> https://openrouter.ai/api + ~typesafe/jev-latest over /v1/systemone (src/lib.ts:554-577); works with just ~/.config/jev/api_key.

Sensible safety design: off-by-default global switch, key never in argv or tool args, key file mode enforced 0600, file root confinement with symlink checks, credential-file name deny list, SSRF guard for URL fetching, ledger with no content.
Fail-open behavior: hooks swallow errors, 5 s timeout and 0 retries, classified errors, skill says carry on without Jev, denied grep is allowed on retry.

Tools fit Jev's actual strengths (ranking/locating/extracting over windows, injection screening via Noul) instead of asking it to reason; batching guidance (up to 16 questions per pass) is aligned with TypeSafe's cookbook.
jev_screen / jev_rank_pages injection screening and withholding of suspicious pages is a real security add for a bypass-permissions user browsing the web.

Reasonable engineering hygiene for a young repo: MIT, 12 test files (~2.9k lines) run offline against a stand-in API, CI on Node 20/22/24 with bundle-matches-source check and npm audit, ledger/status command for measuring cost and savings.
cons: Repo is 5 days old (created 2026-09-25, first commit 2026-09-17), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 2 contributors (one wrote 43 of 50 commits), version 0.14.0; no evidence of real-world use.
Ships opaque 1.8 MB committed bundles that run instead of the readable source, and install.sh does curl|sh (uv) and uv tool installs; marketplace add tracks main of a single-maintainer repo.

Sends whole file contents and grep windows to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; secret filtering is by filename only, so hardcoded secrets in source files go out; unsuitable for client/NDA projects and the global switch is not per-project, so the user must remember to toggle it.

Hook denies the first Grep/rg per prompt, adding a failed tool call and extra turn whenever Claude wants an exact-string search; with GitNexus (Grep|Glob|Bash) and secret-guard hooks on the same matchers, hook ordering and duplicated denials are untested. A node process is also spawned for every Grep/Read/Bash/Web call even while off.

Weak value proposition for this user: Opus-class main model with GitNexus graph search and native Grep already reads code cheaply and precisely; Jev is a probabilistic ranker over windows and its own README says to keep deterministic code when it decides correctly and warns it cannot compute; recall failures in jev_search/jev_locate mean silently missed lines.

Per-prompt reminder (~250 tokens) plus 11 tool schemas (~5-7k tokens if not deferred) and tool results that carry full probability distributions partly offset the tokens saved; the instruction 'say in one line when Jev saved you a read' adds chatter.

Uses the System One API (/v1/systemone), not the alpha Decisions API, and requires the user to run '/jev:jev on' manually each install; the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var, if present, silently outranks OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
Unverified quality claims: no benchmarks of saved tokens or answer recall in repo; Theo's skepticism that Jev may be a small distilled router model is untested here.
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-in-class for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement (hook-enforced grep and WebFetch redirection plus skill) with native, code-verified OpenRouter support, but it is a 5-day-old single-maintainer alpha that ships opaque bundles and sends file contents to a third party. Worth trialling on personal projects only, after reading src/ and bundle provenance; keep it off (or install per-project) for client work, and check the interplay of its hooks with GitNexus first.

gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20.12 (bundled ESM); optional ripgrep (required for jev_search), uv-installed trafilatura and markitdown for jev_rank_pages
gh-maxkimambo-jev-mcp.tests: 12 test files under test/ (about 2.9k lines, node --test), offline against a local stand-in API asserting request bodies, plus a live e2e test; GitHub Actions CI on Node 20/22/24 with typecheck, build, bundle-diff check, npm test and npm audit. I did not run them.

gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.name: aimcc-org/aimcc-jev-mcp (codex-jev-mcp)
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: A Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server ("decision kernel") that turns 6 coding-agent questions into batches of Jev Choice/Noul/Score primitives, sends them to a System-One provider (TypeSafe SDK, OpenRouter /alpha/decisions, generic endpoint, or a local 0.48 GB DeBERTa ONNX model), validates the typed answers, and applies deterministic threshold policies (config/policies.json) to return an accept/reject/collect_evidence/system_two_review/ask_user envelope. It returns advice only. It runs nothing and finishes no task itself.

providerSupport.evidence: src/providers/openrouter.ts:17-20 prefixes the model with typesafe/ and POSTs to `${baseUrl}/alpha/decisions` (default base https://openrouter.ai/api, src/config/env.ts:98) with `Authorization: Bearer ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}` (openrouter.ts:24-25). Body is `{state, questions, model}` (src/runtime/primitive-runtime.ts:299-301). Env vars: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_OPENROUTER_BASE_URL, JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, JEV_MODEL (default jev-1.13) at env.ts:41-56, 83, 91. TypeSafe direct uses @typesafe-ai/sdk TypeSafeClient.systemOne (src/providers/typesafe.ts:6-23) with TYPESAFE_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Note: it does not use /api/v1/systemone. I could not fetch OpenRouter's Decisions API docs (404), so the request and response schema is unverified against the official spec. The repo's tests use mocks only.
providerSupport.others: compatible (JEV_API_KEY + JEV_API_BASE_URL full URL, src/providers/compatible.ts); local OpenJev via @huggingface/transformers (JEV_PROVIDER=local, or auto with no keys, env.ts:52-55). Auto priority is TypeSafe, then OpenRouter, then compatible, then local, so a stray TYPESAFE_API_KEY would override OpenRouter unless JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is set explicitly.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter is a first-class provider. Only the schema against the live endpoint needs a smoke test.

interface.name: verify
interface.purpose: Claims plus evidence (up to 32 claims and 32 items, 200k chars each) mapped to supported/contradicted/not_addressed. Policy returns accept, reject, collect_evidence or system_two_review (min confidence 0.8).

interface.name: rank_candidates
interface.purpose: Rank 2-32 candidates against an objective. Returns continue or system_two_review (min confidence 0.65, margin 0.1).

interface.name: select_capability
interface.purpose: Noul relevance filter over up to 64 capabilities, then a Choice among the survivors. It can make 2 provider calls.

interface.name: assess_task
interface.purpose: Three Score questions (complexity, risk, ambiguity, 4 levels each). Returns continue, ask_user or system_two_review.

interface.name: screen_content
interface.purpose: Content up to 100k chars checked against caller-supplied rules with a Noul per rule. Returns accept, review or reject (block threshold 0.8).

interface.name: completion_gate
interface.purpose: Requirements, evidence and check statuses. Deterministic priority: failed blocking check gives reject, not_run gives run_checks, then a semantic verify.

interface.name: CLI/other
interface.purpose: `node dist/index.js` (stdio MCP) and `pnpm playground`, a local HTTP UI on 127.0.0.1:4317. No hooks, no skills, no plugin.json, no .mcp.json and no install script are shipped.

security: Key is read from env vars only; it is not put in argv. With a `command`/`args`/`env` MCP entry the key stays out of the process list, though it is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ to the same user.
Redacts the API key in HTTP error text (src/providers/http.ts:92-94, 138, 164).
Fail-closed response validation and a response byte cap (1 MB) are implemented. Retries are limited to 408/409/429/5xx.
No shell execution, child_process or telemetry in src (grep clean). Only outbound calls are the provider endpoint and the Hugging Face model download for the local provider.

Supply chain is heavy: needs a local `pnpm install && build` (a pnpm workspace allowBuilds for onnxruntime-node and protobufjs runs native build scripts) and pulls @huggingface/transformers, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (real, published 2026-09-15) and the MCP SDK. Not published to npm, so it is git-clone only. Repo is 8 days old with 2 commits by one author, and the git author email is a personal QQ address. The pnpm allowBuilds rule means build scripts run at install time.
Playground binds to 127.0.0.1 by default (PLAYGROUND_HOST overridable) and has no auth. It is only started manually.

Prompt-injection surface: evidence, claims and content are attacker-controllable text (logs, diffs, web content) that goes into Jev state. This is mitigated only by the deterministic policy, and a poisoned log could steer a completion_gate accept.
Docs say thresholds are unvalidated bootstrap values, not calibrated.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.dataEgress: On every call the whole `state` goes to OpenRouter (then to TypeSafe): claims, evidence text (diffs, test/build logs, file contents, up to about 96k chars per call after reduction), task descriptions, capability descriptions and rule text. Because Claude must fill these arguments, nothing is sent unless the model chooses to call a tool, but each call can include client code and diffs. Headers include HTTP-Referer https://github.com/aimcc-org/codex-jev-mcp and X-Title, so OpenRouter sees an attribution to the repo author. With provider=local (auto without keys) nothing leaves the machine except a one-time Hugging Face download of about 0.48 GB. This is a concern for client projects with confidentiality obligations.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.failureMode: Provider timeout or error is caught per tool and returned as a normal (non-isError) text envelope with status provider_error and action `escalate` (src/mcp/server.ts:28-51, 72-74). It never throws to Claude and never blocks a tool the way a hook could, so it is effectively fail-open advisory. Default timeout is 60 s (JEV_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS, max 300 s) with up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx inside one shared deadline (http.ts:15-33, 119-158). A hung Jev can therefore stall a turn for up to 60 s unless the timeout is lowered, and the smoke test does not cover this. In the local fallback the first call waits for a 0.48 GB download. Missing required env (e.g. provider=openrouter with no key) makes startup fail with an exit code, so the MCP shows as failed to connect.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.contextCost: 6 tools, no server `instructions`, no hook text. Estimated at about 12k chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas, roughly 3k tokens permanently in context (completion_gate and verify are the largest, with enum lists, nested evidence objects and min/max constraints). Descriptions are in Chinese, which is cheap to read but gives Claude no English cue about when to call. Every actual call also costs Opus output tokens to serialize claims and evidence (can be thousands of tokens for diffs), plus about 1-3k tokens of returned JSON with signals and meta.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no proxy. Claude will call it only if a tool description matches its judgment. The Chinese one-line descriptions plus nothing telling Claude to call it after tasks make automatic use unlikely without adding your own CLAUDE.md rule or a Stop/PostToolUse hook. Hooks would still need to build the JSON evidence themselves.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: One extra tool round-trip per use: claimed 70-500 ms model latency plus Claude generating the structured input (seconds for large evidence). select_capability can be 2 sequential provider calls. There is no cost per turn when the tool is unused. With local provider, the first call waits for the model download and every later question is an individual 512-token CPU forward pass.
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.install: git clone, `pnpm install && pnpm run build` (Node 22, pnpm 11.17), then register `claude mcp add jev -e JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -e JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13 -e JEV_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 -- node /abs/path/dist/index.js`. Not on npm (package is private).
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.tests: 9 node:test files (config, context reducer, local OpenJev, MCP stdio smoke, playground, provider, response validator, tools, verify). All use mock HTTP servers, with no live OpenRouter or TypeSafe call. No CI (.github is absent), no releases, no tags. I did not run them (static review only).
pros: Only candidate-type project with a real OpenRouter Decisions API provider: POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/ model prefix (openrouter.ai/api default), so OPENROUTER_API_KEY works with no code patching.
Sound design: Jev is a sensor, deterministic policy decides; strict zod schemas, fail-closed response validation of probabilities and winners, and bounded responses.
Deadline plus limited retries plus key redaction are implemented, and errors return as data instead of crashing the session.
Env-only secrets. No shell exec, no telemetry, no install scripts of its own, MIT.

completion_gate is the one tool with a plausible daily-coding use: a 'is this really done' sanity check that treats failed or not_run checks deterministically and does not let the model grade test results.
Local OpenJev fallback lets you avoid sending client code to any cloud, if you accept a weaker English-only 512-token model.
cons: Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool only, with no hooks or skill, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told. The Chinese-only tool descriptions make spontaneous calls unlikely.

Marginal value for an Opus 5.5 main model: tools like assess_task, rank_candidates and verify just re-ask a small classifier what Opus already judges better, at the cost of Opus writing large structured inputs.
Sends diffs, logs and file contents to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, which is a data-egress risk on client projects, and the beta Jev model is scored by unvalidated bootstrap thresholds (ARCHITECTURE.md).
Very immature: 8 days old, 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no CI, no release, not on npm; OpenRouter request/response schema not confirmed by a live test in the repo.
Default 60 s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn if Jev is slow. It must be lowered by env.
Silent provider drift: auto mode prefers TYPESAFE_API_KEY over OPENROUTER_API_KEY and falls back to a 0.48 GB local model download when no key is set, so pin JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.
Costs about 3k tokens of context permanently for 6 tools, most of which are irrelevant to routine coding (screen_content, select_capability).
gh-aimcc-org-aimcc-jev-mcp.verdict: A well-structured but brand-new proof of concept that supports OpenRouter properly, yet it only exposes model-discretion tools and nothing that makes Claude Code use Jev on its own. It is worth reading as a reference for wiring Jev primitives (especially completion_gate), but not as the primary always-on integration for this user.

gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.name: Mokusei-Hana/Jev-mcp
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, one 241-line server.py) written for Codex that wraps TypeSafe's System One API. It exposes four tools (jev_choose, jev_judge, jev_score, jev_decide) that POST state plus typed questions to a hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone endpoint. It validates the response strictly (answer IDs, probability keys, sum-to-1, choice equals argmax) and adds local needs_review hints from thresholds: confidence below 0.7, or Noul probability between 0.2 and 0.8. There is no hook, skill or proxy layer. README and comments are in Chinese.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_mcp/server.py:139-143 hardcodes client.post("https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}) with no base-URL override. Key is read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.py:123). Model comes from JEV_MODEL, default "jev-latest" (server.py:126). README says the request URL is fixed. providerSupport.others: None. The default JEV_MODEL "jev-latest" is not an OpenRouter id, which expects typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. The parser depends on answers[*].type/choice/confidence/probabilities/noul/score, which matches the TypeSafe native format.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. Change the URL at server.py:140 to an env-driven base (for example OPENROUTER base + /v1/systemone), read OPENROUTER_API_KEY instead of TYPESAFE_API_KEY at server.py:123, and set JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Batch 1-64 independent choice/score/noul questions over the same state in one API call. Takes state (any JSON), questions dict of Question{type, instructions, criteria}, min_confidence, no_threshold, yes_threshold.

interface.name: jev_choose
interface.purpose: Choose among 2-255 named options (state, question, options, min_confidence); returns probabilities plus a needs_review hint.

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Rate one dimension on 2-10 ordered level descriptions (state, question, levels, min_confidence); the score is fractional, 0 to n-1.

interface.name: jev_judge
interface.purpose: Yes/no proposition (state, statement, no_threshold, yes_threshold); returns the noul probability and true/false/null.

interface.name: MCP server instructions
interface.purpose: ~560-char instruction string in the MCP handshake (server.py:102-109), saying to use Jev for small, well-scoped judgments and that results are advisory.

interface.name: examples/AGENTS.snippet.md
interface.purpose: Six-line Chinese prompt snippet for a project AGENTS.md steering Codex toward on-demand use. This is the only auto-invocation mechanism in the repo.

security: API key is read from the process environment (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put on argv. The Codex example passes it via env_vars, which suits Claude Code's .mcp.json env expansion.
httpx redirects are disabled to protect the key (server.py:96). Error bodies are not surfaced, so state and key are not echoed back (server.py:149-155).

The only network egress is the single hardcoded HTTPS POST. No shell execution, no file reads, no telemetry, no postinstall. Source is 241 lines and easy to audit. Dependencies are mcp, httpx[socks] and pydantic, all reputable.

The install is git clone + uv sync from an unpinned default branch, with no release tags. Running uv run executes whatever is on disk, so the user should pin a commit hash and review it before trusting it.

Prompt-injection surface is low: the server returns only numeric or label decisions with no free text. Model-controlled inputs (state, options) are sent outward. The response is strictly validated, and the README states that output is advisory and never authorization.
No license file (licenseInfo null). Default copyright applies, so the code is legally unlicensed for reuse or forking, which matters for client projects.
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes in the tool arguments: state (any JSON: error text, code snippets, diffs, facts), question text and option descriptions. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai; through a patched OpenRouter route it would go to openrouter.ai and then TypeSafe. The server itself reads no files and runs no commands. Nothing is sent automatically. Egress happens only when the model chooses to call a tool, but on client projects Claude can pass proprietary code inside state. The existing secret-leak guard hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it would not cover mcp__jev__* arguments unless the matcher is extended.
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open for Claude, no hang. There is a 15 s total deadline (asyncio.timeout plus httpx timeout, configurable up to 120 s) and no retries (server.py:96,138). Timeout, network error, non-200 or an invalid response becomes an MCP tool error with a short message telling the model to keep reasoning (server.py:144-160). A missing key gives a tool error, not a crash. The Codex example sets tool_timeout_sec=25. In Claude Code a slow Jev only costs one failed tool call, but 15 s is long if it stalls. A missing key only errors at call time, so the server still starts.
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per call: Jev's claimed 70-500 ms plus a Claude tool-call round trip, meaning an extra model turn (roughly 1-3 s of Opus latency and tokens), which usually exceeds the value of a small decision. Server startup through uv run has a 60 s startup timeout in the example and takes a few seconds cold. Zero overhead on turns where Claude does not call it (there are no hooks).
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.contextCost: 4 tools. The tool schemas are dominated by the nested Question model in jev_decide (JsonValue unions), roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens for all tool names, descriptions and schemas (estimated, not measured). Server instructions add about 140 tokens. There are no hooks, so no per-turn injection. Total is roughly 2k tokens resident, which is moderate for a low-utility toolset. Tool search or deferred loading in Claude Code 2.1.x may reduce this.
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. Claude Code will call them if the tool descriptions and server instructions persuade it. There is no deterministic trigger: no hook, skill or proxy. The repo's AGENTS.snippet.md is a Codex-oriented nudge, and an equivalent CLAUDE.md snippet would be needed to raise call frequency. Opus 5.5 rarely delegates small judgments to an external classifier without a strong prompt, so this does not deliver truly automatic use.
pros: Small, readable, well-defended adapter: 241 lines, strict schema validation (server.py:52-86), no redirects, no error-body leakage, and no shell or file access. Realistic to audit in 10 minutes and safe to run locally.
Explicit fail-open design: 15 s hard deadline, no retries, and errors told to the model as 'continue reasoning'. It cannot block a Claude Code session.
Uses the native System One schema (state/questions/answers), which OpenRouter also serves, so the OpenRouter switch is a 3-line patch. jev_decide batches up to 64 questions into one call.
Local needs_review thresholds (confidence under 0.7, Noul 0.2-0.8) give Claude a sane 'don't trust this' signal. The README states plainly that this is not authorization.
Tests use MockTransport (tests/test_server.py) and require no API key.
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint (server.py:140) and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, so it does not work with OpenRouter without editing source. The user has no TypeSafe direct key and wants OpenRouter.
Not automatic in Claude Code. It is MCP-tool-only, so it depends on model discretion. The only nudge is a Codex AGENTS snippet in Chinese, and there is no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md integration.
Built for Codex, not Claude Code: no .mcp.json, no plugin manifest, no Claude Code docs. The user would write the config and patch the code themselves.
Very immature: created 2026-09-22, 2 commits from 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE (legally unusable for client work), and an empty repo description. Unpinned uv sync from main.
Data egress is model-controlled: Claude can put code or diffs from client projects into state. The existing secret guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* calls.

Marginal value for an Opus-class agent: each call costs an extra turn plus about 2k resident context tokens for choices Opus can make itself. The output has no reasoning trace, and the Jev quality claim is disputed (unverified 'flash router' skepticism).
gh-mokusei-hana-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, safe, well-validated but tiny and unlicensed Codex-oriented MCP wrapper. It is TypeSafe-only with a hardcoded URL, and it offers no automatic invocation in Claude Code beyond model discretion. It is usable as a reference implementation of the System One client and response validation, but a poor turnkey pick. If the user wants an MCP, a 3-line OpenRouter fork of it (or a clean rewrite) is realistic, though the license gap means rewriting is safer.
