gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.name: CodeCampusCo/jev-mcp
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Minimal stdio MCP server (TypeScript, ~430 LOC, plain fetch, one runtime dep: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) exposing a single tool `evaluate`. It forwards {model, state, questions} unchanged to the TypeSafe System One endpoint and returns the raw JSON (per-answer probabilities). Retries twice on 408/429/529/5xx with backoff, has a 10s per-attempt timeout and a 4MB response cap. Has optional Axiom logging, off unless AXIOM_API_KEY is set. Not published to npm: requires git clone, npm install and npm run build.

providerSupport.evidence: src/client.ts:15 DEFAULT_API_URL = https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; src/client.ts:36 apiUrl = process.env.TYPESAFE_API_URL || default; src/client.ts:18,37 model default jev-1.13.0, overridable via TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL; src/index.ts:215 only reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY; client.ts:55-56 sends `authorization: Bearer <key>`. No OPENROUTER_* var anywhere. The path /v1/systemone is identical to OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so setting TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 should work with zero code change, but only if OpenRouter's request/response schema matches TypeSafe's (unverified: openrouter.ai docs URLs I tried returned 404, so I relied on the brief). The model can also be set per call via the `model` tool arg.
providerSupport.others: Optional Axiom ingest (https://api.axiom.co/v1/datasets/jev-mcp/ingest, src/log.ts:4) when AXIOM_API_KEY is set.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only: three env vars (TYPESAFE_API_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding the OpenRouter key, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). Caveats: the code comment at client.ts:16-17 says the TypeSafe API requires the three-part id (jev-1.13.0), and OpenRouter's id is typesafe/jev-1.13, which I could not verify. OpenRouter may also apply different rate-limit headers or error bodies. A key is passed as a Bearer token, which is what OpenRouter expects. Unpublished env-var naming is misleading but harmless. If OpenRouter is not schema-compatible, a change in client.ts would be needed.

interface.name: evaluate (MCP tool, mcp__jev__evaluate)
interface.purpose: Args: state (string/object/array, ~32k tokens max), questions (map of id -> {type: noul|choice|score, instructions, criteria}), optional model. Read-only hint, openWorld hint. Returns the API JSON verbatim as text, or isError on 4xx/5xx or transport failure. Only local validation is that state and questions are present.

gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20.12 (uses process.loadEnvFile), TypeScript compiled to dist/ by hand. Node 24 satisfies it. No npm publication and no release.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.tests: 14 tests in test/client.test.js and test/log.test.js (Node test runner, stubbed fetch, no network); CI in .github/workflows/ci.yml on Node 20.12/22/24; all tests unrun by me per the no-execution rule
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/CodeCampusCo/jev-mcp && cd jev-mcp && npm install && npm run build; then `claude mcp add jev -- node /abs/path/jev-mcp/dist/index.js`. Put the key in .env beside the README (loaded by the server from its own directory, not in argv) or pass env via `claude mcp add -e`. Not published to npm, so no npx path. You must rebuild after each git pull.
security: API key handling is good: read from .env resolved relative to the package (client.ts:7) or from the environment, so it never appears in argv or the process list; sent only as a Bearer header to TYPESAFE_API_URL (client.ts:55-56); never logged.
No shell execution, no child_process, no postinstall/preinstall/prepare scripts (package.json checked), no curl|sh installer, nothing written to disk.

Telemetry is opt-in only: Axiom logging fires only if AXIOM_API_KEY is set (log.ts:52-53). If set, it ships full state, instructions, criteria and the hostname to Axiom (README Logging section, SECURITY.md). Leave it unset.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the response is a typed JSON blob with probabilities and no free text. But an API error body is passed back verbatim (index.ts:258), and the `state` the agent sends can contain attacker-controlled repo text that influences the decision. Do not let a Jev decision gate a destructive action.

Outbound channel: anything the agent puts in `state` leaves the machine, including code or secrets from client repos. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and will NOT cover mcp__jev__evaluate.

Single-maintainer, 2-week-old repo, zero stars, so supply-chain trust is low. The code is small enough to audit fully (I read all of it), and dependency surface is just the official MCP SDK. Pin a commit and use package-lock (npm ci).
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.dataEgress: On every `evaluate` call the entire `state` (whatever the model chose to include: code snippets, diffs, file text, tool output, plus questions/criteria) and the API key go to the endpoint in TYPESAFE_API_URL, by default api.typesafe.ai, or openrouter.ai if reconfigured. With OpenRouter, the request is subject to OpenRouter's logging and data-policy settings. Nothing is sent when Claude does not call the tool. Axiom receives a full copy plus hostname only if AXIOM_API_KEY is set. No other telemetry.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: errors come back as an MCP tool error (isError), never a crash, so Claude Code carries on and the model reasons itself. Worst case is about 31s per call (10s timeout x 3 attempts plus backoff) while Claude waits, which is a noticeable stall if Jev is down or hanging. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the server exit at startup with code 1, so the tool silently disappears (a failed MCP connection, not a session failure). There is no circuit breaker, so a dead endpoint costs up to 31s each time the model tries it.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate). Tool name plus description plus schema is about 4,000 chars, roughly 1,000 tokens (DESCRIPTION alone is about 1,550 chars, and the schema property descriptions about 2,300). The server sends no MCP `instructions`. It adds no hooks and injects no text. Claude Code may defer tool loading, in which case only the name is in context until searched for. Each answer adds about 100-400 tokens of JSON. The tool is cheap in context versus e.g. playwright.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Claimed ~300ms per call (README; brief says 70-500ms) plus the MCP stdio hop and one extra model tool-call turn (Claude must author the state and questions JSON, which costs output tokens and seconds on Opus). Zero overhead on turns where it is not called. Worst case about 31s on outage. Cold Axiom drain up to 1.9s at shutdown only, and only if enabled.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, skill or proxy. The tool description is written to make the model use it mid-task ("Reach for this mid-task, the way you would read a file... classifying, routing, scoring, gating") and also says when NOT to. There is no deterministic trigger, so how often Opus 5.5 actually calls it is unpredictable and likely low, since Opus can answer small classification questions itself at no extra cost. To raise the rate you would add a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill, which is contrary to the user's wish for no explicit prompting but is a one-time global setup.
pros: Smallest, cleanest way to expose Jev to Claude Code: one tool, about 1k tokens of context, no server instructions, no hooks, so it will not collide with the existing secret-guard, GitNexus or caveman hooks.
Whole source is about 430 lines and I read all of it. No shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry by default, key never in argv (loaded from .env or env).

The tool description is the best I've seen at telling the model when to use Jev (bounded classification, routing, gating, claim-support check) and when not (prose, code, arithmetic, open answer space), including 'add a none-of-these option'. This gives real model-driven auto-use without prompting.
Provider URL, model and key are env-configurable (client.ts:36-37), and the endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's, so an OpenRouter switch is likely config-only.
Robust client: 10s per-attempt timeout, 2 retries with jitter and Retry-After support, a 4MB response cap, and tool errors returned instead of crashes (fail-open).
MIT, CI on Node 20/22/24, 14 stubbed-fetch tests, signed merge commits, CLAUDE.md/SECURITY.md documenting what leaves the machine.
Batch design: multiple typed questions per call against a single state, which saves round trips.
cons: Not really 'automatic': it is a model-discretion tool. Opus 5.5 can answer most bounded questions itself for free, so it will likely rarely call Jev, and there is no hook forcing it. It also needs the model to build a good state/criteria payload each time, which costs output tokens and a turn.
Not on npm: needs clone, npm install, and manual npm run build after every pull; `claude mcp add` needs an absolute path. No npx one-liner and no release tags.

Very new and single-maintainer (30 of 32 commits by one person, 2 by a bot; 0 stars, 0 forks, 12 days old, version 0.1.0). The project is by CodeCampusCo, not TypeSafe, so it is not the official integration.

OpenRouter is not first-class: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_URL exist, the key var is misnamed for an OpenRouter key, and the default model is jev-1.13.0 (a code comment says the TypeSafe API rejects jev-1.13) whereas OpenRouter uses typesafe/jev-1.13. OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified by me (docs URLs returned 404).

Data egress risk on client projects: whatever Claude puts in `state` (code, diffs) goes to a third party. The user's existing secret-leak hook does not match the mcp__jev__evaluate tool, so it would need a new matcher.
Worst-case stall of about 31s on a hanging endpoint with no circuit breaker. The 10s x 3 retry policy is fine for a batch job but bad for an interactive agent.

Inherits Jev limits and beta status: no 'don't know' answer, poor on arithmetic and dates, accuracy drops with noisy state, 32k limit; the value for coding is niche (routing/triage/claim checks) rather than a daily driver. The Theo/t3.gg skepticism (it may just be a small routed model) is unverified but relevant to how much decisions can be trusted.
gh-codecampusco-jev-mcp.verdict: The best-built and lowest-overhead way to expose Jev to Claude Code (one tool, about 1k tokens, clean and auditable code, config-only OpenRouter path), but it is only a model-discretion tool, so it won't reliably fire on its own. Worth using as the base layer if paired with a CLAUDE.md/skill nudge, a secret-guard matcher for mcp__jev__evaluate, and a check that the OpenRouter endpoint and model id work.

gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.name: itsmostafa/system-one-connector (evaluate MCP server, formerly typesafe-mcp)
gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.whatItDoes: Go single-binary MCP stdio server named "evaluate" exposing ONE tool, `evaluate`, that forwards typed questions (noul / choice / score) plus a `state` blob to Jev (or CLM/Laya/d1 via custom host) and returns the probability JSON. Adds client-side extras: stable probability ordering, a min_confidence abstain threshold, an `items` fan-out (up to 500 records, 8 concurrent, one billed request each), 429/529 retry. `evaluate setup mcp` auto-registers it with Claude Code (user scope), Codex, Hermes and Claude Desktop; `evaluate setup pi` installs a pi extension. It is not a hook or skill: Claude only calls it when the model decides to.

Only OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read, so the user must make sure TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset or it silently goes direct to TypeSafe.

gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.runtime: Go 1.27.1 static binary (MCP go-sdk v1.7.0, cobra); no Node/Python needed. Linux/macOS amd64/arm64 release tarballs.
gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/itsmostafa/system-one-connector/main/install.sh | sh (SHA-256 verified against SHA256SUMS.txt from the same release, so it protects only against corruption, not a compromised release), or `go install github.com/itsmostafa/system-one-connector/cmd/evaluate@latest` (safer: build from source). Then OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... evaluate setup mcp, or manually: claude mcp add evaluate -s user -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -- /path/evaluate mcp
gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.tests: One evaluate_test.go, 940 lines, 24 Test funcs, table-driven over httptest (mock server only; no live API tests). CI workflow only does release-please + cross-build + install.sh verify; no test/vet run on PRs (only `task check` locally per CLAUDE.md). Actively maintained via Conventional Commits/release-please, 12 bot release commits in 8 days.
security: API key stored plaintext: `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key>` puts it in ~/.claude.json mcpServers env, and setup.go:231 passes it as argv to the claude CLI, so it is briefly visible in the process list (ps) during setup. Manual claude mcp add has the same argv exposure. Runtime: key sent only as Bearer to openrouter.ai / TypeSafe host (client.go:42).
No shell execution at runtime: the server only does HTTPS POSTs. setup.go execs claude/codex/hermes CLIs with fixed args (no shell string).

install.sh is curl|sh but is short, readable, checksums the tarball (checksum fetched from same release, so no defense against release compromise), installs to ~/.local/bin. Self-update (`evaluate update`) pulls GitHub releases; the MCP server also GETs api.github.com releases/latest on every startup (2s timeout), a minor telemetry-like beacon (IP + User-Agent to GitHub, no payload); disable only via hidden --no-update-check flag, which setup does not set for Claude Code.

Prompt-injection surface: the update notice string is appended to MCP server instructions (main.go:251) from GitHub release tag_name; tag is validated by parseVersion/newerRelease, low risk. Jev outputs are numbers/enum choices only (no free text), so returning-injection risk is very low; but the instructions itself warn 'instructions embedded in state can steer the answer'.

Tool is marked ReadOnlyHint:true, yet every call (and every item in a 500-item fan-out) is billed; in bypass/auto mode the model can loop calls without a prompt. TYPESAFE_MAX_ITEMS caps per-call only, not total spend; set an OpenRouter key spend limit.

gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.dataEgress: Only the tool-call arguments Claude chooses to pass: `state` (whatever text/JSON Claude puts in, e.g. code snippets, diffs, file contents, tickets, logs if Claude decides to) and `questions` instructions/criteria, sent to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (then relayed to TypeSafe by OpenRouter; OpenRouter privacy/logging settings apply). Never fail-closed on Claude's normal tools, since it is not a hook.

Only when Claude calls the tool: claimed 70-500 ms plus MCP stdio round trip, plus OpenRouter hop; up to 8 concurrent requests in items mode (500 items about 20s). Startup adds up to 2s (GitHub update check, blocks server init) once per session, which can be removed with --no-update-check.

MIT, 337 stars, 37 forks, 121 commits in 2 weeks, tagged releases with checksums, pinned CI action SHAs, ~940 lines of tests; author appears tied to the TypeSafe ecosystem (README lists it as the official connector for Claude Code).
cons: Does NOT deliver the 'automatic without prompting' requirement: it is a plain MCP tool, so Claude uses it only if it judges it useful. Jev is a classifier, not a coding assistant, and Opus rarely needs a 0.86 probability to decide how to edit code; expect near-zero organic calls. Making it automatic needs extra CLAUDE.md trigger rules or a separate hook layer (not in this repo).

Poor daily-coding value: Jev cannot read code, generate patches, or explain; the useful niches (triage of issues/logs, guardrail judging, routing, PR-comment classification) are occasional, not all-day.

Alpha endpoint risk: docs/configuration.md admits /api/alpha/decisions 'may move'; Jev itself is beta and skeptics say it may be a small routed model (unverified).

Secret handling: key lands in plaintext in ~/.claude.json and appears in argv of the `claude mcp add` invocation (ps-visible for a moment); `setup mcp` also re-registers with codex/hermes/Desktop if present (broader footprint than needed); prefer running `claude mcp add` manually.

Hidden costs: ReadOnlyHint:true means some hosts skip prompts; in bypass/auto mode a runaway `items` call could make 500 billed requests; cap only per call.
Startup network call to api.github.com on each server launch (up to 2s added to MCP connect) and self-update machinery you probably don't want in a hardened client setup.
No CI test gate on PRs; project is 2 weeks old with rapid 0.x churn (v0.4.8), API and tool schema may change; only 4 contributors, effectively single-maintainer.
gh-itsmostafa-system-one-connector.verdict: Best available OpenRouter-native way to expose Jev to Claude Code (one tool, small footprint, clean code, uses /api/alpha/decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest), but it is only a model-discretion MCP tool: it will not fire automatically for ordinary coding, and Jev itself has few all-day coding uses. Install it from source (go install) with a spend-limited OpenRouter key and pair it with explicit CLAUDE.md trigger rules or a hook if automatic use is required.

gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: A TypeScript stdio MCP server ("jev-capability-runtime" v0.2.0) that wraps Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives in a programmable "capability" runtime. The connected agent authors typed questions (jev_judge), saves versioned multi-stage workflows with conditional stages, composite scores, routes and ranking (define_capability), runs them over up to 20 items (run_capability), evaluates them against caller-written examples, and stores records in a local SQLite FTS5 store. It ships five starter capabilities (claim_router, inference_warrant, evidence_stance, formalization_fidelity, tool_router) and one SKILL.md. It is a research and experiment lab (inquiry studies, continuity studies, a Graph-of-Thoughts scorer comparison), not a coding-workflow integration. It has no hooks and no code-specific judgments (no commit, diff, test or permission triage).

security: No license file: licenseInfo is null, so it is all-rights-reserved by default. That matters for client projects.

Key handling is decent. The key comes from env or a project-root .env (loaded via process.loadEnvFile, src/server.ts:12-13). It is never in argv. The Codex config forwards env var names only. Error bodies are scrubbed with replaceAll(apiKey,'[REDACTED]') (provider.ts:114). fetch uses redirect:'error' and fixed endpoints, and non-Jev slugs are rejected.

Data on disk: every request (state) and response is persisted in SQLite at <repo>/.jev/jev.sqlite via startRun/event, including exact per-stage requests. Anything the agent sends to Jev, such as code or diffs, is retained in plaintext locally. The .jev directory is gitignored.

No child_process, exec, spawn or telemetry found in src/*.ts (grep). Runtime dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 and zod 4.6.5; devDeps are typescript 7.0.2 and the MCP client. It uses built-in node:sqlite.

No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall. Install is a manual git clone + npm ci + mcp:configure, which writes an absolute-path .mcp.json inside the repo. It cannot be run via npx because Node refuses to run TS from node_modules.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev returns only typed numbers or labels, so the model cannot inject text. The stored-record and guide text is agent-authored. Jev outputs are model judgments that could be mistaken for permission, though the guide says they are not permission. Its tool_router and claim_router outputs steer the agent, a soft-influence vector if you trust them blindly.
Guide notes a transport quirk: hosts may stringify context or sort keys, which shifted borderline probabilities by 0.1-0.2. Results are not order-stable.
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what the calling agent puts in jev_judge state / run_capability items+context, plus the question instructions, goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai). There is no automatic collection of prompts, files, diffs or tool outputs: the server is passive and sees only what Claude chooses to pass. Requests are capped at 40 KB (provider.ts:101) and batches at 250 KB. Because the state is arbitrary JSON, Claude can send code or client data to OpenRouter (and on to TypeSafe) at its own discretion, and nothing screens it. Your existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Locally, everything is also saved unencrypted in .jev/jev.sqlite. The jev_judge description says 'never include API credentials', which is advisory only.
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open and advisory. The server never sits in the tool-call path, so an outage does not block Claude's own tools. Each call has a 20 s timeout (AbortSignal.timeout, provider.ts:111) and at most one retry for 429/500/502/503/529 when Retry-After is 5 s or less (provider.ts:119). 401/402/403/404 mark the run fatal and stop remaining calls (capability-runtime.ts). Failures return an MCP isError result with status failed or partial, so Claude just sees an error and continues. A missing key returns a 'missing_key' RuntimeError on each call, and the server still starts. The worst case is a wasted tool call of up to about 40 s. There are 4 concurrent calls server-wide and a 32-call default budget per run. Response validation is strict, so malformed responses are rejected.
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.contextCost: 10 tools. tool_defs: description text is about 7.2 KB (src/mcp-server.ts lines 77-93). The Zod schemas (runtime-contracts.ts, 14 KB, 49 .describe() calls) are nested unions for questions, rules, composites and routes. My estimate of total tool names+descriptions+schemas is 18-24k chars, roughly 4.5-6k tokens (chars/4), always resident unless Claude Code's MCP tool search defers them. The server 'instructions' string is short, about 300 chars (~75 tokens). The 9 KB guide (~2.3k tokens) is a resource read on demand, and the SKILL.md is 3.9 KB, and only its name and description are loaded up front. No hook-injected text. Note that the tool-count and schema footprint is heavy for what you would use it for.
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a description-triggered skill. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic path. Nothing in the repo makes Claude call Jev on ordinary coding. The tool descriptions say 'Ask agent-authored Choice, Score, or Noul questions... Use this to try a new semantic predicate', so Claude would call it only when it decides to author a question. The suggested habits (run tool_router before substantial tasks, claim_router before reporting findings) live in a resource the model must first fetch (jev://guide), and in a skill that triggers on 'create/test/compose Jev capabilities'. Getting real automatic use would need your own hooks or CLAUDE.md rules, i.e. exactly the prompting you want to avoid. The bootstrapped starter capabilities target research-claim reasoning, not code.
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per Jev call the added latency is the claimed 70-500 ms plus MCP stdio overhead; a stage's questions share one call (question fan-out is free). Multi-stage or multi-item runs add sequential stages per item, with 4 workers/concurrency. Because it is model-discretion only, the added time is one extra tool round-trip (an LLM turn of roughly 1-3 s for Opus to format the call and read the result) each time Claude uses it, likely larger than the Jev call itself. Failure worst case is 20 s x 2 attempts. The 1 h cache is opt-in.
pros: Genuinely OpenRouter-native: default provider is openrouter, endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions and default model ~typesafe/jev-latest (src/provider.ts:3-10, .env.example). It works with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so no patching is needed.

Most thorough client of the Jev API seen: strict response validation (probability sums, choice equals argmax, score equals expectation, label match, provider.ts:49-88), bounded concurrency, per-call cost reporting, pinning of model slug/hash, and floating-alias warnings. This is a solid reference implementation for building your own thin Jev wrapper.

Safe by construction on the write side: it makes no generative calls, calls only fixed Jev endpoints, has no shell execution or child_process, and has a small dependency set (MCP SDK + zod). The key is redacted from stored responses.

Expressive: composites, confidence-gated routes, conditional stages and speculative fan-out map to TypeSafe's documented patterns, so a coding-specific triage capability (for example 'is this diff risky?', 'route this error') could be defined and reused via define_capability and run_capability.

Has tests (5 test files under test/ using node --test), reproducible study artifacts and honest self-reported limitations, including the key-order sensitivity finding (0.1-0.2 shifts on borderline cases).
Reference material: starters/tool-catalog.example.json and the tool_router study (20-server catalog, about 800 chars per routing) is a relevant idea for your MCP-sprawl setup.
cons: Not automatic. It is a passive tool set that Claude must choose to call. The repo has no hooks, and the useful behaviors (tool_router before a task, claim_router before reporting) are 'suggested habits' in a resource the model must read first. That fails your core requirement of Claude using Jev without you asking.

Not built for coding: the bundled capabilities target research reasoning (claim routing, inference warrants, evidence stance, formalization fidelity). None is for code review, test triage, commit-risk, permission decisions or file relevance. You would author the coding capabilities yourself, and the effectiveness is unvalidated.

Heavy footprint for the value: 10 tools with deeply nested schemas (~5k tokens estimated) on every session, in addition to gitnexus and playwright; plus a SQLite record store, run history and versioning machinery that a daily coding flow does not need.

No license (licenseInfo null): all rights reserved. Using or modifying it in client projects has legal ambiguity. A single-author repo (1 contributor, 5 commits in 3 days, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI) and it is very young (created 2026-09-20, last push 2026-09-23). Effectively abandoned-on-arrival risk.

Manual install: git clone + npm ci + a generated absolute-path .mcp.json (gitignored). It cannot be run via npx, must live in a cloned directory, requires Node >=24.12, and stores .jev/jev.sqlite plus a .env in the clone directory. Claude Code reads .mcp.json only when opened in that folder, so you would have to copy the entry into user-scope config with an env block.

Extra data path: any code or diff Claude chooses to judge goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe and is stored plaintext in .jev/jev.sqlite. The mcp__jev__* tools are outside your secret-leak guard matcher. That is a client-confidentiality concern.
Model-discretion tool calls cost a full LLM turn (Opus tokens + latency) per judgment, which cancels most of Jev's 70-500 ms / $0.042 per 1M advantage.

Inherits Jev's beta limits, and its own docs report order and transport sensitivity for borderline cases, so it is unfit for safety or permission decisions (the guide itself says to keep those in code).
gh-angrysky56-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev client found, but it is a research capability workbench with no hooks, so it does not deliver the requested automatic in-Claude-Code use, and it has no license and a single author. Treat it as a reference implementation (provider.ts validation, endpoint and schema) for your own small hook plus minimal MCP wrapper rather than something to install.

gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Single-file (499 lines) Node stdio MCP server exposing 3 tools. search_codebase walks a directory locally, scores files lexically (filename and content substring hits), then sends the top 12 candidates' paths, symbols and 300-char previews to Jev as parallel Noul questions, followed by up to 3 sequential Jev Choice calls to pick a function/line. validate_code_targets asks one Noul per candidate file. judge_with_jev is a thin pass-through for arbitrary Choice/Noul/Score questions. interface.name: search_codebase(query, directory_path?)
interface.purpose: Local lexical candidate scan (max depth 12, max 8000 files, files <500KB read fully) + Jev Noul rerank of top 12 + Jev Choice to pick function/line for top 3 files. Returns paths, target symbol and line, jev_score, plus next_action_steps telling the model not to grep or scan further. Description text: 'MANDATORY FIRST-CHOICE TOOL ... Use this INSTEAD of grep, ripgrep, or find_by_name'.

interface.name: validate_code_targets(goal, candidate_files[])
interface.purpose: Resolves files against process.cwd() (no containment check), sends path + up to 8 symbols per file to Jev as Noul; returns approved_targets (p>=0.4) and rejected_files; tells the model NOT to read rejected files. Description: 'CRITICAL ANTI-HALLUCINATION GATE'.

interface.name: judge_with_jev(instructions, primitive, criteria?, context?)
interface.purpose: Generic pass-through of one Choice/Noul/Score question with caller-supplied context (string or object) to Jev; returns raw answer and usage. This is the only tool aligned with what Jev is actually designed for.

DO NOT read rejected_files', i.e. the server injects imperative instructions into the model's context that suppress verification; a false negative from a low-quality ranker becomes an instruction to skip the right file.
validate_code_targets does path.resolve(cwd, fp) with no containment, so the model can point it at any readable file (only path and up to 8 symbols leave the machine, not contents).

Prompt-injection: file contents (previews, symbols, comments) are interpolated into Jev questions, and results are structured numbers/labels, so injection blast radius is low (wrong ranking) rather than code exec. Query is also interpolated into instructions.

gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.dataEgress: To the endpoint (OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT is repointed, then TypeSafe as upstream provider): search_codebase sends the query, the absolute search root path (root_directory, leaks local dir layout and username), for 12 candidate files the relative path, up to 8 regex-extracted symbols and the first 300 chars of each file; then per top-3 file the query, rel path, extension, first 400 chars, and up to 6 method previews of 60 chars. Files are chosen by keyword score, so a .json or .md with secrets in its first 300 chars could be sent (lines 129-139 read any .kt/.ts/.json/.md etc.; .env has no allowed extension and dot-directories are skipped). validate_code_targets sends goal plus paths and symbols only. judge_with_jev sends whatever instructions/criteria/context the model provides (arbitrary code snippets). No full file contents, diffs or tool outputs are sent automatically. No secrets scan before send. Per-call usage returned by Jev is passed to the model.
gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude level but sloppy: any error is caught and returned as {error} with isError:true (lines 483-488), so Claude sees a failed tool and can fall back to Grep. There is NO timeout on fetch (line 68), so a hung or slow Jev stalls the tool until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout. Missing key throws 'TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable is missing!'. Score-fallback: if all probabilities <0.1, returns the first 2 lexical candidates as if ranked, so a dead or garbage Jev response (missing answers -> ?? 0) silently degrades to arbitrary lexical picks presented as 'exact implementation entry points'. That silent degradation is a correctness risk.
gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: search_codebase: local sync scan of up to 8000 files with full-file reads (can be seconds on big repos) + 1 Noul call with 12 questions + up to 3 sequential Choice calls, so roughly 4 sequential round trips at the claimed 70-500 ms each = ~0.3-2 s network plus scan time, per search. validate_code_targets and judge_with_jev: 1 round trip. Compared with Grep/GitNexus (tens of ms), it is slower and less precise; no hook overhead because there are no hooks.
gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.contextCost: 3 tools. Tool names + descriptions + schemas are about 3.0k chars, i.e. roughly 750 tokens always loaded (or deferred by ToolSearch if MCP tool search is on). No MCP server 'instructions' are sent: instructions.md exists but is never read by index.js (the Server constructor at lines 176-186 passes no instructions), so the README's 'system prompt injection' claim is false. Each search result returns ~1-2k chars of JSON including 3 next_action_steps lines. No hook-injected text.

Automation relies on manipulative tool descriptions ('MANDATORY FIRST-CHOICE TOOL', 'INSTEAD of grep') and a README suggestion to paste rules into CLAUDE.md. With Opus 5.5 and an existing GitNexus graph hook, the model would likely still pick Grep/GitNexus, and the user's requirement of no prompting is only weakly met.
pros: Genuinely Jev-integrated and the endpoint is env-overridable (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT, bin/index.js:51); OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone documents the same request/response schema and Bearer auth, so OpenRouter routing needs zero code change.
judge_with_jev is a correct, minimal exposure of Choice/Noul/Score with caller-supplied criteria, matching Jev's real strengths (typed decisions, calibrated probabilities).

Tool descriptions and result text order the model to skip grep and skip 'rejected_files'; combined with silent fallback to the first 2 lexical candidates when Jev scores are <0.1 or missing (lines 303-309), this can mislead Claude into missing the right files.
Function/line detection uses a regex on fun|func|def|class|interface|fn only for the top 3 files and is keyed to first 6 matches; wrong on TS arrow functions/methods, most JS, Java/C++ methods.

README's npx -y jev-mcp installs an unrelated npm package by another author; the repo is unpublished at v1.0.0 vs npm 0.5.1: high risk of installing the wrong code.
instructions.md is dead (never loaded), README claims contradict the code; zero tests, no CI, no releases, single author, 15 commits in 3 days, no LICENSE file.
Sends absolute project root path and file previews (first 300-400 chars, including from .json/.md) to a third-party model on every search, with no secret filtering, on personal and client code.

gh-y9finsi-jev-mcp.verdict: A small weekend PoC that only lightly uses Jev (reranking a keyword shortlist) and overlaps with GitNexus; its OpenRouter compatibility is real (endpoint env override, same schema) but its aggressive 'use me instead of grep' steering, missing timeouts, .env scraping and the npm name collision make it a poor fit for automatic use on client code. Better to borrow only judge_with_jev-style pass-through, or fork with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and a timeout, rather than adopt as is.

gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.name: wr0x00/jev_mcp
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: A small FastMCP (Python) server, about 700 lines. It exposes 4 tools over Streamable HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8800/mcp: jev_route_task, jev_tool_gate, jev_verify_done and jev_ask. Each tool sends fixed Chinese-language Noul/Score/Choice questions to a Jev endpoint. It then applies threshold policies from config.yaml and returns auto_execute, human_review, block, pass or continue. The design is an "agent control loop" (route, then gate before a tool call, then verify at the end). Nothing in Claude Code invokes it; the calling model has to choose to call the tools. The README calls it "just a demo".

providerSupport.evidence: client.py:250-252 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_BASE_URL and has no OpenRouter key or URL. client.py:271-274 does httpx.post(f"{base_url}/v1/ask", json={context, questions[]}, Bearer key). The README default JEV_BASE_URL is https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, which would give .../v1/systemone/v1/ask; that path is not the documented System One path. The payload shape does not match the documented API. OpenRouter's Decisions API (checked at openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/jev-tutorial.md) needs `model: typesafe/jev-1.13`, `state: {...}` and `questions` as a dict of {type, instructions, criteria}. This repo sends `context` (a string) and `questions` as a list of {name, type, prompt, options}, with no model field. The response parser (client.py:284-302) expects {fields:{name:{value,p}}}, which is an invented schema. config.yaml:8-9 has TYPESAFE_API_KEY set to the URL and JEV_BASE_URL empty, so the shipped defaults are swapped and the server starts unconfigured. The strings 'openrouter' and 'v1/systemone' appear nowhere in the code. The README's 'Jev Cloud API Contract' calls its own /v1/ask schema a guess to be replaced by the official SDK.
providerSupport.others: None. It supports only a generic base URL plus a Bearer key.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. Setting JEV_BASE_URL to OpenRouter is not enough. You would have to rewrite _post_ask and _normalize in client.py. The rewrite means adding the model id, mapping context to state, and converting the question list to a dict with instructions and criteria. It also means parsing the real response (probabilities per option), because the code assumes a single scalar p per field. The Choice p logic (client.py:294) takes one p, but the real API returns per-option probabilities. The templates would also need rewriting. About 100 lines, but it is effectively a new client, and the thresholds in config.yaml were never calibrated against the real API.

interface.name: jev_route_task(request)
interface.purpose: Sends the user request through task_type Choice (direct_query, code_change, research, ops_action, communication, other), difficulty Score and is_urgent Noul. Returns auto_execute or human_review.

interface.name: jev_tool_gate(proposal, tool_name, target)
interface.purpose: Pre-execution risk gate with destructive, exfiltration and scope_breach as Noul and reversibility as Score. Returns auto_execute, human_review or block.

interface.name: jev_verify_done(user_request, result_summary, loop_count)
interface.purpose: Post-execution check with covers_user_request, has_unverified_claim and repeated_action as Noul. Returns pass, continue or human_review.

interface.name: jev_ask(questions, context)
interface.purpose: Generic passthrough of custom typed questions; returns raw probabilities only.

interface.name: GET /health
interface.purpose: HTTP liveness probe. No hooks, skills, plugin.json or .mcp.json ship with the repo.

gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.tests: None. No tests directory and no CI. The code comments say it is 'decoupled for unit testing', but no tests exist. There are no releases and no topics. All 6 commits date from 2026-09-21, the day the repo was created, and 5 of them are README edits.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.install: The README documents start.sh (creates a venv and pip-installs fastmcp>=4.0.0, httpx and pyyaml) or docker compose. Then add a URL entry to .mcp.json (`{"mcpServers":{"jev_mcp":{"url":"http://127.0.0.1:8800/mcp"}}}`). This means you run a long-lived HTTP daemon yourself. Not executed here.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.runtime: Python 3.10+ with fastmcp>=4.0.0, httpx and pyyaml. Runs as a separate HTTP service on port 8800, not stdio. The unpinned fastmcp>=4.0.0 has no lockfile.
security: The MCP HTTP server binds to 0.0.0.0:8800 by default (server.py:226, config.yaml JEV_MCP_HOST, Dockerfile, docker-compose port 8800:8800). It has no authentication in code: FastMCP is created with no auth provider. The README shows a 'Bearer <your-mcp-token>' header, but nothing validates it. On a laptop this exposes an unauthenticated tool endpoint, which is a LAN risk; it would have to be changed to 127.0.0.1.

The API key is read from an env var or from config.yaml, so it is not in argv. The config.yaml `env` section invites putting the key in a file next to the code, and .gitignore does not exclude config.yaml. The shipped defaults have the key and URL fields swapped (config.yaml:8-9).

The prompt-injection defence is weak: sanitize_text (templates.py:110-126) strips control characters, truncates to 8000 chars, and only warns on five regexes without blocking. The gate's `proposal` text is written by the LLM being gated, so a compromised or injected agent can write a benign-looking proposal. The gate is also advisory: nothing enforces it.
Timeouts and failures return human_review, but the calling model can simply ignore that.
No shell execution in the server. No npm postinstall, curl|sh or telemetry. start.sh is a plain venv bootstrap. Dependencies are unpinned.
Docker image runs as root (no USER) on python:3.12-slim.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever text the model puts into the tool arguments, up to 8000 chars per call (safety.max_context_chars). That means the user request, the proposed action, tool name and target, and result summaries. The data goes to JEV_BASE_URL, and the server never checks that the URL is TypeSafe or OpenRouter. The server does not read files, diffs or tool output on its own. Since the args are written by the model, code and secrets can reach the endpoint if the model pastes them in, and there is no secret redaction. The server itself has no telemetry.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-conservative but not fail-open. Client timeout is 4000 ms with 1 retry (config.yaml client, client.py:268-281), so the worst case is about 8 s per call. On any error or when unconfigured, the tools return degraded=true with action human_review (or block if configured). That is a returned value, not an exception, so Claude just sees text. With the shipped config the server starts unconfigured and every call returns 'not_configured'. In practice it soft-fails: it wastes a tool call and adds nothing. Because MCP is a separate daemon, a missing daemon means Claude Code shows the server as failed to connect and the tools are absent, which is harmless.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Each tool call costs one HTTP round trip to Jev, the documented 70-500 ms, plus model time to write the tool call and read the result (a few seconds of LLM turn overhead). The worst case on failure is about 8 s (4 s times 2). The flow suggests 3 calls per task (route, gate on each tool use, verify). Gating every Bash or Edit call would add a full LLM round trip per action, which is unacceptable for daily work.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.contextCost: 4 tools. The description text is Chinese with English Args blocks, about 2,000 chars in total. JSON schemas are small except for jev_ask (list of dicts). Estimate about 800-1,000 tokens of tool definitions (Chinese text tokenizes poorly). It sets no MCP server `instructions` (the FastMCP("jev_mcp") constructor has no instructions argument). No hook-injected text. It is cheap on context, but it is only worth having if it is called.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no SKILL.md and no CLAUDE.md snippet. The tool descriptions say what they do but not when Claude must call them. The README's control-loop pseudocode assumes an external harness that calls route/gate/verify around the LLM, which Claude Code is not. Automatic use would need extra work: hooks (PreToolUse calling the gate, Stop hook calling verify) or CLAUDE.md rules. A hook cannot call an MCP tool, so it would need a separate script that reimplements the HTTP call, which makes the MCP server pointless.
pros: MIT licence, small (about 700 lines), and readable in 10 minutes, so it is easy to audit or fork.
The three-part control-loop framing (route, gate, verify) maps sensibly onto Noul/Score/Choice, and templates.py has reusable questions for destructive, exfiltration and scope_breach checks.
Degrades to human_review on timeout or misconfiguration instead of auto-approving. The client timeout is 4 s with 1 retry.
Low context footprint: 4 tools and about 1k tokens, with no injected hook text.
Includes /health, Docker and cross-platform start scripts, and policy thresholds are in YAML.
cons: It does not work with OpenRouter, and probably not with TypeSafe directly either. It posts an invented {context, questions[]} payload to {base}/v1/ask, while the real API takes `model`, `state` and a `questions` dict with instructions/criteria. It also parses a single scalar `p` per field, which does not fit the real per-option probabilities (client.py:271-302). The README's own default URL would produce .../v1/systemone/v1/ask. There is no evidence anywhere in the repo that it was ever run against a live endpoint.
Shipped config.yaml has the API key and URL swapped (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holds the URL, JEV_BASE_URL is empty), so it starts unconfigured and every call returns not_configured.
It never fires on its own. It is a plain MCP tool with no hook or skill. Claude Code would have to choose to call it, which is the opposite of the user's requirement for automatic use.

Per-action gating through an LLM tool call adds seconds of turn time on every Bash or Edit call. Quality is unproven: the thresholds (exfiltration 0.1, destructive 0.05) are uncalibrated guesses, and the prompts are written in Chinese.
The gate is advisory, and its input `proposal` is authored by the model being gated, so it gives little real protection against prompt injection.
Server binds to 0.0.0.0:8800 with no authentication (the README's Bearer token is never checked), and the design needs a separately managed daemon instead of a stdio server.
Very immature: 0 stars, 1 author, 6 commits all on one day, no tests, CI or releases. The author calls it a demo and points to a sister project (nanojev_mcp) for local use.

The hard-coded question set targets a generic agent loop (support-ticket style task_type). There is nothing specific to coding workflows such as tests, diffs, git or refactors, so it would rarely add value in daily development.
gh-wr0x00-jev-mcp.verdict: Do not use as is. It does not match the real Jev/OpenRouter API, the shipped config is broken, and it has no hooks or skills, so Claude Code would never call it automatically. At most it is a source of question templates (route/gate/verify) to port into a purpose-built hook or a small MCP server that calls openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions.

interface.name: evaluate (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Takes state (string, object or array) and a questions map with up to 16 typed questions (noul, choice with 1-255 options, score with 2-10 levels). Returns typed probabilities, confidence and usage. Marked readOnlyHint and openWorldHint. Source: internal/mcp/tool.go:31-110.

interface.name: select_evidence (MCP tool, only with --enable-selection)
interface.purpose: Takes a task and up to 16 text items. One paid call classifies each as relevant, irrelevant or uncertain. Items are dropped only when P(irrelevant) is at least 0.90. Source: internal/mcp/selection.go:33-100.

interface.name: MCP server instructions (initialize result)
interface.purpose: About 1.2k characters of usage guidance injected into the client (tool.go:44-52, server.go:627). Tells the model to call evaluate only when bounded semantic uncertainty affects a decision.

interface.name: Pi extension adapters/pi/jev.ts
interface.purpose: Registers the Pi tools evaluate and, with --jev-select-root, select_context (line-range retrieval from committed public-files.json, with a paid-call budget of 1-3 per session). Hooks pi.on session_start and session_shutdown. Pi-specific and unusable in Claude Code (jev.ts:3191-3314).

interface.name: CLI flags
interface.purpose: Only --key-file <abs path> and --enable-selection. No help, version, installer or self-update (main.go:60-70, 130-170).

gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.license: MIT (LICENSE, plus NOTICE crediting the upstream itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp v0.4.1)
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.runtime: Go (go.mod says go 1.26, Makefile pins go1.27.1) for the stdio server. Node 22.19 or newer and Pi 0.85 or newer for the adapter. Release artifacts are darwin arm64 and amd64 only. No Linux binary, and no CI (no .github directory).
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.install: No installer by design. The documented path is a manual copy of a darwin release binary plus jev.ts into ~/.pi/agent/extensions. For Claude Code on Linux you would need `git clone`, install Go 1.27.1, edit the Makefile or run `go build ./cmd/jev-mcp`, write the key to a 0600 file, then `claude mcp add jev -- ~/.local/bin/jev-mcp`. That MCP wiring is untested and unsupported by the README.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.tests: Extensive offline tests: Go unit, fuzz and race tests (internal/mcp, internal/typesafe, cmd), plus Pi and TypeScript tests, stdio smoke tests and export tests. Only invalid calls are tested against the real binary. There is no CI. The README admits workflow value, cost savings and 'the model will pick this tool' are not established. I did not run any of it.
security: Key handling is unusually careful: file only, mode exactly 0600, owned by the user, opened with O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK and checked via the descriptor (key_unix.go). It is never read from env or argv, so it cannot leak to `ps`. This conflicts with an OpenRouter workflow, where the key normally comes from OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Network is fixed to one URL. Proxy is nil, so HTTPS_PROXY is ignored. Redirects are not followed, so the bearer token cannot be replayed elsewhere (client.go:57-88). TLS 1.2 or newer. Errors omit HTTP bodies.
Resource bounds: 16 questions, 64 KiB request, 128 KiB response, depth 8, 30s deadline, at most 2 retries and only on 429/529. Child env is HOME, PATH and LANG only.
No postinstall, curl|sh, telemetry or self-update. Zero Go dependencies. Dev-only npm deps are pinned. The MCP server runs no shell.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are structured numbers only, with no free text, so the surface is small. The model does choose which state to send out, and the tool description tells it not to include secrets, but nothing enforces that on the server side.

Provenance risk: 1 author, 0 stars, 10 days old, history-free 'public snapshot' export. Release binaries are darwin-only with SHA256SUMS, unsigned. You would have to audit the code and compile it yourself. The maintainer uses 'ACTION-7' and 'CONTROL-N' internal tags. No SECURITY policy.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts in evaluate.state and the question instructions and criteria, or the items of select_evidence. In practice that means code snippets, diffs, logs, file excerpts and issue or commit text the model chooses to send. This goes to api.typesafe.ai, a direct TypeSafe account, not OpenRouter, so it means a second vendor relationship. That matters for client projects under NDA. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background. Each call is paid and transmits the content. There is no telemetry, and jev.ts in Pi may retain tool args and results in the session transcript.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fails closed and per call. Any error, timeout (30s API deadline, 40s tool-call bound in server.go:73), invalid response, model mismatch or bad distribution returns an MCP tool error (isError) with a generic message. It never returns a guess. The main model sees the error and continues without Jev, so nothing hangs the session. But an invalid or missing key file makes the server exit at startup (main.go run() returns a 'credential:' error), which shows as a failed MCP server. One in-flight evaluation per runner, no queue. The 30s worst case blocks that turn.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate), or 2 with --enable-selection. Approximate token counts are chars/4 estimates. evaluate description is about 1.0k chars and the schema about 2.3k chars, roughly 800-900 tokens. The server 'instructions' are about 1.5k chars, roughly 400 tokens. That is about 1.2-1.4k tokens per session for evaluate alone. With select_evidence add about 2.2k chars, roughly 550 tokens. Claude Code may defer MCP tool schemas via tool search, which would cut the schema part. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero when unused. Per call, one round trip to api.typesafe.ai. Jev is claimed at 70-500 ms, plus roughly 1-3 s of model time to write the structured question payload, plus MCP overhead. The 30s deadline and 429/529 retry backoff bound the worst case. Selection only saves tokens if it runs before the main model reads the corpus, which the README itself notes.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. Claude decides whether to call the MCP tool, guided by the tool description and server instructions. Nothing is deterministic (no hook, skill trigger or proxy). The README says 'the model will pick this tool' is not established. The tool description is written defensively ('Do not call it merely to confirm your conclusion'), which likely lowers the call rate in Claude Code. This does not meet the user's 'automatic without prompting' requirement, except in the weak sense that the tool is always visible.
pros: The best-engineered security posture among Jev clients I can imagine: 0600 key file with O_NOFOLLOW, key never in argv or env, fixed endpoint, no redirects, no proxy, bounded sizes, fail-closed validation, and zero Go dependencies (only stdlib).
Small, readable Go server: about 2.9k non-test lines of Go, easy to audit and fork. The wire schema (state, model, questions) matches System One, so an OpenRouter port is a small patch.
The MCP server is a real, standard stdio server (initialize, tools/list, tools/call), so it can be registered in Claude Code with `claude mcp add` even though only Pi is documented.
Honest README: says workflow value is unproven, lists limits, warns against using Jev for authorization, arithmetic or code generation. Tool descriptions steer away from misuse.
MIT license. Only 1-2 tools, so context cost is modest (about 1.3k tokens). Extensive offline test suite including fuzzing.
cons: No OpenRouter support by design. The README says 'No OpenRouter... no endpoint or model override' and 'alternate providers' are out of scope. It requires a TypeSafe direct account and key, which contradicts the requirement to use the OpenRouter-hosted Jev. An OpenRouter port means maintaining a fork, and the model-pin validator would also need patching (response.go:134).

Target is the Pi agent, not Claude Code. The main adapter is Pi-only and no Claude Code config, plugin, hook or skill ships. Release binaries are darwin only, so on Linux you must build with Go 1.27.1 yourself (the Makefile targets darwin only).

Cannot be automatic. It is a model-discretion tool with a defensive description, and the README says whether the model will pick it is not established. There are no hooks and no deterministic trigger, so it does not meet the 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so' requirement.
Key must be a 0600 file. No env var support, so the OPENROUTER_API_KEY workflow does not fit. Starting the server without the file makes it exit and show as a failed MCP server.
Immature and unproven: 7 commits over 2 days, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no CI, history-free public export, no Linux artifacts, no evidence of real-world value or cost savings.

Data egress to a second vendor (TypeSafe) whenever it is called. The model decides what code or context to send, which is a concern for client projects. There are still no hard guards beyond a prompt-level 'no secrets' rule.

Judgments are only as good as the state Claude writes into the question, and Claude must spend output tokens composing state and rubrics. That can cost more than a direct main-model decision for the small coding tasks Jev suits.
gh-resumocast-jev-mcp.verdict: A well-built but Pi-first, TypeSafe-direct-only, model-discretion MCP with no OpenRouter path and no Claude Code integration, so it fails the two core requirements: OpenRouter hosting and automatic invocation. Worth reading as a reference implementation (its key handling and validators are good) or forking as a base. I would not install it as-is for daily Claude Code use.

gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.name: fast-facts/jev-mcp
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Go stdio MCP server (about 2.9k lines incl. tests, single dependency: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.8.0) that wraps TypeSafe's System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone). It exposes 7 tools. Each is a prebuilt "recipe" of Noul/Choice questions plus local threshold policy: jev_verify (claims vs evidence), jev_screen (prompt-injection/substance/relevance gate for untrusted text), jev_find (rank candidates), jev_pick (choose one or none), jev_extract (pick a verbatim span), jev_classify (batch classify items), jev_ask (raw noul/choice/score escape hatch). Thresholds live in the server (internal/policy), and Jev only returns probabilities.

providerSupport.evidence: internal/config/config.go:9-10 DefaultModel="jev-latest", DefaultBaseURL="https://api.typesafe.ai"; config.go:21-31 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required), JEV_MCP_MODEL, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. internal/jev/types.go:10 PathSystemOne="/v1/systemone". internal/jev/client.go:284 URL = baseURL+PathSystemOne, client.go:288 header "Authorization: Bearer <key>". Request body {model,state,questions}, response {model,answers,usage} (client.go:254, 306-310). grep -i openrouter across the repo: 0 hits. AGENTS.md:128 says "No other LLM provider".
providerSupport.others: None. Only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override; no gateway-specific code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, with no code change, if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same answers shape. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (the client appends /v1/systemone, giving https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone). Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<the OpenRouter key>, since it is sent as a Bearer token. Set JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), because the default "jev-latest" is not an OpenRouter slug. I could not verify that OpenRouter's response schema matches, only the brief's claim that the endpoint exists. The env var name is misleading but works. Nothing is hard-wired to the TypeSafe host.

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Raw escape hatch. Takes state plus named noul/choice/score questions and returns typed answers, probabilities and usage.

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Takes claims[] and evidence, and returns a verdict per claim (verified/contradicted/unsupported) with probabilities, confidence and an auto-vs-review action (auto_accept default 0.8).

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Takes untrusted text and an optional purpose. Returns injection/substance/relevance probabilities and a recommendation of pass/review/block/skip (block_at 0.75, review_at 0.25).

interface.name: jev_find
interface.purpose: Takes a query and up to 250 candidates (2000-char truncation) and returns the top_k ranked hits plus an exists Noul.

interface.name: jev_pick
interface.purpose: Picks at most one candidate or none (Choice with a none option, plus an exists Noul).

interface.name: jev_extract
interface.purpose: Picks one verbatim span from a shortlist, copied and never invented, or null.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Takes items and a class catalog. Returns a class per item with distribution, margin and auto/review decision (0.85 top probability, 0.5 margin).

security: MIT license (LICENSE present).

API key comes from the environment (config.go:21) and is sent only as a Bearer header (client.go:288), so it is not in argv if configured via .mcp.json env. The README example does show putting the key inline in the client config JSON.

No shell execution, no file access and no telemetry found in internal/ or cmd/. The only outbound network call is client.go:290 to baseURL+/v1/systemone. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is arbitrary and unvalidated (an env override, so low risk).

Response body capped at 1 MiB (client.go:295). Error bodies are truncated to 200 chars and returned to the model (client.go:339-347), which is a minor injection or leak surface only if the endpoint is malicious.

Prompt-injection surface: user query/purpose strings are string-concatenated into Jev question text (e.g. pick.go:124, screen.go:386). Output is only numeric or ID-constrained (choice validated against the id set via policy.AcceptPick), so tool output cannot carry attacker prose. jev_screen is a classifier that could be evaded, and it is not a security boundary.

Install path is `go run github.com/fast-facts/jev-mcp/cmd/jev-mcp@latest`. This compiles unpinned, mutable latest code from a 0-star personal repo on every cold start, a supply-chain risk. Pin a tag or commit and build a binary after reading the code.
No prebuilt release binaries (v1.0.1 has 0 assets), so Go is required. go.mod declares go 1.27.1.

Release workflow is a daily cron running `npx semantic-release` with contents/issues/PR write permissions, which is standard, and it only affects the upstream repo. No install scripts affect the user.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what the model passes in a tool call goes to api.typesafe.ai, or to openrouter.ai if repointed. That is candidate texts (up to 250 items, each truncated to 2000 chars, so code snippets, file paths, error text), claims and evidence, text to screen (fetched web pages), classify items, and the query/purpose strings. Nothing is collected automatically: no diffs, tool outputs or prompts are captured unless Claude chooses to pass them as arguments. The server has no hooks or proxy, so it sees nothing else. Under OpenRouter, provider logging and retention settings would apply to those payloads. That matters for client code, so review the data policy before pointing it at client projects.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level. Failures return an MCP tool error to Claude, which can just continue, and nothing blocks the session. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the process exit with log.Fatal at startup (main.go:15), so the MCP server shows as failed to connect, and Claude Code continues without it. HTTP client timeout is 30s per attempt (client.go:230). Up to 3 attempts (maxAttempts=3) on network errors and on 408/429/500/502/503/529, with backoff of 1s and 2s or Retry-After. Worst case is about 93s of blocking on a hung endpoint, which is far above the claimed 70-500ms. There is no circuit breaker and no configurable timeout. A dead or slow Jev stalls whichever turn calls it, but only when Claude decides to call.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.contextCost: 7 tools. Descriptions total about 2.1k chars, and the JSON schemas from struct tags (38 jsonschema annotations, nested Candidate/Class/Item objects, plus `any`-typed fields) probably add another 4-5k chars. Estimate about 6-7k chars, or about 1.5-2k tokens of tool definitions (chars/4), cheaper if Claude Code's MCP tool search defers them. The server sets no MCP "instructions" field (server.go:19 passes nil options). No hooks, so zero injected text per turn. Per-call output is small numeric JSON, though jev_find echoes candidate text back in top hits.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill or proxy. Claude will call jev_* only if it judges the tool descriptions relevant. The descriptions are generic ("Rank candidates...", "Judge fetched or external text...") and are not written to trigger in a coding workflow. Meeting "never say use jev" would need extra glue, such as a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a PostToolUse/PreToolUse hook that calls the tools. Nothing here provides that. The only naturally auto-triggerable tool is jev_screen after WebFetch, but it needs explicit steering.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Only on turns where Claude calls a jev_* tool. That costs one extra model tool-use round trip (seconds of Opus latency) plus Jev's claimed 70-500ms HTTP time, and up to about 93s in the worst failure case. No overhead on other turns.
pros: Cleanest technical fit for OpenRouter of the Jev MCPs. Base URL and model are env-configurable and the path is /v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest should work with zero code changes (unverified end to end).
Small, readable and auditable: about 1.5k non-test lines, one dependency (go-sdk), no shell exec, no file access, no telemetry. The 250-item and 2000-char caps are enforced (candidates.go).

Recipes encode sensible policy locally (none options, an exists Noul guarding against a confident wrong top hit, thresholds and auto/review split, ID-set validation of Jev's choice). This is better than a bare passthrough.
jev_screen (prompt-injection gate on fetched content) and jev_pick/jev_find (which file or which error among N) map onto real coding-agent needs and cost about $0.04 per 1M input tokens.

Failures are tool errors, not session blockers, and the response body is capped. Unit tests cover client, policy and each tool, there is a CI build/test on PRs, and live tests are skipped without a key.
Stdio server that adds no per-turn hook latency and does not disturb existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.
cons: Very young and unproven. Created 2026-09-18, 5 commits in the clone (3 by one author, 2 by renovate), 2 contributors, 0 stars, 0 forks, no description or topics, v1.0.1 published 2026-09-29. The tool set could change quickly.

Not automatic. It is just 7 MCP tools relying on Claude's discretion, with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, no server instructions, and descriptions written for generic agents. It won't meet the goal of Claude using it without prompting unless extra glue is added.

OpenRouter is not officially supported. The docs and AGENTS.md say "TypeSafe key only / No other LLM provider", the env var names are TypeSafe-specific, and the response-schema match with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified. The default model id "jev-latest" would 404 there without an override.

Runtime is awkward. Go must be installed, there are no release binaries, and the documented `go run ...@latest` compiles unpinned code at every cold start, which suits neither a client-project machine nor fast MCP startup. Building a pinned binary is the safe route.
Weak failure bounds. The 30s timeout and 3 retries are hard-coded, so a slow Jev can stall a turn for about 93s, against the claimed 70-500ms.

Limited daily value for an Opus 5.5 workflow. Candidates and results still flow through Claude's context, so there are no token savings. The tools are useful mainly for ranking or classification of shortlists and for a screen gate, and Opus does these well by itself. jev_screen is probabilistic and shouldn't be treated as an injection defense.

Data egress. Code snippets and fetched pages pass to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) whenever the tools are used, which is a concern on client projects and would need a review of the OpenRouter data policy.
gh-fast-facts-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-built and most OpenRouter-friendly Jev MCP audited (env-configurable base URL, model and path, tiny auditable code, sensible recipes), but immature (about 12 days old, 2 contributors, 0 stars) and it only provides model-discretion tools, so automatic use needs extra steering such as a CLAUDE.md rule or skill. Use it pinned and built locally, pointed at OpenRouter after a smoke test, mainly for a jev_screen/jev_pick pattern rather than as a general integration.

gh-wahahaorg-jev-mcp.name: wahahaorg/jev-mcp
gh-wahahaorg-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Python stdio MCP server wrapping browser-use/jev-ultrafast, a web-browsing agent. It drives a Jev-owned background Chrome target for read-only product research (search, filter, extract product cards). Jev decisions go to OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set. jev_decide is a browser-less relay that takes host-supplied page elements and returns Jev's chosen operation and target element. interface.name: jev_browse(url, goal, max_steps=20)
interface.purpose: Opens a Jev-owned Chrome target and runs up to 30 browser-agent steps toward a read-only product-research goal. Returns session_id, page evidence and recent actions.

interface.name: jev_status(session_id)
interface.purpose: Returns URL, visible text, controls and recent actions of a live session without acting.

interface.name: jev_extract_products(session_id)
interface.purpose: Best-effort extraction of visible product cards (name, price, rating, details, link).

interface.name: jev_stop(session_id)
interface.purpose: Closes the Chrome target and drops the session.

interface.name: jev_decide(goal, elements[], page_url, page_title, page_text, operations)
interface.purpose: Relay mode with no browser. Sends host-supplied UI elements to OpenRouter Decisions and returns Jev's choice of CLICK/TYPE_TEXT/SELECT/DONE/BLOCKED plus the target element index (src/jev_mcp/decisions.py:234-301). Elements are capped at 80 and page text at 6000 chars.

security: MIT license; single author (xsz), 5 commits, all on 2026-09-20; 1 star, 1 fork, no releases, no CI, no .github directory.

The OpenRouter key is read from the environment or a .env file via `uv run --env-file .env`, so it is not in argv. README tells users to keep it out of the committed MCP config. A relative .env lookup depends on cwd, so an absolute --directory is needed.

The key is copied into TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY by os.environ.setdefault (decisions.py:131), so the same OpenRouter key is also sent to the text-model endpoint, which is configurable. If TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL points elsewhere (upstream default is api.deepseek.com), the key goes to that host.

Fetches web pages in a real Chrome via browser-harness and remote debugging, so web content is an indirect prompt-injection surface. Mitigations are regex blocklists for goals and actions (safety.py:15-51). They are English/Chinese only and easy to bypass, and they never touch jev_decide, which returns hints only.

Depends on an unreviewed git-pinned dependency (jev-ultrafast at commit 1231850, from browser-use, 21k stars, created 2026-09-16) plus browser-harness. Installing needs `uv sync`, which builds git and PyPI dependencies. No npm postinstall and no curl|sh. I found no telemetry strings in jev-ultrafast Python sources or the uv.lock; browser-harness itself was not audited.

The Chrome CDP target can run with the user's Chrome profile permissions; README says it creates its own background target. A stopped or leaked session leaves a Chrome target open, and sessions live only in memory.
Static analysis only: no code was run. Tests use fakes (6 test functions in tests/test_service.py); there are no tests for the network layer.
gh-wahahaorg-jev-mcp.dataEgress: jev_decide sends the goal text, page URL, title, up to 6000 chars of page text and up to 80 elements (index, role, label, value) that Claude puts in the tool call, to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. Nothing else is read from disk automatically. jev_browse also sends the visited page's DOM snapshot, text, element labels and the last 10 actions to OpenRouter, and goal text plus field context to the TEXT_MODEL endpoint (OpenRouter by default). The whole `request` body is echoed in the decision dict returned to the agent. No code, diffs or tool outputs leave the machine unless Claude passes them as elements or page_text.
