The variable name TYPESAFE_API_KEY is misleading, because it would hold an OpenRouter key. TYPESAFE_API_KEY is required (main.go:177), so the server exits at startup if it is unset.

interface.name: ask
interface.purpose: Batch several typed questions (noul, choice, score) against one state in one request. Returns an answer per id plus 'reliable' flags and the list of unreliable ids. Preferred path.

interface.name: choose
interface.purpose: Pick one option from a set (object name->description or array of names). Returns choice, per-option probabilities, confidence, reliable.

interface.name: score
interface.purpose: Rate on an ordered rubric of 2-10 levels. Returns the probability-weighted score, legend, probabilities, confidence.

interface.name: noul
interface.purpose: Yes/no. Returns P(yes) 0-1 and a yes flag against a threshold (default 0.5). No confidence value.

interface.name: SKILL.md (jev-mcp)
interface.purpose: Skill whose description triggers when the agent faces a closed-set decision such as routing, picking a file, grading risk/severity, triaging logs/diffs, or filtering noise. It tells the agent to prefer batched ask and keep arithmetic in code.

gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.lastCommit: 2026-09-22 (5a1ba95, 'Mark the client as unofficial (#4)'). One author under two git identities, 'Fran' and 'fran'.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.runtime: Go 1.23+ (go.mod says go 1.23). There is no prebuilt release, so you must run make build (CGO_ENABLED=0 go build) yourself. It has zero third-party dependencies. The binary is stdio JSON-RPC, MCP protocol 2024-11-05.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/jfrader/jev-mcp && make install (builds and copies to ~/.local/bin/jev-mcp; requires Go). Then run: claude mcp add jev -s user -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY -e TYPESAFE_MODEL=jev-latest -- ~/.local/bin/jev-mcp. Optionally copy SKILL.md to ~/.claude/skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md. Note that -e values are stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.tests: 9 offline Go unit tests in main_test.go (handshake, batched ask, plain-name options, validation, oversize state, 429 retry, 401 message, 529 retry, config requires key). They use a mock HTTP server. The CI workflow .github/workflows/validate.yml runs gofmt, go vet, build and test. I did not run any of it, per the static-only rule. There are no releases or tags.
security: API key is read from the environment only (main.go:173), never from argv, so it does not appear in the process list. With claude mcp add -e the value is written in plaintext to ~/.claude.json; use a wrapper script that sources a 0600 file to avoid that.

No shell execution or os/exec, no telemetry, no file reads or writes, and no network calls except the single POST to baseURL/v1/systemone. There is no install script or postinstall; the only build step is make build.

TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is unrestricted (any http or https URL), so a poisoned env would send the key and state elsewhere. That is normal for env-configured clients, and http:// is allowed, so keys could go in cleartext if misconfigured.

The tool result is Jev's typed JSON only (no free text), so returned data has a small prompt-injection surface. The input surface is the state that Claude chooses to pass, which can contain untrusted repo content. SKILL.md itself warns that adversarial content can steer answers, so Jev output is a hint and not a guard.
Error bodies are truncated to 300 chars (main.go:257-259) and returned to the model. This is low risk.

Supply chain: brand-new repo, 0 stars, one anonymous-ish maintainer, no releases, and you must build from source. Pin a commit hash and review the ~800-line main.go before building; I read all of it and found nothing malicious.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the 'state' argument plus the question text and criteria. This is an arbitrary JSON or text payload of up to 120 KB, and it could be code snippets, diffs, logs, or file contents that Claude chooses to include. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background, because it is a pure request/response server that only acts on tool calls. It goes to the configured base URL: OpenRouter if you set it, otherwise api.typesafe.ai. With OpenRouter, that traffic is subject to OpenRouter's data policies and to TypeSafe as the model provider. The README says TypeSafe does not train on customer data, which is unverified. For client projects, Claude may forward client code or secrets unless an instruction or a hook stops it. The existing secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__*, so it would not scan Jev payloads, and a matcher for mcp__jev__.* would need adding.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level, because Claude Code just sees an isError tool result and continues. The HTTP client timeout is 30 s (main.go:36), with up to 3 attempts on 429/529 only, and backoff of 0.5 s then 1 s or Retry-After capped at 15 s. Worst case is roughly 30 s per attempt on a network hang, but the retry only triggers on 429/529, so a hang fails after 30 s without retrying. Other 5xx errors are not retried. The process exits at startup if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset, which shows up as a failed MCP connection, but Claude Code itself works normally. It is a synchronous single-threaded loop (run(), one request at a time), and there is no circuit breaker. A slow Jev blocks the server, but not other tools.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero for turns that don't call it, since there are no hooks and no proxying. Each call adds the Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms end to end; unverified) plus MCP stdio overhead of a few ms, and the model must spend an extra tool-call turn, which likely costs 1-3 s of model latency for the call and result. Batching via ask keeps this to one round trip. Worst case is 30 s on a hang.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.contextCost: 4 tools. The tool definitions (names, descriptions and JSON schemas in main.go, about lines 668-735) are about 6-8k characters, which I estimate at roughly 1.5-2.2k tokens when loaded. Claude Code's tool search defers MCP tool schemas, so only the names sit in context until a tool is needed. The server sends no MCP 'instructions' field (initialize returns only protocolVersion, capabilities and serverInfo, main.go:410-415). There are no hooks and no injected text. If SKILL.md is installed, add roughly 100 tokens for the always-listed description, and about 1.4k tokens when the skill is invoked (5.4k chars). Overall a low context footprint.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model discretion only, via the MCP tool descriptions and the optional SKILL.md description trigger. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy, and no forced trigger. Opus decides case by case whether a closed-set decision merits a Jev call, and in practice it will rarely choose to call an external classifier for decisions it can make itself, unless CLAUDE.md contains explicit routing rules. That is the weakness against the user's 'automatic' requirement: it is only as automatic as the model's own habit, and a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge is needed to make it reliable.
pros: OpenRouter works with config only. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api produces the exact /v1/systemone path that OpenRouter documents for the TypeSafe SDKs (main.go:221 versus typesafe-sdk.md). The request schema matches, and bare model IDs such as jev-latest are mapped to typesafe/ by OpenRouter.

Small, auditable and dependency-free. It is one 822-line Go file with no exec, no filesystem access and no telemetry, so I could read all of it. The key comes from env, not argv, and the binary is trivially pinned.

Well-shaped tool surface. Batched ask amortises one request over many questions, and the reliable/min_confidence flag gives the model an act-or-escalate signal. Local guards include a 120 KB state limit, validation, and retry with Retry-After.
Low context cost: 4 tools, no MCP instructions field, no hooks, and it adds nothing to turns that don't use it. Failures are non-blocking (fail-open).

SKILL.md is a well-written trigger for closed-set decisions and includes honest limits (not a calculator, literal, steerable, English-strongest), which suits Jev's real strengths. The tests are offline and cover the retry and 401 paths.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain tool and skill, so Claude Code calls it only if the model decides to. Opus 5.5 can already route, classify and triage in its head, so the tool will likely sit unused unless you add CLAUDE.md rules or a hook. There is nothing deterministic in this repo that fires it.

Very immature: 0 stars, 6 commits in 1 day, one author (git identities 'Fran' and 'fran'), no releases, no tags, no prebuilt binaries. It needs a Go toolchain to build. It is explicitly unofficial and was born as an OpenCode integration ('Initial commit: ... for opencode'), so it has not been tested against Claude Code (README lists OpenCode, Claude Desktop and Cursor). The tools are standard MCP and should work.

Leaks nothing on its own, but the payload is model-chosen, so client code or secrets can flow to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. Your secret guard does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and you would need an extra PreToolUse matcher.
The env var naming is confusing (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holds an OpenRouter key). claude mcp add -e writes the key in plaintext into ~/.claude.json, so use a wrapper script instead.

Built for System One's typed decisions only. It does not use OpenRouter's /alpha/decisions API or the Jev Router, and it has no code awareness, so 'which file holds the bug' still depends on Claude passing sufficient state. State beyond 32k tokens or with unrelated detail degrades accuracy, per its own docs. Value versus just letting Opus decide is unproven, with Theo's 'flash router' claim untested.
Sync and single-threaded with a 30 s timeout and no circuit breaker. A stall blocks the Jev tools and adds an extra model turn per decision, which can cost more time than it saves.
gh-jfrader-jev-mcp.verdict: The best plain MCP building block found for Jev: tiny, readable, and switchable to OpenRouter with three env vars and no code changes. It is only model-discretion, though, so on its own it will not meet the 'Claude Code uses it automatically' goal. Use it as the tool layer, build from a pinned commit after review, and pair it with CLAUDE.md routing rules or a hook (plus an mcp__jev__ matcher on the secret guard) to make invocation reliable.

gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.name: echohello-dev/jev-mcp
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Tiny hand-rolled stdio MCP server (about 500 lines of TypeScript, no deps, no MCP SDK) that wraps the Jev Decisions API in five tools: jev_verify, jev_classify, jev_screen, jev_decide and jev_extract. Each tool builds a {state, questions} body, POSTs it to the provider, and returns the probabilities as JSON text. The optional fail_on argument turns a matching result into isError:true. It is a manual, model-discretion tool: nothing in the repo makes Claude Code call it on its own.

providerSupport.evidence: src/provider.ts:13-14 OPENROUTER_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and model '~typesafe/jev-latest'. src/provider.ts:20-22 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY. src/provider.ts:36-40 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' with body {state, questions, model}. Routing at provider.ts:17-22: TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins if set, otherwise OpenRouter. The TypeSafe URL (provider.ts:11) is https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with model 'jev-latest'. That host is unverified and does not match the console.typesafe.ai host in the brief, so TypeSafe-direct is 'partial'. I checked the wire contract against the OpenRouter API reference (alphadecisions endpoint). Request shape {model,state,questions{type,instructions,criteria}} and response shape {answers{type,choice|noul|score,probabilities,confidence}} both match, apart from the score-range and noul-confidence issues listed in cons.
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe direct only (unverified URL). It does not call OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone. There are no other gateways, and the OpenRouter URL is hard-coded, not overridable by env.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter works today by setting only OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Pinning typesafe/jev-1.13 instead of ~typesafe/jev-latest is a one-line edit at provider.ts:14.

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Takes claim and evidence, asks one noul question ('supports_claim'), and returns {supports, noul, confidence}. fail_on 'true' or 'false' returns isError when the result goes that way (handlers.ts:190-208).

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Takes state, choices[] and optional criteria{}, asks one choice question, and returns {type, choice, probabilities, confidence}. fail_on names a label that triggers isError (handlers.ts:210-226).

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Takes text and asks two questions: a relevance choice (default relevant/off_topic/suspicious) and a risk score over 4 levels (safe/low/medium/high). fail_on{relevance,min_risk} triggers isError (handlers.ts:228-259).

interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Takes state and options{key:description} (at least 2), asks one choice question, and returns the choice plus probabilities (handlers.ts:261-279).

interface.name: jev_extract
interface.purpose: Takes state and fields[] and asks one noul question per field ('does the state mention field X'). It only detects presence and does not extract values (handlers.ts:281-301).

gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.runtime: TypeScript, built with Bun into dist/index.js and run with node (package.json engines says bun>=1.1). No runtime dependencies. Hand-rolled JSON-RPC over stdio, protocol version 2024-11-05, and it only handles initialize, tools/list, tools/call and ping.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.install: The package is NOT on npm: `npm view @echohello/jev-mcp` returns E404. The docs/brief.md line about `npx -y @echohello/jevmcp` is aspirational. To install you clone the repo, run `bun install && bun run build`, and register `node /path/dist/index.js` with env OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Alternatively, download dist/index.js from the release v2026.09.23 (release.yml uploads it). Building needs bun, which the user has not listed in their tooling.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.tests: None. There are no test files, `bun test` has nothing to run, and CI (release.yml) runs only on tag pushes with typecheck + build. There is no PR CI. Repo activity: 3 commits, 1 contributor (the 3rd commit is co-authored by 'opencode', so the code looks AI-generated), 0 stars, 0 issues, 1 PR, 1 release. The repo is 9 days old.
security: The API key is passed through the MCP `env` block, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. It does end up in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or settings.
No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry. The only network call is the provider fetch (provider.ts:34), and there are no runtime dependencies to attack.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The server returns only numbers and labels, but a classify/decide choice string comes from the caller's own input. Provider error text (first 200 chars) is echoed back in the tool result (provider.ts:45), which is a minor channel.

The build uses `bun-version: latest` and softprops/action-gh-release@v2 with unpinned tags, so the supply chain is weak. The release artifact is not signed, and there is no npm provenance because it is not on npm.
No input validation beyond the JSON schema shown to the model. Args are cast blindly (index.ts:418-426), so malformed args cause a caught TypeError and an isError result, not a crash.
Unparseable JSON lines are silently dropped with no response (index.ts:366-369).
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Everything the model puts in `state`, `claim`/`evidence`, `text` or `options` is sent verbatim to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. With this server that means whatever Claude Code chooses to pass: code snippets, diffs, file contents, fetched web content or tool outputs. The server sees nothing else. It does not read files and does not hook into Claude Code events. Key and model ID go in headers and body. OpenRouter/TypeSafe may log requests, and the user works on client projects, so client-confidentiality and zero-data-retention settings matter. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY would silently reroute traffic to TypeSafe direct.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft per call. Any HTTP error, timeout or parse error is caught and returned as a tool result with isError:true and {error: message}. Claude Code sees an error and can continue. The default timeout is 30 s, up to 120 s per call via timeout_ms (tools.ts:75). That is generous compared with the claimed 70-500 ms latency, so a hung provider could stall a turn for 30 s. There is no retry, no circuit breaker and no cache. A missing key gives a JSON-RPC -32603 error on each call, not a startup failure (the server starts fine and only logs to stderr). Caveat: isError is used both for real failures and for a matched fail_on, so the model cannot tell an outage from a verdict without parsing the message.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: No cost unless Claude calls a tool. Each call adds one network round trip (a claimed 70-500 ms through OpenRouter, unverified) plus the model turn needed to decide and read the result. Node startup for the MCP server is about 100 ms once per session. Nothing sits in the critical path of ordinary tool calls, because there are no hooks.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. tools.ts:59-168 defines them in about 4,000 chars of source, so the schemas the client receives come to roughly 1,000-1,300 tokens (chars/4) including the mcp__jev__ name prefixes. There is no MCP `instructions` field (index.ts:375 returns no instructions), and no hook-injected text. That is small and cheap. But the descriptions are terse and do not tell Claude WHEN to use the tools, which matters for auto-use.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, no skill, no server `instructions`, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no proxy. Opus will call jev_* only if it judges a tool description relevant, and the descriptions ('Decide whether the evidence supports the claim...') are generic. In practice Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for a probabilistic classifier when it can just reason, so it would be used only occasionally. Deterministic auto-use would require adding your own hooks, a CLAUDE.md rule, or a skill on top of this server.
pros: Works with OpenRouter today: it uses the right endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), model ~typesafe/jev-latest and Bearer auth, and the request and response shapes match the OpenRouter API reference.
Very small (about 500 lines) and easy to audit or fork. No dependencies, no telemetry, no shell execution, and the key travels via env, not argv.
Cheap on context: 5 tools, about 1k tokens, no injected instructions.
The jev_screen idea (relevance plus risk of fetched content) and fail_on gating are a sensible fit for guarding web or MCP content. It is a useful pattern to copy into a hook.
MIT license. It is a good reference implementation of the wire contract, and forking to add a hook wrapper is easy.
cons: Cannot trigger automatically, which was the user's core requirement. It ships only MCP tools, with no hook, skill or usage instructions, so Claude would use it only if it decides to.
Not installable the easy way: it is not on npm (E404) and needs bun to build. The docs/brief.md claim of `npx -y @echohello/jevmcp` is false today.
Very immature: 9 days old, 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, and no tests. The last commit was refactored with an AI agent. CI runs only on tag push, so nothing runs before a release.

Concrete bugs: jev_screen sends 4 risk levels (safe/low/medium/high, handlers.ts:243), so the score runs 0..3. But the tool description and schema say '0..2' and cap min_risk at maximum 2 (tools.ts:104,119). A 'high' verdict can never be gated by schema-valid input. jev_extract only tests for field presence (the brief promised verbatim extraction). It reads noul confidence, which the API does not return (always undefined).
The state input is typed as a plain string only. The API also accepts an object or array, so structured app state has to be stringified by the caller.

The TypeSafe-direct URL (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) is unverified. If the user later sets TYPESAFE_API_KEY, traffic silently switches provider. The OpenRouter URL and model are hard-coded, so there is no env override, and floating on ~typesafe/jev-latest can change behavior without notice.
Default 30 s timeout with no retry. isError conflates outages with fail_on verdicts. Key in plaintext in the MCP config.
Generic Jev caveats also apply: alpha endpoint, no reasoning trace, and Jev is a classifier and not a coding aid. Of the five tools, only screen/verify have any plausible daily coding value.
gh-echohello-dev-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, minimal and correct-enough OpenRouter wrapper, but it is only five passive tools, so Claude Code will almost never use it without being told, which fails the 'automatic' requirement. Treat it as reference code for the wire contract, or fork it and pair it with hooks and a CLAUDE.md rule. It is not worth adopting as-is, given no npm package, no tests and a few bugs.

interface.name: jev_ask (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Arbitrary state (string/JSON) + map of choice/score/noul questions -> raw JSON response from System One; returned as pretty-printed JSON text. Accepts optional model.

interface.name: jev_health (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models on the configured endpoint to confirm reachability and list models.

interface.name: hooks/pretooluse-guardrail.mjs (PreToolUse, matcher Bash)
interface.purpose: Regex pre-filter for high-stakes commands; if matched sends the full command to Jev with risk (safe/moderate/dangerous) and needs_human questions; emits deny (dangerous, conf>=0.6) or ask (moderate/needs_human>=0.6); otherwise silent. 8s timeout, fail-open.

interface.name: hooks/stop-guardrail.mjs (Stop)
interface.purpose: Sends the entire last assistant message to Jev every turn for quality and accuracy score (0-2); shows summary via systemMessage, appends JSONL (incl. cwd, session_id, 200-char message preview) to ~/.claude/jev-quality-log.jsonl; macOS-only osascript notification; never blocks (SHOULD_BLOCK=false).

Unvetted single-author 0-star repo created 7 days before audit: supply-chain risk for client work; must be read/pinned before installing (small, ~500 lines so easy to audit).
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.dataEgress: MCP: whatever Claude puts into jev_ask state/questions (arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, tool output - model discretion) goes to JEV_BASE_URL (OpenRouter/TypeSafe). PreToolUse hook: full Bash command string, only for regex-matched high-stakes commands (may embed tokens/URLs/creds in args). Stop hook: the entire last assistant message of EVERY turn (can include code, file paths, client details). No egress of user prompts or files by the hooks themselves. On OpenRouter this also passes through OpenRouter's logging policy. Nothing else leaves the machine (no telemetry).
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.failureMode: Hooks fail open: catch -> failOpen() emits systemMessage + additionalContext and exit 0 (lib.mjs:197-205); 8s timeout via AbortController. Bug risk: failOpen emits hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext even for the Stop event, which the author's own comment (stop-guardrail.mjs:191-195) says forces Claude to continue another turn, so an unreachable endpoint / 4xx (e.g. message exceeding 32k context, missing key) could trigger extra continuation turns after every stop (stop_hook_active guard stops loops but wastes a turn). Also uncaught TypeError if response shape differs (e.g. answers.risk undefined) is inside try so fail-open too. MCP tool: errors returned as isError text; no timeout, so a slow endpoint stalls the call. Also SDK-level MCP connect failure just drops the tools.
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: MCP: only when Claude chooses to call it (claimed 70-500ms + tool round trip). PreToolUse: zero for non-matching commands (regex only, but a node process spawn ~50ms per Bash call), +0.1-0.5s (up to 8s on timeout) for matched ones. Stop hook: node spawn + one Jev call (0.1-0.5s, up to 8s on failure) at the end of every turn, plus file append; fires on every turn including trivial ones.
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.contextCost: 2 MCP tools; approx 450 tokens total (jev_ask description ~640 chars + permissive zod schema with passthrough record/union types ~700 chars; jev_health ~250 chars). No MCP server 'instructions' field. Hooks inject nothing on success except Stop systemMessage summary (display only, ~100 chars); on failure additionalContext line (~120 chars) per event.
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Mixed. jev_ask/jev_health are model-discretion MCP tools; the description tells Claude to use them for reliable classification/scoring/yes-no, but nothing in the repo tells Claude WHEN in a coding workflow, so it will rarely call it unprompted. The hooks (PreToolUse Bash for a regex set of high-stakes commands; Stop every turn) are deterministic and truly automatic, but their use cases (risk gating, self-scoring of replies) are weak fits for a classifier model and Stop scoring is purely a dashboard.
pros: Smallest possible integration: ~145-line server, env-only config, so pointing it at OpenRouter is just JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (index.ts:16-18,53), no fork needed.

Ships real deterministic hooks (settings.json snippet in README:125-145) - the only pattern in this repo that gives 'automatic' use without prompting; PreToolUse regex pre-filter keeps non-risky Bash calls at zero API cost.
Fail-open with 8s timeout in hooks (lib.mjs:168,197) so a Jev outage won't block work in bypass/auto mode; low context cost (~450 tokens, 2 tools).
Clean, readable, dependency-light hooks (.mjs, no build) that are easy to audit and adapt; permission decision output uses correct hookSpecificOutput schema and 'ask' rather than only 'deny'.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh; API key only in env.
cons: Brand-new, 0 stars, 4 commits in one day by one author, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file; not published to npm so must clone+build; package-lock.json resolves to a private Skyscanner artifactory, so npm install may break.

Zero OpenRouter awareness: no OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling, hard-coded /v1/systemone path, default model 'kev-latest'; OpenRouter compatibility relies on unverified schema equivalence and users must set three env vars correctly (wrong/missing silently falls back to localhost:8009).

Value proposition for daily coding is thin: the hooks judge shell risk (which the user's existing secret guard and Claude Code's permission system already cover; a 'DeepSeek flash router'-class classifier is a weak safety judge) and score Claude's own replies (Stop dashboard is display-only and pointless for a subscription user).

Stop hook sends every full assistant message (client code included) to a third party each turn and stores previews in an unrotated local log; no truncation for the 32k context; adds latency at every turn end; macOS notification does nothing on Linux.

Probable bug: failOpen emits additionalContext for Stop events which the author himself notes forces a continuation turn; so endpoint failures can cause an extra Claude turn (token cost) rather than a clean skip.

jev_ask is passive: tool description gives Claude no coding-specific triggers, and the schema is loose (z.record(z.any()), passthrough), so the model must invent question schemas itself; likely rarely invoked.
MCP fetch has no timeout; hook overlaps/duplicates existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard on Bash, GitNexus) adding another node spawn per Bash call.
gh-danna-zhou-jev-mcp.verdict: Tiny, readable, env-configurable reference wiring (MCP tool plus Bash risk and Stop-score hooks) that could talk to OpenRouter with just JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL, but it is a week-old zero-star POC with no tests, a possible Stop-hook failure bug, and use cases (risk-gating, self-scoring) that add little for this user. Best treated as a code template to copy and harden (custom hooks, OpenRouter endpoint, truncation) rather than installed as-is.

gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.name: minhgv/jev-mcp
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Repository-blind, read-only stdio MCP server (Node/TS, 9 tools, 8 question-pack resources) wrapping @typesafe-ai/sdk. The calling agent must pass task/observation/diff/claims as tool arguments; the server sends them to Jev as state plus typed Noul/Choice/Score questions, then maps confidences to auto|review|escalate with deterministic TypeScript policy. Also ships a git-collector CLI (context, ci-shadow, doctor, eval) that builds redacted diff bundles for a host/CI adapter. No hooks, no plugin.json, no marketplace.json, no .mcp.json; only a SKILL.md, an AGENTS.md pointer, and Cursor/Codex config examples.

providerSupport.evidence: src/config.ts:40-42 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_MCP_MODEL (default 'jev-latest'), TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. src/typesafe.ts:53-60 builds TypeSafeClient({apiKey, baseURL, defaultModel}) and calls client.systemOne(). The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:513) defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai, POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (line 554) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (line 581), default timeout 10s (518), maxRetries 2 (74). No OpenRouter string anywhere in repo or SDK. The path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API (https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> + JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) would plausibly work with zero code changes, but this was not verified live.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, config-only: base URL is env-overridable and the path is identical (/v1/systemone). Caveats: (1) the env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so an OpenRouter key would be stored under that name; (2) model IDs must be overridden to OpenRouter slugs (default 'jev-latest' is TypeSafe-native) and per-call `model` args from Claude could bypass it; (3) request/response schema parity between TypeSafe /v1/systemone and OpenRouter's is assumed, not verified in code; (4) SDK sends X-TypeSafe-* headers to OpenRouter (harmless); (5) doctor/listModels uses GET /v1/models which OpenRouter serves with a different response shape, so `doctor` will likely fail while the tools work.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only, with a mock mode (JEV_MCP_MOCK=1).

interface.name: jev_coding_loop
interface.purpose: Given task + observation, returns next (continue|retry|ask_user|stop), model_tier (cheap|standard|reasoning), focus, risk score, noul flags done_enough/needs_more_context/tests_likely_fail, and action auto|review|escalate.

interface.name: jev_review
interface.purpose: Score a diff vs the request (correctness, spec-match, test-gap, blast-radius, safe_to_apply). Accepts deprecated flat v1 input or a large v2 {context} object (manifest, sections, verification records, subject_digest sha256, provenance) that an adapter is meant to build.

interface.name: jev_assess_change_risk
interface.purpose: Security/operational/compatibility/scope/reversibility/blast-radius risk of a change from host-supplied context.

interface.name: jev_check_requirement
interface.purpose: Per-criterion covered/partial/not_covered/not_verifiable check of requirements against diff plus verification evidence.

interface.name: jev_classify_issue
interface.purpose: Category, severity, urgency, and allowlisted owner candidate for an issue.

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Per-claim verified|contradicted|unsupported against supplied evidence.

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Prompt-injection probability / substance / relevance for untrusted fetched or pasted text; recommendation pass|review|block|skip. The text to screen has to be passed as a tool argument by the model.

interface.name: jev_rank
interface.purpose: Rank a host-supplied candidate list (max 250 options, 2000 chars each).

interface.name: jev_evaluate
interface.purpose: Escape hatch: arbitrary state plus named noul/choice/score questions.

interface.name: resources jev://packs/{coding-loop,review,verify,screen,rank,change-risk,requirement,issue}
interface.purpose: Read-only question-pack definitions.

interface.name: CLI: jev-mcp doctor | eval | context | ci-shadow
interface.purpose: Debug ping, one-shot eval, git-based context-v2 collector (runs `git` via execFileSync, src/collector.ts:173), and non-blocking CI shadow evaluation.

gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript, ESM); deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod ^4. No npm publish evident and no GitHub release; install is git clone, npm install, npm run build, then point command at dist/index.js (docs/install.md).
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/minhgv/jev-mcp; cd jev-mcp; npm install; npm run build; node dist/index.js doctor; then `claude mcp add jev --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- node /abs/path/dist/index.js` (README shows OpenCode/Cursor/Codex only; docs/install.md says it works with Claude Code). Local build recommended over npx since there is no npm release.
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.tests: 14 test files, roughly 55 test cases, mock-first via JEV_MCP_MOCK=1 (src/mock.ts is a deterministic fake judge, so tests do not exercise real Jev). One opt-in live test (tests/e2e.live.test.ts). GitHub Actions ci.yml runs typecheck, biome lint and mock tests on Node 20/22. No live-calibration evidence; README itself says cost reduction is unmeasured and CI blocking stays disabled until calibrated.
security: API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header; never in argv when set via `claude mcp add --env` in config, but docs/install.md and examples/codex.config.toml also show `codex mcp add jev --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=ts_...` (key in argv/shell history) and hardcoded keys in JSON config; use an env reference instead.
SDK logger is off (logLevel 'off') and custom logger writes to stderr, so no stdout corruption or key logging observed; SDK redacts headers in debug logs.
No telemetry beyond SDK headers (User-Agent, X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime).
No shell execution in the MCP server itself; only src/collector.ts uses execFileSync('git', args) in the CLI collector path (array args, no shell). Server code does no fs reads of the repo.

Redaction (collector.ts:36-49) is regex based (PEM, Bearer, AKIA, JWT, xox, sk-/pk-/key-, ts_/gh*_, keyword=value) and applies only to the collector CLI path; direct MCP tool calls from Claude pass whatever the model puts in the arguments unredacted, so it is not a barrier for Claude Code usage. The user's existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool args (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall. scripts/checkout-d-drive.ps1 is Windows-only and irrelevant.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are typed JSON (probabilities/enums) with little free text, small injection surface. jev_screen is a probabilistic injection filter, not a guarantee. Untrusted third-party code with 1 star and a solo author; would be run locally with full user privileges, and needs a manual npm install of its dependency tree (not audited here; per hard rules nothing was executed).
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in tool arguments is POSTed to the configured base URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai; would be openrouter.ai and then routed by OpenRouter to TypeSafe): task text, observation (test output, diffs, blockers), full diffs up to 200-300k chars for jev_review (truncated to about 32k tokens by limits.ts fitState), requirement/claim text, and text under screening. State is truncated to a 32k-token budget. Nothing is read from disk by the MCP server itself. For client projects this means client code diffs and test output leave the machine to TypeSafe/OpenRouter on every call; redaction only happens if the CLI collector is used, not on MCP tool calls.
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.failureMode: Effectively fail-open for Claude Code. It is an on-demand MCP tool, not a hook or proxy. On timeout (SDK default 10 s, 2 retries with backoff, so worst case around 30 s plus backoff blocking one tool call), 4xx/5xx, or missing key, the tool handler catches the error and returns an MCP error result (server.ts toolError) that Claude can ignore. Missing key throws JevConfigError. Within tool results, malformed Jev output fails closed to 'review'/'escalate' actions and missing or truncated evidence forces 'review' (advisory only; nothing blocks Claude Code). No circuit breaker or configurable timeout env var (timeout is hard-coded to the SDK default, since typesafe.ts passes no timeout).
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.contextCost: 9 tools. Descriptions total roughly 2,000 chars. Input JSON schemas (zod converted): flat tools about 300-700 chars each (about 3.3k chars for the flat ones by my regex count), but jev_review is a union of a legacy flat schema and the v2 changeContext schema (manifest, sections, verification records, provenance, risk signals, with many nested fields), likely 4-6k chars, and jev_assess_change_risk / jev_check_requirement probably reuse the context schema too. Estimate about 3-5k tokens of always-loaded tool definitions (fewer if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch as in this session). No MCP server 'instructions' field observed. No hook-injected text. Resources add small listing overhead. Per-call cost is much higher than definitions: the model must emit the diff or observation as output tokens in the arguments (thousands of tokens), which on Opus is expensive and slow, partly defeating the 'cheap decision' purpose.
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Per invocation: Jev's claimed 70-500 ms plus the SDK's fan-out per question, plus MCP overhead; but the dominant added cost is Opus generating the tool-call arguments (a full diff or test output can be thousands of output tokens, several to tens of seconds) and the extra turn to read the result. Worst case on outage about 10 s x 3 attempts. Zero latency when not invoked.
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no plugin manifest, no proxy. The only steering is the tools' descriptions plus an optional SKILL.md (description-triggered; Claude Code skill in skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md must be copied to ~/.claude/skills) and an AGENTS.md pointer, so Claude may or may not call jev_* on its own; there is no deterministic trigger. Making it automatic would need the user to add a CLAUDE.md rule and/or write their own Stop/PostToolUse hooks that call `node dist/index.js eval|context` (that CLI path is usable from a hook, which is the most valuable reusable part).
pros: Best-documented tool surface among Jev MCPs found: 9 typed recipes (coding_loop, review, change_risk, requirement, verify, screen, rank, issue, evaluate) with real Choice/Score/Noul question packs in src/packs/*.ts, deterministic policy thresholds (JEV_MCP_AUTO_ACCEPT 0.8 / REVIEW_AT 0.5 / BLOCK_AT 0.75) in TypeScript.

Base URL is env-overridable and the SDK path /v1/systemone equals OpenRouter's System One path, so pointing it at OpenRouter looks config-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13).
MIT, small readable TypeScript, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no shell exec in the server, stderr-only logging, readOnlyHint annotations on every tool.
Failures are contained: errors become MCP tool errors, and Jev output that is malformed or evidence that is missing degrades to review/escalate, never a false auto-pass.

Ships a CLI (`eval`, `context`, `ci-shadow`) that can be invoked from a Claude Code hook without MCP, and a git collector with regex secret redaction, useful building blocks for a deterministic Stop-hook diff gate.
jev_screen (prompt-injection probability on fetched text) is a concept that fits Claude Code's WebFetch/Playwright use on client projects.
cons: Not automatic for Claude Code: pure model-discretion tools, no hooks/plugin/marketplace. User's requirement (no prompting) is unmet unless they add their own CLAUDE.md rules and hooks. README and configs target OpenCode, OMP, Cursor, Codex; Claude Code is mentioned only in one line of docs/install.md.

Repository-blind by design: Claude must serialize diffs, test output and claims into tool arguments, costing Opus output tokens and time for every call. The tool that fetches nothing cannot save tokens vs. just reasoning, and the 'cheap routing' premise (jev_coding_loop model_tier) is meaningless for a Claude Code session pinned to Opus 5.5 with no router to act on the result.

Leaks diffs/test output of client projects to TypeSafe/OpenRouter on each call, with no redaction on the MCP path (redaction only in the CLI collector) and existing secret-leak hook does not match mcp__ tool calls.

Extremely young and thin: created 2026-09-17, last commit 2026-09-18, 7 commits, 1 star, 0 forks, no releases, no npm package, tests are mock-only (src/mock.ts) so real Jev behavior is unvalidated; README admits cost savings are unmeasured and CI gate is shadow-only. The v1 review input is already deprecated and slated for removal.

OpenRouter support is inferred, not implemented: key must live in a var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, `doctor`'s GET /v1/models call likely mismatches, default model 'jev-latest' must be overridden, and Claude can pass a per-call `model` arg. Response-schema parity with OpenRouter is unverified.

Heavy, over-engineered contract for jev_review v2 (200-300k char diffs, manifest, sha256 subject digest, provenance, trusted-adapter allowlist) that a model cannot sensibly populate by hand; realistic usage requires the separate `context` CLI adapter, i.e., extra glue.

Tool-definition footprint of roughly 3-5k tokens for 9 tools, most of which (classify_issue, rank, requirement, evaluate) are rarely useful in day-to-day single-developer coding; hard-coded 10 s timeout x 3 attempts can stall a turn during an outage.
gh-minhgv-jev-mcp.verdict: A tidy but very early, client-agnostic MCP wrapper that is worth mining (question packs, thresholds, git collector CLI) and could reach OpenRouter with two env vars, but it does not deliver automatic Claude Code integration and forces the model to hand-feed diffs as tool args. Not recommended as the primary integration; at most use its CLI from your own Stop or PreToolUse hook after verifying OpenRouter response parity.

gh-elyal2-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the `state` argument of decide/classify_batch plus question instructions/criteria, sent to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if repointed). Worst case a single decide blocks about 6x30s + 62s = roughly 4 minutes before returning an MCP tool error. 4xx fails immediately. Since it's an MCP tool (not a hook), Claude just gets an error and continues, so nothing is blocked permanently, but the turn stalls. Tunable via JEV_TIMEOUT and JEV_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS (should be set to about 5-8 s and 1 retry for interactive coding).

No hook or skill ships with the repo, and the descriptions never tell Claude WHEN to consult Jev in a coding workflow (they talk about triaging documents/emails), so Claude will almost never call it unprompted. Two caveats: (1) DefaultModel is hardcoded to "jev-latest" (client.go:103, applied at :209), which is not an OpenRouter model ID, so either every call must pass model="typesafe/jev-1.13" / "~typesafe/jev-latest" (the model is a model-visible optional arg, unreliable) or a one-line patch to DefaultModel is needed; (2) the code's validator and the 'answers' response check assume the TypeSafe schema, and I could not verify that OpenRouter's /systemone response uses the identical shape (question types noul/choice/score, top-level answers map). Also the installer only writes HTTP-transport entries with the token in the header; for stdio you must hand-write the ~/.claude.json/.mcp.json entry (a Go build is needed as well, no prebuilt release exists).

interface.purpose: Batch of several named noul/choice/score questions in one API call; answers keyed by question ID.

Good hygiene in upstream client: Authorization header only, redirects disabled so key never follows a redirect (client.go:198-202), upstream error bodies never echoed, https enforced except loopback, 4 MiB response cap, 1 MiB request cap, bounded retry (429/529, max 3 attempts, <=30 s delay), Origin header rejected on /mcp, token validated to printable ASCII.

Logs contain tool name, success, duration only - no tokens or content (observability.go, server.go:346).

HTTP-mode default bind is 0.0.0.0:8080 (main.go:102, JEV_ADDR); compose binds to loopback, but a bare `serve` exposes an unauthenticated-relay /mcp (any bearer string is accepted and forwarded upstream) plus /metrics to the LAN. Use stdio for local single-user use.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is a JSON of numeric probabilities/choice labels (option labels are chosen by the caller), so returned text is low-risk. Bigger risk is the model itself deciding what state (code, secrets) to send; the repo's secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools unless its matcher is extended.

gh-rudyjunyu-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the `state` and `instructions`/`criteria` arguments of a tool call (arbitrary text/JSON: could be code, diffs, file contents, logs) goes to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai if repointed) together with the API key. Nothing is sent automatically by the server; only on tool calls. In HTTP mode there is an additional hop: Claude Code -> your hub -> upstream, so a remotely hosted hub would also see the content and key. No telemetry, no content logging.

Not a hook, so it can never block a tool call. But the default total timeout is 45 s including retries (main.go:105) with retries on 429/529 sleeping up to 30 s, so a degraded upstream can stall a single tool call for tens of seconds; --timeout should be lowered (e.g. 5-8 s). If the stdio process cannot start (no Go build, missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY exits with error, main.go:121) the MCP server just shows as failed to connect.

Realistically 2-6 s of added wall-clock per use because the calling model must author the typed question. Zero cost on turns where it isn't invoked. Adds no per-tool-call latency like a hook would.

No hooks, no injected text per turn. Cheap (with Claude Code tool search deferral, near zero until used).

The server ships no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet; the only steering is the generic 'instructions' string and short tool descriptions. Claude (Opus) will rarely reach for a probability oracle unprompted, so the user's 'never say use jev' requirement is not met by this repo alone; it would need an external CLAUDE.md rule or skill/hook to make invocation reliable.
pros: Cleanest available primitive mapping: exactly exposes the three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) plus a batch tool, with strict client-side validation (choice 1-255 options, score 2-10 levels, noul true/false) that mirrors the documented System One schema (client.go:127-180).

Stdio transport exists and reads the key from env, and base URL is overridable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so pointing to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 is a config change plus a model-ID workaround, not a rewrite (main.go:104,119).

Fail-open behavior: errors surface as isError tool results, never block Claude Code; tiny context footprint (~4 tools, ~1-1.5k tokens, no hook injection).
Compact, readable code (about 1.6k non-vendored lines) that is easy to fork and patch (DefaultModel, add OpenRouter base, add a hook wrapper).

gh-thedv91-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero when not called (no hooks). judge/verify_claim: one request per call, claimed 70-500 ms plus MCP overhead; rank_candidates one request per candidate (up to 30); review_changes/review_files: "few seconds for three files, minutes for a hundred" (SKILL.md) with concurrency 3. pros: Only candidate so far that is genuinely Jev-shaped: wraps the real /v1/systemone endpoint through TypeSafe's official SDK (src/typesafe.ts, SDK index.mjs:554), covering all three primitives via a generic judge tool.

verify_claim (do the tests pass / is bug fixed evidence check) and judge as a pre-action gate map directly onto real daily-coding decision points; string-match fabricated-quote check costs no model call.
No install scripts, no shell/file/network code beyond the SDK, small readable codebase (~170 KB incl. lock/README), MIT.
Low context footprint versus many MCPs (5 tools, no server instructions, no hooks), and no added latency when unused.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tools plus an optional skill; Claude Code will not reliably call it, contradicting the requirement of automatic use without prompting. Needs extra hooks/CLAUDE.md to enforce.
OpenRouter is not a supported provider in code or docs; compatibility with OpenRouter's System One schema and the model id typesafe/jev-1.13 is untested and unverified.
Extremely immature: 9 days old, 2 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, single npm version; 'jev-agent-mcp' publisher identity differs from GitHub author.

Sends full diffs and file contents of personal and client repos to a third-party model; nothing enforces exclusions and the existing secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool args; client-confidentiality risk.

Review pipelines are heavy fan-out (5 screens per file plus follow-ups, minutes for large diffs) and cost/latency grow with change size; review quality depends on an unproven, possibly router-like model (skeptic claim unverified) and default thresholds are admittedly uncalibrated.
10 s timeout x 3 attempts with no exposed knob and no circuit breaker: a Jev outage can stall a turn ~30 s per call; `npx -y` cold start adds session startup risk.
Jev returns no reasoning or free text, so its value over Opus 5.5 own judgment for coding is unproven; ~4-6k tokens of always-on tool definitions for tools the model may seldom use.
gh-thedv91-jev-mcp.verdict: The most complete Jev MCP found so far and one config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/API_KEY) away from OpenRouter, but it is alpha, untested, model-discretion only, and sends whole diffs off-machine, so it satisfies neither the auto-invocation requirement nor client-safety by itself. Use it only as the tool layer, pinned and audited, paired with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md rule (e.g. Stop-hook gate on verify_claim) if Jev is to be used automatically.

gh-synthet-jev-mcp.name: synthet/jev-mcp
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Small (about 600 lines) Python stdio MCP server that wraps the official typesafe-sdk (pinned to a 0.7.x-era >=0.1,<1 range, lock has 0.7.1) and exposes four tools: jev_choice, jev_score, jev_noul, and jev_system_one (multi-question). It validates the input, builds SDK Choice/Score/Noul objects, calls POST {base_url}/v1/systemone, and returns a normalized {ok, result|error} envelope. It also ships a Claude Code skill (.claude/skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md) with a description-based trigger, plus a workstation installer script. The rest of the repo is unrelated agent-scaffolding boilerplate seeded from the author's synthet-code-framework (dozens of skills, commands, agents, memory and wiki tooling).

Default model jev-1.13.0 (client.py:12, env JEV_MODEL, client.py:42-44). Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and JEV_TOKEN=<OpenRouter key> would therefore hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint. The SDK may also validate response shapes and send X-TypeSafe-* headers, so the OpenRouter response schema needs a live check. JEV_MODEL would likely need an OpenRouter ID such as typesafe/jev-1.13. This is not documented or tested by the repo.

The risk is that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone may differ from TypeSafe's schema or model naming, which I could not verify statically. If needed, the fix is a 3-line change in client.py to pass base_url= explicitly. Because mcp>=2 and typesafe-sdk are third-party dependencies, pinning them would be prudent.

dotenv_util.py:64-70 loads JEV_ENV_FILE / DOTENV_PATH / <project>/.env without overriding the process env. It does not log values. The project_root path computation looks off (parents[1] of src/jev_mcp/cli.py resolves to src/), which is a minor bug.

Third-party dependency surface: mcp>=2,<3 and typesafe-sdk (0.7.1 per uv.lock). The SDK adds X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers and a User-Agent. I saw no telemetry beyond that, and I did not read all the SDK code.

Prompt-injection surface: state and instructions are model-authored, so injected file content could be forwarded to Jev. The output is only typed probabilities and labels, so there is no free-text channel back, which is low risk. The tool result echoes error details, but the messages are static.
Installer script edits ~/.claude.json and user-level configs of several tools and copies files into sibling repos (hardcoded Windows paths). Do not run it; wire the entry by hand.

Repo metadata declares side_effects 'write-capable' and approval_required: true (.mcp.json), but Claude Code does not enforce those fields. It only means the tool would prompt under normal permission mode; in bypass or auto mode it would not.

gh-synthet-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes in the tool arguments leaves the machine: the `state` (string, object or string array), the question `instructions`, the criteria text, and the model name, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if repointed) with the API key in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent automatically from hooks or the filesystem, and there is no whole-transcript egress. Data is limited to what the model chooses to include, so code snippets, diffs or file contents could be sent if Claude puts them in `state` (32k context limit). The response size cap is 512 kB. On a client project this is a third-party data-processor disclosure via TypeSafe and OpenRouter.
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking at the harness level. Any SDK error, including timeout, 5xx and auth failure, is caught (client.py:224-237) and returned as {ok:false, error:{code:'typesafe_error', retryable:true, next_steps}}. A missing key gives {code:'missing_credential'}. The model just sees an error result and continues. The worst case is a stalled turn: the MCP-level timeout defaults to 30 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, client.py:13, 47-66) and the SDK has its own retry policy (RETRY_AFTER headers, so roughly 30 s or more per hung call, not verified). No circuit breaker or caching. A new SDK client is opened per call (client.py:218). A missing key is also detected lazily at first call, not at startup, so the server connects fine and every call fails. That means a silently useless tool until OPENROUTER/JEV key is configured.
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. Tool defs (names, docstrings, schemas from type hints) are about 500-800 tokens total by my chars/4 estimate: the docstrings are one line each, but jev_system_one uses `questions: dict[str, Any]` and `state: Any` with no per-field descriptions, so schemas are compact but the model gets little guidance. No MCP server `instructions` field is set (MCPServer('jev-mcp') only). The skill adds about 90 tokens of always-loaded description plus a body of about 500 tokens loaded on trigger. The repo also ships 40+ unrelated skills, commands and agents under .claude/, .cursor/ and .agents/. These load only if the user opens Claude Code inside this repo, or via the installer. Do NOT copy those; take only .claude/skills/jev-mcp. No hooks, so nothing is injected into prompts.
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call it. On each call there is a Python process spawn via `uv run` at session start (about 1-3 s once), then per call one new httpx client plus TLS handshake (a new SDK client opens per call), plus Jev's claimed 70-500 ms model latency, plus a full extra model round-trip for Claude to issue the tool call and read the result (typically 2-5 s of Opus turn time). Net: a judgment call costs more wall time than Claude just deciding itself. Worst case is 30 s+ on timeout.
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. There are no hooks, so it is not deterministic. Claude decides to call jev_* only if it judges the task to be a typed classification/ranking/verification and the skill or tool descriptions match. In normal coding (edit files, run tests, debug) there is almost no natural trigger, so it would rarely fire without the user asking. The skill's trigger list (reranking, verifying evidence, routing text) is aimed at LLM-app builders, not IDE-style coding. To make it fire automatically for coding you would have to write your own CLAUDE.md or hook policy, which this repo does not provide.
pros: Genuinely Jev-specific and minimal: 4 tools map 1:1 to the Choice, Score and Noul primitives plus a batched multi-question call, all built on the official typesafe-sdk (client.py:201).
Small, readable server of about 600 lines with no shell exec, no file access, no telemetry of its own; easy to audit and to fork in an afternoon.
Key handling is safe: env only, never in argv, .env loader does not override the process env or log values (dotenv_util.py, client.py:26-39).

OpenRouter is reachable without code changes in principle: the SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone (sdk constants.py, transport.py:134), which matches the OpenRouter System One route; only JEV_TOKEN and JEV_MODEL need swapping.
Structured error envelope with retryable and next_steps; a 512 kB response cap; input validation before any network call (client.py:69-165).
Model pinned by default (jev-1.13.0), which is good for calibration-sensitive use; overridable per call.
Mocked unit tests (14 test functions) plus CI (ruff, pytest, CodeQL, dependency-review) in .github/workflows.
cons: Very immature: created 2026-09-22 (8 days old at audit), 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no LICENSE, and no description or topics. Bus-factor of one; the README says it was 'seeded from synthet-code-framework'.

No OpenRouter support in the repo: no base_url parameter, and the default model name (jev-1.13.0) is the TypeSafe name rather than OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13. The OpenRouter path via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is my inference from SDK code and is unverified against OpenRouter's actual response schema. It targets the System One API only, not the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions).

Not automatic: only model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description. There are no hooks and no pre-tool or post-tool integration, so Claude will rarely call Jev during ordinary coding, which is the user's core requirement. Nothing here decides 'when it adds value' for code work.

The skill's example use cases (reranking, evidence verification, routing) target building LLM apps, not editing code. The skill also carries approval_required: true and 'remote_write' metadata, which nudges Claude to ask before use; in bypass or auto mode this is unenforced, so behaviour is inconsistent.

Adds a round-trip through Opus (tool call plus result) for each judgment; Jev's claimed 70-500 ms is dwarfed by model turn time. A 30 s default timeout can stall a turn; no caching or circuit breaker; client is rebuilt per call.

Repo is bloated with unrelated scaffolding (40+ skills, commands, agents, .agent-memory, wiki lint scripts). Installing it 'as a plugin' or opening Claude in it would import that noise. Not a plugin: no plugin.json or marketplace.json. Only the server and one SKILL.md are useful.

Installer script hardcodes D:\Projects Windows paths and the author's sibling repo names (scripts/install_jev_mcp_workstation.py:16-45), and edits ~/.claude.json; unusable as-is on Linux and better avoided.

Data-egress risk on client projects: the model chooses what goes into `state`, so code or confidential content can reach TypeSafe and OpenRouter with no filter and no hook-level secret guard (the user's own PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tool args because its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
Missing-key failure is lazy: the server starts and connects, and every call fails with missing_credential, so it appears healthy in /mcp while doing nothing.
Dependency on mcp>=2,<3, a very new major API (from mcp.server import MCPServer), which may break on ecosystem drift.
gh-synthet-jev-mcp.verdict: A clean, tiny, safe-looking MCP wrapper around the official SDK and the best raw material found for exposing Jev tools to Claude Code, but it is a day-old single-commit POC with no license and no OpenRouter awareness, and as a model-discretion tool it will not give the user automatic Jev use during coding. Use it (or a small fork with an explicit base_url/OpenRouter key and a rewritten skill or hook policy) only as the tool layer, not as the automatic integration.

OpenRouter exposes /api/v1/systemone, so a patch is probably one endpoint constant, a new 'openrouter' branch in config.ts (OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model 'typesafe/jev-1.13') and cache identity tweaks. Risk: parseOutput (cloudflare-jev.ts:67-100) strictly requires usage.input_tokens/output_tokens for typesafe and fails closed to 'review' on any shape difference, and OpenRouter's request/response envelope is unverified here. Needs a fork, since there is no config hook.

interface.name: jev_check_command
interface.purpose: Static policy plus Jev Noul check of a shell command (inputs: command, cwd, environment, target, context). Returns allow/review/deny, riskScore, categories, staticFindings. readOnlyHint true. src/index.ts:369-405.

interface.name: jev_check_test
interface.purpose: Same for test runs: takes command, testCode, diff, framework, isolation/runtime/database/config-cache evidence, safetyProfilePath, testFiles (up to 128), execution, environmentApprovalId. Reads test files under cwd and sends their content to Jev. index.ts:310-367.

interface.name: jev_environment_approve
interface.purpose: Record human approval for a pending test-environment review (index.ts:199).

interface.name: jev_environment_reject
interface.purpose: Reject a pending environment approval (index.ts:222).

interface.name: jev_environment_revoke
interface.purpose: Revoke an active environment approval (index.ts:243).

interface.name: jev_review_approve
interface.purpose: Approve a pending Human Review by ID (index.ts:264). The agent itself can call it, so 'human' approval is not enforced.

interface.name: jev_review_reject
interface.purpose: Reject a pending Human Review (index.ts:287).

interface.name: server instructions
interface.purpose: 'Use jev_check_command before potentially destructive execution and jev_check_test before tests that may touch databases...' (index.ts:194). Advisory text only.

interface.name: CLI verify-test-safety
interface.purpose: npm script running dist/test-safety-cli.js to verify test safety profiles.

gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.runtime: Node.js (TypeScript, ESM), needs the built-in node:sqlite module (Node 22+; Node 24 is fine). Clone, npm install, npm run build. No npm release and no CI (no .github). Dependencies: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, zod.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.install: git clone, npm install, npm run build, then write a .env file and register: claude mcp add jev -- node /path/dist/index.js --env-file /path/.env. README documents Codex only; Claude Code registration is not documented but the standard stdio form works.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.tests: 7 test files in test/ (node --test, mocked Jev; about 70KB of test code) covering config, policy, command checker, test checker, storage, Jev client and MCP server. No CI. Not run here per the static-only rule.
security: Key handling: the API key is read from a .env file (path via --env-file, so it appears in argv but the key itself does not) and is never put in argv or logs. Sent as an Authorization Bearer header; the README claims keys are kept out of logs, caches and responses.

Secret redaction before egress is regex-based (command-checker.ts:34-36, test-checker.ts:119). It covers KEY=val, --token val, private key blocks and DB URLs, but is not comprehensive. Arbitrary secrets inside testCode or diff can still leave the machine.

Prompt-injection surface: command, testCode and diff are placed in Jev state, and the question instructions tell Jev to treat them as untrusted (cloudflare-jev.ts:22-35). Jev returns only a number, which limits injection impact. The MCP tool outputs are structured and include no free text from the model.

No shell execution, no child_process and no postinstall script in package.json. The only network calls go to api.typesafe.ai or api.cloudflare.com (cloudflare-jev.ts:123), with a 30s timeout and a 1 MiB response cap. No telemetry found.
Writes local state: log/jev.log (mode 0600) and cache/jev.sqlite inside the install directory (audit log, fingerprint cache, tickets). Command text is sanitised to 2000 chars in the audit log.
jev_review_approve and jev_environment_approve are exposed to the same agent, so the 'human approval' can be self-approved by the model, especially in bypass mode. This weakens the design.
Unpublished, zero-star, single-author repo created 4 days before this audit, with no releases. Running it needs supply-chain trust in the author plus npm dependencies (a 55KB lockfile).
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai or Cloudflare only (never OpenRouter): for jev_check_command, the redacted command, cwd, environment, target and context. For jev_check_test, the redacted command, full testCode (each test file's contents when testFiles is used, up to a max length), the git diff, framework, context, environment and isolation/runtime evidence (test-checker.ts:119,154-155,297). Nothing is sent unless the model calls a tool, and cache hits skip the network. Whole file contents and diffs from client projects can leave the machine on test checks.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.failureMode: Fail-closed by design, but only advisory. Timeout, network error, HTTP error, invalid JSON, invalid shape or missing usage all return decision 'review' with needsHumanReview=true (command-checker.ts:133-135, cloudflare-jev.ts:129-150). Static denies stay deny. The timeout is 30s (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 30000), with no retry and no failover. Because it is an MCP tool and not a hook, nothing blocks the actual Bash call. A 'review' result only affects Claude if the model chooses to respect it. In bypass mode this means a slow or down Jev adds up to 30s of waiting and then a non-binding 'review'.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.contextCost: 7 tools registered, all always visible. Tool definitions total about 12KB of registerTool source plus large zod schemas for the test tool (isolation, runtime, runtimeDatabase, configCache, runtimeGuard and execution objects). Estimate about 3.5-5k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas, plus about 100 tokens of server instructions (index.ts:194). Most of this is dead weight for daily coding because the approve/reject/revoke tools are rarely used. No hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred tool loading the cost may be lower, but the set is large for two useful tools.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.latencyImpact: Static policy only: milliseconds. With a Jev call: claimed 70-500 ms per call, plus an extra model round trip (tool call and result) of roughly 1-3s of LLM turn time each time. Cache hits avoid the network. Worst case is 30s on timeout. The cost applies only when the model decides to call the tool. Nothing is added to calls it does not make.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The README and examples/AGENTS.md rely on the user adding AGENTS.md/JEV_POLICY.md instructions to each project, plus the short server instructions string. There is no hook, no skill and no proxy, so it is not deterministic. Claude Code would only sometimes call jev_check_command before Bash, and would never be forced to. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PreToolUse Bash hook that calls the check, which this repo does not provide.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for a good-fit typed decision (Noul P(dangerous)) instead of using it as a chat model. Thresholds 0.4/0.8 map it cleanly to allow/review/deny (command-checker.ts:127).
Static deny rules take precedence over Jev, and API failures degrade to 'review', not 'allow' (fail-closed logic, cloudflare-jev.ts and command-checker.ts:133-135).
Zero shell execution, no postinstall, small dependency set (MCP SDK + zod), MIT license, secret-redaction pass before egress, 0600 log file.
Has tests (7 files, mocked Jev) and the request/response parsing is strict, so the TypeSafe System One wire format is already implemented and could be reused.
Already speaks the System One /v1/systemone schema (same path as OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone), so an OpenRouter branch is a small fork.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint (cloudflare-jev.ts:14) and no base-URL env var. You would have to fork it, or would need a separate TYPESAFE_API_KEY from console.typesafe.ai, which conflicts with the goal of using OpenRouter as the Jev provider.

Not automatic: it is a plain MCP tool that depends on the model or on per-project AGENTS.md text. It does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told. There is no PreToolUse hook. Advice is non-binding, and Claude can ignore 'review' or self-call jev_review_approve.

Very narrow use case (destructive-command and test safety). It does nothing for routing, planning, commit/PR decisions or code triage, and duplicates Claude Code's own permission system and the existing secret-leak guard hook.
Adds 7 tools and roughly 4k tokens of always-present context, most of it for an approval workflow (environment/human review tickets) built around Codex, not Claude Code.
Immature: 4 days old, 11 commits, effectively one author, 0 stars, no release, no CI, no npm package, README covers Codex only. Setup needs clone and build, with .env in the install directory.
Config only via a hand-parsed .env file, not process env. It ignores an exported OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and needs a fixed absolute path in the MCP registration.
For jev_check_test it sends test source and diffs from client projects to a third party, guarded only by regex redaction. That is a real concern for client work.
30s timeout and fail-'review' produce stalls in bypass or auto mode where nothing actually gates the command.
gh-fuji-soho-jev-mcp-server.verdict: Well-scoped Jev use (a typed danger probability with a static-deny backstop), but a poor fit for this user. It is TypeSafe/Cloudflare only (no OpenRouter), an advisory model-discretion MCP tool that Claude Code will not reliably call unprompted, immature, and heavy on context for two useful tools. Best treated as reference code for the System One request format and thresholds. Fork it into a PreToolUse Bash hook that calls OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone if a Jev safety gate is wanted.
