gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.name: SantiagoPrada2005/jev-mcp-tool
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.whatItDoes: A remote MCP server meant to be deployed as your own Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object for sessions. It exposes 4 tools (guardrail_gatekeeper, context_pruner, stop_condition_eval, speculative_eval). Each tool wraps one or more Jev noul/choice/score questions. It first calls Cloudflare Workers AI 'typesafe/jev' via the env.AI binding, and only if that throws does it fall back to OpenRouter POST /api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13. The tools are aimed at RAG and agent-safety use cases, not coding. Claude Code cannot connect to it directly. It needs the mcp-remote npx bridge or a native HTTP MCP entry pointing at a Worker URL.

providerSupport.evidence: src/services/jev.service.ts:72 fetch('https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions') with Bearer env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY and body {model, state, questions}; model defaults to typesafe/jev-1.13 (line 70, OPENROUTER_MODEL override). It is only the FALLBACK. The primary path at jev.service.ts:23 is env.AI.run('typesafe/jev') (Cloudflare Workers AI binding, wrangler.jsonc 'ai' binding). The OpenRouter key is a Worker secret (README: 'wrangler secret put OPENROUTER_API_KEY'), not read on the client. src/config/env.ts:1-10 has no TYPESAFE_API_KEY and no /api/v1/systemone. Fallback only runs when the primary throws AND the key is set (line 42). If the primary returns a falsy or answers-less response, it falls through to a hard 'invalid response structure' error (line 60) with no fallback.
providerSupport.others: Cloudflare Workers AI (model 'typesafe/jev'). It is unverified that this model exists on Workers AI. Default deployments may just always throw and fall back to OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial: delete the env.AI.run branch in jev.service.ts and call evaluateWithOpenRouterDecisions directly. But you would still have to deploy and host your own Worker. The request schema is the same {model,state,questions}. The response is assumed to be {answers:{key:{noul|score|choice...}}}, which is not verified against the real OpenRouter Decisions API.

interface.name: guardrail_gatekeeper
interface.purpose: Sends untrusted text to Jev with a noul question 'is injection/jailbreak?' and a 3-level score. Returns {safe, injection_probability, threat_score, confidence, directive: ALLOW|QUARANTINE} (src/tools/guardrail.tool.ts:22-67).

interface.name: context_pruner
interface.purpose: Given a query and chunks[{id,content}], asks one noul relevance question per chunk. Returns which chunks to retain by relevance_threshold (default 0.6). RAG-oriented (src/tools/pruner.tool.ts).

interface.name: stop_condition_eval
interface.purpose: Takes an artifact (code, plan, or diff) plus an ordered acceptance_rubric. Returns PROCEED_FINISH or ITERATE_AND_FIX against pass_threshold (default 1.5). This is a completion quality gate and the only tool with some coding relevance (src/tools/stop-condition.tool.ts).

interface.name: speculative_eval
interface.purpose: Generic fan-out: arbitrary state plus a map of typed questions (noul|choice|score) in one call. This is effectively a raw Decisions API passthrough (src/tools/speculative.tool.ts).

interface.name: HTTP endpoints
interface.purpose: GET /health, GET /sse and /mcp (SSE), and POST /, /mcp, /sse and /message (Streamable HTTP JSON-RPC) with a bearer perimeter token, handled in src/index.ts and src/durable-object/session.do.ts. No hooks or CLI. It ships a .agents/skills/jev-evaluator/SKILL.md, but that directory is gitignored and is not a Claude Code plugin.

gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.license: MIT declared in package.json, but no LICENSE file and GitHub reports licenseInfo null
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.tests: Vitest specs exist (test/tools.spec.ts 193 lines and test/worker.spec.ts 164 lines, about 13 cases, mocked). No CI (.github is absent). Not run, per the static-only rule.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.runtime: TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers plus a Durable Object (SQLite class). Uses @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod. Deployed with wrangler. Needs a Cloudflare account with Workers AI. No stdio server and no local mode.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.install: No package is published to npm and there is no release. You would clone it, run pnpm install and npx wrangler deploy, and set the secrets AUTH_TOKEN and OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Then add to Claude Code either `claude mcp add --transport http jev https://<your-worker>/mcp --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'`, or the README's npx -y mcp-remote ... --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. The mcp-remote form puts the token in argv, so it is visible in the process list.
security: Secret leak: the committed .mcp.json:6 and :19 contain a real-looking bearer token, 'jev_mcp_...', for the author's live Worker (jev-mcp-server.santiagopradamoreno.workers.dev). Anyone can use it. It is a bad-hygiene signal and it means the author's public deployment is not private. Do not reuse it.
Never point Claude Code at that public URL. The author's Worker would see everything you send it, including client code.

The README config puts the token in argv via mcp-remote '--header Authorization: Bearer ...', so it is visible in ps output. The mcp-remote bridge is also an unpinned 'npx -y' that fetches and executes third-party code on every start.

Auth is a single shared static token with a non-constant-time compare (src/index.ts:46). The token is also accepted as a ?token= or ?auth= query param (line 43), which leaks into logs and URLs. CORS is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.

The guardrail_gatekeeper prompt-injection detector is a thin classifier, not a defense. Its output is untrusted model text that decides ALLOW or QUARANTINE, and the instructions in AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md are a prompt-injection surface of their own if pasted into a system prompt.
Cloudflare observability is enabled (wrangler.jsonc), so Worker logs are retained. console.log records model and timing only (jev.service.ts:99), not payloads. No telemetry beyond Cloudflare's.
No shell execution and no postinstall in the repo itself. Tool descriptions are in Spanish and use imperative 'Invoca esta herramienta...' phrasing, which is designed to steer the calling model.
Three .pyc files are committed (skill-creator scripts), and vendored skill-creator scripts are included, but .agents is gitignored. This is repo clutter, not a threat.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in tool arguments is sent over HTTPS to the deployed Worker, and then to Cloudflare Workers AI or to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That means untrusted_text, RAG chunks, the artifact (full code, diffs or plans for stop_condition_eval) and arbitrary state for speculative_eval. Nothing leaves automatically. The model chooses what to send. Because it is a hosted intermediary, you get an extra party: whoever runs the Worker (you, if self-deployed) plus Cloudflare. Your OPENROUTER_API_KEY lives in Worker secrets on Cloudflare. It does NOT go through the OpenRouter key on your machine, so this is not a 'local OpenRouter-key integration'.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but only because it is a model-discretion tool. On errors the DO returns isError:true from tools/call (session.do.ts:222-236) and Claude just continues. There is no explicit timeout or AbortController on the OpenRouter fetch (jev.service.ts:72), so a hung upstream relies on Worker limits. There is no retry. If Workers AI 'typesafe/jev' returns without answers, it hard-fails with no fallback (line 60). If the Worker or mcp-remote bridge is down, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools vanish, as with caveman-shrink. There is no hook, so nothing can block the session.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.contextCost: 4 tools. Estimated about 1.5-2.2k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas (around 6-9k chars of the ~250 lines in src/tools/index.ts plus the long Spanish descriptions). Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas, which reduces the cost. No server 'instructions' field found. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. If the user pastes AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md into CLAUDE.md, add roughly 600-700 tokens of 'MUST delegate' directives on every session, which is not recommended.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.latencyImpact: Per call: Claude to (mcp-remote npx bridge) to Cloudflare edge to Durable Object to Workers AI or OpenRouter, then back. Realistically hundreds of ms to 1-2 s, plus a model-turn round trip for the tool call. On the fallback path, two hops (a failed Workers AI attempt, then OpenRouter) add more. Zero latency when not invoked. The README's 'sub-200ms' is an unverified claim. The cost is a whole extra LLM turn each time the model decides to use it.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tools' Spanish 'Invoca esta herramienta cuando...' descriptions are the only automatic-trigger mechanism. An optional system-prompt paste (AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md) makes it more insistent. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no plugin. The 4 tools do not fit coding events (edit, commit, test), so Claude will rarely or inconsistently pick them without prompting.
pros: Genuinely wraps Jev's typed noul/choice/score primitives and hits the correct OpenRouter endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13) with the right body shape, jev.service.ts:72-85.
speculative_eval is a clean generic passthrough (arbitrary state plus typed questions in one hop) that could be adapted as a building block.
The design of stop_condition_eval (rubric-based completion gate) is conceptually the closest to something useful in a coding agent.
Streamable HTTP plus SSE, session DO, bearer auth, and health endpoint are present, with mock-based Vitest coverage of all four tools and the fallback path.
MIT declared and a small codebase (about 900 lines of src), so it is easy to audit in full.
cons: Requires you to deploy and operate your own Cloudflare Worker with Durable Objects. That is a heavy and unnecessary hop compared with calling openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions directly from a local hook or stdio MCP.
OpenRouter is only a fallback behind an unverified Workers AI model 'typesafe/jev' (jev.service.ts:23). Your OPENROUTER_API_KEY sits as a Cloudflare secret, not locally.
A real bearer token for the author's live Worker is committed in .mcp.json:6/:19. The author's own security posture is weak, and the public URL must never be used.
Tool set is for RAG and agent perimeter security (guardrail, context pruner). No coding-specific tools: no diff/commit risk, test triage, permission gating, or file routing.

Entirely model-discretion auto-invocation. No hooks, so it cannot deterministically fire on PreToolUse, Stop or similar events. It would not satisfy 'Claude Code must use it when needed without my prompt'.
Claude Code needs the unpinned mcp-remote bridge (npx -y) with the token in argv, or native http transport with a static header. There is no stdio option.
No timeout on outbound fetch, no retries, no CI, no release, no LICENSE file (GitHub license null), 1 contributor, 9 commits over one day (2026-09-23), 0 stars. Effectively a weekend PoC.
Sends full artifacts (code, diffs) to third-party infrastructure when stop_condition_eval is used, a problem for client projects.
gh-santiagoprada2005-jev-mcp-tool.verdict: Not recommended for adoption. It is a one-day-old, single-author PoC that needs a self-hosted Cloudflare Worker, uses OpenRouter only as a fallback, has RAG/guardrail tools that do not match coding, and offers only model-discretion invocation. Its only reusable value is as a reference for the /api/alpha/decisions request shape (src/services/jev.service.ts:72-85), which a small local hook or stdio MCP could call directly.

gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.name: kitoutou999/firefox-jev-mcp
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, ~800 lines) plus a Firefox WebExtension that let Claude drive a dedicated Firefox profile. It exposes 8 browser tools. The main one, browse_goal, loops snapshot, then Jev decision, then click or type, using the Jev System One API (Choice over page elements, Noul for 'goal reached?', extra Noul verification when confidence is low). Claude is only called back when Jev hesitates or the action looks risky. It is a browser-automation tool that uses Jev, not a general coding helper.

Calls are all ts.systemOne(...) (jev.ts decide/checkArrival/chooseOption). Dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (I read its dist/index.mjs): the baseURL is fromCodeOrEnv(config.baseURL, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) ?? 'https://api.typesafe.ai' (about line 513), systemOne does POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (line 554) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (line 581), maxRetries default 2. OpenRouter serves POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> should route it with no code change. I did not verify that OpenRouter's request and response schema is identical to the direct one. The model is not chosen by this code, so the SDK's defaultModel or TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL would need to map to typesafe/jev-1.13.

Unverified. Secondary catch: the key is loaded from a project .env via process.loadEnvFile and hasJevKey only checks TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key must sit in that variable name.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only, through the official SDK.

interface.name: browse_goal
interface.purpose: Autonomous multi-step navigation toward a goal (snapshot, Jev decision, action, repeat; params maxSteps, minConfidence 0.6, verifyThreshold 0.8, goalThreshold 0.85, typeText, allowRisky, tabId). Stops with done, need_decision, max_steps or error. Has a regex-based risky-action guard (delete, pay, send, confirm and similar).

interface.name: jev_rank
interface.purpose: Ask Jev to rank the page's elements for a goal without acting. Returns the top 5 candidates, a verification Noul for the top 3, confidence and P(goal reached).

interface.name: browser_snapshot
interface.purpose: List visible interactive elements with refs e1, e2 and so on (limit up to 1000).

interface.name: browser_act
interface.purpose: click, type (optional submit) or select on a ref (annotated destructiveHint and openWorldHint).

interface.name: browser_navigate
interface.purpose: Open a URL in the active or a new tab, or go back.

interface.name: browser_read
interface.purpose: Return the visible page text, up to 50k chars.

interface.name: browser_scroll
interface.purpose: Scroll up or down one screen.

interface.name: browser_status
interface.purpose: Report extension connection, whether a Jev key is set, and the open tabs.

gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.tests: None. There are no tests and no CI (no .github directory). The only checks are tsc --noEmit and web-ext lint. A bench/ directory holds benchmark scripts and result JSON. The benchmark numbers are self-reported: 4 races on one Wikipedia task, Titanic to Tour Eiffel, 14.7 s against 23.4 s.
security: The API key is read from env or a .env file (process.loadEnvFile), never from argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The .mcp.json passes no key in args.
No shell execution and no postinstall script in package.json. The only third-party install is the normal npm install of well-known deps. No curl|sh.

The WebSocket bridge listens on 127.0.0.1:8765 and accepts only Origin starting with moz-extension:// (bridge.ts:33-37). This blocks web pages, but any Firefox extension can connect. The port is fixed, so only one session can run at a time.

The extension asks for permissions ['tabs','<all_urls>'] (manifest.json:15) and can read every page and click or type on it. It is meant to run only in the dedicated profile, but if the user installs it in a daily profile it gets full DOM access to logged-in sessions.

Prompt-injection surface is real: page text, link labels and element names are fed into Jev's state and returned to Claude through browser_read and snapshot output, and browse_goal can click and type autonomously. Mitigations are a regex-based RISKY label filter (agent.ts) and allowRisky=false by default. The regex is easy to bypass and only matches labels.
Synthetic clicks (isTrusted=false) limit what sites accept, which incidentally limits the damage.
Password field values are excluded from element descriptions (content.js:155). There is no telemetry from the repo itself; the SDK sends only API calls to its baseURL.
Tiny, 1-commit, 1-star repo from a single unknown author, so there is no review history. The code is short enough to audit (~1.6k lines including the extension).
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.dataEgress: To the Jev API (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if re-pointed): the goal string, page URL and title, the start of the visible page text (page_text_start), labels, roles, hrefs, placeholders and values (non-password) of the interactive elements, the last 5 steps, any typeText, and previous-page text for arrival checks. This only happens for browse_goal and jev_rank (the README confirms this in its 'Confidentialité' section). Source code, diffs, files and Claude prompts are not sent. Local browser tools (snapshot, read, act) send nothing external. For a logged-in client web app, page contents do leave the machine.
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft per call, and the tool is model-invoked, so it does not block anything else. The SDK client has a 20 s timeout with 2 default retries (jev.ts:72; SDK maxRetries: 2). Errors are caught in browseGoal and return {status:'error', reason, steps so far}. The tools run() wrapper returns isError text. With no key, the server still starts and the plain browser_* tools work, while jev_rank and browse_goal error with 'TYPESAFE_API_KEY absente'. If the Firefox extension is not connected, calls wait up to 4 s and then error. Nothing hooks Claude's normal flow, so a Jev outage cannot stall coding.
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.contextCost: 8 tools. Tool names, descriptions and zod schemas total roughly 4.5k characters, which is about 1.1-1.5k tokens. There are no MCP server 'instructions' and no hooks. Descriptions are in French, which slightly raises token use and may nudge the model. Tool output can be large: browser_snapshot up to 1000 elements and browser_read up to 50k chars per call. It also adds a second browser-automation surface next to the already-installed playwright MCP.
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The browse_goal description says 'À privilégier pour les suites de clics simples', but nothing forces Claude to choose it over playwright. No hook, skill or proxy. It only fires when Claude decides to do browser work, and it needs a Firefox with the extension running. It never helps with ordinary code editing, reading, grep or test runs.
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on normal coding turns, since nothing is in the request path. When browsing, each browse_goal step makes 1 Jev systemOne call, plus a second verification call when confidence is below 0.6 and a third parallel arrival check. The README claims about 181 ms per click and about 1 s per Jev decision. Self-reported end-to-end, it saves Claude turns (4 turns vs 12 in its Wikipedia race).
pros: It is a real, working example of Jev used well: it uses Choice, Noul and multi-question systemOne requests in one call, merges duplicate options, adds a 'none_of_these' option, and does two-pass chunking above 250 options. This is useful reference code for building a custom Jev integration (jev.ts).

Straightforward path to OpenRouter: the official @typesafe-ai/sdk reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, and its systemOne posts to /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, which matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. In principle it is an env-var change with no code edits.

Small and auditable: about 800 lines of server code and about 500 lines of extension, no shell execution, no postinstall, the key is not in argv, and the WebSocket is bound to localhost with an origin check.
Fail-soft design and a risky-click guard (allowRisky=false) suit an agent that can act in a browser. Low context cost (8 tools, roughly 1.3k tokens).
Benchmarks with raw data and scripts are included, so the claimed savings on Claude turns and tokens (20.8k vs 88.5k) can be checked.
cons: Wrong problem for daily coding. It only helps with web-page navigation, not with code review, commit or test decisions, permission triage, routing or classification in the coding loop. Claude Code already has the playwright MCP for browser work, so this would be a duplicate surface.

Not automatic in the sense the user wants: it is a set of model-discretion tools that also needs a dedicated Firefox running with a side-loaded extension and a fixed port 8765, one session at a time. It does not use Jev anywhere Claude Code decides things internally.

Very immature: created 2026-09-23 (7 days old), 1 commit, 1 star, 1 author, no tests, no CI, no releases. It is a personal project, not published to npm. Its benchmark is n=4 on a single Wikipedia-style task with the tool's own author running it.

TypeSafe direct only. OpenRouter use is untested and unclaimed by the repo. The schema and auth compatibility of /api/v1/systemone is assumed, the model must be selected through SDK defaults, and the key has to be stored in a variable named TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

Sends page URL, title, element labels and the start of page text of every visited page to the Jev provider. That is risky on client apps that are logged in. The extension requests <all_urls> plus tabs, and prompt injection from page content flows into an autonomous clicking loop guarded only by a label regex.

Tool descriptions and errors are in French, which is inconsistent with an English-language coding workflow. The 250-option limit, unhandled iframes and non-trusted clicks limit real-world reliability (README 'Limites connues').
gh-kitoutou999-firefox-jev-mcp.verdict: Not a fit for the user's goal. It is a niche Firefox-automation MCP that uses Jev for click selection, so it does not add Jev to coding decisions and only helps if Claude does browser tasks. Worth reading as reference code for calling systemOne with Choice and Noul, and it could be pointed at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, but I would not install it. The playwright MCP already covers the browser use case.

gh-victorperr-jev-mcp-elicitation-autopi.whatItDoes: A fork of the official MCP Inspector v2.8.0 (Apache-2.0/MIT). The fork adds one commit (e935b22c, 2026-09-29) with a `--elicit jev` flag to the Inspector CLI. When an MCP server sends a form elicitation during a tool call, the CLI answers it itself. Each answer is a Jev call to POST /v1/systemone: choice for accept/decline/cancel and enums, noul for booleans. Answers below a probability threshold cancel the run and exit 9. interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Check claims against evidence. Returns a verdict (verified, contradicted or unsupported), a distribution and confidence, and an auto or review action.

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Screen external text for prompt injection, substance and relevance before an agent reads it. Returns pass, review, block or skip.

interface.name: jev_find
interface.purpose: Semantic pick of the best candidate(s) for a query, up to 250 candidates, with no embeddings.

interface.name: jev_rerank
interface.purpose: Score and sort all candidates by relevance in one request.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Batch-assign up to 64 items to a shared label catalog, with an auto or review action.

interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Bounded decision among 2-6 alternatives with evidence, priorities and requirements.

interface.name: jev_compare
interface.purpose: Relate two passages: same_fact, contradicts or different_facts.

interface.name: jev_extract
interface.purpose: Caller-supplied regex finds candidates; Jev picks the true match; values are returned verbatim.

interface.name: jev_review
interface.purpose: Score a proposed diff against the request (correctness, spec match, test gap, blast radius, safe_to_apply). Returns auto, review or escalate. Most relevant to coding.

interface.name: jev_gate
interface.purpose: jev_review plus verification of completion claims against evidence, in one call. Evidence is capped at 16 items and 200k chars.

gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.dataEgress: Whatever Claude passes as tool arguments leaves the machine (via the local service) to the chosen Jev provider, here openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That means diffs (up to 50k chars), the request text, test output, claims, evidence documents (up to 200k chars for gate), candidate lists, and any text given to screen, extract, compare or classify. Only tool-call arguments are sent, so the MCP tool descriptions ask Claude to pass diffs, evidence and text. There are no hooks, so nothing is sent automatically beyond what the model chooses to pass. OpenRouter headers include the fixed Referer https://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp and the X-Title jev-mcp. Locally, the SQLite audit DB (data/jevmcp.db) logs metadata per call (tool, latency, tokens, cost, outcome, token identity). Payload capture is off by default (CALLAUDIT__CAPTUREPAYLOADS=false); if enabled it stores up to 4096 chars per payload for 30 days. For client projects, code and diffs would reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which needs client consent.
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.failureMode: Effectively fail-open for the Claude Code workflow, because there is no hook. If the service is down, the MCP connection fails like caveman-shrink did this session and the tools simply vanish, so Claude proceeds unchecked. If Jev is slow, the HttpClient timeout is 60 s (JevProviderServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:26), with up to 3 attempts and exponential backoff (0.5 s base, 5 s cap) on 429 and 529 only (JevRetryHandler.cs, JevProviderOptions.cs:8-13). A worst-case stall on one tool call is therefore a long block, with no short-timeout circuit breaker. Internally the tools are fail-closed on the verdict: malformed model output becomes invalid_response and truncated input never returns auto. With no credentials the app still starts and /health reports degraded (Program.cs comment, JevProviderResolver.cs:27), and tools then error.
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.contextCost: 10 MCP tools. Tool titles, descriptions and parameter descriptions total about 10.5k chars of string literals in src/JevMcp.Tools/Mcp/*.cs. With JSON schemas (snake_case params, JsonElement evidence unions) I estimate about 3.5-5k tokens always loaded, and less when Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search. I found no MCP server 'instructions' field (grep for Instructions and ServerInfo in the App returned nothing). No hook text injection. Roughly 2-3x the token cost of a 3-4 tool server, because only 2-4 of the 10 tools are useful for coding (review, gate, verify, screen).
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no server instructions in this repo. Claude will call jev_review or jev_gate only if it decides to from the tool descriptions, for example 'before the task is called done' and 'before an agent reads it'. It is not deterministic. The user's requirement of firing without being asked would need a separate Stop or PreToolUse hook, or a CLAUDE.md rule, which this repo does not provide.
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.latencyImpact: Per call, the network hop to OpenRouter is claimed at 70-500 ms for Jev, plus the local ASP.NET service, the SQLite audit write and a possible retry backoff (up to about 0.5 s + 1 s). It adds nothing to turns where no tool is called. Cold start of the .NET container is not per turn. Stateful session init happens once per MCP connection. No hook-based per-turn tax, since there are no hooks.
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.runtime: .NET 10 (ASP.NET Core + Blazor Server + MudBlazor + EF Core SQLite), Docker or dotnet run. No Node or Python. The user has neither the .NET 10 SDK nor Docker mentioned in their tooling, so this needs a new runtime or container.

pros: Native OpenRouter support in code: OpenRouterJevClient posts to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with an sk-or- key, mapping jev-latest to typesafe/jev-1.13. It is the only candidate that fits the user's 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' requirement with no patching, just JEV__PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Tool set is coding-relevant. jev_review (score a diff: correctness, spec match, test gap, blast radius, safe_to_apply) and jev_gate (review plus verification of 'done' claims against test evidence) map directly to a pre-completion check. jev_screen targets web-fetch prompt injection. Its descriptions say 'before the task is called done'.

Policy is in code, not model text: typed thresholds, auto, review and escalate actions, and fail-closed invalid_response handling. The output is compact typed JSON and does not add reasoning noise to context.
All tools are marked ReadOnly = true, so they are safe under the user's bypass and auto permission mode. Nothing is executed or applied locally.
Retry only on 429 and 529, with capped backoff (JevRetryHandler.cs). The provider key is redacted from errors (Secrets.cs). Bearer tokens are hashed at rest. No telemetry found.
Same tool names, schemas and payloads as upstream jkudish/jev-mcp, so it can be swapped for the stdio original later. MIT licence. Sizable test suite (359 tests) for a 4-day-old repo.
Local audit dashboard shows per-call cost, latency and outcomes, which is useful for judging whether Jev adds value (README pricing seed of 0.042 USD per 1M tokens matches the brief).
cons: Wrong deployment shape for Claude Code: a heavy .NET 10 web app (Blazor admin, MudBlazor, EF Core SQLite, cookie login, token store, Scalar, ECharts) that must run as a persistent Docker or dotnet service. A stdio server started by Claude Code (upstream jkudish/jev-mcp via npx) has none of that. The user has Node, Python and uv but no .NET 10, and needs a background service and open port for a 10-tool wrapper.

No automatic invocation of any kind. There are no hooks, no skill, no server instructions and no CLAUDE.md snippet. Firing depends on the model choosing to call jev_review or jev_gate, so it fails the user's core 'automatic, without me prompting' requirement. Opus with 10 unfamiliar tools will often skip them.

Very immature: created 2026-09-22 (8 days old), 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, no CI, no published image. Depends on a beta upstream API. The port's own .cursor/mcp.json is empty. The README says Windows PowerShell 5.1 is the dev gate.

Uses the OpenRouter alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), not /api/v1/systemone. The endpoint is a compile-time const, so it is an alpha surface that can break. The OpenRouter alias is pinned to the hard-coded jev-1.13 and will not follow ~typesafe/jev-latest.

Adds a network service and static Bearer token on the developer machine, with an anonymous /health, /scalar and /openapi and a setup and login surface. That is more attack surface and secrets-in-config (token in ~/.claude.json headers) than a stdio process gives.

Token bloat: 10 tools (about 3.5-5k tokens of schema) are loaded for a coding workflow that would use 2-4 of them. Tools such as jev_find, jev_rerank, jev_classify, jev_decide, jev_compare and jev_extract are generic and mostly redundant with Claude and GitNexus.

Fail-open silently: if the container is down the tools disappear (as caveman-shrink did this session). Worst-case latency is a 60 s timeout with 3 retries, with no short circuit breaker, which can stall a turn.
Sends diffs and evidence (up to 200k chars) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe through model-chosen arguments. This is a data-handling concern for client projects, and there is no path or secret filtering.
Skeptic risk remains. Jev's value as a code-review gate is unproven (calibration claims, the 'DeepSeek flash router' claim), and thresholds are only 'starting points' from cookbooks per the README.
gh-marceloatoledo-jev-mcp-rest.verdict: The only reviewed candidate with native OpenRouter support and a coding-relevant tool set (jev_review, jev_gate, jev_screen), but it is a heavy, days-old .NET web service with no hooks, skill or instructions, so Claude only uses it if it decides to. It cannot deliver the automatic integration the user wants on its own. Better to take its tool contract (or the upstream stdio jkudish/jev-mcp) and add a Stop or PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter directly.

gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.name: jkudish/jev-agent-tools
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.whatItDoes: Zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript/Node (>=22) library exporting ask() and resolveTransport(). It picks a carrier (TypeSafe direct, OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Vercel AI Gateway) from env vars, POSTs {state, questions, model}, and strictly validates the reply (answer IDs, probability distributions, choice = argmax, noul in [0,1], usage, model). security: No postinstall scripts and no runtime dependencies, so supply-chain surface is small.
Key is read from env and sent only as Authorization Bearer to the fixed host (openrouter.ai, or api.typesafe.ai/TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). Nothing goes in argv.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is an unvalidated override, so a poisoned env could redirect state and key to another host (typesafe.ts:8).
Errors are fixed strings with status and byte count only; response bodies and credentials are never echoed, and provider names are whitelisted.
No shell execution, no file reads, no telemetry. SECURITY.md states it makes no other network calls.
Outputs are numbers and IDs only and are strictly validated, so the prompt-injection surface on the return path is minimal.
Sends HTTP-Referer and X-Title (jev-browser) to OpenRouter, which is harmless attribution but mislabels the app in the OpenRouter dashboard.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in state and questions goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai, Cloudflare, Vercel depending on env), plus the OpenRouter key. The library itself reads nothing from disk, so egress equals what the consumer (for example jev-mcp) passes. In a Claude Code setup that could be code, diffs and tool output, which is a client-confidentiality concern.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.failureMode: Fail-closed at the library level: any network error, non-2xx, bad JSON or invalid distribution returns {ok:false, code}, and the consumer decides what happens next. The library has no timeout, no retry and no backoff; it only honours the caller's AbortSignal (jev-mcp keeps its own retry and deadline rules instead of using this layer). There is no fallback across providers, since a JEV_PROVIDER that is set but misconfigured errors rather than falling through.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.latencyImpact: Nothing is added on its own because nothing in Claude Code calls it. When embedded, it adds one HTTPS round trip to OpenRouter (claimed 70-500 ms) plus negligible validation time.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.contextCost: Zero: no MCP server, tools, hooks or injected text.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.autoInvocation: None. It is a library, so nothing invokes it inside Claude Code. Automatic behavior would have to come from a consumer such as jev-mcp (model-discretion MCP tools) or from custom hooks built on top of it.
pros: Correct, code-verified OpenRouter support: POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and Bearer sk-or- key (openrouter.ts:9-15).
Strict fail-closed validation of Jev output (ID match, distribution sums, choice = argmax, noul range, usage). Useful as a reference or building block for a custom hook script.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, small (about 500 lines of source), MIT, and it never echoes bodies or keys.
Explicit JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter avoids silent fallthrough. Injectable JevTransport makes hermetic testing easy.
Could be the basis for a small home-grown PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hook script that calls Jev via OpenRouter.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook or skill. It has no Claude Code integration surface and gives no automatic invocation.
Very new and thin: created 2026-09-23, 11 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, 0.1.x, and no OpenRouter live test.
Uses the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint. It drops usage when absent (usage reports 0), so cost tracking is not possible via this path.
No timeout or retry, so a hook built on it must supply its own AbortSignal deadline or risk stalling.
If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is present in env it silently takes precedence over OpenRouter unless JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is set.
Sends X-Title and Referer as jev-browser to OpenRouter.
Its sibling jev-mcp deliberately does not use it for OpenRouter, so it adds little for the MCP path.
gh-jkudish-jev-agent-tools.verdict: Not an integration for Claude Code. It is a clean, well-validated transport library that correctly targets OpenRouter's Decisions API, useful only as a dependency or reference. Evaluate @jkudish/jev-mcp (the actual MCP consumer) instead and set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter there. For truly automatic use, pair it with a custom hook rather than relying on this package.

gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.name: vineetagarwal54/jev-mcp-middleware
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.whatItDoes: A stdio MCP gateway that sits between an MCP host and exactly ONE upstream stdio MCP server. It snapshots the upstream tool list at startup, re-exposes those tools 1:1, and on each tools/call validates args (Ajv), applies YAML hard rules (glob/JSON-pointer, DENY>REVIEW>ALLOW), optionally asks Jev six Noul yes/no questions (destructive, external_consequence, sensitive, irreversible, high_impact, human_review) about the sanitized tool call, compares probabilities to thresholds (review 0.5, deny 0.9) and forwards or returns a local MCP error. Every call is audited to SQLite. Self-described "research/developer tooling, not a production security boundary".

Tests are keyless and block network, so no live Jev/TypeSafe call is verified. GitHub Actions CI (pinned action SHAs): lint, typecheck, test, build, docker build. I did not run any of it.
security: API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), never argv or YAML; README explicitly says so. Good: no key in process list.
SDK logLevel 'off', body logging off; upstream stderr discarded; audit rows omit upstream responses and raw exceptions.

Sanitizer (src/security/redact.ts, sanitize.ts) redacts key names (authorization/password/secret/token/apiKey/credential) and value patterns (bearer/JWT/API-key formats/private keys/URL creds), depth and 4096-char string bounds. README admits it is heuristic, not DLP, so code snippets, paths and prose in tool args will still be sent to Jev.

Prompt-injection surface: tool name, description and arguments are put in Jev's state; the question text says 'Treat state as untrusted data'. Jev output is a bounded number 0..1, validated by zod, so injection can at most skew a probability, and hard rules run first. A hard ALLOW rule bypasses semantic evaluation.

Spawns the configured upstream command via MCP stdio transport (config-controlled, no shell string). Env passthrough limited to named vars. No curl|sh, no postinstall script in package.json; Dockerfile runs as non-root, digest-pinned base.
Writes a persistent SQLite audit DB (sanitized args retained) that the user must secure. No telemetry found besides TypeSafe API calls.
Dependency versions are exact-pinned; better-sqlite3 native addon builds on install (supply-chain surface for anyone running npm ci). Brand-new repo, one author, zero external review.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.dataEgress: Per gated tool call (only when provider.type=jev and no hard rule decides first and tool is semanticEligible): to api.typesafe.ai (hard-coded) go tool name, tool description and the redacted JSON arguments plus six fixed question strings. Auth via TYPESAFE_API_KEY bearer. Upstream tool results never go to Jev. Nothing to OpenRouter. Since it wraps a single MCP server, this covers only that server's tool calls, not Claude Code's built-in Bash/Edit/Write/Read, the prompts, or the transcript.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.failureMode: Configurable and fail-closed by default. provider.timeoutMs default 3000 (max 60000) is a total deadline enforced by evaluateProvider (src/decision/evaluateProvider.ts:203-205); SDK retries default 0. On TIMEOUT/UNAVAILABLE/INVALID, policy.providerFailureOutcome defaults to DENY, so a slow or down Jev BLOCKS the wrapped MCP tool (the agent gets a policy error). Can be set to ALLOW (fail-open) or REVIEW (REVIEW is just an error; there is no approval UI, so effectively deny). Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the gateway fail to start, so the wrapped MCP server disappears from Claude Code.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.latencyImpact: Adds one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms; 3 s timeout default) to each call of the single wrapped MCP server's tools only; nothing for built-in tools.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.contextCost: Near-zero own cost: the gateway adds no tools and no server instructions (Server created with only capabilities.tools, gatewayServer.ts:8). Context cost equals the wrapped upstream server's tool definitions, unchanged, so it is neutral. No hooks, no injected text. On the contrary, it replaces rather than adds an MCP entry.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy, fully automatic but narrow: once an existing MCP server is re-registered behind it, every call to that server's tools is intercepted with no model discretion. It is NOT a Claude Code hook, so it cannot see built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Write, Read, Grep) where destructive risk actually lives, nor MCP servers not wrapped (one gateway instance per upstream; v0.1 supports one downstream session and one upstream).
pros: Genuinely uses the Jev System One API via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with Noul primitives; typed 0..1 probabilities validated by zod (JevDecisionProvider.ts:9-22), so the integration is architecturally sound and injection-resistant (numeric output only, hard rules first).
Well-engineered failure semantics: hard deadline, explicit providerFailureOutcome (DENY/REVIEW/ALLOW), cancellation never fails open, one audit row per call (router.ts, evaluateProvider.ts).
API key only from env, not argv; sanitizer redacts secrets before egress; audit omits upstream bodies; pinned deps, pinned CI actions, non-root Docker; MIT.
Zero context overhead: adds no tools, no instructions, no hook text.
Good reference implementation of the six-question risk-scoring pattern and threshold policy that could be lifted into a custom PreToolUse hook.
cons: Wrong integration point for this user: it is a proxy for ONE upstream MCP server, not a Claude Code hook. It cannot gate Bash/Edit/Write/Read or any other MCP server, which is where the risky calls happen. The user already has PreToolUse hooks and the existing servers (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) are read-only/browser tools that gain little from a destructive-risk score.

Does not support OpenRouter: hard-coded baseURL https://api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (JevDecisionProvider.ts:28-30); needs a source patch plus a fork, and OpenRouter response-shape compatibility is unverified.
Adds no productivity value (no routing, classification, or code-decision help); it is purely a security/risk gate, and the README itself disclaims it as research tooling and not a security boundary.
Fail-closed default means a Jev outage or slow response blocks the wrapped tool; the missing-key case stops the whole server from starting. REVIEW has no approval UI so it is just a block.

Heavy setup: Node 24 only, native better-sqlite3 build, private package with no release, hand-written YAML per upstream, rewrite of .mcp.json entries, and one gateway process per wrapped server. The catalog snapshot is startup-only (no listChanged), so playwright/gitnexus dynamic tool changes would be missed.

Very immature: 7 commits over 2 days, 2 authors (effectively 1), 0 stars, no releases, no live-Jev test evidence (tests block network; the benchmark is 12 synthetic hand-labelled cases). Persistent SQLite audit of sanitized args on client projects adds a data-retention burden; heuristic redaction can still leak client code/prose to a third party.
Sends tool arguments (potentially client code or paths) to TypeSafe on every gated call, a compliance issue on client projects; sits on the hot path of every call.
gh-vineetagarwal54-jev-mcp-middleware.verdict: Real, competently written but a 2-day-old proof of concept that wraps a single upstream MCP server with a Jev-based risk gate, so it neither covers Claude Code's built-in tools nor supports OpenRouter without patching. Not recommended for daily coding; at most a design reference for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.name: baize7815/jev-mcp-open-source
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.whatItDoes: Self-hosted Cloudflare Worker (D1 for encrypted key store + /admin UI) that exposes a streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint at /mcp with 9 tools. Eight are workflow wrappers (route_intent, rerank_candidates, batch_judge, select_values, verify_evidence, evaluate_options, classify_hierarchy, decide_next_step) that decompose into System One Choice/Noul/Score calls, plus a raw system_one pass-through. The Worker calls api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with model jev-latest, using TypeSafe API keys stored AES-GCM encrypted in D1 and rotated round-robin. Also ships a Codex-style skill (skills/jev-workflows/SKILL.md, in Chinese) and a call-mcp.mjs fallback client.

README.en.md:46 diagram repeats the api.typesafe.ai endpoint.
providerSupport.others: None. Single hardcoded upstream.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The code change is tiny: swap the URL in src/typesafe.js:28 to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and the model to typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest (OpenRouter model ID format differs from bare jev-latest); the bearer-key mechanism would accept an sk-or key unchanged. But the request/response schema on OpenRouter is unverified against this repo (usage.input_tokens/output_tokens parsing, questions shape). It also requires a deploy to your own Cloudflare account (wrangler, D1, secrets), so you would maintain a fork.

security: /mcp is deliberately UNAUTHENTICATED (README.en.md and src/index.ts:72-76): anyone who learns the workers.dev URL can burn your TypeSafe/OpenRouter quota; only /admin needs ADMIN_TOKEN. workers_dev:true in wrangler.example.jsonc makes a public *.workers.dev URL by default. Mitigation requires adding Cloudflare Access/service tokens yourself, and then Claude Code's MCP config must send the header.

API keys are AES-GCM encrypted in D1 with KEY_ENCRYPTION_SECRET (src/keys.js), only last-4 hint shown; decent design. Secrets set via wrangler secret put interactively, not argv. Keys never sit on the user's machine or in Claude Code argv (client only needs the Worker URL).
Admin token is sent as Bearer from the browser page; a login form in an inline HTML page; small surface, but no rate limiting seen and no MFA.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are JSON of probabilities/IDs (no free text from Jev), so injection back-channel is small; but inputs are model-composed from repo content and forwarded off-machine. Tool descriptions themselves are benign.
Deployment requires npm ci + wrangler (deps @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0, agents 0.24.0, zod, wrangler 4.136.0); no postinstall or curl|sh seen. Not executed by me.
Worker observability enabled (logs head_sampling_rate 1) in wrangler.example.jsonc, so request metadata may be logged in your Cloudflare account.

Repo includes scripts/check-privacy.mjs guarding against leaked config; single anonymous author, 7 commits over 2 days, no CI, no releases, no SECURITY policy. Eval/test coverage is small (test/workflows.test.ts, client-config.test.mjs, 13 synthetic eval cases).
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in tool arguments (request/context strings, candidate excerpts up to 128 KB, records, claims and evidence, goals and observations) goes Claude Code -> your Cloudflare Worker -> api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe, not OpenRouter as shipped). Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself; content is model-chosen, so code snippets, file excerpts and client-project text can leave the machine to two third parties (Cloudflare, TypeSafe) beyond Anthropic. Instructions say 'never secrets' but nothing enforces it; the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover mcp__ calls (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Usage counters (token counts, status) are stored in D1. No telemetry to the author was found in the code.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.failureMode: Fail-open at the model level: tool errors return isError with message text (src/index.ts:15-18), SKILL/instructions say 'unavailable -> continue, do not retry'; Claude simply proceeds without Jev. Upstream timeout is 30 s (src/typesafe.js judge default timeoutMs=30000), which is long: a hung upstream would stall a tool call up to 30 s (call-mcp.mjs uses 60 s). No automatic retries (avoids double billing). No caching. Batch items fail individually and are marked failed. If Worker is down, Claude Code MCP connection shows failed and tools vanish; no hard block.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.contextCost: 9 tools; my estimate ~3-4k tokens of tool definitions (descriptions 300-600 chars each, ~4.5k chars, plus zod-derived JSON schemas in src/workflows.ts, which is the bulk: nested routes/candidates/items/questions/criteria) and a ~1k-char server 'instructions' string (src/index.ts:12, ~250 tokens) injected every session. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Tool results are compact JSON. If MCP tool search/deferral is active in Claude Code, the cost drops further.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools. Tool descriptions are explicitly written for autonomous use ('Call proactively ... the user need not mention Jev', 'even if the user never mentions Jev') and the server instructions reinforce it, so Claude Code may call them unprompted, but it is not deterministic: no hook, no proxy. The bundled SKILL.md is a Codex-style skill (frontmatter name/license/description only, Chinese description) that could load as a Claude Code skill by copying to ~/.claude/skills, but its trigger text is Chinese and oriented to KB/RAG/ticket workflows.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.latencyImpact: Extra hop Claude Code -> Cloudflare edge -> D1 key lookup (2 D1 queries: select keys + cursor update, plus a write-back of usage) -> TypeSafe. Estimate 150-800 ms per call for single-judgment tools on top of Jev's claimed 70-500 ms. Composite tools (batch_judge up to 10 items at concurrency 3, evaluate_options, classify_hierarchy walking levels sequentially, select_values) multiply upstream calls, so multi-second turns are plausible. Each MCP call adds a full Claude tool round trip (model decides, emits call, reads result), which dominates.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.install: Not a one-line install: git clone; npm ci; cp wrangler.example.jsonc wrangler.jsonc; npx wrangler login; npx wrangler d1 create jev-mcp; wrangler d1 migrations apply --remote; wrangler secret put ADMIN_TOKEN and KEY_ENCRYPTION_SECRET; npm run deploy; add key in /admin; then claude mcp add --transport http jev https://<worker>.workers.dev/mcp. To use OpenRouter you must first edit src/typesafe.js (and the source .ts) and redeploy.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.runtime: Cloudflare Workers (nodejs_compat) + D1; build tooling Node >=24.11, TypeScript 7.0.2, wrangler 4.136.0; MCP over streamable HTTP JSON (responseMode json)
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.tests: Node test runner: test/workflows.test.ts (~10 KB) and test/client-config.test.mjs; eval/cases.json with 13 synthetic cases (format check only; eval:live spends quota); typecheck script. No CI workflow (.github absent). Not executed by me.
pros: Only candidate so far whose tool descriptions and server instructions explicitly tell the model to call proactively without the user mentioning Jev (src/index.ts:12,24,29,34), which matches the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement as closely as an MCP-only approach can.
Keeps the API key off the workstation and out of argv/process list; keys are AES-GCM encrypted in D1 and the client only needs a URL.

Well-designed typed workflows: rerank_candidates and verify_evidence map onto genuine Jev strengths (typed decisions with confidence), with deterministic weighting in code, failed items marked 'not judged', no auto-retries, and 'never authorizes actions' guard rails.
MIT, small readable codebase (~50 KB source), no postinstall or curl|sh, privacy-check script, clear README in English and Chinese.
Fail-open behavior: errors return isError and the guidance says to continue without Jev.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and model jev-latest (src/typesafe.js:28,33). Directly contradicts the user's requirement; needs a fork and redeploy, and OpenRouter response/usage compatibility is unverified.

Requires running your own Cloudflare Worker + D1 for a single-user tool: a whole infra layer, a second vendor seeing your data, and an unauthenticated public /mcp endpoint by design (anyone with the URL spends your quota). Making it safe needs Cloudflare Access plus header config in Claude Code.

Conceptually aimed at RAG/knowledge-base/ticket triage (default routes answer/search_files/search_knowledge/search_web; examples about photography tutorials, refunds), not code work. Claude Opus 5.5 already routes, ranks and verifies well for coding; the tools duplicate what grep/GitNexus plus the main model do, and add a tool round trip per use.

Model-discretion only: Opus will often skip or over-use the tools; no deterministic hook, so 'automatic' is unreliable. Adds ~3-4k tokens of tool defs plus instructions to every session for marginal use.

Data egress is model-composed and unfiltered: code excerpts and client-project content would go to Cloudflare and TypeSafe; the existing secret-leak hook does not match mcp__ tools, and the worker has full logging enabled in the template.

Very immature: 1 star, 1 author, 7 commits in 2 days, no releases, no CI, version 0.3.0; claims about accuracy are unvalidated (eval:check only validates case format). Skill is Codex-oriented with a Chinese description, not a Claude Code plugin.
Composite tools multiply upstream calls (batch of 10 with concurrency 3, level-by-level taxonomy walk), raising latency and cost versus a single decision call; 30 s upstream timeout is generous.
gh-baize7815-jev-mcp-open-source.verdict: Not recommended as-is: it is TypeSafe-direct only (no OpenRouter), needs a personal Cloudflare Worker with an intentionally unauthenticated /mcp, and targets RAG/KB workflows rather than coding. Its proactive-use tool descriptions are a useful pattern to copy, but you would be better off with a small local stdio MCP or hook pointed at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone.

gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.name: Takamasa045/ctxfilter-jev
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.whatItDoes: A personal, Mac/Codex-specific proof-of-concept that adds an MCP server (Python stdio, one tool classify_records). It reads an allowlisted local JSONL file, extracts bounded excerpts via a separate ctxfilter tool, and sends them to a locally cached jev-mcp@0.4.0 process (tool jev_ask) to label each record relevant, irrelevant or needs_context for a given goal. It does not talk to Jev over HTTP itself. The README says it is not a distributable package and does not work after a plain clone.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter, systemone or decisions endpoint string appears anywhere in the repo (grep -i openrouter|systemone|decisions over outputs/src and outputs/registration returned nothing). The code never makes an HTTP call. outputs/src/ctxfilter_jev/jev_client.py:273-285 spawns a stdio child and calls tools/call name=jev_ask on the cached jev-mcp. constants.py:18 sets KEY_FILE=~/.config/typesafe/key, and provenance.py:74-80 only checks that the file exists and is non-empty. constants.py:19-27 hardcodes /Users/takamasa/.npm/_npx/9bcdfa5b415c6be7/node_modules/jev-mcp and requires jev-mcp@0.4.0, npx and ~/.codex/config.toml. provenance.py:87-88 raises an error if the configured launcher is not exactly that npx jev-mcp@0.4.0. So the provider is whatever jev-mcp@0.4.0 uses, which is TypeSafe direct and not evidenced as OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: None. It delegates entirely to the external jev-mcp npm package.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Hard, and not worth doing. There is no base URL or key to swap in this repo. The dependency is a pinned, cached third-party jev-mcp dist with hardcoded macOS paths, Python 3.14 paths, a Codex config reader and a Jev-launcher identity check. Switching to OpenRouter would mean rewriting jev_client.py to POST to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and removing the provenance checks. That would be a rewrite, not a patch.

interface.name: MCP tool classify_records
interface.purpose: mcp_server.py:_tool_schemas. Takes path (required), goal (max 400 chars), criteria, deterministic, from_byte, identity, max_records (max 16), max_output_bytes (max 16384), max_runtime_ms (max 45000) and max_scan_bytes. Classifies JSONL records as relevant, irrelevant or needs_context, and defers anything ambiguous, low-confidence or failed. It is default-deny unless the file path and hash are on the local allowlist.

interface.name: CLI ctxfilter-jev fingerprint
interface.purpose: Prints path and hash and suggests an allowlist entry. Does not grant permission.

interface.name: CLI ctxfilter-jev allowlist-add / classify / mcp
interface.purpose: Registers a file hash in the allowlist, runs a classification, or starts the stdio MCP server.

interface.name: registration/install-ctxfilter-jev.py and rollback-ctxfilter-jev.py
interface.purpose: Edits and reverts ~/.codex/config.toml. Codex only, no Claude Code .mcp.json, hooks, skills or plugin manifest.

gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.license: None (no LICENSE file; licenseInfo is null, so all rights reserved by default)
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.runtime: Python 3.14 (hardcoded /opt/homebrew path) plus a cached Node jev-mcp@0.4.0 dist, plus an external ctxfilter repo that is not included
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.install: No install path. The README says cloning is not enough. You must edit the hardcoded absolute paths in constants.py, fetch the separate ctxfilter repo (../codex-context-filter-grok46), have jev-mcp@0.4.0 in the npx cache, and have a Codex ~/.codex/config.toml that launches it. The registration scripts target Codex only.
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.tests: About 41 unittest tests (test_classify, test_jev_client, test_mcp_process, test_cli_process, test_extract and others) run against a mock Jev transport. The README reports them as passing on the author's Mac only. There is no CI (.github is absent). I did not run them, per the hard rules.
security: Design is security-conscious: allowlist keyed on path plus hash, default deny, byte/time/record bounds, excerpts capped at 240 to 400 chars, a fixed untrusted-evidence notice, and secret env stripping for the child process (strip_secret_env).
Launcher is pinned to a cached jev-mcp dist and its sha256 is recorded (provenance.py:60-70). The key is read from a file, not argv, and the code only checks file existence.
The Jev child is spawned as a subprocess with a list argv (no shell), start_new_session=True and stderr discarded. Spawn is bounded by a 20 s timeout and a process-group kill.
Fetched JSONL record text goes into the Jev state, so there is a prompt-injection surface. It is mitigated, since Jev returns typed choices, but it is not eliminated.

No LICENSE, hardcoded /Users/takamasa paths, no npm postinstall and no curl|sh installer, no telemetry seen. The registration scripts rewrite ~/.codex/config.toml, which is invasive for a foreign environment.
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.dataEgress: Only for allowlisted JSONL files: excerpts (default 240 chars each, max 400) of up to 8 to 16 records, plus the goal (max 400 chars) and up to 4 criteria rules (200 chars each), sent as a state payload of at most 64 KB via jev-mcp to TypeSafe. The tool does not transmit source code, diffs or general tool outputs. Nothing leaves without an allowlist entry, and the README says the goal and rules need separate approval.
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.failureMode: Fail-safe and defer. Timeout (default 25 s runtime, 20 s Jev), malformed reply, transport error, provenance mismatch or file change during the call all yield a deferred or error result, never a false negative. In Claude Code the tool would simply return an error and Claude carries on. It never blocks like a hook. However, when the launcher check fails (the case on every machine except the author's Mac), Jev is never called at all.
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (classify_records). The description is about 1,000 chars and the schema about 1,600 chars, so roughly 650 to 700 tokens. No server instructions are set that I saw, and no hooks inject text. The optional AGENTS-block.md is Codex-only (about 150 tokens if copied).
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills, plugin manifest or proxy. The description says it is opt-in and that ordinary literal search should use ctxfilter without Jev, so Claude would rarely pick it. Its input is a JSONL file path that must be allowlisted, which is not a normal coding-loop input.
gh-takamasa045-ctxfilter-jev.latencyImpact: The tool starts a Python process, then the ctxfilter extraction, then a Node jev-mcp child with initialize, tools/list and tools/call. It adds process-spawn overhead of hundreds of ms to seconds, plus Jev's 70 to 500 ms claimed latency, per call. It only applies when the tool is invoked, so there is no per-turn overhead.
pros: Careful, well-bounded design for sending untrusted local data to an external inference call: allowlist by hash, size limits, defers on uncertainty instead of guessing negative.

Uses Jev's typed Choice-style answer (relevant, irrelevant, needs_context) with a confidence threshold (ACT_ABOVE 0.8, REVIEW_ABOVE 0.5) as a gate. This is a reasonable pattern to copy for log triage.

security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from env and sent as a Bearer header. It is not passed in argv by the server itself. It is only visible in argv if the host config or scripts/install.py bakes it in.
No shell execution or telemetry found in the package. subprocess is used only to launch Chrome (cdp.py:243), with output sent to DEVNULL.

Prompt-injection surface is real. Untrusted page text goes to the model, and the prompt tells it to treat page text as data (policy.py:30). The server limits agents to observed refs. It has no JS eval or click_at, JS assertions are off by default (JEVMCP_ALLOW_JS=0), and there are domain allow/deny lists and confirm patterns. Uploads are ON by default (JEVMCP_ALLOW_UPLOADS=1), so a hostile page could try to induce file uploads.

Persists a Chrome profile and macros under ~/.jev-ultrafast-mcp. Attach mode can drive the user's real logged-in Chrome (Chrome 144+ DevToolsActivePort). That is a large blast radius on client accounts.
Optional Chrome extension and mcpb/smithery packaging widen the surface. scripts/install.py edits other tools' config files, so review before running.
MIT licence. Single anonymous-ish maintainer, brand-new repo, 2 forks, 19 stars. No supply-chain track record.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.dataEgress: Per browser_goal step, sent to OpenRouter: page URL, title, up to about 6000 chars of page text (JEVMCP_MAX_TEXT), the full element list (ref, role, name, value, options, checked), and the last 10 actions (policy.py:355-389). If TYPE_TEXT or select is used, field name, options and goal go too. If TEXT_MODEL inherits OpenRouter, up to 6000 chars of page text plus goal go to the chat model. It does not send source code, diffs or Claude Code prompts, except whatever the goal string contains. Any logged-in page content (client dashboards, admin panels) is sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe when the browser is in attach mode. The direct tools (open, observe, act, assert) make no external calls.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed per call and non-fatal to Claude Code. The server imports and runs without a key. With no key, browser_goal returns 'turbo_unavailable' and executes nothing, so Claude falls back to the manual tools. The httpx timeout is 30 s, with 3 attempts and backoff on 429/503/529 (policy.py:153-174). Network errors return TurboUnavailable('Decision model unreachable; no action executed'). Malformed or unexpected responses are rejected the same way. Never blocks Claude's other tools.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.latencyImpact: Only when browser_goal is called. Each step is 1 Decisions call (about 70-500 ms claimed) plus Chrome CDP actions, up to 20 steps per goal by default (max_steps=20). Zero added latency to non-browser turns, since there are no hooks and no proxy. A cold Chrome launch adds seconds on the first call.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.contextCost: 10 tools. Tool names, docstrings and args total about 8.5k chars, plus server INSTRUCTIONS of 2,015 chars, so about 2.1k tokens before JSON schema overhead. Realistic estimate is 2.5-3.5k tokens always resident (less if tool search defers MCP tools). The optional SKILL.md adds about 100 tokens to the description list. No hook-injected text.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, strongly nudged. The server INSTRUCTIONS say 'Do not drive a task yourself, click by click; that is what this server is for', and the optional skill description triggers on any browser or URL-plus-action request. Nothing is deterministic, no hooks. It only fires on browser tasks, not on ordinary coding decisions.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code: JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter plus OPENROUTER_API_KEY posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the {model,state,questions} contract (config.py:83-118). No patching needed.
Fail-closed and isolated: with no key or with Jev down, browser_goal returns turbo_unavailable, executes nothing, and Claude falls back to manual tools. The server never breaks a session.

Uses Jev for what a System One model fits: Choice questions with per-option probabilities for 'which ref next', with bounded 30 s timeouts and retries. One of few real Jev integrations that actually runs a decision loop.
Server-side loop keeps page content out of Claude's context, and macro replay uses zero model calls. This is useful for repetitive web QA or check-in flows.
Safety rails are sensible: no arbitrary JS or coordinate clicks, ref-revalidation, JS assertions off by default, domain allow/deny lists, and code-checked verify assertions.
Direct tools need no key. The auto-trigger skill and server instructions mean Claude uses it without being told to.
cons: It is a browser-automation server. Jev is used only to pick clickable elements, so it does not touch coding decisions such as file routing, commit or test triage, or permission classification. It does not deliver the user's stated goal of Jev deciding when it adds value in Claude Code.

Overlaps the Playwright MCP the user already has. Two browser stacks compete for the same tasks, and the strong 'do not drive it yourself' instructions and skill can pull Claude away from Playwright or make it choose inconsistently.
Sends page text and element names (potentially from client apps or authenticated sessions in attach mode) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a client-confidentiality concern.

Very immature: created 2026-09-19, 81 commits from one author in 5 days, 19 stars, 2 forks, v0.1.5, beta. The CI unit-test step is continue-on-error. The author's 'the release the registry would accept' style suggests a rapid-fire, possibly AI-generated codebase (CHANGELOG is 109 KB).
About 2.5-3.5k tokens of always-resident context for 10 tools plus 2k chars of instructions, for a feature used only on browser tasks.

Real browser autonomy driven by an unverified small model (skeptics: possibly a router over a flash LLM) on untrusted pages. Uploads on by default, persistent profile, and attach-to-real-Chrome mode give prompt-injection consequences.
Needs a local Chrome, a paid OpenRouter credit purchase (no :free variant), and the TYPE_TEXT path needs a separate chat model, so it is not fully Jev-only.
Not verified by running; static read only. Live latency and quality are unknown.
gh-jiawei686-jev-ultrafast-mcp.verdict: A real, well-guarded, fail-closed Jev integration with first-class OpenRouter support. It is a niche browser-automation tool that duplicates the user's Playwright MCP and does nothing for everyday coding decisions. It is worth trying in a sandbox for repetitive web flows, but not as the answer to 'Jev used automatically in Claude Code'.
