gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.name: MarkChu-git/typesafe-mcp (npm: typesafe-mcp)
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: A working stdio MCP server (Bun, TypeScript, about 880 LOC of src) that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk and exposes Jev's three primitives as 5 typed tools (jev_check/Noul, jev_classify/Choice, jev_score/Score, jev_ask/batch, jev_models). The server, not Jev, computes a threshold-gated act/review/abstain verdict from certainty (default act_above 0.8, review_above 0.5). The discovery summary "research/scaffolding" is outdated: the repo also has a published npm package (v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 on 2026-09-21), MIT license, CI, and about 18 test files. It is a third-party wrapper by an individual, not a TypeSafe official project.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code in the repo (grep for openrouter/baseURL in src/ returns nothing). src/config.ts:5-9 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS. src/client.ts:22-28 builds `new TypeSafeClient({apiKey, defaultModel, timeout, fetch, logLevel})` without baseURL, so the SDK default https://api.typesafe.ai applies. The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:58 and 513) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai, trailing slashes stripped). It POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (index.mjs:554 and 581). Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would therefore hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the documented OpenRouter System One endpoint. This is inferred from code and not tested (no third-party code was run). Model ids must also be switched to OpenRouter ids (TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). The `model` input is a free string with no allowlist (src/schemas.ts:30-33). docs/research-jev-typesafe-mcp.md:182 says OpenRouter compatibility is unconfirmed.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change needed. It is env-only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus an OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, plus OpenRouter model ids. Remaining risks are that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone request/response schema matches TypeSafe's exactly (the brief says it is the same System One API, but this was not verified), and that the jev_models tool will likely fail. SDK models.list() does GET /v1/models and requires `{models:[...]}` (index.mjs:365-370), while OpenRouter's /api/v1/models returns a different shape. Only the health-check tool is affected. Alternatively, a one-line patch in src/client.ts passing baseURL would make it explicit.
providerSupport.others: Direct TypeSafe API only in docs and defaults (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone). The SDK also accepts defaultHeaders and baseURL in code.

interface.name: jev_models
interface.purpose: Lists models via GET /v1/models and reports the default model. Health check with no inference tokens (src/tools/models.ts:24). Likely broken against OpenRouter because of the response shape.

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Noul: yes/no question about `state`. Returns probability, answer, certainty=|p-0.5|*2, decision, thresholds, model, usage (src/tools/check.ts). Annotated readOnlyHint and idempotentHint.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Choice: pick one of 2-255 options. Returns choice, probabilities, confidence, plus gating fields.

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Score: rate on 2-10 ordered levels. Returns expected score, legend, probabilities, confidence, plus gating fields.

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Batch of mixed Noul/Choice/Score questions against one state in a single upstream call (README claims about 10x cheaper). Returns answers keyed by the caller's ids.

gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.tests: About 17 test files under tests/ (unit tests for client, config, errors, gating, schemas, questions and result; in-process MCP tests for each tool; a stdio test; recorded API fixtures including 401/422/429/529 errors; and a live integration test that skips without a key). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs tsc, oxlint and bun test on Ubuntu, with macOS/Windows advisory. Also CodeQL, dependency review, actionlint and zizmor. Not executed by me.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.runtime: Bun (>=1.2.0, pinned bun@1.4.2). Launched with `bunx typesafe-mcp`, and the npm bin is a Bun-targeted single-file bundle (`bun build --target=bun`). Bun is NOT installed on the user's stack (Node 24, uv). The bundle has a Bun target, so plain `npx` or `node` is not guaranteed to run it, and `bun` would have to be installed. Running from source needs `bun install`.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.install: claude mcp add jev -s user -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- bunx typesafe-mcp (needs Bun on PATH). For OpenRouter, add -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -e TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (untested). Safer for this user is to pin the version (bunx typesafe-mcp@0.1.1), or vendor and build from source after review. `claude mcp add -e KEY=value` puts the key in ~/.claude.json, so prefer env expansion from a shell-exported variable.
security: API key is read only from env (src/config.ts:23) and never placed in argv. The README config passes it via the MCP `env` block, so it is not visible in the process list. It does end up in plaintext in the Claude config file if pasted.

Errors redact keys (README says so; src/errors.ts handles the mapping). The SDK's logLevel is forced to 'warn' (src/client.ts:27), so the request body is not logged (SDK debug level would log bodies and redacted headers).

No shell execution, child_process, eval, or telemetry found in src/. The published bundle (mcpnpm dist/typesafe-mcp.js, 22.5k lines) contains no eval, child_process, or spawn calls. No postinstall scripts in typesafe-mcp or @typesafe-ai/sdk package.json. No curl|sh installer.

Supply chain: 2 runtime deps that matter (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, published 2026-09-15 by the TypeSafe maintainers; @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0) plus zod. Releases use OIDC trusted publishing with provenance. The author is an individual (1 contributor, 1 star), so the trust is in one unknown maintainer plus a very new npm package. Pin the version.

Prompt-injection surface is low: outputs are numeric probabilities and echoed ids, with no free text from the model. The model's answer is constrained. But the tool inputs (`state`) are arbitrary text the agent chooses to send to a third party.

Repo contains committed .claude/.cursor skills and a .claude/settings.json with teamai hooks. These are the author's own dev tooling in the repo, are not shipped in the npm package (files: dist, examples), and are irrelevant unless someone opens the repo in Claude Code.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in the `state` and `question`/`options`/`levels`/`criteria` fields of a tool call goes to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is changed), as JSON POST to /v1/systemone with Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: the server never reads files, diffs or transcripts on its own, and only the text Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine. Extra headers sent: User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK / X-TypeSafe-Runtime (SDK version and runtime name). With OpenRouter, the provider also sees the payload and may apply its own logging or data policies, which matters for client projects. The state limit is about 32k tokens.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-soft per call and not blocking. This is an MCP tool, not a hook, so a Jev outage only returns an isError tool result with a category prefix (TIMEOUT, NETWORK, RATE_LIMIT, OVERLOADED, UPSTREAM, AUTH, CONFIG, VALIDATION) and Claude carries on. Timeout is 10 s per attempt (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS in src/config.ts:13, override via TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS). The SDK retries up to 2 times with backoff (index.mjs:73-74), so the worst case is about 30 s of hang for one tool call. Without a key the server still starts and lists tools, and calls return a CONFIG error. Note that Claude might waste turns retrying or reasoning about the error.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. Tool descriptions total about 1.9k characters. The zod schemas with long .describe() text (state, question, model, thresholds, and a discriminated union in jev_ask) plus outputSchemas add roughly 8-10k characters more. My estimate is about 2.5-3.5k tokens of tool definitions, and it is not measured. No MCP server `instructions` (createServer only sets name and version, src/server.ts:11). No hook-injected text. Loaded lazily via ToolSearch if the user has deferred MCP tools enabled.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code will call jev_* only if the model decides the tool descriptions fit the current situation. The descriptions are generic (an "ask Jev a yes/no question about state"), with no coding triggers, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no skill, and no hook. So it will rarely fire on its own for daily coding, and a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill would be needed to make it fire reliably. The user's requirement "without me prompting" is only weakly met.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Adds nothing to turns where the tool is not called (no hooks, no proxy). When it is called: Jev's claimed 70-500 ms end to end plus MCP stdio overhead, and Bun cold start at spawn. On failure or timeout, up to 10 s x 3 attempts. Each call also costs a model turn (tool_use plus result, about 200-400 tokens), which usually exceeds the latency of Jev itself.
pros: It is the only candidate here with a real, tested, MIT-licensed Jev MCP server that exposes all three primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) plus a batch `jev_ask`, with strict zod input/output schemas and outputSchema on every tool (src/tools/*.ts).

OpenRouter switch is env-only in theory: the official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and sends Bearer to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (sdk index.mjs:58,513,554,581), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key should reach OpenRouter's System One endpoint with no fork.

Sensible engineering hygiene for a week-old repo: pinned GitHub Action SHAs, CodeQL, zizmor, dependency review, OIDC npm provenance, recorded error fixtures for 401/422/429/529, key redaction, stdout kept clean for stdio.

Server-computed act/review/abstain gate with echoed thresholds (src/gating.ts) makes the output easy for an agent to act on deterministically, and `jev_ask` batching keeps calls to one upstream request.
Low risk profile: key via env not argv, no shell exec or postinstall, no telemetry in src or the bundle, readOnlyHint on tools, data sent only when Claude passes it.
Small footprint of 5 tools (about 3k tokens of context), and fail-soft errors so an outage never blocks coding.
cons: Does not meet the core requirement of automatic use: pure model-discretion tools with generic descriptions and no coding-specific triggers, no skill, no hook and no CLAUDE.md snippet, so Claude will seldom reach for it unless told. Integration would need extra glue (a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill written by the user).

OpenRouter is not supported in code or docs (docs/research-jev-typesafe-mcp.md:182 says unconfirmed). The base-URL trick depends on OpenRouter's /v1/systemone schema matching TypeSafe's, and I did not verify that. jev_models will very likely fail because it expects `{models:[...]}` from GET /v1/models (sdk index.mjs:368-371), and the default model ids (jev-latest, jev-1.13.0 hints in src/config.ts:11-12 and schema text) are not OpenRouter ids (typesafe/jev-1.13), so the user has to override the model everywhere.

Requires Bun, which is not in the user's stack (Node 24, uv). The npm bundle is built with `--target=bun`, so npx/node use is not supported by the README. Adds a runtime to install for one small server.

Very immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-21, 15 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 1 fork, v0.1.1 only, SERVER_VERSION constant still says 0.1.0 (src/config.ts:2) although the package is 0.1.1. Roadmap items (HTTP transport, Jev-specific coding tools like jev_gate) are not implemented. Depends on an SDK that is itself only about 2 weeks old (0.6.0, 2026-09-15). Jev is beta.

The MCP server asks for a decision, but for coding the tool result is only a probability. Claude still has to spend a model turn to decide to call it and to read the result, so it is slower and more expensive than just deciding. The Opus main model answers a typed choice in one thought. Value only appears for routing or gating logic in the user's own apps, or for calibrated abstain thresholds.

Sends `state` text (potentially client code or ticket content) to TypeSafe or OpenRouter. No per-project allowlist or redaction, and the user's existing secret-leak guard only covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* tool inputs, so a leak would be possible if Claude passes secrets in `state`.
Failure worst case is a 30 s hang per call (10 s timeout x 3 attempts) with no circuit breaker, and there is no fast-fail mode.
Adds 5 tool definitions (about 3k tokens) to every session for a tool that will rarely be called, unless deferred tools are used.
gh-markchu-git-typesafe-mcp.verdict: The best-built Jev MCP wrapper found so far and almost certainly switchable to OpenRouter with just TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus an OpenRouter key and typesafe/* model ids (inferred from code, not tested), but it is a passive, generic tool that Claude will rarely call unprompted, needs Bun, and comes from a one-week-old single-maintainer repo. Use it at most as a pinned, optional building block behind a CLAUDE.md rule or skill, not as the automatic integration the user wants.

gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.name: teempai/jev-in-codex
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.whatItDoes: A Codex plugin plus stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Node 22+) with ONE tool, jev_label. It reads a JSONL file of {id,text} records (1-256 records, 1 MiB max) inside a configured workspace root. It sends them to TypeSafe System One as 'choice' questions, 8 questions per request, and writes a new id/label JSONL file. It returns counts and the original text of records with confidence below 0.8. The earlier versions had three tools (capability selection, context search, output triage). The author removed them in v0.3.0 (2026-09-20) because benchmarks showed no useful gain. Today it is only batch text classification, not the tool/skill selection or context search in the discovery summary. The discovery summary is out of date.

providerSupport.evidence: src/labelling.ts:53 hardcodes fetch('https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone') with `Authorization: Bearer ${options.apiKey}`. src/index.ts:13 reads only process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY. src/labelling.ts:27 pins MODEL='jev-1.13.0' (the old JEV_MODEL override was removed). There is no base-URL env var. The docs say production has no endpoint override; the test-only redirect is test/fixtures/local-typesafe.mjs. The request body is {model, state:{items}, questions:{q0..:{type:'choice',instructions,criteria}}}. It expects response.answers.qN.{type,choice,confidence,probabilities} (labelling.ts:55-57 and 76-83). grep for 'openrouter' in all source and docs finds nothing.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe only.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial for the transport, unverified for the schema. It needs a 3-line fork edit: change the URL at labelling.ts:53 to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, change MODEL at labelling.ts:27 to typesafe/jev-1.13, and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY at index.ts:13. Nothing in the code depends on a TypeSafe-only feature. It assumes OpenRouter's System One API passes the request and response schema through unchanged, which I could not check from this repo. Tests use a loopback simulator, so they would not catch a schema difference. The patch is worthless if the tool does not fit the use case (see cons).

interface.name: jev_label (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Args: path (relative to workspace root), policy ('feedback_theme' or {question, criteria:{label:definition}} with 2-16 labels), and optional output_path. Labels each JSONL record and writes a new decisions.jsonl. It never overwrites (src/server.ts:15-22, src/labelling.ts:44-105).

interface.name: skills/jev-label/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Codex skill. Its description tells the model to use jev_label for a substantial JSONL text batch and to prefer ordinary tools for small batches. It is not a code-search or tool-selection skill.

interface.name: CLI --help / --root
interface.purpose: src/index.ts. Starts the stdio MCP server. It needs --root or JEV_WORKSPACE_ROOT and exits on failure.

interface.name: No hooks
interface.purpose: The repo has no hooks.json, no Claude Code plugin.json (only .codex-plugin/plugin.json) and no marketplace.json. .mcp.json uses Codex-style 'env_vars' and 'tool_timeout_sec', which Claude Code does not read.

security: API key: read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent only in an Authorization header (labelling.ts:53). It is never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. The bundled README config uses env_vars passthrough.
Redirects rejected (redirect:'error'). Provider error bodies are not exposed. The server logs nothing and has no telemetry and no cache (README, and confirmed by reading the 225 lines of src).
No shell execution and no child processes. The old ripgrep dependency was removed.

Filesystem: workspace-root confinement with realpath and O_NOFOLLOW. It excludes .git, node_modules, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .env*, *.pem, *.key and similar (workspace.ts:5-6). The write uses flag 'wx', mode 0600, and no overwrite. Exclusions are filename-based only; the README admits there is no secret detection.

Prompt injection: records are marked untrusted in the instruction. The model returns only a constrained enum label, so an injection cannot direct actions. The returned review text is original file content that goes back into Claude's context.

Supply chain: private:true (not on npm); it must be cloned and built locally. Two runtime deps (@modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0, zod 4.6.5). CI uses 'npm ci --ignore-scripts' and there is no postinstall. Installation is by cloning and building, or via the agent-driven docs/INSTALL.md prompt. That needs a manual review before use.

Very young repo: created 2026-09-19, 7 commits, 6 stars, no releases, 2 authors (probably one team, Vectordrift/Teemu Paivinen). No independent review; the security review in docs targets the retired implementation.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.dataEgress: Every record's full text in the JSONL file, plus the question and criteria, goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. It only sends what the model chose to put in a JSONL file inside the workspace. It does not send prompts, diffs, tool outputs or the repo automatically. Up to 256 records, 6,000 characters each. The bearer key goes to TypeSafe only.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.failureMode: Fail-closed, but harmless because it is an opt-in tool call. On a missing key, an HTTP error, a malformed answer or an incomplete batch it returns isError with 'No output was created; use ordinary tools or retry later' and creates no file (labelling.ts:49, 75, 85, 88-91). Per-request timeout is 8 s, total deadline 20 s, and the MCP tool timeout in config is 90 s. It never fabricates local labels. It cannot block other Claude Code work, since nothing is intercepted.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.latencyImpact: None on normal turns, because there is no hook or proxy. When called, it takes about 0.5-3 s for 8 parallel requests of 8 questions each, with a hard cap of 20 s. The added time also includes the model composing a JSONL file first. That preparation can cancel the benefit, and the author says so.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (jev_label). The tool description is about 470 characters and the input schema with the policy union is about 900 characters. Server instructions are about 330 characters. The total is roughly 400-500 tokens. There are no hooks and no injected text. The bundled SKILL.md is about 3 KB (about 800 tokens), but the skill only loads in Codex, and its description is about 550 characters.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. In Codex the skill description acts as a trigger. In Claude Code you would only get the MCP tool, and its description says 'Label id/text JSONL text records'. Claude will rarely pick it, because a Claude Code session almost never has a labelling job with a JSONL file. There is no deterministic hook.
pros: Small, readable code: 225 lines of TypeScript in 5 files, easy to audit and to fork.
Careful hardening: the key is passed by env and not argv, redirects are rejected, there is a workspace jail with O_NOFOLLOW, no overwrite, and no shell or telemetry.
Fails closed and never makes up labels.
Only one tool, so a context cost of about 500 tokens.

It really does use Jev's Choice primitive with per-option probabilities and confidence (labelling.ts:55-57, 76-83), so it is a useful reference for the wire format of /v1/systemone: {model, state, questions:{qN:{type:'choice', instructions, criteria}}} -> answers.qN.{choice, confidence, probabilities}.
Honest about limits: the author removed tools that lacked a benchmark gain and states it is synthetic data and alpha.
MIT licence, CI on Node 22 and 24, unit and e2e tests using a loopback simulator.
cons: The discovery summary is wrong. The 'tool/skill selection, context search, output triage' tools were removed on 2026-09-20. What remains is batch JSONL text labelling. That does nothing for daily coding in Claude Code.
Built for Codex: .codex-plugin/plugin.json and a Codex-format .mcp.json (env_vars, tool_timeout_sec). There is no Claude Code plugin or hook config.
No OpenRouter support: URL, model ID (jev-1.13.0) and env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) are hard-coded with no override. A fork is needed, and the OpenRouter schema is unverified.
Can't be automatic: model-discretion tool only, with no hook. Claude would rarely have a 1-256 record JSONL file to label, and the author's own skill says to avoid it for small batches.
Requires a clone and a local build (private:true, not on npm), with no release or version pinning by tag.
Very immature: 6 stars, 7 commits in 2 days of activity (2026-09-19 to 2026-09-21), no releases, and gains are measured only on 64-record synthetic sets with paired runs of n=4.
Sends full record text to a third party; embedded secrets are not detected. That matters for client projects.
The tool writes files, so it would go through permission prompts unless bypass mode is on.
gh-teempai-jev-in-codex.verdict: Not suitable. After v0.3.0 this is a Codex-only batch JSONL labelling tool, not tool/skill selection or context search, and it has no hooks, no OpenRouter support and no reason for Claude Code to invoke it on normal coding turns. Only useful as a small, clean reference for the System One choice-question wire format (a fork to OpenRouter would take 3 lines, but the tool would still be unused).

gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.name: rilfi/token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experimental
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.whatItDoes: Two things in one repo: (1) a stdio MCP server (token-optimizer-jev-mcp 0.1.0, TypeScript, wraps @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing 6 read-only tools for Jev typed decisions (batched jev_ask, jev_choice/score/noul, jev_list_models, jev_server_info) with a local context-budget guard and compact answers; (2) a set of six Node hook scripts (hooks/) plus agent-bridge.mjs that call the MCP server over stdio to run Jev decisions at lifecycle events (destructive-command risk gate, failure triage, completion gate, session profile). The hooks were built and benchmarked for the Hermes agent; Claude Code support is a translation shim in agent-bridge.mjs. Not published to npm.

providerSupport.evidence: Default base URL https://api.typesafe.ai at src/config.ts:26 (DEFAULTS.baseURL); env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (config.ts:12, README 'for a proxy'); key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or JEV_API_KEY (config.ts:10-11, hooks/jev-client.mjs resolveApiKey). No mention of 'openrouter' anywhere in the repo (grep). The @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (sdk/package/dist/index.mjs:548-556, 579-581) does POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and body {...request, model: request.model ?? defaultModel}. That path/auth pair matches OpenRouter's documented POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> + TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 is plausible with zero code change, but that is inferred, not tested; default model 'jev-latest' would not be an OpenRouter id; jev_list_models calls GET /v1/models and expects {models:[...]} (sdk index.mjs:365-370), which would fail or return the OpenRouter catalog shape.
providerSupport.others: None. Hook client passes process.env through to the spawned server, so the same env overrides apply to hooks. It does not use OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions endpoint.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle (env vars only: base URL, key, default model), because SDK path /v1/systemone and Bearer auth match OpenRouter's System One API. Unverified request/response parity; jev_list_models would break (harmless, optional tool).

gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.runtime: Node >=20.12 (TypeScript compiled to dist/, dist is gitignored so it must be npm-installed and built locally); deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.29, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, zod. Hooks are plain .mjs with no npm deps but require ../dist/index.js.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.install: Not installable as documented: `npx -y token-optimizer-jev-mcp` returns npm E404 (package never published; package.json repository points at a different repo name, rilfi/token-optimizer-jev-mcp). Would require git clone + npm install + npm run build (executes third-party build code), then register `node <REPO>/dist/index.js` as MCP and hand-paste the hooks JSON from README with <REPO> substituted.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.tests: Jest unit/protocol/offline-e2e suites (12 test files in src/) plus hooks/selftest.mjs (33 offline cases) and opt-in live tests; no CI (.github absent). Author benchmarks in bench/ (Hermes + deepseek-v4-flash, 6 tasks, n=1 per arm). I did not run any of it.
security: API key from env only, never a tool argument or in argv; hook client spawns the server with key in env (hooks/jev-client.mjs spawn env), not on the command line. Good.
Key resolution fallback reads Hermes config: ~/.hermes/config.yaml and ~/.hermes/.env by regex (jev-client.mjs resolveApiKey) - irrelevant to Claude Code but reads secret files if present.
MCP server itself: no shell, no fs, no path arguments; stdio only; all tools annotated readOnlyHint (README). Small attack surface.
No postinstall/preinstall scripts (package.json). prepublishOnly only. No curl|sh installer. No telemetry in server or SDK beyond X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers.

Prompt-injection surface: MCP instructions are benign, but hooks feed untrusted content to Jev (prompts, tool output) and act on its scores; H2 block reasons/H4 push-back text are static templates plus command text echoed back (truncate 160 chars) - low risk.

Deny-list is naive regex: `\b(shutdown|reboot|halt|poweroff)\b` matches anywhere in a command (e.g. `grep -r halt`, a git commit message), causing false blocks; SAFE_HINT is a prefix match so `cat x; <anything>` short-circuits the Jev gate (deny-list still runs first). Not a real security boundary.

Hook state written to ~/.hermes/state/jev-hooks/ (cache.json, blocked.jsonl, problems.jsonl storing command and result excerpts in plaintext) and ~/.hermes/logs; on this user's machine that creates a new plaintext store of commands from client projects.

Single-author 1-commit repo with 0 stars: no review history, package name/repo mismatch; supply-chain trust is that of an anonymous experiment. Its @typesafe-ai/sdk dependency is the vendor's own SDK.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.dataEgress: MCP tools: whatever `state` and question text the Claude model chooses to send (arbitrary code/diffs/text) to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL only (config.ts; README: only egress). Hooks (if wired): H1 sends the user's prompt (truncated to 4000 chars) on every UserPromptSubmit >=12 chars; H2 sends {tool, cwd, command<=2000 chars} for every non-'safe-shaped' Bash command and non-cwd write path (not file contents, only 'WRITE <path>'); H3 (inert under Claude) would send tool name + 600-char digest of failing output; H4 sends final_response (<=3000 chars) + record digests; H5 sends session-start signals. Commands and prompts can contain secrets or client-confidential text and would go to Jev/OpenRouter. No file contents are read by the hooks themselves.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every hook wraps errors and returns {} (hook-common.mjs runHook); Jev errors/timeouts/no key return allow (jev_pre_tool_call.mjs 'no decision'). Per-call timeouts: H2/H3 6000 ms, H1/H4 8000 ms (JEV_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS), Claude hook timeout suggested 20 s; MCP server per-attempt timeout 30 s with SDK retries. Guards: 12 h decision cache, 400 calls/day (JEV_HOOK_DAILY_LIMIT), 25 calls/session (JEV_HOOK_SESSION_LIMIT), kill-switch JEV_HOOKS_OFF or marker file. Worst case a slow Jev adds up to ~6-8 s per Bash call before allowing. Only the regex deny-list is fail-closed.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.contextCost: MCP: 6 tools with rich zod-described schemas (each judgment tool carries a 6-field option block and long state/criteria descriptions). Estimated ~11-13k chars of tool defs + ~2.4k chars server `instructions` (identity.ts:19-52) = roughly 3-3.5k tokens of always-on context, or less with tool search deferral. Hooks: H1 injects a one-line additionalContext only when P>=0.6 (rare); H5 injects a session-profile line; H4 push-back injects text and buys an extra turn. Author's own benchmark shows H1/H4 raised model cost 1.44x-3.08x, and lean profile (H2/H3/H5/H6) 1.00x with +12% wall time.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.autoInvocation: Two modes. (a) MCP tools: model-discretion only; the author's own three-way benchmark (bench/THREE-WAY.md) found the agent used the Jev MCP tools 0/6 times when the tools merely existed, so this does NOT meet the 'Claude uses it without being told' requirement. (b) Hooks: deterministic (UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop/SessionStart/SessionEnd), which does satisfy automatic invocation, but the Jev decisions are narrow safety/verification gates, and under Claude Code H3 and H4 are effectively dead code because the bridge does not map tool_response to extra.result or provide changed_paths/coding.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.latencyImpact: Each Jev-backed hook spawns node, which spawns a second node process (the MCP server), does initialize + tools/call: author measured 1.3-1.8 s per real decision (Jev ~1.1-1.3 s of it); deny-list/skip paths ~0.01-0.16 s. Serial and blocking in PreToolUse for any Bash command not starting with ls/cat/grep/git status-like prefixes (git commit, npm install, docker, node, etc. all trigger a call unless cached), plus ~1.5 s on every UserPromptSubmit >=12 chars. Bench: wall time +12% (lean) to +41% (all six).
pros: Only candidate found with actual deterministic Claude Code hook wiring for Jev (agent-bridge.mjs maps PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit/Stop/SessionStart/SessionEnd and Bash/Write/Edit names, decision:block + stderr), so automatic invocation is at least architecturally possible.

Hooks fail open with timeouts, 12h cache, daily and per-session call ceilings, per-hook env kill-switches, and a pure-regex deny-list that works with no network or key - sensible engineering for a hook that must not wedge a session.
MCP server is small, read-only, key never in argv or tool args, no postinstall, clean typed error codes, budget guard, batched jev_ask (one call, many questions) matching how Jev is meant to be used.

SDK path (/v1/systemone + Bearer) equals OpenRouter's System One API, so pointing it at OpenRouter is probably just TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key, and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13.

Honest, measured self-benchmarks (including that MCP tools were used 0/6 and hooks raised cost) - useful negative evidence on what does not work; Jev cost itself is negligible (~$0.00001 per decision).
cons: Not published to npm (E404), 1 commit, 1 author, 0 stars, created 7 days before audit, no CI/releases, package.json points to a different repo name: install path in the README does not work and requires cloning and building unreviewed third-party code.
Hooks are Hermes-first: install.mjs is Hermes/Windows only; state goes to ~/.hermes; Claude support is a hand-pasted README snippet with <REPO> paths and a required local build of dist/.

Claude bridge is incomplete: PostToolUse tool_response is never mapped to extra.result and Stop payload has no changed_paths/coding, so H3 (failure triage) never fires and H4 (completion gate) returns 'not a coding turn'; the Stop push-back also ignores stop_hook_active. Real value under Claude Code reduces to H2 + H1 + H5.

Decision value for this user is low: H2 duplicates what bypass/auto permission mode plus a regex deny-list already cover, and the user already has a PreToolUse secret guard; H1's 'irreversible request?' classifier just adds a sentence of warning. Author bench shows accuracy 6/6 with or without Jev, so no measured coding benefit.

Costs real latency on the hot path: ~1.5 s blocking per non-trivial Bash call and per prompt, via double node spawn, versus zero benefit on read-heavy sessions; and sends every prompt and shell command (may contain client secrets/code) to Jev/OpenRouter.

MCP tools alone are not automatic (0/6 agent uses in author's benchmark) and add ~3k tokens of tool definitions to every session; deny-list regex has false positives (word 'halt'/'reboot'/'shutdown' anywhere) and a prefix-based safe-list bypass.
gh-rilfi-token-optimizer-jev-mcp-experim.verdict: Interesting as a reference design for wiring Jev into Claude Code through deterministic hooks with fail-open semantics, but it is a one-week-old, unpublished, Hermes-oriented experiment whose Claude bridge leaves half the hooks inert and whose own benchmark shows no coding gain. Do not install it; at most borrow the hook pattern (small local wrapper calling OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone directly with a strict timeout) rather than the code.

gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.name: ndolinschi/toolgate
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.whatItDoes: Not a Claude Code hook despite the candidate label. It is a 283-line Next.js 15 demo web app (single page plus one POST /api/decide route). You paste a planned tool call as JSON. The route sends it to Jev with 5 fixed questions: a Choice for allow/ask_human/deny, a Score for risk, and 3 Noul questions for exfil, irreversible and policy_violation. It returns the answers. With no TYPESAFE_API_KEY it falls back to a regex heuristic that fakes the same answer shape. It has no MCP server, no hook script, no CLI, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md.

providerSupport.evidence: src/lib/jev.ts:59 const ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"; jev.ts:73 process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY; jev.ts:74 default model "jev-latest"; jev.ts:77-84 fetch with Authorization Bearer and body {state, model, questions}. grep for openrouter across the repo returns nothing. The endpoint host api.typesafe.ai is unverified: the brief lists the direct API as console.typesafe.ai keys and does not name this host. The request body shape {state, model, questions} is the author's assumption and may not match the OpenRouter Decisions or System One schemas. The response parsing (answers.*.probabilities/confidence/noul) is also untested against a real API.
providerSupport.others: None. No other gateway or provider code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial for the HTTP client. It would be a base URL change to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, a Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY and a model id such as typesafe/jev-1.13. The request and response schema would still need checking against OpenRouter's docs. The larger problem is that the repo is a web demo, so the useful part is only the 5 question definitions in src/lib/product.ts:11-45. Those are better reimplemented in your own PreToolUse hook script than patched from this repo.

gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.install: npm i && npm run dev (a local dev web server). There is no Claude Code install path: no hooks.json, no .mcp.json, no plugin manifest.

security: TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read from the server-side env only (jev.ts:73). It is not in argv, and nothing is logged.
/api/decide has no auth, rate limiting or input size cap. If the dev server is bound beyond localhost, anyone can spend the key.

Untrusted tool-call JSON is passed straight into the Jev state with no sanitization. That is prompt-injection surface, but Jev returns typed probabilities rather than free text, so the impact is limited to manipulating the score.

Fail-open demo fallback: with no key, a regex heuristic silently answers instead (jev.ts:105-115). meta.mode marks it, but nothing enforces it. A gate that silently degrades to regexes is a security smell.
Heuristic deny list is trivially bypassable (product.ts:51). It matches strings like 'rm -rf' and 'sudo', but not variants like find -delete or base64 payloads.
No postinstall scripts and no curl|sh. The dependencies are only next, react and tailwind.
No telemetry in the repo code (Next.js itself collects anonymous telemetry unless NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED is set).
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.dataEgress: In live mode, the full JSON in `state` (tool name, args, context, goal) plus the question text goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev.ts:77-84). In this repo, nothing hooks into Claude Code, so nothing leaves automatically. Only what you paste into the web UI is sent.
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.failureMode: If the key is present and Jev is down or slow, fetch has no timeout or AbortSignal (jev.ts:77). It hangs until the platform default, and a non-2xx response throws, which becomes a 500 (route.ts:11-13). If the key is missing, it silently uses fake heuristics. For Claude Code there is no fail-open or fail-closed behavior to evaluate, because there is no hook.
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.contextCost: Zero as shipped. It exposes no MCP tools, injects no hook text, and adds no skill descriptions. If the idea were rebuilt as a PreToolUse hook, the context cost would also be about 0, since hooks add no tokens to the context unless they return additionalContext.
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a manual web demo with no integration into Claude Code at all: no hook events, no MCP tool, no skill trigger.
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.latencyImpact: None to Claude Code, since it is not wired in. The route makes one Jev call per request, and the claimed latency is 70-500 ms. A rebuilt hook would add that per gated tool call.
pros: The question design is a sound template for a Jev-backed PreToolUse gate: one Choice (allow/ask_human/deny), one Score for risk, and Noul flags for exfil, irreversibility and policy violation (product.ts:11-45). It maps directly onto Jev's three primitives.
Its permissionDecision-like outputs (allow/ask/deny) match Claude Code's PreToolUse hook decisions, so porting is conceptually easy.
The client is small and readable (jev.ts, about 115 lines) and has no dangerous install steps.
The key is kept in an env var on the server side, not in argv.
cons: The candidate is mislabeled. It is a Next.js demo UI and has no hook, MCP server, skill or plugin, so it cannot be installed into Claude Code.
There is no OpenRouter support. It is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY. That host and request schema are unverified against the OpenRouter docs.
It has 1 commit, 3 stars, no license, no tests, no CI and a 7-line README, and the last push was 13 days before the audit date. It is a hackathon-style artifact.
The demo fallback silently substitutes regex heuristics when the key is missing. That is fail-open behavior disguised as an answer, which is wrong for a security gate.
No fetch timeout, no retry, no auth or rate limit on /api/decide.

Even as a hook, a per-tool-call gate would be redundant for this user. It would overlap the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook and the bypass/auto permission modes, and it would add 70-500 ms to every tool call.
gh-ndolinschi-toolgate.verdict: Not a usable integration: it is a standalone Next.js demo of a Jev tool-call gate with no Claude Code hook or MCP surface and no OpenRouter support. At most, copy its 5 question definitions as a design reference for a self-written PreToolUse hook.

gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.name: bgivenb/flick-computer-use (Flick)
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Playwright, Swift macOS AX helper) that runs a whole browser or macOS "computer use" goal autonomously. The host agent hands over a goal, exact inputs and completion conditions. Flick then loops observe (DOM or AX tree), then a Jev typed decision (Choice questions bundled into one /v1/systemone request), then execute and verify. It is a GUI automation agent that uses Jev as its per-step policy. It is not a coding-assistant integration or a general Jev decision tool.

providerSupport.evidence: src/providers/typesafe.ts:235 hardcodes fetch('https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone') with Authorization: Bearer ${this.key}. src/config.ts:13-14 read only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_MODEL (default 'jev-latest'). grep found no 'openrouter' string anywhere in src/ or scripts/. The request body is {model, state, questions}, and the response is parsed as {answers, model?, usage.input_tokens?} (typesafe.ts:255-257). Choice answers need {type:'choice', choice, confidence, probabilities}, and Noul answers need {type:'noul', noul} (typesafe.ts:8-9). The server.ts:53,175,189,221 error messages hard-require TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
providerSupport.others: Optional text-helper providers (not Jev): Cerebras qwen-3.8-27b, Groq, OpenAI gpt-6-luna via CEREBRAS_API_KEY / GROQ_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY (src/config.ts, src/providers/text-helper.ts).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, and only for the Jev leg. It is a 3-line patch, because the URL is a single literal and the key and model come from config: change the URL to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the key env to OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and the model to typesafe/jev-latest. This works only if OpenRouter's System One API accepts the same {model,state,questions} to {answers} schema (the brief implies it, but I could not verify it). The maintainer has no OpenRouter path, so it would be a private fork to maintain. The bigger blocker is that the tool is macOS-centric and does not fit the coding workflow (see cons).

gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.runtime: Node >=22 (TypeScript, tsx for tests), Playwright ^1.63 with Chromium, zod, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk; optional Swift helpers built on macOS. package.json is private:true, so nothing is published to npm. It installs from a git clone plus scripts/setup-agent.mjs.
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.tests: About 25 test files in tests/*.test.ts, run with tsx --test and no API key needed. They cover runner, browser, decision contract, workflow and more. GitHub Actions CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) has Linux browser+core and macOS native-build jobs. There are no releases and no tags. It is 6 days old with a single author. The maintainer's own README says "Early developer release... native macOS control is experimental".
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.install: git clone, then node scripts/setup-agent.mjs (npm ci, tsc build, Playwright Chromium download, empty .env.local). Then set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in .env.local and merge the output of `npm run mcp:config` into the MCP config (node /abs/path/dist/cli.js). The README's "install with your agent" prompt asks the agent to star the repo. This is a social-engineering-style instruction, and I ignored it. The installer itself does not star.
security: API key is read from a .env.local file in the install dir via process.loadEnvFile (src/config.ts:10-13) and sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. It is not in argv. The key does not appear in the MCP launch entry, which is good practice.
Redirects are blocked: redirect:'error' (typesafe.ts:236). Response size is capped at 2 MB on the fallback path (typesafe.ts:213).

Inputs whose names look like password, secret, token, api key, pin or otp are filtered out of the verification payload (typesafe.ts verificationInputs). Other inputs, page text and typed values are sent to TypeSafe. The README warns that task traces can contain input values.
No postinstall hooks. Setup runs npm ci, a Chromium download and an optional Swift build. There is no curl|sh.
No telemetry found. The only network calls are to api.typesafe.ai and the optional Cerebras, Groq and OpenAI endpoints.

Prompt-injection surface is large: page and app text feeds Jev's decisions and the writing helper, and Jev drives real clicks, typing and form submits. The system prompt says interface text is evidence and not instructions, but a 15-tool server that clicks, types and submits on the user's browser or (on macOS) desktop is a high-risk primitive, particularly in bypass mode.

The tool description tells the host agent to run a 'postMortem review' after every run and to save local guide lessons. This is agent-directed text in server instructions, and it steers agent behavior.
'existing-chrome' mode, which reuses the user's signed-in profile, is macOS-only (browser.ts:134).
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.dataEgress: Sent to api.typesafe.ai on every decision: the goal, supplied inputs (except keys that look secret), selected interface text (element names, roles, values, page title, URL), task memory and retained text artifacts, recent action history, and milestone evidence (up to 72 KB for the whole-goal check). If a text-helper key is set, the goal, current page text, the observed form and error history go to Cerebras, Groq or OpenAI. Screenshots stay local. OCR is local, on macOS only. Nothing from the user's code repo leaves the machine unless the browser goal displays it. There is no path for Claude Code transcripts, diffs or tool outputs to reach Jev.
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.failureMode: Fail-closed for the task, and the failure is contained. Each Jev call has a 15 s timeout (typesafe.ts:237) and up to 5 attempts, with backoff on 429/503/529 and transient network errors (150 ms x 2^n, 300 ms x 2^n). The last attempt uses a fresh HTTPS connection. After that the run throws a 'TypeSafe request failed' or 'retry budget exhausted' error and the task errors. Individual guarded driver actions have a 10 s timeout (server.ts:44). It is not a hook, so a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code's normal tools. Only computer_* calls fail. Direct inspect and act tools work without a key (server.ts:53).
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary coding turns, because nothing is in the hot path. It only matters when computer_* is called. Then each step costs a Jev round trip (the docs claim a ~6 s median for a 13-14 action synthetic task, so roughly 0.4 s per step) plus browser or AX time. That is a self-run synthetic benchmark on macOS.
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.contextCost: 15 tools registered in src/server.ts and src/app-guide-tools.ts (server.ts:85-262), plus a very long server 'instructions' string of about 2.4k chars (server.ts:33) and long tool descriptions and zod schemas. My estimate is 5-7k tokens (about 27k chars of TS source for the tool definitions, and a good part of that is prompt text that is not exposed to Claude). That is heavy for an MCP that overlaps with the already-installed playwright MCP (about 25 tools). There are no hooks and no injected text per turn. Claude Code's MCP tool search may defer the schemas.
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude calls computer_execute or computer_run when a task needs GUI automation, guided by the server instructions and tool descriptions. It is not a hook, skill trigger or proxy. Even used well, Jev here only drives the browser or desktop and never advises Claude on coding decisions, so it does nothing to serve the user's goal of Jev being used automatically for coding.
pros: Real, readable, tested source (about 3.5k lines of TS, about 25 test files, CI on Linux and macOS). It is a serious reference for how to build Jev Choice/Noul decision contracts (decisionContract in typesafe.ts:56 onward): options keyed by element IDs, per-field value questions, and probability/choice validation.

Batches several related questions into one /v1/systemone request and validates that the returned choice exists in the criteria. Its retry, backoff and fresh-connection fallback handle 429/503/529 sensibly.
MIT licensed, no postinstall, no telemetry, key kept out of argv, redirects blocked.
Runs on Linux for dedicated Playwright browser sessions (CI does this on ubuntu). The INSTALL notes mention the Ubuntu AppArmor Chromium setup.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It is browser and macOS GUI automation, and the user is on Linux doing coding. The native macOS control, existing-Chrome attach, Apple Vision OCR and user-input interruption are all macOS-only. On Linux only the generic Playwright path works, and playwright MCP is already installed.

No OpenRouter support: the URL https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone is hardcoded (typesafe.ts:235), and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_MODEL exist (config.ts:13-14). The user wants OpenRouter as the Jev provider, so this needs a private fork.

It cannot make Claude Code use Jev automatically for coding. Jev is buried inside a sub-agent loop, and Claude only decides whether to call computer_execute. There are no hooks, no gating of tool calls and no use of Jev for code decisions.
Heavy context footprint: 15 tools plus a roughly 2.4k-char instructions block, for an MCP that duplicates the existing playwright server.

Security posture is risky for a bypass-permissions user: an autonomous agent that clicks, types and submits in a real browser, driven by untrusted page text, with client-project browser sessions in scope. The server instructions also tell Claude to run post-mortems and write local guide files after every run.

Immature: 6 days old, 1 author, 24 commits, 23 stars, no releases, private package. The author's own README says 'early developer release' and 'native macOS control is experimental'. It is also 'independent, not affiliated with TypeSafe'.
Its tests stub the Jev calls. The only live checks (test:live) need a real TYPESAFE_API_KEY. I found no evidence that the OpenRouter route works with this schema.
The README install prompt tells the coding agent to star the repository on the user's GitHub account. That is an unrequested social action embedded in the install text.
gh-bgivenb-flick-computer-use.verdict: Not suitable as the Jev integration for this user. It is a macOS-centric GUI computer-use agent hardwired to api.typesafe.ai, not a way to have Claude Code consult Jev during coding, and it duplicates playwright MCP at a 5-7k token cost. Treat it only as a reference implementation for building Jev Choice/Noul contracts and a robust client.

gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.name: mukiwu/jev-search-mcp
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.whatItDoes: A web-search wrapper, not a decision-API integration. It POSTs a plain-language query to a third-party "Jev Search" web app (default https://jev.s1.dev, upstream superagents-lab/jev-search, built on Search1API) at /api/ask and reads back NDJSON results (intent, lane, done). Jev is only the server-side query planner and relevance judge inside that app. The Claude Code plugin uses the early-access "function hooks" API to intercept the built-in WebSearch tool and answer it from Jev Search, falling back to the built-in tool on failure. It also ships a jev_search MCP tool, an npx CLI and a skill. It never calls openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, /api/v1/systemone or the Choice/Noul/Score primitives, so it cannot be used to make typed decisions about code, diffs or agent state.

providerSupport.evidence: The client code has no Jev model API call at all. src/client.js:66 builds `${origin}/api/ask` from JEV_SEARCH_BASE_URL (src/tool.js:17, default https://jev.s1.dev at src/tool.js:6 and hooks/jev.js:9). A grep of src/ and hooks/ for openrouter|typesafe|api_key|systemone|decisions finds nothing. There is no API key in the client, and the only auth-like header is a spoofed same-origin `Origin` (src/client.js:69). The upstream server (superagents-lab/jev-search README) supports Jev providers typesafe (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY), vercel (AI Gateway, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY) and cloudflare (Workers AI). OpenRouter is not listed there either, and it also needs SEARCH1API_API_KEY.
providerSupport.others: Indirect only, via the self-hostable upstream Worker: TypeSafe direct, Vercel AI Gateway, Cloudflare Workers AI, plus Search1API for the search engines.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not patchable in this repo, because the plugin has no Jev API code to re-point. To get OpenRouter-hosted Jev behind it you would have to self-host superagents-lab/jev-search on Cloudflare Workers, add an OpenRouter provider to that Worker (moderate: a new provider branch calling openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone), and buy a Search1API key. You would then point baseUrl at your deployment. That is a large detour for a web-search feature and gives no coding-decision value.

interface.name: function hook tool.call {tool: WebSearch} (hooks/jev.js:85)
interface.purpose: Replaces every WebSearch execution with a Jev Search HTTP call through $.http.fetch. On error, non-2xx or zero hits it calls next(e), so the built-in search runs. Shows a status line and a toast.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_search (src/tool.js:34)
interface.purpose: Web search with query, optional window (any|24h|7d|30d), optional sources (12 enums) and max_results (1-40). Hand-rolled stdio JSON-RPC server (src/mcp.js), 1 tool. Descriptor says 'Use this instead of the built-in WebSearch'.

interface.name: skill jev-search (skills/jev-search/SKILL.md)
interface.purpose: Description-triggered on current-web questions, HN/Reddit/X sentiment, links/papers/repos. Tells the model to prefer WebSearch, then jev_search, then the npx CLI.

interface.name: CLI `jev-search-mcp search "..." [--window --sources --max --json]` (src/cli.js)
interface.purpose: Shell search. The README says to run it via npx, but the npm package is not published (npm registry 404), so the npx path and `claude mcp add ... npx -y jev-search-mcp` fail today. Only the plugin/marketplace or a git clone works.

interface.purpose: Instance URL (default jev.s1.dev), toggle WebSearch interception, results per search.

gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.runtime: Node >=22 for MCP/CLI (zero runtime deps). The function hook runs inside the Claude Code engine (no Node, no DOM), and needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 plus Claude Code >=2.1.271.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.install: Plugin: set env CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, then `claude plugin marketplace add mukiwu/muki-ai-plugins` and `claude plugin install jev-search@muki-ai-plugins`. Note the plugin clones the whole repo and the marketplace is a separate personal repo (muki-ai-plugins) that I did not audit. MCP-only: `claude mcp add --scope user jev-search -- npx -y jev-search-mcp` (currently broken, since the package is 404 on npm). Not installed or run during this audit.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.tests: Present: 8 test files (about 58 test cases) using node:test with a fake Jev server (test/helpers/fake-jev.js), covering client, hook, MCP stdio protocol, CLI, rank and format. CI in .github/workflows/test.yml runs npm test and the hook typecheck on Node 22. I did not run them (static audit only). No releases, no npm publish, 1 contributor, 8 commits all on 2026-09-21.
security: No API keys anywhere in the client, so nothing to leak in argv or process lists. The auth model is only a spoofed same-origin `Origin` header (src/client.js:69), and the upstream README itself says this is 'a browser boundary, not authentication'.

The default endpoint is a public demo run by a third party (jev.s1.dev, 'someone else's bill', about 10 req/min per IP). It is a trust and availability dependency you do not control. The logging policy claim ('does not store queries') is only the upstream README's word.

Prompt-injection surface: web-search snippets returned by the remote server are injected into the model context as tool results. The server can also return arbitrary text, so a compromised or hostile jev.s1.dev or baseUrl can feed the agent instructions. The hook replaces the built-in WebSearch result, so this is a new trust boundary versus Anthropic's search.

The hook injects guidance into the first-message context via prompt.context, plus a modified WebSearch tool description. That is a legitimate but opaque behaviour-steering channel that depends on an early-access API.

No shell execution, child_process, curl|sh or postinstall found in src/ or hooks/ (grep clean). The runtime has zero dependencies. The package.json files list excludes hooks/, so the npm build would not contain the hook.

No telemetry in the client. The plugin install path clones the whole repo and depends on a second unaudited repo (mukiwu/muki-ai-plugins) as the marketplace, and a 1-contributor, 9-day-old repo with no release pinning is a supply-chain risk, since anyone with push access controls hook code that runs inside the Claude Code engine.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.dataEgress: On each WebSearch call, the model-authored query (trimmed to 300 chars at a word boundary, src/client.js:8,34), optional window, and source list or domain filters go as a JSON POST to https://jev.s1.dev/api/ask (or your baseUrl). The upstream forwards that text to Search1API (Google/DDG/Yandex/etc.) and to a Jev provider. No source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent by the client itself, but the model may put project or client-specific terms (error strings, library names, internal product names) into a query. Nothing goes to OpenRouter or TypeSafe from the client. Note that with the hook, ALL WebSearch traffic is rerouted from Anthropic's search to a third-party demo host. That matters for client projects.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by design. In hooks/jev.js:98-103, any thrown error (network, non-2xx including 429, malformed NDJSON) logs a dim line and calls next(e), so the built-in WebSearch runs. It also falls back when 0 hits remain after domain filtering (hooks/jev.js:62,90). It has no explicit client timeout in the hook: it relies on the engine's hook time budget and the server's own 30 s deadline (a slow Jev can stall a search for up to ~30 s before fallback). The MCP path uses AbortSignal.timeout 35 s (src/tool.js:124) and returns failureText telling the model to fall back. There is no retry, no circuit breaker and no local cache, so a down or rate-limited host adds a failed round trip to every search.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.latencyImpact: Only when WebSearch or jev_search is called (no per-turn overhead). Jev Search does an LLM intent pass, then a multi-engine fan-out, then relevance scoring, and the README says it 'answers in a few seconds', with a 30 s server cap. This is likely slower than the built-in search, and worst case (down or slow host) adds up to ~30 s plus the fallback search. The 10 req/min per-IP limit makes agentic multi-search bursts hit 429 and fall back.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (jev_search). Descriptor is about 1.4k chars of description plus about 1.3k chars of schema, so roughly 650-750 tokens per session. The plugin adds a ~1.1k-char always-on context block (~280 tokens) from prompt.context and a small WebSearch description addition (~50-100 tokens). The skill description is ~600 chars (~150 tokens) in the skills list. Total about 1.1-1.3k tokens fixed overhead. The MCP server has no 'instructions' field. Tool results are ranked link lists (default 10 rows, up to 40), which are moderately sized.
gh-mukiwu-jev-search-mcp.autoInvocation: Plugin path: transparent interception. A deterministic function hook replaces every built-in WebSearch call, plus context and tool-description nudges so the model chooses WebSearch. That is automatic in the sense the user wants, but only for web search. The MCP tool and skill are model-discretion and description-triggered.
pros: Genuinely automatic once installed: tool.call hook on WebSearch (hooks/jev.js:85) means zero prompting and no CLAUDE.md edits, and the plugin carries its own guidance (prompt.context).
Fail-open design with explicit fallbacks to built-in WebSearch on error, 429 and empty results, so it cannot brick web search.
Clean, small, zero-dependency codebase (about 1.9k lines including tests) that is easy to audit. No shell exec, no postinstall, no API keys handled, MIT.
Reasonable test suite (about 58 cases, fake upstream server, real stdio MCP test) and CI, unusual for a 9-day-old repo.
Source routing (HN, Reddit, GitHub, arXiv) and per-result relevance percentages could be useful for library and issue research.
A useful reference for how a Claude Code function hook can transparently intercept a built-in tool (the pattern, not the payload).
cons: It is not an integration of the Jev decisions/System One API at all: no OpenRouter, no TypeSafe API, no Choice/Noul/Score. Jev is hidden behind someone else's search web app, so it fails the user's stated goal of OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code.
OpenRouter is not supported, and cannot be patched in at this layer. It would require self-hosting the upstream Cloudflare Worker, adding an OpenRouter provider there and buying a Search1API key.

Default backend is a public rate-limited demo (jev.s1.dev, about 10 req/min per IP) run by a third party, with no auth and no SLA, and it reroutes all WebSearch queries to that host. That is a poor fit for client projects.

Solves web search, which is a minor part of daily coding. It offers nothing for routing, classification, permission or intent decisions, or code-related probabilities, which is where Jev's value lies.

Depends on an early-access, undocumented-in-stable 'function hooks' API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, types snapshot from 2.1.278). It may break on any Claude Code update, and the user's bypass mode does not change that.
README's npx / `claude mcp add ... npx -y jev-search-mcp` instructions are dead: the npm package returns 404, and the 'files' allowlist also omits hooks/.
Immature and single-maintainer: 2 stars, 8 commits in one day (2026-09-21), no releases, and the plugin install pulls from a second unaudited marketplace repo. Adds a hook in the engine's trust zone.

gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.name: tacticocc/Jevbridge (@tactico/jevbridge)
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Node 22+ TypeScript project (run via --experimental-strip-types, about 4.1k lines) that provides (a) a stdio MCP server with 4 tools (jev_decide, jev_gate, jev_computer_use, jev_recipe), 3 resources and 2 prompts, and (b) an ACP (Agent Client Protocol) sidecar/proxy for Zed/JetBrains-style hosts that can wrap claude-agent-acp or codex-acp and gate their tool calls with Jev. It POSTs {model,state,questions} to a System One endpoint and post-processes the typed answers with a local confidence gate (execute/confirm/escalate/abort). If no TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set it silently falls back to another LLM (whichever provider key is in env) posing as System One, or to a keyword heuristic. Mostly a generic wrapper and demo, not a Claude Code-native integration.

Only route is git clone plus a manual 'claude mcp add' with node --experimental-strip-types /abs/path/src/cli.ts mcp. The README's 'npx -y @tactico/jevbridge' path does not work yet. Nothing was executed during this audit.

Tests exercise mocks and the heuristic backend, with no evidence of live Jev or OpenRouter integration tests. I did not run them.

TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT) with 'Authorization: Bearer <apiKey>' and body JSON {model,state,questions}. src/env.ts:4-10 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEVBRIDGE_JEV_MODEL. Secondary path: the LLM adapter (src/llm-adapter.ts, chatOpenAICompat) POSTs to <JEVBRIDGE_BASE_URL>/chat/completions with the JEVBRIDGE_API_KEY and provider 'generic', so it could reach OpenRouter chat completions, but that sends the request as a chat prompt through an emulated System One with a JSON-only prompt, not the native System One endpoint.

interface.name: jev_decide (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Takes a state (text or JSON) plus named noul/choice/score questions, calls Jev (auto: Jev if TYPESAFE_API_KEY, else LLM adapter, else heuristic), and returns typed answers plus a confidence gate. Args include backend, gate, choiceId and destructiveId.

interface.name: jev_gate (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Pure local function with no network call. Takes previously computed answers and applies thresholds (execute >=0.72, confirm >=0.46, abort <0.18, destructive noul >=0.62 forces confirm) to return execute/confirm/escalate/abort.

interface.name: jev_computer_use (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Picks the next GUI action from the closed set click/type/scroll/wait/screenshot/done/abort given goal plus visible control labels. Irrelevant to coding.

interface.name: jev_recipe (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Runs a canned demo recipe (support-route, computer-use, destructive-gate, compaction). Demo only.

interface.name: MCP resources jevbridge://recipes and jevbridge://recipe/{id}; prompts jev_decide, jev_computer_use
interface.purpose: Static recipe JSON and prompt templates that tell the model to call the tools.

interface.name: jevbridge mcp
interface.purpose: CLI: stdio MCP server, newline-delimited JSON-RPC, protocol versions 2024-11-05 to 2025-11-25.

interface.name: jevbridge acp [--upstream claude|codex | -- cmd]
interface.purpose: CLI: ACP server over stdio with Content-Length framing. Sidecar mode classifies each prompt and streams a Jev decision. Proxy mode spawns 'npx -y @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp' (or codex-acp) and intercepts session/request_permission and tool_call notifications, sending each to Jev (choice next + noul is_destructive + score risk) to allow/ask/deny. Built for Zed/JetBrains, not the Claude Code CLI.

interface.name: jevbridge eval <recipe> / recipes / help
interface.purpose: CLI demos.

interface.name: skills/jevbridge/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Skill whose description triggers on routing, gating, scoring, computer use, MCP, ACP, Codex, Claude, Grok, OpenCode, noul/choice/score. Its body only documents the library API and MCP tools. It is not wired as a Claude Code plugin (no plugin.json, marketplace.json or hooks.json).

security: No API key in argv, since keys come from env vars. In the README's Claude Desktop config the key sits in the MCP 'env' block. In claude mcp add, use -e or a settings.json env block.
No shell execution in the MCP path and no postinstall or curl|sh scripts. package.json has only prepublishOnly (tests). No telemetry found.

Proxy mode spawns 'npx -y @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp' (src/acp/upstream.ts), which fetches and runs unpinned third-party code at runtime. It also honors JEVBRIDGE_ACP_COMMAND/ARGS. Not used in the MCP path.

envLlm() (src/env.ts:12-21) picks up ANY of JEVBRIDGE_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_API_KEY from the environment. With 'auto' and no Jev key, state is silently sent to that provider. Default provider is xai, so an OPENAI_API_KEY in env could be sent to api.x.ai as a Bearer token (key/provider mismatch leak).

'auto' silently degrades to a keyword heuristic that the README itself says is not a safety signal (question text overlaps state). A misconfigured key therefore yields fake 'execute' decisions rather than an error.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever the model passes as 'state' goes to Jev, and the output is only numbers. A gate 'execute' is advisory, and Claude can ignore or game it. The ACP proxy can genuinely deny tool calls, but only inside ACP hosts.

Installing means cloning a 3-contributor, 12-day-old repo and pointing an always-on MCP server at a checkout path. Any later 'git pull' changes code that runs with the user's env, so pin a commit and review the diff.
Sessions persist to ~/.jevbridge/sessions in ACP mode (unencrypted JSON of prompts and history). The MCP path writes nothing.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.dataEgress: MCP path: only what Claude chooses to put in the 'state' and 'questions' arguments of jev_decide/jev_computer_use/jev_recipe leaves the machine, sent to the endpoint from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if overridden), plus the key as a Bearer header. jev_gate sends nothing. Nothing is sent automatically, but because Claude authors the state it can include code snippets, diffs, commands or paths. If no Jev key is set, the same payload goes to whichever LLM provider key exists in the environment (xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenCode or a custom base URL). ACP proxy mode would send the user prompt, cwd, tool name and full tool input for every tool call (src/acp/intercept.ts toolCallState), meaning shell commands and file edit contents. That is irrelevant to the Claude Code CLI but a large egress on client projects.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.failureMode: Fail-open by design at the tool level: the MCP tool never blocks Claude Code, because errors come back as isError text results (callMcpTool catch) and Claude proceeds. There are no timeouts, retries or AbortSignal anywhere in src (grep found none), so a hung Jev/OpenRouter connection makes the tool call wait until undici's default timeouts (minutes), stalling the turn. Because MCP tools are model-discretion, a slow Jev only hurts when Claude calls it. Misconfiguration (no key) falls back silently to heuristic or another provider rather than failing loudly, which is a fail-wrong mode. In ACP proxy mode a Jev failure behavior is more complex, but that mode does not apply to Claude Code.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.contextCost: 4 tools (jev_decide, jev_gate, jev_computer_use, jev_recipe): tools array is about 4.3k chars of names, descriptions and schemas, roughly 1.1k tokens. Server 'instructions' string about 480 chars, roughly 120 tokens, and it aggressively says 'Call jev_decide before routing or acting on a closed set. Call jev_gate before executing a tool, shell command, or GUI click', which nudges Claude to add extra calls before shell commands. Total about 1.2-1.3k tokens per session (deferred/ToolSearch reduces it further). Resources and prompts add no context unless used. No hook-injected text. The SKILL.md description is about 60 tokens if the skill were installed separately.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call it. When called: one extra tool round trip of Jev latency (claimed 70-500 ms) plus MCP process overhead plus the model tokens spent composing the questions JSON, realistically 1-3 s of wall clock per call (mostly Claude generating the payload). jev_gate adds only model-token overhead. Node cold-start of the stdio server is about 100-200 ms once per session. If the instructions cause Claude to call jev_gate before every shell command, this becomes a noticeable per-command tax.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by server 'instructions' and tool descriptions ('Use this instead of asking the generating model to classify, route...'). NOT deterministic: no Claude Code hooks (no PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit), no plugin manifest and no proxy for the CLI. The strongest automation (ACP proxy interception of tool calls) only works in ACP clients like Zed/JetBrains, since Claude Code CLI is not an ACP host. The user's requirement of 'Claude Code must use it when needed without prompting' is only weakly met, and there is no clear coding use case for Claude to reach for it (the tools target support routing and GUI clicks).
pros: MIT-licensed, readable, zero-dependency 4.1k-line codebase that I could fully audit statically. There are no postinstall scripts, no shell exec in the MCP path and no telemetry.

Env overrides TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEVBRIDGE_JEV_MODEL (src/env.ts:7-8) plus a Bearer-auth POST of {model,state,questions} make OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone usable with zero code changes, if the schema matches.

Genuinely Jev-specific building blocks worth borrowing: the choice/noul/score question builders, coerceAnswers normalization, and gate.ts thresholds (execute >=0.72, confirm >=0.46, abort <0.18, independent destructive noul >=0.62) map well to a 'should this Bash command run' gate.
The MCP server is protocol-clean (negotiates 2025-11-25 down to 2024-11-05), tools carry readOnlyHint annotations, and there are tests and CI with typecheck.
Small footprint, about 1.2k tokens of context; jev_gate is a local no-network pure function.
The intercept design (src/acp/intercept.ts: choice next + noul is_destructive + score risk over tool_name/tool_input) is a reasonable reference for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls Jev.
cons: Not automatic in Claude Code: only model-discretion MCP tools. The ACP proxy that could deterministically gate tool calls needs an ACP host (Zed/JetBrains), and Claude Code CLI 2.1.x is not one. There is no hooks.json or plugin.json to hook PreToolUse.
Not published: npm 404 for @tactico/jevbridge, no GitHub releases. Install is a manual clone with an absolute path to run unreviewed-upstream code, and later pulls change it.
Very young and thin: 9 commits over 3 days (2026-09-18 to 09-21) by effectively 1-2 people, no tags, 5 issues and 4 PRs total. 46 stars come from Jev hype rather than track record.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; it only works via the undocumented TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env trick, and the OpenRouter response schema equivalence is unverified. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is unsupported. The variable name TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding an OpenRouter key is confusing.

Silent fallbacks are dangerous: with no or wrong key, 'auto' uses the keyword heuristic (self-declared 'not a safety signal') or ships state to any of XAI/OPENAI/ANTHROPIC/OPENCODE keys found in env (default provider xai even with an OpenAI key) — a leak risk on client projects.

Coding value is thin: recipes target support routing, GUI clicks and destructive gating, which duplicate Claude Code's own permission system and the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook. Instructions push Claude to call jev_gate before every shell command, adding latency and tokens for little benefit under bypass/auto permission mode where the gate cannot actually block anything.
The gate is advisory and computed on Claude-authored state, so it is not a real security boundary. There are no timeouts on fetch, so a slow OpenRouter call can hang a turn.
Adds 4 tools, 3 resources and 2 prompts, including computer-use tools irrelevant to coding, and the tool surface is mostly noise beyond jev_decide/jev_gate.
gh-tacticocc-jevbridge.verdict: Only usable as a manual MCP server that the model may or may not call, and it is not yet on npm. It works with OpenRouter only through an undocumented env override (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEVBRIDGE_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). It has silent multi-provider fallbacks, no timeouts and computer-use-oriented tools. It is better mined for its gate thresholds and question shapes to build a small, deterministic PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter System One directly than adopted as-is.

gh-krw82-jev-playwright-mcp.name: krw82/jev-playwright-mcp
gh-krw82-jev-playwright-mcp.whatItDoes: A stdio MCP proxy that spawns the official @playwright/mcp 0.0.81 as a child, re-exposes all its tools unchanged, and adds Jev (System One Choice/Noul/Score) judgments: page-state triage (login_wall/captcha/error/paywall...) via a <jev-insights> block appended to tool results, prompt-injection span masking in page text, goal-based snapshot pruning, and pre-call risk gating of click/type/upload-style calls. Without a key it is a pure passthrough of Playwright MCP. It is a browser-automation guard, not a coding-workflow tool.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev/client.ts:20 hard-codes `const JEV_ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"` and it is used at client.ts:234 (fetch with `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}`). No base-URL env var or flag exists (grep for openrouter/OPENROUTER/baseUrl returns nothing in src/). Key env vars: TYPESAFE_API_KEY, fallback JEV_MCP_API_KEY (.env.example:17-19). Default model sent in body is `jev-latest` (JEV_MCP_MODEL, .env.example:26), which is not an OpenRouter id (would need `typesafe/jev-1.13` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`). Request body is `{state, model, questions}` with answers validated as noul/choice/score (client.ts:149-206), matching the TypeSafe /v1/systemone shape.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, leaning trivial but unverified. Code changes needed: make JEV_ENDPOINT configurable (one line at client.ts:20), send Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and set JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). OpenRouter exposes /api/v1/systemone (a System One API), so the request/response schema is plausibly identical to TypeSafe's, but this was not verified. If OpenRouter's schema differs (wrapper fields, model id format, usage/cost fields required by validateUsage at client.ts:177), the strict response validator would throw and every call would fail open silently. Would need a forked local copy; no upstream flag.
providerSupport.others: None. Only api.typesafe.ai.

Insight markers in page text are neutralized so a page cannot forge <jev-insights> (contracts.ts:309-316).

Fail-safe wrong direction on gating: Jev unreachable means gating fails open (README degradation matrix), so an attacker able to make Jev slow could bypass the destructive gate; but the blockTools list still holds.
gh-krw82-jev-playwright-mcp.dataEgress: Only when a TypeSafe key is set: to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone the proxy sends (a) up to a text_excerpt of each browser tool response (detectors.ts:311 `ctx.text.slice(0, TEXT_EXCERPT_CHARS)`) with url and title, (b) candidate injection sentences found by local heuristics (max 32), (c) region labels and 240-char excerpts of accessibility snapshot regions for pruning (prune.ts:196-201, batch up to 40) plus the session goal string, (d) for gated calls: tool name, compacted arguments (element, text typed, url, value, filename, ref; head+tail 120 chars each) and a 300-char excerpt of the previous page (gate.ts:109-121). So page content and text the agent types into forms (which may include credentials or client data) leave the machine. No source code, diffs or non-browser tool output is sent, because it only wraps Playwright. Not routed via OpenRouter as shipped.

Jev errors, malformed responses, and exhausted budget all fall back to passthrough (README degradation matrix; gate.ts:191 no verdict means allow; toRiskVerdict returns needs_confirmation on bad shape). Per-request timeout 10 s (client.ts:21), up to 2 retries with 500 ms-5 s backoff honoring Retry-After up to 60 s (client.ts:22-28), so a degraded Jev could add roughly 10 s x 3 attempts plus backoff (~35 s worst case per call) before falling open, an undesirable stall on a gated browser action. Session budget cap default $1.
