Applies only to browser tool calls, not to normal coding turns. Worst case with Jev outage about 30+ s per call as computed from timeouts and retries. Not measured by me.

Adds 2 tools (browser_set_goal, browser_jev_status), roughly 250-350 tokens of schema, plus a server `instructions` string of about 300 chars (~80 tokens, proxy.ts:249-253). Tool list of Playwright itself is unchanged (duplicated if both servers are kept: doubles ~25 browser tools, so it should replace, not join). Per-response, appends a <jev-insights> block (one-line hint, up to 3 masked excerpts), tens of tokens; pruning with a goal can save tokens on big snapshots. No hooks.
gh-krw82-jev-playwright-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool layer with transparent proxying: Claude calls the usual Playwright tools and Jev logic runs inside the proxy on every browser call with no prompting (triage/masking/gating are automatic once the key is set). Only browser_set_goal is optional model-driven. It fires only when Claude uses the browser, never on ordinary code editing, searching, or reviewing.
pros: Genuinely automatic: drop-in replacement for the existing `playwright` MCP with identical tool names and schemas (proxy.ts:6), so no prompt changes and Claude never has to be told to use Jev.

Uses Jev for what a typed calibrated classifier suits: injection Noul scan on untrusted page text, page-state Choice, risk Choice for browser actions; outputs are constrained to probabilities so the guard itself can't be prompt-injected into free text.

Sound engineering for a PoC: fail-open with retries honoring Retry-After, response schema validation, content-hash cache, $1 session budget, off/annotate/gate modes, deterministic blockTools for browser_run_code_unsafe, pinned @playwright/mcp version, marker forgery protection.
Cheap: input-only pricing at ~$0.042/1M; typical call fractions of a cent.
No postinstall scripts, no shell-out beyond the pinned child, MIT license, sizable test suite with stubbed Jev.
Relevant to a user with client projects: shields agent from hostile page content when browsing staging/third-party sites via Playwright, and gating protects against accidental destructive clicks.
cons: Browser-only: does nothing for the user's daily coding (editing, grep, tests, git, PR review). Fires only when Playwright is used.

No OpenRouter support: endpoint hard-coded to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (client.ts:20), only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_MCP_API_KEY, default model `jev-latest`. Using the user's OpenRouter key requires forking; and OpenRouter schema parity for /api/v1/systemone was not verified.
Very immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 2 stars, created 13 days before the audit, no releases, no CI, not on npm; needs manual git clone + npm install and tsx-at-runtime (or manual build).
Page text and text typed into form fields (possibly credentials/client data) egress to a third party (TypeSafe) beyond Anthropic; relevant for client work.
Gate fails open: if Jev is down or slow the destructive-action check is silently skipped; worst-case stall of ~30 s per call from 10 s timeout x 3 attempts + backoff.

Gating and masking are LLM probabilities; browser_evaluate (arbitrary JS) is not hard-blocked by default; only browser_run_code_unsafe is. Injection masking claims are unverified against real attacks, and Theo's skepticism about Jev's actual model is unaddressed.
Replaces rather than complements the existing playwright server, so needs config swap; keeping both would duplicate ~25 tools of context.

Comments/docs partly in Korean; single maintainer bus-factor; API pinned to @playwright/mcp 0.0.81 which lags the user's current tool set (e.g. browser_find/browser_drop appear in the user's server), so swapping may drop tools.
gh-krw82-jev-playwright-mcp.verdict: A well-built but narrow, brand-new Playwright guard proxy: it is the only candidate that makes Jev run automatically, but only during browser use, and it is hard-wired to TypeSafe rather than OpenRouter. Worth a fork-and-pin only if you regularly let Claude browse untrusted pages; not a solution for daily coding.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart: .claude/hooks/discover_tools.py

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse: .claude/hooks/post_tool_use.py
interface.purpose: Sends tool_response (first 4000 chars) as observation with goal and catalog to Jev, injects additionalContext suggesting the next tool. Timeout 5 s.

interface.name: Skill harness-router

security: No curl|sh, but the recommended installer is `curl ... main/scripts/install_hook.py | python3 -`: unpinned code from the main branch executes and writes hook scripts that then run on every prompt/tool call (supply-chain surface). It has a symlink refusal and .bak backups, and is project-scoped.
Also installs from `git+https://github.com/...@main` (unpinned); the package is not on PyPI.
API key is read from env only and sent as a Bearer header via httpx, not argv. Good hygiene: the code asserts the key is not in the payload and redacts it from error text (provider.py).

Sensitive data is NOT redacted: only the API key is filtered. Tool output (PostToolUse tool_response[:4000], clipped to ~512 chars per field by RoutingConfig.state_field_limit) and user prompts go to OpenRouter. A Read of .env or command output containing secrets can leak in that snippet.

Hook state written to the project dir: .harness-router/sessions/*.decision.json and .decisions.jsonl contain goal and observation in plaintext and are appended without rotation. The installer adds .gitignore entries, but hooks/ and .claude/hooks are committed unless the user avoids that.
Daemon spawns a detached Python process listening on /tmp/harness-router-<uid>.sock, with no auth beyond filesystem permissions; the socket path is in shared /tmp.

discover_tools.py launches `claude mcp serve` and `claude --print` subprocesses at every SessionStart (including resume/clear/compact), which spawns configured MCP servers (gitnexus, playwright) a second time.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev output is a constrained enum, so low risk, but the deny reason and additionalContext are injected into the Claude context. Tool output influences the routing state (observation) but the router cannot execute anything.
No telemetry found in code. No npm postinstall.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, on UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse (and via MCP route): the user's prompt text (goal, first 1600 chars, clipped to ~512 chars in the router state), the last tool's output text (first 4000 chars from the hook, clipped to ~512 chars by the router), last tool name, and the name plus description (about 96 chars each) of every candidate tool including all MCP tools. File contents and command output that appear in tool responses leak in the snippet; the diff or whole repo is not sent wholesale. This also applies to client projects. OpenRouter/TypeSafe then see the client-code fragments. Secrets are not scrubbed except the API key itself.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: every hook wraps errors and prints nothing or {}. Timeouts are 4 s per Jev call (hook timeout 5 s); MCP tool 2 s; missing key returns fallback. Provider errors become fallback, and an unavailable daemon falls back to a subprocess CLI call. Worst case per event is roughly 4-5 s stall on UserPromptSubmit or PostToolUse if OpenRouter hangs (synchronous hooks). Also fails open if the catalog is missing. However, when the router works but is wrong, PreToolUse actively DENIES Claude's tool call (fail-closed for that call, one retry), which is the bigger risk in practice.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.contextCost: MCP server: 2 tools (route, route_mcts) plus server instructions (~300 chars). route_mcts has a large nested schema (MCTSState, MCTSTransition, RouteCandidate), so estimated ~700-900 tokens of tool defs in total; only ~50 tokens if the MCP is omitted and hooks used. Skill: ~60 tokens of description in the always-loaded listing. Hooks inject additionalContext on every user prompt and every PostToolUse ('Harness Router selected X as the next tool (confidence ...). Use that tool...', ~40-60 tokens each), i.e. roughly 50 tokens x every tool call, and SessionStart injects the catalog path. Deny messages add a whole extra model turn (re-plan), the costly part.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.latencyImpact: Each UserPromptSubmit and each PostToolUse blocks on a fresh python3 process plus up to 4 s of Jev (authors' own measure: mean 454 ms, median 386 ms, max 2756 ms; 128-256-entry cache helps only exact-repeat states). With 30-100 tool calls per turn in daily coding, that is ~0.5-1 s added per tool call, plus process spawn. SessionStart discovery spawns 2 extra claude processes (up to 8-10 s). A PreToolUse deny costs a full extra model round-trip. The authors' own BENCHMARK.md (Codex, skill-driven, 5 vs 5 runs) shows tokens +110% and elapsed 115.8 s -> 228.9 s, 54 of 58 routing decisions fell back. Hook-based Claude variant has no published benchmark.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, PreToolUse, SessionStart). It really is automatic with no user prompting. It is not model-discretion: MCP and skill are optional extras (skill description says rarely/only-when-asked). Caveat: it automates a decision the user does not need, choosing among Claude's own tools, not code-review or classification decisions.
pros: Truly automatic through deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse / PostToolUse), which matches the 'never say use jev' requirement in mechanism.
OpenRouter-native out of the box: correct Decisions API URL, typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY. No patching needed (config.py, provider.py).
Careful engineering on failure: fail-open everywhere, short timeouts, redirect at most once per state, never emits permissionDecision allow, refuses to put API key in payload and redacts errors.
Decent test surface for an alpha (13 test files incl. provider, MCP server, installers) and an honest BENCHMARK.md that publishes a negative result.
Claude hook code is small, readable stdlib Python (about 130 lines per hook), so it is easy to audit or fork.
Discovers the live tool catalog including MCP tools from Claude itself rather than a hard-coded list, so GitNexus/playwright tools would be in scope.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: it routes between tools Opus 5.5 already picks correctly; Jev adds a second opinion over 'Read vs Grep vs Bash', not a real decision (review triage, risk scoring, commit classification) where calibrated probabilities pay off.

Own benchmark (BENCHMARK.md) shows the integration doubled tokens (+105.9% main-model, +109.8% full system) and doubled wall-clock (115.8 s -> 228.9 s); 54/58 routings fell back. The Claude-hook variant is unbenchmarked.

PreToolUse deny+re-plan on a stale prompt-time precompute (30 s TTL, threshold 0.85): a decision made from the user's prompt is compared against whatever tool Claude proposes later, so correct calls can be denied, costing a model turn. In bypass/auto mode this adds friction with no safety benefit.
Data egress on every prompt and every tool result for personal AND client projects: prompt text plus 512-4000 chars of tool output go to OpenRouter with no secret/PII scrubbing except the API key.

Synchronous hook per prompt and per tool call (fresh python3 process + up to 4 s network) adds ~0.5-1 s per tool call on top of existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks; hook ordering/interaction with GitNexus additionalContext is untested.
SessionStart spawns `claude mcp serve` and `claude --print` to enumerate tools on every start/resume/compact, which respawns the user's gitnexus and playwright MCP servers.

Installer is project-scoped and hard-wired to $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks and $ROOT/hooks/pre_decision.py, and commits scripts into client repos; a user-global install requires manual rewrite. README says PreToolUse calls the router MCP, but the shipped pre_tool_use.py only reads the precomputed decision file (docs and code diverge).
Very young and thin: created 2026-09-25, 2 contributors, 19 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, unpinned `main` installs, no test CI, alpha per its own README. Installs via curl | python3 from main.
route_mcts is impractical for Claude (needs a model-authored simulated state graph) and its large schema costs ~500+ tokens for no daily value.
gh-protocol-lattice-harness-router.verdict: Real, OpenRouter-native and genuinely automatic via hooks, but it uses Jev for the least valuable job (second-guessing Claude's tool choice) and the authors' own benchmark shows about 2x tokens and time; it also sends prompts and tool output of client projects to OpenRouter on every step. Do not install as-is. At most mine its provider.py (about 200 lines) as a reference for the Decisions API request/response schema.

gh-qualixar-jev-decision-layer.dataEgress: Nothing leaves on hooks (they only print fixed text). Egress happens only when the model calls an MCP tool, and only to api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai (per config): JSON {model, state, questions}. Depending on tool this is: task text plus candidate ids/descriptions (jev_route), arbitrary state object (jev_typed_decide), a diff up to 16,000 chars (jev_review_diff), source text up to 20,000 chars and the extraction (jev_verify), up to 100,000 chars of text (jev_reduce), passages (jev_rerank), recipe input objects (jev_recipe_try). data_classification (public / internal-minimized / restricted) is model-supplied per call and checked against the workspace's reviewed scope; secret screen is best-effort. Prompts as a whole and full tool outputs are not sent automatically. Local receipts and state stored under user state dir (7-day retention default).
gh-qualixar-jev-decision-layer.failureMode: Fail-open in practice. Hooks: any exception, oversized input, missing cwd, or unenrolled workspace produce no output and exit 0 (claude_hook.py:111-127); launcher exits non-zero silently if no Python 3.11+ at the four hard-coded paths (non-blocking hook error). MCP: provider timeout default 12 s (settings.py:20, configurable 1-30 s), non-200 -> PROVIDER_HTTP_xxx, transport failure -> PROVIDER_TRANSPORT_FAILURE_NO_RETRY (never retried, since call may be billed); tool returns isError text and the model proceeds without Jev. No fallback to another provider (Jev-only never silently falls back to Laya). A stuck call can add up to ~12 s to a turn, and a broker BROKER_VERSION_MISMATCH/START failure surfaces as tool error.
gh-qualixar-jev-decision-layer.latencyImpact: Hooks: one Python 3.11+ process start (python -I -S, imports settings/policy loader) on SessionStart and on EVERY UserPromptSubmit in enrolled workspaces, order of tens of ms, timeout 20 s ceiling, no network. MCP calls: TypeSafe-claimed 70-500 ms provider latency plus local broker/gate overhead, keep-alive HTTPS connection reuse (providers.py:28-32); first call in a workspace also spawns the broker daemon. Each call is an additional model tool-use round trip for Opus (extra turn tokens and seconds) which likely exceeds the Jev latency itself.

gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.name: revsmoke/promptrejectormcp (Prompt Rejector)
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.whatItDoes: Security scanner for prompts, SKILL.md files, MCP tool descriptors and agent capability sets. It combines deterministic pattern checks with Jev Noul/Choice judgments (TypeSafe /v1/systemone) and a Gemini reasoning model. It ships an 11-tool stdio MCP server, an HTTPS REST API (/v2/*), and a Claude Code/Codex plugin with a SKILL.md. It uses Jev as a classifier, not as a coding-assistance decision engine. The agent must call it explicitly; the author states that the application or agent has to invoke the scanner.

providerSupport.evidence: src/ai/providers/TypeSafeAdapter.ts:82 hard-codes url "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone" with `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}` and body {model,state,questions}. There is no base-URL env var or config field. The only key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY (.env.example:12, src/ai/configValidation.ts:37, src/bootstrap.ts:48). A repo-wide grep for openrouter, /decisions and OPENROUTER finds no code matches. Model IDs are constrained by a regex at TypeSafeAdapter.ts:28 (/^jev-\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ or jev-latest/jev-preview), and the response model must equal the requested model at :46. config/ai.active.json pins "jev-1.13.0". The default profile also requires GEMINI_API_KEY for the semantic/reasoning role, and decide() in DecisionPolicy.ts returns unavailable for prompt/skill when the semantic check is incomplete. A Jev-only run therefore gives no usable allow.
providerSupport.others: Gemini (default reasoning), Anthropic and OpenAI adapters for reasoning roles only. These are not Jev providers.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The URL is a single hard-coded literal, and the request shape {model,state,questions} plus the answers envelope may match OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (unverified). The patch touches four places: (1) replace the URL with openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and swap the key env var; (2) relax the model-ID regex to accept the typesafe/jev-1.13 form; (3) relax the resolved-model equality check at :46, since OpenRouter may return a different ID string; (4) confirm OpenRouter's envelope still has model, answers and usage, because parseTypeSafeAnswers uses z.strictObject and rejects any extra fields. Fork maintenance is needed, and the Gemini dependency for the reasoning role remains.

CI is GitHub Actions on a Node 18/22/24/26 matrix running lint and test:offline, plus plugin, release and Claude review workflows. Live Jev smoke results are committed in evaluations/ai/runs/. security: Keys are read from env or .env. The plugin launcher spawns node with env: process.env and no shell (plugins/prompt-rejector/scripts/launch.mjs). Keys are not passed in argv, and the docs say logs and config contain no key values.

Fail-safe design: the decision policy returns 'unavailable' or 'review' rather than 'allow' when coverage is incomplete (DecisionPolicy.ts). The SKILL.md tells the agent not to translate unavailable to allow.

No curl|sh installer and no postinstall script in package.json. CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts. Install is a manual clone, npm ci and build. Dependencies include express, jose, @anthropic-ai/sdk and @google/generative-ai.
update_vuln_feeds and deploy_canary mutate local state. The optional taste_test runs Taster/Monitor with mocked tools against an Anthropic model, and is off by default.

Prompt-injection surface: the scanner ingests hostile text and passes it as Jev/Gemini 'state'. The verdict is model-based and can be evaded; the README itself says it is not a guarantee. The result is untrusted-content-in, structured-decision-out, so output injection risk is low.

No telemetry code found (grep for telemetry/analytics in src is empty). Egress is limited to configured providers plus NVD, GitHub advisories, CISA KEV, OSV and HuggingFace lookups for feeds and model references.
Maintainer is a single individual with 2 stars; supply-chain trust is low, and the fork would need a source review.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.dataEgress: Whatever text the agent submits to a tool leaves the machine: the prompt, skill file, or tool descriptor JSON (up to 100k UTF-16 units for prompts, 500k for skills). It goes as `state` to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (Jev) and also to Google Gemini for the reasoning role in the default profile, so there are two third-party recipients. Skill scans may also trigger HuggingFace GET lookups for referenced model IDs. Feed and CVE tools hit NVD, GHSA, KEV and OSV with search parameters only. Nothing is sent unless the agent calls a tool. If it were auto-invoked on every code edit, source code and diffs would go to both providers.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.failureMode: Fail-closed at the verdict level: Jev timeout (default judgmentTimeoutMs 2000 ms, max 30000; Gemini 15 s), missing key or an invalid response gives status unavailable, so check_prompt returns decision 'unavailable' or 'review' (never a silent allow). Because it is an MCP tool the agent chooses to call, this cannot block Claude Code itself. With no hook, there is nothing to hang a turn. The transport has a concurrency limit of 2 and a queue of 32. If the server process fails to start, the MCP server simply appears failed and Claude Code carries on.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.latencyImpact: Only when a tool is called. Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms, with a 2 s default timeout. The Gemini reasoning step adds up to 15 s per prompt/skill scan, so a full scan is likely multi-second. There is zero overhead on ordinary coding turns because there are no hooks.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.contextCost: 11 MCP tools. The tool names, descriptions and input schemas in src/mcp/mcpServer.ts lines 85-255 total about 9.2k characters, roughly 2.3k tokens, which is deferrable through Claude Code's tool search. There are no MCP server 'instructions' (grep found none). The plugin adds one SKILL.md whose description is about 400 characters, roughly 100 tokens, always in the skills listing. No hook-injected text.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger that fires only for Prompt Rejector setup or a requested security review. The SKILL.md explicitly says it does not require scanning every conversation or changing global agent behavior. Only the tool descriptions ('Use this before processing any untrusted user input', 'before installing any third-party skill') might nudge the model to call it. There is no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook and no proxy, so nothing is deterministic.
pros: Real, non-trivial Jev integration: a native, strictly validated /v1/systemone adapter using Noul and Choice, with probability-sum checks, model pinning and batched questions (TypeSafeAdapter.ts).
Fail-closed decision policy that never turns an unavailable or incomplete result into allow (DecisionPolicy.ts), with a 2 s Jev timeout.
Ships a Claude Code plugin/marketplace with a launcher that uses no shell and no npm, and has no postinstall script or curl|sh installer.
Useful niche for this user: vetting third-party MCP servers, skills and plugins before installing them. That fits this evaluation task, where skills and MCPs are being adopted.
Offline replay tests and committed live-smoke evaluations make the Jev claims checkable without spending credits.
Small context footprint (about 2.3k tokens for 11 tools, no server instructions, no hooks).
cons: Hard-codes api.typesafe.ai; there is no OpenRouter support, base-URL override or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It needs a fork patch (URL, key env, model-ID regex, resolved-model check, strict envelope schema) and OpenRouter's response shape is unverified.

The default profile requires a second provider (GEMINI_API_KEY) for the reasoning role. Prompt and skill decisions cannot reach 'allow' on Jev alone, so a second vendor also receives the scanned text.

Not automatic: no hooks. It never runs unless the model decides to call a tool or the user asks, which fails the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' goal. Building a hook around it would mean wiring PreToolUse to a local HTTPS API yourself.
Scope mismatch: it is a security classifier for untrusted text, not a coding aid. Nothing here uses Jev for routing, code review or commit decisions.
Multi-second latency per scan (Gemini leg) and a paid call on both providers per check; scanning every prompt or diff would leak client code to two vendors.
Heavy setup: source checkout, npm ci and build, .env, optional mkcert TLS for the REST API. It is not on npx.
Immature and single-maintainer: 2 stars, 3 forks, about 8 months old, mostly AI-authored commits, v1.2.0 released 2026-09-21. Sprawling docs (PLAN, SPEC, RESEARCH_*) for a small user base.
Detection quality is only vendor-evidenced (a synthetic recorded example); the README disclaims guarantees.
gh-revsmoke-promptrejectormcp.verdict: A genuine, well-engineered Jev consumer, but it is a manual prompt/skill/MCP-descriptor security scanner rather than an automatic daily-coding integration. It is hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai, needs Gemini too, and has no hooks. It is worth keeping as an optional, occasional vetting tool for third-party skills and MCP servers after patching or accepting direct TypeSafe billing. It is not the answer to 'Jev via OpenRouter, automatically'.

gh-n8mirai-jev2mcp.name: n8mirai/jev2mcp
gh-n8mirai-jev2mcp.whatItDoes: Despite the name and the "router-proxy" label from discovery, it is NOT an MCP server, proxy or Claude Code component. It is a ChatGPT-only Chrome MV3 extension (content script matches https://chatgpt.com/*) plus a local Node HTTP bridge on 127.0.0.1:4328 and a small web companion UI. Before you press Send in ChatGPT it sends your prompt (optionally the last 4 visible messages) plus a hand-configured catalog of tool descriptions to TypeSafe System One as Noul questions (one "needs_tools" plus one per tool). If the probabilities are decisive (<=0.20 or >=0.80) it clicks the matching native ChatGPT "@" picker entries and sends; otherwise it holds the draft. It has no MCP transport, does not discover or connect to MCP servers, and nothing in it references Claude, Claude Code, hooks, or MCP protocol (grep for claude/anthropic/modelcontextprotocol/openrouter returned zero hits). The only reusable idea is the Noul-per-tool routing pattern in src/router.mjs.

Conservative security posture for a local bridge (loopback, token, Origin/Host checks, no logging) and MIT license with zero runtime deps.
Request format is identical to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the pattern could be lifted into your own Claude Code hook with a 3-line change.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: it only targets chatgpt.com via a Chrome extension; there is no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin manifest, and it explicitly does not connect to MCP servers (README: 'does not ... connect directly to MCP servers').
Name jev2mcp is misleading; it selects ChatGPT @ picker entries, not MCP tools, and the catalog is static hand-entered text.
Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter support and no env override for base URL or model.
Very young and thin: 4 commits, created 2026-09-22, 0 stars, one contributor identity split in two, no CI running, macOS-centric launcher, self-described experimental; ChatGPT Work unverified.

Its routing pattern is useless for Claude Code's already-good native tool selection (Claude picks MCP tools itself, and deferred ToolSearch handles large tool sets), so even a port would add latency without clear gain.

gh-micic-mihajlo-jev-tool-runner.name: micic-mihajlo/jev-tool-runner
gh-micic-mihajlo-jev-tool-runner.whatItDoes: Codex-CLI-specific integration of TypeSafe Jev as a tool selector. Main feature (router-cli.ts + router-server.ts) launches a loopback OpenAI-Responses-API proxy and starts `codex` with a temporary custom model_provider pointing at it. Before each coding-model request, Jev (Choice primitive via @typesafe-ai/sdk systemOne) picks one of up to 8 "offered" native read-file calls for files explicitly named in the user message, or hands off. Selected call is synthesised as a fake Responses tool_call so Codex executes it and the OpenAI request is skipped. Also contains a legacy MCP server (single tool run_tools, Jev-driven read-only investigation loop over an internal workspace with rg/read/run_command) and legacy Codex lifecycle hooks (SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop) that pre-inject Jev-gathered evidence. Coverage is intentionally narrow: only numbered reads of explicitly named relative files; no search planning, test selection or arbitrary commands. Upstream is hard-locked to api.openai.com / chatgpt.com, so it cannot front Anthropic/Claude Code traffic.

Router: Jev call has 5s SDK timeout, 0 retries, 6s AbortSignal; on any error or timeout falls back to normal upstream model request (router-server.ts:82,90-93; tool-selector.ts:64). Legacy runner: 15s timeout with 1 retry (jev.ts:22-23); hooks catch all errors and emit only a systemMessage 'Jev hook unavailable' (hook-cli.ts:25-27); on degraded state PreToolUse dedupe is disabled (hooks.ts:145). Stop hook can block up to 2 times to force verification. MCP run_tools returns isError result with status error/time_limit.

Legacy hooks: UserPromptSubmit blocks each prompt for up to settings.timeoutMs (default 15 s, max 30 s) with up to 6 sequential Jev decisions plus rg/file reads; Stop hook adds verification command runtime. Measured benchmarks in docs/benchmarks are explicitly disclaimed by README as not applicable to the native router architecture (small sample).
gh-micic-mihajlo-jev-tool-runner.contextCost: MCP mode: 1 tool (run_tools) ~ 250-400 tokens total (name+description+schema; description embeds configured command ids/argv, mcp.ts:47) plus ~110-token server instructions string (mcp.ts:42). Legacy hooks: SessionStart injects ~150 tokens (hooks.ts:88) and UserPromptSubmit injects up to 18,000 chars (~4,500 tokens) of JSON evidence per prompt (hooks.ts:133,136), a large recurring cost that may duplicate what Claude would read anyway. Native router mode: zero added context (transparent proxy), but Codex-only.
gh-micic-mihajlo-jev-tool-runner.autoInvocation: Native router: transparent proxy (deterministic, automatic) but Codex/OpenAI Responses API only, cannot sit in front of Claude Code. Legacy hooks: deterministic lifecycle hooks (UserPromptSubmit/Stop) but in Codex hook format and installed into Codex config by scripts/codex-integration.mjs. MCP run_tools: model-discretion tool invocation only; the model decides after it has already reasoned, which the README itself says cannot remove reasoning. Nothing in the repo targets Claude Code (grep 'claude': no hits).
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's Choice primitive with sensible validation: candidate-set check, probabilities check, fail-open fallbacks (jev.ts:72-77, router-server.ts:90-93).
Clean, defensive engineering for a POC: loopback-only, token-authenticated proxy, strict upstream allow-list, spawn shell:false with scrubbed env, redaction, atomic 0600 state files, SHA-pinned CI.
Honest README: states narrow coverage and that legacy benchmarks do not prove savings; live-smoke harness asserts Jev actually selected a call.
SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so pointing the Jev call at OpenRouter (/api/v1/systemone) is env-only with no code change, if schema parity holds.
Legacy hook code (hooks.ts) is a useful reference for a deterministic UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse/Stop pattern with Jev fail-open handling that could be re-implemented for Claude Code.
cons: Built for Codex CLI, not Claude Code: the only truly automatic mechanism (model-provider proxy) speaks OpenAI Responses API and rejects non-OpenAI upstreams (router-server.ts:50-52); would not work with a Claude subscription/OAuth session.
Native router only offers numbered reads of files explicitly named in the prompt; README admits no search planning, test selection, or command routing: near-zero value for real daily work with Opus.

Legacy hooks are wired to Codex hook schema and Codex installer (codex-integration.mjs); UserPromptSubmit runs an investigation loop on every prompt and injects up to ~4.5k tokens, with up to 15 s blocking latency, overlapping the user's existing GitNexus graph-context hook and duplicating what Claude's own Read/Grep would do.

MCP run_tools is model-discretion: Claude must decide to call it, contradicting the requirement of no 'use jev' prompting; and it duplicates Claude Code's native Read/Grep/Bash with a slower, less capable investigator.
No OpenRouter awareness or docs; model slug default jev-1.13.0 differs from OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13, needing manual env in a key file; OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
Legacy mode sends file contents/command outputs (up to 22 KB per decision) to a third party with only regex redaction: risky for client projects.
Immature and unlicensed: 3 commits in one day, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, not on npm, private:true, no LICENSE (cannot legally reuse/fork).
TypeSafe cookbook-style demo of Jev as a router; Jev's Choice replaces only a trivial decision (which of <=8 file reads), so it offers negligible cost or latency benefit against Opus 5.5.
gh-micic-mihajlo-jev-tool-runner.verdict: A tidy but narrow, unlicensed, Codex-only proof of concept; its automatic path is an OpenAI Responses proxy that cannot front Claude Code, and its Claude-compatible parts (a single model-discretion MCP tool, Codex-format hooks) are not automatic or useful for you. Worth reading only as a design reference for a fail-open hook that calls Jev via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api.

gh-tontoko-jev-browser.name: tontoko/jev-browser
gh-tontoko-jev-browser.whatItDoes: A Playwright-core based browser-automation SDK, persistent CLI and stdio MCP server (jev-browser-mcp). Roughly 50 MCP tools (browser_*): about 34 native Playwright ops that need no model (click, type, snapshot, assert, tabs, cookies, trace, route, pdf, evaluate...), plus Jev-backed tools (observe, act, extract, semantic_locate/compare/assert and their batch forms, run, resume). Jev is used only for Choice questions that pick one of the page's own candidate elements, options or values. It is a Playwright MCP / Stagehand replacement for browser QA, not a general coding-assistant hook. It has no hook, skill-trigger or proxy component, and it does nothing for code, diffs or Claude Code's own decisions.

providerSupport.evidence: src/decision.ts:33 hostedOrigin='https://api.typesafe.ai'. decision.ts:41 baseURL comes from options.baseURL or JEV_BASE_URL. decision.ts:45 the hosted key (JEV_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY) is used only when url.origin equals hostedOrigin, otherwise only JEV_ENDPOINT_API_KEY. decision.ts:53 model comes from JEV_MODEL. decision.ts:65 calls client.systemOne(). The pinned @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (dist/index.mjs:554) POSTs baseURL + '/v1/systemone' with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' (line 581). OpenRouter docs (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md) say a TypeSafeClient with baseURL 'https://openrouter.ai/api' and an OpenRouter key hits https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the same request shape. Model id in the OpenRouter docs example is 'jev-1.13'. README.md:126 and docs/api.md:9 say a custom endpoint must implement POST /v1/systemone with the state/questions to model/answers/usage envelope. So the OpenRouter config is JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_ENDPOINT_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13. This is by config only and I did not run it. The response validator (decision.ts:28-32) requires answers[id].choice and .confidence, model (string) and usage.input_tokens and output_tokens; extra fields such as OpenRouter's usage.cost are tolerated (non-strict zod). I could not confirm that OpenRouter's response has exactly those field names.
providerSupport.others: No OpenRouter-specific code and no OpenRouter mention anywhere in src/. Any TypeSafe-compatible /v1/systemone endpoint works, including a local one. The key is refused over plain http to non-loopback hosts (decision.ts:47).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no patch is needed: three env vars (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_ENDPOINT_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL) in the MCP server's env block. Only the exact response envelope from OpenRouter is unverified.

It needs a project-local install with peers, which is awkward for a global Claude Code setup.

gh-tontoko-jev-browser.dataEgress: Only when a Jev-backed tool (observe, act, extract, semantic_*, run, resume) runs. Then the natural-language instruction, page URL and title, visible semantic text (each string truncated to 700 chars), element names, row/list/form context, options, href evidence, the action history and the input binding names go to the configured endpoint. That would be openrouter.ai and then TypeSafe (the OpenRouter model page states the data policy). The caller's `values` are withheld by default unless listed in semanticInputs. Text typed into editors and textareas is omitted from neighbouring-context strings. Values echoed by the page, or quoted in the instruction, can still leak, and SECURITY.md says redaction is best-effort. Native tools (snapshot, click, assert, screenshot...) send nothing to Jev. Source code, diffs, repo files and Claude's conversation never go to Jev, because the tool only sees browser pages. Expected literals in semantic_assert are sent.
gh-tontoko-jev-browser.failureMode: Fail-closed per Jev-backed call but isolated. decision.ts:54 sets timeout 15s (options.timeoutMs) with 0 SDK retries. Single-op decisions do not retry. Goals may retry read-only decisions up to decisionRetries=2. On error it throws BrowserError PROVIDER_ERROR (retryable for 408/429/5xx) or INVALID_DECISION, and the MCP tool returns isError JSON to Claude, which can fall back to native tools (snapshot, click). A missing key only fails the Jev tools (CONFIG). Native tools keep working. Mutations are never auto-replayed. MCP calls are serialized in a queue (mcp.ts:16-30), so one slow Jev call blocks all later browser calls until timeout or cancel. Nothing outside the browser tools is affected, so Claude Code as a whole never blocks on Jev.
gh-tontoko-jev-browser.latencyImpact: Zero for normal coding turns, since it hooks nothing. Only browser_* Jev calls add time: claimed 70-500 ms per decision plus the browser round trip. browser_run batches judgments in parallel frontiers so it avoids per-field round trips. Native ops add no model latency. The MCP server launches Chromium lazily on the first tool call (a few seconds for a cold start).

Once rendered to JSON Schema with per-argument descriptions this is roughly 10-15k tokens (my estimate; I did not run the server) of always-on tool definitions if not deferred. Claude Code 2.1.x tool-search deferral may reduce this, but the user already has playwright MCP, which loads about 30 tools. Running both would duplicate the browser surface. The server sets no MCP 'instructions'. No hook-injected text, since it has no hooks.
gh-tontoko-jev-browser.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. Claude picks browser_* when a task involves a browser. The shipped skills/jev-browser/SKILL.md has a description, but there is no plugin manifest, so it would need manual copying to ~/.claude/skills. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy, and no trigger on plain coding work. It fires automatically only in the narrow sense that Claude will choose it for browser/E2E tasks instead of playwright MCP, and only if tool descriptions steer it there.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for what it is suited to: typed Choice questions over a constrained candidate set (which element or option to act on), with confidence thresholds and inconclusive-never-passes semantics (docs/semantic-verification.md). This is a sound use of a System One model, not a chat substitute.

OpenRouter-compatible with config only: the SDK 0.6.0 appends /v1/systemone to baseURL, which matches OpenRouter's documented System One API. JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_ENDPOINT_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL are enough. The key stays out of argv.

Careful data-boundary design: values withheld by default, hosted keys never sent to a custom URL, no telemetry, no postinstall, logging off. The SECURITY.md is honest about limits. 34 native tools work with no key and no egress.

Broad, well-tested surface for a 13-day-old repo: 96 test files, a 7-way OS/browser CI matrix, Apache-2.0, SHA-pinned Actions. A batch API (browser_run, semantic_*_batch) reduces model round trips. Deterministic browser_assert sits beside semantic assertions.
Useful for web E2E and UX verification of the user's own frontend (dougthepug/empat design skills suggest UI work), especially semantic assertions on changing copy.
cons: Wrong layer for the stated goal. It only helps when a browser task occurs. It does nothing for code review, routing, permission gating, commit classification or context triage. Jev never sees code, so it adds no value to daily coding.

Overlaps and would duplicate the existing playwright MCP (about 50 tools versus about 30). It adds a second Chromium stack and a 10-15k token tool-definition footprint unless one of them is removed or deferred.

Not automatic in the sense the user wants. There is no hook or trigger. Claude uses it only if it prefers browser_* here over playwright MCP tools, and it can still choose native or Playwright tools, so Jev calls happen only inside the Jev-backed subset.

Distribution is poor: GitHub Release tarball only, no npm, with peer deps (playwright-core, zod) and a browser download. Setup is per-project or a manual global install. The 13-day-old, single-maintainer, 11-star repo with about 12 releases and heavy bot and AI-authored commits is high churn (pre-1.0, API and removed adapters already noted in docs/migration.md).

OpenRouter path is untested by the project (no OpenRouter mention in code, CI runs keyless). The response-envelope assumptions (usage.input_tokens/output_tokens, model) are unverified against OpenRouter. The model id format (jev-1.13 vs typesafe/jev-1.13) needs a manual check.

Page content plus client-site data (URLs, titles, visible text, form context) would leave the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a compliance question for client projects, and the browser runs with full network reach in bypass mode. Prompt injection from pages remains an inherent risk.
One slow Jev call blocks the serialized MCP queue up to the 15s timeout. Only Choice questions are used, so the Noul and Score primitives, which are the more interesting parts of Jev, go unused.

It does not deliver automatic Jev use across everyday Claude Code work, and it overlaps the existing playwright MCP. Worth trying (about 5 minutes of config) only if the user does a lot of browser E2E or UI verification. For the stated goal, look at hook-based candidates such as permission-prompt gating instead. If adopted, use it as a replacement for playwright MCP, not in addition.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The URL path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the change is one constant (ENDPOINT), the env var name, and the model ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 instead of jev-1.13.0). If OpenRouter wraps or renames those fields, every call fails with 'Invalid response envelope'. That is unverified. Redirects are refused (NoRedirect). Tests and docs assume the fixed endpoint. interface.name: suggest.py catalog
interface.purpose: Scan skill roots or --skill-file entries and write a catalog JSON to a new --out path. Reports warnings for symlinks, oversized files and suspected credentials.

interface.name: suggest.py suggest --mode local|jev
interface.purpose: Recommend one installed skill for --task or --task-file. Local mode does keyword matching with no network. Jev mode makes multi-call Choice/Noul requests. Flags: --allow, --exclude, --require, --prompt-key, --max-calls (default 12), --cache-dir, --trace.

interface.name: SKILL.md description trigger
interface.purpose: Model-discretion skill trigger. The body says to use it only when skill selection is explicitly requested or a large catalog makes selection ambiguous, 'Do not run it on every message'. SKILL.md is in Codex format (frontmatter name/description only) with an agents/openai.yaml sidecar.

interface.name: Status outputs
interface.purpose: suggested, explicit_selection, none, uncertain/ambiguous, local_only, unavailable, incomplete. Exit codes: 0 done, 2 invalid input, 3 incomplete.

security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or getpass, and is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (jev_client.py:92). It never appears in argv. SKILL.md forbids putting keys in command arguments.
Endpoint is hardcoded and redirects are refused (NoRedirect), so credentials cannot be bounced to another host.
No shell execution, subprocess or os.system in the scripts (grep found none). It uses stdlib urllib only, has no dependencies, no install script, no postinstall and no telemetry.
Invoked as python3 -I -B (isolated mode). Reads are bounded: no FIFOs, no final symlinks, 160 KB per entry, 256 skills.
Heuristic credential detection blocks transmission of skills whose text looks like secrets; the docs admit it does not catch every secret. Task text and paths inside prose are not anonymized.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted SKILL.md descriptions and body excerpts go into Jev state. Impact is limited because the output is only a typed distribution and nothing is executed. The design doc says it is not a security certification.
Response validation is strict (probability sums, legend match, sizes). The cache is mode 0600 and stores hashed keys, not request text.
Repo is a single-author, single-commit dump. The reader must review it, since there is no history to audit.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.dataEgress: Only in Jev mode: the task text (up to 12,000 bytes), plus every eligible skill's name, description and content hash. In the detail stage it also sends bounded SKILL.md body excerpts (about 6 KB each, at most 12 candidates). Filesystem paths are omitted. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai; nothing goes to OpenRouter. Code, diffs and tool outputs are not sent unless the caller pastes them into --task. Local mode makes no network calls.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the tool. Any API error or timeout raises ScanError, and the status becomes 'incomplete' with exit code 3. There is one 2-second retry on 429/5xx and a 45 s timeout per attempt, so worst-case latency is about 90 s per call across up to 12 attempts. Auth failures disable the client. Since nothing is wired into Claude Code as a hook, a failure only affects the model's explicit invocation, and the model just proceeds without a suggestion.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.contextCost: Very low. There is one skill, and the frontmatter description is about 150 Chinese characters, roughly 100-150 tokens, always loaded. The SKILL.md body (54 lines, about 1.5k tokens) loads only when the skill is triggered. No MCP tools and no hook-injected text.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at model discretion. It has no hook and the docs say 'no automatic hooks'. Claude Code would load it only if the description matches the situation, which is a narrow case: choosing between many skills. The SKILL.md body also says not to run it on every message. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.latencyImpact: Each invocation is several sequential HTTPS round trips: one ranking call per roster batch (28 KB cap), then one verification call. The design doc itself warns latency may outweigh savings on simple tasks. Estimated 1-5 s with Jev's claimed 70-500 ms per call, and worse with a large catalog. Tool startup is negligible (stdlib Python). Zero latency when not invoked.
pros: Clean, well-validated reference implementation of a real Jev use case (Choice plus Noul, two-stage skill routing), mirroring TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook.
Strong hygiene: stdlib-only, no subprocess, hardcoded endpoint, no redirects, key via env or getpass, bounded reads, strict response schema validation, 24 h cache with 0600 mode.
Explicit user consent model: it separates local (offline) mode from Jev mode, and --require gives a deterministic path for a skill the user named.
Documented failure semantics and call budget (12 attempts, timeouts, exit codes), and a 25-test offline suite plus a CI matrix (py3.10/3.13, macOS).
Very small context footprint, MIT license, and the code is a useful template for a custom hook that reuses the same request builders and validator.
strict validate_response, and a jev_client.py that already speaks /v1/systemone, would carry over to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone if the envelope is identical.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only. No OpenRouter path, and the design doc says 'no custom endpoint'; it needs a fork to change the URL, key env var and model ID, plus verification that OpenRouter's envelope matches.

Not automatic: there is no hook, and the docs explicitly forbid running it on every message. Claude Code would trigger it only via a description match. That conflicts with the user's goal of Jev firing without being asked.

Built for Codex (~/.codex/skills, ~/.agents/skills, agents/openai.yaml). Claude Code skills live in ~/.claude/skills and plugin caches, which need explicit --root/--skill-file flags. Claude Code already lists skill names and descriptions natively, so the value is marginal unless the user has hundreds of skills.
Unnecessary latency and cost on simple tasks (the design doc admits this), plus a Bash invocation and a permission prompt outside bypass mode.
Sends the task text and skill descriptions and excerpts to a third party (TypeSafe), which matters for client projects.

Weak provenance: a single commit, one author, created 2026-09-19 (11 days old), no releases, no issues history. 33 stars are mostly novelty. Its performance is unvalidated (the docs say so), and the docs and README are largely in Chinese.
Solves a narrow problem (skill routing) and does not touch the broader Jev uses: gating tool calls, risk scoring, code-review triage, permission decisions.
gh-win4r-jev-skill-suggester.verdict: A careful, safe reference implementation of Jev skill routing, but it is TypeSafe-only, Codex-oriented, description-triggered rather than hook-driven, and narrow in scope. It does not meet the goal of automatic OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code. Use it as a code template or pattern for a custom hook, not as the integration.

Each harness builds state plus Choice/Score/Noul questions, applies confidence thresholds in code, and returns an action band (auto/confirm/human/block). It is NOT a skill, MCP server, hook or plugin. It has no SKILL.md, .mcp.json, plugin.json or hooks config, and no Claude Code integration. The key is passed in-process to the SDK, not via argv. The optional LLM helper sends the key in x-api-key or Authorization headers (llm.py:107,163), not via argv.

No telemetry in the repo code (the SDK was not audited).

The README itself warns that user-controlled text in state can change Jev's answer, which is a prompt-injection surface for a tool-call gate that puts command strings and conversation summaries in state.
The README says thresholds are not ready for unattended production use.
Pulling in typesafe-sdk is a third-party dependency that was not audited.
gh-kenhuangus-jev-usecases.dataEgress: Only when the user's own code calls it: whatever is put in `state`, sent to api.typesafe.ai. In the library, get_client raises MissingApiKeyError if the key is missing, and CLI errors exit 1 or 2 (fail-closed for the CLI). The gate function has no try/except or explicit timeout around client.system_one, so an outage would raise an exception. The caller would have to decide fail-open or fail-closed. The LLM helper uses a 60 s timeout.
gh-kenhuangus-jev-usecases.contextCost: Zero in Claude Code as shipped, since it registers no MCP tools, hooks, skills or instructions. If it were adapted into a hook, the injected text would be only what the hook chooses to print.

pros: Concrete, readable template of how to phrase Jev questions for a coding agent: coding_agent_guardrails.py uses 8 Noul safety conditions, a risk_class Choice (read_only/reversible/irreversible) and a Score severity, combined with thresholds (deny at or below 0.15, allow at or above 0.75) and a deterministic protected-path pre-check. It could be copied into a PreToolUse hook.

Honest about Jev's limits: it cites TypeSafe's jaggedness notes (literal reading, no counting or date comparison, distraction by unneeded state fields, injection via user text) and says code should do exact checks.
Deterministic checks first, Jev second, and the model never executes anything. This is a sound pattern for a gate.
MIT licensed, small codebase (about 900 lines of core plus use cases), easy to audit.
Fixtures for about 40 use cases show working state and question shapes for agent_trace, function_calling, model_routing and semantic_linting, which are the ones relevant to a coding agent.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. Claude Code cannot use it without the user writing the glue, so it does not meet the requirement of automatic use.

Provider support is TypeSafe direct only. No OpenRouter code path, no base_url on the Jev client, and the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone schema is unverified against typesafe-sdk. The user would need to rewrite the client.
Mostly irrelevant domains (SOC, insurance, recruiting, ad tech, financial crime, about 35 of 40 modules) for a developer's daily coding.

Very young and thinly reviewed: 8 commits over 3 days, 2 contributors, 17 stars, no releases, no CI, no PyPI package. Its own README says the runs check typed responses, not correctness, and that the thresholds are not production-ready.

The gate would send full commands, cwd and conversation summaries (which may include client code and paths) to a third party on every call. The README says accuracy drops when state carries extra fields, and the repo sends conversation_summary anyway.

A PreToolUse gate on the user's already busy Bash|Read|Grep chain (secret guard, GitNexus) would add latency per call. The user runs bypass/auto permission mode, so a fail-open gate adds little real safety, and a fail-closed one adds outage friction. The code has no timeout or fallback handling.
Uses load_dotenv() from the CWD, which could load a client project's .env, a hygiene issue for client work.

gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.name: Gamedirection/JevAI-MCP
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.whatItDoes: A self-hosted Node/TypeScript MCP server (Streamable HTTP, /mcp on ports 8080 and 3001) plus a React dashboard and SQLite request log. It wraps POST {endpoint}/systemone with 5 opinionated tools (jev_decide, jev_route_task, jev_assess_complexity, jev_should_escalate, jev_choose_strategy) that build choice/score/noul questions for coding-agent routing. It maps confidence to use/guidance/independent, retries, supports backup credentials, and has an optional local/cloud LLM fallback. Agent behavior is steered by server instructions and a shipped jev-routing.md to be pasted into CLAUDE.md. It is meant to run in Docker/K8s as an internal service.

providerSupport.evidence: Provider-agnostic on base URL but not named for OpenRouter; there is no OpenRouter mention anywhere in the repo. packages/jev-client/src/client.ts:482 posts to `${credential.endpoint}/systemone` with headers `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}` and body JSON.stringify({model, state, questions}) (client.ts:~483-495). The endpoint comes from DEFAPI_API_ENDPOINT (apps/server/src/context.ts; the env key is mapped in apps/server/src/routes/settings.ts:22), the model from JEV_MODEL, and the key from DEFAPI_API_KEY. Defaults are inconsistent: packages/shared/src/settings.ts:63 uses https://api.defapi.org/v1 with typesafe/jev-1.13, while .env.example and docker-compose.yml:14 use https://api.typesafe.ai/v1 with jev-1.13.0. The response schema is `{model, answers:{choice|score|noul, confidence, probabilities}, usage}` (packages/shared/src/jev-schema.ts). Setting DEFAPI_API_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 would hit /api/v1/systemone.
providerSupport.others: DefAPI gateway (api.defapi.org/v1, dk- keys), TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai/v1), up to 2 backup credential slots (JEV_BACKUP_2/3_*), optional OpenAI-compatible local (Ollama) and cloud fallback LLMs.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial on paper: env-only, no code change (DEFAPI_API_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, DEFAPI_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>). The caveat is that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone request and response schema is assumed to match TypeSafe's, and the strict zod parse in client.ts would reject any divergence with JEV_INVALID_RESPONSE. The repo's real-api.test.ts only targets DefAPI. The API-key redaction regex (secrets.ts) does not cover OpenRouter sk-or- keys unless they match sk-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}, which they likely do.

interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Generic tool: takes a state (string, object or array, up to 200k chars) plus up to 32 named choice/score/noul questions and returns typed answers with probabilities and confidence. The description tells the model to batch related questions.

interface.name: jev_route_task
interface.purpose: Classifies the task as bug, feature, refactor, documentation, investigation, infrastructure, security, testing, deployment or other, with optional custom choices.

interface.name: jev_assess_complexity
interface.purpose: Scores complexity on trivial, small, moderate, complex, high-risk.

interface.name: jev_should_escalate
interface.purpose: Noul probability that deeper or more expensive reasoning, or a human, is warranted. Thresholds: >=0.80 yes, <=0.20 no.

interface.name: jev_choose_strategy
interface.purpose: Picks a first investigation strategy from caller-supplied {name: description} options (logs, git diff, ingress, db and so on).

interface.name: MCP server instructions (SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS)
interface.purpose: About 6 sentences injected into the session that tell the model when to call Jev, to batch calls, and to fail open. This is the only built-in auto-trigger.

interface.name: integrations/claude/jev-routing.md and CLAUDE.md
interface.purpose: Static routing policy the user must copy into CLAUDE.md. Says to pass caller {caller: claude-code}.

interface.name: HTTP dashboard API (/api/*, /health, /metrics)
interface.purpose: Dashboard, requests, logs, settings (writes), integrations ZIPs, Prometheus metrics. There is no login.

security: No auth on /mcp or the dashboard API; README says 'No login. Internal tool only'. Defaults bind 0.0.0.0 (.env.example HOST/MCP_HOST, DEFAULT_SETTINGS mcp.host 0.0.0.0, server.ts bindHost). On a laptop or shared network, any host can call the tools and spend the OpenRouter key.

The settings write API can change jev.endpoint. Cross-origin protection only checks Origin against Host when an Origin header is present (api.ts:57-66), so a non-browser LAN client can repoint the endpoint and capture the Bearer key. There is no DNS-rebinding or Host allow-list on /mcp.

The API key is not visible in argv if supplied via .env or Docker env. If saved via the dashboard, it is stored in SQLite (the README claims 'stored as a hash', but a hash cannot be replayed, so this needs checking in api-key-store.ts). Redaction regexes cover dk-, jv_, apikey_ and sk- patterns (secrets.ts).

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are typed (choice/score/noul), so the injection surface is small. The model composes the state itself, so injected repo text can still influence what gets sent and how it is classified. Then 'strong_yes'/'use' guidance is fed back to the agent.

Optional fallback (JEV_FALLBACK_ENABLED, default false) sends the full state to a configured local or cloud OpenAI-compatible LLM. Off by default. With full storage enabled, state is written to SQLite (truncated to 20k chars).

No postinstall, telemetry or curl|sh found. package.json has an allowScripts entry for esbuild and better-sqlite3 (native build). CI is GitHub Actions and .gitlab-ci.yml. Runs as the node user in Docker. It needs Docker or a build of a monorepo with about 800 KB of source, so there is a large audit surface for a tool that only wraps one HTTP call.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.dataEgress: To the configured endpoint (OpenRouter if repointed) with Authorization: Bearer key, X-Request-Id and User-Agent jevai-mcp/1.0.0: whatever `state` Claude composes (free text, object or array, up to 200k chars) plus the question instructions and criteria. There is no automatic collection of files, diffs or tool outputs; egress is limited to what the model chooses to put in state. Locally it stores metadata (caller, project, repository, session_id, sizes, timings) in SQLite by default, and the exact state (first 20k chars) if REQUEST_STATE_STORAGE=full. There is no telemetry to the author. Fallback LLM egress only happens if enabled.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every tool returns {success:false, error:{type:JEV_UNAVAILABLE, retryable}} and the instructions tell the agent to carry on. Defaults are a 10s timeout and 3 retries (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, JEV_RETRIES) with exponential backoff (300ms base, 5s max) and Retry-After support. Worst case is roughly 40s of blocking in a single tool call (4 attempts x 10s plus backoff), which is bad for a 'fast router', though backup credentials trigger only on 401/403/429. If the local MCP server itself is down, Claude Code just shows the MCP as failed and continues. The MCP-layer health returns 200 degraded.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.contextCost: 5 tools. By my estimate, descriptions come to roughly 3,000 chars and the zod-derived JSON schemas (state union, questions record with discriminated union, caller and metadata) to roughly 4-6k chars, so about 1.8-2.5k tokens of tool defs when loaded (they are deferred via tool search in current Claude Code, so the name-only cost is small). Server instructions come to about 1,000 chars, roughly 250 tokens. No hooks and no hook-injected text. If you also paste jev-routing.md into CLAUDE.md, that adds about 700 tokens on every turn.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Auto-use relies on SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS plus tool descriptions (and optionally a jev-routing.md pasted into CLAUDE.md). There is no hook, no skill and no proxy, so nothing deterministic ensures Jev is called. Opus will often skip calling a routing tool for tasks it can classify itself. The 'do not call for obvious' language further biases it toward not calling.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.latencyImpact: Each call is a local MCP HTTP round trip plus the Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms) plus SQLite writes, so roughly 0.1-0.6 s per call. It is a full model tool-call turn each time (extra assistant output tokens and a reasoning step), which costs more in wall time and tokens than the Jev call itself. It saves nothing on Opus-side tokens for coding, and the 'saves tokens' claim rests on a hard-coded ESTIMATED_AVOIDED_TOKENS=1500 constant rather than measurement.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.runtime: Node 22+ (TypeScript, Hono, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, better-sqlite3), Docker/Helm/K8s manifests, React+Vite dashboard.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.install: Official path is Docker: cp .env.example .env, set DEFAPI_API_KEY, docker compose up --build -d, then `claude mcp add --transport http jevai http://localhost:3001/mcp`. Then paste integrations/claude/jev-routing.md into CLAUDE.md. For OpenRouter, set DEFAPI_API_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. Note that docker-compose.yml maps the dashboard to host port 8081.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.tests: 11 test files (vitest) covering jev-client (retry, credentials, fallback), mcp-tools, database, secrets, context and the web app. CI runs lint, typecheck, vitest, build and a Docker smoke test. real-api.test.ts hits a live API. I did not run any of this (static review only).
pros: Env-only repointing to OpenRouter: the base URL, model and key are all configurable (client.ts:482, settings.ts:63), and the path is `{endpoint}/systemone`, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone in the brief. No code patch is needed, as long as the schema matches.

It is the only candidate I saw with a real design for coding-agent routing. It ships pre-built question templates, confidence-threshold mapping (use/guidance/independent) and batching guidance, and it fails open with typed errors.

Sound client engineering: retry/backoff with Retry-After, backup credential rotation on 401/403/429, strict zod validation of responses, key redaction, request-size limits, metadata-only storage by default, MIT license, and CI with tests.

The MCP server sets `instructions` and tool descriptions that explicitly say when to call and when not to, which is the closest thing to auto-invocation available without hooks. The Claude integration pack (jev-routing.md, CLAUDE.md snippet) is ready to drop in.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh. The tool surface is small (5 tools) and its typed outputs limit injection risk from Jev to the agent.
Local dashboard with per-call log, latency and cost makes it possible to actually measure whether Jev helps.
cons: It is 4 days old with 5 commits, 0 stars, 0 releases and 2 authors. It was clearly built for the author's own environment (docker-compose comment 'port 8080 is taken by octo-ai-web'; inconsistent defaults between README/settings.ts (defapi, typesafe/jev-1.13) and .env.example/compose (typesafe.ai, jev-1.13.0)).

Massive over-engineering for one HTTP call: a Docker service, SQLite, React dashboard, Helm, K8s and Prometheus metrics for a personal dev laptop. You must run a persistent daemon (with `docker compose up`) before Claude Code starts, or the MCP shows as failed. It is awkward for a stdio/uvx-style workflow, since Claude Code has no supervision of it.

No authentication and binds 0.0.0.0 by default. The unauthenticated settings API can repoint the endpoint (and thus exfiltrate the OpenRouter key) and any LAN host can spend your credits. It is unsuitable on a laptop on client networks without setting HOST=127.0.0.1 and MCP_HOST=127.0.0.1 manually.

Auto-invocation is entirely at model discretion. There is no hook, so 'without ever prompting' is not guaranteed; the instructions themselves tell Opus not to call it when things are obvious, so it will rarely fire. Each call also costs a full tool-call turn.

The value proposition is weak for Opus 5.5 daily coding: routing/classifying tasks, complexity and escalation are things the main model does inside its own reasoning at near-zero marginal cost, so Jev adds latency and tokens rather than saving them. The 'saved tokens' metric is a fixed 1500-token constant.

Worst-case blocking is about 40s per call (10s timeout x 4 attempts + backoff), which is a poor fit for a 70-500 ms router. No OpenRouter support has been verified in tests or docs, only DefAPI and TypeSafe, so schema drift on OpenRouter's /systemone would surface as JEV_INVALID_RESPONSE.
Codebase is roughly 800 KB across a monorepo, so auditing a client-facing tool that handles a paid key is expensive. Fallback mode can send state to arbitrary LLM URLs if misconfigured.
gh-gamedirection-jevai-mcp.verdict: It is a well-made but heavy, early-stage (4 days old) Docker+dashboard wrapper. It can technically point at OpenRouter through env vars alone. But it is only model-discretion (no hook), is unauthenticated on 0.0.0.0 by default, and its routing/escalation tools duplicate what Opus already does for free. It is worth using only as a reference for question templates or for measuring Jev, not as the daily integration.

pros: Only candidate here that actually wires Claude Code lifecycle hooks (SessionStart/PreToolUse/Stop) so behavior is automatic rather than requiring a prompt; git commit/push gate on the staged diff is a genuinely sensible Jev use case (Noul/Choice on diff risk).
MIT license, static-only content (markdown + short bash), no build step, no postinstall or curl|sh: easy to read fully in 10 minutes, low direct supply-chain risk from the repo itself.
docs/CONFIDENCE.md gives a clear act/confirm/stop threshold policy, and the idea of pairing Jev's calibrated probabilities with human-approval gates is a good pattern to borrow.
Supports a local TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override convention (could be pointed at a compatible endpoint) and includes an offline mock server.
cons: No Jev/OpenRouter code at all: zero references to openrouter.ai, /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone; everything depends on 6 unaudited third-party CLIs that each need TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it cannot use the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev without patching every downstream tool.

Stop hook exits 2 whenever the working tree is dirty and runs ./scripts/test.sh of whatever project you are in: forces commits/loops on every turn, breaks normal exploratory or client-repo workflows, and executes project scripts each turn. Combined with bypass/auto mode this is disruptive and risky.
PreToolUse commit gate is fail-closed and fragile: without git-jev installed all `git commit`/`git push` (and any Bash text containing both words) are blocked; grep-based JSON parsing; no timeouts.

Bulk: bundles the entire upstream superpowers skill set (20 skills, ~150KB) duplicating jev-* variants, injects an EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT MUST-invoke block every session start/compact, and mandates the workflow (brainstorm gate, human approval) that conflicts with existing GitNexus/caveman setup and a senior user's fast loop; jev-scout is Rust/crates-centric.

gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.name: HyunjunJeon/jev-judgment
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.whatItDoes: Agent Skill (SKILL.md plus one stdlib-only Python script, jev.py) that tells the coding agent to send closed questions to TypeSafe Jev at three points. (1) Before asking the user a closed question, it asks Jev whether context already determines the answer. (2) Before a risky command, it scores destructive, exfiltration, beyond_scope and impact. (3) After a command fails, it classifies the failure and checks for leaked secrets. jev.py is a thin pass-through for POST {base}/v1/systemone. It redacts credentials with regexes, truncates strings, fails open on every network error, and prints the JSON answer. SKILL.md holds fixed thresholds and action tables (for example, auto-answer if P>=0.9 and determined>=0.9; stop if destructive>=0.9 or exfiltration>=0.7). The agent applies these itself, so nothing is enforced.

interface.name: Protocol 1: pick (choice incl. ask_user) plus determined (noul)
interface.purpose: Auto-answers a closed user question when P(pick)>=0.9 and determined>=0.9. Otherwise it puts Jev's pick first as '(suggested)'.

interface.name: Protocol 2: destructive, exfiltration, beyond_scope (noul) plus impact (4-level score)
interface.purpose: Pre-action risk gate. It asks the user to confirm when destructive>=0.9, exfiltration>=0.7, beyond_scope>=0.85 or impact>=2.5.

interface.name: Protocol 3: leaks_secret (noul) plus failure_class (choice)
interface.purpose: After a failed command, it classifies the failure as transient, environment, code_bug, permission or user_error. It also flags secrets in the output.

security: API key is read from env or <cwd>/.env (jev.py:246-251) and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. The state goes via stdin heredoc.
Reading <cwd>/.env (jev.py:234-243) means a client project's .env is parsed for TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. Other entries are not returned, but the file is opened.

Regex redaction (jev.py:70-124) covers PEM, JWT, AWS, gh*, sk-*, Slack, Bearer and KEY=value assignments with 16+ chars. It is best-effort. Secrets in other formats, DB connection strings, and short passwords pass through. The README admits false negatives are possible.

No shell execution inside the script, no curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry. It is stdlib-only, with a single HTTPS call to a user-configurable base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL can redirect traffic anywhere, so a poisoned env or .env could exfiltrate the redacted state and key. Nothing else is in the way.
Installation uses `npx skills add` (third-party skills CLI). That is outside this repo and unaudited, but it is only needed once. The files can also be copied by hand.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output and file facts are put into the state and Jev's verdict then drives agent behaviour. A malicious repo could word its content to push 'destructive' low. The verdict is advisory and the agent can ignore it.
allowed-tools in SKILL.md:18 pre-approves Bash(python3 *scripts/jev.py *), a broad glob that would match any script named jev.py. This is minor, and irrelevant under bypass mode.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in `state`, after regex redaction. Per SKILL.md, that means user_request, last_user_message, chosen facts (file listings, config snippets), the exact tool arguments (the command, path, first 400 chars of content), and the first 2000 chars of failed-command output. Strings are capped at 2000 chars and the whole state at 8000 chars. It goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to the host set in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (OpenRouter, in this user's setup). It is chosen by the model, so it varies per call. On client projects this can include proprietary paths, commands and snippets, and OpenRouter and TypeSafe would both see them. There is no telemetry from the script itself.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.failureMode: Fail-open by design (jev.py:411-446). A missing key, HTTP 401, 422 or 429, another HTTP error, a timeout or a connection error each print {"error":...} with exit 0, and SKILL.md says to behave as if the skill were not installed. The default timeout is 8 s (jev.py:58). There are no retries in the script, and the agent is told to retry at most once. Worst case per failed call is about 8 s blocked, most likely when the network hangs. Exit 2 only on a malformed request or a state over 8000 chars, and the agent is told to fix and resend. There is no fail-closed mode, so Protocol 2 gives no guarantee on Jev outages.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens. The always-loaded cost is the skill name plus description (SKILL.md:2-12, about 690 chars, roughly 175 tokens) plus the compatibility and allowed-tools frontmatter, so about 200 tokens per session. The full SKILL.md (204 lines, about 9.5k chars, roughly 2.4k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. Each trigger also costs the model tokens to author the state and questions JSON (roughly 300-600 output tokens, since instructions and criteria must be written per call), plus the returned JSON (roughly 150-300 tokens). references/questions.md (217 lines) is read on demand, and the model may re-read it. No hook injection and no MCP server instructions.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). Claude Code decides whether to load the skill from the description, then the model decides at each point whether to call jev.py. There is no hook, so nothing is deterministic. Under bypass or auto permission mode the model is not forced to consult Jev before rm or push --force, so the risk-gate protocol is not reliable. Reliability of triggering on 'about to ask the user' or 'command failed' is uncertain because Claude has no strong reason to defer to it. It can be improved by adding a CLAUDE.md line or by wrapping jev.py in a PreToolUse hook, which would require code changes.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.latencyImpact: Claimed p50 about 250 ms and p95 about 600 ms for the API, plus 0.3-0.5 s for TLS and Python startup (api.md:94-99). Realistic added cost per trigger is about 0.6-1.5 s of wall time plus the model's own generation time for the JSON body (roughly 3-8 s of Opus output for 400-600 tokens). This is probably slower than Claude just deciding. A failing network adds up to 8 s. It is paid only when the skill triggers, not on every tool call.
pros: Zero-cost passive footprint: no MCP server, about 200 tokens always-loaded, and no hooks to conflict with the secret-leak guard, the GitNexus hooks or the caveman plugin.
Auto-invocation is at least designed in. The description names concrete moments (before AskUserQuestion, before rm/reset/force-push, after a failed command), so the user never has to say 'use jev'.

jev.py is small, readable and stdlib-only. Fail-open on every network error, an 8 s timeout, redaction of common secret formats, and --dry-run to inspect exactly what would leave the machine (jev.py:407-409).

The OpenRouter switch is config only if the OpenRouter body schema matches: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13 (jev.py:53-57, 267-278, 422). The wire format {model,state,questions} matches the documented System One shape.
MIT licensed and a single file to fork. Adding OPENROUTER_API_KEY support is a 5-line change.
The protocols are well thought out, with an always-ask list (dependencies, remote state, multi-select) and a rule to report every Jev-driven decision. This limits the damage from over-trusting Jev.
Failure-class and secret-in-output checks could complement the existing secret-leak hook.
cons: Not deterministic. It is a skill, not a hook, so Claude decides whether to invoke it. In bypass or auto mode the Protocol 2 risk gate can simply be skipped, which is when it is needed most. It cannot block a command; it only asks the model to self-police.

Very young and unproven: 1 commit, 1 contributor, created and last pushed 2026-09-17, 7 stars, 1 fork, no releases, no tests, no CI. The benchmark cited in questions.md (54 items) is unpublished and self-reported.

Uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL only. OpenRouter needs a misleadingly named key variable and non-default model slugs. Whether OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same answer shape is unverified from the repo. The user's planned OPENROUTER_API_KEY would be ignored.

Poor value for Opus 5.5. Each use costs the model 300-600 tokens of hand-written JSON (instructions, criteria) plus 0.6-1.5 s of network and startup, to answer questions Opus can usually answer itself. Protocol 1 mostly helps agents that ask the user too often, and Protocol 3's failure classification is trivial for a strong model.

Real safety risk of over-trusting a beta model whose behaviour is disputed (the Theo 'flash router' claim). A wrongly confident 'determined' can auto-answer a question the user should have decided. Protocol 2 tells the model to skip mention of Jev when nothing fires, which weakens visibility.

Privacy: commands, snippets, user messages and failed-command output leave the machine on every trigger, including client projects. Regex redaction is best-effort and only covers the listed formats. The model chooses what goes in the state, so egress is unpredictable.

Overlaps with existing controls. The PreToolUse secret guard already deterministically blocks secret leakage. Permission modes already gate destructive commands when not bypassed. There is no code-search, refactor or analysis value, so it does not help with daily coding tasks.
Reads <cwd>/.env for the key (jev.py:251). In client repos this can hit the wrong .env or be surprising.
gh-hyunjunjeon-jev-judgment.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-open skill and the lightest possible way to get Jev into Claude Code (about 200 tokens, no MCP, no hook conflicts). But it is only advisory and model-triggered, one-commit and untested, and it is aimed at agents weaker than Opus 5.5. Use it as a low-risk experiment through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model slug (after verifying the OpenRouter schema with --dry-run and one live call), or as the source for a hook-based fork. Do not rely on it as a safety gate.
