gh-samtay32-jev-system-architect.name: samtay32/jev-system-architect
gh-samtay32-jev-system-architect.whatItDoes: A single SKILL.md (717 lines, ~19 KB) of architecture guidance. It tells a coding agent how to spot places in a codebase where deterministic code needs bounded semantic judgment, and how to turn them into Choice/Score/Noul questions. It covers fit tests, atomic questions, fan-out, confidence gates, evaluation and a review procedure. It never calls Jev. It contains no code, no API calls, no MCP server, no hooks and no scripts. It defers to TypeSafe's docs and official skill for API details. It is a design-time aid for building apps that use Jev, not a way for Claude Code to consult Jev while coding.

There is no endpoint, base URL or env var anywhere, so provider support is not applicable. The skill makes no runtime calls. Its 'Default Instruction to the Agent' (SKILL.md:713-717) tells the agent to inspect systems for Jev opportunities. That can nudge Claude to suggest adding a Jev dependency to client projects, which matters for personal versus client work.

gh-samtay32-jev-system-architect.verdict: This is a safe, well-written but purely advisory design playbook. It has no Jev runtime, no OpenRouter support and no hooks, so it cannot give the automatic use of Jev the user wants inside Claude Code. It is worth installing only as an optional companion skill, alongside TypeSafe's official skill or an MCP/hook that actually calls Jev, and only if the user builds Jev-backed apps.

gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.name: devagrawal09/stanley-code
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.whatItDoes: Standalone Node CLI ("stanley") that takes a natural-language request, uses one Jev Choice call to route it to one of 10 deterministic built-in workflows (check diff vs task, review, test gaps, summarize, security/perf/compat review, find relevant code, triage failures, triage review comments), splits the git diff into hunks and asks Jev fixed-choice questions per hunk. Code, not the model, applies thresholds and produces findings/notChecked. Falls back to the Pi coding agent (if installed) for unsupported requests and queues background self-improvement (agent writes new workflows into .stanley/). It is a CLI, not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin; nothing in the repo integrates with Claude Code.

providerSupport.evidence: src/adapters/jev.ts:1,12-17,20: uses @typesafe-ai/sdk TypeSafeClient({apiKey from TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, retry maxRetries 0}).systemOne(). The SDK (npm @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0, dist/index.cjs:58-59,514,555) defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai, honours env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, and POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with Bearer auth. Stanley itself has no OpenRouter code (grep 'openrouter' in src/scripts: zero hits). Model: src/workflows/types.ts:5 DEFAULT_MODEL='jev-1.13.0', overridable via TYPESAFE_MODEL (src/adapters/config.ts:4-9).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, env-only, no code change: TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, exactly the OpenRouter System One URL), TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. Caveat: I did not verify OpenRouter's System One request/response schema is byte-identical to TypeSafe's; the brief says the same path/name so likely compatible. Stanley requires the var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY so the OpenRouter key would be stored under that misleading name (redact.ts and git.ts scrub that name from diffs/child env, which is fine).
providerSupport.others: None. Optional Pi coding agent (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) with its own model credentials for fallback.

interface.name: stanley "<request>" [--scope worktree|staged|branch] [--base ref] [--input path|-] [--repo dir] [--json] [--no-persist] [--no-agent]
interface.purpose: Single CLI entrypoint (src/cli.ts). Jev routes the natural-language request to a built-in or repo workflow; prints report with findings/parked/notChecked.

interface.purpose: find, check (task/rules/criteria), review, test_gaps, summarize, security, performance, compatibility, triage_failures, triage_comments (src/workflows/*.ts). Internal, not exposed as subcommands.

interface.purpose: Administrative self-improvement: detached worker asks Pi agent to write a new workflow into .stanley candidates; user promotes it.

interface.name: .stanley/workflows/*.ts|js
interface.purpose: Trusted repo-local workflows loaded via tsx (arbitrary code execution with user privileges).

interface.name: library export (src/index.ts)

Pi agent fallback executes an arbitrary coding agent on unsupported requests (pi.ts spawn, shell:false), which in a Claude Code context is a second autonomous agent with its own model provider (would send code to OpenAI/whichever Pi is configured for).
Writes .stanley/runs records to the repo unless --no-persist.

No telemetry found in source; no postinstall scripts; no curl|sh. Prompt-injection surface: diff contents and comments are fed to Jev, but Jev only returns typed choices and code applies thresholds, so injection impact is limited to skewing judgments.
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is repointed): the natural-language request, workflow routing metadata, and per-hunk diff text, file path/metadata plus excerpts of repository files (find workflow), test/CI log blocks, review comments; up to 150 hunks per check, 3000 files screened by path, all after regex secret redaction. If the Pi fallback runs, the request and repo context go to Pi's configured LLM provider (e.g. OpenAI via OAuth in their docs). Nothing is sent from Claude Code itself; only what the CLI is asked to inspect.
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.failureMode: Fail-closed but bounded and non-blocking to Claude Code because it is not wired in: each Jev call has a 30s default timeout (executor.ts:108), SDK retries disabled and retries counted in run budgets by the executor; transport failures classified (auth/transient/too_large/rejected) and surface as incomplete/budget_exhausted/unsupported with notChecked; low-confidence routing yields cannot_tell/unsupported rather than a guess. Missing key throws MissingCredentialError. Exit codes 1 and 2 deliberately unused because exit 2 is a blocking signal in agent hooks (output.ts:15), showing the author considered hook use but there is no hook implementation.
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.latencyImpact: Not applicable to normal Claude Code turns since nothing calls it automatically. When invoked manually via Bash: routing call plus N per-hunk Jev calls (up to 150 hunks for check, many rounds for find), each 70-500 ms claimed, some concurrency unknown, so several seconds to tens of seconds per run, plus Node/tsx startup. Not verified live.
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.contextCost: Zero passive cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no skill. Only cost is output tokens when Claude runs the CLI via Bash and reads the report (text + structured data; --json is machine readable). Claude would have to be told (CLAUDE.md line or skill) that the command exists.
gh-devagrawal09-stanley-code.autoInvocation: Only when prompted / invoked explicitly as a shell command. No hook, MCP tool, skill or proxy in the repo. To be automatic, the user would have to write their own glue (e.g. a Stop or PreToolUse-on-git-commit hook running `stanley "Check these changes..." --json --no-agent --no-persist`, or a CLAUDE.md/skill instruction). That glue is not provided.
pros: Genuine, non-trivial Jev usage: correct use of Choice/Noul/Score-style typed questions with code-side thresholds, so the model never writes free text; matches Jev's System One strengths (bounded classification of hunks).

Useful review-type checks that map to real pre-commit gaps: added test.skip, deleted assertions, weakened expectations, lockfile/CI/config edits, hunks unrelated to the stated task, missing test evidence.

Env-only OpenRouter path: SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone, which is exactly OpenRouter's System One URL; TYPESAFE_MODEL selects typesafe/jev-1.13. No fork needed (schema parity unverified).

Well-engineered: 20k lines with heavy tests, CI on 3 Node versions, pinned action SHAs, explicit budgets, timeouts, honest 'empty findings is not approval' reporting, --no-agent and --no-persist switches, JSON output.
Hook-aware design: avoids exit codes 1/2 (output.ts:15) so it could be wrapped in a hook; no telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh.
MIT license; clean read-only-by-default git usage.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it gives no automatic integration with Claude Code at all; violates the user's core requirement unless the user writes their own hook/skill glue.
Not released: not on npm, no GitHub release; must clone, npm ci and build. 10 days old, single author, 22 commits, README says 'Experimental: every request, report, and interface may change'.
Hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_BASE_URL naming; using OpenRouter means storing an OpenRouter key under a TypeSafe-named variable, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified.

Its own Jev router step duplicates Claude's job: Claude Code already knows whether to review a diff, so Jev-routing a natural-language request adds latency and cost with no benefit; only the diff-analysis workflows are valuable.
Sends diff hunks and file excerpts (post best-effort regex redaction) to a third-party beta model for every run, a concern on client projects; secret scrubber is explicitly not a secret scanner.

Repo-local .stanley/workflows/*.ts are auto-loaded via tsx as trusted code, so running it inside an untrusted client repo is arbitrary code execution; plus detached background improvement worker and optional second coding agent (Pi) with passthrough env, a poor fit for bypass/auto permission mode.
Multi-call design (routing + per-hunk calls, up to 150 hunks) makes runs slow relative to Jev's 70-500 ms claim per call and the hunk-level workflows only run on demand, not per edit.
No MCP means no structured tool schema for Claude; Claude must parse Bash text or --json output.

gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.whatItDoes: Single-file (293 lines) Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, mcp==1.26.0) plus a Codex/Pi-style Agent Skill. It wraps TypeSafe's direct System One endpoint with six code-oriented tools. Each tool packs the caller-supplied code, diff, log or report into 'state' and sends a fixed set of Noul/Choice/Score questions to Jev. Nothing is read from disk by the server, so Claude has to paste the content into the tool call. Written for Codex and Pi. The README never mentions Claude Code.

gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.runtime: Python >=3.10, uv, stdio. The only dependency is mcp==1.26.0 (a uv.lock is included, 184 KB). Installed by git clone plus 'uv sync --locked' into a .venv. There is no PyPI package, no release and no npx or uvx one-liner.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.install: git clone https://github.com/MorenoLand/Moreno.Jev.git && cd Moreno.Jev && uv sync --locked. Then register a stdio server pointing at .venv/bin/python -u -m jev_mcp with cwd set to the clone. For Claude Code that means an entry in .mcp.json or 'claude mcp add' with the key forwarded through env. The README documents only Codex TOML and Pi's pi-mcp-adapter. Copy .agents/skills/jev-review to ~/.claude/skills/ if you want the skill. Nothing was installed or run during this audit.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.tests: None. There is no tests directory and no CI config in the repo (only 8 files: README, LICENSE, pyproject, uv.lock, jev_mcp.py, SKILL.md, .gitignore, .gitattributes).
security: API key comes from the process environment (jev_mcp.py:77), not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The README says to forward it via env_vars/inheritEnv rather than writing it to config.
Bearer key is sent only to the hard-coded host api.typesafe.ai over https. Redirects are blocked (_NoRedirectHandler, lines 21-23), so the key cannot leak through a redirect.
Hard caps: request 512 KB (lines 14, 85-89), response 1 MB (line 95), 45 s timeout (line 16). Error messages are scrubbed to a status code only.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, no logging of bodies. Code inspection confirms the README's 'does not read repository files or persist prompts' claim.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Output is a dict of numeric probabilities and enums, not free text. Real risk is upstream: Claude pastes content into the args, so whatever Claude submits (including secrets that appear in code or logs) goes to a third party. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover MCP tool args.

Supply chain is small: one PyPI dependency (mcp==1.26.0, pinned and locked) and a single 293-line file that is easy to audit. The repo is 3 days old with one author, so there are no external reviews and the maintainer could push changes. Pin a commit SHA if used.
No curl|sh, no postinstall scripts.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.dataEgress: Everything Claude passes as tool args goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter): full code snippets, diffs, test or build logs, bug reports, hypotheses, context strings, and language/command strings, up to 512 KB per call, plus the Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Nothing is sent automatically, since the server reads no files. The volume is whatever the model chooses to paste. For client projects this means client source code leaves the machine to a beta third-party API. If retargeted to OpenRouter, it would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.failureMode: Fail-soft, not a hard block. There is no hook or proxy in the path. On timeout (45 s), HTTP error, invalid JSON or a missing key, the tool raises RuntimeError and MCP returns an isError result. Claude sees a short message and carries on. There is no retry, no circuit breaker and no fallback. The 45 s ceiling is far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms, so an outage would stall a single tool call for up to 45 s. The server never blocks edits or commands.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Estimated ~800-1,000 tokens always loaded (about 3.5k chars of names, docstrings and JSON schemas: 5 tools with 2-5 string params each, and jev_evaluate with free-form Any/dict). Some of this could sit behind deferred tool loading. No server-level 'instructions'. The skill adds ~30 tokens of frontmatter only if installed; its ~1.4k-char body loads only when triggered. No hooks, so no text is injected per turn. Each call also costs its argument tokens (the code or diff Claude must re-emit into the tool call, which can be thousands of output tokens) and a small dict result (~100-200 tokens).
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.latencyImpact: Model-visible tool call: ~1 model round trip (Opus writes the args, which for a diff can take several seconds because output tokens are pasted) plus Jev's claimed 70-500 ms plus TLS and local Python startup (already running as a stdio process). Realistic 3-15 s per invocation, dominated by Claude re-emitting the code, not by Jev. Zero latency on turns where it is not called; no per-tool-call overhead like a hook would add.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The bundled skill is explicitly opt-in ('when the user asks for Jev review'; 'only when the user requests Jev or invokes this skill'), and the README's suggested AGENTS.md text is likewise 'when I ask for Jev review'. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic trigger. To get automatic use you would have to write your own CLAUDE.md or skill-description rules (for example 'after each diff call jev_review_diff') and change the skill wording. Even then it is only as reliable as Claude's compliance, and nothing in the repo gives Claude Code a reason to reach for it.
pros: Tiny, fully readable: one 293-line file, one pinned dependency, MIT license. A full audit takes minutes and forking it for OpenRouter is a ~4-line change.
Good security hygiene for a POC: key from env (not argv), redirects refused, 512 KB/1 MB/45 s limits, sanitized errors, no file reads, no telemetry.

Question design fits Jev's primitives properly. Categories are enums, severity uses Score scales, and there are separate 'evidence_sufficient' and 'needs_human_review' Noul checks. Good templates for hooks or a custom MCP: review_diff, check_hypothesis, and test-output classification map to real daily coding moments.
Includes jev_evaluate as a generic escape hatch for custom Choice/Score/Noul questions.
Non-blocking failure mode: errors are just tool errors, and it cannot break Claude Code sessions.
Low steady-state context cost (~1k tokens for 6 tools) and no per-turn hook injection.
cons: Not automatic: the skill and README explicitly gate use on the user asking for Jev, which contradicts the user's main requirement. Nothing pushes Claude Code to call it, and it has no hooks.
No OpenRouter support. Hard-coded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It needs a fork or patch before it matches the user's OpenRouter-hosted setup, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified.
Claude Code is not a target: only Codex and Pi are documented. It should work as a generic stdio server, but nothing has been tested there.
Very immature: repo created 2026-09-27 (3 days old), 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no tests, no CI, no real-world usage. The 45 s timeout is far above the claimed Jev latency.

The model must paste code or diffs into args. This costs Opus output tokens and adds seconds of latency per call, and leaks whatever it pastes (client code, secrets in logs) to a third party. The secret-guard hook does not inspect MCP args.

Heavy on the review-quality question: Jev returns only probabilities with no reasoning, and Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim is unverified. A 'has_concrete_bug' probability from a small model on a pasted diff is a weak signal versus Opus's own review. Duplicates part of the existing /code-review and gitnexus detect_changes.
Install is a manual git clone plus uv sync into a .venv (no uvx or PyPI package). This makes updates and reproducibility manual, and the path is machine-specific.
gh-morenoland-moreno-jev.verdict: A clean, safe, well-written 3-day-old proof of concept, but it is opt-in by design, TypeSafe-direct only, and untested with Claude Code, so it fails the 'automatic, OpenRouter' requirement as shipped. Its best use is as reference code for the question templates and the hardened request client (no redirects, size caps, env-only key) in a custom OpenRouter-based hook or MCP. As a drop-in install it scores low.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, no code change: JEV_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, and put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY or the key file (misleading name; no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support). No shell injection. Git calls use execFileSync with an args array and `-C cwd` (src/adapters/git.ts, repository-files.ts), and there is no shell.

Dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1, allows GET/HEAD only, serves a fixed allowlist of 3 assets, and sends CSP and nosniff headers. The report JSON is served unauthenticated on loopback, and any local process or browser tab could read it.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted diff and source text is passed as `state` to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities and choices, no free text, so the injection blast radius is limited to skewed scores. The code does not act on model output beyond ranking.
package-lock is committed. The only runtime dependency is the official SDK, which has no postinstall.
No telemetry in the repo. The SDK's logging is not verified beyond a log-level setting.
Repo is 5 commits from one author over one day, so there is no review history or security policy.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.dataEgress: Full file contents (codebase mode, chunked into regions via sourceRegions/SCREEN_REGION_LINES) and full unified diffs with 3 lines of context (changes mode) of every JS/TS file in scope, plus changed test files. This is sent to the configured base URL, api.typesafe.ai by default or OpenRouter if overridden, on every run. Untracked files are included. Only .js/.ts/.jsx/.tsx/.mjs/.cjs files are sent. .env is not sent unless the file is git-tracked and matches SOURCE_FILE, and it does not, but nothing scans for secrets embedded in source. A whole-codebase scan sends the entire source tree, which is a real client-confidentiality issue. Nothing else leaves the machine.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.failureMode: Not connected to Claude Code at all, so nothing to fail-open or closed there. Standalone, it is fail-closed per run. A Jev error during screening throws `Screening <file> failed` (workflow.ts) and aborts the whole review. The save command exits 1 and leaves the previous report unchanged. Profile and locate calls have no try/catch either. The SDK gives 10s per attempt with 2 retries and backoff. Concurrency is 3 and follow-ups are capped at 8. A codebase scan makes about 1 call per source region, plus 5 profiles and up to 8 follow-ups, so it takes minutes on a big repo.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.latencyImpact: None on Claude Code, since it is not wired in. If invoked manually via Bash, a diff review costs roughly N_files screen calls at concurrency 3, then up to 5 profile calls and 8 locate calls. That is about 3 sequential stages, so a few seconds for small diffs and minutes for a codebase scan. It is far too slow for a per-tool-call hook.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.contextCost: Zero as shipped: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no skill. If run through Bash, the JSON report is large (per-file matrix plus findings) and would need to be truncated or summarised.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. Claude Code cannot discover or call it automatically. It could only run if you wrote your own hook or skill that shells out to `npm run review:changes`.
pros: Best available worked example of Jev's real intended pattern: code owns the workflow, and Jev answers many small typed Noul/Choice/Score questions with calibrated probabilities. It can be copied into a Claude Code hook or skill design.

Its code shows concrete prompt/criteria design for a diff-risk gate: per-dimension Noul questions with true/false definitions and examples, thresholds (SCREEN_THRESHOLD 0.7, ROUTE_SEVERITY 1.5, BLOCKING_SEVERITY 2, MIN_LOCATION_CONFIDENCE 0.55), and a Choice over hunk ids with a noMatch fallback (src/domain/config.ts, src/review/judgments.ts).

The SDK it uses reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and posts to /v1/systemone (sdk index.mjs:513-554). That matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone path, so pointing it at OpenRouter with an OpenRouter key looks env-only.
Safe code hygiene: execFileSync with arg arrays, no shell, loopback-only dashboard with a fixed asset allowlist, MIT license, one small dependency, no postinstall.
643 stars and 42 forks in 2 weeks, so it is a visible reference from an ecosystem author (Dev Agrawal).
cons: Not an integration at all. It has no MCP server, hook, skill, plugin.json or .mcp.json, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
Overlaps and duplicates what Opus 5.5 already does with /code-review. Jev returns only probabilities, so there is no explanation or fix, and the README admits findings are review prompts, not proof.
JS/TS only (SOURCE_FILE regex /\.(?:[cm]?[jt]sx?)$/). It ignores Python and other languages, which is a poor match for a user on Node and Python projects.

Sends full diffs and whole-source contents of the repo to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe). That is a client-confidentiality risk for the user's client projects, and there is no redaction or allowlist.
Fail-closed batch design: any single Jev failure aborts the run. Sequential stages with a 10s timeout and 2 retries make it slow for interactive use.

Very immature: 5 commits by 1 author on one day (2026-09-16/17), no tests, no CI, no releases, and private:true, so it is not installable as a package. Star count reflects hype around Jev's launch, not maturity.
Requires a Node 24 clone plus npm install, and a separate .env file for the key. It needs an SDK env override to reach OpenRouter, which is undocumented and untested here.
The dashboard is a manual side workflow outside Claude Code's terminal loop, and adds nothing for headless or agent use.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-review.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration: it is a standalone demo review CLI and dashboard, so it cannot give the user automatic Jev use. Treat it as a design reference for building a Jev-backed PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook or skill (thresholded Noul/Choice gates, with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone), not as something to install.

gh-altryne-jevify.name: altryne/jevify
gh-altryne-jevify.whatItDoes: Community (ThursdAI, Alex Volkov) agent skill, not an official TypeSafe product. SKILL.md tells the agent to use Jev as "System One" during its own work: sift large documents or tool outputs, select evidence from many candidates, check many items against criteria, and rank or score them. It says to do this even if the user never mentions Jev. It ships stdlib-only Python helpers (scan.py ranks text/JSONL, run_cases.py runs request packs, jev_client.py is a concurrent client with cache and retries) plus about 160KB of reference docs on question design and the Choice/Noul/Score primitives. It also covers "Jevify this" product discovery. It is prompt-level: it makes no API calls until the agent chooses to run the scripts.

security: No install script, no postinstall, no curl|sh. Install is 'npx skills add altryne/jevify' (vercel-labs skills CLI, third-party but standard). Manual copy into ~/.claude/skills also works.
Python helpers use only stdlib (http.client to a fixed HTTPS host); no shell execution or subprocess found by grep in scripts/.
API key goes in an Authorization header via env var or a .env file (jev_client.py:47-61, 134). It is never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.

find_key() reads NAME=value lines from ./.env in the cwd (default env_files=('.env',)), a project file that may hold many secrets. It only extracts the named key, but the user's secret-leak guard hook on Read/Bash may interfere or be triggered.
Error bodies are deliberately omitted so submitted data is not echoed (jev_client.py:163-164). Timeout is 30s per attempt.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill tells the agent to run Jev over untrusted documents and tool outputs. Jev only returns typed probabilities, so it is not an instruction channel, but answers used for filtering can be gamed by adversarial text (a missed-evidence risk).

SKILL.md tells the agent to 'reuse task or session authorization for external inference, data, and spending'. In practice, on client projects with bypass or auto permission mode, the agent may ship client code or docs to OpenRouter without asking. It does say to keep credentials and unrelated private data out of request state.
No telemetry in the repo. OpenRouter itself logs per its data policy; the OpenRouter response includes provider and usage.cost.
gh-altryne-jevify.dataEgress: Nothing leaves at install or load time. On a live run, the JSON body {model, state, questions} goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set). The state is whatever text the agent chooses: chunks of documents, tool outputs, log excerpts, candidate code or diffs, chunked in about 4000-char pieces by scan.py with excerpts. The OpenRouter key goes in the Authorization header. There is no automatic capture of prompts or tool calls, and only what the agent explicitly feeds the scripts is sent. The optional --cache-dir cache writes responses locally, keyed by request hash.
gh-altryne-jevify.failureMode: Fail-soft and at the agent's discretion, because there is no hook in the path. jev_client.py defaults to a 30s timeout per attempt, 3 retries with jittered backoff (0.25*2^n s up to 8s) on network errors, and 429/529 with Retry-After up to 30s. Non-retryable HTTP errors return {error, status}. Malformed or partial answers are flagged as 'unjudged', never treated as negative. SKILL.md says to report partial coverage and use the task fallback. A missing key means the agent explains setup once and continues locally. Worst case, one call could stall roughly 30s x 4 attempts, but only inside a script the agent chose to run. Claude Code itself never blocks on Jev.
gh-altryne-jevify.latencyImpact: None on ordinary turns, since it is not in the request path. When triggered, the agent spends extra turns to inspect the input, write or run a script, and read the shortlist (several tool calls). The Jev call itself is claimed to be about 100ms per request, with a 30s per-attempt timeout as the worst case. Net effect is usually faster than reading large inputs in-context, but it adds orchestration overhead on small inputs.
gh-altryne-jevify.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions. There are no hooks and no injected text. Always-on cost is only the skill listing entry: name plus a description of about 620 chars, roughly 150 tokens. When triggered, SKILL.md loads at about 10.8KB, roughly 2.7k tokens. References load on demand (the largest are field-notes at about 14KB and question-design at about 14KB, each around 3.5k tokens). A full task typically costs 3-8k tokens of skill text.
gh-altryne-jevify.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion), the closest thing to the requested 'Claude decides itself' behavior. The description explicitly says 'Trigger when sifting large documents or tool outputs ... even if the user never mentions Jev'. But README:40 states 'installation does not intercept tool outputs automatically', and SKILL.md concedes 'activation depends on the host agent'. Opus 5.5 may often prefer grep/GitNexus/its own reading. Nothing is deterministic.
pros: It is the only found candidate whose skill description is explicitly written to auto-trigger without the user naming Jev, which matches the 'do not make me prompt' requirement.

OpenRouter is natively supported in code (jev_client.py:36-39, 83-97, 125-126), with the correct model mapping to typesafe/jev-1.13 and tests for key selection. The fallback path is already there: set only OPENROUTER_API_KEY and it works.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, no hooks, about 150 tokens always-on. It coexists with the existing gitnexus/playwright/caveman hooks without conflict.
Stdlib-only Python 3 (works with the user's Python 3.13), no npm or pip dependencies, no installers, no telemetry, key never in argv, error bodies deliberately withheld.
Good failure semantics: failures are 'unjudged', not negatives, with retry/backoff/pacing and an atomic cache. Includes unit tests for the client and scanner.

Encodes useful usage doctrine (bulk semantic filtering of logs, tool output, candidate lists; per-item Noul/Score; audit low-ranked samples) that fits large-log and large-search triage in Claude Code.
MIT license, small readable codebase of about 1.4k lines, easy to fork and patch.
cons: It is not a real integration. Claude uses Jev only if it decides to shell out to scan.py. There is no hook or transparent routing, and the README admits it does not intercept tool outputs. Auto-trigger reliability is unproven; evals/evals.json exists but no results are published.
Opus 5.5 already handles grep, GitNexus and file reads well. The bulk-semantic-filter niche (big logs, hundreds of docs) is uncommon in typical daily coding, so real hit rate is likely low.

The skill's prose is aggressive and salesy: 'Default to Jev', 'Assume it is faster and cheaper', and instructions to skip cost comparison. It nudges the agent to use an unvalidated beta model (Theo claims it's a cheap flash-router) for judgments whose errors can silently drop relevant evidence.

Privacy and consent risk on client projects: 'reuse task or session authorization for external inference, data'. In bypass or auto mode the agent may send client code or documents to OpenRouter without an explicit prompt. Needs a deny rule or a CLAUDE.md boundary.

Provider selection is implicit. TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins over OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and a leftover key routes to TypeSafe directly. There is also no way to select the Decisions API, ~typesafe/jev-latest or the Jev Router model without patching. The model is pinned to jev-1.13.0.
The helpers read ./.env in the cwd by default, which on client repos contains unrelated secrets. Safer to export the key in the shell environment. May also trip the user's secret-guard hook.

gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.name: chungsubeen0/jevmcp (jev-mcp)
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.whatItDoes: Local Python MCP server (stdio by default, optional Streamable HTTP) that exposes 7 tools where the frontier model hands over a structured "state" (failure output, diff summary, requirements, findings, candidates) and gets back Jev "noul" probabilities mapped to labels and a "user_decision" advisory. It only uses the Noul primitive (no Choice or Score). It adds validation, input truncation, a SQLite cache, local telemetry and secret redaction. It never edits code. Calls go to POST {base_url}/v1/systemone.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_mcp/providers/typesafe.py:104 builds url = base_url.rstrip('/') + '/v1/systemone' with Bearer auth (l.105-108). The payload is {state, model, questions:{id:{type:'noul',instructions,criteria?}}} (l.72-79, 171-175) and the parser reads answers[id].noul (l.137-157), which matches OpenRouter's documented System One schema (POST /api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, answers[..].noul, usage.input_tokens). Defaults: src/jev_mcp/config.py:62-66 (base_url https://api.typesafe.ai, model 'jev-latest'). Env only: config.py:220-226 (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_MODEL). Host allowlist typesafe.py:17-41 is only api.typesafe.ai unless TYPESAFE_ALLOWED_HOSTS is set (README Environment table). No mention of 'openrouter' anywhere in src (grep). Project YAML cannot set base_url or api_key (config.py:176-177).
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct plus a 'mock' provider (ProviderName = Literal['typesafe','mock'], config.py:15). No other gateways.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and no code change: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_ALLOWED_HOSTS=openrouter.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<the OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. The hostname allowlist accepts it and the schema is the same. Two caveats. (1) OpenRouter's docs list 'criteria' (true/false) as required on noul questions, but jev-mcp sends criteria for only 1 of about 23 questions (tools/triage_failure.py only). It may get HTTP 400, which surfaces as INVALID_PROVIDER_RESPONSE. If so, patching JudgmentQuestion or _questions_payload to add default criteria is a 3-line change. This was not tested, because running third-party code was forbidden. (2) The model alias 'jev-latest' is wrong for OpenRouter; use 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'.

interface.name: jev_triage_failure
interface.purpose: After a test/build/lint failure, returns 6 signals (related_to_current_change, likely_localized, likely_preexisting, requirement_related, same_as_previous_failure, needs_deeper_reasoning) plus classification and user_decision. The caller must pass task goal, failure command/exit_code/output, and changed_files/diff_summary.

interface.name: jev_compare_attempts
interface.purpose: Compares two failed attempts and returns PROGRESSING/UNCERTAIN/LIKELY_STUCK with a CONTINUE/REASSESS/ESCALATE signal (stuck detection).

interface.name: jev_check_completion
interface.purpose: Per-requirement appears_satisfied/evidence_present/possible_gap, giving APPEARS_COMPLETE/REVIEW_REQUIRED/INCOMPLETE.

interface.name: jev_rank_context
interface.purpose: Ranks up to 25 candidate files or snippets into HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW for what to inspect next.

interface.name: jev_classify_findings
interface.purpose: Normalizes reviewer/linter/test findings (likely_valid, security_relevant, requires_code_change and so on).

interface.name: jev_assess_risk
interface.purpose: Says whether a change (auth, payment, schema, public API) warrants a deeper frontier review.

interface.name: jev_judge
interface.purpose: Generic Noul wrapper: caller supplies arbitrary state plus {id, question} list. Rejects generative or planning questions.

interface.name: CLI: jev-mcp / jev-mcp-doctor (--ping) / jev-mcp-benchmark / jev-mcp-export
interface.purpose: Server entrypoint, offline install check, mock benchmark, telemetry and outcome export. Also /health on the HTTP transport.

gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or openrouter.ai after re-pointing), and via OpenRouter on to TypeSafe: the normalized `state` JSON, which is whatever Claude puts in the tool arguments. Depending on the tool this is: the task goal and requirement text; command, exit code and up to ~50k chars of failure output; diff_summary (up to ~25k chars); changed file paths; previous failure summary; findings; candidate file snippets (up to 8k chars each, 25 candidates); and free-form state in jev_judge. The hard cap is max_state_chars = 100,000 (config.py:89). Also sent: the question instructions, the model id and the Bearer key. The MCP has no file-read or shell access, so it only sends what Claude chooses to put in. There is no secret scrubbing of state before sending; redaction applies to logs, errors and telemetry only. Nothing goes to the maintainer, and there is no remote telemetry. Locally it writes hashed telemetry and a cache. For client projects, this means client code excerpts and test output go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (a beta service with 0 promise of data-handling terms verified here).
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors come back as structured JSON (PROVIDER_TIMEOUT, PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE, RATE_LIMITED, INVALID_PROVIDER_RESPONSE, INTERNAL_ERROR with a retryable flag) instead of raising, and Claude continues (tools/_common.py:safe_run; README says "No fabricated probabilities"). Startup never contacts TypeSafe. Defaults: timeout 30 s (bounds 1-120), max_retries 1 for 408/425/429/5xx/529 and timeouts with a 0.2 s sleep (typesafe.py:16, 109-135). Worst case on a hung provider is roughly 60 s of blocked tool call, and 401/403 fails immediately with a "check TYPESAFE_API_KEY" message. The timeout is far above the claimed 70-500 ms, so lowering it to about 3-5 s is advisable. Missing key gives an immediate PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE.
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.latencyImpact: Per call: claimed Jev 70-500 ms plus one HTTPS request, plus about 200 ms Python overhead. This is small next to the real cost, which is that Claude must generate the whole state (failure output, diff summary, requirements) as tool-call output tokens. That can be thousands of Opus output tokens per call, and the seconds this takes probably outweigh Jev's latency. The SQLite cache only helps for identical repeats. The server spawns lazily at session start (Python startup roughly 0.3-1 s).
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.contextCost: 7 tools (jev_triage_failure, jev_compare_attempts, jev_check_completion, jev_rank_context, jev_classify_findings, jev_assess_risk, jev_judge). Descriptions total about 2.1k chars (250-390 each; ~530 tokens). Pydantic-generated input schemas with nested models ($defs for TaskInput, FailureEvent, Attempt, Finding, ContextCandidate, ClientMeta and others; models.py is 3.2k chars of source) add an estimated 8-11k chars, so the total is roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens of tool definitions (estimated statically, not measured). No MCP server `instructions` (FastMCP("jev-mcp") is created without them, server.py:50). No hook-injected text, since there are no hooks. The suggested CLAUDE.example.md adds about 1.7k chars (~430 tokens) each session. With deferred MCP tool loading, the definitions only cost a name-list line until fetched. Each tool result adds JSON with meta, signals and user_decision (probably a few hundred tokens).
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, made "automatic" only by tool descriptions ("Use before broad reasoning when scope is unclear") plus a CLAUDE.md block the user must paste in. There is no hook, no skill, no proxy. Claude Code will not reliably call it after every failing test, since the descriptions are hedged ("Use selectively", "Do not call for trivial decisions"). The README's recommended shadow mode adds an "advisory: treat as telemetry" line to results, so the outputs are explicitly non-binding. A deterministic PostToolUse hook could not call it without writing new code. It also cannot cover Jev's typical uses (routing, gating hooks) since only Noul-on-coding-artifacts is implemented.
pros: Same wire schema as OpenRouter System One (state + questions{type:noul,instructions}, answers[id].noul): jev-mcp typesafe.py:72-79,137-157 vs OpenRouter docs. OpenRouter use needs only 4 env vars (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_ALLOWED_HOSTS=openrouter.ai, key, model typesafe/jev-1.13), no code changes in the likely case.

Best-engineered Jev integration seen so far for coding: injection-aware (project YAML cannot redirect the key, host allowlist, no redirects), fail-open structured errors, bounded timeouts/retries, input truncation with warnings, local hashed-only telemetry, 0600 files.
Read-only by design: no shell, file or write tools, so a compromised Jev response cannot cause actions; responses can't say APPROVED/SAFE_TO_MERGE.

Real test discipline for an early repo: about 33 test files, contract/schema snapshots, adversarial and secret-leak tests, golden corpus, CI with nightly live tests, plus a client-specific Claude Code config and profile (interactive).
MIT licence, stdio by default (no open port), lazy startup with no network on init, doctor script for offline checks, Python/uv-friendly.
Use cases are on point for Claude Code: failure triage, stuck detection across attempts, requirement coverage, risk flagging.
cons: Immature and single-author: 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, not on PyPI, created 2026-09-17 and last pushed 2026-09-18 (about 12 days stale on 2026-09-30). Commits are Cursor-co-authored. No published eval results: eval-results/ has only a README and GATES.md states accuracy numbers are unset, so claimed usefulness and savings are unverified.

Not automatic. Invocation depends on Claude's discretion plus a pasted CLAUDE.md block, and the docs themselves say to call Jev 'less often' in Claude Code. There is no hook to trigger it deterministically after a failing test.

Claude has to serialise the state into tool arguments. Writing failure output and diff summaries as Opus output tokens can cost more than the ~$0.042/M-input Jev call saves, and it adds seconds per call. The design is aimed at cutting Opus reasoning, but the plumbing may erase that.

It maps every question onto Noul via generic prose instructions. Only 1 of about 23 questions defines criteria (true/false), while OpenRouter's docs list criteria as required on noul questions, so calls may 400 on OpenRouter until patched. This is untested.

Default model alias 'jev-latest' and default host api.typesafe.ai are TypeSafe-specific. OpenRouter needs TYPESAFE_* env var names to be reused for an OpenRouter key (confusing but harmless), and a mismatch of model id will produce HTTP 4xx.

Heavy tool surface for uncertain value: 7 tools with nested schemas cost roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens of context, and with the CLAUDE.md block about 3-4k. Rejects planning/architecture/debugging questions by design, so it does not help the most valuable Opus work.

Sends failure output, diffs and file snippets (up to 100k chars per call) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no pre-send secret scrubbing (redaction covers logs/errors only). Sensitive for client projects, and it conflicts in spirit with the user's secret-leak guard hook.

Timeout default 30 s with one retry means a stalled provider can block a tool call for up to about 60 s. Jev is beta and Theo-style skepticism (router-like behaviour) is unresolved, and the outputs are probabilities that the README itself says are not gates.
Only Noul is used, with no Choice or Score. It cannot express routing or gating decisions (for example 'which of N options'), which is Jev's other main strength.
gh-chungsubeen0-jevmcp.verdict: The most careful and best-tested Jev MCP for coding agents, and repointing it to OpenRouter is a config-only change (plus possibly default criteria). However, it is a 1-day-old single-author PoC with no published accuracy data, invocation is model-discretion rather than automatic, and the token cost of Claude serialising state into tool calls may cancel any savings. Worth trying as an opt-in, shadow-mode experiment pinned to a reviewed commit, not as the primary automatic integration.

gh-uehaj-sys1grep.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency single-file Node CLI (sys1grep.mjs, ~170 KB, plus git-sys1grep) that does "grep by meaning": each line (30 per request, 8 requests parallel) is sent to the Jev System One endpoint as a Noul question ("does this line match the meaning X?"), and the returned P(yes) is thresholded. Meanings combine with AND/OR/NOT (-e/-a/-v), can be mixed with local regex prefilters, -Q questions, -g for git log, --dedup, --rank, --unit=function and optional --summarize (pipes the matching lines into a local `claude -p --model haiku` or other LLM CLI). It is not an MCP server or hook. The Claude Code piece is a separate model-invoked skill (plugins/uehaj/skills/sys1grep/SKILL.md in uehaj/uehaj-marketplace, plugin "uehaj") that tells Claude to run `npx -y @uehaj/sys1grep@0.5.0-next.1 ...` instead of Grep/full-file reads for meaning-type questions.

security: API key: read from env SYS1GREP_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.config/sys1grep/.env only; deliberately never ./.env (sys1grep.mjs:21-24) so an untrusted checkout cannot redirect the key. Sent as Bearer to SYS1GREP_URL whatever it is; warns if key goes over plain http off localhost (:559-560).
Key can also be given via --sys1-api-key on argv (visible in ps and shell history); README warns and recommends the .env file. Skill does not use that flag.

Prompt injection: matched lines are untrusted text. Jev only returns probabilities, so injection can at worst skew scores. --summarize runs claude -p with --tools '' --setting-sources '' --strict-mcp-config --safe-mode (:722) so a line can at worst mislead the summary. The Claude-facing risk is the skill output being trusted.
Shell execution: execFileSync for git only (array args, --end-of-options), spawn of the summarizer CLI with array args; no shell string building seen. Reads only files/stdin named by the user.

Supply chain: the skill runs `npx -y @uehaj/sys1grep@0.5.0-next.1`, i.e. downloads and executes a 11-day-old single-maintainer npm prerelease at first use; npm dist-tag latest is 0.5.0-next.0 (a prerelease). Zero deps limits transitive risk, but a compromised publish would run with the user's env (including OPENROUTER key if exported). Pinning a vetted version or cloning and reading the single file is better.

-r mode skips .env*, credential files, keys, .ssh/.aws/.gnupg/.kube/.docker, binaries, lockfiles (:1091, README:165), but explicitly named files are always searched and stdin pipes (cmd 2>&1 | sys1grep) are unfiltered.
No telemetry or analytics found in source (grep for telemetry/analytics empty); only outbound calls are Jev endpoint and the optional summarizer.
No postinstall script in package.json; no curl|sh installer. Skill text itself tells Claude to warn before sending secret-like content (SKILL.md line 6).

Interplay with the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard: it triggers on commands that name .env plus a reader, so setting the key by writing ~/.config/sys1grep/.env must be done by the user outside Claude Code.
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.dataEgress: To SYS1GREP_URL (OpenRouter in this setup): the verbatim text of every searched unit (line by default, chunks of 30 lines per request, each unit truncated to 2000 chars, -M) as `state`, plus the meaning strings as `questions`, plus the model id and the bearer key. With -r over a tree this can be entire source directories (regex prefilter terms limit it to lines that pass the local regex; a term without a regex sends everything; --max-cost default $1 prompts on a terminal or exits 2 without one). git log searches (-g) send commit messages/diffs text units. With --summarize the matching lines (up to 200 KB) additionally go to the summarizer: default `claude -p` haiku (Anthropic, via the user's own Claude login), or an llm/pi CLI or any OpenAI-compatible URL. Nothing is sent to the author. OpenRouter/TypeSafe retention of code is a client-project confidentiality question (client code is uploaded to a third party beyond Anthropic).
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.failureMode: Fail-closed per command, not per session: 60 s fetch timeout per request; retries up to 6 times with exponential backoff (500 ms * 2^n, roughly 31 s of sleeping in total) on 429/529/5xx and connection errors/timeouts; then dies with one line and exit code 2 ('sys1grep: host: error'). A malformed answer is treated as an error, not as 0 (:1289-1291). Claude sees a failed Bash call and would fall back to Grep by itself (nothing is blocking), so Jev being down does not stop Claude Code work, but a slow endpoint can burn up to several minutes inside one Bash call (Bash tool backgrounds at 120 s; the skill says to set timeout 300000). Exit 1 = no match, 2 = error. Author's own issue #132 reports --summarize taking over 120 s when run inside a nested claude -p session, after which Claude fell back to reading the whole file.
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero hooks, no server instructions. The only always-on cost is the skill's frontmatter description in the skills listing: about 750 chars of dense Japanese (~350-500 tokens; CJK tokenizes worse than chars/4) per session. When invoked, the SKILL.md body (6.9 KB, ~2.5-3k tokens, in Japanese) loads once. No text injected by hooks. The heavier hidden cost is turns, not tokens: author measured that every extra tool call re-reads ~40k cached tokens, so one sys1grep run can cost more than it saves (issue #132).
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). The skill is meant to be model-invoked (description says to use it before Grep or whole-file reads for meaning questions), but the author's own measurement (issue #132 comment, SWE-bench Verified, 30 issues, sonnet) shows the model-invoked skill fired 0/30 (0/67 over two wordings) because tasks name identifiers and Claude uses Grep; only a forced prompt or a PreToolUse hook that denies the first Grep got 25-29/30 usage, at higher cost (+$0.035-0.052 median Claude cost, +95-133k context tokens median) and no recall gain. No hook is shipped; it is not deterministic and not transparent.
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.latencyImpact: Claimed: 210 lines in under a second, --summarize ~10 s from a shell. Per invocation: 1 extra Bash tool call (an extra Claude turn, ~40k cached tokens re-read per turn per author) plus npx cold start on first use plus Jev round trips (30 lines/request, 8 parallel; 70-500 ms each per brief). Large -r scans scale linearly and can hit the 120 s Bash background threshold; --summarize adds a nested claude -p haiku call (10 s to over 120 s reported). Worst case retry stalls of ~30 s+ when the endpoint is 429/5xx.
pros: Genuine, working OpenRouter path today: SYS1GREP_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with an sk-or key; three env vars, no patching (README.md:273, sys1grep.mjs:555-558).

Only listed candidate with real measurements: author benchmarked on SWE-bench and on git log (33k tokens/$0.070 for whole log vs 1.3k tokens/$0.005 via sys1grep -g -Q) and publishes negative results honestly.

Hardened for a coding-agent context: never reads ./.env (untrusted checkout), skips secrets/lockfiles/generated files with -r, --max-cost ($1) and --max-filesize guards, summarizer runs with tools, MCP and project settings disabled.
Zero dependencies, single readable file, MIT, no telemetry, no postinstall; easy to audit and to vendor into ~/.local/bin instead of using npx.
Good fit for a real Jev strength: fuzzy, multilingual, negation-aware filtering of large logs/tickets/git history where Grep terms cannot be chosen.
Zero context tax beyond one skill description (~400 tokens); no MCP tool schemas and no hook injection, so it does not conflict with GitNexus/secret-guard/caveman hooks.
Active: 210 commits in 11 days, CI on 3 Node versions, gitleaks in CI, fake-Jev offline tests so behavior is reproducible without a key.
cons: Not a general Jev integration: it exposes only the Noul primitive through /v1/systemone as a grep. No Choice/Score, no routing or decision-gate use for Claude Code (permission decisions, model routing, commit classification).

Fails the user's core requirement (automatic use): the author's own data says the model-invoked skill fired 0/67 times because Claude prefers Grep when identifiers are known, and the forced/hook arms cost more and did not improve recall. Fully deterministic triggering would need a custom PreToolUse hook, which conflicts with the existing GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks.

Positive value case for daily coding is narrow: most code search has identifiers, where Grep and GitNexus are free, exact and faster; each sys1grep call adds a Claude turn (~40k cached tokens) and paid Jev tokens.

Uploads searched source lines to OpenRouter/TypeSafe (and matches to Anthropic via --summarize) - real confidentiality concern for client projects; stdin pipes and explicitly named files bypass the secret skip list.

Skill executes an 11-day-old single-maintainer npm prerelease through `npx -y @uehaj/sys1grep@0.5.0-next.1`; npm 'latest' tag points at 0.5.0-next.0, version churn is rapid (0.1 to 0.5 in 11 days, a rename semgrep->sys1grep), API and flags unstable.

Default model id 'jev-latest' is probably not the OpenRouter slug (typesafe/jev-latest); README OpenRouter example omits SYS1GREP_MODEL and I could not verify it works unmodified; must set it explicitly.

SKILL.md is written in Japanese and README/skill have stale-fact history (issue #132); skill was in flux (open PR #1 rewrite on feat/sys1grep-skill branch), and the marketplace repo has 0 stars and bundles unrelated plugins (run-interactive, playground hooks needing CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS).

Nested-session slowness: --summarize can take >120 s inside Claude Code's Bash, after which Claude falls back to full-file reads (issue #132). Single-maintainer bus factor (2 GitHub accounts, one person) and beta Jev behind it; Theo's skepticism about the model applies to output quality.
gh-uehaj-sys1grep.verdict: A well-built, honest, OpenRouter-capable semantic grep, but it is a search utility with a description-triggered skill that its own author measured as never firing automatically, so it does not meet the "Claude uses Jev by itself" goal. Worth vendoring as an optional, manually-nudged tool for big logs/ticket dumps/git history (pin the version, set SYS1GREP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest, keep client code away), not as the core integration.

gh-huaaudio-jevsim.failureMode: Fail-closed per workflow but bounded: Jev connection error, non-2xx, or invalid response throws Stop (jev_connection_failed / jev_http_N / invalid_jev_response, src/jev.ts:43-46) and the run stops with partial progress reported; missing key gives credentials_missing but exact-identifier steps still work without any key. Whole run has a hard 60 s deadline via AbortSignal.timeout (src/runner.ts:81, workflow timeoutMs max 60000); no separate per-request Jev timeout or retry. Never automatically replays uncertain actions. It cannot affect other Claude Code operations since it only runs when its tool is called.
gh-huaaudio-jevsim.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Descriptions total ~900 chars plus zod-derived JSON schemas (workflowSchema with 5-way discriminated step union, 10 predicates, device fields) roughly 3-4k chars, so about 1.0-1.5k tokens of tool definitions. No server 'instructions' field (server created with only name/version, src/server.ts:86). No hooks and no injected text. Full agent guidance lives in docs, not in context.
gh-huaaudio-jevsim.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. Claude would call it only if a task involves driving an iOS Simulator or Android device, which the tool descriptions and README explicitly scope to.

When invoked, each Jev target decision is one HTTPS call (claimed 70-500 ms) plus repeated accessibility captures (a snapshot before and after every decision and a verification per step); their own benchmark: 10-tap iOS Settings tour median 35.7 s vs 117.3 s pure-agent (n=3, vendor-run, one scenario).
pros: Genuine, non-trivial use of Jev's Choice primitive with strict output validation (sum to 1, argmax, key set equals criteria, src/jev.ts:12-24), a 'none' abstain option, and a 0.90 probability gate: a good reference design for a Jev integration.
Careful safety design: no automatic replay of uncertain actions, redacted results, key not passed to child processes, redirect:'error', stable error codes, pinned dependencies and backend version.
Costs almost no context (3 tools, ~1-1.5k tokens, no hooks, no server instructions) and adds zero latency to normal coding turns.
MIT, no postinstall scripts, no telemetry, reasonable test suite with mock backends and CI.
Reported 3.3x speedup on an iOS Settings navigation task (vendor-run, 3 runs) if the user ever does mobile UI automation.
cons: Wrong domain for this user: it automates iOS Simulator / Android UI, not code editing, search, review, or general development; it would rarely or never be auto-invoked on a Linux dev box.
iOS backend (XcodeBuildMCP + Xcode simulator) requires macOS; README says Linux hosts and physical Android devices are unvalidated; Android needs a separately run Appium 3 + emulator.

No OpenRouter support: api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone is hardcoded (src/jev.ts:38) with no base URL override; using OpenRouter would require forking the package, and TypeSafe direct key is needed as shipped.
Not automatic: it is only a model-discretion MCP tool, and the agent must supply the plan; nothing decides 'when Jev adds value' across general coding.
Extremely immature: created 2026-09-21, 9 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, single 0.1.0 release, 9 days old; Node pinned to exactly >=24 <25; vendor-authored benchmarks (n=3) on a single simulator.
Sends app accessibility text and field values (potentially client data) to TypeSafe on every semantic selection; Appium may log full UI text locally.
Runtime fetches xcodebuildmcp via npx -y for iOS, adding a second unaudited supply-chain hop.
gh-huaaudio-jevsim.verdict: Well-engineered but off-target: a mobile-UI-automation MCP that uses Jev as a control selector, hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, useless for general Linux daily coding and not automatically invoked. Skip it for this setup; at most read src/jev.ts as a reference for validating Choice responses.

gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.name: koosbcom/jev-delegate
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) plus a SKILL.md, packaged for both Codex and Claude Code (.claude-plugin/plugin.json bundles skill + MCP). Exposes two tools. search_and_rank runs ripgrep inside the workspace root, dedups and filters hits, then asks Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter Decisions API) one Noul question per candidate ("does it satisfy the relevance criterion") and returns hits ranked by P(yes). classify_items assigns caller-supplied labels (2-20, plus reserved other/insufficient_context) to up to 200 English text items using Jev Choice questions. On any Jev failure it returns a bounded raw fallback. Narrow scope: not a router, not a general delegate. Despite the name it cannot delegate coding work.
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.install: git clone, npm ci, npm run check (builds dist/, dist is gitignored), then: claude mcp add --scope user jev_delegate -- node "$PWD/dist/server.js"; cp -R skills/jev-delegate ~/.claude/skills/ ; or claude --plugin-dir /path (plugin.json uses ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/dist/server.js, so build is still required). Needs rg on PATH and OPENROUTER_API_KEY exported in the shell that starts claude. No npm/PyPI release; package.json is private:true.
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.runtime: Node >=20 (user has 24), ripgrep required; deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0, zod 4.6.5; dev deps typescript 7.0.2, vitest 5.0.1
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.tests: 6 vitest files (search, classify, jev client, privacy, MCP stdio, opt-in live test). Offline tests only in npm run check. Live test skipped without key. No CI workflow (.github absent). README states: "The live API path has not yet been verified against a user's OpenRouter key, so API behavior may need adjustment."

Request body { model, state, questions } with question types noul and choice (jev.ts:95, 47-64 response schema: answers{noul|choice+confidence+probabilities}, usage{input_tokens,output_tokens,cost}). No TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no console.typesafe.ai, no /api/v1/systemone anywhere (grep empty). Base URL hard-coded, not configurable.
providerSupport.others: None. Hard-coded to OpenRouter only.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed (OpenRouter native). Adding TypeSafe direct would be trivial-to-moderate: one URL string plus key env, but response schema may differ.

interface.name: search_and_rank (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: rg over workspace with patterns[1-10], mode literal|regex, include/exclude globs, relevance_criterion (<=2000 chars), top_k<=25; Jev Noul per hit; returns status ok|fallback, ranked results with probability, raw_match_count, truncated, usage/cost. rg uses --max-count 20 per file, 1M max filesize, caps at 500 raw matches, 200 evaluated (src/search.ts:52-139).

interface.name: classify_items (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Jev Choice classification of up to 200 items (text<=8000 chars each, metadata) into 2-20 caller labels + other/insufficient_context; returns label, confidence, probabilities; items containing secret-like text get blocked_sensitive; uncertain if confidence <0.80 (src/server.ts:121-177, classify.ts).

interface.name: skills/jev-delegate/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Skill description trigger: use when search yields >20 candidates / ~4K tokens or bulk English classification; do not use for prose/code/sensitive/non-English; 'local only' request disables Jev.

interface.name: No hooks
interface.purpose: No hooks.json, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse, no proxy.

security: API key read from env only (config.ts:24), sent only as Bearer header to openrouter.ai; not in argv or process list (no CLI args carry it). .mcp.json/plugin.json pass no key; note plugin.json mcpServers has no env block so child inherits the parent env.

Privacy filters are heuristic: denied path parts (.git, .env*, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, credentials, secrets, id_rsa, id_ed25519) and extensions (.pem .key .p12 .pfx .jks .keystore) in src/privacy.ts:1-30; 7 secret regexes (sk-/AKIA/ghp_/xox/bearer/key=value>=12 chars/PEM) applied to snippets and to criterion/patterns. Misses many secret formats (e.g. Stripe sk_live_ with underscore prefix partially, JWTs, connection strings with passwords, .npmrc, service-account JSON, .netrc); path-denylist does not cover .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, kubeconfig, *.tfstate. README itself warns filters are heuristic. Client-project code snippets leave the machine.

rg spawned via child_process.spawn with args array (no shell) and patterns passed as -e values (search.ts:55,79), so no shell injection or flag injection; globs rejected if absolute or containing '..'; realpath + ensureInsideRoot check. rg respects .gitignore (default) so ignored files excluded. Symlink targets not followed by default.

Prompt-injection surface: repo text (snippets) goes into Jev state, but Jev returns only typed probabilities, so an injected snippet can at most bias a relevance score (could hide/promote a hit); output to Claude is JSON with snippets from the repo (normal untrusted-file-content risk, same as Grep).

Telemetry is local only: metadata JSONL (tool, latency, counts, model, cost, fallback_reason; no content) at ~/.codex/state/jev-delegate/usage.jsonl even under Claude Code (config.ts:38-40, dir mode 0700, file 0600); disable with JEV_DELEGATE_TELEMETRY=off. No network telemetry. Odd Codex path for a Claude Code user.

No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh; installer is manual git clone + npm ci (runs third-party dep tree incl. typescript 7.0.2 / vitest 5.0.1 pins; package-lock present). Uncommon version pins would need review before npm ci.
Default spend guards $0.01/call and $0.25/day (config.ts:32-33), enforced from local telemetry file (bypassable, and counts only when telemetry enabled: with telemetry off, daily guard is always 0).
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.dataEgress: Only to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and then to whichever upstream provider OpenRouter routes Jev to, typically TypeSafe). Sent per call: model id, the relevance_criterion, and for search up to 200 candidates of {relative file path, line number, snippet up to 500 chars}; for classify, up to 200 items of full text (<=8000 chars each) plus metadata, labels and instructions. Not sent: whole files, diffs, Claude's conversation, tool outputs from other tools. But it does send code lines and file paths from personal AND client repos to a third party (OpenRouter + TypeSafe), which matters for client NDAs; secret filtering is regex-based only. Sending is entirely model-initiated (the model decides to call the tool).
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Missing key -> JevError -> status "fallback" with raw ripgrep hits (top_k, unranked, deterministic pattern-count order) and fallback_reason. Per-request timeout 10 s (max 30 s), whole-tool deadline 30 s (config.ts:34-35), 2 attempts with 250 ms backoff on 429/5xx/timeout/transport (jev.ts:109-122). Schema mismatch -> fallback. Caveats: a slow Jev can stall a Claude turn up to ~30 s; rg failure or missing rg, secret-like patterns, or workspace-root failure throw a hard tool error rather than fallback; classify fallback returns items with no label so Claude has to classify itself. Unverified live contract means a wrong payload shape would silently degrade to fallback every time (fail-open masks breakage; only visible via fallback_reason).
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.latencyImpact: Per call: local rg (tens to hundreds ms) + 1 to 4 sequential-ish OpenRouter round trips (batch 50, concurrency 2, so 200 candidates = 4 batches, ~2 waves) at claimed 70-500 ms each plus OpenRouter overhead, so roughly 0.5-2 s typical; worst case 30 s deadline. Plus MCP tool-call overhead. Compared with the native Grep tool (instant), it is slower, and only pays off when the result set would be large.
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.contextCost: 2 tools. Model-visible definitions: search_and_rank description ~250 chars + 6-param schema with constraints (~700 chars), classify_items description ~215 chars + nested item/label schema (~900 chars), titles ~90 chars; total roughly 2.2k chars, about 550-700 tokens (outputSchema is not typically sent to the model). No MCP server-level instructions. Plus the skill: only name + description (~430 chars, ~110 tokens) always loaded; SKILL.md body (~1.7k chars, ~430 tokens) loaded when invoked. No hook-injected text. Total always-on about 700-800 tokens: small. Note the user already runs Playwright and GitNexus MCPs, so this is marginal.
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.autoInvocation: Model-discretion. The tool descriptions say "Use automatically when raw search would exceed 20 candidates or about 4K tokens" and the skill description triggers on search hits >20 candidates, but Claude must first think of the pattern set and relevance criterion BEFORE searching, and Claude Code's native Grep/Glob and the existing GitNexus hook are the default reflex; the model rarely knows the hit count in advance, so triggering will be inconsistent. No deterministic hook, no proxy, no way to intercept Grep results. Not truly automatic in the sense the user wants.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev via OpenRouter today: hard-coded openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-1.13 (jev.ts:135, config.ts:24-25), matching the user's provider choice; model overridable to ~typesafe/jev-latest.
Uses Jev's actual strengths correctly: typed Noul per candidate and Choice with confidence/probabilities, with no free text, and thresholds (0.5 drop, 0.8 include) exposed via env.
Explicitly ships a Claude Code plugin (.claude-plugin/plugin.json bundling skill + MCP) and Claude Code install docs; roots-based workspace detection works in Claude Code.

Well-designed safety: fail-open fallback to raw rg hits, per-call ($0.01) and daily ($0.25) spend caps, request and tool timeouts, retry with backoff, no shell (spawn args array), path traversal guard, secret-regex screening, metadata-only local telemetry, MIT license.

Tiny and readable (about 600 lines src, 52 KB total incl. tests): auditable in minutes; only 2 tools so about 700 tokens of context; no hooks that would interfere with the existing secret-guard/GitNexus hooks.
Good reference implementation of the Decisions API request/response shape (state + questions -> answers) that could be lifted into a custom hook or MCP.
cons: Very young and unproven: created 2026-09-24 (6 days old), 4 commits, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, one human author plus an AI-authored commit; README admits the live OpenRouter API path is not verified against a real key.

Solves a niche problem: re-ranking large ripgrep result sets and bulk English classification. Claude Code's Grep already caps output and the main model reads ~20 hits cheaply; the token saving is small and the value for daily coding (edit/debug/refactor/review) is low. Jev is not used for the decisions that matter in coding (which file to edit, does this diff break X, routing to model tiers).

Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool + skill trigger. The model must guess before searching that the result set will exceed 20 hits, and it will keep defaulting to native Grep/GitNexus. The user's requirement (no prompting, Claude Code uses it when needed) is not met deterministically.

Overlaps with and is weaker than existing tooling: GitNexus already provides graph/semantic context; ranking by a literal-pattern rg pass plus a per-line-snippet Noul (snippet only, max 500 chars, no surrounding code) has limited semantic power and relevance judged from one line is noisy; a wrong 'no' silently hides real matches (results below 0.5 dropped), a risk for refactors.

Sends code snippets and file paths from client repos to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; heuristic-only secret filter with gaps (.npmrc, .netrc, kubeconfig, JWTs, DB URLs); the model, not the user, decides when data leaves. Problematic for client NDA projects without a per-project opt-out beyond the prompt phrase 'local only'.

Fail-open masks breakage: because the Decisions API contract is unverified, a schema mismatch just returns 'fallback' raw hits every call, adding up to 10-30 s of wasted latency with no ranking benefit. Latency added per call ~0.5-2 s versus instant native Grep.

Codex-centric leftovers: telemetry path ~/.codex/state/..., .codex-plugin, openai.yaml, .mcp.json with Codex-only keys (env_vars, tool_timeout_sec); Claude Code would ignore those so the 10 s startup and 4096 output limits are not applied; plugin.json has no env passthrough config (relies on inheritance).

Manual build step (git clone, npm ci, tsc; dist not committed, no npm package), unpinned upgrade path, and running npm ci pulls unusual pinned versions (typescript 7.0.2, vitest 5.0.1) that should be reviewed.
gh-koosbcom-jev-delegate.verdict: Real, clean, OpenRouter-native Jev integration, but a narrow 2-tool MCP (grep re-ranking and bulk classification) that is model-discretion only, six days old, with an unverified live API path; it does not deliver automatic Jev use in Claude Code. Worth reading as a reference for the Decisions API payload and safety patterns, not worth installing as the main integration; install at most as an optional low-priority extra after verifying with a live key, and skip on client repos.

gh-derwells-sieve.whatItDoes: Local Python MCP server (stdio or loopback HTTP; mcp 2.x + typesafe-sdk) exposing 8 Jev-backed tools. jev_ask is the general one: the agent writes a question plus yes/no, choose or score criteria and gets calibrated probabilities per item. jev_grep, jev_rank, jev_search, jev_verify, jev_route and jev_triage_* are shortcuts over the same core, which batches 8-40 items per request, caches answers in sqlite, validates answers client-side and enforces a USD budget. Jev never generates text; the agent reads the survivors itself. jev_grep (rank repo files/functions against a plain-language question) is the coding-relevant tool. Also ships a sieve-ask shell CLI and SearXNG/Brave/codex/claude web-search backends for jev_search.

So OpenRouter POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone should work with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> in ~/.config/sieve/env, provided OpenRouter's endpoint is wire-compatible with the SDK schema (I did not verify that; the SDK's schemas are generated from api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json).
providerSupport.others: Web-search backends only (jev_search): SearXNG, Brave, codex CLI, claude CLI. No other Jev gateway.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to low. Mostly env-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + key). Caveat: model ID. client.py DEFAULT_MODEL='jev-latest' is what MCP tools send in the body, and OpenRouter IDs are 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. That needs a one-line change in sieve/client.py (or the TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL env, but build_client passes model explicitly so the env is ignored for MCP tools; only sieve-ask has a --model flag). Cost accounting is hardcoded at $0.042/M input (jev.py:24), matching the OpenRouter price. Response 'usage' fields must also come back in the same shape, otherwise budget tracking silently reads 0.

security: bin/sieve-mcp:12-16 sources ~/.config/sieve/env AS SHELL CODE with set -a, and values in it override the environment. Fine if the file is mode 600 and yours, but it is code execution from a config file.

API key is never in argv: read from env or env file, so it is not visible in ps. It is sent as Bearer to the base URL only. The claude/codex search backends strip ANTHROPIC_*/OPENAI_* routing env before spawning children (backends/base.py:120-145).

Side effect on user repos: jev_grep appends '.sieve-cache/' to an existing .gitignore in the searched repo (cache.py:19,43-54), otherwise writes to ~/.cache/sieve/<hash>/. Modifies client repos without being asked, though it is documented.

No secret filtering in the walker (enumerate.py:67-68 ALWAYS_SKIP only .git/.hg/.svn/.sieve-cache; rely on .gitignore + binary sniff). Untracked or ignore-missed files such as .env.local, keys or config with tokens would be previewed and sent to the API. The user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tools.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are only ids and probabilities (no free text back), which is a small surface. But jev_search and jev_verify fetch web pages/PDFs (2 MB/25 MB caps, PDF parsed in a child with 30s/1GB limit) and jev_search can spawn `claude -p`/`codex exec` children as search backends (not default unless configured; default falls back to `claude` when no SearXNG/Brave is set).

Install path: git clone + `uv sync` pulls typesafe-sdk, mcp>=2.2.0, tree-sitter-language-pack, pypdf (uv.lock pinned, 130 KB). No curl|sh, no postinstall. No telemetry found in sieve code. Optional bin/sieve-searxng runs a digest-pinned Docker container on loopback.
