gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.name: 0pilatos0/jev-browser-mcp
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server exposing 11 browser tools on a persistent Playwright Chromium/Chrome profile. Pages are turned into an indexed element table; browser_act/browser_run send one TypeSafe systemOne request per step (Choice for operation and target, Noul for goal_met and stuck) and code executes the chosen action. It is a Jev-powered browser agent, not a coding-decision tool. It overlaps with the existing playwright MCP.

providerSupport.evidence: src/decide.ts:4-7,34 uses TypeSafeClient from @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 with no explicit config. decide.ts:25-32 requires process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY. decide.ts:39-42 reads JEV_MODEL and passes it as model. The server hardcodes no URL. In the npm SDK (dist/index.mjs:56-62) env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL overrides baseURL, which defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai (index.mjs:513). systemOne() POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (index.mjs:548-556) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (index.mjs:581). Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is OpenRouter's System One endpoint. Request and response schema equality with OpenRouter is not verified here. The SDK default timeout is 10s (index.mjs:518) with maxRetries 2 (index.mjs:74).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no code patch is needed if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same shape as TypeSafe's. Set env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. The .env loader (env.ts) does not override variables already set in the environment. Risk: model ID format ('jev-latest' vs 'typesafe/jev-1.13') and any response field differences (usage.input_tokens, answers[q].choice/confidence/noul, model). The code reads these fields directly, so a mismatch would throw. Needs a live test with a real key.
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct (default) or any host that mimics its /v1/systemone.

gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.install: git clone, npm install, npx playwright install chromium, npm run build, then `claude mcp add jev -- node /abs/path/dist/index.js`. For OpenRouter also set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and JEV_MODEL in the MCP env.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.tests: No unit tests and no CI (no .github directory). scripts/ holds manual e2e, smoke, and challenge scripts that need a live key or a browser. Not run, per the static-only rule.
security: API key is read from process.env or a project-local .env (env.ts); it is not placed in argv, so it does not show in the process list. Key handling is fine.

Prompt-injection surface is large: browser_act/browser_run feed arbitrary web page text and element labels into Jev, and browser_extract/observe return page content to Claude. The server instructions tell the caller to treat page content as untrusted. Jev returns only typed choices from an enumerated set, and the code re-validates refs, which limits injection to steering clicks and typing. Claude is still exposed to injected page text through observe and extract.
Launches a persistent browser profile at ~/.jev-browser-mcp/chrome-profile (browser.ts:24-29), so cookies and logins persist across sessions and projects.

Stealth patches (browser.ts:10-15, --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled, navigator.webdriver spoofing) evade bot detection. This is ethically and ToS-questionable, and it raises the risk of automated actions on client sites.
browser_type can type arbitrary text and click arbitrary elements with no allowlist. Password fields are excluded from refs. Supplied `values` contents are matched locally and not sent to Jev.

No shell execution or child_process in src, no fetch() calls apart from the SDK, and no telemetry seen in the server code. No postinstall script in package.json. The installer is a manual build, not curl|sh.

The dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk is a first-party TypeSafe package (MIT, 3 versions, published 2026-09-12 to 2026-09-15), so it is young and its supply chain has had little scrutiny. The author 0pilatos0 is an unknown solo developer with a brand-new repo.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.dataEgress: Every browser_act/browser_run step sends to the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe or, if redirected, OpenRouter): the natural-language goal and instruction, the page URL, title, and up to ~6000 chars of visible page text, the numbered list of element labels/roles/current values, the last 4 actions, and the keys (not contents) of supplied values. The README itself warns that page content leaves the machine. No source code, diffs, or Claude conversation are sent unless a page shows them. Deterministic tools send nothing. Via OpenRouter the payload would also pass through OpenRouter and its logging and provider policies.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed per call and only for the Jev-backed tools. If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is missing, decide() throws (decide.ts:29-33). SDK timeout is 10s with 2 retries by default. Errors surface as an isError tool result or as status 'error'/'timeout' in browser_run (loop.ts:428). The deterministic tools (observe, click, type, extract, find) keep working, so Claude can fall back. The server does not crash the session, and nothing blocks Claude's normal work, because no hook is involved.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.contextCost: 11 MCP tools. registerTool blocks (descriptions and zod schemas) come to about 10k chars, plus about 1.7k chars of server `instructions` injected on connect. Estimate roughly 3-3.5k tokens of always-on context (tool names, descriptions, schemas, instructions). This duplicates the 25+ tools of the existing playwright MCP, so total browser tool context grows. No hooks and no hook-injected text.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. Claude Code sees the tool descriptions and instructions and decides whether to call them. There is no hook, no skill trigger, and no transparent proxy, so Claude would use it only when a browser task comes up, and it would still choose between this server and playwright. It cannot cover the coding-time decisions Jev is meant for.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on non-browser turns, since it is not in the hot path. During browser use each step costs one Jev round trip (README claims 150-500 ms) plus Playwright execution and a 500 ms settle wait (loop.ts:356), so multi-step browser_run takes seconds. Two-stage link selection on dense pages adds a second call. Cold start launches Chromium.
pros: Genuine, non-toy use of Jev's Choice and Noul primitives. It fans out several typed questions in one systemOne request (operation, per-kind target choices, goal_met, stuck) and re-validates in code (decide.ts:122-133, 189-193). It is a real reference for the typed-decision pattern.
Provider is swappable by env only. The SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus the /v1/systemone path maps directly onto OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so no fork is needed to try OpenRouter.
No secrets in argv, no shell exec, no postinstall, MIT. Small codebase (~2.4k lines) that is easy to audit. Password fields are never exposed or typed, and supplied value contents never go to Jev.
Fails open for Claude. Errors are contained to the two paid tools, and deterministic browser tools remain usable.
Very cheap per step (about $0.0002 at $0.042/Mtok input), and it saves frontier-model tokens versus screenshot or DOM-dump loops for repetitive browsing.
cons: Not a coding-workflow integration. It only automates web browsing and does not address Claude Code's edit, permission, or routing decisions. The user wants Jev to add value automatically during daily coding, and this does not.

Model-discretion only. Claude must choose to call browser_run, and it will likely prefer the already-installed playwright MCP (about 25 tools) for UI testing. It adds about 3-3.5k tokens of duplicate tool context for little gain.
Day-old solo-author PoC: 8 commits, all on 2026-09-25, 0 stars, no releases, no tests, no CI, not on npm. Requires clone, build, and Playwright download.

Sends page text (up to about 6k chars per step) to a third-party endpoint. That is risky on client projects with authenticated or internal pages. It uses a persistent profile with saved logins, and it includes bot-detection evasion (stealth init script, AutomationControlled disabled).

OpenRouter compatibility is a plausible inference from SDK source, not verified. The model ID format and response schema on OpenRouter may differ, and the code throws on unexpected operations. The default 10s timeout with 2 retries could stall a run.
The stated 'Chrome' default only auto-detects a macOS path (browser.ts:21), so on Linux it silently uses bundled Chromium.
gh-0pilatos0-jev-browser-mcp.verdict: A well-built but narrow proof-of-concept browser agent. It works with OpenRouter with a probable env-only switch (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api), but it does not provide the automatic Jev-in-Claude-Code decision layer the user wants. It is redundant with the playwright MCP and immature, so use it at most as an optional add-on for scripted browsing and as a code reference for Choice/Noul usage.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. Not an env var or base URL swap: the Jev call goes through the AI SDK's gateway-specific experimental_evaluate, the vck_ key regex would reject an OpenRouter sk-or key from the key file, and two call sites (decide.js, read.js) plus the confidence/providerMetadata parsing and the 'did not select' retry logic depend on the gateway response shape. A patch would replace evaluate() with a fetch to POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (mapping the state/questions schema and the confidence field) and swap generateObject for an OpenRouter-compatible provider for the Gemini reader. A cloned client repo whose .env sets TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (config.ts:108) would redirect the OpenRouter/TypeSafe key and all Jev payloads to an attacker host; setting JEV_PLAYWRIGHT_COMMAND (config.ts:61, read after the .env load at :118) makes run_action spawn an arbitrary command via StdioClientTransport (playwright.ts:112). Real risk for a user opening many client repos, especially in bypass mode.

API key handling: setup stores key in ~/.jev/.env with mode 0600 (setup.ts:50), but the documented CLI form 'jev-bro setup --api-key "$OPENROUTER_API_KEY"' puts the key in argv (visible in ps briefly). Under openrouter provider the same key is also written as TYPESAFE_API_KEY (setup.ts:117-120) and can be written into project ./.env with --project-env (setup.ts:145). MCP server itself gets key via env/file, not argv, if configured that way.

Supply chain: documented launch is 'npx --yes' of an unpinned 4-day-old single-author package, which in turn spawns 'npx --yes agentic-playwright-mcp' (also unpinned, same author, created 2026-09-26, 0 stars) at runtime (config.ts:73-74). No postinstall/preinstall scripts (package.json, lockfile grep clean). No curl|sh.

Browser surface: attaches to Chrome at unauthenticated CDP port 127.0.0.1:9223 shared with the agent and user's sessions/cookies; run_action can click through logged-in sessions. Page text is fed to Jev (prompt-injection surface is limited because Jev only returns typed choices, but a malicious page can steer which control is pressed). Server states it never fills passwords/captcha.

File read: contextPaths lets steps read files within cwd allowlist, 64KB cap, .env refused unless explicitly listed (files.ts). TYPE_TEXT helper sends up to 4000 chars of page + goal to a third-party text model (inception/mercury-2.5) via OpenRouter (text.ts).
Debug traces (--debug or debug:true) write every payload and response untruncated to ~/.jev/traces (trace.ts) without redaction.

No telemetry found (grep for analytics/telemetry empty); no child_process exec/eval; only spawn is the MCP stdio transport to the Playwright server. OpenRouter calls send HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers identifying the package (jev.ts:~266).

Also HTTP-Referer/X-Title app attribution to OpenRouter. No prompts/conversation history, tool outputs or hooks data are sent automatically; no local transcript access.
gh-techyaditya-jev-browser-sidekick-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's perspective: tool errors are caught and returned as isError JSON ({error: message}) (mcp.ts use_jev_raw catch), so Claude just proceeds without Jev. SDK timeout 15 s per call with maxRetries 1 (jev.ts:126-131; CHANGELOG claims 'two retries' but code says 1). run_action has call deadline 90 s default (config.ts runTimeoutMs), task 90 s, and a stalled Jev call blocks that tool call up to ~30 s (15 s x 2 attempts) plus possible OpenRouter fallback attempt (another 15 s x 2). Endpoint faults are classified (rate_limit, auth, no_credits, not_found, provider_outage, unreachable, proxy_interstitial, bad_response) and stop run_action series but keep them resumable. Nothing blocks the Claude Code turn beyond the tool call itself since it is not a hook.

Each use_jev_raw call: claimed 70-500 ms Jev plus MCP round trip plus an extra model turn for Claude to read resource guide once and write the questions (likely 3-10 s of model time in practice, my estimate). run_action: one Jev call per non-trivial step (19 decisions for a 26-step run per README) plus browser time; runs in tens of seconds.
gh-techyaditya-jev-browser-sidekick-mcp.contextCost: 2 tools, 2 resources (resources not auto-loaded). Server instructions ~2,940 chars (~730 tokens) always injected; tool descriptions 384 + 1,071 chars; JSON schemas roughly 4.2k chars source (run_action 3.0k, use_jev_raw 1.2k), so total always-on cost approx 8.5-9.5k chars = ~2.2-2.6k tokens (chars/4), unless Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch, in which case only names are resident. gh-techyaditya-jev-browser-sidekick-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The use_jev_raw description is written to nudge autonomous use ('Use whenever a decision has more than one defensible answer and you are about to pick on instinct... which fix to do first, whether a step is risky enough to stop and ask the user'), and server instructions say 'use when about to guess', so Opus may call it unprompted, but there is no deterministic hook, skill trigger or proxy; usage frequency depends on the model's own judgment and is not guaranteed. run_action would compete with the already-installed Playwright MCP.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code with OpenRouter as the default provider: uses both OpenRouter surfaces (/v1/systemone via TypeSafe SDK with baseURL openrouter.ai/api, and /api/alpha/decisions via @openrouter/sdk with typesafe/ model prefix) (jev.ts:121-132, 241, 280-296).

use_jev_raw is a real generic Jev passthrough with full Choice/Noul/Score support, criteria, and documented question-writing guide as an MCP resource; the one component that could be model-triggered for coding forks ('which fix first', 'is this step risky').
Fail-open, classified errors, bounded timeouts (15 s, 1 retry), no telemetry, no postinstall, no shell exec, MIT, sensible file allowlist that refuses .env.
Zero per-turn context overhead from hooks; small footprint (2 tools, ~2.5k tokens).
Has CI, 11 test files, changelog, and a fast-moving single maintainer who clearly reads Jev docs (questions.ts cites jev-1.13 jaggedness and fan-out docs).
cons: Scope mismatch: it is a shopping/browser automation agent (cart, add to cart, Amazon traps) that only incidentally exposes use_jev_raw; run_action duplicates the user's existing Playwright MCP and requires a second unvetted MCP (agentic-playwright-mcp) plus Chrome on CDP 9223.

Automatic use is not guaranteed and not deterministic: only model-discretion; no hooks or skill to gate risky Bash/edits, so it does not satisfy 'Claude Code must use it when needed' beyond a description nudge; a coding model rarely needs a probability oracle and Claude may simply ignore it.

Serious config-injection risk for client repos: project ./.env is auto-loaded into process.env (config.ts:90), letting a hostile repo redirect the API key via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or execute a command via JEV_PLAYWRIGHT_COMMAND (config.ts:61); dangerous in bypass permission mode.

Very immature: repo and package created 2026-09-26, 12 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 issues, 10 versions in 2 days; API surface churning; Jev/OpenRouter endpoints are alpha/beta. Documented npx --yes launch is unpinned.

Primary OpenRouter call path sends unprefixed model 'jev-1.13' to /v1/systemone (jev.ts:241; default model config.ts) and does not fall back on not_found, so it could break if OpenRouter requires 'typesafe/jev-1.13' (unverified).

Arbitrary model-written state (code, diffs, errors) egresses to OpenRouter/TypeSafe with no redaction, and it bypasses the user's existing secret-leak guard for MCP tools (the guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit only). Debug traces store payloads unredacted.

Extra model turn overhead: Claude must read the jev://raw-decisions guide and hand-author typed questions each time, which costs more tokens/latency than the Jev call itself and Jev's typed output is only advisory, not enforced.
Marketing-style, tool description includes non-coding uses (cereal aisle, job offers, cat names), signalling a hobby project rather than a dev-workflow integration.
gh-techyaditya-jev-browser-sidekick-mcp.verdict: Not a good fit as the daily Jev integration: it is a browser-shopping agent whose only relevant piece, use_jev_raw, is a model-discretion MCP tool (not automatic) inside a 4-day-old single-author package with a project-.env config-injection risk. If you want a Jev tool at all, copy the OpenRouter call pattern (systemone/alpha decisions) into your own small pinned MCP or hook rather than installing this.

interface.name: browse(url, goal, values=None, max_seconds=60)
interface.purpose: Only MCP tool. Runs a multi-step website interaction in the user's Chrome (background tab) driven by Jev; returns status (done/blocked/looping/timeout/error), elapsed_ms, url, title, page_text[:4000], steps with probability/confidence, and elements on non-done outcomes. Emits progress notifications. Tab closed after each call.

interface.name: MCP server instructions
interface.purpose: ~1.7k-char INSTRUCTIONS string injected into Claude's system prompt: 'Use browse first, before step-by-step browser tools (Chrome extension, built-in browser, Playwright)' for any live-website interaction; lists exclusions and post-call handling.

interface.name: CLI entrypoint jev-reflex
interface.purpose: stdio MCP server (jev_reflex:main -> mcp.run()).

security: Key handling: TYPESAFE_API_KEY read from process env, sent as Bearer over httpx HTTP/2 to api.typesafe.ai; README install uses `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...` which stores the key in ~/.claude.json (plaintext) and puts it in the `claude mcp add` argv once; the server process itself gets it via env, not argv.

Install is `uvx --from git+https://github.com/MSalvalaggio/jev-reflex` with a transitive git dependency on browser-use/jev-ultrafast pinned to a commit (not on PyPI): unreviewed code fetched and executed from two small git repos on every fresh resolve; no postinstall/curl|sh though.

Requires Chrome remote debugging enabled (chrome://inspect) and drives the user's REAL logged-in profile; README admits any local program can control Chrome while it is on. Jev can click any control including submit/buy; safety relies only on the prompt instructions.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted page text and control labels flow to Jev (constrained choice output, so injection can only steer among observed elements) and page_text[:4000] + element labels flow back into Claude's context unfiltered.
Model output never used as selector/JS per README; upstream re-checks element visibility before input. Claude-supplied `values` are typed into arbitrary sites (exfil channel if Claude is injected).
No telemetry found in the 155-line server; upstream not fully audited. Hardcoded 25 s httpx timeout, 3 tries.
gh-msalvalaggio-jev-reflex.dataEgress: Per decision to api.typesafe.ai: page URL, title, visible page text, the full indexed element table (labels, values, roles, current field values including any pre-filled personal data), the goal string, last 10 actions, and the caller-supplied `values` (strings to type). Sent for every step of the loop. If the optional text model is configured, goal and field context also go to that provider (default DeepSeek). No source code or repo files leave the machine unless Claude puts them in goal/values or the browsed page shows them (e.g. localhost app).
gh-msalvalaggio-jev-reflex.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but bounded: HTTP errors/429/503 retried up to 3 times (0.5s, 1s backoff), 25 s per-request timeout, then RuntimeError -> tool returns status 'error' with elements so Claude can continue with another browser tool; max_seconds default 60 gives 'timeout'; loop detection returns 'looping'. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY raises ToolError immediately. Since it is a discretionary tool, Jev being down only affects browse calls, not other Claude Code work, but a wedged call can block up to ~60+ s. Chrome not reachable -> ToolError.
gh-msalvalaggio-jev-reflex.contextCost: 1 tool (`browse`). Description ~1.0k chars + schema ~0.3k chars, server instructions ~1.7k chars (always in system prompt): roughly 750-800 tokens total. No hooks. Tool results add up to ~4k chars page_text plus steps (and full element table on failure), i.e. ~1-3k tokens per call. Instructions also tell Claude to prefer browse over Playwright, which would displace the user's existing playwright MCP.
gh-msalvalaggio-jev-reflex.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, nudged strongly by server instructions injected into the system prompt (Claude Code adds them automatically); optionally a ~/.claude/rules/jev.md rule. No hooks, no proxy. It would trigger automatically only when a task involves interacting with a live website, which is rare in daily coding.
gh-msalvalaggio-jev-reflex.latencyImpact: Only when invoked: measured by author 1.96 s (example.com, 1 step), 3.4 s (Wikipedia), 13 s (Google Flights, 11 steps) on Windows; each Jev decision claimed ~100 ms plus browser action and page-settle time. Zero latency on ordinary coding turns (no hook). Cold `uvx` start pulls git deps and httpx/mcp (first start may take many seconds).
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's intended System One shape (typed Choice questions with per-option probabilities/confidence), and validates responses strictly (validate_choice checks probabilities sum, range, argmax) before acting.
Auto-invocation is real without user prompting: MCP `instructions` are injected into the system prompt telling Claude when to use `browse`.
Well-bounded runs: max_seconds, 60-action budget, A-B-A-B loop detection, retries with backoff, and a handoff (elements + url) so Claude can take over with Playwright.
Tiny, readable (155 lines), MIT, has offline tests (tests/test_server.py) and CI (ruff + pytest), upstream jev-ultrafast is a 21k-star browser-use project.
Returns verifiable output (page_text, steps with probabilities) and explicitly says 'done' is not proof.
cons: Wrong problem for this user: it is website automation (flight search, forms), not code editing/reading/testing; almost never triggers in daily coding, so Jev would add near-zero value.

No OpenRouter support: api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY hardcoded in server (line 68) and in a pinned third-party dependency (jev_ultrafast/model.py:119); user has only OpenRouter. Needs a fork/monkeypatch, and unverified that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the identical body.
Drives the user's real logged-in Chrome with remote debugging enabled: high risk on client projects/accounts (can click submit/buy/delete); mitigation is prompt text only.

Its instructions tell Claude to use browse BEFORE Playwright/built-in browser for any site interaction, which would override the user's existing playwright MCP behaviour and could send localhost/client-app page content to a third party (though it says not to for local dev servers).

Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 6 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 2 forks, no releases, last push 12 days ago; depends on non-PyPI git-pinned upstream; measurements only on Windows with 'a handful of runs'.

gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.name: carryforward (Dharundp6/jev-carryforward)
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (MCP server + skill + SessionStart hook) that keeps a per-project append-only JSONL ledger (~/.carryforward/<project>.jsonl) of constraints, corrections, decisions, measurements and parked threads. On recall(task), Jev scores each non-pinned entry with a boolean question (P that the entry is still live for the task); >=0.60 is injected in full, 0.30-0.60 as one line, below is omitted. It is a session-memory relevance filter, not a coding-assist router. Jev is used only for scoring ledger entries.

providerSupport.evidence: src/gateway.ts:13 MODEL = 'typesafe-ai/jev'; gateway.ts:20 requires env.AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY (Vercel AI Gateway); gateway.ts:23,37 calls experimental_evaluate({model,state,questions}) from the 'ai' npm package (^7.0.107, package.json); README 'Why Jev' says Vercel AI Gateway chosen for published ZDR terms. No mention of openrouter, OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY anywhere in the repo (case-insensitive grep returned nothing). server.ts:149 and cli.ts hardcode gatewayAsker() so there is no env switch for another provider.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway only (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, model typesafe-ai/jev via AI SDK experimental_evaluate)
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The Asker interface (ask(state, questions) -> {id: probability}) is already pluggable and the library exports recall(entries, task, asker), but the shipped server/CLI hardcode gatewayAsker() at src/server.ts:149, so you must fork and edit ~30 lines: write an Asker that POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or /api/v1/systemone) with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and map the boolean/Noul response to P(yes). The exact OpenRouter request/response schema is not in this repo and differs from AI SDK experimental_evaluate, so it needs verification. Not a config-only switch.

interface.purpose: stdio MCP server, print brief, print ledger path (cli.ts).

gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.runtime: Node >=22 (TypeScript, ESM); deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30, ai ^7.0.107, zod ^3.25; launched via `npx -y carryforward` (plugin.json mcpServers and hook)

No integration test against real Jev; author states no accuracy claim. Tests not run (static audit).
security: Ledger is plaintext, unencrypted, at ~/.carryforward/<slug>.jsonl (slug = cwd basename + sha1 prefix); if the model records a secret it persists (SECURITY.md warns)
Key passed via `claude mcp add -e AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=...` lives in ~/.claude.json, not in argv of the server; hook uses npx with inherited env, no key in argv

`npx -y carryforward` runs unpinned latest npm code at every session start (hook) and MCP launch; supply-chain risk, single-maintainer npm account; version in plugin.json is 0.1.1 but npm shows only 0.1.0 published at review time, so the plugin/hook may resolve a different version than the repo
No shell execution, no postinstall/preinstall script, no curl|sh, no telemetry found in src/

Prompt-injection surface: recall output (ledger text) is injected into context via hook/tool result; any injected text recorded earlier (record is model-discretion) would be replayed as trusted 'Always' rules
Pinned constraints/corrections never sent to Jev (recall.ts pinned filter); husk is that the model decides what to record
No input length cap on entries beyond batching 25 per request
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.dataEgress: Only `recall` with a non-empty task and AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY set. Sent to Vercel AI Gateway (then TypeSafe Jev): the task sentence plus text/ref/refresh/kind/obtained/date/id of every non-pinned (decision, measurement, thread) entry, in batches of 25 (recall.ts:263-272). Constraints and corrections are never sent. `record` and the SessionStart hook (no task) make no network calls. No source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent automatically, only what the model chose to write into ledger entries (which may include file paths, commands, branch names, PR refs).
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.failureMode: Fail-open. No key, no task, or any scorer exception returns the full ledger with an explanatory note (recall.ts:286-300, 312-319). Entries missing from Jev's answer default to 'inject'. No explicit request timeout is set in gateway.ts, so a hung scorer relies on AI SDK defaults and the MCP client's tool timeout; the hook has a 25s timeout (hooks.json) but does not call Jev. Ledger corruption lines are skipped and counted, never deleted.
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.contextCost: Low. 2 MCP tools (record, recall); descriptions ~870 + ~600 chars and schemas ~900 chars, roughly 600-700 tokens total; no server-level 'instructions' field. Skill description ~450 chars (~110 tokens) always listed. SessionStart hook injects the brief (empty ledger prints nothing only with --quiet; the plugin hook.json omits --quiet, so it prints 'The ledger is empty' text every start/clear/compact). Ledger size grows unbounded, so hook output grows with all non-pinned entries one line each.
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.latencyImpact: Hook: npx -y startup on every SessionStart (startup/clear/compact), typically 0.5-3 s cold and needs network to check the registry; no Jev call. recall tool: author reports ~1.4 s for 9 entries (1 request per 25 entries, Jev + Vercel gateway); record: local append, negligible. No per-tool-call overhead on normal coding turns.
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.autoInvocation: Mixed. Deterministic: SessionStart hook (startup|clear|compact) auto-injects pinned rules and unscored one-line entries without the model, but without Jev. Model-discretion: recall/record MCP tools plus skill description trigger. The author's own eval found the agent called recall 0 of 4 times even with tools and skill present, so the Jev-scoring path is not reliably auto-invoked. Not a transparent proxy.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for what a calibrated boolean scorer is good at: ranking ledger entries per task with thresholds exported as constants (recall.ts:245-248)
Excellent fail-open design: every error path returns the whole ledger with a note, so Jev outages never cost information
Hook does the important part deterministically (re-injects rules after compaction) and is honest in the README that the tools alone were not called (0/4 in author's eval)
Small, readable, 2 tools, ~800 lines src, no shell execution or postinstall, MIT, CI on 2 OS x 2 Node versions, pluggable Asker interface makes an OpenRouter scorer a small patch
Pinned constraints/corrections never leave the machine; nothing sent unless a task is given and a key is set
Low context footprint (~700 tokens tools + ~110 skill)
cons: No OpenRouter support: hard-wired to Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, model typesafe-ai/jev, AI SDK experimental_evaluate), so it needs a fork to use the user's OpenRouter key, and the OpenRouter Decisions API schema is not implemented anywhere here

The Jev call happens only in recall(task), which the model must choose to call; the SessionStart hook passes no task so Jev is never used in the only deterministic path. The author's own eval showed recall was not called even with skill installed
Solves cross-session memory, not daily coding decisions; user already has gitnexus graph context, CLAUDE.md and auto memory, so overlap is high and Jev adds little
Very young and tiny (created 2026-09-18, 6 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars), no accuracy evidence (README says only 9 entries x 3 tasks), npm shows only 0.1.0 while repo/plugin is 0.1.1

Depends on the model diligently calling record with well-worded text; ledger is plaintext and could capture secrets or client-project details, replayed as trusted rules in future sessions (injection / client-confidentiality concern across projects sharing the home dir)
`npx -y` unpinned at each session start adds a network-dependent supply-chain hop and cold-start latency on top of the user's existing hooks; hook without --quiet prints 'ledger is empty' noise
Jev is beta and skeptics say it may be a flash-model router, so ranking quality of a 4-line boolean question over free-text notes is unproven
gh-dharun-cohere-jev-carryforward.verdict: Well-engineered but tiny alpha memory ledger whose Jev use is confined to model-invoked recall and is hard-wired to Vercel AI Gateway, not OpenRouter. Not a good fit for automatic Jev use in daily coding; useful only as a design reference for a fail-open Jev relevance scorer (the Asker interface could be repointed at OpenRouter's Decisions API in a fork).

gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.name: Fuwn/typesafe-mcp
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Tiny (~200 line) Node stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} verbatim to POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY and returns the raw JSON (answers, probabilities, confidence, usage) as tool text. Validates question shapes with Zod before sending and checks each returned answer type matches the question type. Nothing else: no hooks, no skill, no routing.

providerSupport.evidence: server.js:160 hardcoded `fetch("https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone", ...)`; server.js:162 `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}`; server.js:193 key only from process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY; server.js:155 model default "jev-latest". No env override for base URL or key name. server.test.js:46 asserts the exact URL. README.md:21 TYPESAFE_API_KEY only.
providerSupport.others: None. No OpenRouter, no other gateway.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, assuming OpenRouter's System One API mirrors the TypeSafe request/response schema (the path /v1/systemone is identical and the brief lists both as System One surfaces; not verified against OpenRouter docs here). Edit two lines: URL at server.js:160 to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY at server.js:193 instead of TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Also change the default model at server.js:155 to `typesafe/jev-latest` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`, since OpenRouter uses vendor-prefixed slugs. Update the URL assertion in server.test.js:46. MIT license permits a fork. Better still, parametrise via env vars (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL) in a private fork. Caveat: the answer envelope check at server.js:176-180 (result.answers[id].type) would break if OpenRouter wraps the response differently, which would make every call return an error.

interface.name: evaluate (MCP tool, only tool)
interface.purpose: Args: `state` (string | object | array evidence), `questions` (map of id -> {type:'noul', instructions, criteria?{true,false}} | {type:'choice', instructions, criteria: {option: desc|null}, 1-255 options} | {type:'score', instructions, criteria: [2..10 level descriptions]}), `model` (default 'jev-latest'). Annotated readOnlyHint:true, openWorldHint:true. Returns JSON string of the upstream response; isError:true on validation, HTTP non-2xx (status only, upstream body not echoed), mismatched answer type, or timeout. Server.js:147-186.

gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.runtime: Node >=22 (user has Node 24); deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0 and zod 3.25.76 (pinned exact); stdio transport; no build step. Not published to npm (package.json private:true), so it must be cloned and `npm ci` run locally.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.install: git clone https://github.com/Fuwn/typesafe-mcp && cd typesafe-mcp && npm ci; then `claude mcp add typesafe -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- node /abs/path/server.js`. Note: putting the key via `-e` writes it into ~/.claude.json; the key is not in argv because it is passed via env. There is no OpenRouter path without patching the source.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.tests: Yes. server.test.js has 7+ node:test cases using mocked fetch and in-memory MCP transport: request shape, malformed-question rejection, HTTP error non-echo and no retry, invalid JSON / missing answers, key redaction, cancellation, stdio entrypoint, missing-key exit. Opt-in live-check.js hits the real API (needs key, costs money). No CI (.github absent). I did not run them (static review only).
security: API key read from env only, never argv; sent only as Bearer header to a hardcoded HTTPS host (server.js:160-162). Redirects disabled (`redirect: "error"`), so key cannot be bounced to another host.
Error text has the key replaced with [redacted] (server.js:184) and upstream error bodies are never echoed (server.js:168-171), which is good hygiene and tested.
No shell execution, no child_process in server.js, no fs access, no postinstall scripts in package.json, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry beyond the single API call.
Exact-pinned dependencies plus a package-lock.json (42 KB); dependency surface is just the MCP SDK and zod.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool returns only numeric/enum JSON from Jev (no free text), so returned content is low-risk. But the tool description asks the caller to 'supply evidence', so the model decides what data goes out; injected text in a repo could steer what gets sent, though egress is only to TypeSafe.

Tool has no output-size or input-size cap client-side (32k context limit is enforced upstream). One-person, 1-star, 8-day-old repo: supply-chain trust rests on Fuwn, so pin a commit or fork after reading (the file is small enough to audit fully, which I did).

In bypass/auto permission mode the tool would run without prompts; combined with model-driven evidence selection this could send arbitrary file contents/secrets to the API. The existing secret-leak guard hook matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__typesafe__evaluate, so it would not cover this tool unless the matcher is extended.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions`/`criteria` (arbitrary text or JSON: could be code, diffs, file contents, logs, tool outputs, prompts). Sent over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe) as-is. The full request body is JSON.stringify(input) (server.js:163), so also the `model` string. Only the API key in the Authorization header besides that. Nothing is sent automatically; egress happens only when the model chooses to call the tool. Client projects: contents leave to TypeSafe's direct API (would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe if patched), so check client confidentiality terms.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level: every failure (missing key at startup exits 1 so the MCP server shows as failed; HTTP non-2xx, bad JSON, mismatched answers, network error, 60 s timeout) is returned as an isError tool result and the model simply carries on without Jev. 60-second deadline (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS, server.js:5) is long relative to the 70-500 ms claim, so a hung upstream would stall a turn for up to 60 s before failing; no retries; honours MCP cancellation (Esc). Nothing blocks tool use.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Description about 450 chars (~110 tokens); input schema (Zod discriminated union of three question types with nested criteria, generated JSON Schema, no per-field descriptions except `state`) roughly 1.5-2.5k chars (~400-600 tokens). Estimate total ~500-700 tokens per session (deferred via ToolSearch if MCP tool search is on, so likely only the name). No MCP `instructions` field is set (McpServer created with only name/version, server.js:145). No hooks, so zero per-turn injected text.
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or triggers a call: no hook, no skill, no system prompt or CLAUDE.md text. Claude will call `evaluate` only if it judges the description relevant, and the description is written for classification/scoring of evidence, not for coding decisions, so on typical coding turns it will almost never be picked. Getting the 'automatic without prompting' behaviour requires adding CLAUDE.md rules, a skill, or hooks around it (not provided by this repo).
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where it is not called. When called: one stdio MCP round trip plus one HTTPS call; the brief claims 70-500 ms end to end for Jev, plus Node process already resident. Worst case 60 s timeout. Model has to spend an extra tool-call turn (output tokens to compose questions, ~200-500 tokens, plus a round trip of the main model, likely 2-8 s of Opus time), which dwarfs Jev's own latency.
pros: Smallest possible correct wrapper: single file (server.js, 199 lines) that I read completely; easy to audit and to fork for private use.

Covers all three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) with proper Zod validation (choice 1-255 options, score 2-10 levels) and answer-type verification, so malformed calls fail locally without spending money.
Good security hygiene: key via env, not argv; redirect:'error'; key redaction; no upstream body echo; no postinstall/shell/telemetry; exact-pinned deps with lockfile.
Fail-open behaviour: errors come back as isError results and never block Claude Code; cancellation propagates to the fetch.
Tiny context footprint (one tool, ~0.5-0.7k tokens, no server instructions, no hooks).
Test suite with mocked transport is meaningful (7+ cases), plus an opt-in live check that verifies probabilities sum to 1.
Patch to OpenRouter is two-line and MIT permits it; the endpoint path /v1/systemone already matches OpenRouter's System One API path.
readOnlyHint:true annotation makes it low-friction in permission modes.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: base URL hardcoded (server.js:160), key env fixed to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter slug. Must be forked/patched; compatibility of OpenRouter's response envelope is unverified.

No automatic invocation mechanism: purely model-discretion. It does not meet the user's requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told. Needs CLAUDE.md rules, a skill, or hooks written separately.
Not published to npm (private:true), no releases, no CI, 2 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 8 days old: version 0.1.0 alpha with bus-factor 1 and no maintenance track record.

Nothing in it is tailored to coding: no code-oriented question templates, no diff/file gathering, no risk/permission-classification helper. The model has to compose questions and evidence itself each time, costing an extra Opus turn that likely outweighs Jev's 70-500 ms benefit.
60 s timeout is far too generous for a 70-500 ms model; a slow upstream would stall a turn. Not configurable via env.

Data egress is model-chosen and unfiltered; in bypass/auto mode with the secret-leak hook not matching mcp__typesafe__* tools, sensitive/client code could be sent out. Would need the hook matcher extended.
Returns the raw JSON blob as text with no summarisation; adds tokens to context per call (answers + probabilities + usage).
gh-fuwn-typesafe-mcp.verdict: A clean, safe, minimal reference wrapper worth forking (two-line change to OpenRouter) as the transport layer, but on its own it is a bare model-discretion tool with no auto-invocation and no coding-specific logic, so it will not deliver the 'Claude uses Jev by itself' goal. Use it, if at all, as the MCP backend under a hook/skill layer you write, not as the integration.

gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.name: nirvana124/typesafe-mcp (npm: system-one-mcp)
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server exposing a single tool, `evaluate`, that forwards {state, model, questions} (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe System One direct (via @typesafe-ai/sdk), OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint, or Vercel AI Gateway. Thin pass-through adapter by a third-party individual (not TypeSafe). Published to npm as `system-one-mcp` because `typesafe-mcp` was taken.

Payload shape sent to /decisions is the System One shape, unverified against the live alpha API (the code comment at openrouter.ts:1-6 asserts it matches).

security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts (npm scripts are only build/dev/test/typecheck); published dist contains the openrouter URL matching the repo (checked tarball).
API key comes from env, not argv, if set via the MCP `env` block (README config). The README's `TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... npx` form is also env-based. No key in the process list.

dotenv loadEnv({quiet:true}) at src/index.ts:27 reads .env from the MCP server's cwd, which for Claude Code is the project directory. A client repo's .env (or a hostile cloned repo's) can inject OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_BACKEND, OPENROUTER_BASE_URL/AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL, so the key could be sent to an attacker-chosen host, or an unrelated project OPENROUTER_API_KEY could be used silently. Real risk on client projects. Host-injected env wins (dotenv does not overwrite).
OPENROUTER_BASE_URL is used as the full POST URL with the bearer key, no host allowlisting (openrouter.ts:36).
npx -y with no version pin runs whatever is latest on npm from a solo maintainer with a brand-new account/package: supply-chain exposure. Pin system-one-mcp@0.1.0 or vendor the source.

Tool output is returned as JSON of numeric probabilities only, so the prompt-injection surface from responses is small; the state sent is model-authored so exfiltration risk is via what Claude chooses to send.
No shell execution, no telemetry in this repo. Transitive @typesafe-ai/sdk is not audited here.
Third-party wrapper, not affiliated with TypeSafe; single anonymous-ish maintainer (Pankaj Yadav).
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and `questions.instructions/criteria` on each evaluate call goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe/Jev), plus the bearer key. It could be code, diffs, file contents, or tool output, because the model decides what to pass; nothing is sent automatically. Client-code confidentiality depends on OpenRouter/TypeSafe data policies. Nothing else leaves the machine (no telemetry in the repo).
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup: the process exits 1 if no credential resolves (src/index.ts:29-40), so Claude Code shows the server as failed with no tools. At runtime, errors are returned as isError tool results (index.ts:75-77), which Claude can read and carry on from, so the agent flow is not blocked. The hand-rolled HTTP path (openrouter/vercel) has a 10s timeout per attempt and 2 retries with 0.5-5s backoff on 408/429/5xx/network errors (http.ts:9-12, 27-56), so worst case is about 30s+ before an error. If OpenRouter relocates the alpha path, every call fails with HTTP 404 (README and code note this).
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Model call only adds latency when Claude chooses to call the tool: roughly 70-500ms claimed API latency plus Node stdio round trip plus Claude's own extra tool-call turn (a few seconds of Opus time per use). npx cold start on first connection (download of package and deps) adds seconds at session start, and MCP startup blocks nothing else. Worst case about 30s on outages.
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool. Tool description 486 chars plus inputSchema, total src/tools/evaluate.json 2230 chars, about 550-650 tokens of tool definition in context (fewer if tool search defers it). The server sets no `instructions` field (Server constructed with capabilities.tools only, index.ts:47-50). No hooks, so no injected text.
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. The tool description says what it does but gives no guidance on WHEN a coding agent should call it (no 'use before X' triggers), so Opus will rarely call it unprompted. Getting auto-use would require adding CLAUDE.md rules or a companion skill/hook. Does not satisfy 'used automatically without prompting' on its own.
pros: Only candidate-type that already has a first-class OpenRouter path: correct alpha Decisions URL https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (openrouter.ts:11,37), and JEV_BACKEND=openrouter forces it.
*_API_KEY_ENV redirect (index.ts:21-28) lets you keep a dedicated OpenRouter key var without colliding with other tools; useful with existing secret-leak hook setups.
Tiny surface (1 tool, about 600 tokens, no hooks, no postinstall, no telemetry, Apache-2.0), easy to audit (about 400 LOC) and to vendor or pin.
Exposes all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) with multi-question parallel calls in one request, matching the Jev brief.
Sensible error handling: 10s timeout, 2 retries with Retry-After, tool errors returned as isError rather than crashing; backend switching to TypeSafe direct later needs only a key change.
cons: Model-ID trap: `model` is a required tool arg (evaluate.json:45) with example "jev-latest", but OpenRouter's IDs are typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest; the OpenRouter default (openrouter.ts:12, lacking the ~) is bypassed and itself likely wrong. Claude will likely hit 4xx on the first call.
Only model-discretion invocation and no guidance on when to call it, so it fails the core requirement 'Claude Code must use it automatically'. You would need CLAUDE.md prompts or hooks anyway.
dotenv loads the project's .env from cwd (index.ts:27); on client repos that can silently swap the OpenRouter key/base URL (key exfiltration or wrong billing). Needs cwd isolation or removing dotenv.

Very immature: 3 commits over about 1 hour, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases or CI, single npm version 0.1.0, third-party (not TypeSafe or OpenRouter official); never verified against the live alpha API (tests only use a mock).

Uses alpha /api/alpha/decisions (may move), not the more stable /api/v1/systemone; no `response_format`-style normalization; returns raw probabilities with no thresholds or decision policy, so Claude must interpret them.
Sends whatever code/diffs Claude puts in `state` to a third party; on client projects that needs contract review. `npx -y` unpinned adds a supply-chain risk.
No Claude-Code-specific value: no code-review, commit-gate or permission-gate recipes; Jev's typed decisions are just exposed generically.
gh-nirvana124-typesafe-mcp.verdict: Cleanest existing OpenRouter-capable Jev MCP wrapper and a reasonable base to fork or vendor (pin version, drop dotenv, fix model ID to ~typesafe/jev-latest, make model optional). By itself it is not automatic: it is a bare model-discretion tool with no invocation guidance, so it needs a hook or CLAUDE.md layer to meet the goal.

gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.name: Bodila51/Jev-chooses-a-LLM (Jev Router for Cursor)
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.whatItDoes: A Cursor-specific plugin (rule + 3 subagents + slash commands + stdio MCP server) that sends a task description to TypeSafe System One (Jev) with a Choice question (cost/balanced/intelligence tier), a Score question (complexity) and a Noul question (needs approval), applies a hard policy layer, and tells the parent agent which subagent to delegate to. It also ships a Cursor SDK runner that picks a Cursor model ID. It is not a Claude Code integration: the model tiers are Cursor model IDs (composer-2.5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5), and Claude Code cannot swap models per subagent through this.

providerSupport.evidence: shared/config.ts:20-24 defaults typesafe.baseUrl to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model "jev-latest", timeoutMs 15000. mcp/typesafe-client.ts:50 reads only process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and :59-67 does fetch(config.typesafe.baseUrl) with Authorization: Bearer. config.example.json also has baseUrl api.typesafe.ai. grep for 'openrouter' across the repo returns no hits. The base URL is overridable via config JSON (JEV_ROUTER_CONFIG), but the key env var name is hardcoded.
providerSupport.others: None. The only other key is CURSOR_API_KEY for the Cursor SDK runner.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The request body is {model,state,questions} and the response is answers.{tier,complexity,needs_approval}. This matches the System One shape that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts (web search of OpenRouter docs and third-party PRs), so a config change to baseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and model=typesafe/jev-latest plus a key is nearly enough. But the key env var is hardcoded to TYPESAFE_API_KEY (workaround: put the OpenRouter key in it). Search results say OpenRouter validates more strictly than TypeSafe. The Score question passes criteria as an array (typesafe-client.ts:95-101), and this could be rejected if OpenRouter needs an object. I could not fetch the OpenRouter schema page, so this is unverified. The larger problem is the payload, not the transport.

interface.purpose: Cursor slash-command markdown files.

gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.runtime: Node >=20, TypeScript run via tsx (npx tsx mcp/server.ts). Single dependency: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. Optional @cursor/sdk.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.install: Cursor-oriented: git clone, cp .env.example .env, npm install, then scripts/setup.sh, which symlinks into ~/.cursor/plugins/local. For Claude Code, the only manual path is `claude mcp add jev-router -- npx tsx <clone>/mcp/server.ts` with a key in .env. Nothing here is packaged for Claude Code, and it has no npm release or tag.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.tests: 3 node:test files (policy, redaction, router; 286 lines in total) that use a mock client. No CI workflow (.github is absent). No live-API test, and no test of the real HTTP client.
security: API key is read from env or from a .env in the repo root (mcp/server.ts:6-29, a hand-rolled parser). It is never put in argv. The key is sent only as a Bearer header to the configured baseUrl. Nothing stops baseUrl in config.json from pointing elsewhere.

No curl|sh, no postinstall script, no telemetry phone-home. Local telemetry is written to ./telemetry/events-DATE.jsonl relative to cwd (shared/telemetry.ts). By default it stores only a length and hash digest (logPromptContent=false). With true it stores the first 500 characters of the prompt, after regex secret redaction.
mcp.json uses `npx tsx` at every start, so it needs npm resolution at runtime (tsx is a devDependency and is fetched by npx). Node is spawned with NODE_OPTIONS=--use-system-ca.

Secret redaction patterns exist (shared/redaction.ts), but they are applied only to telemetry. They are NOT applied to the state sent to Jev; the raw task is sent, truncated to 4000 characters (typesafe-client.ts:113).

Prompt-injection surface: the tool result contains an 'instruction' field that tells the parent agent to delegate everything to a subagent. It is script-generated, not attacker-controlled, but the task text is model-supplied and can be steered by injected content in read files, which would bias the tier.

Silent mock fallback: with no TYPESAFE_API_KEY the server uses regex heuristics and returns a 'jev-mock' route without failing. useMock is set to !process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.ts:156). It would look like Jev is working when it is not.

Config lookup includes cwd/config.local.json and cwd/config.json, so a client repo containing such a file could redirect typesafe.baseUrl and receive the API key and task text (config-injection risk when run from untrusted repos).
Hard-policy keyword detection (detectSensitivity in policy.ts) is regex-based and tuned for email, finance and deploy tasks, not coding.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.dataEgress: The `state` object in every jev_route call goes to api.typesafe.ai (or another baseUrl if configured). It holds task[0:4000] (the raw task text the model passes in), objective, attachment metadata, tool names, and about 12 boolean or flag fields (mcp/typesafe-client.ts:111-132). There are no file contents or diffs unless the model pastes them into `task`. The task text is model-composed, so code or secrets can end up in it, and there is no redaction before sending. Local telemetry files contain digests only by default.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.failureMode: Fail-open. Jev errors, HTTP failures or timeouts (15s default, AbortController at typesafe-client.ts:57) become degradedRouting=true, and the tier falls back to BALANCED (router.ts:62-103). A 15s worst-case stall per route call is a long time for an interactive tool, though it only occurs if Jev hangs. A missing key gives silent mock routing (see security).
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.latencyImpact: One extra MCP tool call before every task, plus one Jev HTTP round trip (claimed 70-500 ms) and an extra model turn to call the tool and read the result. There is also a subagent hop for the delegated work, which adds tokens and loses parent context. The extra cost is per turn rather than per tool call, but it is paid on every prompt, including trivial ones.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Tool defs (names, descriptions, schemas) are about 3.0k characters, roughly 750 tokens. No MCP server 'instructions'. The Cursor rule (about 1.9k characters, about 480 tokens) is not loaded by Claude Code unless it is copied into CLAUDE.md. Each jev_route result adds roughly 300-500 tokens of JSON. If the 3 subagent files were installed as .claude/agents, that adds a few hundred more tokens. Total is about 1-1.5k tokens fixed plus per-turn results.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, and only if the Cursor rule text is copied into CLAUDE.md. The tool description says 'Parent agents MUST call this before delegating work'. In Claude Code there is no hook or deterministic trigger, so compliance is best-effort. Unlike Cursor, there is no alwaysApply rule mechanism, so the rule would have to be manually ported.
pros: Small, readable codebase (about 1.7k lines TS) with a minimal dependency (only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry to third parties, and key handling is env only.

Real use of the System One primitives (Choice, Score, Noul) with a sensible request shape and a clean typed client (typesafe-client.ts). This is a useful reference for building our own OpenRouter Jev call.
Fail-open with a 15s timeout and a BALANCED fallback, and explicit kill switches (enabled:false, /jev-bypass).
Transport is nearly OpenRouter-compatible: the same {model,state,questions} body, so baseUrl and model can be changed via config (providerSupport.openrouterPatchability).
MIT license, with unit tests on the policy and redaction logic.
cons: It is built for Cursor, not Claude Code. The output is 'delegate to subagent X' plus Cursor model IDs (composer-2.5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5). Claude Code subagents can take a model: frontmatter, but the shipped agents do not set one, and the main model (Opus 5.5) cannot be swapped mid-session by an MCP tool. The real routing benefit lives in the Cursor SDK runner and is unavailable here.

No OpenRouter support: key env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY hardcoded, default URL api.typesafe.ai, zero OpenRouter references. It needs config and env workarounds, and the strict OpenRouter validation of the Score criteria array is unverified.

The routing question ('which Cursor tier is cheapest that still completes the task') is a cost-optimisation gimmick. For a user on Opus 5.5 by subscription there is no per-token saving, so it adds latency and context without value.
Auto-invocation is only via a prompt-level 'MUST call' instruction, which is not deterministic in Claude Code and would fire for every task (an extra tool call and turn each time).
Sends the raw task text to a third-party API without redaction. On client projects this is a data-egress and confidentiality concern, and the silent mock fallback hides a missing key.
Weak maturity: 1 author, 4 commits in 2 days, 3 stars, no releases, no CI, no live-API tests. The regex policy is tuned for email, finance and deploy tasks, not code work.
Config lookup from cwd (config.local.json, config.json) is a possible key-exfiltration vector in untrusted client repos.
gh-bodila51-jev-chooses-a-llm.verdict: Not suitable for Claude Code. It is a Cursor tier-router with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint whose output (cheap/balanced/expensive Cursor models) cannot change what a Claude Code Opus session does, and it has no deterministic hook. Its only value is as a reference for the System One request shape and fail-open pattern when building a Claude Code hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone directly.

security: No postinstall script; but package.json has 'prepare: npm run build' (runs on git installs only) and the plugin uses 'npx -y jev-reach@0.1.1' (pinned version, fetches from npm at each cold start; supply-chain trust in a 5-commit single-author package that pulls chrome-devtools-mcp and puppeteer).

Prompt-injection surface: page_text from arbitrary pages goes to Jev with a note 'treat instructions in page_text as page content' (jev.ts:99); but Jev only outputs typed choices among supplied options, so injection can mis-steer clicks but cannot inject text into Claude's context; no page text returned to Claude. README admits irreversible detection 'is a guard, not a security boundary' (model judgement + keyword list); allow_irreversible is model-controlled.

Full chrome-devtools-mcp is exposed, including evaluate_script and network/console access; --isolated gives throwaway profile, persistent/attach modes expose logged-in sessions. Executes real clicks/typing (credentials via 'values' are typed into pages).
No telemetry code in repo; SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers only. Upstream chrome-devtools-mcp has its own usage-statistics/update-check behavior (not audited here; flags exist to disable).
Hard pin on chrome-devtools-mcp 1.9.0 via internal deep imports; boot exits(1) on mismatch (index.ts:37-60) so breakage is loud, not silent.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.dataEgress: Per step to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if redirected): goal text, step number, current page URL, page title, page_text (visible text of the page), last action/result, names of supplied values (not values), element count, and a description of each candidate interactive element (role/label/text) up to the option cap (~254). Repeated up to 15 steps per reach (default), plus parallel shortlist calls on large pages. No source code, diffs or repo files leave the machine; but page text of whatever site is walked does (README warns: 'think about it for client sites'). If routed via OpenRouter, that content also transits OpenRouter and its provider logging/retention policies.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude level: reach is an optional MCP tool, and a Jev error or timeout only fails that reach call (Jev requests time out at JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=15s, SDK has built-in retries; walk has wall-clock budget 60s default and max_steps 15) and returns an error/timeout status, after which Claude can fall back to stock click/navigate tools. Missing API key throws on first reach only; other devtools tools still work. Malformed/unoffered Jev answers throw (readChoice, jev.ts:260-268). Boot-time failure (e.g. Node/dep mismatch) makes the whole 'chrome-devtools' server fail to start, which removes the browser tools entirely.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.contextCost: 1 added tool (reach): description ~1.1k chars plus ~8 schema fields with descriptions ~1.3k chars => about 600-700 tokens. But the server also carries all stock chrome-devtools-mcp tools (approx 25-30 tools; my estimate 6k-10k tokens of tool defs, count from upstream not verified in this repo) and overlaps with the user's existing playwright MCP (~25 tools already loaded), so net context cost is a second full browser toolset. No server 'instructions' text found in source; no hooks, so zero injected hook text.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code sees 'reach' in its tool list and may choose it when a task involves getting a browser to a page state; the tool description is written to encourage this ('Get the browser to the exact place...'). It is not a hook, not a skill, not a transparent proxy, and only fires on browser/frontend-verification tasks, never on ordinary coding, editing or search.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.latencyImpact: Nothing on non-browser turns. Per reach call: README sample shows 4 Jev calls, 3.9s Jev time, 6.6s total for a 3-step login; per Jev step 0.4-2.0s observed (README claims ~300 ms), plus 500 ms network settle per action and Chrome launch. A 15-step walk can be 15-40 s. Saves Claude model turns and snapshot tokens on multi-click walks, but slower than a single direct navigate for trivial cases.
pros: Only candidate audited that is genuinely 'automatic' in the sense Claude picks it on its own: a well-worded model-discretion tool with typed statuses, so Claude will use it whenever a task requires driving a browser to a state (login, cookie banner, nested settings).

Good Jev design: every answer is a Choice among app-supplied options or a Noul, so Jev cannot invent elements or text; credentials passed as 'values' never reach Jev (only names, jev.ts:83); irreversible actions blocked by default (needs_confirmation).
Shares process and Chrome with chrome-devtools-mcp so console and network are recorded for the walk; returns no page text, saving Claude context on multi-click flows.

Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with configurable base URL: OpenRouter routing looks like pure env config (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13), path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One path.
MIT, small readable code (~1.5k lines), pinned deps, unit and e2e tests present, no hooks/postinstall, fail-open at tool level.
cons: Narrow: only helps browser verification of frontend bugs; nothing for everyday edit/search/refactor/commit/permission decisions, which is where this user spends the day.

Extremely immature: created 2026-09-20, 5 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI; depends on chrome-devtools-mcp internals via deep imports pinned to exactly 1.9.0, so upgrades of the stock server will not reach the user.
Requires removing/replacing any chrome-devtools entry, and duplicates the user's existing playwright MCP (second browser stack, ~25-30 more tool defs in context, 2 Chromes if both used).

OpenRouter not supported out of the box; works only if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is byte-compatible with TypeSafe's /v1/systemone (unverified); model id 'typesafe/jev-1.13' vs 'jev-latest' and error/usage shapes need a live test. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY to an OpenRouter key is confusing and easy to misconfigure.

Sends page text and element lists to a third party every step; on client sites this is a data-handling issue, and with bypass/auto permission mode Claude may launch it against logged-in or attach-mode browsers without a prompt.
Latency 0.4-2 s per Jev step in the author's own example, above the 70-500 ms claim; a wrong Jev pick wastes steps and 'irreversible' guard is admittedly not a security boundary.
Playwright MCP already lets Claude do the same walk with accessibility snapshots; the saving is only fewer model turns on long click paths.
gh-rashedint32-jev-reach.verdict: A tidy, honest proof-of-concept that lets Claude auto-delegate multi-click browser walks to Jev, and it is probably OpenRouter-compatible via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, but it only touches frontend browser verification, duplicates the user's playwright MCP, and is a 10-day-old single-author package. Worth trying in a sandboxed project if browser walks are frequent; not a core daily-coding integration.

gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.name: mywwave/cursor-jev
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.whatItDoes: Cursor-only plugin (hooks + stdio MCP + rule + skill, zero npm deps, Node 22.13+) that calls TypeSafe System One (model jev-latest) to gate agent behaviour. Hooks: rewrite/deny Task subagent hops (route by Choice+Noul), deny out-of-scope Write/StrReplace/Delete (scope Noul), split compound prompts, ask before destructive shell, rerank Grep/Glob hits and then DENY any Read outside a top-3 shortlist, and emit a "stop, work is ready" nudge after agent replies. MCP exposes jev_auth, jev_route, jev_judge, jev_ask. State kept in ~/.cursor/cursor-jev.sqlite. Not designed for Claude Code; README says "The plugin is Cursor-only".

providerSupport.evidence: src/client.mjs:3 `SYSTEM_ONE_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"`; src/client.mjs:47-52 POST with `Authorization: Bearer ${key}` and body `{model, state, questions}`; src/roles.mjs:3 `MODEL = "jev-latest"`; src/key.mjs:31,52 only TYPESAFE_API_KEY (env or ~/.cursor/cursor-jev.env). Grep for 'openrouter' across the repo: zero hits.
providerSupport.others: None. Single hard-coded endpoint, single env var.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The call is one fetch in src/client.mjs with a hard-coded URL and model, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-latest is a ~10-line change IF OpenRouter's System One body/response schema is identical to TypeSafe's (state + questions -> answers; unverified here). But the real blocker is not the provider: hook I/O contract, tool names (Task/StrReplace vs Claude Code Agent/Edit), and ~/.cursor paths are all Cursor-specific, so a Claude Code port is a rewrite of hook.mjs/install.mjs, not a URL swap.

security: Key stored in plaintext ~/.cursor/cursor-jev.env with mode 0600 (src/key.mjs:48-54); key passed via env/envFile, not argv (mcp.json envFile), so not visible in ps. set-key CLI prompts (no --key flag found).

Secret filter is weak: looksSecret (src/session.mjs:3) only matches 'apikey_', 'Bearer <tok>', 'TYPESAFE_API_KEY='. AWS keys, GitHub tokens, private keys, client credentials in Write previews, shell commands or search snippets would be sent to the API.
Write hook sends path + first 1200 chars of new content/old_string to a third party (src/hook.mjs:119-126); on client projects this is source-code egress.

Prompt-injection surface: task text, file snippets and agent responses are fed as Jev state; outputs only feed thresholds, but hook injects fixed strings, not model text, so injection risk is low. However an attacker-controlled repo could steer scope/read gates (deny Reads) via crafted content.

Read gate denies any file not in the reranked top-3 allowlist (src/hook.mjs:210-218) - behavioural risk not security: can block legitimate reads. handleReadGate has no try/catch (unlike other handlers), so a SQLite error crashes the hook.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh; install is a local `node bin/cli.mjs install` that edits ~/.cursor config. install.mjs writes ~/.cursor/hooks.json and mcp.json (would need porting).
Uses node:sqlite (experimental-era API) and concurrent WAL access from every hook process.
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on each gate: full Task prompt (<=12000 chars), user prompt (<=4000 chars, every submit), planned Write/Edit path plus 1200-char content preview, non-routine shell command text (1200 chars) plus user ask, search hit paths plus 180-char snippets (up to 16), Task results (1500 chars) and agent response summaries (1200 chars). File bodies of Reads are not sent. README claims secrets are stripped, but the filter is a 3-pattern regex. Sent to TypeSafe directly, not OpenRouter (would go to OpenRouter after a port).
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: missing key, HTTP error, timeout all return allow/{} (src/hook.mjs try/catch; README 'fail open'). Hook timeout 1.8s, 1 attempt (src/roles.mjs:12-13), Cursor-level hook timeout 5s (hooks/hooks.json). Exceptions: Read gate is uncaught, and once an allowlist exists it fails closed on unlisted paths independent of Jev availability. MCP path uses 15s timeout and 3 attempts with 429/529 retry (client.mjs:5-6, roles.mjs:10).
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.contextCost: Low for MCP: 4 tools (~1.2k chars descriptions + ~0.8k chars schemas) plus ~330-char server instructions, roughly 600-800 tokens, plus 2 prompts and 1 resource. Bundled SKILL.md (~2 KB, ~500 tokens when triggered) and an always-on rule (2.5 KB, ~650 tokens; Cursor concept, no Claude Code equivalent). Hooks inject text only occasionally (~30-40 tokens like 'Jev routed:... Jev speed: fast...' prefix on Task prompts, stop/scope nudges), but deny messages cost a wasted turn each.
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.latencyImpact: Each hook = fresh `node` process + node:sqlite open + one HTTPS call (claimed ~100ms, cap 1.8s). Fires on EVERY user prompt, every non-routine shell command, every Write/Edit and every Read (Read is local SQLite only), plus after every agent reply and search. Expect roughly 150-400 ms added per gated call and up to ~2s worst case; stacks on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Fail-open on timeout means slowness costs time, not correctness.
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (Cursor events) do the real work with no model involvement; MCP tools plus a skill/rule are model-discretion. Under Claude Code, none of this fires as-is: the hooks are registered in ~/.cursor/hooks.json using Cursor event names (preToolUse/beforeShellExecution/beforeSubmitPrompt/afterAgentResponse) and Cursor response fields (permission, agent_message, updated_input, additional_context). Only the stdio MCP server would load in Claude Code, giving model-discretion tools.
pros: Only candidate seen so far with a full deterministic-hook design for Jev (gates on prompts, writes, shell, search), i.e. the automatic 'no need to say use jev' pattern the user wants - useful as a design reference.
Sensible Jev usage: closed typed questions with thresholds in one reviewable file (src/roles.mjs), code decides, model never generates; matches Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives.
Hooks fail open on timeout/HTTP error/no key, with 1.8s cap and one attempt.
Zero npm deps, MIT, no postinstall/telemetry, key file 0600, key not in argv; small (~137 KB) and easy to audit; 4 test files (~56 tests) using injectable fetcher.
Central client.mjs makes provider swap mechanically small in code terms.
cons: Cursor-only by the author's own statement; hook events, tool names (Task, StrReplace), response schema and ~/.cursor install paths do not match Claude Code (Agent/Edit, hookSpecificOutput/permissionDecision). Would require a rewrite of hook.mjs/install.mjs.
No OpenRouter support: hard-coded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, jev-latest, TYPESAFE_API_KEY; zero mention of OpenRouter.
Brand new and unproven: created 2026-09-20, 4 commits in one afternoon, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, no CI, no issues history; version 0.1.0.

Value proposition (deny Task hops, deny Reads outside top-3, block writes deemed out-of-scope) mostly addresses Cursor cost/latency, and can actively harm a senior dev on bypass/auto mode: false-positive scope denies and Read denies burn turns and derail client work.
Claims of 'almost useless on one-file tweak' and speed gains are unmeasured; no benchmark of Jev gate accuracy (skeptics say Jev may be a small router model).
Heavy per-event egress of code snippets, prompts and shell commands to a beta third-party API with a weak 3-regex secret filter; risky for client projects under NDAs.
Per-event node cold start plus network on every prompt/shell/write/response adds latency stacked on existing PreToolUse hooks; read gate uncaught exception path.
Overlaps and may conflict with the user's GitNexus grep/glob context hook and secret-guard (competing additional_context / deny decisions).
gh-mywwave-cursor-jev.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code or with OpenRouter without a substantial rewrite; treat it as a design reference for hook-driven Jev gating (scope/split/destructive-shell) rather than something to install. The aggressive Read/Write denial and code-snippet egress make a straight port undesirable for client work.
