gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.name: wangBoYi972/typesafe-mcp
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Single-file Python stdio MCP server (server.py, 343 lines) with 3 model-discretion tools that POST to the TypeSafe System One endpoint with a hardcoded question set. One generic tool (typesafe_classify) plus two hardcoded Chinese-language templates: support-ticket triage and content moderation. Nothing here is aimed at coding work.

providerSupport.evidence: server.py:24-33 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required, exits if missing) and TYPESAFE_API_ENDPOINT, default https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. server.py:56-61 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' with payload {state, model, questions} via requests.post, with no timeout. The payload shape matches the OpenRouter System One schema in the OpenRouter TypeSafe SDK docs page (model/state/questions; choice uses a criteria dict; noul uses instructions). The server does not mention OpenRouter, and the default model 'jev-latest' (server.py:47) is accepted bare by OpenRouter, per those docs.
providerSupport.others: README also advertises 'codex-latest' (server.py:91), a model that is not part of the Jev brief and may be invalid on OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and no code edit: set TYPESAFE_API_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> in the MCP env block. I did not test this against OpenRouter (nothing was run). Caveats: no timeout, and the score questions are built wrongly (see cons).

interface.name: typesafe_classify
interface.purpose: Generic tool. Args: content (becomes state), questions (free-form object the model must build in the System One schema), model enum [jev-latest, codex-latest]. Returns the raw JSON answers (server.py:76-98, 178-196).

interface.name: typesafe_ticket_classify
interface.purpose: Takes title and content. Sends a hardcoded 5-question set (type, priority P0-P3, department, emotion, impact score), with Chinese labels and 'state' text (server.py:99-122, 199-267).

interface.name: typesafe_content_moderate
interface.purpose: Takes content. Sends noul questions for violence, sexual, hate speech and spam, plus a risk score and an approve/review/reject choice, all in Chinese (server.py:123-142, 270-322).

security: API key is passed through the MCP env block (README), not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. Bearer header only.
No install script, no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry. Only deps are mcp and requests (unpinned: mcp>=1.0.0, requests>=2.31.0).
requests.post has no timeout (server.py:61), so a hung upstream blocks a worker thread indefinitely.
The tool result is the raw upstream JSON dumped as text (server.py:191-196), with no sanitizing. Risk is low because Jev returns typed output, not free text.
Errors are caught and returned as 'Error: <exception>' (server.py:168-175). A requests exception message can include the endpoint URL but not the key.
Single-author repo created 2026-09-23 with 1 star and no releases or CI. Supply-chain trust is low, but the code is small enough to audit in 5 minutes, and I did.
README/commit tell users to pip install the requirements and run a checked-out server.py. Fine for a one-file read, but nothing is pinned or hashed.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: On each tool call, only what the model puts into the 'content' or 'questions' arguments (or title/content for the ticket tool) leaves the machine. It goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to OpenRouter if the endpoint is overridden. The server has no hooks and never reads files, diffs or tool outputs itself. Whatever code or text Claude chooses to pass is sent to a third party, and client-project code would be included if Claude passes it.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open in effect. Errors are returned to Claude as an isError tool result, so Claude carries on without Jev. The real risk is that there is no HTTP timeout (server.py:61): a slow upstream can hang the tool call for as long as requests waits. Startup is fail-closed for this server only: it exits with code 1 if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset (server.py:25-28), which shows up as a failed MCP connection. Under mcp 1.x it would also crash, because the code uses the 2.x Server(on_list_tools=...) constructor. requirements.txt allows mcp>=1.0.0, so a pinned 1.x install would fail; I confirmed against mcp 2.2.0 sdist source that those kwargs exist there.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 3 tools. Approx 500-700 tokens of tool names + descriptions + schemas (about 2-2.5k chars of JSON schema). The descriptions are in Chinese, so token counts run higher per character and Claude gets weak triggering signals from them. No MCP server 'instructions' and no hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred MCP tool loading, the cost is lower still.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills or CLAUDE.md snippets. The tool descriptions are Chinese-language and describe ticket triage and content moderation, so Claude has no reason to call them during coding unless the user prompts it. That is exactly what the user wants to avoid.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Adds one MCP tool call (about 70-500 ms upstream plus Python stdio overhead) only when Claude chooses to call a tool. It adds nothing per turn. Startup cost is a Python interpreter plus the mcp import.

gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.install: pip install -r requirements.txt, then add an mcpServers entry to ~/.claude.json: command python, args [/path/server.py], env {TYPESAFE_API_KEY}. pros: Small (343 lines) and easy to audit. No shell exec, no telemetry, no installers.

The System One payload shape (state/model/questions, choice criteria dict, noul instructions) matches OpenRouter's documented schema, so pointing it at OpenRouter is one env var (TYPESAFE_API_ENDPOINT) plus the key.
The API key goes in via the MCP env block, not argv.
The generic typesafe_classify tool lets Claude build its own choice/noul/score questions, so it could serve as a raw System One passthrough (e.g. 'is this diff risky?').
MIT license. The 3-tool footprint is light on context.
cons: Wrong domain for this user: the two purpose-built tools are Chinese-language support-ticket triage and content moderation, which have no use in coding.

No auto-invocation: it is a plain MCP tool, and the descriptions never mention code, diffs, commits, or PRs. Claude will rarely call it unprompted, so the user's core requirement is unmet. It would need extra CLAUDE.md text or a hook.
No timeout on requests.post (server.py:61), so a hung upstream can stall a tool call.

Score questions are malformed: the ticket/moderation templates pass criteria as 3 strings ('影响范围评分','1=个别用户','10=全站影响') plus a 'score':{min,max} field (server.py:247-251, 292-299). The OpenRouter docs describe score as an ordered criteria list of levels, so 3 strings would be read as 3 levels, not a 1-10 scale. Results are likely wrong or misleading.
Requires the mcp 2.x lowlevel API (on_list_tools kwargs); requirements.txt says >=1.0.0, so a pinned 1.x install crashes.
'codex-latest' in the model enum is unexplained and unvalidated.
Not battle-tested: 1 commit, 1 star, created 7 days before audit, no tests or CI. The commit message shows it was AI-generated, and the repo description is just 'typesafe-mcp'.
Anything Claude passes is sent to a third party. On client projects that means code egress at Claude's discretion, with no allow/deny filter.
No caching, retries or rate-limit handling.
gh-wangboyi972-typesafe-mcp.verdict: A tiny, honest, OpenRouter-patchable wrapper, but it targets Chinese ticket triage and moderation, and it is an opt-in MCP tool with no auto-trigger. It would not deliver 'Claude uses Jev automatically'. At most, borrow the typesafe_classify passthrough idea, and write your own coding-focused hook or tool with a timeout and coding-oriented question templates.

security: Created 2026-09-22, 8 days old; 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases or tags. Effectively a weekend proof of concept.
MIT license; unofficial, with a disclaimer in the README.

API key is read from the environment and sent only as a Bearer header to JEV_API_BASE. It is not logged, and error paths return only response text (first 500 chars) and JSON body. Stdio mode with 'env' in the MCP config keeps the key out of argv. The recommended HTTP mode keeps it in the container env or .env instead.

Recommended mode is an unauthenticated HTTP MCP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:8000 (the compose file binds 127.0.0.1). Any local process or browser-origin request to localhost can call it, spending the user's key and sending arbitrary state. Inside the container it binds 0.0.0.0, which is safe only because of the 127.0.0.1 port mapping. The README's 'docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000' is also safe.
JEV_API_BASE is unvalidated: a poisoned env or .env could redirect the key and state to another host. Only a local trust issue.

env.py:9-18 loads a .env from the package's repo root via python-dotenv. With a non-editable pip install this resolves to site-packages parents and is harmless. Under uv/editable use it loads the repo .env.

No shell execution, no postinstall, no telemetry, no curl|sh. Dependencies: httpx, mcp, pydantic, python-dotenv (unpinned lower bounds; mcp>=1.0 in pyproject, but server.py imports mcp.server.mcpserver, which exists only in mcp 2.x. Verified in the mcp 2.2.0 wheel. A resolver picking 1.x would break it).
Prompt-injection surface is small. Output is numeric or enum JSON from Jev with no free text, apart from the echoed error snippets. The main risk is that Claude sends state it should not.

Docker image is published to GHCR on every push to main, tagged latest and by SHA, with no signing or pinning. Pin a SHA or build from source after reading it. Actions are pinned to floating major tags (checkout@v7 etc.).
gh-chrishow2-mcp-jev.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts in the jev_decide arguments: the 'state' JSON or string and the question instructions and criteria. That goes from the local MCP process (or Docker container) to JEV_API_BASE (TypeSafe by default, or OpenRouter if patched). Nothing is sent automatically, and there is no telemetry and no persistence in the server. Whatever Claude decides to classify (code, diffs, tool output, file contents) is exposed to TypeSafe/OpenRouter and their upstream providers. Client-project code therefore needs an explicit data policy. The user's global secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover the mcp__jev__ matcher unless it is extended.
gh-chrishow2-mcp-jev.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level and blocking-heavy in time. Every error path returns a structured error JSON string and never raises, so Claude just sees {error:true}. Missing key returns a 401-style error. Timeout is 30 s per request (JEV_TIMEOUT_SEC), with retries only on HTTP 429/529 (up to 3, sleeps of 1, 2, 4 s or Retry-After) using synchronous time.sleep. A network timeout or connection error (httpx exception) is not retried and is caught by the generic handler as a 500. Worst case is about 4x30 s plus backoff on repeated 429s. If the Docker container is down, the MCP server shows as failed to connect in Claude Code and its tools are simply absent; it does not break other work. There is no circuit breaker and no fallback.
gh-chrishow2-mcp-jev.contextCost: 1 tool (jev_decide). Estimated tool definition about 900 chars, roughly 225 to 300 tokens, covering the name, a one-line description, and schema for state (anyOf string/object/array), questions (object) and model. Plus about 230 chars (about 60 tokens) of server instructions. Total about 300 to 350 tokens per session (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch). No hook-injected text.
gh-chrishow2-mcp-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no proxy. Claude calls jev_decide only if its own judgment says a calibrated yes/no, choice or score fits, and it must also construct the questions JSON itself each time. The generic instruction text gives Claude little reason to reach for it in normal coding turns, so in practice it would fire rarely. To make it automatic the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook on top, which this project does not provide.
gh-chrishow2-mcp-jev.latencyImpact: Zero when unused. Per call: local MCP hop plus Jev's claimed 70-500 ms network round trip, plus one extra model turn for Claude to compose the questions JSON and read the result (about 1-3 s of Opus time). The sync httpx client creates a new connection per request (no client reuse), which adds TLS setup of about 50-150 ms. The streamable-http stateless mode adds negligible overhead.

The user's requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told) is not met, and nothing routes tool calls, prompts or diffs through Jev. The user would have to write the automation (CLAUDE.md rules or hooks) themselves.

Claude must hand-write a full questions JSON (instructions plus criteria) on every call, costing tokens and an extra Opus turn. There are no preset gates such as risky-command check, commit-message classification or test-failure triage.

gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.name: altregubov/jev-antigravity-mcp (jev-mcp-proxy)
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Python (~535 LOC) stdio MCP server built on the mcp SDK (imports mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, i.e. mcp 2.x). Exposes 4 tools that forward a caller-supplied state plus typed questions to TypeSafe System One (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, Bearer auth) and return typed answers: jev_evaluate (batch), jev_choice, jev_noul, jev_score. Retries 429/529 with backoff. Written for Google Antigravity; README has a generic Claude Code/Cursor config snippet. Pure passive tool: no hooks, no skills, no routing logic.

providerSupport.evidence: jev_proxy/client.py:230 DEFAULT_ENDPOINT='https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone'. client.py:269-270 read TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. client.py:272-275: a base ending in /v1 gets '/systemone' appended, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 resolves to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (the OpenRouter System One URL). client.py:299-303 send 'Authorization: Bearer <key>', so an OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY would be sent correctly. Default model 'jev-latest' (server.py:51,87,125,162; client.py:293) is NOT an OpenRouter model id (needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest), so model must be passed on every call or the default patched. Payload is {state, model, questions} (client.py:305-309); it is unverified that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts exactly this schema. grep -i openrouter over the repo: zero hits. Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) not supported.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. Env-only route: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, and force the model id (~typesafe/jev-latest) since the default 'jev-latest' is likely rejected; a 4-line default-model patch fixes that. Only residual risk is request/response schema parity with OpenRouter's System One API, which was not verified against a live call (static analysis only).
providerSupport.others: None. Only TypeSafe direct; any other gateway only through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.

gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.runtime: Python >=3.10 (uv), deps mcp, httpx, pydantic. uv.lock pins mcp 2.2.0, but pyproject says mcp>=1.3.0 while the code needs the 2.x-only mcp.server.mcpserver module. A uvx --from git+... install ignores uv.lock and could resolve an incompatible mcp version.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.install: README: uvx --from git+https://github.com/altregubov/jev-antigravity-mcp jev-mcp (unpinned git HEAD, runs unreviewed code on every fresh resolve), or git clone + 'uv run --directory PATH jev-mcp'. Add via a .mcp.json / claude mcp add stdio entry with env TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No release tags, no PyPI package.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.tests: 3 test files (tests/test_client.py 203 lines, test_server.py 178, test_stdio.py 70) using httpx mock transport. No CI (no .github directory). Not executed by me per the hard rules.
security: API key from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (good, not in argv), but the --api-key CLI flag would expose it in the process list, and every tool takes an optional api_key argument, so the model can put a key into tool-call arguments and transcripts (server.py:52, 90, 128, 164).
No shell execution, no eval, no postinstall or curl|sh. Only outbound httpx POST to the configured endpoint (client.py:320).

Logs to stderr at INFO by default (JEV_DEBUG defaults to '1', client.py:228): endpoint, model, question ids, latency, token counts. On non-200 it logs the full response.text (client.py:349), which could echo request content on 4xx. State content itself is not logged.
No telemetry beyond the User-Agent 'jev-mcp-proxy/0.1.0'.
Prompt-injection surface is small: outputs are numeric or typed labels. The risk is the reverse, since the model decides what state to ship out.
Supply chain: single-author, 1-star, 4-commit repo installed from unpinned git HEAD, no signed releases, no CI. An arbitrary-code-execution trust decision for a client-project machine.

Nothing enforces secret redaction: state is free-form, so if Claude passes file contents or diffs they go to the provider unfiltered (the existing secret-leak guard hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not MCP tools).
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.dataEgress: Exactly what the model puts in the tool arguments: the 'state' (any text or JSON: could be code, diffs, logs, file contents, tool outputs), plus 'instructions' and 'criteria', sent over HTTPS to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe direct by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden, and then OpenRouter and the upstream Jev host both see it). The Bearer key goes in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, but it does not crash the session. Errors (401/422/429/529/network) become ToolError 'Jev routing error: ...' (server.py:74-75), and Claude sees the error and can continue without Jev. Timeout is 30 s per attempt (client.py:265), and max_retries=3 for network errors and 429/529 with backoff 0.5, 1, 2 s or Retry-After, so the worst case is about 2 minutes of blocking on a hung endpoint. 401/422 fail immediately. The timeout is not configurable via env. No circuit breaker, so repeated calls during an outage each pay the full penalty. It never blocks tool use the way a PreToolUse hook could.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.latencyImpact: Per call: about 70-500 ms Jev latency (claimed) plus stdio round trip, plus one model turn to emit the tool call and read the result (typically 1-3 s of Opus turn overhead). Each call opens a new httpx.AsyncClient (no connection reuse), adding TLS handshake cost of roughly 50-150 ms. Cold start with uvx-from-git adds a git resolve and env build on first launch. Zero cost on turns where the model does not call it.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.contextCost: 4 tools plus server instructions. Estimated ~1.2-1.6k tokens always loaded in the session: 4 tool descriptions (~230 chars each) plus JSON schemas with nested Union[str, dict, list] types on state/instructions, plus the ~330-char instructions string (~0.3k). Unless Claude Code tool search defers MCP tools, this is loaded every turn. No hook-injected text.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The sole nudge is a generic server-instructions string ('use whenever a skill needs fast, structured decisions...'), which is written for agent skills, not coding. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no skill. Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for a classifier tool during normal coding, because it has no concrete coding use case (no 'is this diff risky', no 'which file is relevant', no 'should I run tests'). Achieving the user's 'never prompt use jev' goal would require adding your own CLAUDE.md rules or hooks on top.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related and minimal: one small file set (~535 LOC) that is easy to audit; I read all source (server.py, client.py, models.py) and found no shell exec, no telemetry, no installer hooks.
Exposes all three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) plus a batch tool, so the typed-decision surface is complete for building your own gating logic.
Base-URL normalization (client.py:272-275) makes 'TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1' resolve to the OpenRouter /v1/systemone path, so an OpenRouter route is close to env-only.
Key comes from env by default; sane retry and Retry-After handling on 429/529; errors surface as clean ToolErrors so Claude continues without Jev.
MIT licensed; tests exist (client, server, stdio handshake); uv.lock pins deps.
Server-instructions text explicitly tells the model when to use it, which is the only auto-invocation lever an MCP server has.
cons: Age 12 days, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, no CI: PoC-grade for a beta model.

No OpenRouter awareness: default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id, no OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var (must abuse TYPESAFE_API_KEY), and no support for the /api/alpha/decisions API. Schema parity with OpenRouter System One is unverified.
Not automatic: pure model-discretion tools with a generic instruction. Fails the user's core requirement ('Claude Code must use it when needed') without extra hooks or CLAUDE.md rules.

No coding-specific design: it is a generic pass-through, so Claude must compose state and rubrics itself each time, and Jev's 32k context and no-reasoning design gives little value to an Opus 5.5 session doing agentic coding.
Unpinned uvx-from-git install of a 1-star single-author repo is a supply-chain risk on client projects; pyproject 'mcp>=1.3.0' conflicts with the 2.x-only import, so a non-lock resolve may break.

Exfiltration risk: the model can send arbitrary code, diffs or file contents as 'state', and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools. The api_key tool parameter lets keys leak into transcripts.
Timeouts/retries up to about 2 minutes per call with no env config or circuit breaker; a new HTTP client per call (no connection reuse); stderr logging on by default.
~1.2-1.6k tokens of always-on tool and schema context for a tool that will rarely be called.
gh-altregubov-jev-antigravity-mcp.verdict: A clean, small, honest passthrough MCP for Jev, but a 12-day-old one-author PoC that is TypeSafe-direct only, has no auto-invocation beyond a generic instruction, and no coding use cases. Useful at most as a reference, or as a base to fork with OpenRouter defaults and pair with your own hooks or CLAUDE.md gating; not something to install as-is for automatic Jev use.

gh-obrais-cloud-typesafe-mcp.name: Obrais-cloud/typesafe-mcp
gh-obrais-cloud-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP) written for one person's private agent fleet (openclaw/hermes, Mac mini, Tailscale IPs). It exposes 7 tools over the TypeSafe direct API (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13.0): judge (NL request compiled by a private Ollama fleet LLM into a typed noul/choice/score request), rerank, systemone (raw passthrough), quality_judge, compare, classify_push_failure, job_fit (shells out to a personal career-ops script). Also includes cron triage/ledger/router-shadow scripts, launchd plists and a vendored copy of the official TypeSafe SKILL.md. Not a Claude Code plugin, no hooks.

Tools are mostly non-coding (job_fit, quality_judge/compare for LLM-eval, rerank tickets); only classify_push_failure is coding-adjacent and marginal.
No license (all rights reserved), 1 commit author, 1 star, 33 commits in 11 days, no releases/CI/packaging, tests cover only jevkit and ledger; leaks author's infra details in tree.
Extra dead-host latency: up to 4 unreachable probes + 10 s wake before erroring.
Requires Jev to be called through Claude as a tool: an Opus turn to build the request then read probabilities, so cost/latency far exceeds the 70-500 ms Jev call itself.
gh-obrais-cloud-typesafe-mcp.verdict: Not suitable as the Claude Code integration: it is a private-fleet MCP wrapper for TypeSafe direct, with headline tools that depend on the author's Ollama hosts, no OpenRouter path, no license and no automatic triggering. At most, reuse its validation rules and the systemone URL override idea as reference material for a custom minimal hook or MCP.

gh-tomasthrawat-typesafe-mcp-key.name: TomasThrawat/typesafe-mcp-key
gh-tomasthrawat-typesafe-mcp-key.whatItDoes: Personal Vercel-hosted "custom MCP" for a Kotlin mobile app. The committed api/mcp.js (the deployed /mcp function) is NOT a Jev/System One bridge: it exposes health, chat, send-photo and send-file, which forward user text, files and images to OpenRouter /v1/chat/completions using hard-coded free models (nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free, inclusionai/ling-3.0-flash-vl:free). A System One tool (system_one, via @typesafe-ai/sdk) exists only in server.js and api/ask.js. server.js imports the wrong package path ("@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server") that is not in package.json, so it is likely dead code. README and package.json describe System One, but the deployed MCP does something else. It is a hosted relay that receives your API key and content, not a local server.

providerSupport.evidence: OpenRouter is used only for chat completions to free non-Jev models: api/mcp.js:75-77 and api/chat.js:226-228 (https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions), models at api/mcp.js:5-6. No use of openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, /api/v1/systemone or typesafe/jev-* anywhere in the repo. System One is called only through @typesafe-ai/sdk in server.js:40 and api/ask.js:81. The SDK defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai and POSTs /v1/systemone (sdk index.mjs:513,554). Its baseURL is configurable in the SDK, but this repo never passes it. Env vars: TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.js:29, ask.js:60), OPENROUTER_API_KEY (api/mcp.js:16).

gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.name: miskakaskinen/typesafe-mcp (evaluate)
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.whatItDoes: Single static Go binary `evaluate` that runs as a stdio MCP server exposing one read-only tool, `evaluate`. The tool forwards {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} to Jev and returns the raw typed JSON. It picks its backend from env: TYPESAFE_API_KEY goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, otherwise OPENROUTER_API_KEY goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest. It also has `setup mcp` (registers with Claude Code, Codex and Claude Desktop), `setup pi`, `update` and `version`. It is only a thin transport: the host model still has to decide when to call it and what state and questions to send.

providerSupport.evidence: cmd/evaluate/client.go:37-52: `case vars["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"] != ""` -> URL https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, Model jev-latest; `case vars["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"] != ""` -> URL https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, Model ~typesafe/jev-latest. Auth is `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (client.go:82). If both keys are set, TYPESAFE wins (client.go:23-27, README:61). setup.go:163 only copies TYPESAFE_* and OPENROUTER_API_KEY= into the client env. /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter is not used.
providerSupport.others: None. Endpoints are hardcoded, with no base-URL override env var. Codex, Claude Desktop and pi are also supported as hosts.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter works natively when only OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set and TYPESAFE_* is unset. The endpoint is the alpha /api/alpha/decisions path, and the README itself warns it may move (README:61). It is hardcoded, so a path change means editing client.go:47 and rebuilding.

interface.name: MCP tool `evaluate` (read-only, ReadOnlyHint)
interface.purpose: Sends state and a map of typed questions (noul, choice, score) to Jev. Returns raw typed JSON with probabilities, choice, confidence and legend, keyed by question id. Criteria shapes are validated locally (tools.go:114-146).

interface.name: MCP server instructions (evaluateInstructions)
interface.purpose: About 11 guideline lines (tools.go:30-43) injected into the host's system prompt. They explain how to phrase questions, the effect of putting a conclusion in state, batching, and how to read scores.

interface.name: CLI `evaluate mcp`
interface.purpose: Runs the stdio MCP server. It exits with an error if neither key is set, which shows up in Claude Code as a failed server (main.go:87-95).

interface.name: CLI `evaluate setup mcp`
interface.purpose: Runs `claude mcp add evaluate -s user -e KEY=VAL -- <exe> mcp`, and does the same for Codex, and edits the Claude Desktop config. The API key is passed on argv (setup_hosts.go:119-126) and stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

interface.name: CLI `evaluate setup pi`
interface.purpose: Writes a pi extension (~/.pi/agent/extensions/evaluate.ts). Irrelevant for Claude Code.

interface.name: CLI `evaluate update` / `version`
interface.purpose: Self-update from GitHub releases with a SHA256SUMS check (update.go:190-203), and print the version.

security: API key handling: `evaluate setup mcp` calls `claude mcp add ... -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key>` (setup_hosts.go:121-125), so the key is visible in argv and the process list briefly. It is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. This can be avoided by running `claude mcp add` by hand, or by using an env reference or wrapper.
At runtime the key is read from the process env and sent only as a Bearer header to the hardcoded HTTPS endpoint (client.go:82). It is not logged and there is no telemetry in the code I read.
No shell execution in the server path. The only exec.Command calls are the setup adapters, which run `claude` and `codex` with fixed argv (setup_hosts.go:28-30).

The install.sh in the README is a curl|sh installer. It does verify a SHA256SUMS.txt fetched from the same GitHub release, so the checksum protects against corruption but not against a compromised release. The install URL points at PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which returns 404. This repo has no releases at all (releases API returns []). The install.sh and `evaluate update` paths would therefore fail as documented, and the only working path is building from source with Go.

README badges and install URLs reference github.com/PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which does not resolve (404 via gh api). The clone under miskakaskinen is not a fork (fork=false) and has 0 stars. Provenance is muddy: the README says it is maintained by elkaix under PyModel, and nearly all commits are by author elkaix. A future PyModel org could be squatted, and install.sh/update would then fetch binaries from whoever owns that org.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is JSON of probabilities, not free text, so returned content is low-risk. The state the host sends is untrusted repo or tool content that goes to a third party.
Dependencies are Go modules (go-sdk, cobra, jsonschema-go). CI actions are pinned by SHA (ci.yml). Response body is capped at 16 MiB and Retry-After is capped at 60s.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the host model puts in `state` and in the question `instructions`/`criteria`, sent as JSON to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai). This can include code, diffs, logs, tickets and file contents that Claude chooses to pass. It is not automatic, since the server sees nothing except what Claude passes in a tool call. The OpenRouter key goes in the Authorization header. No telemetry was found in the code. `evaluate update` and install.sh contact api.github.com and github.com. On OpenRouter the data is subject to OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies, which matters for client projects.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by nature, since it is a model-discretion tool. The HTTP timeout is 60s (client.go:35). 429 and 529 are retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff starting at 1s, or Retry-After capped at 60s (client.go:101-110). Worst case is about 60s x 4 plus backoff before a tool error is returned to Claude, which then just carries on. Other errors come back as an IsError tool result. If no key is set at startup the server exits and Claude Code shows it as a failed MCP server, but the session continues. There is no hook, so a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code. The 60s timeout is long compared with the claimed 70-500ms latency, so a stalled call would hang a turn.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call the tool. When it does, the cost is one extra tool round trip, about 70-500ms claimed for Jev plus Claude's tokens to author the state and questions JSON (often 300-1500 output tokens) and a further turn to read the result. In practice this is often slower than Claude answering the question itself. Server startup is a static Go binary, so about 10-50ms and no npx cold start.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Tool description is about 690 chars (tools.go:51-56). The input schema with jsonschema tags is about 1.3k chars (tools.go:58-68). Server instructions are about 2.1k chars of guidelines (tools.go:30-43), which the MCP client injects into the system prompt. Total is about 4.1k chars, roughly 1,000 tokens, always present in every session. There is no hook-injected text. That is small compared with playwright and gitnexus.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no proxy. Claude will call `evaluate` when its description ("classification, routing, scoring, extraction, branching, guardrails/judging") seems relevant, but for ordinary coding turns it almost never does, since Opus decides itself and the tool says "Not for prose, code". There is no deterministic trigger. The desired "Claude Code uses Jev automatically when it adds value" is only weakly met, with no code-level rules for when to call. Realistic use is limited to explicit classification or triage tasks.
pros: Native OpenRouter support with the exact endpoint the user wants: OPENROUTER_API_KEY only gives /api/alpha/decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest (client.go:45-52). No patching needed.
Tiny context footprint: one tool, about 1k tokens including instructions. Much cheaper than the user's existing playwright and gitnexus servers.

Well-engineered wrapper: local criteria validation with JSON-path errors (tools.go:114-146), 429/529 backoff, 16 MiB cap, 60s timeout. 117 tests exist (evaluate_test.go, 34 KB, roughly 22 top-level Test funcs by grep). CI runs gofmt, vet and go test -race with SHA-pinned actions.
Single static Go binary, MIT licensed. No Node or Python runtime, and no npx cold start.
Good agent guidance is baked into the server instructions: do not put your verdict in state, batch independent questions, and read noul near 0.5 as uncertain. This reduces misuse of Jev.
The tool is read-only and returns typed JSON only, so the prompt-injection surface from the response is small.
No telemetry found. Failure is fail-open, because a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code.
cons: Not an automatic integration. It is a plain MCP tool that relies on Opus choosing to call it. There is no hook or skill trigger, and the description itself excludes code and prose, so it will rarely fire on daily coding. This directly misses the user's goal of Claude Code using Jev without being prompted.
Very young: repo created 2026-09-20, 62 commits in about 2 days (most commits by one author, elkaix), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases and no tags on the GitHub repo. Maturity is proof-of-concept.

Broken distribution: README, install.sh and `evaluate update` point to github.com/PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which returns 404, and this repo has no releases. The curl|sh installer and updater cannot work as documented. It must be built from source (`go build`, and go.mod may demand a very new Go toolchain, which was not verified). It must also be reviewed and built by the user, since running it here is forbidden.

`evaluate setup mcp` puts OPENROUTER_API_KEY on argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (setup_hosts.go:121-125). It is better to register by hand with an env reference, or a wrapper that reads the key from a secrets store.

Hardcoded alpha endpoint (client.go:47) with no base-URL or model env override. If OpenRouter moves /api/alpha/ the binary must be rebuilt. It does not use the newer /api/v1/systemone route on OpenRouter.

Data egress is model-chosen: Claude decides what code, diff or log to send to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That may violate client confidentiality unless the user restricts it, and the existing secret-leak guard does not cover mcp__ tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).

Adds a round trip and Claude authoring tokens for each use. For most coding decisions Opus 5.5 is both faster and better than authoring a Jev question. The 60s timeout with 3 retries is far above the claimed sub-500ms latency.
Documentation is inconsistent about ownership (miskakaskinen copy, PyModel org, elkaix maintainer). A supply-chain risk if the PyModel org name is claimed by someone else.
gh-miskakaskinen-typesafe-mcp.verdict: The best-written Jev MCP wrapper I inspected for OpenRouter: it supports OPENROUTER_API_KEY natively, has a small context footprint and fails open. It is still a model-discretion tool with no automatic trigger, so it will not deliver "Claude uses Jev when it is useful", and it is a two-day-old repo with no releases and dead install links. Build it from source after review and register it manually so the key stays off argv. Treat it as an optional building block for explicit routing or classification, not as the automatic integration.

gh-djancyp-oido-typesafeai-mcp.name: Djancyp/oido-typesafeai-mcp (oido-typesafe MCP extension)
gh-djancyp-oido-typesafeai-mcp.whatItDoes: Small Go stdio MCP server (about 240 lines plus a 90-line HTTP client) written as a plugin for Oido Studio. It exposes four tools (typesafe_choice, typesafe_noul, typesafe_score, typesafe_ask) that wrap TypeSafe's System One API. Each tool POSTs {state, model, questions} to <BASE_URL>/systemone with a Bearer key and renders the typed answer (choice, probabilities, noul, score, confidence) as plain text. It has nothing Claude-Code-specific: no hooks, skills or plugin.json. It is a plain MCP server that works with Claude Code once built.

providerSupport.evidence: config.go:9-10 defaultBaseURL=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1, defaultModel=jev-latest. config.go:16-30 read OIDO_TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required), OIDO_TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and OIDO_TYPESAFE_MODEL. client.go:59 builds url := c.cfg.BaseURL + "/systemone"; client.go:65-66 sets Authorization: Bearer <key>. client.go:26-30 request body is {state, model, questions}. OpenRouter's System One API is POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, uses the same TypeSafe request/response shapes (model, state, questions -> model, answers, usage) and a Bearer OpenRouter key (confirmed via web search of the OpenRouter/TypeSafe SDK docs, not by running the code). README:35 explicitly says the base URL can point at a 'compatible endpoint'. The code has no OpenRouter code path. It also does not use the /api/alpha/decisions endpoint.
providerSupport.others: Any endpoint that speaks the TypeSafe /systemone schema. The Oido config also accepts a JSON --config flag (main.go:12-31), and env vars take precedence over it.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and no code change. Set OIDO_TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (the client appends /systemone), OIDO_TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<the OpenRouter key>, and OIDO_TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). The model must be set explicitly, because the default 'jev-latest' is the bare TypeSafe name and is probably not a valid OpenRouter slug. The env var name is misleading, since it holds an OpenRouter key. Caveat: I did not run it, and the OpenRouter answer schema was only confirmed indirectly.

interface.name: typesafe_choice
interface.purpose: Pick exactly one option from a map of option -> rubric (at least 2; the code enforces only the minimum, mcp_server.go:109). Returns the choice, the probabilities and the confidence. Note that renderAnswer prints probabilities in Go map order, so the output order is non-deterministic.

interface.name: typesafe_noul
interface.purpose: Yes/no condition -> calibrated P(true). Optional true/false criteria. Instructions are required.

interface.name: typesafe_score
interface.purpose: Rate on an ordered scale of 2-10 level descriptions -> probability-weighted score plus legend.

interface.name: typesafe_ask
interface.purpose: Batch of independent noul/choice/score questions over one shared state, in a single request. The answers are rendered as markdown (mcp_server.go:184-190).

interface.name: commands/typesafe-{choice,noul,score}.toml
interface.purpose: Oido/Gemini-CLI style slash-command templates. They are not used by Claude Code.

interface.name: OIDO.md (contextFileName)
interface.purpose: Guidance text with an 'auto-trigger' section telling the LLM to use the tools for semantic judgments and not for deterministic rules. Oido-specific, so Claude Code does not load it. It would have to be pasted into CLAUDE.md by hand.

Any failure (non-200, network error, or parse error) returns an isError tool result 'Error: ...' (mcp_server.go:235-240) and Claude simply continues. If the API key is missing, the server exits at startup (log.Fatalf, mcp_server.go:52), so the MCP server shows as failed to connect and Claude Code carries on without the tools. A 30 s hang on a slow call would stall the turn, as the timeout is far longer than Jev's claimed 70-500 ms. There is also a nil-pointer risk: if the response lacks the 'q1' key, answers[answerQID] is a zero Answer and renderAnswer returns an empty string, so the model sees an empty success.

gh-djancyp-oido-typesafeai-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where the tool is not called. Each call adds one MCP round trip plus the Jev API latency (claimed 70-500 ms end to end, unverified), plus an extra model tool-call/response step (about 1-3 s of Opus turn time). Worst case is the 30 s timeout.

As a stand-alone answer to 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' it falls short: it is Oido-oriented, invocation is left to the model, and it is a 1-commit, untested, unlicensed prototype. Its best use is as a base or reference (or to fork with a Claude-Code-aware description and hooks), not as the daily-driver integration.

Claude must copy all of it into the tool call, so it also becomes Opus output tokens. Nothing is read from disk by the server. gh-thienle99-dev-typesafe-mcp-server.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level, with no fallback. The SDK timeout defaults to 10s (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS) with 3 retries (TYPESAFE_MAX_RETRIES), so a hung Jev could block one tool call for roughly 40s or more plus backoff. After that, errors propagate as an MCP tool error and Claude just continues without it. Malformed responses throw (src/jev.ts:245,275). The server is a separate process. If it is not running, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools are simply absent. It does not block a session, because nothing is a hook. The confidence gate defaults to 0.97, so most non-trivial decisions come back needsHumanReview=true, which is noise. If the server lacks a key at boot it exits, so it never registers.

Hard-coded questions are weakly designed for the task. select_tests' fallback choice question ('Which test group is highest priority?') is mismatched with the noul flow. Priority is derived from the count of selected groups. confidence for a noul is max(p,1-p). merge_gate takes free-text, model-written summaries, so it is garbage-in/garbage-out. The 0.97 default threshold flags most results as needing human review.

The tasks it covers (classify diff, triage error, route task, pick tests) are things Opus 5.5 already does inline with full repo context. Using this server forces Claude to re-emit whole diffs as output tokens (slow and expensive) for a label that Claude must then still verify. Net latency and token cost are a loss.

It only offers seven model-discretion MCP tools that Opus is unlikely to call unprompted, and it exposes an unauthenticated SSE port. Its only real value is as a reference for how to map Jev choice/noul questions onto coding decisions, and as a config-only OpenRouter patch (TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus typesafe/jev-1.13). For real automation, build a small stdio MCP server or hook that reuses these question definitions.

gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.whatItDoes: Unofficial single-file Rust MCP server (rmcp 0.8, stdio or SSE) that wraps TypeSafe's System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone, GET {base}/v1/models) and adds 10 higher-level tools: bulk filter/rank/classify/dedupe with chunking, choose_one (skim then verify, with rejection), stability_check, verify_output, verify_tool_calls, check_claims, extract_fields. Thresholds, aggregation and clustering are computed deterministically in Rust. Default model "jev-latest".

No mention of 'openrouter' anywhere in repo (grep -ri returns nothing).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Near-trivial, config only for the main path. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> makes the server call https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with a Bearer header, which is exactly the OpenRouter System One surface named in the brief. Caveats: (1) I could not confirm that OpenRouter's request and response schema is byte-identical to TypeSafe's, because the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404, so the schema match is an inference. (2) The default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID (the brief gives typesafe/jev-1.13 and ~typesafe/jev-latest), so either every tool call must pass model, which the LLM would have to remember, or you patch the one-line default_model() at line 104 and rebuild. (3) list_models hits OpenRouter's global /api/v1/models and would return the entire OpenRouter catalogue, which is a large payload of little use. It could be left unused. (4) The env var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY would hold an OpenRouter key, which is confusing but harmless. It needs a Rust toolchain to build, and a one-line patch means maintaining a fork.
providerSupport.others: None. It does not support the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) and no other gateway.

interface.name: systemone
interface.purpose: Evaluate one state against a map of typed questions (choice/score/noul) in one call; returns probabilities, confidence and usage

interface.name: list_models
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models; list model names and aliases for the account

interface.name: filter_items
interface.purpose: Yes/no probability per item against one criterion; chunked (max 1000 items); returns matched and the full probability vector

interface.name: rank_items
interface.purpose: Score each item on 2-10 ordered levels against a query; returns ranked indices and top_k

interface.name: classify_items
interface.purpose: One choice per item over up to 255 categories; returns buckets and per-item confidence

interface.name: choose_one
interface.purpose: Two-pass skim then verify selection over up to 255 candidates, with min_fit rejection

interface.name: stability_check
interface.purpose: Re-run the same questions 2-20 times and report mean, std and modal share

interface.name: verify_output
interface.purpose: Battery over a draft or code snippet: safe_to_share, grounded, consistent_with_sources, complies_with_instructions, plus custom checks

interface.name: verify_tool_calls
interface.purpose: Pre-flight check that planned tool calls are relevant and schema-conformant

interface.name: check_claims
interface.purpose: Classify claims as supported, contradicted or unverified against evidence

interface.name: dedupe_items
interface.purpose: Pairwise same-entity judgments (max 64 items) and clusters

interface.name: extract_fields
interface.purpose: Pull fields from text into fixed option sets

security: Apache-2.0. Single 1839-line src/main.rs, 0 tests in the repo (README claims e2e testing against a mock API, but no test code or CI is committed), no .github directory.

API key is passed via env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or the --typesafe-api-key CLI flag. The flag exposes the key in argv and the process list, and start.sh does this. Use the env form in the MCP 'env' block, which stays out of argv.
Key is only used as an Authorization Bearer header (src/main.rs:493). tracing::info! calls log tool names and counts, not content or key. Log level is info to stderr by default.

No shell execution, no file writes, no Command::new. Egress is only the configured base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is an env override, so a poisoned env could redirect data, but this is standard for a client.

Install requires cargo build --release from source: no prebuilt binaries, no releases (latestRelease null), no crates.io publish found. Building compiles about 200 transitive crates (Cargo.lock), which is a supply-chain surface. No npm/pip postinstall and no curl|sh.
start.sh binds SSE to 0.0.0.0:3391 with no auth. Do not use it; use stdio.

Prompt-injection surface: returns only numeric probabilities and echoed indices or keys, not free text from the model, so the injection surface is small. The state text sent to Jev could contain injected content, but Jev only emits typed decisions.
Self-declared AI-assisted (GLM and DeepSeek). Solo maintainer, 0 stars, 0 forks. Unofficial and not affiliated with TypeSafe.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments leaves the machine, sent verbatim to {base}/v1/systemone: the state (strings, JSON, items lists, draft outputs, code snippets, sources, claims, tool-call schemas) and the question text, plus model name. That is up to 64k chars per chunk. Nothing is read from disk or intercepted automatically. Only what Claude chooses to pass. With the base URL pointed at OpenRouter, this goes to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe. verify_output sends the draft and sources, which may include client code or secrets if Claude passes them, so this must be considered for client projects. No telemetry from the server itself. It sends the User-Agent mcp-typesafe/0.1.2.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.failureMode: Fail-open (see above): MCP tool error, 30 s HTTP timeout, no retry.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.latencyImpact: Nothing added to turns where the model does not call the tool. When called, one MCP round trip plus the API call: the claimed 70-500 ms per request, plus the LLM turn to compose arguments (state, questions) and to read the JSON result, which costs more than the Jev call itself. stability_check with 20 samples is 20 sequential requests (src/main.rs:981-982 in a loop), so about 2-10 s. Bulk tools parallelize chunks.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.contextCost: 12 tools. Tool descriptions total about 5.5k chars on one-line #[tool] attributes (some are multi-line), and the 66 schemars field descriptions total about 10k chars. With JSON schema structure overhead, roughly 21k chars for the tool defs, plus about 2.9k chars of server 'instructions' text (src/main.rs:1502-1530), for about 24k chars, or roughly 6k tokens permanently in context per session (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search, in which case only the names load until needed). No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. Tool results are pretty-printed JSON, and bulk tools return the full probability vector, so results can be large.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The server ships no hooks, no skill and no plugin. The server 'instructions' and tool descriptions steer Claude to use bulk filter/rank tools "instead of reading long lists yourself", but nothing deterministic makes Claude call it. For daily coding, Claude with Opus would rarely reach for these, since typical coding work (edit, grep, test) has no Jev-shaped judgment step.
pros: Only candidate found so far with a typed, tested-by-author wrapper over the full System One primitives (choice/score/noul) plus useful compositions: filter_items/rank_items/classify_items for triaging long lists (logs, search hits, issues) and verify_output/verify_tool_calls/check_claims as an independent second opinion.

OpenRouter path is config-only for the main tool: base URL is a runtime flag/env (src/main.rs:96-97) and the path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One API path, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key should work (schema match unverified).
Deterministic server-side math (thresholds, ranking, clustering, chunking); returns only numeric or typed output, so little prompt-injection surface and small results relative to reading lists.
Low-risk runtime: no shell, no file access, no writes, 30 s timeout, fail-open, Apache-2.0, apart from the one HTTP egress.
Small ~6k-token footprint, no per-turn hook cost or latency, so it does not compete with the existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tools, no hook or skill trigger. Violates the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told, unless paired with a CLAUDE.md nudge or a custom hook (which the repo does not provide).

Default model is 'jev-latest', which is not an OpenRouter model ID (OpenRouter uses typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Without a patch, Claude must pass model on every call, or the call likely fails. list_models on OpenRouter would dump the full OpenRouter catalogue.
OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified (docs 404'd during this audit); the server has no OpenRouter test, so any field difference would surface as runtime errors.

Extreme immaturity: repo created 2026-09-19, 4 commits (3 by sf-stav, 1 by Stav Katsoulis), 1 human contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, no test code in the repo, self-described AI-assisted, unofficial, and the maintainer solicits paid work.

Build-from-source only: needs a Rust >=1.85 toolchain and compiling ~200 crates; no binaries, no crates.io or npm package, and you must not run it blindly as an audited artifact. A default_model patch means owning a fork.
--typesafe-api-key flag and start.sh put the key in argv (env form avoids this). start.sh SSE binds 0.0.0.0 unauthenticated.

Everything Claude passes as state, drafts or sources goes to a third-party API, which is a concern for client code, and verify_output's 'safe_to_share' check would itself require sending the possibly-secret text out.

Use case mismatch for coding: Jev is a judgment engine; most of the 12 tools solve list-triage and agent-pipeline problems that rarely arise in an editing session, and Claude must spend an Opus turn to compose the typed questions, which erodes the latency and cost advantage.
gh-sf-stav-mcp-typesafe.verdict: The most complete Jev MCP wrapper in the discovered set and pointable at OpenRouter by env (plus a model override), but it is a brand-new, untested, one-person Rust project, and being a pure model-discretion tool it cannot deliver the "automatic, without prompting" integration by itself. It is worth using only as a building block (optionally with a pinned fork and a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge) rather than as the solution.

gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also manually installable) with one dependency-free Node script registered on two hook events. PreToolUse(Bash) sends each Bash command plus cwd to Jev as a 3-way Choice (safe/risky/destructive) and forces a permission prompt ("ask") when P(destructive) >= 0.5. UserPromptSubmit sends every user prompt to Jev with 8 questions (1 Score quality, 1 Noul follow-up, 6 Noul prompt-pitfalls taken from the Opus 5.5 prompting guide); it blocks (decision:block) prompts scoring < 1.5/3 or tripping a pitfall until the user resubmits the same text, otherwise shows a one-line "Prompt grade" message.

gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.runtime: Node >=18 (global fetch), single .mjs, zero dependencies; user has Node 24.
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.install: /plugin marketplace add dbadea-heits/jev-claude-code-hooks ; /plugin install jev-hooks@jev-hooks (prompts for TypeSafe key stored in system credential store), or curl the .mjs into ~/.claude/hooks and add two hook entries to settings.json (with key in settings env block). No postinstall scripts; the manual route is a curl of a raw file, not curl|sh.
security: API key is read from env (CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFE_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header from inside Node; never in argv or process list. Plugin route stores it in the credential store (sensitive:true). Manual route README suggests putting the key in settings.json env (plaintext on disk).

No shell execution, no eval, no child_process, no telemetry beyond the Jev call; only outbound host is TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is env-overridable, so a poisoned env/project settings could redirect the key and all prompts/commands to another host.

Every Bash command string and cwd (and every user prompt, up to full pasted text) is sent to the third party. Commands often embed secrets (inline tokens, curl -H Authorization, DB URLs, .env values echoed). This directly undercuts the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and client-project confidentiality/NDA is a concern. Runs alongside that guard in parallel so ordering cannot redact first.

Prompt-injection surface is small: Jev returns typed probabilities, not text, so injected content cannot execute anything; but a command containing a misleading comment could lower P(destructive). Jev is a probabilistic classifier, not a security boundary; false negatives possible, and fail-open lets a slow/down API pass everything.

Hook state files in os.tmpdir()/jev-claude-code-hooks/<sanitized session id>.{held,warned} (hash of held prompt, error message). Session id sanitized to [A-Za-z0-9_-]; on a shared /tmp another local user could pre-create/poison these, low impact.

No LICENSE, single unknown maintainer, day-old repo: auditable in 5 minutes but unmaintained-risk; pin a commit and review before enabling as a plugin (plugin updates would auto-pull code that runs on every Bash call).
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.dataEgress: On every Bash tool call: full command text + cwd. On every non-slash, non-'!' user prompt: the full prompt text (including pasted logs/code/emails). Tool outputs, file contents, diffs and assistant messages are NOT sent. Destination api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (then also retained per OpenRouter/TypeSafe logging policies) if base URL is overridden.
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: missing key, HTTP error, bad JSON, schema mismatch, or 8 s AbortSignal.timeout (jev-hook.mjs:18,33,255-259) lets the command/prompt proceed; a single systemMessage warning per session ('jev-guard inactive: ...') via a marker file. Hook timeout in hooks.json is 15 s, so worst case adds ~8 s to a Bash call/prompt when Jev hangs. Note: in claude -p, a flagged command is denied and a held prompt dropped. Unverified whether permissionDecision:'ask' is honored or auto-resolved under the user's bypass/auto permission modes (README claims it prompts even for allowed commands; bypass mode may skip it, making the guard moot).
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.latencyImpact: One serialized HTTPS round trip per Bash call (blocks execution) and one per prompt (blocks submission), plus Node cold start (~40-80 ms). Claimed Jev latency 70-500 ms, so ~0.15-0.6 s per Bash call typical, up to 8 s on timeout. The prompt call carries 8 questions in one request, so slower than a single question. Runs in parallel with the user's other Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus), so adds max not sum, but still on the critical path of every agent command; agentic sessions issue hundreds of Bash calls/day. Cost negligible (~$0.042/1M input tokens).
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skills. Hooks emit nothing on the common path for Bash (silent when not destructive). The prompt grader emits a systemMessage "Prompt grade: X (n/3)" per prompt, which is displayed to the user and not added to model context. Only when flagged does it show a block reason (to user).
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse:Bash and UserPromptSubmit) fire automatically every time with no model discretion and no user phrasing, which meets the 'never say use jev' requirement, but only for these two narrow judgments.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks.json registers PreToolUse(Bash) + UserPromptSubmit, no prompting needed, zero context-token cost.

Good fit for Jev's design: typed Choice/Noul/Score questions with probabilities and a threshold (P(destructive)>=0.5) is exactly the 'System One' use case; request shape {model,state,questions} is the real /v1/systemone shape.
Env-driven base URL (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and model (JEV_MODEL) make an OpenRouter switch likely env-only since path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API.
Tiny, readable, dependency-free, fails open with 8 s timeout and once-per-session warning; key not in argv; plugin stores key in credential store.
A semantic destructive-command check catches things regex secret/deny lists miss (git reset --hard, force push, redirect overwrites), useful when running in auto mode.
Reusable template: the askJev client and question definitions can be lifted into the user's own hook with extra questions (e.g. secret-in-command, prod-target).
cons: Sends every Bash command and every prompt to a third party; client-project code/secrets in commands and pasted prompts leave the machine, conflicting with the user's secret-leak guard intent.

Prompt grader is opinionated and intrusive for a senior dev: it BLOCKS prompts (resubmit to bypass) based on Opus-5.5-guide heuristics, and the user is on a subscription workflow where terse prompts are normal; extra friction on every prompt plus 8 questions per call. Can be disabled with grade_prompts=false, leaving only the Bash guard.
Only covers two narrow uses; does not add Jev for code decisions (routing, file/test selection, review triage, commit-type choice). Not a general Jev integration.
Adds a network round trip to every Bash call on the critical path (0.15-0.6 s typical, 8 s worst); with GitNexus and secret-guard hooks already there this stacks in agentic loops.
Under bypass/auto permission modes a 'ask' decision may be ignored or auto-handled, so the guard's main value is uncertain (unverified); in auto mode the built-in classifier already vets commands.
Not OpenRouter-native: defaults and userConfig are TypeSafe-only, model default 'jev-latest' lacks the typesafe/ prefix, OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
Very immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-29, no license, no tests, no CI, 0 stars; plugin auto-update pulls unreviewed code that runs on every Bash call.
Fail-open and probabilistic, and Jev is beta/unverified (skeptics claim it is a flash-model router), so it is not a reliable safety boundary.
gh-dbadea-heits-jev-claude-code-hooks.verdict: A clean, minimal, truly automatic hook, but it covers only a Bash destructive-check and an intrusive prompt grader, ships all commands/prompts to a third party, and is a day-old unlicensed single-commit repo. Best used as a reference or copied/pinned (Bash guard only, grade_prompts off, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter) rather than installed as a plugin; does not by itself deliver a broad Jev integration.

gh-geronimo-deploy-cloud-typesafe-tpm-mc.name: typesafe-tpm-mcp (geronimo-deploy-cloud)
gh-geronimo-deploy-cloud-typesafe-tpm-mc.whatItDoes: Small Python MCP server (stdio, mcp v2 MCPServer) that gates work-ticket quality. It sends a structured ticket (title, goal, description, acceptance criteria, scope lists) plus 11 Jev primitives (Noul/Choice/Score) to TypeSafe System One in one batched typesafe_sdk call. Routing (ready_for_execution / needs_revision / needs_human_scoping / blocked_on_dependency), hard gates and fix hints are computed in local Python. It is a ticket/issue-template reviewer for an agent-orchestration workflow, not a general coding aid.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter reference anywhere in the repo (grep found none outside uv.lock). Server code: schema.py:165 `with TypeSafeClient() as client: client.system_one(state=..., questions=...)`; server.py:83 checks only TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It uses typesafe-sdk (README pins >=0.6.0, uv.lock 0.7.0). Read from sdk 0.7.2 sdist: constants.py:3-15 API_KEY_ENV=TYPESAFE_API_KEY, BASE_URL_ENV=TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, DEFAULT_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai, DEFAULT_MODEL_ENV=TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=10.0; _core/constants.py:5 SYSTEM_ONE_PATH=/v1/systemone; _core/endpoints.py:28-33 body {state, model, questions}; _core/transport.py:121 `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; config.py:61 base_url.rstrip('/'). OpenRouter's System One endpoint is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY would map onto it (unverified that OpenRouter's request/response schema is identical to the SDK's).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and no code change: set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) in the MCP env block, because the SDK sends the model in the request body and its default 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID. Risk: the SDK strictly parses responses, so any schema difference on OpenRouter's /v1/systemone would raise, and the server would then fail closed. Should be tested by the user. server.py:83 only checks that the env var is non-empty.
providerSupport.others: Direct TypeSafe API only (api.typesafe.ai) by default.

The guard hook fails open on degraded or missing data. The destructive regex check is fail-closed by design. Risks: the launcher retries the server up to 3 times on early exit; a dropped MCP server leaves the session toolless (the author documented this). In the shipped plugin layout, plugin/hooks/subagent-guard.mjs imports `../plugin/server.mjs`, which resolves to plugin/plugin/server.mjs and does not exist; this looks like a broken import that crashes the hook with a non-blocking error on every Bash/Edit/Write (unverified, static reading only).

gh-cyrusasco-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Hook: a Node process spawn (about 40-80 ms) on every UserPromptSubmit and on every Bash/Edit/Write PreToolUse (the guard is a no-op or crashes outside ZCode subagent sessions, but still pays the spawn). When the pipeline runs: Battery #1 is about 1 s per the README, and the agent spends extra model turns on the Gate, ts_feasible, ts_ask, ts_decide, subgoal check, guard push, judge polling every 15-30 s and review-comment. pros: Genuinely automatic trigger path exists for Claude Code: plugin/hooks/hooks.json registers UserPromptSubmit plus PreToolUse and plugin/.mcp.json auto-wires the MCP server, so no 'use jev' prompting is needed (though it works by nudging, not by hard integration).

Its purpose is a multi-agent dispatch orchestrator that adds a heavy ritual (gate, feasible, ask, decide, subgoal dedupe, guard push, background judge polling, review-comment) to every build-shaped prompt. That is the opposite of low-friction daily coding and burns Opus turns and tokens.

Hook regex is very broad (create|install|implement|refactor|upgrade...) and injects about 1.1 KB of Cantonese imperative text on many ordinary prompts. It also mandates spawning background subagents and sending diffs/specs to DeepSeek/Qwen/codex-cli, which is a client-confidentiality hazard on client projects.

Likely-broken shipped hook: plugin/hooks/subagent-guard.mjs imports ../plugin/server.mjs, a path that does not exist inside the plugin layout, and it only acts on ZCode sess_subagent sessions anyway, so on Claude Code it is dead weight that still spawns Node on every Bash/Edit/Write and conflicts with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks.

The only overridable knob is the model name. There is no base-URL env var, and a grep finds no mention of openrouter anywhere in the repo. security: The API key is read from the env var and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv (.mcp.json has no key), and it is validated as printable ASCII (server.mjs:129). The fetch catch deliberately swallows the error, because Node embeds the header value in the TypeError (lines 144-150).
Error bodies are never echoed into the transcript (lines 152-157). This is a good practice.
Hardcoded HTTPS endpoint with redirect:"error". There is no user-controlled URL, so no SSRF or redirect exfiltration.
No shell execution, no file reads, and no .env loading. The only filesystem write is the truncated result at mkdtemp(tmpdir()/jev-*)/result.json with mode 0600, which can contain echoed evidence.
No postinstall script. The package scripts contain only `test`. No telemetry in the code (grep found no analytics).

`npx -y jev-judge-mcp` in .mcp.json is unpinned, so each start can pull a new version from a single-maintainer, 10-day-old package. That is a supply-chain risk, mitigated by npm provenance and by the small dependency set (MCP SDK + typebox). Pin the version, or vendor and read it.

Prompt-injection surface: `state` is composed by the model and the response is typed JSON with no free text, so the return path is low-risk. The tool description tells the model to 'send only evidence the user's sharing policy allows' and 'keep credentials out', but that is advisory only. There is nothing in the server that scrubs secrets, and it is not integrated with the user's PreToolUse secret guard, which does not cover mcp__ tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
gh-gecm0-jev-judge-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into `state` and the question `instructions` and `criteria` goes to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, with the key as a Bearer token. That can include code snippets, diffs, file contents and tool outputs, at the model's discretion. The server never reads files or forwards session history on its own (README:144-147). Nothing goes to OpenRouter as shipped. Sending client code to TypeSafe raises a per-client data-sharing question, and the user's secret guard does not cover this channel.
gh-gecm0-jev-judge-mcp.failureMode: Fail-loud and fail-open for the workflow. There is a 30 s AbortSignal.timeout (server.mjs:131), no retry and no fallback model. Failures surface as a tool error such as 'Could not reach TypeSafe', 'TypeSafe HTTP 429', or 'Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY' (checked before any network call). Claude sees the error and simply proceeds without Jev, so nothing blocks the session. The tool stays listed even with no key. A hung Jev can stall a turn for up to 30 s, but only when the model chose to call it. It honours MCP cancellation.
gh-gecm0-jev-judge-mcp.contextCost: One tool. Description is about 1,900 chars (~475 tokens). The inputSchema (a typebox union of three question kinds plus record and array descriptions) is roughly 1,500-2,000 chars (~400-500 tokens). The server sets no MCP `instructions`. The skill's frontmatter description is about 550 chars (~140 tokens), always loaded. The SKILL.md body (~113 lines, ~1.5k tokens) loads only when triggered. Total always-on cost is about 1,000-1,200 tokens, which is very cheap. No hook-injected text.

The tool description says 'Reach for it on a close call you cannot settle by running code: choosing among candidate files, symbols or fixes, ... reranking hits, scoring against a rubric, triage', but it also says 'Run the test or the grep where one exists'. Opus 5.5 will only occasionally choose to call it, because it must author state and typed questions itself. There is no deterministic hook, so it does not fully meet the 'Claude Code must use it when needed, without prompting' requirement. The README's own usage example starts with 'Use Jev to...'. gh-gecm0-jev-judge-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero cost when Jev is not called. Per call: the tool-call round trip plus Jev's claimed 70-500 ms end to end (the response includes elapsed_ms), plus the model's time to generate the question JSON (a few hundred output tokens, often 1-3 s on Opus). Batching many questions per call is encouraged and cheap. The worst case is the 30 s timeout.
pros: The most complete and best-designed Claude Code packaging of Jev found here: plugin + marketplace + MCP + skill, install is two `claude plugin` commands.

Careful engineering: strict typebox schema validation before the network call, per-question response validation, no error-body echo, key never in argv, redirect:error, 30 s timeout, cancellation, and a private 0600 temp file for large output (server.mjs:85-199).
Tiny always-on context footprint of about 1k tokens for one tool plus a skill description, so it fits alongside gitnexus, playwright and caveman without bloat.
Fail-open: any Jev outage or missing key becomes a tool error and Claude carries on. It cannot wedge sessions or block hooks.

The SKILL.md is high quality: the one-second test, decomposition, fan-out (cites a 11.5x cheaper, 9.6x faster figure from TypeSafe's cookbook), and probability-to-decision thresholds (>0.9 for destructive actions). It teaches Claude to make good calls.

The tool description explicitly targets coding use cases: choosing among candidate files, symbols or fixes, reranking hits, triage. MIT license, small (245-line) server that is easy to audit and fork, and CI with trusted publishing and provenance.
TYPESAFE_MODEL lets you pin a version such as jev-1.13.0.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter. The endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read (server.mjs:125,137). Using OpenRouter needs a small fork, the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified, and the fork then has to be maintained.

Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool: no hook, no proxy, and nothing forces use. Opus tends to solve close calls by running grep or tests, and the description itself says to do that first. The README example even starts with 'Use Jev to...'. It does not meet the 'never prompt Claude to use jev' goal on its own.
Very new and thin: created 2026-09-19, 8 commits over 2 days, 1 star, 0 forks, one maintainer, no GitHub releases, no live-API test and no accuracy evidence. It is version 0.5.2 for a beta model.
Unpinned `npx -y jev-judge-mcp` in .mcp.json pulls whatever the latest version is on every start, from a single new maintainer. Pin the version or vendor it.

Data egress to a second vendor (TypeSafe direct) with only advisory guidance. Nothing scrubs secrets, and the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover mcp__ tools. Sending client code needs a per-client decision.

Model-authored questions are the bottleneck. Claude must spend output tokens and reasoning to build state and typed criteria, so for most everyday coding it is cheaper to just decide. The value is niche: reranking, triage, rubric scoring.
The tool is currently 'a DeepSeek flash router' per skeptics (unverified), and 32k context caps the state size.

Fork it (about 5 lines) to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, pin the version, and pair it with a CLAUDE.md rule or hook if you want reliable automatic use.

gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.name: eyenpi/actionreflex
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.whatItDoes: Python library (v0.2.0, alpha), NOT a Claude Code hook despite the candidate label. It wraps typesafe-sdk to build a pre-execution "Gate" for agent tool calls: you construct an Action (name, arguments, context) and it sends one Jev System One request containing several policy questions (Noul/Score/Choice). The answers are folded into allow/block/escalate. It ships six built-in policies (destructive_action, intent_mismatch, follows_injected_instructions, contains_pii, scope_of_impact, risk_tier), a @gate.guard decorator, an async gate, and an on_error mode (raise / fail_closed / fail_open). It has no CLI, no MCP server, no hooks.json, no PreToolUse adapter, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md, so it does not plug into Claude Code without you writing a wrapper.
