gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.install: pip install git+https://github.com/eyenpi/actionreflex. This is a library install only, and I did not run it. Nothing in the repo registers it with Claude Code. Making it work means writing your own PreToolUse hook script (Python, using uv or a venv) that reads the hook JSON from stdin, builds an Action and calls Gate.check().
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.tests: Offline pytest suite: tests/test_action.py, test_eval_parsing.py, test_gate.py, test_integration.py (live, needs a key), test_policy_helpers.py and test_verdict.py. The failure modes are run against a real client pointed at a closed port, per the README. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs a 3.10 to 3.13 matrix with ruff and pytest, plus an integration job that needs a repo secret. I did not run the tests. Eval results (eval/results/*.jsonl.gz) are committed. They report R-Judge F1 89.3 and 2,106 of 2,108 InjecAgent attacks stopped. Those figures are self-reported by the author, and the README itself caveats them: the attacks are mostly off-task tool calls, and on-task hijacks are essentially untested.
security: Key handling: the key comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or an api_key argument, and is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (typesafe-sdk transport.py:121). The SDK logging redacts authorization headers. Nothing is placed in argv.
No shell execution, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, and no telemetry found in the 881 lines of src/actionreflex. The SDK adds only User-Agent and SDK/runtime headers.

The tool arguments and context are sent to the model as state JSON. If a hook fed it tool_results, it would be putting untrusted content into a classifier prompt. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so the injection surface is limited to flipping a verdict, not executing anything.
Supply chain: a single-author, 5-commit, 2-star, 12-day-old repo, installed from git without a pinned SHA, and it depends on a pre-1.0 typesafe-sdk. Pin the commit if you use it.
The SDK is pre-1.0 and pinned to a narrow range (>=0.6,<0.8), so it will break on SDK upgrades.

It is a gate, so a false 'allow' is a security failure. The README admits the default thresholds are untuned, that the weak spot is unintended risks (F1 72.7, specificity 55.4), and that on-task injection hijacks are untested.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.dataEgress: Whatever you put in Action.arguments and Action.context is sent as JSON to the configured base URL. That means TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai) by default, or OpenRouter if you override the base URL. Realistically, for a Claude Code hook that would be the tool name plus the full tool_input (Bash commands, file paths, Edit/Write contents and diffs) and, if you add them, the user request and the recent transcript or tool outputs. The library has no redaction and no allowlist. On client projects this sends code and possibly secrets to a beta third-party model provider (and to OpenRouter if it is routed there). Your existing secret-leak guard hook would have to run before it. Because everything is one request, the payload grows with each policy and each piece of context, and input is billed per token.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.failureMode: Configurable via on_error. The default is "raise" (GateUnavailable), which in a hook wrapper would crash the script. Claude Code treats a non-blocking hook error as a non-block, so that behaves as fail-open for the user, but it is accidental rather than designed. "fail_closed" would block every tool call during an outage or rate-limit, which is unacceptable for daily coding. "fail_open" is the sensible mode, but it means no protection when Jev is down. Timeout is None by default (the SDK default applies), so you must set a short timeout, for example timeout=2. There are 2 retries with backoff by default (RetryPolicy), so a slow or down Jev can stall each tool call for several seconds unless you disable retries. All of this is the wrapper author's job.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.contextCost: Zero for the library on its own: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill text. A hand-written PreToolUse hook would inject nothing unless it emitted a block or ask reason. Context cost is effectively 0 tokens in the normal case.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.latencyImpact: Claimed median about 260 ms per check (README and eval), with 70-500 ms published by TypeSafe. On top of that comes Python interpreter and typesafe-sdk import time, roughly 200-500 ms per hook invocation if it is spawned fresh each time (my estimate, not measured), and the network round trip to OpenRouter. It is serial with the tool call, so expect about 0.5-1 s added to every gated tool call. Restricting the matcher to Bash|Write|Edit keeps that manageable. Multiple hooks run in parallel in Claude Code, so it does not add to your existing hooks in sequence.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.autoInvocation: None as shipped. It is a plain library that only runs when other code calls it. It could become a deterministic PreToolUse hook (the best fit for the user's 'automatic, no prompting' requirement), but the user would have to write and maintain that glue themselves.
pros: It is the only candidate here that uses Jev's real strengths, cheap calibrated yes/no/score answers on every action, and its deterministic gate design matches the user's 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement (a PreToolUse hook needs no model discretion).

OpenRouter routing is nearly free. typesafe-sdk honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (constants.py:6) and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key should reach OpenRouter's System One API without a code patch. This is unverified.

Clean, small (881 lines), readable code with no shell exec, no postinstall and no telemetry. MIT licensed. The policies are well-formed Jev questions (Noul/Score/Choice) that can be reused as templates.
One request carries N policies, so adding questions costs input tokens, not round trips. The eval reports $0.19 for 3,584 checks, so cost is negligible.
Published benchmark artifacts (R-Judge, InjecAgent) with committed raw results, and the README is honest about caveats and weaknesses. The on_error fail_open/fail_closed choice is explicit.
Zero MCP tool or context overhead in Claude Code.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration. There is no hook adapter, MCP server, plugin, skill or CLI in the repo, so the candidate label 'hook' is inaccurate. The user would have to write a PreToolUse wrapper (stdin JSON to Action to Gate.check to permissionDecision JSON) and decide the context to pass.

The design targets untrusted agents in production, not a senior developer's own coding agent. The built-in questions (destructive, intent mismatch, injection) overlap with what Claude Code permissions, bypass-mode guards and the existing secret-guard hook already cover, and in bypass/auto mode a Jev 'block' would add friction, not remove it.

False-alarm risk for coding work. Specificity on unintended-risk records was only 55.4 and thresholds are untuned. Normal coding actions like rm -rf node_modules, git reset, migrations and force-push will look 'destructive' and cause noisy escalations. Claude Code has no human review queue, so 'escalate' would have to map to an 'ask' prompt.
Benchmarks are chat/tool-call records (R-Judge, InjecAgent), not Claude Code Bash/Edit traffic, and the author admits on-task hijack injections are untested.
Egress on client projects. Every Bash command, file path and edit body would go to a beta provider with no redaction, and the user has a client-confidentiality concern.

Immature and fragile. It is 12 days old with 5 commits, 1 author and 2 stars, not on PyPI, has no releases, and needs pre-1.0 typesafe-sdk >=0.6,<0.8. Python startup per hook call adds latency, since there is no persistent daemon.
Fail modes need hand-tuning: the default is raise with unbounded timeout and 2 retries, so a slow Jev could stall every tool call unless the wrapper sets a tight timeout and fail_open.
gh-eyenpi-actionreflex.verdict: A well-made but tiny alpha Python library for gating agent actions with Jev. It is not a Claude Code hook or MCP, so nothing works automatically until you write your own PreToolUse glue, and its safety-gate purpose adds little for a developer already running secret-guard and permission modes. It is worth borrowing as a reference for Jev policy design and OpenRouter routing (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), not as the daily integration.

gh-edwardyen724-g-jev-compactor.dataEgress: An abridged copy of the whole conversation (skeleton state up to ~20k tokens; long tool outputs replaced by 'ok, N chars (omitted)' but user/assistant text, commands, code blocks and file paths retained) plus the goal and the generated questions is POSTed to the configured Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if overridden). For check_action, the proposed command text. In the Claude Code MCP flow, the model must additionally serialize the history into the tool-call arguments, so the same content is also re-emitted through the Claude context as output tokens. Nothing goes anywhere else. Sending client-project code and prompts to a beta third party is a compliance concern for client work.
gh-edwardyen724-g-jev-compactor.failureMode: Fail-open by default: no key, 401, timeout or Jev error returns the history unchanged with report.skipped='jev_unavailable' (failClosed:true option throws instead); check_action fail-open falls back to the regex floor only and says so. Configurable timeoutMs, cooldownTurns; SDK retries 408/429/5xx. Compaction only calls Jev when estimated tokens exceed maxTokens (default 15000); the safety gate runs on every call. Since Claude Code will not call it automatically, failure mode matters little in practice.
gh-edwardyen724-g-jev-compactor.contextCost: Low tool-definition cost: 4 MCP tools (compact_context, inspect_context, check_action, self_test). Descriptions plus zod schemas approx 2.5k characters, roughly 600-800 tokens (compact_context ~1.2k chars, inspect ~0.6k, check_action ~0.6k, self_test ~0.5k). No MCP server-level instructions field set (McpServer created with only name/version). No hooks, so zero injected text. Real hidden cost: every compact_context/inspect_context call requires the model to write the whole history (up to tens of thousands of tokens) into tool arguments and then read the same amount back as the result, which increases context rather than reducing it.
gh-edwardyen724-g-jev-compactor.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. There are no hooks (no PreToolUse/PreCompact/UserPromptSubmit), no skill, no plugin manifest, no proxy. Nothing triggers it deterministically; Claude Code would only use it if the model decided to, and would need CLAUDE.md prompting to do so, which the user explicitly does not want. It also cannot swap the harness's own context, since MCP tool results do not replace the conversation.
gh-edwardyen724-g-jev-compactor.latencyImpact: Jev call itself claimed ~300-600 ms (README benchmark 350 ms for 12.7k tokens, 593 ms for 61k). In the MCP flow the dominant latency is Claude generating the serialized message array as tool arguments (tens of seconds for large histories) plus reading it back. check_action is a ~0.3 s Jev call plus a model tool round trip per invocation (a few seconds).

gh-ajasra-jev-hooks.dataEgress: Only to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai). Per event: (1) UserPromptSubmit sends the user's prompt (redacted, capped 1500 chars), an assembled envelope of up to 4000 chars (project goal, session objective, active file path, git branch, first 600 chars of git status, last error, prior context) and skill/knowledge catalog names plus descriptions. (2) PreToolUse sends the raw, unredacted Bash command string and tool name for every Bash call that passes the regex denylist and has no matching stored rule. (3) Verification and lint send code snippets and diff hunks, redacted with a secret regex, up to 8-12k chars. It does not send whole files or tool outputs by default. Note that the prompt and every shell command from client projects go to a third party.
gh-ajasra-jev-hooks.failureMode: Mostly fail-open, with a timeout too tight for Jev. Default semantic timeout is 0.25s (paths.py:105) and the hook deadline is 0.30s (adapters/base.py:142). Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms plus network and a Python cold start, so a large share of calls will time out. On any client exception the safety gate returns ALLOW ('semantic_unavailable', safety.py end) and the router features silently abstain. The regex denylist still runs offline. Fail-closed cases: a malformed PreToolUse event or an unparsable operation returns deny (cli.py:39-42, runtime.py:_safety), and the Codex adapter maps needs_confirmation to a hard deny. Under Claude Code bypass/auto mode there is no interactive approve path, so a false-positive semantic 'destructive' (>=0.5) would block the command outright. Only the `jev authorize` CLI can whitelist it.
gh-ajasra-jev-hooks.latencyImpact: Cold Python process on every hook call (about 50-100 ms) plus a Jev round trip capped at about 250-300 ms. That is roughly 0.1-0.4 s on every Bash call and every user prompt. The README claims 80-270 ms per feature. The Codex hook timeout is 5s. Nothing here is measured for Claude Code.
gh-ajasra-jev-hooks.contextCost: No MCP tools are needed for the hook path (zero tool-definition tokens). The optional MCP server adds 8 tools, roughly 500-800 tokens with short one-line descriptions. Hooks inject up to context_budget=12000 chars (about 3k tokens) on UserPromptSubmit, but only when a feature fires: git status up to 3000 chars, a skill body, a knowledge item. On Codex a telemetry HTML comment footer is appended. With no .agents/skills or .agents/knowledge in the user's projects, nearly nothing is injected; the skill and knowledge features are useless for Claude Code layouts.
gh-ajasra-jev-hooks.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse and others), which is exactly the automatic, no-prompting model wanted. BUT the shipped configs target Antigravity (.agents/hooks.json, Windows `cmd /c` paths) and Codex (.codex/hooks.json with command_windows only). There is no Claude Code settings snippet and no `claude` adapter. Claude Code would need a new adapter plus a settings.json hooks block.
pros: Uses the hook model the user wants: fully automatic, deterministic, no 'use jev' prompting (registry.py FEATURES, .codex/hooks.json).
OpenRouter is first-class in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY selects https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and typesafe/jev-1.13 (client.py:46-62), and the request shape matches TypeSafe's System One API.

The Codex adapter's stdin/stdout JSON is very close to Claude Code's hook protocol (hook_event_name, session_id, cwd, tool_name, tool_input, transcript_path, hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision/additionalContext). A `claude` adapter is probably a ~60-line copy of adapters/codex.py plus a `--harness claude` choice.

Good architecture in places: stdlib-only core, ports and adapters, a deterministic regex floor that runs even when Jev is down, trusted vs project config separation (paths.py), one-use authorization with a digest, and unit tests with a fake client.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to: typed noul and choice micro-decisions (destructive?, needs git?, which skill?), never free text, matching the System One design.
Stdlib-only core and no npm postinstall or curl|sh means low supply-chain risk; a pip -e install of a single-author repo is easy to read and audit.
cons: No Claude Code support at all. `--harness` accepts only antigravity|codex (cli.py:81,101), and the adapters directory has only those two. Reading it is a reference implementation, not an integration.
Windows-first docs and hook configs (cmd /c, mklink, %USERPROFILE%, command_windows). The user is on Linux.

Overlaps the user's existing tools, and its value is thin for this user. The regex safety gate duplicates their existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard and Claude Code permission rules. Speculative git status duplicates the GitNexus hook. The skill and knowledge routers read .agents/skills, not ~/.claude/skills, and Claude Code already does skill selection natively.

The timeout budget (0.25s semantic, 0.30s deadline) is below Jev's claimed 70-500 ms end-to-end once the cold Python start is counted. Most semantic calls will silently fall back to allow, so the 'safety' value is mostly the regex list.

Raw Bash commands go unredacted to OpenRouter (safety.py) on every non-denylisted Bash call. That is a real client-confidentiality exposure for a bypass-mode user with client projects; only the semantic-lint and verification paths redact.
In bypass/auto mode, the Codex mapping of needs_confirmation to hard deny has no human-in-the-loop path. Jev false positives block work, and the escape hatch is a separate CLI command.
Project .env files are parsed into the hook's environment on every run (client.py:15-30).

Immature: 5 days old, 1 author, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE file (README claims MIT), version 0.1.0. RFC-heavy docs (26 proposals, about 300KB) versus about 44 tests. Some hooks (jev_output_pruner) still default to the direct TypeSafe endpoint and Antigravity behavior.
Uses the older /api/v1/systemone surface, not the newer /api/alpha/decisions surface. It sends the whole 'state' as a prompt string or dict with no typed schema.

It is worth reading as a design reference for a Claude Code hook (a few noul questions on Bash and UserPromptSubmit, OpenRouter /systemone, a deterministic fallback), but a small purpose-built hook is safer than adopting this repo (unredacted commands leave the machine, no license, 5 days old).

It shows how to build a compact state payload (build_jev_state) and use Jev confidence to fall back to a bigger model. Good design material.
Careful engineering: durable SQLite tasks, idempotency keys, secret-file support that fails closed, redacted logs, about 30 test files, CI and MIT licence.
The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so the TypeSafe SDK route to OpenRouter is plausibly a base-URL and key swap (unverified).
cons: It is Android UI automation, not a coding tool. It needs a physical USB phone plus adb, and gives Claude Code nothing for editing, reviewing or testing code.

The code only supports the TypeSafe-direct SDK path (TYPESAFE_API_KEY). No OpenRouter code or env var exists in the repo. The OpenRouter path would need an unverified SDK base-URL trick.

gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.name: jev-fuse (0xshikhar)
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.whatItDoes: Python 3.12+ package (PyPI jev-fuse 0.1.0) that wraps TypeSafe Jev in a local governance layer. It has four parts. (1) A FastAPI gateway (`jevfuse serve`) that proxies POST /v1/systemone with a singleflight coalescer, an LRU+SQLite cache and a SQLite/DuckDB audit log. (2) A Claude Code PreToolUse hook for Bash only (`jevfuse hook pre-tool-use`) that runs a shell-command classifier: AST/tokenizer checks, a deterministic denylist and allowlist, then a Jev "split-noul" fallback. (3) A stdio MCP server (`jevfuse mcp`) with 4 tools. (4) A Claude plugin/marketplace manifest and a SKILL.md. Its real function is a bash-command safety gate. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration for coding assistance.

Lines 45-66 read the key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and the base URL from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or JEV_BASE_URL. Line 202 hardcodes the path '/v1/systemone'. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would produce https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with a Bearer header, matching the System One surface. Three problems remain. (a) The model field is hardcoded to 'jev-latest', which needs a code patch to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. (b) OpenRouter's response schema is unverified against SystemOneResponse. (c) The hook's classifier.py:456-462 sends the TYPESAFE_API_KEY to the local gateway (FUSE_URL) and only starts an in-process engine on ConnectError, so the config must be consistent across the hook and the server.

security: Critical: the hook emits legacy/invented JSON ({"allow": true}, {"deny": ...}, {"ask": ...}; hook/pre_tool_use.py, classifier.py:30-37). Current Claude Code docs require hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision for PreToolUse, and top-level allow/deny/ask are not valid. The docs say exit 0 with no valid decision falls through to normal permission flow. So the ALLOW/DENY/ASK verdicts are most likely silently ignored and the gate is a no-op. The tests only assert the invented shape (tests/test_guard_hook.py:30) and never run against a real Claude Code.

The hook command is `uv run jevfuse hook pre-tool-use` (.claude/settings.json). In any project that is not the jev-fuse checkout, uv cannot spawn `jevfuse`. It exits non-zero, and exit code 2 would block every Bash call. This is an inference from the hook contract and was not tested, because running candidate code was forbidden.

Layer 4 never returns ALLOW: every model verdict below the deadband still returns ASK ('Uncalibrated safety verdict'; classifier.py:~505). Jev adds only DENY signals or nothing. In bypass/auto mode an ASK adds friction and is not a real gate.

The gateway enables CORS allow_origins=['*'] with credentials (server/app.py:52-59). It forwards the caller's Authorization header upstream, and there is no local auth on /v1/decide, /v1/traces or /dashboard. It binds 127.0.0.1 by default, but any browser page could reach it, and traces can contain command text.

API key handling is via env vars only, not argv, unless the user copies the README MCP snippet with the key in the env block of the MCP config. The key is then in plaintext in ~/.claude.json and is visible to any process that can read the environment. classifier.py:460 sends the TYPESAFE_API_KEY as a Bearer header to FUSE_URL, which defaults to localhost.

Persistent state is written to CWD-relative files jevfuse_decisions.db and jevfuse_cache.db (engine.py:103-104) in whichever project directory the process runs from. This pollutes client repos and stores command text and prompts on disk.

Dependencies are heavy: fastapi, uvicorn, duckdb, aiosqlite, httpx[http2], mcp and pyyaml. There is no postinstall or curl|sh installer, and no telemetry beyond the dashboard's Google Fonts links (server/app.py:392-394). The single author has no CI, no releases and no SECURITY process beyond a template.

MCP server imports mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer (mcp/server.py:11). I could not confirm this module exists in the pinned mcp>=1.0.0. If it does not, the MCP server would fail at import. Not verified.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.dataEgress: Only the Layer-4 fallback contacts Jev. The payload is 'Command to evaluate: <bash command>\nWorking Directory: <cwd>' plus 4 fixed noul questions, sent to the gateway, which forwards to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default). Commands on the allowlist or denylist send nothing. Commands may embed inline secrets or file paths in their text. The MCP tools can send much more: fuse_verify sends arbitrary statement + context (code/logs), and fuse_prune sends up to 1500 chars of each non-user turn (assistant text, tool outputs, code) to Jev. Everything is also stored locally in unencrypted SQLite/DuckDB files in CWD.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.failureMode: The design is meant to fail closed toward ASK. The hook wraps errors as ASK, and the classifier returns ASK on non-200 responses, timeouts and connection errors (classifier.py). The client timeout is 2.0s for the hook-to-gateway call. On ConnectError it spins up a full in-process JevFuseEngine (SQLite+DuckDB init) per Bash call, which is slow. The provider-level timeout is 10s with 3 retries and exponential backoff (jev.py:30-31), so a stalled upstream can hold the gateway for up to ~40s. Because the ASK/DENY JSON shape is probably not honored by Claude Code, the practical failure mode is fail-open (the normal permission flow, which is bypass for this user). An exit-2 failure when `uv run` cannot find the script would be fail-closed and would block Bash entirely.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.contextCost: MCP: 4 tools (fuse_guard, fuse_prune, fuse_verify, fuse_route). The tool descriptions and schemas total roughly 2,000-2,500 chars, about 500-650 tokens. The MCP server sets no server-level instructions. The optional SKILL.md adds a ~90-word description line to the skill list (~120 tokens) and loads about 1.2k tokens when triggered. The PreToolUse hook injects no text into context, since it prints only JSON or nothing. The plugin install would add the skill, but the repo has no hooks/hooks.json, so the plugin does not install the hook; only the project-level .claude/settings.json in this repo has it.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.autoInvocation: Hook for the gate: PreToolUse on Bash is deterministic, but the verdict format is invalid for current Claude Code, so it is ineffective. The plugin manifest ships no hooks file, so the user must hand-add the hook to settings. The MCP tools (fuse_verify, fuse_route, fuse_prune) are model-discretion only; nothing prompts Claude to use them. The SKILL.md description trigger is the only nudge, and it concerns guard and prune.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.latencyImpact: Each Bash call spawns `uv run jevfuse hook pre-tool-use` (uv resolve/venv check plus a Python 3.12 start and imports). I estimate roughly 0.3-1.5s cold per Bash call, on top of the Jev call for non-allowlisted commands. The README's 0ms figures apply only to in-process rules and exclude process start. Fallback to the in-process engine on ConnectError adds DB init. This is a real overhead across a day of Bash-heavy work with bypass mode, in exchange for no effective gating.
pros: Genuinely reads the real System One wire: POST /v1/systemone with state/questions/answers, and models Noul/Choice/Score (provider/jev.py:194-214). Base URL and key are env-configurable, so a patched OpenRouter path is close.

Its deterministic Bash guard has useful logic: tokenizer/AST checks, a denylist (rm -rf on root/home, git push --force, dd of=/dev, mkfs, curl|sh) and a read-only allowlist. It is a sensible design for reducing prompts in default permission mode.
Fail-closed intent (ASK on any error) and a 2s client timeout in the hook path.
Apache-2.0, has a test suite (about 85 test functions across 11 files, including golden shell-guard fixtures), and the PyPI package exists.
Singleflight and cache logic would cut duplicate Jev calls if a gateway were ever run.
cons: The Claude Code hook output uses a made-up shape ({"allow": true}) that the current docs say is invalid for PreToolUse. The tests verify only the invented shape, so the flagship integration probably does nothing.

Wrong problem for this user: he runs bypass/auto mode with a secret-leak guard hook already installed. A Bash safety gate adds latency for little benefit, and its model tier never returns ALLOW (always ASK).

Does not use Jev for what Jev is good at in coding (routing, triage, tool selection, relevance). fuse_prune/route/verify are thin wrappers that need Claude to choose to call them, and the tool schema leaks real code and tool outputs to a third party.
No OpenRouter support. The model name is hardcoded to 'jev-latest', and the OpenRouter response schema is unverified. It needs code patching plus a running gateway or in-process engine.

Operationally fragile: `uv run jevfuse` only works inside a checkout or with a global tool install. It creates .db files in the CWD of every client project, uses a wide-open CORS gateway, and pulls in duckdb/fastapi/uvicorn for a 2-second check.

Immature and single-author: 50 commits over about 1 day, 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, the pushed date is 2026-09-24. The README makes unsupported claims (35ms P50, 98% cost savings, 'tamper-evident' logs, a Laya provider that has no code).
Overlaps existing tooling: the user's PreToolUse secret guard already covers the secret-path cases, and it would add a second Bash hook chain alongside GitNexus and caveman.
gh-0xshikhar-jev-fuse.verdict: Do not adopt. The project is a day-old, single-author proof of concept. Its Claude Code hook emits a decision format that current Claude Code docs say is invalid, and it has no OpenRouter path. Even if fixed, it only gates Bash commands, which adds latency and gives this bypass-mode user little value. At most, borrow its ideas (denylist, deadband, and the noul question design) for a custom hook.

security: API key: `jev-ra install claude` runs `claude mcp add jev-ra -s <scope> -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<real key> -- uvx jev-ra mcp` via subprocess.run (cli.py:366-377,403), so the key is in argv (visible in process list) briefly and is stored in plaintext in Claude Code's MCP config (~/.claude.json env block). Output is redacted and the displayed command shows $VAR, but argv exposure is real. Mitigation: register manually with the key from a wrapper or config.json (~/.config/jev-ra/config.json is also read, cli skips forwarding when key comes from config.json).
No telemetry/analytics found in grep of jev_ra/, npm/, scripts/. Only outbound calls: the decision endpoint, DuckDuckGo html for search, target sites via Chrome, optional text helper.

Prompt injection: page text is untrusted; SECURITY.md and questions.py state this, and the model only picks among observed operations/element indexes (no selectors, coordinates or JS from model output); password/file/hidden inputs excluded from snapshot; will not invent typed text. Residual risk: injection could steer clicks on legitimate-looking controls; tool results (page text up to 3000 chars in browser_observe, 1500 in summaries) flow into Claude's context as untrusted content. SECURITY.md advises a dedicated Chrome profile not signed into anything valuable.

Shell execution: subprocess used only for Chrome launch (chrome.py:315-332, launches Chrome, may retry with --no-sandbox), desktop notification (present.py), and `claude mcp add`. npm launcher (npm/bin/jev-ra.js:62) can offer `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` after prompting (--yes skips; --no-install refuses). PyPI install itself has no postinstall hook.

It gives Jev no role in coding decisions (routing, commit, permission, test-triage).
pros: Genuine, working OpenRouter integration: default route when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set, uses typesafe/jev-1.13 on /api/alpha/decisions with session_id (config.py:11-13,125-133; client.py:116-122), tests cover key precedence and route selection (tests/test_config.py, test_client.py).

Real use of Jev's typed primitives (Choice for operation/target/value, Noul for prev_ok/goal_achieved) with strict client-side validation of probabilities (client.py:60-103), i.e. the closest thing found to a faithful Jev design pattern.

Solid engineering for a 12-day-old repo: 960 test functions across ~100 test files, CI matrix on Python 3.12-3.14 with real headless Chrome, ruff/ty, dependabot, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG, tagged releases (0.2.8), PyPI + npm launcher, MIT.

Safety design: model can only pick among observed elements, passwords/file/hidden inputs never observed, no invented input, pacing per host, human-handoff for CAPTCHAs, file:// blocked by default, no telemetry found.
Failure is contained: provider errors become structured escalations; direct tools (click/type/observe/extract) never call Jev so browser use degrades gracefully.
Small tool surface (14) and tiny server instructions, lazy startup.
cons: Not a coding-workflow integration: Jev only decides browser clicks. Nothing for routing, permission decisions, test triage, commit classification, code review gating. Fit for a daily coding loop is limited to occasional web tasks.

Not automatic in the sense the user wants: only a model-discretion MCP tool; Claude must choose it over the already-installed playwright MCP, and the user asked for Claude to use Jev when it adds value without prompting. No hook/skill trigger shipped.
Redundant with playwright MCP already configured; adds a second browser stack (separate Chrome profile) and its own Chrome launch/--no-sandbox fallback.
README's own known-gaps: real-site corpus passes 102/120 (85%) vs a stated 90% bar; benchmark speedups are self-reported, single machine, browser-use compared with its single recorded run.
Sends goal text, page URL/title/6000 chars of page text and field values to OpenRouter/TypeSafe every step; unsuitable for logged-in or client-confidential pages without a dedicated profile.

`install claude` puts the raw OpenRouter key in argv of `claude mcp add` and persists it in plaintext in Claude Code's config env; recommended `uvx jev-ra mcp` is unpinned PyPI code from a single-author package created 2026-09-18 (198 of 200 commits by one person, 5 stars).
Depends on the alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions); could break as OpenRouter's alpha route changes. Jev has a 32k context, page text is truncated to 6000 chars.
Quality of Jev decisions unverified independently; skeptic claim (router-like behavior) not tested here.
gh-brnyxx-jev-ra.verdict: Best-in-class example of a well-built OpenRouter-native Jev integration, but it is a browser-automation tool that overlaps the user's playwright MCP, uses Jev only inside web tasks, and is invoked at Claude's discretion, so it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically for coding'. Worth installing only as an optional, pinned, dedicated-profile web tool; not the core integration.

gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.name: Gitmaxd/agent-seek
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.whatItDoes: FastAPI service (MCP Streamable HTTP at /mcp plus REST /v1/search) that runs a You.com web search and then re-ranks the candidates with TypeSafe Jev (Score and Noul questions for answerability, subject match, republisher, prompt-injection risk). It returns a scored URL list and does not write answers. It is a web-search product, not a coding aid, and Jev is used only as a hidden ranking backend.

providerSupport.evidence: packages/core/rank/jev.py:11 SYSTEMONE_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"; jev.py:12 MODEL = "jev-latest"; jev.py:44 base_url is a constructor arg but apps/api/main.py:184 builds `JevClient(s.typesafe_api_key)` with no override, and apps/api/config.py:22 only defines typesafe_api_key (no OPENROUTER_* or base-URL setting). Request body {model,state,questions} with Bearer auth, response read from data['answers'] (jev.py:57-73). grep found no openrouter references anywhere.
providerSupport.others: Also needs a paid You.com key (YDC_API_KEY). Optional OPENAI_API_KEY is used only by the eval harness. Optional Upstash Redis for rate limiting.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The constructor already takes base_url and model, so a fork edit would be small: point base_url at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, use typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest as the model, and load an OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The OpenRouter System One request/response schema is unverified. The code relies on {model,state,questions} -> {answers:{id:{type,noul|score}}} and on the shape of the parse_noul and parse_score_01 helpers. Nothing in the repo lets you switch by config, so you would have to fork and self-host the server.

interface.name: search_web (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Ranked web search. Args q (1-500 chars), k (1-25), max_candidates (1-100), mode snip|deep. Needs a Bearer AGENT_SEEK_API_KEY or OAuth scope search:read. Returns scored URLs, snippets, flags and signals.

interface.name: get_service_health (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Liveness and version check.

interface.name: get_api_docs (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Returns doc links and a contract summary.

interface.name: list_search_capabilities (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Lists modes, caps, signals, gates and OAuth scopes.

interface.name: POST/GET /v1/search, /v1/sandbox, /health, /oauth2/register, /mcp, /.well-known/*
interface.purpose: REST API, OAuth DCR, MCP transport and discovery endpoints.

interface.name: skills/agent-seek/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Agent Skill whose description triggers 'run ranked web search / find and rank sources for research or RAG'. Served from the well-known path; not an installer or a plugin.

security: Not a local stdio server: it is a FastAPI HTTP service to self-host, or a hosted MCP at agentseek.dev. The README publishes a shared demo Bearer key (AS_...) and says to paste it into mcp.json headers. Every query goes through a third-party operator, and the key is public and rate-limited to about 5 lifetime searches per IP.

No install scripts and no postinstall. Plain pip install -r requirements.txt (fastapi, uvicorn, httpx, pydantic, dotenv, pytest). No telemetry found in code. Optional Upstash Redis is used for rate limits.

Prompt-injection surface: web results (title, snippet, and page text in deep mode) are returned into the agent context. The repo's own defence is a Jev prompt_injection gate that drops flagged rows. The gate fails 'flagged' when the parse is missing, but subject_match and is_republisher fail open. The repo has no external verification of the gate.
Deep mode fetches arbitrary URLs server-side (packages/core/fetch/page.py), which is an SSRF surface for a self-hosted instance.
Default CORS_ORIGIN=* and a default AGENT_SEEK_API_KEY of dev-agent-seek-key-change-me in .env.example. OAuth state is in-memory.
TYPESAFE_API_KEY is stored in the server .env, not in argv. The client only sends its Bearer key in the MCP headers config.
MIT license. No pinned dependency versions (>= only).
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.dataEgress: The search query text (q, at most 500 chars) goes to You.com. Titles, URLs, snippets and (deep mode) fetched page text plus the query go to TypeSafe Jev. When the hosted agentseek.dev is used, the query also goes to the operator, whose privacy page says client IP is stored for the demo quota. Nothing from the code, diffs or repo files leaves the machine unless Claude itself puts code into q. If self-hosted, the operator is you.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.failureMode: Fail-open on the Jev side. On total Jev failure it returns HTTP 200 with meta.ranking=raw_fallback (You.com order). The Jev client timeout is 8s per call (jev.py:13, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT), and a full cascade makes several calls (Stage A and B, plus page fetches in deep mode). The MCP tool is model-invoked, so if the server is down Claude simply gets a tool error. Rate limiting fails closed (503) if Upstash is configured and down. No Claude Code hooks are involved.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. The tool definitions are about 1.6k tokens (estimated from the 4 descriptions and schemas in mcp_server.py). The server-level MCP_INSTRUCTIONS string is about 6,000 chars (about 1.5k tokens) and is injected on every session. Total about 3k tokens of standing context. No hook text is injected. Three of the four tools (health, docs, capabilities) add nothing for coding.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool (search_web) plus an optional skill description trigger (SKILL.md, 'ranked web search for research or RAG'). No hooks and no transparent proxy. Claude would call it only when it decides to search the web, and it competes with Claude Code's built-in WebSearch/WebFetch.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.latencyImpact: Each search is You.com discover plus 1-2 Jev cascade rounds (Stage A, Stage B). Deep mode adds up to 12 page fetches. No latency numbers are published in the repo; expect seconds per search rather than the 70-500 ms Jev claim. It adds nothing to non-search turns.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.runtime: Python 3.12+, FastAPI/uvicorn, httpx. Remote HTTP MCP (self-hosted or hosted at agentseek.dev)
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.install: Two routes: (1) hosted, add a Streamable-HTTP MCP entry with url https://agentseek.dev/mcp and a Bearer AS_... header. (2) Self-host: git clone, python -m venv, pip install -r requirements.txt, fill .env with YDC_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, run uvicorn apps.api.main:app --port 8787, then point Claude Code at http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp with a Bearer header. Not installed or run during this audit.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.tests: About 30 pytest files (offline fixtures, no live keys) and a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/test.yml, Python 3.12). One release, v0.3.0 (2026-09-23). The code is very young and single-author (2 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars).
pros: Real, working Jev usage (System One Score and Noul questions) with an actual fallback path (raw_fallback) and offline tests (about 30 test files, CI workflow).
MIT license, small readable codebase. JevClient already has base_url and model parameters, so an OpenRouter switch is a small fork edit.
Single-purpose read-only tools, all annotated readOnlyHint. The prompt_injection scoring of web results is a useful defence idea for research with Claude Code.
Doubles as a reference for how to build typed Jev questions (state + questions dict) for ranking, which the user could reuse.
cons: Not a coding tool. It is web search ranking, so it offers little value in daily coding: no code, diff, PR, test-failure or permission-decision use cases.
Jev is hidden behind a server. Claude Code cannot use Jev directly, only through the search_web tool.

No OpenRouter support: hard-coded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev.py:11) and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. Switching needs a fork and a self-hosted server, and the OpenRouter System One schema compatibility is unverified.
Requires two paid upstream keys (You.com and TypeSafe) to self-host, or trusting a stranger's hosted endpoint with a public shared key limited to about 5 searches per IP.
Model-discretion only. Claude Code must decide to call search_web instead of its built-in WebSearch, so it is not truly automatic, and there is no hook to force it.
Costs about 3k tokens of standing context, of which the 3 non-search tools and the 1.5k-token instructions block are mostly waste. Multi-second latency per search.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 2 stars, created 8 days before the audit date, and no pinned dependencies. Deep mode gives a self-hosted server an SSRF surface.
gh-gitmaxd-agent-seek.verdict: A fresh, single-author web-search reranker that uses Jev as an internal backend. It does not support OpenRouter and does not help with coding, and the model has to choose to call it. Skip it as the Jev integration for Claude Code; at most read the Jev question design as a reference.

gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.name: jev-browser-wingman
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.whatItDoes: Browser-automation MCP server (npm jev-browser-wingman 0.2.1). It attaches to a Chrome over CDP (playwright-core or raw CDP) beside Playwright MCP. It runs a bounded observe/decide/act loop: it enumerates page elements, sends the page state and Choice/Noul questions to the Jev System One endpoint, and clicks or types on the element Jev picks. Values you pass are typed locally and never sent. Irreversible actions are gated by confirm tokens. It is unrelated to code editing, repo navigation or general coding decisions.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.runtime: Node >=22, TypeScript compiled to dist. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, playwright-core, tldts. Published on npm as jev-browser-wingman@0.2.1. No GitHub releases.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.install: npm install -g jev-browser-wingman, then register in Claude Code as {"command":"jev-browser-wingman","args":["mcp"]}. Requires ~/.jev-browser-wingman/config.json with mode "on" (absent means off, and the tool list is then empty). Optional: wrap the Playwright MCP entry with `jev-browser-wingman with-chrome -- npx @playwright/mcp ...`. INSTALL-FOR-AGENTS.md drives an agent-led install with backups and diffs.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.tests: Large test suite in tests/ (about 60 files: loop, gate, policy, jev-client, mcp-server, CDP and Playwright adapter conformance, doctor, egress) run via scripts/run-tests.mjs. No .github directory, so no CI. I did not run any of it. The README benchmark is n=1 and shows no speedup (parity, sometimes slower). bench/ and spike/ dirs hold many result JSONs.

providerSupport.evidence: src/contract/constants.ts:5 ENV.KEY='TYPESAFE_API_KEY', BASE_URL='TYPESAFE_BASE_URL'; :50-52 TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_BASE_URL='https://api.typesafe.ai', TYPESAFE_PATH='/v1/systemone', TYPESAFE_MODEL='jev-latest'. src/core/jev-client.ts:73 baseUrl = opts.baseUrl ?? process.env.TYPESAFE_BASE_URL ?? default; :77 url=`${baseUrl}${TYPESAFE_PATH}`; :84 body JSON {model:'jev-latest', state, questions}; :99 Authorization: Bearer <key>. src/core/config.ts:312 resolveKey reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY (env) or the secrets_file line TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No OPENROUTER_* string anywhere in src/.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Nearly trivial, with one caveat. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the fixed path /v1/systemone gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is the OpenRouter System One route. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY to the OpenRouter key value, since the key env name is hardcoded. The blocker is that the model id is hardcoded to 'jev-latest' (jev-client.ts:84) with no env override. OpenRouter expects 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. It may reject the bare id, and I could not confirm because the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404. That needs a one-line source patch or a local proxy that rewrites the model field. The request and response schema (state, questions, answers[].choice/probabilities/confidence/noul) is TypeSafe-style and probably the same on OpenRouter, but unverified.
providerSupport.others: Custom Jev client can be injected via a plugin module (config `plugin`, exporting wingmanPlugin), which is an official way to supply a different JevAsk without forking.

interface.name: wingman_do
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Runs one bounded goal on the open page (observe, Jev picks element, act, settle) and returns a compact status: done, needs_confirmation, blocked, login, ambiguous, error or fallback. Args: goal, values, url_match, confirm_token, max_steps<=8, max_ms.

interface.name: wingman_check
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Read-only yes/no question about the visible page, returned as a probability (Noul).

interface.name: browse_step
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Proposes 1-3 steps plus a goal. The first Jev round decides, then it continues autonomously up to 24 steps and returns the step to the caller when uncertain (step-uncertain).

interface.name: CLI mcp / run / check / chrome ensure|status|stop|show|hide / with-chrome / doctor / guide
interface.purpose: Runs the stdio MCP server, one-shot goal or check, shared-Chrome lifecycle, Playwright-MCP proxy that starts Chrome lazily, 9-check doctor, prints the agent install guide.

interface.name: skills/jev-browser-wingman/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Skill telling the model to delegate any browsing goal of more than 3 clicks to wingman_do and how to read each status. Its description is not a hook or trigger, only a skill.

security: MIT, single author. I found no postinstall script (package.json scripts are build, test and prebuild only), no telemetry, and no curl|sh installer. I did not do a full audit of the source.

Key handling: read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or from a KEY=VALUE secrets_file. It is sent as a Bearer header in-process, not in argv. INSTALL-FOR-AGENTS says never put the key in synced config, and doctor's registration-portable check flags secret-shaped env in the registration.

Shell and process execution: it spawns Chrome with --remote-debugging-port (default 9222) and a dedicated profile dir. It uses execFile/netstat and process-cmdline inspection to find Chrome holders, and with-chrome spawns the wrapped command. An open local CDP port is an attack surface for other local processes.

Prompt-injection surface: page text and labels feed Jev, but Jev emits no free text, so injection can only bias element selection. Result labels are flagged as untrusted page text. An irreversible-action gate needs a single-use confirm token. The gate can be turned off (gate.mode off), and the sensitive-page policy defaults to OFF.
The tool descriptions and SKILL.md contain strong imperative steering (DEFAULT for any browsing goal, do NOT use raw tools) that pushes the calling model to route work through this tool.
Wrapping the Playwright MCP entry means editing the existing Playwright registration and reusing its user-data-dir, which would expose the logged-in Chrome profile to a second tool.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every step: page origin and path (no query or fragment), page title, element roles and labels (<=80 chars, up to 240 elements), a text excerpt (<=3000 chars), the goal text (<=500 chars), binding names and type hints, and a verb-plus-label history, within a state cap of 24k chars. Per the README it never sends typed values, hidden or prefilled input values, cookies, storage, screenshots or password fields. By default it sends this from all pages, including banking and mail, unless policy.mode is set to 'enforce'. No source code, diffs or repo file contents leave the machine. Only browser page content does. Routing via OpenRouter adds OpenRouter as a second party that sees the same payload.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.failureMode: Fail-open by design. The default Jev client (jev-client.ts) never throws and returns ok:false on timeout, network or invalid-response errors. It does 2 attempts, retrying only on 429 or 5xx after 250 ms or retry-after. The per-call timeout is 10s (jev_timeout_ms, max 10s) and the total loop budget is 45s. The loop turns failures into status 'fallback' (askFailReason, loop.ts:729/968: no-key, budget-time, breaker-open, and similar), and the docs tell the calling agent to use its raw browser tools. With mode absent or off, the tool list is empty. With no key, every call returns fallback/no-key. If Jev is down, it wastes up to a few seconds per call and then falls back. There is no circuit breaker in the default client.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.contextCost: Three tools: wingman_do, wingman_check and browse_step. Descriptions are about 1.4k, 0.6k and 1.6k chars, plus schemas of roughly 1.5k chars, so about 5.5k chars or 1.4k tokens (chars/4). The server sets no MCP 'instructions'. The optional SKILL.md adds a one-line description only until it is invoked. No hooks inject text. Tool results are compact JSON. When mode is off, the tool list is empty and the cost is about 0.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.latencyImpact: Only on browser-tool calls, nothing on ordinary coding turns. The README measures about 1s per step of machinery, of which Jev is a small part, and Chrome attach or start on the first call. Its own benchmark (n=1) shows wall-clock from 22% faster to 95% slower than plain Playwright, and no cost win. Zero latency added to non-browser turns.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools. The tool descriptions and optional SKILL.md are written to make Claude pick wingman_do or browse_step for multi-click browsing goals without being asked. There is no hook or transparent proxy, and Jev is not used for any non-browser coding decision. The with-chrome wrapper only lazily starts Chrome before the first tools/call.
pros: Genuinely Jev-based: it uses Choice and Noul questions against the System One endpoint /v1/systemone and validates the probability output strictly (parseJevAnswers, jev-client.ts:26-54).
The base URL is overridable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (jev-client.ts:73), so pointing it at OpenRouter needs a single env var. TYPESAFE_API_KEY can hold the OpenRouter key value.
Fail-open with bounded timeouts (10s per call, 45s per loop): a Jev outage degrades to fallback, and the calling agent uses raw Playwright.
Tool descriptions and SKILL.md steer Claude to delegate automatically, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.
Typed values stay local. There is an irreversible-action confirm-token gate, and an opt-in sensitive-page policy.
MIT license, no postinstall or telemetry that I found, a large test suite, and it is honest about its own benchmarks (no proven speedup).
Small context footprint (about 1.4k tokens), and about 0 when mode is off.
cons: It only covers browser automation. A senior dev's daily coding (edit, grep, test, git, review) never touches it, so Jev adds no value there.

The model id is hardcoded to 'jev-latest' (jev-client.ts:84) with no override. OpenRouter needs 'typesafe/...' or '~typesafe/jev-latest', so it likely fails against OpenRouter until patched (source patch or rewriting proxy). The OpenRouter body schema is unverified.
The env var names are TYPESAFE_*, with no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support, and the key must be duplicated or renamed.
It is 10 days old, one author, 0 stars, no releases, no CI and no external users. It is alpha, and the Jev API itself is beta.
Its own benchmark shows no gain: wall-clock is parity to 95% slower than Playwright, n=1, and one long-chain run failed on both routes. The README says a speedup is not shown.
It sends page content (titles, labels, text excerpts) to a third-party endpoint, and by default also from sensitive pages. That matters for client projects unless policy.mode is 'enforce'.

Overlaps with the existing Playwright MCP and needs a shared Chrome on a debug port. Wrapping the Playwright entry changes existing config and profile handling, and the alternative is a separate second Chrome profile.
Mode defaults to off and requires hand-written config.json. The steering language ('do NOT use raw tools') can make Claude over-delegate to a beta tool, and it can loop with the with-chrome wrapper.
gh-coderexpert123-jev-browser-wingman.verdict: A real but narrow Jev integration: a browser-step chooser that could be pointed at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a one-line model-id patch. It does nothing for everyday coding, its own benchmark shows no gain, and the project is 10 days old. Skip it unless you do a lot of browser automation and want to experiment on the side.

gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.runtime: Node >=20, TypeScript compiled to committed dist/ (64 tracked dist files), zero runtime dependencies, stdio JSON-RPC MCP server written in-house (src/mcp/jsonrpc.ts)
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.install: claude plugin marketplace add CaptainDigitals/jev-copilot ; claude plugin install jev-copilot@jev-copilot ; then set the key via /plugin -> Configure (stored in the OS credential store), or export OPENROUTER_API_KEY, or run /jev-copilot:configure. No npm install needed because dist/ is committed.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.tests: About 105 node:test cases across 16 files (tests/*.test.ts: hooks, client, runtime, tool-risk incl. a bypass suite, redact, credentials, config, youtube, mcp), plus tests/evals/cases.jsonl for live accuracy calibration. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) on ubuntu/windows/macos: typecheck, build, a check that dist/ is not stale, tests, claude plugin validate, and a secret scan. I did not run any of it (static read only). README claims 84 tests at v0.2.0.
security: API key handling is good: the key reaches the MCP server as an env var from plugin userConfig (sensitive:true, .claude-plugin/plugin.json), so it does not show in argv. Fallback file ~/.jev-copilot/credentials.json is written mode 0600 (credentials.ts). A project .jev-copilot.json cannot override apiKey or endpoint (config.ts:206). The endpoint is https and host-allowlisted to openrouter.ai (client.ts:17).

Outbound redaction of ~15 secret patterns (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, AWS, Slack, Stripe, Google, JWT, private keys, bearer, connection strings, *_SECRET/TOKEN= assignments) via redactValue before every call (runtime/index.ts). It is regex based, so custom or low-entropy secrets pasted into a prompt can still leak. Excluded paths (.env, *.pem, .ssh, .aws, credentials*) are never summarised.

No shell execution in the hook or MCP path. Only execFileSync('git', ...) with a 4 s timeout (context/discover.ts:16) and execFile for yt-dlp with an option allowlist (youtube/ytdlp.ts). No curl|sh, no postinstall (private package, zero deps; the only devDependencies are typescript and @types/node).

Telemetry is local only (telemetry.jsonl in the plugin data dir) and holds hashes, ids, latency and cost, not prompt text. No third-party analytics endpoint in dist (host grep shows only openrouter.ai, youtube.com and github.com strings).

Supply-chain risk: the committed dist/*.js is what runs, not the TypeScript. CI checks dist is not stale, but any install trusts a single anonymous account's compiled JS on every hook with the ability to read your prompts and inject context. It is a 3-day-old repo with no releases, so pin a commit SHA and review dist before installing.

Prompt-injection surface: the hook injects model-derived text into Claude's context (task profile, and Stop-hook 'reason' listing deficiencies). Content is generated from typed numbers and fixed templates, so the surface is small. The YouTube path handles untrusted captions with an explicit neutraliser (youtube/untrusted.ts) and is not relevant unless used.

The Stop hook can return decision:block, so a wrong Jev verdict makes Claude do extra work, capped at 2 loops per task. In strict mode a Jev outage means 'manual review' messaging instead of silent pass.
Plugin skill/command allowed-tools pre-approve only plugin MCP tools plus a Bash(node *configure*) / Bash(node *) pattern in status.md, which is broad but only exists in that command.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, per call: model id, the redacted user prompt (up to 12,000 chars, on nearly every prompt of 40+ chars), a repo summary (up to 40 top-level paths, top 6 file extensions, up to 20 git-diff --name-only changed files), on Stop the request (6000 chars), requirement texts, up to 40 changed-file paths per category, last 10 test commands (300 chars each) and outcomes, and Claude's last assistant message (4000 chars). With jev_context or jev_rank_context: up to 24 candidate paths with summaries (symbol names) and 600-char redacted head excerpts of source files. With tool governance on (off by default): the classified command/path state and the task text (2000 chars). Never full diffs or whole files. OpenRouter and TypeSafe therefore see your prompts and file paths. That matters for client projects: client code names and paths leave the machine, and a per-project .jev-copilot.json can set mode off. HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers identify the app. Response cache and telemetry stay local.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.failureMode: Fail-open by design in assist and enhance. No key means a degraded notice and no calls. Timeout is 8 s per attempt with 1 retry (400 ms base backoff, Retry-After honoured, capped 30 s), so the worst case is roughly 16 s of stall. The runner enforces a wall-clock budget (UserPromptSubmit 15 s, Stop 25 s, PreToolUse 10 s, PostToolUse 3 s), and on budget expiry the hook silently returns nothing (hooks/runner.ts:8-38). Any exception exits 0 with no output. A session budget of $0.25 skips optional calls. Strict mode is the only fail-closed variant: hard tool rules deny, and a Stop review outage tells Claude to flag manual review. Hidden costs: a blocking 20 s UserPromptSubmit hook can freeze the prompt when OpenRouter's alpha endpoint stalls, and the Decisions API is an /alpha path that can change its schema. Responses are schema-validated, and a malformed response is treated as failure and skipped.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.contextCost: MCP: 13 tools (7 general and 6 YouTube). Tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 6.7K chars, roughly 1.7K tokens (my regex estimate of src/mcp/server.ts and youtube-tools.ts register blocks), and the server sets no MCP 'instructions' field. Skills: 4 descriptions of roughly 400-600 chars each (about 0.5K tokens always loaded), bodies 2-4.4 KB on trigger. 15 slash commands add small frontmatter descriptions (about 0.5K tokens), and 1 agent description adds about 0.1K. Total always-on overhead is about 2.5-3K tokens, of which about 1K is YouTube-only clutter. Hook-injected text: SessionStart is about 2 lines (about 120 tokens) once per session. Each substantive prompt injects an ~8-10 line profile plus the requirement line (about 200-300 tokens per turn, accumulating in the transcript). A Stop repair block adds about 150-400 tokens plus the extra Opus turn that follows. It coexists with the existing gitnexus tool set, but the user already pays context for many MCP tools, and YouTube tools have no value here.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.latencyImpact: Blocking, in the critical path. UserPromptSubmit adds one OpenRouter round trip per substantive prompt (claimed 70-500 ms plus node cold start ~50-100 ms and TLS; realistically 0.3-1.5 s, cached hits are about 0 ms). Stop adds one call (~0.3-1.5 s) after any turn that edited files and then possibly forces an extra Opus repair turn (multi-second, extra tokens). PreToolUse and PostToolUse spawn a fresh node process for every Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit call, adding ~50-100 ms each with no network (deterministic path), and this stacks with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus hooks. Worst case on an OpenRouter stall is ~16 s at prompt submit and ~25 s at Stop.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks, with no model discretion needed. UserPromptSubmit fires for any non-trivial prompt and injects a Jev task profile automatically. Stop fires after edits and runs a completion review that can block. PreToolUse fires on every mutating tool call for regex hard rules (Jev only for high-impact actions if governance is enabled). The MCP tools, skills (description-triggered) and slash commands are supplementary and model-discretion. This is one of the few candidates that meets 'never say use jev' literally.
pros: Fully automatic without prompting: hooks.json wires UserPromptSubmit, Stop and PreToolUse to dist/src/hooks/runner.js, so Jev runs on prompts and at completion with zero user phrasing. This matches the stated requirement.

OpenRouter-native and correct for this user: endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and model typesafe/jev-1.13 (defaults.json:3-4), with the key from OPENROUTER_API_KEY or the OS credential store. It does not need a TypeSafe account.

Fail-open and bounded: 8 s timeout, 1 retry, hard wall-clock budgets in hooks/runner.ts, an exit-0 catch-all, a $0.25 session budget and a local content-addressed decision cache. A Jev outage will not break Claude Code in enhance mode.

Solid privacy engineering for a young project: secret redaction on every outbound state, excluded paths, no file bodies or diffs in hooks, telemetry without prompt text, key in env not argv, project config cannot change the endpoint or key, mode 'off' available per project.

Zero runtime deps, no postinstall, no shell exec beyond execFileSync('git') with a timeout, tests plus a CI stale-dist check on three OSes. Cost per session is negligible (about $0.00002-0.00003 per call).

Good design principle in policy code: Jev only supplies typed probabilities, deterministic rules outrank Jev for tool safety, and JEV never invents file paths in context ranking. The Stop hook repair loop is capped at 2.
Removable per project (.jev-copilot.json mode off) and per plugin via the standard plugin uninstall, so client projects can opt out.
cons: Very immature and single-author: created 2026-09-27, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars/forks, no releases or tags, version 0.2.1, three days old on 2026-09-30. There is no community vetting, and the docs (PRD, roadmap, handoff) read as AI-generated scaffolding. The committed dist/ JS runs on every hook, so a supply-chain review or SHA pin is mandatory.

Scope creep: 6 of 13 MCP tools, 7 of 15 commands and a whole skill are a YouTube research engine irrelevant to coding. This costs about 1K tokens of always-on context and extra attack surface (yt-dlp exec).

Weak signal for its cost: the Stop-hook review sees only changed-file names, test outcomes and Claude's last message, never diffs or file contents (runtime/index.ts:155-176). Jev returning 'implementation complete' or 'regression likely' from filenames is close to noise, and each false 'repair' forces another Opus 5.5 turn (real tokens and time). The default thresholds are documented as uncalibrated starting points (defaults.json thresholds, README 'starting points for calibration, not truth').

The UserPromptSubmit profile (task type, complexity, tests needed) largely restates what Opus 5.5 infers itself, while adding a blocking network hop on every prompt (up to ~16 s if OpenRouter stalls) and ~250 tokens per turn. The value for an expert Opus workflow is marginal.

Sends every prompt of 40+ chars, plus file paths and Claude's last message, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on client projects. Regex redaction will not catch client names, proprietary identifiers or non-key secrets. The user needs a per-project opt-out policy.

Hook overlap and friction with the existing setup: a node process spawns on every Bash/Edit/Write on top of the secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks. Its hard rules (credential path access, download-and-execute, recursive delete) duplicate the secret guard and return permissionDecision 'ask', which could interrupt unattended bypass or auto-mode runs. Whether 'ask' overrides bypass mode was not verified.

Depends on OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions (alpha, beta model). Schema drift breaks it, though it fails open. Session-id matching for MCP/CLI uses the most recently modified session file (runtime/index.ts currentSessionId), which can attach to the wrong session with concurrent Claude Code windows.
No releases or CI-proven history, and the manifest pins no marketplace version. The README says npx-less, but the plugin cache path is hard-coded to version 0.2.1 in the docs.

Skepticism about Jev quality (Theo: 'a DeepSeek flash router') would apply directly here, since all value comes from Jev's calibrated probabilities on vague semantic questions and none is verifiable locally.
gh-captaindigitals-jev-copilot.verdict: The only candidate seen that is OpenRouter-native and automatic via hooks, and it is well engineered (fail-open, redaction, budgets, tests). It is still a 3-day-old solo project whose Jev signals (filename-based completion review, prompt classification) add latency, tokens and possible spurious repair loops for little gain over Opus 5.5. Worth trying only with SHA pinning, tool governance and Stop-block disabled or assist mode, and off on client repos. Otherwise treat it as a pattern to copy, not something to depend on.

gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.name: opsiaadi/opnroute-jev
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.whatItDoes: Two tiny (about 5.7 KB and 8.2 KB) single-file Python MCP servers, one stdio and one Streamable HTTP, written for the Hermes agent. They wrap OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev via urllib. The exposed tools are classify, classify_batch and health. The default question set is a hardcoded chat-message classifier (is_crypto, is_support, is_spam, category, urgency, sentiment_score). Nothing in it is coding-specific, and nothing in it triggers automatically.

providerSupport.evidence: jev_classifier.py:41-43 sets OPENROUTER_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, SYSTEMONE_ENDPOINT=f"{OPENROUTER_BASE}/systemone" and MODEL=os.environ.get("JEV_MODEL","~typesafe/jev-latest"). jev_classifier.py:70-85 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY and sends a Bearer header. Payload at :74 is {model, state, questions}. The HTTP variant repeats this at jev_classifier_http.py:70-72 and :98-114. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not used. TYPESAFE_API_KEY and the TypeSafe direct endpoint do not appear anywhere. The key falls back to ~/.hermes/.env (:25-35). The base URL is hardcoded and not configurable. The request/response schema ({model,state,questions} -> .answers) is unverified against OpenRouter docs and is not confirmed by any test, since none exist.
providerSupport.others: None. Sends HTTP-Referer https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com and X-Title headers, so requests are attributed to Hermes on OpenRouter.

gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.openrouterPatchability: Already OpenRouter-only. Adding TypeSafe direct would be trivial, but the user does not need it.

interface.name: classify(text, questions?)
interface.purpose: POSTs text as System One 'state' with default or custom questions (JSON string) and returns the answers JSON. Only with the default questions is it a chat-message classifier for crypto, support, spam, intent, urgency and sentiment.

interface.name: classify_batch(texts, questions?)
interface.purpose: Takes a JSON-array string and makes one sequential HTTP call per text with a 30 s timeout each. Invalid questions JSON is not caught (jev_classifier.py:129), so it raises.

interface.name: health()
interface.purpose: Returns {ready: bool(env key), model, endpoint}. It makes no network call, so it does not verify connectivity.

gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.runtime: Python 3.10+ with the mcp package (imports `from mcp.server import MCPServer`, which the README says needs mcp 2.0+; the stdio file's ImportError hint says pip install mcp[cli]). The HTTP variant also needs uvicorn and starlette. No pyproject or requirements file, no lockfile, no versions pinned, no PyPI or npm package. Install is git clone and run by hand.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.install: git clone https://github.com/opsiaadi/opnroute-jev && pip install mcp uvicorn starlette. Then run `claude mcp add jev -- python3 /path/jev_classifier.py`, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY passed through env. The README only documents Hermes, Claude Desktop and Cursor over HTTP, not Claude Code or stdio for Claude Code.

security: No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry. Only outbound call is to openrouter.ai (urllib, jev_classifier.py:77-88).

Stdio variant: the key can be passed via env, so it stays out of argv (good). The README example for Hermes uses `--env OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...`, which puts the key in the Hermes command line. Claude Code's `claude mcp add -e` avoids that.
Fallback silently reads ~/.hermes/.env (:28-35). The parser only picks the OPENROUTER_API_KEY line, but it is an odd hardcoded path for a non-Hermes user.

HTTP variant: a default of 127.0.0.1 is safe, but the README pushes 0.0.0.0 with no auth by default. MCP_AUTH_TOKEN is optional (jev_classifier_http.py:36-45), and the check is `!=` string compare, not constant-time. transport_security=None disables DNS-rebinding protection (:193). Anyone who reaches the port can spend the user's OpenRouter credits. The HTTP variant is not needed for Claude Code, so use stdio only.
Prompt-injection surface is small. Tool output is JSON probabilities, so it cannot carry free text back into the model, except the raw OpenRouter error body (first 500 chars, :90).
Data sent to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) is whatever text the model passes as 'text', with no redaction and no allowlist. For client projects that is a compliance concern.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.dataEgress: Whatever string Claude passes as the `text` argument, sent as `state` to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (and on to TypeSafe), plus the question definitions. Nothing else. There is no automatic capture of prompts, diffs, files or tool outputs. The scope depends on what Claude chooses to send, and unlike a hook it is not filtered by the user's secret-leak guard, because that guard only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and MCP tool inputs are not covered. Headers include the OpenRouter key and a Hermes HTTP-Referer.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level. Errors (missing key, HTTP error, URLError, bad JSON) are returned as {"error": ...} JSON and not raised. The timeout is 30 s per call and blocking. The stdio server is synchronous inside async tools, so a slow Jev call blocks the server event loop. classify_batch is sequential, so N texts can take up to N x 30 s. TimeoutError and socket.timeout raised while reading the response body are not caught (only HTTPError, URLError and JSONDecodeError are), so the tool can raise. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. Since nothing calls it automatically, failures only affect turns where Claude chooses to use it.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.latencyImpact: Nominally 70-500 ms per classify call (claimed by TypeSafe), plus a fresh TLS connection every call (urllib, no pooling) and one model tool-call round trip (about 1-3 s of Opus turn time). No per-turn or per-tool-call overhead, because it is not a hook. In the worst case, a hung request blocks for 30 s.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.contextCost: 3 tools. Names, descriptions and schemas come to about 250-350 tokens in the HTTP variant, which has docstrings. The stdio variant has no docstrings at all, so its tools are described only by name and args, which is worse for model discretion. Server instructions add about 55 tokens ("JEV Classifier MCP - structured classification ... noul, choice, score"). Total is about 300-400 tokens, negligible. Nothing is injected by hooks.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no routing. The server instructions describe a generic text classifier and never mention coding. Opus would almost never call it unprompted for coding tasks, since the tool descriptions and defaults are about crypto, spam and sentiment. It does not meet the user's 'automatic' requirement.
pros: Very small and fully auditable (about 14 KB of Python), with no shell execution, no postinstall and no telemetry. The only network destination is openrouter.ai.

Uses OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL defaulting to ~typesafe/jev-latest. Model id and env var match the user's chosen provider directly, and the stdio variant can be registered with `claude mcp add -e`.
Custom `questions` passthrough (JSON with type noul/choice/score, instructions, criteria) makes it a usable raw System One client if you supply your own coding-oriented questions.
Errors are returned as data instead of crashing the server in the common cases. MIT license, tiny context footprint (about 300-400 tokens).
cons: Not automatic. Pure model-discretion tool with generic-classifier descriptions (crypto, spam, sentiment). Claude Code will not use it without being told to, which is the exact thing the user wants to avoid.
Default questions are a hardcoded crypto/support/spam chat classifier (jev_classifier.py:45-66) with no coding use case such as risk-gating a Bash command, triaging a diff or picking a test scope.

Built for Hermes. README has no Claude Code instructions, hardcodes the Hermes Referer and X-Title headers and reads ~/.hermes/.env. Depends on `mcp.server.MCPServer` from an mcp 2.0+ API that is not verified and has no pinned version, so a plain `pip install mcp` may fail to import.
Zero tests, no CI, no releases, 0 stars, 4 commits in one day, and an unverified request/response schema that has not been checked against OpenRouter docs. The stdio tools have no docstrings.

Sends arbitrary Claude-chosen text to a third party with no redaction, outside the coverage of the user's secret-leak hook. No timeout tuning, no retry, sequential batch, and a blocking call inside an async server.
Uses only the System One endpoint and not the Decisions API. It offers no Choice-over-tool-calls or permission-hook integration.
HTTP variant encourages an unauthenticated 0.0.0.0 bind that would let others spend the user's credits (transport_security=None). The user would not need it.
gh-opsiaadi-opnroute-jev.verdict: A harmless but tiny Hermes-oriented proof of concept that proves the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone call shape (model + state + questions). It is not an automatic Claude Code integration and has no coding-relevant behavior. Use it at most as reference code for a custom hook or MCP, and do not adopt it.

Each use costs an extra Opus turn to hand-write question JSON (and possibly call question_schema first), likely exceeding Jev's 70-500 ms benefit; Jev is a decision primitive, not something that speeds up code edits.
Worst-case stall: 60 s timeout x 3 attempts per call, no circuit breaker; batch tool doesn't wrap client-init errors.
Data egress is at Claude's discretion: code/diffs it pastes into `state` go to a third party, and the existing secret guard hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover this MCP tool.

gh-gnapse-jev.dataEgress: Only what Claude places in `state` and `questions` arguments of jev_ask/jev_batch leaves the machine: POST to <base>/v1/systemone with the bearer key, sent to api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (and then TypeSafe as its provider) if the base URL is overridden. Nothing is sent automatically: no hooks, no file scanning, no transcript access. Claude decides content per call, so client code, diffs and file contents are sent whenever the model chooses to include them. With the secret-leak guard hook only on Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, MCP calls to jev_* are not covered, so secrets in state would pass through unguarded. OpenRouter's prompt-logging/ZDR settings then apply.
gh-gnapse-jev.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's point of view: errors come back as an MCP tool result with isError:true and a structured error body (code, retryable, http_status), and Claude simply proceeds without Jev. Defaults: per-attempt timeout 10 s (settings.ts:69), total deadline 120 s (settings.ts:70), SDK retries maxRetries 2 with backoff (settings.ts:79), concurrency 4, max 32 outstanding calls. Worst case for a slow or down backend is a call stalling the turn for up to ~120 s (retries x 10 s), unless timeout_ms/deadline_ms are tuned via a config file or CLI flags. Those cannot be set through MCP env vars, only via the `config` file or `jev mcp` flags. If the key is missing, the tool returns an AUTH_ERROR without crashing the server.
gh-gnapse-jev.latencyImpact: None unless Claude chooses to call. When called: the Jev network round trip (claimed 70-500 ms) plus about 0.3-1 s of extra Claude tool-call/reasoning tokens for building the typed request. There is no per-turn overhead since there are no hooks. Server cold start adds ~100-300 ms at session start (Node process; more with npx).

Estimated ~1.5-2k tokens for tool names, descriptions and inputSchemas (descriptions about 1.3k chars, input schemas about 5k chars, roughly 6-7k chars/4). outputSchema is also declared, but it is likely not sent to the model. Server `instructions` are about 300 chars (~75 tokens). No hook-injected text. If the optional SKILL.md (6.4k chars, about 1.6k tokens) is installed, only its description line sits in context until it triggers. There is no hook and no proxy, so nothing deterministic. The optional skill's trigger is tied to 'working with @gnapse/jev or adding classification... to scripts', which is not a general coding trigger. Auto-use in daily coding would be rare and unpredictable unless CLAUDE.md or a hook adds policy (e.g. 'before X, call jev_ask with Choice to classify Y'), which the user explicitly does not want to hand-prompt.
pros: Wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, which POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with a Bearer token (dist/index.mjs:554,579). That path matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so OpenRouter should work via env only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (settings.ts:63) with an OpenRouter key.
