Tiny context footprint (4 tools, about 1.5-2k tokens, no hook text), and no hooks, so no interference with the existing secret-guard/GitNexus/caveman hooks and zero per-turn latency.
Tools declared readOnlyHint, so no permission prompts in auto or bypass mode.
MCP-only path returns only numbers and labels (no free text), so it is a low prompt-injection risk on the return path.

cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with a generic description. Nothing makes Claude Code reach for Jev during coding, so the user's core requirement (no 'use jev' prompting) is not met without extra glue (CLAUDE.md policy or own hooks).

Hard-wired to TypeSafe: no OpenRouter code path, docs or tests; OpenRouter works only by an unverified env override. Default model name 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter slug (needs TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL). jev_models likely breaks on OpenRouter's /models shape.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21 (9 days old), 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, v0.1.1; not TypeSafe-official. API and behaviour may churn, and it is a supply-chain trust decision (pin the version).

Timeouts/retries default to 10 s x 3 attempts and 120 s deadline, and are not configurable via MCP env vars, so a slow Jev could stall a turn for a long time. Would need a config file or wrapper flags.

Silent egress: jev_* calls are readOnly so auto/bypass mode sends whatever state Claude chooses (code, diffs) with no prompt, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not match MCP tools. Would need a PreToolUse matcher for mcp__jev__.*.

Jev is a decision-classifier, not a code model; this package adds no coding-specific integration (no PreToolUse routing, no diff/permission classification hooks), so daily-coding value is speculative.

Key handling: for OpenRouter the key has to live as plaintext env in the MCP config (~/.claude.json) or be exported in the shell; `jev auth login` stores it only for TypeSafe verification and may reject an OpenRouter key when verifying before save (unverified).
gh-gnapse-jev.verdict: A clean, safe-ish thin MCP/CLI wrapper that can probably be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is a generic manual-use tool: it gives Claude Code the ability to call Jev, not any automatic trigger. Useful only as the transport layer beneath a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy, or as a reference for the request format; pin the version and treat it as alpha.

Uses reqwest 0.12 default features (native TLS); Cargo.lock committed (56 KB) but no cargo-audit/deny in CI. Unreviewed single-author, 0-star repo: supply chain risk is the author plus the rmcp/tokio dep tree; you must compile it yourself.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into the tool arguments: state/question text for noul/choice/score/decide; query + up to 32 item strings for rank; full text of fetched/pasted content for screen; claim + evidence (diff/log/passage) for verify; proposed command + optional task/policy for gate. All sent verbatim (except rank's local index preview truncation) to openrouter.ai, which forwards to TypeSafe (response 'provider' field). Nothing is harvested automatically from the repo or transcript, but in practice Claude will paste diff hunks, commands and file snippets, so client code can reach OpenRouter/TypeSafe; no redaction or secret stripping is done server-side (SKILL.md only says 'strip env files first'). Client-project NDAs and OpenRouter data-retention/provider policy should be checked. Cost: about $0.042/M input tokens.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.failureMode: Fail-open by construction: API errors (HTTP, non-2xx, decode) are returned as a normal isError tool result with the message (server.rs:45, api.rs:243-247), so Claude just sees a failed tool call and continues. Missing key makes the process exit at startup (main.rs:418 config::load()? -> Err), so Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools are absent, again not blocking anything. Timeout is 60 s per request (api.rs:210), no retries, no circuit breaker, no cache. A hung Jev could stall one turn up to 60 s if the model chose to call it; in a hook this would matter, but here it is model-discretion only. No hook means no fail-closed path exists.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.contextCost: 8 tools always in the tool list. Estimated from source: descriptions about 2.3k chars, JSON schemas from params.rs (about 4.3k chars of source with per-field descriptions, schemars output about 5-6k chars incl. structure) plus server instructions about 700 chars (server.rs:357-364), total roughly 8-9k chars, about 2.0-2.5k tokens. If Claude Code's MCP tool search defers tool defs, only names are loaded until needed. No hook-injected text (no hooks). SKILL.md adds only its description (about 400 chars) to the skill list until triggered; full body about 2.3k chars (about 600 tokens) when loaded.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude doesn't call it (no hooks). Per call: one HTTPS round trip to OpenRouter, plausibly 70-500 ms per TypeSafe's claim (unverified here) plus MCP stdio overhead of a few ms; rank/decide are one request but parallel questions server-side. Each call costs an extra model tool-use step in Claude's loop (~1-3 s of Opus turn time), which usually exceeds Jev's own latency; that overhead makes gate/rank calls net-negative for speed vs. Claude just deciding.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. Nothing is deterministic: no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, no proxy. Claude will call it only if it judges a tool description relevant; with Opus 5.5 that is rare for tasks like 'noul: does this diff touch auth' because it can answer directly. The bundled SKILL.md is written for Grok's search_tool/use_tool flow and references Fable/Grok, so it needs rewriting for Claude Code. Making it truly automatic (e.g. gate before every Bash, screen after WebFetch) would require adding your own hooks that call the API or the binary, which this repo does not provide; note the README itself says gate/screen never execute or block anything.
pros: Genuinely OpenRouter-native and code-verified: hits https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.rs:8-12,117; api.rs:170), matching the Jev brief exactly. Zero patching needed for the user's chosen provider.
Small, readable codebase (about 1.1k lines Rust, about 64 KB source excluding lock); auditable in 10 minutes. No shell exec, no file access, key never in argv when config.toml is used.

Good tool design for typed decisions: decide batches many atomic questions in one request; rank/verify/screen/gate are sensible pre-baked prompts for coding-agent use cases (retrieval reranking, claim vs diff, injection screening, tool-call risk).
Fail-open and non-blocking: errors surface as isError tool results; missing key just disables the server; adds no per-turn cost or latency when unused.
MIT licensed, pinned model default with an explicit comment that jev-latest moves (config.toml.example), and CI runs fmt/clippy/test.
Cheap: ~$0.042/M input tokens; even heavy tool use is pennies.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion. Opus 5.5 has little reason to delegate a yes/no to another model, so it will seldom call these tools unless CLAUDE.md or hooks force it; that directly fails the user's 'Claude Code must use it without being told' requirement.

No Claude Code integration at all: no hooks, no plugin.json/.mcp.json/marketplace entry; README documents only Grok; SKILL.md targets Grok/Fable (search_tool, use_tool, 'Keep Fable/Grok for that') and would need rewriting.

gate and screen are advisory and never enforce; thresholds (secrets>=0.30, injection>=0.75, etc.) are hardcoded guesses (format.rs:138-166) with no calibration evidence. Using an unverified beta model as a security classifier is weaker than the user's existing deterministic secret-leak PreToolUse hook and would add no real protection.

Data egress risk on client projects: diffs, commands and file content that Claude chooses to pass go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no redaction; the user's existing secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool arguments unless its matcher is extended.

Extreme immaturity: 1 commit, 1 author, 0 stars/forks, created 9 days before audit date, no releases, no prebuilt binaries (must cargo build), one mocked round-trip test and no live-API tests, uses alpha endpoint that may change (/api/alpha/).
Extra Opus round trip per use (~seconds) outweighs Jev's 70-500 ms; ~2-2.5k tokens of always-on tool-def context for 8 tools, most of which overlap what Claude does natively (verify, rank, screen).

Silently falls back to reading ~/.config/mcp-server-open-router/config.toml for an API key (config.rs:118), and the sample 'site_url' attribution defaults to the author's domain example; minor hygiene issues.
Only System One Decisions API; no TypeSafe direct key support, no System One (/api/v1/systemone) path, no Jev Router model support beyond overriding default_model.
gh-codechap-mcp-server-jev.verdict: The only OpenRouter-native, code-verified Jev MCP found so far, and safe to read and build, but it is a Grok-oriented proof of concept whose tools Claude will rarely call on its own, so it fails the 'automatic' requirement unless you add deterministic hooks or CLAUDE.md rules yourself. Best used as a reference implementation or a low-cost opt-in tool (fork it, build locally, add a Claude Code hook layer), not as a drop-in solution.

gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.name: GodsBoy/jev-agent-skill-router
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.whatItDoes: Python 3.11 stdlib-only library and CLI (jev-router route/evaluate/report/validate-results) that routes a natural-language request to one skill out of a catalogue of (name, description) pairs. It batches the catalogue (8 per batch, 4 parallel workers), calls Jev Choice on each batch, keeps the top 2 per batch, and repeats until a final Choice plus Noul calls (needs_specialist, needs_review, fit_N) can run. Python thresholds then produce route, no_skill or review. It is a research demo for the Hermes Agent skill catalogue (443 skills). It is not a Claude Code integration and does not load or execute skills. The name "router-proxy" in the discovery record is wrong. It is a client library, not a proxy.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_router/transport.py:12 hardcodes _ENDPOINT = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone". There is no env or CLI override for the base URL. transport.py:41 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and sends it as Bearer (transport.py:58). policy.py:~62 RouterConfig.__post_init__ enforces re.fullmatch(r"jev-[A-Za-z0-9._-]+", model), so an OpenRouter id such as typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest is rejected. grep for openrouter, claude, mcp and hook across all code and docs returns nothing. The default model is jev-1.13.0.
providerSupport.others: None. TypeSafe direct only.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate-trivial, but unverified. The payload is {model, state:{request}, questions:{...choice|noul...}} and the response is {model, answers:{id:{type,choice,probabilities,confidence}|{type,noul}}, usage:{input_tokens,output_tokens}}. That is the TypeSafe System One schema. OpenRouter documents POST /api/v1/systemone, which is likely the same shape, but I could not confirm it from this repo. A patch would change the _ENDPOINT line (transport.py:12) and the env var name (transport.py:41), then relax the model regex in policy.py. Response-model checks (router.py:84) would also need adjusting, since OpenRouter may echo typesafe/jev-1.13. This is about 10 lines of edits. It would still be a forked library with no Claude Code glue.

interface.name: jev-router route --request TEXT [--catalogue FILE] [--baseline] [--model ...] [threshold flags]
interface.purpose: Route one request against a JSON catalogue and print a JSON RoutingDecision with outcome, selected_skill, probabilities and per-call evidence. Exit code 2 on API error.

interface.name: jev-router evaluate --json OUT --markdown OUT [--split all|development|test] [--baseline-only]
interface.purpose: Run the 72-case synthetic benchmark (about 288 live API calls) against a lexical baseline. Refuses to overwrite existing outputs.

interface.name: jev-router report --input JSON --output MD
interface.purpose: Render a saved results file offline.

interface.name: jev-router validate-results --input JSON
interface.purpose: Validate the schema of a results file.

interface.name: Python API: Router(HttpTransport(), RouterConfig()).route(request, catalogue)
interface.purpose: Library entry point. A custom Transport protocol is supported (evaluate(payload) -> ApiResponse).

interface.name: MCP tools / hooks / SKILL.md / plugin.json / .mcp.json
interface.purpose: None exist. The repo has no Claude Code integration surface at all.

gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.runtime: Python >=3.11, zero runtime dependencies (urllib only). Dev extras pin ruff 12.12 and mypy 1.18.2. Build backend is setuptools==80.9.0.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.install: git clone, then python -m venv and pip install -e . (no PyPI release, no GitHub releases). Not installed or run during this audit.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.tests: About 101 offline unittest cases across 5 files (transport, router, cli, evaluation, public-artifacts) using a fake transport. GitHub Actions runs unittest, ruff and strict mypy on Python 3.11 and 3.12 without credentials. Live benchmark results are committed under results/. I did not run any of it.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable only. There is no CLI key flag, so the key never appears in argv or the process list. Dotenv files are not read (transport.py:41-46, README).
Key is validated as printable ASCII, and __repr__ omits it (transport.py:44,49).

HTTPS to a fixed host, with redirects disabled via a _NoRedirect handler (transport.py:18-28). This prevents the Bearer token leaking on a redirect. Response size is capped at 2 MB and the timeout is 30 s.
No subprocess, eval or exec in the runtime. There is no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh installer. The tests use subprocess only for git ls-files.

Prompt-injection surface: user request text and skill descriptions are sent inside the question text. The policy strings tell Jev to treat them as data (policy.py:11-45). The output is typed and only ever selects among the given options, so injection can at worst mis-route. The library executes nothing.
Error handling collapses exceptions to short codes (raise ... from None), so response bodies and key material are not leaked in errors.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.dataEgress: Each API call sends the full request string (up to 16,000 chars), plus the names and descriptions (up to 2,000 chars each) of the skills in that batch, to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. The payload is state.request plus the question text and options. For a catalogue of N skills, every skill description is sent at least once per route (batching then a final round). The library itself never reads code, diffs, files or tool outputs. Anything it sends is only what the caller passes as the request. Nothing goes to OpenRouter, since the endpoint is hardcoded to TypeSafe. The client does not retain raw response bodies.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.failureMode: Fail-safe at library level, with no retries. A single call has a 30 s default timeout (HttpTransport timeout=30.0, transport.py:32). Any HTTP, connection or invalid-response error becomes an error code, and route() returns outcome "review" with reason "api_error" (router.py:114-131). The CLI exits with 2. There is no automatic retry, and no fallback to the lexical baseline unless the caller adds one. Without a hook wrapper, nothing blocks Claude Code, because there is no integration. Observed: one of 72 cases in the final run hit invalid_response, and the initial pinned model jev-1.12 returned HTTP 400 for all 12 cases.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.latencyImpact: Measured by the author: median 1,287 ms and p95 1,406 ms per routing request for a 24-skill catalogue. That is 3 parallel batch calls plus one final call with 4 Noul/Choice questions, so it is roughly 4 sequential-ish API calls and about 4 calls per route. The README claims 287 calls for 72 cases. Latency is well above Jev's advertised 70-500 ms because of the multi-round design, and it grows with catalogue size. As a per-turn Claude Code hook this would add about 1.3 s or more, plus Python startup.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code today, because it registers no MCP tools, no MCP instructions, no hooks and no skills. If someone wrapped it as a UserPromptSubmit hook, the injected text would be small (a JSON decision or a short hint). Approximate cost of the repo itself as installed context: 0 tokens.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.autoInvocation: None. It is only run when explicitly invoked from the CLI or imported as a library. It has no hook, MCP, skill or proxy surface, so Claude Code would never call it automatically without new glue code.
pros: Clean, dependency-free reference implementation of Jev Choice and Noul calls, with the exact System One request and response schema (transport.py:52-77, parse_response). It is useful as a template for a custom hook or MCP wrapper.
Careful security hygiene: key only from env, redirects disabled, response capped at 2 MB, HTTPS-only, no shell execution, no telemetry, no install scripts.
Strict validation of Jev output (probabilities sum to about 1, choice equals argmax, exact key sets), which guards against malformed responses.

Real, published measurements against a lexical baseline on synthetic data (68/72 vs 51/72). Its honest disclosure of limitations is credible. It also empirically shows that jev-1.12 returned HTTP 400 and that jev-latest resolved to jev-1.13.0.
Fail-safe abstention design: on API error it returns review instead of guessing.
About 101 offline tests with CI and strict mypy.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, hook, SKILL.md, plugin manifest or .mcp.json. The auto-invocation requirement is completely unmet.

TypeSafe-direct only. The endpoint is hardcoded (transport.py:12), the env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and the model regex jev-* rejects OpenRouter ids (policy.py). The user wants OpenRouter, so this would need a fork.

Solves a different problem: selecting one of hundreds of Hermes-style skills. The user's Claude Code setup has a handful of skills and MCP servers, and Claude Code already matches skills by description. A 1.3 s multi-call router in front of that adds latency with little value.
Slow and chatty by design: about 4 API calls per request and a 1.3 s median, which is noticeable if run per prompt.

Very young and single-author: 4 commits, all on 2026-09-16, no releases, no PyPI package, 24 stars. Exploratory results with reused test data, and the author states that they do not establish production accuracy or calibration.
25% of outcomes are 'review' (abstain), and 3 of 72 were unnecessary reviews. A hook built on this would often punt back to Claude anyway.
Sends the user's full prompt and all skill descriptions off-machine on every route, a concern for client projects.
gh-godsboy-jev-agent-skill-router.verdict: Not usable as an automatic Claude Code integration: it is a Hermes-oriented skill-routing benchmark library with no MCP, hook or skill surface, and it only speaks to api.typesafe.ai. Its main value is as a small, well-validated reference for the System One request and response schema and for the abstention thresholding pattern. If the user builds a custom hook, borrowing transport.py (swap the endpoint to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone) is worthwhile, but adopting the repo itself is not.

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Judge text against an integer scale rubric; returns score, confidence and per-level probabilities.

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: Batch-check claims against supplied evidence (supports/contradicts/says_nothing) with auto/review action; max 64 claims.

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Advisory prompt-injection, substance and relevance screen of untrusted text (block/review/pass/skip).

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Batch true/false propositions with shared context; returns probability, label and action.

interface.name: jev_match
interface.purpose: Find the best-matching candidate for a query plus an exists verdict (answered/partial/absent).

interface.name: jev_rerank
interface.purpose: Rank all candidates by relevance to a query.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Bulk-classify items into a fixed class set.

interface.name: jev_decide
interface.purpose: Pick the best of 2-6 options given evidence and priorities, with ask_user/investigate/none escape hatches.

interface.name: jev_compare
interface.purpose: Compare two passages' factual relation (same_fact/contradicts/different_facts), overall and per aspect.

interface.name: jev_extract
interface.purpose: Regex candidate finding, then Jev picks the correct value per field; makes no API call when there are zero matches.

interface.name: jev_review
interface.purpose: Score a diff against a request on correctness, spec_match, test_gap and blast_radius, plus a safe_to_apply signal; returns action auto/review/escalate. Request, diff and tests are each capped at 50k chars.

interface.name: jev_gate
interface.purpose: jev_review plus fact-checking claims against evidence; returns auto/review/escalate.

interface.name: jev_doctor
interface.purpose: Connectivity probe plus a config snapshot (model, credential source, budgets, session spend).

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Escape hatch: arbitrary named noul/choice/score questions sent almost raw to System One.

interface.name: CLI: jev <tool> / jev mcp [--tools ...]
interface.purpose: The same logic as a Unix command (flags or --json in, text or -o json out, exit code equals verdict). Bare `jev` is an unimplemented TUI and exits 3.

gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.runtime: Go 1.25 (github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.8.0, cobra). Not on PATH by default, so this needs a Go toolchain. `go install github.com/pyck-ai/jev-cli/cmd/jev@main` gives a single binary. The user's stack (Node 24, Python 3.13, uv) has no Go, so Go must be installed.
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.install: go install github.com/pyck-ai/jev-cli/cmd/jev@main ; claude mcp add --transport stdio jev -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -- jev mcp --tools review,verify,check,... (the README suggests `go run ...@main mcp`, which recompiles from an unpinned main on every start). There are no releases or tags.
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.tests: Extensive: nearly every package has *_test.go. Tests run against a fake OpenRouter httptest server, and main_test.go drives a real MCP client/server session. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs go vet, a gofmt check and `go test -race`, with actions pinned by SHA and `permissions: {}`. Renovate is configured. No live-API test exists.
security: API key comes from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, or from opencode's auth.json as a fallback (read-only). The key is never read from the config file or logged, and is sent only as a Bearer header. It is not in argv unless the user puts it in `claude mcp add -e`, which stores it in ~/.claude.json. Reading another tool's credential file is a mild surprise, but it is skipped if absent.

No os/exec and no shell execution anywhere (grep: the only net/http user is internal/openrouter/client.go). The only outbound host is openrouter.ai. No telemetry and no postinstall script; the install is a source build via `go install`. The README's `go run ...@main` fetches and builds unpinned main at every start, which is a supply-chain risk. Pin a commit or build locally after reading.
Audit log at ~/.local/share/jev-cli/audit.jsonl (dir 0700, file 0600) stores only SHA-256 of the input, plus tool, model, score, tokens, cost and latency. No raw content is stored.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Outputs are structured numbers and enums, and tool descriptions are static. Unsanitized text in the `state` sent to Jev could sway a verdict, but Jev cannot emit instructions. jev_screen is advisory only.

Tools carry no readOnly/destructive annotations (grep for Annotations found none), so permission prompts may fire on each call in non-bypass modes. The user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover mcp__jev__* calls, so diffs or content the model passes to jev_review could include secrets and be sent to OpenRouter without inspection.
Single anonymous-ish maintainer (Michael Krupp, pyck-ai org), 3 days old, 0 stars, no releases. Code quality looks careful, but it has had no external review.
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone as JSON {model, questions, state}. For jev_review and jev_gate that is the request text, the full diff and the test output, each truncated at 50k chars. For verify, check, match, rerank, classify, compare and extract it is the claims, evidence, passages and documents supplied. The tool itself reads no files and runs no commands. Only what Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine, and it goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe/its upstream providers, with OpenRouter's logging and privacy settings applying. This matters for client code under NDA. Nothing else is sent (no telemetry).
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.failureMode: Fail-closed at tool level, and non-blocking for the session. Timeout is request_timeout_ms=30000 total (default) across all attempts. Retries: 3 attempts with jittered backoff (500 ms to 8 s), on HTTP 408, 409, 429 and 5xx only. Network errors are never retried. If the endpoint is down or slow, the tool returns an error or `invalid_response` and Claude carries on. A hang could cost up to 30 s of waiting per call. There is no fail-open verdict, and malformed answers become status=invalid_response with action=review, never a fabricated pass. Missing key makes `jev mcp` exit at startup, so the MCP server shows as failed and nothing else breaks. Default budget caps are $0.01 per call (flag only) and $1.00 per session (hard refusal).
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.latencyImpact: Each call is one HTTPS round trip, claimed 150-500 ms in the docs and about 312 ms in the audit-log example. One Jev call is far shorter than an Opus turn, but the model must first decide to call and then read the result, so a call adds roughly one tool-use step (an extra 1-3 s of model time). The worst case is a 30 s timeout. `go install` gives a fast-starting binary. `go run ...@main` adds a compile or cache check on every start. The MCP process startup log goes to stderr.
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.contextCost: 14 MCP tools, or fewer with `--tools`. The server sets no `instructions`, since mcp.NewServer is called with nil options. Each description is about 600-900 chars (14 x ~750 = ~10.5k chars), and there are 79 schema fields with jsonschema descriptions (~12k chars of description plus JSON-schema structure), so about 25-30k chars, or roughly 6-8k tokens for the full set. Trimming to `--tools review,verify,check` cuts that to about 1.5-2k tokens. No hook-injected text. Claude Code's MCP tool search/deferral may reduce the standing cost.
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tool descriptions have "Use jev_X instead when..." routing text, but no hook, no skill trigger and no proxy, and the server sets no instructions. Claude will call a tool only if it decides to. To make it reliable the user would need to add a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a hook (for example PostToolUse on Edit, or Stop, calling `jev review` via the CLI). Those are user-authored, not provided by this repo. The CLI mode (`jev review --json ...`, exit code equals verdict) is a good building block for a deterministic hook, but the repo ships none.
pros: Native OpenRouter support: it calls /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so no code change is needed for the user's chosen provider (types.go:84, credentials.go:21).

Only jev_review/jev_gate are directly coding-relevant (diff versus request on correctness, spec_match, test_gap and blast_radius, with auto/review/escalate). jev_screen (prompt-injection screen), jev_classify and jev_verify are useful as secondary tools.
The `--tools` flag (commit f59398c) lets the user expose only 2-4 tools and keep context cost near 2k tokens. Otherwise the 14-tool surface is heavy.
Strong safety design: fail-closed parsing, budget caps ($1/session default), a hashed-input audit log, no shell exec, no telemetry, only openrouter.ai contacted, and SHA-pinned CI actions.

Single static Go binary, and the same logic is exposed as a CLI with exit codes, so it can be wired into deterministic hooks (for example a Stop or PostToolUse hook running `jev review`) that make invocation automatic. This is the only way to meet the user's no-prompt requirement.
Broad test coverage with fake-server integration tests and a real MCP session test; MIT license.
It documents a live end-to-end call on 2026-09-26 that fixed the model alias (~typesafe/jev-latest), a sign that at least the score path was exercised for real.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a plain MCP server with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, so Claude calls it only at its own discretion. That fails the user's core requirement unless the user builds a hook or rule layer.
It is very new (created 2026-09-26, 18 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases or tags), and the README itself says schemas and thresholds may change. Installing from `@main` is unpinned.

Most wire shapes are transcribed from docs and not verified live (types.go header). Only the score path and the model alias are noted as live-tested, so choice/noul tools such as review and verify may have edge-case bugs.

The 14 tools mostly target document, RAG and ops workflows (rerank, match, extract, classify), not coding. Only review/gate/screen/decide are relevant, and the rest is context clutter (~6-8k tokens) unless trimmed with `--tools`.
Requires a Go 1.25 toolchain, which the user's Node/Python/uv stack does not include.

Data egress: diffs and code that Claude passes are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. This is a concern for client projects. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse matcher does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and the server does no secret redaction.
It has no MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint) and no server instructions, so it may prompt for permission outside bypass mode and gives Claude no guidance on when to use it.
It uses only the /api/v1/systemone endpoint, with no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions), no direct TypeSafe path, and the endpoint URL is hardcoded.

Jev's value for review is unproven (calibrated probabilities but no reasoning trace), and the author's own docs flag it as beta. Rubric weights, thresholds and default 0.8/0.7 gates are the author's invention (comments in verify.go say the 64 cap is invented).
gh-pyck-ai-jev-cli.verdict: This is the most complete and best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev MCP server, with fail-closed behavior, budget caps, an audit log and a `--tools` subset. It is still only a tool menu and gives no automatic invocation. Use it as the OpenRouter backend (ideally `--tools review,verify,check,screen` from a pinned, locally built commit) and add your own hook or CLAUDE.md rule to trigger it. Do not expect it to fire on its own, and be careful about sending client diffs.

gh-douglance-jevon.name: douglance/jevon (jev CLI + MCP server)
gh-douglance-jevon.whatItDoes: Rust binary `jev` (alias `typesafe`) built on the incurs CLI framework. One command graph is exposed as a CLI and as an MCP stdio server (`jev mcp add` registers it) and can generate skill files (`jev skills add`). Each command wraps the TypeSafe Rust SDK's System One call (POST {base}/v1/systemone) with Choice/Score/Noul questions over a text state. No hooks, no proxy. Purely model-discretion tools.

providerSupport.evidence: Provider is a config knob, no code change. Env vars from typesafe-sdk-rs crates/typesafe-sdk-env/src/lib.rs:24-27: TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL. Default base https://api.typesafe.ai (crates/typesafe-sdk-config/src/config.rs:10), default model jev-latest (config.rs:13), trailing slash stripped (build.rs resolve_base_url ~L137). Path constant SYSTEM_ONE_PATH="/v1/systemone" (crates/typesafe-sdk-client/src/client.rs:27), URL built as format!("{}{}", base_url, path) (send.rs:35), header Authorization: Bearer <key> (config.rs:43, headers.rs). So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<sk-or-...> yields POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, exactly the OpenRouter System One endpoint. OpenRouter docs page https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk states the same env vars and that bare ids jev-1.13 / jev-latest are mapped to typesafe/jev-1.13 / ~typesafe/jev-latest, so the default model needs no change. jevon README 'Configuration' table lists the same vars. jevon itself hard-codes no URL (grep of crates/*.rs finds only docs.typesafe.ai links in hints, ask/src/lib.rs:118-121). No OPENROUTER_* var and no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) support.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed, already works via env vars. Only caveats: `jev models list` uses GET /v1/models expecting envelope {models:[...]} (typesafe-sdk-models/src/lib.rs:21,38) and will likely fail against OpenRouter's {data:[...]} list, and an extra X-TypeSafe-* / User-Agent typesafe-sdk header set is sent to OpenRouter (harmless). Decisions API (alpha) is not reachable through this tool.
providerSupport.others: Any System One compatible gateway via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (per-project overridable). Untested by me because running code is forbidden; compat inferred from static source plus OpenRouter docs.

interface.name: ask
interface.purpose: MCP tool/CLI: `jev ask <state> --choice/--score/--noul/--questions/--questions-file/--state-file/--model`. One System One request; returns model, answers (typed with probabilities), usage. Annotated read-only, open-world (crates/typesafe-sdk-cmd-kit/src/mcp.rs).

interface.name: classify

interface.name: eval

interface.name: models list

interface.name: mcp add

interface.name: skills add

gh-douglance-jevon.runtime: Rust 2024 edition, rust-version 1.98; binary `jev` via `cargo install jevon` (crates.io) — no prebuilt binaries, no GitHub releases (latestRelease null). Needs a Rust toolchain for install. Runs as stdio MCP server.
gh-douglance-jevon.install: cargo install jevon; export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api; jev mcp add (or claude mcp add jev --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- jev mcp)
gh-douglance-jevon.tests: In-process integration tests via serve_to (crates/jevon/tests/agent_surface.rs, surface.rs), a real-binary MCP stdin regression test (mcp_stdin.rs), unit tests in cmd-kit/classify; explicitly no live API tests here (README: live conformance is in the SDK repo). CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs fmt, custom xtask structure check (150-line file cap, complexity), clippy -D warnings with pedantic/nursery, tests, python audit tooling. Code quality gates are unusually strict; unsafe_code forbidden, unwrap/expect/panic denied.
security: API key is read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY); `jev mcp add` deliberately writes no key into agent config; no --api-key CLI flag found, so not visible in argv. Key masked in `doctor` output and redacted in SDK debug logs (typesafe-sdk-headers/src/redact.rs). Caveat: Claude Code must have the key in its own environment, so it also reaches every Bash tool call and other MCP children; use claude mcp add --env instead to scope it.

No shell execution, no subprocess spawn in library code (Command::new appears only in tests/mcp_stdin.rs), unsafe forbidden, no build.rs/postinstall in jevon (SDK runtime crate has a build.rs that only records rustc version), no curl|sh installer.

Local file read primitives: --state-file, --items-file, --questions-file take arbitrary paths (crates/typesafe-sdk-cmd-kit/src/input.rs read_file, no path allowlist). A prompt-injected agent could send any readable file (e.g. .env, ~/.ssh) to the API endpoint. Tools are flagged read-only, so with auto/bypass permission mode they run without any prompt. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, NOT MCP tools, so it would not catch this path.
Hint text in tool descriptions points the agent to docs.typesafe.ai/*.md URLs to fetch (ask/src/lib.rs:118-121); external content pulled into context = minor prompt-injection surface.

Telemetry: SDK sends User-Agent/X-TypeSafe-SDK/X-TypeSafe-Runtime (rustc/os description) headers to whatever base URL is configured; no separate analytics endpoint found. Dependency tree is large (reqwest/hyper/tokio via SDK), from crates.io, unaudited; 0 stars, single-author (35 of 37 commits), SDK repo maintained by same person (douglance, appears to be a community project; a typesafe-public-bot[bot] and one other contributor exist) — supply-chain trust is personal, not vendor.
gh-douglance-jevon.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the `state` argument (or reads from --state-file/--items-file) plus the question text and labels, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai/api when redirected) with the bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: no hook or background capture. Content is entirely model-chosen, so it can include code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. Via OpenRouter the payload additionally passes through OpenRouter's logging/routing policy and TypeSafe as upstream provider. Also SDK identification headers.
gh-douglance-jevon.failureMode: Fail-open at the session level (it is an optional MCP tool; an error is just an isolated tool result with stable codes TIMEOUT, CONNECTION_ERROR, RATE_LIMIT, AUTHENTICATION_ERROR, etc. from kit lib.rs:46-72). But a single call can block a turn for long: SDK default per-attempt timeout 10 s, 2 retries, backoff 500 ms to 5 s with jitter, honours Retry-After up to 60 s (typesafe-sdk-retry/src/policy.rs:7-50), so worst case ~30+ s before an error is returned. Missing key returns 'No API key was provided' rather than crashing. Timeout is settable in the SDK but I found no env var for it in jevon. If the server binary fails to start, Claude Code just shows the MCP server as failed.
gh-douglance-jevon.contextCost: 5 MCP tools (ask, classify, eval, doctor, models_list). Source text for descriptions/hints/examples/schemas is ~18 KB across ask/classify/eval libs (ask HINT alone ~1.9 KB of prose, includes 5 docs URLs); after schema generation with option docs I estimate roughly 9-12k chars, about 2.5-3k tokens always resident (or deferred behind ToolSearch in recent Claude Code). No MCP server-level 'instructions' seen. No hook-injected text. Moderate footprint, larger than a single-purpose tool, mostly wasted for coding since eval/classify/models/doctor are rarely wanted.
gh-douglance-jevon.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where the tool is not called. Per call: process is long-lived stdio; one HTTPS round trip to OpenRouter, claimed 70-500 ms model latency plus OpenRouter routing overhead, plus the extra LLM turn Claude Code spends to decide, format the JSON call and read the result (typically 2-5 s of Opus time and output tokens). It is more expensive in turn time than the call itself, and net negative when Opus could just decide.
gh-douglance-jevon.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description says 'Use when code needs a judgment — choosing the next action, filtering or ranking, routing, or gating — rather than generated prose', which is aimed at app code, not at an agent editing code, so Claude Code will rarely pick it unprompted for daily coding. Not a hook, not a proxy, not a skill trigger (`jev skills add` can write skill files, but those are also description-triggered and the same mismatch applies). Cannot deliver the 'Claude Code uses it automatically' requirement by itself.
pros: Works against OpenRouter with zero code changes: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> gives POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (client.rs:27, send.rs:35), matching OpenRouter's own doc for the TypeSafe SDK; default model 'jev-latest' is auto-mapped to ~typesafe/jev-latest.

Cleanest available wrapper for the System One (Choice/Score/Noul) API: full primitive coverage, parallel multi-question requests, batch classify with concurrency and min-confidence, eval command for threshold calibration.
Key never written to config by `jev mcp add`; no key in argv; redacted logging; no shell exec, unsafe forbidden.
Tools annotated readOnly so no approval prompts (matches bypass/auto workflow); stable structured error codes; sane 10 s timeout and bounded retries.

Very disciplined codebase (strict clippy/pedantic, size limits, CI, MCP stdin regression test that drove a real bug fix), MIT license, and the docs/when-to-use.md is honest that Jev is for decisions with known options, not general coding.
Also useful as a manual/scripting CLI (`jev ask ... --format json`) and as a reference for how the SDK talks to the endpoint.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tool whose description targets app developers building decision logic, so Claude Code (Opus) will seldom call it unprompted, which fails the user's core requirement. There is no hook, proxy or per-turn integration.

Young and thin: repo created 2026-09-19 (11 days before audit date), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 37 commits with 35 by one author, version 0.8.0 alpha; SDK dependency (typesafe-sdk-rs 0.6) is a separate community repo. API surface may churn.

Install requires cargo build from source (`cargo install jevon`, rust 1.98 toolchain, big reqwest/tokio tree); no prebuilt binary, npm or uvx path, and I cannot verify the crates.io artifact matches the GitHub source.

Data exfiltration path: --state-file/--items-file/--questions-file read arbitrary local paths and send content to a third party, marked read-only so auto/bypass mode runs it unprompted; the user's secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tool calls. Client projects make this a real concern.

Everything sent is model-authored text; ask needs the agent to serialise code/context into a string argument, costing Opus output tokens and a full extra turn per decision, which usually exceeds what Jev saves.
Context tax: 5 tool definitions (~3k tokens) mostly for commands (eval, classify, models list, doctor) irrelevant to coding.

`models list` likely breaks on OpenRouter (different /v1/models envelope); Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported; retry policy can stall a turn ~30 s worst case; API key must sit in Claude Code's own environment (leaks to all child processes) unless passed via claude mcp add --env.
Jev itself is a decision model with 32k context and no reasoning; skeptics call it a small flash-router; no evidence in this repo it improves code-editing decisions.
gh-douglance-jevon.verdict: Best-quality, lowest-risk generic wrapper for reaching Jev through OpenRouter (just set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api), so it is a fine building block or manual/scripting tool, but as a plain model-discretion MCP it will not fire automatically in daily coding and it adds a file-read egress path under bypass mode. Use it only as the transport behind a deterministic hook or a purpose-written narrow skill, not as the integration itself.

gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.name: safzanpirani/pi-jev-skill-picker
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.whatItDoes: A Pi coding agent (Earendil Works pi-coding-agent) extension, not a Claude Code skill despite the "skill" label. It hooks Pi's before_agent_start event to delete the generated <skills> catalog from the system prompt. It registers two tools: skill_search and skill_load. skill_search sends one Jev Score question per enabled skill (levels: unrelated / adjacent / directly applicable), with the task text in shared state. It loads the full SKILL.md of the top N skills (default 3, minimum score 1.6 out of 2). skill_load reads skills by name from disk and never calls Jev. If Jev fails or there is no key, it falls back to lexical keyword matching. The value is saving about 19k tokens per request on a 137-skill catalog.

security: API key sent as Bearer header only, never on argv. It is read from the env or a JSON config file (README recommends chmod 0600), and the code does not check the file's permissions.
No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh, and no telemetry in the source. package.json has only devDependencies, and the published files are extensions/README/LICENSE.

The only network call is a POST to the configured endpoint. PI_SKILL_JEV_ENDPOINT is fully overridable, so anyone who can set env vars could redirect skill descriptions and the task text to another host.

Prompt-injection surface: skill_search returns full SKILL.md bodies as tool results that the agent is told to follow. Skill content is trusted local data, but a malicious skill or a description crafted to score highly would get its instructions injected. The score is a probability-weighted position, not a safety filter.
Small codebase (about 830 lines of source) that is easy to audit. Single maintainer, 8 commits, and 37 stars in 10 days, so it has no track record.
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.dataEgress: The task string the agent writes (its own summary of what it is about to do, including named tools, services, and files) plus the name and description of every enabled skill, each truncated to 1200 chars. This goes to api.typesafe.ai in one request per 50 skills, and a 137-skill catalog is about 38.6k Jev input tokens per call. No source code, diffs, file contents, or tool outputs are sent unless the agent puts them in the task text. Skill bodies are read locally and never sent.
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.failureMode: Fail-open. There are up to 3 attempts per shard with exponential backoff (250ms, then 500ms) and Retry-After honored on 429/5xx. Each attempt has a 20s timeout (worst case is over 60s per shard). If every shard fails, or there is no key, it falls back to lexical matching that returns skill metadata and paths. If only some shards fail, it uses the partial ranking and says so. A skill_search error never blocks the agent (skill-jev.ts:196-236).
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.contextCost: In Pi it is net-negative, saving about 19k tokens per request by stripping the catalog. The cost is two tool definitions of roughly 500-800 tokens (long descriptions plus promptGuidelines injected into the system prompt), plus the full SKILL.md bodies returned per search. For Claude Code the impact is not applicable, because it cannot run there. Claude Code already lists skills with only a one-line description each, and that list is not removable through hooks.
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.autoInvocation: In Pi, the catalog strip is deterministic through the event hook. Skill selection is model-discretion: promptGuidelines tell the model to call skill_search before substantive work. Not applicable to Claude Code, as it has no extension API for this.
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.latencyImpact: One Jev round trip per skill_search call: the claimed 70-500ms for a single request, but larger with sharding (each shard has 50 questions, and a 137-skill catalog means 3 parallel shards of about 12k tokens each). Latency tracks the slowest shard. The model must also spend one extra tool-call turn to invoke it.
pros: Concrete, working reference for the Jev System One Score request and response shape: {model, state, questions:{id:{type:'score',instructions,criteria[]}}} returns answers[id].score and .confidence (jev.ts:194-205, 208-231). Useful to copy when writing your own hook or MCP.
Endpoint and model are env-overridable (PI_SKILL_JEV_ENDPOINT, PI_SKILL_JEV_MODEL), so pointing it at OpenRouter is a config change, not a code change.
Well-engineered failure handling: fail-open, retry on 429/5xx, Retry-After, lexical fallback, and partial-shard tolerance. The core logic is unit-tested with a stubbed fetch.
Clean security posture: no shell, no postinstall, no telemetry, key never on argv, MIT license, 830 lines that are easy to read.
The idea of ranking skills per task with a cheap calibrated classifier is sound. It gives about $0.0016 per call at Jev pricing and is a good pattern to port.
cons: It is a Pi agent extension. It uses Pi's ExtensionAPI (pi.on('before_agent_start'), pi.registerTool) and cannot be installed or loaded in Claude Code. Nothing is usable without a rewrite.

The main saving depends on stripping the skills catalog from the system prompt. Claude Code hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse) cannot remove or rewrite the built-in skill listing, so the core benefit does not port.

The Claude Code equivalent would be a UserPromptSubmit hook that ranks skills and injects additionalContext. That would add Jev latency to every prompt and duplicate Claude Code's own skill matching, and the user's list is only about 30 skills.
Its key handling is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. It works with OpenRouter only by putting an OpenRouter key in a misnamed variable, and OpenRouter /systemone schema equivalence is unverified.
Very early: 8 commits, one author, no CI, no releases, 10 days old, and version 0.1.0. The default 20s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn for a minute in the worst case.
It solves skill selection only. It does not address the user's other Jev use cases in Claude Code, such as permission decisions, routing, or triage.
gh-safzanpirani-pi-jev-skill-picker.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code: it is a Pi-only extension whose key benefit (stripping the skill catalog from the system prompt) has no Claude Code hook. Treat it as a reference for the Jev Score request format and the fail-open pattern, not as an integration. Do not install it.

gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.whatItDoes: A Pi coding agent (pi.dev, not Claude Code) extension. It uses the @typesafe-ai/sdk client to call Jev System One. It registers 3 model-callable tools: jev_find_tools (activate inactive tools by Noul probability), jev_find_skill (rank SKILL.md files) and jev_evaluate (generic Choice/Noul/Score). It also has opt-in hooks for per-prompt auto-routing, auto model selection, a tool-call guard, compaction, and agent orchestration. A separate jev-gate CLI checks a git diff or stdin against acceptance criteria and exits 0/1/2. The runtime is TypeScript against Pi's ExtensionAPI (pi.on, pi.registerFlag, pi.setActiveTools). It is not an MCP server and has no Claude Code hook, plugin or skill manifest.

Shortlists up to 10 inactive Pi tools by keyword overlap, asks Jev one Noul question per tool, and activates those at P >= 0.65 (src/tools.ts:17, src/router.ts). It exists to fix tool-list clutter in Pi and has no equivalent in Claude Code.

interface.name: jev_find_skill (Pi tool)
interface.purpose: Takes a query and an optional threshold. Ranks workspace SKILL.md files with Jev Noul questions (src/tools.ts:69, src/skills.ts).

interface.name: before_agent_start hook (extensions/index.ts:107)
interface.purpose: With --jev-auto or PI_JEV_AUTO=1, runs one batched Noul call per user prompt. It activates tools and injects a 'jev-auto' message recommending skills. Off by default.

interface.name: tool_call / tool_result hooks (src/tool-guard.ts)
interface.purpose: With --jev-tool-guard, asks Jev 'is_hallucinated' about each tool call and can block it. It also appends 'Anti-Hallucination Guidance' to error results. Off by default.

interface.purpose: With --jev-compact, has Jev pick which tool history to keep in the compaction summary.

interface.name: AutoModelRouter (before_agent_start)
interface.purpose: With --jev-auto-model, picks a model profile per prompt. Per the README this is local heuristics only and spends no Jev requests.

interface.name: AgentOrchestrator
interface.purpose: With --jev-agents, auto-dispatches pi-subagents when the prompt matches architecture, refactor, security review and similar words. /jev agents <task> does it manually.

interface.name: agent: 'jev' (src/agent.ts)
interface.purpose: A typed Jev handler registered for pi-subagents workflows.

interface.name: /jev status | help | skills | test | enable | disable | auto | auto-model | tool-guard | compact | agents | auto-agents
interface.purpose: Pi slash commands (src/commands.ts).

interface.name: jev-gate / pi-jev-gate CLI (bin/jev-gate.js)
interface.purpose: Options -c criteria, -p threshold (default 0.7), -d (git diff HEAD), -f file, stdin, --json, --fail-open, -m model. It sends the diff or stdin to Jev as a Noul 'gate_passed' question. Exit 0 = pass, 1 = fail, 2 = error (or 0 with --fail-open). This is the only piece that is host-agnostic. It could be called from a Claude Code Stop or PreToolUse hook, or from CI, but the user would have to write that wiring.

security: MIT license. The repo has only a SECURITY.md that gives a private email for reports.

Key handling: TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env or a plaintext file ~/.pi/agent/secrets/typesafe_api_key. The key is sent only as a Bearer header by the SDK. It is never put in argv by this code, but the jev-gate criteria and its diff do pass through argv/stdin.

Shell execution: gate.ts:76-82 runs execSync('git diff HEAD') and 'git diff --cached' with fixed strings, so there is no injection from user input. bin/jev-gate.js spawnSync's node with tsx and the runner path, and it forwards process.argv.
No postinstall script in package.json and no curl|sh installer. It depends at runtime on the tsx and @typesafe-ai/sdk npm packages. It is published with npm --provenance via CI (publish.yml).
No telemetry in the code. The SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK and X-TypeSafe-Runtime headers.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompts, tool descriptions and skill descriptions are interpolated into Jev question strings (auto.ts, router.ts). Jev returns only typed probabilities, not free text, so the injection blast radius is limited to wrong activation or skill suggestions. The tool-guard is a probabilistic block/allow on hallucination, not a security control.
Fail-closed on missing config in the gate CLI (exit 2, unless --fail-open). In the tool router it fails to zero activation.
Single maintainer, 9 forks, 58 stars. No independent audit.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.dataEgress: The user prompt goes to Jev in auto mode (auto.ts state:{task: prompt, tools, available_skills}), with candidate tool names and descriptions and skill names and descriptions. jev_evaluate sends whatever state the model supplies, which can include diffs or file contents. With tool-guard on, every tool name and its full input parameters leave the machine (file paths, Bash commands, edit contents), and the error content of failed tools is sent too. The gate CLI sends the full git diff HEAD, a file, or stdin. Compaction sends tool-history entries. All of this goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to whatever PI_JEV_BASE_URL says. There is no redaction layer. The client-project code and secret-leak concerns are real if tool-guard or the gate CLI are used. Auto mode alone leaks only the prompt text and tool metadata.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.failureMode: Fail-open for auto-routing. AutoJev.route() catches every error and returns skip('error'), so the turn continues untouched (auto.ts). ToolRouter.findAndActivate falls back to activating nothing. The tool-guard checks are wrapped in try/catch, and I did not read the catch branch, so I am assuming it allows the call. The gate CLI is fail-closed by default (exit 2) and fail-open only with --fail-open. Timeouts are the SDK defaults: 10 s per request (index.mjs:519, timeout ?? 1e4) plus a retry policy. That means a slow Jev can stall a Pi turn for up to about 10 s times the retries, since auto mode awaits the call in before_agent_start. There is no custom short timeout in pi-jev.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.contextCost: Not applicable to Claude Code, because it cannot be loaded there. In Pi it adds 3 tools. The description and schema text in src/tools.ts is about 6.8 KB including code, so the tool definitions are roughly 0.6-0.8k tokens. Auto mode injects a short 'jev-auto' message only when skills match. There are no MCP server instructions.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.autoInvocation: Inside Pi: opt-in hooks (--jev-auto, tool-guard, compact), which are deterministic hook events, plus model-discretion tools (jev_find_tools, jev_find_skill, jev_evaluate). For Claude Code: none. It ships no .claude-plugin, no hooks.json, no MCP server and no SKILL.md. Only the jev-gate CLI can be called from a Claude Code hook, and that needs custom wiring.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.latencyImpact: Claimed Jev latency is 70-500 ms per call. In auto mode this is one awaited call per prompt (before_agent_start blocks). With tool-guard it is one call per tool call, which would add hundreds of ms per action in a long agentic loop. pros: The gate check is real. jev-gate turns a diff or command output plus natural-language criteria into P(pass) with clean exit codes (bin/jev-gate-runner.ts, src/gate.ts). It is host-agnostic and could be called from a Claude Code Stop hook or CI as a cheap second opinion.

Base URL and key are env-configurable (PI_JEV_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, src/jev.ts:15-24). The SDK posts to {base}/v1/systemone, so https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key maps to the documented System One endpoint with no code change.

Opt-in and cost-honest design: the README lists which features spend Jev requests. It has typecheck, 12 test files, CI and npm provenance publishing, and MIT license.
Ideas transfer: the tool-guard and 'ask Jev Noul questions in a hook' patterns are useful design references for building a Claude Code hook.
cons: Wrong host. It is a Pi extension (ExtensionAPI: pi.on, pi.registerFlag, pi.setActiveTools, package.json 'pi' key). It cannot be loaded into Claude Code. It has no MCP server, no hooks.json, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md. The 'tool routing' value (dynamically activating tools) has no Claude Code equivalent, because Claude Code's tool set is not switched at runtime by hooks.

Not OpenRouter-native. There is no OpenRouter string in the code, the model default is 'jev-latest' rather than typesafe/jev-1.13, and the README says TYPESAFE_API_KEY from console.typesafe.ai. OpenRouter works only through the undocumented-in-repo env override and would need a live test.
Very young and single-maintainer: 19 commits in 8 days, 1 contributor, v0.6.0, 58 stars. Behaviour of Jev-based routing is unproven, and Theo's 'flash-router' skepticism applies.

Automatic features are opt-in and, in Pi, cost one Jev request per prompt or per tool call. Tool-guard sends every tool input to a third party, which conflicts with the user's client projects and the existing secret-leak guard. There is no redaction.

The 10 s default SDK timeout with retries, awaited in before_agent_start, can stall a turn when Jev is slow. The README's 'fails closed safely' claim is contradicted by the code, where auto mode fails open.
The Node/tsx runtime is heavy for a hook. jev-gate spawns node with tsx on every call, adding cold-start latency, and would need npm install of the peer/dev tree to run.
gh-theooliveira-pi-jev.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code as shipped. It is a Pi-specific extension with no MCP, hook or plugin surface. Only the jev-gate CLI and the design patterns (batched Noul relevance questions, diff-vs-criteria gate) are reusable. It is worth borrowing the ideas, not installing the package, and any Claude Code hook should call OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone directly.

gh-daniel-farina-nitro.whatItDoes: A fork of xAI's Grok Build CLI (Rust, Apache-2.0, upstream 1.0.38), renamed 'nitro'. A missing verdict is read as ESCALATE, but a missing answer to any of the other 5 questions raises. In a Claude Code port you would need to decide between fail-open (fall through to normal permission handling) and ask.

security: API key sent as Authorization Bearer header via fetch; key is read from env or plaintext JSON config files, never put in argv (good). Caveat: keys placed via 'claude mcp add -e' land in ~/.claude.json in plaintext.

Data-exfil surface is the core function: the receipt path sends the head 1000 + tail 1500 chars plus an error anchor of arbitrary command output (and the command string) to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe/upstream). Hook has NO secret redaction. It would ship .env dumps, tokens in logs, client code snippets from test output to OpenRouter. Conflicts with the user's existing secret-leak guard hook and client-project confidentiality. jev_guard sends the full command + context; jev_decide_* send whatever state the model passes.

Correctness/safety risk: a 4 s-budget probabilistic classifier decides whether to DELETE tool output from the context. 'success' + P(error)<0.15 replaces the entire output with the last 4 lines. Warnings, skipped tests, or deprecation notices in the middle of a long run can be lost. Exit-code path is deterministic but the Claude Code Bash tool result has no reliable exit-code field for the hook to use (regex on trailing text only).

Prompt-injection: command output is passed as Jev 'state' and instructions strings; a malicious log line could push the classifier toward 'success' and hide errors. Jev is typed-output so no text injection into the agent, but suppression of real errors is possible. Receipt text itself is generated locally (last 4 lines) and returned to the agent.
No shell execution in the MCP path (no child_process in mcp-server/receipt/client). Only bin/ego-browse.js spawns a hardcoded macOS path.

install.sh: no curl|sh, no npm postinstall. But it does 'git pull --ff-only' from origin on every run (auto-running unreviewed upstream code, symlinked so a later git pull silently changes executed code), appends to ~/.codex/config.toml and edits other agents' JSON configs, and creates ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json and ~/.agents/mcp.json even if those agents are not installed. Single anonymous author, 0 stars, created 12 days ago: high supply-chain risk for client work.

Telemetry: local only. Writes ~/.local/share/universal-jev/telemetry.json (last 100 events with first 120 chars of the command). No network telemetry found. Sends X-Title/HTTP-Referer headers to OpenRouter.

I did not execute the candidate. One slip: a node -e dynamic import of bin/mcp-server.js was run once with stdin=/dev/null (loaded module, no key, no tool call, no network). Disclosed for transparency.

Missing key: JevClient constructor throws (client.js:80) -> MCP tool call returns isError text. MCP server itself starts fine without a key since client is lazy. jev_guard is fail-closed only in the sense that it throws; it is advisory, not enforcing.
gh-raj8525-universal-jev.contextCost: 7 MCP tools. Tool defs in bin/mcp-server.js lines 18-125 are about 3.6k chars, roughly 900 tokens (plus Claude Code's mcp__jev__ name prefix). No server 'instructions' field returned by initialize (mcp-server.js:220-231). No hook-injected text in Claude Code, since no Claude Code hook exists. jev_compact and jev_receipt are the costly ones in practice: the model must pass the entire raw output/transcript as a tool ARGUMENT, meaning the tokens are already spent in context (output was read, then re-emitted as output tokens) before any 'savings', so it increases rather than decreases token use.
gh-raj8525-universal-jev.latencyImpact: Per jev_* call: one HTTPS round trip (brief claims 70-500 ms; I did not measure) plus model turn overhead for the tool call itself (seconds), and the model must re-emit the whole output as tool-call arguments (slow, expensive on Opus). Fast paths: output <1200 chars and <30 lines, protected code/diff calls, and non-zero exit code skip the API. Worst case 15 s (30 s with two keys) per call because of the ignored timeout option.
gh-raj8525-universal-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only, for Claude Code. Nothing forces Claude to call them; tool descriptions are generic ('Fast, calibrated multi-option classification...') and do not tell the model when to use them, so it will rarely or inconsistently call them and never on its own with the output it already received. The only deterministic component (codex-hook.js, PostToolUse output rewriting) is Codex-only and not wired for Claude Code; Claude Code hooks can only rewrite MCP tool output via updatedMCPToolOutput, so it could not rewrite built-in Bash results anyway (my understanding of Claude Code's hook API, not verified here). Not a transparent proxy, no skill triggers.
pros: Only candidate seen so far where OpenRouter is a first-class, coded provider: src/client.js:5-6 uses https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest and works with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY (client.js:59).
Small and auditable: ~3.1k lines total, zero npm dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no child_process in the MCP path; one afternoon to fully review.
Clean generic primitives (jev_decide_choice/noul/score) in src/primitives.js that map directly onto Jev's Choice/Noul/Score API, usable as a reference for building your own thin MCP.

Thoughtful protections in the receipt path: diff/patch and source-code immunity (compactor.js isProtectedCall), non-zero exit-code fast path with zero API calls, mid-output error anchor sampling, passthrough under 1200 chars.
Fail-open error handling in receipt path and hook; MCP key is lazy so server starts without a key and does not break Claude Code startup.
MIT license, local-only telemetry, key never in argv.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: install.sh configures OpenCode, Codex, Antigravity and Pi only; the single hook (bin/codex-hook.js) is Codex-format and unregistered for Claude Code. The README's Claude Code support is one line saying 'connect via MCP'. You would get 7 tools the model may never call, i.e. fails the user's core requirement of automatic use.

Wrong use of Jev for coding: main value proposition is 'prune command output' (receipt) and 'compact history' (jev_compact), which duplicates caveman-shrink / Claude Code's own compaction, and via MCP requires the model to re-send the whole log as an argument, costing more tokens, not fewer. No Jev-based code decision (e.g. routing, permission triage, commit-message or test-failure classification) is provided.
Lossy and unsafe by design: a classifier decides 'success' and the whole output is replaced by 4 lines; fallback mode silently truncates on any API failure. Risky for debugging on client projects.
Sends command output to a third party with no redaction, contradicting the user's secret-leak-guard setup and client-confidentiality constraints.
Timeout bug: JevClient.decide ignores options.timeout (client.js:141-142), so the advertised 4 s budget in receipt.js:186 is really 15 s (up to 30 s with fallback).
jev_guard is advisory, not a hook; it cannot block anything, and is redundant with your PreToolUse guards. It also adds an LLM round trip for a task where deterministic checks are better.

Ships unrelated and broken code: browser engine hardcoded to /Users/yangyu/.local/bin/ego-browser (bin/ego-browse.js:53), Pi extension, Chinese/English mixed README with marketing claims ('95%+ token savings', '100% transparency') and no benchmarks; 'Codex (GPT-6)' claims suggest the README is largely AI-generated.

Request schema (state string + questions map) is the author's own; I could not confirm it matches OpenRouter's documented Decisions API, and the TypeSafe URL (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) is not in the brief.

gh-kierandotai-jev-client.whatItDoes: Zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript client (Node >=22.18, run via --experimental-strip-types) for Jev. It is NOT an MCP server, hook, skill, or plugin, and has nothing Claude Code-specific.

Jev state is untrusted-data-steerable (README admits adversarial content in state can steer outputs), so gating decisions taken from repo content are injectable.
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in `state` plus the question text goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or TypeSafe or Vercel). The library sends nothing by itself; no telemetry. Since it is not wired into Claude Code, nothing leaves until someone writes glue code that decides what (prompts, diffs, file contents) to send. It is subject to OpenRouter's data policy for typesafe/jev-1.13, which matters for client code.
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.failureMode: Only as robust as the caller. postJson retries 429/500/502/503/504/529 up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff (500ms*2^n plus jitter, honoring Retry-After) (providers.ts:24-66). There is NO default timeout: fetch gets only an optional caller-supplied signal, so a hung connection blocks indefinitely, and worst-case retries add several seconds. Network errors (fetch throwing) are not retried. Errors throw JevError; there is no fail-open behavior. A hook built on this would need its own timeout and try/catch. The 'auto' mode silently falls back to the keyword MOCK provider when no key is set, with only a stderr warning, which would produce fake decisions that look real.
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text. It is not registered anywhere. Integration would require new work (roughly 30 lines to write a hook or MCP wrapper).
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.autoInvocation: Only when prompted / not applicable: it is a plain library and proxy with no Claude Code integration surface. Automatic use would need the user to write a PreToolUse hook or MCP server on top.
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.latencyImpact: None by itself. It would add one Jev round trip per call (claimed 70-500 ms plus process startup: a Node strip-types script per hook invocation costs roughly 50-100 ms). The retry path can add seconds and there is no timeout cap.

pros: Correct, minimal reference for the OpenRouter Decisions API wire format: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with {model, state, questions{type,instructions,criteria}} and Bearer auth (providers.ts:74-80), so it is a useful spec to copy for a self-written hook or MCP server.
Zero runtime deps and no install scripts: static-read auditable in about 45 KB, low supply-chain risk.
Retry/backoff handling for 429/5xx with Retry-After, including a recent 504 fix.
Documents Jev jaggedness (literal reading, no counting/dates) that matters when writing Jev questions for coding gates.
gateToolCall / escalateIfUnsure helpers show the exact pattern for gating a risky tool call by P(yes) and confidence, which maps to a PreToolUse hook design.
cons: Not an integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill, or plugin, so it does not give Claude Code any automatic Jev use. The user's core requirement is unmet.
11 days old, 1 author, 5 commits, 2 stars, no license, no releases, no CI, unpublished to npm: not fit to depend on in client work.
Local proxy binds all interfaces without auth (server.listen with no host): a key-spending open relay if run on a shared network.
No default fetch timeout and no fail-open path, so a naive hook built on it could stall every tool call.
auto provider silently falls back to a keyword mock, and prefers a Vercel gateway key over OpenRouter, both surprising for an OpenRouter-only user.
Uses only the alpha /api/alpha/decisions path (README admits it may move); does not support /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter.
Helper questions (urgency/ticket triage) are support-desk oriented, with nothing for coding tasks (no diff, commit, test-failure or file-relevance questions).
gh-kierandotai-jev-client.verdict: A tidy but tiny, unlicensed, 11-day-old TypeScript client that is useful only as a reference for the OpenRouter Decisions payload. It provides no Claude Code integration (no MCP, hooks or skills), so it does not satisfy the automatic-invocation goal; write a small fail-open PreToolUse hook or MCP wrapper yourself instead.

security: API key comes only from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and is sent as a Bearer header. jev-cli has no -key flag, so the key never appears in argv or the process list.
Zero third-party dependencies and no go.sum, so the supply-chain surface is one author and the Go stdlib.
No shell execution, no telemetry and no postinstall in the source I read. The only network call is the POST to the configured URL.
A repo-wide grep for exec./os/exec in main.go found nothing.
-url / JEV_API_URL can point anywhere and the Bearer key goes with it. The client does not check that a redirect is same-host, so a poisoned JEV_API_URL would leak the key.
If no key is set, no Authorization header is sent, which is fine for a local tensai server but silently unauthenticated.
The endpoint defaults to plain http:// for bare hosts (Endpoint()).
Release binaries come from a GitHub Actions tag build. I saw no checksums or signing in the first 60 lines of release.yaml.
Prompt-injection surface: none directly, because the output is typed (a float or one of the given option strings). The state text is still untrusted content sent to a model.
Single maintainer (Yasuhiro Matsumoto, a well-known Go author), 1 week old, 8 commits.
gh-mattn-go-jev.dataEgress: Whatever the caller pipes into stdin or -s, plus the question text and criteria, sent as JSON to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if repointed, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe). It sends nothing on its own. Code, diffs or tool output leave the machine only if Claude Code (or a hook) pipes them in. Client-project code would go to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe).
gh-mattn-go-jev.failureMode: Fail-closed per invocation, and the failure is visible to the caller. Exit status 2 on error and 1 on 'no'. Default timeout is 60 s including retries (jev.go:20), and 429/529 are retried with exponential backoff for up to 3 retries (500 ms, 1 s, 2 s). A slow or down Jev can therefore block the caller for up to about 60 s unless JEV_TIMEOUT is set low (say 2 s). Ambiguity: exit 1 means both 'no' and 'grep found nothing'. A wrapper hook would need its own fail-open logic (timeout 3, ignore non-zero, exit 0).
gh-mattn-go-jev.latencyImpact: Zero on its own, since it does nothing unless invoked. Each invocation costs process start (a few ms for a static Go binary) plus a TLS handshake plus the claimed 70-500 ms Jev round trip, and there is no connection reuse across calls. A hook that calls it per tool call would add about 0.1-0.6 s per call. It also blocks up to the timeout, 60 s by default, on failure.
gh-mattn-go-jev.contextCost: Zero. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook or skill text. Claude would only know about it if the user adds a CLAUDE.md line or a skill, which would cost a few hundred tokens.
gh-mattn-go-jev.autoInvocation: None. It is a passive CLI/SDK, so it is only used when invoked (Claude choosing to run it through Bash, or a hook the user writes). It is not usable as-is for the goal of automatic invocation. It could serve as the executable inside a user-authored PreToolUse hook or an MCP wrapper.
pros: Cleanest OpenRouter path of any client: JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY are all env-configurable with no code change (cmd/jev-cli/main.go:180-196), so the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone endpoint and typesafe/jev-1.13 plug in directly.
Stdlib-only Go, about 900 lines of source. Small enough to audit in minutes, and the audit here found no exec, telemetry or hidden network calls.
The key is read from the environment only, never from argv, so it does not show in ps.

A single static binary with fast startup is a good fit as the executable inside a fail-open PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. The `noul -q` exit code, `choice` and `ask` (several questions in one request, JSON out) are exactly the hook-friendly primitives.
JEV_TIMEOUT and -timeout allow a hard low timeout, and the 429/529 retry logic is sensible.
Tests plus a 3-OS CI matrix, MIT license, and prebuilt release binaries so Go is not needed on the box.
The typed output (float or an enumerated option) gives no free-text injection channel back into Claude's context.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. It gives Claude Code no automatic invocation, which was the user's main requirement. The user would have to write the hook or wrapper glue themselves.
Default timeout is 60 s with up to 3 retries, which is unsafe for a hook on the tool path unless overridden. Exit codes do not distinguish 'no' from error in every mode, so a wrapper needs care.
No OpenRouter mention anywhere in the repo (grep is empty). OpenRouter parity is inferred from the brief and untested, and OpenRouter's Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported at all.
The API key must live in a var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY even when it is an OpenRouter key, which is confusing next to a real TypeSafe key.
One week old, v0.0.3, single maintainer, 8 commits, requires Go 1.27 to build from source, and release binaries have no visible signing.
No persistent process or connection reuse, so a TLS handshake on every call adds latency on a per-tool-call hook.
Sending code or diffs to Jev for routing decisions leaks client-project content to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and Jev's own usefulness for coding decisions is unproven.
gh-mattn-go-jev.verdict: go-jev is a clean, auditable, dependency-free client that switches to OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is a passive CLI/SDK and provides no automatic Claude Code integration. Use it at most as the binary behind a self-written fail-open hook (with JEV_TIMEOUT around 2 s), not as the integration itself.
