gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.name: Alberto-Codes/judgevet
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.whatItDoes: Unofficial Python client (httpx, pydantic) for TypeSafe's Jev System One API, plus a CLI (`judgevet`) and an optional stdio MCP server (`judgevet-mcp`). The MCP server exposes 4 tools: ask_noul, ask_choice, ask_score and evaluate_policy. evaluate_policy runs a local pass/fail acceptance policy over Jev's probabilities. It is a plain request/response wrapper: Claude must decide to call the tools. There are no hooks, no skill and no plugin manifest.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.runtime: Python >=3.12 (uvx or uv tool install; `judgevet[mcp]` extra needs mcp>=2.2). Deps: httpx, pydantic-settings, structlog, typer, mcp.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.install: claude mcp add --transport stdio --scope user judgevet --env 'JEV_API__KEY=${JEV_API__KEY}' --env 'JEV_API__BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api' -- uvx --from 'judgevet[mcp]==0.15.0' judgevet-mcp   (the docs show only the project-scope form with the TypeSafe host; the OpenRouter base URL is my adaptation)

providerSupport.evidence: Code has no 'openrouter' string anywhere (grep of src/docs/json is empty), but the base URL is fully configurable. src/judgevet/adapters/inbound/settings.py:60 DEFAULT_BASE_URL="https://api.typesafe.ai"; :116-118 base_url with validation_alias AliasChoices("base_url","TYPESAFE_BASE_URL") (env JEV_API__BASE_URL via env_prefix JEV_ and nested delimiter __ at :344-346); https-only validator at :121-150. Key comes from JEV_API__KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY (settings.py:158), JEV_API__KEY_FILE, or a `!command` (credential_command.py). Auth defaults to `Authorization: Bearer` (settings.py auth_header/auth_scheme, gateway.py). The HTTP adapter POSTs to relative path "/v1/systemone" (outbound/http.py:497 and :741). With base_url=https://openrouter.ai/api this becomes https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, exactly OpenRouter's documented System One endpoint (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk says TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api). Payload {state, questions, model} (http.py:155-182) matches OpenRouter's documented body. Response parser (domain/response_parser.py:65-74) reads model, usage.input_tokens/output_tokens and answers by key, and ignores extras such as id, provider and usage.cost. Default model 'jev-latest' (settings.py:61) is mapped by OpenRouter to ~typesafe/jev-latest. Not verified live: STATUS.md records live runs against TypeSafe only. OpenRouter error bodies use a different shape than `detail.error_type`, so errors fall back to the bare HTTP status line.
providerSupport.others: Generic gateway settings (custom auth header/scheme, extra headers, request-id header, proxy, CA bundle) in settings.py:190-215. A SystemOnePort provider seam (used for self-hosted typevet/Gemma) exists. It does NOT use OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions Decisions API.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change. Set JEV_API__BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and JEV_API__KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The wire schema is the same and the model id is mapped server-side. The only cost is that nobody has verified it live, and OpenRouter error messages are less detailed.

interface.name: ask_noul (MCP)
interface.purpose: Yes/no question over a state (string or object) and an instruction; returns P(yes) as NoulAnswer.

interface.name: ask_choice (MCP)
interface.purpose: Multiple choice: state, instruction, optional criteria map (default yes/no); returns chosen label, confidence and per-option probabilities.

interface.name: ask_score (MCP)
interface.purpose: Ordered rubric: state, instruction, optional criteria list (default Poor/Fair/Good/Excellent); returns score, confidence, legend and probabilities.

interface.name: evaluate_policy (MCP)
interface.purpose: Several keyed noul/choice/score questions plus a local JSON acceptance policy (rules with min/max/label bounds); returns answers, pass/fail with per-rule detail, model and usage. Local evaluation only.

interface.name: judgevet [STATE] [QUESTIONS] (CLI)
interface.purpose: Calls System One with state from an arg, file or stdin; JSON output or policy exit status. Subcommands for policy evaluation exist (cli_policy*.py). Usable from a shell hook.

interface.name: judgevet-mcp (entrypoint)
interface.purpose: stdio MCP server. Exit 2 if no key or invalid settings; exit 1 with a fixed 'stage failed (TypeName)' diagnostic on fatal errors.

interface.name: examples/staged-review/review-staged.sh
interface.purpose: Example script that sends `git diff --cached` plus versioned questions and a policy to Jev. Opt-in, not wired into any hook.

security: API key: read from env, file or `!command` into SecretStr; sent only in the Authorization Bearer header. Never in argv when using `--env 'JEV_API__KEY=${JEV_API__KEY}'`, though docs show the key held in the launching shell env. The CLI explicitly warns against putting keys in command arguments.
Base URL validator rejects non-loopback http://; redirects disabled (SECURITY.md). A configured replacement host receives the same data and key.

`!command` credential source runs argv directly with no shell (credential_command.py), bounded stdout, stderr discarded, and a timeout. It is a trusted-config feature, not an attack surface unless the env is attacker-controlled.
No telemetry or phone-home (SECURITY.md); logs are quiet by default and exclude state and question text. Tracebacks and error envelopes may contain content.

No curl|sh installer and no npm postinstall. It is a PyPI package run via uvx; the docs pin ==0.15.0 but transitive dependencies are not pinned. There is a supply-chain workflow (SBOM, uv audit, CodeQL, Dependabot).

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs come from Claude, so injected file content can be steered into a Jev call. Jev returns only typed probabilities, no free text, so the return channel is low-risk. The main risk is exfiltration by sending content to a third-party host.

Optional StateRedactor and a spend cap (spend_max_attempts / spend_max_input_tokens) exist, but the MCP entrypoint wires only the spend cap from settings. No redactor is configured, so state is sent unredacted.
Solo maintainer, 0 stars, 10 days old, pre-alpha classifier. Trust is by code reading only; the author also publishes a release every day or two.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.dataEgress: Whatever Claude passes as `state` and `instruction`/`criteria` in each tool call. Nothing is sent automatically: Claude decides what to include, which could be code snippets, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. It goes as JSON {state, questions, model} to the configured base URL, i.e. OpenRouter and then the TypeSafe or Jev provider. The Bearer key goes in the header. evaluate_policy rules stay local. No telemetry. Retention and training policy of the remote service is not established (SECURITY.md says so). Client work needs a check against OpenRouter data policies and client NDAs.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, and it never blocks the session. A missing key makes the server exit 2 at startup, so the tool shows as failed in /mcp. At call time errors are typed and returned as an MCP error result: JevAuthError, JevRateLimitError, JevServiceError, JevBudgetExceededError. Timeouts are 30 s read and 5 s connect (settings.py:302, http.py:404). Retries default to max_attempts=3 with 0.5-5 s backoff on retryable HTTP errors. Transport-error retry is off by default (retry_transport=False). Worst case a single call could take about 90 s, so tighten timeout_seconds and max_attempts. Since Claude is the caller, it can ignore a failed call and carry on. There is no fail-open hook semantics because there is no hook.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.contextCost: 4 tools. Input-side definitions (names, descriptions, inputSchema) come to about 6-9k chars, roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens. evaluate_policy dominates because it embeds the closed policy JSON Schema and nested question schemas (mcp_schemas.py, 314 lines, 11.3k chars including docstrings). Output schemas (mcp_output_schemas.py, 253 lines) are also declared but Claude Code does not use them. No MCP server `instructions` text (grep found none) and nothing injected by hooks. Tool descriptions say what each tool returns but not WHEN Claude should call it, which weakens discretionary use.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code loads the four tools and Claude may call them if the descriptions look relevant. There is no hook, no skill trigger, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no server instructions telling Claude when to use Jev. In practice it will rarely or unpredictably call ask_noul and friends unless the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook wrapper. That misses the user's goal of Claude Code using Jev when needed with no prompting.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.latencyImpact: Per call: Jev's claimed 70-500 ms plus OpenRouter overhead. Add one extra LLM tool-use round trip on the Opus side (seconds), and uvx cold start on first launch (dependency resolution and download; cached afterwards). Nothing is added to turns that do not call the tools. Startup adds one stdio process to session start. Prefer `uv tool install` over uvx to avoid a cold-start delay.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with no code change: `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`/`JEV_API__BASE_URL` aliasing plus the `/v1/systemone` path match OpenRouter's `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone`, and the response parser ignores OpenRouter's extra fields (settings.py:116-118, http.py:497, response_parser.py:65-74).

The only candidate found with all three Jev primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) exposed as typed MCP tools with output schemas, plus a local policy layer that turns probabilities into pass/fail. That fits a 'gate' use of Jev.
Careful key handling: SecretStr, key file and `!command` sources, https-only base URL, no redirects, no telemetry, and debug logs that exclude state.
Real engineering hygiene for a 10-day-old repo: 148 test files, CI with lint, docs checks, uv audit, SBOM, CodeQL, release-please and a signed publish workflow. MIT licence.

Includes a CLI that could back a deterministic hook (e.g. a PreToolUse or Stop hook gating on `judgevet` exit status) if the user builds one. `examples/staged-review` shows the pattern for `git diff --cached`.
Claude Code was already tried by the author (STATUS.md: v2.1.280 connected and discovered 3 tools; calls blocked only by the author's account spend limit).
cons: Not automatic: no hook, no skill and no server instructions, so Claude uses Jev only if it happens to pick a tool. This directly fails the user's 'never say use jev' requirement without extra glue such as a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook.

OpenRouter was never tested by the author: docs and tests target api.typesafe.ai only, and the evidence in STATUS.md is TypeSafe-direct with jev-1.13.0. OpenRouter error bodies (not `detail.error_type`) degrade to bare status lines.
Ignores OpenRouter's Decisions API (`/api/alpha/decisions`) and the 'Jev Router' model. Only System One is supported.

Solo maintainer, 0 stars, created 2026-09-20, daily releases, pre-alpha classifier, docs marked 'draft'. High churn and bus-factor risk. The pin `==0.15.0` will need bumping, and the MCP path is verified only on the legacy handshake.

No redactor in the MCP path: Claude-chosen state, which could contain client code or secrets, goes to a third party unredacted. The only guard is Claude's judgement, and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover these mcp__ tools unless its matcher is extended.

Generic tools (ask yes/no, choice, score) with no coding-specific presets. Claude must design the question each time, and Jev is not a chat model, so value for edits, refactors or code search is weak.
Adds ~1.5-2.5k tokens of tool definitions to every session for a rarely-called tool. Long worst-case timeouts (30 s x 3 attempts) unless tuned.
Requires Python 3.12+ and uvx cold start, and the transitive dependency set (mcp>=2.2, pydantic-settings, structlog, typer) is not pinned.
gh-alberto-codes-judgevet.verdict: The most complete and best-engineered Jev client/MCP found, and it works on OpenRouter by setting only JEV_API__BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and the key. But it is a passive toolbox, not an automatic integration: use it as the transport layer (MCP or the CLI called from a hook) rather than a standalone answer to the 'Claude must use it by itself' requirement. It also has a solo-maintainer, 10-day-old, pre-alpha risk profile.

gh-docxology-daf-jev.name: docxology/daf-jev
gh-docxology-daf-jev.whatItDoes: Python (httpx) toolkit for the System One /v1/systemone API. It contains a sync/async client, a question builder for noul/choice/score, a concurrent evaluator, confidence and tiered gates, a calibration module, a CLI, a FastMCP stdio server (`daf-jev serve`, 9 tools plus 1 resource) and an agent SKILL.md. It also has a registry of six providers, including openrouter. Much of the repo is research-style extras: a Bayes-net factor elicitation experiment, a manuscript and figures. It is a generic client and toolbox, not a Claude Code coding integration. It has no hooks and no coding-specific questions.

providerSupport.evidence: src/daf_jev/providers.py:216-233 registers provider `openrouter`: default_base_url=https://openrouter.ai/api, api_key_vars=(OPENROUTER_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY), base_url_vars=(OPENROUTER_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), model_vars=(OPENROUTER_MODEL,), default_model=jev-latest. src/daf_jev/client.py:60 SYSTEM_ONE_PATH=/v1/systemone, so the request goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (client.py:221). The direct TypeSafe provider `jev` (providers.py:133-144) uses https://api.typesafe.ai with JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY. README.md:485 and output/experiments/asia/receipts.json report a live end-to-end run with provider openrouter, model jev-latest. The MCP tools take a per-call `provider` arg, default `jev` (mcp_server.py), and the server has no env/CLI default for the provider (the MCP path does not read a provider env var). So for OpenRouter each tool call must pass provider=openrouter. Alternatively set JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and leave provider=jev.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already supported; only config is needed. The Decisions API at /api/alpha/decisions is NOT used. Caveats: default model is the bare `jev-latest`, while the brief's OpenRouter IDs are `typesafe/jev-1.13` and `~typesafe/jev-latest`. Set OPENROUTER_MODEL (or pass `model`) to be safe. Whether OpenRouter accepts the bare alias is unverified here, but the repo's receipts claim it worked. `jev_models` is unsupported through openrouter (per the provider notes).
providerSupport.others: jeff, kev, localjev (GitHub Next), openthai-systemone: self-hosted System One servers

gh-docxology-daf-jev.runtime: Python >=3.10; deps httpx and pyyaml; `mcp>=1.2,<2` is an optional extra. Not on PyPI (as far as inspected); install is `uv sync --extra mcp` in a clone, then `uv run --directory <clone> daf-jev serve`.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.install: git clone https://github.com/docxology/daf-jev ~/tools/daf-jev, then `uv sync --extra mcp`. Register it with `claude mcp add daf-jev -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... -e OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest -- uv run --directory ~/tools/daf-jev daf-jev serve`. Every tool call must then pass provider=openrouter. Alternative: set JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and JEV_API_KEY. The env values would land in ~/.claude.json and, for `-e`, in argv at add time. I did not run any of this.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.tests: Large suite: 35 unit test files in tests/unit plus tests/live, which are skipped without a key. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs ruff, mypy, pytest with a 90% coverage gate, docs-drift checks and a `serve --help` smoke test. The tests were not run here (static review only).
security: API key is read from env or a `.env` in the server's CWD (config.py load_dotenv). It is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (client.py:221), and README says it is never returned in tool output. Nothing was found that puts the key in argv on the server side. The `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` route does expose it briefly in argv and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

The `.env` lookup uses the process CWD, so a `.env` in a client project's directory could be picked up as the source of the key. That is a minor cross-project leak vector, and it conflicts with the user's secret-guard hooks.
No shell execution or subprocess in the server path. The only subprocess use is in manuscript_variables.py, which is a dev script. No curl|sh, postinstall or telemetry found in src (grep).

The MCP tools jev_posteriors_load, jev_reask_plan and jev_docs_verify take arbitrary local file paths and read them (JSON parse). This is a small arbitrary-file-read surface if the model is prompt-injected, and it returns only parsed or validated fields. It is not directly harmful, but it is pointless surface for a coding setup.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is typed probabilities and labels, with no free text from the model. This is low risk. The `state` argument is whatever Claude sends.
The repo commits a PDF, output files and ~280 files. Single-author, brand-new project (13 days old), version 0.6.0. It is unaudited third-party code that would run with the user's OpenRouter key.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.dataEgress: The `state` argument (str or JSON) and the question texts and option descriptions that Claude composes go to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, along with the model name and the OpenRouter key. In practice that means whatever snippets, diffs, file contents or task descriptions Claude decides to put into `state`; nothing is collected automatically. Nothing else leaves the machine, and there is no telemetry. OpenRouter forwards to TypeSafe, so client code could reach third parties. Client-project confidentiality needs care.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.failureMode: When Jev is slow or down, `jev_ask` blocks the tool call for up to 60 s per attempt (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=60.0 in _http.py:60, or JEV_TIMEOUT). There are up to 3 attempts with 0.5-8 s backoff on 429/529 (README config table), which is worst case of about 3 minutes. A failed call returns a tool error, so Claude sees the error and carries on. It is model-discretion, so nothing structurally blocks the session, and this is effectively fail-open. A missing key raises ValueError, which surfaces as a tool error. The circuit breaker in resilience.py is opt-in and is not wired into the MCP server.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call Jev. Each jev_ask call costs one MCP round trip plus the remote latency (claimed 70-500 ms end to end, unverified here), plus the Claude tool-call overhead (an extra model step, a few seconds). On outage it can be up to 60 s per attempt, and up to 3 attempts. There are no hooks, so there is no per-tool-call latency.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.contextCost: 9 tools (jev_ask, jev_evaluate, jev_models, jev_composite_score, jev_confidence_gate, jev_tiered_gate, jev_docs_verify, jev_posteriors_load, jev_reask_plan) plus 1 resource. Docstrings sum to about 4.2k chars and signatures about 0.8k chars; with JSON schema overhead I estimate about 6.5k chars, roughly 1.6k tokens. The server INSTRUCTIONS block (~1.0k chars, about 250 tokens) is injected into the system prompt. Total is roughly 1.9k tokens always-on, or about 0.3k tokens if deferred tool loading (ToolSearch) is active. Six of the tools are irrelevant to coding. Hooks inject nothing, since none exist.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions are generic ("Ask named questions about one state...") and give Claude no coding triggers, so Claude will rarely or never call it unprompted. The SKILL.md description triggers only on daf-jev / System One code work. There is no hook, proxy or deterministic trigger. It does NOT meet the user's "Claude must use it automatically" requirement without extra glue such as a CLAUDE.md rule, or a custom PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook that calls `daf-jev ask`.
pros: Gives a working, source-verified OpenRouter path: providers.py:216-233 targets https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_MODEL. It has a claimed live OpenRouter run in README/receipts.

The client is a generic, well-typed System One client: strict parsing that tolerates OpenRouter's extra id/provider/usage.cost fields, retries on 429/529, a 60 s timeout, and native or spec-string question building. This is useful as a library and as a CLI (`daf-jev ask`) for writing your own hook.
The local gates (jev_confidence_gate, jev_tiered_gate, jev_composite_score) encode confidence-routing patterns that fit turning Jev probabilities into decisions.
Good engineering hygiene for a young project: MIT licence, CI with a 90% coverage gate, ruff and mypy, 35 unit-test files, tagged releases v0.3.0-v0.6.0.
Server is small (493 lines) and readable, with no shell execution and no telemetry, so it is easy to audit and fork.
Multi-provider registry lets one switch to a local or self-hosted System One (jeff, kev, localjev), which is useful if the client code must stay on the machine.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool with generic descriptions and no coding-specific guidance. Claude will not reach for it without being told, which fails the user's core requirement. There are no hooks, no plugin.json and no .mcp.json.

The MCP server has no default-provider setting: the `provider` argument defaults to `jev` (direct TypeSafe) on every tool. The user must set JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_API_KEY hacks, or Claude must pass provider=openrouter every call, or the fork must be patched (a one-line default change in mcp_server.py).

Default model `jev-latest` may not match the OpenRouter IDs (`typesafe/jev-1.13`, `~typesafe/jev-latest`). It also does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions). It uses only the /api/v1/systemone surface. The bare alias is unverified against OpenRouter.

About 1.9k tokens of always-on context for 9 tools, of which 6 have no coding use (docs_verify, posteriors_load, reask_plan, evaluate, models, composite_score). The Bayes-net posteriors tools read arbitrary local paths.

Not a coding-workflow tool at all: no questions for code review, commit triage, test selection, permission gating or intent routing, and no state-shaping guidance for a repo. Much of the repo is research output (manuscript, PDF, figures, Bayes-net experiments) that adds noise. Single-author (79 of 90 commits), 13 days old, 7 stars, unaudited.
Not published to PyPI and needs a clone plus `uv sync`. The `.env` in CWD is auto-loaded, and the key sits in ~/.claude.json env or gets picked up per-project.
Slow-failure behaviour is unfavorable: a 60 s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn if OpenRouter or TypeSafe is degraded, and the circuit breaker is not wired into the MCP server.
gh-docxology-daf-jev.verdict: daf-jev is a real, tested System One client that supports OpenRouter in code. But it is a generic library and toolbox, not a Claude Code integration, and its MCP tools are model-discretion with no coding triggers. It cannot deliver the "automatic, never say use jev" goal. Use it, at most, as a source for the client code and question builders when writing your own thin hook or MCP server (a forked provider default, plus hook-driven calls to `daf-jev ask`), not as the integration itself.

gh-ranjan2829-askjev.name: askjev-mcp (AskJev)
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.whatItDoes: Browser-automation MCP server (npm askjev-mcp 1.7.3, 15 tools) plus a Chrome extension. askjev_do runs a Playwright/CDP autopilot loop. Each step it snapshots the page (URL, title, up to 60 interactive elements with role, name, href and current input value) and sends one fan-out POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. That call asks a Choice (next action), a Choice (target element), a Noul (irreversible) and a Score (progress). It then executes the chosen click or type. It stops when P(irreversible) is 0.65 or higher. Jev drives web browsing here. It is not a coding assistant and does not help with code, diffs or tests.

README (mcp/README.md) confirms api.typesafe.ai.

security: Key handling: the API key is read from env or ~/.askjev/api-key (mode 600, written by the extension's Auto-connect). It is not passed in argv. The extension's Auto-connect writes the key into Claude's MCP config env, which would put it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or the Claude Desktop config.

Instruction hijack: server `instructions` and the askjev_do description say 'ONLY browser automation', 'REQUIRED for any website request' and 'Do NOT use any built-in browser pane... or other browsing tools'. In this user's setup this would fight the existing playwright MCP and is the opposite of a neutral integration.

Prompt-injection surface: page element names, hrefs, titles and read_page text flow into Jev state and into Claude's context. Jev is a typed classifier, so it cannot be told to run arbitrary shell commands. The single-action tools (askjev_act, click, type, navigate) have no guard, and a Claude that has been injected can drive a logged-in browser.
The guard is only a probabilistic P(irreversible) >= 0.65 inside the autopilot loop. It is not a security boundary.

No shell execution of user input. It spawns a browser with --remote-debugging-port, or attaches to ASKJEV_CDP_URL (default 127.0.0.1:9222). An open CDP port gives any local process browser control. Launched browsers use a persistent Playwright profile, and the code comments mention a past profile-corruption incident (cdp-browser.ts ~line 99).

Supply chain: root package.json has a postinstall (`npm install --prefix mcp`) but it belongs to the extension repo. The published npm package has no postinstall. Dependencies are @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, playwright-core, ws and zod. No curl|sh installer was seen. One maintainer, 4 versions published within 2 days.
No telemetry found. The only fetch is to api.typesafe.ai.
MIT license.
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.dataEgress: On each autopilot step, sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone: the goal text (the user's words), page URL, page title, the last 6 actions, and up to 60 interactive elements (role, accessible name, href, input_type, and current_value truncated to 80 chars for form fields). Values typed into form fields, including possibly passwords or PII, can appear in current_value. No source code, diffs or Claude prompts are sent, because it only ever sees what is in the browser tab. Screenshots are returned to Claude, not to Jev. Everything goes to TypeSafe directly, not through OpenRouter.
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.failureMode: Fail-loud for the multi-step tools. Without a key, askjev_do returns a missing_api_key error. There is a 15 s per-attempt timeout and 2 retries with exponential backoff on network errors, 429 and 529. 401 and 422 fail fast. On failure the tool returns an error to Claude rather than silently degrading. Single-step tools never call Jev and keep working. It does not block Claude Code itself, because there is no hook. The failure only affects browsing tasks.
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.contextCost: 15 MCP tools. The descriptions, zod schemas and server instructions add up to roughly 2-3k tokens (estimate from the sizes of index.ts's tool registrations, about 16.8k chars including code, and the instructions string of about 700 chars). It is always loaded, or deferred if tool search is on. No hook-injected text. The instructions text tries to steer Claude away from other browser tools, which would bias against the user's playwright MCP.
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. Claude calls askjev_do only when the task involves a website or browser. It is aggressively worded (REQUIRED for any website request) but never triggers during ordinary coding, so it is not a deterministic hook and never runs by itself.
gh-ranjan2829-askjev.latencyImpact: Zero on non-browser turns. During browser tasks, each autopilot step costs one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms) plus a Playwright snapshot and action. A 25-step cap and 100-step ceiling multiply this to seconds or tens of seconds per goal. Since Jev only picks the next click, a multi-step goal is much slower and less reliable than Claude or playwright MCP planning directly.

It uses structured criteria, confidence gating (ASKJEV_MIN_CONFIDENCE 0.45), an irreversible-action Noul guard at 0.65, and stuck/oscillation detection. It is a good reference for how Jev is meant to be used.

Single-step tools (navigate, snapshot, read_page, screenshot) need no key and never call Jev.

Duplicates the playwright MCP that the user already has. The server instructions explicitly tell Claude not to use other browser tools, so installing it would cause conflicts.
The Jev browser loop is slower and less reliable than Claude planning directly. Jev has no reasoning trace and re-decides every step from a 60-element list.

npmjs-com-package-fast-mcp-gatekeeper.name: fast-mcp-gatekeeper
npmjs-com-package-fast-mcp-gatekeeper.whatItDoes: A stdio MCP proxy wrapper (not an MCP server itself): you prefix another MCP server's command with `fast-mcp-gatekeeper --`. It intercepts JSON-RPC `tools/call` requests, sends the serialized call to a Jev System One endpoint (noul/score/choice questions) and blocks, redacts or allows the call. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or on ANY error or non-2xx response, it silently falls back to a hard-coded keyword 'simulator' (substring checks such as '../', 'curl ', 'secret'). The README's '<50ms' and demo output are therefore simulator numbers (random 30-50ms), not measured Jev latency.

Add a new profile to judge_profiles.json (api_url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, key_env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and copy the calibration numbers) and set SUPERJEV_JUDGE to it. The host check compares against the selected profile's own api_url, so a new profile passes it. Same /v1/systemone path and the same {model,state,questions} body are likely compatible, but that is unverified against OpenRouter. Watch the response field names and OpenRouter's alpha schema. Calibrated thresholds (0.8/0.9/0.85) were measured on the TypeSafe direct model, so they would need re-measuring. The Node twin (src/judge-profile.ts) reads the same JSON. It means maintaining a fork, and the upstream ships changes daily.
providerSupport.others: Laya local judge (open Apache-2.0, keyless, UNCALIBRATED, 1024 token window) as a second profile.

interface.name: Stop hook: skills/super-jev/hooks/stop-gate.sh -> `superjev.py hook gate`
interface.purpose: Claim gate on every final reply. Sends last_assistant_message plus the last 8 tool_results (default; capped by SUPERJEV_GATE_WINDOW_TOK 8000) to Jev. Exit 2 BLOCKS the turn on REJECT or on a confident NOT_SUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED (>=0.80). Fails open on timeout (SUPERJEV_GATE_BUDGET_S 15s) and missing config. Never blocks when stop_hook_active=true. Example only, not auto-installed.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook (matcher Agent): hooks/posttooluse-verify.sh -> `hook verify`
interface.purpose: Verifies a sub-agent's report (git, tests, PR) via an external worker-verify tool (SUPERJEV_VERIFY_CMD), which is NOT shipped. Without it, it fails open or exits 6. Timeout 300s.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook: hooks/userpromptsubmit-verify.sh -> `hook prompt-verify`
interface.purpose: Scans the user prompt for <\teammate-message> blocks and verifies them. Advisory only, always exit 0. Not useful for a solo dev without agent teams.

interface.name: Skill super-jev (skills/super-jev/SKILL.md, 22 KB)
interface.purpose: Commands ask.py / dispatch.py: ask (cache-first retrieval over connected folders), navigate, skills, ask --claim (TRUE/FALSE/CONFLICT), check (claim/draft gate vs evidence files), verify (agent-report verification), help. Trigger is by description text, model discretion.

interface.name: Skills skill-search, super-jev-connect, super-jev-build-cycle
interface.purpose: Suggest installed skills for a request (advisory), onboard/refresh connected folders (prepare_bulk.py, connect_github.py), and a build-cycle skill.

interface.name: Node CLIs (package.json bin/scripts)
interface.purpose: superjev (jev-chat-cli terminal chat), organize, sweep, permit (is this harness action safe to auto-run?), fetch/skill-search/catalog (score a skill catalog), chain (experimental), replay/bench. All are run manually.

security: No API key in argv: key is read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (docs suggest export TYPESAFE_API_KEY="$(cat file)") and sent only as an Authorization header. There is a key-provider file option for hooks.
Key exfil guard: the URL override is refused unless it is the same host as the profile or loopback (lib/jev_client.py _key_may_go_to; src/jev.ts:206). Redirects are disabled (_NoRedirect).

Outbound secret scan: every request is scanned (payload_has_secret) and refused with SecretBlocked before sending. This is a heuristic, not a guarantee, and it is separate from and additional to your own secret-leak hook.

install.sh is a curl|bash installer that clones the repo's default branch and runs `npm install --omit=dev` (only 2 deps: @clack/prompts, picocolors). It has no pinned commit or checksum, so you trust the moving `main` branch. Do not use it. Read-only cloning and manual symlinking is the safer path.

The stop hook parses the model's own last message and tool outputs, so it processes untrusted tool-result content (prompt-injection surface) and feeds it to a classifier that can BLOCK a turn. Blocking requires confidence >= 0.80 and no stop_hook_active.
Shell execution: the verify path runs git, gh and test commands DERIVED from a worker report's text (run twice); this is a command-injection style surface if the report is attacker-influenced.
Writes state to ~/.local/state/super-jev, and skills/super-jev/prepare-cache and ledger in the checkout. Traces are said to be redacted (no file contents).

No telemetry code found. No plugin manifest. SECURITY.md is 2 lines. Some code shells out to `claude -p --model haiku` when the claude CLI exists (GETTING-STARTED.md:76), which is unexpected extra LLM spend.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (not OpenRouter, as shipped): with the Stop hook enabled, EVERY turn end sends the assistant's final reply text plus the content of the last ~8 tool results (file reads, grep and bash output, diffs), up to about 8000 judge tokens, along with the user's last prompt when no tools ran. Secret-scan heuristics filter some of it. With ask/connect: the text of connected files (to describe and check them), descriptions and questions. With check: the claim plus the evidence files. The README states this. On a client project this means code and client data leave to a third party on every turn, which is outside any client-confidentiality boundary unless authorized.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.failureMode: The Stop gate mostly fails open: a missing SUPERJEV_GATE_CMD is a no-op, a budget overrun (default SUPERJEV_GATE_BUDGET_S=15s, timeout 90s) prints "budget exceeded, not judged" and exits 3 (advisory), and a Jev error is a typed error with no verdict (not a pass, not a block). It FAILS CLOSED in one case: a confident (>=0.80) NOT_SUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED/REJECT verdict returns exit 2 and forces Claude to continue the turn. With Jev's calibration only measured on the TypeSafe model, and false-positive misfires documented in the code comments (HAS_LEAKS on plain notes), this can annoy in daily coding. A stop_hook_active loop guard exists. Client retries on 429/529 (4 attempts, 1s doubling) can add multi-second delays. In bypass mode the blocking is the only friction.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 MCP tool definitions and 0 server instructions. Skills: super-jev SKILL.md is ~22 KB (~5.5k tokens), loaded in full when the skill triggers. The frontmatter description is about 300 chars (~75 tokens) always resident, plus skill-search (5.5 KB) and super-jev-connect (12 KB) if linked. The Stop hook injects at most one advisory line, or a block reason, into the transcript, so it is negligible normally. The lookup protocol pushes every question through ask.py and Python output with OUTCOME lines, which costs tokens per use. The SKILL.md prose is extremely dense and hard for a model to follow.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.autoInvocation: Mixed. The Stop hook (if the user pastes the snippet into settings.json) is deterministic and automatic, but it only judges the finished reply for unsupported claims. It is the sole real "Claude Code uses Jev without prompting" element. Everything else (ask, check, permit, skill-search) is a skill triggered by description at model discretion, or a manual CLI. The docs give a "retrieval rule card" to paste into CLAUDE.md to make the model prefer ask/skill-search. No PreToolUse/permit hook is shipped, so the permit gate is not automatic.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.latencyImpact: Stop hook: one Jev call per turn end, claimed 70-500 ms for Jev but wrapped by Python startup and a large superjev.py (about 10k lines). The hook budget is 15s end to end with a 1-call allowance, so typical +1-3s at the end of each turn, worst case 15s. The retry path with 429 can extend this. ask.py can also wait up to 45s on reconnects. There is no per-tool-call latency unless you wire PostToolUse (it fires for Agent only, and the external verify tool is not shipped).
pros: Only candidate here with a real, documented Claude Code hook integration (Stop hook that reads last_assistant_message and transcript_path per the actual hooks payload, honors stop_hook_active to avoid loops, fail-open budgets). It is the one place Jev fires automatically with no user prompt.

Serious hardening for a 2-week-old repo: outbound secret scan before every request, API key locked to same-host or loopback (lib/jev_client.py), no redirects, typed errors so a failure is never reported as a pass, and pinned GitHub Action SHAs.
Judge is abstracted behind judge_profiles.json (typesafe-jev + local laya), so adding an OpenRouter profile is a small JSON edit rather than a rewrite. The Node twin reads the same table.

Large test surface: about 107 Python tests in skills/super-jev/tests, about 45 Node tests, CI on Node 24 plus pytest, gitleaks config and a scorecard workflow. MIT licensed, 275 commits, a release v1.0.12, 113 tags, active daily pushes.
Honest maturity table and 'what 1.0 does not do' in the README, and data-egress documented in a 'What this tool touches' section.
cons: No OpenRouter support. The URL override refuses anything except api.typesafe.ai or loopback, so the user's OpenRouter key and endpoint cannot be used without patching judge_profiles.json and keeping a fork. The calibrated thresholds (0.8/0.9) are measured for TypeSafe direct only, and OpenRouter's alpha endpoint may differ.

Wrong problem domain. It is a document-retrieval, cache and claim-verification system for agent 'brains' (connect folders, approve answers, principals, pointers, ledgers), not a coding router. Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives are used for 'which file answers this?' and 'does this text support this claim?', not for coding decisions such as model routing, permission decisions or test selection. Setup burden is high (setup.py, connect, prepare_bulk, principals, state dir).

Egress risk on client work: the recommended Stop hook ships the final reply plus recent tool outputs (code, diffs, file contents) to a third-party API every turn. It is heuristic secret scanning only, and it duplicates what the user's secret-leak hook guards against.

Can block. Stop-hook exit 2 forces extra turns on a confident NOT_SUPPORTED, and the source itself documents false positives (HAS_LEAKS/SELF_CONTRADICTORY misfires in hand tests 2026-09-24). On a coding session 'tests pass' claims need a trace and the gate derives evidence only from the last 8 tool results, so long sessions get judged on partial evidence.

Two of the three hooks depend on an external 'worker-verify' tool that is NOT in the repo (SUPERJEV_VERIFY_CMD), and the PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit hooks target multi-agent team workflows the user does not run. The permit gate (the only coding-relevant primitive) has no hook wiring.

Complexity and churn: superjev.py is about 10k lines, docs are dense internal changelog prose, SKILL.md is 22 KB, package.json version 1.0.6 vs release v1.0.12, 203 of 275 commits by one author (72 more by 'admin'), age 13 days. It is a one-team daily driver made public, with no plugin manifest or marketplace entry. install.sh is curl|bash from a moving branch. Sole live evidence for Jev is one recorded call on 2026-09-17 (test/fixtures/live-score-2026-09-17.json).
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.verdict: Not recommended as the integration. It is a genuine, well-tested Jev harness, but it targets agent knowledge retrieval and claim verification, hard-locks TypeSafe direct (OpenRouter needs a forked profile), and its only automatic Claude Code piece is a Stop-hook claim gate that ships every turn's replies and tool outputs to a third party and can block turns. Treat it as a reference for a fail-open Stop hook and for keeping the key on the same host, and borrow those ideas rather than installing it.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.install: Manual: git clone, export TYPESAFE_API_KEY, python3 skills/super-jev/setup.py, symlink skills into ~/.claude/skills, and paste the hook snippet into settings.json. Alternative: curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash for the superjev chat CLI only.
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.runtime: Node >=24 (TypeScript run natively, deps @clack/prompts and picocolors) plus Python 3 stdlib (urllib) for the skills and hooks
gh-kevthetech143-super-jev.tests: About 107 Python test files (skills/super-jev/tests), about 45 Node test files (test/, test/enhance/), GitHub Actions test.yml running npm test, demos, pytest and the experiments; gitleaks and scorecard workflows. Not run here (static reading only).

gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.name: ajevt-browser-mcp (XYenon/ajevt-browser)
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server exposing one tool, ajevt_browser. It runs a bounded observe/decide/act loop on a web page through Vercel agent-browser. Each step sends page state plus a finite list of candidate operations and targets to the Jev System One endpoint. Jev answers with choice and noul probabilities, which the tool validates before acting. It is a browser-automation fast path, not a coding-assistance integration. The same core also ships as Pi, OpenCode and Amp plugins.

providerSupport.evidence: src/config.ts:6 DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Overrides: src/config.ts:133 JEV_ENDPOINT, :134 JEV_MODEL, :135 JEV_API_KEY else TYPESAFE_API_KEY, :137 JEV_HEADERS, plus ~/.config/ajevt-browser/config.json decision.{endpoint,model,auth}. src/jev.ts:50-58 POSTs {model,state,questions} with 'authorization: Bearer <key>'. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling and the string 'openrouter' appears nowhere in the repo. Pointing JEV_ENDPOINT at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 should work, but only if OpenRouter's System One schema matches this request and response shape. That is unverified: my fetches of the OpenRouter docs returned 404 and I did not run the code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, config only and no code patch needed. Set JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. The request body is {model, state, questions:{name:{type:'choice'|'noul', instructions, criteria}}}. The response must be {answers:{...}} with choice {choice, confidence, probabilities} or noul {noul}. This looks like the TypeSafe System One schema that OpenRouter's /systemone likely mirrors, but that is unconfirmed. If OpenRouter's response shape differs, validateChoice/validateNoul in src/decision.ts would fail closed, and a small shim would be needed. The config guard at src/config.ts:211 refuses to change the endpoint without also supplying auth, which is sensible.
providerSupport.others: Any HTTPS endpoint via JEV_ENDPOINT, or HTTP on loopback only (src/config.ts:238-243). Custom headers are supported (JEV_HEADERS), for example for OpenRouter attribution headers.

interface.name: ajevt_browser (MCP tool, the only one)
interface.purpose: Runs a bounded browser goal against a URL. Params (packages/mcp/src/index.ts:29-39 and src/schema.ts): goal, url, values, max_steps (1-50, default 12), allow_risky, allowed_domains, ignore_https_errors, ca_cert, proxy, proxy_bypass, host_mappings, session_id, keep_session, require_action, verifiers[]. Returns a text handoff plus structuredContent, with statuses done/likely_done/input_required/ambiguous/needs_confirmation/blocked/stuck/error. Annotations are readOnlyHint false, destructiveHint true, openWorldHint true.

interface.name: notifications/progress
interface.purpose: Emits per-step progress (phase and operation) when the client supplies a progressToken.

interface.name: Config file / env
interface.purpose: ~/.config/ajevt-browser/config.json, AJEVT_BROWSER_CONFIG, JEV_ENDPOINT, JEV_MODEL, JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_HEADERS, JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, JEV_RETRIES, AGENT_BROWSER_BIN.

gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.license: AGPL-3.0-only (repo LICENSE and npm metadata). Fine for personal use. It is a copyleft concern only if you embed it in or redistribute a client product.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript run at runtime through tsx, since bin/ajevt-browser-mcp.js registers tsx/esm). Requires the separate global agent-browser CLI plus 'agent-browser install', which downloads a Chromium build. npx -y ajevt-browser-mcp pulls @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30, tsx and ajevt-browser 0.2.0.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.install: npm install -g agent-browser && agent-browser install, then claude mcp add ajevt-browser -e JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone -e JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 -e JEV_API_KEY=... -- npx -y ajevt-browser-mcp. Better to keep the key in ~/.config/ajevt-browser/config.json using auth:{file:'/abs/path'} (mode 0600 enforced) so it stays out of argv and the process list.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.tests: 16 test files, roughly 105 test cases (loop 36, agent-browser 24, observation 15, and others), using fakes and mocks. The MCP package has 1 server test. CI at .github/workflows/ci.yml runs biome check, typecheck and test on Node 22 and 24, plus the amp build. There are also manual live smoke scripts. No releases on GitHub (latestRelease null); npm has 0.1.0 and 0.2.0. Repo age is 7 days, with 26 commits of which 14 are by the 'Amp' AI agent and 10 by renovate.
security: API key handling is good. The key is read from an env var or a secret file that must be a regular file, at most 16 KiB and mode 0600 (src/config.ts:151-163). Sensitive header names must use env or file references (:73). The endpoint must be HTTPS, or HTTP on loopback only (:241). Reusing credentials when the endpoint changes is refused (:211). Embedded URL credentials are rejected.
Putting the key in the MCP 'env' block of .claude.json or 'claude mcp add -e' stores it in plaintext there. Prefer the auth.file option.

agent-browser is spawned with shell:false and an argument array (src/agent-browser.ts:33), so there is no shell injection. The browser tool itself is destructive/open-world: it drives a real Chromium against arbitrary URLs, and it can fill forms and click.

Prompt-injection surface: page text is fed into the Jev state as untrusted data. The blast radius is limited because Jev only picks from a finite candidate list. The COMMITMENT regex in src/policy.ts blocks pay, delete, send and similar actions unless allow_risky is set. Fresh-snapshot guards and probability validation (src/decision.ts:13-44) apply. The MCP result returns page text to Claude, though, so it is still an injection channel into the main model.
Secret-looking fields (password, token, api key, cvv and so on) are redacted from the Jev payload (src/observation.ts:20,136). Redaction is a heuristic regex.
No postinstall or preinstall scripts. Telemetry: none found in the code. agent-browser and its Chromium download are separate third-party components that I did not audit.
Supply chain: a brand-new package (7 days old) by an individual maintainer, and the code is largely AI-written. Runtime tsx transpile on every start. npm signatures are present.
AGPL-3.0.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (OpenRouter or TypeSafe), per browser step (src/decision.ts:106-120): the goal string, page URL, title and rendered page text (truncated by clean(maxText) and redacted for secrets), the interactive elements (ref, role, name, value with secrets redacted), the candidate labels, recent action history and the question definitions. It does NOT send your prompts, source code, diffs, repo files or other tool outputs. Only browsed web-page content and the goal text leave the machine. The values you supply for TYPE fields stay local (only has_value is sent). The page content itself also goes to Claude as the MCP result, and the browser session contacts whatever sites are visited.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.failureMode: Fails closed per call. The default timeout is 2000 ms per request with up to 5 retries, using exponential backoff of 250 ms to 2 s on 408, 429, 5xx and network errors (src/jev.ts:12-34,47-70). If Jev is invalid, down or misconfigured, the loop returns a handoff with status 'error', or 'Invalid or failed Jev decision; no action executed' (src/loop.ts:376-383). No action is taken. A missing key throws 'No Jev authentication configured', surfaced as an isError MCP result. It cannot block Claude Code sessions, only that one tool call. In a worst case, an outage burns about 6 attempts plus backoff (roughly 15 s or more) per step.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.latencyImpact: Zero for normal coding turns, since it is not in the hot path. It only applies when the tool is called. Each browser step costs one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms, with a 2 s timeout) plus an agent-browser snapshot and action, so about 1-3 s per step. A task of up to 12 default steps takes tens of seconds. Cold start through npx adds seconds to spawn Node and tsx, and the tool description advertises it as a 'fast reflex'.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.contextCost: One tool. The description is about 480 chars, and the input schema with the 9-variant verifier oneOf is about 4.5k chars, so about 1.3k tokens total (chars/4). The server sets no 'instructions' field. There is no hook-injected text. The tool name is shown as mcp__ajevt-browser__ajevt_browser. The result of each call adds a handoff of page text and elements to context, which can be large.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude calls it when the tool description ('Fast browser reflex for clear, bounded tasks with observable completion') fits the task. There are no hooks, skills or proxy behaviour. It competes with the already-installed playwright MCP for the same browser tasks, and Claude will mostly choose playwright or its own reasoning. It is not triggered by coding work such as edits, reviews or commit decisions.
pros: It really is Jev-based and is the only candidate in this audit that drives a real System One choice/noul loop with strict output validation (src/decision.ts:13-44), and it fails closed.
The endpoint, model and key are fully configurable by env or config file (src/config.ts:133-137), so OpenRouter can be tried with no code changes if the request schema matches.
Solid config security: key files must be mode 0600, HTTPS is enforced, and credentials are not reused across endpoint changes.
No hidden data egress of code. Only browsed page content and the goal go to Jev, secrets are redacted, and TYPE values stay local.
Risk policy blocks commitment actions (pay, delete, send) by default, and allowed_domains adds a domain allowlist. Cost is a single tool of about 1.3k tokens.
Reasonable test coverage for a young project (about 105 unit tests with CI on Node 22 and 24).
cons: It only automates browser tasks, so it adds nothing to editing, code review, planning or commit decisions, which is where you spend the day.
It duplicates the playwright MCP already installed. Nothing forces Claude to prefer it, and Opus will normally choose playwright, so automatic value is unlikely.
Model-discretion invocation only, with no hook or deterministic trigger. The user wants automatic use, and this cannot guarantee it.
Needs extra runtime: the global agent-browser CLI plus a Chromium download, and Node runs TypeScript through tsx at startup (slow npx cold start).

OpenRouter is not officially supported and the string never appears in the repo. It relies on OpenRouter's /systemone matching TypeSafe's schema, which I could not verify (docs 404 on the URLs I tried).
Very immature: created 2026-09-23, 2 stars, no GitHub release, 26 commits with 14 by an AI agent, a single human maintainer. Jev itself is beta.
AGPL-3.0 licensing is awkward if the code is reused in client work.

Up to 5 retries with a 2 s timeout can stall a step for a long time when the provider is degraded. Returned page text is a prompt-injection channel into Claude, and destructiveHint is true, so it will likely prompt for permission or run unattended in bypass mode.
gh-xyenon-ajevt-browser.verdict: A real but narrow Jev integration. It is a bounded browser-automation MCP, not a coding-assistant hook, and it needs a separate Chromium runtime. It could probably be pointed at OpenRouter via JEV_ENDPOINT, but that is unverified. It gives no automatic benefit for daily coding and overlaps playwright, so skip it unless you want to experiment with Jev-driven web QA.

Nothing in the code or README mentions OpenRouter. jev-client.js:60 uses `cfg.baseUrl || known.baseUrl`, and jev-config.js:196 reads `baseUrl` from the jev.json config file, so a base URL override is possible. Keys are read only from the config file (jev-config.js:197-198, opencodeApiKey/typesafeApiKey) and sent as a Bearer header (jev-client.js:54-55). No environment variable is read for keys or provider (grep of process.env finds only test and smoke scripts). The MCP tool's `provider` enum is fixed to zen-free|zen|typesafe (mcp-server.js:226-230). The request body is {state, model, questions:{pick:{type:'choice',instructions,criteria}}} and the parser expects answers.pick.{choice,probabilities,confidence} (jev-client.js:47-50,75-82).
providerSupport.others: OpenCode Zen (opencode.ai/zen/v1/systemone), free tier jev-1.13-free used anonymously by DEFAULT, and paid jev-1.13.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate to trivial, but only if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same request/response schema as TypeSafe's, which I did not verify. Config-only route: put a jev.json in ~/.config/jev/ with {provider:'typesafe', baseUrl:'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone', model:'typesafe/jev-1.13', typesafeApiKey:'<OpenRouter key>'}. The key would sit in a plaintext file, because there is no env-var support. The clean fix is a small fork: add an 'openrouter' provider entry and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the environment, roughly 10 lines. One risk: the Zen and TypeSafe shape uses the `questions` and `answers.pick` envelope, and the OpenRouter docs may use different field names.

interface.name: score_options (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Args: question (req), options[] (req, 2 or more), state, autoAnswer, provider. Calls Jev Choice and returns text lines: the top choice, a percentage per option, an enrichedOptions JSON array, and, if autoAnswer is on, a directive 'DO NOT ask the user this question ... Treat <choice> as the user's answer and continue.' (mcp-server.js:216-251,319-326).

interface.name: score_cline_options (MCP tool alias)
interface.purpose: Identical schema and description with a '(Cline compatibility alias)' suffix and a 5-option cap. It duplicates tool definitions in Claude Code's context for no benefit.

interface.name: jev-option-scorer (CLI)
interface.purpose: --state/--question/--option/--provider/--model/--auto. On any error it prints a fake 'mock' equal-split probability table (cli.js:47-52).

interface.name: jev-mcp (bin)
interface.purpose: Starts the stdio JSON-RPC server, protocol 2024-11-05, tools capability only, no server instructions.

interface.name: Cline-only parts in the repo, not in the npm package
interface.purpose: hooks/PreToolUse.cjs and PostToolUse.cjs (Cline ask_followup_question enrichment and a decision trail in ~/.cline), skills/jev-percentages/SKILL.md, cline-plugin.js, install-hook.mjs. None of these target Claude Code events.

security: No npm postinstall script or lifecycle install hooks. The package has zero dependencies and ships only src/, README and LICENSE. The scripts are check, test and smoke, and the smoke script runs only in prepublishOnly.

API keys live in plaintext in jev.json, cline-jev.json or ~/.config/jev/jev.json. There is no env-var path, so the keys cannot come from a secrets manager. They are not put in argv. Keys are read from config and sent as a Bearer header.

Config discovery walks up from cwd to the nearest package.json, .git or .cline and reads jev.json there first (jev-config.js:131-166). A cloned client repo can therefore ship a jev.json that redirects baseUrl to an attacker host and captures state text, or sets autoAnswer:true. This is a real config-injection risk for a user working on client repos.

Prompt-injection and behavior-steering surface: the tool result can append a directive 'DO NOT ask the user ... Treat X as the user's answer and continue' when autoAnswer is true, which can come from a repo-level config file. The output is a probability distribution from a remote model, so a decision could be made on behalf of the user without asking.
The default provider is zen-free, which is an anonymous free endpoint on a third-party host (opencode.ai). Everything in `state` goes to that host with no key and no agreement about retention.

No telemetry, no shell execution and no curl|sh installer in the MCP package. Its CI and publish workflows use OIDC trusted publishing. The npm package was hand-published by a single maintainer, so provenance is minimal.
The CLI silently substitutes a fabricated 'mock' equal split when the API fails (cli.js:47-52). Only the CLI does this. The MCP server returns isError instead.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.dataEgress: The `state` string (which the model chooses, and can include task context, repo facts, code or diffs), the `question` and every option label. All of it goes over HTTPS to opencode.ai/zen (the DEFAULT, anonymous, with no key) or api.typesafe.ai, or to a custom baseUrl from the config file. No file reads or tool outputs are collected by the server itself, and only what the model puts in the arguments leaves the machine. No telemetry. The Cline decision-trail logs (~/.cline/data/logs) are NOT written by the MCP package.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.failureMode: Fail-open. Timeout is 10 s by default (jev-config.js:124, AbortSignal.timeout at jev-client.js:64). On error, timeout or a missing key, the MCP tool returns isError:true with the text 'Jev scoring unavailable ... Proceed without percentages.' (mcp-server.js:329). Nothing blocks Claude Code. The worst case is one tool call stalling for up to 10 s. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. Because it is a model-called tool, a Jev outage only wastes a turn.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.contextCost: 2 MCP tools with an identical schema. Approximately 350 chars of description per tool plus about 800 chars of JSON schema, so about 1,100 chars per tool, or roughly 550 tokens total for both (estimate at chars/4). There are no server instructions. There are no hooks and nothing is injected per prompt. Each call's result is small, about 100-200 tokens.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. The tool description says 'Use BEFORE presenting choices to the user or making a decision', but Claude Code (Opus 5.5) has no mandatory trigger and no deterministic mechanism to call it. The Cline hooks that make it deterministic in Cline (PreToolUse on ask_followup_question) have no Claude Code equivalent in this repo. Claude Code's AskUserQuestion is not covered by anything here. With autoAnswer the tool tells the model to answer for the user, which is a behavior override, not an automatic integration.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.latencyImpact: Approximately 70-500 ms for the Jev call (claimed) plus a model turn to make the tool call and read the result, so about 1-3 s of added turn time each time the model uses it. Node cold start via `npx -y` at every Claude Code launch adds one-off startup latency (network check). It adds zero latency on turns where the model doesn't call it.
pros: Tiny, readable, zero-dependency code (about 400 lines in the npm package), so a full audit takes minutes and there is no supply-chain surface beyond the package itself.
Correct fail-open behavior: errors come back as isError text that says to proceed without percentages, with a 10 s timeout.
Criterion IDs are positional (opt_N) so the option labels cannot collide, which is a real bug fix in 0.3.1 (jev-client.js:17-29).
Has a baseUrl override and a model override, so pointing it at OpenRouter is possible in principle (jev-client.js:60,49).
MIT license, real tests (node --test) and CI with a drift guard between the copied files.
Low context cost: about 550 tokens for two tools and no hooks.
cons: No OpenRouter support: three hard-coded providers, and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY or any env var. A custom baseUrl needs a plaintext key in a JSON file, or a fork.
Exposes only Choice for option scoring. There is no Noul (yes/no) or Score (ordinal) primitive, so it covers the smallest part of Jev.

Automatic use is not achievable. It relies on model discretion, and the real automation (hooks, SKILL.md) is Cline-specific (ask_followup_question, ~/.cline). It does not meet the user's requirement that Claude Code uses it without being told.
Default provider is the anonymous free Zen endpoint at a third party, and `state` would carry client project context to it. A poor default for client work.
A project-level jev.json is trusted and searched first from cwd upward, so a cloned repo can redirect baseUrl or set autoAnswer:true. It is a config-injection risk on client repos.

autoAnswer tells the model to 'DO NOT ask the user' and to treat Jev's top option as the user's answer. That is the opposite of what a careful senior developer wants for code decisions, and a probability model with no reasoning trace should not be answering for the user.
Duplicate tool alias (score_cline_options) wastes context in Claude Code. The server version string is 0.3.0 while the package is 0.3.1.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21, single author, 42 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, first npm version published 2026-09-25, package hand-published by one maintainer. No response-schema check against the OpenRouter API.
The MCP protocol is hand-rolled JSON-RPC (protocol version 2024-11-05, no ping, no cancellation), which risks incompatibility with newer Claude Code clients.
gh-saahmadnejad-cline-option-scorer.verdict: This is a small, honest, fail-open wrapper around one Jev Choice call, but it targets Cline's UX. It has no OpenRouter path except by editing config or forking, and nothing in it makes Claude Code use it automatically, since that depends entirely on the model deciding to call it. It is useful only as a reference for the Choice request/response shape, and a fork or a custom hook would be needed for any real integration.

gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.name: barq-mcp
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.whatItDoes: Browser-automation MCP server (plus Claude Code plugin/skill, CLI and Node library) built on Playwright. The calling agent names an outcome ("Log in") and Jev, called through TypeSafe's System One API, picks each click or keystroke in a loop. It also uses Jev for yes/no page checks (browser_check), multi-option checks (browser_choose) and question-based page reading (browser_read). It is a browser-testing and web-interaction tool, not a coding-workflow helper.

Request: POST JSON {state, model, questions} with Authorization: Bearer <key> (src/jev.mjs:94-110); response read as {answers, usage.input_tokens, model} (src/jev.mjs:124). No mention of openrouter anywhere in the source (grep of the whole repo). OpenRouter's docs page could not be fetched (404) so schema equivalence with openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone was not verified.
providerSupport.others: None. JEV_API_URL allows any System One-compatible gateway; JEV_MODEL overrides the model id; JEV_PRICE_PER_M overrides the price used for cost display.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same answers shape (unverified): set JEV_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and put the OpenRouter key into TYPESAFE_API_KEY (env var name is hardcoded but the value is just sent as a Bearer token). No code change is needed for that. The catch is that the key variable has a misleading name, and the pinned 'jev-1.13.0' thresholds in session.mjs were tuned against TypeSafe's model id and behaviour, so a router alias could shift results.

CI on GitHub Actions (Node 20 and 22), release workflow with commit-pinned actions. Not run by me (static reading only).
security: API key handling: read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env, macOS keychain, or .env in cwd/package root (src/jev.mjs:35-68). Via the plugin it lands as sensitive userConfig, so it is not in argv. With claude mcp add -e it is stored in Claude config, not in argv of the node process. Sent only as a Bearer header to API_URL, which JEV_API_URL can redirect anywhere.
Reading .env from the current working directory means the server parses project .env files (only for the TYPESAFE_API_KEY line), which is a small surprise on client repos.
No postinstall script in package.json; no curl|sh installer. Playwright browser download is a manual step. Publishing to npm is done by hand by the owner (release.yml comment); actions pinned by SHA.

Web prompt-injection surface is large: it reads arbitrary page text and hands control of a real browser, optionally the user's own logged-in Chrome/Edge via remote debugging with a relay process holding an approved connection for 8 idle hours (README). Mitigations exist: allowed_sites, needs_confirmation for pay/send/delete, secrets by reference (keychain:, bw:, env:, autofill) never sent to Jev, tab isolation from the user's own tabs, and site tool output flagged as data.
Runs child processes: security (macOS keychain), bw (Bitwarden), spawns a browser with --remote-debugging-port=0, and a detached relay process (src/browsers.mjs:162, src/relay.mjs:336).

Writes per-step trace files (page decisions, probabilities) to ~/.local/state/barq/traces with 14-day retention (src/trace.mjs), and a recipes file; both can be disabled (BARQ_TRACES=0, BARQ_RECIPES=0). Traces may hold page content.

No telemetry found in source (only fetch calls are to Jev and to the local browser /json/version). Single maintainer, 0 stars, project 10 days old at audit time, so no independent review; it drives a browser holding real logins, so trust in the author matters.
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.dataEgress: To TypeSafe (or whatever JEV_API_URL points to): the extracted page state of every page it works on (visible text, element list with names/attributes/values from the DOM, goal string, the non-secret values passed in `values`, action history) plus question instructions. Secrets passed by reference are claimed not to reach Jev (test/secrets.test.mjs). Nothing about the user's source code, diffs, prompts or Claude tool outputs leaves, because the tool only sees web pages it is told to open. On client projects, if the agent opens an internal or staging app, that page content goes to the Jev provider.
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense that nothing blocks Claude Code: it is an opt-in MCP tool, so if Jev is down the tool call returns isError with a one-line message. Client behaviour in src/jev.mjs:99-135: 60s per-attempt timeout, 2 retries with 800ms*(n+1) backoff, honours Retry-After (capped 15s) for 429/5xx, retries malformed answers, then throws. Tool calls themselves time out at 60s. It never guesses on a malformed answer. Statuses like stuck/ambiguous hand control back to Claude. Worst case a browser_do step stalls up to about 3 minutes before failing.
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.latencyImpact: None on ordinary coding turns, since nothing is injected or intercepted. Only when a browser tool is called: about 300-400 ms per Jev round claimed (README, RESULTS.md) plus browser action time; a browser_do is several rounds. Cold start needs a browser launch or a debugging-port Allow prompt.
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.contextCost: 14 MCP tools registered (browser_open, do, check, choose, snapshot, read, site_tools, call_site_tool, act, screenshot, scan, scan_status, sessions, close). The region of bin/barq-mcp.mjs with server instructions and tool definitions is about 23 KB including handler code, so tool names, descriptions and schemas are roughly 4-5k tokens (estimate, chars/4, not measured exactly). Server instructions are 4 short lines (about 150 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. The SKILL.md description adds about 100 tokens always-loaded; the full skill body of about 1.5k tokens loads on trigger. This overlaps the already-configured Playwright MCP (about 30 tools).
gh-ibrahimhajjaj-barq.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus skill-description trigger (SKILL.md says 'Use for any task that needs a real browser... prefer over screenshot-driven browsing'). Claude decides to call it; nothing deterministic hooks into Edit/Bash/Grep. It only fires when a task involves a real browser, and it competes with the existing playwright MCP for that role.
pros: Genuine, deep Jev use: uses Choice, Noul and Score-style typed answers in a tight loop, with output-shape validation (src/jev.mjs:73-89) and no reliance on free-text output.
URL and model are overridable via JEV_API_URL and JEV_MODEL (src/jev.mjs:11-13), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is likely a config change with no fork.
Solid client engineering: retries with Retry-After, per-attempt timeout, malformed-response rejection, surrogate-safe JSON, token-based cost accounting at $0.042/M.
Good safety design for browser agents: needs_confirmation on irreversible actions, allowed_sites, secrets by reference never sent to Jev, own-tab isolation, robots.txt option for scans.
Only 4 small runtime deps, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry found, MIT, SHA-pinned CI actions.
Claims (self-reported) 66/66 on its own benchmark and 23% cheaper driver tokens than Playwright MCP on 11 tasks; useful if the user does frequent web UI testing/E2E flows.
Ships 20 offline test files and a Claude Code plugin manifest with sensitive-key userConfig.
cons: Does not touch normal coding: no hooks, no code/diff/tool-output classification, so Jev would never be used during edits, commits, permission decisions or routing. It only helps for browser tasks.

Auto-invocation is only a model-discretion tool/skill trigger, and it competes with the user's existing Playwright MCP; Claude will often pick playwright unless Playwright is disabled or the description wins.

Hardcoded TYPESAFE_API_KEY name and default TypeSafe endpoint; OpenRouter is not supported natively and the OpenRouter request/response schema equivalence is unverified (docs fetch 404). Model id pinned to jev-1.13.0, OpenRouter id is typesafe/jev-1.13, so JEV_MODEL must be set.

Consider it only as an optional, on-demand extra for web UI testing, run via JEV_API_URL pointed at OpenRouter after verifying schema compatibility, and not as the core integration.

gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.name: @diegosouzacdv/jev-browser-mcp (npm 0.6.0)
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.whatItDoes: A Node stdio MCP server that drives a real Chrome/Edge through Playwright and uses Jev only as a "which candidate plan or action next?" picker. The calling LLM (Claude) writes declarative UI-test plans (click, type, assert, upload and so on). The MCP takes an accessibility snapshot of the page and sends it to OpenRouter's Decisions API (typesafe/jev-1.13) as a Choice question. It then executes the chosen plan and checks the expected outcome on screen. It is a browser E2E/screen-flow tool, not a general coding-decision layer. With a single candidate plan (fast_path, on by default) Jev is skipped entirely.

The request body (jev-client.mjs:39-55) is {model, state:{requested_flow,current_page_snapshot,completed_steps}, questions:{next_action:{type:"choice",instructions,criteria}}}. The response is read from answers.next_action.choice/confidence/probabilities plus model and usage.cost (jev-client.mjs:59-84). This is a working reference for the OpenRouter Decisions payload shape. It uses no TypeSafe direct endpoint and no /api/v1/systemone.
