gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.runtime: Node >=22 (fine on Node 24). Real Chrome or Edge (default "computer" mode, headed) or a Playwright-downloaded browser (harness mode). Deps pinned exactly: playwright 1.63.0, @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0, @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.1.0, zod 4.6.5.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.install: claude mcp add jev-browser -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY -- npx --yes @diegosouzacdv/jev-browser-mcp@0.6.0 (README recommends a pinned version, or a global npm install so npx does not resolve on every start). It is a pure MCP server, so there is no hook or skill setup. Not executed here, because static audit only.
security: No postinstall or lifecycle scripts in package.json. The only shell-out is spawnSync of Playwright's own cli.js for --install-browser (server.mjs:301-303). On win32 only, it runs powershell.exe to find a Chrome profile owner PID (server.mjs:191). No exec or eval seen in the Jev path.

Key handling is good. The key comes from the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var and is never in argv (only the env-var name is in config). It is sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS only (validProviderUrl in config.mjs rejects non-HTTPS, credentials and query). redirect:"manual" avoids leaking the key on a redirect. toolError redacts the key, Bearer tokens and ?token=/api_key= patterns from error text (server.mjs:145-152). Response body is capped (65536 bytes) and the response is validated against the supplied action IDs.
JEV_PROVIDER_URL can redirect the key to any HTTPS host. That is only a risk if the environment is attacker-controlled.

Prompt-injection surface: web page content goes to Jev, and Jev's output is constrained to a supplied action id, which limits what an injection can do. But run_browser_flow drives a persistent, headed Chrome profile (~/.cache/orquestrador/jev-browser-chrome) that stores cookies. The plan comes from Claude, so a malicious page could still influence Claude via returned snapshots or extraction results. No Jev-side telemetry was seen.

File upload is restricted to JEV_BROWSER_UPLOAD_ROOT, with size caps. Downloads and artifacts go to ~/.cache/orquestrador/. The design says no JavaScript or coordinates are accepted from the harness, though the CSS/XPath selector fallback is allowed with a warning.

Supply chain: a single new unscoped-history author, 11 versions in 3 days, no reachable source repo to verify the tarball against, no provenance visible. The npm signatures exist, but for a package that runs a browser next to your logged-in sessions, that is a real trust cost.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.dataEgress: Only to openrouter.ai (or JEV_PROVIDER_URL), on a Jev decision call: the flow description (<=12000 chars), the accessibility snapshot of the current page (<=12000 chars), the candidate action descriptions (<=32 x 300 chars), the completed step names, the model id, and the Bearer key. No source code, diffs, file contents or Claude tool outputs leave the machine unless Claude puts them into the flow text. Page content of whatever site is being tested is sent, so a client staging site's DOM text or a logged-in page snapshot would go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Playwright itself contacts the target sites, and there is an optional tracker-blocking list. No telemetry endpoint was found in the source.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, and confined to the tool call. Missing key, non-200 response, timeout (30 s default), invalid JSON, or a choice outside the supplied ids each throw a JevBrowserError, which is returned as an MCP isError result (jev-client.mjs:103-129). Claude can then retry or continue, and nothing else in Claude Code is affected. There is a single-plan fast path that avoids Jev entirely. A failed decision does not fall back to a heuristic plan choice. Browser launch failures give clear messages, for example when the profile is locked by another Chrome.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.contextCost: 3 tools. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 2.5-3k chars, roughly 700-900 tokens, of which the run_browser_flow description alone is about 900 chars. The MCP constructor sets only a name/version/description, so there are no server-level instructions. No hook text is injected. The real cost is per call: snapshots and reports returned by run_browser_flow can be large.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. Claude picks it from the tool descriptions when a task involves UI or browser flow verification. There is no hook, skill or proxy, so it cannot be fired deterministically, and the descriptions do not tell Claude to prefer it over the already-installed Playwright MCP. The docs also expect Claude to hand-write candidate_plans in a custom DSL, which is heavy for the model.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.latencyImpact: Zero on normal turns, because it is an opt-in tool. Per flow call: browser startup is cold on the first call and the session is then kept warm. One Jev round trip adds roughly 70-500 ms claimed, with a 30 s timeout. It is skipped when there is a single plan. Overall latency is dominated by Playwright, not Jev.
pros: The only candidate found so far that is OpenRouter-native, and verifiably so in code. It already uses POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It is a working reference for the Decisions API request/response shape (state, questions.{name}.type=choice, criteria; answers.{name}.choice/confidence/probabilities; usage.cost).

Good security hygiene for an early package. The key comes from env and never argv. It uses HTTPS-only, redirect:"manual", bounded response bytes, and validation of the returned id against the supplied set. It redacts secrets in errors, pins exact dependency versions, and has no install scripts. The prompt tells Jev to treat page content as untrusted.
Fails closed per tool call with clear errors and a 30 s timeout, so it cannot hang or break the Claude session. Only 3 tools and about 0.8k tokens of context cost, so cheap to keep loaded.

Jev is used the way the brief describes it: a typed selection among enumerated options with probabilities, not free text. The design keeps consequential actions in Claude's hands, because choose_next_action only returns an id and does not execute it.

Useful if the user does UI/E2E verification work: warm Playwright session, axe accessibility audits, JUnit/Markdown reports, screenshots on failure, and a bounded declarative plan DSL with no arbitrary JS.
cons: Wrong problem for the stated goal. It covers only browser-flow selection, not general coding decisions such as routing, permission or risk gating, or picking between refactor options. Daily coding in Claude Code rarely calls it, so Jev would be used rarely if at all.

Not automatic. It is a plain model-discretion MCP tool. Nothing forces or prompts Claude to use it, and it competes with the Playwright MCP the user already has, which Claude already knows how to use. Getting Claude to write its plan DSL correctly needs the docs loaded as a skill or CLAUDE.md text.

The Jev value is marginal. With one plan the call is skipped, and with a few plans a choice among plans that Claude just authored could be made by Claude itself at no extra cost. A 12k-char snapshot goes to a third party for a minor decision.
Data egress of page content: any client site or logged-in page snapshot is sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. This matters for client projects.

Maturity and trust risk. It is one author, first published 2026-09-26, with 11 versions in 3 days. The GitHub source (diegosouzacdv/orquestrador) returns 404, so it is private or renamed and cannot be audited, and stars, commit history and CI are unknown. No tests ship in the tarball. Docs are in Portuguese. The default config points at Chrome profile paths under ~/.cache/orquestrador, and the default mode is headed "computer" mode with a persistent cookie profile.

Adds a heavy footprint: Playwright 1.63 plus axe plus a second browser lifecycle next to the existing playwright MCP. The config is a strict-key JSON inside the package, so most tuning needs env overrides or a fork. The 2.7k-line flow.mjs is large to audit.
gh-diegosouzacdv-orquestrador.verdict: A real, OpenRouter-native Jev integration whose security handling is careful for an early package. But it only picks Playwright UI-test plans, so it does not deliver the goal of Jev used automatically across daily coding in Claude Code. Treat it as a reference for the OpenRouter Decisions payload, or as an optional UI-testing add-on with a pinned version. It is not the main integration, and its unauditable private source is a real trust cost.

gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.name: decide-mcp
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK 7) exposing one `decide` tool: the calling agent supplies a decision string, context (string/JSON, up to 100k chars) and 2-64 choices with descriptions; the server calls Jev's Choice primitive via AI SDK experimental_evaluate and returns the selected choice plus per-choice percentages (Jev's native probability distribution). Optional config adds bias/policy profiles with a 2-stage router (a first Jev call picks a profile, a second evaluates), optional per-profile tools (decide-default, decide-<profile>), and a language-model fallback (generateText with structured output) that yields model-estimated, non-calibrated percentages. Only the Choice primitive is used; Noul and Score are not exposed.

Dependency @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai@3.0.2 (read from npm tarball, src/typesafe-ai-provider.ts:26-36) defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1 with Bearer auth, and src/typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109 POSTs to `${baseURL}/systemone` with body {model, state, questions}. Setting kind 'typesafe', baseURL 'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1', apiKeyEnv 'OPENROUTER_API_KEY' and model 'typesafe/jev-1.13' would therefore hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint in the brief. No OpenRouter string anywhere in the repo, README or examples; this is inferred from code, not tested. Documented paths are Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, README:9-16) and direct TypeSafe (examples/jev-direct.json, TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY). The openai-compatible kind (providers.ts:50-56) is language-mode only and would call Jev as a chat model, which is wrong for OpenRouter's Jev.

Caveat: unverified against the live OpenRouter route. The AI SDK response schema (typesafeEvaluationResponseSchema) must match OpenRouter's System One response, and the rounding/confidence fields are untested there. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not used.

security: API keys are read only from env vars named in config (apiKeyEnv) and never from argv or committed config files (src/providers.ts:27-31; readme 'Credentials stay in environment variables'). An env-based key is safe from ps output. However, `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` writes the key in plaintext to ~/.claude.json.
Startup is fail-fast: if apiKeyEnv is set but the variable is missing, the server throws and exits (providers.ts:30-31, cli.ts:52-57), which Claude Code shows as a failed MCP connection.
Provider errors are swallowed and replaced with a generic message, so no auth headers or response bodies leak into Claude's context (server.ts:161-171). An e2e test covers redaction.

Prompt-injection surface is small: context is JSON-stringified data and the policy instructs the model to treat it as data (scoring.ts:7-8, 104), but the README admits this is not a security boundary. The output is a choice ID and numbers, with no free text from the provider, so injection into Claude via the return value is minimal. A malicious repo could steer what Claude puts into `decision` and `choices`, and the tool result then biases Claude's next action.

No shell execution. `custom` provider kind does dynamic import() of an operator-configured module (providers.ts:57-77). This is local trusted code, and the config comes from the operator, not from tool input. Do not use it with an untrusted DECIDE_CONFIG_JSON.

Dependencies are exact-pinned (ai 7.0.105, @ai-sdk/*, MCP SDK 1.30.0, zod), but the install pulls 5 provider SDKs you do not need (openai, anthropic, google, gateway, openai-compatible), which widens the supply-chain surface. `npx -y` fetches from npm at every start unless the package is pinned and cached.
Single-maintainer package that is 13 days old, with no CI, no signed releases, no GitHub release and no provenance evidence. The npm package was published seconds after the git commit.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts in the tool arguments is sent to the configured provider: the `decision` string (up to 16k chars), the `context` (string, JSON object or array, up to 100k chars), and each choice id and description (up to 8k chars each, max 64 choices). It goes as the `state` and `questions` body of POST {baseURL}/systemone with a Bearer key (typesafe-evaluation-model.ts:52-63). If profiles and routing are enabled, the same full input is also sent in a first routing call (decision-service.ts:95-115). Nothing is read from disk or the repo automatically and no hook captures tool outputs, so egress is limited to what Claude chooses to include. In practice that can be code snippets, diffs, error text or client details, and there is no redaction or filtering layer in the server. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this: it matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__decide__decide. No telemetry beyond the provider call itself.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's point of view: a provider error, timeout or invalid output returns an MCP tool result with isError true and the text 'Decision failed... No recommendation was produced' (server.ts:161-171), so Claude continues without a recommendation. Defaults: timeoutMs 30000, covering routing, retries and evaluation together (config.ts:100, decision-service.ts:80); maxRetries 2 (config.ts:101). A dead Jev could therefore stall a single call for up to 30 s before it errors. Client cancellation is propagated. Router errors fail the request rather than silently switching policy. Server start is fail-closed: a missing key env var or bad config prevents the MCP server from starting, and the tool is simply absent.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call the tool (no hooks, no proxy). Each `decide` call adds one Jev round trip, claimed 70-500 ms, plus about 1-2 s of Node/npx cold start once per session and the cost of Opus producing the tool-call arguments (choices with descriptions, plus a context summary). That is likely 2-6 s of model generation per use. With profiles and routing enabled it makes 2 sequential Jev calls. Worst case is 30 s on a timeout.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool in the default 'routed' mode. With tools=separate|both it adds 1 + 1 + N profile tools. The `decide` description is 260 chars (server.ts:178-179). The input schema (decision, context union, choices array with id regex and constraints, with output schema) is roughly 1.5-2.5k chars and the outputSchema adds another ~1.5k. Estimate about 700-1000 tokens for the tool definition (chars/4), a single tool. The server sets no `instructions` field (server.ts:126 only name and version), and no hook injects text. Because nothing tells Claude when to call it, effective use needs a CLAUDE.md or rule paragraph (adds ~100-200 tokens per session). Under Claude Code MCP tool search / deferred loading, the definition may only cost its name until needed.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no proxy and no server instructions. Claude calls `decide` only if the tool description (generic: 'Evaluate a decision, context, and choices') persuades Opus 5.5 to do so, so unprompted use will be rare and inconsistent. The design assumes the agent formulates the question and options itself. To get the user's 'use it whenever it adds value' behaviour you would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule, such as 'when choosing between 2+ concrete options call mcp__decide__decide', or wrap it in a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. That is outside this package.
pros: Smallest workable surface for Jev in Claude Code: one read-only tool (readOnlyHint true), ~1k tokens of context, no hooks that can interfere with the user's existing PreToolUse guards or GitNexus hooks.

Uses real Jev probabilities: the percentageSource 'provider-distribution' path passes Jev's native Choice distribution through unmodified (scoring.ts:83-88) and refuses to invent numbers when they are missing ('unavailable'). It is honest about non-calibrated estimates in language mode.

OpenRouter path is a pure config change: kind 'typesafe' plus baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 plus apiKeyEnv OPENROUTER_API_KEY yields POST /systemone (typesafe-evaluation-model.ts:109), which is exactly the OpenRouter System One route. No fork needed, though it is untested.
Secrets are handled correctly: key only via env var name in config, generic error strings, MCP stdio only, no telemetry, no postinstall, exact-pinned deps, MIT.

Good input hygiene: strict zod schemas, unique choice IDs, size caps, timeout that covers retries, abort propagation. Reasonably thorough unit and e2e tests (real MCP client against local HTTP fixtures) for a 1-commit project.
Profiles and routing (bias policies such as 'reliability' or 'cost') are a neat way to encode team risk preferences if wanted, and language-mode fallback lets the same tool work with other models.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with a generic description and no server instructions, so it fails the user's core requirement (Claude Code must use Jev without being told). Getting closer needs CLAUDE.md nudging or your own hook.

Only the Choice primitive. There is no Noul (yes/no) or Score (ordered scale) tool, and no way to feed real app state. `state` is just the model-written decision/context/choices, so Jev is asked to judge Opus's own summary of the situation. The value over Opus deciding directly is unproven, and Jev returns no reasoning trace.

Data egress is unfiltered and model-controlled: up to ~100k chars of context per call can go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, including client code. The user's secret-leak guard does not match this MCP tool's name, so a PreToolUse matcher for mcp__decide__decide must be added before use on client projects.

Immature: 1 commit, 1 star, 1 contributor, no CI, no GitHub release, 13 days old, tied to experimental AI SDK 7 `experimental_evaluate` APIs that the README says may change in patch releases. The @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai adapter is also days old.

OpenRouter is not documented or tested. The default is Vercel AI Gateway, and the OpenRouter routing is inferred from reading the adapter. The only unverified point is whether OpenRouter's /v1/systemone response matches the AI SDK's zod response schema and accepts the model id 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Installs five unused provider SDKs (openai, anthropic, google, gateway, openai-compatible) and an npx cold start, and Node 22+ (Node 24 fine). The default 30 s timeout with 2 retries can stall a turn if Jev is down.
Optional 2-stage routing doubles Jev calls, and the router judges the full payload again, sending it twice. Bias profiles add configuration complexity with little value for coding decisions.
gh-dakdevs-decide-mcp.verdict: A clean, honest, minimal Jev-Choice MCP wrapper, and the best off-the-shelf way to reach OpenRouter's System One route from Claude Code by config alone (untested). It is only a manually-invoked model-discretion tool, though, so it does not satisfy the 'automatic' requirement without extra CLAUDE.md or hook glue. Egress control is also needed for client work. Treat it as a low-risk experimental add-on, not a core integration.

security: License MIT. Single maintainer (hrishi1990). Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, playwright-core, tldts (small). No postinstall/preinstall script in package.json. No telemetry or analytics strings in dist.

API key is read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or a KEY=VALUE secrets_file (core/config.js:274-305). It is not put in argv. The install guide tells agents to keep the key in env or the secret store. A Claude Code registration would use env:{} so the key would need to come from the shell environment.

Shell execution: child_process spawn of the Chrome binary (browser/ephemeral.js:260, chrome.js), lsof/netstat for port owner lookup, and with-chrome spawns the wrapped MCP command. All are local process management, no remote code fetch. Note the wrapped Playwright registration uses `npx -y @playwright/mcp@0.0.80`.

Opens a Chrome remote-debugging port (default 9222) on a dedicated profile. Any local process able to reach that port can drive the browser and its logged-in sessions. Playwright MCP is normally not exposed this way. INSTALL-FOR-AGENTS.md instructs wrapping/editing the user's existing Playwright MCP entry (removes --user-data-dir), which changes existing config.

Prompt-injection surface: page text and labels go to Jev (which emits no free text, so injection can only bias element selection) and result labels are returned to Claude as untrusted page text. Irreversible gate defaults to 'confirm' with single-use confirm tokens bound to URL, element and verb. gate.mode 'off' disables it. In bypass permission mode the user's own confirm flow is the only guard.
policy.mode defaults to 'off', so sensitive pages (banking, mail) are sent to TypeSafe by default. The user must set 'enforce' to fail closed.

INSTALL-FOR-AGENTS.md is written to make an installing agent run commands and edit client config (with a 'show diff, get approval' rule). Treat as untrusted data. The package is 6 days old, so a supply-chain risk exists (new maintainer, no linked repo).
npmjs-com-package-jev-browser-wingman.dataEgress: To Jev (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if base URL is redirected) per loop round: page origin and path (no query or fragment), title, element roles and labels (<=80 chars, up to 240 elements), a text excerpt (<=3000 chars), the goal, binding names and type hints, and a verb+label history; state capped at 24k chars. Never sent: typed values, hidden or prefilled input values, cookies, storage, screenshots, password fields (README Security model). No source code, diffs, repo files or Claude prompts leave the machine. Only browser page content does. If redirected to OpenRouter, that content also passes through OpenRouter.
npmjs-com-package-jev-browser-wingman.failureMode: Fail-open with a bounded time budget. Jev call timeout is 10 s (jev_timeout_ms max 10000) and the client retries once on 429 or 5xx (jev-client.js, MAX_ATTEMPTS 2, 250 ms delay). Failures become status 'fallback' (no browser, no key, breaker open, budget exhausted), and the note tells Claude to use its own browser tools. Whole loop capped at max_ms 45 s (max 50 s) and 24 steps. There is no circuit breaker in the default client. Config errors give an empty tool list and one stderr line. The SKILL tells Claude to call again on fallback or blocked, which can cause repeated calls.

Description plus schema text is about 4,600 chars, roughly 1,150 tokens, always loaded once mode is set (0 tokens if mode is unset because the tool list is empty). Descriptions are long and prescriptive ('DEFAULT for any browsing goal...'). No MCP server-level instructions were found and no hooks are injected. The optional SKILL.md adds a description-level cost of a few dozen tokens plus about 700 tokens when it is triggered.

npmjs-com-package-jev-browser-wingman.latencyImpact: Zero on non-browser turns, since there are no hooks. Per browser step the package's own README puts the machinery at about 1 s (attach, observe, Jev call at 70-500 ms claimed, act, settle up to 3 s). Its own n=1 benchmark shows wall-clock from -22% to +95% versus plain Playwright, i.e. no measured speedup. A wingman_do call can run up to 45 s.
pros: Genuine, narrow use of Jev's Choice/Noul primitives. It does not ask a chat model to write text, and it validates every response strictly (jev-client.js parseJevAnswers).
Auto-invocation without user prompting is plausible for browser work, because the tool descriptions say 'DEFAULT for any browsing goal >3 clicks' and the user already runs Playwright MCP.
Base URL is env-overridable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and the path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the switch may need only base URL and key (unverified).
Security design is careful: typed values never leave the machine, no cookies or screenshots, the irreversible-action gate is on by default, no postinstall script, small dependency set, MIT license.
Fail-open with bounded timeouts and a fallback status telling Claude to use its normal tools, so an outage degrades gracefully.
Plugin hook (wingmanPlugin exporting a custom JevAsk) allows an OpenRouter client without forking.
cons: Only helps browser automation. It gives nothing for coding, refactoring, review, git or test work, which is what the user does all day.

Overlaps with the existing Playwright MCP, and the wingman needs a shared Chrome on port 9222. Its guide wants to rewrite the Playwright MCP registration to `jev-browser-wingman with-chrome -- npx -y @playwright/mcp...`, which changes an existing working setup and opens a debug port on a profile.
The author's own benchmark shows no speed or cost win (n=1: -22% to +95% wall-clock, long-chain failure on both routes). The claimed advantage is unproven.

OpenRouter is not supported natively. It needs TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY set to OpenRouter values, the model is hardcoded to 'jev-latest' (OpenRouter expects 'typesafe/jev-latest'), and response-shape compatibility is unverified. It may need a small patch or a plugin.
Very new and thin: created 2026-09-24, 3 versions in 2 days, single maintainer, no repository field in package.json, no tests shipped in the tarball, not affiliated with TypeSafe. Alpha quality.
Sends page content by default even for sensitive pages (policy.mode 'off' by default). Client browsing of authenticated pages could leak content to a third party. Must set policy enforce.

Bypass or auto permission mode plus gate 'confirm' means irreversible actions rely on Claude relaying the confirm_token flow. The SKILL says 'do not interleave' and 'call again on fallback', which can lock Claude into a failing tool.
Extra ~1.15k tokens of always-on tool definitions for a rarely used capability. SKILL.md is not a hook, so it needs separate installation.
npmjs-com-package-jev-browser-wingman.verdict: A well-built but very narrow browser-automation add-on. It is model-discretion, not a hook, and it does nothing for everyday coding work. It could be pointed at OpenRouter with an env override plus a model-ID fix, but skip it unless the user does heavy multi-step browser automation on top of Playwright.

The README itself says Jev did not beat plain truncation on held-out tasks.

npm ctxjev-mcp: 22 versions in 9 days (0.1.0 to 0.7.1), published by GitHub Actions via npm OIDC (trusted publishing). Dependencies are only zod, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and ctxjev-core, which in turn pulls @typesafe-ai/sdk. I found no postinstall, preinstall or install scripts in package.json. The MCP package has no curl|sh installer.

The API key comes from an env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and is never passed in argv. The .mcp.json variants use ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} expansion. The SDK sends it as a Bearer header and redacts headers in debug logs (redactHeaders).

Secret masking: packages/core/src/redact.ts (redactSecrets) masks common key formats, passwords in URLs, private keys, JWTs, card numbers and values of API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD-like names. It runs in jevClient.ts buildJevRequest on goal, content and toolName, and entry ids are replaced with e0, e1. The README calls it best-effort. There are blind-corpus dev/holdout redaction tests, which is unusual diligence, but any masking is still not exhaustive.

Prompt-injection surface: with the MCP tools, Claude sends entries as tool arguments, and the results are numeric scores only (JSON), so the injection risk is low. The plugin's SessionStart digest re-injects verbatim excerpts of past tool output into context, which is a small replay-of-untrusted-content surface. The sessionStart output and the skills explicitly say to treat the content as data.

Shell execution: the plugin hooks run only bundled node scripts (dist/*.js committed to git, with CI checking that the bundle matches src). The cache in ~/.claude/ctxjev/ holds session excerpts, mode private to the user, with the 50 most recent sessions kept. No telemetry found beyond the Jev call; the SDK adds X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers.

The repo has 47 test files, CI on Node 20 and 22 with pinned action SHAs, lint, a typecheck, boundary brute-force and coverage scripts, SECURITY.md, and four self-audit documents. The audit docs are written in Japanese and were generated inside the repo. I did not run any of it.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.dataEgress: MCP path: nothing leaves the machine unless a tool call uses scorer 'jev', and that is the default for the tools. Then the goal (max 2000 chars) and each entry (role, toolName, content up to 4000 chars each, up to 500 entries, secrets masked best-effort) go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter as the System One `state`. Because Claude must supply the entries itself as tool arguments, the data sent is only what Claude chooses to pass, and it also costs Claude output tokens. Plugin path: no egress by default. With CTXJEV_SCORER=jev plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY, every compaction sends excerpts of the whole transcript since the last compaction: user messages, assistant replies, and tool calls with their outputs (file contents, command output), goal included. For client projects this is a real confidentiality issue on top of the OpenRouter/Jev provider chain.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.failureMode: The MCP server starts without a key (index.ts:216) and returns an isError result telling Claude to use scorer 'local' when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is missing (server.ts:15-27). It fails open at the connection level, but a Jev call error simply surfaces as a tool error, and the SDK default timeout is 10s with retries on 408/429/5xx. The plugin is fail-open by design: PreCompact always exits 0, uses a 20s Jev deadline inside a 25s hook timeout, and falls back to offline keyword scoring. The UserPromptSubmit hook swallows all errors. Nothing here blocks the user's prompt.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.contextCost: MCP: 2 tools (score_relevance, prune_history). Descriptions plus zod-derived JSON schemas (entries array with 6 fields, scorer enum, thresholds, with .describe text) come to about 1.2-1.8k tokens (estimated as chars/4 from server.ts and schemas.ts, about 3.8KB of schema source). I did not read any server 'instructions' field; the McpServer is created without one. Plugin: no per-turn injected text except after a compaction, when the SessionStart digest of about 5 entries is added. Two skills have short descriptions (set-goal is a model-invocable skill; status is disable-model-invocation). The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one node process start (roughly 30-60 ms, estimated, not measured) to every prompt.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.autoInvocation: Two different things. (1) ctxjev-mcp is a model-discretion MCP tool. Claude would have to decide by itself to serialize history into arguments for score_relevance, and nothing in the tool descriptions or server instructions prompts it to. The README itself says this does not save tokens in Claude Code. In practice it will almost never fire automatically. (2) The bundled plugin is a deterministic hook (PreCompact and SessionStart compact), which runs automatically, but only around compaction events, and it is offline (keyword overlap) unless the user sets CTXJEV_SCORER=jev. It is not a per-edit or per-tool-call integration.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.latencyImpact: MCP calls: one Jev round trip per chunk of entries, with the claimed 70-500 ms per request, plus the cost of Claude emitting the whole entries payload as output tokens, which is the dominant latency and cost (up to 500 entries x 4000 chars). Plugin: zero to negligible per turn (a node process on every UserPromptSubmit); at compaction up to 20s with Jev enabled (25s hook cap), a few ms offline. Nothing is on the critical path of normal edit or tool loops.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript, ESM); npm packages ctxjev-mcp 0.7.1, ctxjev-core, ctxjev-cli; plugin dist bundled and committed in git
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.install: MCP: `claude mcp add ctxjev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- npx ctxjev-mcp` (or the marketplace entry; plugins/ctxjev/mcp.json runs `npx ctxjev-mcp@0.7.1`). Plugin: `/plugin marketplace add x96x64/ctxjev`, then install ctxjev. Not executed by me.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.tests: 47 vitest test files across core, cli, mcp-server and claude-plugin, plus live tests that need a real API key (*.live.test.ts). CI runs on Node 20 and 22 with lint, typecheck, README-example checks, boundary brute force and coverage. I did not run any of it.
pros: It is the only candidate so far with a real, working design for a hook-based automatic path in Claude Code (PreCompact plus SessionStart compact). It fails open: it always exits 0, has a 20s deadline, and falls back to offline scoring.

Honest, evidence-based README. The author preregistered a holdout eval and reports that Jev did not beat plain truncation (0 points, CI [0,0]) and kept less than a random ordering on the secondary measure. It is rare for a project to say this, so the claims can be trusted more than most.

Good hygiene: npm OIDC trusted publishing, pinned action SHAs, no install scripts, key kept in env and not in argv, secret redaction with blind-corpus tests, private cache in ~/.claude/ctxjev, and an offline default that sends nothing.

OpenRouter reroute looks near-trivial on paper: the SDK builds `${TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone` with a Bearer key, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and the OpenRouter key is put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (unverified; the model id may also need a change).
cons: The MCP server cannot be invoked automatically in a useful way: it needs Claude to copy history into tool arguments, costing output tokens, and the README admits it saves nothing in Claude Code. There is no instruction or hook that makes Claude call it.

The Jev use case is context pruning/scoring for compaction, not coding decisions, and its own eval says Jev ranking adds nothing over truncation or keyword overlap. The plugin therefore defaults to offline, so the automatic part does not use Jev at all unless CTXJEV_SCORER=jev is set.

With Jev enabled in the plugin, excerpts of every session (user messages, assistant replies and tool outputs including file contents) go to a third party at each compaction. Redaction is best-effort only, which is risky for client projects.

No OpenRouter support in code; it needs an untested env-var trick and possibly a model-id change; only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is checked in the MCP server, so an OpenRouter key would have to be placed in a variable named for TypeSafe. The default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id.

Very young (9 days), 22 npm releases in 9 days, 0 stars, effectively one maintainer with a mostly AI-authored history, and the audit documents are in Japanese. It could conflict with the user's existing compaction handling (caveman plugin hooks) and adds a PreCompact/SessionStart injection of replayed tool output.
gh-x96x64-ctxjev.verdict: Not a fit for the goal of Jev used automatically during daily coding. The MCP tools are model-discretion and will not be called on their own, and the deterministic plugin only touches compaction, is offline by default, and its own eval shows Jev does not help there. Skip it, or at most consider the offline plugin for compaction, which has nothing to do with Jev or OpenRouter.

gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.name: bytesjev (PlanningChecker)
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.whatItDoes: Local stdio MCP server (npm bytesjev 0.2.1) exposing one tool, PlanningChecker. Claude sends the verbatim user request, its plan items (change + rationale) and optional repo_context. The server makes one Jev System One call per plan item, in parallel, with 4-6 yes/no (noul) questions each: necessary, requested, convention, safety, speculative, droppable. Deterministic TS thresholds then turn the probabilities into keep / simplify / review per item. It is advisory only. It also ships a SKILL.md that tells Claude when to call it (after planning, before the first edit), an optional localhost dashboard (port 4310) and a status line. It is an anti-overengineering plan checker, not a general Jev bridge.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code. src/jev/client.ts:328-332 builds `new TypeSafeClient({apiKey, defaultModel, timeout})` from @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 and calls `client.systemOne(...)` at :372. src/config.ts:221-222 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL (default jev-latest); no base URL option in bytesjev itself. The SDK (sdk/package/dist/index.mjs:56-58, 513) reads env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai) and POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (:554, :579-590). So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives exactly https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the OpenRouter System One endpoint. The base URL is only reachable by env var, which `setup` does not set. README and setup only mention typesafe.ai keys. The OpenRouter response shape matching the SDK's parsing is unverified.
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe direct only in documented usage; no other gateways.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change. Register the MCP with env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, e.g. `claude mcp add --scope user -e ... -- npx -y bytesjev`, and skip `setup`. Residual risks: OpenRouter model-id and response-schema parity with the SDK (untested here), and SDK X-TypeSafe-* headers sent to OpenRouter. The SDK's default retry policy may add latency on 429/5xx.

interface.name: PlanningChecker (MCP tool, the only tool)
interface.purpose: Input: user_request (string), plan_items[1..25] {id, change, rationale?}, repo_context? (string). Output: status ok|unavailable|invalid, results[] {id, necessity_score, recommendation keep|simplify|review, reason, evidence[], uncertain}, limitations[]. Annotated readOnlyHint, openWorldHint, idempotentHint. Source: src/mcp/server.ts:49-81.

interface.name: SKILL.md `bytesjev`
interface.purpose: Skill description trigger: 'Check a completed plan for overengineering before editing any file. Use after you have formed a plan for a non-trivial user request...'. Body tells Claude to call the tool exactly once before the first edit and skip it for trivial changes. It also tells Claude to keep secrets out of the payload and to justify overriding a simplify flag in its final summary. Installed by `install-skill` or `setup` to ~/.claude/skills/bytesjev.

interface.name: CLI: bytesjev setup
interface.purpose: Prompts for the key, runs `claude mcp remove` then `claude mcp add --scope user bytesjev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key> -- npx -y bytesjev`, copies the skill, and adds a statusLine to ~/.claude/settings.json only if none exists (src/cli.ts:67-92, 31-46). Present in the 0.2.1 npm build but the statusLine part is only in git HEAD.

interface.name: CLI: bytesjev [mcp]
interface.purpose: stdio MCP server, the default entry.

interface.name: CLI: bytesjev viz
interface.purpose: HTTP dashboard on localhost:4310. Routes: GET /, GET /events (SSE), POST /relay, POST /run.

interface.name: CLI: bytesjev status / install-skill

security: MIT license. Deps are minimal: zod, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (official, MIT), @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No postinstall or preinstall in package.json (checked the npm tarball). No curl|sh.

API key in argv: `setup` runs `claude mcp add ... -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key>` via spawnSync (src/cli.ts:80), which puts the key in the argv of a child process, visible in `ps` briefly. `--key X` is also accepted (cli.ts:50). The key is then stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The server never logs the key (log lines omit it). Env-var registration avoids the argv exposure.

Reads `.env` from the package dir AND process.cwd() (src/config.ts:194-211) and sets ANY unset [A-Z0-9_] variable, including TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. A malicious or client repo with a crafted .env could redirect Jev traffic (request, plan, repo_context) to an attacker host, since the server is launched from the project cwd. Set the vars explicitly in the MCP registration to reduce the risk (existing env wins).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is deterministic TS strings. Reasons and evidence are sentences from Claude's own submitted text, chosen by word overlap, plus fixed templates. Jev returns only numbers, so there is no free-text channel from the remote model. The residual risk is a poisoned plan item, which is Claude's own input.

`setup` modifies ~/.claude/settings.json (adds a statusLine only when none exists) and writes ~/.claude/skills/bytesjev. This user already has hooks, so it would probably skip the statusLine; do not run `setup` blindly.

The dashboard (`viz`) is an unauthenticated HTTP server on port 4310 with no CORS handling. It holds the history of request and plan text in memory. The MCP server POSTs every call's full state to VIZ_URL (default http://localhost:4310) on each call, with a 5s timeout, and disables itself after the first failure. Localhost only, but any local process can read it. It is optional.
Writes ~/.claude/bytesjev/status.txt (item snippets, 44 chars) on every check. Disk cache under the package dir only when BYTESJEV_CACHE=1.
Telemetry: none from bytesjev itself. The SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK / Runtime / User-Agent headers to the configured base URL.

Supply chain: brand-new package (3 versions in one day, single maintainer 'benny.bytes', 0 stars, published 2026-09-27). `npx -y bytesjev` fetches the latest on every launch without a version pin, so pin bytesjev@0.2.1 (or vendor the reviewed source). Version drift: git HEAD says SERVER_VERSION 0.3.0 while npm is 0.2.1, so the published build lacks the status.ts feature.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.dataEgress: Each call sends to Jev (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if base URL is redirected) one request per plan item. The state JSON contains the verbatim user request (cap 4000 chars), repo_context (cap 8000 chars, which Claude composes from what it observed, so it may include file names, paths and code conventions), the item's change and rationale (1000 chars each), and the other items' change text (src/jev/primitives/necessity.ts:500-506). For N items the full request and context are therefore sent N times. No file contents, diffs or tool outputs are sent unless Claude puts them in repo_context. The skill says not to include secrets, but there is no scrubber, so it relies on model compliance; the secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tool payloads. A second local egress goes to http://localhost:4310, the same data to the dashboard, if it is running. Client-confidential requests and paths would go to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter), which needs a policy decision for client projects.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. checkPlan (src/mcp/planning-checker.ts:354-384) catches all Jev errors and returns status 'unavailable' with a category (no_api_key, timeout, network, auth, rate_limit, server_error, unknown), an empty results array and a limitation saying 'proceed without the check'. The skill also says to proceed silently and retry at most once. A missing key gives an immediate 'unavailable' with no network call. The per-call timeout is 20s (BYTESJEV_TIMEOUT_MS, src/mcp/index.ts:227), and the SDK's own retry with backoff sits inside it, so worst-case stall is about 20s per check. Not fail-closed, and it never blocks edits. The relay to the dashboard has a 5s timeout and self-disables. Outside the fail-open path, a malformed Jev answer (e.g. an OpenRouter shape mismatch, `a.necessary!.noul` on undefined) would throw inside assessNecessity, but that is inside the try/catch and would surface as 'unknown'.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.contextCost: Low. One MCP tool. The description is about 1.17k chars, and the input schema (user_request, repo_context, plan_items with id/change/rationale plus describes) and the output schema add roughly 1.5k chars. That is about 650-800 tokens in the tool definition, or fewer if Claude Code defers MCP tools. The server sets no `instructions`. The skill adds a frontmatter description of about 400 chars (~100 tokens) always loaded, and a 4.2k-char SKILL.md body (~1k tokens) loaded only when it triggers. No hooks, so no per-call injected text. The status line and dashboard cost no context. Each invocation costs output tokens for Claude to write the plan items (and repo_context), roughly 300-1500 tokens, plus the ~1k-token result back into context.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion, steered by a skill description trigger. Nothing is deterministic (no hooks). The MCP tool description says 'Call it once after you have a plan and before you edit any file', and the SKILL.md description says 'Use after you have formed a plan for a non-trivial user request'. In a Claude Code session that is bypass or auto mode with little formal planning, Claude may often skip it or make it inconsistently. The skill also requires the verbatim user request, so it is skipped when that cannot be recovered. It could be made near-deterministic only by adding your own hook or CLAUDE.md rule, e.g. a PreToolUse/ExitPlanMode nudge.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.latencyImpact: One MCP round trip per plan, not per edit. All items are judged in parallel, one Jev request each (each carrying the full request and context). Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms, so a check should take about 0.3-1s in the README's own status-line example ('0.3s'), plus MCP and npx cold start on first launch (npx -y resolves the package each session, so a few seconds at startup unless installed globally). Worst case is a stall of about 20s on timeout. The Claude-side cost is the extra turn and the tokens to write out the plan items, probably more than the Jev call itself. Nothing is added to Read/Grep/Bash calls.
pros: It is a real, coherent Jev use case that fits the primitive well: many independent yes/no (noul) questions per item, with the thresholding done in deterministic TS rather than by a chat model (src/jev/primitives/necessity.ts, planning-checker.ts:242-320). It is a faithful demonstration of Jev as a 'System One' decision layer.
Only one tool and about 700 tokens of tool definition. The design is advisory, never edits, and fails open (planning-checker.ts:365-380), so an outage cannot block coding.
Automatic-ish integration: a shipped SKILL.md with a strong trigger phrase plus a self-describing tool description, so the user never types 'use jev'.

Lets it work with OpenRouter with no code change. The official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, and its path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One API once the base is https://openrouter.ai/api (sdk index.mjs:513, 554).
Output is safe from injection because Jev returns only numbers and the reasons are quoted from Claude's own text. Input caps (25 items, 4k/8k chars) and truncation are reported in `limitations`.
Has an offline test suite with a fake Jev (about 34 test cases across 5 files, test/*.ts), and a small readable codebase (~1.3k lines of TS) that is easy to audit or fork. MIT license.
Cheap: about $0.04/M input tokens, so a 6-item plan of about 2k tokens each is roughly $0.0005 per check.
cons: Narrow value for this user. It only critiques plans for overengineering. It does not cover code review, test selection, risk scoring, routing or permission decisions. Opus 5.5 already plans well, and the 'droppable'/'necessary' judgments come from a model that sees only 4k chars of request and 8k of self-reported context, so the signal is only as good as what Claude chooses to write. The README itself says 'false positives are expected'.

Not deterministic: it relies on Claude choosing to call it. There are no hooks, and in bypass/auto mode there is often no explicit plan step, so triggering will be inconsistent. The skill explicitly excludes trivial requests.

No OpenRouter support out of the box. The `setup` command is TypeSafe-key-only and stores the key in argv/~/.claude.json. You must register the MCP by hand with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and a typesafe/jev-1.13 model id. OpenRouter compatibility of request and response shapes is not verified by the project (no OpenRouter tests).

Egress and privacy: sends the user request and Claude-composed repo_context, once per plan item, to a third party. Sensitive for client projects. There is no secret scrubbing beyond a prompt instruction.

Very immature: repo created 2026-09-27, 8 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars/forks/issues, no releases or tags, no CI (.github missing), 3 npm versions in one day. npm 0.2.1 lags git HEAD (0.3.0 in source). Unpinned `npx -y bytesjev` is a supply-chain risk.
The .env loader reads the cwd's .env and can set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/API_KEY from any repo you open, which is awkward for client repos (possible traffic redirection or a stray key).

Extra cost on the Claude side: Claude must write out structured plan items and repo_context, which adds tokens and a turn to every non-trivial task. The token cost probably exceeds the benefit unless the tool catches overengineering often.

Adds a dashboard and status-line machinery (unauthenticated localhost HTTP server, files in ~/.claude) that the user does not need and that `setup` may try to install; also a per-call POST of full state to localhost:4310.
gh-bennyp11-bytesjev.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-open proof-of-concept that is the right shape for Jev, but it addresses a narrow problem (plan overengineering) and triggers only when Claude decides to call it. It is very young (2 days old, 1 author), so at most treat it as an optional add-on. If used, pin the version and register it manually with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and a typesafe/jev-1.13 model id, not via `setup`, and avoid it on confidential client repos. It is not a primary integration.

npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.name: jev-mcp-server (npm, weeeeekdy)
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.whatItDoes: Tiny (about 85-line, 3.5 KB, 3-file) stdio MCP server exposing three generic tools that wrap TypeSafe's System One endpoint: jev_noul (yes/no probability), jev_choice (pick one from a criteria map, with confidence and per-option probabilities), jev_score (ordered levels, with score, confidence and probabilities). Claude must build the `state` string itself, because Jev reads nothing on its own. It is a passive judge tool with no hooks, skills, or policies.

providerSupport.evidence: dist/server.js:5-6 `const API_KEY = process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY; const API_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone";` Both are hard-coded, with no env override for the base URL. dist/server.js:7-10 exits if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is missing. dist/server.js:13-18 sends `Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY}` and the body `{state, model:"jev-latest", questions}`. There is no reference to openrouter.ai or OPENROUTER_API_KEY anywhere. The tarball has no src/ (only dist/, README.md, package.json), so it cannot be rebuilt. The npm page has no repository field, and the GitHub weeeeekdy/jev-mcp-server URL returned 404.
providerSupport.others: None. The PyPI package jev-mcp-server is a different author (wangkuangkuang) and a different codebase.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate to trivial, but unverified. OpenRouter exposes POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which has the same path suffix as api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, so the request and response schema is probably identical. Patching would mean editing 3 lines in dist/server.js: the URL, the env var name, and the model id (`jev-latest` would become `typesafe/jev-1.13` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`). That means maintaining a local fork or vendored copy, since there is no upstream repo. I could not confirm the OpenRouter request schema from public pages (the docs URL returned 404 and the model page shows no schema). A simpler option is to write your own 60-line server against OpenRouter.

security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. The README's `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...` form puts the key in argv at install time and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, and no postinstall script. Runtime dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod.
Ships compiled dist only, with no source or repo, so the published JS cannot be compared against a public git history. It is short enough to read in full, and I found nothing malicious.

Single anonymous maintainer (weeeeekdy, gmail address), package created 2026-09-21 and unclaimed by TypeSafe. This is an unofficial third-party wrapper, so there is a supply-chain and typosquat risk. If you use it, pin the exact version 1.0.0 or vendor the file.

No error handling: an API error message body is thrown verbatim into the tool error. An uncaught fetch failure or a missing `answers` field throws inside the handler, and the MCP SDK returns it as a tool error.
Prompt-injection surface is small because the server only relays text. The `state` Claude sends is whatever it chooses, and the returned probabilities are numbers only.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.dataEgress: Only the `state` string, the `instructions` string, and the criteria/levels that Claude passes in each tool call go to api.typesafe.ai (the direct TypeSafe API, not OpenRouter, as shipped). Whatever code, diff, or text Claude puts into `state` leaves the machine. The server never reads files by itself. There is no telemetry and no other network calls.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup: the process exits 1 if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset, so the MCP server shows as failed to connect. At call time there is no timeout (plain fetch with no AbortSignal), no retry, and no fallback. HTTP errors and network failures raise a tool error to the model, which is non-blocking for Claude Code since it is a model-invoked tool, not a gate. A hung connection could stall a tool call until the undici default timeouts.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.contextCost: 3 tools. The tool names, descriptions and schemas total about 830 chars of quoted strings plus zod schema structure, roughly 350-500 tokens with JSON-schema overhead. The descriptions are in Chinese, which is token-heavier per character and not ideal for an English workflow. The server sets no MCP `instructions`. No hooks inject text. Claude Code 2.1.x with MCP tool search defers these schemas anyway.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or prompts Claude to call it. Its descriptions say nothing about when to use it, and the README's 'gate on noul >= 0.8' guidance is not shipped as a skill or CLAUDE.md snippet. Achieving the user's 'automatic' goal would need extra glue: a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a hook that instructs Claude to call jev_* at certain moments. There are no deterministic triggers.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.latencyImpact: One HTTPS round trip per call, plus the npx cold start once per session (npx -y checks the registry, adding perhaps 1-3 s on first run unless it is installed globally). Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms, plus an MCP tool-call overhead of roughly 1-3 s of model turn time, since Claude has to emit the call and read the result. That is always additive when it is used, and never blocks tools that are not gated.
pros: Very small and easy to audit: one 3.5 KB file with no shell exec, no file reads, and only two runtime deps (dist/server.js).

Exposes the three real Jev primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) with a generic `criteria` map, so it is flexible enough for diff-review gates, error-class routing, and 'does the evidence support the claim' checks.
Cheap context footprint (3 tools, roughly 400 tokens), no MCP instructions, and no hook text injected into every turn.
MIT license, and the README states plainly that Jev is a judge and not a generator.
Simple enough to fork and point at OpenRouter by editing 3 constants.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter. The URL api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY are hard-coded (dist/server.js:5-6), with no env override. It needs a TypeSafe console key, which contradicts the user's OpenRouter-only plan unless the file is patched.

No source, no repo, and no git history on npm (package.json has no `repository`; the guessed GitHub URL is 404). The build script needs src/, which is not published, so a patch has to be made in dist/, and updates cannot be tracked.
Model-discretion only, so it fails the core requirement of automatic use without prompting. Claude has no reason to call jev_* unprompted, and the tool descriptions do not say when to.

No timeout, retry, or graceful fallback, and it crashes on startup without a key. Error handling is minimal, with no validation of the response shape (data.answers.judgment.noul is dereferenced blindly).
Tool descriptions are in Chinese and the error message is in Chinese, which is odd for an English-language workflow and may confuse both the model and the user.

Extra hop with a real per-call model-turn cost (Claude must compose `state`), and Jev only judges what Claude feeds it. There is no automatic diff or file access, so most 'gating' value is redundant with Claude's own judgment.

Brand-new (published 2026-09-21), version 1.0.0 only, a single anonymous maintainer, no tests, no CI, no releases, and no stars or community. There is no evidence the schema is correct against live TypeSafe or OpenRouter, since the response fields (answers.X.noul and others) are unverified.
Unofficial: not affiliated with TypeSafe, and there is a name collision with the PyPI jev-mcp-server, so pin the package name and version.
npmjs-com-package-jev-mcp-server.verdict: A minimal, readable but unofficial wrapper that only talks to TypeSafe's direct API and is purely model-invoked, so it fails both the 'OpenRouter' and 'automatic' requirements as shipped. It is useful at most as a reference or a base to fork (change the URL, env var and model id, then add a hook or skill for automatic triggering), not as a drop-in install.

gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.name: @goldjunge91/jev-code
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server (plus Claude Code plugin/marketplace, Agent Skill, CLI, Pi/OpenCode adapters) exposing five Jev tools (jev_classify, jev_check, jev_score, jev_rank, jev_ask). It batches items into one POST to OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone (model hard-coded to typesafe/jev-1.13) and turns Jev's probabilities into auto/review decisions and yes/no/uncertain verdicts using local thresholds. A bundled SKILL.md tells the model when to call the tools. It is a fork by goldjunge91 of FrancoisChastel/jev-code (32 stars, TypeSafe-direct). The fork's only substantive change is switching the backend to OpenRouter (commit db79fd2).

The published npm dist/core/config.js:9 matches. Base URL and model are constants with no env override. There is no TYPESAFE_API_KEY path and no use of the /api/alpha/decisions Decisions API. The README says 'The endpoint and model are fixed.' CI e2e still reads secrets.TYPESAFE_API_KEY (.github/workflows/ci.yml), a leftover from the upstream fork.
providerSupport.others: None. The upstream FrancoisChastel/jev-code uses TypeSafe direct; this fork removed that.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed, it is already OpenRouter-only. The reverse (adding a base-URL or model override, e.g. ~typesafe/jev-latest or Jev Router) would be a trivial 2-line change in config.ts and client.ts, but is not configurable today, so a model bump means waiting for a new release.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Up to 64 items x up to 250 classes, one label each. Returns label, probabilities, margin, confidence and decision auto|review (defaults auto_accept 0.85, min_margin 0.5). Item text is truncated at 4000 chars.

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Up to 64 yes/no checks over one state. Returns P(yes) and verdict yes|no|uncertain (yes_at 0.75, no_at 0.25).

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Up to 64 items on an ordered scale of up to 20 levels. Returns score, nearest level, confidence and decision (auto_accept 0.7).

interface.name: jev_rank
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Up to 250 candidates (id + excerpt) ranked by relevance to a query. Returns per-candidate relevance, a sorted list, and any_relevant.

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: MCP tool. Raw System One passthrough: mixed noul/choice/score questions over one state.

interface.name: MCP server instructions
interface.purpose: server.ts:20 sends six USAGE_GUIDANCE sentences as MCP 'instructions', e.g. 'keep the workflow in your own reasoning and use Jev for the narrow judgments'. All tools are annotated readOnlyHint, idempotentHint and openWorldHint.

interface.name: skills/jev/SKILL.md (/jev, or /jev-code:jev via plugin)
interface.purpose: Skill whose description lists trigger situations: labelling or routing many items, yes/no checks, scoring, ranking, replacing regex heuristics. The body has workflow and limits, plus 5 reference files (~30 KB).

interface.name: jev-code CLI
interface.purpose: setup [claude|codex|pi|opencode] [--project] [--dry-run] [--no-env]; doctor [--live]; classify|check|score|rank|ask --input file|stdin; mcp; skill.

interface.name: .claude-plugin/plugin.json + marketplace.json + .mcp.json
interface.purpose: Plugin bundling the skill and an MCP server launched as 'npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp'.

interface.name: Pi / OpenCode adapters
interface.purpose: integrations/pi/jev.ts and integrations/opencode/jev.ts, native tool registrations. Not relevant for Claude Code.

security: No install hooks. npm package has no preinstall/postinstall/prepare scripts. Only the 'prepublishOnly' script exists, and it runs at publish time. Runtime deps are just @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod.

No telemetry and no analytics. The only network call is the POST to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. grep of src found child_process only in setup/exec.ts, which spawns claude/codex/pi with fixed args and no shell. There is no eval.

API key handling: read from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, sent as a Bearer header, and masked in doctor. BUT `jev-code setup` by default bakes the key into harness config. src/setup/index.ts:189-212 builds `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key> ...`, which puts the key in argv (briefly visible in the process list) and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. `--no-env` avoids this. The plugin route (.mcp.json) has no env block and relies on inheriting the shell env, which is cleaner.
Do not run `setup` blindly. Register the server yourself with an env reference, or use the plugin, to keep the key out of argv and config.

Supply chain: the .mcp.json and setup use unpinned `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp`, so every Claude Code start resolves the latest version from npm. That is a single-maintainer third-party package (v0.1.0, 4 days old) that runs with your full env. Pin the version, e.g. @0.1.0, or vendor it.

npm dist shows only a registry signature, no provenance attestation, despite publishConfig.provenance:true. The 0.1.0 tarball was evidently published outside the release.yml workflow. The package.json author is still 'François Chastel', while the maintainer is goldjunge91 ([email removed]), so attribution is confusing. SECURITY.md still points to the upstream author's email.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are only numbers, labels and ids echoed back, with no free text from the model, so Jev cannot inject instructions. Item text is caller-supplied, so a hostile file passed as an item could sway the label. Item ids are sanitised. Low risk. The skill even suggests using jev_check to screen for injection.
MIT license (upstream copyright preserved). Dependabot is enabled. CI runs Node 20/22/24 with lint, typecheck, vitest and smoke.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.dataEgress: Only the payload the model puts in a tool call leaves the machine: items[].text (each truncated at 4000 chars), classes, questions, context or state, sent as JSON to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the Bearer key. The whole request is capped at about 120K chars. Nothing is read from disk, git, the session or the environment by the tool itself, so whatever code, diffs, logs or file excerpts Opus chooses to pass goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe/its upstream provider. That matters for client projects under NDA, and the secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* calls (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). The OpenRouter account's data and logging policy applies, and the response contains only usage plus the model id.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level. It is an optional MCP tool, not a hook or proxy, so nothing blocks if it fails. A missing key surfaces as a tool error (isError:true, 'jev_x failed: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set...'), because the client is built lazily (mcp/server.ts:9,23). Each attempt has a 30 s timeout (JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS) and up to 2 retries (JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES) on 408/425/429/5xx/529, timeouts and connection errors, with exponential backoff of 0.5-8 s and Retry-After honoured up to 30 s. Worst case is roughly 90 s or more of stall on a hard-down endpoint, which is long for a 'fast classifier'; lowering the env vars to ~3000 ms and 0-1 retries fixes that. The model then sees the error and proceeds by itself. If the server fails to start (npx offline), the tools are simply absent and the skill falls back to a `jev-code` CLI that does not exist, so it just tells the user to run setup.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.latencyImpact: Zero added latency on turns where the model does not call a tool. When it does, that is one MCP round trip: a single batched HTTPS POST to OpenRouter, claimed 70-500 ms plus the OpenRouter hop (~100-300 ms), plus the extra model turn (tool_use then tool_result, adding a few seconds of Opus time). Cold start of `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp` at session start costs about 1-5 s (npm registry resolution, and a download on first run), and it runs in parallel with other MCP servers. Because batching is encouraged, net time is only saved for large item sets; for single items it is slower than just reasoning.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Estimated at chars/4: tool descriptions about 2.9k chars (~730 tok), JSON schemas including field descriptions about 8-9k chars (~2.2k tok), MCP server instructions (6 sentences) about 1.1k chars (~280 tok). Total is roughly 3.2-3.5k tokens of tool definitions, or about 12-14k chars, if tools are not deferred (Claude Code 2.1.x tool search can defer them and cut this to the names). The skill adds a ~1.4k-char description always listed (~350 tok); the SKILL.md body (8.5 KB, ~2.1k tok) loads on trigger, and the references (~30 KB) load only if read. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Net always-on cost is about 3.5-4k tokens, moderate, and larger than the value of a tool that is called rarely.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, plus a skill-description trigger. There are no hooks and no proxy. Claude Code (Opus) sees the 5 tool descriptions and the MCP server instructions in every session and can call the tools on its own, which meets the 'no need to say use jev' goal in the loosest sense. In practice the description and skill text ('when you notice yourself about to label more than a handful of items...') is a soft nudge that Opus may often ignore in favour of reasoning inline or Grep/Read. There is no deterministic guarantee. Making it reliable would need a CLAUDE.md rule, or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook that you write yourself.
pros: It is the only candidate found here that is wired to OpenRouter by design. Base URL and model are hard-coded to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13 and a Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (config.ts:6-13, client.ts:104,148,181), so it works with just one env var and no TypeSafe account.

A tool set shaped for coding work: batch classify (64 items), check (64 yes/no), score, rank (250 candidates, with any_relevant to avoid trusting a false top hit) and a raw jev_ask escape hatch. Thresholds and decisions are computed locally, so the model gets auto/review flags rather than raw probabilities.

Fully automatic install is possible via the Claude Code plugin marketplace (`claude plugin marketplace add goldjunge91/jev-code`), which bundles the skill and .mcp.json. It is user-level, and you never have to type 'use jev'. Tool descriptions are written as triggers ('triage CI failures', 'pick which files to open').

Sane client engineering: retries with backoff and Retry-After handling, a lazily built client so a missing key is a tool error rather than a crash, local validation of duplicate ids and request size before spending a call, and read-only/idempotent annotations. 81 test cases across tests/ (client, config, tools, MCP server, setup), a CI matrix on Node 20/22/24 and a smoke script.

Small and auditable: about 2.9k lines of TypeScript, 2 runtime deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell execution beyond fixed-argument spawns in setup. MIT licensed, and Jev's calibrated outputs mean it fits the typed-decision design.
cons: Not really automatic. It is a model-discretion tool, so Opus decides whether to call it, and for a strong reasoning model most triage of small lists is cheaper inline. Expect it to be called rarely unless CLAUDE.md nudges it. It only helps in bulk-judgment situations (CI failure triage, many files to rank), which are a small part of daily coding.

Brand-new and single-maintainer. The repo was created 2026-09-26, has 11 commits (8 by the fork owner, 3 by upstream), 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues and no GitHub release. npm 0.1.0 is 4 days old, has no provenance attestation, and carries a mismatched author and SECURITY contact (still the upstream author). It is a fork of a 32-star upstream (FrancoisChastel/jev-code) that could be pulled from directly with a 2-line OpenRouter patch, which would remove trust in a second party.

The default `setup` bakes OPENROUTER_API_KEY into `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...`, so the key lands in argv (transiently visible in the process list) and in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (src/setup/index.ts:189-212). The `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp` launcher is unpinned, so a compromised or updated package would execute with your environment on every session start. Register manually with a pinned version.

Rides on the beta System One endpoint, and there is no way to select ~typesafe/jev-latest, the Jev Router, or the alpha Decisions API, because model and URL are constants. If the doc-cited endpoint changes, the tool breaks until a new release. The retry defaults (30 s x 3 attempts) can stall the tool for over a minute on an outage, so tune JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES.

Code egress to a third party with no guard. Whatever excerpts Opus classifies go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which is a real concern on client projects. Your existing secret-leak hook matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it will not inspect mcp__jev__* payloads; add a matcher for it. About 3.5-4k tokens of always-on context (5 tools with long schemas, server instructions, skill listing) for occasional use, unless tool-search deferral applies. The stated Jev quality is unverified (the Theo/t3.gg 'flash router' skepticism), and its output is an unexplained probability, so review-band items still need Opus.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.verdict: Best-fit OpenRouter-native, well-scoped Jev MCP found so far: safe to try as a user-scope plugin (pinned version, key kept in shell env, short timeout) for bulk triage and file-ranking. However it is a day-old single-maintainer fork whose automatic use is only a soft model nudge, not a deterministic hook, and it needs a hook matcher and vetting before use on client code.
gh-goldjunge91-jev-code.install: Recommended: pin the version and keep the key out of argv. Run `export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...` in your shell profile, then `claude mcp add --scope user jev -- npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code@0.1.0 mcp`. Alternatively use the plugin route: `claude plugin marketplace add goldjunge91/jev-code && claude plugin install jev-code@jev-code`. Avoid the default `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code setup claude`, which copies the key into ~/.claude.json and argv. Lower the retry cost with JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS=4000 and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES=1.

gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.name: jevx-mcp
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.whatItDoes: Tiny (about 10 KB source) stdio MCP server exposing 3 tools that wrap the third-party jevx.org gateway (README states it is an independent playground, not affiliated with TypeSafe). Model-invoked `decide` POSTs state + up to 16 typed questions (choice/noul/score) to https://jevx.org/api/decisions/run using a Bearer JEVX_API_KEY, and formats the returned probabilities as text. Not a hook, skill or proxy, so nothing is automatic.

providerSupport.evidence: src/src/client.ts:60 `BASE_URL = process.env.JEVX_BASE_URL || 'https://jevx.org'`; client.ts:136 `fetch(`${BASE_URL}/api/decisions/run`, {Authorization: Bearer JEVX_API_KEY})` (path hardcoded); client.ts:134 only env key is JEVX_API_KEY. No reference to openrouter.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or console.typesafe.ai anywhere (grep of built dist/*.js confirms only jevx.org URLs). Published npm dist matches the git source.
providerSupport.others: Only jevx.org (third-party reseller/playground with its own credit system: response has `charged` credits).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. JEVX_BASE_URL only swaps the host; the path /api/decisions/run, the `{code, message, data}` response envelope (client.ts:150-152), `charged` credits, and the request body `{state, questions:{name:{type,instructions,criteria}}, model}` are jevx-specific. OpenRouter uses /api/alpha/decisions and a different auth key, and its schema is not verified to match, so a fork would need to change path, key env var and the response parser. Roughly a 20-line change in client.ts if the schemas turn out to be similar, but that is unverified, and it would be a fork of a 0-star repo.
