security: Key is passed via env (JEVX_API_KEY), not argv, so it does not show in the process list. It is sent only as a Bearer header to BASE_URL (client.ts:138).
JEVX_BASE_URL env override is unvalidated. If it is ever set to an attacker-controlled host, the Bearer key and state leak. Low risk for this user, who controls their own env.
No postinstall or install scripts (package.json scripts: build, start, prepublishOnly, test only). No child_process or shell exec in dist. Zero dependencies beyond the MCP SDK and zod.
No telemetry beyond the jevx.org call itself. The utm_source=mcp link is returned as tool text only.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is only formatted numbers plus model/request id, so it is small. But `decide` input is model-authored text sent to a third party.

Supply chain: brand-new single-maintainer npm package (kavel, [email removed]), 1 version, 0 stars, unaffiliated with TypeSafe. `npx -y` without a version pin means a later malicious publish would run with the user's shell privileges.
Unaffiliated third party sits between the user and Jev, so it can see and log all state sent, and bills via its own credit system rather than OpenRouter or TypeSafe.
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever `state` and `questions` Claude puts in the `decide` call (arbitrary text or JSON, so code snippets, diffs, or file contents if Claude includes them) is POSTed to https://jevx.org/api/decisions/run, a third-party site that is not OpenRouter or TypeSafe, with the JEVX_API_KEY. Nothing is sent unless the model calls the tool. No background collection. For client projects this creates a new, unvetted data processor.
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open only in the trivial sense that the tool returns isError text on failure (missing key, non-JSON, code!=0, network throw is caught at index.ts:232). There is NO fetch timeout or AbortController (client.ts:136), so a hung jevx.org could stall the tool call until the MCP client's own tool timeout. No retries. Because the tool is model-invoked, not hook-based, it cannot block Claude Code.
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.latencyImpact: Zero when unused. When invoked, one extra model tool-call round trip plus the jevx.org HTTPS call (unmeasured; claimed 70-500 ms for Jev itself, plus a third-party hop). npx cold start adds seconds at MCP startup the first time, unless the package is cached.
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.contextCost: 3 tools. Approximate tool-definition text is 3.5k characters, so roughly 900 tokens: the decide description of about 430 chars, the decide schema of about 1.2k chars with nested questionSchema (duplicated in validate_questions), and the small open_in_jevx. No MCP server `instructions`. No hook-injected text. Cost is paid every session, and the tools are likely deferred under Claude Code's tool search, which reduces it.
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions never tell Claude WHEN to use Jev (for example, no "use this before branching on X"). Claude would rarely call `decide` unprompted, and it must author a whole question schema each time. It does not meet the user's "automatic without prompting" requirement. There are no hooks, no skill, and no CLAUDE.md snippet in the repo.
pros: Very small and auditable: about 10 KB of source, no postinstall, no shell exec, and the published npm dist matches the git source (verified by grep of the tarball).
Key passed by env, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
`validate_questions` is a free local schema checker that could be useful to a developer prototyping Jev question shapes.
Surfaces the useful semantics: the API's HTTP-200-with-code!=0 refusals become tool errors, and a noul of exactly 0.5 is flagged as 'declined' (index.ts:229; client.ts:150).
cons: Wrong provider: hardcoded to the unaffiliated jevx.org gateway and its own credits (client.ts:136). No OpenRouter or TypeSafe endpoint, and it needs a separate jevx.org account and key. Not the OpenRouter-hosted Jev the user wants.

Not automatic: model-discretion tool with no trigger guidance, so it fails the core requirement. It would need a CLAUDE.md nudge or a wrapping hook or skill, and the user does not want to prompt for it.
Sends model-chosen state, which may include client code, to a third-party site with an unknown privacy policy. That is a serious concern for client work.
No fetch timeout or retry (client.ts:136), 1 commit, 0 stars, 1 unaffiliated maintainer, brand-new (8 days old), a single test file, no CI. Effectively a proof of concept.
`open_in_jevx` is just a referral link and wastes context tokens. The tool schemas cost about 900 tokens per session for minimal gain.
`npx -y` unpinned means a future malicious publish auto-runs. The LICENSE text is nonstandard (GitHub shows 'Other').
gh-hanshs474-jevx-mcp.verdict: Skip. It is a small clean wrapper, but for a third-party gateway (jevx.org), not OpenRouter or TypeSafe. It is a discretionary MCP tool with no auto-trigger, and it sends prompts to an unvetted 8-day-old service. If the user later builds their own integration, the only reusable idea is the question-shape validation and the code!=0 error handling, and it is easy to reimplement.

npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.name: @livx.cc/mcp-jev
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.whatItDoes: Tiny stdio/HTTP MCP server exposing one tool, post_jev_evaluate {state, questions[], provider?}, which forwards to Jev via Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter Decisions API (alpha) or TypeSafe direct, normalizes the answers (choice / score / boolean) and falls through providers on failure. Also ships an MCP resource skill://mcp-jev/workflow (SKILL.md text) and a library export. Purely a model-discretion tool: Claude must decide to call it and must author state + questions itself.

providerSupport.evidence: src/providers/openrouter.ts:43-44: url `${OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_URL || 'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha'}/decisions`, key OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model JEV_OPENROUTER_MODEL || 'typesafe/jev-1.13', body {model,state,questions{id:{type,instructions,criteria}}}, boolean sent as type 'noul'. src/providers/typesafe.ts:11 https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model default 'jev-latest'. src/providers/vercel.ts:14 https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai/evaluation-model with AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. Default order vercel,openrouter,typesafe (src/jev.ts:21) so set JEV_PROVIDERS=openrouter to avoid fall-through to other vendors. Does NOT use the /api/v1/systemone OpenRouter surface.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (evaluation-model endpoint, default first in order)
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed; OpenRouter already supported natively. Pin with JEV_PROVIDERS=openrouter and JEV_OPENROUTER_MODEL=~typesafe/jev-latest if desired.

interface.name: post_jev_evaluate (MCP tool, POST /jev/evaluate)

Returns {ok, provider, model, answers{id: choice/score/probability + probabilities/confidence}, usage?} or {ok:false,error}. Questions validated client-side in src/jev.ts:62-80.

interface.name: library export ./jev

security: API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header to the chosen provider (src/providers/openrouter.ts:24); not in argv if supplied via env; but cli.ts:7-8 loads a .env from the package root (in bunx cache) or --env-path, so best to pass keys via the MCP config `env` block instead

No shell exec, no postinstall/preinstall scripts, no telemetry, no curl|sh; only fetch to provider URLs. URLs overridable by env (OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_URL, TYPESAFE_API_URL, AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL) so a hostile env could redirect the key
Logging is stderr-only and logs failure messages (HTTP body first 500 chars), not keys

Transitive deps are heavy for a 1-tool server: edge.libx.js pulls express 4, libx.js, selfsigned, body-parser, @vercel/edge, @whatwg-node/server, isomorphic-fetch, ua-parser-js; same single maintainer (Elya Livshitz, also ships shraga/agentx); version 0.1.0 published 2026-09-25, 5 days old, no repository field, no tests in tarball, no provenance link to source (gitHead 2a916ae only)
Runs TypeScript directly with Bun-only APIs (import.meta.dir, #!/usr/bin/env bun); bun is not installed on this machine, so it cannot run under Node 24 as is
HTTP mode binds 127.0.0.1 only, no auth on REST/MCP endpoint (any local process could spend the key) - avoid HTTP mode
Prompt-injection surface: state is arbitrary text assembled by Claude; output is numeric/enum only (choice strings limited to declared options), so return-path injection risk is low
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and each question's `instructions`/`criteria` leaves the machine as JSON to openrouter.ai (and, with default JEV_PROVIDERS, on failure to ai-gateway.vercel.sh and api.typesafe.ai if those keys exist; unconfigured providers are skipped). Nothing is sent automatically: only what the model chooses to serialize, which can include code, diffs, file contents or ticket text. No hook reads user prompts or tool outputs. Client projects: OpenRouter data-policy/ZDR settings apply; TypeSafe/Jev is a third-party model behind OpenRouter.
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level: errors are caught and returned as {ok:false,error} (src/app.ts:27-29), so Claude Code sees a normal tool result and continues; in stdio mode it is not a blocker for the turn. However there is NO fetch timeout or AbortSignal in postJson (src/types.ts:53-62), so a hung OpenRouter connection can stall the tool call until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout. Provider fall-through (src/jev.ts:42-56) can add extra latency and unintended egress to other providers if their keys are set. Not a hook, so no fail-closed risk to normal work.
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__mcp-jev__post_jev_evaluate). Tool description about 900 chars plus body-param description about 250 chars plus name/schema, roughly 350-450 tokens; server `instructions` string about 330 chars (~85 tokens); total about 450-550 tokens always loaded (less if MCP tool search defers it). SKILL.md (~1.9k chars, ~480 tokens) only loaded if the resource is read. No hooks, no injected text per turn.
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no Claude Code skill is registered (the SKILL.md sits inside the npm package and is an MCP resource, not installed to ~/.claude/skills). Claude would call it only if its own judgement says a probabilistic decision is useful, which for daily coding is rare, and it must hand-build a state + questions payload each time. To make it 'automatic' the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or write own hooks; this package provides none.
pros: Correct OpenRouter Decisions API wire format (POST /api/alpha/decisions, boolean->noul mapping, model typesafe/jev-1.13) implemented in about 30 lines (src/providers/openrouter.ts) - useful as a reference or to vendor
Small, readable surface: 520 lines total, one tool, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry
Response normalization gives identical choice/score/boolean shape across providers; client-side validation of question shapes gives clear errors to the model
Tool-level failure returns {ok:false,error} instead of crashing the session; keys can be passed via MCP env block
Only ~500 tokens of always-on context, cheap to keep loaded
Can be pinned to OpenRouter only with JEV_PROVIDERS=openrouter, matching the user's stated provider
cons: Requires Bun (shebang #!/usr/bin/env bun, import.meta.dir, TS entrypoint shipped uncompiled); user has Node 24/uvx only and bun is not installed, so npx will not work

Not automatic: single model-discretion tool, no hook, no CLAUDE.md fragment, no installed skill; Claude must invent state and questions schema every call, which contradicts the 'never prompt to use jev' requirement without extra glue
Default provider order tries Vercel then OpenRouter then TypeSafe, so failure can leak the same payload to other vendors if their keys exist; must set JEV_PROVIDERS
No fetch timeout/abort; hung upstream stalls the tool call
Very new and unproven: v0.1.0 published 2026-09-25, single maintainer, no repository link, no tests shipped, no CI/provenance visible; heavy transitive tree (express, libx.js, etc.) for one POST call
Uses the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint with hardcoded model default typesafe/jev-1.13 rather than ~typesafe/jev-latest; alpha API can change
Jev is a decision model with no coding-specific value proposition; a generic 'state + questions' tool gives Claude little reason to prefer it over its own reasoning for code tasks
npmjs-com-package-livx-cc-mcp-jev.verdict: Correct but thin proof-of-concept wrapper: it proves the OpenRouter Decisions API call shape, but it is a Bun-only, model-discretion tool with no hook or trigger, so it does not deliver the 'automatic' integration and is not worth running as-is. Best used as a reference for a small custom Node hook/MCP against openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions.

gh-legostin-jev-browser.name: @legostin/jev-browser
gh-legostin-jev-browser.whatItDoes: Browser-automation MCP server plus skill (not a coding-assistant helper). You give a goal; Jev picks browser actions via the OpenRouter Decisions API, and Playwright or a Chrome extension executes them. The npm package (3 files, 32 KB) is only an installer/launcher shim. It git-clones the real engine from github.com/legostin/jev-browser main, and that repo now returns 404 (private or deleted). The npm package is therefore a dead installer. A sibling public repo, legostin/jev-mcp (MIT, 94 commits, 1 star, created 2026-09-23), holds the same author's earlier browser MCP with the same purpose.

providerSupport.evidence: The candidate's engine source is unreachable, so provider support could not be verified in code. Only the npm README is readable. It says 'On first use, save your OpenRouter key' via `jev configure`, and 'JEV is called through the alpha OpenRouter Decisions API' (README.md, Initial release limitations). It also says the config lives in ~/.config/jev-browser/.env. The shim bin/jev-browser.mjs has no provider code: line 9 sets repository='https://github.com/legostin/jev-browser.git' and lines 44-45 clone it. `gh repo view legostin/jev-browser` and `git clone` both fail with 'Repository not found'. The sibling legostin/jev-mcp (src/core/config/schema.ts:56) defaults to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` with model `typesafe/jev-1.13`. It posts to `${baseUrl}/systemone` (src/core/jev/client.ts:66) and has a second provider at https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (test/core/jev.test.ts:66). Env vars are OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/core/config/store.ts:86-87).
providerSupport.others: The sibling jev-mcp also supports TypeSafe direct (TYPESAFE_API_KEY). The candidate's README mentions only OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter is the native provider. The blocker is that the engine repo is inaccessible, not the provider.

security: Install-time supply chain risk. bin/jev-browser.mjs:44-46 does `git clone --depth 1 --branch main` of an unpinned repo and then runs its scripts/setup.mjs with node. Any main-branch content, including a hijacked or recreated legostin/jev-browser repo, executes on the user's machine. Nothing is pinned or checksummed.
README offers `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash` and a `gh api ... | bash` installer, both curl|sh style. Those are unauditable now because the repo is 404.

Background auto-update is on by default. README: 'MCP starts, checks for updates in the background, at most once a day' from main. Validated builds become current, so unreviewed remote code runs on every MCP launch.
Persistent background service. It survives terminal close and is not tied to the Claude session. Local dashboard link contains an access token.

Chrome extension uses the `debugger`, `tabs`, `nativeMessaging`, `webNavigation` permissions. It gives CDP-level control of the user's real logged-in Chrome, and a Native Messaging host is registered. This is a large attack surface, especially on client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: web page content is fed to Jev, and results and findings are returned to Claude. Passwords can be passed through MCP args into the Claude transcript. README admits: 'MCP arguments may remain in the calling conversation's history'.
API key is stored in ~/.config/jev-browser/.env (0600) and is not put in argv. Setup uses hidden-input `jev configure`. This is good practice, but it is unverifiable in code.
Package has no postinstall script. 'files' ships only bin/. License field is absent from package.json and there is no LICENSE file in the tarball. The repo is inaccessible, so the license is unknown.
Telemetry could not be verified. Not mentioned in the README.
gh-legostin-jev-browser.dataEgress: Only to OpenRouter (Decisions API), per README. Per step it sends a compact page structure (DOM/ARIA groups, labels, field values except password/secret-typed fields), the goal, planned values, browserContext (URLs, clicked elements, typed text, up to 14 KB), and the saved findings. It does not send source code, diffs or Claude prompts, because it is unrelated to the repo. The risk is browsing-session content. It uses the user's real Chrome with existing sign-ins, so private pages, client portals and form data go to OpenRouter and Jev. Local history under ~/.local/share/jev-browser also stores page-derived data. It cannot be exercised or audited for coding tasks, because it has no code-editing surface at all.
gh-legostin-jev-browser.failureMode: Unverifiable in code. README says it fails closed and safe on ambiguity. Below minConfidence (default 0.55) or on an uncertain result it stops with needs_review or needs_input and returns alternatives. It never auto-lowers the threshold and never auto-replays mutations. If GitHub or npm is down, the auto-update keeps the working release. Timeout values for Jev calls are not documented. Tool calls block for up to 25 s (jev_run) and 45 s (jev_wait), so a slow Jev stalls the Claude turn. If the engine repo cannot be cloned, `install` throws and nothing works (bin/jev-browser.mjs:27).

Plus an installed skill (the sibling skill is about 11 KB, or about 2.8k tokens, when loaded). No hooks and nothing injected per prompt. MCP server instructions are unknown. The tools are only useful for browser tasks. The user already has Playwright MCP loaded, so this duplicates and competes with it.
gh-legostin-jev-browser.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. No hooks and no transparent proxy. It fires only when Claude decides that a browser task needs it, which is unlikely in daily coding. It is not a general Jev integration.

npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.whatItDoes: Tiny (about 160 LOC) unofficial npm package with two bins: `jev` (CLI that builds a single-question request) and `jev-mcp` (stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `judge(state, questions)`). interface.name: MCP tool `judge`

POSTs to TypeSafe System One and returns JSON.stringify(answers) as a text content block. security: API key is read from env only, never placed in argv; sent as Bearer header over HTTPS. Not printed. Good.
CLI accepts --state on argv, so state content is visible in the process list (not the key).

No shell execution beyond execFileSync('security', [...]) with fixed args and process.env.USER as an argument (no shell, so no injection). On Linux this call just fails (ENOENT) and yields the 'key not found' error.

No postinstall or install scripts; only dependency is @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30.0 (caret range, no lockfile shipped). `zod` is imported (index.js:5) but not declared in package.json, so it relies on the SDK hoisting it (works with npm/npx today, fragile).

No repository field or provenance link. Single anonymous-ish maintainer (gmail address), package about 9 days old, two versions 30 minutes apart. Supply-chain risk is moderate for a tool that holds an API key; pin an exact version or vendor the 53-line file.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever `state` Claude passes (files, diffs, tool output) goes to Jev, but the output is a numeric structure with no free text, so the injection blast radius on return is small.
No telemetry.
README explicitly disclaims affiliation with TypeSafe.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.dataEgress: Exactly the `state` and `questions` that Claude Code chooses to put in the judge call, sent to api.typesafe.ai (direct TypeSafe, not OpenRouter). This could be code, diffs or file contents if the model decides to pass them. The server never reads files or hooks anything itself. The CLI --file option reads a local file and sends it whole. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup without TYPESAFE_API_KEY: the top-level throw crashes the MCP server, so Claude Code shows it as failed to connect (same status as the caveman-shrink failure you see now). Not a blocking hook, though, so Claude Code keeps working. At call time, HTTP errors and network errors throw and become an MCP tool error, which the model just sees and continues from. There is no timeout, no AbortController and no retry on fetch, so a hung connection would rely on Claude Code's MCP tool timeout (very long by default). Effectively fail-open for the session but with a possible long stall.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Jev is not called (no hooks, no proxy). When called: one HTTPS POST (claimed 70-500 ms) plus about 200 ms of tool-call overhead plus one extra model round trip for Claude to write the call and read the result. Stdio server spawned via node at session start, with a small startup cost from importing the MCP SDK and zod.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__jev__judge). Description about 680 chars plus schema (state unknown, questions record with nested union types, generated JSON schema roughly 1.0-1.5k chars) gives roughly 400-550 tokens in the tool list. No MCP server `instructions`. No hook-injected text. Very cheap.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The description actively suppresses auto-use: 'Call ONLY when ... explicitly required', 'Use it when the caller names Jev'. There is no hook, skill trigger or proxy, so it will rarely fire without you naming Jev. It could be made more proactive by editing the description, but Claude would then still be choosing when to spend an extra round trip.
pros: Smallest possible surface: one tool, about 500 tokens of context, no hooks, no prompt-rewriting, no proxying. Cannot break existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.
Whole implementation is 53 lines (index.js) and readable in a minute; easy to audit, vendor and fork into an OpenRouter version.
Sends the key as a Bearer header from env, not argv; no install scripts; no telemetry.
Tool schema mirrors the real System One contract (noul/choice/score with instructions and criteria), and README examples show the response shapes, so it is a correct thin client.
Batch-friendly: the questions record lets Claude ask several independent typed questions about one state in a single call.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL, model and env var are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (index.js:7-11). It fails your stated requirement unless you fork or patch it.
Uses jev-latest and the TypeSafe direct endpoint; OpenRouter model IDs (typesafe/jev-1.13, ~typesafe/jev-latest) are not accepted without editing.
Description tells the model to use it only when Jev is named, which is the opposite of your goal. Nothing deterministic (hook, skill or proxy) makes it fire automatically.
Linux-hostile key path: the fallback is the macOS `security` command; on Linux the only working path is the env var, and if it is unset the server crashes at import time (index.js:19).
No timeout or abort on fetch; no retries; errors surface as raw thrown text including the response body.
Maturity is very low: created 2026-09-21, 2 versions in 30 minutes, single individual maintainer, no repo link, no tests, no CI, no license field in package.json. Not affiliated with TypeSafe.
Undeclared `zod` dependency and a caret-ranged SDK with no lockfile, so installs are not reproducible.

Offers no coding-specific value on its own: it is a generic judge call, and any code-related question (is this test flaky, which file to edit) requires Claude to hand-write the question schema each time, costing tokens and a round trip.
npmjs-com-package-sunchojack-jev-cli.verdict: A correct but throwaway 53-line TypeSafe-direct wrapper that cannot use OpenRouter without a fork, and whose tool description tells Claude not to use it unless you name Jev. At most, copy index.js as a template for your own OpenRouter-backed MCP or hook. Do not install it as-is.

gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.name: jev-router-mcp (MarcosldcC/Jev_Router)
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.whatItDoes: Zed-first ACP router/supervisor with a secondary MCP bin (jev-mcp). The MCP tool jev_delegate takes a coding prompt, asks TypeSafe Jev (System One) two typed questions (noul "too ambiguous?" and choice low/medium/high complexity), then either returns a clarify/confirm instruction to Claude, or picks a downstream model. If it picks "claude" it hands the task back to the calling Claude Code session with a suggestion to run a subagent with model=claude-haiku/sonnet; if it picks Codex, Gemini or DeepSeek it spawns that ACP agent as a child process and auto-approves its tool calls. Jev is used only for prompt classification and an optional Tool Gate (allow/deny/conditional). It is not used for anything a Claude Code user needs, such as memory, retrieval or code decisions.

It calls client.systemOne({state, questions:{ambiguous: noul(...), complexity: choice(...)}}) at line 36. The SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:56-62 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. Line 513 sets the default base to https://api.typesafe.ai. Line 554 POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Line 512 defaults the model to "jev-latest". Timeout is 10s (line 518) with maxRetries 2 (line 74). Tool count is 2 (dist/mcp/server.js:35,167).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial with no code change, in principle. OpenRouter's System One endpoint is /api/v1/systemone and the SDK appends /v1/systemone to baseURL, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 should work. This is untested and depends on OpenRouter's request/response schema matching TypeSafe's, and on the SDK's response validation. The bigger problem is that a successful switch changes nothing about the design issues below.
providerSupport.others: Delegates to Claude (claude-agent-acp), Codex (codex-acp), Gemini CLI and DeepSeek (dsh-acp) via ACP, each needing its own key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, DEEPSEEK_API_KEY). Nothing goes through OpenRouter.

interface.name: jev_delegate (MCP tool, inputs prompt and cwd)
interface.purpose: Classifies the task through Jev and returns one of three things. (1) A Portuguese 'AÇÃO NECESSÁRIA' instruction to ask the user a clarifying question. (2) A confirm-with-user instruction. (3) A delegation: for Claude, an instruction to run the task in the calling session or a subagent with model=<id>; for others, a real ACP child run with a transcript and audit returned.

security: Repo is 404 on GitHub, single maintainer, single publish 9 days ago. Provenance is weak and the code is not reviewable beyond the npm tarball.

dist/delegation/mcp-child.js: the Tool Gate treats both 'allow' and 'conditional' as auto-approve (allow_once). The comment says there is no live user to ask. 'Conditional' is the risky/destructive bucket, so it is effectively unsupervised.

The Jev-based Tool Gate is only a probabilistic allow/deny. The deterministic block is a title keyword match for database/production/deploy/secret/credential/.env/api_key, which is trivially bypassable.

fs/readTextFile and writeTextFile go through resolvePath(cwd, path). I did not verify it blocks path escapes outside cwd. The child agent can also request terminal/create with an arbitrary command and env: ...process.env. The child inherits the full parent environment, including any keys.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool result text is an imperative 'AÇÃO NECESSÁRIA' block plus a JSON contract that Claude is told to follow. The tool description also tells Claude not to investigate before calling. That is instruction-shaped output injected into the main agent, but it is the author's own text, and the classifier output can steer which model or subagent runs.

API key handling: the key is read from the environment, not argv. Good. The SDK redacts headers in debug logs. No postinstall/preinstall scripts. No curl|sh. No telemetry found in dist. Stdio ownership is safe, and diagnostics go to stderr via log.
The stated purpose in README is Zed. The MCP bridge is described as secondary and 'Claude Code has no equivalent extension point'.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.dataEgress: To TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed: the entire user prompt as `state` on every jev_delegate call, in the noul/choice call at jev-client.js:36. In the Tool Gate path (only for delegated non-Claude agents): tool kind, tool title and the execution contract. No file contents or diffs go to Jev. To other providers: if Codex, Gemini or DeepSeek is chosen, the prompt, the contract and anything that agent reads through fs/terminal goes to that provider, so client code can leave to a third party the user did not choose. The cwd path is passed as a tool argument, so Claude Code sees it as well.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.failureMode: Fail-open, locally. classifyTaskWithJev catches any error and returns the regex heuristic plan (jev-client.js:84-87). The SDK default is a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries, so a slow or down Jev can stall a jev_delegate call for up to about 30 s before the fallback. The jev-mcp path has no startup gate. The 'mandatory key' startup exit only applies to the jev-acp bin. If no downstream provider is keyed, Claude is still always enabled (alwaysEnabledProviders: [claude]). A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently gives heuristics only, so the user would get regex 'Jev' with no warning.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.contextCost: 2 tools: jev_delegate and jev_status. The jev_delegate description is about 1.9k characters and the input schemas are small, so all tool definitions come to roughly 700 tokens. It has no MCP server instructions and no hook text. But each call injects a 300-1500 token instruction block into context, in Portuguese, and Claude is told to act on it.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no transparent proxy. Claude Code would call jev_delegate only if the model chooses to based on the tool description, which says to pass the user's request verbatim on the first call. That is unreliable and drifts across sessions, and it is not the deterministic 'always when needed' behavior the user asked for. A CLAUDE.md line telling Claude to call it is not a real solution either, since the user does not want to prompt for it.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.latencyImpact: Jev call 70-500 ms in the claimed happy path, plus an MCP round trip and an extra model turn (Claude has to make the tool call and then follow the returned instruction). Failures cost up to about 30 s (10 s timeout, 2 retries). If it delegates to Codex, Gemini or DeepSeek, it blocks for the entire downstream agent run inside a single tool call.
pros: Real, working use of the Jev primitives (noul and choice) through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The criteria strings for the ambiguity and complexity questions are sensibly calibrated (jev-client.js:48-52).

OpenRouter repoint is close to trivial on paper. The SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer token, which matches OpenRouter's System One path shape.
The design is fail-soft: a local regex fallback on any Jev error, and the deterministic security keyword floor is checked before Jev.

It is the only candidate here that actually tries to make Claude Code call Jev from inside a session, and it is aware that Claude Code cannot run it as a backing agent. The Claude branch avoids double billing by handing back to the calling session.
MIT license, no install scripts, key kept out of argv, no telemetry.
cons: The GitHub repo is 404, there is one npm publish and one maintainer, and the age is 9 days. There is no way to audit history, tests or CI, and it could vanish.

The core product is a multi-model router for Zed. For an Opus-5.5-subscription user the useful part is tiny: it mostly suggests spawning a subagent with a cheaper Claude model. The Codex/Gemini/DeepSeek branches need extra paid keys and would send client code to other vendors.

Invocation is model-discretion. Nothing forces Claude to call jev_delegate, so it fails the user's requirement of automatic integration without prompting. And when it is called, the tool text asks Claude to skip its own investigation first, which can make results worse.

It puts Jev in the wrong role. Jev is a calibrated decision primitive and this uses it as a preflight gate on every task. That adds a turn and latency to each request for a marginal gain over Claude's own judgement, and 'ambiguous?' gating can stall work with clarification loops, as the SDK comment at jev-client.js:57-69 admits it hit.

Unsafe defaults: the 'conditional' verdict is auto-approved, child agents inherit the full environment, and the deterministic guard is a keyword match on the title. This is worse than Claude Code's own permission system, which the user already has hooks around. It also conflicts with the client-project secret-leak guard.

Instruction-shaped tool output in Portuguese with 'AÇÃO NECESSÁRIA' that Claude is told to obey, plus ~700 tokens of tool definitions. Worst-case blocking is about 30 s with a silent local fallback, so a missing or broken key looks like it works.
Sends the full user prompt (client project details) to the Jev provider on each call, with no opt-out for sensitive projects.
gh-marcosldcc-jev-router.verdict: Not recommended. It is an early, unauditable single-author Zed router whose MCP path is model-discretion, fires an extra turn on every task and auto-approves its own child agents' risky tool calls. Only its jev-client.js pattern (noul plus choice via the SDK with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter) is worth borrowing for a custom hook.

Node/npx cold start ~1-3 s at session start.
gh-tairuframework-mokei.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__system-one__predict). Definition includes the full recursive question-map JSON schema (anyOf choice/score/noul, instructions anyOf string/object/array) plus outputSchema; estimated ~600-900 tokens. No server-level instructions field set. No hooks, no injected text.
gh-tairuframework-mokei.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description ('Classify text with System One typed questions (choice/score/noul)') is generic and gives Claude no guidance on when to use it; without a CLAUDE.md rule or skill it will almost never be called spontaneously, and Claude must construct a valid typed question map each time.
pros: Minimal, readable, MIT-licensed wrapper (3 source files, ~130 lines server + ~850 lines client) that is easy to audit and does exactly one thing
Endpoint path v1/systemone and Bearer auth match OpenRouter's System One API, and base URL/key/model are env-configurable, so OpenRouter-hosted Jev is plausibly a config-only change
Strong schema validation of both inputs and responses (choice/score/noul with probabilities, confidence, act_probability) and structuredContent output with outputSchema
No shell exec, no postinstall, key via env not argv, no telemetry
Actively developed (commits through 2026-09-30) and low context cost (single tool)
cons: Not Jev-specific: built for Laya/laya-serve (default localhost:8000, model 'english'); zero mention of OpenRouter, TypeSafe or Jev in code or docs, so OpenRouter compatibility is inferred, not proven
No deterministic trigger: a bare model-discretion tool with a generic description; Claude will not use it automatically, which violates the user's core requirement
Every call requires Claude to author a full typed question map, costing an extra main-model turn, tokens and latency; poor for routine coding steps
README is thin (npm README empty), only 1 star, single maintainer, package 6 days old (0.13.0 on 2026-09-24), no GitHub releases

No default timeout/retry configured in the MCP server, no fallback behavior; send-what-Claude-chooses egress with no redaction, and would sit beside the existing secret-leak guard without integrating with it
Requires storing the OpenRouter key in MCP env config (plaintext in ~/.claude.json) and npx -y of an unpinned young package
gh-tairuframework-mokei.verdict: A clean but generic System One MCP client aimed at Laya; it can probably be pointed at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone by env vars alone, but as a discretionary MCP tool it cannot deliver the automatic, no-prompt Jev usage the user wants. Useful only as a reference implementation or as the transport underneath a hook/skill that decides when to call it.

gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.name: mcp-jev
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server (Node, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk + zod) that forwards typed Jev questions (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe's /v1/systemone endpoint or to a local Laya server. The candidate summary is stale: v2.0.x (latest 2.0.1) replaced jev_decide/jev_list_models with four tools: decide_predict, decide_preset, decide_status, decide_list_models. Presets (triage, guard, moderation, router, email) are hard-coded question sets aimed at support-ticket, moderation, email and LLM-routing use cases, not coding.

providerSupport.evidence: dist/adapters/jev.js:24 POSTs `${baseUrl}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}` and body {model, state, questions}; dist/adapters/factory.js:108-114 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY (required) and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai). There is no OpenRouter-specific code and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var. Default model is hard-coded "jev-latest" (jev.js:13), and the constructor's model argument is never set from env (factory.js:114). Laya adapter (laya.js:156) also uses /v1/systemone at LAYA_BASE_URL (default http://localhost:8000). Wire-compatibility with OpenRouter was not verified from the OpenRouter docs: both openrouter.ai doc URLs I tried returned 404. The brief lists the OpenRouter endpoint as https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would hit that path if the request/response schemas match.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. No code change is needed for the base URL, since the path /v1/systemone matches the brief and the key travels as a Bearer token; put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The problems are the model ID and the schema. The default "jev-latest" is not an OpenRouter ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and it can't be set by env, so the calling LLM must pass `model` on every call or a one-line fork edit is needed. The response parser (lib.js:35-42) is strict zod and needs {answers, model, usage.input_tokens/output_tokens}; any difference in OpenRouter's response shape fails with ParseError. GET /v1/models (jev.js:46) is unverified on OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: Laya (local HTTP server, pip package laya) via DECIDE_PROVIDER=laya

interface.name: decide_predict
interface.purpose: Send state (string, object or array, up to 200k chars) plus 1-100 typed questions (noul, choice with up to 255 options, score with 2-10 levels) to the provider. Returns raw JSON with per-question probabilities. Optional `model`.

interface.name: decide_preset
interface.purpose: Run one of five hard-coded question sets (triage, guard, moderation, router, email) against a state, using the field names the preset expects (message, prompt, post, request, body).

interface.name: decide_status
interface.purpose: Returns provider, base_url and default model. For Jev it is synthesized from env and makes no network call, so it always says "ok" even when the key is bad or the API is down.

interface.name: decide_list_models
interface.purpose: GET /v1/models from Jev, or the loaded checkpoints from Laya /health.

gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.createdAt: 2026-09-21 (first npm publish; 7 versions from 2026-09-21 to 2026-09-28, 4 of them within 40 minutes of the first release)
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.lastCommit: Unknown. github.com/mndpjm/mcp-jev and user mndpjm both return 404 (deleted, private, or wrong owner). The npm gitHead 96108aa9a621f0259a82b05e3956f1ca14d36357 cannot be checked. Last npm publish was 2026-09-28.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.tests: The package.json declares vitest and the code says lib.ts is exported for tests, but the published tarball contains no tests, no CI config and no source (dist only, 26 files). Could not be verified. The repo is unreachable, so no CI status is available.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.runtime: Node >=20, ESM, stdio transport. Launched via `npx -y mcp-jev`, which fetches from npm at each session start unless pinned.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.install: claude mcp add jev -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -e TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api -- npx -y mcp-jev@2.0.1 (the OpenRouter variant is my inference and is untested; the README documents only the api.typesafe.ai default)
security: No install scripts: package.json has no preinstall/postinstall. The `prepare: tsc` script does not run for registry installs.
Runtime dependencies are only zod and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No child_process, fs or eval in dist/*.js. Only fetch() calls, to the configured base URL.
No telemetry found: outbound requests go only to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (or LAYA_BASE_URL) at /v1/systemone, /v1/models and /health.
API key is read from env (factory.js:108) and sent only as a Bearer header, so it stays out of argv if placed in the MCP `env` block. It is not logged; stderr only shows startup lines.
Any base URL is trusted: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is not validated, so a mis-set URL would send the key and state to another host. The default is HTTPS api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is raw JSON of numbers and enum keys (no free text from the model), which is small. But question text and state are chosen by the calling LLM, so file contents pass through it.

Supply chain: single anonymous-ish maintainer (Gmail address), age of about 9 days, GitHub source missing. `npx -y` without a version pin would auto-run any later malicious release. The code I read looks benign.
Preset definitions are ported from another project (laya/presets.py, convaiinnovations/laya) with a manual sync note.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.dataEgress: Only what the LLM puts in `state` and `questions` (up to 200k chars each call) goes to the provider. With OpenRouter that is the text the agent chooses to send: possibly code, diffs, file contents, user prompts or tool output, plus the OpenRouter key. Nothing is sent automatically. Claude Code's own prompts and tool results are not intercepted, so egress is model-driven and opt-in per call. Client code would reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe only if Claude decides to call the tool with it. This matters for client projects under NDA.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors are caught and returned as an isError text result ("Error: ..."), so Claude continues. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the server call process.exit(1) at startup (index.js:31), so it shows as a failed MCP connection, which is harmless but noisy. Each request has a 30 s timeout (lib.js:6) and 3 attempts on 429/500/502/503/529 with backoff (1 s, 2 s, capped at 60 s total). The worst case is therefore about 90 s plus about 3 s of waits on one call, while a healthy call takes roughly 70-500 ms. There is no circuit breaker. Because it is a tool call, a slow Jev blocks only that call and not other turns.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.contextCost: 4 tools. Descriptions total about 2.3k chars. The JSON schemas from zod (a question discriminated union, state union, model) add roughly 2-3k chars. Estimated total is about 1.2-1.5k tokens of tool definitions per session (chars/4), less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch. No server-level `instructions` field is set. No hook-injected text, since it has no hooks. It is a small footprint, but it pays for tools whose presets are irrelevant to coding.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude calls it if the tool description convinces it to. The description says to call it to "classify or route text", "check a true/false condition" or "rate content on a rubric", which rarely arises in coding work. Opus 5.5 can classify or route text itself for free, so it has little reason to call an external classifier and will mostly ignore it. There is no hook, skill, or proxy, so it will not be used automatically in the sense the user wants unless CLAUDE.md or a hook forces it, and that would be the user telling Claude to use it.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.latencyImpact: Nothing is added to turns unless the tool is called. A call adds the claimed 70-500 ms network round trip plus MCP overhead and one extra Claude tool-call turn (about 1-3 s of LLM time to compose the question and read the result). Cold start via `npx -y` adds around 1-3 s at session start (the registry check and the download on the first run).
pros: Small, readable, benign code: about 30 KB of dist JS, two dependencies, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry, MIT.

Uses the same /v1/systemone path as OpenRouter's System One API and sends a Bearer key, so the base-URL override TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api will probably work with no code change (wire format unverified).

Exposes all three Jev primitives generically through decide_predict, with limits enforced by zod (max 100 questions, 255 choices, 2-10 score levels), so Claude can build custom noul/choice/score questions.
Good errors: 401/403 and 400/422 are not retried, retries are bounded, and there is a 30 s timeout. Failures come back as isError results, so Claude keeps working (fail-open).
Small context cost of about 1.2-1.5k tokens for four tools.
Key stays in the MCP env block and does not show up in argv.
cons: The candidate description is stale. It lists jev_decide and jev_list_models, but the current 2.0.1 has decide_predict, decide_preset, decide_status and decide_list_models. The old v1 tool names would no longer match.

The GitHub source repo and author account return 404, so provenance, commit history and tests cannot be verified. The package is about 9 days old with 7 releases in a week, one anonymous-looking maintainer, and the tarball ships no tests or source.

No OpenRouter support in code. It has no OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The key has to be smuggled in via TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the hard-coded default model "jev-latest" is probably not a valid OpenRouter ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). There is no env to change it, so the LLM must pass `model` every time or you must fork the package.

The response parser is strict (zod requires answers, model, and usage.input_tokens/output_tokens). Any difference in OpenRouter's response envelope breaks every call with ParseError. I could not confirm the shape because the OpenRouter doc URLs I tried gave 404.
decide_status never calls the API and always reports status "ok" for Jev, so it is useless for diagnosing a bad key or an outage.

Presets are built for support tickets, moderation, phishing and email, plus an LLM 'router', and none is for coding. The router preset's model-routing idea does not apply to Claude Code, which can't switch its main model per prompt through MCP.

It is a passive tool that only fires when the model chooses to call it. Opus has no reason to hand simple classification to an external model, so this fails the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement. Forcing it would take CLAUDE.md instructions or hooks, both outside this package.
Data sent is whatever the LLM puts into `state`, so client code could leave the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The tool's own advice is to send only relevant fields, which nothing enforces.
Worst-case retry time of about 90 s per call, with no circuit breaker, and `npx -y` without a version pin runs whatever is latest on the registry at each session start.
gh-mndpjm-mcp-jev.verdict: A clean, small, generic Jev wrapper, but young, of unverifiable provenance (GitHub repo gone), and not OpenRouter-native. Even patched, it is a model-discretion tool with support/moderation presets that Claude Code has no reason to call, so it will not deliver the automatic integration the user wants. It is at best a building block: if used, pin mcp-jev@2.0.1 or vendor the 30 KB and set the base URL and default model. A hook-driven approach fits the goal better.

gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.name: jev-incur-cli
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI + stdio MCP server built on the incur framework. It wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (POST /v1/systemone) and exposes Jev typed questions (noul/choice/score) to agents. It also ships 5 authored Jev "workflow" skills (plan validator, completion gate, metric decomposition, subagent orchestrator, grill-with-docs) that are installed via a wrapper around `npx skills@1.7.0`. It is a generic question-asking tool. It has no hooks and no automatic invocation. The caller supplies the state text and the question.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code in the package. dist/jev/client.js:8 does `new TypeSafeClient(config)` with no config, so all settings come from the SDK env vars. @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:56-62 defines env vars TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. Line 513 defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai. Line 554 sends POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone`. Line 581 sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Line 514 defaults the model to `jev-latest`. dist/jev/errors.js:62 even mentions TYPESAFE_BASE_URL in its NOT_FOUND message.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and it needs no code change if OpenRouter's System One API accepts the same request body and the same {answers, model, usage} response. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OPENROUTER_API_KEY> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) in the MCP `env` block. Schema equivalence is unverified because I cannot run it. Caveat: the `models` command calls GET /v1/models and expects `{models:[...]}` (index.mjs:365-370). OpenRouter's models list has a different shape, so that command would fail. The tools pass `model` through per call, so it is not essential.
providerSupport.others: Only the TypeSafe direct API by default. Any base URL that mimics /v1/systemone works via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.

interface.name: MCP meta-tool search_tools
interface.purpose: incur progressive discovery (Mcp.js:148 in incur 0.5.1). Lists tool names and descriptions. This is the default, because cli.js does not set discovery to 'direct'.

interface.name: MCP meta-tool get_tool_details
interface.purpose: Returns one tool's full input schema (incur Mcp.js:170)

interface.name: MCP meta-tool call_read_tool
interface.purpose: Executes read-only-annotated tools (incur Mcp.js:187). All Jev tools are annotated readOnlyHint.

interface.name: MCP meta-tool call_write_tool
interface.purpose: Executes unclassified tools (incur Mcp.js:199)

interface.name: AskJevQuestions
interface.purpose: Takes an array of {name,state,question:{type,instructions,criteria}}. Runs one concurrent systemOne call per item. Returns {results:[{name,model,answer,usage}]}. One failure fails the whole batch (dist/commands/ask.js:80-98).

interface.name: AskNoulQuestion
interface.purpose: Single yes/no probability sugar (state, instructions) (dist/commands/noul.js)

interface.name: AskChoiceQuestion
interface.purpose: Pick one of the criteria. Internally expands to up to 8 criterion-order permutations in one request and averages the probabilities to reduce position bias (dist/jev/permutation-choice.js:1-40).

interface.name: AskScoreQuestion
interface.purpose: Ordered rubric, returns expected score plus probabilities (dist/commands/score.js)

interface.name: models
interface.purpose: Lists Jev models for the account (GET /v1/models) (dist/commands/models.js)

interface.name: CLI: skills add/list/remove
interface.purpose: Delegates to `npx --yes skills@1.7.0 ...` with the bundled .agents/skills catalog (dist/skills/jev-skills-command.js)

interface.name: skill jev-completion-gate
interface.purpose: Model-discretion skill for deciding which unmet requirements block task completion

interface.name: skill jev-plan-validator
interface.purpose: Validates plans, specs and slices against criteria

interface.name: skill jev-subagent-orchestrator
interface.purpose: Routes subagents by scope, model and effort

interface.name: skill jev-metric-decomposition
interface.purpose: Turns qualitative tasks into hill-climbable metrics. This is the default skill installed.

interface.name: skill grill-jev-with-docs
interface.purpose: Interviews Jev about a plan using supplied docs and code

security: No install-time scripts in the published package. package.json has only a dev-side `prepare: husky`, which does not run on a registry install. Runtime deps are incur ^0.5.1, cross-spawn 7.0.6 and @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. The SDK is MIT, from github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js, created 2026-09-12.

API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header (SDK index.mjs:581). The key never appears in argv. The MCP env block should forward it as `${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}`, but the README says registration does not add this automatically. The user must hand-edit the .mcp.json.
The SDK logger defaults to the console at a configurable level (TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL). debug logs bodies (index.mjs ~line 620), so keep it at the default.

Shell execution is limited to `skills add`, which runs `npx --yes skills@1.7.0` through cross-spawn without a shell. That fetches and runs a third-party installer (Vercel Skills) at install time. The recommended MCP registration also uses `npx --yes --package=jev-incur-cli@latest`, which runs unpinned latest code on every Claude Code start.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev returns only numbers and labels. No free text returns except the criteria labels the caller supplied. That is a low surface. The bundled skills are long instruction documents (29-83 lines each plus references) that steer the agent to run subagents, which is a moderate behavioural-influence surface.

Single-maintainer package. npm publisher stevennevins. Versions 0.1.0 to 0.3.0 were published between 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-22. npm signatures are present. The GitHub source repo is not publicly reachable (gh returns 404 for the repo and the README itself says 'this private Git repository'), so the published dist cannot be checked against source. I read the compiled JS directly.
No telemetry found in the package or the SDK grep (only api.typesafe.ai or the configured base URL).
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.dataEgress: Exactly what the agent puts in the `state` and `question` fields is POSTed to TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is redirected). The README instructs agents to 'read the relevant files yourself, then pass each file's contents inline as an item state'. The typical payload is therefore code and file contents, plans and diffs, and one full copy per question, because the fan-out sends the same file once per item (the README example is 126 concurrent calls with the same file). Choice questions expand to up to 8 permutations. Nothing is sent automatically. Everything is model-authored. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool inputs (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so secrets in a file the model chooses to forward would go out. A client-project NDA implication exists: client code would go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter, and OpenRouter data policy applies.
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, but non-blocking for Claude Code. The SDK defaults are 10 s timeout and 2 retries (index.mjs:74, 518). Worst case is about 30 s or more before the tool returns c.error with a typed code such as TIMEOUT, RATE_LIMITED, AUTH_FAILED or CONNECTION_FAILED and a `retryable` flag (dist/jev/errors.js). AskJevQuestions is all-or-nothing: one failed item discards all results, and in-flight siblings are not cancelled (README and ask.js:80-98). A missing key errors at first use, not at startup. If the MCP server itself fails to spawn (npx fetch on a bad network), the tools are simply absent and the session proceeds normally.
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.latencyImpact: Zero on normal turns, because nothing is hooked. Each use costs 3 extra model round-trips (search_tools, then get_tool_details, then call_read_tool) plus the Jev call itself (claimed 70-500 ms), then the Opus turn to interpret results. The first start incurs an npx cold fetch. That is seconds if `npx --yes --package=jev-incur-cli@latest` is used, and each Claude Code start re-resolves `latest`.
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.contextCost: MCP: 4 top-level tools (search_tools, get_tool_details, call_read_tool, call_write_tool). Their descriptions and schemas are about 1.5-2k chars, so roughly 400-600 tokens in the tool list. This is small thanks to progressive discovery, and there is no server `instructions` string in cli.js. The 5 real Jev tools cost nothing until fetched. Each full schema fetched (AskJevQuestions with its nested union) is roughly 500-800 tokens, added mid-conversation. If the 5 skills are installed, each adds a ~300-char description to the skill listing, so about 400 tokens standing. Invoking one loads 30-80 lines of workflow plus references, several thousand tokens. Hooks: none, so no injected text.
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. It is an MCP tool behind progressive discovery plus optional skill description triggers. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic trigger. Because the tools are hidden behind search_tools, Opus has no standing cue that a Jev tool exists, so auto-use is unlikely unless a CLAUDE.md line or a skill description nudges it. The bundled skills trigger on 'plan validation', 'task completion', 'subagent routing' and 'metric decomposition' phrasing. They fire rarely in ordinary coding and are workflow-heavy.
pros: Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The wire shape is exactly POST /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, so OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone should work by setting only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY (an OpenRouter key) and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. No fork is needed (index.mjs:513, 554, 581).

Covers all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) plus batching. Choice questions get permutation averaging (up to 8 orderings) to cancel option-order bias (permutation-choice.js), which is a real quality feature for a calibrated-probability model.

Low standing context cost (about 500 tokens) because incur's progressive discovery hides the schemas. All tools are marked readOnlyHint, so they should not trigger permission prompts under the user's auto or bypass mode.
Typed error codes with a retryable flag let the agent back off or skip cleanly (errors.js). No install hooks in the published package, MIT license, npm provenance signatures present.
The bundled skills show sensible Jev usage patterns (thresholds left to the caller, 'raw model signals not verified facts'). They are the only agent-usage guidance found so far.
cons: Not automatic. It only offers tools, with no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook and no router. The user's stated requirement, that Claude Code uses Jev without being told, depends entirely on Opus deciding to call it. Progressive discovery makes that less likely, because the model must search_tools, then get_tool_details, then call_read_tool before it can use it.

Not built for the daily coding loop. Its own README example is checklist triage (126 concurrent noul calls against one Solidity file) and 'metric decomposition' and 'plan validation' skills. There is no built-in coding-specific use such as command risk or 'should I run tests' classification.

Sends whatever state the agent passes, and the README tells agents to pass whole file contents inline. The fan-out repeats that content per question. Client-project code would leave the machine, and the existing secret guard does not match mcp__ inputs.

Unpinned npx registration (`--package=jev-incur-cli@latest`) means code from a single new maintainer runs at every session start. It needs manual pinning (jev-incur-cli@0.3.0) and preferably a vendored install.

Source repo is not publicly accessible (GitHub 404; the README calls it private). It is 12 days old with 3 versions and one maintainer, and its tests are not shipped. The README references release availability quirks ('0.1.1 release does not contain this skill' although the registry lists 0.1.0/0.2.0/0.3.0). Maturity is alpha.

`models` command breaks on OpenRouter (different /v1/models response shape). The key must be hand-added to .mcp.json env, and the SDK's 10 s timeout with 2 retries can stall a tool call for 30 s or more. An all-or-nothing batch discards partial results.

The 5 skills are heavy orchestration prompts (routing subagents, gating completion). They add process overhead and could conflict with the user's existing caveman, GitNexus and context-efficiency workflows.
gh-stevennevins-jev-incur-cli.verdict: A competent, thin wrapper around the official SDK that can talk to OpenRouter with env vars alone, but it is an on-demand tool box, not an automatic integration. With progressive discovery and no hooks, Claude Code will rarely call it unprompted. Use it at most as the transport for a custom deterministic hook, and prefer a small direct OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone hook or wrapper of your own that you control.

npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.name: mcp-server-jev (bin: jev-mcp)
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.whatItDoes: Generic stdio MCP server that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (systemOne call) and exposes Jev's three primitives as tools: batched jev_evaluate, single-question jev_choice / jev_score / jev_noul, and jev_models. Not coding-specific: no hooks, no skill, no code/diff awareness. The model must decide to call it and must build the typed question and the self-contained 'state' itself. Ships a short server 'instructions' string telling the model to ask atomic questions, batch them, and read confidence as a second axis.

SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:513) defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai; index.mjs:554 posts to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone`; index.mjs:581 sends Authorization: Bearer <key>. So jevBaseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is exactly the OpenRouter System One endpoint from the brief. README 'Endpoints > OpenRouter' documents this with model jev-1.13 (bare or typesafe/jev-1.13); I could not confirm from code that OpenRouter accepts the bare name, so prefer typesafe/jev-1.13. It does not use the /api/alpha/decisions Decisions API. jev_models does not work on OpenRouter (dist/index.js:144-145, README says so); all other tools do.

security: npm package published 2026-09-24 by a single individual maintainer (mark-haedal <[email removed]>), not a typesafe-ai account; package.json has no repository/homepage/bugs field, so there is no auditable source repo, CI, or issue tracker. Tarball contains only dist/index.js (bundled, deps external), README, LICENSE, package.json (4 files, 30.9 KB). README says releases are manual 'npm publish' with no CI or Git remote. Tests described in README are not in the tarball, so I could not verify them.

No install/postinstall scripts; only prepack/prepublishOnly (publisher side). Dependencies: @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.1.0, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 (official, MIT, repo typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js), commander, zod. Unpinned `npx -y mcp-server-jev` would auto-pull any future malicious version from an anonymous single maintainer: pin the exact version (mcp-server-jev@0.1.0) or vendor dist/index.js.

Read dist/index.js in full (377 lines): no shell execution, no filesystem access, no telemetry of its own, only the SDK HTTP call. SDK sets X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers and User-Agent (harmless metadata) and redacts headers in debug logs.

Key handling: the env-var names are unusual and case-sensitive (jevApiKey, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY). README recommends env block over --jevApiKey because argv shows in ps; via claude mcp add --env the key lands in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, so use a dedicated low-limit OpenRouter key. Could be sourced from shell env instead of a literal.

Prompt-injection surface is small: tool output is just numbers and labels (no free text from Jev). The main risk is the reverse: Jev's low-confidence or wrong probabilities could steer the model's decisions. Tool result echoes user-supplied option labels and legend text only.
Error logging goes to stderr (console.error), never stdout, so the protocol is not corrupted. Server warns on start if no key is set.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts in the tool arguments (state, instructions, criteria/options/levels, optional model) is JSON-POSTed to jevBaseUrl/v1/systemone (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe/its provider) with the bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: no hooks, no file scanning. But 'state' is free-form, so if Claude passes code, diffs, file contents, tool output or secrets into it, all of that leaves the machine to OpenRouter and its upstream. This matters for client projects. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools unless its matcher is extended. The SDK adds SDK version/runtime headers.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.failureMode: Fail-open in practice: any error is thrown as a tool error with an actionable message (dist/index.js:255-262, 119-150) and Claude simply continues. Nothing blocks the session. However the latency worst case is bad: SDK timeout is 10 s per attempt (index.mjs:518) with maxRetries 2 on timeouts, connection errors, 408, 429 and 5xx (index.mjs:74-88), with backoff 0.5-5 s and Retry-After up to 60 s, so a down or slow endpoint can stall one tool call for about 30-40 s or more. Claude's MCP tool timeout applies on top. No option to tune this through the server's config (only jevApiKey, jevBaseUrl, jevModel are exposed). Missing key: server starts, every call errors.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.contextCost: 5 tools. Estimated tool definitions ~9-11k chars, about 2.5-3k tokens (jev_evaluate has the largest schema: discriminated union of 3 question types with long describe() strings; each shortcut tool ~1.2-1.8k chars; jev_models tiny) if all loaded eagerly. Claude Code's MCP tool search can defer them to names only. Server 'instructions' text ~1.3k chars (~330 tokens) is injected every session. No hook-injected text. Adds one more always-on stdio process (Node, ~50-80 MB). A cheaper setup exposes only jev_evaluate via permissions/allow lists.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, skill, or proxy. Claude will call it on its own only if the tool descriptions and server instructions look relevant to the current task. Those texts are generic: 'routing, classifying, gating an action' (not coding-specific), and they say nothing like 'before committing / after tests fail'. Expect rare and inconsistent use unless a CLAUDE.md rule or hook/skill supplies concrete triggers. So it does not meet 'Claude must use it when needed' by itself. It is a good transport layer under a hook or skill, not the automation.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.latencyImpact: Per call: claimed 70-500 ms Jev inference plus OpenRouter hop, plus MCP round trip and the extra model turn Claude spends composing a typed question (dominant cost: output tokens of a question with state, ~1-3 s of Opus time). Batching through jev_evaluate keeps it to one call. Cold start of `npx -y` at each session start adds a few seconds and a network fetch unless pinned or installed globally. Failure or outage worst case ~30-40 s (see failureMode). Nothing runs on every tool call, so idle turns cost nothing.
pros: Only needs config to use OpenRouter: jevBaseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api hits the correct /v1/systemone endpoint, verified in SDK code (index.mjs:554,581), and reuses OpenRouter's key as Bearer.
Small and readable: one 377-line bundled file with no shell, fs, or telemetry code, no install scripts. Statically auditable in minutes.
Built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so request/response schemas match TypeSafe's, with built-in retries and typed errors mapped to actionable messages.

Good tool ergonomics: jev_evaluate batches mixed noul/score/choice questions in one call; structuredContent plus a readable text line; probabilities truncated to keep output small; server instructions teach atomic questions and confidence use.
Fits the 'gate an action' idea: jev_noul can be a cheap yes/no check (for example 'does this diff touch auth?') when something else triggers it.
MIT licensed; the same server also works on TypeSafe direct if OpenRouter is dropped.
cons: Does not satisfy the core requirement: invocation depends on the main model's judgment. There is no hook or skill trigger, and the generic descriptions do not say when to consult Jev during coding, so Claude will mostly ignore it without extra CLAUDE.md prompting, which the user explicitly does not want.

Provenance risk: released 6 days ago (0.1.0, single version), an anonymous individual maintainer, no repository link, no CI, and README-described tests that are absent from the tarball. Unpinned npx would auto-update from that account.

Odd, non-standard env names (jevApiKey/jevBaseUrl/jevModel, case-sensitive) instead of OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The key ends up in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or must be exported in the shell. jev_models is broken on OpenRouter.

Data-leak channel: free-form 'state' can carry code and client data to OpenRouter. The existing secret-guard hook does not cover it without a matcher change, and there is no redaction or size cap in the server (32k context limit is left to the API to reject).
Poor failure bounds: 10 s x 3 attempts plus backoff (up to about 30-40 s) with no config knob to shorten it, and Retry-After up to 60 s honored.

Every question costs an Opus turn to author the typed schema plus its output tokens, likely more than a Jev call saves for typical coding decisions. Jev returns no text or reasoning, so it does not help write, debug or review code directly.

Adds 5 tool defs and about 330 tokens of server instructions to every session for a tool that will rarely fire. Overlaps with the other community Jev MCPs (burnigtm/jev-mcp, jkudish/jev-mcp, Brainwires/jevwire) that appear to target coding loops or ship hooks; this one has no source repo to compare.
npmjs-com-package-mcp-server-jev.verdict: Clean, small, OpenRouter-compatible transport for Jev (config-only, verified in code), but it is a bare model-discretion MCP with no hook or skill triggers and an unauditable one-week-old single-maintainer npm release, so it will not give the user's 'Claude uses Jev automatically' behavior on its own. Usable only pinned (@0.1.0) and paired with a hook or skill that supplies the triggers, or as a reference implementation to vendor.

gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.name: @opengeni/genigrep (ggr)
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.whatItDoes: Code-search tool for agents (CLI `ggr`/`genigrep`, stdio MCP server `ggr mcp` with a single `code_search` tool, library, and an Agent Skill). Given a question plus 6-15 agent-chosen keywords, it runs one ripgrep pass, then uses Jev (Choice/Noul/Score-style probability answers via POST /v1/systemone) to triage up to 240 candidate files, verify up to 80 line-numbered passages, follow definitions one level, and rate the final evidence. It returns verbatim passages with path:line. Jev only scores; it never writes text. It is a port of the code_search engine from Cloudgeni's OpenGeni harness (packages/jev).

providerSupport.evidence: src/engine/client.ts:13-14 defaults JEV_DEFAULT_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai, JEV_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest; client.ts:389 posts to `${baseUrl}/v1/systemone` with Bearer auth and body {state, model, questions}, reads {answers, usage.input_tokens, model}. src/config.ts:10-13 env vars GENIGREP_JEV_API_KEY, GENIGREP_JEV_BASE_URL, GENIGREP_JEV_MODEL, GENIGREP_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS; config.ts:174-175 base URL and model are overridable via env or ~/.config/genigrep/config.json (jevBaseUrl/jevModel). config.ts:66-77 requires https (http only for localhost). No occurrence of 'openrouter' anywhere in src/, README or docs (grep). OpenRouter's System One path is /api/v1/systemone, so GENIGREP_JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus GENIGREP_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) and GENIGREP_JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would produce the same URL suffix. I could not verify that OpenRouter's request/response JSON is identical to TypeSafe's (OpenRouter docs URLs returned 404), so that is inferred from the brief, not confirmed.
providerSupport.others: None. Only TypeSafe direct is documented; custom base URL is allowed (README Configuration table).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Likely trivial, with no code change: three env vars (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, model typesafe/jev-latest, key). Risks: (1) OpenRouter schema parity is unverified; client.normalizeAnswer throws JevUnavailableError if an answer id is missing. (2) warmUp() sends GET {base}/healthz (client.ts:~372), which is probably a 404 on OpenRouter but is harmless (errors swallowed) and only costs the TLS pre-warm. (3) `ggr auth` verification call and `ggr doctor` assume TypeSafe. (4) The engine's 16-way parallelism and 10 s timeout were tuned for TypeSafe direct; OpenRouter rate limits (429) are retried only twice with a 2 s cap. If the schema differs, patching client.ts post() and normalizeAnswer is small (about 1 file, ~100 lines).
