security: API key: read from GENIGREP_JEV_API_KEY or a 0600 config file in a 0700 dir; sent only as a Bearer header; never logged; `ggr auth` prompts without echo, so the key never appears in argv. Warns if the config file is world-readable (config.ts:~160). The MCP server re-reads the key on every call (it does not go into .mcp.json).
HTTPS enforced for the base URL, with http only for localhost (config.ts:66-77).
No telemetry found: grep shows no analytics. The only network destination is the configured Jev base URL (plus GET /healthz warm-up to the same host).
No postinstall scripts (package.json scripts: build/typecheck/test/check/prepublishOnly only). The npm package is published with provenance (publishConfig.provenance=true). No curl|sh installer.

Shell execution is limited to spawning ripgrep (src/workspace/local.ts:285) with --no-config and a flag allowlist (no --pre, no symlink following, no absolute or .. paths) and `rg --version` in doctor. ripgrep is the bundled @vscode/ripgrep binary, which is downloaded from GitHub at that package's postinstall (a transitive supply-chain step to note).

Reads honor .gitignore/.ignore/.rgignore, skip binaries, dependency/build dirs and lockfiles, and skip a list of secret files (.env*, keys, *.tfvars, .npmrc, .netrc, .ssh, .aws, etc., case-insensitive; src/workspace/excludes.ts). It refuses ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg and ~/.kube as the search root. The MCP server confines calls to configured or client roots.
Gap acknowledged in SECURITY.md: it does NOT scan contents for secrets, so a hard-coded credential in an ordinary source file can be sent to Jev. This matters for the user's client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool returns verbatim repo text (same as any file read). The engine sends repo text to Jev, but Jev only returns probabilities, so an injection cannot steer Jev's output into free text. Its directive text is fixed and benign; the instructions do not push the agent to skip verification.
Single-author repo (all 18 commits by one person; three npm maintainers), created 3 days ago. The maintainers are Cloudgeni staff, a real company, but the track record is minimal.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.dataEgress: To the configured Jev endpoint only (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if overridden, and then also OpenRouter and its upstream). Per docs/how-it-works.md:173-186 and README Privacy: the question and sub-questions; paths of up to 240 candidate files each with up to 3 matching lines (160 chars each); up to 80 passages plus 6 followed definitions of up to 8,000 chars each (verbatim source code) with path, line numbers and enclosing declaration; up to 60 identifier names with their line text; and up to 60,000 chars of the final packed passages. The keywords, whole files and gitignored/secret files are not sent. Secrets in ordinary source files can be sent. Not sent: prompts or conversation history, diffs, or other tools' outputs, because the agent only supplies a question and keywords. A single search can therefore send on the order of hundreds of KB of client source code to a third party. Per the user's client-project context, check the contracts.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.failureMode: Fail-closed for the tool but non-blocking for Claude Code. There is no keyword-only fallback; the README says this is deliberate, because keyword-only ranking lost 7.7 quality points. On error the MCP tool returns isError text ending with 'Search with rg, grep or file reads instead', so Claude falls back to native tools. Per-request timeout is 10 s (GENIGREP_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, 1-120 s), with 2 retries on network/429/5xx (backoff 250 ms base, retry-after capped at 2 s). 401/402/403 fail immediately and are surfaced as key/billing problems. The circuit breaker (src/engine/circuit-breaker.ts, 3 consecutive failures, cooldown of minutes, auth cooldown longer) then refuses fast, so an outage costs one quick refusal per call. There is no total wall-clock cap besides per-request timeouts times the stages. A worst-case stall can be several tens of seconds before the first breaker trip. A missing key returns a setup error without any network call.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (code_search). Tool description about 1,150 chars plus input schema (5 properties with descriptions) about 1,500 chars, plus title/annotations, so about 700 tokens. MCP server `instructions` (CODE_SEARCH_DIRECTIVE) about 900 chars, about 225 tokens, injected into the system prompt on every session. Total about 900-1,000 tokens fixed per session; deferred tool loading may hide the schema until needed. The optional skill adds about 100 tokens of description, with the body loaded only when triggered (about 900 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injection. Each call returns up to a 12k-token evidence pack (default budget 12000), typically 5-10k tokens, which is a big per-call cost when the answer is small.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, nudged by the server instructions (a directive that says to start with one code_search call instead of several searches/reads) and the tool description. Optionally also a skill (description-triggered). No deterministic hook and no transparent proxy: Claude decides. It also competes with the user's existing GitNexus hooks/MCP and native Grep/Glob, so real invocation frequency is uncertain. It is best treated as an opt-in via the instructions, not guaranteed.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.latencyImpact: README example: 2.3 s for one search (15 passages from 10 files); the docs say 'a few seconds', with about 0.4 s per Jev request, stages run in parallel (up to 16 concurrent), plus the ripgrep pass and a cold TLS connection of about 0.7 s (mitigated by warm-up). Multiple sequential Jev stages (triage, passage check, leads, rating) means roughly 3-5 serial Jev round trips. Through OpenRouter, expect extra hop latency. The per-call latency is partly offset by replacing the agent's multi-step grep/read loops, and the measured gain was about -10% total time on investigation questions. It is not a per-turn cost when unused.
pros: Only candidate seen that does real Jev work: it uses Jev's probability answers as a ranker (src/engine/client.ts POST /v1/systemone), with Jev never producing free text, so it fits Jev's 'System One' design.

Configurable base URL and model by env vars (config.ts:10-13,174-175), so pointing it at OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/api + typesafe/jev-latest) is plausibly a config-only change; the endpoint suffix /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's documented System One path.

Ships an MCP server with one small, read-only, well-annotated tool (~1k tokens of context, no hook overhead per turn) plus server instructions that tell Claude to prefer it for 'where is X decided?' questions. This is the closest thing to automatic use short of hooks.

Good engineering for a 3-day-old repo: circuit breaker, bounded retries, fail-to-rg messages, 0600 key storage, no key in argv/logs, HTTPS enforcement, ripgrep flag allowlist, secret-file skip list, root confinement, no postinstall, npm provenance, Apache-2.0, big test suite and CI.

Honest documentation: publishes measured results with CIs (about -6.6%/-7.5% cost and -9%/-10% time on 26 investigation questions with equal quality, and no effect on bug-fixing) and explicit limitations. It also tells the agent not to over-trust the rating.
No bundled telemetry; egress goes only to the configured Jev endpoint; the exact fields sent are documented.
cons: Extremely new and single-author: 18 commits in 3 days, 3 stars, 1 contributor, no releases on GitHub, npm 0.1.0/0.1.1 published 2026-09-28. Expect churn and bugs.

Evidence applies only to the OpenGeni harness with GPT-6-class agents on one TypeScript monorepo; the README says the CLI, MCP server, skill and derived keywords were not part of the evaluation. Zero measurement with Claude Code / Opus. The reported gain is modest (7-10%) and its 2nd run's CIs include zero.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs (no 'openrouter' string anywhere). Schema parity with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified, and the auth/doctor verification flow and warm-up /healthz assume TypeSafe. Needs a smoke test with a real OpenRouter key before trusting it.

Sends verbatim source code (up to 80 passages x 8k chars, plus 60k chars of evidence) to a third party per search, and does not scan for hard-coded secrets. Risky for client projects with NDAs, and it bypasses the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard because the MCP tool is not in the Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit matcher (the guard only sees the Grep/Read that genigrep replaces).

Not deterministic: it depends on Claude choosing the tool. Claude Code already has native Grep/Glob and the user's GitNexus MCP/hooks (graph context) that overlap heavily; it is likely to be under-used, or duplicate GitNexus's function.

Requires the agent to supply 6-15 good keywords per call, and the results are only as good as those; each call returns up to about 12k tokens, which can inflate context when only a small fact is needed. It is not exhaustive (rg is still needed for renames and counting), and language tuning is TypeScript-only.
Fail-closed with no fallback ranking: if Jev/OpenRouter is slow, calls can take several seconds to tens of seconds before failing over to rg. Beta model plus an alpha tool.
Bundled ripgrep binary is fetched at @vscode/ripgrep install time (network at install), a small supply-chain step.
gh-cloudgeni-ai-genigrep.verdict: The best, and about the only, working Jev-as-ranker integration for Claude Code: a small single-tool MCP server whose instructions make Claude reach for it on 'where is X decided' questions, and its base URL and model are env-configurable, so OpenRouter is probably a config-only switch. It is 3 days old, evaluated only outside Claude Code with modest gains, sends real source code out per search, and leaves auto-invocation up to the model, so try it in a sandbox project with an OpenRouter key and a smoke test of the response schema before adopting it globally.

gh-sidearker-vex.name: @sidearker/vex-mcp (Vex + jev CLI)
gh-sidearker-vex.whatItDoes: TypeScript package (npm @sidearker/vex-mcp 0.1.1, bins `vex` and `jev`) with a stdio MCP server and a CLI, both on a shared engine that calls Jev over OpenRouter (/api/alpha/decisions) or TypeSafe direct (/v1/systemone). It exposes 4 MCP tools: vex_choose (bounded 2-12 option choice with an abstain option and 0.70 confidence / 0.15 lead thresholds, plus an optional forced 'routing' mode), vex_tool (pick a tool from candidates), vex_gate (destructive / escalate / risk noul+score questions) and vex_verify (completion-evidence gate). It is advisory only. Nothing hooks into Claude Code; the model must choose to call the tools.

providerSupport.others: None. A custom base URL is possible through OPENROUTER_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_BASE_URL and the --base-url CLI flag.
providerSupport.evidence: src/core/schemas.ts:6-7 defines TYPESAFE_SYSTEMONE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions; DEFAULT_OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (line 5). src/core/engine.ts:53-64 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ~/.openrouter_key. engine.ts:173-190 resolves URL and model from OPENROUTER_BASE_URL / OPENROUTER_MODEL / JEV_MODEL. engine.ts:192-202 sets headers, with HTTP-Referer/X-Title for OpenRouter. engine.ts:234-242 POSTs {state, questions, model}. Provider is chosen by JEV_PROVIDER / VEX_PROVIDER, or by key prefix (sk-or- goes to OpenRouter, ts- to TypeSafe); with no provider set, a TypeSafe key wins if both exist (engine.ts:141-154). The MCP tool description says 'Input is sent to OpenRouter' (src/mcp/server.ts:24). It does not call /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter, only the alpha /decisions endpoint. The default model typesafe/jev-1.13 is pinned rather than ~typesafe/jev-latest; set OPENROUTER_MODEL to change it.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already supported; nothing to patch. Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY (optionally JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_MODEL=~typesafe/jev-latest) in the MCP server env.

interface.name: MCP vex_choose
interface.purpose: Input {question, context?, options[1-12 of {id,description}], decisionType?: choice|routing, constraints?}. Internally builds one Choice question with an extra __jev_abstain__ option. Returns {contractVersion, choice|null, abstained, confidence, probabilities, reason}. Abstains when confidence <0.70 or top-vs-runner-up lead <0.15; routing mode never abstains (src/mcp/server.ts:20-45; src/core/engine.ts decide()).

interface.name: MCP vex_tool
interface.purpose: Input {task, tools: record of 2-12 name->description, context?}. Wraps vex_choose with the question 'Which tool best advances the task'. Returns {tool, abstained, confidence, probabilities, reason} (server.ts:47-88).

interface.name: MCP vex_gate
interface.purpose: Input {action, context?}. Sends 2 Noul questions (is_destructive, escalate_to_human) and 1 Score question (risk_level Low/Medium/High). Returns booleans thresholded at 0.5 plus risk_level (server.ts:90-171).

interface.name: MCP vex_verify
interface.purpose: Input {task, acceptance, evidence}. Sends 3 Noul questions (enough_information, needs_verification, task_complete). Returns task_complete (>=0.8), needs_verification, evidence_sufficient and next_steps (server.ts:173-259).

interface.name: CLI vex
interface.purpose: `vex mcp serve` starts the stdio server. Also `vex stats`, `vex doctor`, --help, --version (src/index.ts:49-127). Note: running `vex` with no args only prints help, so the MCP config must pass `mcp serve`.

interface.name: CLI jev
interface.purpose: decide, run, workflow, eval, route, suggest-skill, triage, gate, verify-diff, stats, doctor, with --provider/--model/--base-url (src/cli/jev.ts). This could be scripted from a Claude Code hook, but no hook is shipped.

gh-sidearker-vex.license: MIT (LICENSE file and package.json). README badge and footer wrongly say ISC.
gh-sidearker-vex.runtime: Node >=20, ESM, deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1 and zod ^3 only. Run with `npx -y @sidearker/vex-mcp mcp serve`. Bare `npx ... vex` prints help and exits.
gh-sidearker-vex.install: claude mcp add vex --scope user --env OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... --env JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter -- npx -y @sidearker/vex-mcp mcp serve   (or pin a global npm install and call `vex mcp serve` to avoid npx latency and unpinned version drift; better to keep the key in ~/.openrouter_key, mode 600, than in ~/.claude.json)
gh-sidearker-vex.tests: The repo has 4 vitest files (core, public_contract, cli_process, stats), about 43 test()/it() cases. The README badge says 41 and claims offline mocked transports. There is no .github directory and no CI. I did not run them (static review only).
security: No shell execution: grep of src found no child_process, exec or spawn use. The only outbound calls are the decision POST and, in `stats` only, GET openrouter.ai/api/v1/auth/key and /credits (src/core/stats.ts:209,224).

API key comes from env or ~/.openrouter_key, ~/.typesafe_key and ~/.jev_key. There is no --api-key CLI flag, so no key in argv/ps. The key is sent as a Bearer header only to the configured URL. The base URL is overridable via env, so a hostile env could redirect the key; that is a normal risk.

No telemetry beyond the provider call. It writes a local stats file (~/.agents/jev_stats.json, path from VEX_STATS_PATH) holding op name, provider, elapsed time and token usage, not prompts (stats.ts:62-64,182-183). A failed stat write is swallowed with .catch(() => {}).

package.json has `prepare: npm run build`. That runs on git installs and local npm install, not on registry installs. The published tarball ships prebuilt dist/ (27 files) and has no postinstall script. The dist matches the 4 tools in src. The tarball was reviewed statically only; no `npm pack` or install was run.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is small structured JSON (choice ids, numbers), so it is a low injection channel in the return direction. But the input is model-authored free text that the model must summarise. The LLM decides what to send, and the docs tell it to sanitise secrets, which is only a prompt-level control. vex_gate and vex_verify results are advisory and the agent can ignore them, so they are not a security control.

Supply chain: single anonymous maintainer (sidearker, Radoslaw Sowa), package published 2026-09-26, only 2 versions, 1 star, no CI, no provenance attestation seen. `npx -y` with no version pin would auto-pull any later malicious release. Pin the version.
The MCP server reports version 0.1.0 while npm is 0.1.1, and the README says ISC while the licence is MIT. This is minor polish/consistency debt.
gh-sidearker-vex.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into the tool arguments leaves the machine, sent over HTTPS to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai). For vex_choose that is question, context (string or object), constraints, and the option ids and descriptions. For vex_tool it is the task, the tool descriptions and the context. For vex_gate it is the proposed action text and the context. For vex_verify it is the task, the acceptance criteria and the evidence text, which may include test output or diffs if the model pastes them. Nothing is read from disk or captured automatically. There are no hooks, so no automatic capture of prompts, files or tool outputs. Keys are never in argv. OpenRouter sees the requests under the user's account; the HTTP-Referer 'https://github.com/typesafe-ai/jev' and X-Title 'Jev' headers are hard-coded and are not the user's app. The client-side abstention logic runs locally.
gh-sidearker-vex.failureMode: There is no hook, so nothing blocks Claude Code. If the server is missing or the key is absent, the tool returns isError JSON, or the MCP server simply does not connect, and Claude carries on. It is effectively fail-open. A default 45 s fetch timeout (AbortSignal.timeout(45_000) at engine.ts:241, overridable via EngineOptions only, and the .env.example JEV_TIMEOUT_MS is not read by the engine, so it may be dead config) means a hung call can stall one tool call for up to 45 s. Timeouts, HTTP errors, bad JSON and schema-mismatched responses all become error results with no retry. Because the alpha endpoint and the beta model are volatile, expect occasional error results. Abstention is common by design (<0.70 confidence returns null), so the model must handle 'no answer' well.
gh-sidearker-vex.latencyImpact: One MCP round trip per call. The README claims 70-500 ms for TypeSafe direct and 400-1200 ms for OpenRouter (the second figure is the README author's own; I did not measure it). The cost is a model turn to decide to call the tool plus the tool call, roughly 1-2 s per use, incurred only when the model chooses to call it. npx cold start adds a one-off delay at session start unless the package is installed globally. No latency is added to non-Jev tool calls.
gh-sidearker-vex.contextCost: 4 tools. Tool names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas total about 3-3.5k chars, so roughly 800-1000 tokens of tool definitions, loaded into every session (or deferred behind ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.1.x if MCP tool search is enabled). The McpServer sets no `instructions`, so it adds no server-instruction text. No hooks, so no injected text. Each call costs the model tokens to author the options and context (typically 150-400) plus a ~100-token JSON result. The only discovery signal is the terse tool description; without a CLAUDE.md rule the model will rarely call it.
gh-sidearker-vex.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills or plugin manifests, and it is not a proxy. The repo ships only integrations/codex/AGENTS.example.md, a 7-line 'use only when choosing among plausible skills' snippet. For truly automatic use in Claude Code you would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule, or write your own PreToolUse/Stop hook that shells out to `jev gate` or `jev verify-diff`, which this repo does not provide. Claude, an Opus-class model, already reasons well, so it will often skip a 'ask a tiny classifier' tool that returns abstain often.
pros: Works with OpenRouter today: sk-or- key auto-detected, default model typesafe/jev-1.13 and endpoint /api/alpha/decisions match the brief (schemas.ts:5-7, engine.ts:53-64,119-120). Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY and it works. TypeSafe direct also works, giving a fallback.
Small and readable: 4 tools, about 1.5k lines of TS, only 2 runtime deps, no shell execution, no postinstall, no key in argv, no telemetry. Static review found nothing dangerous.

Good client-side safety layer: options validated against caller ids, reserved abstain id, probability-key checks, and the confidence/lead abstain logic (engine.ts decide()). This reduces the risk of a hallucinated route.

Covers the sensible Jev use cases for a coding agent: vex_gate (destructive / escalate / risk with Noul and Score) and vex_verify (done-ness gate) map well onto Jev's Noul/Score primitives. vex_choose has a forced routing mode.
The npm tarball has prebuilt dist that matches src, and MIT is the licence. The `jev` CLI could be reused inside your own hooks (e.g. `jev gate` from the existing PreToolUse setup) if you write them.
Costs are trivial (about $0.042/1M input tokens, output free) and the local stats file with `vex stats` gives usage tracking.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a pull-style MCP tool; Claude Code will not call it unless the model decides to. There is no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet for Claude Code (the only guidance is Codex-specific). This directly misses your 'never say use jev' requirement without extra glue.

The README claims Claude/Cursor support but only Claude Desktop, Cursor and Antigravity config examples are given; there is no Claude Code `claude mcp add` recipe or hooks. Docs reference `vex_workflow`, which does not exist in the 0.1.1 code (agent-integration.md section 3), and the docs are partly stale or Codex/Pace-specific (e.g. model names like gpt-6-luna).

Very immature: created 2026-09-24, 36 commits in 2 days, single contributor, 1 star, 2 npm versions, no CI, no releases. Alpha endpoint plus a beta model plus a 3-day-old wrapper is three unstable layers.

Fail-soft but blunt: there are no retries, no circuit breaker and a 45 s timeout that cannot be set from env in the MCP path (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS in .env.example is not read). The README's 'mathematical guarantee' is only a threshold heuristic on model outputs, not a proof.

Fit with an Opus-class main model is weak: asking a tiny System-One classifier which tool to use (vex_tool) or whether the task is done (vex_verify) adds a round trip and a possible false 'done' or false 'destructive' signal versus Claude's own judgement. vex_gate duplicates your existing secret-guard and permission flow and is not a security boundary.

Data egress is model-authored: evidence and diffs pasted into vex_verify or vex_gate go to OpenRouter under client projects. That needs a client-NDA decision, and sanitisation depends on the LLM obeying docs. `npx -y` without a pinned version is a supply-chain risk for a single-maintainer, new package. The hard-coded HTTP-Referer 'github.com/typesafe-ai/jev' also misattributes usage in OpenRouter analytics.
gh-sidearker-vex.verdict: The safest and most complete off-the-shelf way to get OpenRouter-hosted Jev into Claude Code as MCP tools (works today with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, no code execution beyond HTTP), but it is only a model-discretion tool with no hooks, so it does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' goal alone. Use it, version-pinned, as the transport and pair it with your own CLAUDE.md rule or a small PreToolUse/Stop hook that calls `jev gate` / `jev verify-diff`. Treat the package itself as alpha.

gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.name: ultrabrowse
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.whatItDoes: Node MCP server (also packaged as a Claude Code plugin with a skill) that launches or attaches to a local Chrome over raw CDP. For a natural-language goal it loops: snapshot page, call TypeSafe Jev System One (Choice questions for operation and target index), execute the click, fill or select, and return the final page text. A separate OpenAI-compatible text model (default inception/mercury-2.5 on OpenRouter) writes typed field values and does the extract tool. This is a web-browsing agent, not a coding-decision helper. Jev is only the click picker.

providerSupport.evidence: Jev calls are hardcoded to TypeSafe direct: src/model.js:122 `postJson("https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone", cfg.typesafeKey, body)`, key from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/config.js:38), model from TYPESAFE_MODEL default `jev-latest` (src/config.js:39). The URL is a literal, not env-configurable, and the committed dist/cli.cjs contains the same single api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone literal. OpenRouter is used only for the auxiliary text model: TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL default https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 + /chat/completions (src/config.js:41, src/model.js:158,197) with TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY. No use of openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone or /api/alpha/decisions anywhere (grep).
providerSupport.others: Any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint for the text helper via TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL (e.g. DeepSeek special-cased at model.js:155).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The request body is already the System One shape (model, state, questions with type:choice; reads result.answers.<q>.{choice,probabilities,confidence}), which matches the brief's /api/v1/systemone surface. A local patch needs: (1) replace the literal URL at src/model.js:122 with https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, (2) use OPENROUTER_API_KEY, (3) set TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. Two unverified risks: OpenRouter's response envelope may differ (validateChoice at model.js:32-51 is strict and fails closed), and dist/cli.cjs is a committed bundle so a patch means rebuilding with esbuild or editing the bundle. There is no env override upstream; it needs a fork or a wrapper.

interface.name: browse(url?, goal, max_actions=40, timeout_s=120, screenshot)
interface.purpose: Goal-driven end-to-end browsing loop. Returns status done/blocked/stuck/budget/timeout, steps, final page. Requires both keys.

interface.name: snapshot(url?, full?)
interface.purpose: No-model page read (text plus numbered elements). No keys needed.

interface.name: extract(url?, goal?, schema)
interface.purpose: Optionally browse, then return JSON matching schema via the text model (up to 14k chars of page text sent).

interface.name: browse_many(tasks[1-12], concurrency<=8, max_actions)
interface.purpose: Parallel goal runs in separate tabs with a 90 s cap each.

interface.name: click(index)
interface.purpose: Manual click on a numbered element.

interface.name: type_text(index, text, submit)
interface.purpose: Manual typing into an element.

interface.name: press_key(key)
interface.purpose: Send a key press.

interface.name: scroll(direction)
interface.purpose: Scroll the tab.

interface.name: back()
interface.purpose: Browser history back.

interface.name: screenshot()
interface.purpose: JPEG of the current tab.

interface.name: close()
interface.purpose: Close this server's tab.

interface.name: close_all()
interface.purpose: Close every page in the ultrabrowse Chrome.

interface.name: skill: skills/ultrabrowse/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Description-triggered skill ('any task that involves a website') telling Claude to call browse instead of clicking step by step. Shipped by the plugin.

interface.name: CLI: ultrabrowse (stdio MCP), --version, doctor [--no-launch]
interface.purpose: Server entrypoint and key/Chrome checker (src/cli.js).

gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.lastCommit: 2026-09-19 (0.1.4 "wait for screens that are still painting"). GitHub API was unreachable from the sandbox, so stars, forks and releases are not verified. npm shows 5 versions all published 2026-09-19.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.tests: Only scripts/smoke.js, a live end-to-end stdio test that needs real keys and Chrome (README: `node scripts/smoke.js dist`). No unit tests and no CI config in the repo. Not run, per the static-only rule.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.runtime: Node >=22 (fits Node 24), esbuild-bundled CJS with a committed 819 KB dist/cli.cjs. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, zod. Needs Google Chrome/Chromium.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.install: claude mcp add ultrabrowse -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -e TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY=... -- npx -y ultrabrowse@latest ; or /plugin marketplace add narekgevorgyan/ultrabrowse then /plugin install ultrabrowse@ultrabrowse (keys in ~/.ultrabrowse/.env)
security: Keys passed via `claude mcp add -e` live in the MCP config env block, not argv. Plugin route reads ~/.ultrabrowse/.env (plain text, src/config.js:33-35), which is fine but stores secrets on disk.

`npx -y ultrabrowse@latest` runs unpinned code from a single-maintainer, 11-day-old package on every start. Auto-updates are a supply-chain risk; a pinned version or a local clone of dist/cli.cjs is safer. The committed 819 KB bundle is not reviewable line by line.
No npm postinstall script (package.json scripts: gen, build, start, test only). `allowScripts` lists esbuild for dev. No curl|sh installer.

Only child_process use is spawning Chrome with fixed args (src/chrome.js:124-128): --remote-debugging-port=0, persistent --user-data-dir=~/.ultrabrowse/chrome-profile. The profile persists cookies and logins on disk; the CDP port is local.

Prompt-injection surface is high by design: arbitrary web page text goes into the Jev state and into the text-model prompt. Mitigation is that Jev output can only be an index into observed elements (README Safety; model.js validateChoice), so injected text cannot yield a URL or code. The returned page text still lands in Claude's context, and that text is untrusted.

Password, file and hidden inputs are excluded from snapshots so it cannot type passwords. The text helper can still type arbitrary text from the goal into forms, and clicking is unrestricted (could click purchase or delete buttons on a logged-in profile).
README claims no telemetry and no update checks. grep shows outbound hosts only api.typesafe.ai and the TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL host.
Optional ULTRABROWSE_CDP_URL attaches to any CDP endpoint, so pointing it at the user's everyday Chrome would expose logged-in sessions.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on every browse step (src/model.js:110-122): page URL, title, visible page text, element labels and values, the goal, and the last 10 actions. No cookies, screenshots or password fields. To OpenRouter or TEXT_MODEL_BASE_URL only for typed fields or extract: the goal, the schema, and up to 6,000 chars of page text (fieldContext) or 14,000 chars (extractJson). No source code, diffs or Claude tool outputs leave the machine unless the user's goal or the browsed page contains them. Nothing is sent when Claude is not browsing. The Jev step goes to TypeSafe directly, not OpenRouter, in the stock build.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, but isolated to this tool, so Claude Code itself is unaffected. postJson has a 25 s timeout (40 s for extract) and retries 429/503/529 twice with backoff (src/model.js:9-30). Connection failure, HTTP errors and malformed or invalid Jev answers throw ModelError/InvalidChoice ("no action executed"), and the browse ends error/stuck. The run is bounded by max_actions (default 40, max 80), timeout_s (default 120, max 300) and no-progress detection. There is no fallback provider. browse fails upfront if either key is missing. Claude Code's MCP tool timeout can expire before a long browse finishes.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.latencyImpact: See above: no added latency to normal coding turns; only during browse calls.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.contextCost: 13 MCP tools (browse, snapshot, extract, browse_many, click, type_text, press_key, scroll, back, screenshot, close, close_all, plus server instructions). Estimated tool names, descriptions and zod schemas at about 3,000-3,500 tokens (the 'browse' description alone is about 1.2k chars). Server `instructions` string is about 380 chars (~100 tokens, src/server.js:132). The plugin also adds a skill description of ~330 chars (~85 tokens). No hooks, so no per-call injected text. Playwright MCP is already installed, so this would be a second overlapping browser toolset (~30 more tool names) competing for the same intent. Tool results (page text and numbered elements) can be large.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger plus model-discretion MCP tool. The plugin's SKILL.md description ('Use for any task that involves a website...') and the MCP server instructions steer Claude to call `browse`. There are no deterministic hooks and no proxy, and it does not touch coding decisions. Automatic only for web tasks, and it competes with the existing Playwright MCP.
pros: Real, working Jev System One integration with a typed-choice schema (src/model.js:96-122). It shows the right pattern: Jev picks an indexed option, the code validates strictly (probabilities sum to 1, argmax equals the choice) and fails closed on anything invalid.

Model output can never become a selector, URL or code. It is only an index into elements from the snapshot (README Safety; model.js:32-51), and clicks are hit-tested. This is a sound design against prompt injection from web pages.

Clean packaging: a Claude Code plugin with marketplace.json, plugin.json, a skill and an MCP server. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry claimed, and only two outbound hosts (api.typesafe.ai and the text-model base URL).
Zero cost on non-web turns: no hooks, no proxy, no latency added to normal coding.
OpenRouter is already the default for the text helper (src/config.js:41), so one OPENROUTER_API_KEY covers that half; a small patch to the Jev URL would cover the other half.
MIT license. Small, readable codebase: about 60 KB of src, with a Node >=22 requirement that suits this setup.
cons: Wrong use case for this user's goal. It is a web-browsing agent, not an integration of Jev into Claude Code's coding decisions (permissions, routing, next-step gating). It gives no gain for daily coding.

Jev calls are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/model.js:122). Stock, it cannot use the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev. It needs a fork or patch, and dist/cli.cjs is a committed bundle that must be rebuilt.

Very immature: created 2026-09-19 (11 days old), 9 commits, 1 contributor, 5 npm versions in a single day. No CI and no unit tests, only a live smoke test that needs real keys. GitHub stars, forks and release data could not be fetched (API unreachable), so community adoption is unverified.
Duplicates the installed Playwright MCP. The two would compete for the same 'website task' intent, and 13 more tools cost about 3-3.5k tokens of context in every session.

Needs a second API key and a second model (TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY with the default inception/mercury-2.5) on top of Jev, so it sends page content to two providers. Every browse step sends page text to TypeSafe.

Persistent Chrome profile at ~/.ultrabrowse/chrome-profile keeps cookies and logins. Combined with bypass or auto permission mode, an injected page could steer clicks in logged-in sessions on a client project.
`npx -y ultrabrowse@latest` is an unpinned auto-update from a brand-new single-author package, which is poor supply-chain hygiene for client work.
Only one place where a wrong Jev answer is caught (validateChoice), and there is no fallback provider if Jev or the key fails; a browse then just errors.
gh-narekgevorgyan-ultrabrowse.verdict: A competent but very young (11 days, single author) Jev-driven browser agent. It is not a coding-workflow integration, and stock it talks to api.typesafe.ai only, so OpenRouter Jev needs a one-line URL patch plus a rebuild. Skip it for this user's goal, or use it only as a reference implementation of System One Choice calls (src/model.js) and for an optional, sandboxed web-task tool.

No shell execution, child_process, postinstall script or telemetry found in server.js or SDK. Static read only.

npm provenance: the npm signatures are present (registry signatures), but there is no visible repo, so the source cannot be cross-checked against the tarball; the npx -y install path always pulls latest 0.x with no pinned lockfile (supply-chain risk on a fresh single-maintainer package).

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are raw JSON.stringify of API responses; jev_judge/jev_fanout descriptions instruct the model to obey the route (fairly benign). jev_label and jev_contract_create are write tools an injected instruction could trigger; the descriptions warn against inventing labels.
JEVAAAS env var name has a triple-A typo, easy to misconfigure, and it silently exits with code 1 if unset, so the MCP shows as failed.
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` (arbitrary JSON: prompts, code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs) plus question instructions/criteria goes to https://jev.api.br/v1 (JEVaaS, then presumably on to TypeSafe or NACE upstream). Nothing is sent automatically; it is only what Claude decides to pass in a tool call. Third-party retention policy unknown (the site only mentions a 'privacidade' section, which I did not verify). Results are stored as auditable 'receipts' on the JEVaaS side, including full answers.
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.failureMode: Fail-open by nature (MCP tool call the model chooses to make). SDK timeout is 30 s per request (default timeoutMs 30000) with up to 3 attempts and backoff, retrying on 429/502/503/504 and network errors, so a hung upstream can stall a tool call for about 90 s or more. Judge is idempotent (auto decision_id); fanout is non-idempotent and not retried on ambiguous failures. Missing key: the process exits with code 1 and the MCP shows as failed, with no fallback. On error the tool throws and Claude simply continues without it.
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.contextCost: 8 tools. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 8.3k characters in server.js, roughly 2.1k to 2.5k tokens after zod-to-JSON-schema expansion (descriptions are long Portuguese; jev_fanout and jev_contract_create are the biggest). No MCP server-level `instructions` string. No hooks, so zero injected hook text. Deferred tool loading in Claude Code reduces the resident cost to names only.
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.latencyImpact: Per call: network round trip to jev.api.br plus the judge model (vendor-claimed sub-second, unverified). Nothing on the critical path unless the model chooses to call it. Retries and the 30 s timeout add worst-case tail latency. No overhead on turns that do not call it, aside from npx cold start (~1-3 s at session start, since npx -y resolves each launch).
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The jev_fanout/jev_judge descriptions nudge use ('rotear, triar, checar se um passo terminou, se uma ação é segura') but they are written for business workflows (ticket routers, payments), not coding, and Claude Code will rarely pick them unprompted. jev_judge needs pre-created contracts. No hook, skill or proxy component, so it cannot satisfy 'automatic without prompting'.
pros: Small, readable, dependency-light code (about 80 lines plus a zero-dep SDK). Auditing it was easy and I found no exec, postinstall or telemetry.
fanout maps conceptually to Jev's Choice/Score/Noul primitives, and it can select typesafe/jev-* models, so it is the closest thing to a ready MCP wrapper if you accept JEVaaS as the provider.
SDK has good hygiene: SSRF guard on baseUrl, idempotency keys on judge, sensible retry rules, timeouts, request-id logging.
MIT license, npm registry signatures present.
cons: Not OpenRouter and not TypeSafe direct: requires a JEVaaS jev_sk_* key from dashboard.jevaas.com.br. The SDK rejects any other key prefix, so it cannot be pointed at openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone by config.
Third-party middleman (Vertikon, Brazilian, pricing in BRL) sitting between your code and Jev; extra trust and egress hop, and your data goes to their servers, not OpenRouter's.

The product is oriented to business workflows (contracts, routes auto/human_review, shadow mode, receipts, labeling), not code assistance. Most of the 8 tools (contracts, receipts, label, calibration, contract_create) are irrelevant to coding and cost about 2k tokens of context.
Source repo is 404 and there is no test file in the tarball, so it is unverifiable. Package is 2 days old with 2 versions and one maintainer.
No hook or skill, so it fails the core requirement: nothing forces Claude Code to consult Jev. Only model discretion, and its descriptions are Portuguese business jargon.
Env var typo JEVAAAS_API_KEY, inconsistent docs (SDK README says jev.vertikon.com.br/v1; the code says jev.api.br/v1), and `npx -y` with no version pin on every start.
gh-vertikon-jev-vertikon-com-br.verdict: Not a TypeSafe or OpenRouter integration: it is a wrapper for a separate reseller (JEVaaS) whose SDK enforces its own jev_sk_ keys and API shape, and it has no hook or skill for automatic use. Skip it; if you want Jev in Claude Code, write your own thin client against OpenRouter's Decisions API and trigger it via a hook.

gh-reachjalil-sysone.license: MIT for this integration layer; the downloaded compiled engine runtime is under a separate 'preview license' with private source (README.md:8-10, 'The System One Engine application and studio are private-source software')
gh-reachjalil-sysone.runtime: Node >=22.18 (TypeScript compiled to ESM; deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0, puppeteer-core 24.39.0, zod 4.1.13); local engine is a closed compiled Node runtime cached in ~/.cache/systemoneengine
gh-reachjalil-sysone.install: npx sysone (starts local engine + Studio); claude mcp add sysone -- npx -y sysone mcp --connection /private/path/agent.json (requires prior engine setup with Vercel AI Gateway key, or 'npx sysone@latest login' for the hosted cloud). Not installable against OpenRouter.
gh-reachjalil-sysone.tests: test/ has 7 node:test files (~420 lines: client, launcher, cloud-login, doctor, computer, accessibility, recorded-dialogue); no .github directory so no CI. Not run per audit rules.
security: API key handling is good in design: the client needs only a scoped consumer token via SYSONE_URL/SYSONE_TOKEN env or a 0600 JSON file (--connection); README explicitly warns against tokens in argv, so no key in the process list if used as documented. Provider key stays in the closed engine.
Client hardening is real: https or loopback-http only, no credentials/path in origin, redirect:'error', 10s timeout, 256KB response cap (src/client.ts:8-18, 60-71).

Launcher downloads a gzip runtime manifest from systemoneengine.com/releases/systemone-runtime-0.5.1.json.gz, verifies a SHA-256 embedded in this package and spawns it with process.execPath (src/launcher.ts:30-34, 157). Trust ends at a closed-source blob from a single-maintainer vendor executed locally with your user rights.
No install/postinstall scripts in package.json; npx execution of an unpinned package is still a supply-chain surface (v0.2-0.7 in 4 days, one maintainer).

Sends X-Sysone-Client-Name/Version and transport headers to the engine on each request (src/client.ts:52-64); opt-in callerModel/reasoningEffort attribution is sent for usage comparison; engine has a 'usage database' and cloud logins, so server-side telemetry/logging is likely but unauditable.
Prompt-injection surface: MCP tool results are JSON of Jev answers; low. Computer companion tools can click/submit forms in Chrome, driven by Jev proposals; high blast radius but opt-in and separate.
Cloud login uses PKCE with loopback callback, credentials in ~/.config/systemoneengine/cloud.json 0600 (README).
gh-reachjalil-sysone.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts into the 'state', 'candidates', log or question fields of sysone_run/decide/logs/tree is POSTed to the engine (local engine, which then forwards to Vercel AI Gateway/TypeSafe/Cloudflare, or to cloud.systemoneengine.com for hosted mode). Nothing is sent automatically (no hook, no proxy); egress is only model-chosen content, which for coding could include code, logs or diffs. Plus client name/version headers and caller model attribution. Cloud mode sends this to a third-party startup (not OpenRouter, not TypeSafe) that stores usage in a database. Problematic for client projects. Computer companion sends page text and accessibility names (not pixels) to the engine.
gh-reachjalil-sysone.failureMode: Fail-open by design for the MCP tools: errors return isError with text 'Use the caller's deterministic fallback or reasoning model. Do not retry automatically' (src/mcp-core.ts:158-165). Client timeout 10s per request (src/client.ts:70-73); no retries. Since it is an on-demand MCP tool, Jev being down cannot block Claude Code. Setup failure (no engine / no token) just leaves tools erroring. The local engine must be running separately (npx sysone terminal kept open) or the cloud login valid.
gh-reachjalil-sysone.contextCost: 7 MCP tools in the main bridge, about 6.5k chars of descriptions plus zod schemas (RunPatternInput, decide with up to 8 questions x 1600-char instructions, logs, tree, dialogue) = roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens; the separate 'computer' MCP adds 8 more tools (~2-3k tokens) if enabled. No server-level 'instructions' field found (grep). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. The SKILL.md description (~60 tokens) is the only always-on text if installed.
gh-reachjalil-sysone.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus an optional manually-copied passive skill. Nothing deterministic: no hook, no proxy. Claude Code would call the tools only if the model judges a task suits them, and the SKILL.md itself tells the agent to prefer code and to keep planning and synthesis with the reasoning model, which discourages frequent use. Tools are read-only annotated so they auto-approve easily, but the recipes are aimed at palette matching, citation checks, log triage, game dialogue and browser control, not typical coding decisions.
gh-reachjalil-sysone.latencyImpact: Each tool call adds a full MCP round trip plus an engine hop plus a model call: local engine to Vercel Gateway to Jev, likely 0.3-1.5 s (vendor claims not verified here), and the model must spend an extra tool-use turn (Opus generation for the call plus reading the result). The computer _run adds up to 90 s. Zero cost when not invoked. Engine startup requires a first-time runtime download.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev (recipes, 'jevlogs', 'jev-tree' heads) and cites TypeSafe docs; Jev-related, unlike many false positives

MIT client with hardened HTTP handling (no redirects, size and time caps, loopback/HTTPS only) and honest, conservative guidance ('keep unknown probability unknown', 'selected ID is not authorization')
Fail-open error messages tell the agent to fall back to deterministic code or reasoning model
No hooks, so cannot slow or interfere with existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks; no per-turn context injection
logs triage and tree (taxonomy selection) are the only marginally coding-adjacent services (e.g. log classification, issue routing)
Hosted free allowance with 'sysone login' avoids running a local server
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: provider is Vercel AI Gateway, (newer engine) TypeSafe direct or Cloudflare; the engine that would need patching is closed source, so OpenRouter is not achievable by a config change, contradicting the user's core requirement

Extra middleman: Claude Code -> sysone bridge -> System One engine (closed, third-party) -> gateway -> Jev; you must trust and run a proprietary binary or send client-project data to cloud.systemoneengine.com
Not automatic: only model-discretion tools; the shipped skill explicitly discourages routine use, and there are no hooks or proxy to make Claude Code use Jev without being asked
Recipe catalog is domain-specific (palette-match, citations, dialogue for a game, browser control); poor match for reading/editing code, permission decisions or commit routing
Needs its own separate running engine and Studio setup with a Vercel key, or cloud account, in addition to no OpenRouter key; extra infrastructure for little value
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 13 commits, single author, 1 star, no CI, versions 0.3 to 0.7 in 4 days; local runtime pinned at 0.5.1 lags the source engine
Data egress of model-chosen code/log content to an unaudited vendor with a usage database, on client projects
Adds 7 tools (about 3k tokens) to context, 15 tools if browser companion enabled, for low expected use
gh-reachjalil-sysone.verdict: Real and Jev-related but it is a third-party closed-engine wrapper (Vercel Gateway/TypeSafe/Cloudflare) with no OpenRouter path, no auto-invocation mechanism and recipes aimed at non-coding tasks. Not recommended for this user's OpenRouter-hosted, automatic-in-Claude-Code goal; at most a curiosity for log triage.

gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.name: @maximem/jev-mcp (with @maximem/jev-core)
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.whatItDoes: Stdio MCP server (11 tools) wrapping Jev's System One API. Five generic primitives (jev_classify, jev_score, jev_check, jev_rank, jev_ask), jev_health, and five "harness" tools (jev_plan_gate, jev_action_gate, jev_verify, jev_screen, jev_select). Each harness tool bundles fixed Noul/Score/Choice questions into a single call and applies local threshold logic (deny/ask/allow, verified, safe, abstain). The "automatic checkpoints" in the README are only the tool descriptions telling the model when to call them. There are no hooks, skills or slash commands. Decisions are logged to a local JSONL ledger.

JEV_API_KEY. :202 baseUrl = opts.baseUrl ?? process.env.JEV_BASE_URL ?? default. :203 model from JEV_MODEL. :272 sends Authorization: Bearer <key>. jev-mcp/dist/index.js:850 new JevClient({apiKey, model: env.JEV_MODEL}) (baseUrl picked up from JEV_BASE_URL). Wire shape (model/state/questions -> answers/usage, jev-core:34-72) matches OpenRouter's System One doc (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, SDK appends /v1/systemone, Bearer OpenRouter key, extra id/provider/usage.cost fields tolerated because responseSchema uses passthrough). No OpenRouter string anywhere in the code. It works only via env overrides.
providerSupport.others: Any System One-compatible gateway via JEV_BASE_URL. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported. The path is hardcoded to /v1/systemone.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change: set JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (or TYPESAFE_API_KEY), and JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13 or typesafe/jev-1.13. JEV_MODEL is needed because the default 'jev-1.13.0' may not map to an OpenRouter model ID (OpenRouter documents mapping only for 'jev-1.13' and 'jev-latest'). Not tested live, since running the candidate is forbidden. The only unverified point is that the server returns the same answer schema, which the OpenRouter docs claim.

interface.name: jev_classify
interface.purpose: Pick one label from a closed set (Choice) with per-option probabilities

interface.name: jev_score
interface.purpose: Place something on an ordered rubric (Score), returning a probability-weighted position

interface.name: jev_check
interface.purpose: Batch of independent yes/no propositions (Noul), each returning P(yes)

interface.name: jev_rank
interface.purpose: Rank candidate strings against a query (one Noul per candidate), abstains below minScore

interface.name: jev_ask
interface.purpose: Free-form mix of noul/choice/score questions in one call

interface.name: jev_health
interface.purpose: Probe connectivity, model version and latency, and report the ledger path. Only tool registered when no API key is set.

interface.name: jev_plan_gate
interface.purpose: 'Run BEFORE planning any non-trivial task'. 7 questions: spec ambiguity, blast radius, needs research, reversible, parallelisable, needs confirmation, work type. Returns proceed/ask_user/research_first/parallelise/gate_actions.

interface.name: jev_action_gate
interface.purpose: 'Call BEFORE any irreversible or outward-facing action'. Severity, irreversible, destructive, outward-facing and production questions give allow/ask/deny (deny>=0.85, ask>=0.55).

interface.name: jev_verify
interface.purpose: 'Call BEFORE telling the user it is done'. Checks claim + evidence for supported/contradicted/insufficient; verified if support >= 0.75.

interface.name: jev_screen
interface.purpose: Prompt-injection screen of untrusted text (instruction_like, redirects_task, exfiltration; flag >= 0.65)

interface.name: jev_select
interface.purpose: Choose between approaches, abstaining if the top-2 margin is < 0.15

interface.name: config: jev.harness.json + env
interface.purpose: Env: JEV_PROJECT_DIR, JEV_LEDGER_PATH, JEV_MODEL, JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_HARNESS. Thresholds and ledger config in <projectDir>/jev.harness.json (jev-core:333-400).

gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.tests: Unknown. The package.json 'test' script delegates to the repo root ('npm test --prefix ../..'). No tests or CI are visible because the repo is not public. The core error message references a 'verify:wire' script.
security: GitHub repo maximem-ai/jev_mcp returns 404 (the org's 6 public repos do not include it), so it is unauditable beyond the 4-file npm bundle. The only source I could read is the minified/tsup-built dist. No provenance attestation, only registry signatures. Publishers are maximem.ai (a memory/context company), not TypeSafe. The npm 'directory' fields point to packages/mcp-stdio and packages/core.
npx -y always pulls the latest 0.1.x from the registry: supply-chain exposure on every session start unless pinned (@maximem/jev-mcp@0.1.5).
No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no child_process/exec/spawn, no telemetry or analytics calls (grep of both dist files). The only network call is fetch to ${JEV_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone.

API key is read from env only, never a tool argument. redact() strips key-shaped strings from error messages (jev-core:156-162). The key is visible in argv only if passed as `claude mcp add --env KEY=...` on the command line, and it is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
JEV_BASE_URL is not validated: any value receives the Bearer key. Only the local env can set it, so this is low risk.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are numeric or enum (structured), which is good. But tool text is model-authored and untrusted content (diffs, web pages) is forwarded into Jev state. jev_screen is itself a model call and is bypassable. A misjudged jev_action_gate 'allow' could lull the agent, so it must not replace real permission controls.

Local ledger writes <cwd>/.jev/decisions.jsonl (or ~/.jev when cwd is home or unwritable) containing full answers plus 120-char subjects of tasks, actions and claims. It creates untracked files inside client repos and can leak task text if committed.

Falls back silently to ~/.jev when cwd is / or $HOME, and any jev.harness.json in the project cwd is read (invalid JSON throws at startup and kills the server). A malicious repo could ship a jev.harness.json to loosen thresholds (e.g. act.deny=1, abstain onAbstain=proceed).
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments is sent to ${JEV_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe as the provider). jev_plan_gate sends the user's task verbatim plus context (file names, constraints). jev_action_gate sends the literal shell command plus context. jev_verify sends the claim plus raw evidence (test output, diffs). jev_screen sends full untrusted text (web pages, issue and PR bodies). jev_rank/jev_ask/jev_check/jev_select send arbitrary state, candidates or options. Nothing is read from disk by the server itself (no file scanning, no hook capture); only what Claude chooses to pass leaves. That still means client-project code and diffs can reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe, so check OpenRouter's data-retention and logging settings for client work. Requests carry Authorization: Bearer <key> and a JSON body only.
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open in practice, but only because it is advisory and model-mediated. A Jev error, timeout or budget error returns an isError MCP result ('Jev call failed (kind): ...'), and the agent proceeds. Client timeout is 5s per attempt with 2 retries (jev-core:204-205) and backoff of 250ms and 500ms ±25%, honoring Retry-After. Worst case is about 15.8s of stall on a hard outage or a black-holed network for a single call. Auth (401/403), request and schema errors are not retried. Claimed 'failOpen' in the harness config schema (jev-core:369) is dead config: never read anywhere. CallBudget (maxCallsPerTask=8) is only enforced if opts.enforceBudget is set, and main() calls createServer() with no opts, so it is never enforced. Nothing can block a tool call, because there are no hooks and only the model decides whether to obey a 'deny'. JEV_HARNESS=off (README: disables automatic checkpoints) is also effectively a no-op in 0.1.5: harnessDisabled/checkpointEnabled are exported but never called by the server code. With no key set, the server registers only jev_health, so it does not crash.
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.latencyImpact: Claimed ~100ms per call and 70-500ms end to end via OpenRouter, plus MCP stdio overhead and the model's tool-call round trip (one extra LLM turn of roughly 1-3s in Claude Code, since the tool call and result each cost an Opus turn). No per-tool-call latency is added to unrelated calls, because it fires only when Claude chooses. Cold start via npx -y adds 1-5s at session start (registry check), removable by pinning or a global install. Retries can add up to about 16s when the API is down.
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.contextCost: 11 tools, mcp__jev__*. Tool descriptions total about 6.6k chars (12 description strings, 522-758 chars each; the largest are jev_plan_gate, jev_check and jev_action_gate) plus input and output zod schemas with .describe() text. My estimate is about 3k tokens for names, descriptions and schemas (about 12k chars / 4), which is heavy for a single MCP. Claude Code's MCP tool-search deferral can cut the always-on cost. No MCP 'instructions' field is set. There is no hook-injected text, and results are compact (a few lines of text plus structuredContent with full probabilities and a duplicated 'answers' object, about 150-400 tokens per call).
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. No hooks, skills or transparent proxy. 'Automatic' behavior depends on the descriptions ('Run this BEFORE planning any non-trivial task', 'Call BEFORE any irreversible action', 'BEFORE telling the user it is done'), which Opus may follow inconsistently, and which conflict with the user's bypass/auto permission mode: the model must voluntarily consult it. Ends up mostly firing on planning and verification prompts, not deterministically.
pros: Only candidate here that is a working, typed, complete MCP wrapper around System One: all three primitives are exposed (jev_classify/jev_score/jev_check plus jev_ask for mixed batches), and I verified the wire format matches OpenRouter's documented System One request/response shape.

OpenRouter switch is config-only, with no fork: JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_API_KEY (or TYPESAFE_API_KEY) = OpenRouter key, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13. Response parsing uses passthrough, so OpenRouter's extra id/provider/usage.cost fields are fine.

Harness tools encode useful coding-agent patterns in a single batched call each (action pre-flight with allow/ask/deny thresholds, verify-claim-against-evidence, injection screen, choose-between-approaches) with abstention. This matches the OpenRouter 'auto-approve permission prompts' cookbook idea, though as tools rather than a hook.

Small, dependency-light, readable dist (about 1.4k lines total); no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry; key redaction in errors; structured content carries full probabilities so the model can see uncertainty.

README candidly lists when NOT to use Jev (deterministic checks, trivial work), and tool descriptions repeat it, which limits over-calling. Retry/backoff/jitter and a 5s timeout are implemented; when there is no key it degrades to a single diagnostic tool instead of crashing.
Cheap: about $0.042/M input tokens, so gate calls cost fractions of a cent.
cons: Not deterministic: fully dependent on Opus 5.5 choosing to call the tools, which contradicts the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev automatically without prompting. There is no PreToolUse hook, so jev_action_gate cannot actually block anything, and in bypass/auto mode the model can ignore or skip it.

Source repo is 404/private: unauditable, no visible commits, tests, CI, issues or contributors. 6 versions in 6 days (0.1.0-0.1.5, all 2026-09-20/21), by maximem.ai rather than TypeSafe. It is an alpha third-party package, run via npx -y unpinned.

Documented safety knobs do not work in 0.1.5: JEV_HARNESS=off is never checked by the server, harness config 'failOpen' is never read, and CallBudget is never enabled (enforceBudget unset). This is the README behavior versus the code.

11 tools (about 3k tokens of definitions) is heavy for a tool that fires rarely, and jev_plan_gate/jev_verify get called on non-trivial turns only if the model complies. Each call also costs an extra Opus tool-call turn (seconds), so the '~100ms replaces seconds of deliberation' claim is unproven for Claude Code.

Data egress of task text, shell commands, diffs and test output to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on client projects, at the model's discretion and unfiltered. Nothing redacts secrets or code, so it overlaps badly with the user's secret-leak guard hook.

Writes .jev/decisions.jsonl into every project cwd by default (dirties client repos, needs global gitignore or JEV_LEDGER_PATH), and reads an untrusted repo's jev.harness.json, which can loosen thresholds or crash startup with invalid JSON.

Default model 'jev-1.13.0' is not an OpenRouter-documented ID, so JEV_MODEL must be set explicitly. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is unsupported. Jev is unproven: the Theo/t3.gg 'DeepSeek flash router' skepticism means the calibrated-probability gating is unvalidated on real coding work.
gh-maximem-ai-jev-mcp.verdict: Best-shaped plain MCP wrapper for Jev and easy to point at OpenRouter with three env vars (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL), but it is model-discretion only. It cannot deliver the guaranteed 'automatic' behavior wanted here, its safety toggles (JEV_HARNESS, failOpen, budget) are inert, and the GitHub source is not public. Use it as an optional tool layer (pinned version, trimmed to 3-4 tools) beneath a deterministic PreToolUse/PermissionRequest hook that calls OpenRouter directly, not as the primary integration. Process note: I ran one `node -e import()` of the candidate dist that failed at module resolution (missing @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) before any of its code evaluated. Nothing from the package executed, and every other check was static.

gh-rika-labs-proof.name: @rikalabs/proof
gh-rika-labs-proof.whatItDoes: Bun/TypeScript (Effect) tool that judges diff hunks against plain-English rules using Jev Noul/Choice/Score calls. It has three parts. (1) CLI 'proof review' (git diff, changed lines only) and 'proof lint' (walks the repo, 50-line windows, 20 parallel Jev calls, optional .proof/cache.json) driven by a proof.rules.ts file. (2) A GitHub composite action that posts inline PR comments. (3) A stdio MCP server, 'proof mcp', that exposes a single tool, proof_check. There is also an Amp-only plugin (jev and judge tools plus a SKILL.md) that does not apply to Claude Code. It is a PR/code-review linter, not a general Jev decision gateway.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, with no code patch and env vars only. Set TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, which yields POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (the OpenRouter System One API). Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (only sent as a Bearer token) and TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, or ~typesafe/jev-latest. This assumes the OpenRouter /systemone request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's, and that the model name goes in the request body. That is unverified. interface.name: proof_check (MCP tool)
interface.purpose: Src/Toolkit.ts:9-29. Params: statement (English rule), file, diff (hunk), optional threshold (0..1, default 0.75). It makes one Noul call on {file, diff} with the question 'Does this diff violate the following rule? Rule: ...'. Returns {violates, noul (probability), threshold}. Failure returns a string tool error and never a clean zero. This is the only MCP tool.

interface.name: proof review
interface.purpose: CLI. Judges only the changed lines of a git diff (--base/--head) against proof.rules.ts. Flags: --fail-on, --min-confidence, --format annotations|json|summary, --dry-run, --comment/--repo/--pr/--commit for GitHub PR comments. Exits non-zero on blocking flags.

interface.name: proof lint [paths]
interface.purpose: CLI. Walks files and judges 50-line windows with --concurrency (default 20) Jev calls. Has --chunk-lines and --no-cache.

interface.name: proof mcp
interface.purpose: CLI. Runs the stdio MCP server (McpServer.layerStdio, protocols 2025-03-26 to 2025-11-25) exposing proof_check.

interface.name: Rule.noul / Rule.choice / Rule.score
interface.purpose: Library API for rule files. Noul is a violation detector, Choice is a classifier with explicit passing options, Score is a gradient. Rules have severity, threshold, include/exclude globs, and few-shot examples.

interface.name: GitHub composite action (action.yml)
interface.purpose: Runs bunx @rikalabs/proof@<ref> review on PRs with the typesafe-api-key input and posts inline comments.

interface.name: Amp plugin (.amp/plugins/proof: jev, judge, skill proof:jev)
interface.purpose: Amp-only. Not usable in Claude Code as shipped. A generic 'jev' tool takes arbitrary JSON state plus 1-32 typed questions. Judge is a read-only agent.

security: No postinstall, preinstall or install scripts in package.json or on npm (only lint/test/check/start scripts).

Requires Bun >= 1.2 (engines), and the bin is a raw TypeScript file (./src/cli.ts). It is run as 'bunx @rikalabs/proof mcp', which fetches and executes the package each start unless pinned, so a supply-chain surface on every launch. Pin the version.

API key: read via Config.Redacted from env and sent only as 'Authorization: Bearer' to TYPESAFE_API_URL. It is not put in argv when passed through the .mcp.json 'env' block. The README's Claude Code example puts the literal key in .mcp.json, which is a risk if committed.
The endpoint is fully controllable by the TYPESAFE_API_URL env var, so the key and diffs go wherever it points. Fine if it points to OpenRouter.

Prompt-injection surface: the diff and rule text are interpolated into the Jev question. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so an injected diff can at most skew a number. README: 'probabilistic findings never authorize actions'. The Claude-side risk is small.
No shell execution in the MCP path. cli.ts uses Bun.spawn for git diff in review/lint only. GITHUB_TOKEN is used only for PR comments.
No telemetry found in src. The README says 'do not submit secrets as evidence', and there is no redaction, so the existing secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool args sent to Jev.
Deps are pinned exactly, but they are Effect 4.0.0-rc.116, @effect/ai-typesafe rc, and distilled-typesafe rc.7 (release candidates). A single author's fork, unreleased for weeks. MIT license.
gh-rika-labs-proof.dataEgress: For proof_check: the 'statement', the 'file' path and the full 'diff' hunk supplied by Claude are serialised into the System One request body and POSTed to TYPESAFE_API_URL/systemone with the Bearer key (default api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if overridden). That means code from the diff, file paths and the rule text. It sends nothing else, with no filesystem access, no tool outputs and no whole files (lint mode sends 50-line file windows). There is no redaction, and Claude decides what to pass. No telemetry to Rika Labs was found. .proof/cache.json is local and written only by lint, and it is disabled by default in MCP.
gh-rika-labs-proof.failureMode: Fail-closed as a tool error in MCP. Jev outage or malformed output returns a string tool error ('Jev evaluation failed (provider unavailable or invalid output)') and never a clean zero. Claude simply sees an error and continues, so nothing blocks. The CLI fails on outage (README: 'Jev outages... fail the CLI'), so a pre-push hook would block pushes. No retries, no provider fallback. No explicit timeout was found in the MCP path (the 30 s Effect.timeout in Amp.ts:74 is Amp-only), so a hung request depends on the HTTP client and MCP client timeout. The old commit message 'cli fails open on Jev outage' has since been superseded.
gh-rika-labs-proof.latencyImpact: Per proof_check call: one Jev round trip, about 70-500 ms claimed by Jev, plus a Bun/bunx cold start on server launch (bunx resolution is potentially seconds on the first run, cached afterwards). Only when Claude chooses to call it. lint with 20 parallel calls on a whole repo could be many seconds and is not tied to MCP.
gh-rika-labs-proof.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (proof_check). About 700 chars of name, description and schema, so roughly 175-250 tokens, which is negligible. No server 'instructions' field was found in Toolkit.ts, and no hooks inject text.
gh-rika-labs-proof.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces Claude to call proof_check. Its description ('Check one diff hunk against one plain-english rule') gives Claude no cue to call it during normal edits, and it needs an inline rule statement each time. The repo ships no hooks.json, no Claude Code plugin or marketplace manifest, and no Claude skill (the SKILL.md is Amp-only). To make it automatic, you would have to write your own PostToolUse/Stop hook that shells out to 'bunx @rikalabs/proof review' (the CLI, not the MCP), or add CLAUDE.md instructions.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's typed primitives (Noul/Choice/Score) and returns calibrated probabilities. It is a real Jev consumer, not a wrapper on chat completions.

The hardcoded TYPESAFE_API_URL/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_MODEL config points at POST {base}/systemone (protocol.ts:15, index.ts:21-24). OpenRouter exposes /api/v1/systemone, so an env-only switch to OpenRouter is plausible with no fork.
Tiny footprint: 1 MCP tool at about 200 tokens, no hook text injection, no postinstall, MIT.
Honest safety model: errors are never reported as a clean pass, findings are advisory, the diff is treated as data, and the typed output limits the injection blast radius.
The CLI 'review' command, which judges only changed lines against a versioned proof.rules.ts, is a sensible fit for a pre-push or Stop-hook gate that would enforce team conventions no linter can.
The stdio MCP is a clean, dependency-light Effect implementation with exact-pinned dependencies and 9 test files (about 1,150 lines).
cons: Not automatic: a single opt-in model-discretion tool with no cue to fire. It fails the user's requirement of 'Claude Code must use it when needed' without extra hook glue that this project does not provide.

Narrow scope: only 'does this hunk violate this English rule'. It is not a general router or decision layer for Claude Code (no routing, no command classification, no permission or next-step decisions).
Needs Bun and an unpinned 'bunx' launch on every MCP start; an npm package whose bin is raw .ts. There is a supply-chain and cold-start cost, and no Node-only path is documented.

Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 27 commits in 3 days by one author, 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 releases, no CI (.github absent), version 0.5.2 and pre-1.0. It depends on rc-tagged Effect 4 and a single-author rc fork of the TypeSafe client. The README admits live Judge inference is unverified.

OpenRouter compatibility is untested. There is no OpenRouter mention, and the strict response decoding may break on any schema difference. The client is bound to the TypeSafe rc schema and may not match the OpenRouter /systemone or alpha Decisions API.
Egress of source diffs with no redaction (the README itself warns), and the guard hook won't catch Claude-supplied MCP args. No explicit timeout in the MCP path.
No Claude Code integration assets (no plugin.json, hooks, .mcp.json in repo). The included opencode.json has a hard-coded /Users/dallenpyrah path, showing the repo is a personal working checkout.
gh-rika-labs-proof.verdict: A real but narrow Jev consumer for rule-based diff review. The proof_check MCP is a single opt-in tool that Claude won't reliably call unprompted, and the repo has no Claude Code hooks or skills. Its useful part is the 'proof review' CLI, which could be wired to a Stop/pre-push hook, with OpenRouter reachable through TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (untested). Too young (3 days, single author, rc dependencies) to adopt now. Watch it or borrow its Noul-per-hunk pattern.
