gh-remotehostai-jg.name: @remotehost/jg (jevgrep)
gh-remotehostai-jg.whatItDoes: Node CLI `jg` plus a stdio MCP server (`jg mcp <workspace>`) exposing one tool, search_code, for semantic code search. It chunks local files (TS AST / Python AST / line windows), shortlists with a local BM25 ranker (or evaluates everything with all=true), and POSTs batches of snippets (max 16 per request, 24k chars) to the vendor's own hosted backend (default https://jevgrep.com/api/v1/grep). That backend calls Jev via Vercel AI Gateway with server-side credentials. The client gets back one relevance probability per snippet and returns the snippets above a threshold. It is a hosted SaaS wrapper. The client is not a generic Jev client, and it does not use OpenRouter or the TypeSafe API.

providerSupport.evidence: src/src/score in search.mjs:221 `fetchImpl(`${endpoint}/api/v1/grep`...)` with header `authorization: Bearer ${token}`. Default endpoint auth.mjs:18 `'https://jevgrep.com'`. Env vars are only JEVGREP_ENDPOINT, JEVGREP_TOKEN, JEVGREP_CONFIG_DIR, JEVGREP_CACHE_DIR (README config table, auth.mjs:7,18,20; cache.mjs:5). grep for openrouter, typesafe, systemone, api/alpha and AI_GATEWAY in src/ finds only the README line 'Not affiliated with TypeSafe, Vercel or OpenAI.' README: 'The server calls Jev through Vercel AI Gateway using server-side credentials.' There is no model ID or Jev prompt/schema in the client.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (server-side only, inside the vendor's closed backend). JEVGREP_ENDPOINT accepts only an HTTPS origin with no path, so it cannot be pointed at openrouter.ai/api/v1.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Hard. The client does not talk to Jev. It sends {query, snippets[]} to a proprietary /api/v1/grep and expects {probabilities[]}. The Jev prompt/Choice-Noul-Score framing, model ID and gateway call live in the closed backend, which is not in the repo. Switching to OpenRouter would mean rewriting score() to build Jev Noul requests against /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone and parse the response. It would also drop the device-login auth and add an OpenRouter key. That amounts to a fork or rewrite, not a config change. Note the README says 'Old Jevgate logins', so the backend was a rebrand of an earlier project.

interface.name: MCP tool search_code
interface.purpose: Semantic search by behavior. Inputs: query (1-2000 chars), paths[] (default ['.']), limit (1-100, default 5), threshold (0.5), broad, all (judge every snippet; 'may take minutes'), max_evaluations (up to 20000), dry_run, no_cache, max_output (1024-64000, default 8000), debug, full, dump_candidates. Returns JSON with matches (path, startLine, endLine, symbol, text, probability), coverage and truncated (mcp.mjs:97-127). It is annotated readOnly but openWorld.

interface.name: jg [flags] "query" [paths]
interface.purpose: CLI semantic search; --all, --dry-run, --json, --files, --limit, --threshold, -g globs.

interface.name: jg exact <rg args>
interface.purpose: Passthrough spawn of ripgrep (cli.mjs:43-46).

interface.name: jg mcp [workspace-root]
interface.purpose: Start the stdio MCP server. The workspace root is realpath-validated and search paths must stay inside it.

interface.name: jg login / logout / status
interface.purpose: Device-code browser login to jevgrep.com. The token is saved at ~/.jevgrep/config.json (0600). logout revokes the token; status calls /api/v1/me.

gh-remotehostai-jg.license: MIT (CLI client only; backend closed and hosted). The first commit was titled 'Publish proprietary jevgrep CLI preview'. MIT was added on 2026-09-21 in 1.0.1.
gh-remotehostai-jg.runtime: Node >=22 (user has Node 24), needs ripgrep (rg) on PATH; Python 3 for Python parsing. Deps: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0, zod 4.6.5, typescript 5.9.3 (pinned).
gh-remotehostai-jg.install: npm install -g @remotehost/jg; jg login (browser email login on jevgrep.com); then `claude mcp add jevgrep -- jg mcp /abs/workspace`. The MCP server is bound to a single workspace root, so a per-project registration or a wrapper is needed. There is no plugin, hook or skill, and the README documents only Codex registration.
gh-remotehostai-jg.tests: None in the public repo (README: 'Development and tests are maintained internally'). No CI in the repo, only github-actions[bot] commits that sync a generated distribution. 9 npm versions in 2 days, no GitHub releases.
security: No npm postinstall or install scripts; the only script is `start`. The tarball is the same 11 files as the repo, and package.json differs only by private:true vs false.

Token handling is sound: config file mode 0600 in a 0700 dir, atomic write, token sent only as a Bearer header (never argv), credentials bound to the origin, redirect:'error', HTTPS-only endpoint (localhost HTTP allowed), 10s timeout on auth calls. JEVGREP_TOKEN can be supplied via env.
Shell exec is limited to execFileSync('rg', ...) with an argv array (no shell), spawn of xdg-open on login, and `jg exact`, which forwards raw args to rg. rg --files is scoped to the validated paths.

MCP paths are realpath-checked to stay inside the workspace root. rg respects .gitignore and hidden files are skipped, but the tool does not filter secrets: any non-ignored, non-hidden UTF-8 text file under 1 MiB (for example config.json, credentials.ts, tracked *.pem or tokens in source) can be chunked and uploaded. It has no secret scanner and no allow/deny list, and explicit file paths bypass ignore rules.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool returns source excerpts from the repo (untrusted content) into the agent context, the same as Read. Output is JSON of matches, and no LLM free text comes back from the server.

Hosted third-party trust: a closed backend (jevgrep.com, run by a two-person 'Remotehost' shop) plus Vercel AI Gateway. Claims 'source and query text are not stored in Jevgrep's database'. This is unverifiable, and there is no security or privacy policy in the repo.
Response validation is strict (probability array length and range checked). The cache stores only sha256 keys and numbers, with a 10 minute TTL.
gh-remotehostai-jg.dataEgress: On every non-dry-run search_code call, the query text and the source text of every candidate snippet go to https://jevgrep.com (then Vercel AI Gateway and Jev). Each snippet is up to about 2,000 chars plus surrounding 'context'. Shortlist mode sends the top 48 BM25 snippets. all=true can send up to 20,000 snippets, which is the whole repo up to 32 MiB, in 16-snippet batches with 3 concurrent requests. Uncommitted working-tree contents are included. File paths stay local, though symbol names and code inside snippets are sent. The bearer token identifies the account (email). Nothing goes to OpenRouter. Client-side telemetry: none found. Server-side usage metadata is stored per the README. This is a client-confidentiality problem for the user's client projects: the vendor's server is a third party that is not OpenRouter and not TypeSafe, so client code would leave the machine to a two-day-old startup backend.
gh-remotehostai-jg.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but non-blocking overall. It is a model-invoked MCP tool, so an error comes back as isError text and Claude falls back to Grep or Read. Timeout is 30s per request, with one retry on 502/504 or network TypeError after 300ms. There is no partial result: any batch failure aborts the whole scan (429 gateway rate limit throws). A missing login throws 'Run jg login'. The MCP server stays up when the backend is down, and no session hang is likely. all-mode 'may take minutes', so a long tool call can stall a turn.
gh-remotehostai-jg.latencyImpact: Adds a network round trip to a third-party backend plus a Jev call for each search_code call. Shortlist mode does 3 batches (48 snippets / 16) with 3 concurrency, so about 1-3 s per call is a plausible estimate (not measured). all=true on a mid-size repo means hundreds to thousands of requests, so minutes. Each search also does local rg discovery (15s cap) and reads and parses all files under the paths, including TypeScript AST parsing, on every call. Zero latency on turns where the tool is not called (no hook).
gh-remotehostai-jg.contextCost: 1 tool (search_code). Tool description of about 420 chars, an input schema with 13 params of about 1,500 chars, and an outputSchema that MCP clients may not send to the model. Server instructions of about 480 chars. About 600-800 tokens total (chars/4), small. Deferred tool loading in Claude Code makes the cost lower still. Per-call output is capped at 8,000 chars (max_output default) of JSON, so about 2k tokens per result. No hook-injected text.
gh-remotehostai-jg.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The description and server instructions nudge use for 'behavior-based discovery when exact names are unknown', but Claude will still often prefer Grep, Glob, or the user's existing GitNexus query tool and hook. There is no hook, skill trigger or proxy, so invocation is not deterministic. Note the user has GitNexus, which already covers semantic and graph code discovery locally.
pros: Genuinely Jev-powered, and it is one of the few real Jev consumers: it uses Jev as a per-snippet relevance probability (a Noul-like use), which fits Jev's typed-probability strength better than chat.
Small, readable, dependency-light client (about 1,000 lines of ESM, pinned deps, no postinstall). I found no obfuscation, no telemetry and no hidden network calls.

Good security hygiene in the client: 0600 token, no key in argv, origin-bound credentials, redirects blocked, workspace-root path validation, and dry_run/dump_candidates to see exactly what would be sent.
Honest coverage reporting (evaluated/eligible/selected, warnings that no match does not prove absence). Cache reduces repeat cost.
Cheap context footprint: one tool, about 700 tokens.
MIT license on the client, and it works with Claude Code via a plain stdio `claude mcp add`.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter, and there is no TypeSafe key path. Auth is only the vendor's own jevgrep.com login. The user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev requirement is not met, and the OpenRouter key would be unused. Retargeting means a rewrite (the Jev prompt lives in the closed backend).

Sends the user's code (queries, snippets, uncommitted files) to a closed third-party backend, jevgrep.com, then Vercel AI Gateway, with no secret filtering. This is unacceptable for client projects without contractual clearance, and it is an extra hop beyond OpenRouter/TypeSafe.

Very immature: repo created 2026-09-20, 10 commits, 2 committers (one is a bot), 6 stars, 9 npm versions in 2 days, no tests or CI visible, and the first commit was labelled 'proprietary'. The relicense to MIT came only in 1.0.1. The README admits it does not establish measured task speedup.

Vendor and availability risk: the service depends on a single small company's backend. The README notes prior rebrands ('Jevgate' logins not migrated). Accounts, quotas and pricing are undocumented in the repo.

Not automatic: it is only a model-discretion MCP tool. Claude will default to Grep or GitNexus, and there is no hook or skill to force use. It is bound to one workspace root per registered server, which is awkward for a many-project user.

Redundant with GitNexus (already installed, local, graph and semantic query) and with Claude's own Grep or Explore agents. A hosted per-snippet LLM scan costs latency (seconds, minutes with all=true) for something the local index does for free.

Local scans re-read and re-parse the repo on each call (rg plus TS AST), with no persistent index. Shortlist recall depends on a hand-tuned BM25 with a 12-group synonym table, so semantic search only judges the top 48 lexical hits.
gh-remotehostai-jg.verdict: A real Jev-powered semantic-grep MCP, but it is a closed SaaS wrapper, not an OpenRouter integration: it only talks to jevgrep.com, so it would send client code to an unvetted startup backend and cannot use the user's OpenRouter key. It is also not automatic and overlaps with GitNexus, so skip it for daily use, and treat it at most as a reference design for a Jev Noul-based relevance reranker to build yourself against OpenRouter.

gh-smlayero-jev-debtgate.name: jev-debtgate
gh-smlayero-jev-debtgate.whatItDoes: Tech-debt gate for agents and CI. Local code (git diff plus ast-grep AST pass) collects metrics, sends a compact "state" (stats, file list, static-analysis findings, up to 12,000 chars of raw diff) plus fixed Jev typed question packs (choice/noul/score) to the TypeSafe System One endpoint, then a local policy turns per-option probabilities into allow/review/block, a confidence floor and a suggested model tier. Exposes 3 MCP tools over stdio, a CLI (diff/gate/file/init/doctor), a GitHub Action, and an agent skill pack written for Cursor (.cursor/skills).

security: API key read from env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (or a cwd .env parsed by hand in src/env.ts:61-84); placed in Authorization header, not argv. If configured through .mcp.json env block it stays out of process argv (README pattern uses npx -y jev-debtgate mcp, key in env). Note the .mcp.json.example ships a literal empty key field, tempting people to paste the key into a project file.

With DEBTGATE_FAIL_OPEN=1 it returns verdict review with confidence_floor 0 and fail_open:true (assess.ts:26-37). No fetch timeout/AbortSignal (src/jev.ts:29), no retry on network errors; a stalled request can block the tool call for minutes. Backoff sleeps up to ~6 s on 429.

gh-smlayero-jev-debtgate.verdict: A tidy, well-scoped PoC that really uses Jev's typed primitives, and it can run against OpenRouter through env vars alone, but it is a narrow tech-debt reviewer that fires only at model discretion and ships raw diff excerpts off-machine. gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.name: jev-for-all (emirbartu)
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.whatItDoes: Multi-harness Jev wiring (OpenCode plugin is the primary product; Claude Code, Hermes, pi adapters are secondary). The Claude Code adapter (adapters/claude-code, plugin id "system-one") is a hooks-only plugin: on every UserPromptSubmit it asks Jev (via @openrouter/sdk client.alpha.decisions.create, model ~typesafe/jev-latest) which single skill from ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills fits the prompt (1 Choice + 4 Noul gates, optional rerank) and injects that skill body (max 8000 chars) as additionalContext; if Jev confidently says "none" it injects a note and a PreToolUse hook denies the Skill tool until the next prompt. Optional Stop hook (off by default) checks whether a completion claim is backed by a passing check and blocks the stop with a hint. Also ships a browser_task MCP server (needs separate jev-ultrafast checkout + CDP browser). Tool-subset routing is OpenCode-only and cannot be done in Claude Code. The npm package jev-for-all 0.2.1 only ships the OpenCode plugin (files: index.ts, src, spec, bin); the Claude adapter exists only in the git repo.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev.ts:1 imports OpenRouter from @openrouter/sdk; src/jev.ts:39 default model "~typesafe/jev-latest"; src/jev.ts:45 client.alpha.decisions.create (POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions per AGENTS.md); adapters/claude-code/hooks/system-one.ts:41 reads process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY and returns undefined (inert) if missing; :46 optional SYSTEM_ONE_SERVER_URL override passed as serverURL (src/jev.ts:50). No TYPESAFE_API_KEY or api.typesafe endpoint anywhere in code. AGENTS.md mentions /api/v1/systemone only as a possible replacement transport.
providerSupport.others: None. OpenRouter-only by design; OpenRouter is exactly the user's desired provider.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: N/A, already OpenRouter. Switching to /api/v1/systemone or TypeSafe direct would be moderate: replace the SDK call in src/jev.ts with a fetch and the response shape may differ.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook (hooks/system-one.ts, bun run, timeout 10s)

interface.purpose: Single tool browser_task(goal,url,max_steps): natural-language browser goal executed by jev-ultrafast policy loop; requires ~/jev-ultrafast checkout with its own .env

interface.name: Skill browser-task (skills/browser-task/SKILL.md)

security: API key read only from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var in the hook (system-one.ts:41); not put in argv by the Claude adapter. The OpenCode installer accepts --key on argv and can write apiKey into opencode.jsonc plaintext (irrelevant for Claude Code).

No shell exec in hooks; browser-mcp spawns `uv run ... jev-runner.py` via subprocess and passes goal via env vars (jev-runner.py header says creds stay in checkout .env, not on cmd line). browser_task drives a real CDP browser with model-chosen clicks and typed values: high prompt-injection and account-action surface.

No npm postinstall, no curl|sh. Marketplace entry uses a symlink to the parent dir (marketplace/system-one -> ..). Hooks import ../../../src/jev and ../../../spec, and .mcp.json uses ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/../browser-mcp, so a plugin install that copies the plugin dir into Claude's cache (rather than --plugin-dir in place) will likely break these relative paths (inferred, unverified).

Prompt-injection: skill bodies from ~/.claude/skills and project .claude/skills are injected as additionalContext; a malicious repo's .claude/skills is auto-scanned and can be injected based on the prompt (project skills are already trusted by Claude Code, but roster text and first 700 chars of bodies also go to a third party). Jev is not an instruction follower, but its answer steers which text is injected.
Local decision/usage log at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA:-$TMPDIR:-/tmp}/system-one-cc/decisions.jsonl (prompt length, chosen skill, tokens; not prompt text). Falls back to world-readable /tmp.

No telemetry found besides the OpenRouter call itself. Repo is 12 days old, single maintainer plus an AI agent account (67 of 93 commits authored by 'OpenCode Agent'); unreviewed code that runs on every prompt with full env access.
Hook could deny the Skill tool session-wide (see cons) which is an integrity/availability risk rather than a confidentiality one.
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.dataEgress: UserPromptSubmit: the full user prompt text (every prompt, including client-project prompts), the roster of skill ids/names/descriptions from ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills, and when rerank runs the first 700 chars of each shortlisted skill body -> openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (then to TypeSafe/whatever provider OpenRouter routes Jev to). Injected skill body stays local. Stop hook (only if SYSTEM_ONE_VERIFY=1): last 2000 chars of transcript incl. text, tool-call names and tool-result bodies plus final assistant message. browser_task: goal, URL and each step's page URL/title/visible text/controls to the policy model. No code files or diffs are sent by default, but prompts routinely contain code/snippets/secrets and the existing secret-leak guard does NOT cover UserPromptSubmit egress.
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: no API key, timeout, HTTP error, malformed answer, low confidence, unknown skill id, empty roster, cap of 500 calls/session all print nothing and exit 0 (hooks/system-one.ts main().catch, lib/decide.ts:41). Per-request timeout is 1000 ms (src/jev.ts:48; the 2500 ms default applies only to the OpenCode plugin, index.ts:88), retries disabled, so on slow OpenRouter calls the hook simply skips; hook command timeout 10 s bounds worst case. Caveat: fail-open covers Jev failure but not Jev being wrong: a confident false 'none' blocks the Skill tool for the whole turn/session (state persists until the next prompt overwrites it).
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.contextCost: Very low static cost: 0 tools from the hooks, 1 MCP tool (browser_task, ~150-300 tokens of description/schema, optional; can be removed by not loading .mcp.json), 1 skill description (~60 tokens), no MCP server instructions. Dynamic cost per prompt: an injected skill body up to 8000 chars (~2000 tokens) when Jev picks a skill (duplicates what Claude would load itself via Skill tool), or a ~20-token 'skills routed externally' note when Jev says none. Roster covers only ~/.claude/skills and project .claude/skills (plugin skills are not scanned).
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse:Skill, optional Stop) fire on every prompt with no user action, matching the 'never say use jev' requirement, but only for skill routing and the optional completion gate. browser_task is model-discretion MCP tool plus a description-triggered skill. No tool-catalog routing, no coding/decision help for edits, commits, permissions, or model routing.
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.latencyImpact: Synchronous on every user prompt: bun cold start (~50-100 ms) + directory scan of skill folders + 1 OpenRouter round trip (author measures ~0.6 s average per skill-route run; docs claim 70-500 ms), and a second call when roster >40 skills or top probability <0.5. Hook budget 10 s, request cap 1 s, so worst case adds ~1 s per prompt; nothing per tool call except a trivial local file read for PreToolUse:Skill. Stop hook adds ~0.7 s per completion claim only if enabled.
pros: Only candidate so far with a real, automatic Claude Code integration: hooks fire per prompt without the user ever saying 'use jev' and the code is fail-open with an inert no-key path (hooks/system-one.ts:41, lib/decide.ts).
Uses OpenRouter natively via @openrouter/sdk alpha.decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, exactly the user's provider; no rewrite needed.

Sensible use of Jev (typed Choice/Noul, cheap wrong-is-harmless hints), spend cap of 500 calls/session, local JSONL usage log, 31 adapter tests plus fixtures/L1 evals, and honest WHERE-JEV-WINS.md listing losses.
Optional Stop verification gate (claim/ran/passed) is a genuinely relevant daily-coding idea for a bypass-mode user, default off, fails open, and reuses shared spec/decisions.json thresholds.
Very small static context footprint (no server instructions, 0-1 MCP tools) and MIT license; cost about $0.0001 per decision.
cons: Value is narrow for this user: skill routing only. Claude Code already auto-triggers skills from descriptions; Jev adds a ~0.6-1 s blocking hop on every prompt to save little. Tool-subset routing, the headline feature, is impossible in Claude Code (README 'Harness ceiling').

Roster blind spot: only scans ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills, not plugin skills (gitnexus-*, caveman:*, anthropic-skills:*). If Jev answers a confident 'none', PreToolUse denies the Skill tool for the turn, blocking legitimate plugin/marketplace skills the user relies on (roster.ts:199-201, system-one.ts:114-126). Highest-risk behavior for this setup.
Sends every prompt (client-project content included) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every turn, outside the user's secret-leak guard; Stop gate would send transcript tails including tool results.

Immature and fragile install: 12 days old, 6 stars, 2 authors (67/93 commits by an 'OpenCode Agent' account), no releases/tags, no CI, Claude adapter not in the npm package, README paths hard-coded to /home/gerius/..., hooks depend on ../../../src and bun (not in the user's stated toolchain: Node 24 / uv) plus an undocumented `bun install` for @openrouter/sdk; the marketplace symlink/relative-path layout probably breaks under a cached plugin install, so --plugin-dir or a fork would be needed.
Request timeout is 1000 ms in the hook (src/jev.ts:48) so cold OpenRouter calls will often silently no-op; the hook does not pass the 2500 ms used by the OpenCode plugin.
browser_task duplicates the already-installed Playwright MCP, needs an external ~/jev-ultrafast checkout with its own .env, and lets a small policy model drive clicks/typing on real sessions.
Jev is an unverified/beta model (Theo's 'router' claim), and all accuracy numbers here are author-reported on the author's own corpora (64 cases).
gh-emirbartu-jev-for-all.verdict: Best-in-class for 'automatic, no prompting' on OpenRouter because it is real hooks-based Claude Code glue, but it only routes skills (plus an optional stop-time verification gate) and its Skill-tool denial can block the user's plugin skills. Worth borrowing the pattern (fork the Stop verify gate, fix roster/deny logic, use Node instead of bun), not installing as-is.

gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.name: jev-dev-harness
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.whatItDoes: TypeScript/Node stdio MCP server plus CLI (jev-dev) that wraps Jev-style Noul/Score/Choice calls into 5 dev-workflow tools: context ranker (per-file relevance scoring), tool-manifest pruner, shell-command guard (regex classifier, Jev only for unknown commands), git-diff patch reviewer, and semantic linter. It also ships a git pre-commit hook, an opt-in local reverse proxy that can inject tool hints into Anthropic API requests, a telemetry dashboard, and rule files (CLAUDE.md etc.) telling agents to call its tools. Despite the README's "hooks" talk there are NO Claude Code PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks, only a git pre-commit script. Automatic invocation relies entirely on the model reading instruction text.

providerSupport.evidence: src/shared/typesafe-client.ts:266-292 executeOpenRouterDecisions() POSTs https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with {model,state,questions}, but it is only used when the model slug starts with typesafe/ or ~typesafe/ (:449-455). The default OpenRouter model is deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash (:208, README 'OpenRouter Emulator'), routed to executeOpenRouterChat() at https://openrouter.ai/v1/chat/completions with a system prompt telling a generic LLM to emit Jev-shaped JSON (:337-395). Actual Jev is used only if the user sets OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. In that case any HTTP 400 or 'does not exist' error silently falls back to the DeepSeek emulator (:462-470). The System One endpoint /api/v1/systemone is NOT used anywhere. Env vars: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_MODEL, OPENROUTER_EFFORT, JEV_PROVIDER, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. Native path uses @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 TypeSafeClient (:260-270), default model 'jev-latest'. A Vercel AI Gateway path is also present (:236-254). Provider auto-detection order at :153-184 picks Vercel, then TYPESAFE key, and only then OPENROUTER key.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/typesafe, model typesafe-ai/jev). Deterministic offline heuristic fallback.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. Set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) to reach the real Decisions API without code changes. A small patch would remove the silent DeepSeek fallback on 400 and add error visibility, so the user does not unknowingly get a chat-model emulation. The Decisions API response mapping (json.answers) assumes the same shape as the SDK result, which is not verified.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_rank_context
interface.purpose: Rank repo files by relevance to a task. Stage A walks the tree, Stage B does heuristic scoring, Stage C makes one Jev call PER candidate file, sending path and a snippet up to 1200 chars (src/context-ranker/stage-c-jev.ts:101-113,164). Results are cached.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_rank_tools
interface.purpose: Prune a passed-in tool manifest to the top-N tools for a task (src/tool-ranker/). The agent must pass the tool list itself, so this is not a transparent MCP-tool-search replacement.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_guard_check
interface.purpose: Classify a shell command as read-only, modify-local, destructive-local, network or production-sensitive with a regex classifier. Jev is called only for 'unknown' commands (tool-guard/index.ts:31-45). Advisory only: it does not block anything unless the agent voluntarily calls it.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_review_patch
interface.purpose: Audit a git diff (staged, range, or raw) for regression risk, scope creep, auth/DB changes, missing tests and secrets. Runs git via execSync (diff-extractor.ts:123). Returns a risk score and status.

interface.name: MCP tool jev_lint_semantic
interface.purpose: Run 6 built-in semantic rules over a diff (secrets, dangerous migration, UI/DB mixing, auth boundary, generated-file edits, missing tests).

interface.name: CLI jev-dev setup / provider / doctor / compare / dashboard / update / uninstall
interface.purpose: Wizard that writes API keys to ./.env AND ~/.jev-dev/config.json in plaintext (cli/setup.ts:215-250), registers the MCP server in Codex, Claude Desktop, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Trae and Cline/Roo configs. It does NOT register with Claude Code (~/.claude.json or `claude mcp add`).

interface.name: CLI jev-dev context rank / guard check / patch review / lint semantic / tools rank / proxy
interface.purpose: Same pipelines as the MCP tools. The proxy is a local reverse proxy (127.0.0.1:8789 for Claude) that forwards to api.anthropic.com and appends '[Jev Router Hint...]' to the last user message (proxy/server.ts:97-107, router.ts). It is opt-in and needs ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.

interface.name: CLI jev-dev hooks install
interface.purpose: Writes a .git/hooks/pre-commit shell script that runs `jev-dev patch review --staged` and blocks the commit on exit 2 (src/hooks/index.ts:10-48). It is a git hook, not a Claude Code hook.

interface.name: Rule/skill files (CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills/typesafe-ai, .agents/skills/jev-tool-guard, jev-patch-reviewer, jev-context-ranker)
interface.purpose: Prose instructing agents to call the tools before running commands and to append a mandatory '### Eficiencia Jev' block (in Portuguese) to every answer. Claude Code loads it only if the user copies it into their project or ~/.claude.

security: Repo is 9 days old (created 2026-09-21), 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor (55 commits), 17 npm versions in 4 days (0.1.0 to 0.2.7). Not vetted by anyone else.

API key is stored in plaintext in ./.env in the CURRENT project directory and in ~/.jev-dev/config.json (cli/setup.ts:215-250). On client projects that risks committing the key, and the wizard does not add .env to .gitignore.
typesafe-client.ts:21 calls process.loadEnvFile() on import, so it loads whatever .env sits in the cwd of the MCP process, i.e. every project's secrets.

MCP server config written by setup places the key in an `env` block (visible in the config file, not argv). Recommended launch is `npx -y jev-dev-harness`, which runs unpinned latest code from npm on every session start, so a supply-chain risk given a single-maintainer, 9-day-old package.

No npm postinstall script (package.json scripts: build, prepublishOnly, dev, test). No curl|sh installer. `jev-dev update` runs execSync `npm install -g` (cli/index.ts:517). git is run via execSync with string-built args (diff-extractor.ts:123): check for injection through commitRange, which the model controls via MCP args.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results (JSON) embed `instructionForAgent` text ('OBRIGATORIO: ...present the block') that steers the main model (mcp/server.ts:234,316). The README-mandated Portuguese efficiency footer would be added to every answer. File snippets and diffs go to the Jev model, and their content could try to manipulate scores.

Redaction is regex-based (redaction.ts:7-70) covering PEM keys, JWT, ghp_/sk-/xox tokens, bearer headers, DB URLs and key=value. It is applied to state before sending (typesafe-client.ts:435 redactState). It will miss unusual secrets, client PII and proprietary code.

Telemetry is local only: appends to ~/.jev-dev/telemetry.jsonl, including the raw command strings and task text (telemetry.ts:229-412). The only external call besides Jev is the npm registry update check (update-checker.ts:114). No phone-home found.

Proxy mode forwards all request headers, including Authorization / x-api-key / OAuth bearer, to upstream. It sits in the path of all Anthropic traffic, is HTTP on localhost, and has no auth. It also buffers whole bodies (streaming is pumped manually), which is risky for a subscription/OAuth login.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.dataEgress: To the Jev provider only, redacted by regex: (1) jev_rank_context sends the task text, plus for each candidate file its relative path, extension, size, matched symbols and up to 1200 chars of the file snippet, one request per candidate, concurrent via Promise.all; (2) jev_guard_check sends the command string and task, only for commands the regex classifier could not classify; (3) jev_review_patch and jev_lint_semantic send diff content and the task; (4) the proxy sends the last user message (800 chars), the tool names and 150-char descriptions to the Jev provider. On OpenRouter with the default config, this code goes to whatever deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash provider OpenRouter routes to, not to TypeSafe. Also sent: HTTP-Referer 'https://github.com/marcelo/jev-dev-harness' and X-OpenRouter-Title headers. Local: telemetry.jsonl with commands and tasks. npm registry: version check.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.failureMode: Fail-open by design. SafeJevClient.systemOne() catches every error and returns {ok:false,fallback:true} (typesafe-client.ts:514-524). Default timeout 15000 ms (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, :119), the proxy uses 4000 ms, and the SDK path does 1 retry. The context ranker falls back to heuristics only (stage-c-jev.ts:153-160). The guard falls back to the regex classifier, and unknown commands then require confirmation. The proxy passes the request through unchanged. With no key it silently runs in offline heuristic mode. Downside: a slow API can stall a tool call for up to 15 s, and a wrong OpenRouter model name silently degrades to DeepSeek or heuristics with no loud error. The MCP server is a stdio child of Claude Code, so if `npx -y` cannot fetch the package at startup, the server fails to connect.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.contextCost: 5 MCP tools (jev_rank_context, jev_rank_tools, jev_guard_check, jev_review_patch, jev_lint_semantic). The TOOLS array is about 4,850 chars, roughly 1,200 tokens of tool definitions, and the server sets no `instructions` field (mcp/server.ts:169-179). Each tool call returns pretty-printed JSON (JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)) plus an efficiencyReport with a long Portuguese instructionForAgent, adding several hundred tokens per call and pushing the model to add a footer to answers. No Claude Code hooks are installed, so hooks inject nothing. The proxy appends a ~60-char hint to the last user message only when the proxy is used. The CLAUDE.md/skill files, if copied in, add about 500-1,000 tokens to every session.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by prose rule files (CLAUDE.md / SKILL.md). The only deterministic pieces are a git pre-commit hook and an opt-in Anthropic reverse proxy (hint injection, not a real tool call). There are no Claude Code PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks. This does NOT meet the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev automatically without prompting, unless the user adds their own hook wrapper around the CLI (`jev-dev guard check`) or a CLAUDE.md instruction, which still depends on the model complying.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.latencyImpact: Guard: under 1 ms for regex-classified commands, but an unknown command adds one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms, 15 s timeout ceiling). Context ranker: one Jev call per candidate file, run concurrently, so a burst of N requests to OpenRouter with a rate-limit risk. The README claims 280 ms, and the code comment says 'reduces from 40s+ to under 3s'. With the DeepSeek emulator path each call is a full chat completion, so expect 1-3 s or more. Patch review is claimed at about 750 ms. The proxy adds a Jev round trip (up to 4 s) to EVERY Claude API turn if enabled. The npx cold start of the MCP server may add several seconds on the first launch. The token savings claims (92% reduction, ~$1400 to $107) are hard-coded estimates (`initialCandidates*1200 - selected*900`, server.ts:210), not measurements. Claude Code with GitNexus and Grep/Glob already avoids reading dozens of files.
pros: Real code that calls the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) with typesafe/ or ~typesafe/ model slugs (typesafe-client.ts:266-292, 449-455), so real Jev on OpenRouter works with a single env var change (OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13).

Wraps Jev in sensible, well-structured Noul/Score/Choice question sets (file relevance, command destructiveness, patch risk, tool routing) and shows how to compose all three primitives. This is a good reference for writing our own hook.
Fail-open everywhere with timeouts, a redaction pass before egress and result caching, so it will not block work when Jev is down.

Tool-guard's deterministic regex classifier (classifier.ts, 270 lines) runs locally and only escalates unknown commands to Jev; the design fits a PreToolUse Bash hook, and the CLI (`jev-dev guard check`) could be called from a hook script.

MIT licence, only 4 runtime dependencies (MCP SDK, @typesafe-ai/sdk, commander, ignore), no postinstall. 142 vitest tests across 22 files exist (tests/), including mcp server, hooks, redaction and typesafe-client error tests, though I did not run them.
Small MCP surface (about 1.2k tokens) which is cheap in context.
cons: Not automatic in Claude Code: no PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks, no plugin.json or marketplace, setup does not register with Claude Code (only Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex etc.). It relies on the model choosing to call the tools, which is the opposite of the 'never prompt to use jev' goal, and with Opus 5.5 in bypass mode a tool the model doesn't need simply gets ignored.

OpenRouter default is an emulator: the default model is deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash via chat completions with a made-up JSON schema, so the returned 'probabilities' are not calibrated Jev outputs. Any 400 from the typesafe/ slug silently falls back to DeepSeek (typesafe-client.ts:462-470). Provider auto-detect prefers TYPESAFE/Vercel keys over OpenRouter, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone yields DeepSeek, not Jev.

The tools duplicate what Claude Code already does well. The context ranker sends a Jev call per file (N calls, 1200-char snippets of possibly client code) to save tokens Claude already saves with Grep/Glob/GitNexus; the guard duplicates the user's existing secret-leak and permission setup and is advisory only; and in bypass/auto mode it never gates anything.

Jev is a poor fit for the large-text jobs: the patch reviewer and semantic linter feed diffs (32k context limit, no reasoning trace) to a beta System One model; the false-positive/negative rate is unmeasured, and the README numbers (92.4% token cut, 5x faster, $15,500/yr) are simulator constants, not benchmarks.

Tool results force a Portuguese 'Eficiencia Jev' footer onto every reply via instructionForAgent, which is intrusive noise and a prompt-injection-style side channel into the main model. It is bad for client-facing sessions.

Very immature and single-author: created 2026-09-21, 0 stars, 1 contributor, 17 releases in 4 days, CI only for a lint workflow (no test CI), and server version string hard-coded '0.1.0'. Running unpinned `npx -y` from it on client projects is a supply-chain risk.
Setup writes the API key to ./.env in the project dir and process.loadEnvFile() ingests project .env files, which is unsafe for client repos; the wizard does not gitignore it.

The proxy mode would sit in front of the Anthropic subscription/OAuth traffic, forwarding all headers, and adds a Jev round trip per turn plus a hint suffix that could disturb prompt caching; the user's setup (OAuth login) makes ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL routing awkward and risky.
gh-celolopes-jev-dev-harness.verdict: Not a good primary integration: it is an alpha, single-author MCP toolkit whose 'automatic' behaviour is just prose telling the model to call its tools (no Claude Code hooks), and its OpenRouter path defaults to a DeepSeek chat emulator rather than real Jev. Its value is as a reference for the Jev question designs and OpenRouter Decisions API call shape (with OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13), not as something to install.

gh-tupe12334-holstered.name: holstered
gh-tupe12334-holstered.whatItDoes: A single Rust binary (`holstered`) that runs as a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook, and also for Codex, Gemini CLI, Hermes and Cline through the polyhook crate. On each prompt it scans SKILL.md files under ~/.claude/skills, ~/.codex/skills, ~/.agents/skills, ~/.gemini/skills and ~/.hermes/skills. It shortlists the top 20 by BM25 over name and description, then sends the shortlist to Jev as one Choice question (skills plus a "none" option). If Jev picks a skill, that SKILL.md body (capped at 8,000 bytes, shared across picks) is injected as additionalContext. Up to 2 runner-up skills are injected when their probability is at least 0.2. On none, error, timeout or missing key it injects nothing and passes the prompt through. Its role is skill routing, not general Jev decision support such as gating tool calls, picking models or triaging.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev.rs:57-58: DEFAULT_URL = "https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions", JEV_MODEL = "~typesafe/jev-latest". src/jev/endpoint.rs:25-27 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY (Jev is disabled if it is unset) and lets HOLSTERED_JEV_URL override the URL. src/jev/ask.rs:64-66 sends `authorization: Bearer <key>`. The request body (src/jev/request.rs:94-102) is {state:{user_prompt}, model, questions:{skill:{type:"choice", instructions, criteria}}}, and the answer is read from answers.skill.choice and answers.skill.probabilities (pick.rs:42-45, runners_up.rs:76). There is no TYPESAFE_API_KEY handling and no console.typesafe.ai endpoint. HOLSTERED_JEV_URL could point to another Decisions-compatible URL, but the key variable is fixed to OPENROUTER_API_KEY and the model is hard-coded. HOLSTERED_KEV_URL selects a local Kev System One server with no key.
providerSupport.others: Local Kev (jaredpalmer/kev, open weights) through HOLSTERED_KEV_URL. If both are set, Kev wins. It does not use the /api/v1/systemone endpoint on OpenRouter; only the alpha /decisions endpoint.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed: OpenRouter is the native default.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook: `holstered` (no args, reads hook JSON on stdin)
interface.purpose: The only real interface, declared in plugins/claude-code/hooks/hooks.json as {type:command, command:"holstered"}. It returns additionalContext with `SKILL SELECTED by holstered: <name> (<path>). Follow it for this task.` followed by the SKILL.md body (src/inject.rs:23-27), or an empty approve response.

interface.name: CLI flag: -v / --version, -h / --help
interface.purpose: Only flags parsed by clap (src/main.rs:19-29).

interface.name: Claude Code plugin `holstered@holstered`
interface.purpose: Installed with `/plugin marketplace add tupe12334/holstered` then `/plugin install holstered@holstered`. It ships only the hook config and requires the `holstered` binary on PATH (npm -g, cargo, brew or go).

interface.name: Env vars
interface.purpose: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, HOLSTERED_JEV_URL, HOLSTERED_KEV_URL, HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS (default 8000), HOLSTERED_PICK_THRESHOLD (unset by default), HOLSTERED_RUNNER_UP_THRESHOLD (0.2 on Jev, 0.15 on Kev), HOLSTERED_SKILLS_DIRS. There are no MCP tools and no skill of its own.

gh-tupe12334-holstered.runtime: Rust, single static binary (ureq, bm25, polyhook, walkdir, gray_matter). Distributed through npm (a bin/holstered.js wrapper plus per-platform @holstered/holstered-linux-x64 and similar packages as optionalDependencies, with no install scripts), crates.io, Homebrew, and a Go shim that downloads the release binary and checks it against SHA256SUMS. Needs no Node or Python at runtime.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.install: npm install -g holstered   (or cargo install holstered), then in Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add tupe12334/holstered ; /plugin install holstered@holstered ; and export OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment Claude Code starts from (for example the "env" block of ~/.claude/settings.json).
gh-tupe12334-holstered.tests: Integration tests in tests/ (agents, fallback, inject, kev, passthrough, runners_up, timeout, version, help) use assert_cmd and mockito against a fake endpoint. There are unit tests for bm25, pick, runners_up, prompt and skills. An eval harness (evals/eval.rs, cases.json, cassettes, baseline.json) covers a 38-prompt set. CI runs cargo fmt, clippy -D warnings and cargo test, plus go vet and go test. release.yml uses npm provenance/trusted publishing and a smoke test of the packed install. I did not run any of it.
security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from the environment only and sent as a Bearer header via ureq (src/jev/ask.rs:64-66). It is not in argv, so it does not show up in the process list. Error strings carry only the status or transport failure, not headers (ask.rs:61-62).

There is no telemetry, no shell execution, no postinstall script (npm view shows no scripts) and no curl|sh installer. The hook only reads local files and makes one HTTPS POST. The Go shim downloads a release binary and verifies SHA256SUMS. The npm packages use provenance.
HOLSTERED_JEV_URL is an unrestricted override, so anyone who can set the env can redirect prompts and the key to another host. That only matters if the environment is already compromised.

Prompt-injection surface: the chosen SKILL.md bodies (up to 8KB) are injected verbatim into context with 'Follow it for this task'. Any file in ~/.claude/skills or the other scanned roots, including third-party skills, is therefore trusted. The skill descriptions (the criteria sent to Jev) are attacker-influenced text only if a malicious skill is installed. Jev's output is a constrained choice, and unknown names are dropped (pick.rs:50), so the model cannot inject free text.
Skills are walked with follow_links(true) up to depth 5, so symlinks in skill dirs are followed, and any SKILL.md with a description is read.

Supply chain: a single maintainer, 4 stars, project less than a week old (created 2026-09-25, npm 1.2.0 published 2026-09-26). The hook is a binary that runs on every prompt with access to the key, so it needs review or a pinned version. A Rust build from source (cargo install --locked) would be safer than a prebuilt npm binary, which I did not inspect.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions on every submitted prompt (skipped only if the prompt is empty, no skill has a BM25 match, or the key is unset): the user prompt clipped to its first 500 and last 1,500 characters (src/prompt.rs:122-133, so up to 2,000 chars; CONFIGURATION.md wrongly says first 2,000), the name and description of up to 20 shortlisted skills, and the API key. It sends no file contents, diffs, tool outputs or conversation history. Pasted logs or code in the prompt do go out, so for client projects any pasted secrets or proprietary code in the prompt reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe. OpenRouter's data policy applies. Setting HOLSTERED_KEV_URL to a local Kev keeps everything on the machine.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.failureMode: Fail-open. Any read error, missing key, HTTP error, timeout or unparsable answer leaves the prompt untouched (src/main.rs:33-39, src/select.rs:104-106 prints the error to stderr, tests/timeout.rs and tests/fallback.rs). The default timeout is 8s (HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS), well under Claude Code's default hook timeout, which the docs put at 60s. A slow Jev delays every prompt by up to 8s before it gives up. It retries nothing and has no circuit breaker, so a Jev outage costs 8s of latency per prompt. Lowering HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS to about 2000 is advisable.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.latencyImpact: Synchronous, blocking, once per user prompt (not per tool call). Its own numbers are a median of 915 ms per prompt and about 0.7-1s extra per prompt with a shortlist, from the README and CONFIGURATION.md. I did not measure it. BM25 and the skill scan are local and fast. Worst case is 8s on a timeout. Prompts that match no skill terms cost nothing extra.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.contextCost: No MCP tools, so there are no tool definitions and no server instructions. The hook injects text only when Jev picks a skill: up to 8,000 bytes (about 2k tokens) total, plus about 30 tokens of header, and up to 2 runner-ups share that budget. It is often zero on chit-chat prompts. Because a hook re-injects on every matching prompt, a long session can accumulate several skill bodies, since the same skill is not deduplicated across turns.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), with no model discretion. It runs on every prompt without the user saying anything. The hook itself is deterministic, and Jev is called inside it.
pros: Fully automatic: a UserPromptSubmit hook fires on every prompt with no 'use jev' wording, which is exactly the requested integration model, and it coexists with the existing PreToolUse and GitNexus hooks.
Native OpenRouter support with the right endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) and model (~typesafe/jev-latest), using only OPENROUTER_API_KEY. No code patching is needed.
Fail-open by design (empty response on any error, timeout or missing key), it never blocks a prompt, and its tests cover timeout and fallback.
Zero context cost when it declines, no MCP tool definitions, and injection is capped at 8KB. Runtime is a static Rust binary, so there is no Node or Python startup and no postinstall script.

Uses Jev for what it is designed for: a typed Choice with probabilities, with a pick threshold and runner-up threshold you can tune. The README reports 29/32 correct picks and 6/6 correct abstentions on its own 38-prompt set, with a 915 ms median.
Small, readable codebase (about 700 lines of source) that is easy to audit or fork. MIT, npm provenance, CI with clippy and fmt.
cons: Solves a narrow problem: routing prompts to local SKILL.md files. It only helps if you keep many custom skills under ~/.claude/skills. It does not scan project-level .claude/skills or plugin-provided skills, because roots.rs:155-161 only looks in $HOME dirs, so the plugin and skills available in this environment are largely ignored unless HOLSTERED_SKILLS_DIRS is set. Claude Code already auto-triggers skills from their descriptions, so the marginal value is modest.

Sends every prompt (up to 2,000 chars, including pasted logs or code) plus skill descriptions to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. This is a real concern on client projects, and there is no redaction or per-project opt-out except unsetting the key. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
Adds about 1s of blocking latency to every prompt, up to 8s during a Jev outage, with no circuit breaker. Jev is in beta and the OpenRouter endpoint is 'alpha', so the URL and schema may change.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-25, 48 commits, 4 stars, 1 contributor, 3 npm versions in 3 days). There is no independent evidence beyond its own small eval, and I did not run any of it. Installing an unreviewed prebuilt binary that handles your API key on every prompt needs some care.

Documentation inconsistency (CONFIGURATION.md says the first 2,000 chars are sent; the code sends head 500 plus tail 1,500). Skill bodies are injected verbatim with 'Follow it', so any third-party skill becomes trusted instructions.

It does not use Jev for other daily-coding decisions such as permission or tool-call gating, model routing, or task triage. The 'Jev' part is limited to one Choice call. It also needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment Claude Code starts from, which is not configured yet.
gh-tupe12334-holstered.verdict: The best fit found so far for 'automatic, no prompting': a deterministic, fail-open hook that already targets the OpenRouter Jev Decisions API correctly. Its scope is only skill routing over ~/.claude/skills, and it sends every prompt to OpenRouter, so it is worth using only if you keep a large personal skill library; audit or build it from source, set a shorter timeout (about 2s), and avoid it on sensitive client repos.

The model decides what to send, and per the built-in instructions this will typically be code snippets, diffs, user requests, and tool traces. With client projects, that content can be client source code going to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user should check OpenRouter's data-policy and ZDR settings and avoid sending secrets or NDA code. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool calls unless its matcher is extended to mcp__typesafe__evaluate.
npmjs-com-package-y0usaf-typesafe-mcp.failureMode: Fail-open by construction. It is an optional tool: a missing key, a network error, an HTTP error or a timeout returns an isError text result (index.js:154-179) and Claude continues without Jev. It never blocks the turn as a hook would. The default timeout is 30 s (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS), so a hung API can stall one tool call for up to 30 s. Set TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS=3000-5000. There are no retries and no circuit breaker, and if Jev is down Claude may retry the tool repeatedly. If the server crashes at startup (for example an npx fetch failure), the tools are unavailable but the session continues.
npmjs-com-package-y0usaf-typesafe-mcp.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate). Tool definition is about 1.1k chars of description plus about 2k chars of JSON schema, roughly 800 tokens. Server instructions are about 1.7k chars, roughly 430 tokens, added to the system prompt. Total is about 1.2-1.3k tokens per session, or somewhat less if tools are deferred via ToolSearch. The 3.4k-char guide resource is not auto-loaded. No hook-injected text. Cost per call is small: the state Claude serializes into the call, plus about 100-300 tokens of JSON back.
npmjs-com-package-y0usaf-typesafe-mcp.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. There is no hook and no proxy. Claude Code decides whether to call evaluate based on the tool description and server instructions, which say to use it for "classification, detection, scoring, routing, verification, ranking, context selection". Nothing in the package forces invocation. Coding turns rarely have a natural "typed decision" step, so real-world call rates are likely low unless CLAUDE.md or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook reinforces it. That would be extra work outside this package, and it would conflict with the goal of never having to prompt for it.
npmjs-com-package-y0usaf-typesafe-mcp.latencyImpact: Claimed 70-500 ms API latency per call, about 100 ms per the guide. Real cost per use is the extra tool-call round trip plus model tokens to write the questions, roughly 1-4 s of Opus time. No latency on turns where the tool is not called. Worst case is the 30 s timeout.

npmjs-com-package-y0usaf-typesafe-mcp.verdict: The best available minimal bridge: it is clean, safe by inspection, and works with OpenRouter through env vars only. gh-carter1111-jevcore.name: jevcoreagent
gh-carter1111-jevcore.whatItDoes: Local Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server plus CLI (jevcore / jev-guard) that acts as a risk and safety gate for coding agents, not as a general coding helper. It composes a deterministic regex hard-policy (secrets, rm -rf, force push, DB migrations, auth, payments, CI privilege, web3) with one batched TypeSafe System One call (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0: Choice for task domain, Score for 4-level risk, several Noul questions for risk factors and security review). It returns a typed decision (execute / plan_first / approval_required / block). The Claude Code adapter is only templates: an optional PreToolUse Bash hook that runs the deterministic `jev-guard check` (no Jev call), and an advisory CLAUDE.md telling the model when to call the MCP tools. Built Cursor-first; the runtime dir is ~/.cursor/jev-coding-guard/.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter code or string anywhere in src/. The provider builds `new TypeSafeClient({apiKey: config.apiKey, baseURL: config.baseURL, ...})` and hardcodes `this.model = config.model ?? "jev-latest"` (src/provider.ts:222-228), then calls `client.systemOne({model, state, questions})` (provider.ts:250). The MCP server constructs `new TypeSafeProvider({ timeoutMs })` with no baseURL or model (src/mcp-server.ts:~608), so config comes only from the SDK env. SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:56-62, 513, 554, 579-581): env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai), POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> would hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the same path as the OpenRouter System One API.
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe direct only (api.typesafe.ai). No other gateways.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The base URL and key can be switched by env alone (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY) if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the SDK's request and response shape, which I did not verify. The model is hardcoded to the bare id "jev-latest" in provider.ts:228 and is not env-configurable, because TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL is bypassed when the provider passes the model explicitly. OpenRouter expects typesafe/jev-latest or ~typesafe/jev-latest, so a one-line patch is needed, and the MCP entrypoint does not forward the model at all. OpenRouter may also reject some SDK headers or fields. Untested.

interface.name: jev_assess_task (MCP)
interface.purpose: Typed decision for a coding task: domain, execution mode, risk 0..1, security-review flag, confidence. Inputs: userTask, repositoryContext, changedFiles?, diffSummary?, testSummary?, batchItems? (batch mode).

interface.name: jev_assess_command (MCP)
interface.purpose: Typed decision for a proposed shell command. The command is treated as text evidence only and is never executed.

interface.name: jev_review_diff (MCP)
interface.purpose: Typed decision over changedFiles and diffSummary, intended to be called before declaring a risky change complete.

interface.name: jev_guard_report (MCP)
interface.purpose: Local SQLite evidence report (7d/14d/30d/all). Only works if JEV_GUARD_LOCAL_EVIDENCE=1. Never calls TypeSafe.

interface.name: CLI: jevcore check [--stdin] [--json]
interface.purpose: Deterministic policy gate with no network. Exit 0 allow, 1 block, 2 approval_required, 3 plan_first, 4 fail-closed error.

interface.name: CLI: init / doctor / decide-many / evidence (status|purge|reset)
interface.purpose: Dry-run install planner, diagnostics, batch decisions, local evidence management. `init --apply --agent claude` writes project-scoped files only.

interface.name: Hook: PreToolUse (matcher Bash) pretooluse-jev-check.mjs
interface.purpose: Spawns `node dist/cli.js check --stdin --json` per Bash call and maps the exit code to permissionDecision allow/deny/ask. Deterministic, no Jev call. Denies if the binary is missing or on error (fail-closed).

interface.name: Advisory adapters/claude-code/CLAUDE.md
interface.purpose: Instructs the model to call jev_assess_task before implementation work, jev_assess_command before mutating or high-impact commands, and jev_review_diff before finishing risky changes, and to print a 'JEVCore:' block verbatim.

interface.name: hooks/jev-write-policy-check.mjs
interface.purpose: Cursor preToolUse Write/Delete gate. Cursor-format stdin and stdout, not wired for Claude Code.

gh-carter1111-jevcore.runtime: Node >=20 (uses experimental node:sqlite when evidence is enabled). Deps: @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0, @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0, zod ^4.6.5. Requires a local clone plus `npm run build`, or npx jevcoreagent.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.install: npx jevcoreagent init (dry-run) and `init --apply --agent claude --project-dir <dir>`. This writes project-scoped .mcp.json, hook and CLAUDE.md only, never ~/.claude.json. User scope is a printed `claude mcp add --scope user --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... jev-coding-guard -- node <repo>/dist/mcp-server.js`. The hook additionally needs JEV_GUARD_BIN set.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.tests: About 60 node:test files in tests/ (engine, MCP in-process, policy, claude-adapter, telemetry). They use a fake provider, so no live-API tests run in CI. There is no .github directory, so no CI. The repo has tools/ for latency, corpus and threshold evals, but I saw no published results. I did not run any of it.
security: API key: read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var by the SDK. The MCP config example uses env `${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}` expansion, and `claude mcp add --env KEY=...` would place the key in the argv and process list, which is the documented pattern. The key is stored in ~/.claude.json in plaintext unless the env-expansion form is used. Docs say the server never exposes the key.
No postinstall/preinstall scripts. package.json scripts are build/test/tools only. No curl|sh installers. The npm tarball contains dist, src and adapters (237 files).

Shell execution: the server itself runs none. context-router.ts runs `git` via spawnSync to list candidate paths in the cwd, and setup.ts runs `node --check` (doctor). The PreToolUse hook spawns node with the command on stdin, not on argv.
Telemetry: none to third parties. Opt-in local SQLite (JEV_GUARD_LOCAL_EVIDENCE=1) with de-identified metadata, off by default. The only network egress is the TypeSafe/SDK call.

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs (userTask, diffSummary, repositoryContext) come from the model and go into the Jev state, so injected text can skew the classification. Hard-policy regexes run first and can only escalate. Output is typed, but the CLAUDE.md tells the model to print 'agent.headline/plan' text verbatim, which is a small model-echo surface.

Hard policy is regex-based, so it is evadable, and it is prone to false positives (any 'auth', 'token', 'DELETE FROM', 'migration', 'deploy' mention triggers approval_required or block). Secret redaction is also regex-based.

Single anonymous-ish maintainer (npm '[email removed]', git author 'Carter Macbook'), brand-new package (about 8 days old), 1 star. SECURITY.md says 'once the public repo exists'. It is an unvetted supply-chain dependency that would receive task text and your API key.
The hook's fail-closed behavior denies every Bash call if JEV_GUARD_BIN is misconfigured (default path resolves relative to the adapter dir).
gh-carter1111-jevcore.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL host): a Bearer key plus JSON state {task, touchedFiles[], mentionsProduction, context} and the question definitions. The task, command, diffSummary and testSummary strings are model-authored and pass through redactSecrets (regex) first (policy.ts:881-896, engine.ts:245). Preflight `block` rules (secret paths, rm -rf and similar) send nothing. Not sent: raw file contents or full diffs, unless Claude puts them in diffSummary or repositoryContext. File paths of touched files are sent. Fan-out (default on) can make a second call, and context rerank (default on) can make an extra call with candidate path identifiers. For client projects, task descriptions and repo paths still leave the machine via OpenRouter to TypeSafe, and OpenRouter logs metadata.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.failureMode: Fail-safe, not fail-open. The MCP provider timeout is 25 s (15 s for the rerank) and the SDK also retries. On provider failure or invalid output, the engine falls back deterministically: ordinary tasks become plan_first, elevated-risk ones become approval_required, and block comes only from hard policy. Under CLAUDE.md, plan_first means show a plan and wait, and 'do not continue with high-risk actions while the assessment is unavailable'. A slow or down Jev therefore stalls or nags the workflow instead of silently passing. An MCP tool error is reported to the model as isError. The PreToolUse hook fails closed (deny) on a missing binary or errors. It calls no network, timeout 15 s inside a 30 s hook limit.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (jev_assess_task, jev_assess_command, jev_review_diff, jev_guard_report). The estimate for tool names, descriptions and input schemas is about 1.2-2k tokens (12+ .describe fields, batchItems and batchStrategy options), plus outputSchemas if the client includes them. There are no MCP 'instructions' (capabilities: {tools:{}} only). The advisory CLAUDE.md adds about 700 tokens on every session if merged into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Every assess result includes an `agent` Contract block (headline, plan, choices, actions) that the CLAUDE.md asks Claude to print verbatim, adding hundreds of tokens per call. The hook injects only a short reason string on ask or deny.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.latencyImpact: Each MCP assess call is one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms, with up to 2 calls for fan-out plus an optional rerank call), plus a model turn to call the tool and print the block, so roughly 1-3 s per invoked turn in practice. The PreToolUse hook adds a node process spawn of about 50-150 ms to every Bash call, with no network. I did not measure any of this, and the repo's latency-bench results are not published.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.autoInvocation: Mixed. (a) MCP tools are model-discretion, steered by an advisory CLAUDE.md that you would have to merge yourself (no automatic install into ~/.claude). Claude may skip or ignore them, and the README itself says the hook is the hard gate and the CLAUDE.md is advisory. (b) The optional PreToolUse Bash hook is deterministic and automatic but does not call Jev, only regex policy. Jev is therefore not on any deterministic path. There is no UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse or Stop hook and no skill.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's typed primitives (Choice, Score, Noul) in one batched systemOne call, and code owns the workflow. That matches the intended use of System One, with a real question pack in src/question-packs.ts.

The Jev call goes through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with a configurable TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. The path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the switch is plausible with env changes plus one model-id patch.
Hard-policy runs first, offline and deterministic. Blocking rules make zero model calls, and the model can never override a block. Secrets are regex-redacted before egress.
Fail-safe design: provider errors and invalid risk scores degrade to plan_first, never clamp or fabricate. Fail-closed hook.

Ships an explicit Claude Code adapter (MCP config, PreToolUse hook, CLAUDE.md, dry-run installer) that never touches ~/.claude.json, and a Jev-independent `jevcore check` CLI usable as a secret and destructive-command guard.
About 60 test files with a fake provider, Apache-2.0, no install scripts, opt-in local-only telemetry. Read-only tool annotations.
Local evidence and report tool could later show how often Jev changed the mode.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for daily coding: it gates risk (approve, plan, block), it does not help write, find or review code. It gives Claude no code-quality signal, only a domain label and a risk number.
Not automatic in the way you want. Jev is only reached if Opus chooses to call an MCP tool following an advisory CLAUDE.md. The one deterministic piece (the Bash hook) does not use Jev at all.

Conflicts with your bypass/auto permission workflow. The policy returns approval_required for any auth, migration, deploy, payments, npm publish, CI secrets or terraform work, and the hook maps that to `ask`. It also stacks a fourth Bash hook next to your secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks. Regex rules produce false positives on ordinary client work.

OpenRouter is not supported out of the box: no OpenRouter code, the model is hardcoded to bare 'jev-latest' (provider.ts:228) and the MCP entrypoint does not pass a model. It needs a patch or fork and an untested compatibility check of the request/response shape.

Cursor-first codebase: the runtime dir is ~/.cursor/jev-coding-guard, docs use `zsh -lc`, the Write hook uses Cursor's protocol. The Claude Code parts are templates that the user must wire up by hand.

Very immature: repo and npm package created 2026-09-22, 4 commits in one day, 1 star, one anonymous maintainer, no CI, 0.1.x alpha. Not vetted for a client-project dependency that receives your task text and API key.
Sends task descriptions, file paths and context summaries of client projects to TypeSafe via OpenRouter, with no way to keep it fully local other than skipping Jev.

Latency and context tax on invoked turns: an extra tool call plus a mandatory verbatim 'JEVCore:' print block per assessment, and a fail-safe fallback that downgrades to plan_first when Jev is slow or down.
Its own README says 'IDE/CI integration beyond that is still future work', and the Jev value claims (latency, calibration) are not backed by published results.
gh-carter1111-jevcore.verdict: Real Jev integration (Choice/Score/Noul via the official SDK) but it is a risk-gate/approval layer, not a coding accelerator, and the Claude Code side is advisory templates plus a hook that does not call Jev. npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.name: jev-sudo
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.whatItDoes: A standalone Node CLI wrapper (jev-sudo <command>) that sends a shell command to a "Jev System One" endpoint (noul isDestructive, score riskLevel, choice actionPolicy) and then blocks, prompts, or execSync-runs the command. It is not a Claude Code hook, MCP server or skill. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or on any fetch failure or non-2xx response, it silently falls back to a hard-coded keyword-matching "simulator" (rm -rf, drop table, git push --force, etc.) that fakes 35-60ms latency and reports "Jev System 1" in the output.

npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.tests: 4 node:test cases (test/guardian.test.ts), all run against the built-in keyword simulator, so they never exercise the live API. No CI seen. The README claims "<80ms" and "Zero-Latency" and the simulator invents the latency number with Math.random (client.ts:49).

security: No postinstall, no runtime deps, no telemetry, no curl|sh. Tarball has 23 files and about 34 KB, all readable.
Sends the full command string, cwd, USER and SHELL to api.typesafe.ai in the live path (guardian.ts:142-147). Bearer key is read from an env var, not argv, so it is not exposed in the process list.

Silent fail-open to a naive substring matcher when the API is unreachable or returns an error (client.ts:43-46). The output still says 'Jev System 1' (model label 'jev-system1-sim' appears only in JSON), so the user can believe Jev vetted a command when a keyword list did. This misrepresents the protection.

The simulator is trivially bypassed. Only literal substrings are matched, so 'rm -r -f /', 'find / -delete', 'shred', 'git push -f origin' without spaces, encoded or base64 payloads, and 'rm -rf $HOME' variants may get 'allow' (e.g. 'rm -rf ~' matches 'rm -rf' but not the '/' catastrophic branch). Any command not in the list is 'allow' with 0.96 confidence.

The command is passed as a joined string to execSync (shell), so quoting and argv boundaries are lost. Wrapper args like -f are stripped from the wrapped command, corrupting commands such as 'git push -f' (the -f is treated as the tool's own force flag and removed, changing behavior).

Not a hook, so it does not intercept anything by itself. It only guards commands the user or agent explicitly prefixes with jev-sudo. The interactive y/N prompt needs a TTY and would hang or fail under Claude Code's Bash tool.
Single-maintainer, zero-adoption package (162 weekly downloads, 0 dependents, 0 stars), published 10 days ago, with unverified provenance of the endpoint. Supply-chain trust is low.
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.dataEgress: Live mode only (requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY): the command string, cwd, username and shell go to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Nothing else (no code, diffs or file contents). In simulator mode nothing leaves the machine. Nothing goes to OpenRouter.
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.failureMode: Fail-open to the keyword simulator on any exception or non-OK response. There is no fetch timeout (no AbortSignal), so a hung connection blocks the command indefinitely. A malformed 200 response falls back to defaults: isDestructive 0.05, riskLevel 'low', policy 'allow' (guardian.ts:174-179), which is also fail-open.
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.contextCost: Zero if used as a plain CLI, since it adds no MCP tools, no skills and no hook text. It also adds no automatic behavior. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PreToolUse hook wrapper around `jev-sudo --eval "$cmd" --json`.
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or manually prefixed. It ships no hook config, MCP server or skill. It would need a custom PreToolUse Bash hook that calls it, and that hook would parse the JSON output, since the CLI itself exits 0 in --check mode regardless of policy (cli.ts:265-267).
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.latencyImpact: Node cold start of roughly 50-100 ms plus, in live mode, a network round trip (claimed 70-500 ms). In simulator mode it adds only the process start, and the reported 35-60 ms latency is fabricated. Per Bash call in a hook, roughly 100-600 ms. No timeout guard.
pros: Tiny, fully readable codebase (about 400 lines of TS, no runtime deps, no postinstall, MIT), so it is easy to audit and to fork.

The Noul/Score/Choice bundle in one call (guardian.ts:149-172) is a sensible illustration of how a Jev decision gate for risky shell commands could be shaped. It could be borrowed as a template for a custom PreToolUse Bash hook that calls OpenRouter.
Has --eval --json output that a hook could parse.
Command-risk gating is a legitimate Jev use case (a low-latency typed decision) that complements the existing secret-leak guard.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no hook, MCP or skill, so it cannot be automatic without custom glue.

No OpenRouter support. It targets api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a request schema that does not match the OpenRouter System One or Decisions APIs as described, and the base URL is not configurable by env.

Default and fallback mode is a hard-coded keyword matcher that prints 'Jev System 1' and invents 35-60 ms latency (client.ts:49). This is misleading for a safety tool, and the tests only cover that fake path.
Silent fail-open with no timeout. Any 200 response missing fields defaults to 'allow'.
Interactive y/N prompt and execSync of a re-joined string break in Claude Code's non-TTY Bash tool. It also strips -f from wrapped commands.
Effectively no adoption or vetting: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 162 weekly downloads, and it does not exercise the real API in tests. Its superiority over a plain deny-list hook is unproven.
Redundant with Claude Code's own permission modes, and in bypass mode a guard has value only if implemented as a hook, which this is not.
npmjs-com-package-jev-sudo.verdict: Skip it: a single-commit CLI wrapper, not a Claude Code integration, with no OpenRouter support. Its default path is a fake keyword matcher labelled Jev, and it fails open with no timeout. The only thing worth keeping is the idea of a Jev Noul/Score/Choice gate for risky Bash commands, which should be built as a small custom PreToolUse hook against OpenRouter with a strict timeout and an explicit fail-open or fail-closed policy.

gh-verhex-xerify.name: xerify-cli
gh-verhex-xerify.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI, library and stdio/HTTP MCP server for cross-provider claim verification. Three MCP tools: xerify_ask, xerify_verify, xerify_capabilities. Jev is one built-in verify-only backend next to codex, claude, cursor, openai-api, anthropic-api, openai-compatible and generic command adapters. A verify call sends {claim, context} as the Jev state with one fixed 3-way Choice question (confirmed/refuted/unclear); Jev probabilities/confidence are thresholded (p>=0.90, conf>=0.80, no tie, else 'unclear'). It is a claim-checker, not a general Jev decision gateway: no Noul, Score or arbitrary typed questions. The model must decide to call the MCP tool itself; nothing is automatic.

Returns verdict confirmed/refuted/unclear plus decision{probabilities, confidence, policy} for Jev. Annotated readOnly, openWorld.
