gh-dizk-jev-lens.name: jev-lens
gh-dizk-jev-lens.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (monorepo also has a host-independent core and a pi extension). A PostToolUse hook on Read|Bash|Grep intercepts tool results of about 1200 tokens or more, builds candidate views from the output's own lines (outline, focus, testlog, matches, head/tail and others, using tree-sitter for code), and asks Jev (Noul/Choice questions via TypeSafe SDK systemOne) which is the smallest view that still serves the agent's next step. The hook then replaces the tool output via updatedToolOutput, with a footer that points to a `recall` MCP tool for the full text. It never generates or summarizes text. Claimed 79% token reduction on large tool results, measured on 500 OpenHands trajectories via the pi harness. The Claude Code plugin itself is explicitly not yet measured on Claude Code sessions.

providerSupport.evidence: No OpenRouter or endpoint string exists in the repo. packages/core/src/classifier.ts:91 and packages/core/src/lens.ts:105 both call `new TypeSafeClient({ apiKey })` from @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 and pass no baseURL. In the SDK tarball (dist/index.mjs:56-58, 513) baseURL falls back to env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, then `https://api.typesafe.ai`. The request is `POST ${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <apiKey>` (index.mjs:554, 581), body {state, questions, model}. Key resolution is env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, then ~/.claude/jev-lens/key.json (packages/core/src/config.ts:105-107). The model name comes from JEV_LENS_MODEL and defaults to `jev-latest` (config.ts:170). The classifier reads answers.<q>.noul (classifier.ts:93-94), so it depends on the response shape.
providerSupport.others: None. The code uses the TypeSafe SDK only and has no other gateway.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial on paper, needs a live check. OpenRouter's System One API is POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the SDK path /v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, using an OpenRouter key as the bearer token, and JEV_LENS_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) should route it with no code change. Unverified: whether OpenRouter accepts the same request and response schema (state, questions, answers.*.noul, choice), and whether it accepts the SDK's X-TypeSafe-* headers. Do not put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the Claude env, because Bash children inherit it. Put it in ~/.claude/jev-lens/key.json instead, and set only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEV_LENS_MODEL under settings.json env.

interface.name: PostToolUse hook, matcher ^(Read|Bash|Grep)$ -> node src/hook.ts
interface.purpose: Compresses large tool results by returning hookSpecificOutput.updatedToolOutput. Timeout 40s in hooks.json, internal cap JEV_LENS_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS=30000. statusMessage 'jev-lens is choosing a view'.

interface.name: UserPromptSubmit hook (shell: cat >> events.jsonl)
interface.purpose: Appends every user prompt (the raw hook JSON) to events.jsonl in the data directory, so Jev gets the task context. Prints nothing.

interface.name: MessageDisplay hook (shell: cat >> events.jsonl)
interface.purpose: Appends each batch of assistant text to events.jsonl. It fires on every assistant message, not only on large tool results.

interface.name: MCP tool recall(id, lines?, pattern?)
interface.purpose: Returns the stored full output of a compressed result, or a line-range or pattern slice. Its description is the constant RECALL_DESCRIPTION, about 70 tokens.

interface.name: MCP tool stats()
interface.purpose: Reports what was compressed and the tokens saved.

interface.name: Slash command /jev-lens:stats
interface.purpose: Calls the stats MCP tool and prints the result.

interface.name: src/statusline.ts
interface.purpose: Optional status-line segment showing tokens saved, compressed/considered counts and recalls. The user wires it into their own statusLine command.

interface.name: src/trajectory.ts
interface.purpose: Exports Claude Code transcripts as benchmark trajectories.

security: MIT licence, 1 author (Didrik Rognstad). Repo created 2026-09-18, 79 commits in about 2 days, 1 star, 1 fork. Several commits are co-authored by Claude.

No postinstall or preinstall scripts (grepped all package.json). Installed through the Claude Code marketplace, which runs npm ci from the standalone packages/claude-code/package-lock.json. Dependencies are jev-lens core, @typesafe-ai/sdk, web-tree-sitter, @vscode/tree-sitter-wasm and @binclusive/tree-sitter-kotlin-wasm (a small third-party wasm package). Supply chain is thin and brand new.
The key is read from env or from key.json (mode 0600 when written by storeKey). It is sent only as an HTTP Authorization header, not in argv. The hook and MCP server take no key argument.
The core's loadDotEnv only reads .env from the package or monorepo root, never from the target project. With the plugin installed under node_modules this is safe.

The MCP server is dependency-free JSON-RPC over stdio. recall and stats read only the local store. Recall ids come from tool_use_id and are used as file lookups. I did not audit sanitization of the id, so path traversal is unchecked.
The hook does no shell execution beyond node. The two logging hooks run `cat >> events.jsonl`.

Prompt injection surface: the tool output previews and the user and assistant text go into the Jev state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injected text can at worst sway a view choice, for example hide lines. It cannot inject text into Claude, because the replaced output consists only of lines from the original plus a fixed footer.

Local data at rest: events.jsonl holds every user prompt and assistant message in plaintext, pruned at 4MB. Stored full outputs of every compressed result stay under ~/.claude/jev-lens for 90 days (JEV_LENS_KEEP_DAYS) and can include secrets that appeared in Bash or Read output. The log records the cwd.
No telemetry beyond the API calls. The SDK sends User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai, or to OpenRouter if the base URL is overridden, one or two systemOne calls per large (about 1200 tokens or more) Read, Bash or Grep result. The state contains: the first user request (600 chars), the latest user message (400 chars), the assistant text before the call (600 chars), the tool name, the tool args (300 chars, which include file paths and shell commands), and previews of each candidate view (about 900 chars each, the full view up to 1500 chars) drawn from the actual file or command output. For code, a second call sends block signatures plus 240-char previews. Small outputs, Edit, Write, images and MCP tools send nothing. Per-call egress is a few KB of source snippets, command output and prompt text, and this repeats all day on client code. Whether the provider retains or trains on it is unverified. The user's PreToolUse secret guard blocks reads of secret files, but secrets that show up in Bash output (env dumps, logs) would still be previewed to the provider.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.failureMode: Fail-open. Any exception, non-2xx response, missing key, or exceeding the 15s per-request SDK timeout (systemOne timeout 15000, SDK maxRetries 2 with backoff, so worst case is far above 15s) ends with exit 0 and no output, and Claude gets the original result. The hard cap is 30s (JEV_LENS_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS), and the hook config timeout is 40s. This means a slow or down provider can stall a large Read or Bash result by up to about 30s before it falls back, so no timeout is tight. Without a key it silently uses a deterministic mock classifier (size and tool-type rules) and still compresses, which is not fail-open in the sense of 'no change'. JEV_LENS_CLASSIFIER=mock or JEV_LENS_DISABLED=1 turns it off.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.contextCost: Small. There are 2 MCP tools (recall and stats), and the server sends no `instructions`. Tool definitions are about 150-250 tokens total. The footer added to each compressed result is about 60-100 tokens, but it replaces thousands of tokens. UserPromptSubmit and MessageDisplay hooks print nothing, so nothing is injected. The net effect is a reduction in context. It removes a large share of large tool results, as claimed by the author (79% on the benchmark, 31% on their own sessions). The risk is a lossy view that forces a recall round trip, which costs a tool call.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.autoInvocation: Deterministic PostToolUse hook. It fires on every Read, Bash and Grep result of about 1200 tokens or more, with no model discretion and no prompt needed. The recall MCP tool is model-discretion, prompted by the footer text in the compressed result.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.latencyImpact: Per the README, about 0.1s node startup plus one or two Jev calls of 0.4-0.8s, so roughly 0.5-1s added to each large Read, Bash or Grep result (more if code needs a second block-expansion call). Small results exit before loading the core, at only the node startup cost of about 50-100ms for the process. There is also one shell `cat` per user prompt and per assistant message for the logging hooks. In the worst case (provider slow or down) a large result waits up to 30s.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.runtime: Node >=22.18 (runs TypeScript directly, no build step for the plugin). The user has Node 24. Core dist is fetched by npm from the registry when the plugin installs.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.install: /plugin marketplace add dizk/jev-lens ; /plugin install jev-lens@jev-lens ; key: echo '{"apiKey":"..."}' > ~/.claude/jev-lens/key.json && chmod 600 (or TYPESAFE_API_KEY). For OpenRouter add env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and JEV_LENS_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest) in settings.json env, then test in a scratch project first.
gh-dizk-jev-lens.tests: Vitest suites exist: 8 files in packages/claude-code/test (hook, mcp, store, events, transcript, claude, statusline, trajectory), 7 in packages/core/test, 7 in packages/pi-jev-lens/test. GitHub Actions CI runs typecheck and tests with JEV_LENS_CLASSIFIER=mock, so the real Jev path is not exercised in CI. There is an eval harness with 500-trajectory benchmarks and a 45KB STATUS.md research log. I did not run anything.
pros: This is the only candidate so far that gives fully automatic use of Jev inside Claude Code: a deterministic PostToolUse hook on Read|Bash|Grep. There is no prompting and no reliance on the model deciding to call a tool, which is exactly what the user asked for.

The Jev usage plays to Jev's strength: typed Noul questions and a Choice over candidate views return probabilities, with no free text. Code applies the thresholds. Cost is negligible at about $0.042 per 1M input tokens.
Fail-open by design: any error returns the original output. Code is sent in full unless Jev is confident. Every retained line is byte-for-byte original, and a recall tool fetches the rest.
Compression happens before the first send, so it does not break the prompt cache. The author measured that post-send pruning cost 17% more money and left it out of the Claude Code plugin.

The context footprint is tiny (2 MCP tools, no server instructions, no output from the logging hooks), and the net effect is fewer tokens in context. This helps on long sessions on a subscription plan.

OpenRouter routing is likely a config-only change. The code passes no baseURL, and the SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and POSTs /v1/systemone, matching OpenRouter's System One path. The model is overridable via JEV_LENS_MODEL.

Tunable and switchable: JEV_LENS_DISABLED=1, per-kind thresholds, min tokens, hook timeout. The stats tool, /jev-lens:stats and the statusline segment let the user measure recall rate before trusting it. Small readable code (about 830 lines in the plugin), MIT, no postinstall scripts, dependency-free MCP server.
cons: Very immature: repo created 2026-09-18, 1 contributor, 1 star, 79 commits in 2 days, partly AI-authored. The Claude Code plugin has explicitly not been measured on Claude Code sessions. The headline 79% comes from an OpenHands/pi benchmark, and even there 2 of 26 later edits missed their block.

Lossy on the main model's inputs. Opus sees a partial Read of client code, and an edit whose old text is a line it never saw fails. The mitigation is thresholds and recall, but the risk is real for a senior dev doing precise edits, and a recall costs an extra round trip and tokens.

Not OpenRouter-native. OpenRouter compatibility rests on the assumption that the /v1/systemone request and response schemas are identical to TypeSafe's. This is unverified, and the model id may need changing to typesafe/jev-1.13. It needs a live test with a real OpenRouter key.

Data egress: previews of source files and command output, plus the user's prompts and assistant text, go to a third party on every large tool result, all day, on personal and client code. This may breach client confidentiality or NDA terms. Bash output can contain secrets that the PreToolUse guard does not stop, since it guards inputs.
Plaintext local copies: events.jsonl (all prompts and assistant messages) and all compressed outputs are kept for 90 days in ~/.claude/jev-lens, and may hold client code and secrets.

Latency and failure timing: 0.5-1s on each large result, and a Jev outage can stall a result for up to 30s (SDK retries plus the 15s timeout) before the fail-open fallback. Silent fall-back to a mock classifier when no key is found means it compresses anyway with crude rules.

Interaction risk with existing hooks: GitNexus already has a PostToolUse hook on Grep|Bash. Two hooks that rewrite or augment the same tool result can conflict, and this needs an ordering test. Also, updatedToolOutput for built-in tools is a newer hook feature that I could not verify on 2.1.285. Two extra hooks (UserPromptSubmit, MessageDisplay) fire on every prompt and message.

Another dependency chain to trust: Node TypeScript execution in the plugin cache, the tree-sitter wasm packages including a third-party Kotlin build, and the marketplace fetching from a single-author GitHub repo (pin a commit or version).
gh-dizk-jev-lens.verdict: The best-fitting automatic integration found so far: a deterministic, fail-open PostToolUse hook that uses Jev's typed decisions in the way Jev was designed for, and it should reach OpenRouter with only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEV_LENS_MODEL overrides (needs a live check). Trial it on personal projects first, watching recall counts and edit failures, and hold off on client code until the data-egress and lossy-Read risks are accepted.

npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.name: jev-prompt-enhancer
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.whatItDoes: Single-file Node CLI (cli.mjs, 216 lines) that registers as a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook. For every user prompt it calls Jev (OpenRouter Decisions API) with a noul question ("needs refinement?") plus a choice question (typos, ambiguous, missing_context or none). If P>=0.6 and the problem is not "none", it calls inception/mercury-2 via OpenRouter chat/completions to rewrite the prompt. A second Jev call scores whether the meaning changed (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH). HIGH rejects the rewrite. Otherwise it injects the rewritten prompt as additionalContext ("FYI the user's request could be phrased as..." or, with --auto, "Treat the user's request as..."). It is a prompt-quality tool. It does not use Jev for any coding decision.

No TYPESAFE_API_KEY or console.typesafe.ai endpoint anywhere. Response parsed as d.answers[k] with .noul / .choice / .confidence fields (cli.mjs:40, 80-81, 93). I could not verify that response shape against the OpenRouter docs: the docs pages I tried returned 404.

npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.runtime: Node >=18, zero dependencies, ESM. Uses global fetch.
security: No npm postinstall or install scripts. It has zero dependencies and no shell execution in the CLI itself. The OpenCode plugin it writes uses spawnSync with an argv array, so there is no shell injection.
The API key is read from the env var only and never appears in argv. It is sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS to openrouter.ai only. No telemetry and no other hosts.

--init claude (cli.mjs:139) does s.hooks.UserPromptSubmit = [...], which clobbers any existing UserPromptSubmit hooks. It then rewrites the whole ~/.claude/settings.json with JSON.stringify and makes no backup. This is risky for this user's carefully built global config.

Prompt-injection surface: the model's rewritten text is injected into Claude's context as trusted-looking guidance. With --auto it says 'Treat the user's request as...'. The rewrite comes from Mercury, a small diffusion LLM, and the only guard is a Jev check that scores meaning change. A wrong or drifted rewrite would silently steer Opus. A prompt that contains instructions is also passed to Mercury.
The raw user prompt is interpolated into the Jev and Mercury prompts inside triple-quote delimiters, and a prompt that contains those delimiters can break out of them (low impact).
The README says 'the decision stays yours', but there is no approval UI in hook mode. additionalContext is applied automatically, and the user can only object afterwards in chat.
Single anonymous-ish maintainer (aleksvega), 8 days old, no source repo. Supply-chain trust is low. The code is small enough to audit fully (I did), but future versions are unvetted.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.dataEgress: Every user prompt, in full, goes to openrouter.ai for the Jev call. That includes prompts on client projects and any code, paths or secrets the user pastes. When refined, the prompt is also sent to inception/mercury-2 through OpenRouter (a second provider behind OpenRouter), and then the rewrite goes out again for the fidelity check. It sends only the prompt text (stdin .prompt). It does not send file contents, diffs or tool outputs. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit, so a pasted secret would leave the machine. Data policy for the Mercury/Inception route on OpenRouter is unverified.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.failureMode: Fail-open in the code: the try/catch prints '{}' and exits 0 (cli.mjs:192-194), and a missing key throws inside the try and is treated the same. There is NO timeout: fetch has no AbortSignal (cli.mjs:32, 49). If OpenRouter or Jev hangs, every prompt submission stalls until the Claude Code hook timeout, which I did not verify and which is generous by default. Add a wrapper such as `timeout 3` or a hook "timeout" setting. HTTP 4xx/5xx from the alpha endpoint (an unstable API) fail open silently, so the tool can quietly do nothing. Also fail-open on a wrong response shape, because ?. chains default to 0 and produce no enhancement.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.latencyImpact: Added to EVERY prompt turn, synchronously, before Claude sees the prompt. Node startup is about 50 ms, plus one Jev call. The README claims ~0.5 s for prompts left untouched and ~2 s for refined ones (Jev + Mercury + Jev). These figures are the author's own and I did not measure them. Per turn this is small next to Opus latency, but it is dead time on every message, and the retry-less no-timeout design gives a bad worst case.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. The hook injects text only when a refinement fires: about 30-300 tokens of additionalContext per refined prompt ("FYI the user's request could be phrased as: ..."). It injects nothing for clear prompts. Context cost is negligible, but the injected paraphrase duplicates the user's own prompt, which is noise for Opus.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), fires on every user prompt with no model discretion. It meets the 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement literally, but only for prompt rewriting.
pros: Truly automatic: a real UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.
Already OpenRouter-native: a single OPENROUTER_API_KEY, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13:latest. This matches the user's constraint exactly, with no patching.
Tiny (216 lines), zero dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry. Fully auditable in minutes. Fail-open on errors.
Good illustration of the Decision primitives (noul, choice and score all used correctly in the request shape), and a cheap gate: clear prompts pass untouched at about $0.00002 per call.
The gate avoids the rewrite step for most prompts, so the added cost per turn is one small Jev call.
cons: Solves a problem this user barely has. A senior dev on Opus 5.5 writing precise English prompts gains almost nothing from typo or vagueness rewriting, and Opus already handles ambiguity or asks.

Weak fit for the goal: Jev is used for prompt hygiene, not for coding decisions (which files to load, whether to run tests, risk of a tool call, context pruning, routing). It does not make Claude Code better at daily coding.
Ships every prompt, including client-project prompts, to OpenRouter and (when refined) to the Inception Mercury model, on every turn. It adds a second vendor and a data-privacy question.
No timeout on fetch, so a slow or down OpenRouter alpha endpoint blocks every message. Fail-open only applies to thrown errors, not to hangs.
--init claude clobbers existing UserPromptSubmit hooks and rewrites settings.json without a backup. It must not be used with this user's existing hook set.

Injected 'refined' text can drift from intent (the README's own limits admit the 0.6 threshold is calibrated on 5 examples). The claimed 'you approve / reject / rework' flow is not implemented in hook mode.
Uses a beta alpha endpoint, and the response field names (answers.*.noul / .choice) were not verified. A schema change would silently disable it because everything fails open.
8 days old, v0.1.0, one maintainer, no source repository, no tests, no CI. The README's evidence is 5 hand-run examples, several in Russian.
The Mercury dependency (inception/mercury-2) means a paid second model and a second failure point.
npmjs-com-package-jev-prompt-enhancer.verdict: Only OpenRouter-native, truly automatic Jev integration in this set, but it uses Jev for the least valuable job (rewriting prompts for a senior dev). It adds latency and sends every prompt to two third-party models. Skip it as a primary integration. If you want its idea, copy the 60-line Jev call into your own hook with a 2-3 s timeout, and point Jev at higher-value decisions instead.

gh-allan-nava-hookgate.name: hookgate
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (also Codex CLI) with three zero-dependency Node hook handlers that ask TypeSafe Jev typed questions. (1) PreToolUse on Bash: Choice{allow,ask,deny} plus Noul "destroys data/state outside repo?" gives ask/deny; a confident allow passes through by default. (2) Stop: Noul "does the final message claim completion that git status does not support?" can block a stop once per prompt, behind a local regex prefilter (EN+IT). (3) PostToolUse on WebFetch|WebSearch|Read|Bash, off by default: Noul prompt-injection screen adding additionalContext. Also audit log, per-session cache, rule-promotion suggestions, doctor, report. Ships in audit mode by default (0.0.3): judges and logs but never blocks until mode=enforce is set in ~/.hookgate.json.
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.tests: About 770 lines of node:test in test/ (e2e against a local fake HTTP server via HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT, handlers, gates, redact, scorecard) plus `hookgate check` manifest validation. CI: Node 18/20/22/24 matrix, npm pack dry-run, CodeQL, OpenSSF scorecard, release-drift. README admits the real-Jev benchmark has NOT been run (needs key), so Jev accuracy on real commands is unmeasured; only the no-key fall-through and fake-server paths are tested. Not executed by me (static read only).
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.runtime: Node >=18, zero runtime deps, ESM, native fetch
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.install: /plugin marketplace add Allan-Nava/hookgate ; /plugin install hookgate@hookgate ; export TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the env Claude Code runs in ; {"mode":"enforce"} in ~/.hookgate.json to make it act. npm 0.0.3 also exists (npx hookgate doctor/report).

security: No MCP server, no shell execution of user input; only execFileSync('git', ['status','--porcelain','--branch']) with 1.5 s timeout (handlers.mjs:15). No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, zero runtime dependencies, no telemetry found (grep).

API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, sent as Bearer header via fetch; never placed in argv (hook command is `hookgate.mjs pre-tool-use`, payload via stdin). Not visible in process list. Key must be exported to the Claude Code process env.

Redaction before egress (redact.mjs:4-34): private keys, sk-/rk-/pk- keys, GitHub/AWS/Slack/Google tokens, Bearer/Basic, JWTs, KEY/TOKEN/SECRET=value assignments, --password/--token flags, URL passwords, 40+ hex. Regex-based, so novel secret formats and secrets in file contents (injection gate on Read) can slip through.
Repo-level config hardening: a cloned repo can only tighten, cannot set failClosed/model/timeout/mode=audit (config.mjs:40-93). Good against malicious-repo config, a thoughtful design.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command and (optionally) tool output are fed into a Jev question as state. Injected text in a command could try to sway a classifier; the defense is that a confident allow only passes through and never widens permissions. Being fed untrusted content to a small classifier is a bypass surface, so it is a narrowing heuristic, not a security boundary.
Audit log ~/.hookgate/decisions.jsonl (or CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA) stores verdicts and a command prefix, not full command; session cache files store answers keyed by hash. Local only.

Single unknown maintainer, 0 stars, 8 days old, npm shows 0.0.1 dated 2026-03 then 0.0.2/0.0.3 same day as repo creation. Supply-chain trust is low; plugin runs on every Bash call with your env (incl. the API key) so pin a commit if installed. npm publish uses OIDC (workflow log hints).
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.dataEgress: One HTTPS POST per uncached decision to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT). Command gate (all Bash calls): redacted shell command (up to 12k chars), its description, last two segments of cwd, permission_mode. Stop gate (only when local prefilter sees a completion claim, ~2/3 of stops by their own measurement): agent final message (max ~7.2k chars) + stop_reason + first 60 lines of git status --porcelain (file names/branch), redacted. Injection gate (off by default): redacted tool output of WebFetch/WebSearch/Read/Bash up to 12k chars, which would include file contents and web pages. Never transcript or session id. For client projects: file paths, branch names, command contents (paths, hostnames, table names) leave the machine to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if routed there, which adds a second party). Per-session cache dedups identical commands, though their measurement puts real repeat rate at about 0%.
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.failureMode: Fail-open by design (README, hooks.json description, hookgate.mjs:14-17). No key, timeout, HTTP error, malformed JSON, exception -> exit 0 with empty stdout, so Claude Code's normal permission flow applies. Fetch timeout 2000 ms default (config.mjs:17, range 100-10000), hook timeout 5 s in hooks.json; note Claude Code's own hook timeout kills the process if exceeded (non-blocking error). failClosed:true only in enforce mode makes command gate 'ask' on outage (user-level config/env only). Slow Jev costs up to 2 s per Bash call before falling open. Bad answer shape -> decision null -> pass. Stop gate: stop_hook_active guard plus one-block-per-prompt marker prevents loops.
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.latencyImpact: Their own measurement (README, evals/local.mjs, 30 spawns): ~59-61 ms Node start per Bash call with no key or on cache hit, ~79 ms to a local fake Jev; plus real Jev network round trip (TypeSafe claims 70-500 ms; via OpenRouter probably slightly more). So roughly 150-600 ms added to EVERY Bash tool call in enforce/audit mode (audit still waits for the call, it does not run async), and on ~2/3 of turn ends for the Stop gate. Matcher is Bash only, so Read/Edit/Grep are unaffected unless injection gate enabled (then WebFetch|WebSearch|Read|Bash all pay). Their own numbers: 27,246 Bash commands across 102 sessions, i.e. hundreds per day for a heavy user.
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.contextCost: Zero tool-definition cost (no MCP tools, no skills). Hooks inject text only when acting: ask/deny reason (~150-250 chars) on flagged commands, Stop block reason (~300 chars) when it blocks, rule-promotion systemMessage after 3 confident verdicts on the same prefix, and additionalContext (~250 chars) if injection gate enabled and positive. In audit mode (default) nothing is injected except promotion messages. Statusline text shows 'hookgate: judging the command' during each Bash call.
gh-allan-nava-hookgate.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PreToolUse(Bash), PostToolUse(WebFetch|WebSearch|Read|Bash), Stop, registered via plugin hooks/hooks.json. Fully automatic, no prompting, no model discretion. Only effect-producing after mode=enforce.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks fire on every Bash call and every Stop with no prompt from the user, exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' requirement, and zero context/tool-schema cost.

Genuine, well-chosen Jev use case: calibrated Choice/Noul for a small binary/ternary decision where a full LLM hook would cost seconds (their measured type:prompt judge on opus: 3.5 s p50, $0.129 per decision).
Fail-open everywhere with hard timeouts (jev.mjs:22, hooks.json timeout 5), no key -> silent no-op; will not wedge a bypass-mode session on a Jev outage.
Ships in audit mode: you can run it for days, run `hookgate report` for false-positive rates on YOUR real commands before enabling enforce. Safe rollout path.
Endpoint and model are overridable (HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT, HOOKGATE_MODEL), so pointing at OpenRouter is likely env-only; key var needs aliasing.

Careful security engineering: redaction before egress, repo config can only tighten, command >12k chars asked rather than partially judged, no postinstall, zero deps, small readable ~1000-line code base I read fully.
The Stop 'unverified completion' gate is a novel, useful idea for Opus-driven long sessions (catches 'all tests pass' with dirty tree), and Italian/English lexicon suits this user.
cons: Solves safety gating, not coding productivity: it never routes work, retrieves context, or improves code; value is only in preventing destructive commands and false 'done' claims.

Largely redundant/overlapping with the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and in bypass/auto permission mode the user has chosen not to be prompted: an 'ask' output would re-introduce prompts (possibly annoying) while only 'deny' is effective. Confident 'allow' does nothing by design.

Adds latency to EVERY Bash call (~60 ms Node spawn + Jev RTT, up to 2 s timeout), plus a Stop-time call on ~2/3 of turns, with Claude Code running hundreds of Bash calls/day; real-Jev latency and accuracy are unmeasured by the author.

Accuracy is unproven: README says benchmark not run, defaults to audit, and author's rule is 'under ~90% agreement it ships ask-only'. Skeptic claim that Jev is a small router model makes false positives on odd but legit commands (chained pipes, scripts) a risk; their own data says 94% of real commands are chains/pipes/scripts.

Data egress for client projects: every Bash command (redacted by regex only), cwd tail, git status file names and final assistant messages go to a third party (TypeSafe, and OpenRouter if routed). Injection gate would send file contents. Could breach client NDAs.

Very immature: 8 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0.0.3, no real-Jev tests, README claims about Codex verified live but nothing about Claude Code 2.1.285 with `args` array in hooks.json (untested by me; verify the plugin hook format is accepted).
Hard-coded TYPESAFE_API_KEY name (no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support) and OpenRouter wire compatibility with /api/v1/systemone unverified; model id format differs (jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-latest).
Stop gate can block finishing and cost extra agent turns (Opus tokens) on false positives; one block per prompt limits damage.

Worth trying in audit mode via HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT/TYPESAFE_API_KEY aliasing to OpenRouter (pin a commit, review with `hookgate report`), not something to enforce blindly on client repos.

npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.name: jev-assist
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.whatItDoes: Single-file Node CLI (scripts/jev.mjs, 531 lines, zero deps) plus a SKILL.md. Since 1.0.0 it is skill-only: no hooks and no MCP server. The agent pipes grep/git/test output on stdin (one candidate per line) into `jev noul|choice|score '<question>'`. The CLI batches the lines into Jev Decisions API calls (concurrency 8, 45k-token budget per request) and prints a banner with exact totals, then rows sorted by calibrated probability with a cut line (widest-gap "cliff", else p>=0.70, else top 10). Verdicts are cached locally. The pitch is that the agent reads about 30 rows instead of thousands of grep hits. It does not search. It classifies what the agent already found.

providerSupport.evidence: scripts/jev.mjs:31-38. Key prefix 'sk-or-' selects OpenRouter: url 'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions', model '~typesafe/jev-latest'. Any other key goes to 'https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone' with model 'jev-latest'. JEV_API_URL and JEV_MODEL override both (:34-36). The body is {state:{question}, model, questions:{q0..}} with per-question {type:'noul'|'choice'|'score', instructions:<line>, criteria}, sent with Authorization: Bearer <key> (:57-61). The key comes from env JEV_API_KEY or ~/.config/jev/key (:40-50). OpenRouter is a first-class path with no patching needed. It targets the alpha Decisions endpoint (not /api/v1/systemone), and the response readers guess field names (`a.noul ?? a.probability`, `a.choice ?? a.label ?? a.option ?? a.value`, lines 223-238), which suggests the schema was reverse-engineered and not fully pinned.
providerSupport.others: Any gateway via JEV_API_URL (name reported as 'custom'). Note the direct TypeSafe default URL api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone differs from the console.typesafe.ai host in the brief; not verified.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter already works via the sk-or- prefix or JEV_API_URL.

interface.name: jev key <API_KEY>
interface.purpose: Writes the key to ~/.config/jev/key (dir 0700, file 0600). The key ends up in argv, so it is visible in the process list and shell history at setup time. Using env JEV_API_KEY avoids this.

interface.name: jev noul '<statement about one candidate>'
interface.purpose: Returns P(yes) per stdin line, sorted, with a cut line. The 'flood filter' for grep hits and TODOs.

interface.name: jev choice '<q>' --opt name:criteria ...
interface.purpose: Assigns each stdin line a label from a fixed set (2 or more options), grouped by label. Example uses: which layer owns a file, whether a test failure is a flake or a real bug.

interface.name: jev score '<q>' --level N:criteria ...
interface.purpose: Assigns each stdin line an ordered rubric level (expected position), grouped by level.

interface.name: flags --top N | --by-file [N] | --by-dir [N] | --json | --fresh
interface.purpose: Fix the cut; census of selected rows by path/dir; emit every row as JSON (banner goes to stderr); skip cache reads while still merging verdicts.

interface.name: SKILL.md description trigger
interface.purpose: Model-discretion skill. Description (about 900 chars) says: use when a search returns a flood, or when about to write `grep -v`. The agent must call the script by absolute path, because the skill install does not put `jev` on PATH.

npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.tests: test/jev.test.mjs: 329 lines, about 25 unit cases covering helpers only (batching, argv parsing, cut, census, readers, provider selection). There are no HTTP or integration tests. CI is GitHub Actions on Node 18/20/22 running `npm test`. Note: the published npm tarball lists test/ in package.json "scripts" but does not ship it (files: scripts/, SKILL.md).
security: No postinstall or lifecycle scripts in package.json. Network calls go only to the chosen Jev endpoint (fetch in ask(), :57). No telemetry, no shell execution, no child_process, no eval.

Key handling is mostly good. The key file is 0600 in a 0700 dir, JEV_API_KEY takes precedence, and the key is masked on echo (`sk-or-…xxxx`, :496). The weak spot is `jev key <API_KEY>`: it puts the secret in argv, visible in ps and shell history, and an agent running it would also have the key in its transcript. Use the env var instead.

Prompt-injection surface: candidate lines are sent as `instructions` to a typed classifier. The SKILL.md itself admits 'no prompt-injection defence' and that comments and fixtures in the repo can move an answer. Consequence: a poisoned line can only skew a probability (silent false negatives), not execute anything. However, the Claude agent reads the sorted output and may skip rows it should have read.
The output echoes candidate lines JSON-quoted into Claude's context, so repo text still reaches the model, as with plain grep.

The skill tells the agent to run a script via absolute path and to pipe grep output into it. That is fine under bypass or auto mode, but it means a repo-wide flood of code is sent off-machine on each use.

The cache is ~/.cache/jev/cache.json, keyed by sha256(model, cmd, spec, line). It holds hashes and verdicts, not plaintext code. It grows without eviction (author's own 'ponytail' note, :14) and is written non-atomically without locking, so parallel runs can clobber each other.
Single anonymous maintainer (glud123, 163.com email), 4 stars, package 10 days old, 1 version. npm signatures are present, but there is no provenance attestation on the tarball listing.
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.dataEgress: Per call, to openrouter.ai (via the sk-or- prefix): the OpenRouter API key, the question text, the raw candidate lines (for example `path:line:code snippet` from grep, file paths from git ls-files, test failure lines, diff hunks), the model id, and the criteria/options. No whole files unless the agent pipes them in (SKILL.md tells it not to). Nothing is sent when every line is a cache hit. On the OpenRouter side the payload is subject to the account's data-policy settings. For client projects, the client's source lines leave the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, which needs a client-policy decision. The tool's own doc says: 'If the repo must not leave the machine, do not point jev at it.'
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.failureMode: Fail-closed per invocation, but harmless to Claude Code because it is not on the tool path. A missing key exits 1 in milliseconds with a message (:54, :395). Any non-OK HTTP status (401, 429, 5xx) calls die(), exiting 1 with the first 400 chars of the body, with no retry or backoff. The only retry is halving a batch on `max_tokens_exceeded`. fetch has no timeout or AbortController, so a hung endpoint hangs the Bash tool call until Claude Code's own Bash timeout. There is no fallback to plain grep. That fallback is the agent's own behaviour. Because it is a voluntary skill, an outage just means the agent falls back to reading grep output. A malformed API response produces a loud die() and not a fake result. With one worker failing, the whole run dies and partial results are lost (the cache is only written after all batches finish).
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens and no server instructions. The skill listing costs only the frontmatter description: about 900 characters, about 230 tokens, permanently in every session. When invoked, the full SKILL.md is loaded: 183 lines, about 2.5k tokens. No hook-injected text in 1.0.0. The earlier 0.x SessionStart and PreToolUse hooks were removed. Each call's output is capped to about 30 rows or 50 rows, so it typically costs 0.5-2k tokens instead of the tens of thousands a flood would cost.
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.latencyImpact: Nothing in the normal path, because it is opt-in. When it runs, the README shows about 1s for a 4-line pool (1046ms) and the SKILL.md says 'a few thousand lines takes tens of seconds' (concurrency 8, 45k-token batches). Cache hits are instant. This is slower than the brief's claimed 70-500ms because it includes node startup, batching and multiple sequential model round trips. Net effect can be positive if it saves the agent from a multi-grep loop, but it adds a step when the pool is small.
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger only (SKILL.md description). There are no hooks in the current version. This matters: the author's own git history (commit 3a5d3c5, 2026-09-22) records that a session with the description in the skill listing, a full SessionStart injection and a memory note still ran nine hand-written greps and never invoked the skill, and the description lever was called 'exhausted'. The author then added a PreToolUse hook (asks once per session on repo-wide file-listing greps) and removed it again in 1.0.0 (7f3679b), which deleted install-hook.mjs, pretool.mjs, session-start.mjs. So the shipped package does not meet the user's 'automatic without prompting' requirement on its own, and the author's data suggests it would rarely fire. A custom PreToolUse hook could be layered on top, but that means writing our own code and colliding with the existing Grep|Glob|Bash hooks.
pros: Direct OpenRouter support in the code: sk-or- key prefix routes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest (jev.mjs:31-38). It needs no patching, only JEV_API_KEY=sk-or-... in the environment.
Cheapest possible context footprint: no MCP server, no tools, about 230 tokens for the skill description, and output capped at about 30-50 rows regardless of pool size.

Uses Jev for what it is actually good at: batched typed classification (noul/choice/score) of many short candidates with calibrated probabilities, rather than free-form chat. Counts are computed in JS, so the model is never asked to count.

Honest, well-documented failure modes: short lines score low, multi-hop questions degrade, no injection defence, noul and choice are not comparable. Good guidance on when NOT to use it (under a dozen candidates, anything a linter decides).
Small, dependency-free, readable code (531 lines) with no postinstall, no shell exec and no telemetry. Key stored 0600 outside the repo, and cache holds hashes only.
Real batching and resilience details: token-budget batching, halve-and-retry on max_tokens_exceeded, concurrency 8, dedupe, local verdict cache so re-runs are free and cheap ($0.042/1M input).
Works with any agent that reads SKILL.md and can call it via `node /abs/path/jev.mjs`, so it can be dropped into ~/.claude/skills with no interference with the existing gitnexus/caveman hooks.
cons: Not automatic. It is a description-triggered skill only. The author's own commit message (3a5d3c5) documents the agent ignoring it and running nine hand-written greps, then 1.0.0 deleted the hooks that tried to fix it. That is direct evidence against the user's core requirement.

Solves a narrow problem (triaging huge grep/TODO/test-failure floods). Opus 5.5 plus GitNexus (already installed) already narrows search results, so the 'flood of thousands of lines' case is rare in normal daily coding. Value is occasional, not constant.

Sends real source lines (grep hits, diff hunks, paths) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every uncached call. This is a data-egress problem for client projects and there is no per-project allow/deny switch ('There is no per-project config').

Fragile API coupling: uses the alpha Decisions endpoint and guesses response field names with fallbacks (`noul ?? probability`, `choice ?? label ?? option ?? value`). A schema change breaks it, or worse, it defaults a choice probability to 1 when the field is missing (jev.mjs:231-232).
No fetch timeout, no retry/backoff on 429/5xx, and one failed batch kills the whole run with no partial results. Poor for a tool that fans out 8 concurrent requests on large pools.

A classifier on short lines is unreliable (author states short candidates score systematically lower, especially CJK), so the sorted cut line can hide true positives. There is no prompt-injection defence, so a hostile repo comment can skew the ranking, and the agent is told to trust the cut.

Single-maintainer, 10-day-old, 4-star project, 40 commits in 4 days, 1 npm version, 0.x churn that ended in removing its own automation. Test coverage is unit-level only. Authored with heavy AI assistance ('Co-Authored-By: Claude Code' throughout).
`jev key <KEY>` puts the secret in argv, and the skill install does not put `jev` on PATH, so the agent must be given an absolute path.
npmjs-com-package-jev-assist.verdict: Clean, safe, OpenRouter-ready CLI skill for one niche job (triaging grep/test floods), but not an automatic integration: it is a description-triggered skill, and the author's own history shows the agent ignoring it and the hooks removed. Worth installing only as an optional low-cost helper (key via env var, not on client repos) and never as the main Jev integration.

gh-edoproch-compact-jev.name: compact-jev
gh-edoproch-compact-jev.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (early-access "function hooks" module, TypeScript) adding a manual /compact-jev [goal] slash command. It sends the transcript state (user/assistant text, tool inputs, 240-char excerpts of tool outputs) plus 2 boolean questions per tool call (still needed? keep full result?) to Jev via Vercel AI Gateway /v1/evaluate. It then drops stale tool calls and truncates stale results, keeping user/assistant messages verbatim with no summary, by hooking session.compact and vetoing the built-in summarizer during its own run. It also ships a TS library (npm compact-jev 0.5.4) with a pluggable JevAsker/baseUrl.

gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin built on the early-access "function hooks" (mods) API. The brief says OpenRouter exposes POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, the same path suffix, so the patch is: change ENDPOINT (scout.js:7), use model id `typesafe/jev-latest` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`, read OPENROUTER_API_KEY in register.ts:48 (and cli.mjs:133). Risks: the OpenRouter response envelope (answers/usage field names) may differ from TypeSafe's native one; plugin runs in the function-hooks sandbox whose declared env-reads/http hosts are validated (README 'What it can reach' lists env reads), so the extra env var and host must be allowed; and a fork means losing marketplace updates. tests/register.test.ts mocks http.fetch, so a swap can be tested offline.

However skill names/descriptions from installed third-party plugin SKILL.md files are placed into the Jev request and the winner name is interpolated into the context line unescaped; a hostile skill name could inject text into the model context (low risk, requires malicious installed skill).

gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.dataEgress: On every typed prompt of >=12 chars (not starting '/'), to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone: the full prompt text (cut to 4000 chars, scout.js:49), a 400-char recent_context field (currently passed '' by the hook), all installed skill names plus descriptions (400 chars each), and on the 2nd call the first 700 chars of the top 3 SKILL.md bodies. Not sent: source files, diffs, tool outputs, assistant replies. Still, prompts on client projects routinely contain code snippets, paths, error text and business details, so every client prompt leaves the machine to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter plus provider if patched). The audit CLI sends all historical human prompts from ~/.claude/projects (21.4M input tokens in the author's run) after a cost confirmation.
gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Per-call abort plus Promise.race timeout, default 4000 ms (register.ts:68-83, scout.js:122-143); on timeout, HTTP error, exception, no key, empty roster or short prompt the original prompt proceeds untouched and is entered exactly once (register.ts:105-109). Cost of a slow Jev is added latency up to ~4 s per prompt before the model starts (status line shows 'no answer in N ms'). No retries by default (retries=0). Disabled with no key.
gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-schema tokens, no MCP server instructions. Only per-prompt injection when a skill is picked: a ~55-token `<skill_relevance>` block (about 200 chars) appended as context. Nothing injected on 'no skill' turns. Adds nothing to the static prefix so prompt caching is unaffected. Plugin has no skills/agents/commands of its own.
gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.latencyImpact: Two sequential HTTP round-trips to the API on gated turns (one on gate-fail turns) before the model starts. Author reports median ~850 ms for both calls, 2-3 s from India, 'well under a second' from the US; Jev claimed latency 70-500 ms per call. Hard cap 4 s. Applies to every typed prompt, not every tool call, so ~0.5-2 s per turn. Blocking (the hook awaits the result before the prompt is entered).
gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: function-hook on session.start and prompt.submit fires on every typed prompt with no model discretion and no user phrase needed. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. It only nudges Claude to load an existing skill; Claude still decides.
pros: Truly automatic: prompt.submit hook fires on every typed prompt; meets the 'never say use jev' requirement without model discretion or MCP tool descriptions.
Near-zero context cost: no tools, ~55 tokens only on turns where a skill is picked; does not touch the static prefix so caching holds.
Fail-open with hard 4 s timeout and 'enter prompt exactly once' guard (register.ts:105); will not block work if Jev/OpenRouter is down.
Shadow mode (`shadow`/JEV_SKILL_SCOUT_SHADOW=1) lets the user watch picks in the status line before allowing injection, and the audit can measure obedience before/after.
Real Jev use-case that matches its design (typed Choice/Noul decisions over an app state) and follows TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook; thresholds configurable via plugin settings.
Small, readable, dependency-free, no shell execution, no postinstall, MIT; static review is easy (~1.7k LOC total).

User has many skills (gitnexus-*, caveman, design skills), so skill-miss reduction is a plausible daily win; audit gives evidence on the user's own transcripts before committing (about $0.9 for 3k prompts).
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (scout.js:7, register.ts:48); no OpenRouter support, so the user's chosen provider needs a fork/patch, and the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified.

Depends on Claude Code function hooks, an early-access API that may change without notice and needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; validated on 2.1.278, user on 2.1.285, so may silently stop working after an update (README: builds without it ignore the modules key).
Narrow scope: only nudges skill loading. Does not offer Jev for code decisions (permission auto-approval, routing, review risk scoring, commit type, etc.) which is where most daily value might be.
Sends every typed prompt (client project text included) to a third party; a NDA/client concern, plus the audit uploads entire prompt history.

Adds blocking latency (two sequential calls, ~0.5-3 s) to every typed prompt for a benefit the author's own data says is ~50% precise (15/30 hand-labelled misses right) and the 'miss rate' metric is Jev-judged, not ground truth.
Cannot suggest Claude Code's bundled skills (code-review, simplify, etc.) since they are not on disk (README Limits), and only affects typed prompts, not subagent/tool loops.
Immature: 0 stars, 1 contributor, ~11 days old, no CI, no releases; overlaps with typesafe-mod and skillranker which do the same thing, so it is one of three competing implementations.
Uses Opus 5.5 main model, which loads skills well already; the cookbook gain (16.8% to 7.3% wrong-skill loads) was measured on Haiku, so benefit for this user is uncertain.
gh-karanb192-jev-skill-scout.verdict: Best-in-class proof that Jev can run automatically inside Claude Code (deterministic prompt.submit hook, fail-open, near-zero context cost), but it is skill-suggestion only, hardwired to api.typesafe.ai, and rides an early-access flag. Worth trying in shadow mode with a small OpenRouter fork (swap ENDPOINT/key/model) and running its audit first; do not rely on it as the sole Jev integration.

gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.name: @maromocooo/skill-dispatch (skilldispatch)
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI (skilldispatch) that registers user-level Claude Code (and Codex) UserPromptSubmit hooks. On each prompt it discovers the native skill catalog (local, plugin, synced skills), sends the RAW prompt plus each skill's name/description/agent/scope to Jev as one Noul question per skill (via @typesafe-ai/sdk client.systemOne), applies a threshold policy (0.75, max 4 skills) and either only logs a trace (shadow, default) or, in opt-in advisory mode, injects a 'consider invoking these skills with the native Skill tool' additionalContext listing skill names (max 4096 bytes). Also adds PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure observers that record native Skill invocations locally, plus trace analytics and an eval harness. It is a skill router/observability tool, not a general coding-decision integration.

gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.dataEgress: On every UserPromptSubmit: the full RAW user prompt text plus, for each candidate skill (up to 48 per chunk, chunked, concurrency 2), name, description, agent ('claude-code'), scope are POSTed to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe direct) with Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/providers/jev/questions.ts:14-17,26-31; client.ts:59-82). Not sent: skill bodies, file paths, cwd, code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs (README 'Privacy and security'; docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md). The prompt is repeated in every chunk request. Traces stay local. With a patched OpenRouter path, OpenRouter would also see the same payload. Client projects: raw prompts (which may include pasted code/secrets/client names) leave the machine.
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: hook wrapped in try/catch (src/hooks/runtime.ts:37-43,108-110) returns nothing on parse/setup/provider/timeout/storage errors. Defaults: request timeout 1800 ms, overall routing budget 2500 ms, retries 0 (options.ts:22-23, README), hook registration timeout 5 s. Missing key produces a doctor warning and routing fails open (no silent mock fallback). In default shadow mode the hook is registered async so Jev slowness/outage never blocks the turn; in advisory mode a slow Jev delays prompt by up to ~2.5 s and on timeout injects nothing (partial/degraded results not injected: runtime.ts:117-120).
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.latencyImpact: Shadow (default): ~0 on the critical path (async hook), background process spawn per prompt only. Advisory: synchronous, adds one Jev round trip per prompt (claimed 70-500 ms, plus Node startup ~50-150 ms, catalog discovery scan of local/plugin skills every prompt), bounded at 2.5 s worst case; only once per user prompt, not per tool call. Observer hooks (Pre/PostToolUse on Skill) are async local-only.
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-definition tokens, no server instructions. Shadow mode injects nothing. Advisory mode injects at most 4096 bytes (about 1000 tokens max, typically about 100-150 tokens: ~330-char intro/conclusion boilerplate plus up to 4 '- skill-name' lines) as UserPromptSubmit additionalContext only when at least one skill clears the 0.75 threshold.
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt with no user action (fully automatic once installed). But Jev's output only nudges Claude toward skills via advisory context; Claude retains discretion, and shadow (default) does nothing visible to the agent.
pros: Truly automatic: UserPromptSubmit hook, no need to tell Claude to 'use jev'; install command is idempotent and edits user settings while preserving existing hooks (src/registration/document.ts, manage.ts).

Genuine Jev usage via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 systemOne with Noul primitives (the right primitive for 'does skill apply', calibrated P(yes)); Jev is a good fit for cheap yes/no relevance gating (~$0.042/1M input tokens).

Careful engineering: fail-open on everything, 1.8s/2.5s timeouts, async shadow default, no shell in hook command (exec-form argv), no postinstall, sanitized errors, sane privacy defaults (HMAC prompts, 0600 files), pinned CI action SHAs, ~397 tests, Node 20+24 CI.
Zero context cost in shadow mode and small bounded injection (<=4096 B) in advisory mode; no MCP tools bloating context.

Built-in observability (recommended vs injected vs actually-invoked Skill calls, eval harness with recall/precision gates) lets you measure whether Jev routing actually helps before enabling advisory.
MIT license; code is small and readable so a fork adding OpenRouter is feasible.
cons: No OpenRouter support: baseURL hardcoded to https://api.typesafe.ai (src/providers/jev/client.ts:61), only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read, and the model regex rejects OpenRouter IDs containing '/' (options.ts:8). User wants OpenRouter-hosted Jev, so a local fork/patch (3 small edits + local build) is required; OpenRouter response compatibility with the SDK is unverified.

Narrow use case: only routes to Claude skills. It does not use Jev for other coding decisions (permission/risk gating, whether to run tests, which files, plan vs act). Value depends on how many skills the user has; with a handful of skills benefit is marginal, and native Claude skill selection via descriptions already exists. Tool-call-level decisions, where Jev could add most value, are out of scope.

Sends the raw prompt to an external service on every prompt, repeated per 48-skill chunk; for client projects this is a real confidentiality issue and the existing secret guard (PreToolUse) does not filter UserPromptSubmit prompts. README itself warns sensitive prompts should not be routed.

Advisory mode is synchronous (extra 100-500 ms+ Node spawn and full catalog rescan each prompt, up to 2.5 s); shadow mode, the default, injects nothing so Claude never benefits automatically until user opts in and reinstalls.

Extremely immature: repo and npm created 2026-09-23 (one week old), 2 commits, single author, 0 stars/forks, 0.1.0; README states no measured Jev accuracy and 'no superiority over native Claude routing is claimed'; labels in benchmark are AI-assisted drafts; single 'smoke test' anecdote.
Only recommends; Claude may ignore it, and the observed-invocation evidence is positive-only, so measured benefit is hard to prove.

Installs seven+ hook registrations into global ~/.claude/settings.json (UserPromptSubmit plus Pre/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure observers), adding a Node process spawn on each Skill tool call; more moving parts alongside gitnexus/caveman/secret-guard hooks. Bypass/auto permission mode does not affect it but debugging hook interplay costs time.
Depends on TypeSafe SDK 0.6.0 workaround for an Undici tee crash on Node 20/22 (client.ts:29-51); user is on Node 24 so likely irrelevant but indicates SDK fragility.
gh-maromocooo-skill-dispatch.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context-cost UserPromptSubmit hook that really calls Jev, but it only does skill recommendation, is one week old, hardcodes api.typesafe.ai (needs a small fork to reach OpenRouter), and ships raw prompts out on every turn. Worth reading as a reference implementation or running in shadow mode after patching, not a core daily-coding integration.

gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.name: compactio
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.whatItDoes: Claude Code plugin (npm compactio 0.2.3, MIT) with deterministic PostToolUse hooks that rewrite large tool outputs (Bash, Read of data files, Grep, WebFetch, WebSearch, mcp__*) via updatedToolOutput. Lossless cleanup (ANSI strip, repeated-line collapse) always runs. For outputs of 6k chars or more, it asks Jev (Choice primitive with levels full/errors/headtail/stub) how much to keep, then cuts locally and stores the original under ~/.compactio/store, retrievable via a "node cli.ts show ID" line. It also skips unchanged re-reads. An optional "Sweep" local proxy on 127.0.0.1:8787 (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) asks Jev which old tool results in the history to replace with tombstones. Jev is used as a System-1 decider, and the tool is not an MCP server.

Overrides: COMPACTIO_JEV_URL, COMPACTIO_JEV_MODEL. Body at jev.ts:58 is {model, state, questions} with Bearer auth; questions are {type:'choice', instructions, criteria}. TypeSafe wins if both keys are set. Caveat: I could not fetch the OpenRouter docs (404) to check the body schema. interface.purpose: 'key' prompts for a hidden key and writes it in plaintext into ~/.claude/settings.json env. The agent itself runs 'show ID' to fetch the full output

security: No MCP server, no npm postinstall script, no curl|sh installer. The plugin runs TS source directly with node (needs Node >=22.18; you have 24). CI publishes to npm with provenance and OIDC trusted publishing.

API key is read from env or from ~/.claude/settings.json env (install.ts:153-156) and sent as a Bearer header from fetch(), so it does not appear in argv. 'compactio key' saves the key in plaintext in settings.json (backup written as settings.json.compactio-bak).

Redaction is regex-only (src/redact.ts): private-key blocks, sk-/pk-/rk- tokens, gh*_ tokens, AWS AKIA, Google AIza, JWTs, Bearer/Basic, and NAME=value for names containing KEY/TOKEN/SECRET/PASSWORD. SECURITY.md admits it does not catch every secret. Client code snippets and paths in a 6 KB preview still leave the machine.

Sweep proxy (sweep.ts:serve) sits between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com. It sees every API request including OAuth/API-key auth headers and forwards them; README says it does not store them. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only. POST /_compactio/quit exits it, requiring a custom header as CSRF mitigation. Dropped outputs are stored unencrypted on disk in ~/.compactio/store and never pruned.

Sweep edits settings.json (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5[1m]) and creates a systemd user service. If the proxy dies mid-session, Claude Code loses API access (not fail-open). Routing OAuth/subscription traffic through a third-party proxy is a policy and ToS grey area, which I did not verify.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev is asked with instructions plus attacker-controllable tool output preview. Jev returns only a typed choice, so injection can at worst make it wrongly cut or keep output; low severity. Cut outputs are replaced with 'compactio: ... Full output: node .../cli.ts show ID' text, which the agent will execute via Bash. The ID is only a random uuid slice and safe() sanitises it.
Telemetry: none beyond Jev calls; logs stay local in ~/.compactio/log.jsonl. Data-file cut heuristics can hide the middle of long logs from Claude.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.dataEgress: With an OPENROUTER_API_KEY, each Bash/Grep/WebFetch/mcp output of 6,000 chars or more (after lossless cleanup) sends to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions: the last user prompt (up to 2000 chars, redacted), the tool name, the tool_input (up to 600 chars, redacted), and a preview of about 6,000 chars (first 30 lines, error lines, last 20 lines, redacted). No key means nothing is sent. Sweep additionally sends, per batch of up to 16 old tool results, the goal and 2,400-char previews, but only when at least 40k chars of old results are open. Nothing is sent when the output is under 6k chars, for code Reads that are not data files, or for images/PDFs. Note that this covers client code and command output, and redaction is best-effort.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.failureMode: Hooks are fail-open. A Jev timeout (COMPACTIO_TIMEOUT_MS default 1500 ms), HTTP error, unknown choice or confidence below 0.6 all leave the full output unchanged, and errors are logged as engine=fail-open. The main() catch exits 0. The hook timeout is 5s. Without a key, a local-only mode applies head+tail only to outputs over 24k chars. The Sweep proxy is fail-open for its own logic errors (the original body is forwarded, Jev timeout 3000 ms) but fail-closed if the process is down: ECONNREFUSED breaks Claude Code until 'sweep off'. Systemd Restart=always and the SessionStart guard mitigate this.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server, so no tool definitions, no server instructions, and no skill descriptions. There are 3 slash commands (setup/sweep/gain) with one-line descriptions, about 100 tokens in total. Hooks inject no additional text on the happy path. They only shorten tool results, adding a one-line note of about 40 tokens ('[compactio: kept "errors" view of N lines. Full output: node ".../cli.ts" show ID]') where output is cut. Net effect is a context reduction, in exchange for occasionally hiding data.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PostToolUse on Bash|Read|Grep|WebFetch|WebSearch|mcp__.*, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart). Jev is called automatically without the model choosing or being prompted, which matches the user's requirement. The optional Sweep is a transparent proxy.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.latencyImpact: Every matching tool call spawns a fresh node process (about 40-80 ms, estimated, not measured) even when the output is small. Outputs under 2k chars exit immediately. Calls from 6k chars add one Jev round trip, capped at 1.5 s (claimed 70-500 ms). Sweep adds up to 3 s per API request when it asks Jev (and only when at least 40k chars of old results are open), plus proxy hop overhead. UserPromptSubmit adds a small node spawn per prompt.
pros: Only candidate here that satisfies 'Claude Code must use Jev automatically': deterministic hooks that never need a 'use jev' prompt.
OpenRouter is a first-class provider (jev.ts:29-42) using ~typesafe/jev-latest on /api/alpha/decisions. It sends the attribution headers and is a zero-patch integration for the user's key setup.
Sensible use of Jev's actual strength: a typed Choice decision with calibrated confidence, gated by MIN_CONFIDENCE 0.6, at negligible cost ($0.042/M input tokens).

Conservative by design: never cuts Read of code the agent may edit (hook.ts:159-178), skips images/PDFs/notebooks, and exempts commands containing 'compactio'. Originals are recoverable by 'show ID'. Hook path is fail-open with a 1.5 s timeout.
Zero context cost (no MCP tools) and it reduces context. It works with a subscription/OAuth login when using hooks only.
Clean, small (about 1.7k lines total), readable source and MIT licensed. Unit tests use a fake Jev and fake API. CI runs on Node 22 and 24, and npm publishing uses provenance.
Works without a key in a lossless-plus-24k head/tail local mode, so it is safe to try before enabling Jev.
cons: Very young and unproven: repo created 2026-09-25 (5 days old), 26 commits by one author in a single day, 3 stars, no releases and no issues history. README admits 'a real session where Jev drops a result is not tested yet'.

The Jev integration is not evidenced against the OpenRouter Decisions schema: I could not verify the {model,state,questions} body from OpenRouter docs (404), and the README does not say which provider its live test used. Test it with a small curl before trusting it.

Sends redacted client-code previews (last prompt, tool input, 6 KB of output) to OpenRouter and its upstream on every large output. It uses regex redaction that SECURITY.md itself says is incomplete, which is a real concern for client projects under NDA.

Sweep proxy is high-risk for this user: it redirects all Anthropic traffic (including OAuth) via localhost, pins ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL to 'claude-opus-5-5[1m]' (stale when Opus changes), and edits settings.json plus installs a systemd Restart=always service. If the proxy fails, Claude Code has no API. Its cache-rewrite gate can cost more than it saves. It is macOS/Windows untested and has a permanent-tombstone problem.

It conflicts in practice with the user's stack: it also mutates tool output through PostToolUse updatedToolOutput on Bash/Grep, the same events where the GitNexus and caveman hooks run, so hook ordering and multiple rewriters are unverified. Its matcher also covers mcp__.* (gitnexus, playwright output).

Cutting risk: Jev sees only head/errors/tail, so it can misjudge a middle-critical output. A short 'continue' prompt gives it a poor goal. Hidden log lines can cause wrong debugging, and the agent must remember to run 'show ID'.

Node process spawn on every Bash/Read/Grep/WebFetch/mcp call. In auto/bypass sessions with hundreds of calls, that costs tens of ms each. Its value is token savings, not better coding decisions, so it does not deliver Jev for routing, permission or review decisions.
Key handling: 'compactio key' writes the key in plaintext into ~/.claude/settings.json. No tests were run by me (static review only); the token-savings claims are unverified.
gh-ramaaditya49-compactio.verdict: A real, automatic hook-based Jev integration with native OpenRouter support, low context cost and a fail-open design. It is also brand-new, single-author and lightly tested, and it sends redacted code previews off-machine. Reasonable to try hooks-only (never enable Sweep, and keep it off client repos) after verifying the OpenRouter call and hook ordering with GitNexus; skip the proxy entirely.

It applies the answer by appending an effort-only system message (beta mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01) as the last message, re-inserting earlier markers so the prompt cache prefix is preserved. Jev may only lower effort below the session /effort by default. It is a cost-saving research tool that also ships `stats` (spend breakdown), `bench` (6 coding tasks) and `doctor`. It does NOT give Claude Code any Jev-powered decision tools, review, routing of model choice, or planning help; it only tunes thinking effort.

security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts and no runtime dependencies (package.json scripts only has test); no curl|sh installer.

Proxy binds 127.0.0.1 on random port for the session only (src/proxy.mjs:277 listen host default 127.0.0.1); Claude credentials (OAuth bearer / API key) pass through untouched and are stated as never stored or logged. Any local process that finds the port could still send requests through it but the proxy adds no creds.

Jev key: stored in ~/.config/jev-effort/config.json mode 0600 (config.mjs:209-218), or read from env/file; setup takes --key-file/--key-stdin/hidden prompt, so the key is never in argv (setup.mjs:46-84). Key only sent as Bearer to the configured route with redirect:'error'.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs/prompts are fed to Jev as state, but Jev returns only a constrained choice (parseDecision validates effort in allowed list and lease in allowed set, jev.mjs:58-71) and instructions mark history as untrusted; worst case is a manipulated effort level, not code execution. Jev can never exceed session effort by default.

Rewrites API requests: appends a system message and beta header; on API 400 it resends the original, and after two rejections disables rewriting (proxy.mjs:235-241, docs/how-it-works.md failure table).
Unofficial dependency on undocumented Claude Code request shape (per-turn-control-2026-07-01 beta); TESTED_CLAUDE_CODE = 2.1.280 while the user runs 2.1.285. doctor warns on newer versions.
Optional JEV_EFFORT_DUMP_DIR writes full request bodies (off by default).
Local logs ~/.local/share/jev-effort/logs contain counts, efforts, timings, Claude session ids; state holds hashes only; no telemetry. Single unvetted maintainer, 1 week old, 3 stars.

Behind any custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL Claude Code disables Remote Control, server-managed settings and claude.ai-backed tools (Artifacts), and asks for server-side auto-mode review differently (docs/usage.md Limitations). Notably relevant to a subscription/OAuth + auto-mode user and to client work with managed settings. It also bypasses (runs plain claude) if ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL/HTTPS_PROXY/Bedrock etc. are set (environment.mjs:213-228).
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.dataEgress: To OpenRouter/Jev per uncached decision: model name, allowed efforts, latest user prompt (up to 8,000 chars), original task plus up to 5 earlier prompts (trimmed), up to 8 of Claude's visible replies since latest prompt, and the last 6 tool calls with inputs and head+tail output previews (~1,000 tokens each). That is real code, file contents, command outputs and client-project text (typically ~1-5K input tokens per call, README says avg ~5K in long sessions). No thinking traces. Also everything to Anthropic goes through localhost proxy unchanged except the appended effort message. Client projects: source excerpts leave to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (provider pinned to typesafe, no fallback) on every non-leased step, with no secret redaction; the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover this path.
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Jev error or timeout (default 5 s, jevTimeoutMs, min 500) -> that step uses Claude Code's own effort (policy.mjs fallback). Circuit breaker: 3 consecutive failures -> Jev skipped for 2 minutes (jev.mjs:83-105). Internal errors forward the original request; API 400 on rewrite -> resend original, after 2 rejections drop to shadow. Missing key -> plain claude. But the proxy itself is in the critical path of every Anthropic request: if the proxy process crashes mid-session, Claude Code is stuck with a dead ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (no automatic fallback).
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.contextCost: Zero tools, zero MCP instructions, zero hook-injected text, no SKILL.md. The only prompt effect is the tiny appended effort-only system message (empty content). Side effects are worse than the cost: any custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL makes Claude Code disable MCP tool search (README measured 27K -> 281K-500K token fresh sessions); jev-effort mitigates by setting ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, fine-grained tool streaming and gateway hint headers when upstream is api.anthropic.com (environment.mjs:190-210), and about 4K fewer tokens per request because claude.ai-backed tools drop. The user already has gitnexus and playwright MCP servers (large tool sets), so relying on the ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH restoration matters.
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.latencyImpact: Apply mode adds a synchronous Jev call before each non-leased step: docs/usage.md reports 747 ms median and 3.8 s p95 in real sessions (how-it-works cites ~300 ms on TypeSafe route; README reports 601 ms median / 793 ms p95 in benchmark). Zero added wait during leases (up to 10 steps) and in shadow mode. Timeout ceiling 5 s per call. Lower thinking at max effort can offset the wait (benchmark wall time -58% at max; +6% at high).
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy, fully automatic once Claude Code is started through `jev-effort` (alias claude=jev-effort). No prompting, no model discretion; it acts on every model step. Caveat: it is a launcher wrapper, not a plugin or settings.json entry, so plain `claude`, IDE extensions and the desktop app are not covered unless `jev-effort serve` plus ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set. Setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in ~/.claude/settings.json makes it step aside.
pros: Genuinely automatic once aliased: no per-prompt instruction, decides per step with leases, and its own docs claim it never resets the prompt cache (0 unexpected misses in 411 checked steps).

Real OpenRouter support in code: openrouter route with sk-or- auto-detect and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/jev.mjs:5-8, src/config.mjs:170,221), matching the user's chosen provider, and it is the only Jev use that leverages Jev's Choice primitive in the way it was designed (typed decision, probabilities).

Careful engineering for a small tool: zero deps, no postinstall, localhost-only, key never in argv, 5 s timeout, circuit breaker, fail-open, 400-retry fallback, shadow mode to try it with zero effect, doctor and stats.

Honest, reproducible research: the author's own results say at high effort the saving is about 1% and the real-session estimate is 4-9% at max; it can be evaluated in shadow mode before applying anything.
Restores MCP tool search under the proxy (ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true) which matters for the user's gitnexus and playwright MCP servers; adds no tools or context of its own.
Cheap: Jev costs about $0.12 for 470 steps of a 92-minute session.
cons: Only tunes reasoning effort; it does not give Claude Code any Jev decision capability (no code-review gating, no risk scoring, no routing between models or subagents). Most of the 'use Jev when it adds value' idea is not delivered.

Savings are small for this user: at high effort about -1%, and even at max only 4-9% in a long session because cached context is ~82% of spend; and the user is on a subscription so dollar savings are not billed, and quality risk at max on real client work is 'untested' per the author.

Wrapper/proxy architecture: must launch via `jev-effort`; behind ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL Claude Code disables Remote Control, server-managed settings and claude.ai-backed tools such as Artifacts (usage.md limitations) and changes auto-mode review behavior (needs CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0), which the user relies on daily (auto permission mode, Artifacts). Explicit warning: don't use if a client org relies on server-managed settings.

Fragile coupling to undocumented Claude Code internals: verified only on 2.1.280 and Opus 5.5 (user is on 2.1.285); the marker must be the last message and depends on beta headers per-turn-control-2026-07-01 and mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01, so a Claude Code update can silently disable it (falls back to no-op, not breakage).

Sends prompts, replies and 6 tool-output previews (real code, potentially secrets from command output) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe every non-leased step with no redaction; bad fit for client projects and bypasses the user's secret-leak hook.
Adds 0.6-0.75 s median (3.8 s p95) wait per non-leased step in apply mode.
Very immature: created 2026-09-23, 15 commits by 1 author, 3 stars, no releases on GitHub, npm latest (0.1.6) lags repo HEAD (0.1.7); README itself says 'isn't recommended as a way to save money'.

The 'function hooks' native path (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, turn.step) documented in how-it-works.md would remove the proxy but is early-access and unimplemented here; sibling repos (jev-opus, jev-model-router, effort-router) cover the same niche.
gh-ifoster01-jev-effort.verdict: Technically sound, safe-by-design (fail-open, localhost, no deps, OpenRouter supported) but it only tunes thinking effort with a 1-9% saving that the author himself says does not justify using it, and the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy costs this user Artifacts, Remote Control, server-managed settings and pipes code excerpts to a third party. Worth running once in --jev-shadow mode as a measurement, not as the daily integration.

Plugin runs as in-process TypeScript inside Claude Code with access to the function-hook surface ($.fs, $.shell 'CLI only', $.http, $.settings); trust is entirely in the aleksvega fork author, whose npm/GitHub identity is 1 week old
