Prompt injection: Jev output is only numeric probabilities so it cannot inject text into Claude; but attacker-controlled tool output could bias keep/drop decisions (e.g. get a constraint dropped). jev-qa/jev-find embed file contents/paths in the state
Compaction is destructive: dropped calls/results are deleted permanently (state prompt says so); a wrong Jev decision loses context silently with no summary

gh-aleksvega-fast-jev-compaction.dataEgress: Hook path: on every compaction, the whole conversation state (up to maxStateTokens=25k est. tokens) goes to the Jev endpoint, resent in full with every batched request: all user prompts and assistant text (verbatim, abridged head+tail only if over budget), goal (last 3 user prompts), and every tool call's name and input (Bash commands, file paths, Edit/Write content truncated to 1000/200/60 chars only when over budget); tool RESULTS are replaced by 'ok, N chars (omitted)' so file contents and command output are not sent. So code appears only via Edit/Write inputs and pasted user text; secrets typed in prompts or Bash commands (env vars in commands) would leave the machine, and the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover $.http.fetch. Destination as shipped: api.typesafe.ai (needs TypeSafe key); after patch: openrouter.ai (OpenRouter's data policy applies). CLIs: jev-qa sends source file contents; jev-find sends directory listings plus first line of each file; jev-gate sends git diff of last commit.
gh-aleksvega-fast-jev-compaction.failureMode: Hook is fail-open by design: any Jev error, malformed JSON, missing key, state that cannot be fitted, or <25% reduction => toast 'fallback to built-in summary' and next(event) hands off to Claude's normal compaction (fast-jev.ts:283-289). Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY it falls back every time (missing key = plugin silently does nothing beyond a toast). No timeout or AbortSignal anywhere in the TS path (grep: none in src/ or hooks/) - a hung request stalls compaction until the host's fetch gives up; concurrent batches via Promise.all. turn.complete swallows errors. jev-gate.py is fail-CLOSED (API failure => BLOCK, 60s timeout) which would block pushes if wired in a hook; jev-qa/jev-find have no timeout.
gh-aleksvega-fast-jev-compaction.contextCost: Essentially zero tokens: no MCP server, no tools, no server instructions, no SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit text injection. Only a UI toast/log line per compaction. Root SKILL.md (~1.5k chars, ~370 tokens if loaded) is not registered by plugin.json. If the user instead wires the CLIs through AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md prose, cost is a few hundred tokens but then it is model-discretion again.
gh-aleksvega-fast-jev-compaction.autoInvocation: Deterministic function hooks (session.compact, turn.complete) that fire automatically with no user prompting, but only for context compaction. Everything else (jev-qa, jev-find, jev-gate, jev-enhance) requires the agent to choose to shell out per SKILL.md/AGENTS.md prose, or the user to script a git hook, i.e. not automatic. Function hooks require the early-access env flag CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 (README, hooks/README.md) and were type-generated against Claude Code 2.1.274 while the user runs 2.1.285 (API drift risk, unverified).
gh-aleksvega-fast-jev-compaction.latencyImpact: Only on compaction events (roughly 1-3 s estimated with 25-30k token payloads); nothing on normal turns.

gh-ipecter-jev-runway.name: jev-runway
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.whatItDoes: Local HTTP proxy (127.0.0.1:8788) that sits between the OpenAI Codex CLI/app and its upstream (ChatGPT backend, OpenAI API or custom provider). Once at least 32k chars of new tool output accumulate, it asks Jev two Noul yes/no questions per old tool call (does the call still matter; is the full output still needed) and on every later /responses request cuts unneeded outputs to a 300-char head plus a note pointing to an archived copy under ~/.codex/jev-runway/archive. It also drops reasoning items for fully trimmed steps, trims Codex compaction requests, and can use a WebSocket upstream. Codex-only: it parses OpenAI Responses requests, not Anthropic Messages, so it does nothing for Claude Code as shipped. Idea is derived from tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev.ts:34-41 ROUTES = typesafe https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (model jev-latest, env TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and vercel-ai-gateway https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai/evaluation-model (model typesafe-ai/jev, env AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY). JevProvider type is a closed union (jev.ts:4) and parseJevProvider throws on anything else (jev.ts:44-52). grep -i openrouter across src/, scripts/, README: zero hits. Request body for typesafe route is {model,state,questions:{name:{type:'noul',instructions}}} with Bearer auth (jev.ts:96-104); reply read as answers[name].noul (jev.ts:140-151). jevCaller has a baseUrl option (jev.ts:165,190) but it is not wired to any env var: codex-proxy.ts:143 only passes {...loadDaemonCredential(), model: JEV_RUNWAY_MODEL, timeoutMs, signal}.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Jev side is trivial-to-moderate: the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone body is described as the same System One shape as TypeSafe's /v1/systemone, so adding a third 'openrouter' route in jev.ts (url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, key OPENROUTER_API_KEY) plus extending the provider union/auth.ts/parseJevProvider is roughly 20-40 lines; the 'noul' reply parsing and 32k budget (JEV_BUDGETS) likely carry over, but the OpenRouter response schema was not verified from this repo. The real blocker is not the Jev provider: the proxy only understands OpenAI Responses (endpointOf matches /responses and /responses/compact only, codex-proxy.ts:498-499; responses.ts 430 lines) so Claude Code (Anthropic /v1/messages, tool_use/tool_result blocks, cache_control) would need a new request parser and rewriter, i.e. a rewrite of the core, plus ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL wiring that does not exist.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (the second supported Jev route, with a 4.5k-token request budget because it 503s on large requests).

Trim decision is driven by an LLM classifier reading untrusted repo content in tool inputs and messages: a prompt-injection or model error can silently hide tool output from the main model; mitigated by 300-char head, archive copy and the note telling the model where to re-read, but the note relies on the model doing so
Archives (full trimmed outputs) and trims.jsonl (first 200 chars of each call input) written under ~/.codex/jev-runway/, 0600, pruned after 7 days; may retain secrets from tool output on disk

No postinstall script seen; npm ships prebuilt native binaries in optional platform packages (opaque, unauditable from source alone); self-update downloads tarball from npm registry (honours npm_config_registry) and verifies integrity hash (update.ts:11,54)

Telemetry: no third-party telemetry found; metrics stay local and exclude prompts/keys per README (only network calls are Jev, upstream, npm registry)
Not executed; static reading only
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.dataEgress: To Jev provider (TypeSafe or Vercel AI Gateway): full conversation text (user and assistant messages, task/goal) plus tool-call names and inputs, with tool outputs replaced by size notes, in batches of Noul questions (judge.ts, README Privacy). Whole request bodies still go to the user's model upstream as before (with trimmed outputs). Local disk: archived full tool outputs, trim ledger. Nothing else observed leaving the machine. If ported to Claude Code, it would additionally see Anthropic OAuth/API auth headers because it must proxy /v1/messages.
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.failureMode: Fail-open by design: Jev evaluation runs between turns in the background so no request waits on it; on Jev error/timeout (default 15s per call, jev.ts:180, retries on 503) or an unreadable request, the request goes upstream exactly as Codex sent it. A missing key is reported as an auth JevError. The proxy itself is a single point of failure though: if the local service is down while ~/.codex/config.toml points at 127.0.0.1:8788, Codex requests fail (service has KeepAlive/ThrottleInterval 5s restart).
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero hook text, so no context cost in Claude Code (it would not run at all there). In Codex it reduces context by trimming stale tool output (author claims 46% fewer input tokens over a real workload, 66-76% on replayed sessions; self-reported, provider-count based). Downside: trimming rewrites earlier history, which changes the prompt prefix and can cost cache hits; author reports 92% cache reads so far on Codex/OpenAI, but that is not evidence for Anthropic cache_control behavior.
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.latencyImpact: Claimed no added waiting: Jev decisions are made asynchronously between turns; per-request overhead is a local proxy hop plus JSON rewrite (a few ms sizing per code comment at codex-proxy.ts ~431). Jev calls themselves take up to 15 s timeout, parallel 4, several batches for long sessions. Not measured by me.
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (fully automatic once Codex is pointed at it). For Claude Code the equivalent would be ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at a local proxy, which this project does not implement.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev with the right primitive (Noul yes/no per tool output) for a real, measurable problem: stale tool output re-billed every turn
Fail-open, off the request path: Jev is consulted between turns so a slow or down Jev never blocks the coding loop (README, codex-proxy.ts)

Lossless design: full output archived locally and the note tells the model where to re-read it; first message and the 6 newest items never trimmed; includes trims ledger and status/quality metrics (re-run rate 0.9% in author's data)

Clean, well-typed Jev client (jev.ts) with hard deadline that survives fetch ignoring abort, retries, budget-aware batching for the 32k window, and a baseUrl option, so adding an OpenRouter route is small on the Jev side
Substantial test suite (~3.5k lines, mocked Jev) and MIT license; architecture idea is portable and directly relevant to a fully automatic, prompt-free Claude Code integration
No MCP/skill/hook footprint on the context window
cons: Codex-only: parses OpenAI Responses (/responses, /responses/compact) and Codex config.toml/session ids; cannot be pointed at Claude Code, which speaks Anthropic /v1/messages with tool_use/tool_result and cache_control (no such code found in src/)
No OpenRouter support at all (zero references); only TypeSafe direct and Vercel AI Gateway, both closed provider unions; baseUrl exists in code but no env var/CLI reaches it

Would require porting the core (responses.ts, codex-proxy.ts, WebSocket upstream, compact handling) to the Messages API and proxying Claude Code auth; for a subscription/OAuth user the proxy must forward OAuth headers, increasing risk and ToS/stability questions

Trimming old tool_result content invalidates Anthropic prompt-cache prefix; cache savings vs token savings tradeoff is untested for Claude Code, and Claude Code already does its own microcompaction/auto-compact
Very immature: 5 commits over 5 days, 1 author, 3 stars, no releases, no PR CI, npm package first published 2026-09-24; 'private: true' package.json; unverified self-reported savings
Sends full conversation text and tool inputs from client projects to a third-party beta model (Jev), a confidentiality issue for client work; archives of raw tool output kept on disk for 7 days
Persistent background service + rewriting the agent's base URL is invasive and adds a local single point of failure; binary distributed prebuilt via npm (opaque)
gh-ipecter-jev-runway.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code: it is a Codex/OpenAI-Responses proxy with no OpenRouter route, no MCP/hook/skill surface, and only 5 days of history. Its only value is as a design reference (async Noul 'is this tool output still needed?' with fail-open trimming), which would need a fresh Anthropic-Messages implementation and cache-behavior validation to be useful here.

gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.name: claude-jev-model-router
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.whatItDoes: Local Node HTTP proxy (127.0.0.1:8787) placed between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. For the first request of each subagent (x-claude-code-agent-id header) it sends the delegation prompt (latest user turn, max 4000 chars) plus 6 fixed Noul yes/no questions to Jev /v1/systemone, combines P(yes) with hand-set weights in code into a score, and maps it to Haiku/Sonnet/Opus tiers with margin gates. Only the `model` field is rewritten; everything else is relayed byte-for-byte and streamed. Main conversation is never touched by default. Observe-only by default (logs what it would do); --enable applies routing. Does model-cost routing for subagents, not code intelligence.

Would need a fork or local patch of the npm dist (dist/classify.js:13,60,77 mirror the source); no upstream support, no plugin seam. security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts (npm scripts only dev/build/check/prepublishOnly); only 2 runtime deps (undici, smol-toml); no child_process/eval in src.
Binds 127.0.0.1 by default (config.ts defaultConfig), but --host is configurable; no auth on the local listener, so any local process can use it as an Anthropic relay.

Proxy sees every request incl. the OAuth/Bearer Authorization header and the full conversation; it forwards headers unchanged (relay.ts buildUpstreamHeaders) and does not log them. Decision log (decisions.ts, server.ts:110-125) records metadata only (ids, models, tool counts, tokens, reasons), no prompt text.

API key handling: README's first-listed method is `--env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...` on the command line, which exposes the key in the process list / shell history; safer options are env var or ~/.claude-model-router/.env.

envfile.ts loads ./.env from the CURRENT DIRECTORY first (index.ts loadDotEnv ['.env', ~/.claude-model-router/.env]) into process.env, so launching the proxy from a client project dir pulls that project's .env into the proxy process (not sent anywhere, but surprising).

Prompt-injection surface is small: Jev output is only numbers (P(yes)) combined by fixed code; a malicious delegation prompt can at worst bias the tier choice. Readonly tool sets skip Jev entirely; mutation-capable downgrades to Haiku need margin >=0.3.

Extremely new single-author package (npm 0.1.0 on 2026-09-20), no signed releases, no LICENSE file, no CI: supply-chain trust is low; pin version and review dist/ before use. No telemetry found in source.
Rerouting to a different Claude model is a behavioural risk: a wrong Haiku verdict on an editing subagent could produce worse edits (mitigated by margins, mid-tier fallback).
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.dataEgress: To Jev (TypeSafe direct as shipped; OpenRouter after patch): once per new subagent that has exec or mutation tools, the latest user-turn text (the delegation prompt Claude Code wrote for the subagent, truncated to 4000 chars, context.ts MAX_TURN_CHARS) plus turn index, model id and 6 fixed question strings. No transcript, files, diffs or tool outputs by design, but the delegation prompt often contains file paths, symbol names and task descriptions, which matters for client projects; with OpenRouter it passes through OpenRouter and its provider. Read-only subagents send nothing. To Anthropic: the normal Claude traffic (all of it) transits the local proxy unchanged except model. Local: JSONL log ~/.claude-model-router/decisions.jsonl (metadata only, no prompt text). Auth header is forwarded, not stored.
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.failureMode: Jev failure is fail-open: 3000 ms timeout (router_timeout_ms; code default in JevRouter is 400 but config passes 3000), HTTP >=400, non-JSON or no answers become RouterError, caught in policy.consultRouter, and the request falls back to the static tier (cheap for readonly/exec agents, mid for mutation-capable). Low margin also falls back. Jev being down never breaks a Claude request. BUT the proxy process itself is a single point of failure: if it is not running while ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points to it, all Claude Code API calls fail (connection refused); upstream failure returns 502 (server.ts:146-159). Needs a supervised service. Observe mode still calls Jev for every subagent request each time (not sticky), adding latency without benefit.
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.latencyImpact: Main-thread turns: only local proxy hop (negligible, streamed unbuffered) with no Jev call. Subagent start: one Jev call, claimed 70-500 ms, budget up to 3 s (default.toml comment says observed 0.3-2.0 s in practice, 400 ms timed out every time); blocks the subagent's first request only, then sticky for 12 h TTL. Sticky state is in memory and lost on restart.
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.contextCost: Zero tokens in Claude's context: no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill, no injected text. It is a transparent network proxy. Indirect effects: setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to a non-Anthropic host may change some Claude Code client behaviour (e.g. features gated on first-party base URL such as MCP tool search); unverified, worth testing. Also the GET /v1/models catalogue returned by the proxy lists only the 3 tier IDs.
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: fully automatic once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set and the daemon runs; no prompts, hooks or tool calls needed. Only acts on subagent requests (x-claude-code-agent-id), never the main thread by default. This is the only category in the candidate set that satisfies 'Claude Code uses Jev without being asked', but what it automates is model-tier routing for subagents, a narrow use of Jev.
pros: Truly automatic and zero-prompt: transparent proxy triggered by the x-claude-code-agent-id header, no MCP/hook/skill overhead in context (0 tokens).
Uses Jev the way its brief says it should be used: typed Noul questions to get calibrated P(yes), with arithmetic and thresholds in deterministic code (signals.ts:141-164) and nothing free-text.

Conservative design: main thread never touched, sticky per-subagent decision protects prompt cache, tool-set gates (readonly capped cheap, Write/Edit agents need margin >=0.3 to go to Haiku, fallback mid), fail-open on any Jev error.
Observe-only by default with JSONL decision log and a `savings` report; you can watch decisions for a day before --enable.

Request body handling is careful: only `model` rewritten, undici.request for byte-exact relay, backpressure, unbuffered SSE, error bodies untouched, anthropic-* headers forwarded as an open list; passes the OAuth Authorization header straight through so subscription login should keep working.
Tiny, readable codebase (~2k LOC src, 2 deps, no postinstall), easy to audit and to patch for OpenRouter.
Jev call happens once per subagent so cost is negligible (~400 tokens at ~$0.042/M input).
cons: Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY with no OpenRouter path; needs a local patch/fork (trivial, but you then own an unmaintained fork of a 10-day-old, 6-commit, single-author, 1-star project).

No LICENSE file despite MIT metadata, no CI, git package.json (0.1.2) lags npm (0.1.3), README says subagent_router defaults to jev but code default is none (config.ts defaultPolicy) unless a TOML config is passed.

Narrow value: only affects subagent model choice. Gains are cost/quota savings on Explore-type subagents; for a subscription/OAuth user there is no per-token bill, only quota, and Opus 5.5 subagents may be deliberately wanted. No help with code intelligence, review, or decisions in the main loop.

Classifier only sees the delegation prompt (README admits this), so difficulty is prompt-level; wrong downgrades to Haiku on editing agents are possible. Six hand-tuned weights and thresholds are unvalidated, and the author's own comments show tuning trouble (400 ms timeout on every call, margin 0.25 rejecting nearly all).

Operational burden: a persistent local daemon must be running (systemd user unit) or every Claude Code call fails; ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL must be exported in the environment or settings.json env; non-first-party base URL may alter Claude Code features; the proxy handles your OAuth bearer token and all conversation content for personal and client projects.

Hardcoded tier IDs (claude-sonnet-5.5, claude-opus-5.5, claude-haiku-4-5) use dotted names not verified against the real API IDs used by Claude Code 2.1.285; a mismatch would make routed subagents error (model-not-found) once --enable is on. Unverified, must check the observe log's model_in values first.
Delegation prompt text (possibly client code names/paths) goes to a third-party inference endpoint; only mitigated by size cap and readonly-skip.
--env KEY=... documented as the first option leaks the key to the process list; ./.env from cwd is auto-loaded.
gh-andrei10k-claude-jev-model-router.verdict: The only genuinely automatic, zero-context-cost Jev integration in this set, and its design is careful and fail-open, but it automates just subagent model-tier routing, is 10 days old with a single author, and needs a small patch to use OpenRouter instead of api.typesafe.ai. Worth running in observe mode with a patched OpenRouter key only if you spawn many subagents and want quota savings; not a general Jev integration for daily coding.

npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.name: @barmajja/jclaude
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.whatItDoes: Node CLI (commander, zod) from one person (am33ma / Barmajja). Its main purpose is a controller that asks Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter) Choice/Score/Noul questions to pick a Claude model and effort for a task, then launches `claude -p <task> --model X --effort Y` as a subprocess. It also ships a `jclaude hook <event>` subcommand that acts as a Claude Code hook handler. The hook events are user-prompt-submit, pre-tool-use, stop, subagent-stop, post-tool-batch, post-tool-use-failure, permission-request, task-created and task-completed. The repo also has a SQLite/JSON ledger, an offline Jaccard-similarity project memory, a skill catalog, a test selector, and a PKCE login for OpenRouter keys. Its wrapper of `claude` is a zsh function in the source repo. That function is not in the npm tarball and only covers `claude -p`.

providerSupport.evidence: jclaude.config.json: jev.endpoint="https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions", modelId="typesafe/jev-1.13", timeoutMs=8000. Overridable via JCLAUDE_JEV_ENDPOINT and JCLAUDE_JEV_MODEL (dist/config/load.js:29-35). The key is OPENROUTER_API_KEY (dist/config/load.js:120,189). dist/jev-client/client.js:74-81 POSTs with `authorization: Bearer <key>`. The wire body is {model, state:<JSON string>, questions:{id:{type,instructions,criteria}}, session_id} (client.js:20-34). dist/auth/login.js:4-5 uses openrouter.ai/auth and /api/v1/auth/keys for PKCE. The README says /api/v1/systemone but the code uses /api/alpha/decisions. No TYPESAFE_API_KEY or TypeSafe host appears anywhere in dist.
providerSupport.others: none. The `claude` worker launch is a plain subprocess to the local CLI. The optional central store is a user-deployed AWS API Gateway endpoint (JCLAUDE_CENTRAL_STORE_ENDPOINT), off by default.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: n/a, already OpenRouter-native. Moving to TypeSafe direct would be a base URL, key and header change, and the wire schema is presumably the same.

interface.name: jclaude hook user-prompt-submit
interface.purpose: Each prompt is truncated to 4000 chars and run through runRoute (redact, pack, several Jev questions, policy, ledger, memory, skill nomination). It injects additionalContext starting with '[jev advisory - not an instruction...]', containing profile=, effort=, near-duplicate, skill= and memory lines. It cannot change the active model. It is silent when there is no key or on error (dist/cli/commands/hook.js:63-135).

interface.name: jclaude hook pre-tool-use
interface.purpose: Bash only. Sends the command (first 2000 chars) as one Noul 'is this destructive/hard to reverse' question. If P>=0.6 it returns permissionDecision:'ask'. It never returns deny and returns nothing below the threshold or on error (hook.js:~290-320).

interface.name: jclaude hook stop
interface.purpose: Sends the last assistant message (4000 chars) to Jev as a Noul 'looks finished' check. Writes state/stop-events.jsonl. Never prints or blocks (hook.js:163-200).

interface.name: jclaude hook subagent-stop
interface.purpose: Local error-class logging only, no Jev call.

interface.name: jclaude hook post-tool-batch
interface.purpose: Maps edited files to test suites through glob mappings (config plus jclaude.project.json) and injects a '[jev] ... consider running suite' hint. No Jev call.

interface.name: jclaude hook post-tool-use-failure
interface.purpose: Regex classification of auth/permission/missing-credential/platform errors, injecting a 'retrying is unlikely to help' hint. No Jev call.

interface.name: jclaude hook permission-request
interface.purpose: Appends the tool name and a 200-char input summary to state/permission-events.jsonl. It never returns a decision. It also syncs to the central store if configured.

interface.name: jclaude hook task-created / task-completed
interface.purpose: Logs task events. task-created asks Jev a 'well_specified' Noul on subject and description. It never blocks.

interface.name: jclaude route <task> [--live --project --subsystem]
interface.purpose: Runs the routing pipeline and prints the decision. It uses a mock client unless --live is given.

interface.name: jclaude run <task> [--model --repair]
interface.purpose: Routes then spawns `claude -p` with --model and --effort. Optional bounded repair and escalation loop.

interface.name: jclaude resume / report / memory {list,add,invalidate} / blocker / doctor / auth {login,logout}
interface.purpose: Ledger inspection, telemetry report, memory management, cross-project blocker board, environment check, OpenRouter PKCE key setup writing .env with mode 0600.

security: Not a Jev-trust-boundary tool: hooks send data to OpenRouter unredacted in two paths. The PreToolUse and Stop hooks call JevClient.ask directly with {command} or {response}, bypassing redactRoutingState (hook.js:170-172, ~305). Only the UserPromptSubmit route path applies the regex redactor (decision-contract/redact.js). It covers sk-, ghp_, AKIA, KEY=value and PEM patterns, plus any 40+ char alphanumeric run.

API key is read from .env in JCLAUDE_HOME, the install dir of the package (cli/index.js:277), not from the process env or argv. Nothing appears in the process list. It is written with mode 0600 and never printed. With a global npm install that dir is inside node_modules, and the ledger and state (prompts, commands, permission-event summaries) are written there in plaintext.

No postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry to the author. Deps are only zod, dotenv and commander. Optional central store POSTs hook events (task/permission/stop) to a user-configured AWS endpoint, off by default.

Prompt-injection surface: the UserPromptSubmit advisory injects memory titles, near-duplicate request summaries and cross-project blocker summaries into model context. Those records come from a shared ledger and central store, so poisoned entries would enter context as hook additionalContext (labelled 'advisory').

Shell execution: spawns `claude -p` (run only) and git via execFileSync with an args array, no shell string. Log-reducer spawn is shell-less. The wrapper function shadows `claude` globally in zsh (source repo only).

No license field in package.json or npm metadata (unlicensed by default). Source repo Barmajja/barmajja-aios is not public: gh returns 404, so the only reviewable artifact is the npm tarball with source maps.
Single maintainer account, published 7 versions within about 2 hours on 2026-09-23 and untouched since. The README says the design is copied from another repo without history.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.dataEgress: The user-prompt-submit hook sends the first 4000 chars of EVERY user prompt (regex-redacted) plus memory evidence and a session/project id to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, as a JSON string in `state` with 4-5 questions. The pre-tool-use hook sends every Bash command (first 2000 chars, NOT redacted). The stop hook sends the last assistant message (first 4000 chars, NOT redacted), so it can carry code, file contents and tool-derived text. task-created sends the task subject (500 chars) and description (2000 chars). All of that goes to OpenRouter and the TypeSafe/Jev provider behind it. It is also stored locally in plaintext under JCLAUDE_HOME/state (ledger, stop-events, permission-events, task-events). The central store is opt-in and would send events to the user's own AWS endpoint. No source files or diffs are sent, except what appears in prompts, commands and assistant messages. The repair loop diff module reads git diffs, but only in `run --repair`.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. Hooks return null on any error, and a missing key means no call is made at all. The JevClient timeout is 8000 ms (config timeoutMs) via AbortController. The CLI has an internal 10 s cap, which is under Claude Code's hook timeout. On a Jev failure, route returns jevError and the prompt hook emits nothing. In `route` a failure resolves to a fallback or review-pause decision. The PreToolUse hook can add an 'ask' prompt for Bash, which in bypass or auto mode may interrupt unattended runs on a false positive. The stop hook is shadow-only and never blocks. In the worst case Jev is slow, so each prompt waits up to 8 s and each Bash call waits up to 8 s before proceeding. Nothing is cached per call.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.contextCost: 0 MCP tools and no MCP server instructions, so no per-session tool-definition cost. The cost is hook-injected text. UserPromptSubmit adds a '[jev advisory ...]' block of about 2-8 lines (roughly 60-200 tokens) on EVERY prompt, and more when memory, near-duplicate or blocker lines appear. post-tool-batch and post-tool-use-failure add one line (~40 tokens) only when they match. The advisory content is mostly routing telemetry (profile=haiku/sonnet/opus, effort=) that Claude Code cannot act on in an interactive Opus session, so it is nearly pure noise.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, Stop, etc.), with no model discretion involved. This is the only candidate mechanism here that satisfies 'Claude Code uses it without me prompting'. BUT the npm package ships no hooks.json or settings snippet, so you would hand-write the ~/.claude/settings.json entries (command: node <pkg>/bin/jclaude.mjs hook <event>). The routing purpose (pick model or effort) cannot take effect in an interactive session. README lines 339-343 say hooks cannot swap the model, and the only model-switching path is the zsh `claude -p` wrapper.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.latencyImpact: Each prompt adds one Jev round trip, which the README claims is 70-500 ms, but several questions are packed per call, plus Node cold start (~100-200 ms), SQLite/ledger opens and memory retrieval, so roughly 0.3-1 s per prompt and up to 8 s on a timeout. Each Bash tool call adds a serial Jev call (~0.3-0.8 s, up to 8 s on timeout) on top of your existing secret-guard and GitNexus Bash hooks. The stop hook adds another call at every turn end. The hooks are synchronous unless configured async. That is significant overhead for an all-day agentic session with hundreds of Bash calls.

npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.install: No documented install for consumers. README says clone the repo, then npm install and npm run build. The npm tarball ships dist/ and bin/jclaude.mjs, so `npm i -g @barmajja/jclaude` works. Then add hook entries manually pointing at `jclaude hook <event>`, and run `jclaude auth login` to write the OpenRouter key. The global zsh wrapper is not in the tarball.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.tests: The README claims 216 vitest tests, all offline/mocked, plus a 36+16 task live pilot (52 real route calls, $0.0016 total). The tarball has no test files and no CI config, and none could be verified. The hook handlers have not been shown to run under a real Claude Code session; the README admits `run --live` was never exercised.
pros: It is the only candidate that uses Claude Code hooks (deterministic UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse and Stop events) to call Jev without you ever mentioning it, so the automatic-invocation requirement is met by design.

Real OpenRouter code path with the wire schema empirically corrected against the live endpoint (state as string, questions keyed by id, Score criteria as level labels, dated model-suffix acceptance). It hits /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 pinned, and the base URL and model are env-overridable. It is a working reference for the request/response shapes.
Uniform fail-open: 8 s abort timeout, errors swallowed, no call when there is no key, and PreToolUse can only 'ask', never 'deny'. A Jev outage will not wedge a session.

Sensible Noul-question design ideas to borrow: destructive-Bash risk (P>=0.6 gives ask), 'looks finished' check on the last message, 'well specified' check on tasks. Also a PKCE headless OpenRouter key flow that avoids pasting keys into sessions.
Small dependency footprint (zod, dotenv, commander), no postinstall, no telemetry to the author, key stored 0600 in .env and not exposed in argv.
cons: The core value (route to haiku/sonnet/opus and effort) is useless for an interactive Opus 5.5 subscription session. The README states hooks cannot swap models, and routing only applies to `claude -p` through a zsh wrapper that is not in the package. The hook output is a passive advisory the model has no reason to act on.

Only the UserPromptSubmit route path redacts secrets. PreToolUse (Bash commands) and Stop (last assistant message) send raw text to OpenRouter and the Jev provider, a real problem for client projects with tokens in commands or env output. Your existing secret-leak guard would not cover these calls.

Latency: one to two extra network round trips per prompt, plus one per Bash call (up to 8 s on timeout), stacked on your GitNexus and secret-guard Bash hooks. Jev's Noul destructive check is much weaker than your deterministic guard and may add false-positive 'ask' prompts, which break bypass and auto mode.

No hook config or settings snippet ships, and the package has no docs (docs/ and shell/ are not in the tarball). The source repo is private, there is no license, and it is a one-maintainer package with 7 releases in about 2 hours on 2026-09-23 and no updates since. It is tightly coupled to Barmajja's projects (config test mappings, skill catalog, AWS central store, Arabic RTL memory examples).

JCLAUDE_HOME is the install dir, so keys, ledger and plaintext prompts/commands land inside node_modules or the global prefix. It also creates a persistent local store of every prompt and permission request, plus an opt-in remote store.

Injects context on every prompt and cross-project 'blockers elsewhere' lines from a shared store, a prompt-injection and context-pollution surface that the user did not ask for. The README itself mislabels the endpoint (/api/v1/systemone) while the code uses /api/alpha/decisions, and the claimed 216 tests could not be verified from the tarball.
Never exercised as an actual Claude Code hook in a real session; per the README the nested-claude path was refused by the permission system.
npmjs-com-package-barmajja-jclaude.verdict: Not recommended for adoption as-is. Its model/effort routing does nothing for an interactive Opus subscription session, and its hooks send unredacted Bash commands and assistant messages to OpenRouter with per-call latency. It is worth reading only as a reference for OpenRouter Jev wire format, fail-open hook patterns and Noul question wording, then reimplementing a minimal hook of your own (e.g. one PreToolUse risk check).

gh-rajdhakad9826-jev-router.name: jev-model-router (npm, rajdhakad9826)
gh-rajdhakad9826-jev-router.whatItDoes: A ~200-line TypeScript library (npm jev-model-router 2.0.1). Router.route(query) calls TypeSafe Jev via @typesafe-ai/sdk systemOne() with a single Score question ("Which model tier should handle this query?") whose levels are your 2-3 model descriptions. It then applies confidence thresholds to pick a model name. It is NOT a Claude Code integration. gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.whatItDoes: TypeScript library (npm jev-harness-router 1.1.2) that, for each agent turn, makes ONE Jev /v1/systemone call with about 20 Noul/Score/Choice questions (via @typesafe-ai/sdk). Pure code (policy.ts) turns the answers into a model tier, effort level, tool subset and skill suggestion. It has a hard deadline (default 600 ms) with a regex-heuristic fallback, a local cache, and 0 ms shortcuts for acks and "/" commands. An adapter, toQueryOptions(), maps the route onto Claude Agent SDK query() options (model, effort, tools, systemPrompt.append). It is NOT an MCP server, hook, plugin or skill, and it has no Claude Code CLI integration. It is meant for people who build their own harness on the Agent SDK. The catalogue (models, tools, skills) has to be hand-written. The shipped default is the author's own 24-skill catalogue, in Spanish and English.

Single unaudited author, 3 stars. Supply-chain trust is low. The tarball and SDK were fetched and inspected statically, and no install scripts were found in the SDK.
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.dataEgress: Per routed turn, one POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is repointed. The body is state (latest_user_message truncated to 1200 chars, recent_context truncated to 600 chars of the previous assistant reply, session facts, unavailable_tools) plus the ~20 questions, which embed the catalogue descriptions (about 4,000 input tokens per call by the README's measurement). It does not send file contents, diffs or tool outputs unless the harness puts them into recentContext or openFiles. openFiles is capped at 8 paths and is sent as-is. Client-project prompts and paths would leave the machine for TypeSafe or OpenRouter, so this needs a client-confidentiality check. The two warmup calls send only the string "warmup".
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.failureMode: Fail-open by design. The deadline defaults to 600 ms (HARNESS_ROUTER_DEADLINE_MS, calibratable) and is a raced timer (src/jev.ts:~195). There are no retries (maxRetries 0). On a timeout, API error, network error or missing key, the local regex heuristic answers. A late answer still lands in the cache and is not aborted, so as not to break the TLS connection. Fallback rate is 0-16% depending on the day. Fallback quality is worse: under-provisioned tiers go from 7.4% to 31.5%, and skill accuracy from 90.7% to 81.5% by the author's own numbers. A missing key throws MissingKeyError unless MOCK=1.
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.latencyImpact: Author-measured p50 351-376 ms, p95 444-1006 ms, max about 470-605 ms (bounded by the deadline), from Buenos Aires. It should be similar or somewhat lower from Europe. A cold start is about 1.15 s, so prewarm is needed (2 calls). Shortcuts and cache hits cost 0 ms. The cost is roughly $0.17 per 1,000 turns. This would be added to every turn IF it could be wired in, and it cannot be wired into interactive Claude Code, since only the Agent SDK takes per-call model, effort and tools.
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped, because it registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills. If wired through the Agent SDK it appends a skill-suggestion block to the system prompt each turn, and restricting tools would shrink the tool definitions. Both effects belong to the SDK harness, not to the interactive CLI.
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.autoInvocation: None for the Claude Code CLI. It is a library that a custom harness calls before each query(). It is deterministic when embedded in your own Agent SDK program, but it is not a hook, MCP tool, skill or proxy. Getting it into interactive Claude Code would need custom glue. A UserPromptSubmit hook can inject additionalContext, but it cannot change the session model, effort or tool set. A transparent proxy through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is impossible because the user is on subscription/OAuth. Only the skill-suggestion text could be reproduced through a hook.
pros: Uses Jev's real strengths (Noul, Score and Choice in one batched call). It reports Jev beating a regex baseline on 181 labelled turns: skill exact 90.0% vs 59.4%, tier too-cheap 3.3% vs 19.9% (README table; self-reported, single labeller).
Well-engineered failure handling: a hard deadline, no retries, a heuristic fallback, and a late answer that still lands in the cache (src/jev.ts).
Cheap: 4,015 input tokens per call, about $0.17 per 1,000 turns (README).
The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer key (sdk index.mjs:513,554,581). Pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api is likely a config-only change.
Includes toQueryOptions() for the Claude Agent SDK, with type-checked options (tests), and 113 offline tests.
MIT, one runtime dependency, no install scripts, no argv secrets. Small and readable (about 4k lines).
Its README findings are useful design lessons for any Jev integration: without recentContext Jev routing is worse than regexes, don't abort on the deadline, and prewarm with two calls.
cons: It does not integrate with interactive Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hooks.json, plugin.json, SKILL.md or settings snippet. It only targets the Agent SDK's query() options, where the harness is your own program. The user's goal is automatic use inside the Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5 on a subscription.

Interactive Claude Code hooks cannot apply its outputs. The model, effort and tool set cannot be changed per turn from a hook. Only additionalContext text (the skill suggestion) could be reproduced, and even that needs custom glue. The user's OAuth subscription cannot be redirected to a proxy either.

Even where it could work, routing to Haiku or Sonnet would fight the user's wish to use Opus 5.5 as the main model. The value is cost savings, not coding quality. The user is on a subscription, so there is no per-token bill to save.

Sends the user's prompt, the previous assistant reply (600 chars) and up to 8 open file paths to a third party on every turn. That is a confidentiality concern on client projects, and it adds 0.35-1 s of latency per non-shortcut turn.

Fitted to one Spanish/English author's 24 skills and 181 turns, all labelled by that same person. Thresholds, the deadline and the catalogue are not transferable (the README says so). You would have to hand-write a catalogue of your own tools and skills and re-run the eval.
Immature: 12 days old, 3 stars, one author (17 commits, the last on 2026-09-21), no CI, no issues or community. Its only sample of the SDK path is examples/agent-sdk.ts.

OpenRouter is not native. Compatibility rests on the assumption that OpenRouter's systemone response has the same shape as api.typesafe.ai (usage.input_tokens, model, answers). The default model ID jev-1.13.0 differs from OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13, so the env override needs to be set. Unverified.
Restricting tools (the default `restrict` mode) risks stripping Bash, Edit or Write on a misroute.
gh-joacomarc-jev-harness-router.verdict: A well-built per-turn Jev router for people writing their own Claude Agent SDK harness, and the best reference for how to structure batched Jev calls, deadlines and fallbacks. It is not a drop-in for interactive Claude Code, since it ships no hook, MCP or skill, and a hook cannot change the model, effort or tools per turn. It is worth borrowing ideas from (recentContext, the deadline pattern, and a skill-suggestion hook built on the same questions), not installing.

gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.name: reflex-router
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI (`reflex`) that launches the real `claude` behind a loopback proxy (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL -> 127.0.0.1) with a temporary merged --settings file. At the start of each user-typed prompt or subagent it sends a redacted, truncated task to Jev (POST {base}/v1/systemone, Choice question for the cheapest adequate tier haiku/sonnet/opus plus a Score question for reasoning demand). In the default shadow mode it only records what it would do. In opt-in route mode it rewrites the model field to a cheaper Anthropic model, with a prompt-cache cost guard. It also records outcome signals (correction, failed test, reverted edit) and has `reflex report`. It is a cost/latency model-router, not a way for Claude to consult Jev for coding decisions.

gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.dataEgress: To Jev (only at start of work: typed main-chat prompt or a subagent's first request): JSON {state:{task (user prompt, default cap 4000 chars head+tail, redacted), previous_assistant_reply (main chat only, last 1000 chars tail, redacted), context:{requesting_tier, is_subagent}}, model, questions}. No system prompt, tool list, file contents, tool outputs, diffs or session ids (docs/privacy.md, asserted by tests). Plus a keyless HEAD / to the backend host at startup and every 60 s keep-alive. To Anthropic: the normal Claude Code traffic through the proxy (byte-identical in shadow mode). Locally: ~/.reflex/decisions.jsonl with hashes/counts/tiers, no prompt text by default.
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.failureMode: Fail-open by design and by tests. Decision deadline REFLEX_JEV_DEADLINE_MS default 1500 ms (hard, includes connect); on timeout/HTTP error/invalid response the request is forwarded unchanged on the requested model (jev.ts:159-211, BackendError). Circuit breaker (src/worker/breaker.ts), worker supervisor with restart backoff, crash loop -> passthrough, front door forwards directly to the API. No key -> passthrough (effective-mode.ts:21). Caveat: a new turn waits up to 1.5 s in route mode; a killed launcher ends the session connection; pins are lost on worker restart.
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.contextCost: No MCP tools, no skills: 0 tool-definition tokens. Hook-injected text: none by default; with opt-in REFLEX_DELEGATE=1 about 3 lines (~80-100 tokens) added per typed prompt. Hidden cost risk: proxying via a non-first-party ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL makes Claude Code disable MCP tool search, so reflex sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (launch.ts:53-59) to avoid the README-measured 32k -> 67k /context inflation. Route mode can also break prompt cache continuity when switching models (cache write penalty, guarded).
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy plus injected hooks: fully automatic once `claude` is aliased to `reflex` (no prompting needed). But Jev is only used to pick a model tier for each turn, not consulted by Claude for coding decisions, and it does nothing if you start plain `claude`.
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.latencyImpact: Shadow mode: decision runs but the request is not held for it per README ('Route mode adds a wait'); loopback proxy hop overhead small. Route mode: each new turn/subagent waits for Jev up to 1500 ms. Measured by author (from Turkey, TypeSafe direct): p50 823 ms / p95 1136 ms on fresh connection, p50 382 / p95 408 ms reused (n=11-12; tiny samples). Adds nothing to tool-loop steps, which are pinned.
pros: The only candidate so far that is truly automatic: a transparent proxy/hook layer needing no 'use jev' prompt once claude is aliased.

Real Jev wire client in src/backend/jev.ts with strict answer validation, keep-alive, hard deadline, no retries, key and body never logged; base URL is configurable (REFLEX_JEV_BASE_URL) and the path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's.

Well-engineered fail-open design (front door, supervisor, breaker, byte-identical passthrough), tested under a network-blocking guard, CI on 2 OSes x 3 Node versions; MIT; zero runtime deps; no telemetry; no postinstall.
Shadow mode default: can observe for a few sessions what Jev would decide, with `reflex report`, before enabling any rewriting.
Privacy controls: allow-listed state, char budgets, secret redaction, 0600 logs, TypeSafe key stripped from child env.
Honest documentation: README says no cost saving has been measured; maintainer's own 3-day log showed net about $0.03 estimated saving.
cons: Wrong use of Jev for this user's goal: it only routes Anthropic model tier (Opus->Sonnet/Haiku) and reasoning effort; it does not let Claude Code use Jev typed decisions during coding (permission triage, file choice, etc.).

Value is cost saving, but the user appears to be on a subscription/OAuth login with Opus 5.5 as main model; per-token savings are moot, and the author's own data says 73% of tokens are main-chat tool-loop continuations that routing cannot touch, with 2-turn sessions all judged opus.

No OpenRouter support in code: key must start with apikey_ (config.ts:352), model regex ^jev- rejects typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.ts:259), only TYPESAFE_API_KEY; OpenRouter's System One schema not verified equal, so a fork/patch is required and untested.

Puts an alpha, 10-day-old, single-maintainer proxy in the path of every Claude Code request for personal and client work; wire format 'is not a public contract', fixtures only up to CC 2.1.284 while user runs 2.1.285; route mode degrades to shadow on major version drift.
Route mode risks: Sonnet 5.5 refusals that poison the session, prompt-cache losses on switch, up to 1.5 s added wait per new turn, pins lost on worker restart.
Prompt text (up to 4000 chars per turn, from client projects) goes to a third party (Jev/OpenRouter) even in shadow mode; redaction is best-effort.

Requires launching via `reflex` (alias) and injects its own --settings hooks/status line, which may clash with the user's existing statusLine and hook stack (GitNexus, secret guard, caveman); README notes it skips its status line only if the user has their own, and hook ordering interplay is untested.
Adds ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true and a proxied base URL; any Anthropic-side change to request shape, beta headers or OAuth handling can break passthrough.
gh-ziyacivan-reflex-router.verdict: Best-engineered automatic Jev integration found, but it solves a different problem (cheaper-model routing) than making Claude Code consult Jev, gives little for a subscription Opus-main user, needs a fork to work with OpenRouter, and puts an alpha proxy in front of all traffic. At most run it in shadow mode on personal projects to see what Jev decides; do not adopt for client work.

gh-ruban-24-switchboard.name: @ruban24/switchboard
gh-ruban-24-switchboard.whatItDoes: Node/TypeScript CLI (`switchboard claude` / `switchboard codex`) that launches Claude Code behind a local loopback proxy. On each new conversation it extracts the user task, sends it to Jev (System One, one request with about 6 Choice questions: taskType, complexity tier, sufficientContext, per-model effort) and applies a local deterministic policy to pick model (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus 5.5, Fable) and reasoning effort. It rewrites the model and effort fields in the /v1/messages request forwarded to api.anthropic.com and pins that pair for the whole conversation. Jev is used only as a model/effort router, not as a general decision tool.

gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.name: claude-autorouter
gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.whatItDoes: Local 127.0.0.1 Anthropic-Messages proxy launched via `claude-autorouter claude`, which sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to itself and spawns `claude`. For every /v1/messages request it sends a bounded state excerpt (up to 12,000 chars: latest human task, first task, 1000-char system excerpt, up to 8 recent messages incl. tool results) to Jev /v1/systemone as a single `choice` question (haiku/sonnet/opus), then rewrites the request `model` to the chosen Claude tier and streams the response back. It is a Haiku/Sonnet/Opus cost router, not a general decision tool for Claude Code. Low-confidence (<0.75) picks are bumped to at least Sonnet. It also has an experimental local Ollama (nimble/tev1) evaluator, a status line, and savings estimates.

gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.dataEgress: To the Jev evaluator (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed) on every inference request: up to 12,000 serialized chars of latest human prompt, first prompt, system-prompt excerpt (up to 1000 chars), up to 8 recent messages (up to 3000 chars each) including tool_result text (file contents, command output, diffs), plus message_count and tool_count. Images, documents, thinking blocks and tool_use inputs omitted. Because client-side secret guards are hooks on tool calls, secrets that appear in tool results or prompts will be included in these excerpts, which matters for client projects. Anthropic still receives the full request as before. Large/multimodal requests also hit Anthropic count_tokens. Local Ollama evaluator keeps classification on-machine (3000 bytes).
gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.failureMode: Fail-open, but slow. Jev call has a 1500 ms timeout (AUTOROUTER_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, max 10000) with redirect:error; on timeout/HTTP error/invalid JSON the router returns fallback: Sonnet, or Opus if the client model is Opus, and keeps the pinned/sonnet+ model for continuations (router.mjs:214-223, 297). Requests are never blocked by a Jev outage. Note that the classification is awaited before the request is forwarded, so a slow Jev adds up to 1.5 s to each request. Decisions are cached 5 min by body hash; turn pins for 30 min keep tool continuations on one model.
gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.latencyImpact: One awaited Jev round trip per inference request (each tool-loop step is a request; cache hits only on identical bodies), claimed 70-500 ms plus loopback proxy hop; worst case +1.5 s on timeout. Large requests (>150 KB) may add a parallel count_tokens call. README status-line example shows Jev at 210-290 ms.
gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.contextCost: Zero context cost for tools: registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills, injects no text into the model context. Side effects on session config instead: forces ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5, MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 (compatible profile), adds a temporary statusLine via --settings (may replace the user's own status line unless AUTOROUTER_STATUSLINE=0), optional CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP.
gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: fully automatic once Claude Code is started through `claude-autorouter claude` (could be aliased as `claude`), with no prompting needed. Plain `claude` launches bypass it entirely, and it does not use the existing hooks. It is not deterministic per tool call but per API request.
pros: Truly automatic with no prompt wording: a per-request Jev decision is made by a proxy, not by model discretion, and the design fails open (router.mjs:214-223)
Real Jev usage matches the brief: a `choice` question with per-option criteria and confidence, and a 0.75 confidence threshold that bumps uncertain cases to Sonnet+ (router.mjs:205-208)
Zero context cost: no MCP tool defs, hooks or skill text added, so it does not interact with gitnexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks
Endpoint, model and key are all env/config-overridable (AUTOROUTER_JEV_URL/MODEL, saved config keys), so repointing to OpenRouter is a config change with no code patch

gh-frapposelli-claude-autorouter.verdict: A well-built but narrowly scoped Haiku/Sonnet/Opus cost router that transparently uses Jev via the System One choice API; it is automatic and fail-open, and repointing it to OpenRouter is plausibly a three-variable config change. For a subscription Opus 5.5 user it mostly risks quality and adds latency, so it is a curiosity rather than a daily driver, and it is far too new and closed-source to route your OAuth traffic and client code through.

gh-jevrouter-jevrouter.name: @jevrouter/jevrouter (npm only, no GitHub repo)
gh-jevrouter-jevrouter.whatItDoes: Local Rust daemon (axum, SQLite, launched via a ~1 KB Node shim) that listens on 127.0.0.1:3479 and exposes Anthropic /v1/messages and OpenAI /v1/chat/completions. It asks Jev (Choice over small/medium/large slots) how hard the request is, then forwards to the upstream configured for that slot. It escalates the slot if the upstream fails, and falls back to simple routing if Jev is unavailable. It is a model-tier router, not a coding assistant integration.

providerSupport.evidence: Static strings of the darwin-arm64 binary (Linux binary is not on npm). Jev endpoint is hard-coded as https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, with env JEVROUTER_JEV_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY and model default 'jev-latest'. Zero occurrences of 'openrouter', 'api/alpha/decisions' or 'openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone'. Config struct JevConfig has api_key_env, model, timeout_ms, min_confidence, cache_ttl_s, max_state_chars; SlotConfig has provider_base_url, api_key_env, match_models (so the upstream model slots can point at OpenRouter's /v1/chat/completions, but the Jev call itself cannot).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Hard for Jev itself: the Jev base URL is not a config field (only the slot upstreams have provider_base_url). Switching requires editing and rebuilding Rust source, but no source is public (GitHub repo jevrouter/jevrouter does not resolve; org has 0 public repos). Also the OpenRouter Jev API response schema may differ from the TypeSafe one, which is unverified. Slot upstreams pointing to OpenRouter are possible, but that only affects the coding models, not Jev.

gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.name: jevrouter-ai (Abishek0070/JEV-model-router)
gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.whatItDoes: A small Node/Fastify gateway (about 1,500 lines of TypeScript, 4 dependencies) that exposes OpenAI-style /v1/chat/completions and a non-streaming Anthropic /v1/messages. For model "auto" it sends the last 6k chars of the conversation to Jev and asks a Choice question, tier = fast | balanced | powerful, plus a Noul "escalate" question. A policy engine and a cost/latency scorer then pick a concrete model from a YAML config (groq-llama, gemini-flash, gpt-mini, claude-haiku, claude-sonnet, gpt-reasoning, mock-echo), and the gateway dispatches to that provider with your own API keys. It is an LLM cost router, not a Claude Code integration. Jev only supplies a coarse tier signal. There is a local regex-heuristic fallback.

providerSupport.evidence: src/src/jev/openrouter.ts:16-18 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_BASE_URL (default https://openrouter.ai/api/v1) and OPENROUTER_JEV_MODEL (default 'typesafe/jev-1'), so the model id is stale (real ids: typesafe/jev-1.13 and ~typesafe/jev-latest). Line 26 POSTs to `${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, which is the chat endpoint, not /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone. Lines 32-37 use a system prompt 'Return ONLY JSON {tier,confidence}' with max_tokens 60 and regex-parse the text reply. That is the wrong contract for a typed-decision model and returns no Choice probabilities. The default timeout is 800 ms (index.ts:21 passes cfg.jev.timeoutMs, which is 3000 in config.example.yaml:89-90). typesafe.ts:24 uses https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with the correct {state, model, questions:{route:{type:'choice',criteria},escalate:{type:'noul'}}} shape and reads answers.route.{choice,confidence,probabilities} (lines 37-67). jevmodel.ts:98 uses https://jevmodel.org/v1/systemone, a third-party host. .env.example:59 lists JEV_TYPESAFE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/decisions, which contradicts the code default. Default order is [jevmodel, typesafe, openrouter, local] (config.example.yaml:89). The OpenRouter path is therefore a best-effort chat-completions shim, not a real Decisions/System One client.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The correct System One wire shape already exists in typesafe.ts. Pointing JEV_TYPESAFE_URL at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the OpenRouter key and model typesafe/jev-1.13 should work if OpenRouter's schema matches, but I could not verify that from this code. The env vars are shared (JEV_API_KEY alias), so you would need to fork or set the URL and key per provider. Patching only fixes Jev tier selection. It does not solve the Claude Code proxy problems listed under cons.
providerSupport.others: jevmodel.org (unknown operator; /v1/systemone, JEVMODEL_API_KEY) and a local regex heuristic. LLM backends: OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, Ollama and mock.

security: Keys are read only from env or .env and are sent as Bearer headers. They do not appear in argv. The startup log reports only booleans for configured keys (server.ts:27-46).

Gateway auth is open by default: checkAuth returns true when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty (ingress/auth.ts:7). The server binds 0.0.0.0 (server.ts:313) with CORS origin:true (server.ts:23). On a dev machine this exposes an unauthenticated proxy that spends your upstream provider keys to anyone on the LAN or any web page.
The quota is in-memory only. addSpend records spend but there is no enforcement of the '$1/day' comment.
Gemini's API key is placed in the URL query string (providers/native.ts, generateContent?key=...), which can leak into logs and proxies.

Default jev.order puts jevmodel.org first (config.example.yaml:89). Any key set as JEV_API_KEY is sent as a Bearer token to that non-TypeSafe host as well as api.typesafe.ai (index.ts:19-20). An OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone is not sent there.

Telemetry logs routing metadata via pino, not prompt bodies. However, the exact cache stores full responses in memory keyed by a hash of the prompts. /v1/telemetry/recent is unauthenticated when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty.

No postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json scripts: build, start, dev, eval, typecheck, prepublishOnly). There is no telemetry phone-home beyond the configured providers. npm dist matches src for the endpoints (diffed).
The prompt-injection surface on the Jev call is small, because Jev returns only a typed tier. Untrusted conversation text can only bias the tier; the regex fallback is easy to game.

gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.dataEgress: Two destinations. (1) To Jev: up to 6,000 chars (jevmodel.ts slices to 8,000) of the concatenated 'role: content' conversation is sent as `state`. In router/pipeline.ts the state is messages.map('role: content').join('\n').slice(0, 6000), so system prompt, user text and pasted code all go out. Jev goes to jevmodel.org, api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai depending on which key is set and the order. (2) To the chosen LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq or Ollama), the full messages array with your keys. In a Claude Code setup that would mean sending your entire agent context (files, diffs, tool outputs) to a non-Anthropic model chosen by the router. This matters for client projects.
gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.failureMode: Jev failures are fail-open. JevRouter.decide (jev/index.ts:41-60) walks the order, skips providers with an open breaker (5 fails then 30 s cooldown), and always falls back to the local regex heuristic. The per-call Jev timeout is 3 s in the example config (800 ms constructor default), so a slow Jev can add up to 3 s per request per failing provider. The order tries jevmodel, typesafe and openrouter in sequence; a missing key throws immediately, so only configured providers cost time. The LLM dispatcher does 2 attempts per model with 100/300 ms backoff and a 30 s timeout, then falls back to the other models in route.allow. If the gateway itself is down, Claude Code would fail closed, because ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL would point at a dead port with no direct path.
gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.latencyImpact: The README claims router_ms of 0.8-4 ms warmed, excluding Jev. A remote Jev call adds roughly 70-500 ms (claimed) up to the 3 s timeout on every uncached request. Claude Code makes many requests per turn, and a synchronous Jev call would sit in front of each one. The non-streaming /v1/messages also removes token streaming, so the UI would only show output when the whole response is done.
gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks and no skills, so 0 tokens of tool definitions and no injected text. Its effect is on the transport, not the context window: it would replace Claude Code's Anthropic endpoint with an OpenAI/Anthropic-style proxy. This is not a workable path for Claude Code 2.1.x. The gateway's /v1/messages has no streaming (server.ts:269), which Claude Code needs. It drops tool_use/tool_result blocks and ignores the tools array (server.ts:272-276, 278-286), so agentic tool calls break. It returns fixed stop_reason 'end_turn' and does not implement count_tokens, thinking or prompt caching. Model names like claude-opus-5-5 are not in its config.
gh-abishek0070-jev-model-router.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy only. Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000 and every request goes through it. That would be automatic, but it would break Claude Code: with a subscription/OAuth login, Claude Code authenticates to api.anthropic.com, so it will not work through this proxy, and the proxy needs its own ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. It also downgrades Opus 5.5 to whatever the tier map picks. It does not use Jev as a decision aid for Claude's own workflow (hooks/MCP), which is what the user asked for.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related: typesafe.ts and jevmodel.ts implement the documented System One Choice + Noul request shape (state, model, questions with criteria) and parse choice, confidence and probabilities (typesafe.ts:37-67). That is a usable reference for a typed Jev client.
Fail-open design with a circuit breaker and a local heuristic fallback (jev/index.ts:41-60). Jev outages would not block traffic by themselves.
Tiny codebase (about 1.5k lines), 4 runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, MIT license. It can be read in about 15 minutes.
Jev is called only for a coarse tier. It never picks a provider, and the policy/scoring stages are deterministic and inspectable (/v1/routing/decision dry run).
OPENROUTER_API_KEY is at least recognised as a Jev provider (openrouter.ai/api/v1 with typesafe/* model), so the design does not lock you to a TypeSafe key.
cons: Wrong tool for the goal. It is an LLM cost router (send easy prompts to cheap models). It does not give Claude Code a Jev decision capability, so it cannot support things like 'should I run tests / is this safe / which files matter'.

It cannot front Claude Code. /v1/messages rejects stream:true with HTTP 400 (server.ts:269), which Claude Code always uses. It also flattens content to text and drops tool_use and tool_result (server.ts:272-276), so the agent loop breaks. It ignores tools, thinking and cache_control.

Subscription/OAuth login does not work through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to this gateway. It would need a separate Anthropic API key, and routing sends most turns to groq-llama, gemini-flash, gpt-mini or claude-haiku instead of Opus 5.5. That is a large quality regression on client work.

The OpenRouter Jev adapter is a chat/completions hack (openrouter.ts:26-46) using a stale model id typesafe/jev-1 and a JSON-in-prompt contract. It uses neither /api/alpha/decisions nor /api/v1/systemone, so it likely does not work against a typed-decision model, and errors silently drop to the regex fallback (local.ts), which is not Jev at all.
Default order sends conversation state to jevmodel.org first, an unaffiliated third-party endpoint that also receives JEV_API_KEY. No documented relationship to TypeSafe.
Unauthenticated, network-exposed by default: binds 0.0.0.0, CORS origin:true, gateway auth open when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty. Dangerous next to client code and provider keys.
Data egress: the full agent context would be relayed to OpenAI, Gemini, Groq or Anthropic, which may violate client confidentiality terms.

Immature: 9 commits over 3 days, single author, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, docs contradict code (.env.example JEV_TYPESAFE_URL is /v1/decisions vs code /v1/systemone). The README claims Claude Code support but the code does not deliver it.
Adds latency on every request with no UI benefit: up to 3 s Jev timeout, no streaming.

Use it only as a reference for the System One Choice/Noul request shape (typesafe.ts:37-67), and build any real Claude Code integration as a hook or MCP server that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.

security: API key from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env only, sent as Bearer header via urllib (jev.py:145); never in argv, so not visible in the process list. Hook only works if the key is in the env of the Claude Code process itself (shell profile export), meaning every Bash child process inherits it.
No shell=True, subprocess, eval or os.system in jev.py; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall (package.json has no install scripts), no telemetry or analytics found (grep clean).

hook --write (bin/claude-x-jev.js:150) does fs.copyFileSync(settingsPath) unguarded: throws if ~/.claude/settings.json does not exist; it then rewrites settings.json with JSON.stringify (reformats file, drops comments). Backup is kept as settings.json.bak-claude-x-jev.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command text is fed to Jev as state, so an attacker-controlled command string (e.g. from a poisoned repo) can carry text that steers the serves_task/reversible noul answers. Jev returns numbers only, but an 'allow' at >=0.9 skips the human prompt. A regex-free probabilistic model deciding allow on arbitrary shell is a weak control (e.g. 'reversible' definition includes 'only reads or changes files inside cwd', so curl|sh of a local file, or git-tracked destructive edits, may score high).
Hook 'allow' from an alpha 5-day-old single-author project auto-approves commands; the default 0.9 is unvalidated (tune command exists but needs labelled data).

Installer copies files to ~/.claude only; write scope is limited (skill dir, commands dir, settings.json). SKILL.md declares allowed-tools [Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash, WebFetch, AskUserQuestion, Skill, Task], broad but only when the skill is invoked.
Error log at $TMPDIR/jev-gate.log (default /tmp, world-readable dir) gets stderr: exception text incl. up to 400 chars of API error body; not the key.
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.dataEgress: For the hook: every gated Bash call sends to openrouter.ai (then TypeSafe, per OpenRouter provider routing) the JSON {tool:'Bash', tool_input: json.dumps(tool_input)[:4000], cwd, task?}. That is the full command line (heredocs, inline tokens/passwords/URLs, file contents written via cat<<EOF) truncated to 4000 chars, plus the absolute project path (jev.py:512-521). No file contents otherwise, no prompts, no diffs, no tool outputs. It runs BEFORE the user's secret-leak guard result is known (hooks run in parallel), so a command containing a secret still goes out. Batch commands (/jev-classify etc.) send whatever fields of the input items the preset lists (up to max_chars each) — explicit user data, dry-run offered. Client-project concern: command text and cwd path leave the machine per call; check OpenRouter data-policy/ZDR for TypeSafe endpoint.
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.failureMode: Intended fail-open-to-human: no key, network error, bad JSON, non-Bash tool all print nothing and exit 0 (jev.py:500-502, 545-548), leaving normal permission flow. In bypass permissions mode that means fail-open to full auto-execution, i.e. same as today. Weakness: latency, not correctness. decide() retries 4 times with 1/2/4/8s backoff on 429/5xx/network, per-request timeout 20s (gate default, jev.py:667), so a slow or down Jev can stall a Bash call for up to about 115s worst case; the Claude Code hook default timeout (60s for command hooks; hooks.json here sets no timeout) would likely kill it and treat as non-blocking error. No circuit breaker, so every Bash call re-pays the stall during an outage. Also, on 'ask', bypass mode may or may not honour it; in auto mode it forces prompts.
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server, 0 tools. Always-on: skill description 916 chars (~230 tok) + 13 command stub descriptions ~1700 chars (~425 tok) + names, roughly 700 tokens in the skill/command listing every session. SKILL.md body (7.7KB ~1.9k tok) and task files load only on invocation. Hook injects no context text; only a short permissionDecisionReason ('jev: reversible=0.97, serves_task=0.91') shown to the user/tool result.
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.autoInvocation: Only the PreToolUse Bash hook is deterministic and automatic (a permission gate, not a value-add coding helper). The 13 commands are only-when-prompted (slash) or skill-description trigger on phrases like 'classify these', 'score these'; there is no automatic use of Jev for coding decisions (routing, code review triage, test selection, etc.).
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.latencyImpact: Hook adds one synchronous HTTPS round trip plus Python interpreter startup (~30-50 ms) to every Bash call: claimed 0.3 s typical (README), Jev claim 70-500 ms; TLS setup per call since new process each time. Over a heavy day with hundreds of Bash calls that is minutes of added wall time. Worst case about 115 s with retries (see failureMode). No caching of repeated identical commands.
pros: Correct OpenRouter integration out of the box: hardcoded /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (jev.py:35-52), no patching needed, matches the user's provider choice.
Truly automatic path exists: PreToolUse hook needs no prompting; deterministic, runs on every Bash call, adds zero context tokens and zero tools.

Fail-safe design intent: any error prints nothing and exits 0; key never in argv; stdlib-only Python, no third-party deps, no postinstall, no telemetry; small, readable code (one 30KB script + 11KB installer) that is easy to audit and vendor.

Sound Jev usage patterns worth copying: noul-question tool-gate preset (tool-gate.json), threshold semantics (allow >=0.9, deny <=0.1, else ask), retry/backoff, hook JSON output shape (hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision).
Installer is idempotent, keeps a settings.json backup, preserves user presets on update, offers --project scope.
MIT license; low cost per call (about $0.00004 per gate call at Jev pricing).
cons: Wrong center of gravity for coding: 12 of 13 commands are for inbox/lead/comment triage and batch classification with manual slash invocation. Nothing wires Jev into coding decisions automatically (no code-review triage, test selection, file routing, commit/PR gating beyond Bash).

The one auto feature is a permission gate that duplicates what the user already has: user runs bypass/auto mode with a secret-leak guard hook. Jev 'allow' adds nothing in bypass mode (already allowed), 'ask' would ADD prompts the user does not have today, and 'deny' at <=0.1 is the only real value. The default and shadow settings (JEV_GATE_APPROVE=1.01) make almost every non-obvious Bash call return 'ask', i.e. prompt spam in a workflow that currently has none.

Documentation contradicts code: tasks/gate.md says the hook 'logs every decision to $TMPDIR/jev-gate.log', but the hook only appends stderr on errors (pre-tool-gate.sh:32, jev.py:545); decisions are never logged, so the recommended shadow-mode review of 'what would have been allowed' cannot be done.

Latency and outage exposure: sync call on every Bash, no timeout in the hook config, retries 4x with backoff and 20 s timeouts (up to about 115 s stall), no circuit breaker or cache; competes with GitNexus and secret-guard hooks on Bash matchers.

Sends full Bash command text (up to 4000 chars) and cwd to a third party on every call, in parallel with (not after) the secret-leak guard; unacceptable default for client projects without confirming OpenRouter/TypeSafe data policy.

Only gates Bash by default; Write/Edit/MCP tools require JEV_GATE_TOOLS and env vars (state kept in env, not in the settings entry), and JEV_GATE_TASK is a static env string that cannot know the current task, so serves_task is mostly 'is this routine dev work'.

Immature: 3 commits in one day, 1 author, no CI, no real tests (npm test just parses the file and lints one preset), no releases on GitHub, npm 0.1.1 published 5 days ago; hook --write crashes if settings.json is missing; the marketing benchmark (216 of the author's emails) is self-reported. Promotional content in README (community links).
Depends on OPENROUTER_API_KEY being exported in the environment Claude Code launches from; key then leaks to every child process, and GUI/desktop launches won't see it.
gh-charlesdove977-claude-x-jev.verdict: Not a good fit as a whole: it is an ops/inbox-triage skill whose only automatic feature is a Bash permission gate that is redundant or noisy under bypass/auto mode. Worth mining as a reference implementation (correct OpenRouter endpoint, hook JSON shape, noul tool-gate preset, threshold logic) for a custom, narrowly scoped deny-only hook with a short timeout and no retries, rather than installing it.

gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.name: jev-classifier
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.whatItDoes: Local Node HTTP gateway (default port 8080) that sits between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/oauth/claude. For every POST /v1/messages that carries tools, it rebuilds a compact state (user texts, actions taken, tool results clipped to 600 chars) and calls Jev (choice over ALL tool names/descriptions plus a 'done' noul). In enforce mode it rewrites the request body to tool_choice={type:tool,name:X} before forwarding upstream; if confidence is below MIN_CONFIDENCE (0.5) it uses tool_choice auto and appends a 'Routing hint' to the system prompt. Every decision is appended to a JSONL log. The MCP mode (advisory jev_choose_next_tool) exists only for Cursor and Antigravity, not for Claude Code. It launches via a wrapper (jev-classifier run claude), not through hooks or plugins.
