They use mocks and fixtures only, with no live Jev or Anthropic calls. CI on GitHub Actions runs ubuntu, macos and windows with Node 22 and 24 (typecheck plus tests). I did not execute anything. No test or code handles extended thinking, prompt caching or the size of Claude Code's real requests.
security: No install or postinstall scripts (package.json scripts: build/test/start/prepack only); no curl|sh installer.

Jev key stored in plain text in ~/.config/jev-classifier/config.json (dir 0700, file 0600, src/settings.ts:96-103); keys are entered via setup prompt or env, not argv. Child agent env is stripped of JEV/TYPESAFE/OPENROUTER/AI_GATEWAY keys (agents.ts:78).

With OAuth mode the gateway receives and forwards Claude Code's subscription bearer token. It forwards headers except hop-by-hop ones (server.ts:69-85), does not persist them, and the optional --capture mode stores only allow-listed non-credential headers plus the full request body to .jev-classifier/captures. The gateway listens on a local port, so any local process that can reach it can use it as an authenticated relay to the user's Anthropic account when the user's token is attached. It does not attach the token itself, so risk is low.

OAuth path is locked to https://api.anthropic.com by default and rejects '..' and encoded dot segments (upstream.ts:36-40). Upstream/base URLs can be overridden by env or config (UPSTREAM, CLAUDE_OAUTH_UPSTREAM). A config poisoned to point elsewhere would exfiltrate the subscription token.
Jev call uses redirect:'error' and does not put provider error bodies into logs (jev.ts:91-101). Decision log stores tool names, confidences and timings, not content.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results and user text are sent to Jev as data and only steer which tool is forced. In low-confidence mode it appends a fixed 'Routing hint' to the system prompt built only from tool names. Injected text in a tool result could bias Jev toward a chosen tool name, and enforce mode then makes Claude call that tool, although with any tool's arguments still model-generated.
Single-maintainer, 6 commits in about one day, unaudited; wide-permission daemon that sees every prompt. Optional XDG autostart entry persists the daemon across logins.
Under bypass permissions, forced tool_choice can push Claude toward a tool call such as Bash that would not otherwise be chosen, with no human gate.
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (POST /api/alpha/decisions, jev.ts:79-90) on EVERY Claude Code /v1/messages request that has tools (that is basically every main-loop turn, including subagents): (1) the concatenated text of ALL user messages in the conversation, not clipped and joined with '---' (router.ts buildState; this includes Claude Code's injected system-reminder blocks such as CLAUDE.md and hook output, since those live in user-message text blocks); (2) every tool call's name and full raw input (not clipped: file paths, bash commands, edit contents, written file bodies); (3) every tool result clipped to 600 chars each (file snippets, command output, grep hits); (4) assistant text clipped to 300 chars each; (5) the name and full description of every available tool (Claude Code built-ins plus gitnexus, playwright, caveman MCP tools, roughly 60 to 80 tools; descriptions of built-ins run to thousands of chars each). The system prompt is not sent. Code and client data therefore go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on each turn, on top of Anthropic. The direct Anthropic traffic still flows as normal. That is a real problem for client projects under NDA.
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.failureMode: Fail-open for Jev errors: any classify exception (missing key, HTTP 4xx/5xx, invalid or incomplete probability distribution, timeout) is caught and the original body is forwarded unchanged (server.ts:206-212). Jev fetch timeout is 30 s (jev.ts:83), so a slow OpenRouter stalls each turn up to 30 s before falling through. Fail-closed for the gateway itself: if the local daemon is down or the port is taken, Claude Code (pointed at ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) gets connection refused and cannot reach the API at all, and with upstream errors returns 502 (server.ts:233-238). There is no circuit breaker or negative cache, so each turn repeats a failing Jev call (for example, a 32k-context overflow error) and pays its latency. A launch with 'run claude --no-proxy' or JEV_PROXY=0 bypasses it.
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no hooks in Claude Code, so no extra tool-schema tokens (MCP server exists only for Cursor/Antigravity). The real costs are elsewhere. (a) In enforce mode the gateway changes tool_choice per request, and Anthropic invalidates cached message blocks when tool_choice changes, so prompt-cache hit rates and subscription usage suffer. I inferred this from Anthropic's documented caching rules and did not measure it. (b) Forcing {type:tool} means the model cannot emit text or thinking before the call. (c) Extended or adaptive thinking (which Opus uses in Claude Code) is documented as incompatible with tool_choice any/tool and returns an HTTP 400. grep -rn -i thinking over src finds no handling in the adapter (only 'shadowReason' for OpenAI previous_response_id), so enforce mode will very likely break turns with thinking on. Low-confidence turns append a small system-prompt hint (about 30 tokens).
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.latencyImpact: Adds one serial round trip to Jev via OpenRouter before every model request, not overlapped with the model call. The docs claim 70-500 ms for the model itself, and OpenRouter alpha routing adds more. The request payload holds the full tool catalog (tens of KB) plus history, so it is bigger than typical Jev calls. Plus about 0 to 2 ms local proxy hop and SSE tap. Worst case is a 30 s stall on timeout. Over an agent session with 50 to 200 turns this is +10 to +100 s of pure waiting, with no overlap possible because the choice must precede the call. Multiple subagent turns each pay it too.
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at the gateway, it classifies and rewrites every tool-bearing request with no prompting and no model discretion. That is the closest match to the 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement of all candidate types. But it is not a Claude Code hook or plugin. Startup requires either the 'jev-classifier run claude' wrapper or a persistent ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, and it needs the daemon running (startup enable gives a desktop autostart on Linux).
pros: Truly automatic: transparent proxy on ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, so no user prompt or model cooperation is needed. Claude Code's model, login and OAuth stay unchanged, and the docs say the OAuth token is only forwarded, never stored (src/upstream.ts, server.ts:69-85).
First-class OpenRouter support: JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model ~typesafe/jev-latest, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions (jev.ts:5). Set-up is a one-key change.

Shadow mode (JEV_MODE=shadow) classifies and logs whether Jev's pick matches what Opus actually called (record.actual and match, server.ts:288-297), so you can measure Jev's value on real sessions before enforcing anything. That is a useful evaluation harness.

Fail-open on Jev errors and validates probability distributions strictly; only forces a tool when confidence >= 0.5, else falls back to auto plus a hint. Also a 'done' gate stops premature respond_to_user.
No install scripts, MIT, small readable codebase (about 2.5k LOC src), cross-platform CI, per-session env injection instead of editing ~/.claude, key stripped from the child env.
Local decision log and metrics/dashboard (jevMs p95, match rate), and a doctor --check command.
cons: Forces tool_choice={type:'tool'} on Claude Code's main loop. Per Anthropic's API rules this is incompatible with extended/adaptive thinking (Opus 5.5) and there is no thinking check in the adapter (src/adapters/anthropic.ts:57-59 just sets body.tool_choice). Expect 400 errors or degraded behaviour, and no text/plan before tool calls. Not verified by running (static-only audit).

Semantically wrong fit: Jev sees only Claude Code's tool NAMES plus descriptions and picks one, overriding Opus 5.5's own judgement on what to do next. A cheap router picking tools for a stronger model reduces quality (Bash vs Edit vs Task vs MCP), and it has no notion of arguments, so a forced Read or Bash still relies on Opus to fill them.

Payload size: sends the entire tool catalog (built-ins plus gitnexus, playwright and caveman MCP tools, likely 60-80 tools, ~15-30k+ tokens of descriptions) and unclipped user messages and tool inputs on every turn to a 32k-context beta model. Likely to hit HTTP 400/context limits often, and with no circuit breaker each turn repeats the failing call. Also 255-option cap silently truncates the tool list (router.ts:limitOptions), dropping tools beyond the first 254 in order of appearance.
Serial extra latency on every turn (Jev + OpenRouter alpha routing), up to 30 s on timeout; adds real wall-clock cost over long agent sessions.

Data egress: full user text (including CLAUDE.md/system-reminder content and hook output), raw tool inputs and 600-char tool results go to OpenRouter/TypeSafe every turn. Unacceptable for client projects without a data-processing agreement.

Fail-closed for the gateway: if the daemon dies or the port is used, Claude Code cannot reach Anthropic at all. The user must keep a background service running and set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL globally. Breaks the 'simple subscription OAuth' setup if the env leaks into other tools.
Changing tool_choice per request breaks Anthropic prompt-cache reuse for messages, raising subscription usage and latency (inferred from documented cache invalidation rules).

No Claude Code MCP or hook integration: the MCP server refuses any client except cursor and antigravity (mcp.ts:14), and it's not a plugin or skill. Very immature: 6 commits over ~1 day, 1 contributor, 4 stars, v0.1.2, no release notes; derivative of jev-eval-agent; depends on a beta model and on the 'alpha' OpenRouter endpoint.

Interaction risk with the existing tooling: forced tool selection would collide with the GitNexus and secret-guard hooks' assumptions, and with the ToolSearch/deferred-tool flow, subagents and plan mode, none of which are tested.
gh-felpsdev-jev-classifier.verdict: The only candidate that is truly automatic in Claude Code (a transparent ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy with native OpenRouter support). But it forces tool_choice on every turn, which very likely conflicts with Opus thinking and prompt caching, and it ships the whole conversation and tool catalog to a 32k-context beta model on each request. Use it at most in JEV_MODE=shadow on a personal project to measure Jev's agreement with Opus; do not enforce it for daily or client work.

npmjs-com-package-usemilo.name: usemilo (Milo routing gateway onboarding CLI)
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.whatItDoes: usemilo is a 3-file, single bundled ESM CLI (bin: milo) that rewrites Claude Code / Codex / pi config so the harness's MAIN model traffic goes to a third-party hosted gateway (https://milo-gateway.fly.dev) with model "milo/auto". The gateway uses a small "decision model" (Jev, per its root JSON: decisionBackend "jev") to classify task type and difficulty, picks a tier (fast/mid/frontier) from a roster of cheap OpenRouter models (deepseek-v4-flash, glm-5.3-flash, gpt-5.6-luna, gemini-3.8-flash, etc.), and forwards the request to OpenRouter with the user's OpenRouter key. So Jev is used only as an internal model-tier router; it is not exposed to Claude Code as decisions/tools. For Claude Code it sets env ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=gateway, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=milo/auto, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" plus apiKeyHelper reading OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It replaces the Anthropic backend rather than adding Jev alongside Opus.

No openrouter.ai URL, no TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no /decisions or /systemone call anywhere in the package; OpenRouter is only reached server-side by the hosted gateway. Live GET https://milo-gateway.fly.dev/ returns decisionBackend:"jev", endpoints /v1/messages /v1/chat/completions /v1/responses /v1/roster /v1/memory /v1/decisions/:id.

No CI, no public repo (docs point to github.com/bananaman614305/milo which gh cannot resolve; a different account militoromero10/milo-gateway exists on GitHub and is unrelated/unverified). README has dangling relative links ../../README.md and docs/onboarding.md.
security: No postinstall script, no telemetry in the CLI, no curl|sh; CLI only edits config files and spawns the harness (child_process.spawn with stdio inherit) - static read of dist/cli.js.

Key handling in the CLI is decent: OPENROUTER_API_KEY read from env and not written; a prompted key is stored in a 0600 file (mode 384) .milo-openrouter.key in the global ~/.claude dir and read via apiKeyHelper 'sh -c cat <path>'. milo run passes the key via env ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, not argv.

BUT the OpenRouter key is sent as Bearer to an unaudited third-party gateway (milo-gateway.fly.dev) run by an anonymous npm maintainer ([email removed], package created 2026-09-20). The operator can log/keep the key and spend your OpenRouter credit. Gateway has /v1/memory and /v1/preferences endpoints that persist per-key data server-side.

Setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in settings.json makes every prompt, file content, diff, and tool result of the main agent traverse that gateway: full source-code exfiltration surface for client projects (NDA/contract risk).
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='' plus base URL override overrides subscription/OAuth login behavior; the session stops using the Opus 5.5 subscription.

Hosted service can return arbitrary model output including tool_use blocks; in bypass/auto permission mode a compromised or mis-routed gateway response is effectively remote command execution on the dev machine.

skill.md / setup.md served by the gateway are written for agents and instruct an agent to ask about models and PUT rosters using the user's key: agent-addressed instructions in untrusted remote content (prompt-injection surface if ever fetched).
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.dataEgress: Everything Claude Code sends to its model endpoint: full conversation, system prompt, CLAUDE.md, file contents read, diffs, bash outputs, tool results, plus the OpenRouter API key, all to milo-gateway.fly.dev; then forwarded to whichever cheap OpenRouter model the router selects (DeepSeek, GLM, MiMo, Tencent HY3, etc. per roster). Jev sees the request content for classification. Nothing goes to Anthropic once base URL is overridden.
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.failureMode: Fail-closed for the whole session: the gateway is the sole model backend (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL). If fly.io gateway is down, slow, or the key is missing, Claude Code cannot run at all (no fallback to Anthropic). No timeouts or fallback logic in the CLI; internal gateway timeouts unknown/unauditable. Mitigation: milo off restores config from .milo-backup.
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.latencyImpact: Adds a network hop (Claude Code -> fly.io gateway -> Jev classify -> OpenRouter -> model) on EVERY model request, not just occasional decisions; Jev's claimed 70-500 ms is added serially to each turn plus gateway proxying, and streaming through a proxy may degrade. Estimated +0.1-0.7 s per call; not measured (did not execute).
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero hook-injected text, no MCP server instructions. But the model swap is the cost: Opus 5.5 is replaced by whatever cheap model milo/auto routes to; Claude Code warns milo/auto is not in the model catalog; features tied to Anthropic models (prompt caching, extended thinking, exact tool-use semantics, 1M context) may break or degrade.
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. After 'milo on', every Claude Code model call is routed automatically without prompting, which satisfies 'no user prompt needed' literally, but it uses Jev as a model-tier router and replaces the main model, not as an extra decision aid Claude Code consults.
pros: Truly automatic: a transparent proxy needs no 'use jev' prompt; project-scoped enabling via ./.claude/settings.local.json is reversible (milo off restores .milo-backup) and milo run is a zero-persistence one-shot.
Small and auditable CLI: 3-file tarball, MIT, no dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, spawn-only; key kept out of settings.json (0600 key file / env), not in argv.
OpenRouter-native: uses the user's OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OpenRouter models, and does actually put Jev in a real routing loop (gateway reports decisionBackend jev).
Gateway exposes Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages plus /v1/decisions/:id and x-milo-* headers so routing decisions are inspectable.

Its own skill.md states the sensible design: keep the frontier planner (Opus) and route only sub-task implementation through Milo, which points at the right pattern even though the shipped CLI does the opposite for Claude Code.
cons: Wrong role for Jev here: it replaces the user's main model (Opus 5.5 on subscription) with cheap DeepSeek/GLM/MiMo-class models chosen by a router, degrading quality on client work; Claude Code's own ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL takeover also kills OAuth/subscription usage.
Does NOT call OpenRouter's Jev Decisions API or System One API and does not expose Choice/Noul/Score to Claude Code; no typed-decision value for hooks, permission gating, or task triage.

Sends all prompts, source code, diffs and the OpenRouter key to an anonymous, unaudited hosted gateway (fly.dev) whose source is not accessible (gh 404); unacceptable for client projects; bypass/auto mode magnifies risk of malicious tool_use in responses.
Single point of failure, fail-closed, no fallback; Jev + proxy latency added to every turn.

Very immature: package created 2026-09-20, 5 versions in 2 days, single anonymous maintainer, no public repo, tests or CI, dangling README links; 'milo/auto' unknown to Claude Code catalog; the router's tier policy is a black box (policyVersion v4).
Matches Theo's skeptic framing: it is essentially a DeepSeek-flash-centric router product rather than a Jev integration.
npmjs-com-package-usemilo.verdict: Not suitable: usemilo swaps Claude Code's entire model backend for an unaudited third-party gateway that routes to cheap models via Jev, rather than giving Claude Code Jev-based typed decisions. Only conceivably useful as a reference for the (hosted-service) routing idea or as a throwaway experiment via 'milo run claude-code' on a personal non-sensitive project with a limited-credit OpenRouter key; do not use on client work.

gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.name: rlcd-gateway
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.whatItDoes: Self-hosted Go binary (npm/PyPI wrappers around prebuilt binaries) that sits between Claude Code and the model provider via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. It forwards Anthropic/OpenAI-format traffic, keeps the subscription login as passthrough, and can (a) prune stale tool_result blocks from context, (b) route requests to other models via rules, (c) proxy/audit Jev-style System One calls (POST /v1/systemone) with calibration stats, mirror and dashboard. Jev is used in three ways: as the 'economy model' selector that scores per-block keep probabilities (noul questions) for pruning, as the answerer for 'decision rules' that route requests (choice/score/noul), and as an audited passthrough for the user's own apps. It is a general LLM gateway that uses Jev as an optional decision backend, not a Jev tool for coding tasks (no code review/commit/permission gating). A small MCP server (rlcd_recall) lets the model restore pruned blocks.

providerSupport.evidence: Jev defaults are TypeSafe-direct: gateway/internal/config/config.go:187 SelectorPreset(jev) = BaseURL https://api.typesafe.ai, TokenEnv TYPESAFE_API_KEY, Model jev-latest; README.md:193 table lists only api.typesafe.ai for jev. The System One client posts to strings.TrimRight(BaseURL,"/")+"/v1/systemone" with Authorization: Bearer <token> (gateway/internal/selector/selector.go:82-88, body {state, questions, model}). OpenRouter is supported only as an LLM route (config.go:201 BaseURL https://openrouter.ai/api, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), not as a named Jev backend; provider.go:34/48 detect openrouter.ai and typesafe.ai hosts only for labeling. Because the base URL is free-form (decisions/settings.go Backend{base_url, token, token_env, auth}), setting base_url=https://openrouter.ai/api, auth=key, token_env=OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model=typesafe/jev-1.13 yields https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, exactly the documented OpenRouter System One endpoint (bare jev-1.13/jev-latest are also mapped by OpenRouter). Not tested by the project; no README mention of OpenRouter-hosted Jev. Provider label would fall to 'open-rlcd' unless provider:typesafe is set (settings.go:55-66), which affects only pricing/labels (pricing.go:84 uses $42/1B input).
providerSupport.others: open-rlcd (self-hosted System One) is the default selector (config.go:205 http://127.0.0.1:8000); LLM routes for Anthropic, OpenRouter, OpenAI, Groq, Together, DeepSeek, Mistral, Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio.

A decisions backend with base_url https://openrouter.ai/api + OPENROUTER_API_KEY + model typesafe/jev-1.13 hits the correct URL path with identical request schema. No telemetry found in Go source (grep for telemetry/analytics empty)
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.dataEgress: To the LLM provider: unchanged Claude Code requests (or pruned in enforce mode; or rerouted to another provider/model if a rule/route says so, in which case the subscription is dropped and an OpenRouter/other key is used). To the Jev backend (prune selector, plan.go:160-163): state {goal = up to last 3 user turns, each head 1200 + tail 300 chars, recent_activity = last 8 tool-call summaries (tool name + file path/command/pattern/url clipped to 100 chars)} plus one noul question per candidate old block whose instructions contain the block's description and a 1000-char (700 head + 300 tail) excerpt of the tool result/text, per epoch. For decision rules (router/decision.go): latest_user_text/goal/recent tool calls/context_tokens/client per rule (default only on conversation start). So code snippets, file excerpts, command output and user prompts do leave the machine to the Jev backend (OpenRouter if configured) in addition to Anthropic. Local disk: full request/response bodies under ~/.rlcd-gateway/.
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.failureMode: Two layers. Jev-side: fail-open. Prune selector timeout 3000 ms (selector_timeout_ms, max 30 s) and any error keeps everything (ReasonFailOpen, plan.go:~170); decision rules have timeout_ms 2000 with else-branch/next-rule on error, timeout or low confidence; selector HTTP client timeout 30 s with one retry on connection failure (selector.go:58,95). Gateway-side: fail-closed for the whole session. If the local gateway process is not running or crashes, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to 127.0.0.1:4777 cannot reach the API at all (no autostart, no built-in fallback to api.anthropic.com from the client side). It has upstream error recovery (clamping, backoff, route fallbacks) but a single point of failure and an extra hop for every request including streaming.
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.latencyImpact: Proxy hop on every model call: local, small (single Go binary) but nonzero and untested here. Jev prune call only at 'epochs' (context growth since last epoch, above floor), up to 3 s cap, blocking the request that triggers it (the request waits for the selector). Claimed Jev 190-314 ms in README traces. Decision rules with evaluate=conversation_start add ~200-500 ms once per conversation; every_request would add it each turn and also break prompt cache and signed thinking. Mirror is post-response so free.
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.contextCost: Zero tool-definition cost by default: the recall MCP server is optional and exposes one tool (rlcd_recall, roughly 100-250 tokens of schema/description); no hooks; no injected text. Net effect on context is negative-cost when pruning is enforced (replaces stale tool_results with ~40-token markers), with prompt-cache invalidation risk that the project mitigates with sticky decisions and epochs. Default mode is shadow, so no change to what Opus sees until switched to enforce.
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.autoInvocation: transparent proxy. Once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at the gateway, Jev is consulted automatically and invisibly (pruning epochs, decision rules) with no user prompt and no model discretion. But it is infrastructure-level (token/cost optimization and model routing), not a coding-value feature: Jev never gates commits, reviews diffs, classifies user intent for skills, or acts inside Claude Code's decision points.
pros: Truly automatic and prompt-free: base-URL proxy is the only approach that needs no model cooperation, matching 'Claude Code must use it when needed' literally
Keeps subscription/OAuth login (passthrough route forwards credentials unchanged), with documented settings-level and credential-order handling in setup/claude.go
Jev usage is fail-open: 3 s selector timeout, error keeps all context; decision rules fall to else/next_rule on timeout or low confidence

Jev endpoint config is free-form: base_url https://openrouter.ai/api + auth key + token_env OPENROUTER_API_KEY + model typesafe/jev-1.13 produces the exact OpenRouter POST /api/v1/systemone URL (selector.go:82), so OpenRouter-hosted Jev is a config change

Decision rules give a real, concrete Jev use case: route trivial vs hard requests (score) between Haiku and Opus, or keep sensitive data local (noul), with min_confidence and audit/calibration (ECE) of every Jev answer
Pruning starts in shadow mode (default) so you can see 'would have saved' before enforcing; sticky per-conversation decisions and epoching designed around Anthropic prompt-cache economics
Reversible install: setup writes a timestamped backup and 'undo' restores the previous ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL; no npm postinstall; npm provenance attestation; Apache-2.0; 46 test files
Loopback-only with Host/Origin checks, gateway keys hashed (SHA-256), tokens never returned by the API
Good observability dashboard for token/cost per request, which helps evaluate whether Jev-driven routing actually saves money
cons: Not a Jev integration for coding value: Jev only scores 'keep this old tool_result?' and 'how hard is this request?'. It does not review code, gate destructive commands, triage tasks, or decide commit/PR actions
Single point of failure for every Claude Code call: if the local process is not running, Claude Code cannot reach the API (fail-closed at the proxy level); no autostart/systemd unit found

Man-in-the-middle for the subscription OAuth token and all client code, from a repo created 2026-09-23 with 1 contributor, 2 stars, 3 npm versions in 13 minutes on 2026-09-24; prebuilt binaries via optionalDependencies cannot be inspected at runtime

log_bodies defaults to true: full prompts, file contents and any secrets Claude reads are persisted to ~/.rlcd-gateway for 14 days (2 GB); unacceptable default for client projects, and it sidesteps the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard because the proxy sees tool_result contents after the fact
Code excerpts (1000 chars per candidate block plus last 3 user turns) are sent to the Jev backend/OpenRouter in addition to Anthropic; extra third party in client-data flow

Enforce-mode pruning changes what Opus sees; a 700+300-char preview decides drops permanently per conversation ('a kept block is never reconsidered'), quality risk on long agentic sessions; Jev's fitness for judging code relevance is only validated on tiny self-run sets (12, 10, 20 prompts) by the author

Model-routing rules that send requests to OpenRouter models require a 'key' route, which drops the Claude subscription for those turns (spend real money) and switching models mid-conversation invalidates prompt cache and signed thinking blocks (their own warning)

OpenRouter-hosted Jev is not documented or tested by the project: defaults and pricing labels assume api.typesafe.ai/TYPESAFE_API_KEY; provider label falls back to 'open-rlcd' unless overridden; you must manually configure decisions backend, token_env and model id
Prune value is small for this user: subscription billing means token savings are not cash savings, and Opus context savings do not justify added latency (up to 3 s per epoch) and risk
No CI test workflow; release-only pipeline; alpha (v0.1.2); heavy scope (33k LOC, dashboard, resilience, keys) to trust for a security-sensitive position
Overlaps with existing tooling (caveman-shrink MCP, GitNexus context hooks) that already reduce context without a proxy
gh-jimmywesley-rlcd-gateway.verdict: The only candidate that is fully automatic (transparent ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy, fail-open Jev calls, OpenRouter reachable via a config-only backend), but it uses Jev merely for context pruning and request-complexity routing, adds a fail-closed single point of failure and logs full prompts to disk by default, and comes from a 1-week-old single-maintainer repo. Reasonable to trial in shadow mode on personal projects with log_bodies=false, not something to put in front of client work or your subscription login yet.

npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.name: jev-skill-router
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.whatItDoes: Single-file Node CLI (cli.mjs, 258 lines, zero dependencies) that sends one OpenRouter Jev Decisions request per user request (state = request + catalog of up to 60 local SKILL.md name/description pairs; questions = complexity score, use_skill choice, confidence score) and prints JSON telling the agent which skill to load. Also has a skill supply-chain scanner (Jev choice questions for prompt injection and dangerous commands on the first 6 KB of each SKILL.md) and a GitHub SKILL.md installer. Despite the "skill" label it is NOT a SKILL.md or plugin. It is a CLI, and it only reaches the model if the user pastes a rule into CLAUDE.md telling Claude to run it.

providerSupport.evidence: cli.mjs:24 const API = 'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions'; cli.mjs:25 const MODEL = 'typesafe/jev-1.13'; cli.mjs:87 key = process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY (only env var); cli.mjs:89-93 fetch POST with Bearer key, body {model,state,questions}. The URL, model and key variable are hardcoded, so there is no TypeSafe-direct or configurable base URL. Model is pinned to jev-1.13 rather than ~typesafe/jev-latest.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed for OpenRouter. Adding TypeSafe direct or the ~typesafe/jev-latest alias would be trivial (edit 2 constants, about 3 lines), but the package has no repo link, so a local fork would be required.
providerSupport.others: none

interface.name: jev-skill-router "<request>"
interface.purpose: Default mode. Discovers skills, makes one Jev call, prints JSON {complexity, use_skill, skill_name, instruction, confidence}. Fail-open on error (cli.mjs:226-258).

interface.purpose: List discovered skills (name :: desc) (cli.mjs:163)

interface.name: --init <claude|codex|opencode|hermes|generic>
interface.purpose: Prints a paste-in rule for CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md telling the agent to run the CLI before every non-trivial request. It does NOT write the file (cli.mjs:209-218).

interface.name: --install owner/repo[/ref] [--scan]
interface.purpose: Fetches every SKILL.md (up to 200) from a GitHub repo via the API and raw.githubusercontent.com into ~/.jev-skill-router/library, optionally auditing them (cli.mjs:106-126,170-190)

interface.name: --scan [--dir X]
interface.purpose: Jev prompt_injection / dangerous_commands audit of discovered skills, 8 parallel calls, writes ./skills-security-report.json into the cwd (cli.mjs:192-207)

npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.createdAt: 2026-09-21 (npm created; 3 versions 0.1.0, 0.1.1 and 0.2.0 all published within about 15 minutes; last modified 2026-09-21T20:01Z)
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.lastCommit: n/a (no repository field in package.json or npm metadata; npm gitHead e360f3ff but no linked repo)
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.runtime: Node >=18, ESM, zero dependencies (Node 24 is fine), 18.9 KB unpacked, 4 files
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.install: npm i -g jev-skill-router; export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...; add the rule from --init claude to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (manual). No postinstall script, no repo link.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.tests: None. No test files, no CI, no repo. README claims of "verified on a real setup" are unverifiable.
security: API key read from env only (cli.mjs:87), never in argv, which is good. The user request text IS passed as argv, so it is visible in ps and process lists (one more leak surface next to the secret-leak guard hook).
No timeout or AbortController on fetch (cli.mjs:89). The fail-open catch only handles errors, so a hanging connection stalls the Bash tool call until the tool timeout.
No postinstall or install scripts. The package is clean and only uses fs, path, os, fetch. No child_process, no eval, no telemetry beyond the OpenRouter call and, for --install, GitHub.

--install pulls unpinned SKILL.md content (ref HEAD) from arbitrary GitHub repos and writes it under ~/.jev-skill-router/library. That directory is not a Claude Code skill dir, so nothing is auto-loaded, but discoverSkills() reads it and the catalog is fed to Jev, so a hostile skill description is a prompt-injection surface into the router. It only affects a choice among names, low blast radius.

The security audit is a probabilistic classifier on the first 6 KB of a skill (cli.mjs:131). Content past 6 KB is unscanned, and Jev is a typed-decision model, not a code-audit tool. It gives false assurance (TRUSTED) and README marks API errors as UNKNOWN but does not block. Treat it as a heuristic.

The router output is instructions fed back to Claude ('Load the X skill and follow it'). The skill name is chosen from the local catalog, so it cannot inject free text, but any attacker who controls a SKILL.md name or description can steer the routing.
--scan writes skills-security-report.json into the cwd, so it can pollute client repos.
Anonymous single maintainer (aleksvega, [email removed]), package 9 days old, no source repo, so provenance is weak. Pin the version or vendor the 258 lines rather than installing globally.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai only (plus api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com for --install). Routing call sends: (a) the request string Claude passes on the command line, truncated to 4000 chars (cli.mjs:239), which is whatever Claude paraphrases and could contain client project detail; and (b) name plus first 140 chars of description for the 60 skills with the LONGEST descriptions from ~/.claude/skills, ~/.codex/skills, ~/.opencode/skills, ~/.jev-skill-router/library and ./skills (cli.mjs:234-237). Nothing is sent about code, diffs or file contents unless Claude pastes them into the request. --scan sends the first 6 KB body of every discovered SKILL.md. Note the plugin skills dir is skipped (walkMd excludes 'plugins', cli.mjs:47), so the user's caveman, gitnexus and other plugin or project skills are likely not in the catalog.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.failureMode: Fail-open on missing key, HTTP errors and JSON errors: prints {use_skill:false,...} and exits 0 (cli.mjs:256-258). There is NO fetch timeout and NO retry, so a slow or hanging OpenRouter stalls the Bash call until the tool-level timeout (default 2 min). It is also fail-open at the agent level in the sense that nothing enforces the rule: if Claude skips the CLAUDE.md instruction, routing simply does not happen.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.contextCost: Zero tool-definition cost: no MCP server, no tools, no server instructions. Only the pasted CLAUDE.md rule (about 70 tokens, recurring every session). Per user request, if Claude obeys, there is one extra Bash tool_use plus a JSON result of about 80 to 120 tokens, roughly 200 tokens of transcript per turn, accumulating over a long session. No hook-injected text.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.latencyImpact: One synchronous Bash call per non-trivial user request: Node startup (~50 ms) + skill dir walk + Jev call. README claims 0.5 to 1.5 s (1.1 s for the sample). It adds one model turn (tool_use, then result, then continue), so about 1.5 to 4 s per prompt in practice, all serial before Claude starts real work. Unbounded if OpenRouter hangs (no timeout).
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. The mechanism is a pasted CLAUDE.md instruction ('Before answering any non-trivial request, run jev-skill-router ...'), which depends on Claude choosing to comply on every turn and deciding what counts as 'non-trivial'. There is no hook, no MCP tool, no SKILL.md trigger and no proxy. A CLI is not a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, though a 5-line hook wrapper around this CLI or its API call could be made deterministic.
pros: Correct Jev usage: exact Decisions endpoint and model from the brief (cli.mjs:24-25), OpenRouter key only, and a sensible use of typed Choice/Score primitives, with cheap cost per call.
Tiny and auditable: 258 lines, zero dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, no child_process or eval. The whole thing can be read in 5 minutes, so vendoring or forking is easy.
Fail-open on API errors and a missing key (cli.mjs:256-258) so it never blocks Claude.
Zero context cost from tool definitions, since there is no MCP server.
Reusable pieces: the request shape (state + questions with choice/score, cli.mjs:238-245) and the skill-audit prompts are a good reference for writing a proper UserPromptSubmit hook.
cons: Solves a problem Claude Code already handles natively: Claude Code lists skills with descriptions in context and triggers them itself. This user has about 40 skills, which is cheap in context, so routing adds latency and a network hop for little value.

Not automatic: it requires a pasted CLAUDE.md rule and Claude's compliance every turn. That contradicts the requirement 'Claude Code must use it without me prompting'. Also there is no --init that writes the file, it only prints.

Discovery misses the user's real skills: it scans ~/.claude/skills but explicitly skips any dir named 'plugins' (cli.mjs:47), so plugin-provided skills (caveman, gitnexus, etc.) are invisible. Project-level .claude/skills is not scanned, only ./skills.

Catalog is cut to the 60 skills with the LONGEST descriptions (cli.mjs:234-235), not the most relevant ones, so short-described skills are silently unroutable. Descriptions are truncated to 140 chars, which throws away trigger phrases.
No fetch timeout (cli.mjs:89): a slow OpenRouter call stalls a Bash tool call up to the tool timeout on every turn.
Request text appears in argv (ps-visible) and 60 skill names plus the user prompt go to a third party on client projects; there is no opt-out or redaction.
Adds a full extra model turn (about 1.5 to 4 s and about 200 tokens) to every non-trivial prompt, which is bad for an all-day workflow; in bypass mode the user might not even notice it.
Immature and unverified: 3 versions in 15 minutes, no repo, no tests, no CI, single anonymous maintainer, README claims are unverifiable. The pinned jev-1.13 model, not jev-latest.

Only covers skill routing and skill auditing. It does nothing for real coding decisions (which file, whether to run tests, risk gating, permission decisions, model or subagent routing), where Jev's calibrated probabilities are actually useful.
Security scanner is a heuristic on the first 6 KB of a skill and is likely to give false TRUSTED verdicts; the 'UNKNOWN' state does not block anything.
npmjs-com-package-jev-skill-router.verdict: A small, honest, correctly wired OpenRouter-Jev CLI, but it is a poc that only auto-runs via a pasted CLAUDE.md rule, misses plugin skills, and duplicates Claude Code's built-in skill triggering. Not worth installing; at most use it as a reference for the Decisions request shape and vendor a UserPromptSubmit-hook version with a timeout if skill routing is ever wanted.

gh-aleksvega-jev-stack.name: jev-stack (aleksvega umbrella installer)
gh-aleksvega-jev-stack.whatItDoes: Not a skill or integration itself. It is a 134-line zero-dependency Node CLI (npx jev-stack) that only git-clones five separate third-party repos (fast-jev-compaction, jev-ultrafast, jev-prompt-enhancer, jev-skill-router, cdp-browser-launcher) into the current directory, and runs "npm install -g --prefix <dir>" inside two of them (fast-jev-compaction, jev-prompt-enhancer). It ships an AGENT_PROMPT.md that asks an agent to walk the user through the same installs. It has no MCP server, no hooks, no SKILL.md and no plugin manifest, and it wires nothing into Claude Code. The payload repos are the real tools. The most Claude-Code-relevant one is jev-prompt-enhancer, whose "--install" writes a UserPromptSubmit hook that can rewrite every user prompt. The npm keywords list "claude" and "codex".

providerSupport.evidence: jev-stack itself makes no API calls. bin/jev-stack.js:55-62 (ROUTING text) and README.md 'Routing' only document 'typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions' with OPENROUTER_API_KEY. In the payload repos (read via gh api, not cloned): jev-gate.py:15,51 uses os.environ OPENROUTER_API_KEY and POSTs https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with urlopen timeout=60. jev-prompt-enhancer cli.mjs:19-21 has API='https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions', MERCURY='inception/mercury-2', KEY=process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It also calls https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions (cli.mjs:49). No TYPESAFE_API_KEY or console.typesafe.ai path was seen. README claims 'direct mode' via OPENAI_API_KEY, which is not Jev and was not verified.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already OpenRouter-native (Decisions API), so no patching is needed. Only the payload repos were sampled, not fully audited.
providerSupport.others: README claims OPENAI_API_KEY 'direct mode' (non-Jev), unverified. The prompt enhancer also sends prompts to a second model, inception/mercury-2, via OpenRouter chat completions.

Payload jev-prompt-enhancer states it is fail-open, returning the original prompt on error (cli.mjs header). jev-gate.py uses a 60 s urlopen timeout (jev-gate.py:57), and a slow API would stall a push. Fail-open or fail-closed for jev-gate was not determined.

The other CLIs (jev-compact, jev-gate, jev-qa, jev-find) are invoked manually or via git hooks, not automatically by Claude Code.

Payload prompt enhancer: adds an OpenRouter Jev call plus a Mercury rewrite plus a user approval step on every prompt, likely 1-several seconds and an interactive interruption per turn. jev-gate: a network call on each push, with a 60 s worst-case timeout.

Zero-dependency installer that is short (134 lines) and fully readable, with no postinstall and no telemetry in the installer.
The jev-prompt-enhancer payload does have a real Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook design (updatedPrompt / block), and its fail-open stated behavior fits the 'automatic' goal.
States the sensible rule that deterministic checks (tsc, builds, secret scans) are never replaced by a Jev decision.
cons: It is only an installer that git-clones other repos into cwd. It adds no MCP tool, hook, skill or plugin to Claude Code by itself, so it delivers no automatic integration.

The automatic piece (prompt enhancer) rewrites the user's prompt and then asks for approval. That is the opposite of a silent, zero-friction integration, and it feeds every prompt (including client code and secrets) to two extra models.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, created 2026-09-22, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file. The payload repos are equally new, with 0-1 stars.
Supply-chain risk: unpinned HEAD clones plus 'npm install -g --prefix' run lifecycle scripts from personal repos on a machine that holds client code.

Uses Jev for tasks it is not designed for (compaction, code QA, NL file search, browser steps) with claims like '~100x cheaper' and 'same reliability' that are unbenchmarked in the repo. Jev is a typed decision model, not a free-text summarizer, so the compaction claim is doubtful.

Does not overlap with the user's needs: a Claude Code user with Opus already has /compact and GitNexus. The pre-push guard duplicates the existing secret-leak hook. The browser agent duplicates Playwright MCP.
README/AGENT_PROMPT are marketing-heavy; the AGENT_PROMPT asks an agent to run installs, an unnecessary prompt-injection-shaped path.
The payload fast-jev-compaction hooks.json is only {modules:['./fast-jev.ts']}, which is not a Claude Code hook schema, so Claude Code integration of that tool is unclear.

gh-fsans-jev-skill.name: jev-skill (fsans)
gh-fsans-jev-skill.whatItDoes: Agent Skill (SKILL.md plus a stdlib-only Python 3 CLI, scripts/jev.py) that wraps Jev judgments for coding agents. Commands are detect-intent, rank, check (security, readability, performance, testability gate), safety, ask (custom noul, choice or score question) and doctor. It calls OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions by default, or the direct TypeSafe API. It adds a 1h disk cache, retry/backoff, and a confidence-to-action policy (auto-apply, confirm, escalate). It also ships an npm installer, jev-skill, that only copies files into ~/.agents/skills or a chosen dir. There is no MCP server, no hook and no proxy. A Claude Code session has to decide to run the CLI through Bash.

It does not use /api/v1/systemone. I could not fetch OpenRouter's docs (both WebFetch attempts returned 404), so the wire format is unconfirmed independently. The README says the format was verified live, and the fixtures tests/fixtures/openrouter_check.json exist.
providerSupport.others: None. It supports only the OpenRouter Decisions API and the direct TypeSafe endpoint.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed: OpenRouter is the first-class, recommended backend. The URL and model are overridable through JEV_OPENROUTER_URL and JEV_MODEL. To pin the exact model, set JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 or leave the default alias.

interface.name: jev.py rank --query Q --candidates-file F [--criteria]
interface.purpose: Choice among candidates (JSON array of id, label, code, description) plus a reserved 'none' option. Returns winner, ranking, confidence.

interface.name: jev.py check --code-file F [--standards-file] [--checks security,readability,performance,testability]
interface.purpose: Quality gate. Security and testability are noul questions, readability and performance are 0-3 score questions. Returns passed (overall >= 2.0), overall_score, dimensions, weakest.

interface.name: jev.py safety --code-file F | --text T
interface.purpose: Noul question 'is it safe to execute or apply this?'. Returns safe and probability. Uses stricter thresholds (auto >= 0.95, confirm >= 0.7).

interface.name: jev.py ask --question Q --type noul|choice|score [--criteria JSON]
interface.purpose: One custom typed question, optionally with state.

interface.name: jev.py doctor [--json]
interface.purpose: Checks key presence, backend, cache and connectivity (makes a live API call). Exit 1 with setup help when there is no key.

interface.name: global flags --backend, --no-cache, --verbose
interface.purpose: Select the backend, bypass the cache, include the raw API response.

interface.name: exit codes 0/1/2
interface.purpose: 0 usable judgment, 1 error, 2 uncertain (action=escalate).

interface.name: SKILL.md description trigger
interface.purpose: The only automatic hook. Claude may load the skill for 'judgment-shaped subtasks (classify intent, pick best candidate, gate code quality, check safety)'. No hook events, no MCP tools.

interface.name: npm jev-skill install|uninstall|path [--to DIR] [--link] [--force]
interface.purpose: Copies (or symlinks) skills/jev into a skills dir. Default is ~/.agents/skills, NOT ~/.claude/skills, so use --to ~/.claude/skills. No postinstall script.

gh-fsans-jev-skill.runtime: Python 3 stdlib only (urllib) for the skill. Node >=14 only for the optional npm installer. No dependencies.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.install: Static copy, no code run: git clone https://github.com/fsans/jev-skill && cp -r jev-skill/skills/jev ~/.claude/skills/jev. Or: npx jev-skill install --to ~/.claude/skills. There is no postinstall script (package.json scripts are only sync-version and prepack). The key goes in ~/.config/jev/.env or in the environment.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.tests: The repo has 116 pytest test functions across tests/ (builders 21, cache 11, client 24, cli 32, interpret 26, live 2), all mocked except test_live.py. I did not run them (hard rule). There is no CI (no .github), no GitHub releases, and only one npm version, 0.1.0 (published 2026-09-20).
security: API key is never accepted on argv: it is read from the environment or a .env file and sent only in the Authorization header (config.py docstring, client.py:139-146). Nothing sensitive shows up in the process list.

Config loads .env from cwd first, then the skill dir, then ~/.config/jev/.env (config.py:57-61). A project's own .env (client repos) containing OPENROUTER_API_KEY would silently be used, and only known keys are picked up. Env vars win over files. Real env var OPENROUTER_API_KEY beats all files.
No shell execution in the CLI (no subprocess, os.system, eval or exec in scripts/). No telemetry beyond the X-Title: jev-skill header, plus an optional HTTP-Referer, sent to OpenRouter.
npm installer only copies files (skips .env, pyc), has no postinstall and no network access. It defaults to ~/.agents/skills and would not land in Claude Code's dir without --to. Not curl|sh.

Disk cache at ~/.cache/jev-skill stores the full request-derived response as JSON, plus the raw API response. The key is a sha256 of the payload, so code is not stored verbatim in the key. Files are created with default umask, not 0600 (mkstemp gives 0600, then os.replace keeps that).

Prompt-injection surface: the code or prompt goes into Jev's 'state' as structured JSON. The outputs are only numeric probabilities and enum keys, so a hostile repo cannot make Jev emit instructions. The SKILL.md itself tells the agent 'an unsafe verdict always stops the planned action', which lets a false-positive block work.
Single-author, zero-star, one-commit repo. A supply-chain risk on updates. Pin to a reviewed commit and copy the files rather than using npx.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.dataEgress: Only what the agent passes to the CLI leaves the machine, and only when the skill is invoked. detect-intent sends the user prompt text (state.user_request, plus optional context). check and safety send the full code snippet from --code-file (state.code, plus standards). rank sends every candidate's id, label, code and description plus the query. ask sends the question plus arbitrary state. All of it goes to openrouter.ai (which routes to TypeSafe) and is retained by nothing in the skill except the local 1h cache. There is no automatic full-repo, diff or tool-output upload, but for client projects each check or safety call sends client code to two third parties (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe). The secret-leak guard hook would not see the file contents, because they are read by python, not by the Read or Bash tool arguments.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but slow to fail. With no key, doctor prints setup help and exits 1. Errors return {"error":...} with exit 1, and Claude simply continues. Timeout is 30 s per attempt (JEV_TIMEOUT), with 3 retries and exponential backoff on 5xx, 429 (honours Retry-After, up to 30 s) and URLError (client.py:_post_json). The worst case is roughly 30 s x 4 attempts plus about 7 s of sleep, roughly 2 minutes of blocked Bash on an outage. Exit 2 (uncertain) is a soft signal. Tune JEV_TIMEOUT=5 and JEV_RETRIES=1 to bound it. The cache gives a 1h hit for identical payloads. There is no circuit breaker.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.contextCost: Small. One skill: about 480 chars of frontmatter description (about 120 tokens) sits permanently in the skills listing. The full SKILL.md is about 4.7 KB (about 1.2k tokens) loaded only when the skill is invoked, plus references/*.md on demand. It adds no MCP tools or server instructions and injects no hook text. Each CLI call costs about 100-300 tokens of JSON output, plus the tool-call overhead.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.latencyImpact: Each call is a Bash tool round trip: python startup (about 50 ms) plus the Jev call (claimed 70-500 ms), plus an extra model turn to decide, run and read the result. That is roughly 1-3 s and about 300-500 tokens per use. Cache hits are instant. Because it is model-driven, it adds latency on top of Opus 5.5 turns rather than replacing any. The skill's own advice 'prefer check after writing non-trivial code' would add a round trip after most edits if followed.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at model discretion. Claude Code lists the skill's description and may load SKILL.md when a task looks judgment-shaped. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no MCP tool. Triggering will be inconsistent, because Opus usually just decides such things itself. To make it reliable you would have to add your own hook or CLAUDE.md instruction.
pros: Native fit for OpenRouter: default backend, default model ~typesafe/jev-latest, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions (config.py:28,104-107). No patching needed and one env var (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) to switch on.
Very low context cost: a single skill with a 480-char description and no MCP tool schemas, unlike an MCP server that adds many tool defs.
Stdlib-only Python and static files: easy to audit (about 1,600 LOC in total), no postinstall, no shell exec, and keys never go on argv.

Sensible handling of Jev semantics: noul certainty is derived as abs(2p-1) because noul has no confidence field, the performance-scale inversion is fixed, and escalate/confirm/auto-apply thresholds exist. That is better than naive use of raw probabilities.
Bounded, typed outputs (enums and numbers only), so the prompt-injection risk from Jev's responses is small. The disk cache also reduces cost for repeated identical checks.
Reasonable test footprint (116 mocked tests) for a v0.1 project. Timeouts and retries are configurable via env.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a skill triggered only at Claude's discretion, so it cannot meet the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told. A SessionStart or PreToolUse hook or a CLAUDE.md rule is still needed.

Its use cases duplicate what Opus 5.5 already does for free inside the turn: intent detection is pointless when the main model reads the prompt itself, and rank, check and safety by a 'System One' model are weaker signals than the main model's own review. Nothing gets cheaper, since each use adds a call.

Sends client code (check, safety, rank) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every use, which is a real problem for client projects. Nothing in the skill gates or redacts (no path or secret filtering), and the existing secret-leak hook cannot see the file contents.

Weak evidence for the 'safety' and 'check' verdicts: the questions are hand-written prompts (builders.py:build_check, build_safety) and Jev is a beta model with no published calibration on security review. The skill tells the agent to STOP on any 'unsafe' verdict, which risks false-positive blocks in bypass/auto mode.

Immature and unproven: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 10 days old, no CI, no releases, and the direct TypeSafe endpoint (api.typesafe.ai/v1/judge) is unverified by the author. The OpenRouter wire format could not be confirmed independently, since the docs pages I tried returned 404.
No use of /api/v1/systemone, only the alpha Decisions endpoint. If OpenRouter changes the alpha API the skill breaks (URL is env-overridable but the payload shape is not).

Worst-case failure blocks Bash for about 2 minutes under defaults (30 s x 3 retries). The cwd .env lookup means a client project's .env could override the OpenRouter key without warning. The npm installer defaults to ~/.agents/skills, not Claude Code's skills dir.
gh-fsans-jev-skill.verdict: A tidy, safe-to-read reference wrapper with first-class OpenRouter support and a sound way to interpret Jev's probabilities. But it is only a description-triggered skill, so it does not deliver automatic use, and its judgments mostly duplicate Opus. Use it as a source of code (the interpret/config logic and the payload shapes) for a hook-based integration, not as the integration itself; if installed, copy pinned files, set JEV_TIMEOUT to about 5 and JEV_RETRIES to 1, and avoid it on client code.

gh-leighefford-jev-kit.name: @leighefford/jev-kit
gh-leighefford-jev-kit.whatItDoes: Novelty toolkit of 7 MCP tools (stdio; optional HTTP mode) plus CLI and local web UI that call Jev's System One endpoint: laugh_track (simulated 200-person audience for speeches/jokes), steer_check (per-sentence off-goal/filler/invented-fact check of a draft), semantic_bisect (git bisect judged by Jev; runs a user-supplied shell command in a temp git worktree), physics_interact/physics_sandbox (game-physics judgments), collision_engine (pairwise idea scoring of notes), and jev_ask (raw typed noul/choice/score query). providerSupport.evidence: src/jev.js:9-16 hardcodes GATEWAY = https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/typesafe/v1/systemone (model typesafe-ai/jev) and DIRECT = https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (model jev-latest). Env: AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/jev.js:95-96), macOS Keychain, ~/.config/jev-kit/config.json (src/jev.js:43-58). No 'openrouter' string anywhere in the repo (grep). Undocumented-for-OpenRouter escape hatch: JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL (src/jev.js:73-84, README 'Experimental: a local model'); url = base + '/v1/systemone' unless base already ends in /systemone. So JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 JEV_API_KEY=<OR key> should hit https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with Bearer auth and body {model,state,questions} (src/jev.js:157-170). Untested by author and OpenRouter's request/response schema equivalence to TypeSafe's is unverified (not executed per audit rules).
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (default, also required for audio transcription via openai/whisper-1), any self-hosted System One-compatible server (Laya).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial-to-easy: env-only via JEV_BASE_URL (treated as 'local', so cost display says 'no API cost (local)' and the 'via' label is wrong, cosmetic). A 3-line patch adding an OPENROUTER_API_KEY branch to resolveConfig would make it first-class. Main risk is whether OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same {model,state,questions} body and returns {answers} in the same shape; the client already tolerates both noul and probability shapes (src/jev.js:220-223).

pros: Real, working, well-tested Jev integration using all three primitives (choice, score, noul) on real decisions (which plan is stronger, is another review needed, who finalizes) - a good reference for how to phrase Jev questions.

Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with env-based base URL override (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is probably config-only; --judge-model allows typesafe/jev-1.13.
Sensible hardening of the spawned claude: plan mode, Read/Glob/Grep only, --strict-mcp-config, provider keys stripped from child env.
MIT, no postinstall, one runtime dependency, CI + CodeQL, active (83 commits in 9 days).
Useful for occasional big-task planning where two-model cross-review is wanted, and shows cost/latency numbers of a Jev call (~1.2s).
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin; cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
Ships as a heavy batch workflow (spawns codex and nested claude sessions, minutes per run, 2N+1 LLM calls) - costs extra Anthropic/OpenAI quota and does not fit daily edit-loop use.
Requires a second agent (Codex CLI login or DeepSeek/Kimi/GLM key); user has none configured, and sending client repo material to those providers is a data-governance risk.
Still hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming and default model 'jev-latest'; OpenRouter use is untested and doctor's /v1/models probe may fail; OpenRouter Decisions API not used.
Single-maintainer, 9 days old, 0 stars, unpinned reusable-workflow release pipeline; README 'claude25 jev91' benchmark claim not found in repo docs I could grep and is unverified.
Jev is used only as an arbiter of LLM-written plan text (a judgment over long free-text), not on structured app state where System One is strongest; Jev outage aborts the run (no fallback).
gh-rxova-jev-planner.verdict: A legitimate but standalone multi-agent planning CLI that uses Jev as judge; it has no Claude Code hook/MCP/skill surface and is manual, slow and quota-hungry, so it does not deliver automatic Jev integration. Useful at most as a reference for Jev question design or an occasional manual planning tool (with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter).

gh-vercel-ai.name: @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai (vercel/ai packages/typesafe-ai)
gh-vercel-ai.whatItDoes: Vercel AI SDK provider for TypeSafe System One / Jev. It exposes only an experimental evaluationModel (used via experimental_evaluate from the ai package) that POSTs Choice, Score and Boolean (mapped to Noul) questions against a shared state to {baseURL}/systemone. The output is typed answers with probabilities. It is a TypeScript library for app developers. It has no MCP server, hooks, skills or CLI, so it cannot be wired into Claude Code as-is.

providerSupport.evidence: src/typesafe-ai-provider.ts:24-27 and :36: baseURL is configurable and defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1. src/typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109: url = `${baseURL}/systemone`, so createTypeSafeAi({baseURL:'https://openrouter.ai/api/v1', apiKey}) hits POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint. Key env var is TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY (provider.ts:40) and is checked again at model.ts:99. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY, no alpha/decisions endpoint and no other gateway in the source (grep 'openrouter|alpha/decisions' returned nothing). Model id defaults to 'jev-latest' (model.ts:26); the OpenRouter form would be 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. The request body is {model, state, questions} with question type 'noul' (model.ts:111-122). Whether OpenRouter's /systemone body and response match this schema is unverified, since the Jev brief says nothing about it. The response schema is copied from the official typesafe-sdk-js (evaluation-api.ts:1-3).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial at the SDK level: pass baseURL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, apiKey=<OpenRouter key> and modelId typesafe/jev-1.13. This assumes OpenRouter /systemone uses the same body and response schema as TypeSafe's, which is unverified. Apart from that config there is no code to patch, and no Claude Code integration exists to patch.

Key handling: Bearer token in the Authorization header, loaded from TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY via loadApiKey. It is never placed in argv. The user agent is 'ai-sdk-typesafe-ai/<version>'.

Prompt-injection surface is small because the output is typed (choice, probabilities, numbers) with no free text. But the caller-supplied state is sent to a remote model, and a hostile state can bias the decision.

Response schema is validated with zod, and errors go through createJsonErrorResponseHandler.
gh-vercel-ai.dataEgress: Only what the calling code puts in `state` (string or JSON) plus the question instructions and criteria, sent as one POST body to {baseURL}/systemone with model id and bearer token. Nothing is collected automatically. If someone built a Claude Code integration on this, the egress would be whatever code, diffs or tool output that glue code chose to send. That would need a size cap and a secret scrub, and would matter for client-confidential projects.
gh-vercel-ai.failureMode: Library behavior only: failures throw APICallError. Core experimental_evaluate retries transient errors (429, 529) up to maxRetries=2 by default. There is no provider-side retry loop (docs/105-typesafe-ai.mdx "Errors and retries"). No default timeout is set, only abortSignal passthrough. Fail-open or fail-closed depends entirely on caller code, and no Claude Code integration exists here.
gh-vercel-ai.contextCost: Zero as shipped, because it has no MCP tools, hooks or skills. A custom wrapper (for example a small MCP server built on it) would add its own tool definitions, likely 1 to 3 tools at roughly 300 to 800 tokens.
gh-vercel-ai.autoInvocation: Not applicable: it is a library with no trigger of its own. Automatic use in Claude Code would need extra glue, such as a hook script or MCP wrapper calling it. A deterministic hook is the only truly automatic route, and this package provides none.
gh-vercel-ai.latencyImpact: None as shipped. Any wrapper would add one HTTPS round trip per evaluate call (claimed 70 to 500 ms end to end) plus Node startup (about 100 to 300 ms) if it is spawned per hook call.
pros: Confirms the wire format from code: POST {baseURL}/systemone with {model,state,questions}, question types choice/score/noul, and answers with probabilities and confidence (model.ts:108-122, api.ts:8-30). This is a useful spec for writing your own thin Claude Code hook or MCP wrapper.
baseURL is overridable (provider.ts:36), so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 is a one-line change for the /systemone endpoint, if OpenRouter's schema matches.
Small and auditable: about 6 KB of dist, 2 pinned dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, npm provenance, Apache-2.0, maintained by Vercel with an active release cadence.
Sound typed-output handling: limits of 255 choice options and 2 to 10 score levels are enforced client-side, and the two-decimal rounding is declared.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration at all. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI and only plugs into the ai package's experimental_evaluate. The user's automatic-use requirement is unmet.

Reads TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY only (provider.ts:40, model.ts:99). There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY fallback, so you must pass apiKey and baseURL explicitly. The default endpoint is api.typesafe.ai, not OpenRouter.
Covers only the /systemone shape. No use of OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions endpoint or of the Jev Router model, and it is unverified that OpenRouter's /systemone accepts the 'noul' body.

Explicitly experimental: 'Evaluation is experimental' in the README, and the ai package's experimental_evaluate API may change. The package is 14 days old with 12 releases, and only 17 commits touch it, most of them bot releases.
Requires the ai package and zod as runtime dependencies. That is heavy for a hook or MCP script, when a plain fetch of about 30 lines would do.
No timeout, and retries depend on the core, so a slow or down Jev could stall a hook unless the caller sets an abortSignal.
gh-vercel-ai.verdict: This is a real Vercel-published Jev SDK provider, but it is an app-developer library and not a Claude Code integration, so it gives no automatic invocation. Its only value here is as a verified reference for the /systemone request and response schema, which a small custom hook or MCP wrapper pointed at OpenRouter could reuse.

gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.name: @fleeex/jev-orchestrator
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.whatItDoes: A Claude Code skill (SKILL.md plus a Node CLI helper) that treats Jev as a cheap decision layer for orchestrating coding workers. Claude writes a compact JSON state and runs `jev-orchestrator decide <strategy|parallel|worker|retry|review|completion|stuck>`. The CLI sends a projection of that state to TypeSafe POST /v1/systemone through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. It applies code-level policy overrides and confidence tiers, then prints a recommendation. It can also launch OpenAI Codex CLI workers in git worktrees, and it logs sessions and estimated cost to JSONL. Its whole purpose is delegate/parallelize/retry/review decisions for Codex workers. It does not do general per-turn coding decisions.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev/client.ts:141 calls TypeSafeClient.systemOne(); the SDK (sdk/package/dist/index.mjs:554) does POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (line 581) and defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai (line 513). The SDK also reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (line 58). The tool has an override, `jev.baseUrl` in config (src/config/schema.ts:19, wired in src/jev/engine.ts:12). Env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (src/config/paths.ts:13, src/security/secrets.ts:90). There is no OpenRouter string anywhere in src. Setting jev.baseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api and putting the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY would map to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which matches the path in the brief. Not verified: whether OpenRouter's response matches the zod schema in client.ts:59-63, and my WebFetch of OpenRouter docs returned 404. Also, config jev.model defaults to `jev-latest` (schema.ts:4), which would have to be changed to `typesafe/jev-1.13` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`. `setup` and `doctor` validate the key via GET /v1/models, and the SDK expects `{models:[...]}` (index.mjs:370), which OpenRouter's /v1/models probably does not return. So they would likely fail, but `decide` does not call them.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial to moderate. The config-only route needs jev.baseUrl, jev.model and TYPESAFE_API_KEY set, with no code change. The response-schema match is unverified. The setup and doctor key check would break, so use `decide` directly or patch two lines.

security: The skill pre-approves exactly one command, its own helper shim (allowed-tools: Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/jev-orchestrator *)). The shim only runs `node <recorded cliEntry>` and never fetches code (src/skill/installer.ts:56-78). That is a good design, but the pre-approved wildcard also covers `codex run`, which launches Codex workers.

API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var first, else from ~/.config/jev-orchestrator/secrets.json (mode 0600). It is passed to the SDK in memory and sent as a Bearer header, not put in argv. The key is stripped from Codex worker environments and redacted from their output (README, src/security/secrets.ts:104-114). Config files reject secret-like keys (schema.ts:112).
Child processes use spawn() with argument arrays and task text goes over stdin (src/util/exec.ts:50). No shell string execution seen. No postinstall script in package.json, only prepublishOnly.

Prompt-injection surface is small, since Jev returns typed probabilities only. The state is built by Claude, and worker summaries and test output (up to 4000 chars) are passed into it. Code-level policy forces irreversible or sensitive-file tasks back to Claude.

Codex workers run in a sandbox (read-only or workspace-write) with no approval-bypass flags. That is separate from Claude Code's own permissions, so with the user's bypass mode a delegated Codex run is only limited by Codex's sandbox.

No telemetry to third parties found. Local JSONL logs go in .jev/sessions/ inside the repo and default to no state recorded (recordState:false). This adds a .jev/ directory to client repos, and src/git/exclude.ts appears to manage git excludes. I did not verify that in detail.
Single maintainer, 6 commits in one day, so supply-chain trust is low. The npm scope @fleeex is new and the SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk is at 0.6.0.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.dataEgress: Only the projected state per `decide` call goes to the endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or the override URL) with the question text and rubric. For strategy that is userGoal, currentPlan, repositorySummary (max 2000 chars), task/subtask ids, titles, file paths and a codexAvailable flag. For review, retry and stuck it also includes worker summaries, changedFiles and test or build output truncated to 4000 chars (src/orchestration/state.ts, strategy.ts:50-60). No source files or diffs are sent automatically, but Claude composes the state, so task descriptions, file paths and test output from client projects can leave the machine, and the user's secret-leak hook does not see the CLI's payload. The user prompt goal text is sent. Codex workers separately send task prompts and code to OpenAI (not Jev). Nothing goes to any other host.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.failureMode: Fail-open by design. There is a 5 s default timeout (DEFAULT_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=5000, schema.ts:5) and the SDK does 2 retries on 429/5xx/timeouts (client.ts:27,131). After that `decide` exits non-zero with a hint, and SKILL.md says to continue with Claude's own judgment. A missing key gives the exit code EXIT.jevUnavailable. Worst-case added latency on failure is about 15 s or more (three attempts at 5 s plus backoff). Confidence under 0.60 is treated as a fallback tier and ignored. Nothing blocks Claude's tools, because it is a skill-invoked CLI and not a hook.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns, since it is not in the hot path. When the skill fires it adds a model-authored JSON state file and a Bash call per decision, plus the claimed 70-500 ms Jev round trip (README example shows about 415 ms mean). The Claude-side turn cost (writing the state, extra tool calls, reading the result) is likely larger than Jev's latency, and roughly 5 KB of SKILL.md is loaded on each activation. A full orchestration run adds about 5-8 decision calls.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.contextCost: No MCP tools and no hooks. The always-on cost is the skill's frontmatter (name, description and when_to_use, about 1.3k chars, roughly 330 tokens) in the skill listing. When invoked, SKILL.md is about 5.1k chars (roughly 1.3k tokens), and the references (decisions.md 5.1k, orchestration.md 4.7k, codex-workers.md 3.6k chars) load only on demand (about 3.3k tokens if all are read). Each decide call returns a small JSON block (a few hundred tokens). Total 330 tokens per session and about 1.5-5k tokens per activation.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, meaning model discretion. The description says "Use proactively when a task may benefit from delegation...". The README itself admits invocation is 'a suggestion to the model, not a guarantee'. There is no deterministic hook and no transparent proxy. The user must also still install it once.
pros: Genuinely automatic in the sense the user asked for: a skill with a when_to_use trigger that needs no 'use jev' prompt, and it costs only about 330 tokens of always-on context.

Real Jev code path: uses the official SDK against POST /v1/systemone with typed Choice and Noul questions. src/orchestration/*.ts has worked examples of rubric-based choice options, and the confidence tiers (>=0.85 autonomous, 0.6-0.85 advisory, <0.6 fallback) with hard policy overrides are a sound way to use calibrated probabilities.
Fail-open, 5 s timeout, no network fetch under the pre-approved permission, and a single pre-approved command. Security posture is careful for a v0.1.
Small data footprint: the state projection is field-limited (no code or diffs), state recording is off by default, and there is a cost report ($0.042/M in, output free).
jev.baseUrl and jev.model are configurable, so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs no code change, subject to the response shape matching (not verified).
MIT, has tests and CI on two OSes, and includes a mock engine and demo so it can be evaluated without a key.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It only decides how to delegate to Codex workers (strategy, parallel, worker, retry, review, stuck). Its value depends on OpenAI Codex CLI plus worktrees, and the user has Opus 5.5 as the main model with no mention of Codex. Without Codex, Jev's only output is a nudge to 'do it yourself', which Claude already knows.
No benchmark and no evidence it improves outcomes. The README's Limitations section says so, and the Jev step adds tool calls and JSON state writing that a frontier model could answer in one thought.
Auto-invocation is best effort: model discretion via skill description, not deterministic. Claude will often skip it, or fire it on multi-file tasks where it adds only overhead.

No OpenRouter support in code: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and https://api.typesafe.ai. OpenRouter works only through the baseUrl and model overrides and an unverified response shape, and the stock `setup` and `doctor` key validation (GET /v1/models) will likely fail against OpenRouter. Storing the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY is confusing.

Very immature: one developer, 6 commits made in one day (2026-09-17), 1 star, 0 forks, npm 0.1.0. A pre-approved Bash wildcard that also launches Codex workers, plus writing .jev/ into client repos, is a lot of surface for questionable benefit.

With the user's bypass/auto mode, Claude-side permission rules that the README calls authoritative are largely inactive, so only Codex's own sandbox limits delegated runs. Client project goals and file lists are sent to a third-party endpoint via a path the secret-leak hook does not inspect.
Bundles heavy machinery unrelated to Jev (worktree manager, Codex adapter, session log). Little reusable for a lean Jev-in-Claude-Code integration beyond the pattern.
gh-fleeexcorp-jev-orchestrator.verdict: A well-built, security-conscious but very young skill whose entire job is deciding when to hand work to Codex workers. It is a poor match for a Claude-only daily coding flow and gives no OpenRouter support out of the box (only a baseUrl/model override, untested). Worth reading as a reference for wiring Jev's Choice/Noul primitives, but not worth installing for automatic daily use.

gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.whatItDoes: A small (about 870 lines of TypeScript) Node CLI named `jev` plus 8 SKILL.md files (policy, gate, route, guard, verify, triage, review, act). Each skill tells Claude to build a System One request (state plus choice/noul/score questions, with presets from `jev questions <usecase>`), run `jev --file request.json`, and apply one fixed policy. Stop if harm.score >= 1.5. Proceed if the pick probability >= 0.9 and determined.noul >= 0.9. Otherwise ask. The CLI redacts secret-shaped strings from state before sending. On a missing key or transport error it returns source:"fallback" (fail-open). It is not an MCP server and has no hooks. Claude only runs it through Bash, when a skill description matches or the user asks.
