security: API key is read only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/judge.ts:13-20) and never goes in argv. The error path scrubs the key from the message (judge.ts:106-108). The key is not visible in the process list.

State redaction (src/redact.ts): drops the value of any object key matching api-key/token/secret/password/authorization/credential, and regex-scrubs sk-*, jv_live_*, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... and 'Bearer ...' strings. It is best-effort only: free-text secrets of other shapes (AWS, GitHub ghp_, private keys, DB URLs) pass through, so it is weaker than the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard.

No exec, no child_process, no eval. Runtime is only fetch to one hardcoded host. There is no postinstall. `prepare` runs tsc only on git or local install, not on npm tarball install. No curl|sh installer.
No telemetry (README and SECURITY.md say so; grep finds no other network call).

Prompt-injection surface: the model-facing policy lives in SKILL.md. The command and diff text that Claude places in `state` is untrusted, but Jev returns only probabilities, so the injection impact is limited. The bigger risk is over-trust: the skill tells Claude to skip asking the user when Jev says 'proceed'. A probabilistic classifier could therefore weaken an ask/confirm step.
The package is a 2-day-old single-author npm package with a scoped name and no provenance. Pin the version and read the dist before use.
The 'In the wild' table links 11 third-party repos (jev-mcp, jev-skill-gate and others). The author says they were not run. They are not endorsements.
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.dataEgress: Only what Claude writes into the `state` JSON, and only when Claude decides to invoke the CLI. Typically that is the exact shell command, cwd and task (guard), a claim plus test receipts (verify), a diff or diff summary (review), or the user request plus skill names (route). If Claude puts a full diff or file contents in state, that leaves the machine, redacted only by the secret-key and regex scrubber. It goes to api.typesafe.ai today, and it would go to openrouter.ai after patching, where it is then subject to OpenRouter's provider routing and logging. Nothing else is collected. There is no automatic capture, and no hook sends tool outputs.
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.failureMode: Fail-open by design for missing key, HTTP or network exception, or non-Jev body (judge.ts:30-43, 66-70). The result is source:"fallback" and Claude is told to decide on its own or ask. There is NO timeout or AbortSignal on fetch (judge.ts:55). A hung TypeSafe or OpenRouter connection would block the Bash call until the Bash tool timeout (default 2 min). readBody swallows non-JSON and HTTP errors into {status}, which then becomes 'not_jev_answers' fallback. Fail-open on the guard skill means the 'safety' check silently vanishes when Jev is down (the skill says to ask the user before anything hard to undo).
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no hook text. The 8 SKILL.md files total about 11.3 KB (about 2.8k tokens) if all are read. Claude Code injects only name+description at startup: about 8 descriptions of roughly 300-450 chars each, which is about 3.2 KB or about 800 tokens of always-on skill listing. The full body of a skill (about 300 tokens each, the policy one about 800) loads only on trigger. Cheap. Each use also costs a Bash call plus the JSON it prints.
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, i.e. model discretion. Claude reads the descriptions and decides to load a skill, then decides to run the CLI. That fits 'do not have to say use jev' only loosely and is not deterministic. There are no hooks, so nothing fires at PreToolUse. The skill text itself says to skip Jev when a file or command already answers the question, and for a known-dangerous command to ask the user without Jev. In practice the model will rarely invoke it, and jev-guard/jev-verify depend on the model remembering to self-check. It also needs a global `jev` binary and the key exported in the Claude Code environment.
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.latencyImpact: Per invocation: Node cold start (about 50-100 ms) plus the claimed Jev 70-500 ms end to end, plus one extra model turn for Claude to write the request JSON, run Bash and read the output (several seconds of Opus time and tokens). Because invocation is model-driven, the cost falls only on turns where the skill triggers. There is no per-tool-call overhead like a hook would add. No timeout is configured, so the worst case is unbounded until the Bash timeout.
pros: Very light footprint: 0 MCP tools, no hooks, about 800 tokens of always-on skill descriptions, no interference with the existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).
Small, readable code (866 lines TS, no runtime deps, no exec, one hardcoded host). It is easy to audit and to patch in about 5 lines for OpenRouter.
Sensible, codified policy: numeric cutoffs (0.9/0.9/1.5, stop wins) are shared by code (src/branch.ts) and skill text. It never invents a probability on failure. Explicit fail-open contract.
Redacts secret-shaped keys and tokens from state before the body is built. The key is read from env only, not argv, and scrubbed from errors.
Good use-case fit for the Jev primitives (choice, noul, score): guard, verify and gate are closed decisions. Ships request templates and offline fixtures so the wiring can be dry-run without a key.
MIT, no telemetry, CI on Node 20 and 22, and tests cover the request and response contract.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint (src/defaults.ts:114) and key var (src/judge.ts:13) are hardcoded to TYPESAFE. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider, so a fork or patch is mandatory, and the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified against parse.ts.

Not automatic: it relies on the model choosing to load a skill and run a Bash CLI. There is no hook, so the guard and verify checks are not deterministic. This misses the user's core goal of Claude Code using Jev without being prompted.

Adds a full extra LLM round trip (Opus writes the request JSON, runs Bash, reads the result) for each Jev call, which is likely slower and costlier than the 70-500 ms Jev call itself. It is a poor fit for high-frequency decisions.
No fetch timeout and no retry. A stalled connection blocks until the Bash tool timeout. The fail-open guard silently removes safety when Jev is down.

Redaction is a narrow regex list (sk-, jv_live_, Bearer, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=) and misses AWS, GitHub, JWT and private keys, so client-project secrets in diffs or commands could leak to a third party. It duplicates but is weaker than the user's own secret guard.

Policy asks Claude to skip user confirmation when Jev says proceed at >=0.9. That is risky in bypass or auto mode and rests on an unvalidated, beta, 'possibly a flash router' model. Nothing has been benchmarked, and the README itself says the linked projects are not endorsed.

Immature and thin: 6 commits over 1 day, 1 author, 2 stars, alpha 0.1.1, no release tags or provenance. `jev` must be installed globally and put on PATH by hand, since the skills give no path or npx form.

Overlaps with existing tooling: gate/route/triage/review/act duplicate what Claude already does natively or via GitNexus. Only guard and verify add a distinct 'second opinion' value, and that is better done as a deterministic hook.
gh-aitofy-dev-jev-awesome-skills.verdict: A clean, tiny, well-scoped reference client and skill catalog, but it is a skill (model-discretion Bash CLI), not an automatic integration, and it is hardwired to api.typesafe.ai. Use it at most as a source of question presets and policy cutoffs (jev-guard and jev-verify) for a custom OpenRouter-based PreToolUse/Stop hook. Don't install it as the daily integration.

gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.name: @typesafe-ai/sdk (official TypeScript SDK)
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.whatItDoes: Official zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript/JS client for the TypeSafe API. TypeSafeClient.systemOne({state, questions, model?}) POSTs to {baseURL}/v1/systemone using choice()/noul()/score() question builders, and client.models.list() does GET /v1/models. It gives typed answers, retries, timeouts and logging. It is a library only. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI, so it does nothing inside Claude Code by itself. You would have to write a wrapper (an MCP server or a hook script) around it.

providerSupport.evidence: src/env.ts:2-9 env vars TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai), TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL. src/client.ts:41 DEFAULT_BASE_URL=https://api.typesafe.ai; :42 DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest; :270-272 apiKey and baseURL come from config or env; :321 POST /v1/systemone; :354 Authorization: Bearer <key>. baseURL is configurable and OpenRouter's System One API is https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so baseURL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key plus model typesafe/jev-latest matches the same path and auth scheme. grep for openrouter in the source gives 0 hits. Not verified against a live OpenRouter response. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported by the SDK.
providerSupport.others: Only the TypeSafe direct API is built in. The default model jev-latest has no vendor prefix, so it must be overridden for OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-latest). Discovery says it is wrapped by @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai (not inspected here).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial in principle, with no code change: set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest. This assumes OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same request and response schema (state, questions, model), which is unconfirmed.

gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.tests: 13 files under test/ (vitest unit tests, dist tests for ESM and CJS, type tests, and an integration suite that needs a real key). Coverage runs in the check script. The repo is a public mirror with only 5 commits, and the npm history is 0.5.7 to 0.6.0 within 3 days.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.install: npm install @typesafe-ai/sdk (as a dependency of your own wrapper). Nothing to install into Claude Code directly. Do not run the install for this audit.
security: No install scripts: grep of package.json found no postinstall or preinstall.
Zero runtime dependencies, so the supply-chain surface is small.
npm 0.6.0 is published with SLSA provenance attestation from GitHub Actions. The publish workflow pins actions by SHA and uses OIDC id-token.

The API key is held in a private field (#apiKey, src/client.ts:236) and sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (:354). It is never put in argv or the URL. If used from an MCP server, pass the key via env, not args.
Default log level is warn. At debug level the SDK logs request and response bodies (client.ts:335-340 area), which would expose state content in logs.
No telemetry found: grep for telemetry and analytics in src gave 0 hits. It sends only X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime and User-Agent headers.
No shell execution and no file reads in the SDK.
Prompt-injection surface: none by itself. The output is typed probabilities, not free text. Any wrapper still passes untrusted repo text as state.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.dataEgress: Whatever the wrapper puts in the state and questions fields goes to the configured baseURL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if overridden). The SDK reads no files on its own. Data leaving would be exactly what the integrator passes in (prompts, diffs, file contents, tool outputs). With OpenRouter it would pass through OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which matters for client projects under NDA. The header X-TypeSafe-Runtime reveals the runtime name.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.failureMode: The SDK does not decide fail-open or fail-closed. It throws APITimeoutError, APIConnectionError or APIError. The defaults are a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries on 408, 429, 5xx and connection errors, with 500 ms backoff up to 5 s, so the worst case is about 30 s or more of blocking (src/retry.ts:5-21). A hook wrapper must set timeout to 1-2 s and maxRetries to 0 and catch every error to fail open. Otherwise a hook would stall Claude Code turns.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.latencyImpact: The SDK overhead is negligible. The vendor claims 70-500 ms end to end. A Node cold start for a command hook adds about 50-100 ms per invocation. With the default retries a bad network could add 10-30 s unless tuned.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.contextCost: Zero on its own, since it has no tools, instructions or injected text. Any MCP wrapper built on it would add its own tool definitions (roughly 300-800 tokens for 1-3 tools). A hook wrapper could add zero tokens except the text it chooses to inject.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.autoInvocation: Not invocable from Claude Code at all. It is a library that only becomes automatic if you build a deterministic hook (PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit script) or an MCP server around it.
pros: Official, MIT-licensed, zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, npm provenance attestation: the safest building block for a custom Jev hook or MCP server.

baseURL and key are env-configurable and the path is /v1/systemone, the same path OpenRouter documents, so pointing it at OpenRouter should need only 3 env vars and no fork (src/env.ts, src/client.ts:321).
Typed choice/noul/score builders match Jev's three primitives exactly, so a wrapper is about 50 lines.
Configurable timeout and retry (per client and per call), so a hook can be made fail-open with a short deadline.
Fully typed answers and typed errors. The API key stays out of argv and the URL.
cons: It is only a library. It gives Claude Code no MCP tools, hooks or skills, so it achieves none of the automatic integration goal without custom code.
Young and thin: repo created 2026-09-04, 5 commits, 2 human contributors, npm versions 0.5.7 and 0.6.0 within 3 days. The API may change before 1.0.

No OpenRouter awareness: default model jev-latest lacks the typesafe/ prefix, so it must be overridden. There is no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) support, and OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified.
Default 10 s timeout with 2 retries is hostile to interactive hooks and must be tuned by the integrator.
The SDK gives no guidance on when Jev adds value for coding. That policy layer (which questions, which triggers) must be written by the user, and Jev is a classifier, not a chat model.
Debug logging would print state bodies, which may include client code.
gh-typesafe-ai-typesafe-sdk-js.verdict: Best foundation if you build your own thin wrapper (a fail-open hook or a tiny MCP server) and point it at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and model typesafe/jev-latest. But by itself it does nothing inside Claude Code and is not an integration. For a plain hook, raw fetch to OpenRouter would work about as well, since the SDK saves little code.

gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.name: @fiale-plus/jev-cli
gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.whatItDoes: Unofficial Node CLI (bin `jev`) and TS re-export layer over the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. Sends state + typed questions (noul/choice/score) to System One, prints JSON with probabilities, and adds an offline "decision pipeline": bundled packs (verify, screen, route), a fail-closed policy gate with exit codes (0 accept, 2 review, 3 deny, 4 abstain), decision records (state hashed not stored), replay, JSONL batch, doctor, lint. It is not an MCP server and has no hook, skill or plugin manifest. Its CLAUDE.md states "No MCP surface: deliberately out of scope".

providerSupport.evidence: The CLI hardcodes no endpoint. src/utils/validation.ts:2 reads flag or TYPESAFE_API_KEY. src/commands/doctor.ts:38 reads --base-url or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, default https://api.typesafe.ai. src/api/client.ts:37 passes baseURL to TypeSafeClient. The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:513) defaults baseURL to https://api.typesafe.ai, POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (l.554) with `Authorization: Bearer` (l.581), and GETs /v1/models (l.365). OpenRouter's page https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md says to point the TypeSafe SDK at OpenRouter by setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, with the same schema, and that bare IDs like jev-latest map to typesafe/. I did not run it live. Caveat: `jev models` and `doctor --live` use GET /v1/models, which the SDK expects as {models:[...]} (index.mjs:370); OpenRouter's /v1/models likely returns {data:[...]}, so those two likely fail. Inference commands should work.
providerSupport.others: TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai). Any base URL that speaks /v1/systemone, such as the bundled stub at tools/stub-server.mjs:67.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial. Set the env vars TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY, or pass --base-url. No code change is needed. The only breakage is the /v1/models listing.

interface.name: jev noul|choice|score <instructions>
interface.purpose: Single typed judgment. State comes from --state, --state-file, --stdin or trailing positional args. Choice takes --option name=desc. Score takes --level.

interface.name: jev ask
interface.purpose: Batch many questions over one state in one API call. Takes --questions, --pack, --pack-file, --request and --record.

interface.name: jev decide
interface.purpose: Run inference plus a pack policy in one call. Exit code is the decision. --format decision prints only accept, review, deny or abstain.

interface.name: jev batch
interface.purpose: JSONL of independent requests with bounded concurrency (default 4, max 32).

interface.name: jev gate
interface.purpose: Offline policy evaluation of a saved response or record. Exit 0/2/3/4. Makes no API call.

interface.name: jev replay
interface.purpose: Re-emit a stored record with replayed:true. No API call.

interface.name: jev packs
interface.purpose: List or dump the bundled packs verify, screen and route, with content hashes.

interface.name: jev lint
interface.purpose: Structural validation of a questions file. No API call.

interface.name: jev doctor [--live]
interface.purpose: Config check. --live authenticates, lists models and times a probe.

interface.name: jev models
interface.purpose: List models via GET /v1/models.

interface.name: Library exports (src/index.ts)
interface.purpose: Re-exports TypeSafeClient, noul/choice/score, evaluatePolicy, loadPack, readRecord, buildRecord and GATE_EXIT.

security: MIT license.
One runtime dependency, the official @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. No postinstall or preinstall script. `prepare` (npm run build) runs only on git installs or local npm install, not on a registry install.
No child_process, exec, spawn, telemetry or analytics, and no direct fetch in src/ (grep). All network traffic goes through the SDK.

Key handling: env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY is supported, but `--api-key <key>` is also accepted. That would expose the key in argv and the process list, and Claude's transcript, so use the env var only. doctor reports key presence and source, never the value.
SDK logger is forced to stderr (client.ts:48-62). At debug level it may log request details.
Prompt-injection surface: the CLI outputs only numbers and enums, no free text, which limits injection back into Claude. The `screen` pack is documented as advisory, not a security boundary.
Publishing uses npm trusted publishing (OIDC) with staged publish and manual 2FA approval. The CI security workflow runs npm audit weekly.
Single maintainer (Pavel Fadeev, npm user bearmug). Unofficial. Repo is 13 days old.

Whether that blocks Claude depends on the caller, because the CLI is not a hook. Gate and decide are fail-closed (a missing answer abstains, exit 4), which fits approval gates but would block a workflow if wired blindly into a hook. There is no fail-open mode. gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.autoInvocation: Only when prompted, or via instructions the user adds. The package ships no hook, skill or MCP, so nothing fires by itself. Claude Code would call `jev` through Bash only if CLAUDE.md or a skill tells it to. A deterministic PreToolUse hook could call `jev decide`, but the user would have to write it. The official typesafe-ai/skills repo (linked from the CLI help) is the more suitable trigger layer.
gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.latencyImpact: Claimed 70-500 ms per call (unverified), plus Node startup of about 100-200 ms per `jev` process and TLS to OpenRouter. As a Bash tool call it adds a full model tool-call round trip of a few seconds to the turn. As a hook it would add about 0.3-1 s per triggering event. Nothing is added unless invoked.

gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.tests: About 1100 lines across 5 node:test files (client, cli, contract, gate, integration). Mocked fetch with real Response objects, and contract.test.ts spawns the real CLI. The CI test workflow runs on Node 22 and 24, plus a weekly npm audit. The integration job on main uses a TYPESAFE_API_KEY secret. I did not run the tests.
pros: The only candidate here with a working, evidence-based OpenRouter route. The SDK posts to ${baseURL}/v1/systemone with Bearer auth, and OpenRouter documents exactly this env-var swap (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api).
Zero context cost. It is a plain CLI with no MCP tool schemas, which suits a user who already runs gitnexus, playwright and caveman-shrink.
Decision-oriented design: exit codes 0/2/3/4, `decide --format decision` printing one word, and fail-closed gating. This is easy to wrap in a small PreToolUse hook for gating risky actions.
The `route` and `screen` packs (handler routing, prompt-injection screening of untrusted content) are directly relevant to agent workflows.
Thin and auditable. One runtime dependency (the official SDK), no postinstall, no shell exec, no telemetry. Records hash the state instead of storing it.
Hard-coded price estimate of $42 per 1M input tokens matches the brief's ~$0.042 per 1M (the code comment says per Btok, but the value is the same). Each response carries cost.estimated_usd.
cons: No automatic integration. It ships no hook, skill, MCP or plugin. The user's requirement of Claude Code using Jev without being told is unmet unless the user writes their own hook or CLAUDE.md rules.
Very young and single-maintainer: 13 days old, 11 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, v0.2.0, and the maintainer's own 'unofficial' disclaimer. The API surface is churning (0.1.0 to 0.2.0 in 2 days).
`jev models` and `doctor --live` probably break on OpenRouter, because they call GET /v1/models expecting {models:[...]}. I did not verify OpenRouter's response shape.

It is a bare wrapper over the official SDK with no OpenRouter-specific logic, and it does not use the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions). It also does not mention OPENROUTER_API_KEY anywhere. The user must remember the misleading TYPESAFE_* env names.
The `--api-key` flag puts the key in argv. The existing secret-leak guard hook watching Bash would flag this.
Not fail-open. The SDK default is a 10 s timeout with 2 retries, and gate abstains with exit 4. Wired naively into a hook it could stall or block Claude Code.

Weak daily-coding value. Jev answers only typed decision questions (route, verify, noul/choice/score), not code. The best case is gating or routing, and the model quality is unverified (the skeptic claim that it is 'a DeepSeek flash router' remains unresolved).
Sending code, diffs or tool output to a third party (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe) from client projects has data-policy implications.
gh-fiale-plus-jev-cli.verdict: A clean, honest CLI that is the most reliable way to reach OpenRouter-hosted Jev through the official SDK, since only two env vars need changing. But it is a building block rather than an integration: it has no hook, skill or MCP, so it cannot deliver 'Claude uses Jev automatically' on its own. Use it as the engine behind a custom hook or skill, pinned to a version, and treat it as alpha software.

gh-muthuishere-jevx.name: @muthuishere/jevx
gh-muthuishere-jevx.whatItDoes: A Go CLI (jevx, stdlib only, closed to 1 author) plus an installed Agent Skill (SKILL.md) and an optional set of Claude Code hook "plugins". The CLI posts {model,state,questions} to any System One URL and prints verdicts (yes/no/unsure, pick key, score level) with exit codes 0 yes, 1 no, 3 unsure, 4 error. Commands: is, pick, filter, rank, ask (batch, saved questions), judge, question, context, defaults, cache, plugin, hook, profile, stats, install/uninstall. `jevx install` copies the skill to ~/.claude/skills, ~/.agents/skills (and ~/.codex/skills), and writes one `jevx hook run EVENT` entry per plugin event into ~/.claude/settings.json (with a .bak file). Shipped plugins (all disabled, shadow mode first): stop-judge (Stop), bash-guard (PreToolUse:Bash), injection-screen (PostToolUse:WebFetch|WebSearch), route (UserPromptSubmit, tells Claude to delegate simple requests to a haiku sub-agent). There is no MCP server. Default endpoint is TypeSafe direct (https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest, key TYPESAFE_API_KEY); custom endpoints are added as profiles.

providerSupport.evidence: Built-in profile is TypeSafe only: core/core.go:253-254 `BuiltinProfile = Profile{URL: "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone", Model: "jev-latest", Headers: {"Authorization": "Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY"}}`; NeedKeyHelp core.go:332-333 only mentions TYPESAFE_API_KEY. No string 'openrouter' appears anywhere in code (grep); only in docs/reference/comparison.md:17,33, where it is credited to jkudish/jev-mcp. But profiles take any URL + model + arbitrary headers with $VAR expansion at request time (core.go:73-81, 604-614; cmd/jevx/main.go:563 `--header "Authorization: Bearer $JEV_API_KEY"`), and the request body is exactly {model,state,questions} (core.go:637), which matches OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone schema (state + questions{type,instructions,criteria}, model; per openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/systemone/submit-a-system-one-request.md and the 'Point the TypeSafe SDK at OpenRouter' guide: 'Change the base URL and the API key. Everything else stays the same'). So: jevx profile add openrouter https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone --model typesafe/jev-1.13 --header 'Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY' && jevx profile use openrouter. Untested by me (static audit only); the response parser (core.go:568-576: type/noul/choice/score/probabilities/confidence) matches the TypeSafe wire format OpenRouter says it is compatible with. Model ID: OpenRouter maps bare jev-1.13 / jev-latest to typesafe/ namespace per its docs.
providerSupport.others: Any System One-compatible URL (local model, self-hosted, jevless, open-jev). No Cloudflare/Vercel-specific code.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, no code change: one `jevx profile add` line (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13 or jev-1.13). Caveat: OpenRouter /systemone is beta and adds a hop; the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is NOT used by jevx.

security: No API key in argv: keys are referenced as $VAR in profile headers and expanded from env only at request time (core/core.go:604-614); profile list prints the literal. Good.
No telemetry or update check per docs/reference/privacy.md; only network call is the configured System One URL (core.go:673-678, http.Client with per-request timeout).

Folder plugins load from the nearest .jevx/plugins.json walking up from cwd with NO trust prompt (core/core.go:351-368 LocalDir, core/plugin.go LocalPlugins/AllPlugins); a plugin may carry `exec` (runExec -> `sh -c <command>`, plugin.go ~runExec) and `enabled:true, mode:act`. A cloned client/third-party repo shipping .jevx/plugins.json therefore gets arbitrary shell execution on every matching hook event once jevx hook entries are installed (they are, globally, by `jevx install`). Same for .jevx/questions.json changing question wording. Real supply-chain/prompt-injection-adjacent risk on client repos; user runs bypass mode.

Installers: npm postinstall downloads a binary from GitHub Releases and runs `jevx install` (npm/install.js) with NO checksum/signature verification (release publishes checksums.txt but neither install.js nor install.sh checks it); install.sh is curl|sh. Binary is unsigned, fetched over HTTPS from the author's repo; a compromised release = code exec. postinstall exits 0 on failure. The npm package itself has provenance (OIDC trusted publishing in release.yml) but the binary trust is separate.

`jevx install` rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json (writes .bak-jevx-<ts> backup, validates JSON, atomic rename; core.go:1071-1090) and adds hook entries for Stop, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit with no tool matcher (filtering is inside the binary), timeout 20s. Touches the user's global hook setup alongside the secret-guard/GitNexus/caveman hooks.

Redaction exists (core.go:799-815: private keys, xox, AKIA, AIza, JWT, bearer, KEY=value) and is applied by cut() for hook states (plugin StateOf) but README/privacy docs say 'Redaction is your job today' for skill-driven --in/stdin content: whatever Claude pipes into jevx is sent verbatim.

Hook 'state' up to 2000 chars is written to ~/.local/share/jevx/verdicts.jsonl (AppendLog, mode 0600) in shadow/act runs: commands and prompts persisted locally in plaintext (redacted-pattern only). Shadow mode also writes the hook payload to a temp file in os TempDir (0600 via CreateTemp, deleted after 3s).

Skill text is a prompt-injection surface only in the usual sense (it instructs Claude to run shell commands); jevx answers are numbers/keys, not free text, so model output cannot inject instructions except through the 'route' plugin's static template. Skill tells Claude never to use it as a safety gate.
gh-muthuishere-jevx.dataEgress: To the configured endpoint (OpenRouter if you add the profile): the question text, the full input Claude passes (stdin, --in, each line of --lines/--states files, so log lines, ticket text, file excerpts, diffs, anything Claude chooses to pipe in; unredacted), merged `## Jev` sections from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, ~/AGENTS.md and the nearest folder AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, plus --context text. Note: only the ## Jev section is read, not the whole CLAUDE.md. For plugins (if enabled): PreToolUse = tool name + tool_input JSON cut to 3000 chars + cwd (every Bash command, or file content for Write/Edit if you add such a plugin); PostToolUse = tool_input 1500 + tool_response 3000 chars; UserPromptSubmit = user prompt cut to 3000 chars; Stop = last request + agent text + last 25 action summaries in ~1600 chars. Hook states pass through Redact(); skill-driven input does not. Request also carries model name and the Authorization header. Local-only: answer cache (~/.cache/jevx, hash-named, stores answers not inputs), content-free ledger (~/.local/share/jevx/calls.jsonl), verdicts.jsonl (state up to 2000 chars). No other outbound calls.
gh-muthuishere-jevx.failureMode: Fails open for hooks and closed for the CLI. Plugin Run() returns Decision{allow} on any error, including missing key, network, invalid reply (core/plugin.go Run fail()). Per-request timeout default 60s with 3 tries on 429/5xx/network with 0.5s*try^2 backoff (core.go:106,648-655), but the installed hook entry has timeout 20 s in settings.json, so in act mode a hung Jev can stall a tool call up to 20 s before Claude Code abandons the hook (non-blocking error). Shadow mode is detached (only ~50ms added) and cannot delay the agent. CLI (skill path): exit 4 on any error, never read as 'no'; strict reply validation (exact question ids, probabilities in [0,1] summing to ~1, choice must be an offered key; core.go:693-728). Missing key: exit 4 with help text naming TYPESAFE_API_KEY (would confuse an OpenRouter-only user unless the profile is default).
gh-muthuishere-jevx.latencyImpact: Skill path: one Bash tool call per use; cold call ~0.35-0.7 s vs 7 ms cached (authors' own numbers: median 577 ms in privacy.md ledger example, direct TypeSafe; OpenRouter hop adds some). Batches parallel (default 8). Hooks: disabled entries still spawn a tiny Go process for every Stop/PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit event (loads config, exits; ms-level) . Enabled in act mode: +0.4-0.7 s per matching event inline (bash-guard on every Bash call; route on every prompt). Shadow: ~50 ms sleep per event. No claim verified by me against OpenRouter.
gh-muthuishere-jevx.contextCost: No MCP server, so zero tool-schema cost. Skill: name+description always in the skill listing (~700 chars, ~180 tokens); full SKILL.md (~13.7KB, ~3.4k tokens) loaded only when the description matches, scenarios.md (~10KB, ~2.6k tokens) on demand. Hooks: no injected text unless a plugin fires; route plugin injects ~50 tokens as additionalContext on simple prompts; warn/context decisions add a one-line reason. Each jevx CLI call adds its stdout (small table/lines) to context.
gh-muthuishere-jevx.autoInvocation: Two mechanisms. (1) Skill description trigger: model-discretion, Claude loads the skill when it judges the task is classify/triage/filter/rank/'ask the user A or B'/'before handing back a turn', then runs `jevx ...` via Bash. Most daily coding (edit, debug, refactor) rarely matches, so it will fire only occasionally, and Opus 5.5 may decide to just reason itself. (2) Deterministic hooks (Stop, PreToolUse:Bash, PostToolUse:WebFetch, UserPromptSubmit) that run without any prompting, but ship disabled and need `jevx plugin enable X` + `mode X act`; this is the only truly automatic path. No transparent proxy / router.
pros: Only candidate reviewed here that is both an auto-triggering skill AND a deterministic hook layer in one install, with zero MCP tool-definition context cost (no tools list; only ~180 tokens of skill description permanently).

OpenRouter switch is genuinely trivial from code: profiles take any URL/headers with $VAR expansion, and the request body {model,state,questions} matches OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone schema; one `jevx profile add` + `profile use`.

Fail-open hooks with shadow-first rollout: plugins start disabled, then shadow (detached, logs only, ~50ms), and only `mode act` can deny/ask; `plugin test`, `plugin log` let the user calibrate on their own sessions before trusting it.
Honest verdict semantics: unsure band and exit code 3, errors exit 4 and are never 'no', strict fail-closed response validation, retries on 429/5xx.

Keys never in argv or config file (env $VAR expanded at request time); content-free ledger, no telemetry, local answer cache makes repeated identical calls free; installer backs up settings.json and removes only its own hook entries on uninstall.

Read-only per-repo context via the `## Jev` section of existing CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md means no extra config files to maintain; folder .jevx/questions.json lets calibrated questions be committed per repo.
MIT, Go stdlib only (no third-party deps to audit), small readable codebase (~2.5k lines of Go); npm publish uses OIDC provenance.
cons: Very new and single-author: repo created 2026-09-27 (3 days before audit), 37 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 1 fork, npm 0.10.0 to 0.11.0 in two days, INPROGRESS.md documents constant churn (renamed jevcli to jevx mid-flight). Its own docs say 'MCP: none, keychain: none, eval: none'.

Thin test/CI coverage: 9 Go test functions across 6 files; the only workflows are release.yml (build + publish, no `go test` step) and pages.yml. Nothing verifies the hook/settings.json rewriter beyond a few unit tests.

Undisclosed-by-default RCE surface for client work: .jevx/plugins.json in any repo (walked up from cwd, no trust prompt) can define an enabled `exec` plugin that runs `sh -c` on hook events; `jevx install` registers those hooks globally. Cloning a client repo or a third-party repo that ships .jevx/ is enough. Combined with bypass permission mode this is worse than the average skill.

No checksum/signature verification of the downloaded binary in npm postinstall or install.sh despite checksums.txt being published; npm postinstall also auto-runs `jevx install`, which edits ~/.claude/settings.json (global hooks with no matcher, so a process spawn on every tool call/prompt/stop even while disabled). Conflicts with the 'do not modify settings' comfort level and with the existing hook stack (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).

The value for daily coding is unproven and small: skill tasks are batch classification (log lines, ticket triage) that a coding session rarely needs; Opus 5.5 will usually just reason. The author's own notes cite negative evidence that Jev second-guessing a strong model lost accuracy (194 to 173 of 200) and that Stop-judge claims need an eval first. Thresholds (0.35/0.65, destroys 0.8) are uncalibrated defaults; 'act' mode risks false denies on legit commands, and bash-guard duplicates the user's existing secret-leak guard (and Claude Code's own permission system).

Data egress on client projects: skill-driven input is sent verbatim to OpenRouter with no redaction (docs: 'Redaction is your job today'); enabled plugins send every Bash command (3000 chars), prompts (3000 chars) and web tool results to the third party. Privacy-sensitive for client code.

Latency and cost in act mode: +0.4-0.7 s inline on every Bash call (bash-guard) or every prompt (route), hook timeout 20s so a slow Jev can stall up to 20 s; route plugin costs one paid call per prompt. Beyond negligible token price, the latency compounds in long agentic sessions.

Default and error messages are TypeSafe-centric (TYPESAFE_API_KEY help text); OpenRouter needs manual profile setup and model naming (typesafe/jev-1.13 vs jev-latest, which OpenRouter says it doesn't serve as an alias per the jev-mcp docs) and is untested by the author. Uses /v1/systemone, not the Decisions API.
gh-muthuishere-jevx.verdict: A clever, clean-code skill+hook layer that is the closest thing to 'Claude Code just uses Jev' without an MCP tool tax, and switching to OpenRouter is a one-line profile. But it is 3 days old with one author, has an unvetted .jevx/plugins.json exec path and unverified binary downloads, and its real auto-invocation (hooks) needs opt-in per plugin; treat as an experiment: install skills only (JEVX_NO_HOOK=1, and do not let npm postinstall touch settings), pin an OpenRouter profile, and try shadow mode before considering act.

gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.whatItDoes: Tri-runtime (Python/TS/Rust, same logic) "System 1.5" gate toolkit for coding agents: CLI + stdio MCP server + git pre-commit hook + optional Claude Code plugin/skill. Six gates: test-failure triage, abort/doom-loop check, model-tier routing, completion verification, reasoning-effort modulation (produces provider params for GPT/DeepSeek/etc., not applicable to Claude Code), nudge/continue. Deterministic regex heuristics run first and offline (default, no key). With a key it calls Jev System One (Choice/Noul/Score questions) for ambiguous cases and falls back to the offline engine on any failure. It is a wrapper that sends only the test-failure log or step text to Jev; it does not intercept Claude Code itself.

security: API key sent as Bearer header only; never placed in argv when supplied via OPENROUTER_API_KEY env (MCP server has no key flag). CLI --api-key style flags not verified; the MCP path is env-only.

Credential discovery reads .env files walking up 4 parent dirs from cwd (client.ts:397-421) plus .jev.json api_key and ~/.config/jev/credentials.env and ~/.commandcode/auth.json. It parses only key names it knows, but it does open client-project .env files, which conflicts with a secret-leak guard philosophy; also a hostile repo's .jev.json/.env can silently choose the provider/key (repo-controlled config can redirect which key is used, and .jev.json can set model).
Request body: redactSecrets() strips API keys, JWTs, GitHub/AWS tokens, DB URLs, private keys before sending (client.ts:145,464); shape-based only, README admits it is not DLP.
Error text is scrubbed of the key (client.ts:541,645).

Prompt-injection: input logs treated as data, gates escalate on text that addresses the judge (gates.ts:65-76) and adversarial tests exist; outputs are typed enums, so the model output cannot inject free text. BUT skip_llm=true returns an action_recommendation string like 'pip install X' / 'npm install -D X' derived from the log; docs tell Claude to execute it immediately without deliberation, which is a real supply-chain/typosquat and injection vector when logs come from untrusted code (agent auto-installs a package named in an attacker-controlled error message).

No postinstall script (package.json scripts only build/test); zero runtime dependencies; MIT; npm Sigstore provenance badge. Recommended MCP command is `npx -y` unpinned, so every session pulls whatever the latest publish of a 1-maintainer, 9-day-old package is (18 versions in 9 days).

Writes local state: ~/.config/jev/session.json (0600, contains short error snippets), <repo>/.jev/ cache and receipts (hashes only), `init` edits .gitignore and writes .git/hooks/pre-commit. Nothing runs shell in the MCP server itself; only the pre-commit hook runs `sh -c` on the user-configured test command.
No telemetry to the author found in client code; the only outbound host is the chosen provider endpoint (plus triage GitHub Action not used here).
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.dataEgress: Offline default: nothing leaves the machine. Live (OPENROUTER_API_KEY present): HTTPS POST to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions containing model, the typed questions, and the state = redacted failure log (head 2,000 + tail 4,000 chars per README privacy matrix) or, for other gates, the proposed step / attempts summary / task description / criteria+evidence text / nudge transcript tail, all as supplied by Claude in the tool call. Payload cap MAX_STATE_CHARS about 32k tokens. OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe (provider.only=['typesafe'], no fallbacks). Not sent automatically: source files or diffs, unless Claude passes them as evidence to jev_verify_completion. Because the model chooses what to put in tool args, egress is model-discretion, not bounded by a hook.
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.failureMode: Fail-open by default (failOpen=true, client.ts:279): 401/403 -> immediate fallback to offline simulation with stderr warning and degraded_reason auth_N; 429/5xx/timeout/network/malformed -> retry up to maxRetries=3 with exponential backoff (500 ms base, cap 5 s, honors Retry-After up to 30 s) then offline fallback. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (timeoutMs default). Worst case on a hung endpoint about 45 s plus about 1.5 s backoff for a single tool call, during which Claude Code blocks on the MCP call. Responses carry is_mock / degraded_reason so the model can see it degraded. Never blocks Claude permanently; the offline heuristic answer is returned. No circuit breaker across calls, so each call re-pays the timeout during an outage.
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.latencyImpact: Only when Claude chooses to call a tool. Offline: under 1 ms in-process, but MCP server cold start via `npx -y` adds a registry check per session start (roughly 1-3 s, first run downloads). Live: README claims about 0.5-1.0 s measured on free tier, provider claim 70-500 ms; one extra model round trip (tool call + result) of a few seconds of Opus turn overhead per invocation. No per-tool-call tax on unrelated calls because there are no hooks.
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. TOOLS_MANIFEST (mcp.ts lines 20-180) about 8.9 KB of names, long descriptions (Use when / Do NOT use when / Returns), and schemas, roughly 2.2k tokens (chars/4), always resident (or deferred behind ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.1.x, which lowers baseline cost). No MCP server `instructions` field (initialize returns only capabilities.tools). No hook-injected text. If the recommended CLAUDE.md snippet (about 5 lines) is added, minor. Outputs duplicate every field in snake_case and camelCase (skip_llm/skipLlm, is_mock/isMock, etc., mcp.ts result mapping), inflating each tool result.
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger in the Claude Code plugin (skill triggers on test failure / about to declare done / repeating failed approach). No deterministic hook: the repo ships no hooks.json, no PostToolUse/PreToolUse/Stop config for Claude Code. Its own guide advises pasting a CLAUDE.md protocol block, i.e. the user must instruct Claude. This fails the user's requirement of guaranteed automatic use unless the user writes their own PostToolUse(Bash) hook that pipes failed test output to `jev-harness test-gate` (the CLI exit-code contract makes that feasible) and a Stop hook around `verify`.
pros: Real, working OpenRouter support against the correct Decisions endpoint (client.ts:22, :301, :502 with provider.only=['typesafe']), default model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY env; no patching needed.
Offline-first and fail-open: works with zero key, zero network, never leaves Claude stuck; degraded_reason and is_mock make degradation visible to the model.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, secrets redaction before egress, key scrubbed from errors, local state at 0600.
Ships a Claude Code plugin (plugin.json, .mcp.json, SKILL.md) with a sensible trigger description, and CLI exit-code contract (0/1/2) that is easy to wrap in your own PostToolUse hook.
Real test suite, tri-runtime parity tests, CI matrix, calibration replay harness with ECE, npm provenance; unusually rigorous for a 9-day-old repo.
Uses Jev the way it is designed (typed Choice/Noul/Score questions, probabilities, uncertainty/entropy thresholds) rather than as a chat replacement.
cons: Not automatic: MCP tools plus a skill rely on Opus deciding to call them; no hooks.json shipped; docs recommend editing CLAUDE.md to tell Claude to use it, which is exactly what the user wants to avoid.

Value proposition is mismatched to this user: goal is saving frontier tokens on missing-package/flaky errors, but Opus 5.5 on a subscription resolves 'ModuleNotFoundError' in one turn anyway; the tool call round trip can cost more than it saves. Most gates (route tiers, reasoning-effort provider params for GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen) cannot be applied to Claude Code's own model.

Overwhelmingly offline regex heuristics; Jev is only consulted for ambiguous cases, and the published accuracy numbers come from engine=mock, so they do not validate Jev; effort and nudge gates measured 0.625 accuracy.

skip_llm=true plus 'execute the recommended command without deliberating' guidance creates an auto-install path driven by log text (typosquat/injection risk), risky on client projects in bypass/auto permission mode.

Credential resolver reads .env from cwd and 3 parent dirs, .jev.json (repo-controlled) and other providers' keys with fixed precedence (TYPESAFE > CMD > VERCEL > OPENCODE > OPENROUTER), so it may reads client .env files and pick the wrong provider; conflicts with a secret-leak guard mindset.
Unpinned `npx -y` in recommended MCP config from a single-maintainer, 10-star, 9-day-old package with 18 releases; supply-chain and cold-start latency exposure.
Fail-open path can stall a call up to about 45 s during outages (15 s timeout x 3 attempts) with no cross-call circuit breaker.
Tool payloads duplicate every field in snake_case and camelCase; 6 tool descriptions about 2.2k tokens resident.

README contains marketing claims (80-90% token savings, up to $5 saved) that are estimates, and doc/emoji volume plus AGENTS/openspec scaffolding suggest heavily LLM-generated repo; Foreman/CommandCode/OpenCode-specific features are irrelevant to Claude Code.
gh-ismaelsoilet-jev-harness.verdict: Best-engineered of the Jev wrappers on OpenRouter support, offline fallback and tests, but it is a model-discretion MCP/skill toolkit aimed at saving tokens on other vendors' frontier models, not an automatic Claude Code integration. Useful only as a source of a `test-gate` CLI you might call from your own PostToolUse hook; do not adopt as the primary integration.

gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.name: jev-acp
gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.whatItDoes: A standalone Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent, run over stdio, that wraps the @typesafe-ai/sdk. You use it from an ACP client or IDE such as JetBrains, vscode-acp or acp-ui. It runs a human-driven guided workflow (Choose one, Score against a rubric, Check a statement, plus saved templates). Once the user replies "Run", it calls Jev System One and shows the typed decision, probabilities and confidence. It is a chat-UI front end for humans, not a tool or hook for another coding agent. Claude Code is not an ACP client, so this cannot plug into it.

providerSupport.evidence: jev-acp has no endpoint or provider code of its own. src/engine.ts:11-30 calls `new TypeSafeClient()` and then `client.systemOne({state, questions}, {signal})` with no config. The SDK is @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (dist/index.mjs, which I read from the npm tarball). Lines 56-62 read TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL. Line 513 sets the default base URL to https://api.typesafe.ai. Line 514 sets the default model to `jev-latest`. Lines 554-556 POST to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` and a body of {state, questions, model}. The default timeout is 10s (line 518) and there is a retry policy (lines 72-120). There is no OpenRouter string anywhere in jev-acp or the SDK.
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai) is supported natively. Any other base URL comes through the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL variable.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no code patch is needed. OpenRouter serves POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, and the SDK appends /v1/systemone to its base URL. So set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest (the default `jev-latest` has no vendor prefix). This is inferred from the code plus the brief. I did not run it, and I did not verify that OpenRouter's request/response schema is identical to TypeSafe's. It only works if the client is ACP, which Claude Code is not, so it does not matter for this user.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Only text the human types (or embedded text attachments) is sent to Jev. File links are not fetched. Jev returns typed output with no free text, so nothing can steer Claude Code. Since Claude Code cannot call this agent anyway, the exposure is nil.

gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.dataEgress: Only the text the user sends in the ACP chat for the current task (options, question, criteria, state or attached text), packaged as {state, questions, model} and POSTed to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. That URL can be redirected to OpenRouter through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. It does not read repository files, diffs or tool outputs on its own, and it does not send the chat transcript or other tasks' drafts. Templates stay local in ~/.jev-acp.
gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.failureMode: Not applicable to Claude Code, because it is not in the tool loop. Inside an ACP client, errors surface as chat messages and the guided input is kept so the user can retry (README "Session configuration"). Underneath, the SDK uses a 10s timeout and retries with backoff, and cancellation goes through AbortSignal. A slow or down Jev only affects that ACP chat turn.
gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.contextCost: Zero in Claude Code, because nothing loads. It registers no MCP tools, no hooks, no skills and no injected text. It is a stdio ACP agent and Claude Code has no way to connect to it as an agent.
gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.latencyImpact: None to Claude Code. Jev's claimed 70-500 ms would apply per decision inside an ACP chat, plus a manual Run step and a possible 10s timeout with retries.
gh-formulahendry-jev-acp.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. A human must select a task in an ACP client, type the input and reply "Run". There is no hook, no model-discretion tool, no skill trigger and no proxy. It is unusable for the goal of automatic invocation in Claude Code.
pros: Small, readable, MIT-licensed code. About 2.3k lines of TypeScript with unit tests and a CI matrix on Node 22 and 24. It uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk rather than hand-rolled HTTP.

A correct reference for how the typed System One request looks: POST /v1/systemone with {state, questions:{choice|noul|score}, model} and a Bearer key. Its prompt-to-question parsing in src/parser.ts and src/validation.ts is reusable if someone builds a real MCP server or hook.
OpenRouter switching needs no code change. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL are honored by the SDK.
Low security risk: no shell, no postinstall, no telemetry in the package, and only user-typed text leaves the machine.
cons: Wrong protocol for this user. It is an ACP agent (a chat UI for humans), and Claude Code is neither an ACP client nor able to delegate to one. It cannot be wired into Claude Code via .mcp.json, hooks or skills.

Human-in-the-loop by design: pick a task, type options, reply Run. The README says it will not 'automatically select a task for you' and is not a general assistant. That is the opposite of the automatic use the user wants.

No OpenRouter support in code. It works only through the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL variable, and the default model name `jev-latest` needs a prefix change to `typesafe/jev-latest` for OpenRouter. Both are unverified against OpenRouter's live schema.

gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.whatItDoes: The npm package jev-code@0.0.1 is a placeholder (does nothing). The GitHub repo (now named devagrawal09/stanley-code) holds "Stanley", a standalone Node CLI that takes a natural-language request (for example "check whether these changes fix X"), uses Jev (via the @typesafe-ai/sdk systemOne call) to route it to one of 10 built-in read-only diff/log workflows (check, review, test gaps, summarize, security, performance, compatibility, triage failures, triage review comments, find relevant code) or to trusted repo workflows in .stanley/workflows/. Deterministic code gathers hunks or log blocks and asks Jev fixed-choice questions (choice/noul/score); code applies thresholds. It is a competing standalone agent CLI.

gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.dataEgress: To TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if base URL is redirected): first the redacted request text, input shape, diff presence, redacted routing metadata of available workflows and option names; then for the selected built-in, the task plus bounded evidence: individual diff hunks (first ~150 by policy), file excerpts and path/metadata for the top-3000 lexical candidates in shards of 20 for 'find', failure-log sections, review comments. So actual code and diffs leave the machine, redacted best-effort. If Pi fallback triggers, the whole request and repo context go to Pi's separately configured model provider (unknown to Jev). README tells users to review TypeSafe's data terms before using private/regulated code, which matters for the user's client projects.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.failureMode: Mostly fail-safe by design but not a Claude Code hook: executor retries (default 2, clamp), per-call timeout default 30 s (src/core/executor.ts:107-108), hard budgets on request count/tokens/time; transient errors are classified (src/adapters/jev.ts classifyError); low-confidence or unavailable routing returns 'unsupported' / cannot_tell (exit 64) rather than guessing; SDK retries set to 0 so the executor owns them. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY throws MissingCredentialError and every command fails (commit 'Require TypeSafe API key for all commands'). Since it is invoked explicitly as a subprocess, a Jev outage only degrades that one call; nothing blocks Claude Code. With Pi installed, a Jev routing failure can trigger the expensive agent fallback (up to 600 s).
gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.latencyImpact: Not automatic, so zero passive latency. Per explicit invocation it is heavy: one routing Jev call plus N per-hunk/per-file Jev calls (concurrency 4, up to 64 calls/run for workflows, top-3000-file 'find' screening in rounds, up to 40 failures/100 comments judged), each 70-500 ms claimed end to end plus Node/tsx startup. Likely several seconds to tens of seconds per run on a real diff, plus git subprocess calls. Fallback to Pi can add up to 600 s.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.contextCost: Zero MCP/tool-definition cost: there are no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no skills. Claude would only see a CLI via Bash if the user added a CLAUDE.md line or their own skill. Output can be large JSON (findings, parked, notChecked, coverage) unless trimmed; text mode is smaller.
gh-devagrawal09-jev-code.autoInvocation: only when prompted: Claude Code will never call it on its own. It has no hook, MCP tool or skill description. To get automation one would have to write a separate skill/hook wrapper (for example a PostToolUse/Stop hook that runs `stanley ... --json`), which this project does not ship. It also duplicates Claude's own review role and would compete with the Pi fallback agent.
pros: Genuinely reads Jev-native: uses choice/noul/score fixed-choice questions per diff hunk, thresholds in code, no free-text from Jev (src/workflows/*, README flowcharts). It is a well-considered pattern for how to use a System One model that could be borrowed for a custom hook.

Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk /v1/systemone call, and the SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (sdk index.mjs:513), so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api with an OpenRouter key is env-only and needs no code patch (untested).

The agent forms a defect hypothesis and selects source excerpts; tracecheck_verify asks Jev if the concern is supported and returns support, impact, uncertainty and a missing-evidence category. security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json (only prepack/prepublishOnly, which do not run on consumer install). Runtime is a single 2.2 MB esbuild bundle dist/plugin.mjs committed to the repo; CI checks bundle matches fresh build (ci.yml 'node scripts/build.mjs --check'), but the bundle is hard to audit by eye.

API key read only from env (JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/OPENROUTER_API_KEY), sent in an Authorization header, never in argv. No .env autoload, no key persistence (README:412). Plugin .mcp.json has no env block, so the server inherits the shell environment Claude Code was started from.

TYPESAFE_BASE_URL must be HTTPS unless loopback and cannot contain credentials/query/fragment (src/jev.ts:92-103) - prevents key exfil to plain HTTP, but an attacker who controls env could still point it at any HTTPS host.

Outbound secret screening on every string sent (src/safety.ts assertSafeOutbound: private keys, AWS/GitHub/OpenAI/Slack/Google/Stripe/npm tokens, key=value assignments, URL passwords); it fails closed with an error naming the field, and the collector skips files with credentials, symlinks and binaries. Best-effort per its own comment, not DLP.

File reads hardened: O_NOFOLLOW, realpath inside root, TOCTOU identity check, 256 KB per file cap (safety.ts readSource). Git invoked via execFile/spawn with --literal-pathspecs, --no-ext-diff, --no-textconv and SAFE_CONFIGURATION; README:501-505 documents that a hostile checkout's .git/config can still name commands for git (only relevant for untrusted repos, e.g. client code you did not author).
Response handling bounded (512 KB cap, zod validation, probability sum check); error bodies not surfaced because they may echo source.

Prompt-injection surface: reviewed source/comments go to Jev, which returns typed numbers, not text, so injection can at worst skew a verdict; tool output to Claude is structured JSON. README/benchmark explicitly does not claim injection resistance.
No telemetry found in src (grep for telemetry/analytics empty); only network egress is the Jev endpoint.

gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.dataEgress: On tracecheck_verify: hypothesis text, contract, up to 12 source excerpts (max 60 KB) and the target quote, chosen by Claude. On tracecheck_assess: task, diff, files (path+content) and repositoryContext supplied by Claude. On tracecheck_review: collected changed files, their base versions, related callers/tests/dependencies (~60k chars per packet in the author's example, 180 KB request cap, 32k-token model context). Sent to openrouter.ai (which forwards to TypeSafe) with the user's OpenRouter key. Failing the local secret-pattern screen blocks the request. Nothing else leaves the machine; the project has no backend and no telemetry. For client projects this means client source is sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (two processors) whenever a tool fires.
gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's perspective (advisory tool): errors come back as MCP tool errors and Claude continues without a verdict; nothing blocks edits or commits. Per-request timeout 45 s default (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, max 1 h) including retries; up to 3 attempts on network errors and 429/5xx/529 with backoff 500 ms*2^n; honors Retry-After only up to 10 s, otherwise errors out. Overall deadlines: verify VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS, assess 90 s, review 300 s. Incomplete reviews are reported as 'Review incomplete for packet' limitations and not cached. Local secret-screen hit or >180 KB request fails closed (no send). If no key is set the server still starts; preview works, live tools error with a setup message. In the worst case a tool call stalls Claude for the timeout duration (tens of seconds).
gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (tracecheck_verify, _assess, _preview, _review). Descriptions are long (~350-500 chars each, ~1.7k chars total) and input schemas are big (verify: evidence array of 5-field objects, target, missingContext; review/preview share a scope object with base/includeUntracked/task/repositoryContext/collection plus long describe() strings; assess: task/diff/files/repositoryContext/scope/previousEvaluation with nested metrics record). Estimate roughly 3,000-4,500 tokens of tool definitions loaded per session (about 12-18k chars / 4), unless Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch, in which case only names are resident. Server sets no 'instructions' text (createServer passes only name/version, src/mcp.ts:117). Skill adds only name+description (~330 chars, ~80 tokens) to context until triggered; body is 3.5 KB plus a references/tool-usage.md loaded on first call. No hooks, so no per-call injected text. Tool results are JSON reports (can be several KB each, and assess returns 19 metrics).
gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.latencyImpact: No latency on normal turns (no hook, no proxy). Only when Claude decides to call a tool: author's benchmark reports review-stage p50/p95 of about 194/569 ms per request for verify-sized packets, and 820 ms for one 33k-token 19-dimension request (docs/accuracy.md); end-to-end via OpenRouter adds network hop; worst case up to 45 s per request with retries. tracecheck_review over a multi-packet change makes several requests (concurrency 4) and can take seconds to minutes. Local collection/preview adds git and file reads.
gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: an MCP tool set plus a description-triggered skill ('Verify suspected code defects with Jev after an implementation checkpoint, during a code review, or after a repair'). No hooks, no proxy. Claude may pick it up unprompted when reviewing or finishing an implementation, but firing is non-deterministic and the skill workflow is heavy (agent must write hypothesis, collect excerpts, then call verify). Hard automatic triggering would require adding your own Stop/PostToolUse hook, which the project does not ship. The package also has no default-on behavior.
pros: Genuine OpenRouter support in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with no patching (src/jev.ts:36-37,63-67), and it strips OpenRouter's relayed max_tokens_exceeded error correctly (jev.ts:172-176).

Uses Jev for what it is good at: typed, calibrated yes/no and scored judgments as a second opinion on a specific hypothesis, not free-text generation; response schema (choice/noul/score with probabilities summing to 1) is strictly validated against the question set.

Most security-conscious candidate profile: outbound secret screening that fails closed, symlink/TOCTOU-safe reads, HTTPS-only base URL, key only in env and header, bounded responses, no telemetry, no install scripts.
Advisory and read-only (readOnlyHint, never edits or runs code), so nothing can break the working tree; fail-open when Jev is slow or down.
Only 4 tools and no hooks, so it does not conflict with existing GitNexus/secret-guard PreToolUse hooks and adds zero per-turn latency.

Real engineering rigor for its age: 19 test files, CI on Node 22/24, pinned action SHAs, bundle-drift check, calibration and accuracy docs with honest negative results (recall 7/12 full-file, 0/12 false positives on clean variants).
Ships a Claude plugin manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json, marketplace.json pinned to v0.4.0, .mcp.json using ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}) so install is a plugin add rather than hand-editing.
Local preview shows request count and bytes before any code is sent, and maxRequests budget caps spend/egress.
cons: Automatic use is weak: relies on Claude choosing to invoke the skill/tools; the workflow requires the agent to author a hypothesis plus evidence packet, so it will fire rarely and inconsistently unless you add a custom hook or CLAUDE.md rule. Does not meet 'must use Jev when needed' on its own.

Narrow use case (code review/defect verification only); does nothing for routing, permission decisions, commit/PR classification, or other System One primitives users may want daily. Most of Jev's Choice/Noul/Score value is not exposed as generic tools.

Measured accuracy is modest: 58% recall counting abstentions (5/24 abstentions), a full-repo review returned inconclusive on 18 of 19 dimensions (docs/accuracy.md); the benchmark used a private repo so it cannot be reproduced, and author admits injection resistance is not established.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-17, 2 stars, 1 fork, 1 contributor, 183 commits in 13 days, v0.4.0 only; README itself says native Claude UI install was not exercised end to end (docs/integrations.md:93).
Tool schema/definitions are large (~3-4.5k tokens) for a rarely-used feature, unless MCP tool search defers them.

Client-code egress: every call ships source to OpenRouter plus TypeSafe with the same key; the regex screen is best-effort and is not a substitute for client NDAs. Needs a per-project allow/deny decision.
Uses the System One /v1/systemone API, not the newer Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions); could lag if OpenRouter changes the alpha surface.
Default model 'jev-latest' floats, so results are not reproducible unless JEV_MODEL is pinned; a stray TYPESAFE_API_KEY in env silently overrides OpenRouter.
2.2 MB minified bundle is what actually runs; auditing requires rebuilding from src, and it is fetched via npx/plugin from a single npm publisher.
gh-bmccarn-tracecheck.verdict: Best-built and safest Jev integration for code review, with real OpenRouter support and no hook or latency cost, but it is a narrow advisory review tool that Claude invokes at its own discretion, not a broad automatic Jev layer. Worth installing pinned at v0.4.0 (with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL pinned) as one component, but to get true automation you must add your own hook or rule, and think twice before enabling it on client repos.

gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.name: @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails (repo codebam/jev-guardrails)
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.whatItDoes: Monorepo by a single author. (1) @codebam/jev-guardrails: a TypeScript library that asks Jev typed guardrail questions (screenInput, assessAction, screenObservation, verifyClaim) and maps the probabilities to allow/review/block; it has transports for TypeSafe direct, OpenRouter Decisions, and a hosted service. (2) @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails (the audited npm package): an `eval-jev` CLI plus OpenCode, Hermes Agent and DeepSeek Harness pre-tool-call hook installers. These hooks only talk to a paid third-party proxy, https://eval.seanbehan.ca (Cloudflare Worker + D1 + Stripe, prepaid credits), not to OpenRouter. (3) @codebam/dsh-jev-guardrails: a DeepSeek Harness plugin. (4) apps/eval-site: the Worker source for the proxy. There is no Claude Code integration anywhere in the repo, and the word "claude" appears nowhere in it.

providerSupport.evidence: The audited package eval-jev-guardrails does NOT support OpenRouter or TypeSafe direct. packages/eval-jev-guardrails/src/version.ts:8 sets DEFAULT_BASE_URL='https://eval.seanbehan.ca'. client.ts:76 says it calls /v1/evaluate, /v1/systemone, /v1/credits and /v1/me, with env EVAL_API_KEY / EVAL_BASE_URL (config.ts:92-94). The sibling library packages/jev-guardrails does support OpenRouter: src/openrouter.ts:15 endpoint 'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions', :18 default model '~typesafe/jev-latest', :157 'authorization: Bearer'. src/client.ts:67-68 reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY is used for the typesafe provider (client.ts:97). The library's default timeout is 5000 ms (guardrails.ts:87). The library does not call the /api/v1/systemone endpoint on OpenRouter; it uses the Decisions endpoint. apps/eval-site/src/provider.ts (lines 2-12, 49) shows the paid proxy itself forwards to OpenRouter Decisions using OPENROUTER_MODEL.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Library: already supported, so no patch is needed. Hook package: not trivial. You would have to write a Claude Code hook yourself, because there is no Claude Code adapter. You would do that by calling createGuardrails({provider:'openrouter'}).assessAction() from a small Node script that reads Claude Code's PreToolUse JSON on stdin. That is about 30-60 lines, but it means installing and trusting the unpinned @codebam/jev-guardrails library plus @typesafe-ai/sdk, or copying the code. Pointing eval-jev at OpenRouter by setting EVAL_BASE_URL will not work, because the proxy speaks its own /v1/evaluate schema (an {action,reason} verdict), not the Decisions schema.

gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.runtime: Node >=20 (TypeScript compiled to ESM); Hermes plugin in stdlib-only Python; server side is a Cloudflare Worker + D1
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.install: npx -y @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails login && npx -y @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails install opencode (OpenCode only). No Claude Code installer. For the OpenRouter route you would install @codebam/jev-guardrails and write your own hook.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.tests: There are tests: node --test suites with fake providers and local HTTP servers, covering client, doctor, install, opencode, hermes, d1, stripe, github, and the library's cache, guardrails, heuristics, openrouter and redact. There is no CI (no .github directory). No release tags; npm 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 were both published on 2026-09-20. Version drift: src/version.ts says PACKAGE_VERSION 0.1.0 while package.json says 0.1.1. I did not run the tests.
security: Key handling: the eval_ key is stored in ~/.config/eval-jev/config.json with mode 600 and dir 700 (config.ts:152-154). It is sent as a Bearer header, not in argv. The OpenRouter transport also uses a Bearer header (openrouter.ts:157).

Egress trust: with the audited hook package, every tool call goes to a single individual's hosted service. Its D1 schema has an evaluations table with request_hash, verdict_json, tokens and cost, and a global cache keyed by request hash. Full request state may or may not be logged, and the hook cannot verify that. The operator holds the OpenRouter key and can read all traffic.

No client-side redaction in the hook package: grep for redact finds nothing in eval-jev-guardrails/src. Only the library has redact.ts (best-effort patterns for AWS, GitHub, sk-, JWT, bearer and private keys). The hosted hooks send raw tool arguments, including Write contents, Bash commands and inline secrets.
The threat model doc admits the agent can edit the plugin or key, and that fail-open is not a safety guarantee (docs/threat-model.md).

Prompt injection: the block reason is returned to the model as text. The verdict text comes from the remote service, which is a low-risk injection channel if the service is compromised. Jev itself returns typed output.
Shell execution: the CLI runs only xdg-open/open (cli.ts:287-290). No postinstall or preinstall scripts (only prepublishOnly). No curl|sh installer.
Supply chain: an unknown single maintainer, a 10-day-old package, 0 stars, and no CI or provenance information. The @typesafe-ai/sdk dependency is pulled in by the library.
Telemetry: no client telemetry found in the code I read, but the server does bill and log each evaluation.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.dataEgress: The audited hook package sends, for each guarded tool call, {side:'action', state:{tool, arguments (full tool input: Bash commands, Write/Edit contents, file paths, URLs), workspace (cwd path)}, sessionID/callID} to https://eval.seanbehan.ca/v1/evaluate. It is not redacted client-side. The Worker then forwards it to OpenRouter Decisions with its own key. The library route with provider 'openrouter' would send a redacted state directly from your machine to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your key, which is better. Tool results and prompts are not sent by the OpenCode/Hermes hooks (only actions), unless you use the library's screenObservation or screenInput.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.failureMode: Fail-open by default (hook.ts:15, DEFAULT_FAIL_MODE='open'). EVAL_FAIL_MODE can be open, review or closed. The client timeout is 5000 ms by default (client.ts:232-238, EVAL_TIMEOUT_MS). A `review` verdict is denied by default, which risks false-positive blocks. The library has retries: 2 retries with backoff, up to 5 s, which adds delay before failing. With the worst-case timeout of 5 s per tool call, an outage could stall every call before it falls open.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.contextCost: Nothing in Claude Code today: the package ships no MCP server, skill or Claude Code hook. A custom hook built on the library would add 0 tool definitions and 0 context tokens, except when it blocks; the reason text (~50-80 tokens) is fed back to the model. Any Claude Code hook that emitted extra additionalContext would add tokens.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.latencyImpact: Per guarded tool call: one HTTPS round trip to the Worker, which makes a second hop to OpenRouter. The claimed Jev latency is 70-500 ms, and the proxy adds a Cloudflare hop and D1 writes (credit reserve, evaluation start/finish), so roughly 200-800 ms per call estimated (not measured). Retries or a timeout can push it to 5 s or more. A direct library-to-OpenRouter hook would avoid the proxy hop. A PreToolUse hook on every Bash/Read/Edit call, stacked on the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks, would add up over a day.
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook in OpenCode/Hermes/dsh (tool.execute.before, pre_tool_call, tools/pre-execute). For Claude Code it is NOT available out of the box. A PreToolUse command hook (deterministic, fires every tool call, model never prompted) could be built on the library, but that is custom work.
pros: Shows a working pattern: a deterministic pre-tool-call hook that asks Jev a typed Choice/Score question and maps its probabilities to allow/review/block with a fail-mode setting. That is the kind of automatic, prompt-free integration the user wants (a Claude Code PreToolUse hook could reuse the decision table in hook.ts).

The library @codebam/jev-guardrails has a real OpenRouter Decisions transport (openrouter.ts) using the ~typesafe/jev-latest model, with retries, an OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var and the correct endpoint /api/alpha/decisions. It is the only candidate I saw that implements the Decisions API with the right schema.
The library has a best-effort secret redactor (redact.ts) that runs before state is sent, and a cache (cache.ts) that reduces repeat calls and cost.
Configurable: fail-open/review/closed, review allow/deny, and tool skip and allow lists (EVAL_SKIP_TOOLS / EVAL_GUARD_TOOLS) are useful for tuning the hook to skip Read/Grep.
MIT license, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, an honest threat-model doc, and a test suite included in the repo.
cons: No Claude Code support at all: the hooks are for OpenCode, Hermes and DeepSeek Harness. Zero occurrences of 'claude' in the repo. There is no stdin/stdout PreToolUse adapter, no hooks.json snippet and no settings.json installer.

The packaged hooks route via the author's paid proxy eval.seanbehan.ca (prepaid Stripe credits, EVAL_API_KEY), not OpenRouter. That conflicts with the user's stated wish to use OpenRouter-hosted Jev, and it sends raw tool arguments (client code, commands, possible secrets) from client projects to an unknown individual's server. That is a serious client-confidentiality problem.
No client-side redaction in the hook package, unlike the library.

Only guards (a safety classifier for tool calls). It gives no other Jev value in daily coding: it does not route work, pick tools, triage or rank. With Opus 5.5 in auto/bypass mode it duplicates the existing secret-leak guard and Claude Code's own permission classifier.

Fail-open default with a 5 s timeout and retries, and `review` denied by default: a slow Jev stalls every tool call, and false positives will block legitimate calls like rm -rf node_modules or curl|bash in scripts.

Immature: 10 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 15 commits, no CI, no releases, and a version string mismatch. It is a commercial side product that could disappear or change pricing; it needs a paid key before the first call.
Adds one network hop per tool call on top of the existing three global PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).
gh-codebam-jev-guardrails.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code as shipped and not OpenRouter-native: the eval-jev hooks target OpenCode, Hermes and dsh and route all tool-call data through the author's paid proxy. The only reusable part is the @codebam/jev-guardrails library (OpenRouter Decisions transport plus redaction), which someone could wrap in a custom PreToolUse hook for a narrow safety-check use. Treat it as a reference implementation, not an install.

gh-fallow-rs-fallow-verdict.name: fallow-verdict
gh-fallow-rs-fallow-verdict.whatItDoes: Node CLI (npm fallow-verdict 0.1.0) that runs the Fallow JS/TS SAST scanner, then sends each security finding (metadata plus numbered source excerpts) to Jev's System One endpoint as fixed Noul/Choice/Score questions. Deterministic policy code turns the probabilities into survivor, dismissed or needs-human-review verdicts and writes a Markdown/JSON report.
