gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.name: decisionkit-core (DecisionKit)
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.whatItDoes: Installer + library (npm decisionkit-cli / decisionkit-core 0.1.2) that wires Jev-backed typed decisions into coding agents. For Claude Code, `npx decisionkit-cli init --agent claude` writes per-repo PreToolUse, PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit command hooks into `.claude/settings.json`, adds a `decisionkit_locate` stdio MCP server to `.mcp.json`, and npm-installs decisionkit-core into `<repo>/.decisionkit/hooks`. Tiers: (1) Guardrail: Jev Noul/Score on each tool call, and it denies calls it rates destructive. (2) S0 context: on each user prompt it runs a local grep/rg sweep, sends candidate cards to Jev, and injects a digest as additionalContext. (3) Read triage: advisory note that a read is likely irrelevant. (4) Critic: note on empty tool results. Every decision is logged to `.decisionkit/receipts.jsonl`. This is the only candidate found so far that gets automatic, prompt-free Jev use in Claude Code through deterministic hooks.

Direct path: @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 `client.systemOne` (decisionkit.ts:123-125). It does NOT use /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter, only the alpha Decisions endpoint.
providerSupport.others: None. Only TypeSafe direct and OpenRouter. There is a base-URL override, so a proxy is possible.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter is a first-class fallback, chosen automatically when only OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set. Caveat: TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins if it is also present (env or the project's `.env`), so pin `DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER=openrouter`.

interface.name: hook PreToolUse (hook.mjs pre)
interface.purpose: Installed with no matcher, so it fires for EVERY tool: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Agent and mcp__*. Only a read-only bash allowlist skips Jev (host-hook.ts:165-174). Everything else makes a Jev call (host-hook.ts:175) with the full tool_input, using Noul 'destructive' plus Score 'severity'. It emits permissionDecision:deny when both scores exceed the thresholds. The block message tells the model to stop and ask the user.

interface.name: hook PostToolUse (hook.mjs post)
interface.purpose: For the Read tool it makes a Jev triage call per read and, if the file is judged irrelevant, adds an advisory additionalContext note. host-hook.ts:187-190 passes taskContext=worktree (the cwd path), not the real task, so the relevance question has no task to judge against. For other tools, a non-empty result takes a local fast path with no Jev call. An empty result triggers the Jev critic, which adds a corrective note.

interface.name: hook UserPromptSubmit (hook.mjs prompt)
interface.purpose: S0 pre-turn context: for prompts of 4000 chars or fewer it does a local rg/grep sweep and builds candidate cards (path, matched lines, outline). It sends 1-3 Jev calls (gate, pick, sufficiency) and injects the digest as additionalContext. Disable with DECISIONKIT_S0=0.

interface.name: MCP tool decisionkit_locate
interface.purpose: Ranks rg filename matches for a query and task via Jev. Description: 'Find files relevant to a query. Cheaper than multiple grep+read rounds...'. It is a model-discretion tool that competes with Grep/Glob and gitnexus.

interface.name: CLI decisionkit-cli init|remove|test|matrix
interface.purpose: Installs or removes the adapter (init runs npm install in .decisionkit/hooks). `test` runs eval sets against the live Jev API (spends money).

interface.name: Skills decisionkit-calibrate, decisionkit-bench-fixture
interface.purpose: Copied into .claude/skills by init. Used for per-repo pack calibration and benchmark fixture authoring. Neither is useful for daily coding.

interface.name: Env kill switches
interface.purpose: DECISIONKIT_ENABLE=0 disables every tier. DECISIONKIT_S0=0 disables S0 only. DECISIONKIT_PACK overrides the question pack. DECISIONKIT_DEBUG=1 enables debug output.

Then export OPENROUTER_API_KEY and DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER=openrouter in the shell that launches Claude Code. NOT executed by me (static audit only).
security: API key handling is good: the key comes from process env or the cwd `.env` and is sent only as an `Authorization: Bearer` header over fetch (providers.ts:209-213). It is never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
Hook commands are `node "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.decisionkit/hooks/hook.mjs" pre|post|prompt` (init.ts:371-372). Nothing is passed on the command line.

init runs `npm install` in `.decisionkit/hooks` (init.ts:397), pulling decisionkit-core from npm at install time. Its transitive dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk is a supply-chain surface. Hooks execute that node_modules code on every tool call, so a compromised release would run with the user's privileges and see all tool inputs. I found no postinstall script in the repo's package.json files, but I did not audit the SDK.

The installer edits `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` inside the client repo, and it creates `.decisionkit/` (node_modules, receipts.jsonl) there. I found no gitignore handling in init.ts, so this risks committing hook config and receipts into client repos.
Receipts in `.decisionkit/receipts.jsonl` can include command previews (120 characters) and S0 paths. That file may leak into git.

Prompt-injection surface: the S0 digest and critic/triage notes are injected into model context as additionalContext. The digest contains file excerpts from the repo, so hostile repo content could be echoed to the model with tool-like authority. The guardrail deny is driven by Jev probabilities, which are non-deterministic and could be manipulated by content in the tool input.

Reads `.env` from cwd (providers.ts:95) and parses the whole file into memory, though it looks up only its own keys. If a client repo `.env` contains TYPESAFE_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY, it silently picks that up, which is a key mix-up risk.
No telemetry code found (grep for telemetry/analytics came back empty). Network egress is only to OpenRouter or TypeSafe.
Claude Code project-level hooks and MCP servers require a trust prompt for the repo. Repo-committed hook config would make cloned repos run this code.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.dataEgress: Everything below goes to openrouter.ai (or TypeSafe) as JSON `state`. (a) Guardrail: `{tool, input: <full tool_input>}` for EVERY non-read-only-bash tool call (host-hook.ts:175-178, decisionkit.ts:193-194). That includes full Edit/Write/MultiEdit contents (new_string, file content), non-allowlisted bash commands (which may embed secrets, tokens and DB URLs), Read/Grep/Glob arguments, and mcp__* tool arguments. (b) S0: the full user prompt (up to 4000 chars), the cwd, and candidate file cards (relative paths, matched line excerpts of about 60 chars, export outlines, digest summary) via decisionkit.ts:455-500. (c) Read triage: file path plus the worktree path (decisionkit.ts:291, not file content). (d) Critic, on empty results only: tool, tool_input, empty result preview. (e) MCP locate: task text plus candidate file names. No wholesale file contents are sent for reads, but Write/Edit payloads and prompts are sent. For client projects this is a real code and IP egress to a third-party model provider on every edit, and it is not gated by any per-repo opt-in besides installing the hooks per repo.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. There is no key, timeout, HTTP error, or JSON parse failure that blocks the agent: runHostHookStdin swallows all errors and exits 0 with no output (host-hook.ts:228-250), and no-key gives a permanent fail-open (decisionkit.ts:103-108). Per-attempt hard timeout is 2000ms (decisionkit.ts:31) with one retry for 408/422/429/5xx and network errors (150ms backoff; a timeout abort is not retried). Worst case per hook is roughly 2s, or about 4.2s with a transient error plus retry, and a guardrail miss lets the tool call through. The installed Claude hooks set no `timeout` field (only the Codex hooks do, init.ts:469-471), so they rely on Claude Code's default hook timeout. Because each hook is a fresh process, the verdict caches do not apply on the Claude path. Blocks are stochastic: a false-positive deny on a legitimate rm/git reset/migration in bypass mode would stall the agent.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.latencyImpact: Per tool call: node cold start plus SDK import (my estimate is 100-250ms, not measured) plus the Jev round trip. The README's field data (pi host) shows p50 427-942ms and p95 1040-1581ms per call, with one 2102ms outlier. Because the PreToolUse hook has no matcher, this hits all non-read-only-bash tools (Edit, Write, Read, Grep, Glob, Agent, mcp__*), so a 50-tool turn could add on the order of 20-45s serially. The per-prompt S0 hook adds about 3.5-3.8s (3 serial calls) before the first turn (measured on pi). Read triage adds another call per Read. The gains the README reports (2-4x fewer input tokens) were measured on pi with cheap models (glm-5.3-flash), not on Claude Code with Opus and its native Explore/Grep, so they may not carry over.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.contextCost: Low from MCP: 1 tool (decisionkit_locate, about 60 tokens of definition) and the MCP server sends no `instructions` field (mcp.ts:82-91). Hook-injected text costs more. S0 injects a digest of about 1.2k chars (about 300 tokens; the README measured 1245 chars) plus a trailer on most prompts. The guardrail deny message is about 60 tokens per block. Triage/critic notes are short. The two installed skills add a small description footprint (2 skills). Net context is likely modest, but the digest can steer Opus toward the wrong files. The README's token savings compare against pi baselines, not Claude Code.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit) that fire without any user prompting. This is what the user wants. The only model-discretion piece is the decisionkit_locate MCP tool.
pros: Only candidate found that gives fully automatic, hook-driven Jev use in Claude Code, with no need to say 'use jev'. It targets the official hook surfaces (PreToolUse deny, UserPromptSubmit additionalContext).

OpenRouter is a real first-class transport in code: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone selects `POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions` with `typesafe/jev-1.13`, and DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER pins it. No patching is needed.
Fail-open everywhere, with a 2s hard timeout and one bounded retry. It cannot brick a session, and kill switches exist (DECISIONKIT_ENABLE=0, DECISIONKIT_S0=0).
Static read-only bash allowlist and non-empty-result critic fast path avoid Jev calls on the most common cases (tax-fastpath.ts). The API key is never in argv.
A guardrail tier is attractive in bypass/auto mode, since a probabilistic 'is this destructive' gate adds a safety net on rm/DROP/force-push, and receipts give an auditable log.
Uses the Jev primitives correctly (Noul, Score, Choice), and pack wording is data-driven with a per-host Claude pack.
MIT licence, npm provenance and signatures on 0.1.2, CI matrix on Node 20/22, and about 60 unit tests.
cons: Extremely young: repo created 2026-09-21, 8 commits, 1 author, 3 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases, 0.1.x on npm. The README says BETA and calls the Jev API alpha. There is no field data on Claude Code, and all benchmarks are pi with cheap models.

PreToolUse has no matcher, so nearly every tool call, not just Bash/Edit/Write, incurs a fresh node process plus a Jev round trip. There is no cross-invocation cache (each hook is its own process). That is a lot of serial latency in an all-day session.

Data egress is broad: full Edit/Write/MultiEdit contents and all non-allowlisted bash commands (possibly with secrets), plus prompts and match excerpts, go to OpenRouter and the Jev provider on client projects. It conflicts with the user's own PreToolUse secret-leak guard philosophy, and the hooks would run in parallel with it, so the secret guard cannot pre-filter what Jev sees. A client NDA would probably forbid it.

The Claude Read-triage tier is effectively broken: host-hook.ts:187-190 passes taskContext=worktree (the cwd path) as the 'task', so a per-Read Jev call judges relevance with no real task. It costs latency and can steer Opus away from files it needs.

Guardrail duplicates or fights existing protections and is stochastic (thresholds on Jev probabilities). False-positive denies interrupt work; false negatives give false safety. Blocks tell the model to stop and ask the user, which can stall autonomous bypass-mode runs.

S0 digest duplicates what Opus 5.5 with Claude Code's own Explore/Grep, plus the user's GitNexus graph hook, already do. It adds 3+ serial Jev calls (about 3.5s) to every prompt and can inject a wrong file pick. The overlap with gitnexus and its hooks is likely.

The installer is per repo and invasive: it edits `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json`, creates `.decisionkit/` with node_modules, runs `npm install`, adds skills, and does not gitignore. It is a poor fit for client repos; global/user-level install is not supported by init.ts, so you would hand-write a user-level settings entry.
Installed Claude hooks have no `timeout` set, and the retry doubles worst-case latency.
The decisionkit_locate MCP tool adds a redundant, model-discretion search tool alongside Grep/Glob/gitnexus, and the two calibrate/bench skills are noise.
Uses only the alpha /decisions endpoint on OpenRouter, a moving target.
gh-tawfeks-decisionkit.verdict: The only OpenRouter-capable, hook-driven, prompt-free Jev integration for Claude Code, and its fail-open design is sound. But it is a 9-day-old single-author alpha whose broad, matcher-less hooks send full edit and command payloads to a third party and add serial latency on every tool call, and it duplicates GitNexus and the user's own guards. Do not run `init` as-is on client repos. At most, hand-cherry-pick a narrow user-level PreToolUse guardrail (matcher `Bash`, with a timeout of about 3s) on personal projects, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER=openrouter, and disable S0 and triage.

npmjs-com-package-blazejkustra-softlint.name: @blazejkustra/softlint
npmjs-com-package-blazejkustra-softlint.whatItDoes: GitHub Action (plus a small CLI, `softlint`) that reviews PR diffs against plain-English rules in softlint.json. It splits the diff into hunks, asks Jev one Noul (yes/no) question per (hunk x rule), then a Choice question to pick the offending added line. It emits GitHub warning annotations for findings at or above a threshold (default 0.8). Real Jev use: Noul + Choice via the System One endpoint. Not an MCP server, hook or skill.

gh-luantak-is-malicious.name: is-malicious
gh-luantak-is-malicious.whatItDoes: npm CLI (is-malicious 0.1.1) plus a skills.sh agent skill that scans a repo for covert or data-stealing code. It walks eligible text files, packs them into chunks and sends full file contents to Jev's System One endpoint. Each request asks all check categories as Noul questions, plus a Score for overall risk and Choices for category, hot file and reason. Suspicious chunks get a second pass over line windows. It prints findings with file, line range, category, probability and confidence. Exit codes are 0 clean, 1 high finding, 2 error or skipped chunk. It is a one-shot security vetting tool for unfamiliar code, not a coding-assistance helper.

providerSupport.evidence: The SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.x does the HTTP; the candidate only wraps it. sdk/dist/index.mjs:513 baseURL defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai (env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, line 58). Line 554 POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone`. Line 581 sends `Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}`. The key is read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY. src/src/cli.ts:31-45 adds --base-url (http/https only), and scan.ts:40 falls back to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. src/src/jev.ts:31-46 passes apiKey/baseURL/timeout 60s to TypeSafeClient.systemOne. README says any service implementing POST /v1/systemone works. There is no OpenRouter string anywhere in the code. scan.ts:41-42 treats only https://api.typesafe.ai as a TypeSafe endpoint, so on other hosts cost is reported as unknown (the token counts still print). The default model is the hardcoded 'jev-latest' (scan.ts:~57). SKILL.md mentions TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, but no code reads it.
providerSupport.others: Any TypeSafe-compatible /v1/systemone server, such as a local one.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial, and no code patch is needed. OpenRouter serves POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with Bearer auth, which matches the SDK path. Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, and pass --model typesafe/jev-1.13 (or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Two caveats. The env var name is misleading (an OpenRouter key goes into TYPESAFE_API_KEY). And the default model string 'jev-latest' must be overridden on every call, because the skill's run.sh has no --model passthrough and the TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL env it documents is not implemented. Also unverified: whether OpenRouter's response shape (answers/usage) exactly matches the SDK's parser.

Not run, per the static-only rule. No .github/workflows in the repo, so no CI. Only two releases (0.1.0 and 0.1.1) over 5 days.

security: Key handling is sound. The key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var only. It never goes in argv or the process list, and it is sent as a Bearer header to the configured base URL.
--base-url and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL let all file contents and the key go to any http(s) host, including plain http. Fine for OpenRouter, but a poisoned env var would exfiltrate the code.

The skill pushes `npx --yes is-malicious` on every run. That fetches and executes the latest npm version unpinned. Each scan is a supply-chain trust decision on a 2-maintainer, 5-day-old package (npm maintainer luantak, one account).
No npm postinstall script (package.json has only build, prepack, scan, test). No curl|sh. The only shell in the skill is run.sh, which is benign and uses exec.

No telemetry in the candidate code; the SDK's own telemetry was not verified beyond the endpoints found. Discovery skips .env and .env.* files, lockfiles and binaries. Commit 'fail closed and protect sensitive configs' shows credential-like JSON is filtered. Other secrets embedded in source files are still uploaded, and that filtering is best-effort.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted repo code is put into the Jev state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, which limits injection impact, but a hostile repo can still try to bias scores toward clean. The skill also tells the agent that high findings mean 'stop', so a crafted repo could cause a denial of work.
The tool is an anti-malware scanner whose own output is probabilistic. A clean report is not proof, and the README says so.
gh-luantak-is-malicious.dataEgress: Full contents of every eligible text file: source, config, build and CI files. Files are chunked, with extra blank lines collapsed, so the whole repo is uploaded, up to 400 KB per file. .env files, lockfiles, binaries, gitignored files and dist/lib/build output are excluded. Also sent: review rules, check prompts and line-window text on the second pass. Sent to api.typesafe.ai, or to whatever base URL is configured (OpenRouter, in the user's setup). Nothing else leaves the machine. This is a heavy upload for CLIENT projects, and it needs client consent and NDA review.
gh-luantak-is-malicious.failureMode: Fail-closed for the scan. The SDK retries twice (maxRetries 2) with a 60s per-request timeout. Any chunk that cannot be scanned is listed as skipped and the CLI exits 2. The skill instructs the agent to say so and 'not invent a result'. It is not in the coding critical path: it is a standalone command, so a Jev outage cannot block edits or tool calls. Only the pre-install vet is affected. A missing key makes run.sh exit 2 immediately.
gh-luantak-is-malicious.latencyImpact: None on normal coding turns. When it does fire, a full-repo scan makes many requests (12 in parallel, plus second-pass escalations) and takes tens of seconds to minutes. --diff-from limits it to changed files. Jev latency is claimed at 70-500 ms per call.
gh-luantak-is-malicious.contextCost: Small. One skill: the frontmatter description (~400 chars, about 100 tokens) is always in context. The SKILL.md body (~3.3k chars, about 800 tokens) loads only when the skill fires. No MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text. Report output (a few hundred to a few thousand tokens) lands in context only when a scan runs.
gh-luantak-is-malicious.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, model-discretion. The description says to use it 'immediately after git clone' and before install or run, so Claude Code will load it on its own after a clone. It is not a deterministic hook. A PostToolUse hook on Bash matching `git clone|gh repo clone` could make it deterministic. Nothing about it is Jev-as-decision-maker for normal coding.
pros: Genuine, working Jev integration that uses all three primitives (noul, choice, score) in a sensible way, so it is a good reference for how to build typed-question prompts (src/jev.ts).

Auto-trigger is real and needs no user prompt. The SKILL.md description fires after git clone or gh repo clone and before npm install. This is a legitimate use case for a senior dev who pulls in unfamiliar repos.

OpenRouter works with no code change: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus a --model override. The SDK POSTs /v1/systemone with a Bearer header, which is the same surface OpenRouter exposes. The author added the base-url support explicitly (commit #5, 2026-09-23).
The key stays in env, never in argv. No postinstall. MIT licensed. Excludes .env, lockfiles and gitignored files. Cost is cheap: about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, and the report prints token usage.
--diff-from lets you vet only changed files. The exit-code contract (0/1/2) is clean, and the skill fails closed and says so instead of inventing results.
Has 13 test files, and the fail-closed and sensitive-config commits show some hardening.
cons: Wrong problem for daily coding. It only fires on git clone or on an explicit 'is this repo safe' question, so it adds nothing to editing, review, refactor or debugging turns. It does not use Jev to improve Claude Code's own decisions.
Uploads the ENTIRE repo contents to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter). Unsuitable for client projects without consent, and of little use on the user's own code.
Model-discretion skill only, not a hook. Trigger reliability depends on Claude noticing the clone. In bypass or auto mode Claude may skip it, or may run npm install first.

Needs manual patching for OpenRouter. The key must go in a misnamed TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL must be set, and run.sh has no --model passthrough. The documented TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL is not implemented, so the default 'jev-latest' would probably fail on OpenRouter, where the id is typesafe/jev-1.13. That means editing run.sh or calling the CLI directly.

Runs unpinned `npx --yes is-malicious`, executing third-party code from a 5-day-old, 2-maintainer, 2-release package with 33 stars, on the machine that holds the user's secrets. This is the same risk the tool claims to mitigate. Pin the version, or vendor it.

Immature and unreliable as a security control. No CI, beta model, and skeptics say Jev behaves like a small router model. Heuristic probabilities give both false negatives (a clean report gives false comfort) and false positives (the skill says 'stop, do not install' on high findings). The README concedes that a clean report is not proof.
Untrusted-repo content is fed to the model, which is a prompt-injection or score-biasing surface.
The instruction to stop on findings can interrupt legitimate workflows, and hidden cost accrues on large monorepos (400 KB files, 12-way concurrency, second passes).
gh-luantak-is-malicious.verdict: A real, cheap, OpenRouter-compatible (via base-url and model overrides) Jev skill with a genuine auto-trigger, but it only solves pre-install malware vetting after git clone. It does nothing for everyday coding, and it uploads whole repos and runs unpinned npx code. Treat it as an optional, pinned, niche add-on for unfamiliar third-party repos, not a core Jev integration, and never point it at client code without consent.

Each rule in a YAML config is one narrow Choice, Noul or Score question. Every changed hunk is sent to Jev as a numbered-line state. Plain code, not the model, turns the probabilities into findings, a composite score and a verdict. Comments come from templates and are never generated. The CLI reviews the local branch, staged changes, a stdin diff or a GitHub PR, and prints text, markdown, json or SARIF. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill.

gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.runtime: Node >=20 (or Bun); esbuild single-file bundle dist/cli.js, about 2.2 MB, with the SDK, undici and octokit bundled in; 5 files in the npm tarball
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.install: npx @itsoltech/jev-code-review (not run). For Claude Code, wrap it yourself in a hook or skill; the package ships none.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.tests: 8 vitest files (test/unit and test/pipeline: policy, evaluate, config, cli, diff, jev-and-report, calibration, run), plus a large eval/calibration dataset directory. CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs typecheck, tests and checks that dist/ is not stale. Release is by semantic-release with npm trusted publishing (OIDC).
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or .env, never from argv, so it does not show in the process list; CLI has no --api-key flag.
Auto-reads .env in cwd when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset (src/cli/main.ts:144), which is a mild surprise in client repos.
SDK log level is forced to 'warn' so request bodies (the diff) are not logged even with TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug (jevPort.ts).
Config is loaded from the PR base commit, so a PR cannot relax its own rules. A built-in jev:base prompt-injection guard is included.
Comments are template-generated, so diff text cannot inject free-form output into PR comments. Jev returns typed probabilities, so the model-output injection surface is small.
The package.json postinstall script and telemetry: I found none in package.json; no analytics or sentry strings in dist/cli.js.
Runs git via a Git port (src/cli/git.ts) and, with --pr, the gh CLI for `gh auth token`; no execution of reviewed code.
Single-file 2.2 MB minified-free bundle is hard to audit versus src; 1 star, 2 npm maintainers, published 1 week ago, so supply-chain risk is not established.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points at): the review-rule question text, the PR title and description (or oldest commit subject and commit messages), the config's project_notes, and the numbered diff lines of each changed hunk with file paths. Diffs only, not whole files, and not Claude Code prompts, transcripts or tool outputs. With --pr it also calls the GitHub API using gh's token. Excluded and binary files are skipped. Client code diffs would go to the Jev provider, and to OpenRouter and its upstream if routed there.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.failureMode: Fail-open by default. policy.on_error defaults to 'neutral' (src/config/schema.ts:266), so Jev or GitHub failures give a neutral result. Setting on_error: fail makes exit code 1. SDK per-request timeout is set from budget.request_timeout_seconds (default 30 s), with retries on 408, 429 and 5xx (maxRetries 3 in jevPort.ts, backoff 500 ms to 5 s, Retry-After honoured up to 60 s). Timed-out or too-large requests are split in two. The run has a 600 s budget (run_timeout_seconds) and a token budget; skipped work is reported in the summary. A CLI wrapper would still need its own hook timeout.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.latencyImpact: Not per-call. It is a batch review of a whole diff: one request per hunk (up to 16 questions per request, 64k tokens), run concurrently. Probably several seconds to tens of seconds for a normal diff, and up to a 600 s cap. Jev's claimed 70-500 ms applies per request only. Suitable for a pre-commit or pre-PR gate; too slow for every tool call.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-schema tokens, because it is a CLI. No hooks or server instructions. Cost appears only if you add a hook or skill; the JSON or text output (findings list) would then be injected into context, plausibly 200 to 2000 tokens per review depending on findings. A skill description would add about 50 to 100 tokens.
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or wired by the user. The package has no hooks, MCP server or skill of its own. Automatic use would need a custom PreToolUse hook matching `git commit` / `gh pr create` that runs `jev-review --staged --format json`, which the README hints at with 'for a pre-commit hook' but does not ship.
pros: Real, working Jev integration: the SDK call is `client.systemOne` on POST /v1/systemone with typed Noul/Choice/Score questions (src/jev/jevPort.ts, dist/cli.js:29332). It is the most complete example found of using Jev the way it was designed.
Code-side policy, thresholds and needs_human_band: findings are deterministic, calibrated by the code, and comments are templated, so there is no hallucinated review text.
OpenRouter can very likely be used with no code change, via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and a Bearer key, since the SDK reads the base URL from env and OpenRouter serves /v1/systemone under /api.
CLI mode gives a natural Claude Code hook target: --staged, --diff - and --format json/sarif, with clear exit codes (0, 1, 2) and no writes without --post.
API key stays out of argv and logs; SDK debug logging (which would log the diff) is force-disabled.
Fail-open by default (on_error neutral), so an outage does not block commits. Good retry, backoff, splitting and budget handling.
Zero context cost, with no MCP tool definitions or server instructions.
MIT licence, CI-checked builds, semantic-release with OIDC npm publishing, and substantial calibration datasets under eval/ that show the rules were actually measured.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin.json. Automatic use needs custom glue, and this is a rule-based PR linter rather than a general coding aid.
Very young and tiny: created 2026-09-23, 13 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 4 npm versions in 1 day, all from one author; the API is likely to change.

TypeSafe-first: OpenRouter is not mentioned anywhere in the source, docs or defaults. The default model is jev-latest, the README uses jev-1.13.0, and OpenRouter wants typesafe/jev-1.13; the env-var trick is untested.
Env var naming is misleading: an OpenRouter key must be put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It also auto-loads .env from the current directory.
It sends client diffs, PR text and file paths to a beta third-party model via OpenRouter; there is no consent or allowlist layer, and the secret-leak guard hook does not cover this path.
Latency is batch-like (per-hunk requests, seconds to minutes), so it only fits commit or PR-time checks and not the interactive loop.

The value is mostly in GitHub Action / PR-review use; for a local Claude Code session it overlaps with Claude's own code-review, which is stronger on free-form reasoning, so Jev adds a cheap second opinion at best.
The committed dist/cli.js is a 2.2 MB bundle; npx runs it unreviewed, and I did not run it (static audit only).
gh-itsoltech-jev-code-review.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration, but the best-engineered real-world Jev consumer found: a CLI reviewer that could sit behind a custom pre-commit or pre-PR hook and probably works on OpenRouter with only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY set. It is too young and PR-review-specific to be the core integration, so use it at most as an optional commit-time gate after testing the OpenRouter route.

gh-jammaru-jev-affected.name: jev-affected
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.whatItDoes: CLI and library (npm jev-affected 0.3.0) that takes a git diff, sends it plus your natural-language "when:" conditions to Jev as Noul questions via the @typesafe-ai/sdk, and turns P(true) into a run/skip plan for your own shell task commands (tests, build, codegen). It is a CI/test-selection tool, not an MCP server or Claude Code plugin. It ships a passive SKILL.md for agents. The README says no MCP server is planned.

providerSupport.evidence: src/provider.ts:1,20-37 builds `new TypeSafeClient({apiKey, logLevel:'off', timeout, retry:{maxRetries:0}})` and calls `client.systemOne({model, state, questions:{id: noul(q)}})`. The base URL is not set in jev-affected code. The SDK (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, dist/index.mjs:58,513) reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, defaults to https://api.typesafe.ai, POSTs to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (line 554) with `Authorization: Bearer <key>` (line 581). Keys are read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or TYPESAFEAI_API_KEY (src/config.ts:5,101-108). There is no OPENROUTER string anywhere in src/. README Privacy section says 'TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is honored by the official SDK'. In principle TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api with the OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY hits /api/v1/systemone. That path matches OpenRouter's System One surface, but I did not verify that the request and response schema is identical. Blocker for plan(): src/planner.ts:~127 rejects any response whose model does not match /^jev-\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ ('Missing actual model version'), so OpenRouter-style ids like typesafe/jev-1.13 would trip provider-fallback and make every task RUN. Config `model` default 'jev-latest' is also TypeSafe-style, not typesafe/jev-latest. `doctor` calls client.models.list() (src/cli.ts:~220), which will probably not work against OpenRouter.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate but small (~10 lines) and needs a fork or vendored patch. Needed changes: (1) set the SDK baseURL and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY, or export TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment; (2) relax the model-version regex in planner.ts and the cache pin check to accept 'typesafe/jev-x.y' (OpenRouter's id 'typesafe/jev-1.13' has only two version components); (3) map the model name to typesafe/jev-latest or typesafe/jev-1.13; (4) skip or replace doctor's models.list. Zero of this is documented, and the maintainer has no OpenRouter support planned (README: 'Jev is the only supported production provider' and TypeSafe-only).
providerSupport.others: Only TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai). Uses the SDK's systemOne API, not the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions).

security: API key read only from process env (src/config.ts:101); YAML keys named apiKey/api_key are rejected (config.ts:89). The key is never put in argv; the SDK sends it as a Bearer header. SDK logging is off (logLevel 'off'), retries are 0.

Sensitive-file guard: default exclude globs for .env*, *.pem, *.key, *credentials*, *secret*, *token* (config.ts:16-23); when such a file is in the diff, all tasks RUN and no semantic request is sent (git.ts:~198). It cannot catch secrets embedded in ordinary source files, which the SECURITY.md admits. Overall this is better than a naive diff uploader.

Runs configured task commands with shell:true, so it is only as safe as the repo's jev-affected.yml. This is a code-execution vector on a cloned untrusted repo if the agent runs `jev-affected run`. The SKILL.md says to treat the commands as repository code.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The diff is sent to Jev, which returns only probabilities, so there is no free-text output for an agent to obey. The main risk is a poisoned skip decision, which is fail-open toward RUN for low P only if the model is wrong.

No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh, no telemetry (README Privacy; nothing in the code). Dependencies: @typesafe-ai/sdk, picomatch, yaml, zod. The SDK is TypeSafe's own package and was not audited beyond baseURL/auth. A repo-controlled TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env var could redirect diffs, so the README warns to inspect it.

Release workflow uses npm provenance-style permissions (id-token: write), gated on the repo variable ENABLE_RELEASES. SECURITY.md has no private reporting channel set up yet ('Once the public repository is configured').
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.dataEgress: On plan/why/run (and eval --live) it sends to the Jev endpoint the sanitized git state: base and head SHAs, the list of changed files (paths plus status) and the unified diff text, capped at analysis.maxDiffBytes (default 100000 bytes). It also sends your configured natural-language task conditions. Prompts, tool outputs and the full repo are not sent; only the diff. Files matching secret globs make it skip the request entirely. `inspect` and `cache` are local, and `doctor` only hits the models list. Client code diffs would go to the provider (OpenRouter or TypeSafe), which matters for client-confidentiality.
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.failureMode: Fail-open toward RUN, which is the safe direction. A missing key, timeout (default analysis.timeoutMs 10000, SDK timeout, retries 0), provider error, invalid probability or missing model version all mean every semantic candidate task runs, with a warning (planner.ts catch block, README Safety). Policy keys can only be 'run'. Worst-case added delay is 10 s per plan call. With OpenRouter the model-regex check would make this fallback fire permanently, silently disabling the benefit.
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. The only Claude Code context cost is the SKILL.md description (about 60 tokens always loaded) plus the roughly 500-token body when it triggers. It installs no hooks. Real cost appears only if the skill fires: the agent runs the CLI, and `plan --json` output is small.
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and even that is not wired up: nothing is installed into ~/.claude/skills automatically (the README says to point an agent at or copy the directory). It would fire only when the repo has jev-affected.yml or the user asks which tests a change affects, and the model decides whether to follow it. There is no deterministic hook, no MCP tool and no proxy. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PostToolUse/Stop hook that runs `jev-affected plan --working-tree`.
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.latencyImpact: One API call per plan (7 live-eval calls totalled 2,126 ms in EVALUATION.md, so about 300 ms each), plus git diff collection. The cache only works for pinned jev-x.y.z models. With the moving alias jev-latest (the default) there is no cache, so every invocation does a network call. There is no per-tool-call latency inside Claude Code unless you add a hook.
pros: Uses Jev for what it is suited to: typed Noul yes/no probabilities on a diff, with no free text and a fail-open RUN policy and hard thresholds. It is a real, concrete use of a System One model.

Good security hygiene for a v0.3: env-only key, YAML key rejection, secret-file globs that suppress the request, `inspect` to preview egress, no telemetry, no postinstall, small codebase (about 1,600 lines) that is easy to audit.
Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, which honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and hits /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, so pointing it at OpenRouter's System One surface is close to a config change.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, no hooks, one small skill.
Tests (core, cli, provider), a CI matrix on 3 OSes and Node 20/22, a live-eval methodology with a zero-false-skip gate. MIT.
cons: It is not an integration into Claude Code. It has no MCP server or hook, and the README explicitly says none is planned. Automatic use inside Claude Code would need your own hook glue.

Solves test and CI task selection, not general coding assistance. For a developer who already runs the test suite via Claude, the saving is wall-clock test time, and it needs a per-repo jev-affected.yml with hand-written conditions and trusted commands.

OpenRouter is not supported out of the box. The model-version regex /^jev-\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ (planner.ts) would reject OpenRouter ids like typesafe/jev-1.13, which forces every task to RUN. You would need a fork, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY would have to hold your OpenRouter key (confusing, and it risks sending the key to the wrong host if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is unset).
The skill's `run` executes shell commands from the repo config. On client repos or freshly cloned untrusted ones that is an execution risk under bypass permissions.

Very immature: created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 8 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 3 npm versions in about an hour. The 'Public Beta' claim rests on 7 synthetic-fixture live evals with a 50% unnecessary-run rate. The README itself says offline eval verifies plumbing, not accuracy.
Sends client diffs (up to 100 KB) to a third party on every plan. Secret filtering is filename-based only.
Alias jev-latest disables the cache, so it makes a network call every time; the default 10 s timeout could stall a Stop or PostToolUse hook.
gh-jammaru-jev-affected.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-safe Jev use case for CI/test selection. It is not a Claude Code integration and cannot run automatically, and it is not OpenRouter-ready without a small fork. It is worth borrowing as an example pattern (diff -> Noul -> thresholded action) but not as your daily-coding Jev integration.

gh-gordan-code-jev-entropy-gate.name: jev-entropy-gate
gh-gordan-code-jev-entropy-gate.whatItDoes: Standalone Node CLI (jevg) for large code migrations. It finds candidate sites with a regex or ast-grep rule from a YAML file. It sends each site (file, line, snippet plus context lines, task text) to Jev's System One API with one Choice question (rewrite_class: deterministic, judgment or manual) and one Noul question (can_safely_automate). It computes normalized Shannon entropy from the Choice probabilities and buckets each site as auto, assisted or manual. `apply` rewrites the auto sites with the rule's own replacement string or AST fix, with no model involved. `record` and `calibrate` refit thresholds from human feedback. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin.

A grep for 'openrouter' across src returns nothing.
providerSupport.others: None. The base URL and model are not configurable through env vars or flags.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate-to-trivial code change. Change the two constants (endpoint to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model to ~typesafe/jev-latest or typesafe/jev-1.13) and read OPENROUTER_API_KEY. That would need a fork or a local patch of the bundled dist/index.js. Two unknowns remain: whether OpenRouter's /systemone request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's, and whether it supports the `criteria` field. Either would have to be tested. Even patched, the tool does not fit the user's goal (see verdict).

security: API key is read from the JEV_API_KEY env var only and sent as a Bearer header. It is not passed in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
No telemetry found. The only network call is fetch to api.typesafe.ai.
No postinstall or preinstall script in package.json. Runtime dependency is a single pinned native module, @ast-grep/napi 0.45.3.
The only child_process use is Windows ACL verification in src/apply/windows-acl.ts, which does not run on Linux.

Prompt-injection surface: repo snippets and comments go into Jev's `state`. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so text injection cannot steer output beyond skewing the numbers. A hostile repo could still make a risky site score as auto.
Write risk: `apply --write` rewrites files in the target repo. The transaction code has safety checks, but a wrong 'auto' verdict silently changes client code.

gh-gordan-code-jev-entropy-gate.contextCost: Zero. It has no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill and no server instructions, so it adds no tool definitions or injected text. Adding it to Claude Code would need the user to write a skill or CLAUDE.md note, which would cost a few hundred tokens.
gh-gordan-code-jev-entropy-gate.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a plain CLI with no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin manifest. Claude Code would call it only if the user or a custom skill told it to run `jevg` via Bash. This fails the requirement of automatic use with no user prompting.
pros: It is a real Jev integration. It uses the Choice and Noul primitives properly and derives normalized entropy from the Choice probabilities (src/entropy.ts, src/classify.ts:53-81). That makes it a concrete example of using Jev calibration for a decision.
Small egress footprint: snippets with context lines rather than whole files. The key is only in an env var and a Bearer header, with no telemetry and no install scripts.
Reasonable engineering for a young repo: 16 test files, a 6-OS CI matrix with SHA-pinned actions, a transactional apply with a dry-run default, an incremental cache and a calibration loop.
The Jev call is a single small HTTP client (src/jev/client.ts), so the request and response schema is easy to lift as a reference for our own Jev integration.
MIT license, and the CLI is unlikely to break other Claude Code tooling because it doesn't touch ~/.claude.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. Nothing lets Claude Code call it automatically, so it directly fails the user's 'no prompting, must trigger itself' requirement.
It solves one narrow batch problem: bulk migrations such as fetch to apiClient or console to logger, each needing a hand-written YAML rule. This user's daily coding rarely matches that use.

Not OpenRouter-compatible. The endpoint api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and model jev-latest are hardcoded (client.ts:3-4) and only JEV_API_KEY is read. Using OpenRouter would need a fork or a patch to the bundle, and OpenRouter's /systemone schema parity is unverified.
Sends client code snippets to a third-party API. Through the direct TypeSafe endpoint that is a data-handling decision for client projects.

Alpha and single-maintainer: 0 stars, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-21, 2 npm versions. The thresholds (entropy about 0.65, Noul veto) come from the author's own 'real-run entropy ladder' rather than an independent evaluation, so a confident wrong 'auto' can silently rewrite code under `apply --write`.

Installing it means a global npm install of a native-module package from an unknown publisher.
gh-gordan-code-jev-entropy-gate.verdict: A genuine but narrow Jev demo: a batch migration triage CLI with no MCP, hook or skill surface, so it can never fire on its own inside Claude Code. It is also hardcoded to TypeSafe's direct API. Don't adopt it for the OpenRouter-based auto-integration. At most, read client.ts and schema.ts as a reference for the System One request format.

Stop hook injects a one-line status per stop when done-check is enabled (e.g. 'System 1 done-check: 2 of 3 criteria met') and a blocking reason when it blocks. gh-dzhng-jevgrep.name: @dzhng/jevgrep (jg CLI + jevgrep skill)
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.whatItDoes: Node CLI `jg` that answers natural-language repository questions ("where is auth checked?") by walking the repo hierarchy and asking Jev many boolean (Noul) relevance questions per folder/file/declaration (tree-sitter/TS parsing), then prints a ranked file list plus verbatim source excerpts to stdout. It is not an MCP server or hook. Claude Code integration is a separate SKILL.md (installed with `jg skill`, which runs `npx --yes skills add dzhng/jevgrep --skill jevgrep`) whose description tells the model to run `jg` first for "how/why/where does X work" questions.

OpenRouter is selectable via `jg auth --provider openrouter --stdin` (apps/cli/src/args.ts, auth.ts:139-160; tests args.test.ts:54, process.test.ts:123). Only the Noul primitive is used; Choice/Score unused. Env vars are NOT read (README: 'Environment-based credentials and endpoint overrides are not used'); key lives only in ~/.config/jevgrep/credentials.json (auth.ts:19-21,84-97).

Prompt-injection surface is small: repo source and paths go INTO Jev requests with 'data, never instructions' guidance (requests.ts), and Jev returns only probabilities. Output to Claude is verbatim repo excerpts, same trust class as Read/Grep output.

Sensitive filtering is heuristic: skips hidden files, ignore-listed, binary, sensitive names (.pem/.key/.p12/.pfx and a name list, filesystem.ts:51-65,117-123,320) and content matching PRIVATE KEY blocks (filesystem.ts:381); README itself says filters are not a guarantee. `--include-sensitive` is opt-in.

gh-dzhng-jevgrep.dataEgress: Eligible source content is sent to the selected provider (OpenRouter to TypeSafe Jev) on every search: directory listings and file names, file previews, sampled content, parsed declarations and source blocks, plus the natural-language query (requests.ts navigationRequest/evidenceRequest/fileAssessmentRequest). On big roots this can be most of a repo's non-ignored text (issue #38 measured median ~5M input tokens per query on a 2.7k-file repo). Does not send the Claude conversation, diffs or tool outputs; only the query string Claude writes and repo files under the chosen root. For client projects, full code goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (and any upstream), which is a contract/NDA question. Local answer cache in ~/.cache/jevgrep. No other telemetry found.
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: on provider errors jg prints an incomplete/error status (exit 2 or 1) and the skill tells Claude to treat missing context as unknown and use grep/read instead. Per-request timeout 15 s for non-TypeSafe providers (60 s for direct typesafe, evaluator.ts:46), 2 attempts, Retry-After honored on 429 (waits up to 60 s), 401/403 aborts the whole search, request cap 50,000 (evaluator.ts:85-89). No global wall-clock limit: a large-repo search runs ~65-80 s (issue #38) with up to 32 concurrent requests, so failure mode is slow rather than blocking forever; HTTP 402 (out of credit) surfaces mid-query. If jg is missing or the model ignores the skill, it silently falls back to grep.
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.contextCost: Very low. No MCP tools, no hooks. Only the skill frontmatter name+description (~490 chars, ~120 tokens) sits in the skills list permanently; the ~2.9 KB SKILL.md body (~750 tokens) loads only when triggered. The real cost is the search output itself: verbatim excerpts to stdout, capped by --max-source-bytes (render.ts) but issue #41 reports a 5 MB output for a no-match query; a typical invocation adds several thousand tokens.
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). The description says to start behavioral discovery with jg before broad text searches or git history and to tell subagents to use jg, so no per-prompt 'use jev' is needed. Evidence is thin: the author's pilot (evals/results/skill-trigger-2026-09-29.md) ran on Codex with a shim, 3 repeats, ceiling effect, and 'jg before ANY other search' scored 0/6 because agents did filename discovery first; not verified on Claude Code/Opus. Not deterministic: Opus 5.5 with GitNexus, Grep hooks and other skills may prefer gitnexus query, Grep or Explore subagents.
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.latencyImpact: Per invocation: small repo (~165 files) 2-4 s and 8-55 Jev requests; large repo (2.7k files) 7-79 s (median 65 s), 215-1,483 requests, ~5M tokens (~$0.2) per query per issue #38, with discovery often incomplete (resource_limit). Author speed study: native TypeSafe median 140 ms per request vs Vercel Gateway 330 ms; OpenRouter not benchmarked and adds a hop. Zero latency on turns where it is not invoked (no hooks).
pros: Only candidate audited that is actually wired to the Jev System One API through OpenRouter out of the box: `jg auth --provider openrouter --stdin` calls https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with model typesafe/jev-1.13 (providers.ts:12-16; SDK typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109). No patching needed.
Uses Jev as designed: many parallel typed boolean (Noul) probabilities, no free text, so no hallucinated answers and injection cannot alter output beyond scores.
Solves a real daily-coding task (finding relevant code in unfamiliar repos) and is passive: skill description auto-triggers on how/where questions and excludes exact-symbol lookups.
Near-zero standing context cost (one ~120-token description, no MCP tools, no hooks), so no conflict with the secret-leak guard or GitNexus hooks.

Fail-open, timeouts, retry/backoff, 401 abort, key redaction, 0600 key file, stdin key entry; unit tests plus Docker installed-package tests; SHA-pinned CI with tag-based npm release; MIT; 1.8k stars; 13 releases in 4 days.

Author benchmark on 10 SWE-bench tasks: same 8/10 solves at ~25-30% lower total cost including Jev (evals/results/total-cost-2026-09-28.md, speed-2026-09-28.md); small repos cost cents (~$0.002-0.018 per query at $0.042/M).
Filesystem filters respect .gitignore, skip hidden/dependency/binary/obvious credential files and PRIVATE KEY content; `jg files` gives an offline scope estimate; `--exclude` for sensitive paths.
cons: Sends repository source (previews, declarations, blocks) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every search; for client projects this is a real data-egress/NDA problem, and sensitive-file filtering is heuristic (README admits it).

Scales poorly: issue #38 measured median ~65 s, ~5M tokens, ~$0.22 and 215-1,483 requests per query on a 2.7k-file repo, with 19/20 runs ending 'discovery incomplete'; issue #41 reports 5 MB output and 40% of files marked relevant when nothing matches. No spend readout in CLI output.

Auto-invocation is only a soft skill trigger; author's evidence is from Codex with a shim and a tiny sample, none from Claude Code/Opus. With GitNexus hooks, Grep and Explore available, Opus may not choose jg; nothing is deterministic.
Ignores OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var by design; needs one interactive/stdin `jg auth` writing a plaintext key file. Cannot be configured via Claude Code settings/env.

Overlaps with existing GitNexus (graph query/context) and Grep/Glob, adding a second retrieval path with a different cost profile. Quality claims come from the author's tuned Python SWE-bench tasks plus one user report, not independent tests.

Very young: created 2026-09-26, 179 commits in 5 days, 174 by one author, 9 open issues, 0.1.0 to 0.7.0 in 3 days; GitHub latest release v0.6.0 vs npm 0.7.0. Needs global npm install; skill may run unpinned `npm install --global @dzhng/jevgrep@latest` unprompted in bypass mode; `jg skill` executes `npx --yes skills add`.

Uses only Noul (boolean); does not use Choice or Score, so it does nothing for other Claude Code decisions (routing, permission gating, classification). No total wall-clock limit, so one search can stall a turn for over a minute.
gh-dzhng-jevgrep.verdict: The only audited option that genuinely runs Jev through OpenRouter's System One endpoint out of the box and is auto-triggered by a skill description, with tiny context cost and fail-open behavior. Treat it as a supplementary code-discovery tool for small/medium personal repos (pin the version, use `jg files` and --exclude, avoid client code and big monorepos until the ~65 s/5M-token scaling and egress issues are addressed), not a core integration.

gh-dakdevs-lintrules.name: @dakdevs/lintrules
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.whatItDoes: A Rust CLI (shipped on npm as prebuilt native binaries, plus a GitHub Action) that lints a repo against Markdown rules in .lintrules/. Each rule has YAML front matter (title, globs, optional applies-to). For every matching file it sends the rule body and the numbered file source to Jev as Noul yes/no questions ("does the file violate the rule?", "does this rule need cross-file context?"). It turns the returned P(yes) into violation, pass or inconclusive using thresholds (violation 0.8, pass 0.2, inapplicable 0.1). It prints file:line findings or JSON and exits non-zero on failure. With --base it reports only findings on changed files and lines. It is a CI/pre-commit style code linter. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or Claude Code plugin.

providerSupport.evidence: Three hardcoded adapters, no base-URL override and no OpenRouter adapter. crates/lintrules-provider-typesafe/src/lib.rs:188 posts to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (line 189), default model 'jev-latest' (line 178), body {model,state,questions}. crates/lintrules-provider-vercel/src/lib.rs:112 posts to https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai/evaluation-model with AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and custom ai-gateway-* headers (default model typesafe-ai/jev). crates/lintrules-provider-cloudflare/src/lib.rs:221 posts to api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{id}/ai/run with CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. crates/lintrules-core/src/config.rs:11-15 defines the ProviderName enum as Typesafe|Cloudflare|Vercel only. Provider registry: crates/lintrules-core/src/provider.rs:28-34. Shared POST uses bearer auth: crates/lintrules-provider/src/lib.rs:79.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (default in README and in the repo's own config), Cloudflare Workers AI (typesafe/jev)

gh-dakdevs-lintrules.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The TypeSafe adapter body {model,state,questions} matches the System One shape, so an OpenRouter adapter should be about a 30-line crate: URL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13. That assumes OpenRouter's request and response schema (answers.<id>.noul) is identical to TypeSafe's, which I did not verify. It still needs a Rust fork, a ProviderName variant, a registry entry and a local cargo build. The npm package ships only prebuilt binaries, so config alone cannot switch it. The README documents how to add a provider.

CI workflows: ci.yml, build-native.yml, lintrules.yml (dogfooding), release.yml. Not executed here.
security: No postinstall or install scripts; the README states none are needed, and package.json only has prepublishOnly. scripts/install-cli.sh is used only by the GitHub Action and runs npm install --ignore-scripts.

The npm tarball contains about 8-9 MB opaque prebuilt binaries per platform. I cannot verify they match the GitHub source. The package has a registry signature, but I did not confirm provenance attestation. Two npm versions were published within 16 minutes (1.0.0, 1.0.1). package.json in the repo is already 1.0.2, so the registry is behind the repo.

API keys are read from env vars and sent as a bearer header (crates/lintrules-provider/src/lib.rs:79). They are not passed in argv, so they do not show in the process list. The wrapper passes process.env through to the binary.

Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted file contents and rule text go into the state sent to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities and no free text, so an injection can only flip a verdict, not run tools. Outputs are used only as yes/no gates.
Local writes: .lintrules/.cache.json, which stores full provider responses keyed by a sha256 of the request. Nothing is executed from repo content.
No telemetry found in the source I read. I did not grep the whole tree for it. Single maintainer, 1 star, 11 days old, so supply-chain trust is low.
Uses the native TLS path via reqwest to the hardcoded provider endpoints only.
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.dataEgress: Full source of every file matching a rule's globs is sent to the provider, line-numbered, together with the rule text (scan.rs:200, 254-256, 292). In cross-file mode all matched files go in one request, up to max_context_chars=100000 (about 25k tokens). It respects .gitignore, so untracked secrets in ignored files are excluded. Committed .env or config files matched by a glob such as '**/**' would be sent. Nothing is sent from Claude Code's prompts, tool outputs or conversation, since the tool is not connected to Claude Code. With --base, only changed files are checked, but the whole file is still sent. Traffic goes to the chosen provider (TypeSafe, Vercel AI Gateway or Cloudflare), never to OpenRouter. For client projects this means whole-file source leaves the machine.
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.failureMode: Fail-closed by design: provider errors, invalid JSON, HTTP non-2xx, inconclusive probabilities (between the pass and violation thresholds) and oversized context all count as check failure (README: 'failed provider calls all fail the check'). The HTTP client timeout is 45 s with no retries (crates/lintrules-core/src/provider.rs:70; post() in lintrules-provider/src/lib.rs:72-90). That suits CI, but in an interactive hook a Jev outage would block or noisily fail every edit unless the hook wrapper swallows the exit code. The cache reduces repeat calls and skips caching for inconclusive answers.
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.latencyImpact: Each call is a blocking HTTPS round trip (Jev claims 70-500 ms), with up to max_concurrency=4 parallel calls. Per-file mode means roughly N files x rules calls plus one 'cross_file' applicability call per rule. A small diff takes a few seconds and a whole-repo scan with many rules takes tens of seconds to minutes, which is too slow to run on every tool call. It could only be run on demand or on Stop or commit. Cache hits are instant.
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.contextCost: Zero for MCP or skill tokens: no MCP server, no tool definitions, no instructions, no hook-injected text unless the user writes a hook. If wrapped in a hook or Bash call, its stdout (file:line findings) is the only cost. That output is short and structured, and --format json is available.
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or wired up by the user. It has no Claude Code integration. Automatic use would require the user's own hook, for example a PostToolUse/Stop hook or a git pre-commit hook that runs `lintrules --base HEAD --format json`. It would run deterministically but coarsely. It cannot make Claude Code decide 'use Jev when it adds value'.
pros: Real, MIT-licensed, typed Rust code that uses Jev for what it is suited to: Noul yes/no verdicts with calibrated probabilities and thresholds (scan.rs, config.rs). It is not a chat-model wrapper.

A well-scoped use case: natural-language project conventions ('forms show inline validation errors') checked semantically. Static linters cannot do this, so it could run as a post-edit or pre-commit gate.
Sensible design: --base reports only introduced findings, a result cache skips repeat calls, honest 'no silent truncation' behaviour, and an inconclusive band instead of guessing.
No install scripts. API keys are not in argv. Jev's typed output limits the prompt-injection impact.
Adding a provider is a documented, small Rust change, and the TypeSafe adapter body shape is a near match for OpenRouter's System One API.
Cheap to run: at about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, a 100k-char file scan costs a fraction of a cent.
cons: No OpenRouter support: three hardcoded providers (TypeSafe, Vercel, Cloudflare) with no base-URL override. Using OpenRouter needs a Rust fork and local build, and the user said OpenRouter is the desired provider and no other key exists yet.

Not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. It cannot make Claude Code call Jev on its own, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic, model-decided use. At best the user hand-writes a hook.
Whole-file egress: it sends full file source to a third party gateway. That is a risk on client projects, where it is unsafe unless globs are narrowed and secrets are gitignored.
Fail-closed with a 45 s timeout and no retry, and per-file calls with up to 4-way concurrency. That is too slow and brittle to run per edit. It suits CI, not an interactive loop.

Very immature: 11 days old, 1 star, single maintainer, 24 commits, all on 2026-09-18/19. The npm tarball is a 42 MB bundle of opaque binaries that cannot be verified against source, and it lags the repo (1.0.1 vs 1.0.2).
Value depends on the user writing and maintaining a .lintrules/ rule set in each project; it does nothing for general coding assistance or Claude's own decisions.
It duplicates something Claude can already do by reading the rule and the code, at higher latency, and Jev is unproven (a possible DeepSeek-flash router, per the brief).
gh-dakdevs-lintrules.verdict: A legitimate but narrow Jev-based semantic linter aimed at CI and PR checks. It has no OpenRouter provider (hardcoded TypeSafe, Vercel and Cloudflare) and no Claude Code hook, MCP or skill surface, so it cannot deliver the requested automatic, model-decided Jev use. Treat it as an optional pre-commit or CI gate at most, and only after forking to add an OpenRouter adapter.

gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.name: jev-intent-review
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.whatItDoes: A Rust-only PR intent reviewer, shipped as a CLI (jev-intent-review) and a GitHub Action. It reads a requirement from a spec, issue or PR body. It then builds candidate call sites (changed functions, callers one hop out, callees, siblings) using tree-sitter, and asks Jev fixed Choice questions about each. The report sorts calls into worth checking, not settled, read as holding, and not required. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill. The README says maintenance stopped on 2026-09-29 after it lost its own sealed evals: against a frontier model it found fewer known defects (-0.47, 2 wins and 15 losses over 17 repos), and it detected 0 of 17 past defects.

providerSupport.evidence: No 'openrouter' string anywhere in src/, docs or the README (grep -i over the .ts, .md, .yml and .sh files returned nothing). src/judgments/client.ts:55-56 has FIXED_URL typesafe=https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and vercel=https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/typesafe/v1/systemone. client.ts:60 (in docs/usage.md:60) has cloudflare=https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/<id>/ai/run. Env vars, client.ts:160-161 and 237-240: JEV_PROVIDER (cloudflare|typesafe|vercel), TYPESAFE_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, JEV_API_URL plus JEV_API_TOKEN (custom endpoint). client.ts:365-371 makes the client throw EndpointError if a named host is used with a URL other than its fixed one. docs/usage.md:71 says only Cloudflare was ever called for real; the TypeSafe and Vercel paths are untested against live endpoints.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The escape hatch is JEV_API_URL plus JEV_API_TOKEN, which client.ts:287-293 accepts for https URLs, but the README says it must serve the 'Workers AI run request' form. The typesafe/vercel path posts a body shaped for /v1/systemone (answers at top level, unwrapAnswers in jev.ts:9-17). OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone is the same System One name and probably a similar schema, so pointing a custom JEV_API_URL at it might work. That is unverified, and the model name sent is a fixed alias (jev-latest or typesafe/jev), not OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13. A small patch would add an 'openrouter' entry to PROVIDERS, FIXED_URL and HOSTS, and an OPENROUTER_API_KEY entry to PROVIDER_KEYS. Even then the tool is unmaintained and Rust-only.
providerSupport.others: Cloudflare Workers AI (the only host measured), Vercel AI Gateway, custom endpoint via JEV_API_URL

gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.dataEgress: Per judgment, a redacted state containing the requirement text plus code evidence goes to the chosen Jev host. The evidence is function bodies, callers, callees and diff excerpts from a Rust repo, with secrets redacted by pattern. --candidates-only sends nothing. Nothing goes to Anthropic or to OpenRouter. The optional JEV_TRACE_FILE keeps a local copy of the request state.
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.failureMode: Fail-loud in a CLI run. It uses a 30s per-request timeout (client.ts:379, AbortSignal.timeout at :467) and retries with Retry-After or backoff, including on 529. It has a run-wide deadline and a request and byte budget, and errors are typed (timeout, network, budget, bad_response). It has no interaction with Claude Code, so there is nothing to fail open or closed inside the session.
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.contextCost: Zero: it registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills. Only if the user wrapped it themselves would the cost be one Bash call's output.
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a CLI or a CI Action, with no hook, MCP or skill trigger. Automatic use in Claude Code would need custom glue.
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.latencyImpact: A per-PR batch. Each run makes many judgments (one request per candidate call), each up to 30s. It is minutes-scale, not the 70-500 ms interactive scale, and it would only be paid if invoked manually.
pros: It is real, well-engineered Jev client code. It has strict response validation (readChoice checks probabilities in [0,1] and choice membership), typed errors, a retry and budget layer, and it records the Jev model version returned.
Its own README documents that typesafe/jev on Cloudflare is the measured path, which is useful as calibration data. It also records that 'jev-latest' on TypeSafe may be a different version.

Its measurements are an honest negative result for Jev-as-PR-reviewer: it found fewer defects than a single frontier-model request, with 2 wins and 15 losses, and 0 of 17 past defects. That is useful evidence against relying on Jev for code review.
The redaction and sensitive-path exclusion design is careful, and the fixed-URL key binding is a good pattern to copy.
Dual licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, with about 69 test files and CI on Node 22 and 24.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook or skill, so it cannot integrate with Claude Code automatically.
Maintenance stopped on 2026-09-29 and the npm release stays at v0.1.1. It is 11 days old with 0 stars, 0 forks and 1 contributor.
It is Rust-only, with two question types. The user's stack is unknown but is likely mostly non-Rust.
There is no OpenRouter support. Only Cloudflare, TypeSafe direct and Vercel are wired. TypeSafe and Vercel were never verified live, and a custom JEV_API_URL expects the Workers AI form.
It fails its own evals against a frontier model, so it adds little beyond what Opus 5.5 already does for PR review.
It is batch and slow, with many requests per PR. It sends code evidence off-machine to a third party, which matters for client projects.
The repo is still worth mining as a reference for Jev request and response shapes, but it should not be installed.
gh-yottayoshida-jev-intent-review.verdict: Not usable for this goal: it is a stopped, Rust-only PR-review CLI and Action with no Claude Code integration and no OpenRouter path. Its own sealed evaluation shows it losing to a single frontier-model call (2 wins and 15 losses). Treat it as a reference and cautionary data point only.

gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.name: jev-audit
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.whatItDoes: Independent (not TypeSafe-affiliated) npm CLI plus a SKILL.md that audits a codebase to find LLM call sites that are really decisions and could be replaced by Jev. A zero-dependency regex scanner writes jev-scan.json. The skill then has the agent read each call site, tier it (Replace / Hybrid / Keep LLM / Pure code), estimate savings and write JEV_AUDIT.md. It never calls Jev. It is a one-off migration-planning tool for apps that use LLMs, not a runtime integration of Jev into Claude Code.

providerSupport.evidence: No network calls anywhere: bin/jev-audit.js and skill/jev-audit/scripts/scan.js only use fs/os/path. The only Jev endpoint is documentation in skill/jev-audit/references/jev-reference.md:22-23 (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, Bearer $TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and :98 (TypeSafeClient reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY), used to draft code for the audited app. scan.js:46 and scan.js:49 match openrouter.ai/api and OPENROUTER_API_KEY only as detection patterns for existing LLM calls. scan.js:59 treats api.typesafe.ai and @typesafe-ai/sdk as already-Jev. No mention of openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not applicable, since there is no runtime provider call. Editing the code samples in jev-reference.md to the OpenRouter endpoints and model IDs would be trivial, but it would not integrate Jev into Claude Code.
providerSupport.others: Detects, and does not call, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Cohere, Groq, xAI, Together, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Ollama and Bedrock.

security: Scanner privacy leak: scan.js:46-49 and :105 store line.trim().slice(0,160) for every matching line, and .env* files are scanned (scan.js:75). A line such as OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-live-... therefore lands verbatim in jev-scan.json. That file is written to the cwd and could be committed or read by the agent, which clashes with the user's secret-leak guard.

No network, no exec, no child_process, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry (verified in bin/jev-audit.js and scan.js). Local file writes only: jev-scan.json in the cwd, the skill directory on install, and JEV_AUDIT.md.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill makes the agent read every LLM call site, prompt and system message in the audited repo, and write conclusions into a report. Malicious repo content could steer the report, but the skill grants no new tools.
Report template footer embeds a promotional line (npx jev-audit) that SKILL.md says to keep intact, so client repos would carry vendor-style advertising unless it is removed.

Supply chain: single-maintainer brand-new package (das_vicky), 0 stars, published 2026-09-19. Provenance publishing is configured in CI. The README claims independence from TypeSafe, and the scan-output examples are self-reported.
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from the tool itself (no network code). The skill runs inside Claude Code, so code and snippets it reads go to Anthropic as ordinary session context. Nothing goes to Jev, OpenRouter or TypeSafe.
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.failureMode: Not applicable, since Jev is never called. If the skill is not triggered, nothing happens. The scanner fails silently on unreadable files (try/catch returns []) and skips files over 2 MB.
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.contextCost: Only the skill listing: about 700 chars of description (name plus the long trigger sentence), roughly 175 tokens, always present in the skills list. The body (about 6.8 KB) plus two references (about 11.6 KB) load only when triggered, adding roughly 4.5k tokens. There are no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text.
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.latencyImpact: None on normal turns. When triggered, the audit is a multi-minute agent session (scan plus reading every call site).
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only. Claude loads it when the user talks about auditing or reducing LLM usage or mentions Jev or System One. It never makes Jev calls, never runs as a hook, and does nothing during ordinary coding.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related and honest: the README says it does not call Jev and is independent of TypeSafe, and the code matches that (no network, no exec).
Very low footprint: about 175 tokens of always-on context, zero dependencies, MIT licence, no postinstall, and an OIDC/provenance npm publish workflow.
Useful for the user's client projects that contain OpenAI or Anthropic classification, routing or moderation calls: it gives a cited inventory, tier table and shadow-mode migration plan.
scan.js already recognises openrouter.ai/api endpoints and OPENROUTER_API_KEY as existing LLM calls, and the reference docs have accurate primitives (choice, noul, score) and the batching advice.
cons: Does not integrate Jev into Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hook or proxy, so Claude Code gains no ability to call Jev, which is the user's core requirement.
No OpenRouter support: the reference points to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the OpenRouter Decisions and System One endpoints and typesafe/jev-1.13 model IDs are absent.
Manual, occasional use, and it only fires on audit or cost-cutting phrasing, which is the opposite of the automatic in-flow use requested.
Scanner writes raw matching lines, including .env values, into jev-scan.json (scan.js:75, :105), a secret-leak risk that the user's guard hook might block or flag.
Immature: 4 commits in one day, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, v0.1.0. The savings numbers it produces rest on claimed Jev pricing and latency, which are unverified.
The mandated promotional footer in generated reports is unwanted in client deliverables, and the skill is only relevant to repos that make LLM calls.
gh-magicbeansai-jev-audit.verdict: Not the requested integration: it is a static auditing skill that never calls Jev, and it has no OpenRouter path, hook or MCP tool. It is safe and cheap to install as an optional skill for client projects that call LLMs, but it does not deliver automatic Jev use in Claude Code and should not be counted as part of the solution.

gh-darkmatter-adhere.name: @drkmttr/adhere
gh-darkmatter-adhere.whatItDoes: A CLI linter (Bun-compiled binary, npm launcher) that checks a repo against natural-language rules in .adhere/rules/*/RULE.md (Must/Never code examples). Each source file is sent to Jev via the System One API as Noul/Choice questions; rules whose P(violation) exceeds a threshold (default 0.8) are reported with a located section. Results are cached in .adhere/cache/. It is a linter for a repo, not a Claude Code integration: it ships no MCP server and no hooks. It ships 3 skills (adhere, adhere-setup, adhere-fix) that teach an agent to run the CLI and fix findings. Written by TypeSafe-adjacent author (Cooper Maruyama, darkmatter), README says "powered by Typesafe".

providerSupport.evidence: src/services/Jev.http.ts:46 hardcodes `const SYSTEM_ONE = "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone"`; used at :207 (HttpClientRequest.post(SYSTEM_ONE)) with bearerToken. src/services/Credentials.ts:81 reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY (else ~/.config/adhere/credentials.json from `adhere login`, file mode 0600). grep for openrouter/OPENROUTER across src, scripts, README returns nothing. Model id default `jev-latest` (src/config.ts:281), overridable via config `model` (config.ts:157) but the base URL is not configurable and there is no env override.
providerSupport.others: none
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: moderate: the request body is {model, state, questions} and responses decode as {answers:{key:{noul|choice}}}; if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same schema it is a 2-line patch (base URL + key env var + model id typesafe/jev-1.13). But that requires forking and building/compiling with Bun (the npm package ships prebuilt binaries in optional platform packages, src is only used in a git checkout), and the OpenRouter schema is unverified to match. Not a user-config change.

Prompt-injection surface is small for Claude Code itself (Jev returns only typed numbers), but the bundled adhere-fix skill tells the agent to run `adhere lint --yes` unattended and 'never ask before a run ... never stop to report its cost', and README recommends piping it into `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` / `codex exec --yolo`.
