RULE.ts rules (and appendState hooks) are executable TypeScript run under Bun on every lint; `adhere install org/repo` copies rules from arbitrary GitHub repos incl. RULE.ts that then run on lint (install.ts, README) - arbitrary code execution vector from installed shared rules.
Shells out to git clone --depth 1 for install/list; no telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics in src empty). Retries transient errors 3x with exponential backoff; 30s timeout per request.
Native prebuilt binary distributed via optional npm deps: supply-chain trust in the @drkmttr scope; package 8 days old with 20 versions in a week.
gh-darkmatter-adhere.dataEgress: Full text of every source file judged (comments blanked), split into ~30-line numbered sections as `state.code`, plus rule descriptions and Must/Never example code, sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Custom RULE.ts appendState hooks can add arbitrary extra file content (e.g. schemas). Nothing from Claude Code prompts, tool outputs or conversations is sent - only repo files when adhere lint runs. Results cached locally in .adhere/cache/ (meant to be committed).
gh-darkmatter-adhere.failureMode: Fail-closed for the CLI: JevUnavailable refuses the whole run with a non-zero exit (Jev.http.ts:65,149); per-request timeout 30s, 3 retries with exponential backoff from 500 ms; a 400 max_tokens_exceeded skips the file; a Cloudflare 403 block page is reported as JevBlocked. Not a hook, so it can never block a Claude Code tool call unless the user wires it into one; all-cached runs need no network or key.
gh-darkmatter-adhere.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text. Only cost is 3 skills: their descriptions sit in the skills listing (~150-250 tokens total; the 'adhere' description is ~90 words); SKILL.md bodies (adhere ~2.7k tokens, adhere-fix longer) load only on invocation. Nothing installed into ~/.claude automatically - `adhere skill <name>` merely prints them.
gh-darkmatter-adhere.latencyImpact: None to normal Claude Code turns. When run manually, a full lint of a repo is many requests (per file x rules, batched under 32k-token context), typically tens of seconds to minutes plus per-request 70-500 ms Jev latency; cached re-runs near-instant. Not suitable for a per-edit hook without --filter on changed files.
gh-darkmatter-adhere.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (adhere skill: 'Use when writing or editing adhere rules...'; adhere-fix: 'Use when adhere, or CI running it, reports errors...'). Claude will only use it in repos that already have .adhere/ rules. No hook or MCP tool; nothing fires on ordinary coding. It could be wired as a PostToolUse/Stop hook by the user, but that is not provided.
pros: Real, non-trivial, purpose-built Jev consumer: uses Noul and Choice primitives correctly (Jev.http.ts NoulAnswers/ChoiceAnswers/LocateAnswers), a good reference for how to frame typed questions with numbered code sections and thresholds.

Active and fairly well tested for its age: 194 commits by mainly one author, 20 npm versions in 8 days, ~4.1k lines of tests, CI on every PR, MIT licensed, and an eval/ directory with measured studies (e.g. only 1 of 20 findings real on one rule, which the skill honestly discloses).
Content-keyed judgment cache (.adhere/cache/) that can be committed means repeated runs and CI pay nothing and need no key or network - cheap at ~$0.042/M input tokens.

Ships Claude Code-compatible skills (adhere, adhere-setup, adhere-fix) with descriptions that trigger on relevant tasks, at negligible context cost; adds no MCP tools, hooks, or context injection, so it will not collide with the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks.
API key handling is careful (env or 0600 file, Redacted, not in argv), no telemetry found, no postinstall script.
cons: Hard-codes https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (Jev.http.ts:46) and only reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY: no OpenRouter support at all, no base-URL override, so it cannot satisfy the 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' requirement without forking and rebuilding the Bun binary.

Not an automatic Claude Code integration: no MCP server, no hook. It only activates via skill description in repos that already have .adhere/ rules; it does not use Jev to help Claude decide anything during normal coding (routing, gating, classifying tool calls).

It is a repo-wide linter, the wrong shape for interactive daily coding: whole files are uploaded to a third party and full runs cost many requests and seconds-to-minutes; the docs say typical false-positive rate is high for some rules and the fix skill says to verify every finding.
Sends full client source code to api.typesafe.ai (README:45) - a data-egress and contract concern for client projects, with no local/offline judging mode.

Risky agent guidance: adhere-fix says to run unattended, ignore cost, and README promotes `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` piping; RULE.ts from `adhere install` executes arbitrary code on lint. On the user's bypass-permission setup this widens the attack surface.

Very young and single-author (152 of 194 commits from one person, 2 stars, repo created 2026-09-22, Effect 4 release candidates and TypeScript 7 pinned); requires a native binary from optional npm dependencies.
gh-darkmatter-adhere.verdict: A well-built but narrow Jev-powered repo linter that only talks to api.typesafe.ai directly; it is not an MCP/hook integration and cannot use OpenRouter without a fork. Skip it for the automatic OpenRouter-Jev goal; at most use it as a design reference for Noul/Choice question framing, or later as an opt-in CI linter on personal repos.

Unverified: response field names on OpenRouter (answer.noul, answer.probabilities, legend) and the extra X-TypeSafe-* headers being tolerated (they should be). No native OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var.

security: API key is read from env/config and sent only as Authorization Bearer header via the SDK (not argv), so it does not appear in the process list; SDK redacts headers in debug logs (redactHeaders).
Custom base URL is blocked unless client.allowCustomBaseUrl===true (jev-evaluator.ts:106), a good guard against key redirection, but the guard is itself set in a config file that is executed as code.

jev-spec.config.ts/js is loaded via jiti and EXECUTED in every run including --dry-run (README states this). Any repo you open with a hostile config gets code exec when the tool runs; for client projects it only matters if config is untrusted. The jev-spec-init skill also tells the agent to run npm install and npx.

Child processes use execFile without a shell (git ls-files, git show :path), revision ranges pass --end-of-options (src/context/git-diff.ts, docs/specs/security.md REQ-GIT-01/03). Path root-jail, symlink not followed, .env/.git/*.pem/*.key/SSH keys excluded by filename only.
No redaction of file contents: README and jev-spec-init SKILL.md say all matched files are sent as-is; a hard-coded secret in a matched file goes to the API.

Prompt-injection surface: spec and code are wrapped in <specification_context>/<untrusted_source_code> tags plus an ignore-embedded-instructions preamble (src/evaluator/prompt-security.ts); the README calls this 'a mitigation, not a guarantee'. Since Jev emits only numbers, injection can only skew probabilities, not exfiltrate.

No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json; no telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics in src is empty). SDK adds X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers only. npm publish uses provenance. Single maintainer, 6 versions in 10 days, so a supply-chain trust question for a new package.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.dataEgress: On a live check (not dry-run/mock): for each in-scope target, the full text of the Markdown spec (tables replaced with '[table omitted]'), the full contents of every file matched by codePaths (up to 500 files, 2 MiB each, 120,000 chars total per target), the rubric questions/options, and the model name go in one JSON POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or the custom base URL such as OpenRouter). With OpenRouter this means code goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. No git diffs are sent (--staged/--diff only select targets; the whole target is sent), and Claude Code prompts/tool outputs are not involved. Nothing is sent for untouched targets in --staged mode. No redaction.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.failureMode: Fail-closed by design (docs/specs/fail-closed.md): any error yields exit 2, unreadable/NaN answers fail assertions, oversize targets abort the run before anything is sent, missing API key aborts unless --mock/--dry-run. Default SDK timeout is 10 s (jev-evaluator.ts:218 timeoutMs ?? 10_000) with SDK maxRetries 2 and backoff (sdk index.mjs:74), so a slow or down Jev could stall a hook for tens of seconds, then return 2 and block a commit. Claude Code would only be blocked if you wire it into a pre-commit or Claude Code hook yourself and treat 2 as blocking.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.latencyImpact: README claims 0.3-0.9 s per target live request (maintainer's laptop, unverified) plus about 0.1 s Node startup; a pre-commit run adds roughly 0.5-1.5 s per touched target. Zero latency on ordinary Claude Code turns because nothing is wired into Claude Code automatically; the skills only run when triggered.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. Two skills add only their name+description to the always-on listing: about 402 + 508 chars, roughly 230 tokens total. Full SKILL.md bodies load only when triggered: jev-spec-init 20,429 bytes (about 5k tokens) and jev-spec-fix 10,427 bytes (about 2.6k tokens). No hook-injected text.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model-discretion). jev-spec-init fires when the user talks about spec checks, setup or CI gating; jev-spec-fix when a jev-spec check fails. Neither makes Claude Code call Jev on its own during ordinary coding. The CLI itself runs only if the project has a jev-spec.config.ts and something (git pre-commit hook, CI, or the agent following the skill) invokes it. No deterministic hook, no MCP tool, no proxy is shipped.
pros: Real, working, well-tested Jev consumer using the correct System One primitives (noul/choice/score) with per-target thresholds and deterministic exit codes; genuinely fits Jev's typed-decision design rather than pretending it is a chat model.

Talks to the same /v1/systemone path with a Bearer key (SDK index.mjs:554,581), and the base URL, key and model are all overridable, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api is a config-only change (allowCustomBaseUrl:true, model 'typesafe/jev-1.13').
Cheap and fast for a commit gate: one request per touched target, --staged/--diff skip untouched targets and need no key, --dry-run validates offline.

Strong safety posture for its size: fail-closed exit codes, execFile without shell, root-jail and symlink checks, custom-URL opt-in guard, npm provenance, no postinstall, no telemetry, ~195 tests plus self-spec probes.
Tiny always-on context footprint (~230 tokens for both skill descriptions), no MCP tool schemas.

Skills are cleanly written and could help the agent set up and fix spec gates in spec-driven projects; the pre-commit use case can be wired outside Claude Code (git hook) so it is deterministic and not dependent on model discretion.
cons: Not an integration of Jev INTO Claude Code: no MCP server, hook, plugin manifest or router. It gives Claude Code no automatic Jev usage during coding; automatic behaviour requires you to write a git pre-commit or Claude Code PreToolUse/Stop hook yourself.

Only useful in repos that have Markdown specs with requirement IDs and a hand-written jev-spec.config.ts (rubrics per requirement, tuned thresholds). Most personal and client projects have no such specs, so utility for daily coding is narrow; the jev-spec-init workflow is heavy (20 KB skill, threshold tuning against the live model).

OpenRouter support is only by inference: no OpenRouter code path, docs or tests, key must go into a TYPESAFE_*-named variable or config apiKey, and the response schema on OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified against what mapAnswers expects (answer.noul, probabilities, legend).

Sends entire matched source files unredacted to a third party (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe if routed that way); for client projects this is a confidentiality/contract issue, and the default 10 s timeout with 2 retries could make a hook hang before failing closed.
Executes jev-spec.config.ts via jiti on every run, including dry-run, so cloning an untrusted client repo and running the tool executes its code.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-20, 6 npm versions in 9 days, 11 stars, 54 of 115 commits by 'Cursor Agent'), explicitly unaffiliated with TypeSafe; accuracy claims (29/29 probes) come from its own author, and its own README lists Jev accuracy limits (large targets, non-English, tables not sent, literal question phrasing needed).
Probabilities are non-deterministic-ish gating signals: false positives will block commits and false negatives give a false sense of safety; pre-commit gating on a beta model adds friction.
gh-nozomi-koborinai-jev-spec.verdict: A solid, safe, honest spec-drift linter that genuinely uses Jev, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with a config-only change, but it is a niche CI/pre-commit tool rather than a Claude Code integration and will not make Claude use Jev automatically. Worth adopting only for spec-driven repos, wired as a git pre-commit hook; do not count it as the answer to the automatic-integration goal.

gh-lpliu-art-kestrel.name: kestrel-review
gh-lpliu-art-kestrel.whatItDoes: Open-source (community, explicitly not affiliated with TypeSafe) code-review CLI `kestrel` (npm kestrel-review 0.4.3). A deterministic pipeline reads the git diff, matches builtin rule packs (TS/JS, Python, Java, Go, Rust, C#), compiles each rule into typed Jev Choice/Noul/Score questions, sends redacted diff hunks to Jev, bands the probabilities into report/uncertain/drop, and emits line-anchored findings (terminal, JSON, SARIF, Markdown, PR gate). Ships a SKILL.md and two slash commands (/kestrel review, explain) for Claude Code that just shell out to the CLI; Claude writes the prose. It is a code-review-on-diff tool, not a generic Jev decision layer.

Overlaps with Claude Opus itself, which already reviews well; value is a cheap second-opinion gate, not a Jev-in-the-loop for Claude's own decisions; findings are template text from rules, coverage limited to shipped rule packs
gh-lpliu-art-kestrel.verdict: A legitimate but very young, community-made Jev-based diff reviewer that could be pointed at OpenRouter with a base-URL override and is cheap on context, yet it is only a manually or phrase-triggered review skill, not an automatic Jev integration. Treat it as an optional pinned CLI (installed globally, not via npx) behind your own commit/Stop hook rather than the core solution.

gh-hemanth-tool-prune.name: tool-prune
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.whatItDoes: Tiny JS/Python library (not an MCP server, hook, or plugin). Given a query and a tool catalog, it returns the best-matching tool(s) with probabilities, and can prune a large tool list to the top-K before the list goes to an LLM. It has two engines: an offline TurboQuant vector search, which is the default, and a cloud call to TypeSafe System One (Jev) that uses a Choice question over the tool descriptions plus a Noul 'requires_generation' question. It also has dispatch(), which runs a handler directly when confidence is at least 0.85. It has no Claude Code integration at all.

The API key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or options and goes in an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv.
The library does not read .env. Only the bench script bench/run.mjs:11-16 does, and it regex-parses TYPESAFE_API_KEY out of a .env file. That is bench code and is not shipped in the npm package.
No telemetry found in the library code.
The optional dependency turboquant-search is loaded by dynamic import, which adds a supply-chain surface if it is installed.
There is no timeout or AbortController on fetch. A hung request hangs the caller.
Tool descriptions and the query go into the request. A poisoned tool description could steer selection, and dispatch() would then auto-run a handler when confidence >= 0.85.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.dataEgress: Only with the typesafe engine (an API key is set): the whole `state` object (the raw query string, or whatever object the caller passes, e.g. {intent: prompt}) and the full criteria map (every tool name and description), sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. With no key, everything runs offline and nothing leaves the machine. Any Claude Code wrapper would have to send the user prompt and the tool catalog, and possibly code context, to a third party.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the library. A non-2xx response throws 'tool-prune API error', and network errors propagate. There is no timeout, no retry, and no automatic fallback to the offline engine. The engine is chosen only by whether a key is present, so a failing cloud call does not degrade to turboquant. A wrapper would have to add try/catch and a timeout.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.contextCost: The library adds 0 tools and 0 tokens to Claude Code, because it is not wired in. Its only relevance to context is as a technique: pruning MCP tool schemas before they reach the LLM. Claude Code's MCP tool search and deferred tools already do this natively. The user's setup (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) has roughly 60 tools that are already deferred.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.latencyImpact: Cloud engine: about 189 ms per call by the README's own BFCL table, a self-reported figure I did not verify. Offline engine: under 20 ms. Nothing is added to Claude Code today. The library would only matter if someone builds a wrapper such as an MCP server, hook or proxy around it, and each call would then add the 70-500 ms network round trip.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.autoInvocation: None. It is a library that a developer imports into their own agent code. There is no hook, MCP server, skill or proxy, so it cannot be invoked automatically by Claude Code. Claude Code would need a custom wrapper, and the model plans and selects its own tools, so tool routing is not something Claude Code lets an external component do.
pros: MIT, zero required dependencies, no install scripts. The published npm tarball matches the repo source (I diffed lib/).

It shows a concrete Jev request shape: choice with a criteria map, plus a noul question, posted to /v1/systemone with Bearer auth. That is a useful reference for writing an OpenRouter System One client (js/lib/router.js:77-101).
A sensible offline fallback engine, and the calibrated 'confidence >= threshold' dispatch idea is reasonable as a design.
Small and easy to audit (334 lines of router code).
cons: It is not an integration. There is no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it gives Claude Code no automatic behavior.

It solves a problem Claude Code does not have. Claude Code chooses tools itself, and its native deferred tool search already handles large MCP catalogs. An external router cannot intercept or restrict the tool list per turn.
It talks only to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY. There is no OpenRouter support, and the model default 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID.
Fail-closed and no timeout: the cloud call has no fallback to the offline engine and no AbortController.
Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 15 commits, 1 contributor, 7 stars, no releases, CI only deploys the docs site, and the PyPI version lags npm.
The headline benchmarks (100% top-1, 97.5% end-to-end) are self-reported, run on BFCL and synthetic catalogs, and I did not verify them. The Python package is at 0.2.0 against JS 0.3.0.
Sending the user's prompts and tool catalog to a third party would be a data-egress problem on client projects, in exchange for no clear gain.
gh-hemanth-tool-prune.verdict: Not usable for the goal. It is a tool-routing library for people building their own agents, with no Claude Code integration and no OpenRouter support. Skip it, but keep js/lib/router.js:77-129 as a reference for the Jev choice/noul request and response shape when building a custom OpenRouter-based hook.

gh-guschi18-turnprune.name: @turnprune/core (TurnPrune)
gh-guschi18-turnprune.whatItDoes: Agent-neutral library that, once per user turn, sends the previous turn's tool outputs to Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via the OpenRouter Decisions API, one Noul question per output: "is this needed for the current request?") and replaces outputs with relevance below 0.4 by a fixed placeholder to cut context cost and preserve the prompt-cache prefix. The only shipped adapter is for OpenCode 2 (@turnprune/opencode). The Claude Code adapter is only listed as "planned" in docs/architecture.md and the README. So the core is not usable in Claude Code today.

providerSupport.evidence: packages/core/src/selector.ts:7-8: JEV_MODEL = 'typesafe/jev-1.13'; DECISIONS_URL = 'https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions'. selector.ts:227-233: POST with 'Authorization: Bearer ${apiKey}', JSON body {model, state:{current_request, active_goal, repository}, questions:{relevance_N:{type:'noul', instructions, criteria}}}, AbortSignal.timeout(1500). Key comes only from the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var (pruner.ts:482 throws if missing; README says 'never read from config files'). SelectorOptions has a url override (selector.ts:~208) but no env var for it. No TypeSafe direct endpoint or TYPESAFE_API_KEY in code.
providerSupport.others: None. Only OpenRouter Decisions API. The README documents Jev on OpenRouter alpha endpoint only.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Already OpenRouter. The Decisions API request shape here (noul questions with instructions/criteria plus a state object) is a useful working reference for the user's own hook, but it is not a drop-in for Claude Code.

security: MIT license (LICENSE present).
API key from env var only, sent as Bearer header over HTTPS. Not in argv, so not visible in the process list.
No runtime dependencies in core. opencode package depends only on @turnprune/core. No postinstall/preinstall scripts (grep of package.json files).
No child_process, exec or telemetry found in packages/*/src.

Secret handling: regex redaction (private keys, api_key/token/password=..., Bearer, sk-/ghp_/github_pat_, AKIA) and a sensitive-path blocklist (.env, .npmrc, id_rsa, *.pem, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh) that pins such tool work and never sends it. Pattern-based only, so secrets in unusual formats can still leak.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output content (untrusted file/log/web text) is embedded in the Jev request as candidate.content. Jev returns only numeric probabilities, so injection can at worst bias a keep/drop decision. It cannot execute anything. A drop can hide needed context from the main model, though.
Repo is 4 days old, single author, 0 stars, no releases, no security review or signed provenance. Alpha Decisions endpoint.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.dataEgress: Per README Privacy section and selector.ts: to openrouter.ai only, the candidate tool outputs (redacted, capped 20,000 chars each, up to 60 per batch, 200 kB, 20 batches), the user's current message (redacted, capped) used as current_request and active_goal, and the repository path. Anything matching secret patterns or credential-file paths is not sent. This means source code, logs and test output from client projects go to OpenRouter and Jev on every user turn. That may conflict with client confidentiality terms. The main model provider still gets the whole context.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.failureMode: Fail-open. The Jev call has a 1500 ms timeout (configurable 500-5000). Missing key, HTTP error, timeout or invalid answer means the context goes out unchanged, or with the already-frozen prefix. The tool loop adds about 1 ms and makes no Jev call. Once per user turn the hook blocks for the Jev round trip (README: p95 0.9-1.6 s). Under context pressure (80% of window) it re-judges on every request.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.contextCost: Zero tool or MCP context cost, because it is not an MCP server or skill (no tool defs, no server instructions, no hook-injected text). Its effect is the opposite: it removes stale tool outputs from the prompt. It replaces them with a 95-character placeholder. But this only works where the host allows rewriting the message list before each model request (OpenCode's context hook). Claude Code has no equivalent hook today (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit can add context or block, but cannot rewrite prior tool_result content already in the transcript). So even a Claude Code adapter would need an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy in front of the API.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.autoInvocation: Transparent in-process context hook, fully automatic in OpenCode 2 (no user prompting). For Claude Code there is no integration. The only route would be a custom local proxy pointed to by ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL that rewrites /v1/messages bodies with the core. That is not built, and the user's subscription/OAuth login makes a base-URL proxy awkward.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.latencyImpact: About 0.9-1.6 s p95 once per user turn (README measurement, capped at timeoutMs, default 1.5 s). About 1 ms per tool-loop step. Re-judging on every request when the context is above 80% of the window. There is also an indirect cost: pruning rewrites part of the prompt cache once per turn, so short sessions can cost more than they save.
pros: Real, working use of Jev on OpenRouter: the correct endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions), a correct noul request shape, the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var, and typesafe/jev-1.13 (selector.ts:7-8, 227-233). It is a useful reference for the request format.

Well-thought-out safety design: fail-open on every error, 1.5 s hard timeout, secret redaction plus credential-file pinning before anything is sent, a kill switch, content-free state storage, no runtime dependencies and no postinstall.
Cache-aware policy (prune only behind the cached prefix, reuse in tool loops, cost check before refresh) and a reproducible metric replay. This is more careful than a naive context trimmer.
Honest README with measured numbers: about -21% billed cost on a 200k-token session, and an explicit warning that short sessions can cost more.
CI on ubuntu Node 22 and 24, macOS and Windows; about 1,400 lines of tests (core.test.ts, pruner.test.ts, stats.test.ts, plugin.test.ts, cli.test.ts). Jev cost is about $0.004 per session.
cons: No Claude Code adapter exists. docs/architecture.md says 'Claude Code / Codex: planned', and no Claude Code file, hook config, plugin.json or .mcp.json exists in the repo (grep for 'claude' returns only planning text). It cannot be installed into Claude Code today.

Claude Code has no context-rewrite hook. Integrating would need an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy that mutates /v1/messages requests. That is a new project, it conflicts with subscription/OAuth login, it breaks prompt-cache assumptions if done wrong, and it is risky for client work.

Mutating the transcript changes what Opus sees. Jev only sees the new user message, so a short 'ok continue' can drop something needed later. The README admits this, and the cost is extra tool re-runs.
Sends tool outputs (source code, logs) and the repo path to OpenRouter every user turn. Redaction is regex-based and could miss secrets, and it may not be acceptable for client projects.

Savings claims come from a single OpenCode session on cheap models (glm-5.3-flash, gpt-5.6-luna) with 16 prompts. Claude with an already-efficient cache and auto-compaction may see much less benefit. Added latency of about 1 s per turn.

Very immature: created 2026-09-25, 12 commits by one author in 2 days, npm 0.1.0 to 0.1.3 published within 4 hours on 2026-09-26, 0 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases. It targets the alpha Decisions endpoint, which may change.
It solves a narrow problem (pruning old tool output). It is not a general Jev integration for routing, permission decisions or code-review classification.
gh-guschi18-turnprune.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code: only an OpenCode adapter ships, the Claude Code adapter is unbuilt, and Claude Code offers no hook to rewrite prior tool results without a custom API proxy. Treat it as a well-engineered reference for the OpenRouter noul request shape, fail-open design and secret redaction, not as something to install.

gh-kelbie-hunch.name: @kelbie/hunch
gh-kelbie-hunch.whatItDoes: CLI (hunch, npm @kelbie/hunch) plus an Agent Skill (skills/hunch/SKILL.md, installed via `npx skills add Kelbie/hunch`). `find` chops the repo into chunks and asks Jev a yes/no (Noul) or 5-facet task question (edit/contract/caller/test/precedent) about EVERY chunk, returning scored file:line locations (semantic grep / context gathering). `check` reviews diffs or whole files against plain-English rules (Noul/Choice/Score), usable in CI/GitHub App, with rule packs, hunch.lock compiled AGENTS.md guidance, and `eval` for precision/recall. Providers in code: Vercel AI Gateway (AI SDK experimental_evaluate, model typesafe-ai/jev), TypeSafe direct REST (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone), and local SemIf (open model). No MCP server, no hooks.

Credential store allows only AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (packages/cli/src/credentials.ts:10). schema.ts:167 default model 'jev-1.13.0'.

providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial-to-moderate. typesafeClient already accepts opts.baseUrl (jev.ts:102) and posts to `${base}/systemone`, which matches OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone path with a request body of model/state/questions. A ~6-line patch in provider.ts (baseUrl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, key OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model 'typesafe/jev-1.13') should work if OpenRouter's response schema equals TypeSafe's (answers[id].type noul/choice/score, .noul/.choice/.probabilities, usage.input_tokens) since responseSchema (jev.ts:142-152) is strict zod; unverified. Requires forking/vendoring since baseUrl and key names are not exposed via env/config and `npx @kelbie/hunch` would ignore local patches; also credentials.ts key allowlist and isAuthError regex need extending.

gh-kelbie-hunch.dataEgress: `find` and `check --all` send the source text of every in-scope chunk of the repository (whole-file chunks with line numbers, plus the question) to the selected provider: Vercel AI Gateway, api.typesafe.ai, or nothing with SemIf. `check` sends changed diff hunks plus configured reference context. Not just the user's prompt: whole client codebases leave the machine on a broad sweep (find.md tells the agent NOT to narrow scope; use --dry-run to price). Respects hunch include/ignore config; no secret scanning of chunks, so .env-like files not in ignore could be sent (the existing secret-leak guard hook would not see this since it runs inside a Bash subprocess of npx, though Bash matcher might catch some patterns). gh-kelbie-hunch.failureMode: Fail-loud rather than fail-open for the agent: exit 2 = could not run/incomplete ("never report a clean review"). No auth/402/ZDR errors stop the run on the first request; 429s retried (gateway: 5 retries, 90s cap per call; typesafe: 3 attempts, 45s cap); 8 consecutive failures = outage abort with partial results and notice; per-chunk failures recorded as unsearched. Automatic provider fallback chain gateway/typesafe -> SemIf if nothing answered yet (--no-fallback disables). Because it is an on-demand CLI call from a skill, a hung or slow Jev only stalls that one Bash call (Bash tool timeout 2-10 min), not every tool call; nothing blocks normal Claude Code operation.
gh-kelbie-hunch.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero hook text. Skill listing entry ~ 1,000 chars description (~250 tokens) always in context; when triggered SKILL.md is 14,122 chars (~3.5k tokens) and it instructs reading a per-verb reference (find.md etc., several k more tokens); find output (default top 12 with source excerpts, or --top 0 all matches) adds further tokens per call. Modest and lazy compared with an MCP server.
gh-kelbie-hunch.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). SKILL.md instructs 'Run it early... on unfamiliar code find is the cheapest way...', so Claude may reach for it on exploration tasks without being told 'use jev', but nothing deterministic: no hook, no MCP, no proxy. GitNexus/grep habits of Claude Code will compete. Even the autoinvoked path calls `find`, which is a whole-repo sweep, not a cheap per-decision call.
gh-kelbie-hunch.latencyImpact: Per invocation, not per tool call. Jev's claimed 70-500 ms per request is amortised across thousands of chunks. Docs explicitly say 'do not promise a fixed price or latency'. Blocks the Bash call for the duration.

security: No MCP server and no hooks, so no new tool surface or PreToolUse interaction. The only agent-facing artifact is a markdown skill.
API key is read from env (PERCH_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv. doctor prints only the key length and never its value (src/checks.js:37).
Shell execution is limited to git via execFile/spawn with an argument array and '-c core.hooksPath=/dev/null' (src/git.js:12,67). There is no shell string and no curl|sh installer.

The published package has a 'prepare' script (node build.mjs), but it does not run for a registry install and build.mjs is not in 'files'. No postinstall. The tree-sitter pack downloads parsers from GitHub releases at first use, a runtime network fetch of native or wasm code from a third party.

Prompt-injection surface: the Jev output is typed and probabilistic, with no free text, so findings cannot carry instructions. The skill does tell the model to read the code before changing it and never to rewrite working code to satisfy a probability. Rule files under .perch/rules are repo content, so a hostile repo can define rules, but they only become model questions.

Default credential path (no PERCH_BASE_URL) is Perch Cloud, a separate third-party SaaS at dash.perchscan.com. It also receives repository name and scan results (/v1/scans/start|append|finish). Avoid it, or set PERCH_BASE_URL.
Explicit telemetry: none found in grep. The Cloud path reports scans by design.
Young project. The npm maintainer is a single account (jfbrown95), and there were 11 versions in 8 days, so supply-chain risk is not negligible.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.dataEgress: In direct mode (PERCH_BASE_URL set) the following goes to the configured endpoint (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe): for each method or file, the request body is {model, state:{path, name, line, source: full method or file source, plus 'seen' context such as callees, callers and neighbours}, questions:{rule text and criteria}} (src/units.js:319, src/systemone.js:34). That is real source code, up to 24k tokens of state per request, across many requests per scan. Only methods changed or tracked in git HEAD are read, using git cat-file at the committed HEAD, but 'check' reads files from disk. Diffs, conversation text and tool outputs are not sent, and neither are .env files, unless they are committed and in scope. Results are cached locally in .perch/. With the Cloud default, the same content plus organizationId, repositoryId and the git remote name goes to dash.perchscan.com. For client projects, OpenRouter (and TypeSafe behind it) sees client source code, so check the client's policy. OpenRouter's logging and data-collection settings are a separate control.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.failureMode: Not in the critical path of Claude Code: perch is a separate CLI that only runs when the model or the user invokes it. The client retries network errors and HTTP 429/5xx up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff, starting at 2 s and honouring Retry-After (src/systemone.js:38-52). 401/402/403 abort the whole run at once with an AuthenticationError. The direct-mode fetch has NO per-request timeout (AbortSignal.timeout only in the Cloud paths, cloud-auth.js:17,76,163), so a hung TCP connection can stall a scan. Errors exit 1, and findings exit 3, which the skill tells the agent to read as a result and not a crash. In practice it fails open with respect to Claude Code, since the agent just sees an error from a Bash call. It is not a gate unless it is wired into CI or hooks, and the user would need to add that.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.latencyImpact: Zero on ordinary turns, since it is invoked only via a Bash tool call. A scan or check adds seconds to minutes, because it makes one request per method (a rolling pool of 32 concurrent, commit 7e1c704), and Jev claims 70-500 ms per call. The first run also downloads the tree-sitter parsers. 'perch check' on one method is about 2 requests, and the skill says it costs a fraction of a cent (README example: 5k tokens, $0.0002). A scan of a branch costs about $0.0004 in the skill's example. A whole-repo scan is hundreds of requests.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. The skill adds only its name and description (about 90 words, roughly 130 tokens) to the always-loaded listing. The full skill.md (188 lines, roughly 1.9k tokens) loads only when the description triggers. There are no hooks and no injected text per turn. It is the cheapest option in context terms. The per-project .claude/skills copy means it only appears in repos where perch setup was run, unless the file is copied to ~/.claude/skills.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model-discretion). The description says 'verify code changes in flight, scan a branch or diff, check one method right after editing, confirm a fix landed before opening a PR'. Claude Code loads the skill on its own judgement, and then Claude runs the perch CLI via Bash. There is no deterministic hook. The perch author observed for Cursor that description matching is unreliable and worked around it with alwaysApply: true (src/setup.js:38-46). Claude Code has no such option, so triggering will be probabilistic. To make it automatic and reliable you would add your own PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write or a pre-PR/Stop hook that runs perch check, and that is not shipped.
pros: Truly uses Jev for a coding job (bug and semantic-rule detection with calibrated probabilities), which is the most direct 'Jev inside coding workflow' example found, and it matches Jev's typed-decision design (Choice/Noul/Score) rather than misusing it as a chat model.

OpenRouter works by configuration alone: PERCH_BASE_URL and PERCH_API_KEY are honoured (src/cloud-client.js:110,121), and OpenRouter documents /api/v1/systemone as TypeSafe-SDK compatible with bare model IDs mapped to typesafe/. This has not been tested end to end.

Very cheap on context: no MCP tools, no hooks, about 130 tokens of always-on skill description, and a small footprint that will not interfere with the existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks.

Not in the critical path: an outage cannot block Claude Code. Retries with backoff are built in, and 402/401 abort the run cleanly with a clear message. Exit-code semantics (3 = findings, not a failure) are documented for agents.
Incremental and cached: unchanged methods are skipped, --since origin/main scopes to a branch, and check works on uncommitted code, so post-edit checks are about $0.0002 and quick.

Active and reasonably engineered for its age: 137 commits (130 by one author) in 14 days, 316 stars, 34 test files, CI with lint, typecheck, tests, CodeQL and release-please, MIT license, and a clean source tree with an execFile array and a hardened git call (core.hooksPath=/dev/null).
Rules are user-definable (perch.yaml), so client-specific conventions can be encoded as semantic lints and reused.
cons: Auto-invocation is only probabilistic. It is a skill triggered by description and is not a hook, and the author's own note in src/setup.js says description matching can miss ('fix this bug' does not read as semantic linting). Achieving 'always used when needed' needs a self-built PostToolUse or Stop hook, which is not provided.

Sends real source code (full methods plus callers and neighbours, up to 24k tokens per request, many requests) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a client-confidentiality decision for client projects, and there is no local-only mode. The default path without PERCH_BASE_URL sends it to a third-party SaaS (Perch Cloud) as well.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-16, 11 releases in 8 days, 0.x API, pre-1.0 CLI flags will churn. It was published by one npm account, and the dependency chain includes a runtime parser download from GitHub releases. Treat it as beta.

No per-request timeout in direct mode (src/systemone.js uses bare fetch), and a whole-repo scan means hundreds of requests, so cost and time can surprise. It is opt-in per scan, and the skill warns against scanning everything.

Only a linter or reviewer, not a general decision or routing layer. It does not cover the broader ideas for Jev in Claude Code (tool choice, routing, permission classification, commit triage), and its quality depends on Jev's bug-detection model, whose claims (the Theo skepticism) are unverified. Finding noise is possible: the docs explain how rules can answer 'in the sixties' about everything.

Bug/finding quality for your stack is unverified. Tree-sitter language coverage and first-run parser download add friction, and it needs a git repo with at least one commit (scan reads HEAD, not the worktree, except for check).

OpenRouter compatibility (usage and charge fields, the 128-option Choice limit, 24k state) is inferred from docs only. Perch's message strings and limits mention Perch Cloud's bug model, so a quirk on OpenRouter is plausible.
gh-lakeday-org-perch.verdict: The best-fitting Jev tool for actual daily coding found so far: a cheap, non-invasive skill and CLI that works with OpenRouter through two env vars and costs almost nothing in context. However, auto-invocation is only description-triggered, and for real automation you would need to add a small PostToolUse or pre-PR hook yourself. Use it as a complement (post-edit or pre-PR semantic lint) rather than as the whole integration, and only on repos where sending source to OpenRouter is acceptable.

Default model is 'jev-1.13.0' (config.ts:6). Nothing in the source, docs or tests mentions OpenRouter.
providerSupport.others: None. Only api.typesafe.ai.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate, and it needs a fork. Three changes: (1) src/jev.ts:29 baseURL to `https://openrouter.ai/api` (the SDK appends /v1/systemone, matching OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone), or read it from an env var; (2) src/config.ts to accept OPENROUTER_API_KEY; (3) `--model typesafe/jev-1.13`. The third is a problem because src/cache.ts:16 only enables the persistent cache for ids matching /^jev-\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/, so an OpenRouter id like typesafe/jev-1.13 would silently turn off the cache and make repeated searches pay every time. The regex must also be changed. Whether OpenRouter's systemone response matches what src/jev.ts:12-20 parses (`answers.<id>.type=='noul'`, `.noul` as a number, `usage.input_tokens` and `output_tokens`) is unverified. It probably matches, because the OpenRouter route is described as the same System One API, but a shape mismatch would surface as `protocol_error`. I ran nothing, so none of this is tested.

gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.runtime: Node >=22 (TypeScript compiled to dist/). Dependencies: @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, commander, dotenv, ignore, picomatch.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.install: npm install --global nlgrep, or npx nlgrep. Not needed for this audit and not run. The package has no postinstall script (the only scripts are build, test and prepack).
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.tests: 48 offline tests in test/*.test.ts (about 500 lines across 9 files) using mocked HTTP. CI runs check plus package smoke on Node 22 and 24, with actions pinned by SHA. The live eval is synthetic: 40 queries over 120 tiny files (6.7 KB total). Result: 39/40 correct at threshold 0.8. This is self-labelled and not independently reviewed. Author-reported spend across 233 calls is about $0.01.
security: API key is read from JEV_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment, or from a `.env` in the current directory only (src/config.ts). It is never taken from argv, so it does not show in the process list. It is sent as a Bearer header via the SDK. The SDK logLevel is off.

A cwd `.env` fallback means a key sitting in a client project's .env could be picked up. nlgrep itself always excludes .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa* and id_ed25519* from scanning (README). The README says filename exclusion is not real secret detection, so secrets inside ordinary source files are sent to the API.
No child_process or exec anywhere in src (grep hit nothing). No telemetry found in src or in the SDK. It makes no outbound calls other than the systemone POST. There is no postinstall and no curl|sh.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents go into the Jev state. Jev returns typed probabilities only, not free text. src/prompt.ts tells the model to treat source as data. The worst case is a manipulated probability (false positive or negative). The model cannot run commands or choose paths.
The local cache in .nlgrep/cache-v1/ stores only hashes, probabilities and model names, not source text (README, cache.ts).

Supply-chain risk: a brand-new single-maintainer package (npm maintainer ethan98), published 2026-09-20 with 3 versions in 40 minutes. Auto-publish from main via GitHub Actions. Pinned dependencies. The transitive @typesafe-ai/sdk is the vendor SDK.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.dataEgress: On every uncached search these leave the machine for api.typesafe.ai: the query text; each file's relative path, line count and content hash; and the raw source text of every scanned file or 40-line window, up to 24 KiB per request. The scan covers everything not gitignored, hidden, binary or in the built-in exclusion list, and it is capped by --max-bytes (20 MiB) and --max-requests (1000). Nothing else is sent. It does not send the Claude Code conversation, diffs or tool outputs unless the user pipes them via stdin. For client projects this means bulk upload of proprietary source to a third-party beta inference vendor, and to OpenRouter as well if patched. Cache hits send nothing.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.failureMode: Fail-closed, but inside a subprocess. Each HTTP call has a 30 s timeout, SDK retries are off, and nlgrep has one own retry layer that honors retry-after and counts toward --max-requests. When the API is down, slow or the key is missing, nlgrep prints an error to stderr and exits 2 with partial results (`complete=false`). Nothing hangs beyond the timeouts. Since nlgrep is only a CLI, Claude Code would see a failed Bash call and fall back to Grep/Glob. Nothing global is broken.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.latencyImpact: Per search, not per turn. There is zero cost when it is not invoked. A search does about ceil(scanned bytes / 24 KiB) API calls at concurrency 4, each roughly 70-500 ms by TypeSafe's claim, so a search over a large directory takes seconds to minutes. Author-reported: 120 files became 40 calls, and the eval returned 73,680 input tokens for the 40-query run. Repeat searches over unchanged files hit the local cache and are instant.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.contextCost: Zero if used as a plain CLI, because there is no MCP server and no tool definitions. If the user makes their own skill or CLAUDE.md line for it, that costs roughly 100-300 tokens. Output is grep-style and capped by --top 20, so results are small. No hook-injected text.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a bare CLI. Claude Code would call it through Bash only if a CLAUDE.md line or SKILL.md description told it to prefer nlgrep for fuzzy or semantic queries. That is model-discretion at best, and it does not meet the user's "no explicit prompt" requirement without a wrapper. A deterministic PreToolUse hook that rewrites Grep to nlgrep would be a bad idea, because Grep takes exact regexes and every call would cost money and latency. There is no MCP, hook or skill packaging in the repo.
pros: Real, working Jev integration that is well written and small (about 980 lines of TypeScript). It uses the Noul primitive properly, with a typed per-window P(yes) and a threshold.

Cost and safety controls are unusually good: --dry-run, --max-requests, --max-bytes, a persistent hash-keyed cache with no source text stored, and a 30 s timeout. Cache hits make repeat searches free.
No key in argv, no shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall, MIT license, SHA-pinned CI actions. Auditable in 15 minutes.
Zero context-window cost and no effect on the existing hooks (gitnexus, secret guard) or MCP servers. It is opt-in and fails cleanly.

Useful niche for queries grep and GitNexus handle poorly: 'code that awaits fetch in a loop' or 'auth check missing in this handler', run against a narrowed path, or a log pipe such as `tail -2000 app.log | nlgrep ...`.
Its Noul-per-window pattern is a good reference design for a custom wrapper.
cons: Hard-coded https://api.typesafe.ai (src/jev.ts:29). It does not work with OpenRouter as shipped. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL cannot override it, and a fork is required. The cache regex in src/cache.ts:16 would also break on OpenRouter model IDs.
Not an integration into Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hook or skill, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic use without prompting.
Sends bulk raw source to a third-party inference vendor. That is a real problem for client projects under NDA, and the path filter is not secret detection.

Pays and waits on every uncached search. Claude Code's Grep and GitNexus are free, instant and exact, and this is slower and probabilistic. Semantic search is what GitNexus 'query' and Opus reading files already do.
Weak evidence of quality: a synthetic 120-file corpus with self-written labels and a prompt tuned on the same data. There is no run on a real repository and no external review.

Very immature: 4 commits, 1 contributor, 4 stars, all created 2026-09-20 and published 3 versions in 40 minutes. It depends on the beta 0.x TypeSafe SDK. Judgments only see 40-line windows or batches, so absence claims across files are unreliable (the README concedes this).
Docs like SPEC.md, SCENARIOS.md and EVALUATION.md are in Chinese.
gh-yehuitang0316-jev-nlgrep.verdict: A tidy, safe-looking semantic-grep CLI built on the Noul primitive. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill, so it cannot integrate into Claude Code automatically, and it hard-codes the TypeSafe endpoint, so OpenRouter needs a fork plus a cache-regex fix. Treat it as a reference implementation or an optional manual tool, not the daily-coding integration.

gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.name: jev-firewall (PyPI, realahsanshah / jev-action-firewall)
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.whatItDoes: Python library (not a Claude Code hook or MCP server) that gates an agent framework's tool calls: hard local regex floors, then one Jev System One call (severity Choice, is_irreversible Noul, matches_stated_goal Noul) over redacted tool name, args and one-line goal, mapped to ALLOW/HOLD/DENY via policy.yaml, with fail_mode, approval channels and a JSONL audit log. Adapters exist for LangGraph, LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK and Semantic Kernel only. There is no Claude Code integration in the source (grep for Claude Code, PreToolUse and settings.json finds nothing). A CLI 'eval' subcommand exists, so a user-written PreToolUse hook wrapper could shell out to it.

providerSupport.evidence: src/jev_firewall/jev/__init__.py:43-50 ROUTE_DEFAULTS: direct -> TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model jev-1.13.0; openrouter -> OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model ~typesafe/jev-latest, base_url https://openrouter.ai/api; vercel -> AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; cloudflare -> CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN + CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID. build_jev_client reads the key only from the route's env var (or jev.api_key_env). It goes through typesafe_sdk.AsyncTypeSafeClient(base_url=...) in src/jev_firewall/jev/sdk_backend.py:35-52, i.e. the SDK's System One endpoint under the OpenRouter base URL (presumably /v1/systemone; the path is inside the typesafe-sdk dependency and was not read). policy.yaml selects it with 'jev: {route: openrouter}'. The OpenRouter route was only tested with mock HTTP transports (tests/test_jev_backends.py); live tests need TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
providerSupport.others: Vercel AI Gateway (typesafe-ai/jev), Cloudflare Workers AI (typesafe/jev, own REST client src/jev_firewall/jev/cloudflare.py).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Not needed. OpenRouter is a built-in route, selected by config.

gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.tests: About 100 offline pytest tests (FakeJevClient plus mock HTTP transports) across 15 files. CI runs ruff, mypy strict and pytest on Linux and Windows with Python 3.11 to 3.13. Live-Jev tests are opt-in (JEV_LIVE_TESTS=1) and have never been run. The README says live accuracy, end-to-end latency and false-positive rates are not measured. Hard patterns alone catch 19 of 50 seeded harmful cases (0 of 40 benign blocked). The 'adversarial demo' uses an offline keyword stand-in, not Jev.
security: Key is read from the environment only (OPENROUTER_API_KEY for the openrouter route), never from argv. Keys are kept per route so a TypeSafe key is not sent to a gateway.

Redaction of args before they go to Jev or the audit log (src/jev_firewall/redact.py): sensitive key names, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Stripe, Slack and Google keys, JWTs, PEM keys, URL credentials, KEY=value secrets, PII. Long strings are truncated. This is regex-based, so misses are possible. Redaction is a useful complement to the user's existing secret-leak hook.

Prompt-injection posture is deliberate: local hard-pattern floors run first and cannot be lowered by Jev, and the rubric tells the model that tool_args are data. The README admits Jev is moved by adversarial text and that hard patterns alone catch only 19 of 50 harmful cases.
Data leaves the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe or its upstream. No telemetry beyond the Jev call. Audit log is local JSONL, append-only.
No postinstall or curl|sh installer; pure-Python wheel built with hatchling. Dependency chain is typesafe-sdk and httpx2 (both new, unaudited here).
The 'eval' CLI takes the tool args as a JSON argv string, so a hook wrapper would expose command text in the process list. Prefer the Python API, or a small stdin-based wrapper.
Single anonymous-ish maintainer, 3 days old, 0 stars, so supply-chain trust is low. Pin the version and hash if used.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.dataEgress: Per gated call, to the configured route (OpenRouter for this user), so on to TypeSafe: the tool name, the redacted tool arguments (for Bash this means the command text, for Write/Edit the file path and truncated content), and a one-line agent_goal (first user message by default). No conversation history, no tool outputs, no file contents beyond what appears in the tool args. Request is about 680 input tokens (estimated). Redacted args still reveal client project paths and command details. Nothing else is uploaded.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.failureMode: Explicit and required in policy.yaml (fail_mode: open|closed, per-tool override). Jev timeout, error, rate limit or malformed reply resolves through fail_mode: closed means DENY, open means ALLOW (hard-pattern floors still apply). timeout_s (example 1.0 s) is enforced three ways (SDK per-request timeout, retry budget, asyncio.timeout) with max_retries 1. For an unattended bypass or auto session, 'closed' would stall Claude on any OpenRouter blip and 'open' would degrade to hard patterns only. HOLD needs an approval channel (CLI prompt, webhook, timeout_deny). None of these map to Claude Code's permission 'ask' without custom glue.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.latencyImpact: Library overhead is about 1 ms (measured on Windows, no network). Live latency is unmeasured by the author. Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms per call, so roughly 70-500 ms added per gated tool call, times the many Bash/Edit/Write calls in a day. If run as a fresh 'jev-firewall eval' process per hook, add Python startup plus imports of typesafe-sdk, httpx2 and pydantic (a few hundred ms is likely; not measured). Read-only tools can be allowlisted ('read_*': action allow) to skip Jev.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.contextCost: Zero for the library or CLI: no MCP tools and no server instructions. A hook only adds text if the wrapper emits a deny reason or additionalContext. Nothing is injected by default.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.autoInvocation: None out of the box. It is a library wired into agent frameworks that the user owns the code of, and it cannot hook Claude Code, which is closed. To make it automatic in Claude Code you would write your own deterministic PreToolUse hook (a stdin JSON wrapper) that calls Firewall.evaluate and maps ALLOW/HOLD/DENY to allow/ask/deny. That is a deterministic hook design, but it is custom code, not this project.
pros: Native OpenRouter route with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model ~typesafe/jev-latest and base URL https://openrouter.ai/api (jev/__init__.py:44). Config-only switch, no patching.

Built for exactly the Jev use case: typed Choice/Noul questions on a minimal redacted state, thresholds in code. Good reference for a well-formed rubric (rubric.py) and for the Jev 1.13 guidance on wording.
Disciplined design: explicit fail_mode with no default, hard-pattern floors that Jev cannot lower, per-tool allowlists to skip Jev for reads, secret and PII redaction, JSONL audit.
Apache-2.0, typed, strict mypy, CI on Linux and Windows, about 100 offline tests.

Its policy.yaml, rubric and redaction could be reused as ideas or code for a custom Claude Code PreToolUse hook (a 'risk gate' for Bash) that fits the user's bypass/auto workflow. Python 3.13 and uv are already available.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no hook, MCP server, plugin or skill. Adapters cover only LangGraph, LangChain, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK and Semantic Kernel. Claude Code's own tool loop cannot be wrapped by these. Using it means writing and maintaining your own hook glue.

Solves a different problem than the user asked for. It is a safety gate for the agent's actions, not a way to have Claude use Jev for coding decisions. It only vetoes or escalates, and it adds no coding value.

Unproven with live Jev: accuracy, false-positive rate and end-to-end latency are all 'not measured'. Repeated false HOLDs or DENYs on ordinary Bash and Edit in a coding session are a real risk. Hard patterns catch only 19/50 harmful cases, so the remaining protection depends on Jev, which the README says can be moved by adversarial text.

Fail-mode dilemma for an unattended auto/bypass workflow: closed can block work during an OpenRouter outage, open weakens the gate. HOLD has no clean mapping to Claude Code's 'ask' without extra code.
Adds 70-500 ms network latency per gated call, plus process startup if run per call via CLI. The 'eval' CLI passes tool args in argv, which is visible in the process list.
Sends Bash commands and file paths (redacted only by regexes) from client projects to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a possible client-confidentiality problem.

Very immature: created 2026-09-27, 22 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, alpha, two releases on PyPI. Dependencies (typesafe-sdk 0.7.x, httpx2) are new. It overlaps with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, and Claude Code already has a permission system and its own auto-mode classifier.
gh-realahsanshah-jev-action-firewall.verdict: A well-designed but very young (3 days old, alpha, single author) Python guardrail library with a real OpenRouter route for Jev. It cannot be dropped into Claude Code, because it has no hook or MCP layer and only supports other agent frameworks. It gates actions rather than adding coding value, so it is only a reference for a custom PreToolUse risk-gate hook and not a solution to the user's goal.

You pipe or pass state (stdin, --state, --state-file, --state-json, --attach files) plus named --noul/--choice/--score questions, and it prints the official System One JSON to stdout. It is a plain shell tool, with no MCP server, hook or skill shipped. Its README only offers a 'skill blurb' to paste into your own CLAUDE.md or skill. The GitHub repo github.com/nikheal25/jev-kit returns 404 (private, deleted or never public), so only the npm tarball is auditable.

providerSupport.evidence: Not native, but env-patchable with no code change. dist/core/run.js:12 builds new TypeSafeClient({apiKey, defaultModel: model, fetch: logFetch}) with no baseURL. SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 dist/index.mjs:56-58 maps apiKey to TYPESAFE_API_KEY and baseURL to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Line 513 defaults the base URL to https://api.typesafe.ai. Line 554 does POST `${baseURL}/v1/systemone`. Line 581 sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. So TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, which is the OpenRouter System One URL in the brief. credentials.js:59 reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so an OpenRouter key can go there. Model: dist/core/run.js:8-11 reads JEV_KIT_MODEL, default 'jev-latest'. For OpenRouter set it to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest'. Unverified: that OpenRouter's /v1/systemone request body matches the SDK's {state, model, questions}. Also, cli/doctor.js:114 calls client.models.list() (GET /v1/models), and set-key validates the same way, so these may behave differently on OpenRouter (see security note on key handling).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Trivial if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is schema-compatible with TypeSafe's /v1/systemone (the brief suggests it is). providerSupport.others: None. Hard-wired to the TypeSafe SDK. Any other gateway works only through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.

gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.runtime: Node >=22 (user has Node 24). One dependency: @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. No postinstall or preinstall scripts. 'prepare: husky' is a dev-time script, but it would run on a git-clone install, not from the npm tarball.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.install: npm install -g jev-kit (README). The user's rules forbid running this in the audit. Recommended: pin the version, e.g. npm i -g jev-kit@0.1.30, or vendor the ~900 lines after reviewing them.
security: API key: env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or a saved key in ~/.jev-kit/config.json (dir 0700, file 0600, chmod before write; dist/config/credentials.js:73-88). There is no key CLI flag, so the key is never in argv or the process list. Good.

Sensitive-data log: EVERY run appends the full request body (all state, including piped diffs, test output and attached source files), the full response body and the response headers to ~/.jev-kit/logs/jev-kit-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (0600), with 14-day retention (dist/log/write-log.js:50-215). On a client-code machine this is a plaintext copy of code sent to Jev. Disable with JEV_KIT_LOG=off. Response headers are logged unredacted, but the request Authorization header is not captured, because only the body is recorded.

Prompt injection: state comes from untrusted diffs, logs or files and goes into a model that returns only typed probabilities. Injection can skew the numbers but cannot run anything. The help text says never to eval a Choice label. The real risk is that Claude over-trusts a skewed gate.
No shell execution, child_process, telemetry or extra network endpoints in jev-kit's own dist (grep). The only egress is through the SDK, to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or https://api.typesafe.ai.

set-key on OpenRouter: it validates via models.list() against whatever base URL is set. If it is run without TYPESAFE_BASE_URL set, it would send the OpenRouter key to api.typesafe.ai and fail. Set the env var in the same scope, or skip set-key and use env only.
Single unknown maintainer, repo unavailable, no npm provenance, so supply-chain trust is low. Pin the version and review the tarball. The tarball itself is small and clean.

Hook conflict: the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) may block or flag commands that pipe files or .env-like paths into jev-kit. Expect friction when using --attach on sensitive paths.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.dataEgress: Whatever the agent pipes or attaches goes to the endpoint in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (Bearer key in the header), plus the question text. That can include git diffs, test and lint output, and full source files via --attach or --state-file. There is a 32k-token state limit per request. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when Claude runs the command. Locally, the same content is written to the ~/.jev-kit/logs JSONL, which is not sent anywhere. Via OpenRouter, the OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies apply to client code.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.failureMode: Fail-open by nature, because it is a plain command Claude runs. On a Jev failure it exits 4 (no key/config) or 5 (E_API) with one stderr line and nothing on stdout, so Claude just gets a failed Bash call and carries on. Timeout is the SDK default of 10 s per attempt with maxRetries 2 (dist/index.mjs:74,518), so the worst case is roughly 30 s plus backoff. The wrapper adds no timeout override, and no flag exposes one. The logFetch wrapper is a passthrough that cannot break the call. There is no hook, so Jev can never block Claude Code.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.latencyImpact: Only when invoked. Node cold start is about 100-150 ms plus one HTTPS call (claimed 70-500 ms), so about 0.3-0.8 s per call. Zero when not invoked (nothing on every turn). Each invocation costs one Bash tool round trip for the model, so about 1-3 s of model time in total.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.contextCost: Close to zero standing cost. There are no MCP tools and no hooks. The only injected text is whatever the user adds: the README's 'skill blurb' is about 90 words (~130 tokens) in CLAUDE.md or a SKILL.md description. Claude should run `jev-kit --help` once per session, about 4.5k chars (~1.1k tokens), because the blurb says 'read jev-kit --help first'. The JSON output is about 300-600 chars per call.
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. No hook, MCP, skill or proxy ships with the package. To make Claude Code use it 'automatically' you must write your own CLAUDE.md rule or SKILL.md with a description trigger (for example 'before finishing a code change, run the jev-kit gate'), and Claude may still skip it. For a deterministic path you would need to add a Stop or PostToolUse hook that calls jev-kit yourself, which the package does not provide.
pros: Zero standing context cost, because it ships no MCP tools or hooks. Unlike an MCP server, it adds nothing to every turn.

Right primitive fit: pipes diffs, test output or logs straight into Noul/Choice/Score with named answers, so it maps well to gates such as 'unrelated changes?', 'risk category', 'is this file relevant' and skill routing.

OpenRouter-compatible with zero code change: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (dist/index.mjs:58) and posts `${base}/v1/systemone` (line 554), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> plus JEV_KIT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 matches the OpenRouter System One route.
Small and readable: about 890 lines of compiled JS, one dependency (the first-party TypeSafe SDK), no postinstall, no shell exec and no telemetry. Easy to audit or vendor.
Sane key handling: no key flag, so nothing appears in argv or the process list. The saved key file is 0600 in a 0700 dir. Doctor and set-key never write the run log.
Stdout is JSON only, stderr is diagnostics, and stable exit codes 2/3/4/5/70. It is scriptable with jq and safe to wrap in a Stop hook you own.
The README recipes (code-handoff gate, file shortlist by per-file Noul, injection check) match how a senior dev might use a System One model.
cons: Not automatic: nothing triggers it. You need a hand-written CLAUDE.md rule or skill, and Claude will decide when to run it, which contradicts the 'never tell Claude to use jev' requirement unless you add your own hook.

Not OpenRouter-native. It relies on an SDK env var and the unverified assumption that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone body and response match TypeSafe's. doctor and set-key call GET /v1/models, which may behave differently on OpenRouter. Default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID, so you must set JEV_KIT_MODEL.
Unconditional plaintext logging of full request and response bodies (code, diffs, test output) to ~/.jev-kit/logs for 14 days. That is a real leak on client projects unless JEV_KIT_LOG=off is set.

GitHub repo is 404 and there is a single unknown maintainer with no npm provenance. It was created 2026-09-20, ten days old at audit, with 9 versions (0.1.0 to 0.1.30) in 5 days. Tests and CI claims are unverifiable and the package is unstable.

Extra latency and tokens per use: a Node cold start, a Bash round trip and about 1.1k tokens for --help. The SDK timeout is 10 s times 3 attempts, so a slow Jev can stall a Bash call for about 30 s and there is no timeout flag.
32k-token state cap and documented accuracy loss with irrelevant detail. Large diffs must be split by the caller.
Only the System One /v1/systemone route: no Decisions API, no Jev Router, no streaming or batching.
The user's secret-guard PreToolUse hook may block piping sensitive files into it. Jev's usefulness for an Opus-class coding agent is narrow anyway (gates and routing, not code generation).
gh-nikheal25-jev-kit.verdict: A tidy, low-risk, cheap-to-context CLI that could serve as the execution primitive for a self-authored Jev gate (for example a Stop hook or skill) through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter. On its own it is not an integration: it is not automatic, has an unavailable repo, a brand-new solo maintainer, and logs all state to disk by default. If used, pin 0.1.30, set JEV_KIT_LOG=off, and set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_KIT_MODEL, or better, reimplement the ~20-line fetch call yourself.

pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.name: jevguard-mcp (PyPI: jevguard-mcp / GitHub: seb4ez/jevguard-mcp)
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.whatItDoes: Zero-dependency Python stdio MCP server (JSON-RPC, MCP 2024-11-05) wrapping TypeSafe's System One API. It exposes 6 tools: 3 canned task wrappers (shell-command safety, code-patch verification, option choice) and 3 generic ones (evaluate, calibrate, prune_state, cache_fingerprint). Each wrapper sends a hard-coded noul/score/choice question set to the endpoint. It then post-processes the answer with local heuristics: neutral-escape injection, dispersion/ambiguity thresholds, and a SQLite SHA-256 result cache in ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db with a 1h TTL. Third-party single-author project, not official TypeSafe. README says "Official" but it is by Seb4Ez. Repo seb4ez/jevguard-mcp, created 2026-09-20; PyPI 1.0.0 to 1.0.2 (2026-09-22 to 09-23); GitHub HEAD is 1.1.0, unreleased on PyPI.

providerSupport.evidence: tools.py:1535 api_key = os.environ TYPESAFE_API_KEY. tools.py:1538 endpoint = TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT or JEVGUARD_ENDPOINT or default https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. tools.py:90 is_authorized_endpoint hard-allows only api.typesafe.ai and typesafe.ai, plus hosts from JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS (no wildcards, https only, no userinfo). tools.py:2072-2090 sends 'Authorization: Bearer <TYPESAFE_API_KEY>' with the payload {model, questions, state}. The default model string is 'jev-latest', overridable only by the jevguard_evaluate/cache_fingerprint 'model' arg; the wrapper tools always use the default. No OpenRouter string anywhere in the code or README (grep). Verified from HEAD (src/jevguard_mcp/tools.py:90,1772,1866) as well as 1.0.2.
providerSupport.others: None. The OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) and the OpenRouter model ids (typesafe/jev-1.13, ~typesafe/jev-latest) are not referenced.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. Config-only path exists with no code edit: TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS=openrouter.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>. Works only if OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepts the same {model, questions, state} body and returns {answers:{...}} in TypeSafe's shape. That is unverified: the server reads data.answers (tools.py:1608) and the OpenRouter response shape was not checked here. The wrapper tools hard-code model 'jev-latest', while OpenRouter wants '~typesafe/jev-latest' or 'typesafe/jev-1.13', so the wrapper tools would likely 400 unless the code is patched (about 1 line, DEFAULT model). Patching means forking a 3-day-old single-author package.
