pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.tests: One file, test_mcp_server.py, with about 134 test functions, kept in the repo and not shipped in the sdist. There is no CI (no .github directory). Tests use mock_answers, so the real upstream path is not covered. The package claims 'Production/Stable' but is 3 days old, has 22 commits in 6 days, and its commit log is repeated 'audit fix / harden' commits.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.runtime: Python stdlib only, >=3.8, no dependencies, no postinstall. Run as `uvx jevguard-mcp` or `python -m jevguard_mcp.server`. Both entry points would fetch or execute third-party code, so neither was run in this audit.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.install: claude mcp add jevguard -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... -- uvx jevguard-mcp. For OpenRouter, add -e TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone -e JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS=openrouter.ai. Claude Code is not documented in the README, only Claude Desktop, Cursor and LibreChat. Env-var form would keep the key out of argv. Not run.
security: Good: the API key is read only from env and never from tool args (tools.py:1534). HTTPS-only endpoint allowlist that rejects userinfo and wildcards (tools.py:82-105). Redirects blocked to avoid Authorization leakage (NoRedirectHandler, tools.py:63). mock_answers verdict forgery is refused unless JEVGUARD_TEST_MODE=1 (tools.py:1359, 1541).
Key never appears in argv if passed through the MCP env block. Stdlib-only, no shell/subprocess/eval/exec, no telemetry, and the only network egress is the configured endpoint.

Local plaintext SQLite cache at ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db stores answers keyed by hash. It stores hashes and results, not prompts, so the leak risk is low. The wrapper tools set bypass_cache=true for commands.

Prompt-injection surface: the command and diff text is placed as raw 'state' in a request to a classifier, and the verdict (ALLOW_AUTONOMOUS / APPROVE) is then trusted by the agent. An attacker-controlled diff or command comment could steer the classifier. The output is not a security boundary.

Trust: a 3-day-old single-author package with 0 stars, no CI, no signed releases and a self-declared 'Production/Stable' label. The README claims 'Official', which is misleading (author Seb4Ez, not TypeSafe). Supply-chain risk on `uvx` because it always pulls the latest version unless pinned. Pin ==1.0.2.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.dataEgress: Per call to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe or OpenRouter): the full shell command string, working_dir and sudo flag (safety tool). The full unified diff and target file path (verify_code_patch). Free-text context, question and options (evaluate_decision). Arbitrary state/questions (evaluate). Whatever Claude passes is sent, which can include secrets that appear in commands or diffs, and client code. On OpenRouter the key and payload go to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe (or a routed model). The retention policies of both apply, and this matters for client projects under NDA. Nothing leaves without the model choosing to call a tool. There is no telemetry to the author.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level: on missing key, timeout or HTTP error the tool returns isError=true with verdict/fallback_action MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED (tools.py:1613-1617, server.py:254-275). There are 3 retries with exponential backoff (about 0.5+1+2 s) and a default 30 s timeout per attempt (tools.py:2071-2128), so the worst case is over 2 minutes of blocking on a hung endpoint. 400/401/403/404 fail immediately. Because it is a model-called tool, failure only stalls that single tool call and the agent can continue. The SKILL.md rule 'status==error -> REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL' would cause an approval prompt in bypass mode. If the MCP process fails to start (uvx fetch), Claude Code just marks the server disconnected, as with caveman-shrink.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.contextCost: 6 tools. The tools/list JSON in tools.py:1051-1326 is about 8.8k chars, so roughly 2.2k tokens of tool definitions on every session (less with Claude Code's deferred MCP tool loading). No MCP `instructions` field is returned (server.py:153-169 has none). No hooks, so no injected text per turn. The SKILL.md (about 4k chars) costs only its ~50-token description until triggered, but it is not shipped on PyPI.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. The tool descriptions say 'Use ONLY to ...', and the optional SKILL.md nudges Claude to call safety/patch/decision tools. There is no deterministic hook, no PreToolUse integration and no transparent proxy. In bypass or auto mode, nothing forces the model to call these tools, and Claude would rarely do so for routine Bash. Wiring the safety tool into a PreToolUse hook would need your own script.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.latencyImpact: Per uncached call: one HTTPS round trip. The README claims ~740 ms direct WAN on its benchmark; the Jev brief says 70-500 ms. Add MCP tool-call overhead and Python startup on first use (stdlib only, so light). Cache hits cost about 0.1 ms, but the safety tool bypasses the cache by default, and repeated code diffs rarely hit. If used as a per-Bash gate it would add roughly 0.5-1 s per command. Model-initiated calls also cost an extra LLM turn.
pros: Only Jev-specific MCP found that is installable in one line, with no dependencies, no shell exec, no telemetry, and a small readable codebase (about 2.5k lines) I could audit fully.
Sensible security hygiene: key from env only, HTTPS host allowlist, redirects blocked, mock forgery blocked, fail-closed error payloads (tools.py:63-105, 1534-1551).

Endpoint is env-configurable (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT + JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs no fork for the generic jevguard_evaluate tool with model='~typesafe/jev-latest'.
The task-shaped wrappers (command safety, patch verify, choice) map to Jev's noul/score/choice primitives and give ready-made question sets.
Local calibration and caching add value where Jev is noisy: escape option, ambiguity thresholds, 0.1 ms cache hits for repeated state.
cons: Not OpenRouter-native and not official: only TypeSafe and its allowlist are supported. The wrapper tools hard-code model 'jev-latest', which is not an OpenRouter id, and the OpenRouter response shape compatibility is unverified. Real use needs a fork or patch.

No automatic integration: it is model-discretion MCP tools only. There is no hook, and the SKILL.md is not in the PyPI package. This misses the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told). Claude Code is not even in the README.

Poor fit for Claude Code semantics: it duplicates your PreToolUse secret guard, and a Jev classifier cannot judge 'is this Bash command safe' or 'does this diff regress' from a diff alone. The prompts are generic canned rubrics, so results are shallow and vulnerable to prompt injection. Its verdict could create false confidence in bypass mode.

Data egress: full diffs, commands and context go to a third-party endpoint (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe), which is a real NDA problem on client projects. Secrets in commands are sent too, and there is no redaction.

Immature: 3 days on PyPI, 0 stars, one author, no CI, tests are all mocked, 'Production/Stable' and 'Official' are overclaimed, PyPI lags GitHub (1.0.2 vs 1.1.0), and version churn is heavy. `uvx` unpinned pulls whatever is latest.

Worst-case stall of over 2 minutes (30 s x 4 attempts) on a slow endpoint; roughly 2.2k tokens of tool definitions per session for 6 tools, 3 of which (calibrate, prune_state, cache_fingerprint) are local utilities the LLM never needs.
pypi-org-project-jevguard-mcp.verdict: Skip it as the primary integration. It is a tidy, safe-looking, stdlib-only MCP, but it is a discretionary-tool wrapper for TypeSafe's own API, written by a single unofficial author, with a 3-day history and no hook or OpenRouter support. If you want to experiment, pin ==1.0.2, set the OpenRouter env overrides and call only jevguard_evaluate with an explicit OpenRouter model id. Do not rely on it to gate Bash or diffs, and do not send client code through it.

gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.whatItDoes: Python runtime (Reactor loop, policy toolkit, question packs) plus an MCP gateway, jev-reactor-mcp, that sits in front of OTHER MCP servers listed in a YAML config. For each tools/call to a downstream MCP tool it applies an allowlist, JSON-schema validation, hard rules (permissions, amount limits, duplicates, approval for irreversible tools), then one Jev system_one request (relevant, redundant, task_complete, injection_suspected, next_action, etc.). Only allowed calls are forwarded. Denied calls return isError with a reason. It is a proxy, not a tool provider: it exposes zero tools of its own. It cannot see Claude Code built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Read, Grep) because those are not MCP calls.

Author openly says heuristics are not proofs and Jev can be swayed.

SECURITY.md cites TypeSafe MCA 2.3(b) forbidding use of Jev outputs for training/distillation and 2.3(g) forbidding security testing.

gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.dataEgress: Per gated tools/call, one request to the Jev provider (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points to, e.g. OpenRouter then OpenRouter/TypeSafe both see it) containing: the configured goal, the proposed tool name, redacted arguments, tool description, tool risk metadata, and capped excerpts of recent tool calls/results (history_max default 50) as fixed state fields. Only MCP downstream tool traffic is affected: for gitnexus/playwright that could include code snippets, file paths, DOM content and page text. Does NOT see Claude Code built-in Read/Edit/Bash/Grep, user prompts or the conversation. Redaction is regex best-effort. Optional local JSONL of decisions (digest of state by default; redacted state only if state: redacted). No other network calls found.
gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.failureMode: Fail-closed by risk tier, configurable. Default deadline 1.0 s per decision, zero SDK retries, plus asyncio.timeout and a circuit breaker. If Jev is slow/down/errors: write tools go to review, irreversible tools are blocked, read tools get fallback which in enforce mode (default) is NOT run (the model is told the decision service was unavailable); in guard/observe mode fallback lets the call run. Auth errors open the breaker immediately. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY raises MissingApiKeyError at startup (server fails to build). So with default enforce mode, an OpenRouter or Jev outage stalls all gated MCP tools; recommended to run observe or guard. The MCP server itself failing to start makes the gated downstream tools unavailable to Claude Code entirely.
gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.contextCost: Very low itself: 0 tools of its own; server instructions about 330 chars (about 80 tokens). It re-exposes downstream tools you allowlist, with descriptions truncated to 400 chars each, so cost is roughly that of the allowlisted subset (about 50-150 tokens per tool, e.g. 10 gitnexus tools ~ 1-1.5k tokens) and can be lower than the raw server if you truncate/replace descriptions. Every tool call result gains a small _meta decision block (not shown to the model text unless held back). No hooks, so no injected text. Tool names get prefixed server__tool when >1 downstream, which changes mcp__ names and breaks any existing allow rules/hooks/skills referencing mcp__gitnexus__* (e.g. GitNexus skills and the user's hooks).
gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.latencyImpact: Adds one Jev round trip (claimed 70-500 ms; adapter default budget 1.0 s) to every gated MCP tool call, plus a downstream stdio hop (spawns and holds child server processes). Local hard-rule checks are negligible. In fail states, up to 1 s wasted before the fallback. It does not add latency to built-in tools or model turns.
gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy for MCP tools only. Once registered in Claude Code it decides automatically on every call to the allowlisted downstream tools without any user prompt, because Claude Code talks to the gateway as if it were the real server. But this is a gate on other MCP tools, not a way for Claude Code to consult Jev. It does not intercept Bash/Edit/Write/Read/Grep, and it gives Claude no way to ask Jev questions. It would also require removing the original gitnexus/playwright registrations (otherwise the agent just calls the original), and its 'goal' is fixed per gateway in YAML.
pros: Genuinely automatic once wired: transparent MCP proxy, no 'use jev' prompting; decisions happen deterministically in code on every gated call (docs/mcp.md).

Well-engineered safety design for its age: hard rules run before Jev, fail-closed per risk tier, Jev can only make decisions more cautious, approval via sealed MCP elicitation, hostile-description quarantine (SECURITY.md threat table with named tests).
Env-only key handling (no argv exposure), no telemetry, no install scripts, Apache-2.0, strict typing, ~4.3k lines of offline tests, CI with pip-audit.
observe mode lets you log what Jev WOULD have blocked before enforcing; JSONL decision log defaults to digests, not state.

OpenRouter routing looks feasible without code changes because typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 builds URL as base_url + /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, matching OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone; base URL, key and model are all env-overridable.
Zero tools of its own and ~80 tokens of instructions, so no context bloat by itself; description truncation could even shrink downstream tool schemas.
cons: Scope mismatch for daily coding: only gates MCP tools. The user's high-volume, risky actions (Bash, Edit, Write, Read, Grep) are built-in tools and never pass through it; the user's own secret-guard PreToolUse hook already covers those deterministically and for free. The only MCP servers are gitnexus (read-only graph queries), playwright, caveman-shrink, so the gate would judge mostly harmless read calls.
Does not give Claude Code a Jev capability (no Choice/Noul/Score tool for routing, review triage, commit classification, etc.); it is a guardrail, not an integration that 'uses Jev when needed'.

Relevance/redundancy judgments need a fixed per-gateway goal string in YAML, but a coding session changes tasks constantly; 'goal' cannot vary per conversation, so relevance/task_complete signals will be poorly grounded. Docs admit it is unmeasured against live Jev and thresholds are uncalibrated.

Must replace, not add to, existing MCP registrations (else agent bypasses the gate); prefixed tool names change mcp__gitnexus__* to mcp__gateway__gitnexus__* and would break the user's GitNexus skills, hooks and permission allow rules. Also playwright stdio children with allow-listed env only.

Default enforce mode is fail-closed for reads: any OpenRouter/Jev hiccup, 1 s deadline miss, missing key, or schema mismatch blocks gitnexus/playwright calls and can make the agent loop or stall; the redundancy check may wrongly refuse legitimate repeated reads (e.g., re-running a graph query after edits).

Adds a Jev round trip on every gated call, and sends tool arguments plus recent tool result excerpts (code, DOM text from client projects) to a third-party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) with regex-only redaction: client-confidentiality risk. TypeSafe MCA forbids using outputs to train/distill and security testing.

Immature and single-author: 9 commits all on 2026-09-21, 1 star, 0 forks, no GitHub release, alpha classifier, Windows-oriented CI but no live-Jev evidence. Hard-pinned to typesafe-sdk 0.7.x and mcp>=2.2,<3 (very new major); needs Python venv separate from the user's uv workflow (uvx/pipx would work but was not run).

OpenRouter path untested by anyone; TypeSafe direct is the only supported provider, so 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' is unproven and needs a smoke test; the SDK's strict response models may reject OpenRouter's envelope.
gh-knambiardjsc-jev-reactor.verdict: Solid, security-minded but very young MCP guard proxy that is only useful if you want Jev to gate calls to third-party MCP tools; it does not touch Claude Code's built-in Bash/Edit/Read tools nor give Claude a way to consult Jev, so for this user's daily coding it adds latency, data egress and tool-renaming breakage for little benefit. It could be worth a low-risk observe-mode experiment via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, and its ideas (question packs, risk tiers) are more useful as a reference than as the integration itself.

gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.name: jev-style (lawrence3699/jev-style, PyPI jev-style)
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.whatItDoes: Third-party (chaoliangUNSW / lawrence3699) project that fine-tunes small Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B models to imitate Jev's System One interface and serves them locally via a FastAPI server exposing POST /v1/systemone on 127.0.0.1:8765. It is NOT hosted TypeSafe Jev and never calls OpenRouter. It ships a Claude Code plugin marketplace with two plugins: jev-style (6 skills plus a 5-tool stdio MCP server for decide/noul/choice/score/model_info) and jev-style-guard (a PreToolUse hook that sends every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call to the local model with noul/score safety questions and returns allow/ask/deny, plus regex hard rules). Its own benchmark says hosted Jev scores 86.6% versus 73.6% for its 2B model and about 64% for the default 0.8B.

providerSupport.evidence: grep for openrouter/typesafe across jev_style/*.py returns nothing. The only endpoint is the local server: jev_style/server.py:87 (@app.post("/v1/systemone")), default http://127.0.0.1:8765 (guard_config.json server_url; jev_style/mcp_server.py:44 DEFAULT_URL). Env vars are JEV_STYLE_URL, JEV_STYLE_API_KEY, JEV_STYLE_GUARD_URL and similar (client.py:61,152; guard.py:57,457; mcp_server.py:222-236). The guard hardcodes the request model name "jev-style-0.8b-decision-v3" (guard.py:~500) and POSTs to url + "/v1/systemone" (guard.py:~465). Non-loopback hosts are refused unless allow_remote_server (guard.py:455) or --allow-remote (mcp_server.py:71) is set.
providerSupport.others: Only its own local server, plus any server that implements POST /v1/systemone (README line ~158). Weights are downloaded from Hugging Face via huggingface_hub.snapshot_download (models.py:226-237).
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate. The MCP server and guard use a bearer key from an env var and a configurable URL, so a config-only hop to the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone URL is plausible for the MCP tools: --url https://openrouter.ai/api --allow-remote --api-key-env OPENROUTER_API_KEY. That still needs checking, because the client appends /v1/systemone, sends the model name jev-style-..., and the response schema may differ. The guard would additionally need allow_remote_server=true. That would send every tool call over the network, and the guard is not designed for that with an 8 s default timeout. So it is patchable, but it defeats the project's local design and adds per-call cost and latency.

security: Hook input to the guard is the full tool_input (whole Bash command, whole Write/Edit contents, WebFetch URLs). It goes to the local server, and only to a loopback host unless allow_remote_server is set (guard.py:455). Good default.
Bearer key is read from an env var (api_key_env), never from argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The server compares it with hmac.compare_digest.

The hook command is a shell one-liner (`J=$(command -v jev-style || echo $HOME/.local/bin/jev-style); $J guard || printf ...`). It runs whatever jev-style is first on PATH, so it is a PATH-hijack-style trust point but not unusual.
Guard writes a JSONL log with 300-char previews of every tool call to ~/.local/state/jev-style-guard/guard.jsonl. Client code and secrets fragments can land in that log.

Prompt-injection surface: the model reads attacker-influenced command and file text. The guard drops the Bash `description` field to reduce self-persuasion, and hard regex rules can only tighten verdicts, which is well thought out. A 0.8B classifier is still gameable, and it produces false allows and false asks.
Model weights come from Hugging Face (huggingface_hub, unpinned revision) as safetensors, GGUF or MLX, with a torch and transformers>=5 dependency. Trust in the author's HF repos is required.
No telemetry found in the Python source (grep for telemetry/analytics returned nothing). No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall; PyPI wheel via hatchling.
Dependency footprint is heavy: fastapi, uvicorn, httpx, huggingface_hub, numpy, tokenizers, mcp>=2.0, and torch or mlx optionally.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.dataEgress: With defaults nothing leaves the machine except the one-time Hugging Face weight download. Guard payloads (full tool inputs, including file contents being written and commands) go only to 127.0.0.1:8765. Nothing is sent to TypeSafe, OpenRouter or any telemetry endpoint. If the user switched the URL to OpenRouter with allow_remote_server, every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call, including whole file contents and secrets in commands, would leave the machine, with up to 25.6k tokens per call. That is unacceptable for client projects.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.failureMode: Fail-safe but noisy, in the guard. The server being down, a timeout (timeout_s 8 inside a 20 s hook timeout), a 4xx/5xx, a bad body, a missing CLI or an oversized call all produce on_error=ask (configurable to deny, never allow). With the server down every guarded tool call turns into a permission prompt, which is heavy friction in bypass or auto permission mode. The MCP server's HTTP backend has a 120 s timeout, and a failing tool call just returns an error to the model.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.contextCost: MCP: 5 tools with a server-instructions block of about 0.9k chars, and tool defs plus docstrings of about 4.9k chars, so roughly 1.5k tokens always loaded (5.8k chars divided by 4). The 6 skills add short descriptions of about 500-700 chars each, about 0.9k tokens. The guard hook injects no text when it allows (emit_allow=false, so it prints nothing). Ask and deny add a short reason string. Total is roughly 2.5k tokens of static context.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.autoInvocation: Two distinct modes. The guard is a deterministic PreToolUse hook that fires on every Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit/Read/WebFetch/mcp__ call, with no user prompting. It is a safety gate, not a productivity feature. The MCP tools and skills are model-discretion: the skill descriptions only trigger when the user is writing classification or routing code or mentions jev-style, so Claude has no reason to call them during ordinary coding.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.latencyImpact: Documented example latency is about 194 ms per decision (README line ~122), and the guard runs on every matched tool call. That is likely hundreds of ms to seconds on CPU-only Linux with the torch backend (not measured; it depends on hardware). There is a cold-start cost of loading a 0.5-3.8 GB model, and each guard call also spawns a Python process. The hook is synchronous and sequential to the tool call. It is added to every Bash/Read/Edit call, on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.runtime: Python >=3.10 (works on 3.13); needs a resident `jev-style serve` process with torch/CPU-CUDA or MLX or llama.cpp; uvx is possible for the MCP stdio server only

gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.tests: About 53 pytest test functions across 9 files (api, cli, client, eval, guard, mcp, releases, server_json, shortcuts), run with the fake engine only, so the real model is never tested in CI. CI matrix is ubuntu and macOS on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13, plus a CLI smoke test and JSON-manifest validation. There is a release workflow and v0.3.0 was released 2026-09-27. Guard tests are thin (3 test functions for a 693-line guard.py), though there is a guard-replay harness with labelled_commands.jsonl.
pros: The only candidate that hooks Claude Code deterministically with no user prompting. The PreToolUse guard fires on every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call, so the 'automatic' requirement is met mechanically.

Fail-safe design. on_error never resolves to allow, and hard regexes are checked in code and can only tighten verdicts. Loopback-only by default, dry_run mode, a JSONL audit log and a disable env var. Careful engineering for a 4-day-old repo.
No data leaves the machine by default, which is good for client projects. The API key is passed by env var, not argv. No telemetry found.
Apache-2.0, an official-looking MCP registry server.json and a clean plugin marketplace layout. Cheap in static context (about 2.5k tokens), and the hook adds nothing when it allows.
The guard's emit_allow=false default means it only adds ask or deny on top of Claude Code's own permission system and never widens it. Useful as a second safety opinion in bypass mode.
cons: It is not TypeSafe Jev and has no OpenRouter or TypeSafe code path. It is a Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B imitation, and by its own README it scores 64% (0.8B, the default) or 73.6% (2B) against hosted Jev's 86.6% on its benchmark. It fails the user's core ask of using OpenRouter-hosted Jev.

The guard does a job the user already covers: a secret-leak PreToolUse hook exists. Adding a probabilistic 0.8B classifier over every tool call yields false asks. In bypass or auto mode a false 'ask' or an outage (default on_error=ask) interrupts the flow, and a false 'allow' gives a misleading sense of safety.

It requires a resident local server with a 0.5-3.8 GB model and torch. On CPU-only Linux the per-call latency is unknown, and it stacks on the existing hooks on Bash/Read. Each hook invocation also spawns a Python process.

Repointing it at OpenRouter would ship whole file contents and commands to a remote API on every tool call. That is a data-egress problem for client work and adds per-call cost and latency, and the design (8 s timeout, request model name hardcoded to jev-style-0.8b-decision-v3, the default model IDs) is not built for it.

The MCP tools and skills are only model-discretion or triggered by classification-code tasks, so they will rarely be used in ordinary daily coding. Nothing here routes or gates coding decisions with Jev automatically apart from the guard.

The plugin manifests are at version 0.1.0 while the package is 0.3.0. There is a heavy dependency stack (mcp>=2.0, transformers>=5, torch) and the weights come from the author's personal HF account.
gh-lawrence3699-jev-style.verdict: Not an OpenRouter or hosted Jev integration. It is a local Qwen imitation, and its only genuinely automatic piece is a security guard that duplicates the user's existing secret-leak hook. Skip it for the stated goal. At most, consider the guard idea (not this implementation) as inspiration for a fail-open Jev hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

security: API key is sent only as an Authorization header over HTTP(S) (typesafe.py:162). It is never put in argv. It is read from env / the harness .env (chmod 600 advised). The request log is redacted (typesafe.py:84-98), and a custom endpoint never inherits the TypeSafe key implicitly (config.py:445-461).
Text-backend subprocesses (claude -p / codex exec) run with a scrubbed env, a private cwd and start_new_session (textgen.py:194,262). Their argv carries no keys.
jev.base_url rejects credentials, query strings and fragments. Redirects are not followed. Plain http:// is allowed with a doc warning.

Prompt-injection surface: it snapshots arbitrary web page text and feeds it to Jev and (after a miss) to an LLM text backend. Jev returns typed choices only, which limits injection. Commit gate (send, pay, delete, book) and sensitive-field blocking are heuristic and the README admits they lower risk but do not remove it. It drives the user's signed-in Chrome via CDP.

Side effects on install: `jev-browse install` writes a helper block into the browser-harness workspace and symlinks the skill into ~/.claude/skills and ~/.codex/skills (install.py:101-160, refuses to overwrite). The setup skill has the agent run uv tool install and edit .env. The optional global pointer edits ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
Telemetry: none in jev-browse itself. It only reads `browser-harness telemetry status` and warns (install.py:185). browser-harness has its own telemetry setting.
Supply chain: a two-person young repo with PyPI trusted publishing workflow, gitleaks and CodeQL, but 0 vetting time. The runtime has no dependencies, which helps.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.dataEgress: Per Jev decision to the configured SystemOne server (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if repointed): visible page text, element labels, non-personal field values, URL and title of the web page being automated (README 'Safety and privacy'). After a miss, to the text backend: the goal, field labels and up to 2000 chars of page text, and by default to Anthropic via the claude CLI (text.fallback=auto can also send them to Anthropic when a local backend fails). Sensitive and personal fields are excluded. Source code, diffs, repo files and Claude Code tool output are not sent, because the tool never touches the codebase. It is browser-only.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.failureMode: Fail-open, and it only matters in the tool's own workflow. It is not a hook, so it cannot block Claude. Per-request socket timeout is at most 25 s (MAX_SOCKET_TIMEOUT), 3 retries with 0.5 s exponential backoff on 429/503/529 (typesafe.py:16-17), and run deadline defaults to 90 s / 30 actions / 60 requests. On outage or a missing key it returns a typed hand-back (service_error, auth error, no action executed), and Claude then falls back to driving browser-harness itself. A missing key raises MissingKey and hands back cleanly.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.contextCost: Skill mode: one skill description line in the system prompt (about 60 tokens). SKILL.md is 4.7 KB (about 1.2k tokens) loaded only when triggered, reference.md is extra. The optional global pointer adds about 500 tokens permanently. The setup skill adds about 900 tokens on invocation. MCP mode: 8 tools with long param descriptions, estimated 2-3k tokens (mcp_server.py 210 lines, no server 'instructions' seen). No hooks are injected. It requires the separate browser-harness skill and tooling as well.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, which is model discretion and gated on a browser-harness task. The author's own measurement shows that even with browser-harness loaded, the skill was used unprompted 0/5 without the CLAUDE.md pointer and 2/5 with it. No hook. For this user's coding work it would almost never fire, since he already has the playwright MCP for browser tasks.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.latencyImpact: None on normal coding turns, since it only runs on explicit browser sub-tasks. Within fast_run each decision is one Jev request (claimed 70-500 ms), whole tasks took about 25-31 s vs 70 s in the author's benchmarks. A cold MCP or CLI call has browser-harness startup and a Chrome remote-debugging prompt on first use.
pros: Real, working use of Jev: it makes many small typed Choice/Noul decisions per task, a good fit for Jev's design (typedecisions.py-style validate_choice/validate_noul in typesafe.py:49-80).

Custom SystemOne base URL with path prefix and configurable key env var and model (config.py:86-95, typesafe.py:112), so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY should be config-only.

Clean engineering for a young project: zero runtime deps, about 460 tests, CI on 4 Python versions, gitleaks, CodeQL, redacted logs, key never in argv, key scoped so it is not forwarded to other endpoints.
Fail-safe design: typed hand-backs, commit gate, sensitive-field exclusion, owned background tabs only, host allow-list, bounded actions/time.

Available as a Claude Code plugin marketplace, a skill and an MCP server, and it ships a benchmark (2.1-5.3x cheaper, 1.6-3.0x faster browser tasks vs Claude driving the harness alone, author-reported, N=3).
cons: Scope mismatch: it is about browser automation, not coding. It does not help with file edits, tests, code search, permission or commit decisions, or plan routing. Daily coding value is close to zero. The user already has playwright MCP for browser work.

Not truly automatic: the skill trigger depends on a browser-harness task, and the author measured 0/5 unprompted use without a CLAUDE.md pointer and only 2/5 with it. This fails the user's 'Claude must use it without me saying so' requirement.

Heavy prerequisite stack: browser-harness plus Chrome remote debugging ('Allow remote debugging' prompt) plus uv tool plus a helper block injected into the harness workspace, plus symlinks into ~/.claude/skills. Duplicates playwright MCP capability.
No OpenRouter code path for Jev (only the text-backend chat-completions route), and OpenRouter's SystemOne request schema compatibility is unverified. It is a config bet, not documented support.

Egress concerns for client projects: page text and URLs of whatever site is automated go to the Jev provider, and text.fallback=auto sends page excerpts to Anthropic through the claude CLI. It also drives the user's signed-in Chrome, and the commit gate is only a heuristic.
Very new and alpha: created 2026-09-24, 8 stars, 11 commits, 2 contributors, 2 PyPI releases, benchmarks only by the author on a fixture hotel site and Google Flights.
gh-danielnc-jev-browse.verdict: A competent, well-tested but niche browser-automation skill that happens to use Jev for page-step decisions. It has no bearing on code-editing workflows, and its own data shows the agent rarely invokes it unprompted. Skip it for the daily-coding integration. Consider it only as an optional add-on if the user later does heavy browser form automation, and then point it at OpenRouter via JEV_BROWSE_JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api after a doctor check.

gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.name: jev-model-router (jev-claude)
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.whatItDoes: Python stdlib launcher `jev-claude` that starts a 127.0.0.1 HTTP proxy, sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to it, and spawns the real `claude` with a sentinel "JEV Router" model (jev-router) in /model. On each genuinely new user turn it strips system-reminder blocks, POSTs the prompt plus current model and context size to Jev (System One choice question plus 3 score questions), applies a local policy (confidence floor, no downgrade on big context, prompt overrides like "use opus"), and rewrites body.model to a Haiku, Sonnet or Opus id before forwarding to api.anthropic.com. It is a per-turn Claude model router and does nothing else. It has no MCP tools, hooks, or skills for Claude Code (only a Codex skill).

providerSupport.evidence: stdlib_router.py:27 `_ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("JEV_ENDPOINT", "https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone")`. config.py:142 `API_KEY_ENV = "TYPESAFE_API_KEY"`, the only key read (JEV_API_KEY is rejected, config.py:144,154). stdlib_router.py:96 sends `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. config.py:166 `JEV_MODEL = "jev-latest"` is hard-coded, sent as top-level `model` (stdlib_router.py:88), with no env override. `grep -ri openrouter` across the repo returns zero hits. Request body is the System One schema (state, questions {type, instructions, criteria}). Response is parsed as `result["answers"]["model"]` with choice and confidence, and `answers[...]["score"]` (stdlib_router.py:121-125).
providerSupport.others: Optional JEV_CLIENT=sdk path uses typesafe-sdk with base_url derived from JEV_ENDPOINT (sdk_router.py:46-52). Anthropic upstream is fixed at api.anthropic.com (proxy.py:41). Also has a Codex proxy (chatgpt.com/api.openai.com), which is irrelevant here.
providerSupport.openrouterPatchability: Moderate to trivial, needs unverified assumptions. Set JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and put the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (Bearer auth is the same). The blocker is JEV_MODEL, hard-coded to "jev-latest". OpenRouter wants `typesafe/jev-1.13` or `~typesafe/jev-latest`, so a one-line patch or fork is needed. It also assumes OpenRouter's /v1/systemone returns the same `answers.<name>.{choice,confidence,score}` shape, which I did not verify. The direct TypeSafe path has been tested by the author, and only a fake_jev.py stand-in appears in the screenshots.

interface.name: jev-claude [claude args]
interface.purpose: Loads .env files, starts the local proxy, sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=jev-router, ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION*, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_GATEWAY_MODEL_DISCOVERY and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_UNKNOWN_MODEL_WINDOW_ENFORCEMENT, then runs `claude` as a child process (bin/jev_claude.py:83-127). Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY it runs plain claude.

interface.name: jev-explain <session-id>
interface.purpose: Prints the last routing decision report from the /tmp/jev-claude status file (explain.py, bin/jev_explain.py).

interface.name: jev-codex
interface.purpose: Same routing for OpenAI Codex (experimental, codex_proxy.py). Not relevant to this user.

interface.name: jev_statusline (module)
interface.purpose: Status-line command injected via a temp --settings file (bin/jev_claude.py:48-76). It is skipped if the user already has a statusLine in project or user settings.

interface.name: /model row 'JEV Router' (sentinel jev-router)
interface.purpose: The user must select this row, or start via jev-claude, to activate routing. Any other model is passed through untouched (proxy.py:294-298).

interface.name: prompt overrides
interface.purpose: Regex phrases such as 'use opus', 'switch to sonnet', 'with haiku' force a tier (config.py:128-138).

gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.runtime: Python >=3.11 (classifiers list 3.11 and 3.12), stdlib only, zero runtime dependencies. Optional typesafe-sdk extra. The user has Python 3.13, which is untested but likely fine. Also distributed as a Docker image on GHCR.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.install: pip install jev-model-router (or uv tool install jev-model-router), then `echo TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... > ~/.jev-router.env` and run `jev-claude` instead of `claude`. No postinstall scripts. setuptools build, PyPI 0.1.1 published 2026-09-26.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.tests: About 100 pytest functions in tests/live/ (hardening 31, mvp 17, proxy 14, policy 13, sdk 7 and others). CI runs pytest on Python 3.11 and 3.12 in GitHub Actions. I did not run them, per the hard rules. Tests use a local fake Jev server. Live tests are gated by JEV_LIVE_TESTS. No evidence of a test against OpenRouter or a real Jev in CI.
security: API key is read from env or a .env file, never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list. Loader order is cwd/.env, ~/.jev-router.env, ~/.jev-claude.env, and existing env wins (env_file.py:28). A project-local .env in any client repo is auto-read, so a malicious repo could plant TYPESAFE_API_KEY or override JEV_ENDPOINT. That is a config-injection vector, and JEV_ENDPOINT is read at import time from the environment.

Local proxy binds 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port with no auth (proxy.py:265). Any local process can use it as an Anthropic forwarder, but it holds no credentials and only forwards the caller's own headers.

Claude Code's Authorization / x-api-key OAuth token passes through the proxy to api.anthropic.com. The proxy also reuses those headers for its own GET /v1/models call (proxy.py:165-222). It stays on the local machine and there are no third-party hops, but the proxy sits in the trust path for all model traffic.

Modifies ~/.claude/settings.json on exit: restore_saved_model rewrites the file if the sentinel model got saved (settings.py:35-42). It reads settings.json for statusLine detection. It writes a temp --settings file with a statusLine command, in a verified 0700 dir under /tmp/jev-claude.

Status files at /tmp/jev-claude/<session>.json contain the full prompt and the exact Jev request/response for the last 20 turns. They are 0600, owner-checked, and pruned after 7 days (status.py). JEV_DEBUG=1 additionally logs prompt excerpts to ~/.jev-claude.log.

No shell=True. It only runs `claude` via subprocess.run with a list, and no curl|sh or postinstall. No telemetry found in the source (grep for http hits only the proxy, the Jev call and the Codex proxy). Pure stdlib means a small supply-chain surface.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Jev returns typed choice and score output, and the policy validates the tier name and confidence (policy.py:202-214). The only injected content, though, is the user's own prompt text.
SECURITY.md is pre-1.0 boilerplate and still says 'no tagged releases yet' although 0.1.1 exists. Single maintainer plus AI-authored commits (19 commits by 'Claude'). Repo is 6 days old.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or a JEV_ENDPOINT override such as OpenRouter) on each new user turn goes the user's typed prompt text with system-reminder and slash-command blocks stripped and NOT truncated (proxy.py:103, stdlib_router.py:89-92), plus current model id, an estimated context token count and the list of available model ids, plus the routing question text. Tool results, file contents, diffs and prior assistant messages are not sent, but any code the user pastes into a prompt is sent. Nothing is sent for tool-loop continuation requests or resent turns. The Bearer key goes to the Jev host. All normal Claude traffic (full conversation and code) still goes to api.anthropic.com, now via the local proxy. Nothing goes to other third parties. For client projects this is a new third-party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter) recipient of prompt text.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.failureMode: Fail-open. Per-attempt timeout is 1.5 s, wall-clock deadline 3 s, and there is one retry for 5xx/timeout only (config.py:90-92, stdlib_router.py:98-113). Any error, missing key, malformed response or unknown choice yields the model already in use, and the first turn falls back to Opus (policy.py:202-203, config.py:36). Any routing exception falls back to the account's newest Opus (proxy.py:369-376). Upstream Anthropic failure returns a synthetic 502. So a slow Jev adds up to about 3 s to the first request of a turn. Only the Jev call is fail-open. The local proxy itself is a new single point of failure for all Claude traffic if it crashes.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.latencyImpact: One blocking Jev round trip (synchronous, before forwarding) on each new user prompt only. The code comments measure 300-350 ms warm and 900-1000 ms cold TLS, and the worst case is 3 s. There is nothing on tool-call continuations, so it is per turn, not per tool call. Additional hidden cost: switching models invalidates the prompt cache, which the code measures at about 23.6k cache-creation tokens when switching into Opus (config.py:83-86), so downgrades and upgrades cost tokens and time on the following request.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero hook-injected text, and no skill for Claude Code. The context cost is nil. The side effect on Claude Code is NOT nil: setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to a non-first-party host changes client behavior. The repo itself needed sanitize_schema hacks for MCP tool schemas because Claude Code skips its normal conversion behind a custom base URL (proxy.py:54-73). I expect other first-party-only client features to degrade, such as MCP tool search / deferred tool loading, which is not verified in this audit but is worth testing with the user's gitnexus and playwright MCP servers. The repo was verified only against Claude Code 2.1.281/2.1.282, and the user is on 2.1.285.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy, but only when Claude Code is launched through `jev-claude` (or an alias that replaces `claude`) AND the "JEV Router" sentinel model is the active model. Plain `claude` is never affected, so the user must change how they launch. Picking a real model in /model turns routing off (proxy.py:294). There is no hook, MCP or skill route. Once launched, it is fully automatic per turn with no user prompting.
pros: Only candidate here that is truly automatic and prompt-free: a transparent per-turn decision with no 'use jev' phrasing. This matches the user's core requirement in mechanism.
Uses Jev exactly as designed, as a typed Choice plus Score decision with confidences, and the 3 s fail-open deadline means Jev outages never block work (stdlib_router.py:98-113, proxy.py:369-376).
Handles the subscription/OAuth login. It forwards Claude Code's own credential and reads /v1/models with the same headers, so no separate Anthropic key is needed (proxy.py:188-222).

Zero dependencies, no shell execution, no postinstall, key kept out of argv, prompt-only egress with no code or tool outputs, private 0600 status files. All of it is small enough to audit in an hour (about 1.5k lines of source).

Sensible guards: never downgrades on low confidence or big context, keeps a model for the whole tool loop, honors manual /model choice and 'use opus' overrides, Fable is opt-in (policy.py, config.py:74).
Tunable in one file (config.py) and JEV_ENDPOINT is env-overridable, so pointing at OpenRouter is a small patch. MIT license, about 100 tests, CI, signed commits, releases.
cons: Wrong goal for this user's daily coding value: it only chooses Haiku, Sonnet or Opus per turn to save cost. It adds no Jev decisions inside the coding workflow. The user runs Opus 5.5 by choice, and the router will actively downgrade turns to Sonnet or Haiku, risking quality on client work.
Requires launching via `jev-claude` and selecting the sentinel model, so it is not automatic inside a plain `claude` session. It cannot be enabled through settings.json hooks.

No OpenRouter support: the endpoint defaults to api.typesafe.ai and the key var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. The model id `jev-latest` is hard-coded (config.py:166), so OpenRouter needs a patch or fork (JEV_ENDPOINT plus a model-id change). Compatibility of OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone response shape with `answers.model.choice` is unverified.

Puts a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in front of Claude Code. Risk of degraded first-party features, MCP tool-search behavior, and breakage on Claude Code updates. It was validated only up to 2.1.282 and relies on undocumented env vars (ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION*, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_UNKNOWN_MODEL_WINDOW_ENFORCEMENT), and the sentinel still triggers an 'unrecognized_model' warning (bin/jev_claude.py:35-39).

Prompt text of client projects goes to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every turn, unstripped and untruncated. Model switches cost about 23.6k tokens of cache rebuild per switch (config.py:83-86), so a per-turn router can cost more than it saves on a subscription.
Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-24, 2 stars, 1 fork, effectively one maintainer with 19 AI-authored commits, SECURITY.md stale, no evidence of tests against real OpenRouter or Jev.

Modifies ~/.claude/settings.json on exit and auto-loads a .env from any cwd (config injection risk on untrusted repos). Together with the existing PreToolUse and GitNexus hooks, the status-line injection is a further interaction to check.
Subscription users gain little from cost routing: the subscription is flat-rate, and downgrading mainly reduces usage-limit burn, not spend.
gh-himanshu231204-jev-model-routers.verdict: Real, well-written, and the only fully transparent Jev integration found, but it solves cost-routing between Claude tiers, not helping day-to-day coding, and it needs a `jev-claude` launcher, a base-URL proxy, and a fork patch for OpenRouter. For a user who wants Opus 5.5 by default, it is a low-priority optional add-on, not a core integration.
